title: November 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On November 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee.

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and may take four or more business days to be completed across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances may not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Feature

EKM health monitoring

You can now monitor EKM health and configure alerts for EKM-related issues using Cloud Logging. For more information, see EKM health monitoring.

App Engine flexible environment Python

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

App Engine standard environment Python

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

Backup and DR

Feature

Support for automating resource protection for Compute Engine instances and disks at scale in Backup and DR is generally available (GA). By using auto-protection policies and resource labels, you can automatically assign a backup plan to qualifying resources across projects based on user-defined labels. For more information, see Automate resource protection.

BigQuery

Feature

You can now monitor the performance, adoption, latency, and costs of your data agents and their conversations by using Google Cloud Observability in BigQuery. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports BigQuery AI, ML, and object functions and statements in generated Dataform SQLX pipelines and agent instruction files.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Distributed tracing with Cloud Trace is available in Preview for Global external Application Load Balancers, Regional external Application Load Balancers, Regional internal Application Load Balancers, and Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers. Attach a telemetry policy to a load balancer's forwarding rule to generate trace spans that conform to W3C Trace Context and OpenTelemetry, and get end-to-end visibility into requests from clients through the load balancer to your backends. For more information, see Distributed tracing overview.

Feature

For mutual TLS (mTLS) on Application Load Balancers, frontend mTLS validation relaxations are generally available.

The ALLOW_VALIDATION_RELAXATIONS client validation mode on the Client Authentication (ServerTlsPolicy) resource allows you to configure specific X.509 certificate validation exceptions to standard client certificate validation rules. This simplifies migrations of legacy workloads while maintaining an active security posture.

This mode supports the following client certificate validation relaxation parameters:

  • ALLOW_MISSING_EKU: Bypasses Extended Key Usage validation if the EKU extension is absent in the client certificate.

  • ALLOW_SHA1_HASHING: Permits client certificates signed with the legacy SHA-1 algorithm.

  • ALLOW_EXPIRED_LEAF_CERTIFICATE: Evaluates expired leaf certificates by validating them as of 1 second prior to their actual expiration time.

This feature is available for all Application Load Balancer types.

For more information, see Client validation modes.

Cloud NGFW

Feature

Advanced malware sandbox (WildFire) integrates dynamic machine learning (ML) and cloud-based behavioral sandboxing to perform deep inspection of network-routed file transfers and block zero-day malware before it reaches your workloads. Advanced malware sandbox is available in the Cloud Next Generation Firewall Enterprise tier. For more information, see Advanced malware sandbox overview and Configure Advanced malware sandbox in your network.

This feature is available in General Availability.

Cloud Run

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

Cloud Run functions

Feature

Support for the Python 3.15 runtime is in Preview.

Datastream

Feature

Datastream is now available in the africa-south1 (Johannesburg) region. For the list of all available regions, see IP allowlists and regions.

Feature

Datastream is now available in the asia-southeast3 (Bangkok) region. For the list of all available regions, see IP allowlists and regions.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Knowledge Studio in Knowledge Catalog is available in Preview. Knowledge Studio lets you explore data assets and semantic relationships using natural language and an interactive context graph, run automated enrichment tasks to generate and curate metadata from schemas, query logs, and enterprise knowledge signals, and package curated domain knowledge into context sets to ground AI agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or Knowledge Catalog APIs.

For more information, see Knowledge Studio overview, Context sets overview, and About enrichment tasks.

Model Armor

Feature

Support for template-specific exclusion rules in streaming sanitization (StreamSanitizeUserPrompt and StreamSanitizeModelResponse) is available in Preview. You can use dictionary and regular expression exclusion rules in buffered mode (STREAMING_MODE_BUFFERED) with partial or full matching, and in real-time mode (STREAMING_MODE_REALTIME) with partial matching, to mitigate false-positive detections for prompt injection and jailbreak detection and responsible AI filters.

For more information, see Exclusion rules in streaming sanitization.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

Oracle Database@Google Cloud supports creating custom DNS domains for your ODB Networks. You can use custom Domain Name Systems (DNS) to control the names of your resources and delegate DNS resolution within your organization. For more information, see Create and manage custom DNS domains.

You can use custom DNS domains only for Exadata VM clusters.

This feature is generally available (GA).

title: v0 now reads npm credentials from shared environment variables
description:
v0 now installs private packages from npm and custom registries using credentials stored as shared environment variables on Vercel.

This makes it easier for teams to build with their existing design systems, component libraries, and internal packages directly in v0.

To get started, add one of the following as a shared environment variable on Vercel, scoped to Development and/or Preview:

  • Use NPM_TOKEN for private packages hosted on registry.npmjs.org.

  • Use NPM_RC to configure custom or multiple registries.

NPM_RC supports scoped registries and references to other environment variables. For example, configure an organization scope such as @acme for GitHub Packages, or direct package requests through a private JFrog Artifactory registry.

Credentials can be marked sensitive, and v0 never exposes them to the model or writes them to the sandbox filesystem.

You can view the integration status from Settings → Integrations in v0.

Learn more in the private dependencies docs.

Read more

Opt tools in by adding them to the experimental_webMcp object:

Then load the script from your MCP endpoint with the ?webmcp-script parameter:

The script registers those tools with the page and proxies each call back to your MCP server as the signed-in user, so authenticated tools work without a browser-side OAuth flow.

title: Spend Management expands to Enterprise Flexible Commitment plans
description:
Enterprise teams on Flexible Commitment plans can now use Spend Management, already available on Pro, at no additional cost.

You can set a budget at any time in Spend Management settings.

Set a budget per billing cycle, and when your team's metered usage approaches or crosses it, Spend Management can send email notifications, trigger a webhook, or pause the production deployments of all projects. The amount governs the metered usage that draws down from your prepaid balance. Setting an amount does not stop usage on its own; pausing is opt-in, and it does not stop AI Gateway or v0 usage.

Learn more in the Spend Management docs.

title: AI Gateway now supports TypeSafe clients and an HTTP API for Jev
description:
You can now call Jev from TypeSafe AI through AI Gateway using an existing TypeSafe client or the HTTP API, in addition to the AI SDK.

  • TypeSafe client: Point an existing TypeSafe client at AI Gateway without changing its evaluation calls.

  • HTTP API: Call Jev directly from any language or framework.

  • AI SDK: Call Jev from a TypeScript application using AI SDK.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software. State goes in, and typed answers come out with probabilities attached, so there's no generated text to parse. Requests are billed through AI Gateway on all three paths, so they appear alongside your other model calls in usage and observability.

Migrate an existing TypeSafe client

Change the base URL and API key. Your systemOne calls, noul questions, and response shapes stay exactly as they are.

Start a new integration

New integrations name the model as typesafe-ai/jev and ask one of three question types: boolean returns a probability from 0 to 1, choice picks one option from a set you name, and score rates against a scale you define. This example asks whether an agent should keep working after fixing a bug and passing its tests.

With the HTTP API, POST to /v1/evaluate:

With the AI SDK, run the same evaluation through evaluate:

You can also use Jev through eve, a framework for building and deploying agents with sandboxed compute, human approvals, and evaluations already built in. eve uses Jev as the default evaluation model for automatic model selection, typed evaluations, and automated tool approvals.

See the TypeSafe-compatible API guide to migrate a client, or the evaluation guide for the HTTP API or AI SDK.

To see the same breakdown from the CLI, update to version 59.23.1 or later with npm i -g vercel@latest, then run vc inspect:

title: Vercel Connect now supports Microsoft Teams
description:
Vercel Connect now includes a managed connector for Microsoft Teams. Creating one gives your organization a Teams bot that your apps and agents run. People can @mention it in channels or message it directly, and your code receives the message and replies as the bot.

As a Vercel Managed Connector, Vercel registers the Entra app and Azure Bot resource in your tenant, so there's no client secret to store. A tenant administrator with an Azure subscription completes setup once. Incoming Teams activities are verified and forwarded to your project as Connect trigger.

Create a connector from the dashboard or Vercel CLI:

Once the connector is set up, your code requests a token only when it needs one. Use it with the @vercel/connect SDK, eve channel or Chat SDK adapter:

Each token is scoped to what you request and refreshed automatically, so there's nothing to rotate by hand. Connectors only work in the environments you attach them to, and you can revoke access at any time with vc connect revoke-tokens.

Read the Vercel Connect documentation, view details about the Teams connector in the Vercel Connect catalog, or create a Teams connector to get started.

Read more

title: Claude Opus 5.5 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Claude Opus 5.5 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway as anthropic/claude-opus-5.5.

Opus 5.5 is Anthropic’s strongest Opus model for agentic coding, long-running agent tasks, and professional knowledge work. It communicates progress, findings, and next steps clearly, making extended work easier to supervise.

It has a 1M-token context window and supports up to 128K output tokens. Compared with Opus 5, Anthropic has stated that Opus 5.5 performs at a similar level to Fable 5.1, but is ~30% faster and ~40% cheaper per task than Opus 5.

The new model includes two API changes that can turn previously valid requests into HTTP 400 errors:

  • Thinking is always adaptive. Requests that disable thinking or set a fixed thinking budget are rejected. Use an effort level and prompting to control reasoning depth.

  • Forced tool choice is unsupported. Requests cannot require a tool call or force a specific tool. Use automatic tool selection and prompt the model when it should call a tool. If you previously forced a tool call to return JSON, use structured outputs instead.

To use Claude Opus 5.5:

For lower latency, enable fast mode with speed: 'fast' or use anthropic/claude-opus-5.5-fast. In Claude Code, run /fast to toggle it for the session.

Opus 5.5 also supports regional inference and Zero Data Retention through AI Gateway. Try it in the model playground.

title: Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now in public beta
description:
Drives for Vercel Sandbox are now available in public beta on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. It isn’t tied to a single sandbox, so you can reuse the same Drive across runs and different sandbox instances.

Use Drives to preserve an agent's workspace or on-disk memory, or to reuse datasets, models, and dependency trees.

Create and mount a Drive

Create or retrieve a Drive and mount it at a path when starting a sandbox. Read and write files through the sandbox filesystem at that path.

Anything stored under /data remains on the Drive after the sandbox stops.

Share Drive data across sandboxes

A Drive supports one read-write mount at a time. After the Drive has been written to, multiple sandboxes can read from it concurrently by mounting point-in-time, read-only snapshots.

Each snapshot reflects the Drive at the moment it's mounted. Later writes aren’t included; mount a new snapshot to access them.

Limits and pricing

Each sandbox can mount up to four Drives at separate paths. Drives default to a maximum size of 1 TiB (1 GiB on Hobby) and can be configured up to 16 TiB, with higher limits available by request.

Drives are available in every Sandbox region. Each Drive stays in the region where it was created. Sandboxes that mount it must run in that region and can’t use failover regions.

Drive pricing is based on storage, reads, and writes, with rates varying by region. In iad1, storage costs $0.05 per GB-month, reads $0.0015 per GB, and writes $0.004 per GB. Hobby includes 15 GB of Drive storage and 30 GB each of reads and writes per month. See Sandbox pricing for regional rates and plan details.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Unlimited Vercel Blob stores on every plan
description:
You can now create as many Vercel Blob stores as you need. The previous limits of 100 stores on Hobby, 500 on Pro, and 1,000 on Enterprise no longer apply.

Blob store creation is now billed alongside other Blob Advanced Operations, including put(), copy(), and list() calls. On Pro that's $5.00 per million. On Hobby it counts toward the 2,000 free operations you get each month. Deleting a store is free.

Create a new store whenever you want a hard boundary instead of a pathname convention:

  • Separate production, staging, and preview data, and hand each environment its own credential.

  • Create a store per customer in a multi-tenant app, so you can export or delete one tenant's data in a single call.

  • Spin up a store for a preview branch or a migration, then delete it when you're done.

Storage, operations, and data transfer are still billed on what you use, so splitting the same data across more stores costs the same.

Store creation shows up under Blob Advanced Operations on your usage page and in the Observability dashboard.

Learn more in the Vercel Blob Pricing documentation.

title: Vercel Connect now supports TanStack AI
description:
Agents built with TanStack AI can now call OAuth-protected MCP servers through Vercel Connect, with no credentials for you to store or rotate.

The new @vercel/connect/tanstack-ai subpath exports connectMCPTransport, which takes a TanStack transport config and attaches a Connect-backed auth provider. The provider is called before every MCP request, so the token is always fresh.

If the user has not granted access, createMCPClient fails with a consent challenge before the model runs. Catch it with getConsentChallenge and redirect to Connect's consent URL. Otherwise, a consent error raised within a tool call would reach the model as an error string rather than the user as a redirect.

Read the TanStack AI integration docs to get started, or see the full list of supported frameworks and adapters for Vercel Connect.

title: How Klaviyo shipped 356 internal apps in two weeks on Vercel
description:
Klaviyo on Vercel

  • Built a platform for shipping internal apps

  • 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks

  • Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default

  • Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes

Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. It brings marketing, service, agents, and data together in one platform so brands can deliver customer experiences at scale. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program.

In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali.

Guardrails instead of walls

Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way.

Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. Every builder is managed through Klaviyo's identity provider, which Vercel made possible through Enterprise Managed Users.

Implementing safeguards across the stack

Secure Compute gives Vercel deployments a private network path into Klaviyo's own infrastructure. Apps built in the program read from and write to Klaviyo's databases without any traffic crossing the public internet. That's what made bring-your-own-database work for Klaviyo.

On top of that connection, Vercel Passport and Klaviyo’s identity provider give every app the same access defaults, with nothing for the builder to configure:

  • Apps are private and SSO-gated through Okta

  • Sensitive environment variables are set at the team level, out of builders' hands

  • Klaviyo's hardened GitHub security is inherited by every project

  • Wiz scans every project, and findings feed Klaviyo's SIEM

  • Public deployment is granted case-by-case, so sales can share microsites with prospects, while internal tools stay private

How Klaviyo's app platform turns an idea into an app

Klaviyo wanted anyone with an idea to be able to describe it in plain language, from Slack, Claude, or Cursor, and get back a working app. They designed K:Forge, an in-house pipeline built on the Vercel SDK, to handle everything in between.

K:Forge creates a GitHub repo, deploys the app on Vercel, connects data through Secure Compute, and applies every security default. The output is a live, SSO-gated app, and the builder never touches infrastructure. Changes work the same way: mid-thread in Slack, someone can tell K:Forge what should be different, then it makes the change and redeploys.

Klaviyo built the pipeline and deliberately didn't build the layer under it. CDN behavior, preview environments, analytics, global scale: all of it is R&D Vercel had already done, so builders and engineers at Klaviyo don't have to think about it.

For bigger builds, citizen developers take an app about 80% of the way, and Klaviyo's platform team steps in for the last 20%, for fine-tuning and safety review. The platform team went from being the bottleneck to being the finishing touch. "We don't worry about scale," Mohamed says. "If 100,000 people hit an app, Vercel already solved that."

What people at Klaviyo are building

Employees build everything from microsites that rework a sales process to full-stack apps for problems too niche for any vendor tool. For K:BOS, Klaviyo's flagship event, the team skipped off-the-shelf registration tooling and built its own. Engineering barely touched it.

Klaviyo was one of the first customers of Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents. The platform gave the company a way to let anyone build full-stack apps, with security handled by default.

What's next

Klaviyo sets a high bar for AI fluency. One in five employees has shipped an app so far, and Mohamed intends to get even more people building. The team is also going deeper into Vercel, with MCP and AI Gateway.

About Klaviyo: Klaviyo is an autonomous B2C CRM that powers more valuable customer experiences. We unify a flexible, scalable data platform, intelligence that gets smarter with every interaction, and action across Marketing and Service to help businesses turn real-time customer data into personalization at scale.

title: The Vercel Bug Bounty Program is now publicly available
description:
In 2022, we launched a private bug bounty program through HackerOne. Over the last several years, we've worked with HackerOne's VIP program to refine our process, targets, and scope, onboarding thousands of their best researchers and hardening security across our platform.

We've translated those learnings into several public bounty programs:

  • The $1 million React2Shell hacker challenge

  • The $1 million Vercel Sandbox hacker challenge

  • Our OSS bug bounty program

Today, we are combining our private and OSS bounty programs into a single, public Vercel bug bounty program.

Why now

AI has fundamentally changed the nature of bug bounty programs, exponentially increasing the number of reports, both valid and invalid. Some companies are responding by moving to private programs.

At Vercel, we’ve found that public reports are still surfacing real, valuable findings. AI enables a much wider range of researchers to discover vulnerabilities, and we believe in evaluating reports on their own merit, so making our entire program public was the logical choice.

In preparation for the public launch, our security engineering team has streamlined our process and built tooling to filter out noise and expedite remediation. We have improved every step, from triaging reports to shipping and verifying fixes.

Our team and processes have been battle tested through our private program and several large public programs in the recent past. We are ready to open a comprehensive program to the public and have the best researchers out there responsibly explore every part of the platform.

What is covered

All products across the Vercel platform and our open-source projects are now part of our unified public program. Read the Scope page on HackerOne for full details on what is covered.

Consolidation makes sense for our processes, but we also received feedback from the research community that having multiple programs made disclosure confusing because there were multiple places to submit reports. A single program simplifies reporting across our platform and open-source projects.

New findings in our open-source projects should be reported to the main Vercel program, but if you already have submissions to the previous OSS program, you don't need to copy them over. We will still review every submission that was made through that program.

How to participate

If you’re a security researcher, visit our HackerOne program page for details, bounties, and guidelines.

To file a report, submit your findings through HackerOne with clear reproduction steps. Our security team reviews every submission and works with researchers via the disclosure process. We're committed to fast response times and transparent communication.

We appreciate the researchers who take the time to dig into our code and report issues responsibly. We would also like to thank all the researchers who have been working in our private program. You have helped build the foundation for this public program, and nothing will change for you. We look forward to your future submissions.

Learn more about security at Vercel.

Join our security team

If this kind of work excites you, we are hiring. Apply to join the Vercel security team.

title: State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.

  • Function and industry findings describe a classified sample rather than the full catalog.

  • Each analysis uses the latest complete data available. Figures may be revised as the underlying data and methodology improve.

title: Push images to Vercel Container Registry from GitHub Actions
description:
You can now push container images from GitHub Actions to Vercel Container Registry (VCR) without storing long-lived registry credentials.

The new vercel/vcr-action/login action authenticates your workflow using GitHub OIDC. It exchanges the workflow’s OIDC token for a short-lived Vercel access token, then uses that token to log in to vcr.vercel.com. When the job ends, the action logs out and revokes the Vercel token.

To start:

  • Create an OIDC policy on your Vercel team that matches the GitHub repository and workflow, and grants read-write access to VCR.

  • Store your Vercel team ID as a GitHub repo variable, for example VERCEL_TEAM_ID, along with the team slug, project slug, and repo name used in the image tag.

  • Give the workflow or job id-token: write permission.

Then add the login step before you build and push and the image:

The action authenticates Docker by default. Pass engines to use Podman or Buildah instead.

After VCR finishes preparing a linux/amd64 image, you can use it as a custom Vercel Sandbox image. Within the same project, reference it as <repository>:<tag>.

Learn more in the VCR documentation and the GitHub Actions guide.

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

description:

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

description:

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". title: interview questions and answers based on real interview for Jibek
description:
TELL ME ABOUT YOURSELF

My name is Zhibek. I am a DevOps Engineer with more than 5 years of experience in AWS cloud. I started at Yelp in 2021, where I worked 4 years on high traffic consumer apps. I built AWS infrastructure, ran Kubernetes on EKS, and improved our CI CD pipelines with GitHub Actions. With blue green deployments and automatic rollback, I made deployments 35 percent faster. I also mentored junior engineers and wrote runbooks for the team. Now I work at Zulily, where I build Terraform for dev, staging and production, run EKS with autoscaling, and build secure pipelines with approval steps. I have AWS Solutions Architect Associate and CKAD certifications. Now I am ready for the next step, to lead a team as a player coach, and that is why this role at Herc Rentals is very interesting for me.

DAY TO DAY RESPONSIBILITIES

My day starts with checking CloudWatch dashboards and alerts to see if anything broke at night. Then we have a standup with the team. Most of the day I work on Terraform changes, like new environments, network changes or new services. I review pull requests from other engineers. I help developers when their pipeline fails or their app does not scale well on EKS. I fix production issues when they happen and do root cause analysis after. I also update documents and runbooks so the team knows how to handle things. Sometimes I meet with security or app teams to plan new projects.

TELL ME ABOUT YOUR PROJECT

At Zulily the team needed a private database that is easy to repeat in all environments. I wrote Terraform modules for Amazon DocumentDB, put it in private subnets, and used security groups and IAM so only approved apps on EKS can connect. I added it to GitHub Actions with plan, review and approval before production. I set CloudWatch alarms for CPU, connections and storage. The result was the same setup in dev, staging and production, no public access, and new environments now are built much faster.

Second project if they ask, at Yelp. Deployments were slow and risky. I optimized GitHub Actions with caching and parallel jobs, added blue green deployments, and added automatic rollback if health checks fail. Deployments became 35 percent faster and we had fewer failed releases.

TECHNICAL QUESTIONS AND SHORT ANSWERS

What is Terraform state and why remote state
State is a file where Terraform keeps what it created. I keep it in S3 so the whole team uses the same state, and DynamoDB locks it so two people cannot change at the same time.

How do you structure Terraform for many environments
I use reusable modules and separate folders or workspaces for dev, staging and production, with different variable files. Same code, different values.

What is Terraform drift and how do you handle it
Drift is when someone changes things by hand in the console. I run terraform plan regularly to find it, and then fix it in code, not by hand.

Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep
CloudFormation is only AWS, Bicep is only Azure, Terraform works on many clouds. For a multi cloud company like Herc, Terraform is the best choice for one standard.

What is a landing zone
It is a ready secure base for cloud accounts, with account structure, network, IAM, logging and guardrails. In AWS it is Control Tower and Organizations. New teams get a safe account fast.

How does Kubernetes autoscaling work
HPA adds more pods when CPU or memory is high. Cluster Autoscaler adds more nodes when pods cannot fit. Together they handle traffic changes.

A pod keeps crashing, what do you do
I run kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs. Common reasons are wrong config, missing secret, out of memory, or failing health checks. Then I fix and redeploy.

What is Helm
Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. It uses templates and values files so we deploy the same app to many environments in a standard way.

Blue green vs canary
Blue green has two full environments and you switch all traffic at once, easy rollback. Canary sends small traffic first to the new version, then more if it is healthy.

How do you design a CI CD pipeline
Build, unit tests, security scan, terraform plan, approval for production, deploy, health check, and automatic rollback if it fails.

How do you keep secrets safe in pipelines
Never put secrets in code. Use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and GitHub OIDC to get short time AWS credentials instead of long keys.

Explain VPC design
Public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for apps and databases, NAT gateway for outbound internet, security groups to control traffic, many availability zones for high availability.

Security group vs NACL
Security group works on instance level and is stateful. NACL works on subnet level and is stateless, so you need rules both ways.

What is hybrid connectivity
Connecting on premise data center to the cloud with Site to Site VPN or Direct Connect in AWS, ExpressRoute in Azure, FastConnect in OCI. Transit Gateway helps connect many VPCs.

What is IAM least privilege
Give only the permissions needed, nothing more. Use roles, not users with long keys, and review permissions often.

How do you do disaster recovery
First know RTO and RPO, how fast to recover and how much data you can lose. Then backups, multi AZ, cross region copies, and test the recovery regularly, not only on paper.

How do you reduce cloud cost
Right size instances, autoscaling, Savings Plans or Reserved Instances, spot for non critical work, delete unused resources, tagging for each team, and monthly cost reports to leadership.

How do you handle a production outage
First stop the impact, maybe rollback. Communicate to stakeholders. Find root cause with logs and metrics. After that write a postmortem with no blame and fix so it does not happen again.

Do you have Azure or OCI experience
Be honest. My deep experience is AWS, but the concepts are the same. VPC is VNet, IAM is Entra ID and RBAC, EKS is AKS or OKE. Terraform works on all of them, so I can learn fast. I already started learning Azure basics.

How do you use AI in your work
I use Claude AI to help draft pipelines, review Terraform and write documentation. I always review and test before using it. I think AI can help the team move faster when used carefully.

MANAGER QUESTIONS

How do you handle a low performer
Talk early in one on one, understand the reason, set clear goals with time, give support, and follow up. If no change, work with HR.

How do you prioritize when everything is urgent
Production issues and security first, then business priorities agreed with leadership. I make the work visible so everyone sees the tradeoffs.

How do you manage contractors
Clear scope, same standards and code review as full time, and documentation so knowledge stays in the company.

Two engineers disagree on a design, what do you do
Let both explain, compare by facts like cost, risk and simplicity, maybe do a small test, then decide and move forward together.

What will you do in first 90 days
First 30 days listen and learn the team, systems and pain points. Next 30 days find quick wins like standards and runbooks. Last 30 days make a roadmap with leadership.

How do you measure team success
Deployment frequency, failed changes, time to recover, uptime, cloud cost, and team happiness.

title: The Timeout Math That Breaks Your Retry Loop
description:
Your client has a 10-second timeout and three retries. You expect a worst case of roughly 30 seconds. Your caller, who put a 30-second deadline on the whole operation, disagrees — and finds out when their request dies anyway.

The problem is that most retry loops treat timeouts as per-attempt values with no global budget. By the end of this article you'll be able to compute a real worst-case latency for a retried call, split a deadline across attempts, and propagate that deadline through your call stack.

Why per-attempt timeouts lie

A timeout on a single HTTP attempt bounds one connection. It says nothing about the total time of the operation. A retry loop that sleeps between attempts adds backoff on top, and any pre-request work (DNS, token refresh, payload serialization) adds more.

Worst case for "10s timeout, 3 retries, 1s backoff":

attempt 1: 10s  + 1s backoff
attempt 2: 10s  + 1s backoff
attempt 3: 10s
total:     32s

That's before TLS handshakes, connection pool queuing, or a slow middleware layer. A caller with a 30-second deadline doesn't get a slow response — they get an exception from a layer that had no idea a budget existed.

Budget the deadline, not the attempt

Flip the model. Start from the total time you're willing to spend, then divide it across attempts. In Python, time.monotonic() gives you a clock that won't jump when NTP corrects the system time.

import time
import httpx

def get_with_budget(url: str, budget_s: float, max_attempts: int = 3):
    start = time.monotonic()
    per_attempt = budget_s / max_attempts

    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        remaining = budget_s - (time.monotonic() - start)
        if remaining <= 0:
            raise TimeoutError("deadline exhausted before final attempt")

        timeout = min(per_attempt, remaining)
        try:
            return httpx.get(url, timeout=timeout)
        except (httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.TransportError):
            if attempt == max_attempts:
                raise
            time.sleep(min(0.5 * 2 ** (attempt - 1), remaining / 2))

Three details matter here. The timeout for each attempt is capped by the remaining budget, so attempt three can never outlive the caller. The backoff sleep is also capped by the remaining budget, so you never wait two seconds when you have 800 milliseconds left. And a transport error (reset connection, DNS failure) retries too, because those are usually transient as well.

Propagate the deadline down the stack

A budget only works if every layer knows it. If your handler has 5 seconds and it calls three services, each service call should get roughly a third of what's left — not a hardcoded 5 seconds each.

class Deadline:
    def __init__(self, budget_s: float):
        self._expires = time.monotonic() + budget_s

    def remaining(self) -> float:
        return max(0.0, self._expires - time.monotonic())

def handler(deadline: Deadline):
    # each downstream call shares the same budget
    user = fetch_user(deadline)      # gets ~1.6s of a 5s budget
    orders = fetch_orders(deadline)  # gets whatever is left
    return render(user, orders)

This is the same idea as gRPC deadline propagation and the Server-Timing-aware patterns in distributed tracing: the deadline travels with the request. If you're on gRPC already, use it natively — pass the deadline into the context rather than setting a fixed timeout per call.

Where this approach still fails

Budget division has real tradeoffs. Know them before you adopt it:

Tradeoff What happens Mitigation
Equal division starves the last call A slow first call leaves the third service almost nothing Give critical calls a reserved floor
Parallel calls can't share a budget Three concurrent 1.6s calls each need 1.6s, not a third Divide by fan-out, not by call count
Server work is invisible Your budget expires mid-response; you paid for the work and can't use it Budget only the wait, accept partial loss

The last row deserves emphasis. A timeout you enforce client-side doesn't cancel server-side work. If a call times out and you retry, you can stack duplicate work on the backend. Make retried writes idempotent — an Idempotency-Key header or a deterministic request ID — before you tune budgets.

Set sane defaults at the client level

Keep a default budget for calls where the caller didn't specify one, so an unconfigured code path can't hang forever:

DEFAULT_BUDGET_S = 10.0

def fetch(url: str, deadline: Deadline | None = None) -> httpx.Response:
    budget = deadline.remaining() if deadline else DEFAULT_BUDGET_S
    return get_with_budget(url, budget)

Pair this with httpx.Timeout(connect=2.0, read=None, ...) when you do configure per-phase values: connection establishment and response reads usually deserve different limits, and a single flat number hides that distinction.

Key takeaways

  • A per-attempt timeout bounds one connection, not the operation; the true worst case is attempts plus backoff plus overhead.
  • Compute each attempt's timeout from the remaining budget on time.monotonic(), and cap backoff sleeps the same way.
  • Propagate deadlines through your call stack so downstream calls share the budget instead of each carrying a hardcoded maximum.
  • Client-side timeouts don't cancel server work; make retried writes idempotent before tightening budgets.

Source

Stop Hardcoding Your Timeouts — I added working budget-splitting code, deadline propagation through a call stack, and the tradeoff and idempotency failure modes the original doesn't cover.

title: When the Freezers Went Warm: Did a Maintenance Connection Expose Europe's Cold Chain?
description:
When the Freezers Went Warm: Did a Maintenance Connection Expose Europe's Cold Chain?

Somebody turned Europe's supermarket freezers up to 50 degrees without setting foot in a single store. That is not a freezer failure. That is what happens when you wire the cold chain to the internet for convenience and forget to ask who else can reach it.

On 2 November, staff at an ICA Kvantum in Sjöbo, Sweden, walked in to find their fridges "hacked" overnight and their food ruined — temperatures remotely raised to 50°C, spoiled stock wheeled out in carts. It was not one shop. Coop confirmed tampering at a handful of its Swedish stores. Ahold Delhaize reported refrigeration temperatures adjusted across dozens of supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg. Colruyt and Carrefour Belgium reported hits too. And this was billed as a second wave: three weeks earlier, France saw somewhere between 300 and 700 supermarkets hit, with spoilage estimated in the millions — tens of millions by some counts — and even fires at some sites.

The connection that was supposed to help is the whole story

Modern refrigeration is online by design. Technicians monitor units remotely, get failure alerts, and service systems without driving to every store. That is a genuinely good idea — until it is also the attack surface. In Belgium, refrigeration contractor Sabcobel told Belga the units had been switched into defrost mode, with technicians dispatched from about 1 a.m. and fixes discussed including physical modifications and moving units to a secure internet connection. Read that twice: the fix for the connected system is, in part, making it less casually connected.

Nobody will say the same word, and that tells you everything

One Swedish store said "hacked." Coop said "unauthorized tampering." Ahold Delhaize said "IT incident." Those are not synonyms — they are a map of the gap between what is known and what is suspected. No group has claimed responsibility. No authority has named a suspect or an entry point. The French incidents involved older Danfoss controllers that no longer receive software or security updates, which is a polite way of saying part of Europe's food infrastructure runs on abandoned software. Are the waves linked, or just lookalikes reported together? Still unconfirmed. The honest description is narrower than the headlines, and the companies' vocabulary is doing quiet work to keep it that way.

This was never really about freezers

The freezer is just the most literal version of a design choice repeated across every industry: put the ordinary machine online so a technician never has to travel, and you have also built a door that someone uninvited can open. The first sign of trouble is not an alarm — it is a morning shift, a cart full of ruined food, and a display reading 50 degrees. Until the entry routes and the full scale are confirmed, the question is not whether the cold chain can be reached from outside. The reported temperature changes suggest it already was.

Go deeper

Read the full story on Agentic Affairs: When the Freezers Went Warm: Did a Maintenance Connection Expose Europe's Cold Chain?

Originally published on Agentic Affairs (https://agentic-affairs.com)

title: A guardrail that decides at the door lets the intruder walk in later
description:
I report security bugs in AI-agent guardrails, and I keep finding the same shape of bug. This is the first one that's fully public, so I can show you the whole thing — the finding, the fix that shipped, and why I think the design itself is the problem.

The finding (airlock, now public)

airlock is a prompt-injection guardrail in the Hermes plugin catalog. Its job is to stop an agent from doing dangerous things without a human's say-so: in its default approvals_off: block mode, an action that needs approval should be blocked until a person approves it.

The problem I reported: that block could be skipped entirely.

When the Hermes gateway runs a hermes -z turn, the turn is marked unattended in one place (gateway.session_finite) but not in the flag airlock was reading (HERMES_YOLO_MODE). So airlock looked at its usual signal, saw nothing that said "a human is driving this," and let an approval-required action run with no approval at all — even though the whole point of block mode is that nothing dangerous runs unattended.

The maintainer triaged it and shipped a fix in airlock 0.2.3: it now asks the approval layer why Hermes would approve on its own, and it covers CLI subagents under delegation too. The fix is merged into the Hermes plugin catalog (PR #144871), and the advisory is public as GHSA-mgf8-gh7g-q4rg. Coordinated disclosure, credited. That's the system working, and the maintainer was great about it.

The pattern underneath

Here's why I care beyond this one bug. Most agent guardrails work the same way: they decide at the door. Something reads the pending action, matches it against a signal — a mode flag, a regex, a list of paths, a YARA rule — and then either waves it through or stops it. The tool itself runs with whatever access it already had.

Every bug I find in this category is a gap between the signal the guard reads and the effect that actually happens:

  • the action is dangerous, but the signal says "attended," so it runs;
  • the path points at a secret, but it's spelled a way the matcher doesn't recognize, so it's missed;
  • the input is an injection, but it's phrased in a form the rule doesn't cover, so it passes clean.

Same shape every time. The guard is reasoning about a string or a flag that stands in for the real thing, and anything that changes the representation without changing the effect slips past. When these fail, they fail open: no match, no block, action runs. I've started calling this class "stringly-typed guardrails," and once you see it you see it everywhere.

A door-check can be made tighter — airlock's fix did exactly that — but tightening one gap doesn't change the design. There's always another spelling of the dangerous thing.

What I build instead

I'm the author of CleiMesh, and it exists because I got tired of finding this bug. CleiMesh doesn't decide at the door. Two things are different:

The permission becomes the sandbox. An agent runs under a signed, delegable token that says exactly which tools it may call and which directories or network it may touch — and the tool runs inside a WebAssembly sandbox configured from that token, default-deny. There's no "the guard waved it through but the tool still had full access," because the tool never had the access. A subagent can only get a narrower token, never a wider one. A prompt injection can ask for more all it likes; the grant doesn't widen.

Every call leaves a receipt you can replay. Each tool call produces a signed, hash-chained receipt. You can verify the chain offline, and — the part no gateway offers — you can re-run a call from its receipt and compare the result byte for byte. You don't have to trust the log; you re-execute it. That's also what makes it an auditable record for GDPR/LGPD: a report per data subject, from evidence, not from a dashboard someone could edit.

They're complementary, honestly — a door-check catches the obvious stuff fast. But if the door-check is the only thing between an injected agent and your keys, every bug like the one above is a hole. CleiMesh is the layer that doesn't have that failure mode, because there's nothing to "miss."

Why I'm writing this

Because finding these quietly and moving on makes me the nice guy who does free security work for other people's tools and gets nothing for it. I'd rather be clear about what I do: I audit agent guardrails, I report what I find responsibly, and I build the thing that enforces instead of guesses. If you run agents that touch real data — in Claude Code, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes — and "the guardrail checked it" is your whole story, I'd look harder at what the guardrail actually checks.

CleiMesh is free and open (MIT/Apache-2.0): https://github.com/cleitonaugusto/cleimesh. There are two ClawHub skills that set it up — cleimesh-setup for an agent's own file tools, and cleimesh-mcp for the MCP servers it already uses. I also do paid security reviews; the repo README says how.

airlock is the first public one. I have other coordinated disclosures in flight with different maintainers right now; when those patches ship, I'll write them up the same way.

— Cleiton Augusto Correa Bezerra (github.com/cleitonaugusto)

title: Inside Plants vs. Zombies 2: Understanding RSB, RTON, and Rijndael Encryption
description:
Ray Tian — University of Waterloo, Honours Mathematics (Co-op)

I explain how the resource files of Plants vs. Zombies 2 are layered (RSB, RTON, Rijndael), build a small RTON decoder from scratch, and check the container layers of a real build.

1. Introduction

In middle school (around Grades 8–9), I started looking at the data files of the Chinese version of Plants vs. Zombies 2. A new mode, Penny's Pursuit, had just come out, and I wanted to understand how the game stores its level data, for example how the spawns of a level can be described as data. That curiosity led me into binary file formats.

This article explains three separate layers that a PVZ2 asset passes through:

Decryption keys and decryption steps are deliberately left out of this article.

The formats were mapped out by the modding community; the sources are in References. My part is the explanation, a small decoder I built to learn the RTON layer, and a record of what I verified on the container layers of a real build. The code is on GitHub.

I did this analysis locally, for learning. No game files, account data or session tokens are published, and the test data for my decoder is synthetic; the code is in the appendices.

2. Understanding RSB

2.1 What a "resource bundle" is

A game ships thousands of small assets (images, sound, data). Reading them one by
one from the filesystem is slow on a phone, so the engine packs them into a few big
files. An RSB is such a container. The unpacking tools you see in the community read
the container's index and then write each entry out as its own file.

2.2 RSB is not ZIP

Both are "many files in one file", but they differ in structure:

  • A ZIP has a central directory of entries and compresses each file individually.
  • An RSB, as implemented by the community tool Pvz2Tool, has a fixed-size header of offsets, a file list, and a table of resource groups (RSGP). Compression is applied to parts of a group, not to each file separately.

[Source: Pvz2Tool, RsbHeadInfo.kt, RsgpHeadInfo.kt.]

2.3 The header

All fields are 32-bit little-endian integers. The first fields of the RSB header, as
read by Pvz2Tool, are in this order:

# Field Meaning
0 magic 0x72736231, which are the bytes 31 62 73 72 = ASCII 1bsr
1 version an integer (the tool accepts up to 4)
2 (zero) must be 0
3 headLength header size
4 fileList_Length size of the file-name list
5 fileList_BeginOffset where that list starts
6–7 (zero) must be 0
8 rsgpList_Length size of the group-name list
9 rsgpList_BeginOffset where it starts
10 rsgp_Number how many resource groups
11 rsgpInfo_BeginOffset where the group-info records start (each record is 0xCC bytes)
… composite / autopool / ptx tables more Number + BeginOffset pairs

The idea to take away is offset + length: the header does not contain the data, it
contains where to find the data. Everything a parser needs is reachable by
jumping to an offset and reading a known number of bytes.

[Source: Pvz2Tool RsbHeadInfo.kt. I verified the magic value by converting the
constant 1920164401 to bytes myself: little-endian gives 1bsr.]

Version differences are real. The same source notes in a comment that the PTX
info record is 0x10 bytes normally but 0x18 in the "Chinese-version second
generation RSB". A parser that works for one build can fail on another; this is why I
mark my own reproduction by exact version.

2.4 Resource groups (RSGP)

Each group record points to an RSGP block with its own header, magic 0x72736770
(70 67 73 72 = ASCII pgsr). It stores a version, flags, a file offset, and two
parts, each as Offset, ZSize (compressed size) and Size (uncompressed
size), plus its own file list. Pvz2Tool's README describes zlib compression and 4 KB
alignment.

So the recovery procedure for one file is:

  1. Read the RSB header → find the group table.
  2. For each group, jump to its RSGP block → read the part offsets and sizes.
  3. If ZSize differs from Size, inflate the bytes with zlib.
  4. Use the group's file list to cut the decompressed region into named files with their paths.

In the package used for this article, the RSB is wrapped in an extra .smf container and the resource groups do not use zlib compression; see §6.

I am deliberately not claiming what every flags bit means; I have not verified it.

2.5 Checking the layout on a real RSB

Everything above came from other people's source code. To see whether it holds on a real file, I parsed the 147,292,160-byte RSB from §6 with a short script (Appendix D). What came out:

  • The header says version 4 and 30 resource groups. The group records are 204 (0xCC) bytes each and start at offset 383,936 (0x5DBC0). headLength is 397,312 (0x61000).
  • The first group starts exactly at headLength. Every group starts where the previous one ends, and the last group ends exactly at the end of the file. So headLength + (sum of group sizes) = 397,312 + 146,894,848 = 147,292,160: the header accounts for the whole file. A parser can use this as a cheap sanity check.
  • Every group offset and size is a multiple of 4096, which matches the "4 KB alignment" in Pvz2Tool's README.
  • 24 groups use only part0 and 6 use only part1. I do not know what the two parts mean in this build, so I do not interpret them.
  • 19 groups have a first part that begins with the two bytes 10 00: Packages and the 18 WorldPackages_* groups. That is the encrypted-RTON marker from §5.

3. Understanding RTON

RTON is a binary serialization format: a compact encoding of JSON-like structured
data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans). A JSON file spells everything as
text; RTON spells each value as a one-byte type tag followed by its payload.

3.1 Layout 

"RTON"  | version (uint32 LE, usually 1) | entries … | FF | "DONE"

3.2 Type tags (subset I implement)

Tag Meaning
00 / 01 false / true
08 / 0A int8 / uint8, 1 byte
10 / 12 int16 / uint16, 2 bytes (byte order assumed little-endian)
20 int32, 4 bytes (byte order assumed little-endian)
21 int32 zero, no payload (listed as unconfirmed in the notes; supported provisionally)
24 unsigned varint
25 signed varint
81 string: varint byte-length, then bytes
90 / 91 define a cached string / refer to cache entry by index
85 … FF object … end
86 FD count … FE array

[Source: h3x4n1um/RETON format notes. The notes themselves mark several other tags
(09, 0B, … zero-value variants, RTID 83) as uncertain, so I leave them out.]

3.3 Varints

A varint stores a number in as few bytes as needed: each byte carries 7 payload bits,
and the top bit says "another byte follows", least-significant group first.

Example: FE 01 → 0x7E + (0x01 << 7) = 126 + 128 = 254.

The signed form maps the decoded value n to n/2 if even and -(n+1)/2 if odd, so
25 03 → n = 3 → −2. Small magnitudes, positive or negative, stay short.

3.4 String cache

The first time a key such as "Value" appears it is written with 90 and added to a
table; later occurrences are just 91 index. This is why files with many repeated
keys stay small — and why a decoder must keep state while it reads.

3.5 How a parser turns bytes into JSON

A parser keeps a position pos. Loop: read one byte (tag) → the tag decides how many
more bytes to read and how to interpret them → advance pos. Objects and arrays are
recursion: seeing 85, call "read an object" until FF. When finished, pos must
equal the file length — a cheap but powerful correctness check.

3.6 A sample RTON, byte by byte

This is a complete 237-byte RTON that I built with a small encoder. Every value in it is made up, but its shape follows the typical object file: a version, then an array of objects with uid, objclass and objdata. An annotator I wrote (Appendix E) explains each line. Indentation shows nesting; offsets are in hex.
