Things worth noticing:

  • The first object defines 21 strings with 90. The second object recalls the keys and the repeated value "DemoData" with 91 and an index, so it is much shorter. This is the string cache at work.
  • An empty array is just 86 FD 00 FE.
  • zero and x are 21: one byte, no payload.
  • A negative number such as -75 is stored as 25 followed by a varint: 95 01 is 149, which is odd, so it decodes to -(149 + 1) / 2 = -75.
  • Fixed-width integers (08, 10, 20) appear in my tests rather than here, because this sample uses the compact varint forms.

4. Building a Minimal RTON Decoder

How it was built. I wrote the decoder with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), starting from the community format notes and my own earlier ideas about the format, and went through every function myself (§4.1).

Design. A Reader class holds the bytes and a cursor pos. Every read_*
method consumes bytes and advances pos; read_value looks at the tag and
dispatches. Objects and arrays call read_value recursively, so nesting works
without special cases. The decoder rejects anything it does not recognise instead of
guessing.

Tests first. Twelve fixtures in tests/fixtures.py are hand-computed byte strings
with their expected Python values, each annotated byte by byte. A further eleven
tests cover errors: bad magic, bad version, missing footer, trailing bytes, truncated
string, bad cache index, unsupported tag, missing array end, runaway varint,
excessive nesting, invalid UTF-8.

Result. python -m unittest runs 14 tests, all passing (run on 2 Nov 2026).

Scope. Supported tags: 00 01 08 0A 10 12 20 21 24 25 81 85 86 90 91. Floats, 64-bit integers, UTF-8 strings (82, 92, 93) and RTID are the next things to add. The synthetic fixtures check the decoder against my reading of the spec. This article does not decode real game files.

4.1 Reading the decoder, function by function

The full code is in Appendix A. This is what each part does and why.

Reader. Holds data, the cursor pos, and the string cache. Keeping cache on the object, not in a global, means two decodes cannot interfere with each other.

read_bytes(n). The only place that touches data and moves pos. It checks pos + n against the length first, so a truncated file raises RtonError("truncated ...") instead of quietly returning fewer bytes. Everything else is built on it, so the bounds check exists exactly once.

read_int(size, signed). Converts size bytes with int.from_bytes(..., "little", signed=...). This is where the little-endian assumption lives, in one place.

read_uvarint(). The loop from §3.3: take the low 7 bits (byte & 0x7F), shift them into place, stop when the high bit is 0 (byte < 0x80), otherwise add 7 to the shift. It gives up past 63 bits so a file full of FF bytes cannot loop forever.

read_svarint(). Reads an unsigned varint n and applies the mapping: n // 2 if even, -(n + 1) // 2 if odd.

read_string(tag). Three tags share one function. 81 reads a length-prefixed string. 90 does the same and appends the result to cache. 91 reads an index and returns cache[index], raising RtonError if the index is out of range.

read_value(tag, depth). A chain of if checks, one per supported tag. Anything not listed ends in raise RtonError("unsupported tag ..."): the decoder refuses to guess. depth is passed down so deeply nested input stops at 64 levels instead of exhausting Python's stack.

read_object and read_array. They call read_value for each child, so nesting needs no special code. An object reads a key (always a string tag) and then a value until it meets FF. An array requires FD, reads a count, reads that many values, and requires FE.

decode(data). Checks the magic and version, reads the top-level object, then requires DONE and that pos equals the file length. The last check catches files with trailing bytes.

The design choice that matters most: every function either returns a correct value or raises. There is no "best effort" path, so a wrong tag shows up as an error with an offset, not as quietly wrong data.

5. Understanding Rijndael Encryption

5.1 Rijndael vs. AES

Rijndael is a family of block ciphers designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. AES
is the standardised subset: block size fixed at 128 bits, keys of 128/192/256 bits.
Rijndael itself allows block sizes 128, 192 or 256 bits independently of the key
size. So "AES" and "Rijndael" are not interchangeable when the block size is not
128 bits.

5.2 Rijndael in this game: what is publicly known

Community research has documented two things about the encrypted RTON files of this game: they start with the two marker bytes 10 00, and they use Rijndael in CBC mode with a 192-bit (24-byte) block. A practical consequence is that a standard AES library, which fixes the block at 128 bits, cannot be used for them as it is; you need a Rijndael implementation that supports the other block size.

5.3 Keys and IVs: what they are, and what this article leaves out

A key is the secret value the cipher is parameterised by; Rijndael accepts 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. An IV (initialization vector) is a starting value for CBC and has the same size as the block. A key can be written as raw bytes, as ASCII text or as hex, and mixing these up is a classic source of bugs: 32 ASCII characters are 32 bytes, while 32 hex characters are only 16.

This article does not publish, derive or search for any key, and it does not walk through decrypting any game file. Its subject is the structure of the containers and the decoder for the decrypted form of the format. Where a step would need a key, I say so and stop.

5.4 What the design teaches

Whatever the algorithm, a client application that decrypts its own data has to hold the key somewhere on the device. Client-side encryption therefore deters casual reading, but it is not a strong protection, and anything that really matters belongs on a server. That is a lesson about system design; it is not a how-to.

5.5 My own exploration

What I did back then (from memory). In middle school I opened the APK with MT Manager on my phone and browsed its contents, and I learned that the game's data files were encrypted and that community tools could read them. I did not write those tools. I no longer remember their names or the order of my steps, and this article does not repeat any of them.

5.6 CBC, step by step

CBC (cipher block chaining) cuts the data into blocks of the cipher's block size, 24 bytes here. Decrypting works like this:

plaintext[i] = Decrypt(key, ciphertext[i]) XOR ciphertext[i-1]      with ciphertext[-1] = IV

Each block is decrypted on its own with the raw cipher and then XORed with the previous ciphertext block; for the first block the "previous block" is the IV. Three consequences are useful in practice:

  1. The IV only matters for the first block. A wrong IV garbles block 0 but leaves every later block correct, which is a handy way to tell a wrong IV from a wrong key.
  2. Decrypting block i needs only two ciphertext blocks, so long inputs can be processed in pieces.
  3. Identical plaintext blocks encrypt differently, because each is mixed with the previous ciphertext. That is the reason to use CBC rather than encrypting block by block (ECB).

This section describes the mode, not any particular file.

6. Verifying the container layers on a real build

Input. One Chinese-version Android APK (baokai_4.2.7_1885_715_dj2.0-4.0.1.apk, 2,271,163,986 bytes, SHA-256 7c09515d…90a5d7), downloaded from the game's website https://pvz2.hrgame.com.cn/ on 2 Nov 2026 and analysed locally. I look only at the container layers (the wrapper, the RSB header and the group table). I do not decrypt or decode the game's own data here.

An extra layer I did not expect. The RSB files in this APK are not stored bare: assets/dynamic.rsb.smf begins with the ASCII magic RSLB. It is a block container: a 32-byte header, a table of 36-byte block records, then one raw LZMA1 stream per block (32 MiB blocks, LZMA properties lc=3 lp=0 pb=2). I found the layout in a community decompressor's comments and wrote my own decompressor; it produced exactly the 147,292,160 bytes the header declares. So the chain for this build is:

APK -> .rsb.smf (RSLB, LZMA blocks) -> RSB -> RSGP -> RTON files (encrypted; not covered here)
Step Result on this APK
Unwrap dynamic.rsb.smf 147,292,160 bytes; starts with 1bsr; matches the declared size
Read RSB header version 4, 30 resource groups, group records 0xCC bytes, PTX records 0x18 bytes (the "second-generation" variant noted in Pvz2Tool)
Compression In every one of the 30 groups ZSize == Size: no zlib was involved in this build. I did not exercise zlib at all
Read one RSGP (WorldPackages_beach) magic pgsr, version 4; its first part begins with 10 00, the encrypted-RTON marker

What's next.

  • Read the RSGP file-name table to recover full paths.
  • Add floats, 64-bit integers, UTF-8 strings and RTID to the decoder, with new synthetic fixtures.
  • Exercise zlib on a build whose groups are compressed.

6.1 The RSLB container, field by field

The .smf file is 69,183,497 bytes and expands to 147,292,160. All numbers are little-endian. The header:

Offset Field Value in this file
0x00 magic RSLB
0x04 version 1
0x08 total uncompressed size 147,292,160
0x10 packed size 69,183,465 (= file size − 32)
0x18 block size 33,554,432 (32 MiB)
0x1C block count 5

After the header comes a table of 36-byte records, one per block. Decoded for this file:

Block Uncompressed start Uncompressed size Data offset Compressed size LZMA dictionary
0 0 33,554,432 212 10,267,186 33,554,432
1 33,554,432 33,554,432 10,267,398 22,168,257 33,554,432
2 67,108,864 33,554,432 32,435,655 18,241,763 33,554,432
3 100,663,296 33,554,432 50,677,418 14,198,046 33,554,432
4 134,217,728 13,074,432 64,875,464 4,308,033 13,631,488

Each block's data begins with 5 bytes of LZMA properties (5D plus a 4-byte dictionary size) followed by a raw LZMA1 stream with no end marker; the table supplies the size to stop at. The properties byte 0x5D = 93 unpacks as lc = 93 mod 9 = 3, lp = (93 div 9) mod 5 = 0, pb = 93 div 45 = 2.

Checks that came out right: block 0's data starts at 212 = 0x20 + 5 × 36, right after the table; each block starts where the previous one ends (212 + 10,267,186 = 10,267,398); the five uncompressed sizes add up to 147,292,160; and the five compressed sizes plus the 212-byte header and table add up to the file size. The last block is shorter and uses a smaller dictionary; I do not know why.

6.2 What went wrong first

I kept the failures because they show what the checks are for. The scripts were written and run with the AI assistant described in §4.

  1. One stream or many? The first attempt decompressed the .smf as a single LZMA stream after the header. It started well (1bsr, so the idea was right) and then failed with "Corrupt input data" after about 33.6 MB. The container is chunked into 32 MiB blocks; the fix was to read the block table.
  2. A wrong header offset. The first end-to-end script read the first part's offset from the wrong position in the RSGP header. The 10 00 marker check failed at once. I fixed the offset and added an assertion that the RSGP header and the RSB's group record agree.

Neither would have been caught by synthetic tests alone.

6.3 Reproducing the container checks

You need an Android APK of the game that you are entitled to use and Python 3. The scripts are in the appendices.

  1. An APK is a zip file. Take out assets/dynamic.rsb.smf (unzip app.apk assets/dynamic.rsb.smf).
  2. python3 rslb.py dynamic.rsb.smf dynamic.rsb (Appendix C). For the build I analysed, expect 147,292,160 bytes starting with 1bsr. Other builds will differ.
  3. python3 rsb_probe.py dynamic.rsb (Appendix D). Expect version 4 and 30 groups, with Credits_1200 first.
  4. Or run steps 1 to 3 and the consistency checks in one go with python3 inspect_build.py app.apk (Appendix F).

If a step gives a different number, trust your number and check which build you have: that is the point of recording the SHA-256 of the APK.

7. Lessons Learned

This project gave me a more complete picture of how mobile apps are packaged. What I analysed here was an Android APK: at bottom it is a zip archive holding native libraries (.so), assets and configuration. In Grade 9 I also looked at iOS app packages (IPA) and learned how Apple's code signing works; that is outside this article's experiments.

It was also my first fairly systematic contact with encryption concepts: key and IV lengths, how block ciphers differ, and how AES relates to Rijndael (here the block size is not the AES one, so a standard AES library does not fit).

On method, writing tests from the spec before the code paid off: the fixtures forced me to work out varints and the string cache by hand before any decoder code existed. Annotating a sample file byte by byte also taught me to read structured binary data.

Next I want to treat the network protocol (encrypted HTTP requests) as a separate study: finish reproducible experiments first, then write a second article.

8. FAQ and glossary

Is the RSB itself encrypted? Not in this build. After the .smf wrapper is removed, the RSB header parses normally and the groups are stored uncompressed. The RTON files inside carry the 10 00 marker, which marks them as encrypted.

Is Rijndael the same as AES? AES is Rijndael restricted to a 128-bit block. This game uses a 192-bit block, so a standard AES library does not fit.

Does this article show how to decrypt the game's data? No. It covers the container layers and a decoder for the decrypted form of the format, tested on synthetic samples. It contains no keys and no decryption steps.

Does the decoder work on real PVZ2 files? This article does not test that. It handles the documented subset on synthetic samples. Floats, 64-bit integers, UTF-8 strings and RTID are not implemented, and I do not know which of those other files use.

Is the decoder original work? It is my implementation of a documented format, written with an AI assistant and read and understood by me. It is not a new discovery; see §4 and the references.

Glossary

  • Magic number: fixed bytes at the start of a file that identify its type (1bsr, pgsr, RTON, RSLB).
  • Offset / length: where data starts and how many bytes it spans; the basis of almost every binary format.
  • RSB: a PopCap resource bundle holding many files in resource groups.
  • RSGP: one resource group inside an RSB.
  • SMF / RSLB: the wrapper seen in this build that stores an RSB as LZMA-compressed blocks.
  • RTON: PopCap's binary serialization format for JSON-like data.
  • Varint: a variable-length integer; small numbers take fewer bytes.
  • Block cipher / block size: an encryption algorithm that works on fixed-size chunks; Rijndael allows 128, 192 or 256 bits.
  • IV (initialization vector): the starting value that CBC mixes into the first block.
  • CBC: cipher block chaining; each block is mixed with the previous ciphertext block.

9. References

  • h3x4n1um, RETON — RTON format notes. https://github.com/h3x4n1um/RETON
  • DreamMoonCai, Pvz2Tool (MIT) — RSB/RSGP header definitions. https://github.com/DreamMoonCai/Pvz2Tool
  • apples1949, PvZ2ModdingGuide — community guide. https://github.com/apples1949/PvZ2ModdingGuide
  • J. Daemen, V. Rijmen, The Design of Rijndael (Springer).
  • NIST, FIPS 197, Advanced Encryption Standard.
  • Python zlib, hashlib documentation.

Appendix A: the decoder (mini_rton/decoder.py)

MIT licence, copyright 2026 Ray Tian. Only the tags listed in §4 are supported; anything else raises RtonError.

"""A minimal RTON decoder covering a documented subset of the format.

Format notes: https://github.com/h3x4n1um/RETON (see docs/rton-scope.md).
Supported tags: 00 01 08 0A 10 12 20 24 25 81 85 86(FD..FE) 90 91.
Anything else raises RtonError instead of guessing.
"""

MAGIC = b"RTON"
FOOTER = b"DONE"

TAG_FALSE, TAG_TRUE = 0x00, 0x01
TAG_INT8, TAG_UINT8 = 0x08, 0x0A
TAG_INT16, TAG_UINT16 = 0x10, 0x12
TAG_INT32 = 0x20
TAG_INT32_ZERO = 0x21
TAG_UVARINT, TAG_SVARINT = 0x24, 0x25
TAG_STRING = 0x81
TAG_OBJECT = 0x85
TAG_ARRAY = 0x86
TAG_CACHE_DEFINE, TAG_CACHE_RECALL = 0x90, 0x91
TAG_ARRAY_BEGIN, TAG_ARRAY_END = 0xFD, 0xFE
TAG_OBJECT_END = 0xFF

MAX_DEPTH = 64


class RtonError(ValueError):
    """Raised for malformed or unsupported input."""


class Reader:
    """A cursor over bytes: every read advances `pos`."""

    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.pos = 0
        self.cache = []  # strings defined by tag 0x90, indexed by 0x91

    def read_bytes(self, n):
        if n < 0 or self.pos + n > len(self.data):
            raise RtonError(f"truncated: need {n} bytes at offset {self.pos}")
        chunk = self.data[self.pos:self.pos + n]
        self.pos += n
        return chunk

    def read_u8(self):
        return self.read_bytes(1)[0]

    def read_int(self, size, signed):
        return int.from_bytes(self.read_bytes(size), "little", signed=signed)

    def read_uvarint(self):
        """7 payload bits per byte, low group first; high bit = more bytes."""
        result = 0
        shift = 0
        while True:
            byte = self.read_u8()
            result |= (byte & 0x7F) << shift
            if byte < 0x80:
                return result
            shift += 7
            if shift > 63:
                raise RtonError(f"varint too long at offset {self.pos}")

    def read_svarint(self):
        n = self.read_uvarint()
        return n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else -(n + 1) // 2

    def read_string_body(self):
        length = self.read_uvarint()
        raw = self.read_bytes(length)
        try:
            return raw.decode("utf-8")
        except UnicodeDecodeError as exc:
            raise RtonError(f"invalid string bytes before offset {self.pos}") from exc

    def read_string(self, tag):
        """Read a string-valued tag (81, 90, 91) whose tag byte is already consumed."""
        if tag == TAG_STRING:
            return self.read_string_body()
        if tag == TAG_CACHE_DEFINE:
            text = self.read_string_body()
            self.cache.append(text)
            return text
        if tag == TAG_CACHE_RECALL:
            index = self.read_uvarint()
            if index >= len(self.cache):
                raise RtonError(f"cache index {index} out of range ({len(self.cache)} entries)")
            return self.cache[index]
        raise RtonError(f"expected string tag, got 0x{tag:02X} at offset {self.pos - 1}")

    def read_value(self, tag, depth):
        if depth > MAX_DEPTH:
            raise RtonError("nesting too deep")
        if tag == TAG_FALSE:
            return False
        if tag == TAG_TRUE:
            return True
        if tag == TAG_INT8:
            return self.read_int(1, True)
        if tag == TAG_UINT8:
            return self.read_int(1, False)
        if tag == TAG_INT16:
            return self.read_int(2, True)
        if tag == TAG_UINT16:
            return self.read_int(2, False)
        if tag == TAG_INT32:
            return self.read_int(4, True)
        if tag == TAG_INT32_ZERO:
            return 0  # no payload; listed as unconfirmed in the format notes
        if tag == TAG_UVARINT:
            return self.read_uvarint()
        if tag == TAG_SVARINT:
            return self.read_svarint()
        if tag in (TAG_STRING, TAG_CACHE_DEFINE, TAG_CACHE_RECALL):
            return self.read_string(tag)
        if tag == TAG_OBJECT:
            return self.read_object(depth + 1)
        if tag == TAG_ARRAY:
            return self.read_array(depth + 1)
        raise RtonError(f"unsupported tag 0x{tag:02X} at offset {self.pos - 1}")

    def read_object(self, depth):
        """Read key/value pairs until FF. The opening 85 is already consumed."""
        result = {}
        while True:
            tag = self.read_u8()
            if tag == TAG_OBJECT_END:
                return result
            key = self.read_string(tag)
            result[key] = self.read_value(self.read_u8(), depth)

    def read_array(self, depth):
        """86 FD <count> <values...> FE. The opening 86 is already consumed."""
        marker = self.read_u8()
        if marker != TAG_ARRAY_BEGIN:
            raise RtonError(f"expected FD after array tag, got 0x{marker:02X}")
        count = self.read_uvarint()
        items = [self.read_value(self.read_u8(), depth) for _ in range(count)]
        end = self.read_u8()
        if end != TAG_ARRAY_END:
            raise RtonError(f"expected FE at array end, got 0x{end:02X}")
        return items


def decode(data):
    """Decode RTON bytes into Python objects (dict at the top level)."""
    reader = Reader(bytes(data))
    if reader.read_bytes(4) != MAGIC:
        raise RtonError("bad magic: not an RTON file")
    version = reader.read_int(4, False)
    if version != 1:
        raise RtonError(f"unsupported version {version}")
    result = reader.read_object(0)
    if reader.read_bytes(4) != FOOTER:
        raise RtonError("missing DONE footer")
    if reader.pos != len(reader.data):
        raise RtonError(f"{len(reader.data) - reader.pos} trailing bytes after footer")
    return result

Appendix B: synthetic test fixtures (tests/fixtures.py)

Every byte is annotated or built by a small encoder. The error-handling tests are omitted here for length.

"""Hand-built RTON byte strings, each with its expected decoded value.

Every byte is annotated so you can check it against docs/rton-scope.md.
These are synthetic: they contain no game data.
"""

HEADER = bytes.fromhex("52544F4E" "01000000")  # "RTON" + version 1 (uint32 LE)
FOOTER = bytes.fromhex("444F4E45")              # "DONE"

# name -> (bytes, expected decoded Python value)
FIXTURES = {
    # {}   -- just the end-of-object marker FF
    "empty": (HEADER + bytes.fromhex("FF") + FOOTER, {}),

    # {"a": true, "b": false}
    #   81 01 61   string, 1 byte: "a"      01  true
    #   81 01 62   string, 1 byte: "b"      00  false
    "bools": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 01 61 01  81 01 62 00  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"a": True, "b": False},
    ),

    # {"name": "Zombie"}
    #   81 04 6E616D65         "name"
    #   81 06 5A6F6D626965     "Zombie"
    "string": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 04 6E616D65  81 06 5A6F6D626965  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"name": "Zombie"},
    ),

    # {"n": -2, "u": 200}
    #   08 FE   int8 0xFE = -2 (two's complement)
    #   0A C8   uint8 0xC8 = 200
    "small_ints": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 01 6E 08 FE  81 01 75 0A C8  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"n": -2, "u": 200},
    ),

    # {"a": {"a": 1}}  -- cache define (90) then recall (91 00) inside a nested object
    #   90 01 61  define "a" (index 0)   85  object start
    #   91 00     recall index 0 ("a")   08 01  int8 1
    #   FF FF     inner end, outer end
    "nested_cache_recall": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("90 01 61  85  91 00  08 01  FF  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"a": {"a": 1}},
    ),

    # {"a": [1, 2]}  -- 86 FD <count=2> 08 01 08 02 FE
    "array": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 01 61  86 FD 02  08 01  08 02  FE  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"a": [1, 2]},
    ),

    # {"w": -300, "i": 70000}
    #   10 D4 FE  int16 LE: 0xFED4 = -300
    #   20 70 11 01 00  int32 LE: 0x00011170 = 70000
    "wide_ints": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 01 77 10 D4 FE  81 01 69 20 70 11 01 00  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"w": -300, "i": 70000},
    ),

    # {"mX": 0, "mY": -150}  -- 21 = int32 zero (no payload);
    # 25 AB 02 -> varint 0x2B + (2 << 7) = 299 (odd) -> -(299+1)/2 = -150
    "int32_zero_and_signed": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 02 6D 58 21  81 02 6D 59 25 AB 02  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"mX": 0, "mY": -150},
    ),

    # A made-up sample with the same *shape* as a typical object file: a version, then an array of
    # objects (uid / objclass / objdata). The second object reuses keys and values through the string
    # cache (91). Built with a small encoder; annotated byte by byte in the article (section 3.6).
    "showcase": (
        bytes.fromhex(
            "52 54 4f 4e 01 00 00 00 90 07 76 65 72 73 69 6f 6e 24 01 90 07 6f 62 6a 65 63 74 73 86 fd 02 85"
            "90 03 75 69 64 90 05 31 2e 30 2e 31 90 08 6f 62 6a 63 6c 61 73 73 90 08 44 65 6d 6f 44 61 74 61"
            "90 07 6f 62 6a 64 61 74 61 85 90 04 6e 61 6d 65 90 04 64 65 6d 6f 90 05 69 74 65 6d 73 86 fd 00"
            "fe 90 04 66 6c 61 67 01 90 05 63 6f 75 6e 74 24 f4 03 90 06 6f 72 69 67 69 6e 25 95 01 90 04 7a"
            "65 72 6f 21 90 03 62 6f 78 85 90 01 78 21 90 01 79 25 95 01 90 01 77 21 90 01 68 24 c8 01 ff ff"
            "ff 85 91 02 90 05 31 2e 30 2e 32 91 04 91 05 91 06 85 91 07 90 05 64 65 6d 6f 32 91 09 86 fd 02"
            "24 01 24 02 fe 91 0a 00 91 0b 24 07 91 0c 21 91 0d 21 91 0e 85 91 0f 24 05 91 10 25 01 91 11 21"
            "91 12 24 09 ff ff ff fe ff 44 4f 4e 45"
        ),
        {'version': 1, 'objects': [{'uid': '1.0.1', 'objclass': 'DemoData', 'objdata': {'name': 'demo', 'items': [], 'flag': True, 'count': 500, 'origin': -75, 'zero': 0, 'box': {'x': 0, 'y': -75, 'w': 0, 'h': 200}}}, {'uid': '1.0.2', 'objclass': 'DemoData', 'objdata': {'name': 'demo2', 'items': [1, 2], 'flag': False, 'count': 7, 'origin': 0, 'zero': 0, 'box': {'x': 5, 'y': -1, 'w': 0, 'h': 9}}}]},
    ),

    # --- varint fixtures ---
    # {"Value": 61}: key via cache-define 90, value unsigned varint 24 3D (0x3D = 61)
    "varint_cached_key": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("90 05 56616C7565  24 3D  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"Value": 61},
    ),
    # {"n": -2}: signed varint 25 03 -> n=3 is odd -> -(3+1)/2 = -2
    "signed_varint": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 01 6E  25 03  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"n": -2},
    ),
    # {"x": 254}: varint FE 01 -> 0x7E + (1 << 7) = 254
    "varint_two_bytes": (
        HEADER + bytes.fromhex("81 01 78  24 FE 01  FF") + FOOTER,
        {"x": 254},
    ),
}

The scripts for unwrapping the .smf, reading the RSB table, annotating an RTON and inspecting a build (Appendices C to F) are in the original post and in the GitHub repo: https://jelly-raytian.github.io/systems/pvz2-resource-analysis/

title: What If Your Voice Could Command Machines in 1.2 Seconds? Meet Apriel Voice 27B
description:
Apriel Voice 27B — The First Open‑Source Model That Turns Speech Directly Into Action

One 27‑billion‑parameter transformer that lets you speak, see, think — and act—without stitching together a dozen separate services.

A Voice‑First Revolution in Real‑Time

Imagine a maintenance engineer on a noisy factory floor saying, “Show me the temperature map of valve #12, then log a ticket if it’s above 80 °C.” In a traditional stack that request would bounce through three separate services—ASR, a text‑only LLM, and an orchestrator—adding latency, cost, and points of failure. Apriel Voice 27B collapses that chain into a single, end‑to‑end model that listens, interprets visual context, and emits a ready‑to‑run JSON command in just 1.2 seconds on a 4‑GPU A100 node. The result is a faster, cheaper, and far more reliable voice‑first experience.

Why It Matters Right Now

  • Speed: End‑to‑end latency ≈ 1.2 s on a 4‑GPU A100 node, matching a Whisper + GPT‑3.5 pipeline.
  • Cost: One model, one endpoint → eliminates two ASR/orchestration services.
  • Access: Apache 2.0 licence; weights, scripts, and a Docker image are on the Hugging Face Hub.

These three data points answer the “what’s in it for me?” question before you even finish reading.

1. One‑Model Voice Assistant in Action

Scenario: A maintenance engineer on a noisy factory floor asks, “Show me the temperature map of valve #12, then log a ticket if the reading exceeds 80 °C.”

Traditional stack (3 hops):

  1. Whisper‑large → transcript the audio.
  2. Text‑only LLM (e.g., Gemini‑Flash) → parse intent, build JSON.
  3. Orchestrator → call the drone camera, evaluate temperature, create a ticket.

With Apriel Voice 27B (single hop):

  • The raw 16 kHz waveform streams into one endpoint.
  • The model ingests the audio, attends to the live visual frame from the drone, and outputs a ready‑to‑run JSON command: 
{
  "action": "create_ticket",
  "parameters": {
    "device_id": "valve_12",
    "severity": "high",
    "description": "Temperature 82°C exceeds threshold"
  }
}
  • The engineer hears, “Ticket created for valve #12,” and moves on.

Result: 1.2 s latency, no extra integration points, and a 30 % reduction in engineering overhead.

2. Core Innovations

What How It Works Why It Counts
Native audio ingestion A 1 B‑parameter speech adapter (conv front‑end + sinusoidal positions) feeds raw waveform directly into the frozen Gemma‑4 26B‑A4B backbone. Cuts out the separate ASR stage; saves memory and latency.
Unified multimodal reasoning Audio, text, and image embeddings share the same attention matrix. The model can link a spoken command to a visual cue in a single pass.
Direct tool‑use output Two decoders emit (a) OpenAI‑style function‑call JSON, (b) raw shell‑command tokens. Eliminates post‑processing; the model talks to your APIs out of the box.

The entire architecture fits on a 4‑GPU A100 node with ≈12 GB per replica, leaving headroom for batching or concurrent users.

3. Performance Snapshot

  • Speech‑to‑text: 6.8 % WER on LibriSpeech test‑clean, 12.4 % on multilingual CommonVoice (vs. Whisper‑large’s 7.2 % / 13.1 %).
  • Reasoning: 78 % on MMLU (↑4 pts vs. frozen Gemma‑4), 71 % on GSM‑8K with tool calls (↓13 pts without).
  • Tool‑call accuracy: 94 % correct JSON on the new VocalBench suite (Mistral‑NeMo‑Speech‑7B = 78 %).
  • Throughput: 8 concurrent streams per GPU at batch‑size 1; linear scaling with tensor‑parallelism.

Bottom line: Apriel Voice 27B delivers “pipeline‑level” speed and cost with “model‑level” reasoning power.

4. Multilingual Reach

Training data span English, Mandarin, Spanish, Hindi, plus 30+ low‑resource languages. On CommonVoice subsets the model narrows the error gap to Whisper‑large by 0.5 % on average, proving the speech adapter learns language‑agnostic acoustic patterns while the frozen text backbone supplies cross‑lingual semantics.

5. Community Toolkit

  • HF Hub: Model weights, training scripts, Docker image.
  • VocalBench: 1 k spoken prompts with expected JSON; ready‑to‑run evaluation scripts.
  • Fine‑tuning guide: Jupyter notebooks for domain‑specific adaptation (medical dictation, automotive voice control).

These resources lower the barrier for startups and labs to ship voice‑first products without negotiating costly API contracts.

6. Risks & Open Questions

Issue What It Means Mitigation
Transcription accuracy Slightly higher WER than Whisper‑large on clean English. Use a hybrid fallback ASR for legal/closed‑captioning workloads.
Hallucinated tool calls 6 % of generated JSON target the wrong entity (e.g., wrong calendar event). Enforce schema validation + optional human‑in‑the‑loop confirmation for high‑risk actions.
Compute footprint 27 B parameters still require multi‑GPU servers. Community‑driven quantization/distillation for edge deployment.
Data‑privacy Fine‑tuning on proprietary audio can expose voice data. Adopt secure fine‑tuning pipelines; explore differential‑privacy techniques.
Licensing dependencies Some tokenizer libraries carry restrictive licences. Perform a full dependency audit before commercial release.

7. Looking Ahead

Apriel Voice 27B proves that a single, open‑source model can listen, think, and act—without the usual patchwork of services. If the community tightens hallucination safeguards and delivers lighter‑weight variants, this model could become the default foundation for:

  • Voice‑first SaaS platforms
  • Hands‑free AR/VR experiences
  • Accessibility tools that require real‑time action

The next question for developers will no longer be “How do we stitch ASR, LLM, and orchestration together?” but “What new experiences can we build when the model already knows how to listen, reason, and execute?”

Prepared by a senior tech columnist, data‑driven analysis based on the Aprium Lead Tech Analyst Brief (2 Nov 2026).

title: Green plan, red deploy: the subnet that is not there yet
description:
terraform plan answers one question: does this configuration match what Terraform already manages? It does not answer the one that breaks the deploy: does the network this cluster needs exist yet, with a way out to the Internet, in the tenancy this credential can reach?

Control Cloud runs that second question before the first one, against the live inventory of the account, and shows the answer as a list you can act on.

Read from the account, not from the plan

The pre-flight walks the template's dependencies and looks each one up in the provider: the network, the subnets, the firewall rules, the egress path. A subnet that is not there is red with the reason written next to it ("does not exist yet and is needed before deploying") and a button that opens the canvas where you create it. A private subnet with no NAT is a warning, because the deploy would succeed and the nodes would never pull an image.

What a green plan hides

A plan references the subnet by ID and trusts it. The failure shows up minutes into the apply, half the resources created, the other half waiting on something that was never going to appear. Catching it before any Terraform runs costs one read of the API with the read-only credential you already connected.

Where it runs

From the app: the canvas and the Pre-Deploy page, on the template you are about to deploy. It does not replace plan; it looks at what lives outside the state. Quotas are not checked yet; that one is on the roadmap and we say so.

Watch the 25-second clip · Full 60-second demo

Request access

Solo plan is free: 1 operator, 1 provider, no card. Team comes with a 7-day trial. Read-only access to map and check; write access only where you grant it.

title: Lovable or Cursor? The Real Difference Between AI App Builders and AI Coding Tools
description:
"Lovable vs Cursor" is a confusing search because the two tools aren't really competing for the same job.

Lovable, Bolt, Replit Agent, v0, Emergent and Base44 are AI app builders: you describe an app in a browser, and the vendor writes it, runs it, and hosts it. Cursor, Claude Code and GitHub Copilot are AI coding tools: they work on a codebase that lives wherever you put it — your machine, your repo, your host.

The question that actually matters before you pay for either category: can you get your code out? We checked every vendor's own pricing and docs pages as of October 2026, and the answer varies more than you'd expect:

  • Lovable and v0 sync to GitHub on their free plans.
  • Emergent only unlocks GitHub integration at its $20/month Standard tier.
  • Base44 promises "two-way GitHub sync" in its FAQ, but its own plan table only lists GitHub integration from the $40/month Builder plan up — on Free or Starter, your code stays in Base44.
  • Bolt's pricing page says nothing about GitHub or export at all, so that one needs checking inside your actual project before you build anything you intend to keep.

That one detail — export, not raw capability — is the thing that decides whether a prototype becomes a real asset or a dead end you have to rebuild from scratch.

The common path that works: prototype in a builder with GitHub sync, get a working demo fast, then clone the repo into Cursor or Claude Code once the project needs real backend logic, scheduled jobs, unusual auth, or tests — things builders don't model well. Claude Code runs $20/month via Claude Pro; Cursor's current tiers are Free, Plus $8 (Grok-only), and Premium $30; GitHub Copilot Pro is $10/month and the cheapest way into real code if you already use VS Code.

A realistic first-month budget doing both: about $45 — Lovable Pro ($25) to prototype, Claude Pro ($20) once the repo exists and matters.

Full breakdown of all six builders (pricing, credit limits, where people get stuck) and the three coding tools, plus a step-by-step migration guide for moving a builder project into a real repo without losing work: https://devtoolsreview.com/best-for/ai-app-builders-vs-ai-coding-tools/

No vendor named here is paying for placement in this piece — pricing and limits are sourced directly from each vendor's own pages, linked inline.

title: Weekly Threat Recap: Social Engineering to Supply Chain Poisoning
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

Analysis of critical attack vectors this week spanning device-code phishing, Linux DDoS botnets, Android spyware, and supply chain poisoning. Attacker perspective on why social engineering remains devastatingly effective.

Weekly Threat Recap: Social Engineering to Supply Chain Poisoning

Executive Summary

This week's threat landscape demonstrates a critical lesson for defenders: attackers don't always need sophisticated zero-days. They weaponize the friction points that organizations accept as unavoidable-shared links, device-code flows, trusted browser extensions, default credentials, and human psychology.

From a red team perspective, the most effective campaigns this week combined multiple attack primitives. A single compromise vector often chains into infrastructure access, lateral movement, and persistence. We're seeing attackers exploit the gap between security theory and operational reality.

Attack Vector Analysis

The primary attack chains this week fell into three categories:

Social Engineering & Phishing (MITRE ATT&CK T1566 - Phishing)

Device-code phishing attacks represent a sophisticated mutation of traditional OAuth abuse. Attackers generate device codes through legitimate OAuth 2.0 flows, then social engineer targets via fake support calls or messages to authenticate on attacker-controlled applications. Once the target enters that device code, attackers gain session tokens without ever intercepting credentials.

The attack works because device-code flow (RFC 8628) was designed for headless devices-TVs, IoT platforms, printers. The authentication happens on a secondary device (the user's phone), creating a disconnect that social engineers exploit. A convincing support call ("We detected suspicious activity on your account, enter this code to verify your device") is sufficient. The target never realizes they're authenticating an attacker's application.

Related to this: Passkey Bypass Chains show how attackers target authentication ecosystems rather than individual mechanisms.

Linux DDoS Botnet Infrastructure (MITRE ATT&CK T1053 - Scheduled Task/Job, T1583.002 - Infrastructure as a Service)

Linux botnet activity spiked this week with variants targeting exposed Docker sockets, vulnerable package managers, and misconfigured SSH services. These aren't new techniques-they're effective because default configurations persist. A Docker socket exposed to the host network with no authentication becomes a pivot point into containerized infrastructure, then lateral movement to the host.

Botnets this week leveraged Alpine Linux GitLab RCE vulnerabilities and similar supply chain weaknesses to seed initial infections across development infrastructure. Once planted in CI/CD pipelines, they establish persistent DDoS capacity while remaining silent from application monitoring.

Trusted Extension Exploitation (MITRE ATT&CK T1176 - Browser Extensions)

Browser extensions remain one of the most underestimated compromise vectors. Extensions run with the same privileges as the user's browser session and can access all traffic, cookies, and DOM content. Attackers compromise legitimate extensions through supply chain attacks (developer credential compromise, malicious pull requests) or create fake "security extensions" that users install voluntarily.

This week saw variants stealing OAuth tokens, API keys, and session cookies. The critical detail: users grant these permissions explicitly during installation, then never revoke them.

Android Spyware & Mobile Persistence (MITRE ATT&CK T1533 - External Remote Services)

Android spyware campaigns distributed via trojanized apps and SMS phishing links established persistent access to SMS, call logs, location, and camera. The attack chain typically involves:

  1. Phishing link to trojanized APK
  2. User enables unknown sources (or sideloading vulnerability)
  3. Installation with Device Admin permissions (or accessibility service abuse)
  4. Persistence through boot-complete receiver
  5. Command-and-control via SMS or HTTP callbacks

From an attacker's perspective, Android's permission model creates friction but doesn't prevent determined compromise. Accessibility services (T1598 - Phishing for Information) can capture screen content and keystroke patterns without explicit security warnings.

Technical Deep Dive

Device-Code OAuth Exploitation

The attack exploits RFC 8628 semantics:

Attacker initiates:
POST /oauth/device_authorization HTTP/1.1
client_id=attacker_app&scope=openid profile email

Server responds:
device_code: ABCD1234
user_code: WXYZ
verification_uri: https://auth.service.com/device

Attacker calls target:
"Hi, this is [Company] Security. To verify your account,
go to auth.service.com/device and enter: WXYZ"

Target enters code at verification_uri.
Authenticator backend matches user_code to device_code.
Attacker polls:
POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1
client_id=attacker_app&device_code=ABCD1234&grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code

Server issues:
access_token: eyJ0eXAi...[JWT]...
refresh_token: [token]

Attacker now has authenticated session impersonating target.

The critical flaw: nothing in the flow proves the code entry location. The target authenticates an attacker's application while believing they're verifying their own account.

Linux Botnet Persistence via Systemd

# Attacker plants persistent service
cat > /etc/systemd/system/system-updater.service << EOF
[Unit]
Description=System Update Service
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/system-update
Restart=always
RestartSec=10
User=root
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable system-updater
sudo systemctl start system-updater

# Payload masquerades as legitimate service
# Executes DDoS commands while maintaining low visibility

The sophistication is minimal-attackers rely on misconfigurations and lack of behavioral monitoring. Detection requires baseline monitoring of process execution and network connections from unexpected services.

Android Accessibility Service Abuse

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE" />

<!-- Service definition -->
<service
 android:name=".SuspiciousAccessibilityService"
 android:label="@string/accessibility_service_label"
 android:permission="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE">
 <intent-filter>
 <action android:name="android.accessibilityservice.AccessibilityService" />
 </intent-filter>
 <meta-data
 android:name="android.accessibilityservice"
 android:resource="@xml/accessibility_config" />
</service>

Once enabled, this service can:

  • Intercept all screen touches
  • Capture UI hierarchy and text
  • Inject synthetic events
  • Monitor SMS and call logs
  • Exfiltrate screen content periodically

Android 11+ added restrictions, but accessibility services on older devices remain extremely powerful.

Detection Strategies

OAuth Anomaly Detection

  • Monitor device_code authorization endpoints for:
    • Multiple failed code entries before success
    • Unusual geographic locations for subsequent authentication
    • Time deltas between code generation and redemption (instant use = automated attack)
    • Access to sensitive scopes (email, profile) from new applications

Botnet Indicators

  • Linux host monitoring:
    • New systemd services with obfuscated names
    • Unexpected outbound connections from system services
    • High CPU/bandwidth consumption from processes running as root
    • SSH key generation in unexpected locations (/dev/shm, /tmp)

Extension Compromise Signals

  • Browser telemetry:
    • Extensions accessing OAuth tokens or sensitive sites
    • Network traffic from extensions to known C2 infrastructure
    • Extension manifest changes without user action
    • DOM manipulation targeting login forms or password managers

Mobile Spyware Indicators

  • Android device monitoring:
    • Accessibility services from non-system apps
    • Device Admin apps installed from unknown sources
    • Unexpected location data queries
    • SMS/call log access without user interaction
    • Processes holding camera/microphone permissions during idle state

Mitigation & Hardening

Organizational Controls

  1. OAuth Flow Validation: Implement device-code restrictions. Require step-up authentication for sensitive scopes. Log all device_code redemptions with geographic and temporal context.

  2. Endpoint Security: Deploy behavioral monitoring on production Linux infrastructure. Alert on new systemd service creation, especially with restart policies. Monitor container escape attempts and Docker socket abuse.

  3. Browser Policy: Restrict extension installation to allowlists. Implement ChatGPT Work-to-Chat Consolidation principles-minimize third-party integrations that expand attack surface. Revoke extension permissions regularly.

  4. Mobile Device Management: Enforce Android 12+ on corporate devices. Disable sideloading. Use MDM to prevent accessibility service installation from unknown apps. Monitor for rooted devices.

  5. Training: Red team perspective-social engineering works because people trust perceived authority. Treat device-code phishing as a baseline threat. Simulate fake support calls during awareness programs.

Individual Contributor Hardening

  • Never enter verification codes from incoming calls or unsolicited messages
  • Review browser extensions monthly; remove unused ones
  • Disable unknown sources on Android devices
  • Enable password managers that prevent OAuth token exfiltration
  • Use security keys for critical accounts

Key Takeaways

  • Social engineering remains the highest-ROI attack vector. Device-code phishing chains OAuth flows with human psychology. A 5-minute call costs attackers nothing but yields session access.

  • Default configurations are attacker checklists. Exposed Docker sockets, unpatched SSH services, and missing service monitoring enable botnet persistence at scale.

  • Trust models break under targeted pressure. Browser extensions and accessibility services were designed for legitimate use. Attackers exploit this trust with supply chain compromises and trojanized apps.

  • Mobile platforms are less defensible than desktops. Limited monitoring, granular permissions, and user-controlled sideloading create persistent infection vectors.

  • Detection requires baseline behavioral understanding. Knowing what normal looks like for your infrastructure is prerequisite to identifying command execution from unexpected services or unusual OAuth patterns.

Related Articles

  • LXD/MicroCloud Certificate Impersonation: CVSS 10.0 Authentication Bypass
  • North Korean TraderTraitor: $6.43B Binance Heist & Insider Threat Analysis
  • Claude Code Cursor Marketplace: 11-Hour SSH Backdoor Supply Chain

title: Which Cursor model is best for everyday work?
description:
Not one model. In my 5-test Cursor run, Gemini won 4 tests (on low effort; medium/high errored), Claude built the best landing page, and Grok high was slowest and not worth the wait.

Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I4qA5bXzHpM (@janekzarin)

Summary: Cursor recommends Grok by default. I wanted to check that on normal, day-to-day work, the kind that actually helps a small business sell: a shop calculator, a landing page, an edit that doesn't break the page. Not an official benchmark, just my first-impression ratings.

What I tested

Five models side by side in Cursor: Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5, Gemini, Muse and GPT. Each got a completely fresh folder, so it could only use what it generated itself. Same one-shot prompts:

  1. A single-file HTML game
  2. A business calculator for an online shop (VAT, taxes, costs)
  3. Drawing with code: an SVG of a moose riding a scooter through a forest
  4. A single-file landing page for a cordless garden tool shop
  5. Edit without breaking: add a currency switcher with a fixed rate to that shop

It is not the fairest setup. Effort levels differed: Grok and Muse on high, the others started on medium.

What broke

  • Gemini kept erroring in Cursor on medium and high, two or three times in a row. Low effort worked, so most Gemini results are on low.
  • My own mistake: on the first calculator run I forgot to switch the model, so the "Gemini" folder actually had Grok code. I made a new folder and re-ran it with real Gemini.
  • Grok high was slow. On the game it finished last and the result looked about like Claude's. Grok high-fast was much faster on the next test.

Results (my ranking)

  • HTML game: Gemini first, then Claude. Grok's was similar to Claude's but not worth the wait.
  • Shop calculator: Gemini (low) was the cleanest, one I'd use and not be afraid to sell. ChatGPT looked the most "sellable as a product"; Grok and Muse did nice simple ones.
  • SVG drawing: Gemini 1, Claude 2, ChatGPT 3, Muse 4. Grok lost this one.
  • Landing page: Claude best (working links, Q&A section, animation), Muse second, Gemini third, Grok fourth (more blog than shop), ChatGPT last (colors didn't match).
  • Currency switcher edit: Gemini first, Claude second, Grok third with its own unique solution. ChatGPT's switcher worked but was really ugly.

The marketing takeaway

If you use AI to build things that get you sales (calculators, landing pages, quick page edits), don't just take the default model. For a one-shot shop page, Claude gave me the most ready-to-use result. For quick tools and edits, Gemini did best even on low effort. Pick the model per task, and do a second prompt before you judge a page.

At the end of the video I show this month's Cursor usage. Other models ran four against one Grok, so the percentages aren't one-to-one.

title: Nodus vs Northflank: which is better for GPU training?
description:
If the training job is the whole point, use Nodus; if it is one service inside an app you already deploy on Northflank, stay on Northflank. Nodus lists lower NVIDIA L4, A100, H100 and B200 rates than Northflank Cloud and restores your checkpoint on a new machine when one is lost. Northflank lists the lower 8 x H200 rate and runs GPUs across more kinds of your own cloud accounts.

We build Nodus, so we kept this checkable. Every Northflank fact links to its own pricing page or docs, the arithmetic is shown once, and there is a full section on where Northflank is the better pick.

How do Nodus and Northflank compare at a glance?

They start from different places. Northflank is a full deployment platform: services, jobs, databases, builds and pipelines, where a GPU is a resource you add to a service or job. Nodus is an AI compute platform: you hand it a command or a TrainingJob, and it picks capacity, saves checkpoints and replaces lost machines until the run finishes.

Northflank Nodus
What you launch A service or job in a GPU-enabled project, from a Git repo or container image A Job or TrainingJob that Nodus places for you
Billing Per second, pay as you go; GPU deployments need at least $50 of account credit Prepaid credits; a dry-run estimate before any paid work
GPUs on its own cloud L4, A100 40GB and 80GB, H100, RTX PRO 6000, H200, B200 RTX 3070 up to B300 on the pricing page
H100 80GB listed rate $2.74 per GPU-hour, sold as 8 GPUs per container Listed at $2.60/hr, from 1 GPU (--gpu H100 or --gpu H100:8)
Machine lost mid-run Job restarts up to its Retry Limit; your code resumes from files it saved to a persistent volume New attempt on new capacity with /nodus/state restored; urgent checkpoint on a reclaim notice
Spend cap per run Time Limit per job, in seconds --max-cost in USD plus --timeout
Your own cloud GPUs in AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle, CoreWeave and Nebius accounts, $1.00 per GB of VRAM per month Run work in a connected AWS account, GCP project or Azure subscription (Beta)
Coding agents Hosted MCP server via nf agent setup for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode MCP server via nodus mcp install for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor

Sources: Northflank pricing, GPUs on Northflank's managed cloud, Northflank jobs, Northflank MCP, Nodus pricing, Nodus attempts and recovery, Nodus cloud accounts. Prices checked November 2, 2026.

Is Nodus cheaper than Northflank per GPU-hour?

On four of the five GPUs both list, yes. Northflank Cloud lists the NVIDIA L4 at $0.80, A100 80GB at $1.76, H100 at $2.74, H200 at $3.14 and B200 at $5.87 per GPU-hour. The Nodus pricing page lists the same GPUs at $0.43, $1.09, $2.60, $3.593 and $5.50.


The gap is widest on the smaller GPUs; on the H200, Northflank's listed rate is lower.

The gap matters most for single-GPU work. A LoRA fine-tune on one A100 80GB pays a 38% lower listed rate on Nodus. On the H100 the difference is about 5%, and on the H200 Northflank is cheaper. Northflank GPU plans also bundle a fixed amount of CPU and system RAM per GPU, so compare the full estimate, not only the GPU line.

What do four real training jobs cost on each?

We priced four common jobs at list rates. The math is GPUs x hours x the listed rate, nothing else.

Job Northflank Nodus
LoRA fine-tune, 1 x A100 80GB, 12 h 12 x $1.76 = $21.12 12 x $1.09 = $13.08
Full fine-tune, 8 x H100, 10 h (80 GPU-hours) 80 x $2.74 = $219.20 80 x $2.60 = $208.00
Large run, 8 x H200, 10 h 80 x $3.14 = $251.20 80 x $3.593 = $287.44
Large run, 8 x B200, 10 h 80 x $5.87 = $469.60 80 x $5.50 = $440.00


Nodus wins three of four jobs at list price; the 8 x H200 run is $36.24 cheaper on Northflank.

The decision rule we take from this table: if your run fits on one or two GPUs, the listed rate is the biggest lever and Nodus usually wins clearly. At 8 GPUs the rates are close, so recovery and idle time decide the bill more than the hourly price does.

What happens if the machine fails halfway through training?

The difference is who writes the resume logic. Northflank's GPU guide says services and jobs are stateless and recommends saving checkpoints to persistent volumes. A job's Retry Limit sets how many attempts it gets, and a Time Limit ends it regardless of retries.

On Nodus, a Job writes its state to /nodus/state and Nodus saves and restores that directory. When a machine is reclaimed, Nodus asks for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement at the same time. A machine that goes silent for 60 seconds on shared capacity is replaced. The run loses at most the work since its last committed checkpoint, as the attempts and recovery docs describe. We cover the failure modes in more depth in what happens when GPU capacity runs out.

Here is why that matters on the 8 x H100 job above. If the machine is lost at hour 7 and nothing was checkpointed, you redo 56 GPU-hours: $153.44 at Northflank's listed H100 rate, $145.60 at Nodus's. With a checkpoint every 30 minutes, you redo at most 4 GPU-hours. Northflank can get you there too, but you mount the volume and write the resume path yourself.

Can you use your own cloud account with either?

Yes, and Northflank goes further here. Its bring-your-own-cloud option runs GPUs in your AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle, CoreWeave or Nebius accounts, your provider bills the GPUs, and Northflank charges $1.00 per GB of VRAM per month. For one 8 x H100 80GB node that fee is 640 GB x $1.00 = $640 a month on top of your cloud bill.

Nodus can run work in a connected AWS account, GCP project or Azure subscription so it spends your cloud credits before Nodus capacity. That mode is in Beta, and the cloud accounts docs list exactly what each connection can do. If your committed spend sits with Oracle or CoreWeave, Northflank covers that today and Nodus does not.

Where is Northflank the better choice?

Pick Northflank when the GPU is one piece of an application. If your inference API, Postgres database, preview environments and CI/CD already live there, adding a GPU job to the same project is less work than adding a second platform.

Northflank is also the better pick in these cases:

  • You want 8 x H200 and price is the deciding factor. Its listed $3.14 per GPU-hour is below Nodus.
  • You need GPUs in Oracle, CoreWeave or Nebius accounts under one control plane, or timeslicing in your own cluster.
  • You need an Enterprise contract with your VPC, on-premises or air-gapped deployment, SAML, SCIM and a custom SLA, all listed on its pricing page.
  • You serve models with autoscaling services and want training and serving on the same platform.

Pick Nodus when the job is the product. That means a fine-tune or training run that should finish at a low listed rate, survive a lost machine without your own resume code, and stop at a dollar cap. For other ways to run training, see our Modal alternatives for training and Nodus vs RunPod comparisons.

How do you move a training job from Northflank to Nodus?

If your Northflank job runs a container with a training command, the move is one command. Install the CLI with pip install nodus-compute, run nodus login, then preview the estimate from the directory holding your script:

nodus run --name finetune --gpu H100:8 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 250 --timeout 12h --dry-run -- torchrun train.py

Drop --dry-run to start it. To get recovery, write your model, optimizer and step to /nodus/state and load them on start, as the checkpoints guide shows. The flags are copied from the Nodus CLI reference; --max-cost 250 is a cap we picked to sit above the $208.00 estimate, not a quote.

FAQ

Does Northflank offer single H100 GPUs?

Not on Northflank Cloud as of the date above. Its pricing page lists the H100, H200 and B200 at 8 GPUs per container, while the L4, A100 and RTX PRO 6000 come in 1, 2, 4 or 8. Nodus lists the H100 per GPU, so a one-GPU job runs on one GPU.

Does Northflank Cloud use spot GPUs?

Its pricing page describes Northflank Cloud GPUs as on demand, billed by the second. Spot nodes are a bring-your-own-cloud feature, where workloads need a spot tag to land on them. On Nodus, --interruptible takes allow, prefer or never for each run, and recovery handles the reclaims.

Can I try Northflank for free?

The free Sandbox plan includes up to $20 a month of resources on Northflank Cloud, but GPU deployments need at least $50 of account credit. Nodus shows the estimated cost of a run with --dry-run before anything is charged.

Can a coding agent launch training on either platform?

Both have MCP servers. Northflank's sets up with nf agent setup --agent claude, and Nodus installs with nodus mcp install. On Nodus the agent sees the cost estimate before it runs, and a --max-cost cap bounds what it can spend, as covered in how to cap an agent's GPU spending.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Your AI apps should answer to you, not to their lab
description:
I use models from four labs every week, and every one of them wanted my accounts connected inside its own app, with its own idea of what was allowed. I couldn't see what any of them did with that access, and there was no single switch to stop them.

So I put one layer in the middle that I control. This post walks through how it works, in case you want to build the same thing. I also built one you can use, called Kin.

Connect everything to the layer once

The layer holds every connection, whether that's an MCP server by its address, an API from its OpenAPI document, or the tools and commands on your own machine. You sign in once, in one place, and the AI apps never hold your tokens. They talk to the layer and it makes the call.

This also keeps the model's context small. If every MCP server you add puts its tools in front of the model, ten servers can mean hundreds of tool definitions and a model that picks the wrong one. Giving the AI a few fixed tools works better. It searches for the action it needs, gets back that one schema, and calls it, so adding more connections doesn't add to the context.

Give every action one setting

Each action gets one of three settings. It runs on its own, it waits for you to approve that exact request, or it can't run at all. Actions that can't run are hidden from the AI, so it doesn't keep trying them.

OAuth scopes tend to bundle read and delete together, and permission grids with dozens of options don't get filled in. One setting per action is quick to set and still makes sense a month later.

Setting actions one at a time gets old fast, so each account starts from a preset like read only, ask before any change, or ask only before something goes out to other people. Under every preset, anything that deletes asks first or is blocked.

Let approvals wait instead of fail

When an action needs your approval, the tool call stays open while the request goes to your phone. You see the app, the account, the action and the exact details it wants to send. You approve or deny it, and the original call gets the result.

Clients give up eventually, some after about 45 seconds, so the wait needs a limit. If it runs out, nothing is approved, and the agent picks up your answer the next time it checks. An approval runs that one request once, and if the agent retries with the same request key it gets the first result back, so nothing runs twice.

Check the rule on the server every time

If the rules live in each AI app's settings, every app has its own version of them. Checking on the layer's server at call time means one set of rules holds everywhere, and a change applies to the next call. It's worth checking again right before the action runs too, in case the rule changed while a request was waiting.

Log everything and keep a stop switch

Every request goes in one log with what ran, what waited, what was approved and what was blocked. Kin let me see that my ChatGPT account tried to pull data the day after I canceled it. Yikes. You also want one switch that pauses every agent at once.

Switching AI apps

Since the connections, rules and history live in the layer, you can swap the AI app out. When a better model ships you add it and it follows the rules you already have, and removing an app ends its access right away. Work carries over too. When one agent hits its usage limit, another can pick up its notes and next step.

Trying it with Kin

Kin is one remote MCP server, so any AI app that can add one can use it. In Claude Code it's two commands.

claude mcp add --transport http kin https://app.kinlab.ai/mcp
claude mcp login kin

Then connect what you already use, either an MCP server by its address or a service from the catalog, pick a preset, and change the few actions you care about.

What it doesn't cover

The layer only governs what goes through it. If an account is also connected directly inside an AI app, or a coding agent has your shell and credentials, that path follows the app's own controls. A few MCP servers also only accept clients they already know. To keep an account under your rules, connect it only through the layer.

Kin has a free plan, and rules and approvals are on it. https://kinlab.ai/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=community-1102

I'd like to hear where this breaks down for how you work!

title: I benchmarked my own agent skill, and today's Claude barely needed it
description:
I wanted to write an agent skill that makes coding agents better at data analysis. The kind of mistakes I had in
mind are the ones that produce a confident, wrong number: a "Total" row summed together with the countries, a join
that duplicates orders, averaged p99s, timed-out requests that vanish from the latency percentiles, an A/B test that
was supposed to split 50/50 and came back 50.7/49.3.

Every rule in the skill comes from a paper or official documentation. But before claiming it helps, I wanted to
measure it.

The benchmark

I built 30 realistic cases, each with one planted trap and a correct answer computed by code:

  • 19 data-analysis traps (subtotal rows, join fan-out, average of averages, NA parsed as null when it's Namibia, partial weeks, sample ratio mismatch, segment fishing, Simpson's paradox, …)
  • 8 performance and reliability traps (closed-loop load tests, a saturated load generator, retries counted as requests, tail-sampled traces, regression to the mean after a "perf sprint", …)
  • 3 tasks where the agent measures its own work (fix a flaky test and confirm it, report a speedup, measure logging overhead)

Each case ran with and without the skill on Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, graded by an LLM judge (Sonnet,
3 votes per grader).

The result

With skill Without skill
Haiku 5.5 61/61 58/61
Sonnet 5.5 61/61 60/61

Today's Claude models already avoid nearly all of these traps, including the harder performance ones. The skill
fixed every baseline miss (-1 timeout sentinels, which both models missed, plus a closed-loop load test hiding a
stall and an overhead number reported without uncertainty on Haiku) and introduced no new failures. But with one
run per arm, that's "catches occasional slips", not a large effect. That's what the README says.

What I learned

1. Skills help most where the model's knowledge is weakest. The same week I wrote a skill for upgrading to
TypeScript 7, which shipped after the models' training cutoff. There the gains were real: graders passed went from
10/18 to 17/18 on Sonnet and 7/18 to 15/18 on Haiku, on small samples with offline agents. Mainstream analysis
practice is already in the model. Post-cutoff releases and exact operational details are not.

2. Check your test cases before you trust a baseline failure. Across both projects, several of the
"failures" I first saw were flaws in my own cases: an effect I hadn't intended in the data generator, a grader
that was too strict, a premise that contradicted itself. Once, Haiku correctly pointed out that a case's premise
was wrong.

3. A skill that doesn't activate doesn't help. In the benchmark the skill activated by itself in 22/30 Haiku
runs. Its description listed data types and trap names. The prompts it missed asked for an action: "should we
roll back?", "confirm it's fixed", "measure the overhead". I rewrote the description to say when to load it ("at
the start of any task whose answer will include a number … before reading files, running benchmarks or editing
code"). In a short trigger test on Haiku (first 3 turns, 2 rounds), activation on 10 queries the description
was never tuned on went from 7/20 to 20/20, with no activations on 10 unrelated queries.

Try it

The benchmark runs against any agent, with or without the skill. If you run it on another model or agent, I'd
like to see the results: https://github.com/boranfurkan/trustworthy-data-analysis

title: Why your INP can fall after one more click
description:
By Aditya Reddy

You record a slow click, change no code, click again, and the page's Interaction to Next Paint (INP) score drops. The slow interaction is still there. The calculation just picked a different one.

A dashboard gives you one number. A browser trace gives you a lot of events. I opened a PR to explain the INP calculation in the Event Timing specification, and it is still under review. Here is the calculation with actual numbers.

One click can leave several entries

Event Timing exposes PerformanceEventTiming entries. A gesture can produce several related entries, grouped by a nonzero interactionId. An entry with an ID of zero does not belong in this interaction calculation. The Event Timing specification describes that grouping.

Take these made-up entries from one page visit:

Interaction ID Event Duration
7 pointerdown 320 ms
7 pointerup 296 ms
7 click 280 ms
14 click 480 ms
21 keydown 240 ms

Interaction 7 contributes 320 ms. Adding its three entries would produce 896 ms and count overlapping time more than once. Use the longest duration for the group.

That leaves three interaction latencies: 480, 320 and 240 ms, sorted from longest to shortest.

The fiftieth interaction changes the selection

INP leaves out one longest interaction for each complete group of 50 interactions. Google's INP explanation describes why pages with many interactions get this treatment.

Keep those three slow interactions, and suppose every other interaction takes less than 240 ms.

Total interactions in the visit Longest values skipped Selected latency
49 0 480 ms
50 1 320 ms
99 1 320 ms
100 2 240 ms

At the fiftieth interaction, a fast click can move the score from 480 to 320 ms. Nothing became faster.

The selection in web-vitals uses a descending list and a zero-based index:

const skip = Math.floor(interactionCount / 50);
const index = Math.min(skip, descendingLatencies.length - 1);
const candidate = descendingLatencies[index];

This fragment needs at least one candidate. It only covers selection. A complete INP collector needs more.

Keep interactionCount separate from your list length. The count covers interactions across the visit, though your collector may only receive and keep some of them. web-vitals keeps up to ten of the longest interactions.

Lowering the threshold does not recover the past

For entries of type event, Event Timing buffers and exposes durations of 104 ms or above by default. Registering an observer with durationThreshold: 16 lowers the threshold for subsequent delivery. Asking for buffered entries still only recovers the earlier events kept under the default threshold. The specification explains this distinction in when events are measured.

Fast interactions can therefore increase the total count without adding entries to your observed list. A late observer cannot reconstruct the missing durations just by asking for a lower threshold.

For production collection, start with web-vitals, which handles more than this selection step. First-input handling, page visibility and back/forward cache restores matter. A calculation for one window also cannot see every interaction inside an embedded frame.

Keep the score and the debugging evidence

When checking your calculation, keep the selected interaction's latency and ID alongside the total interaction count. Then you can see whether the interaction got faster or the calculation picked a different one.

If your fix is meant to speed up the 480 ms interaction, compare that interaction before and after the change under similar conditions. Another fast click can lower the visit score without fixing the slow interaction.

The proposed specification section covers grouping and selection, plus the observer threshold and the limit on retained candidates.

title: TypeScript 7 upgrade: the two silent default changes and the missing compiler API
description:
TypeScript 7.0 shipped in July: the Go-native compiler, about 10x faster type-checking, still installed as
typescript and still run as tsc. Most of its breaking changes were announced as deprecations in 6.0, so the
upgrade looks easy. Three things catch people anyway.

1. types now defaults to []

Before 6.0, TypeScript loaded every @types/* package in node_modules. Now it loads none unless you list them.
The symptom:

error TS2580: Cannot find name 'process'.
error TS2582: Cannot find name 'describe'.

even though @types/node and @types/jest are installed. The fix is to list them:

"compilerOptions": {
  "types": ["node", "jest"]
}

If you'd rather keep the old behaviour, "types": ["*"] brings it back. Listing them is better: test globals
like describe belong in the test tsconfig, not the one that builds your app.

2. rootDir now defaults to the tsconfig's directory

It used to be inferred as the common directory of your input files, usually src/. Now it's the directory that
contains tsconfig.json. If your tsconfig sits at the project root, src/server.ts is emitted to
dist/src/server.js, and node dist/server.js or your "main" field breaks.

"compilerOptions": {
  "rootDir": "./src"
}

If a test config extends this one and includes test/, it needs its own rootDir (for example "."), or the test
files fall outside rootDir.

3. 7.0 ships without a compiler API

This is the big one. The 7.0 release notes say it plainly: 7.0 does not ship with an API. A new, different API is
planned for 7.1. Anything that loads typescript as a library can't run on 7.0: typescript-eslint (type-aware
rules), vue-tsc and other Volar-based tools, ts-jest, ts-node, ts-patch transformers, and your own scripts that call
ts.createProgram. As of early November typescript-eslint still doesn't support TS 7.

You don't have to choose. The TypeScript team publishes @typescript/typescript6, which re-exports the 6.0 API
and installs a tsc6 binary. Alias it as typescript so library consumers keep getting 6.0, and install 7.0 under
another name for the fast tsc:

{
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6",    // what typescript-eslint, vue-tsc, ts-jest import (bin: tsc6)
    "@typescript/native": "npm:typescript@^7.0.2"   // the 7.0 compiler (bin: tsc)
  },
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",                    // 7.0
    "typecheck:vue": "vue-tsc --noEmit"             // still 6.0 via the alias
  }
}

Be explicit about which command runs on which version. In a Vue project, for example, the slow check is usually
vue-tsc, which stays on 6.0, so the 10x speedup may not show up where you expected it.

The hard errors (quick list)

Deprecated in 6.0, errors in 7.0, and "ignoreDeprecations": "6.0" won't save you:
target: es5, downlevelIteration, moduleResolution: node/node10/classic, baseUrl,
esModuleInterop: false, allowSyntheticDefaultImports: false, alwaysStrict: false, outFile,
module: amd/umd/system/none, the module keyword for namespaces, and import asserts (use with).

The safe order

  1. Upgrade to 6.0 first. Turn on "stableTypeOrdering": true, remove ignoreDeprecations, fix everything. Code that compiles cleanly there should compile the same on 7.0. (The flag can slow 6.0 by about 25%; it's a diagnostic step, not a permanent setting.)
  2. Set rootDir and types explicitly.
  3. Move to 7.0, keeping API-dependent tools on 6.0 with the alias.
  4. On small CI runners, --checkers <n> (default 4) limits the parallel type-checkers.

Why I wrote this down

TypeScript 7 shipped after the training cutoff of today's coding agents. In my tests, Claude knew the general
direction but hedged or guessed on these details, especially the @typescript/typescript6 setup. So I packaged
the facts from the official release notes as an agent skill. In small offline evals it raised graders passed from
10/18 to 17/18 on Sonnet and 7/18 to 15/18 on Haiku. Two runs per arm, and agents with web access may find
the facts themselves, so read those numbers as a hint, not a result:
https://github.com/boranfurkan/typescript-7-migration

Sources: Announcing TypeScript 7.0,
Announcing TypeScript 6.0,
typescript-eslint #12518.

title: UK CMA Requires Google to Provide AI Search Click Data to Publishers
description:
The UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has required Google to give publishers more detailed reporting on how people engage with their content in AI-driven Search features. The requirement covers impressions, clicks and click-through rate (CTR) when Search Content is used in features including AI Overviews and AI Mode.

The change matters because publishers have had limited visibility into whether AI search results generate visits to their sites. Under the CMA's Publisher Conduct Requirement, Google must provide data that is separated from traditional organic Search reporting and broken out by publisher. Google has until 3 December 2026 to comply with the reporting requirement.

What Google must report to publishers

The CMA's Publisher Conduct Requirement requires Google to provide detailed, disaggregated engagement metrics for publisher content used in its AI features. The specified measures are:

  • Impressions
  • Clicks
  • Click-through rate

The data must be separated from organic search data and available at the publisher level. The CMA indicates that Google can provide the reporting through a platform such as Google Search Console.

This distinction is important. A publisher may currently see overall Search performance, but aggregate figures do not show whether an impression or click came from a conventional web result or from an AI-generated search experience. Separate reporting should make it possible to evaluate those channels independently rather than infer AI search performance from changes in total traffic.

The requirement does not mean that the new reporting is available now. Reporting ahead of the decision noted that Google had not announced additional AI click data, and the compliance deadline remains in December 2026. Publishers should therefore avoid treating existing Search Console reports as a complete measurement of engagement with AI Overviews or AI Mode.

The deadline and the related publisher controls

Google's deadline for the data-reporting obligation is 3 December 2026. The CMA also requires Google to offer controls that let publishers opt their content out of being used to train or ground AI systems. Google has an additional three months to roll out page-level controls, taking that part of the implementation to roughly March 2027.

The CMA's measures also require Google to publish information about attribution and factuality in its AI-driven search features. Google is expected to provide compliance reporting at least every six months during the first year.

Requirement What it means for publishers Timing stated by the CMA
Disaggregated AI engagement metrics Separate impressions, clicks and CTR for Search Content used in AI features By 3 December 2026
Controls over AI use Options to opt content out of AI training or grounding Page-level controls roughly by March 2027
Compliance reporting Updates on Google's implementation of the requirements At least every six months in the first year

Why separate AI data changes the measurement conversation

An AI Overview impression is not equivalent to a website visit. A user may find enough information in an AI-generated response to end their search, or they may choose one of the cited links. Without separate click data, publishers cannot reliably quantify the difference between appearing in an AI answer and receiving referral traffic from it.

The CMA's requirement addresses that measurement gap for affected publishers. It should allow teams to calculate AI-feature CTR and compare it with their organic Search CTR, provided Google implements the data in a sufficiently usable form.

That comparison will still need care. A lower CTR from AI features would not, by itself, establish that AI results reduced total clicks. Query mix, ranking changes, seasonality, devices and changes to the Search results page can all affect performance. Equally, high AI impressions may indicate prominent use of a publisher's content without demonstrating conversions, subscriptions or revenue.

The requirement is a transparency measure, not a guarantee of traffic. It also does not establish that data from the UK implementation will necessarily be offered in the same way to publishers elsewhere.

How publishers can prepare before reporting arrives

The deadline gives publishers time to strengthen their measurement baseline. The most useful preparation is not to guess at AI clicks, but to document existing performance so future data can be interpreted in context.
