1. What Is TypeScript?

TypeScript is a programming language developed by Microsoft.

It is a superset of JavaScript, meaning that valid JavaScript code is generally valid TypeScript code.

TypeScript adds a static type system to JavaScript.

Consider this JavaScript function:

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

add(10, 20);
add("Hello", "World");

JavaScript allows both calls.

But what if the function is supposed to work only with numbers?

TypeScript allows us to express that intention:

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

add(10, 20);

// TypeScript error
add("Hello", "World");

Now TypeScript can detect an incorrect function call before the application runs.

Does TypeScript run in the browser?

No. Browsers execute JavaScript, not TypeScript.

TypeScript code must be transformed into JavaScript before execution.

TypeScript
    ↓
Type checking and compilation
    ↓
JavaScript
    ↓
Browser

Tools such as Vite, Next.js, and other build systems handle this transformation.

Important: TypeScript types are primarily checked during development and are erased from the generated JavaScript. They do not automatically validate data coming from an API at runtime.

2. JavaScript vs. TypeScript

JavaScript:

function getUserName(user) {
  return user.name;
}

TypeScript:

function getUserName(user: { name: string }): string {
  return user.name;
}

The TypeScript version tells us:

  • user must have a name property.
  • name must be a string.
  • The function returns a string.

TypeScript helps developers catch mistakes earlier, improve autocomplete, and understand code more easily.

3. Type Annotations

A type annotation tells TypeScript what type a variable, parameter, or return value should have.

The syntax is:

variableName: Type

Examples:

let username: string = "Hamed";

let age: number = 26;

let isActive: boolean = true;

Now consider:

let age: number = 26;

age = 30;

// TypeScript error
age = "Thirty";

The variable is declared as a number, so assigning a string causes a type error.

Function parameters 

function greet(name: string) {
  return `Hello, ${name}`;
}

greet("React Developer");

Function return types 

function multiply(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a * b;
}

The : number after the parameter list specifies the function's return type.

4. Basic TypeScript Types

String 

let firstName: string = "John";

Number 

let score: number = 100;

TypeScript uses number for integers and floating-point numbers.

Boolean 

let isLoggedIn: boolean = false;

Null and Undefined 

let emptyValue: null = null;

let missingValue: undefined = undefined;

These types are especially important when working with optional values.

Object 

let user: {
  name: string;
  age: number;
} = {
  name: "John",
  age: 25,
};

Any 

let value: any = "Hello";

value = 100;

value = true;

any disables type checking for that value.

It can be convenient temporarily, but using it everywhere removes many of TypeScript's benefits.

We'll discuss safer alternatives later.

5. Type Inference

TypeScript can often determine a variable's type automatically.

This is called type inference.

let username = "John";

TypeScript understands that username is a string.

Therefore, writing this is usually unnecessary:

let username: string = "John";

Both examples work, but the first is more concise.

Another example:

let count = 10;

count = 20;

// TypeScript error
count = "Twenty";

TypeScript inferred count as a number.

When should you explicitly define a type?

Use explicit types when they improve clarity or when TypeScript cannot infer the intended type.

Common examples include:

  • Function parameters
  • Component props
  • API response models
  • Complex objects
  • State that can contain multiple types
  • Reusable functions and hooks

In React, you'll often see type annotations around component props and state.

6. Arrays and Objects

Arrays

An array of strings:

const names: string[] = ["John", "Sarah", "Alex"];

An array of numbers:

const scores: number[] = [10, 20, 30];

Another syntax uses Array<T>:

const names: Array<string> = ["John", "Sarah"];

Both approaches are valid.

For most React applications, string[] and number[] are easier to read.

Arrays of objects

Imagine an application displaying a list of users.

type User = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
};

const users: User[] = [
  {
    id: 1,
    name: "John",
    email: "john@example.com",
  },
  {
    id: 2,
    name: "Sarah",
    email: "sarah@example.com",
  },
];

Now every user must follow the User structure.

const newUser: User = {
  id: 3,
  name: "Alex",
  email: "alex@example.com",
};

This becomes extremely useful when rendering lists in React.

{users.map((user) => (
  <div key={user.id}>
    <h2>{user.name}</h2>
    <p>{user.email}</p>
  </div>
))}

7. type vs. interface

Both type and interface allow you to describe the structure of an object.

Using type 

type User = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
};

Using interface 

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

For this example, both behave similarly.

Extending an interface 

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

interface Admin extends User {
  permissions: string[];
}

Now Admin includes the properties from User and adds permissions.

const admin: Admin = {
  id: 1,
  name: "John",
  permissions: ["read", "write"],
};

Extending a type 

type User = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
};

type Admin = User & {
  permissions: string[];
};

The & operator combines types. This is called an intersection type.

What's the difference?

  • interface is commonly used to describe object shapes.
  • type can describe objects, unions, primitives, tuples, and more.
  • Interfaces can be reopened and merged through declaration merging.
  • Type aliases cannot be reopened in the same way.

For React projects, either is perfectly acceptable.

A common convention is:

interface ButtonProps {
  label: string;
}

type Status = "loading" | "success" | "error";

The most important thing is consistency within your project.

8. Union Types and Literal Types

A union type allows a value to have more than one possible type.

let value: string | number;

value = "Hello";

value = 100;

The | symbol means OR.

Union types in React

Imagine a component that receives either a username or a numeric user ID.

type UserIdentifier = string | number;

function getUser(id: UserIdentifier) {
  console.log(id);
}

Both calls are valid:

getUser("john");

getUser(123);

Literal types

Literal types restrict a value to specific options.

type Status = "loading" | "success" | "error";

Now:

let status: Status = "loading";

status = "success";

// TypeScript error
status = "completed";

Literal unions are extremely useful in React.

type ButtonVariant = "primary" | "secondary" | "danger";

interface ButtonProps {
  variant: ButtonVariant;
  children: React.ReactNode;
}

function Button({ variant, children }: ButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button className={`button button-${variant}`}>
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

Now the component only accepts the supported variants.

<Button variant="primary">Save</Button>

<Button variant="danger">Delete</Button>

// TypeScript error
<Button variant="banana">Click</Button>

9. Optional Properties

Sometimes an object does not need every property.

Use ? to make a property optional.

interface User {
  name: string;
  age?: number;
}

Both objects are valid:

const user1: User = {
  name: "John",
};

const user2: User = {
  name: "Sarah",
  age: 25,
};

The age property may be present or absent.

However, accessing it requires care:

console.log(user1.age);

The result may be undefined.

Optional properties in React 

interface GreetingProps {
  name: string;
  subtitle?: string;
}

function Greeting({ name, subtitle }: GreetingProps) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello, {name}</h1>

      {subtitle && <p>{subtitle}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

Usage:

<Greeting name="John" />

<Greeting
  name="Sarah"
  subtitle="Welcome back!"
/>

10. Functions and Return Types

TypeScript allows us to define the types of function parameters and return values.

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}

The function accepts two numbers and returns a number.

Arrow functions 

const subtract = (a: number, b: number): number => {
  return a - b;
};

Functions that return nothing 

function logMessage(message: string): void {
  console.log(message);
}

void indicates that the function's return value is not intended to be used.

Function types 

type Calculator = (a: number, b: number) => number;

const multiply: Calculator = (a, b) => {
  return a * b;
};

This is useful for callbacks and React props.

interface ButtonProps {
  onClick: () => void;
}

The onClick property is a function that accepts no arguments and returns nothing meaningful.

11. Reusable Types

Instead of repeatedly writing the same object structure, create reusable types.

Without a reusable type:

function getUserName(user: {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}) {
  return user.name;
}

function getUserId(user: {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}) {
  return user.id;
}

This creates unnecessary duplication.

With a reusable type:

type User = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
};

function getUserName(user: User): string {
  return user.name;
}

function getUserId(user: User): number {
  return user.id;
}

This becomes especially valuable in large React applications.

You might define types for:

  • User
  • Product
  • Post
  • API response
  • Form values
  • Component props

A common project structure might look like:

src/
├── components/
│   ├── Button.tsx
│   └── UserCard.tsx
├── types/
│   └── user.ts
└── App.tsx

Example user.ts:

export interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

Then import it:

import type { User } from "../types/user";

The import type syntax explicitly imports a type rather than a runtime value.

12. Type Narrowing

Type narrowing means making a broad type more specific after checking its value.

Consider:

function printValue(value: string | number) {
  console.log(value);
}

The value could be a string or a number.

But what if we want to call a string-specific method?

function printValue(value: string | number) {
  if (typeof value === "string") {
    console.log(value.toUpperCase());
  } else {
    console.log(value.toFixed(2));
  }
}

TypeScript understands:

  • Inside the first branch, value is a string.
  • Inside the second branch, value is a number.

This is called type narrowing.

Narrowing with typeof 

function formatValue(value: string | number) {
  if (typeof value === "number") {
    return value.toFixed(2);
  }

  return value.toUpperCase();
}

Narrowing with in 

type Admin = {
  role: "admin";
  permissions: string[];
};

type User = {
  role: "user";
  name: string;
};

function displayAccount(account: Admin | User) {
  if ("permissions" in account) {
    console.log(account.permissions);
  } else {
    console.log(account.name);
  }
}

Type narrowing is important when working with API responses and complex React state.

13. Generics

Generics are one of the most powerful TypeScript concepts.

They allow you to create reusable functions, types, and components while preserving type information.

Imagine this function:

function getValue(value: number): number {
  return value;
}

It only works with numbers.

We could create another function for strings:

function getString(value: string): string {
  return value;
}

But this duplicates logic.

Generics solve this problem.

Basic generic function 

function identity<T>(value: T): T {
  return value;
}

The T represents a type that will be determined when the function is used.

const numberValue = identity(100);

const stringValue = identity("Hello");

TypeScript understands:

numberValue // number
stringValue // string

T is a convention, not a special keyword. You could use another name, but T is commonly used for "Type".

Generic arrays 

function getFirstItem<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

const firstNumber = getFirstItem([10, 20, 30]);

const firstName = getFirstItem(["John", "Sarah"]);

TypeScript infers the type from the array.

Generics in React

Imagine a reusable list component.

interface ListProps<T> {
  items: T[];
  renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode;
}

function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: ListProps<T>) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item, index) => (
        <li key={index}>
          {renderItem(item)}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Usage:

const names = ["John", "Sarah", "Alex"];

<List
  items={names}
  renderItem={(name) => <span>{name}</span>}
/>

TypeScript infers that name is a string.

For a more complex example:

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

const users: User[] = [
  { id: 1, name: "John" },
  { id: 2, name: "Sarah" },
];

<List
  items={users}
  renderItem={(user) => <span>{user.name}</span>}
/>

Now user is automatically typed as User.

You don't need to manually annotate it.

14. TypeScript with React Components

React components are functions that return React elements.

A simple component:

function Welcome() {
  return <h1>Hello React!</h1>;
}

TypeScript can infer the return type.

In most cases, you don't need to explicitly write:

function Welcome(): JSX.Element {
  return <h1>Hello React!</h1>;
}

Modern React projects typically allow TypeScript to infer the component return type.

The most important thing to type explicitly is usually the component's props.

15. Typing React Props

Props are values passed from a parent component to a child component.

JavaScript:

function UserCard(props) {
  return <h2>{props.name}</h2>;
}

TypeScript:

interface UserCardProps {
  name: string;
  age: number;
}

function UserCard({ name, age }: UserCardProps) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>{age}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

Usage:

<UserCard name="John" age={25} />

Incorrect usage:

<UserCard name="John" age="Twenty-five" />

TypeScript detects that age must be a number.

Why destructuring works

This syntax:

function UserCard({ name, age }: UserCardProps) {
  // ...
}

Means:

  1. The component receives an object.
  2. The object must follow UserCardProps.
  3. We extract name and age from that object.

You can also write:

function UserCard(props: UserCardProps) {
  return <h2>{props.name}</h2>;
}

Both approaches are valid.

16. Optional Props and Default Values

A component might have required and optional props.

interface ButtonProps {
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
}

Usage:

<Button label="Save" />

<Button label="Save" disabled={true} />

You can provide a default value:

interface ButtonProps {
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
}

function Button({ label, disabled = false }: ButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button disabled={disabled}>
      {label}
    </button>
  );
}

Now disabled defaults to false.

This is a common pattern in React components.

17. Typing Children

React components often receive content between their opening and closing tags.

<Card>
  <h2>Hello</h2>
</Card>

That content is called children.

The common type for arbitrary renderable React content is React.ReactNode.

import type { ReactNode } from "react";

interface CardProps {
  children: ReactNode;
}

function Card({ children }: CardProps) {
  return <div className="card">{children}</div>;
}

Usage:

<Card>
  <h2>User Profile</h2>
  <p>Welcome back!</p>
</Card>

ReactNode can represent many kinds of renderable content, including:

  • React elements
  • Strings
  • Numbers
  • Arrays of renderable nodes
  • null
  • undefined

Optional children 

interface CardProps {
  children?: ReactNode;
}

Use this when the component can be rendered without children.

ReactNode vs. ReactElement

ReactNode is broader and generally used when a component accepts arbitrary renderable content.

ReactElement describes a React element object.

For most component children props, ReactNode is the practical choice.

18. Typing React Events

React event handlers are one of the most important TypeScript topics.

Consider:

function Input() {
  return <input onChange={(event) => console.log(event)} />;
}

React and TypeScript can often infer the event type automatically.

However, sometimes you need to define it explicitly.

Input events 

import type { ChangeEvent } from "react";

function Input() {
  const handleChange = (event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
    console.log(event.target.value);
  };

  return <input onChange={handleChange} />;
}

The type:

ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>

means this is a change event associated with an HTML input element.

Textarea events 

import type { ChangeEvent } from "react";

function TextArea() {
  const handleChange = (
    event: ChangeEvent<HTMLTextAreaElement>
  ) => {
    console.log(event.target.value);
  };

  return <textarea onChange={handleChange} />;
}

Select events 

import type { ChangeEvent } from "react";

function Select() {
  const handleChange = (
    event: ChangeEvent<HTMLSelectElement>
  ) => {
    console.log(event.target.value);
  };

  return (
    <select onChange={handleChange}>
      <option value="react">React</option>
      <option value="vue">Vue</option>
    </select>
  );
}

Click events 

import type { MouseEvent } from "react";

function Button() {
  const handleClick = (event: MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => {
    console.log(event.currentTarget);
  };

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>;
}

Form events 

import type { FormEvent } from "react";

function LoginForm() {
  const handleSubmit = (event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) => {
    event.preventDefault();

    console.log("Form submitted");
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <button type="submit">Login</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Common React event types

Event Type
Input change ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>
Textarea change ChangeEvent<HTMLTextAreaElement>
Select change ChangeEvent<HTMLSelectElement>
Button click MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>
Form submission FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>
Keyboard event KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>

You usually don't need to memorize every event type. TypeScript autocomplete and your editor can help.

19. Typing useState

useState is one of the most common React hooks.

TypeScript can infer the state type from the initial value.

import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
      {count}
    </button>
  );
}

TypeScript understands that count is a number.

Therefore:

setCount(10);

is valid, but:

setCount("Ten");

is not.

Explicit state types

Sometimes the initial value doesn't tell TypeScript enough.

For example:

const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);

Here:

type User = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
};

The state can contain either a User or null.

Later:

setUser({
  id: 1,
  name: "John",
});

State with multiple possible values 

type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error";

const [status, setStatus] = useState<Status>("idle");

Now only those four values are allowed.

Array state 

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);

You can update it:

setUsers((previousUsers) => [
  ...previousUsers,
  {
    id: 1,
    name: "John",
  },
]);

Important

Don't add explicit types unnecessarily.

This is usually enough:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

But this is useful:

const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);

20. Typing useEffect

useEffect is used to synchronize a component with external systems, such as APIs, subscriptions, or browser features.

TypeScript usually infers the types inside useEffect.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

function Example() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    console.log(count);
  }, [count]);

  return <p>{count}</p>;
}

No additional type annotation is necessary.

Cleanup functions 

import { useEffect } from "react";

function Timer() {
  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      console.log("Tick");
    }, 1000);

    return () => {
      clearInterval(timer);
    };
  }, []);

  return <p>Timer running</p>;
}

TypeScript understands the cleanup function automatically.

The important lesson: you usually don't need to manually type useEffect.

21. Typing useRef

useRef is commonly used to access DOM elements or store values that persist between renders.

Accessing an input element 

import { useRef } from "react";

function SearchInput() {
  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

  const handleFocus = () => {
    inputRef.current?.focus();
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <input ref={inputRef} />

      <button onClick={handleFocus}>
        Focus input
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

Let's understand this:

useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)

The reference points to an HTML input element.

Initially, it is null because the DOM element hasn't been attached yet.

That's why the type is effectively:

HTMLInputElement | null

The optional chaining operator:

inputRef.current?.focus();

checks whether current exists before calling focus().

Other DOM elements 

useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);

useRef<HTMLTextAreaElement>(null);

Storing values 

const countRef = useRef<number>(0);

This stores a number without causing a component re-render when it changes.

22. Typing useReducer

useReducer is useful when state logic becomes more complex.

import { useReducer } from "react";

type State = {
  count: number;
};

type Action =
  | { type: "increment" }
  | { type: "decrement" }
  | { type: "reset" };

const initialState: State = {
  count: 0,
};

function reducer(state: State, action: Action): State {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "increment":
      return {
        count: state.count + 1,
      };

    case "decrement":
      return {
        count: state.count - 1,
      };

    case "reset":
      return initialState;

    default:
      return state;
  }
}

function Counter() {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{state.count}</h2>

      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "increment" })}>
        Increment
      </button>

      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "decrement" })}>
        Decrement
      </button>

      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "reset" })}>
        Reset
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

Notice this:

type Action =
  | { type: "increment" }
  | { type: "decrement" }
  | { type: "reset" };

This is a discriminated union.

The type property identifies which action is being handled.

TypeScript can understand which action is active inside each case.

If you try:

dispatch({ type: "delete" });

TypeScript will report an error.

23. Typing Context API

Context allows components to share values without passing props through every level.

import {
  createContext,
  useContext,
  useState,
} from "react";

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

interface AuthContextType {
  user: User | null;
  login: (user: User) => void;
  logout: () => void;
}

const AuthContext = createContext<AuthContextType | undefined>(
  undefined
);

Now define the provider:

function AuthProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);

  const login = (user: User) => {
    setUser(user);
  };

  const logout = () => {
    setUser(null);
  };

  return (
    <AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, login, logout }}>
      {children}
    </AuthContext.Provider>
  );
}

Create a custom hook:

function useAuth() {
  const context = useContext(AuthContext);

  if (!context) {
    throw new Error("useAuth must be used within AuthProvider");
  }

  return context;
}

Now components can access the context:

function Profile() {
  const { user, logout } = useAuth();

  if (!user) {
    return <p>Please log in</p>;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{user.name}</h2>

      <button onClick={logout}>
        Logout
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

The context type guarantees that consumers receive the correct structure.

24. Typing Custom Hooks

Custom hooks are reusable functions that use React hooks.

TypeScript makes custom hooks safer and easier to reuse.

import { useState } from "react";

function useToggle(initialValue: boolean = false) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue);

  const toggle = () => {
    setValue((previousValue) => !previousValue);
  };

  return {
    value,
    toggle,
  };
}

Usage:

function App() {
  const { value, toggle } = useToggle();

  return (
    <button onClick={toggle}>
      {value ? "ON" : "OFF"}
    </button>
  );
}

TypeScript infers the return type of the hook.

You don't need to manually write it unless there's a specific reason.

Custom hook with generics 

import { useState } from "react";

function useArray<T>(initialValue: T[]) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState<T[]>(initialValue);

  const addItem = (item: T) => {
    setItems((previousItems) => [...previousItems, item]);
  };

  const removeItem = (index: number) => {
    setItems((previousItems) =>
      previousItems.filter((_, i) => i !== index)
    );
  };

  return {
    items,
    addItem,
    removeItem,
  };
}

Usage:

const { items, addItem } = useArray<string>(["React", "TypeScript"]);

addItem("Next.js");

This hook works with different data types:

const numbers = useArray<number>([1, 2, 3]);

numbers.addItem(4);

25. Typing Forms

Forms are an essential part of React applications.

Let's create a login form.

import { useState } from "react";
import type { ChangeEvent, FormEvent } from "react";

interface LoginForm {
  email: string;
  password: string;
}

function Login() {
  const [form, setForm] = useState<LoginForm>({
    email: "",
    password: "",
  });

  const handleChange = (event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
    const { name, value } = event.target;

    setForm((previousForm) => ({
      ...previousForm,
      [name]: value,
    }));
  };

  const handleSubmit = (event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) => {
    event.preventDefault();

    console.log(form);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input
        name="email"
        type="email"
        value={form.email}
        onChange={handleChange}
      />

      <input
        name="password"
        type="password"
        value={form.password}
        onChange={handleChange}
      />

      <button type="submit">
        Login
      </button>
    </form>
  );
}

The LoginForm interface defines the structure of the form state.

The event handler receives a React change event.

The submit handler receives a React form event.

A note about dynamic property updates

This expression:

[name]: value

uses a computed property name.

It allows us to update the field whose name matches the input.

For more complex forms, libraries such as React Hook Form can provide additional structure and validation.

26. Typing API Requests

One of the most important real-world TypeScript use cases is working with APIs.

Imagine an API returns this JSON:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@example.com"
}

Create a type:

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

Then use it with Axios:

import axios from "axios";
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

function UserProfile() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    async function fetchUser() {
      try {
        const response = await axios.get<User>(
          "https://api.example.com/users/1"
        );

        setUser(response.data);
      } catch (error) {
        console.error(error);
      }
    }

    fetchUser();
  }, []);

  if (!user) {
    return <p>Loading...</p>;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{user.name}</h2>
      <p>{user.email}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

This part is important:

axios.get<User>(...)

The generic tells Axios what type you expect the response data to have.

However, this is only a compile-time expectation.

TypeScript does not verify that the server actually returned a valid User.

If the API returns unexpected data, TypeScript won't automatically detect it at runtime.

For runtime validation, libraries such as Zod can help.

Typing fetch 

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

async function getUser(): Promise<User> {
  const response = await fetch("/api/user");

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Failed to fetch user");
  }

  const data: User = await response.json();

  return data;
}

This example describes the expected type, but it still doesn't validate the JSON received from the server.

For production applications, consider validating external data at runtime.

27. Utility Types

TypeScript includes built-in utility types that help transform existing types.

These are especially useful in React projects.

Partial

Partial<T> makes every property optional.

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

type UpdateUser = Partial<User>;

Now:

const update: UpdateUser = {
  name: "Sarah",
};

This is useful for update forms and partial updates.

Pick

Pick<T, Keys> selects specific properties.

type UserPreview = Pick<User, "id" | "name">;

Result:

type UserPreview = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
};

Omit

Omit<T, Keys> removes selected properties.

type UserWithoutEmail = Omit<User, "email">;

Readonly

Readonly<T> makes properties readonly.

type ReadonlyUser = Readonly<User>;

Now:

const user: ReadonlyUser = {
  id: 1,
  name: "John",
  email: "john@example.com",
};

// TypeScript error
user.name = "Sarah";

Record

Record<Keys, Value> creates an object type with specific key and value types.

type UserRoles = Record<string, string>;

Example:

const roles: UserRoles = {
  john: "admin",
  sarah: "editor",
};

Another example:

type Status = "success" | "error" | "loading";

type StatusMessages = Record<Status, string>;

const messages: StatusMessages = {
  success: "Operation completed",
  error: "Something went wrong",
  loading: "Please wait",
};

ReturnType

ReturnType<T> extracts the return type of a function.

function createUser() {
  return {
    id: 1,
    name: "John",
  };
}

type CreatedUser = ReturnType<typeof createUser>;

This is useful when you want to reuse a function's return type.

28. Enums vs. Literal Unions

TypeScript supports enums.

enum Status {
  Loading,
  Success,
  Error,
}

Usage:

const currentStatus = Status.Loading;

But in many React applications, literal unions are a simpler alternative.

type Status = "loading" | "success" | "error";

Usage:

const currentStatus: Status = "loading";

Literal unions are often preferred because:

  • They are simple.
  • They work naturally with string values.
  • They don't require an enum declaration.
  • They are convenient for component props and state.

Enums are still useful in certain situations, but you don't need to use them everywhere.

29. any, unknown, and never

These three types are important to understand.

any 

let value: any = "Hello";

value.toUpperCase();

value = 100;

value.someRandomMethod();

TypeScript stops checking many operations involving any.

This can hide bugs.

Avoid using any unless you have a specific reason.

unknown

unknown is a safer alternative to any.

let value: unknown = "Hello";

You cannot use the value freely without checking its type.

if (typeof value === "string") {
  console.log(value.toUpperCase());
}

This makes unknown useful when handling data whose type is not known yet.

For example:

function handleError(error: unknown) {
  if (error instanceof Error) {
    console.log(error.message);
  } else {
    console.log("An unknown error occurred");
  }
}

This is a good pattern for handling errors in TypeScript.

never

never represents a value that should never occur.

One common use is exhaustive checking.

type Status = "loading" | "success" | "error";

function handleStatus(status: Status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "loading":
      return "Loading...";

    case "success":
      return "Success!";

    case "error":
      return "Error!";
  }
}

A helper for exhaustive checking:

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unexpected value: ${value}`);
}

function handleStatus(status: Status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "loading":
      return "Loading...";

    case "success":
      return "Success!";

    case "error":
      return "Error!";

    default:
      return assertNever(status);
  }
}

If someone adds a new status and forgets to handle it, TypeScript can help detect the missing case.

30. Type Assertions

Sometimes you know more about a value than TypeScript does.

A type assertion tells TypeScript how you want to treat that value.

const value = document.getElementById("username") as HTMLInputElement;

Now TypeScript treats value as an input element.

But be careful.

A type assertion does not perform runtime validation.

It does not convert a value into another type.

For example:

const value = "123" as unknown as number;

This does not convert the string into a number.

The value is still a string at runtime.

Use assertions carefully

Assertions are sometimes necessary, but they can hide errors if used incorrectly.

Prefer proper type narrowing when possible.

31. Common TypeScript Mistakes in React

Mistake 1: Using any everywhere

Bad:

function UserCard({ user }: any) {
  return <h2>{user.name}</h2>;
}

Better:

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

interface UserCardProps {
  user: User;
}

function UserCard({ user }: UserCardProps) {
  return <h2>{user.name}</h2>;
}

Mistake 2: Overusing explicit types

Unnecessary:

const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);

Usually enough:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

TypeScript already knows the type.

Mistake 3: Forgetting null

Incorrect:

const [user, setUser] = useState<User>(null);

Correct:

const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);

Mistake 4: Confusing type annotations with runtime validation 

const user: User = await response.json();

This does not validate the API response.

It only tells TypeScript to treat the value as User.

Mistake 5: Using React.FC everywhere

You may encounter:

const Button: React.FC<ButtonProps> = ({ children }) => {
  return <button>{children}</button>;
};

This is valid.

But modern React with TypeScript doesn't require React.FC.

You can simply write:

function Button({ children }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button>{children}</button>;
}

This is a common and straightforward approach.

32. Recommended Learning Path

You don't need to master every advanced TypeScript feature before starting React.

Focus on the following order:

Level 1 — Essential TypeScript

  • string
  • number
  • boolean
  • Arrays
  • Objects
  • Type annotations
  • Type inference
  • Functions
  • type
  • interface
  • Optional properties

Level 2 — React TypeScript

  • Component props
  • Props destructuring
  • Children
  • Optional props
  • Event types
  • useState
  • useEffect
  • useRef

Level 3 — Intermediate React TypeScript

  • Union types
  • Literal types
  • Type narrowing
  • Generics
  • Context API
  • useReducer
  • Custom hooks
  • API response types

Level 4 — Advanced TypeScript

  • Utility types
  • Discriminated unions
  • unknown
  • never
  • Type assertions
  • Generic components
  • Runtime validation

Final Thoughts

TypeScript isn't about adding complicated syntax to JavaScript.

It's about making your code easier to understand, safer to maintain, and more predictable as your application grows.

When working with React, the most important TypeScript concepts are:

  • Typing component props
  • Understanding objects and interfaces
  • Working with union types
  • Typing state correctly
  • Handling React events
  • Understanding generics
  • Typing API responses
  • Using utility types
  • Avoiding unnecessary any

You don't need to memorize every TypeScript feature.

Learn the fundamentals, practice them in React components, and gradually introduce more advanced concepts as your applications become more complex.

The goal isn't to write the most complicated types.

The goal is to write clear, maintainable, and reliable React code.

Happy coding! 🚀

What TypeScript concept was the most confusing when you started learning React?

Share your experience in the comments. Let's help each other become better developers.

TypeScript #React #JavaScript #WebDevelopment #FrontendDevelopment

title: PostgreSQL document compression: TOAST thresholds, storage policies, and page size
description:
A common way to store documents in PostgreSQL is a table with an ID and a JSONB column. The open-source DocumentDB extension instead stores BSON, the binary document format used by MongoDB, to provide more data types and MongoDB compatibility.

Both approaches commonly combine two patterns that do not perfectly fit what SQL databases were designed for:

  • Rows with a single variable-length column, whose values can range from a few dozen bytes to many megabytes.
  • Repeated data or metadata, such as similar field names and arrays of objects with the same schema, like time-series buckets.

MongoDB's storage engine, WiredTiger, packs many documents into B-tree leaf pages. The default maximum page sizes — 32 KB for leaf pages and 4 KB for internal pages — are limits on the uncompressed page image fed to the block compressor, not on individual documents: MongoDB configures leaf_value_max=64MB, so a document larger than 32 KB simply produces a larger leaf page rather than overflow storage. Snappy compresses each page image for ordinary collections (time-series collections use Zstd, which ignores the global compressor setting), and the compressed result is written in multiples of the 4 KB allocation_size. Because compression runs over the whole page image, several small documents — including their repeated field names — contribute redundant byte sequences to the same compression input.

A JSON or BSON document can contain substantial byte-sequence redundancy: repeated field names, common name prefixes, and repeated values or structures. LZ77-family compressors such as Snappy and LZ4 can replace matching sequences with backreferences to earlier bytes. They don't need to understand JSON, and matches aren't restricted to the beginning of a document.

Binary does not mean compressed: BSON includes field names, and repeated embedded objects repeat those names. JSONB can contain similar redundancy. PostgreSQL can compress those sequences in JSON, JSONB, or a BSON extension type. However, the decision to attempt compression is not driven by document redundancy. It belongs to TOAST's generic heap-row storage policy: reduce a wide row, trying column compression before storing permitted attributes externally in chunks.

This distinction matters for small documents. It also makes increasing the page size potentially counterproductive: the same document can stop being compressed on a larger-page build.

I will reproduce both effects, then compare the SQL controls with the hardcoded values. The examples use PostgreSQL 19 and core JSONB, so they can run without an extension or a custom patch. The distinction between whole-row activation and individual-column compression also applies to the TOAST-backed BSON values stored by DocumentDB.

What is compressed, and what is measured?

TOAST measures the whole tuple (row) to decide whether to start. However, compression acts on individual eligible column values, not on the entire row or all the documents in a page.

PostgreSQL's ordinary table storage uses fixed-size pages, 8 KB by default. A row cannot span those pages. Large column values can instead be moved to an associated TOAST table, and the main row then contains a pointer to access the chunks in the TOAST table by index scan.

JSONB still contains compressible byte sequences. It is a binary representation, not an already-compressed JSON string. Within one object, it normalizes key order and duplicate keys, but an array of similarly structured objects can repeat the same field names. No shared key dictionary exists across those objects or across independently stored JSONB rows.

The distinction between repeated names within a document and repeated names across documents is important. PostgreSQL compresses one column value at a time. PostgreSQL calls each value a datum in its source code. That per-datum compression can use the former repetition, not the latter.

MongoDB's WiredTiger storage engine uses Snappy block compression on disk by default for ordinary collections. Small documents can share a page, so one block-compression input can include repeated names and structures from several documents. This is not a separate compression call per small document. Other codecs can be configured, and time-series collections have different defaults. This is a difference in compression scope, not a capability reserved to Snappy.

This post measures stored datum representations, not table allocation or query performance. I use:

  • pg_column_size(doc::text::jsonb) to reconstruct an uncompressed logical JSONB datum for these ordinary JSON inputs
  • pg_column_compression(doc) to report the actual accepted method
  • pg_column_size(doc) for its stored representation
  • pg_column_toast_chunk_id(doc) IS NOT NULL to identify external values

The last function is available in PostgreSQL 19. For an external value, pg_column_size is not the inline pointer size. The on-disk pointer in the main row occupies 18 bytes. The external size excludes the outer four-byte varlena length word, which explains some four-byte differences below without attributing them to the codec.

Reproduce the environment and output

All SQL needed for the experiments is included below. Run the statements in order in a fresh test database. For each page-size comparison, start a separate PostgreSQL instance.

I use aligned ASCII output, with NULL displayed as (null). To reproduce that format, start an existing server's session with these options:

psql -X -P pager=off -P 'null=(null)' -P format=aligned \
  -P linestyle=ascii -P border=1 -U postgres -d postgres

These are the initial settings on the source-built 8 KB server:

postgres=# SHOW server_version;

 server_version 
----------------
 19rc1
(1 row)

postgres=# SHOW block_size;

 block_size 
------------
 8192
(1 row)

postgres=# SHOW default_toast_compression;

 default_toast_compression 
---------------------------
 lz4
(1 row)

The selected codec is explicit in every test. PostgreSQL 14-18's upstream default is pglz, but an LZ4-enabled PostgreSQL 19 RC1 build defaults to LZ4. SET COMPRESSION has been available since PostgreSQL 14.

LZ4 is a sensible starting choice when compression/decompression CPU matters, but the workload still determines the trade-off. It does not always produce the smallest result. DocumentDB's current setup/tuning configuration selects default_toast_compression = 'lz4' when supported. This is a launcher-chosen PostgreSQL setting, not a property of BSON, nor a guarantee that every installation is configured that way. Check the live server and column settings rather than assuming them from a product name.

A compressible document below the activation threshold

I construct a JSONB array containing eight objects with repeated temperature and humidity names. Both rows receive the same document. The only difference is an unrelated column stored PLAIN, so it cannot be compressed or moved externally.

postgres=# CREATE TABLE small_documents(
    id integer, doc jsonb, other text
);

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE small_documents
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE small_documents
            ALTER COLUMN other SET STORAGE PLAIN
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# INSERT INTO small_documents
    SELECT id,
           jsonb_build_object('samples', (
             SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('temperature',20,'humidity',60))
             FROM generate_series(1,8)
           )),
           repeat('q', CASE id WHEN 1 THEN 0 ELSE 1600 END)
    FROM generate_series(1,2) AS g(id)
;

INSERT 0 2

postgres=# SELECT id,
           pg_column_size(doc::text::jsonb) AS logical_bytes,
           octet_length(other) AS other_bytes,
           pg_column_compression(doc) AS compression,
           pg_column_size(doc) AS stored_bytes,
           pg_column_toast_chunk_id(doc) IS NOT NULL AS external
    FROM small_documents ORDER BY id
;

 id | logical_bytes | other_bytes | compression | stored_bytes | external 
----+---------------+-------------+-------------+--------------+----------
  1 |           508 |           0 | (null)      |          508 | f
  2 |           508 |        1600 | lz4         |          109 | f
(2 rows)

The first 508-byte JSONB datum remains uncompressed. The second compresses to 109 bytes, even though its uncompressed document bytes are identical. The additional 1,600-byte column made the tuple large enough to enter TOAST processing.

This proves both points:

  1. Repeated field names and values in JSONB are compressible.
  2. PostgreSQL does not independently ask whether that small JSONB datum would benefit from compression. The enclosing tuple controls activation.

I used an unrelated column for academic purposes. Of course, I'm not suggesting that adding more data to trigger compression is a good idea.

The hardcoded gate is not the per-table target

In the PostgreSQL source, the ordinary values are derived as follows:

#define TOAST_TUPLES_PER_PAGE 4
#define TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD MaximumBytesPerTuple(TOAST_TUPLES_PER_PAGE)
#define TOAST_TUPLE_TARGET TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD

MaximumBytesPerTuple(4) accounts for page headers, line pointers, and alignment. It is not exactly block_size / 4. Here are the values for the default 8 KB page size and for PostgreSQL builds with 16 KB or 32 KB pages:

PostgreSQL page size Fixed tuple activation threshold Default tuple target Maximum native TOAST chunk payload
8,192 bytes 2,032 bytes 2,032 bytes 1,996 bytes
16,384 bytes 4,080 bytes 4,080 bytes 4,044 bytes
32,768 bytes 8,176 bytes 8,176 bytes 8,140 bytes

These are the values for the tested eight-byte-aligned builds. The chunk capacities were also observed from actual external data, not inferred from page size alone.

Both heap_prepare_insert and heap_update check the fixed threshold before invoking the toaster for fresh inline tuples. Inside the toaster, toast_tuple_target provides the reduction target, after subtracting tuple header overhead.

It’s not simply "compress when the row cannot fit on a page.” A tuple just over 2 KB can still fit on an 8 KB page. By default, wide rows are reduced earlier, with the goal of keeping their size consistent with roughly four tuples per page. This is a row-density and oversized-attribute policy, rather than a separately tunable document-compression policy.

These are fresh values with one eligible document column. If a row has several eligible columns, the toaster works in phases rather than compressing the entire row as one object.

Change the target without changing activation

The following input view constructs fresh JSONB values from repetitive text. It deliberately samples several payload sizes. It is not intended to represent a natural document distribution.

A view is used rather than copying stored compressed values from another table. Reusing an existing compressed datum would confound a test of whether the destination attempts compression.

postgres=# CREATE TEMP VIEW input_documents AS
    SELECT n, jsonb_build_object('v', repeat('x', 1024 * (1 << n))) AS doc
    FROM (VALUES (0),(1),(2),(6),(9),(10),(11)) AS sizes(n)
;

CREATE VIEW

postgres=# CREATE TABLE extended_default(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
);

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# CREATE TABLE extended_200(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
)
    WITH (toast_tuple_target=200)
;

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# CREATE TABLE extended_4k(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
)
    WITH (toast_tuple_target=4096)
;

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE extended_default
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE extended_200
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE extended_4k
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# INSERT INTO extended_default
    SELECT * FROM input_documents ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 7

postgres=# INSERT INTO extended_200
    SELECT * FROM input_documents ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 7

postgres=# INSERT INTO extended_4k
    SELECT * FROM input_documents ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 7

postgres=# SELECT policy, 1 << n AS payload_kib,
           pg_column_compression(doc) AS compression,
           pg_column_size(doc) AS stored_bytes,
           pg_column_toast_chunk_id(doc) IS NOT NULL AS external
    FROM (
      SELECT 1 AS position, 'default' AS policy, * FROM extended_default
      UNION ALL SELECT 2,'target_200',* FROM extended_200
      UNION ALL SELECT 3,'target_4096',* FROM extended_4k
    ) AS cases
    ORDER BY position,n
;

   policy    | payload_kib | compression | stored_bytes | external 
-------------+-------------+-------------+--------------+----------
 default     |           1 | (null)      |         1041 | f
 default     |           2 | lz4         |           39 | f
 default     |           4 | lz4         |           47 | f
 default     |          64 | lz4         |          288 | f
 default     |         512 | lz4         |         2083 | t
 default     |        1024 | lz4         |         4139 | t
 default     |        2048 | lz4         |         8252 | t
 target_200  |           1 | (null)      |         1041 | f
 target_200  |           2 | lz4         |           39 | f
 target_200  |           4 | lz4         |           47 | f
 target_200  |          64 | lz4         |          284 | t
 target_200  |         512 | lz4         |         2083 | t
 target_200  |        1024 | lz4         |         4139 | t
 target_200  |        2048 | lz4         |         8252 | t
 target_4096 |           1 | (null)      |         1041 | f
 target_4096 |           2 | (null)      |         2065 | f
 target_4096 |           4 | lz4         |           47 | f
 target_4096 |          64 | lz4         |          288 | f
 target_4096 |         512 | lz4         |         2087 | f
 target_4096 |        1024 | lz4         |         4139 | t
 target_4096 |        2048 | lz4         |         8252 | t
(21 rows)

The default JSONB storage strategy is EXTENDED, which permits both compression and external storage.

Three observations distinguish the decisions:

  • Even with a 200-byte target, the 1 KB-payload document still remains uncompressed and inline at 1,041 bytes. Its tuple did not enter TOAST because it is smaller than the hardcoded MaximumBytesPerTuple(4).
  • Once TOAST is active, lowering the target externalizes values sooner: the 64 KB payload is inline with the default target but external with the 200-byte target.
  • With a 4 KB target, the 2 KB-payload document remains uncompressed at 2,065 bytes. Its tuple enters TOAST, but already meets the larger target. The same document compressed to 39 bytes in the other two tables.

Raising the target is therefore not an independent "retain more compressed documents inline" control. It can also prevent a compression attempt.

The default and 200-byte cases report 288 and 284 bytes respectively for the same compressed 64 KB-payload document. This is the inline/external varlena accounting difference, not a better compression result.

Storage strategies: what SQL can control

There are four column storage strategies:

Strategy Compression External storage
EXTENDED Permitted, attempted in the first phase when reduction is needed Permitted
EXTERNAL Not permitted Permitted
MAIN Permitted, attempted in a later phase when needed Last resort
PLAIN Not permitted Not permitted

MAIN does not guarantee inline storage. MAIN attributes are also skipped during the first compression pass: they get their own compression round only after EXTENDED/EXTERNAL attributes have been compressed and externalized. They are likewise skipped by the out-of-line loops until the last-resort pass, which uses TOAST_TUPLE_TARGET_MAIN (MaximumBytesPerTuple(1) ≈ 8,160 bytes on an 8 KB build). EXTERNAL does not mean "externalize every document,” and an explicit LZ4 method cannot override its prohibition on compression.

Here EXTERNAL and MAIN use the same 4 KB target, making the comparison independent of an accidental target difference:

postgres=# CREATE TABLE external_4k(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
)
    WITH (toast_tuple_target=4096)
;

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# CREATE TABLE main_4k(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
)
    WITH (toast_tuple_target=4096)
;

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# CREATE TABLE plain_case(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
);

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE external_4k
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE main_4k
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE plain_case
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE external_4k
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET STORAGE EXTERNAL
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE main_4k
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET STORAGE MAIN
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE plain_case
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET STORAGE PLAIN
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# INSERT INTO external_4k
    SELECT * FROM input_documents ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 7

postgres=# INSERT INTO main_4k
    SELECT * FROM input_documents ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 7

postgres=# INSERT INTO plain_case
    SELECT * FROM input_documents WHERE n<=2 ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 3

postgres=# SELECT policy, 1 << n AS payload_kib,
           pg_column_compression(doc) AS compression,
           pg_column_size(doc) AS stored_bytes,
           pg_column_toast_chunk_id(doc) IS NOT NULL AS external
    FROM (
      SELECT 1 AS position,'EXTERNAL' AS policy,* FROM external_4k
      UNION ALL SELECT 2,'MAIN',* FROM main_4k
      UNION ALL SELECT 3,'PLAIN',* FROM plain_case
    ) AS cases
    ORDER BY position,n
;

  policy  | payload_kib | compression | stored_bytes | external 
----------+-------------+-------------+--------------+----------
 EXTERNAL |           1 | (null)      |         1041 | f
 EXTERNAL |           2 | (null)      |         2065 | f
 EXTERNAL |           4 | (null)      |         4109 | t
 EXTERNAL |          64 | (null)      |        65549 | t
 EXTERNAL |         512 | (null)      |       524301 | t
 EXTERNAL |        1024 | (null)      |      1048589 | t
 EXTERNAL |        2048 | (null)      |      2097165 | t
 MAIN     |           1 | (null)      |         1041 | f
 MAIN     |           2 | (null)      |         2065 | f
 MAIN     |           4 | lz4         |           47 | f
 MAIN     |          64 | lz4         |          288 | f
 MAIN     |         512 | lz4         |         2087 | f
 MAIN     |        1024 | lz4         |         4143 | f
 MAIN     |        2048 | lz4         |         8252 | t
 PLAIN    |           1 | (null)      |         1041 | f
 PLAIN    |           2 | (null)      |         2065 | f
 PLAIN    |           4 | (null)      |         4113 | f
(17 rows)

For EXTERNAL, the 2 KB payload is still inline, but the 4 KB payload is external without compression.

For MAIN, the 1 MB payload compresses to 4,143 inline bytes. It can stay inline because MAIN postpones externalization to its last-resort target: the maximum tuple size that fits on one page. The larger 2 MB-payload document still becomes external after compression.

For PLAIN, no value compresses or becomes external. A row that cannot fit on the heap page fails. Run this separate statement expecting an error:

postgres=# INSERT INTO plain_case
    VALUES (3,jsonb_build_object('v',repeat('x',8192)))
;

ERROR:  54000: row is too big: size 8240, maximum size 8160
LOCATION:  RelationGetBufferForTuple, hio.c:531

The 8,160-byte maximum in this error is the heap-page tuple limit, not the 2,032-byte TOAST activation threshold. They answer different questions.

This is the complete SQL control surface relevant to these cases:

Control Scope Changes the fixed activation threshold?
ALTER COLUMN ... SET STORAGE ... Column's permitted/preferred representation No
ALTER COLUMN ... SET COMPRESSION pglz/lz4 Codec when compression is attempted No
default_toast_compression Default codec when the column has no override No
ALTER TABLE ... SET (toast_tuple_target=...) Whole-tuple reduction target after entry No
TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD, TOAST_TUPLES_PER_PAGE Compiled activation policy Source change
TOAST_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE, EXTERN_TUPLES_PER_PAGE Compiled external chunk capacity Separate from activation
BLCKSZ Compiled page size Changes several defaults together

Changing page and chunk sizes requires a freshly initialized cluster. They are not runtime GUCs. Changing only a main-tuple threshold is not inherently an on-disk page-format change, but a correct implementation still has to consider all heap entry paths and TOAST-table creation.

The compression algorithm still matters after activation

Compression is an attempt, not a storage guarantee. Pglz's default strategy has a 32-byte minimum input, a 25% minimum reduction policy, and a 1,024-byte encoded-output first-success limit: it aborts if it has emitted that much without finding a match.

Those are pglz strategy rules, not user-configurable document thresholds. LZ4 does not impose pglz's first-success or minimum-rate rules. Both must still pass TOAST's header/alignment savings check.

Changing the column codec does not rewrite existing values:

postgres=# CREATE TABLE codec_example(
    id integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
);

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE codec_example
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION pglz
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# INSERT INTO codec_example
    VALUES
      (1,jsonb_build_object('v',repeat('x',4096)))
;

INSERT 0 1

postgres=# ALTER TABLE codec_example
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# INSERT INTO codec_example
    VALUES
      (2,jsonb_build_object('v',repeat('x',4096)))
;

INSERT 0 1

postgres=# SELECT id, pg_column_compression(doc) AS compression,
           pg_column_size(doc) AS stored_bytes
    FROM codec_example ORDER BY id
;

 id | compression | stored_bytes 
----+-------------+--------------
  1 | pglz        |           71
  2 | lz4         |           47
(2 rows)

The old value remains pglz. The freshly constructed new value uses LZ4. An update that leaves the document unchanged, or a copy of an already compressed datum, need not recompress it. Therefore, changing the setting is not proof that existing data now uses the new codec.

Larger pages: fewer documents become compression candidates

Larger pages can reduce the number of external chunks. That does not mean they preserve compression behavior.

I rebuilt PostgreSQL 19 RC1 with --with-blocksize=8, 16, and 32, keeping the other configure options the same, then initialized fresh clusters.

Do not reuse a data directory across page sizes. A different page size also requires rebuilding linked extensions against that PostgreSQL installation. This comparison deliberately uses core JSONB rather than mixing extension versions or a stock image with a different source-built baseline.

8 KB: all but the smallest repeated-field document compress

The samples array now contains 8, 64, 128, or 256 similarly structured objects. All tests explicitly select LZ4. One table retains the build's default target. The other sets it to 2040.

postgres=# CREATE TEMP VIEW page_inputs AS
    SELECT n, jsonb_build_object('samples', (
             SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object('temperature',20,'humidity',60))
             FROM generate_series(1,n)
           )) AS doc
    FROM (VALUES (8),(64),(128),(256)) AS counts(n)
;

CREATE VIEW

postgres=# CREATE TABLE page_default(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
);

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# CREATE TABLE page_target(
    n integer PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb
)
    WITH (toast_tuple_target=2040)
;

CREATE TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE page_default
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# ALTER TABLE page_target
            ALTER COLUMN doc SET COMPRESSION lz4
;

ALTER TABLE

postgres=# INSERT INTO page_default
    SELECT * FROM page_inputs ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 4

postgres=# INSERT INTO page_target
    SELECT * FROM page_inputs ORDER BY n
;

INSERT 0 4

postgres=# CREATE VIEW page_observations AS
    SELECT policy, n AS objects,
           pg_column_size(doc::text::jsonb) AS logical_bytes,
           pg_column_compression(doc) AS compression,
           pg_column_size(doc) AS stored_bytes,
           pg_column_toast_chunk_id(doc) IS NOT NULL AS external
    FROM (
      SELECT 1 AS position,'default' AS policy,* FROM page_default
      UNION ALL SELECT 2,'target_2040',* FROM page_target
    ) AS cases ORDER BY position,n
;

CREATE VIEW

postgres=# SELECT * FROM page_observations
;

   policy    | objects | logical_bytes | compression | stored_bytes | external 
-------------+---------+---------------+-------------+--------------+----------
 default     |       8 |           508 | (null)      |          508 | f
 default     |      64 |          3868 | lz4         |          126 | f
 default     |     128 |          7708 | lz4         |          150 | f
 default     |     256 |         15388 | lz4         |          198 | f
 target_2040 |       8 |           508 | (null)      |          508 | f
 target_2040 |      64 |          3868 | lz4         |          126 | f
 target_2040 |     128 |          7708 | lz4         |          150 | f
 target_2040 |     256 |         15388 | lz4         |          198 | f
(8 rows)

16 KB: the 3,868-byte JSONB document no longer compresses

The complete setup is unchanged. This is the same final query on the 16 KB build:

postgres=# SELECT * FROM page_observations
;

   policy    | objects | logical_bytes | compression | stored_bytes | external 
-------------+---------+---------------+-------------+--------------+----------
 default     |       8 |           508 | (null)      |          508 | f
 default     |      64 |          3868 | (null)      |         3868 | f
 default     |     128 |          7708 | lz4         |          150 | f
 default     |     256 |         15388 | lz4         |          198 | f
