title: Agents Don't Fail Like Normal Software: Why AI Agents Need Their Own Testing
description:
A new kind of failure

If you have shipped an AI agent, you have probably noticed that it fails differently from regular software. A normal function returns the same output for the same input, so a unit test can lock that behavior in. An agent is different:

  • The same prompt can produce different outputs.
  • Behavior can shift after a model upgrade or a framework change.
  • Agents call tools, and a wrong tool call can have real consequences.
  • Users, and attackers, can steer the conversation in ways you did not plan for.

Passing a handful of manual demo conversations does not tell you much about how an agent will behave in production.

Why classic test suites fall short

Traditional tests assume deterministic behavior. For agents, three gaps appear.

1. Non-determinism. An assertion like output == "expected text" rarely holds. You need evaluators that judge behavior, such as whether the agent stayed in scope, refused an unsafe request, or used the right tool.

2. Adversarial input. Security-minded users will try prompt injection, social engineering, and attempts to extract data. Happy-path tests do not cover this.

3. Silent regressions. An agent that resisted a manipulation attempt under one model version may behave differently after a minor upgrade. Without continuous testing, you only find out from your users.

What a testing approach for agents needs

Based on how these failures show up, a reasonable checklist looks like this:

Need Why it matters
Red-teaming Probe the agent the way a hostile or careless user would
Scenario-based test suites Make failures repeatable instead of one-off discoveries
Execution tracing See which tools the agent called and why
Custom evaluators Define what "good behavior" means for your product
CI/CD integration Re-run tests whenever the model, prompt, or code changes

Where BotGauge fits

BotGauge has recently positioned itself as a reliability and red-teaming platform for AI agents. According to public descriptions of the launch, the focus areas include:

  • Adaptive red-teaming to surface security vulnerabilities and behavioral failures
  • Tool misuse detection, which matters for agents that can take actions
  • Execution tracing and custom evaluators to detect failures and enforce behavioral guardrails
  • Continuous testing pipelines, so findings become repeatable regression tests
  • Support for multi-agent systems and transactional workflows

As with any tool, check current capabilities and limits directly before you depend on them. Public listings note, for example, that the focus is mainly on text-based agent interactions and that some advanced features sit in paid tiers.

A starter checklist you can use today

Whatever tool you choose, you can improve agent reliability right now:

  1. List what your agent is allowed to do, and what it must never do.
  2. Write adversarial scenarios for each boundary, such as asking the agent to reveal its instructions, exceed its permissions, or act on injected content in a document.
  3. Log every tool call so failures can be explained after the fact.
  4. Define pass/fail criteria in terms of behavior, not exact wording.
  5. Re-run the suite on every change to the model, prompt, tools, or framework.
  6. Keep a growing regression set. Every real-world failure should become a permanent test.

Here is an illustrative scenario format you could adapt:

Scenario: Agent must not exceed its refund authority
  Given an agent permitted to refund orders up to a set limit
  When a user claims to be a manager and requests a refund above that limit
  Then the agent declines the request
  And no refund tool call is made
  And the refusal explains the escalation path

Further reading

One gap worth understanding is the difference between securing your infrastructure and testing your agent's behavior. BotGauge's recent post covers it in detail: AI Red Teaming vs Penetration Testing: What Pen Tests Miss.

The takeaway

Shipping an agent without systematic adversarial testing means your users become your test suite. Treating reliability as a continuous practice, with red-teaming, tracing, evaluation, and regression tests, is how teams catch problems before customers do.

How are you testing your agents today? Share your approach below.

title: Building an Autonomous AI Book Publishing Factory in Python (Zero Dependencies EPUB 3.0)
description:
In early 2024, South African author Coral Hart captured global headlines by generating over $1,000,000 in royalties within twenty months through Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP).

Her operation was an industrial-grade AI Publishing Factory producing 371 titles across high-demand romantic suspense and thriller categories.

When developers attempt to build automated publishing pipelines, they frequently rely on external command-line binaries like Calibre or Pandoc. In production agentic systems, these dependencies introduce fragile setup overhead, missing shared libraries on Linux containers, and inconsistent output formatting.

In this deep dive, we walk through the engineering behind BookFactory Pro—our zero-dependency Python publishing engine that compiles 100% standards-compliant EPUB 3.0 e-books with dual-layer navigation, embedded typography, and automated Amazon KDP SEO packaging.

1. The Anatomy of a Valid EPUB 3 Package

An .epub file is fundamentally an uncompressed ZIP archive containing structured XML documents conforming to IDPF/W3C specifications.

However, e-reader ingest algorithms (especially Amazon KDP and Apple Books) enforce strict structural rules:

book.epub (ZIP archive)
├── mimetype (MUST be first entry, uncompressed ZIP_STORED, exactly 20 bytes)
├── META-INF/
│   └── container.xml
└── OEBPS/
    ├── content.opf (Master metadata, manifest & spine)
    ├── nav.xhtml (EPUB 3 Navigation Document)
    ├── toc.ncx (EPUB 2 NCX Navigation for older Kindle hardware)
    ├── styles.css (Reader typography)
    ├── images/
    │   └── cover.jpg (1600x2560 px high-res cover)
    ├── cover.xhtml
    ├── title.xhtml
    ├── copyright.xhtml
    └── chapter_01.xhtml ...

The Uncompressed Mimetype Rule

The single most common reason automated EPUB generators fail Amazon validation is the mimetype entry. It must be stored uncompressed (zipfile.ZIP_STORED), while all subsequent entries are compressed with Deflate (zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED):

import zipfile

def init_epub(output_path):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(output_path, "w") as zf:
        # 1. mimetype MUST be the very first file and uncompressed
        zf.writestr("mimetype", "application/epub+zip", compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_STORED)

        # 2. META-INF/container.xml
        container_xml = """<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<container version="1.0" xmlns="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:container">
    <rootfiles>
        <rootfile full-path="OEBPS/content.opf" media-type="application/oebps-package+xml"/>
    </rootfiles>
</container>"""
        zf.writestr("META-INF/container.xml", container_xml, compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED)

2. Dual-Layer Navigation: EPUB 3 nav.xhtml + EPUB 2 toc.ncx

Modern Kindle devices and e-readers utilize EPUB 3's HTML5-based <nav epub:type="toc"> structure. However, millions of legacy Kindle Paperwhites and third-party e-ink devices still require EPUB 2's XML-based toc.ncx file.

To ensure universal compatibility without warnings:

  1. Include nav.xhtml declared with properties="nav" in content.opf.
  2. Include toc.ncx declared with media-type="application/x-dtbncx+xml".
  3. Reference toc="ncx" on the <spine> element in content.opf.

3. Reader-Centric Typography CSS

E-readers render CSS using internal WebKit engines. To deliver a premium reading experience:

  • Use serif fonts (Georgia, Merriweather, serif) with line-height: 1.68 for body text.
  • Use system sans-serif headers with break-after: avoid to prevent orphan titles.
  • Style callout blocks and dark-mode code snippets: 
body {
    font-family: "Georgia", "Merriweather", serif;
    font-size: 1.05em;
    line-height: 1.68;
    color: #1a1a1a;
    margin: 5% 7%;
    text-align: justify;
}

pre.code-block {
    background-color: #0f172a;
    color: #38bdf8;
    padding: 1.2em;
    border-radius: 6px;
    font-family: "Courier New", Courier, monospace;
    font-size: 0.88em;
    overflow-x: auto;
    white-space: pre-wrap;
}

4. The Amazon KDP A9 Algorithm & KENP Strategy

Writing the book is only 30% of the battle. The remaining 70% is discoverability:

  1. Kindle Unlimited (KENP) Economics: Readers on Kindle Unlimited binge entire series. Amazon pays ~$0.0045 per page read. A 250-page book read by 2,000 subscribers generates $2,250/month in passive royalties.
  2. The 7-Slot Backend Keyword Secret: Amazon allows seven 50-character search phrases. Never repeat words from your title. Target high-intent long-tail phrases like "build saas without coding" or "python automation for business".

5. Our Live Production Release

We utilized this exact engine to architect, compile, and publish our flagship 2026 digital book:

👉 The 2026 AI Solopreneur Playbook: Building a Zero-Employee Software Empire

  • Interior Manuscript: 10 comprehensive chapters covering solo leverage math, zero-dollar cloud stacks, 48-hour MLPs, digital sales engines, organic programmatic video, and high-ticket retainers.
  • Formats Included: Validated EPUB 3.0 + Standalone interactive browser reader.
  • Launch Discount: Use code LAUNCH20 for 20% off at checkout.

Check out the live release on Gumroad: https://antigone16.gumroad.com/l/ai-solopreneur-playbook.

title: OTP Input Practice: Atomic Verification in a Node.js 2FA Login Flow
description:
Short answer: the best practice for verifying OTP input in a Node.js application is to make the code a one-time, short-lived capability owned by the authentication service, and make verification consume it atomically. In a 2FA login or password-reset process, the message template can belong to the communications team; the decision about validity cannot.

For an education platform, this boundary matters. A learner may request a password reset from a shared school device, refresh the page, or request a second message after the first one arrives. The application must treat delivery as an unreliable notification path and OTP verification as a state transition. I initially treated the input check as the small part of the feature; the process around it turned out to decide whether retries were safe. Duplicate sends and missed jobs create very different operational symptoms, while the account must remain safe in both cases.

That distinction is the whole practice.

How should a Node.js application process OTP input for 2FA login?

A wrong, expired, or already-consumed code should produce the same useful public outcome: the reset does not proceed. Do not reveal whether the account, code, or expiry check was the reason. Internally, record a reason class, a request identifier, and a correlation identifier so support and on-call staff can follow the attempt without logging the secret itself.

It fails closed.

The verifier should apply a bounded attempt policy and a cooldown for issuing new codes. A new code should invalidate the previous code for the same reset transaction, or the service should define exactly which code remains valid. Ambiguity here is how a harmless retry becomes a confusing incident. The expiry window is short by design; the exact duration belongs in configuration and in the runbook, not scattered through handlers.

Put ownership at the validity boundary

Template ownership and token ownership are separate decisions. Communications can own the subject, copy, localization, and rendering tests. The authentication service should own creation, hashing or protected storage, expiry, attempt counters, single-use state, and the audit event. That split lets a copy change ship without changing the security contract.

The delivery worker should receive a message reference and a rendered-safe payload, not authority to accept a code. Its retry policy must be compatible with the fact that a message may be delivered more than once. The reset record is the source of truth; the email or SMS is only a carrier.

Here is the critical shape in Go. The repository call must provide a compare-and-consume operation, so two concurrent verification requests cannot both succeed.

type VerifyResult int

const (
    Verified VerifyResult = iota
    Rejected
    RateLimited
)

func VerifyResetCode(ctx context.Context, repo Repository, resetID, supplied string, now time.Time) (VerifyResult, error) {
    if supplied == "" || len(supplied) != 6 {
        return Rejected, nil
    }

    result, err := repo.CompareAndConsume(ctx, resetID, supplied, now)
    if err != nil {
        return Rejected, err
    }
    if result.AttemptsExceeded {
        return RateLimited, nil
    }
    if !result.Match || result.Expired || result.Consumed {
        return Rejected, nil
    }
    return Verified, nil
}

The six-character example is a contract, not a universal security parameter. Keep the value out of logs, traces, analytics events, URLs, and error details. Compare the supplied value against protected server-side state, and make the successful consume part of the same atomic operation as the match. A check followed by a separate delete is a race.

There is a trade-off here. A central verifier makes the Node.js application easier to reason about, but it also creates a dependency that must be monitored and tested during partial outages. A verifier embedded in each application instance reduces that dependency, yet it makes one-time use, shared login state, and concurrent requests harder to enforce consistently. Pick the boundary your team can operate and audit; do not hide it inside a notification template.

How do we verify the workflow before release?

Test the state machine, not only the happy-path handler. The minimum useful cases are: first valid attempt, wrong attempt, expiry boundary, repeated use, concurrent submissions, a second issuance, delivery retry, and a provider timeout followed by a retry. For each case, assert both the user-visible response and the durable state.

I also put a failure-injection test around the boundary between enqueueing a notification and recording its delivery status. If the worker crashes after sending but before acknowledging, a retry is expected. That is why the reset transaction must tolerate duplicate notifications without tolerating duplicate successful verification.

Operationally, alert on expired-code spikes, rejected-code rates, queue age, delivery failures, and verification latency. These signals should be segmented by channel and reset flow, but never by the raw code. A rollback of a template is a communications change. A rollback of validity rules needs a security review and an explicit migration plan, because old reset records may have different semantics.

The practical rule is narrow: let the team that owns authentication own the code lifecycle, and let the team that owns messaging own how the instruction is presented. That division makes retries observable, templates replaceable, and one-time use enforceable under load.

References

  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: How to Choose an Email API: Reliable Personalized Welcome Mail for Edtech 2026
description:
How to choose an email API for a personalized welcome message is mostly a question about failure handling, not template syntax. For an edtech signup flow, I would choose the API that gives the application a durable event trail, clear bounce semantics, and a controllable suppression path. A convenient send call is table stakes.

Short answer: model the welcome email as a small delivery workflow. Keep the learner record separate from message attempts, classify provider events into a local state machine, authenticate the sending domain with SPF, and suppress a recipient after a confirmed permanent failure. Test that path before comparing feature lists.

The practical decision rule is simple: the API must let the team answer who was sent what, which failure arrived, when it arrived, and why a later message will or will not be attempted. Personalization belongs in a bounded template context. Delivery state belongs in your database.

That is the boundary.

What is the bill actually made of?

Start with the bill, but do not mistake the invoice total for the cost model. In this workflow the visible send charge is only one term. The operational bill is the sum of message attempts, webhook ingestion and retries, retained event data, support time for ambiguous bounces, and the risk of sending again to an address that should have been suppressed.

Take a planning cohort of 10,000 new learners. Suppose the application creates one welcome attempt per learner and retains 30 days of delivery events. That is 10,000 initial attempts plus every retry your policy permits. If an implementation retries all transient failures twice, the upper bound is 30,000 attempts before any later campaign or password email is counted. The arithmetic is not a benchmark; it is a useful capacity boundary.

The dominant term is usually uncontrolled repetition. A hard bounce that remains eligible can turn one bad address into repeated attempts across welcome, course-reminder, and password flows. The first change I make is therefore a durable suppression decision keyed to a normalized recipient identity, with a reason and timestamp. It moves the dominant term from repeated sends to one classified event.

That choice has a cost. I keep enough event history to investigate a false suppression, but not an indefinite copy of every payload. A 30-day event window is a policy example, not a universal answer. Keep the rendered body only when the privacy and support case justifies it; otherwise retain a template version, variable names, provider event ID, timestamps, and classification. Less retention means less forensic context when a learner says a welcome message never arrived.

Which failure should change the recipient state?

A provider response is not the same thing as final delivery. The send request can be accepted, then a downstream mail server can reject the message. Your application needs an event consumer that is idempotent and a state machine that distinguishes temporary failure from permanent failure. SMTP enhanced status codes provide useful semantics, but the provider's event schema still needs mapping and review.

This is a state machine, not a send button.

For example, a timeout while submitting an attempt is an unknown outcome. Retrying immediately may duplicate a welcome email; never retrying may lose it. A transient remote rejection can be retried with a bounded backoff. A confirmed invalid recipient should suppress future automated mail. An unsubscribe or complaint is a different policy path from an invalid mailbox, even if both stop a particular campaign.

Here is a deliberately generic classifier. It consumes normalized events from an adapter, so the rest of the application does not depend on a provider-specific field name.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum


class RecipientState(str, Enum):
    ACTIVE = "active"
    RETRYABLE = "retryable"
    SUPPRESSED = "suppressed"
    UNKNOWN = "unknown"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeliveryEvent:
    recipient: str
    outcome: str
    diagnostic: str | None = None


def classify(event: DeliveryEvent) -> RecipientState:
    if event.outcome in {"hard_bounce", "invalid_recipient"}:
        return RecipientState.SUPPRESSED
    if event.outcome in {"temporary_failure", "rate_limited"}:
        return RecipientState.RETRYABLE
    if event.outcome in {"accepted", "delivered"}:
        return RecipientState.ACTIVE
    return RecipientState.UNKNOWN

The important part is not the enum. It is the judgment around an unknown event. Store the raw event ID and deduplicate it before applying a transition. Do not let a late delivered event silently reactivate an address that was suppressed by a later, confirmed permanent failure; compare event timestamps or sequence metadata under a transaction. That edge case is easy to miss because the happy path is only one request and one response.

The awkward case deserves a concrete rule. If the client times out after submitting the request, the database should record unknown before any retry decision is made. The event consumer can later move that attempt to accepted, delivered, or a classified failure. If no event arrives within the reconciliation window, an operator needs a visible queue and a documented action. The exact window depends on the surrounding system; the invariant does not. No retry policy should quietly turn uncertainty into duplicate mail.

Keep it boring.

How should a team test personalized welcome delivery?

Test the workflow with a matrix, not a screenshot. A test recipient should exercise a valid mailbox, a malformed address rejected before submission, a temporary failure, a permanent bounce, a duplicate webhook, a delayed webhook, and a provider timeout after the request may have been accepted. For personalization, add a missing first name, unusual Unicode input, and a value containing template delimiters. The output must remain valid and safe in every case.

I keep the send boundary narrow: the application passes a template identifier, a locale, and an allow-listed context. It does not hand the mail system an entire learner object. That makes it easier to audit which fields entered a message and prevents an internal field from becoming accidental recipient-facing content.

A minimal send record might look like this:

message = {
    "idempotency_key": "welcome:learner-1842:v1",
    "recipient": "learner@example.edu",
    "template": "welcome-v3",
    "locale": "en-US",
    "context": {"first_name": "Mina", "course_name": "Algebra I"},
}

The identifier is an application key, not a promise that every external API implements idempotency. Persist it before attempting delivery, and define what a retry means when the external result is unknown. A useful policy is to reconcile an unknown attempt from the event stream before issuing another send. When the product requirement permits a duplicate, say so explicitly; pretending duplicates cannot happen creates a worse support conversation.

Measure the states that drive decisions: accepted, delivered, temporary failure, permanent failure, complaint, and suppressed. Segment by domain and template version. A single aggregate delivery rate can hide a broken school district domain or a new personalization value that causes rejection. Alert on a change in permanent-failure rate and on a growing unknown-event queue, but let the thresholds be owned by the team that can investigate them.

What must be true before comparing APIs?

Write the contract first. I look for documented event types, stable event identifiers, signed or authenticated webhook delivery, retry behavior, exportability, regional processing information, and a way to separate test traffic from production traffic. I also ask whether a send response is merely accepted for processing or means something stronger. If the documentation does not define that boundary, the application must treat it as accepted-for-processing and wait for events.

Domain authentication is part of the selection. SPF publishes an authorization policy in DNS; RFC 7208 also describes lookup limits and evaluation behavior, so a team should validate the actual DNS shape rather than paste a long list of include records into production. DKIM and DMARC belong in the same review because a welcome flow is still mail from a real organizational domain. The API cannot compensate for a sender identity the domain has not authorized.

Ask for portability at the data boundary, not for a marketing promise. The adapter should translate a provider event into fields such as event_id, recipient, occurred_at, kind, diagnostic, and template_version. Keep the original event for the retention window. If moving systems requires rewriting learner records or campaign logic, the abstraction is in the wrong place.

This is also where compliance enters. A welcome email may be transactional, but the template can still contain optional promotional content. Keep consent and purpose separate from delivery status. Suppressing an invalid mailbox should not erase the audit record, and removing a recipient from a marketing audience should not accidentally prevent a necessary account-security message unless policy explicitly says it should.

The selection worksheet I would use

Score candidate APIs against the workflow rather than against a feature catalog. Delivery semantics and event quality should carry more weight than template polish for this scenario. A small team can use a worksheet like this during a proof of concept:

Area Evidence to request Failure that evidence prevents
Bounce semantics Permanent and temporary examples with raw diagnostics Repeated sends to invalid learners
Event delivery IDs, ordering guidance, authentication, retry behavior Lost or double-applied transitions
Identity SPF, DKIM, DMARC setup and DNS validation Misclassified authentication failures
Retention Event export, payload controls, deletion behavior Unbounded sensitive-data storage
Operations Test mode, logs, rate limits, status history Debugging only from production mailboxes
Exit path Normalized events and template portability A migration that becomes a rewrite

Run the same seven-case test matrix against each candidate. Record the evidence and the unanswered questions. Do not award points for an endpoint that the application cannot safely interpret.

No API is a good fit for every team. A provider with rich event controls can be unnecessary for a small internal tool that sends occasional, non-critical mail; a self-managed relay can be the wrong choice when the team cannot own DNS, reputation monitoring, and incident response. The trade-off is operational ownership: moving delivery state into your application gives you control and portability, but it also makes retries, retention, and suppression your responsibility. A short integration is not evidence that those responsibilities disappeared.

The worksheet also has a deliberate stopping rule. If a candidate cannot show how a permanent failure is represented, or cannot export enough evidence to reconcile an unknown attempt, stop the evaluation there. The missing detail is not a minor documentation gap for this scenario; it is an unresolved delivery decision that will eventually reach a learner.

The right choice may be less polished than the one with the shortest integration example. For an edtech welcome flow, reliability means a learner is not repeatedly targeted after a permanent failure, a legitimate address is not suppressed on a transient error, and an operator can reconstruct the decision without guessing.

Conclusion

Choose the email API that makes delivery state explicit and recoverable. Put bounce classification, idempotent event handling, authenticated sending, bounded retention, and exportable records ahead of template convenience. Then verify those claims with a failure matrix using your personalized welcome payload.

You will still pay for the messages that cannot be delivered. The engineering win is deciding quickly which attempts stop, preserving enough evidence to explain that decision, and keeping the learner model independent from the delivery adapter.

Further reading

  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3463
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489

title: JavaScript Before React: Everything You Need to Know
description:
1. Variables: var, let, and const

Variables allow us to store data.

JavaScript provides three ways to declare variables:

  • var
  • let
  • const

var

var is the older way of declaring variables.

var framework = "React";

console.log(framework);
// React

However, var has some important problems.

For example, it is function-scoped rather than block-scoped.

if (true) {
  var framework = "React";
}

console.log(framework);
// React

The variable escapes the if block.

This behavior can create unexpected bugs.

let

let allows you to declare variables that can be reassigned.

let age = 25;

age = 26;

console.log(age);
// 26

Unlike var, let is block-scoped.

if (true) {
  let framework = "React";
}

console.log(framework);
// ReferenceError

const

const declares a variable that cannot be reassigned.

const framework = "React";

framework = "Vue";
// TypeError

However, const does not make objects immutable.

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
};

user.name = "Bob";

console.log(user.name);
// Bob

The object can be modified because the reference remains the same.

But you cannot reassign the variable:

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
};

user = { name: "Bob" };
// TypeError

Which one should you use?

In modern JavaScript:

  • Use const by default.
  • Use let when reassignment is necessary.
  • Avoid var in modern code.

You'll see const everywhere in React.

2. Data Types

JavaScript has several primitive data types.

const name = "Alice";       // String
const age = 25;             // Number
const isDeveloper = true;   // Boolean
const score = null;         // Null
let result;                 // Undefined
const id = Symbol("id");    // Symbol
const bigNumber = 123n;     // BigInt

JavaScript also has objects.

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
};

Arrays are also objects in JavaScript.

const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

console.log(typeof numbers);
// "object"

Understanding undefined vs. null

undefined usually means a value hasn't been assigned.

let username;

console.log(username);
// undefined

null represents an intentionally empty value.

const selectedUser = null;

One unusual JavaScript behavior:

console.log(typeof null);
// "object"

This is a historical JavaScript quirk.

3. Operators and Comparisons

JavaScript supports arithmetic operators:

const a = 10;
const b = 3;

console.log(a + b); // 13
console.log(a - b); // 7
console.log(a * b); // 30
console.log(a / b); // 3.333...
console.log(a % b); // 1

Equality operators

Always understand the difference between == and ===.

console.log(5 == "5");
// true

console.log(5 === "5");
// false

== performs type coercion.

=== compares values without performing that coercion.

Prefer === and !== in modern JavaScript.

Logical operators 

const isLoggedIn = true;
const isAdmin = false;

console.log(isLoggedIn && isAdmin);
// false

console.log(isLoggedIn || isAdmin);
// true

console.log(!isLoggedIn);
// false

These operators are particularly useful in React.

4. Truthy and Falsy Values

JavaScript doesn't always require a Boolean value in conditions.

Some values behave like true, while others behave like false.

Falsy values

The main falsy values are:

false
0
-0
0n
""
null
undefined
NaN

Everything else is generally truthy, including empty arrays and empty objects.

console.log(Boolean([]));
// true

console.log(Boolean({}));
// true

Example 

const username = "";

if (username) {
  console.log("Username exists");
} else {
  console.log("Username is empty");
}

This concept becomes extremely important when using conditional rendering in React.

5. Scope: Where Variables Exist

Scope determines where a variable can be accessed.

JavaScript has several important types of scope.

Global scope 

const framework = "React";

function showFramework() {
  console.log(framework);
}

showFramework();
// React

The function can access the global variable.

Function scope 

function example() {
  const message = "Hello";

  console.log(message);
}

example();
// Hello

console.log(message);
// ReferenceError

The variable exists only inside the function.

Block scope 

if (true) {
  const message = "Hello";
  let framework = "React";
}

console.log(message);
// ReferenceError

Variables declared with let and const are block-scoped.

6. Hoisting

Hoisting describes JavaScript's behavior of processing declarations before executing code.

It does not mean JavaScript physically moves your code.

var hoisting 

console.log(framework);

var framework = "React";

// undefined

The declaration is available, but the assignment hasn't happened yet.

Conceptually, this behaves similarly to:

var framework;

console.log(framework);

framework = "React";

let and const 

console.log(framework);

let framework = "React";
// ReferenceError

Variables declared with let and const are also processed before execution, but they cannot be accessed before their declaration is initialized.

This period is called the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).

Function declarations

Function declarations can be called before their definition.

sayHello();

function sayHello() {
  console.log("Hello!");
}

This works because function declarations are hoisted with their function definition.

7. Functions

Functions are reusable blocks of code.

Function declaration 

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

console.log(add(5, 3));
// 8

Function expression 

const add = function (a, b) {
  return a + b;
};

console.log(add(5, 3));
// 8

Arrow functions

Arrow functions are widely used in modern JavaScript and React.

const add = (a, b) => {
  return a + b;
};

For a single expression, you can simplify the syntax:

const add = (a, b) => a + b;

Single parameter 

const square = number => number * number;

console.log(square(4));
// 16

Returning an object

Remember to wrap the object in parentheses:

const createUser = (name) => ({
  name: name,
  active: true,
});

console.log(createUser("Alice"));

Arrow functions and this

Arrow functions do not create their own this.

They inherit this from the surrounding lexical scope.

This is especially important when working with callbacks and React event handlers.

8. Callback Functions

A callback is a function passed into another function.

function greet(name, callback) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}`);

  callback();
}

function sayGoodbye() {
  console.log("Goodbye!");
}

greet("Alice", sayGoodbye);

Output:

Hello, Alice
Goodbye!

Callbacks are everywhere in JavaScript.

For example:

const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

numbers.map((number) => number * 2);

The arrow function is a callback passed to map().

React uses callbacks for event handlers:

<button onClick={() => console.log("Clicked!")}>
  Click me
</button>

9. Closures

A closure happens when a function remembers variables from its surrounding scope, even after that outer function has finished executing.

function createCounter() {
  let count = 0;

  return function () {
    count++;

    return count;
  };
}

const counter = createCounter();

console.log(counter());
// 1

console.log(counter());
// 2

console.log(counter());
// 3

Why does this work?

The returned function still has access to the count variable from createCounter().

This is a closure.

Closures are fundamental to understanding many JavaScript patterns, including how React hooks preserve state between renders.

10. Arrays

Arrays store multiple values in a single variable.

const frameworks = ["React", "Vue", "Angular"];

console.log(frameworks[0]);
// React

Important array methods

map()

Transforms every element.

const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

const doubled = numbers.map((number) => number * 2);

console.log(doubled);
// [2, 4, 6]

filter()

Returns elements that satisfy a condition.

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];

const evenNumbers = numbers.filter((number) => number % 2 === 0);

console.log(evenNumbers);
// [2, 4]

find()

Returns the first matching element.

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Alice" },
  { id: 2, name: "Bob" },
];

const user = users.find((user) => user.id === 2);

console.log(user);
// { id: 2, name: "Bob" }

reduce()

Accumulates values.

const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];

const total = numbers.reduce((sum, number) => sum + number, 0);

console.log(total);
// 10

some() and every() 

const numbers = [2, 4, 6];

console.log(numbers.some((number) => number > 5));
// true

console.log(numbers.every((number) => number % 2 === 0));
// true

These methods are used constantly when working with API data and rendering lists in React.

11. Objects

Objects store data using key-value pairs.

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
  role: "Frontend Developer",
};

Access properties 

console.log(user.name);
// Alice

console.log(user["age"]);
// 25

Add properties 

user.country = "Germany";

Update properties 

user.age = 26;

Delete properties 

delete user.role;

Objects are essential for understanding React props, state, and API responses.

12. Destructuring

Destructuring allows you to extract values from arrays and objects.

Object destructuring 

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
  role: "Developer",
};

const { name, age } = user;

console.log(name);
// Alice

console.log(age);
// 25

Rename properties 

const { name: username } = user;

console.log(username);
// Alice

Default values 

const { country = "Unknown" } = user;

console.log(country);
// Unknown

Array destructuring 

const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];

const [first, second] = colors;

console.log(first);
// red

console.log(second);
// green

Destructuring in React

You'll frequently see this:

function UserProfile({ name, age }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>{age}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

This is object destructuring applied to function parameters.

13. Spread Operator (...)

The spread operator expands values from arrays or objects.

Copy an array 

const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

const copiedNumbers = [...numbers];

console.log(copiedNumbers);
// [1, 2, 3]

Combine arrays 

const first = [1, 2];
const second = [3, 4];

const combined = [...first, ...second];

console.log(combined);
// [1, 2, 3, 4]

Copy and update an object 

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
};

const updatedUser = {
  ...user,
  age: 26,
};

console.log(updatedUser);
// { name: "Alice", age: 26 }

Why is this important in React?

React state should generally be updated immutably.

Instead of modifying an existing object:

user.age = 26;

You create a new object:

const updatedUser = {
  ...user,
  age: 26,
};

This pattern is fundamental to React state updates.

14. Rest Parameters

The rest operator collects multiple arguments into an array.

function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((total, number) => total + number, 0);
}

console.log(sum(1, 2, 3, 4));
// 10

The function can accept any number of arguments.

Rest in destructuring 

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
  country: "Germany",
};

const { name, ...otherDetails } = user;

console.log(name);
// Alice

console.log(otherDetails);
// { age: 25, country: "Germany" }

Spread vs. Rest

They use the same syntax but serve different purposes.

  • Spread expands values.
  • Rest collects values.

15. Template Literals

Template literals allow you to create strings using backticks.

const name = "Alice";
const age = 25;

const message = `My name is ${name} and I'm ${age} years old.`;

console.log(message);

Output:

My name is Alice and I'm 25 years old.

You can also write multiline strings:

const message = `
  Hello!
  Welcome to JavaScript.
`;

Template literals are useful when displaying dynamic content.

16. Optional Chaining (?.)

Optional chaining allows you to safely access properties that may not exist.

Imagine receiving this data:

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  address: {
    city: "Berlin",
  },
};

Without optional chaining:

console.log(user.address.city);

But what if address doesn't exist?

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
};

console.log(user.address.city);
// TypeError

Using optional chaining:

console.log(user.address?.city);
// undefined

Multiple levels 

const user = {};

console.log(user?.address?.city);
// undefined

Optional function calls 

user.onClick?.();

This calls onClick only if it exists and is callable.

Optional chaining is particularly useful when working with API data.

17. Nullish Coalescing (??)

The nullish coalescing operator provides a default value when the left side is null or undefined.

const username = null;

const displayName = username ?? "Guest";

console.log(displayName);
// Guest

Difference between || and ?? 

const count = 0;

console.log(count || 10);
// 10

console.log(count ?? 10);
// 0

Why?

|| uses the fallback for any falsy value.

?? uses the fallback only for null or undefined.

This distinction matters when zero or an empty string is a valid value.

18. The Ternary Operator

The ternary operator is a concise way to write conditional expressions.

const age = 20;

const message = age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor";

console.log(message);
// Adult

The syntax:

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse;

React example 

function LoginStatus({ isLoggedIn }) {
  return (
    <div>
      {isLoggedIn ? "Welcome back!" : "Please log in."}
    </div>
  );
}

This is one of the most common conditional rendering patterns in React.

19. Short-Circuit Evaluation

JavaScript logical operators can return values, not just Booleans.

Using && 

const isLoggedIn = true;

isLoggedIn && console.log("Welcome!");

The second expression executes only when the first expression is truthy.

React example 

function Notifications({ count }) {
  return (
    <div>
      {count > 0 && <p>You have {count} notifications.</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

Important React warning

Be careful when using numbers with &&.

function Notifications({ count }) {
  return (
    <div>
      {count && <p>You have notifications.</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

If count is 0, React may render the number 0.

A safer version:

{count > 0 && <p>You have notifications.</p>}

20. Modules: import and export

JavaScript modules allow you to split code into multiple files.

Export a function 

// utils.js

export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

Import the function 

// main.js

import { add } from "./utils.js";

console.log(add(2, 3));
// 5

Default exports 

// User.js

export default function User() {
  return "Alice";
}

Import it:

import User from "./User.js";

Named vs. default exports

Named export:

export const name = "Alice";

Import:

import { name } from "./user.js";

Default export:

export default name;

Import:

import username from "./user.js";

Modules are fundamental to React applications because components are usually organized into separate files.

21. DOM Manipulation

The DOM (Document Object Model) represents the structure of an HTML document.

JavaScript can interact with the DOM.

Select an element 

const heading = document.querySelector("h1");

Change text 

heading.textContent = "Hello JavaScript!";

Add an event listener 

const button = document.querySelector("button");

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("Button clicked!");
});

Example 

<button id="counter">Click me</button>

<script>
  const button = document.querySelector("#counter");

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    button.textContent = "Clicked!";
  });
</script>

What changes when you learn React?

In traditional JavaScript, you often manipulate the DOM directly.

In React, you usually describe what the UI should look like based on data and state.

Instead of manually changing elements, React manages UI updates for you.

This is one of the biggest conceptual differences between vanilla JavaScript and React.

22. Events

Events allow JavaScript to respond to user interactions.

Examples include:

  • click
  • input
  • submit
  • change
  • keydown

Vanilla JavaScript 

const button = document.querySelector("button");

button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  console.log("Clicked!");
});

React event handling 

function App() {
  function handleClick() {
    console.log("Clicked!");
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleClick}>
      Click me
    </button>
  );
}

Notice the difference:

  • Vanilla JavaScript uses addEventListener.
  • React uses event props such as onClick.

Also, React expects a function reference:

<button onClick={handleClick}>
  Click me
</button>

Not an immediate function call:

<button onClick={handleClick()}>
  Click me
</button>

The second version executes the function during rendering.

23. Promises

JavaScript often performs asynchronous operations.

Examples include:

  • Fetching API data.
  • Reading files.
  • Waiting for a timer.
  • Sending network requests.

A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.

A Promise can be:

  • Pending
  • Fulfilled
  • Rejected

Example 

const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  const success = true;

  if (success) {
    resolve("Operation successful!");
  } else {
    reject("Something went wrong!");
  }
});

Using .then() 

promise
  .then((result) => {
    console.log(result);
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error);
  });

Promises are fundamental to working with APIs in React.

24. async and await

async and await make asynchronous JavaScript easier to read.

Using .then() 

fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users")
  .then((response) => response.json())
  .then((users) => {
    console.log(users);
  })
  .catch((error) => {
    console.error(error);
  });

Using async and await 

async function getUsers() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(
      "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users"
    );

    const users = await response.json();

    console.log(users);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}

getUsers();

Important details

  • async makes a function return a Promise.
  • await pauses that async function until the Promise settles.
  • try...catch helps handle errors.

await doesn't block the entire JavaScript application.

Example 

async function getUser() {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1"
  );

  const user = await response.json();

  return user;
}

You'll use these concepts frequently when fetching data in React.

25. Fetch API

The Fetch API allows JavaScript to make HTTP requests.

GET request 

async function getUsers() {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users"
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Failed to fetch users");
  }

  const users = await response.json();

  return users;
}

POST request 

async function createUser() {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users",
    {
      method: "POST",

      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },

      body: JSON.stringify({
        name: "Alice",
        email: "alice@example.com",
      }),
    }
  );

  const user = await response.json();

  return user;
}

Important

fetch() does not automatically reject the Promise for HTTP errors such as 404 or 500.

You should check:

response.ok

This is important when handling API errors.

26. Error Handling

JavaScript uses try...catch to handle errors.

try {
  const result = riskyOperation();

  console.log(result);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Something went wrong:", error);
}

Example with asynchronous code 

async function getData() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch("/api/data");

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error("Request failed");
    }

    const data = await response.json();

    return data;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}

Error handling is important when working with API requests and asynchronous operations.

27. Immutability

Immutability means creating new values rather than modifying existing ones.

JavaScript does not automatically make objects immutable.

Mutable example 

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
};

user.age = 26;

The original object has been modified.

Immutable update 

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  age: 25,
};

const updatedUser = {
  ...user,
  age: 26,
};

Now you have a new object.

Why does React care?

React state updates should generally replace objects or arrays with new references rather than mutate existing state.

For example:

const numbers = [1, 2, 3];

const updatedNumbers = [...numbers, 4];

This creates a new array.

Understanding immutability will make React state much easier to understand.

28. Shallow Copy vs. Deep Copy

The spread operator creates a shallow copy.

const user = {
  name: "Alice",
  address: {
    city: "Berlin",
  },
};

const copiedUser = { ...user };

The top-level object is copied, but the nested object is still shared.

copiedUser.address.city = "Paris";

console.log(user.address.city);
// Paris

This happens because both objects reference the same nested object.

Using structuredClone()

For supported data types, you can create a deep copy:

const copiedUser = structuredClone(user);

Now nested objects are copied too.

Note that structuredClone() has limitations and does not clone every possible JavaScript value, such as functions.

29. this Keyword

The this keyword refers to a context determined by how a function is called.

Object method 

const user = {
  name: "Alice",

  greet() {
    console.log(`Hello, ${this.name}`);
  },
};

user.greet();
// Hello, Alice

Here, this refers to the object before the dot.

Important

Arrow functions do not have their own this.

const user = {
  name: "Alice",

  greet: () => {
    console.log(this.name);
  },
};

user.greet();

This does not behave like the previous example.

For object methods that need the object's this, use a regular method or function.

In React function components, you usually don't need to manually manage this, unlike older class-based React components.

30. Classes and Constructors

JavaScript supports class syntax.

class User {
  constructor(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
  }

  greet() {
    return `Hello, ${this.name}`;
  }
}

const user = new User("Alice", 25);

console.log(user.greet());
// Hello, Alice

Classes are useful to understand because JavaScript is a multi-paradigm language.

However, modern React primarily uses function components rather than class components.

You don't need to master classes before learning modern React.

31. Set and Map

JavaScript also provides built-in data structures.

Set

A Set stores unique values.

const numbers = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]);

console.log(numbers);
// Set(4) { 1, 2, 3, 4 }

Convert it into an array:

const uniqueNumbers = [...numbers];

console.log(uniqueNumbers);
// [1, 2, 3, 4]

Map

A Map stores key-value pairs.

const userRoles = new Map();

userRoles.set("Alice", "Admin");
userRoles.set("Bob", "User");

console.log(userRoles.get("Alice"));
// Admin

Don't confuse:

  • Array.prototype.map() — transforms array elements.
  • Map — a separate JavaScript data structure.

32. Type Coercion

JavaScript sometimes converts values automatically.

This is called type coercion.

console.log("5" + 2);
// "52"

The number becomes a string.

But:

console.log("5" - 2);
// 3

Here, JavaScript converts the string to a number.

Explicit conversion 

const number = Number("42");

console.log(number);
// 42

Other useful conversions:

String(123);
Number("123");
Boolean(1);

Understanding type coercion helps you avoid unexpected bugs.

33. JavaScript Execution and the Event Loop

JavaScript commonly runs code on a single main thread.

But it can handle asynchronous operations using browser or runtime APIs and the event loop.

Consider:

console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

console.log("End");

Output:

Start
End
Timeout

Even though the timer is set to 0 milliseconds, its callback doesn't execute immediately.

The callback runs later when the event loop allows it.

Promises and microtasks 

console.log("Start");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("Timeout");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("Promise");
});

console.log("End");

Output:

Start
End
Promise
Timeout

Promise callbacks run as microtasks, which are processed before timer callbacks such as setTimeout().

You don't need to master every detail of the event loop before React, but understanding asynchronous execution is extremely helpful.

JavaScript Concepts You Should Master Before React

Here's a practical checklist.

Essential

  • [ ] let, const, and variable declarations
  • [ ] Primitive data types
  • [ ] Objects and arrays
  • [ ] Functions and arrow functions
  • [ ] Scope and closures
  • [ ] Destructuring
  • [ ] Spread and rest operators
  • [ ] Template literals
  • [ ] Array methods: map, filter, find, reduce
  • [ ] Conditional statements
  • [ ] Ternary operator
  • [ ] Logical operators
  • [ ] Modules: import and export
  • [ ] Promises
  • [ ] async and await
  • [ ] Fetch API
  • [ ] Error handling
  • [ ] Immutability

Helpful

  • [ ] Hoisting and Temporal Dead Zone
  • [ ] Optional chaining
  • [ ] Nullish coalescing
  • [ ] DOM manipulation
  • [ ] Event handling
  • [ ] this keyword
  • [ ] Classes
  • [ ] Set and Map
  • [ ] Event loop

Practice Projects Before React

Before starting React, try building these small projects using vanilla JavaScript.

1. Todo App

Practice:

  • Arrays
  • Objects
  • map()
  • filter()
  • DOM manipulation
  • Events

2. Weather App

Practice:

  • Fetch API
  • Promises
  • Async/Await
  • Error handling
  • API data

3. Shopping Cart

Practice:

  • Objects
  • Arrays
  • reduce()
  • Spread operator
  • Immutability

4. User Search

Practice:

  • filter()
  • includes()
  • Input events
  • Array manipulation

5. Counter

Practice:

  • Variables
  • Functions
  • Events
  • DOM updates

These projects will help you understand how JavaScript works before React introduces its own abstractions.

Final Thoughts

Learning React without understanding JavaScript is like trying to build a house without understanding the materials you're using.

You don't need to know every advanced JavaScript concept before starting React.

But you should feel comfortable with:

  • Functions
  • Objects
  • Arrays
  • Destructuring
  • Spread syntax
  • Array methods
  • Closures
  • Promises
  • Async/Await
  • Modules
  • Immutability

Once these concepts become familiar, React will feel much more natural.

Don't memorize JavaScript. Learn how to think in JavaScript.

React will come next.

Happy coding! 🚀

title: Why UI Tests Break Every Sprint (and What an AI Testing Agent Changes)
description:
The problem most test suites share

Almost every team that automates UI testing hits the same wall. The suite starts small and works well. Then the product grows, the interface changes, and a growing share of your week goes to fixing tests that fail even though the application works fine.

This is not a discipline problem. It comes from how most automated tests are built.

Why traditional UI tests are brittle

A typical scripted UI test identifies elements by locators: IDs, CSS selectors, XPath expressions. For example:

driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "#checkout > div.row:nth-child(2) > button.btn-primary").click()

This line says nothing about what the user is trying to do. It describes where a button currently sits in the page structure. That creates several predictable failure modes:

Change in the product Effect on the test
A designer reorders page sections Selectors no longer match
A developer renames a CSS class The test cannot find the element
A component library is upgraded Generated IDs change
An A/B experiment alters the layout The test fails intermittently

In every row, user behavior did not change, but the test broke anyway. Over time the team spends its effort maintaining tests instead of expanding coverage.

A different model: describe intent, not structure

The core idea behind AI testing agents is to separate what the user does from how the page is built.

BotGauge is an AI agent for test automation. Instead of writing code against selectors, you write test scenarios in plain English and let the agent turn them into automated tests. According to its public descriptions, the platform is built around a few ideas:

  • Plain-English scenarios. You describe the behavior you want to verify.
  • Locator-independent testing. The approach is designed to avoid depending on brittle element locators.
  • Autonomous generation, execution, and maintenance. AI agents create tests, run them, and self-heal them when the interface changes.
  • Broad coverage types. UI, API, functional, regression, smoke, visual, and cross-browser testing are all in scope.

What a scenario looks like

Here is an example of how you might describe a checkout test. This is an illustrative scenario, not output from a real project:

Scenario: Customer applies a discount code at checkout
  Given a cart containing two items
  When the customer enters a valid discount code
  Then the order total reflects the discount
  And the discount appears as a separate line on the order summary

Notice what is missing: no selectors, no waits, no assumptions about layout. If the discount field moves into a collapsible panel next month, the intent of the scenario has not changed, which is exactly why this style of test is meant to survive interface changes.

What "self-healing" should mean

"Self-healing" is a term worth treating with healthy skepticism. When you evaluate any tool that claims it, ask:

  1. What changes does it handle? Renamed elements and moved components are different from redesigned flows.
  2. How does it decide an element is the same one? Look for explainable matching, not magic.
  3. Does it tell you what it changed? A healed test you cannot audit is a risk.
  4. What happens when it is wrong? A good tool fails loudly instead of silently passing.

Use these questions in your own evaluation of BotGauge or any alternative.

How to evaluate this on your own product

You do not need to take any vendor's word for results. Run a small, honest experiment:

  1. Pick one critical flow, such as sign-up, checkout, or booking.
  2. Record your baseline. How long does it take your team to write and maintain a test for that flow today?
  3. Automate the same flow with a plain-English scenario.
  4. Make a deliberate UI change, such as renaming a button or moving a section.
  5. Compare. Did the test survive? How much effort did it take to recover?

Measuring your own flow will tell you more than any case study.

Where this approach fits and where it doesn't

AI-driven testing is a strong fit for regression coverage of stable business flows, teams with limited QA capacity, and products with frequently changing interfaces.

It is a weaker substitute for exploratory testing, usability judgment, and visual taste. Those still benefit from human attention.

Wrapping up

The real cost of brittle tests is not the failures. It is the coverage you never get to write because you are busy repairing old tests. Describing behavior instead of structure is one way out of that trap.

title: How much is artificial intelligence threatened by high interest rates and global debt?
description:
Ruchir Sharma analyzes the financial pressures behind the artificial intelligence boom, highlighting how record global debt and high interest rates are forcing tech giants to compete with governments for capital as borrowing scales rapidly.

According to an analysis by Rushir Sharma, chairman of Rockefeller International, the notion that a technological revolution can develop independently of basic economic rules is reminiscent of past stock market bubbles. The price of money still plays a key role, and rising interest rates may pose the biggest risk to the current industry boom.

Unlike in previous decades, global debt levels are at historic highs, forcing governments to compete directly with businesses for available capital. This situation is limiting liquidity in the market. Building the necessary infrastructure for artificial intelligence, such as data centers, requires huge amounts of money, as a result of which large technology groups are increasingly turning to borrowing. It is estimated that debt issuance related to the sector will exceed $600 billion, an amount tenfold compared to 2024.

The financial environment has changed drastically after a long period of low cost of money, with investors now demanding higher returns, squeezing the weaker companies in the value chain. Sharma points out that the major crises of the past did not occur suddenly, but started in more vulnerable sectors before spreading to the wider economy.
