title: Pulling Daily Google Ads Cost by Country Into a CSV With Python
description:
Teams advertising in several countries often need one simple daily file: date, country, campaign, cost, clicks and conversions. Finance wants it for reconciliation, growth wants it for ROAS checks. Exporting by hand every morning does not scale. The Google Ads API can produce it with one query.

Setup

You need a developer token, OAuth credentials and the customer ID of the account (or a manager account with access). Install the official client library and store credentials in a google-ads.yaml file outside your repository.

pip install google-ads

The query

Google Ads Query Language looks like SQL. The geographic view gives cost per country.

from google.ads.googleads.client import GoogleAdsClient
import csv, datetime

client = GoogleAdsClient.load_from_storage("google-ads.yaml")
svc = client.get_service("GoogleAdsService")
CUSTOMER_ID = "1234567890"

yesterday = (datetime.date.today() - datetime.timedelta(days=1)).isoformat()
query = f"""
SELECT segments.date, geographic_view.country_criterion_id, campaign.name,
       metrics.cost_micros, metrics.clicks, metrics.conversions
FROM geographic_view
WHERE segments.date = '{yesterday}'
"""

rows = []
for batch in svc.search_stream(customer_id=CUSTOMER_ID, query=query):
    for r in batch.results:
        rows.append([r.segments.date, r.geographic_view.country_criterion_id,
                     r.campaign.name, r.metrics.cost_micros / 1_000_000,
                     r.metrics.clicks, round(r.metrics.conversions, 2)])

with open(f"gads-{yesterday}.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["date", "country_id", "campaign", "cost", "clicks", "conversions"])
    w.writerows(rows)

Map country IDs to names

The API returns criterion IDs such as 2840 for the United States. Download the geo targets CSV from Google once and join on it, or query geo_target_constant for the IDs you see.

Currency and time zone

Cost is reported in the account currency and the account time zone. If you run accounts in different currencies, add a currency column and convert in a separate step with a fixed daily rate, so finance can audit the conversion. Never mix time zones in one file without saying so.

Schedule it

Run the script once a day with cron or a scheduled cloud function, and write the files to shared storage. Add a simple check that alerts you when yesterday's cost is zero or more than double the seven-day average; that catches broken tracking, paused billing and runaway campaigns early.

Use it

With daily cost by country in one place, you can compare ROAS per market and decide where to move budget. If you want to sanity-check targets before scaling, our ad budget and ROAS calculator turns margin and conversion rate into a break-even ROAS.

Published by PandaWM, an overseas marketing team based in Hong Kong.

title: Goravel deploy: Docker, Caddy and GitHub Actions
description:
Part 19 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-19.

So far in this series, we have run everything on our own machine. But a real application has to be deployed somewhere, so that others can reach it from the internet. So we are going to deploy the full setup on a production server. That means the API, the queue worker and the scheduler, with Postgres and Redis behind them and HTTPS in front. It also means a way to ship new versions without losing the jobs in flight.

Start from the Scheduling & Commands code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-18
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"

A production Docker image

TaskFlow has had a Dockerfile since the first part. Before we ship it, let's build it and look at what ends up inside. It copies our .env into the image, so every secret from the laptop ships with it:

$ docker build -t taskflow .

$ docker run --rm --entrypoint cat taskflow /www/.env | grep -E "APP_KEY|JWT_SECRET|DB_PASSWORD"
APP_KEY=d2RP1W…
JWT_SECRET=kdKMdI…
DB_PASSWORD=secret…

If we ship this image, our .env ships with it, and anyone who can pull the image can read these secrets. So the image should hold only the code, and the settings come from the server when the container starts. Let's rewrite the Dockerfile with that in mind, as a multi-stage build that compiles in one image and ships only the result in another:

Dockerfile

-FROM golang:alpine AS builder
-
-ENV GO111MODULE=on \
-    CGO_ENABLED=0
+FROM golang:1.25-alpine AS builder

 WORKDIR /build
+COPY go.mod go.sum ./
+RUN go mod download
 COPY . .
-RUN go mod tidy
-RUN go build --ldflags "-s -w -extldflags -static" -o main .
+RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags "-s -w" -o main .

-FROM alpine:latest
+FROM alpine:3.22

 WORKDIR /www

-COPY --from=builder /build/main /www/
-COPY --from=builder /build/.env /www/.env
-COPY --from=builder /build/public/ /www/public/
-COPY --from=builder /build/resources/ /www/resources/
+LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
+RUN adduser -D -u 10001 app
+COPY --from=builder /build/main ./main
+COPY --from=builder /build/public ./public
+COPY --from=builder /build/resources ./resources
+RUN mkdir -p storage/app storage/logs && chown -R app:app storage
+USER app

-ENTRYPOINT ["/www/main"]
+ENV APP_ENV=production APP_HOST=0.0.0.0 APP_PORT=3000
+EXPOSE 3000
+ENTRYPOINT ["./main"]
  • The build stage copies go.mod and go.sum first and downloads the modules, so Docker reuses that layer until the dependencies change.
  • golang:1.25-alpine and alpine:3.22 are pinned, so a build next month starts from the same Go and Alpine versions.
  • The final image has the binary, public/ and resources/. The binary reads both from its working directory at runtime. resources/ holds the views and the email templates, so without it the home page answers 500 and the first email panics.
  • The app runs as the user app, not root, and owns only storage/.
  • LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source names the repository the image comes from, so GHCR links the package to it and shows the source on the package page. Use your own repository here.
  • APP_HOST=0.0.0.0 makes the server listen on every address in the container. The default, 127.0.0.1, only accepts connections from inside the container itself.

.dockerignore keeps the rest out of the build, the local .env first:

.dockerignore

.git
.env
.env.*
storage
tests
main

Now let's build the image again and check that it holds only what the app needs to run:

$ docker build -t taskflow .
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint ls taskflow -a
.
..
main
public
resources
storage

There is no Go toolchain in the image, so go run . artisan doesn't work there. The compiled binary is the app, and it runs Artisan commands itself: ./main artisan migrate runs the migrations and exits without starting the server. ./main is the image's entrypoint, so with Docker the same command is docker run taskflow artisan migrate.

Configuration from environment variables

Goravel reads each setting from the environment first, and from .env only when the file is there. So on the server we keep the settings in their own .env file, and Docker passes them to the containers when they start. The image itself never has them.

Two settings in TaskFlow's config are written in code, so we can't change them from the environment yet. The first one is the logs. Right now they only go to a file in storage/logs, and in a container nobody reads that file. With print on, every log line also goes to stdout, so docker compose logs shows it:

config/logging.go

 // ... 29 lines not shown
                "path":      "storage/logs/goravel.log",
                "level":     config.Env("LOG_LEVEL", "debug"),
-               "print":     false,
+               "print":     config.Env("LOG_PRINT", false),
                "formatter": "text",
            },
            "daily": map[string]any{
                "driver":    "daily",
                "path":      "storage/logs/goravel.log",
                "level":     config.Env("LOG_LEVEL", "debug"),
                "days":      7,
-               "print":     false,
+               "print":     config.Env("LOG_PRINT", false),
                "formatter": "text",
            },
        },
    })
 }

The second is which runners a process starts, so one image can run as the API, the worker or the scheduler.

Web, worker and scheduler containers

go run . starts three runners in one process: goravel:http for the API, goravel:queue for the worker and goravel:schedule for the scheduler from Scheduling & Commands. That's fine on a laptop, but on a server it causes two problems. A panic in one queue job stops the whole process, so the API goes down with it. And each runner needs a different number of containers: the scheduler must run in exactly one, while the worker is what we add more of when jobs pile up.

So we are going to run the same image as three containers, each with one runner on. Goravel skips every runner listed in app.disabled_runners, and we read that list from the environment, so each container can turn off the other two:

config/app.go

 // ... 29 lines not shown
        "debug": config.Env("APP_DEBUG", false),

+       // Disabled Runners
+       //
+       // The runners this process should not start, as a space-separated list
+       // of signatures, for example "goravel:queue goravel:schedule".
+       "disabled_runners": config.Env("APP_DISABLED_RUNNERS", ""),
+
        // Application Timezone
        //
        // ... 41 lines not shown

Now we need Docker to start those three containers, along with Postgres and Redis. In front of them goes Caddy, a web server we use as a reverse proxy. Every request from the internet reaches Caddy first, and Caddy passes it on to web. It also sets up HTTPS by itself, getting a free certificate for our domain and renewing it before it expires.

A Compose file describes all six containers. The server needs only this file and a couple of others, not TaskFlow's code, so we keep them in a deploy/ folder and copy just that folder over. Here's deploy/compose.yml:

deploy/compose.yml

x-app: &app
  image: ${TASKFLOW_IMAGE:-taskflow}
  env_file: .env
  restart: unless-stopped
  stop_grace_period: 60s
  depends_on:
    postgres:
      condition: service_healthy
    redis:
      condition: service_healthy

services:
  web:
    <<: *app
    environment:
      APP_DISABLED_RUNNERS: goravel:queue goravel:schedule
    volumes:
      - storage:/www/storage/app
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://localhost:3000/healthz"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3

  worker:
    <<: *app
    environment:
      APP_DISABLED_RUNNERS: goravel:http goravel:schedule
    volumes:
      - storage:/www/storage/app

  scheduler:
    <<: *app
    environment:
      APP_DISABLED_RUNNERS: goravel:http goravel:queue

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_DATABASE}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  redis:
    image: redis:8.10-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes:
      - redis:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  caddy:
    image: caddy:2.10-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    environment:
      DOMAIN: ${DOMAIN}
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy:/data
    depends_on:
      web:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  storage:
  postgres:
  redis:
  caddy:
  • x-app is the part the three app services share: the image, the settings from .env, the restart policy and the wait for Postgres and Redis. &app names the block, and <<: *app copies it into each service. Compose's docs call these fragments. Compose skips anything starting with x-, so it doesn't run as a container of its own.
  • Each service turns off the two runners it doesn't need with APP_DISABLED_RUNNERS.
  • stop_grace_period: 60s gives a process a minute to finish its work when it's stopped, so a deploy doesn't cut a job off halfway.
  • Only Caddy publishes ports. Web is reachable only through it.
  • Redis runs with --appendonly yes, its append-only file, so the queued jobs survive a restart, and its image is pinned like the others.

Web and worker also share one volume, storage:/www/storage/app, because the worker writes each export's file, as in Queues & Jobs, and web is the one that serves the download. Without the shared volume, the export shows done but its download fails. Attachments live in that volume too, so they survive when a new version replaces the web container.

deploy/compose.yml is a second Compose file. The one at the project root is only for development, where it starts Postgres, Redis and Mailpit for the app we run with go run .. We pin Redis there too, so both use the same version:

docker-compose.yml

 # ... 12 lines not shown

   redis:
-    image: redis:alpine
+    image: redis:8.10-alpine
     restart: always
     ports:
       # ... 17 lines not shown

Health checks

Caddy should only start sending traffic once web is up and healthy, but TaskFlow has no route that says whether it is. So let's add one. It checks the two things the app can't run without, Postgres and Redis:

app/http/controllers/health_controller.go

// ... 11 lines not shown

type HealthController struct {
    // Dependent services
}

func NewHealthController() *HealthController {
    return &HealthController{
        // Inject services
    }
}

func (r *HealthController) Show(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    c, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    checks := map[string]string{"database": "ok", "redis": "ok"}
    status := http.StatusOK

    db, err := facades.Orm().DB()
    if err == nil {
        err = db.PingContext(c)
    }
    if err != nil {
        checks["database"] = err.Error()
        status = http.StatusServiceUnavailable
    }

    client, err := redisfacades.Instance("default")
    if err == nil {
        err = client.Ping(c).Err()
    }
    if err != nil {
        checks["redis"] = err.Error()
        status = http.StatusServiceUnavailable
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(status, checks)
}
  • Both checks share a two-second timeout, so a database that hangs can't hang the health check too.
  • Each check writes its error into the response, and either failure turns the status into 503.

The route sits outside api/v1, because it isn't part of the API:

routes/api.go

 // ... 16 lines not shown
    notificationController := controllers.NewNotificationController()
    exportController := controllers.NewExportController()
+   healthController := controllers.NewHealthController()
+
+   facades.Route().Get("healthz", healthController.Show)

    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("register", authController.Register)
        // ... 29 lines not shown

When Postgres or Redis is down, web stays up, but the check answers 503 with the error, and Docker marks the container unhealthy through its healthcheck. Docker doesn't restart it for that. The check is what docker compose up --wait and Caddy's depends_on wait for before they go on.

Only Docker needs this route, so we keep it off the internet. A failed check names our database user and internal hostnames, and every request runs two pings, so it shouldn't be open to anyone. Caddy answers 404 for it, while Docker still reaches it from inside the network:

deploy/Caddyfile

{$DOMAIN} {
    respond /healthz 404
    reverse_proxy web:3000
}

{$DOMAIN} is read from the DOMAIN setting, so the same Caddyfile works for any domain. Caddy gets the certificate for whatever name it holds.

Migrations in production

Migrations have to run once per release, and before the new version starts, because the new code expects the new tables. If each app container ran them when it started, all three would try at once, and again on every restart. We run them in a one-off container instead. docker compose run starts a fresh container from the web service, with the same image and settings, and runs one command. --rm removes it when it's done:

$ docker compose run --rm web artisan migrate
 SUCCESS  Migration success

A VPS with HTTPS

Caddy and the containers need a server with a public IP. Any VPS provider works, with:

  • Ubuntu 24.04 on x86 (amd64), which is what the image is built for;
  • the smallest plan, which is plenty for TaskFlow's six containers;
  • your SSH key added when you create it. GitHub's guide shows how to generate one.

Caddy needs the domain to point at the server before it can get a certificate, so we add an A record with the server's IP. Below, the server is 203.0.113.10 and the domain is taskflow.example.com.

First we log in as root once and prepare the server. It gets Docker, a deploy user that runs the app from here on, and a firewall that only lets in SSH, HTTP and HTTPS:

$ ssh root@203.0.113.10

On the server, as root:

curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" deploy
usermod -aG docker deploy
install -d -m 700 -o deploy -g deploy /home/deploy/.ssh
install -m 600 -o deploy -g deploy /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/deploy/.ssh/
install -d -o deploy -g deploy /opt/taskflow
ufw allow OpenSSH
ufw allow 80/tcp
ufw allow 443/tcp
ufw --force enable

ufw guards the server itself, but ports that Docker publishes skip it. That's one more reason only Caddy publishes any.

Then we copy the deploy/ files to the server, where .env starts as a copy of the example:

$ scp deploy/compose.yml deploy/Caddyfile deploy/deploy.sh deploy/.env.example deploy@203.0.113.10:/opt/taskflow/
$ ssh deploy@203.0.113.10
$ cd /opt/taskflow
$ cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env

deploy/.env.example

DOMAIN=taskflow.example.com
TASKFLOW_IMAGE=ghcr.io/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow:latest

APP_NAME=TaskFlow
APP_ENV=production
APP_KEY=
APP_DEBUG=false
APP_URL=https://taskflow.example.com
LOG_LEVEL=info
LOG_PRINT=true

JWT_SECRET=

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=postgres
DB_PORT=5432
DB_DATABASE=taskflow
DB_USERNAME=taskflow
DB_PASSWORD=

QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis
REDIS_HOST=redis
REDIS_PORT=6379
REDIS_PASSWORD=

FILESYSTEM_DISK=local

MAIL_HOST=
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=
MAIL_PASSWORD=
MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS=taskflow@example.com
MAIL_FROM_NAME=TaskFlow

We fill in the secrets on the server, so they never leave it. Each line replaces one empty setting in .env with a random value from openssl. APP_KEY must be exactly 32 characters, and rand -hex 16 gives that:

$ sed -i "s#^APP_KEY=.*#APP_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16)#" .env
$ sed -i "s#^JWT_SECRET=.*#JWT_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)#" .env
$ sed -i "s#^DB_PASSWORD=.*#DB_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 16)#" .env

grep shows that all three are now filled in:

$ grep -E "^(APP_KEY|JWT_SECRET|DB_PASSWORD)=" .env
APP_KEY=767289…
JWT_SECRET=467d20…
DB_PASSWORD=bf5a2f…

The rest is ours to set: DOMAIN and APP_URL for the domain, TASKFLOW_IMAGE for the image, and the MAIL_* lines for an SMTP provider.

CI and deploys with GitHub Actions

The server runs the app as an image it pulls from a registry. We use GitHub's container registry, GHCR, and let GitHub Actions build the image, push it there and deploy it on every push to main. That way every release passes the tests first, and nothing is built or deployed by hand:

.github/workflows/deploy.yml

name: Test, build and deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_DB: taskflow_test
          POSTGRES_USER: goravel
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
        ports: ["5433:5432"]
        options: --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
      redis:
        image: redis:8.10-alpine
        ports: ["6380:6379"]
      mailpit:
        image: axllent/mailpit:v1.27
        env:
          MP_SMTP_AUTH_ACCEPT_ANY: 1
          MP_SMTP_AUTH_ALLOW_INSECURE: 1
        ports: ["1025:1025", "8025:8025"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
      - run: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing

  image:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    outputs:
      name: ${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}
    steps:
      - id: name
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}:latest

  deploy:
    needs: image
    if: vars.DEPLOY_ENABLED == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    concurrency: deploy
    environment: production
    steps:
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        env:
          SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}
          KNOWN_HOSTS: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS }}
          HOST: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_HOST }}
          IMAGE: ${{ needs.image.outputs.name }}:${{ github.sha }}
        run: |
          install -m 600 /dev/null key
          echo "$SSH_KEY" > key
          echo "$KNOWN_HOSTS" > known_hosts
          ssh -i key -o UserKnownHostsFile=known_hosts -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$HOST" \
            "cd /opt/taskflow && ./deploy.sh $IMAGE"
  • test runs the tests against real Postgres, Redis and Mailpit, started as services on the ports .env.testing expects. Mailpit gets the same two settings as in docker-compose.yml, so it accepts the mailer's login.
  • image runs only when the tests pass. It lowercases the repository name first, because image names must be lowercase and GitHub keeps the owner's capitals. Then it builds the image and pushes it with two tags: the commit, so every release can be found again, and latest. GITHUB_TOKEN can push because the job asks for packages: write.
  • deploy runs only when the DEPLOY_ENABLED variable is true. It logs in to the server as deploy, checking the server's host key first, and runs deploy.sh with the commit's image. environment: production records each run as a deployment on the repository page, and concurrency: deploy makes a second push wait until the first deploy is done.

deploy.sh is what the deploy job runs on the server. It pulls the image and runs the migrations, then checks what migrate printed, so a failed migration stops the release before the new containers start:

deploy/deploy.sh

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

image="${1:?usage: ./deploy.sh <image>}"
export TASKFLOW_IMAGE="$image"

docker compose pull web

out=$(docker compose run --rm web artisan migrate 2>&1) || true
echo "$out"
if ! echo "$out" | grep -q "Migration success"; then
  echo "migrate failed, keeping the running version"
  exit 1
fi

docker compose up -d --wait
sed -i "s#^TASKFLOW_IMAGE=.*#TASKFLOW_IMAGE=$image#" .env
docker image prune -af
  • TASKFLOW_IMAGE is set for this run only. .env gets the new image after the containers are healthy, so if the new web fails its check, .env still names the last good image and docker compose up -d brings it back. Migrations the release already ran stay applied.
  • || true keeps set -e from ending the script when the migrate container can't even start, so the script still prints why before it stops.
  • docker image prune -af removes images no container uses, so each release doesn't leave its image on the disk.

The workflow runs in your own repository, so the code has to live there. Create an empty repository on GitHub and point origin at it, but don't push yet. First put your own username in place of krishankumar01, in the Dockerfile's LABEL and in deploy/.env.example:

$ git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<you>/goravel-taskflow.git

The deploy job needs three secrets. We add them to the production environment under Settings → Environments, and limit its deployment branches to main. Then only a deploy from main can read them, and that matters: deploy is in the docker group, so the deploy key works as root on the server.

  • DEPLOY_HOST is the server's IP.
  • DEPLOY_SSH_KEY is a private key made just for CI, so it can be removed without touching our own. It's made the same way as in GitHub's SSH key guide.
  • DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS is the server's host key. Every run starts on a fresh machine, so without it the job would trust whatever answers on that IP. 
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ci_deploy -N "" -C "github actions"
$ ssh-copy-id -i ci_deploy.pub deploy@203.0.113.10
$ ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 203.0.113.10 > known_hosts
$ ssh-keygen -lf known_hosts

ssh-keygen -lf prints the key's fingerprint, which must match the one SSH showed on our first login. The private half, ci_deploy, goes into DEPLOY_SSH_KEY and known_hosts into DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS, and we delete both from our machine afterwards.

Last, the deploy job only runs when the repository variable DEPLOY_ENABLED is true, set under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions. Turning it off stops deploys, while tests and images keep running on every push.

The first deploy

With the secrets and the variable in place, we push:

$ git push -u origin HEAD:main

That starts the first run, and its image job creates the package on GHCR. The workflow publishes it from a public repository, so the package is public too, and the server pulls it without logging in. If your repository is private, keep the package private. The server then logs in once with docker login ghcr.io, using a classic token with only the read:packages scope, as GitHub's guide on authenticating to the registry shows.

The three jobs run one after another. gh run view shows them in the terminal, and the repository's Actions tab shows the same:

$ gh run view
✓ main Test, build and deploy · 41200199938

JOBS
✓ test in 1m53s
✓ image in 2m0s
✓ deploy in 28s

On the server, web, worker and scheduler now run the commit's image, while Postgres, Redis and Caddy carry on untouched:

$ docker compose ps --format "table {{.Service}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}"
SERVICE     IMAGE                                                                              STATUS
caddy       caddy:2.10-alpine                                                                  Up 12 hours
postgres    postgres:15-alpine                                                                 Up 12 hours (healthy)
redis       redis:8.10-alpine                                                                  Up 12 hours (healthy)
scheduler   ghcr.io/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow:64af961d3cd87192f6f5d97d9f43c4072caceeb0   Up About a minute
web         ghcr.io/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow:64af961d3cd87192f6f5d97d9f43c4072caceeb0   Up About a minute (healthy)
worker      ghcr.io/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow:64af961d3cd87192f6f5d97d9f43c4072caceeb0   Up About a minute

Caddy already has a certificate from Let's Encrypt, and /healthz stays hidden from outside:

$ curl -sv https://taskflow.example.com/ -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E "subject:|issuer:"
*  subject: CN=taskflow.example.com
*  issuer: C=US; O=Let's Encrypt; CN=YE2

$ curl -sI https://taskflow.example.com/healthz
HTTP/2 404

Everyone who registers through the API is a member, so Ana registers first:

$ curl -X POST https://taskflow.example.com/api/v1/register -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
{…,"id":1,"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","role":"member",…}

One SQL update then makes her the first manager. After that she logs in, and we keep her token in ANA as in earlier parts:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U taskflow -d taskflow -c "UPDATE users SET role = 'manager' WHERE email = 'ana@example.com'"
UPDATE 1

A separate database user for migrations:

Right now the app and the migrations log in to Postgres as the same user. That user owns every table, so if someone ever gets the API to run a query of their choosing, they could drop a table as easily as read one. So in production we usually split it into two users. The app gets one that can read and write rows but can't change tables, and migrations keep running as the owner, only when we deploy.

On the server, the owner keeps its name and password, in a file of its own that only Postgres and migrate will read:

$ printf 'POSTGRES_USER=taskflow\nPOSTGRES_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$(sed -n 's/^DB_PASSWORD=//p' .env)" > .env.owner
$ chmod 600 .env.owner

Then the owner creates the app user with a new password, and .env switches to it:

$ pw=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U taskflow -d taskflow -c "
CREATE ROLE taskflow_app LOGIN PASSWORD '$pw';
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO taskflow_app;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO taskflow_app;
GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO taskflow_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO taskflow_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO taskflow_app;"
$ sed -i "s#^DB_USERNAME=.*#DB_USERNAME=taskflow_app#; s#^DB_PASSWORD=.*#DB_PASSWORD=$pw#" .env

The first two grants cover the tables there now. The ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES lines cover the ones later migrations create, so a new table doesn't need a new grant. Postgres 15 also stops ordinary users from creating tables in public, so the app user can't add tables of its own.

In compose.yml, Postgres gets the owner from .env.owner, and a migrate service logs in as the owner, setting DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD from the owner's values just before it runs. profiles: [tools] keeps it out of docker compose up, so it only runs when we ask:

deploy/compose.yml

+  migrate:
+    <<: *app
+    env_file: [.env, .env.owner]
+    profiles: [tools]
+    restart: "no"
+    entrypoint: ["sh", "-c", "DB_USERNAME=$$POSTGRES_USER DB_PASSWORD=$$POSTGRES_PASSWORD exec ./main artisan migrate"]
+
   postgres:
     image: postgres:15-alpine
     restart: unless-stopped
+    env_file: .env.owner
     environment:
       POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_DATABASE}
-      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME}
-      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
     volumes:

deploy.sh then runs the migrations through it:

deploy/deploy.sh

-out=$(docker compose run --rm web artisan migrate 2>&1) || true
+out=$(docker compose run --rm migrate 2>&1) || true

The next deploy migrates as the owner, and the app user gets turned away the moment it tries to change a table:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U taskflow_app -d taskflow -c "DROP TABLE tasks"
ERROR:  must be owner of table tasks

Backups:

Postgres keeps all of TaskFlow's data in one volume, so losing the server loses the data. pg_dump writes the whole database to one file while the app keeps running:

$ docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U taskflow -Fc taskflow > taskflow.dump

-T runs it without a terminal, so the dump reaches the file unchanged. -Fc writes Postgres's compressed custom format, which pg_restore reads.

A dump is only useful if it restores, so we restore it into a scratch database, check the data is there, and drop the scratch database again:

$ docker compose exec postgres createdb -U taskflow taskflow_restore
$ docker compose exec -T postgres pg_restore -U taskflow -d taskflow_restore < taskflow.dump
$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U taskflow -d taskflow_restore -c "SELECT count(*) FROM users"
 count
-------
     1
(1 row)

$ docker compose exec postgres dropdb -U taskflow taskflow_restore

To take one every night, we make a backups/ folder in /opt/taskflow and add one line to the deploy user's crontab with crontab -e. It runs at 03:00 server time, names each file by its date and deletes files older than a week. In a crontab, % has to be written \%:

0 3 * * * cd /opt/taskflow && docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U taskflow -Fc taskflow > backups/taskflow-$(date +\%F).dump && find backups -name "*.dump" -mtime +7 -delete

These files sit on the same server, so they're lost with it. Copy them somewhere else too, such as another machine or object storage. Attachments and exports live in the storage volume, which a database dump doesn't cover.

Graceful shutdown during deploys

A deploy replaces the worker, and the worker may be in the middle of a job when it happens. Docker stops a container by sending it SIGTERM first, and Goravel's worker answers by finishing the job it's running before it exits. Docker waits for that up to stop_grace_period, and only after that does it kill the process.

Let's watch it with an export. A handful of tasks export in an instant, so first we add 100,000 test tasks, which makes the export take a while:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U taskflow -d taskflow -c "INSERT INTO tasks (created_at, updated_at, created_by, title, description, status) SELECT now(), now(), 1, 'Task ' || g, 'A task to export.', 'pending' FROM generate_series(1, 100000) g"
INSERT 0 100000

Then we ask for an export, and while it runs, we replace the worker the same way a deploy does:

$ curl -X POST https://taskflow.example.com/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":1,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate worker
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Recreate
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Recreated
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Starting
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Started

The old worker finished the export before it exited, so the export is done:

$ curl https://taskflow.example.com/api/v1/exports/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{"created_at":"2026-10-31 12:06:39","updated_at":"2026-10-31 12:06:53","id":1,"user_id":1,"status":"done"}

Now let's set the grace period to 2 seconds and try again. Docker reads the grace period from the container it stops, so docker compose up -d first gives every container the new value:

$ sed -i "s/stop_grace_period: 60s/stop_grace_period: 2s/" compose.yml
$ docker compose up -d

This time Docker kills the worker in the middle of the export. The export never finishes: it stays pending, and its job sits in Redis's reserved list, where nothing picks it up again:

$ curl -X POST https://taskflow.example.com/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate worker
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Recreate
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Recreated
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Starting
 Container taskflow-worker-1 Started

$ curl https://taskflow.example.com/api/v1/exports/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{"created_at":"2026-10-31 12:07:07","updated_at":"2026-10-31 12:07:07","id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ docker compose exec redis redis-cli zcard TaskFlow_queues:redis_default:reserved
1

The exports:prune command from Scheduling & Commands deletes an export stuck like this after an hour, but the user never gets the file. So the grace period has to be longer than the slowest job. Put it back to 60 seconds, with docker compose up -d again, before moving on.

A release can also lose a job that's new in it. The worker only runs jobs it knows, and while a deploy is running, the new web can send a job the old worker has never heard of. So a new job type ships one release before anything sends it.

TaskFlow now runs on a server with HTTPS, and every push to main is tested, built and deployed.

title: Goravel scheduling and Artisan commands
description:
Part 18 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-18.

So far, everything in TaskFlow has started with a request: a client calls the API, and Goravel handles it. But some work has no request to start it. For example, nothing reminds assignees when a task is close to its due date. And export files pile up because nothing deletes them, while an export whose job fails all its tries stays pending forever. For work like this, we write a command and let the scheduler run it at a set time.

Start from the Mail & Templates code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-17
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

A command for reminders

An Artisan command is something we run with go run . artisan, like make:migration or package:install. The scheduler runs these too, so we are going to write the reminder as a command of our own, and make:command creates one:

$ go run . artisan make:command RemindDueTasks
  SUCCESS  Console command created successfully
  SUCCESS  Console command registered successfully

It writes a placeholder command to app/console/commands and registers it in a new bootstrap/commands.go, so Artisan can find it. It also adds WithCommands(Commands) to bootstrap/app.go, which hands that list to the app:

bootstrap/commands.go

package bootstrap

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/console"

    "taskflow/app/console/commands"
)

func Commands() []console.Command {
    return []console.Command{
        &commands.RemindDueTasks{},
    }
}

By default, make:command turns the name we gave it into a signature, app:remind-due-tasks, which is what we type after artisan. We give it a shorter one, tasks:remind, and fill in the empty Handle, which sends a Mailable we write next:

app/console/commands/remind_due_tasks.go

 package commands

 import (
+   "fmt"
+
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/console"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/console/command"
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/support/carbon"
+
+   "taskflow/app/enums"
+   "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/mails"
+   "taskflow/app/models"
 )

 type RemindDueTasks struct {
 }

-// Signature The name and signature of the console command.
 func (r *RemindDueTasks) Signature() string {
-   return "app:remind-due-tasks"
+   return "tasks:remind"
 }

-// Description The console command description.
 func (r *RemindDueTasks) Description() string {
-   return "Command description"
+   return "Email each assignee their open tasks that are due soon"
 }

-// Extend The console command extend.
 func (r *RemindDueTasks) Extend() command.Extend {
-   return command.Extend{Category: "app"}
+   return command.Extend{
+       Category: "tasks",
+       Flags: []command.Flag{
+           &command.IntFlag{
+               Name:  "hours",
+               Value: 24,
+               Usage: "remind about tasks due within this many hours",
+           },
+       },
+   }
 }

-// Handle Execute the console command.
 func (r *RemindDueTasks) Handle(ctx console.Context) error {
-   
+   hours := ctx.OptionInt("hours")
+
+   var tasks []models.Task
+   err := facades.Orm().Query().With("Assignee").
+       Where("assigned_to IS NOT NULL").
+       Where("status <> ?", enums.StatusDone).
+       Where("due_at BETWEEN ? AND ?", carbon.Now().StdTime(), carbon.Now().AddHours(hours).StdTime()).
+       OrderBy("due_at").
+       Find(&tasks)
+   if err != nil {
+       return err
+   }
+   if len(tasks) == 0 {
+       ctx.Info("No tasks are due soon.")
+       return nil
+   }
+
+   var assignees []uint
+   due := map[uint][]models.Task{}
+   for _, task := range tasks {
+       id := *task.AssignedTo
+       if _, ok := due[id]; !ok {
+           assignees = append(assignees, id)
+       }
+       due[id] = append(due[id], task)
+   }
+
+   var rows [][]string
+   for _, id := range assignees {
+       assignee := *due[id][0].Assignee
+       if err := facades.Mail().Send(mails.NewDueSoon(assignee, due[id])); err != nil {
+           return err
+       }
+       rows = append(rows, []string{assignee.Email, fmt.Sprint(len(due[id]))})
+   }
+
+   ctx.Table([]string{"Assignee", "Tasks"}, rows)
+
    return nil
 }
  • Category puts the command under tasks: in go run . artisan list.
  • Extend declares a --hours flag. IntFlag makes it a number, and Value sets its default. Usage is the help text that --help prints. ctx.OptionInt("hours") reads it in Handle.
  • The query finds open tasks with an assignee and a due date in the next hours hours. It calls carbon.Now() twice, because AddHours changes the date it's called on instead of returning a new one.
  • The loop groups the tasks by assignee, so each person gets one email that lists all their tasks.
  • Mail().Send sends the email right away. The command runs outside any request, so nothing waits on it and there's no reason to queue the email.
  • When Handle returns an error, the command exits with status 1 from the terminal, and the scheduler writes the error to the log.
  • ctx.Table prints who got an email and how many tasks it listed. The console context also has prompts, progress bars and spinners, listed under writing output in the Goravel docs.

The email is a Mailable like the ones from Mail & Templates, with views that extend the same layout:

app/mails/due_soon.go

// ... 8 lines not shown
type DueSoon struct {
    assignee models.User
    tasks    []models.Task
}

func NewDueSoon(assignee models.User, tasks []models.Task) *DueSoon {
    return &DueSoon{assignee: assignee, tasks: tasks}
}

// ... 8 lines not shown
func (receiver *DueSoon) Content() *mail.Content {
    return &mail.Content{
        HtmlView: "due_soon.html",
        TextView: "due_soon.txt",
        With: map[string]any{
            "Name":  receiver.assignee.Name,
            "Tasks": receiver.tasks,
        },
    }
}

func (receiver *DueSoon) Envelope() *mail.Envelope {
    return &mail.Envelope{
        To:      []string{receiver.assignee.Email},
        Subject: "Your tasks due soon",
    }
}

func (receiver *DueSoon) Queue() *mail.Queue {
    return &mail.Queue{}
}

resources/mail/due_soon.html

{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block content %}
<p>Hi {{ Name }},</p>
<p>These tasks are due soon:</p>
<ul>
{% for task in Tasks %}<li><strong>{{ task.Title }}</strong>, due {{ task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString }}</li>
{% endfor %}</ul>
{% endblock %}

resources/mail/due_soon.txt

{% autoescape off %}Hi {{ Name }},

These tasks are due soon:
{% for task in Tasks %}
- {{ task.Title }}, due {{ task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString }}{% endfor %}{% endautoescape %}

To try it, we start from the same setup as Mail & Templates, with Ana's token in ANA and Ben as user 5. Then we give Ben a task due in three hours, one due tomorrow and one due in three days. due_at has to be in the future, so pick UTC times of your own around those:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Fix the login page","description":"Due soon.","assigned_to":5,"due_at":"2026-10-28 22:00:00"}'
{…,"id":8,…,"due_at":"2026-10-28 22:00:00"}

The other two are the same request with "Write the release notes", due tomorrow, and "Plan the next sprint", due in three days. Only the first two are due in the next 24 hours. Seeded tasks get random due dates, so the table can list other members too:

$ go run . artisan tasks:remind
╭─────────────────┬───────╮
│ Assignee        │ Tasks │
├─────────────────┼───────┤
│ ben@example.com │ 2     │
│ dmason@hart.org │ 1     │
╰─────────────────┴───────╯

Ben's email in Mailpit lists his two tasks:

Hi Ben,

These tasks are due soon:

- Fix the login page, due 2026-10-28 22:00:00
- Write the release notes, due 2026-10-29 15:00:00

With --hours 4, only the task due in three hours is left:

$ go run . artisan tasks:remind --hours 4
╭─────────────────┬───────╮
│ Assignee        │ Tasks │
├─────────────────┼───────┤
│ ben@example.com │ 1     │
╰─────────────────┴───────╯

The schedule

We don't want to run the reminder by hand every morning, so we let Goravel's scheduler run it. To use Goravel's scheduler, let's install its package first, the same way as mail:

$ go run . artisan package:install Schedule
  INFO    Schedule depends on Log, Cache, they will be installed simultaneously
  SUCCESS  Facade Schedule installed successfully

package:install adds the facades.Schedule() facade and the schedule service provider. The schedule itself goes in WithSchedule in bootstrap/app.go, as a list of events. Each event names a command and says when it runs:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 11 lines not shown
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/schedule"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/foundation"
    // ... 13 lines not shown
 func Boot() contractsfoundation.Application {
    return foundation.Setup().
        WithCommands(Commands).
+       WithSchedule(func() []schedule.Event {
+           return []schedule.Event{
+               facades.Schedule().Command("tasks:remind").DailyAt("09:00"),
+           }
+       }).
        WithJobs(Jobs).
        WithRules(Rules).
        WithSeeders(Seeders).
        WithMigrations(Migrations).
        // ... 48 lines not shown
        Create()
 }
  • DailyAt("09:00") runs the reminder at 09:00 every day.
  • The times follow timezone in config/app.go, which is UTC in TaskFlow.
  • The schedule has methods for other times, like EveryFiveMinutes(), Hourly(), Weekly(), or Cron("0 9 * * 1-5") for an expression of our own. The Goravel docs list them all.

schedule:list shows each event as a cron expression, with the time left until its next run:

$ go run . artisan schedule:list
  00 09 * * *  artisan tasks:remind ................. Next Due: 13 hours after

00 09 * * * means minute 0 of hour 9, on every day of every month.

The scheduler starts with the app, next to the HTTP server and the queue worker, so go run . or air runs it with nothing else to start. To watch it run without waiting for 09:00, we change DailyAt("09:00") to EveryMinute() and restart the app. At the next full minute, the terminal running the app shows the scheduler waking up, then the command's table. The SUCCESS lines print because APP_DEBUG is true:

 SUCCESS  wake [now 2026-10-28 19:22:00.000082959 +0000 UTC]
 SUCCESS  run [now 2026-10-28 19:22:00.000082959 +0000 UTC entry 1 next 2026-10-28 19:23:00 +0000 UTC]
╭─────────────────┬───────╮
│ Assignee        │ Tasks │
├─────────────────┼───────┤
│ ben@example.com │ 2     │
│ dmason@hart.org │ 1     │
╰─────────────────┴───────╯

It runs again every minute after that, and each run sends Ben the same email, which is why the real schedule runs it once a day. After the test, change it back to DailyAt("09:00").

Goravel also has go run . artisan schedule:run, which starts a scheduler on its own in the terminal. We don't need it, because the app already starts one. Running both at once gives two schedulers, so each command runs twice and Ben gets every email twice.

Cleaning up exports

The export job from Queues & Jobs writes a file for every export, but nothing deletes the files or their rows. And when the job fails all three tries, the worker moves it to failed_jobs without touching the export, so the export stays pending and its download answers 409 forever.

To see an export get stuck, we replace storage/app/exports with a plain file, so the job can't write there, and then ask for an export:

$ mkdir -p storage/app && rm -rf storage/app/exports && touch storage/app/exports

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":1,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ sleep 13
$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/1/download -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{"error":"The export is not ready yet."}

In the terminal running the app, the job gave up ten seconds after it started, and export 1 stayed pending:

  2026-10-28 19:22:58.237 export_tasks ............................... RUNNING
  2026-10-28 19:23:08.253 export_tasks .......................... 3.526ms FAIL

So we are going to write a second command, exports:prune, that cleans up both. make:command PruneExports creates it the same way as the reminder and adds it to bootstrap/commands.go:

app/console/commands/prune_exports.go

// ... 14 lines not shown
type PruneExports struct {
}

func (r *PruneExports) Signature() string {
    return "exports:prune"
}

func (r *PruneExports) Description() string {
    return "Delete old exports and exports stuck in pending"
}

func (r *PruneExports) Extend() command.Extend {
    return command.Extend{
        Category: "exports",
        Flags: []command.Flag{
            &command.IntFlag{
                Name:  "days",
                Value: 7,
                Usage: "delete exports older than this many days",
            },
        },
    }
}

func (r *PruneExports) Handle(ctx console.Context) error {
    var old []models.Export
    err := facades.Orm().Query().
        Where("created_at < ?", carbon.Now().SubDays(ctx.OptionInt("days")).StdTime()).
        Find(&old)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for _, export := range old {
        if export.Path != "" && facades.Storage().Exists(export.Path) {
            if err := facades.Storage().Delete(export.Path); err != nil {
                return err
            }
        }
        if _, err := facades.Orm().Query().Delete(&export); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }

    stuck, err := facades.Orm().Query().
        Where("status", enums.ExportPending).
        Where("created_at < ?", carbon.Now().SubHour().StdTime()).
        Delete(&models.Export{})
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    ctx.Info(fmt.Sprintf("Deleted %d old exports and %d stuck in pending.", len(old), stuck.RowsAffected))

    return nil
}
  • The first query finds exports older than --days, 7 by default. For each one, it deletes the file and then the row. Deleting only the file would leave a done export whose download fails with a 500.
  • Exists comes before Delete, because Delete returns an error for a file that's already gone.
  • The second query deletes pending exports older than an hour. The job's three tries take about ten seconds, so an export still pending after an hour is stuck.

To try it, we turn storage/app/exports back into a folder, so a second export can finish and write its file. Then SQL moves export 1 back two hours and export 2 back eight days:

$ rm storage/app/exports

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel taskflow -c "update exports set created_at = now() - interval '2 hours' where id = 1; update exports set created_at = now() - interval '8 days' where id = 2"

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel taskflow -c "select id, status, path, created_at from exports order by id"
 id | status  |     path      |       created_at
----+---------+---------------+------------------------
  1 | pending |               | 2026-10-28 17:23:13+00
  2 | done    | exports/2.csv | 2026-10-20 19:23:13+00

The prune deletes the stuck export and the old one, file included:

$ go run . artisan exports:prune
  INFO    Deleted 1 old exports and 1 stuck in pending.

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel taskflow -c "select id, status, path, created_at from exports order by id"
 id | status | path | created_at
----+--------+------+------------
(0 rows)

$ ls storage/app/exports

To run the prune every night, we add it to the schedule with Daily(), which runs it at midnight:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 31 lines not shown
            return []schedule.Event{
                facades.Schedule().Command("tasks:remind").DailyAt("09:00"),
+               facades.Schedule().Command("exports:prune").Daily(),
            }
        }).
        // ... 54 lines not shown

Running on more than one server:

Every copy of the app runs its own scheduler. TaskFlow runs as one copy, but with two, each command would run twice. OnOneServer stops that:

facades.Schedule().Command("tasks:remind").DailyAt("09:00").OnOneServer()

Before an event runs, the scheduler takes a lock named after the command and the hour and minute it runs at, in the default cache store. Only the copy that gets the lock runs the command. TaskFlow's cache store is Redis, which every copy shares, so the lock works across them.

Tests

The tests in tests/feature/schedule_test.go fix the time with carbon.SetTestNow, then call each command with facades.Artisan().Call. They check that:

  • the reminder lists only open tasks due within 24 hours;
  • --hours changes that window;
  • the prune deletes old and stuck exports, and keeps recent and in-progress ones;
  • the schedule has both cron expressions.

The reminder tests send real email, so Mailpit has to be running, like Postgres and Redis:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  1.901s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.360s

TaskFlow now emails each assignee their tasks due in the next day, every morning at 09:00. Every night it also deletes old exports and the ones stuck in pending.

title: Goravel mail: Mailables, templates and queues
description:
Part 17 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-17.

So far an assignee learns about a new task only from GET /notifications, and the owner of an export has to ask GET /exports/{id} until its file is ready. To solve it, we are going to notify them a different way: by email. Each email will have an HTML part and a plain-text part, and it will use templates to add the dynamic data.

Start from the Queues & Jobs code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-16
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

Mail on a laptop

Goravel sends mail over SMTP, so to work in this part we are going to use a tool for development called Mailpit. It accepts every email and shows it on a web page instead of delivering it to the recipient.

To use Goravel's mail package, let's install it first:

$ go run . artisan package:install Mail
  INFO    Mail depends on Log, Cache, Orm, Schema, DB, Queue, they will be installed simultaneously
  SUCCESS  Facade Mail installed successfully

package:install adds config/mail.go, the facades.Mail() facade and the mail service provider. It also adds empty MAIL_ keys to .env and .env.example, which we fill in below.

Next, we need to add Mailpit to docker-compose.yml, so that it runs on our machine next to Postgres and Redis:

docker-compose.yml

 # ... 19 lines not shown
       - redis_data:/data

+  mailpit:
+    image: axllent/mailpit:v1.27
+    restart: always
+    environment:
+      MP_SMTP_AUTH_ACCEPT_ANY: 1
+      MP_SMTP_AUTH_ALLOW_INSECURE: 1
+    ports:
+      - "1025:1025"
+      - "8025:8025"
+
 volumes:
   postgres_data:
   redis_data:

We need the two settings because Goravel always logs in to the SMTP server on a port other than 465 or 587, even with an empty username. Mailpit offers no login by default, so Go's SMTP client stops with smtp: server doesn't support AUTH. The settings make Mailpit accept any username and password without TLS.

Now we point TaskFlow at Mailpit with the MAIL_ keys. Fill them in .env the same way, and add them to .env.testing so the tests send to Mailpit too:

.env.example

 # ... 28 lines not shown
 REDIS_PASSWORD=
 REDIS_PORT=6380
+
+MAIL_HOST=127.0.0.1
+MAIL_PORT=1025
+MAIL_USERNAME=
+MAIL_PASSWORD=
+MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS=taskflow@example.com
+MAIL_FROM_NAME=TaskFlow
  • MAIL_HOST and MAIL_PORT are where Mailpit listens for SMTP.
  • MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS and MAIL_FROM_NAME fill the From line of every email.
  • MAIL_USERNAME and MAIL_PASSWORD stay empty, because Mailpit accepts any login.

Then start Mailpit with docker compose up -d mailpit. Its inbox is at http://localhost:8025, where every email from this part shows up.

The first email

We start with the assignment email. TaskFlow already fires TaskAssigned whenever someone assigns a task, from Events & Listeners. So we are going to add a second listener for this event, called EmailAssignee:

$ go run . artisan make:listener EmailAssignee
  SUCCESS  Listener created successfully

app/listeners/email_assignee.go

// ... 13 lines not shown

type EmailAssignee struct {
}
// ... 12 lines not shown

func (receiver *EmailAssignee) Handle(args ...any) error {
    taskID, ok1 := args[0].(uint)
    assignedTo, ok2 := args[1].(uint)
    assignedBy, ok3 := args[2].(uint)
    if !ok1 || !ok2 || !ok3 {
        return errors.New("email assignee: the ids must be uints")
    }
    if assignedTo == assignedBy {
        return nil
    }

    var task models.Task
    err := facades.Orm().Query().FindOrFail(&task, taskID)
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return nil
    }
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var assignee, manager models.User
    if err := facades.Orm().Query().FindOrFail(&assignee, assignedTo); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := facades.Orm().Query().FindOrFail(&manager, assignedBy); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return facades.Mail().
        To([]string{assignee.Email}).
        Subject(fmt.Sprintf("%s assigned you a task", manager.Name)).
        Content(mail.Content{Text: fmt.Sprintf("%s assigned you %q.", manager.Name, task.Title)}).
        Send()
}

Handle makes the same checks as NotifyAssignee, so a manager who takes a task themselves gets no email.

We build the email with facades.Mail(), which starts a new email on every call. It gives a fluent API: each method sets one part of the email and returns the email again, so the calls chain until Send:

  • To takes the recipients' addresses.
  • Subject sets the subject line.
  • Content sets the body. With only Text, the email has a plain-text part and no HTML.
  • Send sends it over SMTP right away.

The chain also has Cc, Bcc, Attach, Headers and From. This email doesn't need them, and without From it uses MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS and MAIL_FROM_NAME.

Queue returns Enable: true, as in NotifyAssignee, so the listener runs on the worker and sending the email doesn't hold up the request that assigned the task.

A listener runs only once WithEvents lists it, so we add it after NotifyAssignee in bootstrap/app.go:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 36 lines not shown
        WithEvents(func() map[contractsevent.Event][]contractsevent.Listener {
            return map[contractsevent.Event][]contractsevent.Listener{
-               &events.TaskAssigned{}: {&listeners.NotifyAssignee{}},
+               &events.TaskAssigned{}: {&listeners.NotifyAssignee{}, &listeners.EmailAssignee{}},
            }
        }).
        // ... 41 lines not shown

To try it, we start from the same setup as Queues & Jobs:

  1. Reset the database with migrate:fresh --seed, which adds Ana as the manager, plus three members and seven tasks.
  2. Register Ben. He gets id 5.
  3. Log in as Ana and as Ben, and save each token in a variable, ANA and BEN.

Now when Ana assigns a task to Ben, an email arrives in Mailpit. /view/latest.txt shows the plain-text part of the newest email:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Fix the login page","description":"The error message overlaps the button & the logo.","assigned_to":5,"due_at":"2026-11-06 09:00:00"}'
{…,"id":8,…,"title":"Fix the login page",…}

$ curl http://localhost:8025/view/latest.txt
Ana assigned you "Fix the login page".

A Mailable

Building the email inline in the listener works for one line of text. But real emails are more complex, with HTML and styles. And if we send the same email from more than one place, we have to write the same code in each of them. So we are going to use a Mailable, a struct that holds all of this for one email. TaskFlow's unit test, for one, builds the same assignment email without sending it:

$ go run . artisan make:mail Assignment
  SUCCESS  Mail created successfully

app/mails/assignment.go

// ... 9 lines not shown

type Assignment struct {
    task     models.Task
    assignee models.User
    by       models.User
}

func NewAssignment(task models.Task, assignee, by models.User) *Assignment {
    return &Assignment{task: task, assignee: assignee, by: by}
}

func (receiver *Assignment) Headers() map[string]string {
    return map[string]string{}
}

func (receiver *Assignment) Attachments() []string {
    return []string{}
}

func (receiver *Assignment) Content() *mail.Content {
    return &mail.Content{
        HtmlView: "assignment.html",
        TextView: "assignment.txt",
        With: map[string]any{
            "Name": receiver.assignee.Name,
            "By":   receiver.by.Name,
            "Task": receiver.task,
        },
    }
}

func (receiver *Assignment) Envelope() *mail.Envelope {
    return &mail.Envelope{
        To:      []string{receiver.assignee.Email},
        Subject: fmt.Sprintf("%s assigned you a task", receiver.by.Name),
    }
}

func (receiver *Assignment) Queue() *mail.Queue {
    return &mail.Queue{}
}
  • NewAssignment takes the task and both users, so the Mailable has everything the email shows.
  • Content names the two views, one for the HTML part and one for the text part. With is the data they can use.
  • Headers, Attachments and Queue come from make:mail and stay empty. Queue matters later, when we queue the export email.

In the listener, Send now takes the Mailable in place of the inline calls:

app/listeners/email_assignee.go

 package listeners

 import (
    "errors"
-   "fmt"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/event"
-   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/mail"
    frameworkerrors "github.com/goravel/framework/errors"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/mails"
    "taskflow/app/models"
 )
 // ... 41 lines not shown
        return err
    }

-   return facades.Mail().
-       To([]string{assignee.Email}).
-       Subject(fmt.Sprintf("%s assigned you a task", manager.Name)).
-       Content(mail.Content{Text: fmt.Sprintf("%s assigned you %q.", manager.Name, task.Title)}).
-       Send()
+   return facades.Mail().Send(mails.NewAssignment(task, assignee, manager))
 }

The listener no longer deals with the email's text. That now lives inside Assignment, so it changes in one place.

Views

In a Mailable, or in an email built with the chain, the body goes in Content. It can be inline, with Text and Html, or as complex as a full HTML page. For that, Goravel has email views, set with HtmlView and TextView, which the template engine set in config/mail.go renders. Its default engine, html, looks for the views in resources/views/mail and reads them as Go templates. The With data fills them: {{.Name}} prints the Name value, and {{.Task.Title}} prints a field of the task:

resources/views/mail/assignment.html

<p>Hi {{.Name}},</p>
<p>{{.By}} assigned you <strong>{{.Task.Title}}</strong>.</p>
{{if .Task.DueAt}}<p>It's due {{.Task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString}}.</p>{{end}}
<p>{{.Task.Description}}</p>

resources/views/mail/assignment.txt

Hi {{.Name}},

{{.By}} assigned you "{{.Task.Title}}".
{{if .Task.DueAt}}It's due {{.Task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString}}.
{{end}}
{{.Task.Description}}
  • {{if .Task.DueAt}} prints the due-date line only when the task has a due date.
  • {{.Task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString}} calls a method on the date, the one the export uses for its CSV.
  • Goravel renders the views with html/template, which escapes the values it prints, so a title with a < can't add HTML to the email.

The same assignment now arrives with both parts, but the last line of the text part shows & where the description has &:

Hi Ben,

Ana assigned you "Fix the login page".
It's due 2026-11-06 09:00:00.

The error message overlaps the button & the logo.

Goravel's engine has two limitations for these emails:

  • It renders the text view with html/template too, so it escapes the & as if the text were HTML.
  • It parses each view from its own file, so the export email can't share a layout with this one.

Another template engine

We can get past both by swapping the engine. Goravel's custom driver plugs in any template engine with a Render(name, data) method. We use pongo2, a Go engine with Django's template syntax, because its views can extend a layout and switch escaping off for the text part:

$ go get github.com/flosch/pongo2/v6

To plug pongo2 in, we write a small type in app/mails that hands each view to pongo2:

app/mails/pongo.go

// ... 7 lines not shown

type Pongo struct {
    views *pongo2.TemplateSet
}

func NewPongo(dir string) *Pongo {
    return &Pongo{views: pongo2.NewSet("mail", pongo2.MustNewLocalFileSystemLoader(dir))}
}

func (receiver *Pongo) Render(name string, data any) (string, error) {
    with, ok := data.(map[string]any)
    if !ok {
        return "", errors.New("pongo: the mail's With must be a map")
    }

    view, err := receiver.views.FromCache(name)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }

    return view.Execute(pongo2.Context(with))
}
  • NewPongo loads the views from one folder, resources/mail.
  • FromCache parses a view the first time it's used and keeps it for later emails.
  • Render gets the Mailable's With as any, but pongo2 needs a map, so any other type returns an error.

The views move to resources/mail and change to pongo2's syntax. First comes the layout, which every HTML email shares. It's built from HTML tables with inline styles, because email clients show those more reliably than a style sheet. {% block content %} marks where each view goes:

resources/mail/layout.html

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

resources/mail/assignment.html

{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% if Task.DueAt %}<p>It's due {{ Task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString }}.</p>{% endif %}

resources/mail/assignment.txt

{% autoescape off %}Hi {{ Name }},

{{ By }} assigned you "{{ Task.Title }}".
{% if Task.DueAt %}It's due {{ Task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString }}.
{% endif %}
{{ Task.Description }}{% endautoescape %}
  • {% extends "layout.html" %} puts the view's content block into the layout.
  • {{ Task.Title }} prints a value, and pongo2 escapes it for HTML, as html/template does.
  • {% if Task.DueAt %} is false when DueAt is nil. {{ Task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString }} calls the method, with no parentheses.
  • {% autoescape off %} turns that escaping off for the text view, so the & stays as typed.

Last, we need to tell Goravel to use our engine. We can register the custom engine in config/mail.go as pongo, with the custom driver. Goravel calls its via function once to get the engine, and default makes it the one every email uses:

The same assignment now keeps its &, and the HTML part in Mailpit has the TaskFlow header and footer around it:

$ curl http://localhost:8025/view/latest.txt

Ana assigned you "Fix the login page".
It's due 2026-11-06 09:00:00.

The error message overlaps the button & the logo.

Queueing mail

Next, we email the owner of an export once its file is ready, so the email goes at the end of the export job. In EmailAssignee we used Send, because sending the email is the only thing that listener does. The export job is different, because it also builds the file. If we use Send here and SMTP fails, the whole export fails, and every retry builds the file again. So instead we use Queue, which sends the email as a job of its own:

app/jobs/export_tasks.go

-   return facades.Orm().Query().Save(&export)

    return attempt < 3, 5 * time.Second

Queue renders the views right away and puts the finished email on the queue. The worker then sends it as a separate job, goravel_send_mail_job, so an SMTP failure fails only that job and leaves its own row in failed_jobs.

$ curl http://localhost:8025/view/latest.txt

Your export of all tasks is ready. Download it with GET /api/v1/exports/1/download.

To check that, we stop Mailpit and ask for another export. The export still finishes, and only the email job fails:

$ docker compose stop mailpit

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ sleep 2
$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"done"}

  2026-10-27 23:23:44.45 export_tasks ........................... 6.719ms DONE

  2026-10-27 23:23:44.454 goravel_send_mail_job ................. 1.049ms FAIL

The failed email waits in failed_jobs, with the connection error:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel taskflow -At -c "select exception from failed_jobs"
dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1025: connect: connection refused

queue:failed lists the failed job with its uuid:

$ go run . artisan queue:failed
  2026-10-27 23:23:45 aef68b21-e435-43ea-9f9e-b840b1e8cd37 ..... redis@default

Once Mailpit runs again, queue:retry puts that job back on the queue, and the worker sends the email:

$ docker compose start mailpit

$ go run . artisan queue:retry aef68b21-e435-43ea-9f9e-b840b1e8cd37
  INFO    Pushing failed queue jobs back onto the queue

Hi Ana,

Your export of all tasks is ready. Download it with GET /api/v1/exports/2/download.

A queue of its own for mail:

facades.Mail().Queue puts the job on the default connection and queue. A Mailable picks others by returning them from its own Queue method, such as &mail.Queue{Queue: "mail"}. A queue other than the default needs a worker of its own, as in Queues & Jobs.

Tests

We test the emails in two ways:

  • tests/unit/mails_test.go renders the assignment email through the pongo2 engine and sends nothing. It checks the recipient, the escaped HTML, the text part as typed and the due-date line.
  • tests/feature/mail_test.go sends real email to Mailpit and reads it back through Mailpit's API, with the helpers in tests/mailpit.go. It checks that the assignee gets an email, that a manager who takes a task gets none, and that a finished export emails its owner.

The feature tests send real email, so they need Mailpit running, like Postgres and Redis:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  2.020s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.461s

TaskFlow now emails the assignee of each assigned task and the owner of each finished export. All of them still go to Mailpit, because MAIL_HOST points there.

title: Goravel queues and jobs: retries and failed jobs
description:
Part 16 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-16.

This part adds a CSV export of all tasks. A big export takes a while, so the request doesn't build it. It only queues a job and returns. The job builds the file in the background, and the client downloads it when it's done.

Start from the Events & Listeners code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-15
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

A job, not an event

An event announces what happened, and whoever listens decides what to do about it. That fit Events & Listeners, where the notification was one reaction to assigning a task, and more could be added later without touching the handler. For an export, the handler already knows the one thing that has to happen, and the export isn't done until the file is built. So it names that work directly by sending a job. The job runs on the same queue and worker as the queued listener.

The exports table

Each export is a row with its owner, its status and the file's path. The path stays out of the JSON:

app/enums/export_status.go

package enums

type ExportStatus string

const (
    ExportPending ExportStatus = "pending"
    ExportDone    ExportStatus = "done"
)

app/models/export.go

package models

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"

    "taskflow/app/enums"
)

type Export struct {
    orm.Model
    UserID uint               `gorm:"not null" json:"user_id"`
    Status enums.ExportStatus `gorm:"type:enum('pending','done');default:'pending';not null" json:"status"`
    Path   string             `gorm:"size:255" json:"-"`
}

make:migration builds the migration from a model, but it only finds models listed in Models in bootstrap/app.go, so Export goes there first:

bootstrap/app.go

            facades.Schema().Extend(schema.Extension{
-               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}, models.Attachment{}, models.Notification{}},
+               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}, models.Attachment{}, models.Notification{}, models.Export{}},
            })

            // ... 34 lines not shown

$ go run . artisan make:migration create_exports_table -m Export

make:migration builds the columns from the model, and one more line adds the foreign key to users:

database/migrations/20261026231209_create_exports_table.go
