$ go run . artisan migrate

The job

make:job creates the job and registers it:

$ go run . artisan make:job ExportTasks
 SUCCESS  Job created successfully
 SUCCESS  Job registered successfully

WithEvents registers each listener with its event. A job has no event, so make:job registers it in a new bootstrap/jobs.go:

bootstrap/jobs.go

package bootstrap

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/queue"

    "taskflow/app/jobs"
)

func Jobs() []queue.Job {
    return []queue.Job{
        &jobs.ExportTasks{},
    }
}

It also adds WithJobs to bootstrap/app.go. Without it, the worker can't find the job:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 26 lines not shown
 func Boot() contractsfoundation.Application {
    return foundation.Setup().
+       WithJobs(Jobs).
        WithRules(Rules).
        WithSeeders(Seeders).
        WithMigrations(Migrations).
        // ... 50 lines not shown

The job takes the export's id, writes the CSV to the disk from File Storage and marks the export done:

app/jobs/export_tasks.go

// ... 16 lines not shown

type ExportTasks struct {
}

func NewExportTasks(exportID uint) (*ExportTasks, []queue.Arg) {
    return &ExportTasks{}, []queue.Arg{
        {Type: "uint", Value: exportID},
    }
}

// Signature The name and signature of the job.
func (receiver *ExportTasks) Signature() string {
    return "export_tasks"
}

// Handle Execute the job.
func (receiver *ExportTasks) Handle(args ...any) error {
    exportID, ok := args[0].(uint)
    if !ok {
        return errors.New("export tasks: the argument must be the export id")
    }

    var export models.Export
    err := facades.Orm().Query().FindOrFail(&export, exportID)
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return nil
    }
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var tasks []models.Task
    if err := facades.Orm().Query().With("Assignee").OrderBy("id").Find(&tasks); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    rows := [][]string{{"id", "title", "status", "assignee", "due_at"}}
    for _, task := range tasks {
        assignee, dueAt := "", ""
        if task.Assignee != nil {
            assignee = task.Assignee.Name
        }
        if task.DueAt != nil {
            dueAt = task.DueAt.ToDateTimeString()
        }
        rows = append(rows, []string{strconv.Itoa(int(task.ID)), task.Title, string(task.Status), assignee, dueAt})
    }

    var file bytes.Buffer
    if err := csv.NewWriter(&file).WriteAll(rows); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    path := fmt.Sprintf("exports/%d.csv", export.ID)
    if err := facades.Storage().Put(path, file.String()); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    export.Status = enums.ExportDone
    export.Path = path

    return facades.Orm().Query().Save(&export)
}
  • NewExportTasks builds the job and its args together, as NewTaskAssigned does for the event in Events & Listeners. Every call then passes the export's id, and always as a uint.
  • Signature is the job's name, export_tasks. The worker finds the job by it and prints it.
  • Handle reads the export's id from its args and checks its type. Args have to be plain values, as with the queued listener, so the job gets the id and loads the export itself. If the export is gone, an error would only put a job that can never succeed in failed_jobs, so it returns nil.
  • It writes one CSV row per task to exports/<id>.csv and marks the export done.
  • Returning an error tells the worker the job failed.

Starting an export

POST /exports saves a pending export and sends the job. It then answers 202 Accepted, which means the request was accepted but the work isn't finished. The client reads the status from GET /exports/{id}, and once it's done, GET /exports/{id}/download sends the file:

app/http/controllers/export_controller.go

// ... 28 lines not shown
    export := models.Export{
        UserID: authuser.From(ctx).ID,
        Status: enums.ExportPending,
    }
    if err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().Create(&export); err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not start the export.",
        })
    }

    err := facades.Queue().Job(jobs.NewExportTasks(export.ID)).Dispatch()
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not start the export.",
        })
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(202, export)
}

// ... 20 lines not shown
func (r *ExportController) Download(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var export models.Export
    // ... 14 lines not shown
    if export.Status != enums.ExportDone {
        return ctx.Response().Json(409, map[string]any{
            "error": "The export is not ready yet.",
        })
    }

    content, err := facades.Storage().GetBytes(export.Path)
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the export.",
        })
    }

    disposition := mime.FormatMediaType("attachment", map[string]string{"filename": fmt.Sprintf("tasks-%d.csv", export.ID)})

    return ctx.Response().
        Header("Content-Disposition", disposition).
        Data(200, "text/csv", content)
}
  • NewExportTasks gives Job the job and its one arg, the export's id, and Dispatch puts the job on the queue.
  • Show and Download only look among the user's own exports, so an export id that belongs to someone else gives 404.
  • Download answers 409 Conflict until the export is done.

routes/api.go

    notificationController := controllers.NewNotificationController()
+   exportController := controllers.NewExportController()

+           router.Post("exports", exportController.Store)

See it work

The run starts from the same setup as Gates & Policies:

  1. Reset the database with migrate:fresh --seed, which adds Ana as the manager, plus three members and seven tasks.
  2. Delete storage/app/exports, so files from an earlier run can't stop the failure later on.
  3. Register Ben. He gets id 5.
  4. Log in as Ana and as Ben, and save each token in a variable, ANA and BEN.

The export is pending when the request returns, and done a moment later:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":1,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ sleep 2
$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":1,"user_id":1,"status":"done"}

$ curl -D - http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/1/download -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=tasks-1.csv
Content-Length: 466
Content-Type: text/csv
Date: …

id,title,status,assignee,due_at
1,Review the pull request,done,Francesco Bradley,2026-11-04 09:00:00
2,Review the pull request,pending,Francesco Bradley,2026-11-25 09:00:00
…

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"error":"The export does not exist."}

The seeder makes up names and dates, so the CSV rows differ after each reset.

The worker runs inside the app, so its lines show up next to the server's own output. It prints one line when a job starts and one when it ends, each with the job's signature:

  2026-10-27 00:09:53.215 export_tasks ............................... RUNNING
  2026-10-27 00:09:53.222 export_tasks .......................... 6.121ms DONE

When the job fails

The job can't create a file in a read-only folder, so chmod 555 on storage/app/exports makes it fail. POST /exports still answers 202, because it only queues the job, but the export stays pending and Download refuses the file:

$ chmod 555 storage/app/exports

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"pending"}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/2/download -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{"error":"The export is not ready yet."}

The worker tries the job once and gives up:

  2026-10-27 00:09:55.231 export_tasks ............................... RUNNING
  2026-10-27 00:09:55.235 export_tasks .......................... 3.839ms FAIL

The worker saves a failed job in the failed_jobs table, with its args and the error. queue:failed lists those jobs but not the error, so psql reads it from the table:

$ go run . artisan queue:failed
  2026-10-27 00:09:57 00950ba2-2c5b-43dd-9cd8-d757ce5d198b ..... redis@default

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel taskflow -At -c "select exception from failed_jobs"
open …/storage/app/exports/2.csv: permission denied

Nothing marks the export as failed, so it stays pending. Once the folder is writable again, queue:retry takes the job's uuid, the one queue:failed listed, and puts that job back on the queue. The worker then runs it and finishes the export:

$ chmod 755 storage/app/exports

$ go run . artisan queue:retry 00950ba2-2c5b-43dd-9cd8-d757ce5d198b
  INFO    Pushing failed queue jobs back onto the queue

  00950ba2-2c5b-43dd-9cd8-d757ce5d198b ........................... 2.91ms DONE

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{…,"id":2,"user_id":1,"status":"done"}

queue:retry also takes several uuids at once, and with none it retries every failed job.

Trying again by itself

Some failures go away after a few seconds, like a database that's restarting, so ShouldRetry lets the job try again:

app/jobs/export_tasks.go

 package jobs

 import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/csv"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "strconv"
+   "time"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/queue"
    // ... 67 lines not shown
    return facades.Orm().Query().Save(&export)
 }
+
+// ShouldRetry gives a failed export two more tries, five seconds apart.
+func (receiver *ExportTasks) ShouldRetry(err error, attempt int) (bool, time.Duration) {
+   return attempt < 3, 5 * time.Second
+}

After each failed try, the worker calls ShouldRetry with the error and the try's number, starting at 1. ShouldRetry returns whether to try again and how long to wait. Here attempt < 3, 5 * time.Second means another try after tries 1 and 2, each five seconds later. After the third failed try, the worker saves the job in failed_jobs.

The worker runs one job at a time, and it sleeps through each five-second wait itself. So a job queued behind a failing export has to wait for all three tries. The block below makes the folder read-only again, starts an export, then assigns a task, which queues a notification:

$ chmod 555 storage/app/exports

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/exports -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
202

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Fix the login page","description":"The error message overlaps the button.","assigned_to":5}'
201

$ sleep 2
$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"data":[],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":0}}

$ sleep 10
$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"data":[{…,"id":1,"user_id":5,"task_id":8,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Fix the login page\"","read_at":null}],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":1}}

The notification only ran after the export gave up, as the worker's log shows:

  2026-10-27 00:10:06.816 export_tasks ............................... RUNNING
  2026-10-27 00:10:16.839 export_tasks .......................... 6.905ms FAIL
  2026-10-27 00:10:16.842 notify_assignee ............................ RUNNING
  2026-10-27 00:10:16.847 notify_assignee ........................ 4.77ms DONE

The figure steps through both cases, an export that works and this one:

Interactive figure on DevChalk: An export that works, then one that fails three times while a notification waits behind it.

An export that works: the client sends POST /exports, the API saves a pending export in Postgres, puts an export_tasks job on Redis and answers 202. The worker takes the job, loads the tasks, writes the CSV to the disk and marks the export done. An export that fails: the API answers 202 as before, but the worker can't write the file, waits five seconds and tries again, three times, then saves the job in failed_jobs. The notification job waits on Redis the whole time and runs only after the export gives up.

Two jobs at once

concurrent is a key on a connection in config/queue.go. It sets how many jobs the worker runs at the same time, and it defaults to 1. The redis connection doesn't set it, so it runs one job at a time until it's set to 2:

config/queue.go

 // ... 21 lines not shown
            "database": map[string]any{
                "driver":     "database",
                "connection": config.Env("DB_CONNECTION"),
                "queue":      "default",
                "concurrent": 1,
            },
            "redis": map[string]any{
                "driver":     "custom",
                "connection": "default",
                "queue":      "default",
+               "concurrent": 2,
                "via": func() (queue.Driver, error) {
                    return redisfacades.Queue("redis") // The `redis` value is the key of `connections`
                },
            // ... 13 lines not shown

With the same two requests, the notification is there after 2 seconds. In the log, it starts at once, while the export is still retrying:

  2026-10-27 00:10:25.057 export_tasks ............................... RUNNING
  2026-10-27 00:10:25.057 notify_assignee ............................ RUNNING
  2026-10-27 00:10:25.074 notify_assignee ...................... 17.074ms DONE
  2026-10-27 00:10:35.08 export_tasks ........................... 6.471ms FAIL

Make the folder writable again with chmod 755 storage/app/exports.

A queue of its own for exports:

Exports could also go on a queue of their own with OnQueue:

facades.Queue().Job(jobs.NewExportTasks(export.ID)).OnQueue("exports").Dispatch()

The worker that app.Start() runs reads one queue, the one named by the default connection's queue key. That's default in TaskFlow, as the start-up line says: Processing jobs from [redis] connection and [default] queue. A job on exports needs a second worker for that queue, which a runner added in WithRunners can start. With its own worker, a slow export never holds up the jobs on default.

Sending a job later with Delay:

Delay sends a job later:

facades.Queue().Job(jobs.NewExportTasks(export.ID)).Delay(time.Now().Add(time.Hour)).Dispatch()

On redis, the job waits until then. On sync, which the tests use, Dispatch itself sleeps until then, so a test with that delay would take an hour. An export should start as soon as it's asked for, so TaskFlow doesn't use Delay.

Tests

The tests are in tests/feature/export_test.go. They use the sync connection from Events & Listeners, so the job runs inside POST /exports. They check that:

  • the export is done
  • the download is the CSV
  • other users get 404
  • a pending export can't be downloaded 
$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  1.542s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.398s

Exports now run in the background and retry when they fail. An export that fails every try still shows as pending.

Previous: 15. Events & Listeners
Next: 17. Mail & Templates
Series: Goravel

title: Can your Node.js repository survive a fresh clone? I'm looking for developers to test my open-source tool
description:
A project works perfectly on your machine. The tests pass, the application starts, and everything seems fine.

Then someone discovers your GitHub repository, clones it, follows the README, and encounters:

  • A missing or outdated lockfile.
  • A test command that doesn't actually exist.
  • An undocumented environment variable.
  • Conflicting Node.js version declarations.
  • Dependencies or setup instructions that don't match the actual project.

For open-source maintainers, these problems can make the first contribution unnecessarily difficult.

I've been working on an open-source tool called Clone-Proof to help identify these issues before someone else encounters them.

The tool is now publicly available, and I'm looking for developers and repository maintainers willing to test it on real projects.

What exactly is Clone-Proof?

Clone-Proof is a repository readiness checker for Node.js and TypeScript projects.

Its central question is:

Can someone take a fresh clone of your repository, install its dependencies, and run its declared tests?

It approaches this through two execution modes.

1. Static repository inspection

The default check mode performs a read-only inspection without executing the target repository's code.

It examines things such as:

  • Package manifests and lockfiles.
  • Package-manager consistency.
  • Test scripts and README commands.
  • Node.js runtime declarations.
  • Environment-variable documentation.
  • Gitignored core files.
  • Browser-test and service dependency indicators.

Instead of simply returning a generic score, Clone-Proof produces findings with file-and-line evidence, explanations and recommendations.

2. Controlled Docker verification

For developers who want more than static inspection, Clone-Proof also offers opt-in Docker verification.

It attempts to install dependencies using npm ci --ignore-scripts and execute the declared test workflow inside a pinned, restricted container.

The execution profile includes:

  • A non-root user.
  • Dropped Linux capabilities.
  • A read-only source mount.
  • Resource and execution-time limits.
  • Network isolation by default.
  • Container and temporary-file cleanup.

Docker verification currently focuses on the root npm workflow. It is not a universal build system or a complete security sandbox.

3. Native GitHub Actions integration

Clone-Proof also provides a native GitHub Action.

You can integrate it into your existing CI workflow to receive:

  • Workflow annotations.
  • GitHub Actions Job Summaries.
  • Static check results.
  • Optional Docker verification.
  • Reproducibility receipts.

The idea is to make repository readiness checks part of the normal development workflow rather than another command someone has to remember to run.

How can you test it?

You don't need to install Clone-Proof globally.

Requirements: Node.js 22.19.0 or newer. Docker is required only for Docker verification.

Option 1: Test your own repository

Navigate to your Node.js or TypeScript project and run:

npx cloneproof-check check .

You can also inspect a public GitHub repository directly:

npx cloneproof-check check https://github.com/OWNER/REPO

Option 2: Try Docker verification

For repositories you own or trust, you can opt into controlled execution:

npx cloneproof-check verify . --docker --execute

Network access is disabled by default. Some repositories require external dependencies during installation; network access can be explicitly enabled when appropriate:

npx cloneproof-check verify . --docker --execute --allow-network

Docker verification executes repository test code inside the container. Docker is not a complete security boundary, so only use it on repositories you trust.

Option 3: Add it to GitHub Actions

You can also integrate Clone-Proof directly into a workflow:

name: CloneProof Check

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  cloneproof:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Check repository readiness
        uses: psuvraneel-cyber/Clone-Proof@v0.2.4
        with:
          mode: check

The static check can run on pull requests. Docker verification has stricter event and runner restrictions because it executes repository code.

I've tried to validate the tool against real repositories

I didn't want Clone-Proof to be a collection of checks that only works against artificial examples.

I've conducted field testing against public Node.js and npm repositories, including a 100-repository evaluation.

One of the most useful lessons was that the tool itself could produce false positives.

Rather than hiding those results, I investigated the findings, corrected the detection logic, added regression tests and reran the evaluation.

The current implementation also documents its limitations and distinguishes between problems it can identify, situations it cannot verify and repositories it must safely refuse to inspect.

The field-test methodology and results are available in the repository.

I consider this an ongoing engineering process, not proof that Clone-Proof is universally accurate.

What I need from you

This is where I'd particularly appreciate help from people who maintain actual software projects.

I'm looking for developers willing to run Clone-Proof against their own repositories and challenge its results.

I'd appreciate feedback in five areas:

1. Accuracy

Did Clone-Proof identify genuine setup problems? Did it report anything incorrectly? Did it miss an obvious issue?

2. Usefulness

Would these findings actually help a new contributor get your project running?

3. Developer experience

Were the commands, output and recommendations understandable?

4. GitHub Actions integration

Would you consider using Clone-Proof in your repository's CI workflow? What would need to change before you trusted it?

5. Limitations

What did you expect it to detect that it currently cannot?

I'm particularly interested in unusual repository structures, edge cases, false positives and real-world projects that expose weaknesses in the scanner.

Negative feedback is genuinely welcome. Finding something Clone-Proof gets wrong is useful feedback, not a failed test.

Project links

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/psuvraneel-cyber/Clone-Proof
  • GitHub Marketplace: https://github.com/marketplace/actions/cloneproof-check
  • npm package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cloneproof-check
  • Previous field-test article: https://dev.to/psuvraneelcyber/we-fresh-cloned-the-top-100-npm-packages-the-biggest-problem-we-found-was-in-our-own-tool-55i8

A request to the community

Clone-Proof is an independent open-source project that I've been developing and improving through testing against real repositories.

At this stage, I'd rather have ten developers critically evaluate it than a hundred people simply star the repository.

Could you try it on your project and tell me what it gets right, what it gets wrong, and what would make you actually use it?

You can leave feedback in the comments, open an issue on GitHub, or share the findings directly.

Thank you for giving it a try.

title: Goravel events and listeners for notifications
description:
Part 15 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-15.

Right now, when Ana gives Ben a task, nothing tells him about it. This part sends him a notification, but the task handler doesn't write it itself: it announces the assignment as an event, TaskAssigned, and a separate listener writes the notification. The listener starts out inside the request and later moves to the background, so Ana's request no longer waits for it.

Start from the File Storage code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-14
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

Why an event

The simplest way would be to write the notification in the handler, right after the task is saved, and for one notification that's fine. But an assignment usually leads to more than that, like an email or a message in a chat app. If each of those goes into the task handler, it keeps growing, and every request has to wait for all of them to finish.

An event splits that work up. The handler only announces what happened, that Ana assigned task 8 to Ben, and the listeners decide what to do about it. Sending an email as well would then mean adding one more listener, without touching the handler at all.

Installing events

A new Goravel app doesn't have events yet. Install them like any other facade:

$ go run . artisan package:install Event
  INFO    Event depends on Log, Cache, Orm, Schema, DB, Queue, they will be installed simultaneously
 SUCCESS  Facade Event installed successfully

The queue is on that list because a listener can run on it. TaskFlow has had the queue since Installation & Project Architecture, so only the event pieces were added: app/facades/event.go, and the event service provider in bootstrap/providers.go.

The notifications table

This is the table Installation & Project Architecture planned. A notification is one row with who it is for, which task it is about and the text to show, plus read_at, which stays empty until the user has read it:

app/models/notification.go

package models

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/support/carbon"
)

type Notification struct {
    orm.Model
    UserID  uint             `gorm:"not null" json:"user_id"`
    TaskID  uint             `gorm:"not null" json:"task_id"`
    Message string           `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"message"`
    ReadAt  *carbon.DateTime `json:"read_at"`
}

Register the model next to the others, as in File Storage:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 34 lines not shown
        WithCallback(func() {
            facades.Schema().Extend(schema.Extension{
-               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}, models.Attachment{}},
+               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}, models.Attachment{}, models.Notification{}},
            })

            // ... 34 lines not shown

Then generate the migration from the model:

$ go run . artisan make:migration create_notifications_table -m Notification

The columns come from the model, but the two foreign keys don't, so add them. The one on task_id uses CascadeOnDelete, so when a task is deleted, Postgres deletes its notifications along with it. Without that, Postgres would refuse to delete any task that has a notification:

database/migrations/20261026214627_create_notifications_table.go

// ... 16 lines not shown
func (r *M20261026214627CreateNotificationsTable) Up() error {
    if !facades.Schema().HasTable("notifications") {
        return facades.Schema().Create("notifications", func(table schema.Blueprint) {
            table.TimestampTz("created_at").Nullable()
            table.TimestampTz("updated_at").Nullable()
            table.BigIncrements("id")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("user_id")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("task_id")
            table.String("message", 255)
            table.TimestampTz("read_at").Nullable()

            table.Foreign("user_id").References("id").On("users")
            table.Foreign("task_id").References("id").On("tasks").CascadeOnDelete()
        })
    // ... 9 lines not shown

$ go run . artisan migrate

The event

Generate the event:

$ go run . artisan make:event TaskAssigned

A Goravel event has two parts: a struct whose name says what happened, and a list of args with the details. TaskAssigned keeps its struct empty, for a reason the Gotcha below explains, so the details all go in the args: the task, who got it and who gave it:

app/events/task_assigned.go

package events

import (
    "errors"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/event"
)

type TaskAssigned struct {
}

func NewTaskAssigned(taskID, assignedTo, assignedBy uint) (*TaskAssigned, []event.Arg) {
    return &TaskAssigned{}, []event.Arg{
        {Type: "uint", Value: taskID},
        {Type: "uint", Value: assignedTo},
        {Type: "uint", Value: assignedBy},
    }
}

func (receiver *TaskAssigned) Handle(args []event.Arg) ([]event.Arg, error) {
    if len(args) != 3 {
        return nil, errors.New("task assigned: needs the task id, the assignee id and the id of who assigned it")
    }
    for _, arg := range args {
        if _, ok := arg.Value.(uint); !ok {
            return nil, errors.New("task assigned: every id must be a uint")
        }
    }

    return args, nil
}
  • NewTaskAssigned builds both parts at once, so every call passes all three ids, in the same order and as uints. When Ana gives task 8 to Ben, the call is NewTaskAssigned(8, 5, 1): task 8, Ben (user 5) and Ana (user 1).
  • Type: "uint" isn't used yet. It matters once the listener runs on the queue, where the job is stored as JSON and the worker reads Type to turn 8 back into a uint.
  • Handle runs before any listener, so bad args fail right away at Dispatch, in the handler, and not later inside a listener. NewTaskAssigned always gets the args right, so the check is there for a call that builds them by hand.

The listener

Generate the listener:

$ go run . artisan make:listener NotifyAssignee

A listener is the code that reacts to an event. Here is NotifyAssignee:

app/listeners/notify_assignee.go

package listeners

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/event"
    frameworkerrors "github.com/goravel/framework/errors"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/models"
)

type NotifyAssignee struct {
}

func (receiver *NotifyAssignee) Signature() string {
    return "notify_assignee"
}

func (receiver *NotifyAssignee) Queue(args ...any) event.Queue {
    return event.Queue{
        Enable:     false,
        Connection: "",
        Queue:      "",
    }
}

func (receiver *NotifyAssignee) Handle(args ...any) error {
    taskID, ok1 := args[0].(uint)
    assignedTo, ok2 := args[1].(uint)
    assignedBy, ok3 := args[2].(uint)
    if !ok1 || !ok2 || !ok3 {
        return errors.New("notify assignee: the ids must be uints")
    }
    if assignedTo == assignedBy {
        return nil
    }

    var task models.Task
    err := facades.Orm().Query().FindOrFail(&task, taskID)
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return nil
    }
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var manager models.User
    if err := facades.Orm().Query().FindOrFail(&manager, assignedBy); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return facades.Orm().Query().Create(&models.Notification{
        UserID:  assignedTo,
        TaskID:  task.ID,
        Message: fmt.Sprintf("%s assigned you %q", manager.Name, task.Title),
    })
}
  • Signature names the listener notify_assignee. Once the listener runs on the queue, the worker finds it by this name.
  • Queue returns Enable: false for now, so the listener runs right away, inside the request.
  • Handle writes the notification from the args, which arrive in the order the event put them in. It skips a manager who takes a task themselves, and it checks the type of every arg and returns an error instead of crashing; the Gotcha in the queue section shows why.

Firing the event

The event and the listener exist now, but nothing connects them yet. WithEvents in bootstrap/app.go does that, by listing each event with the listeners that react to it. One event can have several listeners, and in the request they run in the order listed here:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 7 lines not shown
    contractsaccess "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/auth/access"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/schema"
+   contractsevent "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/event"
    contractsfoundation "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/foundation"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/foundation"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/http/limit"

    "taskflow/app/enums"
+   "taskflow/app/events"
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/http/authuser"
+   "taskflow/app/listeners"
    "taskflow/app/models"
    "taskflow/app/policies"
    // ... 11 lines not shown
            routes.Web()
        }).
+       WithEvents(func() map[contractsevent.Event][]contractsevent.Listener {
+           return map[contractsevent.Event][]contractsevent.Listener{
+               &events.TaskAssigned{}: {&listeners.NotifyAssignee{}},
+           }
+       }).
        WithProviders(Providers).
        WithConfig(config.Boot).
        // ... 39 lines not shown

Gotcha Goravel finds an event's listeners by its pointer, so the &TaskAssigned{} the handler fires has to match the one in WithEvents. They're two separate values, and they only match because Go usually puts every empty struct at the same address. Add a field, like TaskID uint, and each one gets its own address, so Goravel finds no listeners:

event &{0} doesn't bind listeners

That's why the struct stays empty and the ids go in the args.

Now the task handlers fire the event. A task gets an assignee in two places: when Ana creates it, in Store, and when she changes it, in Update. Both fire TaskAssigned only when someone new is assigned, so renaming a task sends nothing:

app/http/controllers/task_controller.go

 package controllers

 import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "taskflow/app/enums"
+   "taskflow/app/events"
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/http/authuser"
    // ... 60 lines not shown
            "error": "Could not load the task.",
        })
    }

+   if saved.AssignedTo != nil {
+       err := facades.Event().Job(events.NewTaskAssigned(saved.ID, *saved.AssignedTo, authuser.From(ctx).ID)).Dispatch()
+       if err != nil {
+           facades.Log().Error(err)
+       }
+   }
+
    return ctx.Response().Json(201, saved)
 }
 // ... 108 lines not shown

    changes := validator.Validated()
+   var assignedBefore uint
+   if task.AssignedTo != nil {
+       assignedBefore = *task.AssignedTo
+   }
    response := facades.Gate().WithContext(ctx).Inspect(policies.UpdateTask, map[string]any{
        "task":    &task,
        // ... 22 lines not shown
            "error": "Could not load the task.",
        })
    }

+   if saved.AssignedTo != nil && *saved.AssignedTo != assignedBefore {
+       err := facades.Event().Job(events.NewTaskAssigned(saved.ID, *saved.AssignedTo, authuser.From(ctx).ID)).Dispatch()
+       if err != nil {
+           facades.Log().Error(err)
+       }
+   }
+
    return ctx.Response().Json(200, saved)
 }
 // ... 35 lines not shown
  • Job(...) gets the event ready and Dispatch() sends it: first the event's Handle runs, then each listener. NewTaskAssigned returns the event and its args, which is exactly what Job takes.
  • Update(changes) writes the new values into task itself, so the old assignee is copied into assignedBefore before the save. Without that copy, the handler couldn't tell that the assignee changed.
  • If Dispatch returns an error, the task is already saved, so the handler only logs the error and still answers 201 or 200.

Reading notifications

Each user reads their own notifications at GET /notifications, newest first. They pile up, one for every assignment, so the list comes in pages, like the task list in Task CRUD. POST /notifications/{id}/read marks one as read:

app/http/controllers/notification_controller.go

// ... 24 lines not shown
func (r *NotificationController) Index(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    validator, err := ctx.Request().Validate(map[string]any{
        "page":     "bail|filled|integer|min:1",
        "per_page": "bail|filled|integer|min:1|max:100",
    // ... 16 lines not shown
    var notifications []models.Notification
    var total int64
    err = facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().
        Where("user_id", authuser.From(ctx).ID).
        OrderByDesc("id").
        Paginate(page, perPage, &notifications, &total)
    // ... 16 lines not shown

func (r *NotificationController) Read(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var notification models.Notification
    err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().
        Where("user_id", authuser.From(ctx).ID).
        FindOrFail(&notification, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
            "error": "The notification does not exist.",
        })
    }
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the notification.",
        })
    }

    if notification.ReadAt == nil {
        notification.ReadAt = carbon.NewDateTime(carbon.Now().StartOfSecond())
        if err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().Save(&notification); err != nil {
            facades.Log().Error(err)
            return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
                "error": "Could not save the notification.",
            })
        }
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(200, notification)
}
  • Both handlers look only among the user's own notifications, so when Read gets another user's id, it answers the same 404 as for an id that doesn't exist.
  • Read sets read_at only once, so it keeps when the user first read it. StartOfSecond drops the fraction of a second: the column keeps whole seconds and Postgres rounds, so without it the answer could show a different second from the one saved.

routes/api.go

 // ... 14 lines not shown
    userController := controllers.NewUserController()
    attachmentController := controllers.NewAttachmentController()
+   notificationController := controllers.NewNotificationController()

    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("register", authController.Register)
        // ... 15 lines not shown
            router.Delete("tasks/{id}/attachments/{attachment}", attachmentController.Destroy)

+           router.Get("notifications", notificationController.Index)
+           router.Post("notifications/{id}/read", notificationController.Read)
+
            router.Get("users", userController.Index)
            router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
        })
    })
 }

See it work

Set up as in Gates & Policies, with one more member:

  1. Reset the database with migrate:fresh --seed. The seeder adds Ana, the manager, and three members.
  2. Register Ben and Cat. They get ids 5 and 6.
  3. Log in as Ana, Ben and Cat, and save each token in a variable: ANA, BEN and CAT.

Ana creates a task for Ben, and his notification is there as soon as the request returns. Cat can't mark it as read, but Ben can:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Fix the login page","description":"The error message overlaps the button.","assigned_to":5}'
{…,"id":8,…,"assigned_to":5,…,"title":"Fix the login page",…}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"data":[{…,"id":1,"user_id":5,"task_id":8,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Fix the login page\"","read_at":null}],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":1}}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications/1/read -H "Authorization: Bearer $CAT"
{"error":"The notification does not exist."}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications/1/read -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{…,"id":1,"user_id":5,"task_id":8,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Fix the login page\"","read_at":"2026-10-26 21:50:12"}

Then Ana renames the task, gives it to Cat, and finally takes it herself. Of those three changes, only giving it to Cat sends a notification:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"title":"Fix the login form"}'
200

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"assigned_to":6}'
200

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"assigned_to":1}'
200

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $CAT"
{"data":[{…,"id":2,"user_id":6,"task_id":8,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Fix the login form\"","read_at":null}],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":1}}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{"data":[],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":0}}

Ben still has only his first notification, now read.

When a listener fails:

Listeners in the request run one after another, and as soon as one returns an error, the ones after it are skipped. A listener that always fails makes this easy to watch. Make one with make:listener AlwaysFails, and have its Handle return an error:

func (receiver *AlwaysFails) Handle(args ...any) error {
    return errors.New("this listener always fails")
}

Then put it in front of NotifyAssignee in WithEvents:

&events.TaskAssigned{}: {&listeners.AlwaysFails{}, &listeners.NotifyAssignee{}},

Ana gives Ben one more task. It is saved and she gets her 201, because the handler only logs the error, but NotifyAssignee never runs, so Ben's list still has only his first notification:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Update the README","description":"Add the new endpoints.","assigned_to":5}'
{…,"id":9,…,"assigned_to":5,…,"title":"Update the README",…}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"data":[{…,"id":1,"user_id":5,"task_id":8,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Fix the login page\"","read_at":"2026-10-26 21:50:12"}],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":1}}

$ grep local.error storage/logs/goravel-*.log
[2026-10-26 21:50:19.486] local.error: this listener always fails

Goravel's docs call this "stopping the propagation". On the queue, each listener is a job of its own, so if AlwaysFails were queued too, it would fail in the worker and NotifyAssignee would still run. Take AlwaysFails out of WithEvents again before going on.

Running the listener in the background

As long as the listener runs inside the request, Ana's request waits for it. Writing one row is quick enough that she won't notice, but an email can take seconds, and if the mail server is down, she'd be waiting on that too. A queue fixes this: the handler leaves a job on a list and answers right away, and a worker picks the job up a moment later and runs the listener.

TaskFlow already has both halves. The config/queue.go that came with the project sets default to redis. Of its three connections, sync runs a job straight away, inside the call, and database and redis keep jobs in Postgres or Redis:

config/queue.go

// ... 8 lines not shown
func init() {
    config := facades.Config()
    config.Add("queue", map[string]any{
        "default": "redis",

        // Queue Connections
        //
        // Here you may configure the connection information for each server that is used by your application.
        // Drivers: "sync", "database", "custom"
        "connections": map[string]any{
            "sync": map[string]any{
                "driver": "sync",
            },
            "database": map[string]any{
                "driver":     "database",
                "connection": config.Env("DB_CONNECTION"),
                "queue":      "default",
                "concurrent": 1,
            },
            "redis": map[string]any{
                "driver":     "custom",
                "connection": "default",
                "queue":      "default",
                "via": func() (queue.Driver, error) {
                    return redisfacades.Queue("redis") // The `redis` value is the key of `connections`
                },
            },
        },
// ... 11 lines not shown

Whenever the default isn't sync, app.Start() also runs a worker next to the HTTP server, which is the line air prints when it starts:

  INFO    Processing jobs from [redis] connection and [default] queue

A listener's Queue method decides whether it uses that queue:

  • Enable puts the listener on the queue when it is true.
  • Connection picks one of the connections above. Empty means the default one.
  • Queue picks a queue on that connection, for example to keep slow jobs apart from quick ones. Empty means the default connection's queue, which is default.

So to put NotifyAssignee on the queue, only Enable changes:

app/listeners/notify_assignee.go

 // ... 20 lines not shown
 func (receiver *NotifyAssignee) Queue(args ...any) event.Queue {
    return event.Queue{
-       Enable:     false,
+       Enable:     true,
        Connection: "",
        Queue:      "",
    }
 // ... 33 lines not shown

Ana gives Ben a third task, and Ben checks his list straight away and again a second later. Paste the four commands together, because the worker looks for new jobs about once a second, and typed by hand, even the first check would come too late:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Write the API docs","description":"Start with the auth routes.","assigned_to":5}'
{…,"assigned_to":5,…,"title":"Write the API docs",…}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"data":[{…,"id":1,…,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Fix the login page\"",…}],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":1}}

$ sleep 1
$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/notifications -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"data":[{…,"id":3,…,"message":"Ana assigned you \"Write the API docs\"","read_at":null},{…,"id":1,…}],"meta":{"page":1,"per_page":15,"total":2}}

Ana's request came back before the listener ran, and the worker prints the job it ran a moment later, under the listener's signature:

  2026-10-26 21:50:26.42 notify_assignee ............................. RUNNING
  2026-10-26 21:50:26.428 notify_assignee ....................... 8.159ms DONE

Three things change once a listener is on the queue:

  • Errors no longer reach the handler. Dispatch only fails if the job can't be put on the queue, so if the listener fails later, only the worker knows.
  • The args must be plain values. The job is saved in Redis as JSON, and the worker rebuilds each value from its Type. That works for plain values like numbers and strings, which is why the event passes ids and not a Task or a User.
  • The world may change before the job runs. By then the task may have been renamed, given to someone else or deleted. That's why the listener takes the assignee from the args, which say who was assigned at that moment, and why it stops quietly, without an error, when the task is gone.

Gotcha A panic in a queued listener stops the whole app. The worker runs inside the same process as the HTTP server and doesn't recover from a panic, so an unchecked args[0].(int) on a uint brings both down:

panic: interface conversion: interface {} is uint, not int

The process exits, so the API is down until it's started again. That's why the listener checks every type and returns an error instead.

Why not a model observer:

Goravel can also run code whenever a model is saved, with an observer. A TaskObserver's Created and Updated methods could write the notification when assigned_to is set or changes. But an observer fires on every save, wherever it comes from, so the seeders would send notifications too, and it runs inside the save, not on the queue. Only the task handler knows "Ana just gave this task to Ben", so TaskFlow fires the event there.

Here is the whole trip, first with the listener in the request, then on the queue:

Interactive figure on DevChalk: Two assignments.

In the request: the client sends the new task, the API saves it in Postgres, fires TaskAssigned, NotifyAssignee inserts the notification, and only then does the API answer 201. On the queue: the API saves the task, puts a notify_assignee job on Redis and answers 201 at once. The worker takes the job from Redis and NotifyAssignee inserts the notification a moment later.

Note Goravel 1.19 is set to add its own notifications. Until then, an event and a listener do the job.

Tests

The tests for this part are in tests/feature/notification_test.go in TaskFlow. They check who gets a notification after each kind of change, that users only see and mark their own, that deleting a task removes its notifications, and that the event turns down bad args.

The tests don't start the app, so no worker runs, and a queued listener would never run at all. The sync connection runs it straight away instead, so the queue's default now comes from an env variable, and the tests set it to sync:

config/queue.go

 // ... 8 lines not shown
 func init() {
    config := facades.Config()
    config.Add("queue", map[string]any{
-       "default": "redis",
+       "default": config.Env("QUEUE_CONNECTION", "redis"),

        // ... 34 lines not shown

.env.example gets the line with redis, and an .env without it falls back to redis too:

.env.example

 # ... 23 lines not shown

 FILESYSTEM_DISK=local
+QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis

 REDIS_HOST=127.0.0.1
 REDIS_PASSWORD=
 REDIS_PORT=6380

and the tests get sync:

.env.testing

 # ... 29 lines not shown
 HASH_ROUNDS=4
 FILESYSTEM_DISK=testing
+QUEUE_CONNECTION=sync

If the tests ran on redis, their jobs would wait in the shared Redis, and a running server could take them and write into the wrong database, so the test case refuses any queue but sync, the same way it refuses the wrong disk:

tests/test_case.go

 // ... 19 lines not shown
        panic("the tests delete uploaded files, so they only run on the testing disk: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing")
    }
+
+   if facades.Config().GetString("queue.default") != "sync" {
+       panic("the tests check what queued listeners wrote, so they only run on the sync queue: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing")
+   }
 }

 type TestCase struct {
    testing.TestCase
 }

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  1.299s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.401s

Assigning a task now sends a notification, written by a listener that runs on the queue, while the task handler only says what happened.
