title: Goravel file uploads and downloads with Storage
description:
Part 14 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-14.

So far, a task in TaskFlow is only text. A bug report often needs more, like a screenshot of the error or a PDF of the spec. In this part, tasks get attachments: Ben uploads a screenshot to his task, downloads it and deletes it. Each file is saved on a disk, and Postgres keeps a row saying which task it belongs to and who uploaded it.

Start from the Feature Testing code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-13
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

Where the files go

Goravel saves files through facades.Storage(). It saves them to a disk. A disk is a named place for files, set up in config/filesystems.go. A new app comes with this config:

config/filesystems.go

// ... 10 lines not shown
    config.Add("filesystems", map[string]any{
        // Default Filesystem Disk
        // ... 4 lines not shown
        "default": "local",

        // Filesystem Disks
        // ... 6 lines not shown
        "disks": map[string]any{
            "local": map[string]any{
                "driver": "local",
                "root":   path.Storage("app"),
            },
            "public": map[string]any{
                "driver": "local",
                "root":   path.Storage("app/public"),
                "url":    config.Env("APP_URL", "").(string) + "/storage",
            },
        },
    })
}
  • default is the disk facades.Storage() uses when the code doesn't name one. Here it is local. To use another disk, name it: facades.Storage().Disk("public").
  • Each disk has a driver. The driver decides where the files really go. The local driver keeps them in a folder on the server, its root. Both disks here use it: local saves to storage/app, and public to storage/app/public. Other drivers save files somewhere else, like Amazon S3 (see S3 and other cloud disks below).
  • public also has a url, for links to its files. It is meant for files anyone can open, like avatars. But no route serves that folder yet: routes/web.go only serves ./public.

Attachments should only reach the people working on the task. So TaskFlow keeps the local disk. No route serves storage/app, so a file only leaves the server when a handler sends it. And the handler sends it only when the policy allows it.

Make default come from .env, so the tests can use their own disk. Then add that testing disk:

config/filesystems.go

 // ... 14 lines not shown
        // by the framework. The "local" disk, as well as a variety of cloud
        // based disks are available to your application. Just store away!
-       "default": "local",
+       "default": config.Env("FILESYSTEM_DISK", "local"),

        // Filesystem Disks
        // ... 6 lines not shown
        "disks": map[string]any{
            "local": map[string]any{
                "driver": "local",
                "root":   path.Storage("app"),
            },
+           "testing": map[string]any{
+               "driver": "local",
+               "root":   path.Storage("framework/testing/disks/local"),
+           },
            "public": map[string]any{
                "driver": "local",
                "root":   path.Storage("app/public"),
                "url":    config.Env("APP_URL", "").(string) + "/storage",
            },
        },
    })
 }

Add the setting to .env and .env.example:

.env

FILESYSTEM_DISK=local

S3 and other cloud disks:

TaskFlow stays on the local disk in this series. In production, files usually go to cloud storage, so they are not lost when the server is replaced. Goravel has driver packages for Amazon S3, MinIO, Alibaba Cloud OSS and Tencent COS. For S3:

go run . artisan package:install github.com/goravel/s3

This adds an s3 disk that reads AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_SECRET, AWS_REGION, AWS_BUCKET and AWS_URL from .env. It also sets default to "s3", replacing the FILESYSTEM_DISK line.

The handlers in this part only use facades.Storage(), so they work on S3 unchanged. On S3, TemporaryUrl gives the client a link that expires. On the local disk, it just returns Url.

The attachments table

Each file gets a row in Postgres. The row says which task the file belongs to and who uploaded it. It also keeps the file's original name, its place on the disk, its size and its type:

app/models/attachment.go

package models

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
)

type Attachment struct {
    orm.Model
    TaskID     uint   `gorm:"not null" json:"task_id"`
    UploadedBy uint   `gorm:"not null" json:"uploaded_by"`
    Name       string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"name"`
    Path       string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"-"`
    Size       int64  `gorm:"not null" json:"size"`
    MimeType   string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"mime_type"`
}

json:"-" keeps Path out of every response, like the password in Register & Login with JWT. Clients don't need to know where a file sits on the disk.

As in Relationships: Belongs To, make:migration -m only reads registered models, so register Attachment next to the others:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 34 lines not shown
        WithCallback(func() {
            facades.Schema().Extend(schema.Extension{
-               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}},
+               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}, models.Attachment{}},
            })

            // ... 29 lines not shown

Then generate the migration from the model:

$ go run . artisan make:migration create_attachments_table -m Attachment

The columns come from the model, but the foreign keys don't, so add them. CascadeOnDelete on task_id tells Postgres to delete a task's attachment rows when the task is deleted. uploaded_by gets a plain foreign key, like created_by on tasks:

database/migrations/20261026070447_create_attachments_table.go

 // ... 16 lines not shown
 func (r *M20261026070447CreateAttachmentsTable) Up() error {
    if !facades.Schema().HasTable("attachments") {
        return facades.Schema().Create("attachments", func(table schema.Blueprint) {
            table.TimestampTz("created_at").Nullable()
            table.TimestampTz("updated_at").Nullable()
            table.BigIncrements("id")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("task_id")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("uploaded_by")
            table.String("name", 255)
            table.String("path", 255)
            table.BigInteger("size")
            table.String("mime_type", 255)
+
+           table.Foreign("task_id").References("id").On("tasks").CascadeOnDelete()
+           table.Foreign("uploaded_by").References("id").On("users")
        })
    }

    // ... 7 lines not shown

Run it. db:table shows the two foreign keys. cascade on task_id means deleting a task deletes its rows:

$ go run . artisan migrate
$ go run . artisan db:table attachments
  …
  Foreign Key .......................................... On Update / On Delete
  attachments_task_id_foreign task_id references id on tasks  no action / cascade
  attachments_uploaded_by_foreign uploaded_by references id on users  no action / no action

A task has many attachments, so Task gets the other side, as in Relationships: Has Many:

app/models/task.go

 // ... 19 lines not shown
    Status      enums.Status     `gorm:"type:enum('pending','in-progress','done');default:'pending';not null" json:"status"`
    DueAt       *carbon.DateTime `json:"due_at"`
+   Attachments []Attachment     `json:"attachments,omitempty"`
 }

 func (t *Task) Factory() factory.Factory {
    return &factories.TaskFactory{}
 }

omitempty leaves attachments out of the JSON when it is empty. Only the single-task response loads the files, so the task list doesn't send "attachments":null.

Who can attach files

The rules follow the task rules from Gates & Policies. Whoever works on a task can add and download its files. A member can only delete files they uploaded:

manager member
attach a file to a task yes own tasks only
download a file yes own tasks only
delete a file yes files they uploaded

Members still see which files a task has, because they can read every task. Only the task's assignee and managers can open them.

Ana is a manager, and Before already lets managers through. So the policy only decides for members:

app/policies/attachment_policy.go

package policies

import (
    "context"

    "taskflow/app/http/authuser"
    "taskflow/app/models"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/auth/access"
    contractsaccess "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/auth/access"
)

type AttachmentPolicy struct {
}

func NewAttachmentPolicy() *AttachmentPolicy {
    return &AttachmentPolicy{}
}

func (r *AttachmentPolicy) Create(ctx context.Context, arguments map[string]any) contractsaccess.Response {
    user := authuser.From(ctx)
    task := arguments["task"].(*models.Task)

    if user == nil || task.AssignedTo == nil || *task.AssignedTo != user.ID {
        return access.NewDenyResponse("You can only attach files to tasks assigned to you.")
    }

    return access.NewAllowResponse()
}

func (r *AttachmentPolicy) View(ctx context.Context, arguments map[string]any) contractsaccess.Response {
    user := authuser.From(ctx)
    task := arguments["task"].(*models.Task)

    if user == nil || task.AssignedTo == nil || *task.AssignedTo != user.ID {
        return access.NewDenyResponse("You can only open files on tasks assigned to you.")
    }

    return access.NewAllowResponse()
}

func (r *AttachmentPolicy) Delete(ctx context.Context, arguments map[string]any) contractsaccess.Response {
    user := authuser.From(ctx)
    attachment := arguments["attachment"].(*models.Attachment)

    if user == nil || attachment.UploadedBy != user.ID {
        return access.NewDenyResponse("You can only delete files you uploaded.")
    }

    return access.NewAllowResponse()
}

Name the three abilities:

app/policies/abilities.go

 package policies

 const (
    ViewUsers  = "view-users"
    CreateTask = "create-task"
    UpdateTask = "update-task"
    DeleteTask = "delete-task"
+
+   CreateAttachment = "create-attachment"
+   ViewAttachment   = "view-attachment"
+   DeleteAttachment = "delete-attachment"
 )

And register them in bootstrap/app.go:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 63 lines not shown
            facades.Gate().Define(policies.UpdateTask, taskPolicy.Update)
            facades.Gate().Define(policies.DeleteTask, taskPolicy.Delete)
+
+           attachmentPolicy := policies.NewAttachmentPolicy()
+           facades.Gate().Define(policies.CreateAttachment, attachmentPolicy.Create)
+           facades.Gate().Define(policies.ViewAttachment, attachmentPolicy.View)
+           facades.Gate().Define(policies.DeleteAttachment, attachmentPolicy.Delete)
        }).
        Create()
 }

Uploading a file

A file comes in a multipart/form-data request. It is what a browser form with a file input sends. Make a form request and a controller for it:

$ go run . artisan make:request StoreAttachmentRequest
$ go run . artisan make:controller AttachmentController

Then three routes under each task:

routes/api.go

 // ... 13 lines not shown
    taskController := controllers.NewTaskController()
    userController := controllers.NewUserController()
+   attachmentController := controllers.NewAttachmentController()

    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("register", authController.Register)
        // ... 11 lines not shown
            router.Delete("tasks/{id}", taskController.Destroy)

+           router.Post("tasks/{id}/attachments", attachmentController.Store)
+           router.Get("tasks/{id}/attachments/{attachment}", attachmentController.Show)
+           router.Delete("tasks/{id}/attachments/{attachment}", attachmentController.Destroy)
+
            router.Get("users", userController.Index)
            router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
        })
    })
 }

The rules for a file

The form request checks the file before the handler saves it:

app/http/requests/store_attachment_request.go

package requests

import (
    "mime/multipart"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
)

type StoreAttachmentRequest struct {
    File *multipart.FileHeader `form:"file" json:"file"`
}

func (r *StoreAttachmentRequest) Authorize(ctx http.Context) error {
    return nil
}

func (r *StoreAttachmentRequest) Rules(ctx http.Context) map[string]any {
    return map[string]any{
        "file": "required|file|max:5120|mimes:png,jpg,pdf,txt",
    }
}
  • File holds the upload. Its type is Go's *multipart.FileHeader. It has the file's name and size, and can open the file.
  • file passes only when a file came in the file field.
  • max:5120 is in kilobytes when the value is a file, so the limit is 5 MB. For a string, the same rule counts characters.
  • mimes:png,jpg,pdf,txt looks at the first bytes of the file to find its real type. A shell script renamed to photo.png still fails, because its first line shows it is a script. A plain text file passes with any name, because txt is on the list. Store then saves it as .txt. The extensions rule only checks the end of the name, so it would let the script through.

The handler

The handler loads the task, asks the policy, runs the rules, and only then saves the file:

app/http/controllers/attachment_controller.go

package controllers

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "mime"
    "os"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/http/authuser"
    "taskflow/app/http/requests"
    "taskflow/app/models"
    "taskflow/app/policies"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
    frameworkerrors "github.com/goravel/framework/errors"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/filesystem"
)

type AttachmentController struct {
    // Dependent services
}

func NewAttachmentController() *AttachmentController {
    return &AttachmentController{
        // Inject services
    }
}

func (r *AttachmentController) Store(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var task models.Task
    err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().FindOrFail(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
            "error": "The task does not exist.",
        })
    }
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the task.",
        })
    }

    response := facades.Gate().WithContext(ctx).Inspect(policies.CreateAttachment, map[string]any{
        "task": &task,
    })
    if !response.Allowed() {
        return ctx.Response().Json(403, map[string]any{
            "error": response.Message(),
        })
    }

    var request requests.StoreAttachmentRequest
    validationErrors, err := ctx.Request().ValidateRequest(&request)
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not save the file.",
        })
    }
    if validationErrors != nil {
        return ctx.Response().Json(422, map[string]any{
            "errors": validationErrors.All(),
        })
    }

    file, err := filesystem.NewFileFromRequest(request.File)
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not save the file.",
        })
    }
    defer os.Remove(file.File())

    size, err := file.Size()
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not save the file.",
        })
    }
    mimeType, err := file.MimeType()
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not save the file.",
        })
    }

    path, err := file.Store(fmt.Sprintf("attachments/%d", task.ID))
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not save the file.",
        })
    }

    attachment := models.Attachment{
        TaskID:     task.ID,
        UploadedBy: authuser.From(ctx).ID,
        Name:       file.GetClientOriginalName(),
        Path:       path,
        Size:       size,
        MimeType:   mimeType,
    }
    if err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().Create(&attachment); err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        if err := facades.Storage().Delete(path); err != nil {
            facades.Log().Error(err)
        }
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not save the file.",
        })
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(201, attachment)
}

// ... 94 lines not shown
  • request.File is the upload the rules just checked. filesystem.NewFileFromRequest turns it into a Goravel file, which has Size, MimeType and Store.
  • Store saves the file under attachments/<task id>, with a random 40-character name. The extension comes from the file's content. If the type is unknown, it comes from the client's name. The client's name is never used in the path. So two files called login-error.png don't overwrite each other, and a name like ../../.env can't put a file outside the folder.
  • The row saves the client's file name from GetClientOriginalName. The download uses it later.
  • If the row can't be saved, the handler deletes the file, so a failed upload doesn't leave a file behind.

A file belongs to a task. So first, Ana creates a task for Ben. Then Ben uploads files to it. The setup is the same as in Gates & Policies:

  1. Reset the database with migrate:fresh --seed. The seeder adds Ana and three members.
  2. Register Ben. New accounts are members, and Ben gets the next id, 5.
  3. Log in as Ana and as Ben, and save each token in a variable, ANA and BEN.
  4. As Ana, create a task for Ben. 
$ go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Ben","email":"ben@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
{…,"id":5,"name":"Ben",…,"role":"member",…}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"password"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}
$ ANA=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ben@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}
$ BEN=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Fix the login page","description":"The error message overlaps the button.","assigned_to":5}'
{…,"id":8,"created_by":1,…,"assigned_to":5,…,"title":"Fix the login page","description":"The error message overlaps the button.","status":"pending","due_at":null}

Ben uploads a screenshot to his task, task 8. Any PNG works; here it's login-error.png:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN" \
  -F file=@login-error.png
{…,"id":1,"task_id":8,"uploaded_by":5,"name":"login-error.png","size":93,"mime_type":"image/png"}

curl -F sends a multipart/form-data request. @ tells curl to read the file from disk. The file is now in the task's folder, under a random name:

$ find storage/app -type f
storage/app/attachments/8/L1D5yFohfKVrSjYqRYGfCMGvrVz3dBvOMnj9XswQ.png

A shell script renamed to fake.png, any PDF over 5 MB and a file for someone else's task are all refused:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN" -F file=@fake.png
{"errors":{"file":{"mimes":"The file field must be a file of type: png, jpg, pdf, txt."}}}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN" -F file=@big.pdf
{"errors":{"file":{"max":"The file field must not be greater than 5120 kilobytes."}}}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1/attachments -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN" -F file=@login-error.png
{"error":"You can only attach files to tasks assigned to you."}

Gotcha NewFileFromRequest copies the upload into Go's temp folder. That is $TMPDIR if it is set, and /tmp if not. ctx.Request().File does the same copy. Goravel never deletes it, so the handler deletes it with defer os.Remove(file.File()). Without that line, each upload leaves one file in the temp folder. Its name starts with APP_NAME. After three uploads:

$ ls $TMPDIR | grep Goravel_
Goravel_2906077324.png
Goravel_3355795916.png
Goravel_438708143.png

These files stay after the request ends, and even after the server stops. On a busy server, they fill up the disk. This happens with both HTTP drivers, Gin and Fiber.

body_limit doesn't limit the upload:

config/http.go has body_limit: 4096. It looks like a 4 MB limit, but it isn't one. Goravel reads the whole form the first time anything reads the request. In TaskFlow, that is the auth middleware, when it reads the Authorization header. It keeps up to 32 MB in memory and writes the rest to temp files. Go deletes those after the request. Gin only uses body_limit to decide how much of a form stays in memory, and by then Goravel has already read the form. So it never limits anything. So a 50 MB upload is read in full, even with no token:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN" -F file=@huge.pdf \
  -w ' [%{http_code}] sent %{size_upload} bytes\n'
{"errors":{"file":{"max":"The file field must not be greater than 5120 kilobytes."}}} [422] sent 52429012 bytes

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments -F file=@huge.pdf \
  -w ' [%{http_code}] sent %{size_upload} bytes\n'
{"error":"authentication token is invalid"} [401] sent 52429012 bytes

To stop a large upload before the app reads it, limit the request size in front of the app. In nginx, that is client_max_body_size.

Downloading a file

A file on the local disk has no public URL. So the client asks the API for it. The handler checks the policy before it sends the file:

app/http/controllers/attachment_controller.go

// ... 120 lines not shown
func (r *AttachmentController) Show(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var task models.Task
    err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().FindOrFail(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
            "error": "The task does not exist.",
        })
    }
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the task.",
        })
    }

    response := facades.Gate().WithContext(ctx).Inspect(policies.ViewAttachment, map[string]any{
        "task": &task,
    })
    if !response.Allowed() {
        return ctx.Response().Json(403, map[string]any{
            "error": response.Message(),
        })
    }

    var attachment models.Attachment
    err = facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().
        Where("task_id", task.ID).
        FindOrFail(&attachment, ctx.Request().RouteInt("attachment"))
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
            "error": "The file does not exist.",
        })
    }
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the file.",
        })
    }

    content, err := facades.Storage().GetBytes(attachment.Path)
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the file.",
        })
    }

    disposition := mime.FormatMediaType("attachment", map[string]string{"filename": attachment.Name})

    return ctx.Response().
        Header("Content-Disposition", disposition).
        Data(200, attachment.MimeType, content)
}

// ... 39 lines not shown
  • Where("task_id", task.ID) only finds the file if it belongs to the task in the URL. A file from another task gives a 404, even for Ana.
  • GetBytes reads the file through the disk, so it works on the local disk and on S3. ctx.Response().Download can also send a file, but it only opens files on the server's own hard drive. With S3, the files aren't on the server, so Download would stop working.
  • Content-Disposition: attachment makes the browser save the file under its original name, instead of opening it. mime.FormatMediaType builds the header, so names with spaces or accents still work. 
$ curl -D - -o /dev/null http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=login-error.png
Content-Length: 93
Content-Type: image/png

File 1 is not under task 1, so even Ana gets a 404:

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1/attachments/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
{"error":"The file does not exist."}

A single task now lists its files. The client gets the file ids from there:

app/http/controllers/task_controller.go

 // ... 78 lines not shown
        With("Creator").
        With("Assignee").
+       With("Attachments").
        FindOrFail(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
            "error": "The task does not exist.",
        // ... 160 lines not shown

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{…,"title":"Fix the login page",…,"attachments":[{…,"id":1,"task_id":8,"uploaded_by":5,"name":"login-error.png","size":93,"mime_type":"image/png"}]}

Deleting files

A file has two parts: the row in Postgres and the file on the disk. Deleting it removes both:

app/http/controllers/attachment_controller.go

// ... 175 lines not shown
func (r *AttachmentController) Destroy(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var attachment models.Attachment
    err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().
        Where("task_id", ctx.Request().RouteInt("id")).
        FindOrFail(&attachment, ctx.Request().RouteInt("attachment"))
    if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
        return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
            "error": "The file does not exist.",
        })
    }
    if err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not load the file.",
        })
    }

    response := facades.Gate().WithContext(ctx).Inspect(policies.DeleteAttachment, map[string]any{
        "attachment": &attachment,
    })
    if !response.Allowed() {
        return ctx.Response().Json(403, map[string]any{
            "error": response.Message(),
        })
    }

    if _, err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().Delete(&attachment); err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not delete the file.",
        })
    }

    if err := facades.Storage().Delete(attachment.Path); err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
    }

    return ctx.Response().NoContent()
}

The row is deleted first. If deleting the file fails after that, the client still gets 204, and the error goes to the log. A file with no row only wastes space. A row with no file would be a broken download.

Ana uploads a text file, notes.txt, to Ben's task. Ben can't delete her file, but he can delete his own:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA" -F file=@notes.txt
{…,"id":2,"task_id":8,"uploaded_by":1,"name":"notes.txt","size":19,"mime_type":"text/plain; charset=utf-8"}

$ curl -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
{"error":"You can only delete files you uploaded."}

$ curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8/attachments/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $BEN"
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

When a task is deleted

CascadeOnDelete deletes a task's rows, but Postgres doesn't know about the disk. Ana deletes task 8. Its row is gone, but notes.txt is still in its folder:

$ curl -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ANA"
$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel taskflow -c "select count(*) from attachments where task_id = 8"
 count 
-------
     0
(1 row)

$ find storage/app/attachments -type f
storage/app/attachments/8/MyNSQ6l8gjPiwTvZA7JO9qZ6OH5EurXPcJrYy62K.txt

Each task's files are in one folder. So the task's Destroy deletes that folder after the row:

app/http/controllers/task_controller.go

 package controllers

 import (
    "errors"
+   "fmt"

    "taskflow/app/enums"
    // ... 209 lines not shown
 func (r *TaskController) Destroy(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var task models.Task
    // ... 18 lines not shown

    if _, err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().Delete(&task); err != nil {
        facades.Log().Error(err)
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not delete the task.",
        })
    }

+   if err := facades.Storage().DeleteDirectory(fmt.Sprintf("attachments/%d", task.ID)); err != nil {
+       facades.Log().Error(err)
+   }
+
    return ctx.Response().NoContent()
 }

Here is the whole trip, from the upload to the delete:

Interactive figure on DevChalk: An upload, a download and a task delete, one message at a time.

Upload: the client sends the file as multipart/form-data, the API checks the policy and the rules, copies the file into the temp folder, stores it on the disk under attachments/8 with a random name, inserts a row in Postgres, removes the temp copy and answers 201. Download: the API loads the row for the task, reads the file from the disk and sends it with a Content-Disposition header. Delete the task: Postgres deletes the task and, through the cascade, its attachment rows, and the API deletes the folder attachments/8 from the disk.

Tests

The tests for this part are in tests/feature/attachment_test.go in TaskFlow. They upload, download and delete files, check every rule in the table above, and check that no temp file is left behind. They run on the testing disk:

.env.testing

 # ... 28 lines not shown
 CACHE_STORE=memory
 HASH_ROUNDS=4
+FILESYSTEM_DISK=testing

Each test deletes the attachments folder first. So the test case only runs on the testing disk, just as it only runs on a database whose name ends in _test:

tests/test_case.go

 // ... 15 lines not shown
        panic("the tests drop every table, so they only run on a database whose name ends in _test: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing")
    }
+
+   if facades.Config().GetString("filesystems.default") != "testing" {
+       panic("the tests delete uploaded files, so they only run on the testing disk: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing")
+   }
 }

 type TestCase struct {
    testing.TestCase
 }

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  1.491s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.756s

Tasks now have files. They are saved on a private disk under random names. Only the people working on the task can download them, and they are deleted with the task.

title: Goravel feature testing for a REST API
description:
Part 13 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-13.

So far, every rule in TaskFlow was checked by sending curl requests by hand. After twelve parts there are many rules, and a change in one part can break a rule from another, for example a policy change that lets Ben delete Ana's tasks. This part adds tests that send the same requests and check the answers, so one go test run checks the rules again after any change.

Start from the Gates & Policies code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-12
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed

A database for the tests

The tests need a database of their own. Each feature test starts from empty tables, by rolling the migrations back and running them again, and on the dev database that would wipe Ana, her tasks and everything else, so the tests get their own database, taskflow_test:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "CREATE DATABASE taskflow_test"
CREATE DATABASE

The tests also need settings that point at that database. Goravel reads .env.testing instead of .env when go test gets --env=.env.testing. It starts as a copy of .env.example:

$ cp .env.example .env.testing

These lines change:

.env.testing

 APP_NAME=Goravel
-APP_ENV=local
-APP_KEY=
+APP_ENV=testing
+APP_KEY=2Nr9bpCIal8Dj0qYE7IviHcYcwzmVqoh
 APP_DEBUG=true

 # ... 8 lines not shown
 APP_PORT=3000

-JWT_SECRET=
+JWT_SECRET=xRQKZ4WHIu8bIHANdQVnskdTsa47cya8

 DB_CONNECTION=postgres
 DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
 DB_PORT=5433
-DB_DATABASE=taskflow
+DB_DATABASE=taskflow_test
 DB_USERNAME=goravel
 DB_PASSWORD=secret

 REDIS_HOST=127.0.0.1
 REDIS_PASSWORD=
 REDIS_PORT=6380
+
+CACHE_STORE=memory
+HASH_ROUNDS=4

The two new settings do nothing yet, since config/cache.go always uses Redis and config/hashing.go always uses 12 rounds. Both now read their value from the env and keep the old value as the default, so only the tests get the new settings:

config/cache.go

 // ... 9 lines not shown
    config := facades.Config()
    config.Add("cache", map[string]any{
-       "default": "redis",
+       "default": config.Env("CACHE_STORE", "redis"),

        // Cache Stores
        // ... 27 lines not shown

config/hashing.go

 // ... 23 lines not shown
        // hashing time versus attacker time are diminishing, so choose your cost factor wisely.
        "bcrypt": map[string]any{
-           "rounds": 12,
+           "rounds": config.Env("HASH_ROUNDS", 12),
        },

        // ... 12 lines not shown
  • CACHE_STORE=memory keeps the tests' cache in memory. The tests empty the cache before each test, and with Redis that would empty the whole Redis server, including the dev app's logged-out tokens and login counts.
  • HASH_ROUNDS=4 makes bcrypt cheap. Every test user and every login hashes a password, and at the usual 12 rounds the suite takes about 6 seconds instead of 1.

.env.testing goes into git, so a fresh clone can run the tests once the database exists. Its APP_KEY and JWT_SECRET are made up, and any 32 characters work, so nothing in it is a real secret. .gitignore skips every .env.* file except .env.example, so add an exception:

.gitignore

 .idea
 .vscode
 .DS_Store
 .env
 .env.*
 !.env.example
+!.env.testing
 storage
 tmp

A test case that boots the app

A test needs the app started the way main.go starts it, with its config, database and routes. Goravel's Testing package does that. Lite only installs the facades picked when the project is created, and Installation & Project Architecture didn't pick Testing, so install it now with package:install:

$ go run . artisan package:install Testing
INFO    Testing depends on Log, Cache, Schema, Orm, Hash, Http, RateLimiter, Session, Storage, Validation, View, Route, they will be installed simultaneously
SUCCESS  Facade Testing installed successfully

The packages Testing depends on are already installed, so it only adds these:

  • tests/test_case.go, with the TestCase struct every test embeds.
  • tests/feature/example_test.go, a placeholder test to delete.
  • &testing.ServiceProvider{} in bootstrap/providers.go. It sets up what RefreshDatabase and Http need.
  • app/facades/testing.go, the Testing facade, and testify in go.mod.

The new test case boots the app in init. The feature tests wipe every table, so a check there stops the run unless the database is a test database:

tests/test_case.go

 package tests

 import (
+   "strings"
+
    "github.com/goravel/framework/testing"

+   "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/bootstrap"
 )

 func init() {
    bootstrap.Boot()
+
+   if !strings.HasSuffix(facades.Config().GetString("database.connections.postgres.database"), "_test") {
+       panic("the tests drop every table, so they only run on a database whose name ends in _test: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing")
+   }
 }

 type TestCase struct {
    testing.TestCase
 }
  • Go runs init once in each test package that imports taskflow/tests, before its tests. bootstrap.Boot() is the call main.go makes, so the tests run the real app.
  • The check reads the database name from the config. If the name doesn't end in _test, the run stops with the guard's message. That catches a plain go test without --env, and an .env.testing that still says taskflow.
  • Embedding Goravel's testing.TestCase gives every test Http for requests and RefreshDatabase for the empty tables.

Unit tests for the custom rules

A unit test checks one piece of code on its own, without the database or a request. The custom rules fit that well, because a rule's Passes gets a value and returns true or false. They are MaxBytes from Register & Login with JWT and FutureDate from Validation with Form Requests. make:test creates their test file:

$ go run . artisan make:test unit/RulesTest
 SUCCESS  Test created successfully

It writes a testify suite, a struct whose methods are the tests:

tests/unit/rules_test.go

package unit

import (
    "testing"

    "github.com/stretchr/testify/suite"

    "taskflow/tests"
)

type RulesTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    tests.TestCase
}

func TestRulesTestSuite(t *testing.T) {
    suite.Run(t, new(RulesTestSuite))
}

// SetupTest will run before each test in the suite.
func (s *RulesTestSuite) SetupTest() {
}

// TearDownTest will run after each test in the suite.
func (s *RulesTestSuite) TearDownTest() {
}

func (s *RulesTestSuite) TestIndex() {
    // TODO
}
  • RulesTestSuite embeds suite.Suite, which gives it testify's checks like s.Equal, and tests.TestCase from the last section.
  • TestRulesTestSuite is the only function go test itself runs. Its suite.Run then calls every method on the struct whose name starts with Test.
  • SetupTest and TearDownTest run before and after each of those methods, and TestIndex is a placeholder.

The rules need no setup, so the file becomes one test per rule:

tests/unit/rules_test.go

package unit

import (
    "context"
    "strings"
    "testing"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/support/carbon"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/suite"

    "taskflow/app/rules"
    "taskflow/tests"
)

type RulesTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    tests.TestCase
}

func TestRulesTestSuite(t *testing.T) {
    suite.Run(t, new(RulesTestSuite))
}

func (s *RulesTestSuite) TestMaxBytes() {
    cases := []struct {
        name   string
        value  any
        passes bool
    }{
        {"72 bytes", strings.Repeat("a", 72), true},
        {"73 bytes", strings.Repeat("a", 73), false},
        {"18 emoji are 72 bytes", strings.Repeat("🔒", 18), true},
        {"19 emoji are 76 bytes", strings.Repeat("🔒", 19), false},
        {"not a string", 12345, false},
    }

    rule := &rules.MaxBytes{}
    for _, c := range cases {
        s.Equal(c.passes, rule.Passes(context.Background(), nil, c.value, "72"), c.name)
    }
}

func (s *RulesTestSuite) TestFutureDate() {
    cases := []struct {
        name   string
        value  any
        passes bool
    }{
        {"tomorrow", carbon.Now().AddDay().ToDateTimeString(), true},
        {"yesterday", carbon.Now().SubDay().ToDateTimeString(), false},
        {"not a date", "soon", false},
        {"not a string", 12345, false},
    }

    rule := &rules.FutureDate{}
    for _, c := range cases {
        s.Equal(c.passes, rule.Passes(context.Background(), nil, c.value), c.name)
    }
}
  • Each case has a name, a value, and whether the rule should pass it. This table-driven style is common in Go tests, and when a case fails, s.Equal prints the case's name.
  • 🔒 is 4 bytes, so 18 of them are exactly 72 bytes and pass. 19 of them are only 19 characters but 76 bytes, and that case fails because the rule counts bytes, not characters.

The tests run with go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing. Without --env, the guard stops the run before any test, the unit tests included, since they import taskflow/tests too, and its init boots the app. Here and below, the output shows only the test lines:

$ go test ./tests/...
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
panic: the tests drop every table, so they only run on a database whose name ends in _test: go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
FAIL    taskflow/tests/unit 0.714s
FAIL

With it, both tests pass. -v lists each one:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing -v
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
=== RUN   TestRulesTestSuite
=== RUN   TestRulesTestSuite/TestFutureDate
=== RUN   TestRulesTestSuite/TestMaxBytes
--- PASS: TestRulesTestSuite (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestRulesTestSuite/TestFutureDate (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestRulesTestSuite/TestMaxBytes (0.00s)
PASS
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.398s

Note Go also lets a unit test sit next to its code, like app/rules/max_bytes_test.go, and a plain go test ./app/rules/ runs it. Either way works, and TaskFlow keeps every test in tests/ so one command runs them all.

Requests without a token

A feature test sends a request through the routes, the middleware and the handler, as curl did, and checks the answer. The first one checks the simplest rule, that every route behind the auth middleware refuses a request without a valid token. make:test creates its file:

$ go run . artisan make:test feature/AuthTest
 SUCCESS  Test created successfully

It writes the same suite as RulesTest. Replace it with the checks:

tests/feature/auth_test.go

package feature

import (
    "testing"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/support/http"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/suite"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/models"
    "taskflow/tests"
)

type AuthTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    tests.TestCase
}

func TestAuthTestSuite(t *testing.T) {
    suite.Run(t, new(AuthTestSuite))
}

func (s *AuthTestSuite) SetupTest() {
    s.RefreshDatabase()
}

func (s *AuthTestSuite) TestRoutesNeedAToken() {
    for _, path := range []string{"/api/v1/tasks", "/api/v1/tasks/1", "/api/v1/users", "/api/v1/me"} {
        response, err := s.Http(s.T()).Get(path)
        s.Require().NoError(err)
        response.AssertUnauthorized()
    }
}

func (s *AuthTestSuite) TestABadTokenIsRefused() {
    response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken("not-a-token").Get("/api/v1/tasks")
    s.Require().NoError(err)
    response.AssertUnauthorized()
}

func (s *AuthTestSuite) TestAWrongPasswordIsRefused() {
    var ana models.User
    s.Require().NoError(facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&ana, map[string]any{"Email": "ana@example.com"}))

    body, err := http.NewBody().SetFields(map[string]any{"email": "ana@example.com", "password": "wrong"}).Build()
    s.Require().NoError(err)
    response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithHeader("Content-Type", body.ContentType()).Post("/api/v1/login", body.Reader())
    s.Require().NoError(err)
    response.AssertUnauthorized()
}
  • SetupTest calls RefreshDatabase, so every test starts with empty tables in taskflow_test.
  • s.Http(s.T()) is Goravel's test client. It hands the request straight to the router, with no server and no port, so air doesn't need to run.
  • The login request's body is built with Goravel's http.NewBody(): SetFields takes the fields as a map, and Build turns them into JSON, so no JSON is written by hand. body.Reader() is what Post sends, and body.ContentType() is the header that goes with it.
  • AssertUnauthorized checks for a 401.

The run now includes the feature tests:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  0.769s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.653s

The test client and its assertions:

s.Http(s.T()) starts a request. These are the methods the tests here use, and Goravel's HTTP tests docs list the rest:

  • WithToken sends a Bearer token, and WithHeader any other header.
  • Get takes the path, and Post, Patch and Delete also take a body, an io.Reader, or nil for none.
  • Bind fills a struct from the response's JSON.
  • AssertStatus checks for any code, and the common ones have their own name, like AssertOk, AssertCreated, AssertUnauthorized and AssertNotFound.
  • AssertFluentJson checks top-level keys with Where, so a nested value like errors.title needs Bind.

Goravel's assertions, like testify's assert, mark a test as failed and let it carry on. testify's require, called as s.Require(), stops the test at the first failure instead. The tests use it to check each request's error, since a failed request has no response to check.

Every role rule in one table

The next test checks every role rule from Gates & Policies. Each rule is one row in a table, saying who sends which request and the status it should get, so a broken rule fails under its own name. make:test creates the file:

$ go run . artisan make:test feature/TaskTest
 SUCCESS  Test created successfully

Replace the new suite with the table and the users it needs:

tests/feature/task_test.go

package feature

import (
    "fmt"
    "testing"

    contractshttp "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/testing/http"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/support/http"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/suite"

    "taskflow/app/enums"
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/models"
    "taskflow/tests"
)

type TaskTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    tests.TestCase
    ana     models.User
    ben     models.User
    benTask models.Task
    catTask models.Task
}

func TestTaskTestSuite(t *testing.T) {
    suite.Run(t, new(TaskTestSuite))
}

func (s *TaskTestSuite) SetupTest() {
    s.RefreshDatabase()
    s.Require().True(facades.Cache().Flush())

    var ana, ben, cat models.User
    s.Require().NoError(facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&ana, map[string]any{"Email": "ana@example.com", "Role": enums.RoleManager}))
    s.Require().NoError(facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&ben, map[string]any{"Email": "ben@example.com"}))
    s.Require().NoError(facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&cat, map[string]any{"Email": "cat@example.com"}))

    var benTask, catTask models.Task
    s.Require().NoError(facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&benTask, map[string]any{"CreatedBy": ana.ID, "AssignedTo": &ben.ID}))
    s.Require().NoError(facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&catTask, map[string]any{"CreatedBy": ana.ID, "AssignedTo": &cat.ID}))

    s.ana, s.ben, s.benTask, s.catTask = ana, ben, benTask, catTask
}

func (s *TaskTestSuite) login(email string) string {
    body, err := http.NewBody().SetFields(map[string]any{"email": email, "password": "password"}).Build()
    s.Require().NoError(err)
    response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithHeader("Content-Type", body.ContentType()).Post("/api/v1/login", body.Reader())
    s.Require().NoError(err)
    response.AssertOk()

    var login struct {
        Token string `json:"token"`
    }
    s.Require().NoError(response.Bind(&login))
    s.Require().NotEmpty(login.Token)

    return login.Token
}

func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestRoles() {
    ana := s.login("ana@example.com")
    ben := s.login("ben@example.com")
    benTask := fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/tasks/%d", s.benTask.ID)
    catTask := fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/tasks/%d", s.catTask.ID)
    newTask := map[string]any{"title": "Write the tests", "description": "Cover every role rule."}

    cases := []struct {
        name   string
        token  string
        method string
        path   string
        body   map[string]any
        status int
    }{
        {"a member reads tasks", ben, "GET", "/api/v1/tasks", nil, 200},
        {"a member can't list users", ben, "GET", "/api/v1/users", nil, 403},
        {"a manager lists users", ana, "GET", "/api/v1/users", nil, 200},
        {"a member can't create a task", ben, "POST", "/api/v1/tasks", newTask, 403},
        {"a manager creates a task", ana, "POST", "/api/v1/tasks", newTask, 201},
        {"a member changes the status of his task", ben, "PATCH", benTask, map[string]any{"status": "done"}, 200},
        {"a member can't rename his task", ben, "PATCH", benTask, map[string]any{"title": "Renamed"}, 403},
        {"a member can't change someone else's task", ben, "PATCH", catTask, map[string]any{"status": "done"}, 403},
        {"a member reads a task", ben, "GET", benTask, nil, 200},
        {"a manager reads a task", ana, "GET", benTask, nil, 200},
        {"a member can't see a user", ben, "GET", fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/users/%d", s.ana.ID), nil, 403},
        {"a manager sees a user", ana, "GET", fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/users/%d", s.ben.ID), nil, 200},
        {"a member can't reassign his task", ben, "PATCH", benTask, map[string]any{"assigned_to": s.ana.ID}, 403},
        {"a manager changes any task", ana, "PATCH", catTask, map[string]any{"title": "Renamed"}, 200},
        {"a member can't delete a task", ben, "DELETE", catTask, nil, 403},
        {"a manager deletes a task", ana, "DELETE", catTask, nil, 204},
    }

    for _, c := range cases {
        s.Run(c.name, func() {
            body, err := http.NewBody().SetFields(c.body).Build()
            s.Require().NoError(err)
            request := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(c.token).WithHeader("Content-Type", body.ContentType())

            var response contractshttp.Response
            switch c.method {
            case "GET":
                response, err = request.Get(c.path)
            case "POST":
                response, err = request.Post(c.path, body.Reader())
            case "PATCH":
                response, err = request.Patch(c.path, body.Reader())
            case "DELETE":
                response, err = request.Delete(c.path, nil)
            }
            s.Require().NoError(err)
            response.AssertStatus(c.status)
        })
    }
}
  • SetupTest creates Ana, Ben and Cat with the user factory from Factories & Seeding, so each has the password password. Ben and Cat each get a task.
  • login logs in through POST /api/v1/login, the way a client does, and reads the token with Bind.
  • Each row's body is a map, or nil when the request sends none. Every row builds a body, so the loop stays the same for all of them, but only POST and PATCH send it.
  • The login limit from Auth Middleware & Rate Limits counts attempts in the cache, and RefreshDatabase doesn't touch the cache. Cache().Flush() resets the counts, so one test's logins don't use up the next test's.
  • s.Run runs each row as its own test, named after the row.
  • The rows share the same tasks, so Ana's delete comes last.

AuthTest logs in too, so it gets the same Flush, and each suite starts with clean counts whichever runs first:

tests/feature/auth_test.go

 // ... 22 lines not shown
 func (s *AuthTestSuite) SetupTest() {
    s.RefreshDatabase()
+   s.Require().True(facades.Cache().Flush())
 }

 // ... 24 lines not shown

With -v, each row shows as its own test:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing -run TestTaskTestSuite -v
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
--- PASS: TestTaskTestSuite (0.09s)
    --- PASS: TestTaskTestSuite/TestRoles (0.09s)
        --- PASS: TestTaskTestSuite/TestRoles/a_member_reads_tasks (0.00s)
        --- PASS: TestTaskTestSuite/TestRoles/a_member_can't_list_users (0.00s)

To see the table catch a mistake, in app/policies/task_policy.go, change Delete to return access.NewAllowResponse(), so members may delete, and run the tests again:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
--- FAIL: TestTaskTestSuite (0.05s)
    --- FAIL: TestTaskTestSuite/TestRoles (0.05s)
        --- FAIL: TestTaskTestSuite/TestRoles/a_member_can't_delete_a_task (0.00s)
        Expected response status code [403] but received 204.
        --- FAIL: TestTaskTestSuite/TestRoles/a_manager_deletes_a_task (0.00s)
        Expected response status code [204] but received 404.
FAIL
FAIL    taskflow/tests/feature  0.845s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.677s
FAIL
  • The member's row names the rule and the status it got.
  • Ana's delete then gets a 404, because Ben's went through and the task is gone.

Change Delete back before going on.

Checking the body and the database

A status code doesn't show everything a request did. A 201 could carry the wrong creator, and a 204 could come back without deleting anything, so most of the new tests check the body or the database, and two more cover a missing task and logging out:

tests/feature/task_test.go

 // ... 112 lines not shown
            response.AssertStatus(c.status)
        })
    }
 }
+
+func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestCreateSetsTheCreator() {
+   body, err := http.NewBody().SetFields(map[string]any{
+       "title":       "Write the tests",
+       "description": "Cover every role rule.",
+       "assigned_to": s.ben.ID,
+   }).Build()
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(s.login("ana@example.com")).WithHeader("Content-Type", body.ContentType()).Post("/api/v1/tasks", body.Reader())
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+
+   response.AssertCreated()
+
+   var task models.Task
+   s.Require().NoError(response.Bind(&task))
+   s.Equal("Write the tests", task.Title)
+   s.Equal(s.ana.ID, task.CreatedBy)
+   s.Equal(s.ben.ID, *task.AssignedTo)
+   s.Equal(enums.StatusPending, task.Status)
+}
+
+func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestAMissingTaskIsNotFound() {
+   response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(s.login("ana@example.com")).Get("/api/v1/tasks/999")
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response.AssertNotFound()
+}
+
+func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestBadInputIsRefused() {
+   body, err := http.NewBody().SetFields(map[string]any{"description": "No title.", "due_at": "yesterday"}).Build()
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(s.login("ana@example.com")).WithHeader("Content-Type", body.ContentType()).Post("/api/v1/tasks", body.Reader())
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+
+   response.AssertUnprocessableEntity()
+
+   var refused struct {
+       Errors map[string]any `json:"errors"`
+   }
+   s.Require().NoError(response.Bind(&refused))
+   s.Contains(refused.Errors, "title")
+   s.Contains(refused.Errors, "due_at")
+}
+
+func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestUpdateChangesOnlyTheSentFields() {
+   path := fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/tasks/%d", s.benTask.ID)
+   body, err := http.NewBody().SetFields(map[string]any{"status": "done"}).Build()
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(s.login("ana@example.com")).WithHeader("Content-Type", body.ContentType()).Patch(path, body.Reader())
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+
+   response.AssertOk().AssertFluentJson(func(json contractshttp.AssertableJSON) {
+       json.Where("status", "done").
+           Where("title", s.benTask.Title).
+           Where("description", s.benTask.Description)
+   })
+}
+
+func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestDeleteRemovesTheTask() {
+   path := fmt.Sprintf("/api/v1/tasks/%d", s.catTask.ID)
+   response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(s.login("ana@example.com")).Delete(path, nil)
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response.AssertNoContent()
+
+   count, err := facades.Orm().Query().Model(&models.Task{}).Where("id", s.catTask.ID).Count()
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   s.Equal(int64(0), count)
+}
+
+func (s *TaskTestSuite) TestLogoutEndsTheToken() {
+   token := s.login("cat@example.com")
+
+   response, err := s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(token).Post("/api/v1/logout", nil)
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response.AssertNoContent()
+
+   response, err = s.Http(s.T()).WithToken(token).Get("/api/v1/me")
+   s.Require().NoError(err)
+   response.AssertUnauthorized()
+}
  • Bind reads the created task into a models.Task, and the test checks that its creator is Ana, its assignee is Ben and its status is pending.
  • A task id that doesn't exist gets a 404.
  • The bad-input test checks which fields have errors, not the messages, so a reworded message doesn't break it.
  • The update test uses AssertFluentJson to check that the title and description are still the same after a status-only change.
  • After the 204, the delete test counts the task's rows in the test database, and Count must be 0.
  • In the logout test, Cat logs out and then sends her token again, and that request gets a 401.

The whole suite passes:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?       taskflow/tests  [no test files]
ok      taskflow/tests/feature  1.071s
ok      taskflow/tests/unit 0.713s

Gotcha testify keeps one suite struct for all its tests, so after the first test s.ana still holds an id, and that's why SetupTest creates the users into new variables first. Creating Ana straight into s.ana would save her with that old id, but the emptied tables start their ids from 1 again, so the next new user gets the same id:

$ go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing
?     taskflow/tests  [no test files]
--- FAIL: TestTaskTestSuite (0.21s)
    --- FAIL: TestTaskTestSuite/TestBadInputIsRefused (0.03s)
        ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_pkey" (SQLSTATE 23505)

New variables start with no id, so the database gives each one a fresh id.

Why the tests use the real database:

Goravel can swap facades.Orm() for a mock, but then every query has to be scripted by hand. These tests run the real app against taskflow_test instead. That's slower, but the tests get the same answers a client would.

When a test must not touch a service, such as an email provider, Goravel can replace a facade with a mock. Code that takes its dependencies as arguments instead of calling facades can be given a fake directly.

One go test ./tests/... --env=.env.testing now checks every role rule from Gates & Policies, the token checks and the main task endpoints, in about a second.

Previous: 12. Gates & Policies
Next: 14. File Storage
Series: Goravel

title: I built rboto: async-only, fully typed Python clients for 34 AWS services, powered by Rust
description:
About a year ago, I had an idea for a Python ORM for DynamoDB. I wanted a good developer experience, async support, and strong typing, but I also wanted to move expensive work out of the Python layer. That became pydynox, with a Rust core handling serialization and other CPU-heavy work.

More recently, I started thinking about the SDK underneath applications that use several AWS services. Especially with agents, a workflow might combine model calls with documents in S3, state in DynamoDB, and messages in SQS. Async calls and clear input and output types matter there too. Whether a developer or a coding agent writes the code, I want a type checker to help catch mistakes.

So I built rboto.

rboto 0.1.0 is now on PyPI — its first official release. It provides async-only Python clients powered by Rust, with 34 service clients available, including S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, SQS, Bedrock Runtime, EventBridge, Scheduler, and Pipes.

It’s still alpha. The API may change. I’ll try to preserve compatibility where possible and document breaking changes.

Install the services you need:

pip install "rboto[s3,dynamodb]==0.1.0"

Here’s a small example fetching object metadata and a DynamoDB item concurrently. It assumes configured AWS credentials and an existing bucket and table:

import asyncio

from rboto import DynamoDBClient, S3Client


async def main() -> None:
    s3 = S3Client(region="us-east-1")
    dynamodb = DynamoDBClient(region="us-east-1")

    document, user = await asyncio.gather(
        s3.head_object(
            bucket="my-bucket",
            key="documents/report.pdf",
        ),
        dynamodb.get_item(
            table_name="users",
            key={"pk": {"s": "USER#123"}},
        ),
    )

    print(document.content_length)
    print(user.item)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

The method arguments and returned objects have built-in types. Your editor knows that document.content_length is int | None, for example. There’s no separate package of type stubs to install.

A few things included in this release:

  • Typed inputs, outputs, service exceptions, and async paginators.
  • Async byte streams and event streams for supported operations.
  • Global JSON logging with per-service controls, and async interceptors.
  • Pydantic and dataclass usage patterns for application-defined inputs and outputs, without requiring Pydantic.
  • Wheels for Python 3.12–3.15 on Linux and macOS, including ARM64 and musl Linux.

Network requests run on Tokio. Regular outputs stay in Rust until their fields are accessed, and response bodies can be consumed in chunks. There’s still synchronous work in input conversion, response materialization, and callbacks; reducing copies and event-loop pauses with larger payloads is ongoing work.

I’m excited to get this first release out and hear from people using it in their own applications. Which service or workflow would you try first? Where does the API feel awkward?

GitHub · Documentation · PyPI

rboto is an independent project maintained by Ferrumio, not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon Web Services.

title: Turning Support Tickets Into FAQ Content With a Small Python Script
description:
Support tickets are the most honest keyword research you have. Customers write questions in their own words, in their own language, and they repeat the ones your website fails to answer. Those same questions are what people type into ChatGPT or Perplexity. This post shows a small script that groups ticket subjects into question clusters so a content team can turn the biggest clusters into FAQ answers.

Export and clean

Most helpdesks can export a CSV with a subject and a body. We only need the subject and the first customer message. Strip signatures, order numbers and email addresses before doing anything else; you do not want personal data in a content workflow.

import csv, re
from collections import defaultdict

def clean(text):
    text = re.sub(r"\S+@\S+", " ", text)          # emails
    text = re.sub(r"#?\d{5,}", " ", text)          # order or ticket numbers
    text = re.sub(r"https?://\S+", " ", text)      # links
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip().lower()

rows = []
with open("tickets.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for r in csv.DictReader(f):
        rows.append(clean(r["subject"] + " " + r["body"][:300]))

Cluster with TF-IDF

You do not need embeddings for a first pass. TF-IDF plus a simple clustering step is fast, cheap and easy to explain to non-engineers.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=3)
X = vec.fit_transform(rows)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=25, n_init=10, random_state=1).fit(X)

clusters = defaultdict(list)
for text, label in zip(rows, km.labels_):
    clusters[label].append(text)

terms = vec.get_feature_names_out()
for label, items in sorted(clusters.items(), key=lambda x: -len(x[1])):
    centre = km.cluster_centers_[label].argsort()[-5:][::-1]
    print(len(items), [terms[i] for i in centre], items[0][:90])

The output is a ranked list: cluster size, its top terms, and one example ticket. The top ten clusters usually cover more than half of all tickets.

From cluster to FAQ entry

For each large cluster, a person writes one question in the customer's phrasing and a direct answer of 40 to 80 words, followed by detail. Keep the answer specific: numbers, steps, limits. Publish the questions as visible text, and add FAQ markup only for what is shown on the page.

Multilingual tickets

If you serve several markets, run the script per language rather than translating everything into English first. The phrasing differs by market, and those differences are exactly what you want on localised pages.

Repeat quarterly

Rerun the script every quarter. New clusters signal product changes or confusing pages; shrinking clusters show which FAQ entries worked. This loop is one of the cheapest ways to produce content that both customers and answer engines find useful. It sits naturally inside a broader GEO process such as our ten-step GEO checklist.

Published by PandaWM, an overseas marketing team based in Hong Kong.

title: Goravel gates and policies for role permissions
description:
Part 12 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-12.

In Task CRUD, any signed-in user can do everything, even delete a task a manager planned. In this part only managers create, assign and delete tasks, and members can only change the status of their own. Anything else gets a 403 that says why.

Start from the Task CRUD code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-11
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

The rules

Who can do what:

manager member
read tasks yes yes
create or delete tasks yes no
change a task's details or assignee yes no
change a task's status yes own tasks only
list or look up users yes no

Goravel checks permissions with gates and policies. A gate is a function with a name, like view-users, that answers yes or no. A policy is a struct that groups those functions for one model, like TaskPolicy with Create, Update and Delete. The users list needs a single check, so a gate is enough. Tasks need one per action, so they get a policy.

Testing the rules needs a manager and a member. Ana is the manager from the seeders.

  1. Reset the database with migrate:fresh --seed.
  2. Register Ben. New accounts are members, and Ben gets id 5.
  3. Log in as Ana and as Ben, and save each token in a variable, ANA and BEN. 
$ go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed

  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}
$ ANA=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \

After, Any and None:

  • facades.Gate().After runs after every check. Its answer is used only when the check itself returned nil.
  • Any asks whether at least one of several abilities is allowed.
  • None asks whether none of them is.

Why not Authorize in the form request:

Every form request has an Authorize method, and Validation with Form Requests left it returning nil. It runs before the handler loads the task, so it can't check the update rule, which needs the task and the changes. The checks go in the handlers instead, where the task is already loaded. Store's check could go in Authorize, but keeping every check in the handlers means there is one place to look.

Members can read every task, and change only the status of their own.

Updating a task

Routing & Responses listed PUT for Update. PUT replaces the whole task, and PATCH changes only the fields that are sent. Marking a task done sends only the status, so TaskFlow uses PATCH. Its rules go in a form request:

$ go run . artisan make:request UpdateTaskRequest
 SUCCESS  Request created successfully

Fill it in, and delete Messages, PrepareForValidation, its validation import and the sample field:

app/http/requests/update_task_request.go

package requests

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
)

type UpdateTaskRequest struct {
}

func (r *UpdateTaskRequest) Authorize(ctx http.Context) error {
    return nil
}

func (r *UpdateTaskRequest) Filters(ctx http.Context) map[string]any {
    return map[string]any{
        "title":       "trim",
        "description": "trim",
    }
}

func (r *UpdateTaskRequest) Rules(ctx http.Context) map[string]any {
    return map[string]any{
        "title":       "sometimes|required|string|max:255",
        "description": "sometimes|required|string",
        "assigned_to": "bail|sometimes|nullable|integer|exists:users,id|regex:^[0-9]+$",
        "due_at":      "bail|sometimes|nullable|date|future_date",
        "status":      "sometimes|required|in:pending,in-progress,done",
    }
}

func (r *UpdateTaskRequest) Attributes(ctx http.Context) map[string]string {
    return map[string]string{
        "assigned_to": "assignee",
        "due_at":      "due date",
    }
}

UpdateTaskRequest has no fields. A struct can't tell an assignee that wasn't sent from one sent as null, so the handler reads what was sent from the validator instead.

  • Every rule starts with sometimes, so a field the body leaves out skips all its rules.
  • nullable lets a client send null for the assignee or the due date, to clear it.
  • The filters and field names match StoreTaskRequest.

[2026-10-24 20:52:07.441] local.info: [2.634ms] [rows:1] UPDATE "tasks" SET "status"='in-progress',"updated_at"='2026-10-24 20:52:07.438' WHERE "id" = 8

Rename it with spaces around the title, and clear the assignee:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"  Ship v2.0  ","assigned_to":null}'
200

[2026-10-24 20:52:08.48] local.info: [0.875ms] [rows:1] UPDATE "tasks" SET "assigned_to"=NULL,"title"='Ship v2.0',"updated_at"='2026-10-24 20:52:08.479' WHERE "id" = 8

The title was trimmed before it was saved, and null cleared the assignee.

Try to make user 3 the creator while marking the task done:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status":"done","created_by":3}'
200

[2026-10-24 20:52:09.512] local.info: [0.699ms] [rows:1] UPDATE "tasks" SET "status"='done',"updated_at"='2026-10-24 20:52:09.511' WHERE "id" = 8

created_by has no rule, so only the status changed.

An empty body answers 200 with the task unchanged, and the log has no UPDATE:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'
200

[2026-10-24 20:52:10.557] local.info: [0.441ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."id" = 8
[2026-10-24 20:52:10.558] local.info: [0.309ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 1
[2026-10-24 20:52:10.558] local.info: [0.762ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."id" = 8

Bad values get a 422, and a task that doesn't exist gets a 404:

$ curl -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"   ","status":"finished","assigned_to":99}'
{"errors":{"assigned_to":{"exists":"The assignee does not exist."},"status":{"in":"The selected status is invalid."},"title":{"required":"The title field is required."}}}

$ curl -X PATCH http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/99 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status":"done"}' 
{"error":"The task does not exist."}

Deleting a task

Deleting a row that doesn't exist is not an error in Goravel. It just deletes nothing. So Destroy looks the task up first with the same FindOrFail check as Show:

app/http/controllers/task_controller.go

 // ... 193 lines not shown
    return ctx.Response().Json(200, saved)
 }
+
+func (r *TaskController) Destroy(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
+   var task models.Task
+   err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().FindOrFail(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
+   if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
+       return ctx.Response().Json(404, map[string]any{
+           "error": "The task does not exist.",
+       })
+   }
+   if err != nil {
+       facades.Log().Error(err)
+       return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+           "error": "Could not load the task.",
+       })
+   }
+
+   if _, err := facades.Orm().WithContext(ctx).Query().Delete(&task); err != nil {
+       facades.Log().Error(err)
+       return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+           "error": "Could not delete the task.",
+       })
+   }
+
+   return ctx.Response().NoContent()
+}

NoContent() answers 204, as Logout does. Add the route and a request:

routes/api.go

 // ... 27 lines not shown
            router.Get("tasks", taskController.Index)
            router.Patch("tasks/{id}", taskController.Update)
+           router.Delete("tasks/{id}", taskController.Destroy)

            router.Get("users", userController.Index)
            router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
        })
    })
 }

requests.http

 # ... 73 lines not shown
 {
   "status": "in-progress"
 }

+### Delete task
+DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
+
 ### List users
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users
 Authorization: Bearer {{token}}

 # ... 6 lines not shown

Delete the new task:

$ curl -i -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

[2026-10-24 20:52:16.782] local.info: [1.450ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."id" = 8
[2026-10-24 20:52:16.784] local.info: [1.675ms] [rows:1] DELETE FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."id" = 8

It is gone, so both a second delete and a read get a 404:

$ curl -X DELETE http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"error":"The task does not exist."}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/8 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"error":"The task does not exist."}

Soft deletes:

TaskFlow removes the row. With soft deletes, a model embeds orm.SoftDeletes and the migration adds a deleted_at column. Delete then only fills in deleted_at, and queries skip those rows. WithTrashed includes them, Restore brings one back, and ForceDelete removes it for good.

TaskFlow's tasks can now be listed, created, read, changed and deleted, by anyone who is logged in. A member can still change or delete a manager's task.
