title: Goravel auth middleware and login rate limiting
description:
Part 10 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-10.

In Register & Login with JWT, the token routes learned who is calling, but the task and user routes still answer anyone. Me and Logout also start with the same lines to read the token. In this part we move that check into a middleware that guards every route that needs a login, hand the signed-in user to the handlers, and limit how fast anyone can guess a password.

Start from the Register & Login with JWT code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-09
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
go run . artisan jwt:secret
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
go install github.com/air-verse/air@latest
air

The auth middleware

A middleware is code that runs before the handler. It either passes the request on or answers it, so one login check can guard every route that needs it.

$ go run . artisan make:middleware Auth
 SUCCESS  Middleware created successfully

It writes app/http/middleware/auth.go:

app/http/middleware/auth.go

package middleware

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
)

type Auth struct{}

func (m *Auth) Signature() string {
    return "Auth"
}

func (m *Auth) Handle(ctx http.Context) {
    ctx.Request().Next()
}
  • Signature names the middleware.
  • Handle runs for each request. ctx.Request().Next() passes the request on to the next middleware, or to the handler.

Fill in Handle with the Parse check from Me:

app/http/middleware/auth.go

 package middleware

 import (
+   "taskflow/app/facades"
+
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
 )

 // ... 6 lines not shown
 func (m *Auth) Handle(ctx http.Context) {
+   if _, err := facades.Auth(ctx).Parse(ctx.Request().Header("Authorization")); err != nil {
+       ctx.Response().Json(401, map[string]any{
+           "error": err.Error(),
+       }).Abort()
+       return
+   }
+
    ctx.Request().Next()
 }
  • If the token is missing, changed, expired or logged out, the middleware answers 401 with the reason.
  • Abort stops the request there, so the handler never runs.

Protecting routes

Register and log in stay open, since nobody has a token yet. Refresh stays open too, because it must accept an expired token, which the middleware refuses. Every other API route goes into a group behind the middleware:

routes/api.go

 package routes

 import (
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/http/controllers"
+   "taskflow/app/http/middleware"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/route"
 )
 // ... 6 lines not shown
    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("register", authController.Register)
        router.Post("login", authController.Login)
-       router.Get("me", authController.Me)
        router.Post("refresh", authController.Refresh)
-       router.Post("logout", authController.Logout)

-       router.Post("tasks", taskController.Store).Name("tasks.create")
-       router.Get("tasks/{id}", taskController.Show)
-       router.Get("tasks", taskController.Index)
+       router.Middleware(&middleware.Auth{}).Group(func(router route.Router) {
+           router.Get("me", authController.Me)
+           router.Post("logout", authController.Logout)

-       router.Get("users", userController.Index)
-       router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
+           router.Post("tasks", taskController.Store).Name("tasks.create")
+           router.Get("tasks/{id}", taskController.Show)
+           router.Get("tasks", taskController.Index)
+
+           router.Get("users", userController.Index)
+           router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
+       })
    })
 }

router.Middleware(&middleware.Auth{}) returns a router whose routes all run Auth first.

Without a token, the task list is refused now:

$ curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 43

{"error":"authentication token is invalid"}

Log in as Ana from the seeders, whose password is password, and keep the token in TOKEN as in Register & Login with JWT:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"password"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}

$ TOKEN=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…

With the token, the list answers:

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"filters":{},"page":1,"status":""}

In requests.http, the task and user requests need the header too:

requests.http

 # ... 39 lines not shown
 ### Create task
 POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
 Content-Type: application/json

 # ... 5 lines not shown
 ### Create task with bad data
 POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}
 Content-Type: application/json

 # ... 6 lines not shown
 ### Show task
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}

 ### List tasks
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks?status=done&page=2&filters[priority]=high
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}

 ### List users
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}

 ### Show user
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users/2
+Authorization: Bearer {{token}}

 ### Hello
 GET http://localhost:3000/hello

Middleware on every route:

router.Middleware puts a middleware on some routes. A middleware for every route, like one that logs each request, goes in bootstrap/app.go with WithMiddleware. See global middleware.

Laravel also has a guest middleware, which keeps logged-in users away from the login page. An API with tokens has no such pages, so TaskFlow doesn't need one.

One place to check the token

The middleware has parsed the token by the time Me and Logout run, so they can drop their own Parse lines. Refresh keeps its own:

app/http/controllers/auth_controller.go

 // ... 115 lines not shown
 func (r *AuthController) Me(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
-   if _, err := facades.Auth(ctx).Parse(ctx.Request().Header("Authorization")); err != nil {
-       return ctx.Response().Json(401, map[string]any{
-           "error": err.Error(),
-       })
-   }
-
    // ... 41 lines not shown
 func (r *AuthController) Logout(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
-   if _, err := facades.Auth(ctx).Parse(ctx.Request().Header("Authorization")); err != nil {
-       return ctx.Response().Json(401, map[string]any{
-           "error": err.Error(),
-       })
-   }
-
    if err := facades.Auth(ctx).Logout(); err != nil {
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": "Could not log out.",
        })
    }

    return ctx.Response().NoContent()
 }

They still work, because Parse leaves the token's claims on the request for User and Logout to read:

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"created_at":"2026-10-24 18:48:20","updated_at":"2026-10-24 18:48:20","id":1,"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","role":"manager","created_tasks":null,"assigned_tasks":null}

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/logout -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"error":"authentication token has been disabled"}

Gotcha Json only builds the answer. .Abort() stops the request and sends it. Leave Abort out and the 401 is never sent, and the handler runs as if the middleware weren't there. With no token, the task list answers and /me fails with a 500:

$ curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 35

{"filters":{},"page":1,"status":""}

$ curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/v1/me
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 36

{"error":"Could not load the user."}

Nothing warns you, so every answer in a middleware needs Abort.

A token for a deleted user

Parse checks the token's signature, its expiry and the logged-out list in Redis. It never asks Postgres, so a token keeps working after its user is gone. Register Dan, log him in, and delete him while his token is still valid:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Dan","email":"dan@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
{"created_at":"2026-10-24 18:48:29","updated_at":"2026-10-24 18:48:29","id":5,"name":"Dan","email":"dan@example.com","role":"member","created_tasks":null,"assigned_tasks":null}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"dan@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}

$ TOKEN=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "DELETE FROM users WHERE email = 'dan@example.com'"
DELETE 1

The task list still answers him, and only /me notices, because it is the one handler that loads the user:

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"filters":{},"page":1,"status":""}

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"error":"The user no longer exists."}

Goravel's usual way is to call facades.Auth(ctx).User(&user) in the handlers that need the user. That only checks the routes whose handlers remember to call it, and each call runs its own query. Loading the user in the middleware checks every protected route, and the handlers get the user without asking again.

Passing the user to handlers

ctx.WithValue attaches a value to the request, and ctx.Value reads it back by its key. A small package that owns the key means the user can only be set and read through its two functions:

app/http/authuser/authuser.go

package authuser

import (
    "context"

    "taskflow/app/models"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
)

type key struct{}

func Set(ctx http.Context, user *models.User) {
    ctx.WithValue(key{}, user)
}

func From(ctx context.Context) *models.User {
    user, _ := ctx.Value(key{}).(*models.User)

    return user
}
  • The key is key{}, a type only this package can make. A string like "user" could clash with other values on the request, the framework's included. Go's context docs advise the same.
  • Set takes Goravel's http.Context. Its WithValue changes the request in place. Go's own context.WithValue returns a new context, which the handler would never see.
  • From takes any context.Context, so code that only has a context.Context, such as a gate, can read the user too.
  • From returns nil when no user was set. Only call it in a handler behind Auth.

In the middleware, load the user after Parse and store it:

app/http/middleware/auth.go

 package middleware

 import (
+   "errors"
+
    "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/http/authuser"
+   "taskflow/app/models"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
+   frameworkerrors "github.com/goravel/framework/errors"
 )

 // ... 6 lines not shown
 func (m *Auth) Handle(ctx http.Context) {
    if _, err := facades.Auth(ctx).Parse(ctx.Request().Header("Authorization")); err != nil {
        ctx.Response().Json(401, map[string]any{
            "error": err.Error(),
        }).Abort()
        return
    }

+   var user models.User
+   if err := facades.Auth(ctx).User(&user); err != nil {
+       if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
+           ctx.Response().Json(401, map[string]any{
+               "error": "The user no longer exists.",
+           }).Abort()
+           return
+       }
+
+       ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+           "error": "Could not load the user.",
+       }).Abort()
+       return
+   }
+
+   authuser.Set(ctx, &user)
    ctx.Request().Next()
 }

The two error answers come from Me, which becomes one line that reads the stored user with From:

app/http/controllers/auth_controller.go

 package controllers

 import (
    "errors"
    "sync"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/http/authuser"
    "taskflow/app/http/requests"
    "taskflow/app/models"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/auth"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
-   frameworkerrors "github.com/goravel/framework/errors"
 )

 // ... 100 lines not shown
 func (r *AuthController) Me(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
-   var user models.User
-   if err := facades.Auth(ctx).User(&user); err != nil {
-       if errors.Is(err, frameworkerrors.OrmRecordNotFound) {
-           return ctx.Response().Json(401, map[string]any{
-               "error": "The user no longer exists.",
-           })
-       }
-
-       return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
-           "error": "Could not load the user.",
-       })
-   }
-
-   return ctx.Response().Json(200, user)
+   return ctx.Response().Json(200, authuser.From(ctx))
 }

 // ... 34 lines not shown

Log in as Ana again and ask for /me:

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

GET /api/v1/me

{
  "created_at": "2026-10-24 18:48:20",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-24 18:48:20",
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Ana",
  "email": "ana@example.com",
  "role": "manager",
  "created_tasks": null,
  "assigned_tasks": null
}

The /me request adds one query to the query log, from the middleware:

[2026-10-24 18:48:39.64] local.info: [1.189ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = '1'

Register Dan again, log him in and delete him. His token is now refused on the task list too:

$ curl http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
{"error":"The user no longer exists."}

A query on every request:

A JWT can be checked without the database, and that is much of its appeal. TaskFlow already asks Redis on each request whether the token was logged out, and now it reads the user from Postgres too, even for /tasks, which doesn't use it. That is one lookup by primary key, and a deleted user is shut out at once.

Limiting login attempts

Nothing stops a script from trying passwords at login all day. A rate limiter gives a rule a name, and the built-in Throttle middleware applies it to a route. Register it in the WithCallback from Models & Migrations:

bootstrap/app.go

 package bootstrap

 import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/schema"
    contractsfoundation "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/foundation"
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/foundation"
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/http/limit"

    // ... 17 lines not shown
        WithCallback(func() {
            facades.Schema().Extend(schema.Extension{
                Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}},
            })
+
+           facades.RateLimiter().For("login", func(ctx http.Context) http.Limit {
+               email := ctx.Request().Input("email")
+
+               return limit.PerMinute(5).By(email).Response(func(ctx http.Context) {
+                   ctx.Response().Json(429, map[string]any{
+                       "error": "Too many login attempts. Try again in a minute.",
+                   }).Abort()
+               })
+           })
        }).
        Create()
 }
  • PerMinute(5) allows five tries a minute.
  • By sets what is counted, here the email. A script guessing one account gets five tries a minute. In return, anyone who knows an email can keep its owner locked out by sending five requests a minute.
  • Response sets the answer once the limit is hit. Without it, the client gets a 429 with an empty body.

Put Throttle("login") on the login route. Goravel's middleware package has the same name as TaskFlow's, so it is imported as httpmiddleware:

routes/api.go

 package routes

 import (
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/http/controllers"
    "taskflow/app/http/middleware"

    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/route"
+   httpmiddleware "github.com/goravel/framework/http/middleware"
 )
 // ... 6 lines not shown
    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("register", authController.Register)
-       router.Post("login", authController.Login)
+       router.Middleware(httpmiddleware.Throttle("login")).Post("login", authController.Login)
        router.Post("refresh", authController.Refresh)
 // ... 10 lines not shown
            router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
        })
    })
 }

Try a wrong password six times:

$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"wrong"}'; done; echo
401 401 401 401 401 429

The sixth gets 429. Logins that work count too, because Throttle counts every request. Counting only failures would mean moving the limit into the Login handler.

The email as it was typed

The limiter counts the email exactly as it was sent, so check whether another spelling gets past it. Within the minute, log in as Ana with the right password, then with capitals, then with a space in front:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"password"}'
{"error":"Too many login attempts. Try again in a minute."}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ANA@EXAMPLE.COM","password":"password"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":" ana@example.com","password":"password"}'
{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}

Ana's email is blocked, but both other spellings work. The limiter reads the email before the form request trims and lowercases it, so each spelling gets a counter of its own. Redis shows three:

$ docker compose exec redis redis-cli --scan --pattern '*throttle*'
Goravel_cache:throttle:login:0:ANA@EXAMPLE.COM
Goravel_cache:throttle:login:0:ana@example.com
Goravel_cache:throttle:login:0: ana@example.com

Before passing the email to By, trim it and lowercase it, as the form request's filters do:

bootstrap/app.go

 package bootstrap

 import (
+   "strings"
+
    // ... 28 lines not shown
            facades.RateLimiter().For("login", func(ctx http.Context) http.Limit {
-               email := ctx.Request().Input("email")
+               email := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(ctx.Request().Input("email")))

                return limit.PerMinute(5).By(email).Response(func(ctx http.Context) {
                    ctx.Response().Json(429, map[string]any{
                        "error": "Too many login attempts. Try again in a minute.",
                    }).Abort()
                })
            })
        }).
        Create()
 }

Wait a minute for the old counters to run out. Now five wrong tries in different spellings share one counter, and the right password is refused too until the minute is up:

$ for email in "ana@example.com" "Ana@Example.com" " ana@example.com" "ANA@EXAMPLE.COM" "ana@example.com "; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"email\":\"$email\",\"password\":\"wrong\"}"; done; echo
401 401 401 401 401 

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"password"}'
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Retry-After: 60
X-Ratelimit-Limit: 5
X-Ratelimit-Remaining: 0
X-Ratelimit-Reset: 1792867791
Content-Length: 59

{"error":"Too many login attempts. Try again in a minute."}
  • X-Ratelimit-Limit and X-Ratelimit-Remaining say how many tries the minute allows and how many are left.
  • Retry-After is the number of seconds until the next try.
  • X-Ratelimit-Reset is when the counter starts again, in Unix time.

There is one key in Redis now:

$ docker compose exec redis redis-cli --scan --pattern '*throttle*'
Goravel_cache:throttle:login:0:ana@example.com

Register Eve and log her in. Her email has its own counter, so she gets through, with four tries left:

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Eve","email":"eve@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
{"created_at":"2026-10-24 18:48:52","updated_at":"2026-10-24 18:48:52","id":7,"name":"Eve","email":"eve@example.com","role":"member","created_tasks":null,"assigned_tasks":null}

$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"eve@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
X-Ratelimit-Limit: 5
X-Ratelimit-Remaining: 4
Content-Length: 171

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9…"}

What the email limit doesn't stop:

It doesn't stop one client from trying a common password against many emails, and register still tells anyone whether an email has an account. Both need a limit per client, and Goravel counts a client by IP. Throttle does that when a limiter has no key, counting by ctx.Request().Ip() and the path.

Counting the email and the IP together, as Laravel's starter kits do, is weaker than the email alone. With the Gin driver, Ip() trusts the X-Forwarded-For header from any client, so a client can send a new IP on every request, and one account gets unlimited tries. Change the key to the email and the IP:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 33 lines not shown
            facades.RateLimiter().For("login", func(ctx http.Context) http.Limit {
                email := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(ctx.Request().Input("email")))

-               return limit.PerMinute(5).By(email).Response(func(ctx http.Context) {
+               return limit.PerMinute(5).By(email + "|" + ctx.Request().Ip()).Response(func(ctx http.Context) {
                    ctx.Response().Json(429, map[string]any{
                        "error": "Too many login attempts. Try again in a minute.",
                    }).Abort()
                })
            })
        }).
        Create()
 }

Lock Ana's email, then send a new header on each try:

$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"wrong"}'; done; echo
401 401 401 401 401 429 

$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/v1/login -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$i" -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"wrong"}'; done; echo
401 401 401 401 401 401

Every try gets a counter of its own, so the email never locks. Change the key back to By(email). TaskFlow counts by email only. A per-IP limit falls to the same header. A limit per client needs an IP the client can't fake, which means telling the server which proxies to trust.

The task and user routes now turn away anyone without a valid token, handlers get the signed-in user from the middleware, and login allows five tries a minute per email. A member can still do anything a manager can.

title: Goravel factories and seeders with fake data
description:
Part 7 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-07.

So far every row came from psql, typed by hand, and had to be typed again each time the tables were rebuilt. A factory describes one fake row, and a seeder uses factories to fill the database. With both, one command rebuilds the database and fills it with users and tasks.

Start from the Relationships: Has Many code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-06
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate

The user factory

Users come first, because every task needs one. Create a factory for them:

$ go run . artisan make:factory UserFactory
 SUCCESS  Factory created successfully

It creates database/factories/user_factory.go with an empty Definition. Fill it in, using gofakeit for the fake values:

database/factories/user_factory.go

package factories

import (
    "github.com/brianvoe/gofakeit/v7"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
)

type UserFactory struct {
}

// Definition Define the model's default state.
func (f *UserFactory) Definition() map[string]any {
    password, _ := facades.Hash().Make("password")

    return map[string]any{
        "Name":     gofakeit.Name(),
        "Email":    gofakeit.Email(),
        "Password": password,
        "Role":     "member",
    }
}
  • The keys are the model's field names, like DueAt, not the column names, like due_at.
  • Every fake user gets the password password, hashed with the Hash facade. bcrypt is slow on purpose, which is fine for a few rows. Feature Testing lowers its cost for the tests, where the hashing adds up.
  • The role is the plain string "member", not models.RoleMember. The model will import this package, and Go does not let two packages import each other. When the task endpoints need these values too, we move them into a package of their own.

Then run:

$ go mod tidy

The model finds its factory through a Factory method:

app/models/user.go

 package models

 import (
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/factory"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
+
+   "taskflow/database/factories"
 )

 // ... 7 lines not shown
 type User struct {
    orm.Model
    Name     string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"name"`
    Email    string `gorm:"size:255;unique;not null" json:"email"`
    Password string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"-"`
    Role     Role   `gorm:"type:enum('manager','member');default:'member';not null" json:"role"`

    CreatedTasks  []Task `gorm:"foreignKey:CreatedBy" json:"created_tasks"`
    AssignedTasks []Task `gorm:"foreignKey:AssignedTo" json:"assigned_tasks"`
 }
+
+func (u *User) Factory() factory.Factory {
+   return &factories.UserFactory{}
+}

The task factory

Tasks get a factory the same way:

$ go run . artisan make:factory TaskFactory
 SUCCESS  Factory created successfully

Fill in its Definition:

database/factories/task_factory.go

package factories

import (
    "github.com/brianvoe/gofakeit/v7"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/support/carbon"
)

type TaskFactory struct {
}

// Definition Define the model's default state.
func (f *TaskFactory) Definition() map[string]any {
    title := gofakeit.RandomString([]string{
        "Fix the login bug",
        "Write the API docs",
        "Review the pull request",
        "Plan the next release",
        "Update the dependencies",
        "Add tests for tasks",
        "Clean up old logs",
        "Reply to support emails",
    })
    status := gofakeit.RandomString([]string{"pending", "in-progress", "done"})
    due := carbon.Now().AddDays(gofakeit.Number(1, 30)).StartOfDay().SetHour(9)

    return map[string]any{
        "Title":       title,
        "Description": gofakeit.HackerPhrase(),
        "Status":      status,
        "DueAt":       carbon.NewDateTime(due),
    }
}
  • Due dates are 1 to 30 days from today, at 9:00.
  • Status is a plain string too, for the same reason as the role.
  • There is no CreatedBy or AssignedTo. Both need real users, so the seeder sets them.

Link the factory to the Task model:

app/models/task.go

 package models

 import (
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/factory"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/support/carbon"
+
+   "taskflow/database/factories"
 )

 // ... 7 lines not shown

 type Task struct {
    orm.Model
    CreatedBy   uint             `gorm:"not null" json:"created_by"`
    Creator     *User            `gorm:"foreignKey:CreatedBy" json:"creator"`
    AssignedTo  *uint            `json:"assigned_to"`
    Assignee    *User            `gorm:"foreignKey:AssignedTo" json:"assignee"`
    Title       string           `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"title"`
    Description string           `gorm:"type:text;not null" json:"description"`
    Status      Status           `gorm:"type:enum('pending','in-progress','done');default:'pending';not null" json:"status"`
    DueAt       *carbon.DateTime `json:"due_at"`
 }
+
+func (t *Task) Factory() factory.Factory {
+   return &factories.TaskFactory{}
+}

The user and task seeders

Make two seeders, one for users and one for tasks. Keeping them apart lets you run one alone, for example to add more tasks without touching the users:

$ go run . artisan make:seeder UserSeeder
 SUCCESS  Seeder created successfully
 SUCCESS  Seeder registered successfully
$ go run . artisan make:seeder TaskSeeder
 SUCCESS  Seeder created successfully
 SUCCESS  Seeder registered successfully

Like make:migration, make:seeder registers what it creates. It lists the seeders in a new bootstrap/seeders.go:

bootstrap/seeders.go

package bootstrap

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/seeder"

    "taskflow/database/seeders"
)

func Seeders() []seeder.Seeder {
    return []seeder.Seeder{
        &seeders.UserSeeder{},
        &seeders.TaskSeeder{},
    }
}

db:seed runs them in this order. You made UserSeeder first, so the users exist before the tasks. make:seeder also added WithSeeders(Seeders) to bootstrap/app.go:

bootstrap/app.go

 package bootstrap

 // ... 11 lines not shown
 func Boot() contractsfoundation.Application {
    return foundation.Setup().
+       WithSeeders(Seeders).
        WithMigrations(Migrations).
        // ... 11 lines not shown
        Create()
 }

Fill in Run in database/seeders/user_seeder.go:

database/seeders/user_seeder.go

package seeders

import (
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/models"
)

type UserSeeder struct {
}

// Signature The name and signature of the seeder.
func (s *UserSeeder) Signature() string {
    return "UserSeeder"
}

// Run executes the seeder logic.
func (s *UserSeeder) Run() error {
    var manager models.User
    err := facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&manager, map[string]any{
        "Name":  "Ana",
        "Email": "ana@example.com",
        "Role":  models.RoleManager,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var members []models.User
    return facades.Orm().Factory().Count(3).Create(&members)
}
  • The first Create makes Ana, the manager.
  • The map overrides what the factory would pick, so Ana always has the email ana@example.com.
  • Her password is password, like every fake user's.
  • Count(3) then makes three members with fake names.

TaskSeeder can run alone, so it reads the users back from the database instead of getting them from UserSeeder. Fill in database/seeders/task_seeder.go:

database/seeders/task_seeder.go

package seeders

import (
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/models"
)

type TaskSeeder struct {
}

// Signature The name and signature of the seeder.
func (s *TaskSeeder) Signature() string {
    return "TaskSeeder"
}

// Run executes the seeder logic.
func (s *TaskSeeder) Run() error {
    var manager models.User
    err := facades.Orm().Query().Where("role", models.RoleManager).FirstOrFail(&manager)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    var members []models.User
    err = facades.Orm().Query().Where("role", models.RoleMember).Find(&members)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    for _, member := range members {
        var tasks []models.Task
        err = facades.Orm().Factory().Count(2).Create(&tasks, map[string]any{
            "CreatedBy":  manager.ID,
            "AssignedTo": &member.ID,
        })
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }

    var unassigned models.Task
    return facades.Orm().Factory().Create(&unassigned, map[string]any{
        "CreatedBy": manager.ID,
    })
}
  • If there is no manager yet, FirstOrFail stops the seeder with record not found. First would hand back an empty user instead.
  • AssignedTo takes &member.ID because the field is a pointer.
  • One more task is made by Ana and assigned to nobody.

Running seeders with db:seed

db:seed runs every registered seeder:

$ go run . artisan db:seed
  ERROR   fail to run seeder: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_unique" (SQLSTATE 23505)

It fails because Ana is still in the table from the earlier parts, and emails must be unique. A seeder only adds rows. It does not clear the tables first. If you started from the code at the top of this part, your tables were empty and it worked.

Resetting the database with migrate:fresh

migrate:fresh drops every table and runs all the migrations again, and --seed then runs the seeders. Run it either way, so your ids match the ones below:

$ go run . artisan migrate:fresh --seed
 SUCCESS  Dropped all tables successfully
  INFO    Running migration
  INFO    Running: 20210101000002_create_jobs_table
  INFO    Running: 20261022221906_create_users_table
  INFO    Running: 20261023063944_create_tasks_table
 SUCCESS  Migration success
 SUCCESS  Database seeding completed successfully.
 SUCCESS  Migration fresh success

The tables now hold the seeded rows:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "SELECT id, name, email, role, left(password, 7) AS hash FROM users" \
    -c "SELECT id, assigned_to, title, status, due_at::date AS due FROM tasks"
 id |      name      |           email            |  role   |  hash   
----+----------------+----------------------------+---------+---------
  1 | Ana            | ana@example.com            | manager | $2a$12$
  2 | Darion Whitney | francis.hansen@jensen.name | member  | $2a$12$
  3 | Joany Silva    | cpowell@richards.org       | member  | $2a$12$
  4 | Cleora Grady   | ruby.murphy3@harris.io     | member  | $2a$12$
(4 rows)

 id | assigned_to |          title          |   status    |    due     
----+-------------+-------------------------+-------------+------------
  1 |           2 | Add tests for tasks     | in-progress | 2026-11-06
  2 |           2 | Write the API docs      | done        | 2026-11-05
  3 |           3 | Update the dependencies | done        | 2026-10-25
  4 |           3 | Fix the login bug       | pending     | 2026-11-15
  5 |           4 | Update the dependencies | in-progress | 2026-10-28
  6 |           4 | Write the API docs      | in-progress | 2026-11-02
  7 |             | Reply to support emails | in-progress | 2026-11-15
(7 rows)

Your names, emails and dates are different, because they are random. The passwords start with $2a$12$, the start of a bcrypt hash, so they are real hashes now, not x.

Running one seeder

--seeder runs only the seeders you name, by the name their Signature returns. To get more tasks for the same users, run TaskSeeder alone:

$ go run . artisan db:seed --seeder=TaskSeeder
 SUCCESS  Database seeding completed successfully.
$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow -c "SELECT count(*) FROM tasks"
 count 
-------
    14
(1 row)

The same users got seven more tasks. Running UserSeeder alone would fail on Ana's email, just like before. Run migrate:fresh --seed again whenever you want the starting data back.

One command now rebuilds the database and fills it with users and tasks. The API still takes whatever data a client sends.

Next: 08. Validation with Form Requests

title: Goravel has many relationships and N+1 queries
description:
Part 6 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-06.

In Relationships: Belongs To, each task loaded the user who made it and the user it is assigned to. In this part we go the other way, from a user to their tasks, and use the query log to find and fix the N+1 problem.

Start from the Relationships: Belongs To code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-05
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate
docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO users (name, email, password, role) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com', 'x', 'manager'), ('Ben', 'ben@example.com', 'x', 'member');" \
    -c "INSERT INTO tasks (created_by, assigned_to, title, description, due_at) VALUES (1, 2, 'Ship v1', 'The first release', '2026-11-02 09:00:00+00'), (1, NULL, 'Write the docs', 'Nobody has it yet', NULL);"

The three tasks you add below get ids 3 to 5, not 4 to 6.

Has many relationships

A task belongs to a user because the task row holds the user's id. From the user's side, that same link is called has many, because one user can have many tasks. A user has two such lists, the tasks they made and the tasks assigned to them. Add both:

app/models/user.go

 // ... 13 lines not shown
 type User struct {
    orm.Model
    Name     string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"name"`
    Email    string `gorm:"size:255;unique;not null" json:"email"`
    Password string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"-"`
    Role     Role   `gorm:"type:enum('manager','member');default:'member';not null" json:"role"`
+
+   CreatedTasks  []Task `gorm:"foreignKey:CreatedBy" json:"created_tasks"`
+   AssignedTasks []Task `gorm:"foreignKey:AssignedTo" json:"assigned_tasks"`
 }
  • CreatedTasks holds the tasks the user made. Its foreignKey:CreatedBy names the field on Task that holds this user's id.
  • AssignedTasks holds the tasks assigned to the user, linked by AssignedTo.
  • Without foreignKey, GORM looks for a UserID field on Task. There is none, so every query that reads users fails, even GET /tasks/1.
  • They are slices, not pointers like Creator, because a user can have many tasks.

There is no migration this time. The ids already live in the tasks table, so the users table needs nothing new.

Test data

Right now there are two tasks, and only one of them is assigned to anyone, so a list of users would not show much. Add a third user, Cleo, and three more tasks, all made by Ana. One of the tasks assigned to Ben is done. We use it later, when we leave done tasks out:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO users (name, email, password, role) VALUES ('Cleo', 'cleo@example.com', 'x', 'member');"
INSERT 0 1
$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO tasks (created_by, assigned_to, title, description, status) VALUES (1, 2, 'Fix the login bug', 'Users get logged out', 'in-progress'), (1, 3, 'Review the API', 'Check every endpoint', 'pending'), (1, 2, 'Plan the next release', 'Pick what goes in', 'done');"
INSERT 0 3

Three tasks are now assigned to Ben, and one to Cleo.

Loading a has many relation

The project's UserController is still the sample it came with. Add a Show method to it that loads a user with both lists:

app/http/controllers/user_controller.go

 package controllers

 import (
+   "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/models"
+
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
 )

-type UserController struct {}
+type UserController struct{}

 func NewUserController() *UserController {
    return &UserController{}
 }

 func (r *UserController) Index(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    return ctx.Response().Success().Json(http.Json{
        "Hello": "Goravel",
    })
 }
+
+func (r *UserController) Show(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
+   var user models.User
+   err := facades.Orm().Query().
+       With("CreatedTasks").
+       With("AssignedTasks").
+       Find(&user, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
+   if err != nil {
+       return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+           "error": err.Error(),
+       })
+   }
+
+   return ctx.Response().Json(200, user)
+}

Then its route:

routes/api.go

 // ... 9 lines not shown
 func Api() {
    taskController := controllers.NewTaskController()
+   userController := controllers.NewUserController()

    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("tasks", taskController.Store).Name("tasks.create")
        router.Get("tasks/{id}", taskController.Show)
        router.Get("tasks", taskController.Index)
+
+       router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
    })
 }

Add a request for Ben, user 2:

requests.http

 # ... 9 lines not shown
 ### Show task
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1

 ### List tasks
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks?status=done&page=2&filters[priority]=high

+### Show user
+GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users/2
+
 ### Hello
 GET http://localhost:3000/hello

If air is not running, start it, as in Routing & Responses. Then send Show user. Here is the response, formatted:

GET /api/v1/users/2

{
  "created_at": null,
  "updated_at": null,
  "id": 2,
  "name": "Ben",
  "email": "ben@example.com",
  "role": "member",
  "created_tasks": [],
  "assigned_tasks": [
    {
      "created_at": null,
      "updated_at": null,
      "id": 1,
      "created_by": 1,
      "creator": null,
      "assigned_to": 2,
      "assignee": null,
      "title": "Ship v1",
      "description": "The first release",
      "status": "pending",
      "due_at": "2026-11-02 09:00:00"
    },
    ...
  ]
}

Ben made no tasks, so created_tasks is an empty list. He has three in assigned_tasks. Inside each task, creator and assignee are null, because Show does not load them.

The query log shows one query for the user and one for each list:

[2026-10-23 07:49:41.261] local.info: [1.316ms] [rows:3] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."assigned_to" = 2
[2026-10-23 07:49:41.262] local.info: [0.691ms] [rows:0] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."created_by" = 2
[2026-10-23 07:49:41.262] local.info: [6.399ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 2

Loading relations for a list

A list of users is where loading relations starts to cost queries. Replace the sample's Index with one that lists every user, and leave out With for now, to see what an unloaded list looks like:

app/http/controllers/user_controller.go

 // ... 15 lines not shown
 func (r *UserController) Index(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
-   return ctx.Response().Success().Json(http.Json{
-       "Hello": "Goravel",
-   })
+   var users []models.User
+   err := facades.Orm().Query().Find(&users)
+   if err != nil {
+       return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+           "error": err.Error(),
+       })
+   }
+
+   return ctx.Response().Json(200, users)
 }

 // ... 14 lines not shown

Add its route:

routes/api.go

 // ... 9 lines not shown
 func Api() {
    taskController := controllers.NewTaskController()
    userController := controllers.NewUserController()

    facades.Route().Prefix("api/v1").Group(func(router route.Router) {
        router.Post("tasks", taskController.Store).Name("tasks.create")
        router.Get("tasks/{id}", taskController.Show)
        router.Get("tasks", taskController.Index)

+       router.Get("users", userController.Index)
        router.Get("users/{id}", userController.Show)
    })
 }

Index now answers /api/v1/users, so remove the sample's /users route from web.go:

routes/web.go

 package routes

 import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/support"

-   "taskflow/app/http/controllers"
    "taskflow/app/facades"
 )
 // ... 9 lines not shown

-   userController := controllers.NewUserController()
-   facades.Route().Get("/users", userController.Index)
-
    facades.Route().Get("hello", func(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
        return ctx.Response().Json(200, facades.Route().Info("tasks.create"))
    })
 }

Add a request for it:

requests.http

 # ... 9 lines not shown
 ### Show task
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1

 ### List tasks
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks?status=done&page=2&filters[priority]=high

+### List users
+GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users
+
 ### Show user
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users/2

 ### Hello
 GET http://localhost:3000/hello

Send List users. Here is the response, formatted:

GET /api/v1/users

[
  {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Ana",
    "email": "ana@example.com",
    "role": "manager",
    "created_tasks": null,
    "assigned_tasks": null
  },
  {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 2,
    "name": "Ben",
    "email": "ben@example.com",
    "role": "member",
    "created_tasks": null,
    "assigned_tasks": null
  },
  {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 3,
    "name": "Cleo",
    "email": "cleo@example.com",
    "role": "member",
    "created_tasks": null,
    "assigned_tasks": null
  }
]

Every list is null, which means it was not loaded. [], like Ben's created_tasks above, means it was loaded and is empty. As with Creator, reading user.AssignedTasks later does not fetch it. If you forget With, you get null and no error.

The N+1 problem

Goravel has Load, which loads a relation onto a model you already have. Calling it in a loop is a common first try. Load the assigned tasks, the work each user has to do:

app/http/controllers/user_controller.go

 // ... 15 lines not shown
 func (r *UserController) Index(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var users []models.User
    err := facades.Orm().Query().Find(&users)
    if err != nil {
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": err.Error(),
        })
    }

+   for i := range users {
+       if err := facades.Orm().Query().Load(&users[i], "AssignedTasks"); err != nil {
+           return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+               "error": err.Error(),
+           })
+       }
+   }
+
    return ctx.Response().Json(200, users)
 }

 // ... 14 lines not shown

Send List users again. It works, but look at the log:

[2026-10-23 07:50:15.892] local.info: [5.191ms] [rows:3] SELECT * FROM "users"
[2026-10-23 07:50:15.894] local.info: [1.312ms] [rows:0] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."assigned_to" = 1
[2026-10-23 07:50:15.894] local.info: [2.469ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 1
[2026-10-23 07:50:15.896] local.info: [0.738ms] [rows:3] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."assigned_to" = 2
[2026-10-23 07:50:15.896] local.info: [1.474ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 2
[2026-10-23 07:50:15.897] local.info: [0.528ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."assigned_to" = 3
[2026-10-23 07:50:15.897] local.info: [1.150ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 3

Seven queries for three users. This is called the N+1 problem. There is one query for the list, and then a separate load for each of the N users.

Here each user costs two queries, because Load reads the user again, together with their tasks. With 100 users, this would be 201 queries for one request.

Eager loading a list

Take the loop out and use With on the list, as in Relationships: Belongs To:

app/http/controllers/user_controller.go

 // ... 15 lines not shown
 func (r *UserController) Index(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var users []models.User
-   err := facades.Orm().Query().Find(&users)
+   err := facades.Orm().Query().
+       With("AssignedTasks").
+       Find(&users)
    if err != nil {
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": err.Error(),
        })
-   }
-
-   for i := range users {
-       if err := facades.Orm().Query().Load(&users[i], "AssignedTasks"); err != nil {
-           return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
-               "error": err.Error(),
-           })
-       }
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(200, users)
 }

 // ... 14 lines not shown

Send List users again. Ana has no tasks, Ben has three and Cleo has one, the same as with the loop. The log has two lines:

[2026-10-23 07:50:29.602] local.info: [1.504ms] [rows:4] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."assigned_to" IN (1,2,3)
[2026-10-23 07:50:29.602] local.info: [7.835ms] [rows:3] SELECT * FROM "users"

One query reads the users. The other reads the tasks of all of them at once, with assigned_to IN (1,2,3), and GORM hands each task to its user. It stays two queries however many users there are.

Filtered and nested loads

With can do more than load a whole relation. It can leave some rows out, and it can load relations of the loaded rows. A done task is no longer work to do, so leave done tasks out. Then load who made each task:

app/http/controllers/user_controller.go

 package controllers

 import (
    "taskflow/app/facades"
    "taskflow/app/models"

+   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/orm"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
 )

 // ... 6 lines not shown
 func (r *UserController) Index(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var users []models.User
    err := facades.Orm().Query().
-       With("AssignedTasks").
+       With("AssignedTasks", func(query orm.Query) orm.Query {
+           return query.Where("status <> ?", models.StatusDone)
+       }).
+       With("AssignedTasks.Creator").
        Find(&users)
    if err != nil {
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": err.Error(),
        })
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(200, users)
 }

 // ... 14 lines not shown
  • The function given to With filters what it loads. Here it leaves out tasks whose status is done.
  • AssignedTasks.Creator loads each task's creator too. The dot goes one relation deeper.

Send List users again. The done task, "Plan the next release", is gone, and each task has its creator.

GET /api/v1/users

[
  {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Ana",
    "email": "ana@example.com",
    "role": "manager",
    "created_tasks": null,
    "assigned_tasks": []
  },
  {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 2,
    "name": "Ben",
    "email": "ben@example.com",
    "role": "member",
    "created_tasks": null,
    "assigned_tasks": [
      {
        "created_at": null,
        "updated_at": null,
        "id": 1,
        "created_by": 1,
        "creator": {
          "created_at": null,
          "updated_at": null,
          "id": 1,
          "name": "Ana",
          "email": "ana@example.com",
          "role": "manager",
          "created_tasks": null,
          "assigned_tasks": null
        },
        "assigned_to": 2,
        "assignee": null,
        "title": "Ship v1",
        "description": "The first release",
        "status": "pending",
        "due_at": "2026-11-02 09:00:00"
      },
      ...
    ]
  },
  ...
]

Three queries this time:

[2026-10-23 07:50:47.458] local.info: [0.760ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 1
[2026-10-23 07:50:47.458] local.info: [4.612ms] [rows:3] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."assigned_to" IN (1,2,3) AND status <> 'done'
[2026-10-23 07:50:47.458] local.info: [9.377ms] [rows:3] SELECT * FROM "users"

The filter is part of the tasks query. All the tasks were made by Ana, so one more query, for user 1, loads every creator. With more creators it is still one query, using IN.

Users now load with their open tasks and who made each one, in a fixed number of queries. The test rows still have to be typed in by hand with psql.

Previous: 05. Relationships: Belongs To
Next: 07. Factories & Seeding
Series: Goravel

title: Goravel belongs to relationships and foreign keys
description:
Part 5 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-05.

TaskFlow has a users table. A task is made by one user and can be assigned to another. In this part we create the tasks table with foreign keys to users, load a task with both of its users, and keep each user's password out of the JSON.

Start from the Models & Migrations code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-04
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
docker compose up -d
go run . artisan migrate

The model

A task needs its own table, and like users it starts as a model:

$ go run . artisan make:model Task
 SUCCESS  Model created successfully

Then add the fields from the database design:

app/models/task.go

 package models

 import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/support/carbon"
 )

+type Status string
+
+const (
+   StatusPending    Status = "pending"
+   StatusInProgress Status = "in-progress"
+   StatusDone       Status = "done"
+)
+
 type Task struct {
    orm.Model
+   CreatedBy   uint  `gorm:"not null"`
+   Creator     *User `gorm:"foreignKey:CreatedBy"`
+   AssignedTo  *uint
+   Assignee    *User  `gorm:"foreignKey:AssignedTo"`
+   Title       string `gorm:"size:255;not null"`
+   Description string `gorm:"type:text;not null"`
+   Status      Status `gorm:"type:enum('pending','in-progress','done');default:'pending';not null"`
+   DueAt       *carbon.DateTime
 }

A task belongs to a user when the task row holds that user's id. Ours belongs to two users, so it has two pairs of fields:

  • CreatedBy holds the id of the user who made the task, and Creator is that user.
  • AssignedTo holds the id of the user who has to do it, and Assignee is that user.
  • Creator and Assignee are pointers, so they stay nil until we load them.
  • AssignedTo and DueAt are pointers too, because a new task may have nobody and no due date yet. As Models & Migrations showed, a pointer field gives a nullable column.
  • DueAt is a carbon.DateTime, the same type orm.Model uses for its timestamps.
  • Status has its own type with three values, like Role on the user.

The foreignKey tag tells GORM which field holds the user's id. Without it, GORM looks for a field named CreatorID (the relation name plus ID), finds none, and every load of the task fails with:

invalid field found for struct taskflow/app/models.Task's field Creator: define a valid foreign key for relations or implement the Valuer/Scanner interface

We use CreatedBy because the column in the database design is created_by.

The migration

make:migration -m only reads the models you register, as Models & Migrations showed. Add Task next to User:

bootstrap/app.go

 // ... 22 lines not shown
        WithCallback(func() {
            facades.Schema().Extend(schema.Extension{
-               Models: []any{models.User{}},
+               Models: []any{models.User{}, models.Task{}},
            })
        }).
        Create()
 }

Then generate the migration from it:

$ go run . artisan make:migration create_tasks_table -m Task
 SUCCESS  Created Migration: create_tasks_table
 SUCCESS  Migration registered successfully

This is the migration it wrote. As in Models & Migrations, yours has a different number:

database/migrations/20261023063944_create_tasks_table.go

// ... 16 lines not shown
func (r *M20261023063944CreateTasksTable) Up() error {
    if !facades.Schema().HasTable("tasks") {
        return facades.Schema().Create("tasks", func(table schema.Blueprint) {
            table.TimestampTz("created_at").Nullable()
            table.TimestampTz("updated_at").Nullable()
            table.BigIncrements("id")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("created_by")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("assigned_to").Nullable()
            table.String("title", 255)
            table.Text("description")
            table.Enum("status", []any{"pending", "in-progress", "done"}).Default("pending")
            table.TimestampTz("due_at").Nullable()
        })
    // ... 9 lines not shown

Every column is there, but there are no foreign keys. Creator and Assignee are not columns, so make:migration skips them. And despite its name, the foreignKey tag adds nothing to the table. It only tells GORM how to load the user. To stop a task from pointing at a user who does not exist, the table needs real foreign keys.

Add the two foreign keys yourself:

database/migrations/20261023063944_create_tasks_table.go

 // ... 16 lines not shown
 func (r *M20261023063944CreateTasksTable) Up() error {
    if !facades.Schema().HasTable("tasks") {
        return facades.Schema().Create("tasks", func(table schema.Blueprint) {
            table.TimestampTz("created_at").Nullable()
            table.TimestampTz("updated_at").Nullable()
            table.BigIncrements("id")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("created_by")
            table.UnsignedBigInteger("assigned_to").Nullable()
            table.String("title", 255)
            table.Text("description")
            table.Enum("status", []any{"pending", "in-progress", "done"}).Default("pending")
            table.TimestampTz("due_at").Nullable()
+
+           table.Foreign("created_by").References("id").On("users")
+           table.Foreign("assigned_to").References("id").On("users").NullOnDelete()
        })
    }

    return nil
 }

 // ... 4 lines not shown
  • created_by must be the id of a user. Postgres also refuses to delete a user who still has tasks they made. That is what Postgres does when no rule is given, so the created_by line has none. We could tell it to delete their tasks with them instead, but then deleting a user would quietly delete their work.
  • assigned_to must be the id of a user too, or empty. With NullOnDelete, when that user is deleted, the task stays and has nobody assigned.

Run the migration 

$ go run . artisan migrate
  INFO    Running migration
  INFO    Running: 20261023063944_create_tasks_table
 SUCCESS  Migration success

Only the new migration runs, in batch 2:

$ go run . artisan migrate:status
  Migration name .............................................. Batch / Status
  20210101000002_create_jobs_table ................................... [1] Ran
  20261022221906_create_users_table .................................. [1] Ran
  20261023063944_create_tasks_table .................................. [2] Ran

db:table lists the foreign keys at the end:

$ go run . artisan db:table tasks
  public.tasks ...............................................................
  Columns .................................................................. 9
  Size .............................................................. 0.016 MB
  Column ................................................................ Type
  created_at timestamptz, nullable ............... timestamp(0) with time zone
  updated_at timestamptz, nullable ............... timestamp(0) with time zone
  id autoincrement, int8 ............ nextval('tasks_id_seq'::regclass) bigint
  created_by int8 ..................................................... bigint
  assigned_to int8, nullable .......................................... bigint
  title varchar ....................................... character varying(255)
  description text ...................................................... text
  status varchar ......... 'pending'::character varying character varying(255)
  due_at timestamptz, nullable ................... timestamp(0) with time zone
  Index ......................................................................
  tasks_pkey id ....................................... btree, unique, primary
  Foreign Key .......................................... On Update / On Delete
  tasks_assigned_to_foreign assigned_to references id on users  no action / set null
  tasks_created_by_foreign created_by references id on users  no action / no action
  • set null comes from NullOnDelete.
  • no action is the default.
  • created_by and assigned_to are bigint, not unsigned, because Postgres has no unsigned numbers.

Test data

TaskFlow has no endpoint that saves tasks yet, so add two users and two tasks with psql:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO users (name, email, password, role) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com', 'x', 'manager'), ('Ben', 'ben@example.com', 'x', 'member');"
INSERT 0 2
$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO tasks (created_by, assigned_to, title, description, due_at) VALUES (1, 2, 'Ship v1', 'The first release', '2026-11-02 09:00:00+00'), (1, NULL, 'Write the docs', 'Nobody has it yet', NULL);"
INSERT 0 2

Ana made both tasks. Ship v1 is assigned to Ben, and Write the docs has nobody yet. The password x is only a placeholder until we build register and login.

Now check that the foreign keys work. First, add a task made by user 99, who does not exist:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO tasks (created_by, title, description) VALUES (99, 'Ghost', 'No such user');"
ERROR:  insert or update on table "tasks" violates foreign key constraint "tasks_created_by_foreign"
DETAIL:  Key (created_by)=(99) is not present in table "users".

Then try to delete Ana, who still has tasks:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1;"
ERROR:  update or delete on table "users" violates foreign key constraint "tasks_created_by_foreign" on table "tasks"
DETAIL:  Key (id)=(1) is still referenced from table "tasks".

Finding a row with Find

Show, the handler from Reading Request Data, only returns the id. Make it read the task from Postgres:

app/http/controllers/task_controller.go

 package controllers

 import (
+   "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/models"
+
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/http"
 )

 // ... 26 lines not shown
 func (r *TaskController) Show(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
-   id := ctx.Request().RouteInt("id")
+   var task models.Task
+   err := facades.Orm().Query().Find(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
+   if err != nil {
+       return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
+           "error": err.Error(),
+       })
+   }

-   return ctx.Response().Json(200, map[string]any{
-       "id": id,
-   })
+   return ctx.Response().Json(200, task)
 }

 // ... 11 lines not shown

Find reads the row with that id into task. If the query itself fails, Show answers 500 with the error. Sending err.Error() to the client is fine while we build, but it can show table and column names. We replace it when we build the task endpoints.

In requests.http, change the show request to task 1:

requests.http

 # ... 8 lines not shown

 ### Show task
-GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/5
+GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks/1

 ### List tasks
 GET http://localhost:3000/api/v1/tasks?status=done&page=2&filters[priority]=high

 ### Hello
 GET http://localhost:3000/hello

If air is not running, start it, as in Routing & Responses. Then send Show task from requests.http. Here is the response, formatted:

GET /api/v1/tasks/1

{
  "created_at": null,
  "updated_at": null,
  "id": 1,
  "CreatedBy": 1,
  "Creator": null,
  "AssignedTo": 2,
  "Assignee": null,
  "Title": "Ship v1",
  "Description": "The first release",
  "Status": "pending",
  "DueAt": "2026-11-02 09:00:00"
}

The ids are there, but Creator and Assignee are null. Goravel never loads a related model unless you ask for it. Unlike Laravel, reading task.Creator later does not fetch the user. It stays nil.

The timestamps are null too. Goravel fills them when it saves a row, and these rows came from psql.

Ask for a task that does not exist, like /tasks/9, and Find returns no error. You get 200 OK and a task full of zeros. We turn that into a 404 when we build the task endpoints.

Eager loading with With

With tells the query to load a relation along with the task. This is called eager loading:

app/http/controllers/task_controller.go

 // ... 35 lines not shown
 func (r *TaskController) Show(ctx http.Context) http.Response {
    var task models.Task
-   err := facades.Orm().Query().Find(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
+   err := facades.Orm().Query().
+       With("Creator").
+       With("Assignee").
+       Find(&task, ctx.Request().RouteInt("id"))
    if err != nil {
        return ctx.Response().Json(500, map[string]any{
            "error": err.Error(),
        })
    }

    return ctx.Response().Json(200, task)
 }

 // ... 11 lines not shown

The name in With("Creator") is the field name, not the column name. GORM reads CreatedBy from the task and loads that user. Run the request again:

GET /api/v1/tasks/1

{
  "created_at": null,
  "updated_at": null,
  "id": 1,
  "CreatedBy": 1,
  "Creator": {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 1,
    "Name": "Ana",
    "Email": "ana@example.com",
    "Password": "x",
    "Role": "manager"
  },
  "AssignedTo": 2,
  "Assignee": {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 2,
    "Name": "Ben",
    "Email": "ben@example.com",
    "Password": "x",
    "Role": "member"
  },
  "Title": "Ship v1",
  "Description": "The first release",
  "Status": "pending",
  "DueAt": "2026-11-02 09:00:00"
}

Both users are there, and so are their passwords. Here they are x, but once real password hashes are stored, anyone who asks for a task would get them.

The keys are mixed, too. id and created_at are lowercase, but Title and CreatedBy are not. orm.Model gives its fields JSON names, and our fields have none, so Go uses the field name as it is.

JSON field names

A json tag sets the name a field gets in the JSON, and json:"-" leaves the field out. Add them to the user:

app/models/user.go

 // ... 14 lines not shown
    orm.Model
-   Name     string `gorm:"size:255;not null"`
-   Email    string `gorm:"size:255;unique;not null"`
-   Password string `gorm:"size:255;not null"`
-   Role     Role   `gorm:"type:enum('manager','member');default:'member';not null"`
+   Name     string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"name"`
+   Email    string `gorm:"size:255;unique;not null" json:"email"`
+   Password string `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"-"`
+   Role     Role   `gorm:"type:enum('manager','member');default:'member';not null" json:"role"`
 }

And to the task:

app/models/task.go

 // ... 15 lines not shown
 type Task struct {
    orm.Model
-   CreatedBy   uint  `gorm:"not null"`
-   Creator     *User `gorm:"foreignKey:CreatedBy"`
-   AssignedTo  *uint
-   Assignee    *User  `gorm:"foreignKey:AssignedTo"`
-   Title       string `gorm:"size:255;not null"`
-   Description string `gorm:"type:text;not null"`
-   Status      Status `gorm:"type:enum('pending','in-progress','done');default:'pending';not null"`
-   DueAt       *carbon.DateTime
+   CreatedBy   uint             `gorm:"not null" json:"created_by"`
+   Creator     *User            `gorm:"foreignKey:CreatedBy" json:"creator"`
+   AssignedTo  *uint            `json:"assigned_to"`
+   Assignee    *User            `gorm:"foreignKey:AssignedTo" json:"assignee"`
+   Title       string           `gorm:"size:255;not null" json:"title"`
+   Description string           `gorm:"type:text;not null" json:"description"`
+   Status      Status           `gorm:"type:enum('pending','in-progress','done');default:'pending';not null" json:"status"`
+   DueAt       *carbon.DateTime `json:"due_at"`
 }

The gorm tags stay as they were, so the table does not change. Run the request again:

GET /api/v1/tasks/1

{
  "created_at": null,
  "updated_at": null,
  "id": 1,
  "created_by": 1,
  "creator": {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Ana",
    "email": "ana@example.com",
    "role": "manager"
  },
  "assigned_to": 2,
  "assignee": {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 2,
    "name": "Ben",
    "email": "ben@example.com",
    "role": "member"
  },
  "title": "Ship v1",
  "description": "The first release",
  "status": "pending",
  "due_at": "2026-11-02 09:00:00"
}

Every key is lowercase, and the passwords are gone.

The query log

APP_DEBUG is true in your .env, so Goravel writes every query it runs to a log file named after the day. Watch it in a second terminal, then send the request again:

$ tail -f storage/logs/goravel-$(date +%F).log
[2026-10-23 06:40:35.843] local.info: [1.498ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 2
[2026-10-23 06:40:35.844] local.info: [0.726ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 1
[2026-10-23 06:40:35.844] local.info: [7.740ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."id" = 1

Three queries: one for the task, and one for each With. The task query runs first, but its line comes last, because Goravel writes a line when a query finishes and the task query waits for its users.

Ask for task 2, which has nobody assigned:

GET /api/v1/tasks/2

{
  "created_at": null,
  "updated_at": null,
  "id": 2,
  "created_by": 1,
  "creator": {
    "created_at": null,
    "updated_at": null,
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Ana",
    "email": "ana@example.com",
    "role": "manager"
  },
  "assigned_to": null,
  "assignee": null,
  "title": "Write the docs",
  "description": "Nobody has it yet",
  "status": "pending",
  "due_at": null
}

The log gets two new lines:

[2026-10-23 06:40:36.885] local.info: [0.475ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "users"."id" = 1
[2026-10-23 06:40:36.885] local.info: [2.427ms] [rows:1] SELECT * FROM "tasks" WHERE "tasks"."id" = 2

Two queries this time. With only runs a query when there is an id to look up.

A task now loads with both of its users, and no password leaves the API. A user can't list their own tasks yet.
