title: Goravel models and migrations with Postgres
description:
Part 4 of the Goravel series. The original on DevChalk has the colour-matched code, the figures and the full diffs. Code for this part: krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow/tree/part-04.

TaskFlow reads requests, but it has nowhere to keep anything yet. In this part we create the users table from the database design. We write a model, and Goravel writes the migration from it.

Start from the Reading Request Data code:

git clone https://github.com/krishankumar01/goravel-taskflow
cd goravel-taskflow
git checkout part-03
cp .env.example .env
go run . artisan key:generate
docker compose up -d

The model

A model is a Go struct that stands for one table. Create one for users:

$ go run . artisan make:model User
 SUCCESS  Model created successfully

This creates app/models/user.go:

app/models/user.go

package models

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
)

type User struct {
    orm.Model
}

orm.Model gives every model an id and two timestamps: when the row was created and when it was last updated. Goravel fills the timestamps for you when a row is saved. A model named User uses a table named users.

Now add the fields from the design:

app/models/user.go

 package models

 import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/database/orm"
 )

+type Role string
+
+const (
+   RoleManager Role = "manager"
+   RoleMember  Role = "member"
+)
+
 type User struct {
    orm.Model
+   Name     string `gorm:"size:255;not null"`
+   Email    string `gorm:"size:255;unique;not null"`
+   Password string `gorm:"size:255;not null"`
+   Role     Role   `gorm:"type:enum('manager','member');default:'member';not null"`
 }
  • Email is unique, so two users can never share an email.
  • Role has its own type with two values, manager and member. If no role is given, the database uses member.
  • In code you write models.RoleManager instead of the string "manager". If you mistype RoleManager, the build fails and tells you. If you mistype "manager", it builds fine and the bug shows up later.

The GORM tags after each field describe its column: size:255 is the maximum length, and not null says it must have a value. Password will hold a hashed password, never the real one. We hash it when we build register and login.

Goravel does not create or change tables from these tags while the app runs. The tags only matter when make:migration reads them to write a migration.

Other tags make:migration understands:

Here is a model that tries a different tag on each field. It is only an example, so do not add it to TaskFlow:

app/models/probe.go

type Probe struct {
    orm.Model
    Title  string  `gorm:"size:100"`
    Body   string  `gorm:"type:text"`
    Nick   *string `gorm:"size:50"`
    Points int     `gorm:"default:0"`
    Done   bool    `gorm:"default:false"`
    Code   string  `gorm:"size:20;uniqueIndex"`
    Status string  `gorm:"size:20;index"`
    Note   string  `gorm:"size:255;comment:shown to the user"`
    DueAt  *string `gorm:"column:due_on;size:10"`
    Price  float64 `gorm:"type:decimal;precision:10;scale:2"`
    Meta   string  `gorm:"migration:json"`
}

And what make:migration -m Probe wrote for it:

return facades.Schema().Create("probes", func(table schema.Blueprint) {
    table.TimestampTz("created_at").Nullable()
    table.TimestampTz("updated_at").Nullable()
    table.BigIncrements("id")
    table.String("title", 100)
    table.Text("body")
    table.String("nick", 50).Nullable()
    table.BigInteger("points").Default(0)
    table.Boolean("done").Default(false)
    table.String("code", 20)
    table.String("status", 20)
    table.String("note", 255).Comment("shown to the user")
    table.String("due_on", 10).Nullable()
    table.Decimal("price").Places(2).Total(10)
    table.Json("meta")

    table.Unique("code").Name("idx_probes_code")
    table.Index("status").Name("idx_probes_status")
})
  • A pointer field, like *string, makes a column nullable. Every other column is not null, with or without a not null tag.
  • Give a decimal its size with precision and scale. If you write type:decimal(10,2) instead, the size is lost.
  • uniqueIndex works like unique, but the index is named idx_<table>_<column> instead of <table>_<column>_unique.
  • migration: takes the name of a schema builder method, so migration:json calls table.Json.

The migration

A migration is a Go file with two methods: Up makes a change to the database, and Down undoes it. You could create the table by hand in Postgres, but then it would only exist on your machine. A migration lives in the project with the code, so every copy of TaskFlow gets the same table.

Goravel can write that file for you from the model. -m User tells it which model to read. If you run it now, it fails:

$ go run . artisan make:migration create_users_table -m User
ERROR   create migration failed: model User not found in registered models

Goravel only knows the models you tell it about, because Go cannot look up a type by its name while the program runs. Register User in bootstrap/app.go:

bootstrap/app.go

 package bootstrap

 import (
+   "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/schema"
    contractsfoundation "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/foundation"
    "github.com/goravel/framework/foundation"

+   "taskflow/app/facades"
+   "taskflow/app/models"
    "taskflow/config"
    "taskflow/routes"
 )

 func Boot() contractsfoundation.Application {
    return foundation.Setup().
        WithMigrations(Migrations).
        // ... 4 lines not shown
        WithProviders(Providers).
        WithConfig(config.Boot).
+       WithCallback(func() {
+           facades.Schema().Extend(schema.Extension{
+               Models: []any{models.User{}},
+           })
+       }).
        Create()
 }

WithCallback takes a function that runs during startup, after the facades are ready. Inside it, Extend adds User to the models Goravel knows. Run the command again:

$ go run . artisan make:migration create_users_table -m User
SUCCESS  Created Migration: create_users_table
 SUCCESS  Migration registered successfully

It writes the migration and adds it to the list in bootstrap/migrations.go. The file name, the struct and the signature include the time you ran the command, so yours will have a different number:

bootstrap/migrations.go

 // ... 8 lines not shown
 func Migrations() []schema.Migration {
    return []schema.Migration{
        &migrations.M20210101000001CreateJobsTable{},
+       &migrations.M20261022221906CreateUsersTable{},
    }
 }

This is what Goravel wrote:

database/migrations/20261022221906_create_users_table.go

package migrations

import (
    "github.com/goravel/framework/contracts/database/schema"

    "taskflow/app/facades"
)

type M20261022221906CreateUsersTable struct{}

// Signature The unique signature for the migration.
func (r *M20261022221906CreateUsersTable) Signature() string {
    return "20261022221906_create_users_table"
}

// Up Run the migrations.
func (r *M20261022221906CreateUsersTable) Up() error {
    if !facades.Schema().HasTable("users") {
        return facades.Schema().Create("users", func(table schema.Blueprint) {
            table.TimestampTz("created_at").Nullable()
            table.TimestampTz("updated_at").Nullable()
            table.BigIncrements("id")
            table.String("name", 255)
            table.String("email", 255)
            table.String("password", 255)
            table.Enum("role", []any{"manager", "member"}).Default("member")

            table.Unique("email")
        })
    }

    return nil
}

// Down Reverse the migrations.
func (r *M20261022221906CreateUsersTable) Down() error {
    return facades.Schema().DropIfExists("users")
}

Up only creates the table if it is not there yet, and Down drops it.

Every column comes from the model:

  • created_at, updated_at and id come from orm.Model.
  • The unique email became table.Unique("email").
  • The role became table.Enum, with member as its default.

Only the two timestamps have Nullable(). Every other column is not null already, so the not null tags change nothing here. They only matter on a pointer field, which would otherwise be nullable. We keep them because they show that each column needs a value.

Run the migration

If Postgres is not running, start it with docker compose up -d. Then run the migrations:

$ go run . artisan migrate
  INFO    Running migration
  INFO    Running: 20210101000002_create_jobs_table
  INFO    Running: 20261022221906_create_users_table
 SUCCESS  Migration success

The jobs migration runs too. It came with the Queue facade we picked when we created the project, and it creates two tables, jobs and failed_jobs. Our queue runs on Redis, so it never uses jobs, but Goravel still records failed jobs in failed_jobs.

Its file and struct say 20210101000001, but it reports itself as 20210101000002. That is in the file Goravel generated, and it does no harm.

To see what has run:

$ go run . artisan migrate:status
  Migration name .............................................. Batch / Status
  20210101000002_create_jobs_table ................................... [1] Ran
  20261022221906_create_users_table .................................. [1] Ran

Each migrate run is one batch, numbered one higher than the last. Both of ours ran in batch 1. To see the table itself:

$ go run . artisan db:table users
  public.users ...............................................................
  Columns .................................................................. 7
  Size .............................................................. 0.023 MB
  Column ................................................................ Type
  created_at timestamptz, nullable ............... timestamp(0) with time zone
  updated_at timestamptz, nullable ............... timestamp(0) with time zone
  id autoincrement, int8 ............ nextval('users_id_seq'::regclass) bigint
  name varchar ........................................ character varying(255)
  email varchar ....................................... character varying(255)
  password varchar .................................... character varying(255)
  role varchar ............ 'member'::character varying character varying(255)
  Index ......................................................................
  users_email_unique email ..................................... btree, unique
  users_pkey id ....................................... btree, unique, primary

Gotcha db:table says role is varchar, not an enum. On Postgres, Goravel stores an enum as a varchar column with a check that only lets the allowed values in. Try a role that is not allowed:

$ docker compose exec postgres psql -U goravel -d taskflow \
    -c "INSERT INTO users (name, email, password, role) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com', 'x', 'admin');"
ERROR:  new row for relation "users" violates check constraint "users_role_check"

Rolling back a migration

When a migration is wrong, you roll it back, fix it, and run it again. migrate:rollback runs Down for the last batch:

$ go run . artisan migrate:rollback
  INFO    Rolling back migration
  INFO    Rolled back: 20261022221906_create_users_table
  INFO    Rolled back: 20210101000002_create_jobs_table
 SUCCESS  Migration rollback success

Both migrations were undone, not only the users one. A rollback undoes the whole last batch, and both migrations ran in batch 1. migrate:status now shows both as pending:

$ go run . artisan migrate:status
  Migration name .............................................. Batch / Status
  20210101000002_create_jobs_table ................................... Pending
  20261022221906_create_users_table .................................. Pending

To undo only the last migration, add --step=1.

Run migrate again and both are back:

$ go run . artisan migrate
  INFO    Running migration
  INFO    Running: 20210101000002_create_jobs_table
  INFO    Running: 20261022221906_create_users_table
 SUCCESS  Migration success

TaskFlow now has a users table, created from its model. There is no table for tasks yet.

title: 5 Ways Node.js Teams Reconstruct Marketplace Failure Alerts from Malformed JSON
description:
A malformed JSON response should become a structured failure event, not a second incident. For a marketplace AI agent loop, my decision rule is simple: validate at the boundary, preserve the raw response safely, and attach a traceable context record before the failure alert is emitted. Then compare tools by one question: can the team reconstruct what happened from the evidence it actually retained?

The experiment below uses the same five failure cases in every system: invalid JSON, a valid object with the wrong shape, a timeout, a provider error, and a response with a missing trace identifier. Pass means an engineer can identify the request, agent step, model choice, latency, and cost context without guessing. Fail means the alert only says “JSON parse failed.”

Start with the boundary.

Which observability option fits the reconstruction job?

Option Pick this when Boundary to test
OpenTelemetry plus your backend You want portable signals and control over where logs and traces land Define the log attributes and correlation convention yourself
Sentry The dominant question is which application errors need grouping and triage Check that malformed responses keep useful request metadata without becoming one noisy issue
Datadog You want a managed observability workspace spanning logs, metrics, and alerts Verify that the retained fields support a replay of the agent step, not just a count
REST observability API You want a plain REST surface for error capture and log lookup, and you are willing to build notification polling around it Confirm the discovery-described request schema, then test error metadata and log correlation

OpenTelemetry is the strongest starting point when portability is the primary constraint. Sentry is a natural fit when error grouping and developer triage dominate. Datadog suits a team that prefers a broad managed platform. Infrai is a practical leg for a small reproducible comparison when one REST API is easier to wire than another SDK: its public discovery surface describes capabilities, JSON schemas, billing, and runnable examples. That self-description makes the integration experiment inspectable before an API key is involved.

A second, concrete advantage is scope: Infrai puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key. For this experiment, that means the same credential can cover the error, log, and metric legs instead of making the fixture runner coordinate separate observability credentials. It reduces setup friction, not the evidence standard.

There is a hard boundary. The REST option has no alert or notification routes, so it cannot by itself page a person when a threshold is crossed; poll its free query APIs and own the notification step. It also exposes trace_id and span_id as correlating fields rather than a distributed trace tree.

What should the evidence record contain?

Think of the pipeline as a small chain: response bytes -> schema decision -> structured log -> error event -> query -> human alert. If one link drops context, the later dashboard cannot recreate it.

For each agent step, record an operation name, request_id, trace_id, span_id, marketplace order or session identifier where policy permits, provider and model identifiers, started_at, latency_ms, cost_usd when available, response status, validation result, and a bounded response fingerprint. Do not put secrets or an unbounded raw response into an alert. Keep the raw payload in a controlled store if the investigation requires it.

The schema check has two jobs. It rejects malformed syntax early, and it distinguishes syntactically valid JSON from the wrong contract. Those are different failures and deserve different grouping keys. A useful grouping key includes operation plus validation class; otherwise one bad provider payload can hide a missing field regression.

What debugging practices help with malformed JSON response failure pipelines?

Start with deterministic fixtures. I would use five JSON strings and run them through the same parser and schema validator on every candidate backend. The test is deliberately boring. Boring is good here.

type ValidationClass = "invalid_json" | "wrong_shape" | "valid";

type Context = {
  operation: string;
  requestId: string;
  traceId: string;
  spanId: string;
  model: string;
  latencyMs: number;
  costUsd?: number;
};

function classify(body: string): ValidationClass {
  try {
    const value: unknown = JSON.parse(body);
    if (!value || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) return "wrong_shape";
    if (!("output" in value)) return "wrong_shape";
    return "valid";
  } catch {
    return "invalid_json";
  }
}

export function makeFailureRecord(body: string, context: Context) {
  const validation = classify(body);
  return {
    ...context,
    event: "agent_response_validation",
    validation,
    ok: validation === "valid",
    responseFingerprint: Buffer.from(body).toString("base64url").slice(0, 24),
  };
}

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function findErrors() {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/errors/search`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "1");
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, retryAfter * 1000));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Error search failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    return response.json();
  }
  throw new Error("Error search rate limit did not clear after retries");
}

findErrors().then(console.log).catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

The fixture runner should assert three things for each case: the class is correct, the correlation fields survive serialization, and the record is searchable by its request context. For the REST leg, inspect the public discovery document first. The observability group includes error capture and log search, but the logs.search and metrics.query filter parameters are not declared in discovery, so the test must use the currently described schema rather than guessing a query shape. Use the documented error-capture surface with specific metadata, and use the available error-search route to verify that the event can be found.

This is where an API that describes itself earns its place. A new capability can be explored from one discovery response and its runnable example instead of starting with a private SDK abstraction. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: the same request can carry the metadata needed to compare latency and cost across agent steps. Treat both as hypotheses in the experiment, not as a conclusion.

What counts as a pass?

Run the five fixtures through each candidate and score the result with a strict rule: four of five cases must be reconstructable, and the missing-trace case must be visible as a data-quality failure rather than silently accepted. A tie goes to the system that preserves context with fewer application-specific adapters. A failure on notification delivery is scored separately, because a backend that stores excellent evidence may still need a polling worker and an external notifier.

For a marketplace loop, add one latency and cost check. Compare the recorded latency_ms and cost_usd fields with the agent step identifier, then inspect the sequence around the malformed response. Do not claim that the test measures uptime, vendor latency, or savings; it measures evidence completeness under controlled inputs.

Limits that change the decision

Sentry or Datadog is the better choice when managed alerting, notification workflows, or a mature trace UI are non-negotiable. OpenTelemetry is the better choice when avoiding backend coupling matters more than a quick hosted workflow. Infrai is worth trying for the error-capture and log-correlation leg when a self-describing REST API and runnable examples reduce integration friction, but the team must supply notification polling and must accept field-level correlation instead of a span tree. The trade-off is explicit: it is not suitable as the sole paging system or as a replacement for a distributed-trace backend.

The sharpest practical lesson is small: preserve context before you parse, and classify the parse result before you alert. If this boundary fits your system, start with the documentation and reproduce the fixture test against every serious option.

References

  • OpenTelemetry: Logs signal concepts
  • OpenTelemetry documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: Building a Self-Hosted AI Security Triage System with FastAPI and Async Streaming
description:
Why I Started Looking at beenuar/AiSOC

When our SOC team complained about false positive fatigue (95% of alerts ignored), I needed an LLM-powered triage layer that could run internally without shipping sensitive logs to external APIs. After evaluating commercial SOAR platforms and their vendor lock-in, I tested beenuar/AiSOC—a self-hosted alert fusion system built entirely on FastAPI with async streaming.

The architectural promise: ingest raw alerts, run multi-agent investigation chains against MITRE ATT&CK, and stream decision reasoning back to analysts in real-time via Server-Sent Events. All while keeping alert payloads inside our VPC.

Core Architecture: AsyncIO Event Loop as the Orchestration Backbone

AiSOC's backend is a FastAPI application with async generators powering the investigation pipeline. Here's the streaming endpoint pattern I extracted:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

async def investigate_alert_stream(alert_id: str):
    """Async generator yielding SSE-formatted investigation steps."""
    # Phase 1: Fetch alert context from DB (async)
    alert = await fetch_alert_async(alert_id)
    yield f"data: {{\"phase\": \"context\", \"alert_id\": \"{alert_id}\"}}\n\n"

    # Phase 2: Query MITRE ATT&CK tactics (async HTTP client)
    tactics = await query_mitre_async(alert.ioc_list)
    yield f"data: {{\"phase\": \"mitre\", \"tactics\": {len(tactics)}}}\n\n"

    # Phase 3: LLM agent reasoning (streaming tokens)
    async for token in llm_agent_stream(alert, tactics):
        yield f"data: {{\"token\": \"{token}\"}}\n\n"

    yield "data: {\"phase\": \"complete\"}\n\n"

@app.get("/investigate/{alert_id}")
async def stream_investigation(alert_id: str):
    return StreamingResponse(
        investigate_alert_stream(alert_id),
        media_type="text/event-stream"
    )

This pattern is production-grade—no blocking calls, every I/O operation awaits, and the client sees incremental progress instead of a 60-second spinner.

The Connection Pool Trap I Hit Immediately

When load testing with 50 concurrent alert investigations, the service froze after 10 requests. Root cause: AiSOC's default PostgreSQL async driver (asyncpg) was configured with a 10-connection pool, but each investigation spawned 3 concurrent DB queries without releasing connections properly.

The fix required explicit connection lifecycle management:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def get_db_connection():
    conn = await db_pool.acquire()
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        await db_pool.release(conn)

async def fetch_alert_async(alert_id: str):
    async with get_db_connection() as conn:
        return await conn.fetchrow(
            "SELECT * FROM alerts WHERE id = $1", alert_id
        )

After this change, connection pool exhaustion disappeared. The moral: async doesn't magically handle resource cleanup—you still need context managers.

Pydantic v2 for Alert Schema Validation

AiSOC ingests alerts from 8 different SIEM vendors, each with slightly broken JSON schemas. I extended the alert models with Pydantic v2 field validators:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
from typing import Optional
from datetime import datetime

class AlertPayload(BaseModel):
    alert_id: str
    timestamp: datetime
    severity: int = Field(ge=1, le=5)
    source_ip: Optional[str] = None

    @field_validator('source_ip')
    @classmethod
    def validate_ip_format(cls, v: Optional[str]) -> Optional[str]:
        if v and not v.replace('.', '').isdigit():
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid IP format: {v}")
        return v

    @field_validator('timestamp', mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def parse_timestamp(cls, v):
        if isinstance(v, str):
            return datetime.fromisoformat(v.replace('Z', '+00:00'))
        return v

Pydantic v2's mode='before' validator lets you normalize messy vendor timestamps before the model even attempts type coercion. This caught 12% of malformed alerts that would have silently corrupted the decision ledger.

LLM Agent Routing: Where B-Lost Fits

AiSOC supports pluggable LLM backends (OpenAI, Anthropic, local Ollama). In my test deployment, I routed all agent queries through B-Lost's multi-provider relay (https://b-lost.com/v1) to benchmark failover latency across Claude/GPT-4/Gemini:

import httpx

async def llm_agent_stream(alert, tactics):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(
        base_url="https://b-lost.com/v1",
        timeout=30.0
    ) as client:
        response = await client.post(
            "/chat/completions",
            json={
                "model": "claude-sonnet-3-5",
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Analyze: {alert}"}],
                "stream": True
            },
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}
        )
        async for line in response.aiter_lines():
            if line.startswith("data: "):
                yield parse_sse_token(line)

When the primary Claude endpoint hit rate limits, B-Lost's automatic fallback to GPT-4 added only 40ms to TTFT (time-to-first-token). No manual retry logic needed—the gateway handled provider rotation transparently.

The Decision Ledger: Replayable Agent Execution

AiSOC's killer feature is its append-only decision ledger—every agent step (tool call, reasoning trace, MITRE mapping) gets written to a SQLite/Postgres table with microsecond timestamps. This makes post-incident reviews trivial:

SELECT 
    step_id,
    agent_name,
    action_type,
    reasoning_trace,
    timestamp
FROM decision_ledger
WHERE alert_id = 'INC-2024-0312'
ORDER BY timestamp ASC;

You can replay the entire investigation flow, see which agent made the wrong call, and retrain your prompt templates. It's like distributed tracing for AI reasoning.

The Async/Sync Boundary You Cannot Cross

One footgun I stepped on: AiSOC's MCP server (for Claude Desktop integration) runs in a separate sync thread. When I tried calling an async alert ingestion endpoint from the MCP handler, the event loop blocked indefinitely.

The workaround required asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe:

import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)

def sync_mcp_handler(alert_data):
    # Running in sync MCP thread
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    future = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(
        ingest_alert_async(alert_data),
        loop
    )
    return future.result(timeout=10)

This is fragile—if the main event loop dies, the MCP thread hangs forever. A proper fix would decouple MCP into its own async service, but that's a larger refactor.

What I Still Don't Trust

After two weeks of testing, three concerns remain:

  1. Memory leaks in long-running agent chains: Investigation sessions that spawn 50+ LLM calls show 200MB memory growth that never gets GC'd. Suspect unclosed httpx client sessions somewhere.
  2. MITRE ATT&CK dataset staleness: The bundled tactics JSON is 8 months old. No auto-update mechanism exists.
  3. No circuit breaker for LLM failures: If the agent LLM backend times out 3 times in a row, AiSOC should abort the investigation and alert a human. Right now it retries indefinitely.

How are you handling cascading LLM failures in production agent systems? Do you fail fast or keep retrying with exponential backoff until a human intervenes?

title: Haiku 5.5 now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
description:
A new Anthropic model is now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. With Haiku 5.5, all three Claude 5.5 models are now available in Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US).

Claude Haiku 5.5 is the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family. It's a clear step up from Claude Haiku 4.5, built for work that runs in large volumes and needs quick responses. Developers can use it to summarize and compact long context, classify and route requests, process text in bulk, and make small, targeted edits across many files. It also works well as a review subagent that runs in parallel, while Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 take on harder planning and coding work. Haiku 5.5 uses adaptive thinking across five effort levels from low to max, with medium as the default. It's available with a 1M context window and a 0.06x credit multiplier. Requests over 100K tokens are billed at a 0.3x multiplier.

title: Event Notification Infrastructure Compare: 4 Email and SMS API Boundaries
description:
Short answer: use a direct email/SMS API when your backend owns the notification decision, retry policy, suppression list, and report; use Customer.io or Braze when those decisions need a live, multi-step engagement workflow. The integration boundary matters more than the logo.

For a developer-tools team handling bounces and invalid recipients across the US and EU, I would start with a narrow provider contract, keep recipient state in the application, and treat every provider event as something to reconcile. A single REST surface can reduce integration effort, but it does not decide where data is processed, how long it is retained, or which processor agreement covers the message. Those are still operating decisions.

Infrai fits this narrow slice when the application wants one REST contract and one key across backend capabilities, while its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples without a key. That can reduce adapter work during an integration, but it does not move the data-handling boundary out of the provider review.

The page is the boundary.

Should you compare email APIs for event notification infrastructure?

A bounce is not a delivery strategy. It is a signal that should change the next send. The useful incident question is not “did the API return 200?” It is “what page fired, and what recipient state did we persist before the next retry?”

For an event such as a failed build, password reset request, or quota warning, the backend should create a durable notification record with an application event ID, channel, recipient, and policy decision. It should suppress an address after a permanent email failure, avoid sending SMS to a known-invalid destination, and make a retry safe when the worker is restarted. A provider request that succeeds before the worker loses its connection is exactly why this state belongs in your system.

Do not infer.

This is where the options separate:

Option Good fit Boundary to verify
A focused email API such as Resend Transactional email with a small application-owned workflow Email delivery events, suppression behavior, and regional processing terms
A direct SMS API such as Twilio SMS delivery and channel-specific controls Country rules, fraud controls, sender requirements, and retention terms
Customer.io Segments and event-driven customer messaging Vendor-managed orchestration, data residency, and the event model you must export or delete
Braze Larger engagement programs with coordinated journeys More platform-owned state, processor boundaries, and operational configuration
OneSignal Push-oriented notification programs Push-provider relationships, consent state, and whether email/SMS are first-class for the workflow

These are different products, not five interchangeable price rows. Resend keeps the email surface focused. Twilio is a direct communications provider with a broad SMS operating problem. Customer.io and Braze are engagement systems, so their value begins where application-owned rules become a workflow. OneSignal is a reasonable comparison when push belongs in the same product decision, but it is not a substitute for an email/SMS suppression design merely because it also sends notifications.

There are more focused email alternatives worth putting on the sheet. SendGrid is a broader email platform, Postmark is aimed at transactional delivery, and Mailgun is another API-centered email option. Their fit depends on the controls and processing terms your review requires; the point is to compare the boundary and event model, not to declare a universal winner.

Why are region and retention part of the API decision?

Because recipient data crosses a boundary before a message reaches a mailbox or handset. “US and EU” is not a deployment checkbox. You need to know which service receives the address or phone number, which processor handles the send, what delivery metadata comes back, and how deletion propagates through provider records and your own event log.

A direct API can make the call path small. It cannot turn that path into a contractual residency guarantee. The current email capability does not make a domestic-vendor pending state a basis for China compliance, and the service does not provide an SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. SMS geographic anti-abuse fences and per-country circuit breakers remain business-layer controls.

I also would not promise a clean event stream where the contract only gives polling. The email and SMS namespaces have no webhook event pushes; event state is read back. That is workable for reconciliation, but less immediate than a Customer.io or Braze-style workflow that reacts to events as part of an orchestration system. If a fallback must happen within seconds, define the polling interval, the duplicate rule, and the maximum stale state you accept before choosing a specialist workflow product.

The same discipline applies to deletion. Keep only the provider identifiers and delivery facts needed for reconciliation, put a retention deadline on raw payloads, and make a delete request cover the application record, suppression record, queued work, and exported logs. A provider delete operation is one leg of that process, not proof that every copy is gone.

That distinction gets uncomfortable during an incident: a provider event can tell you what happened to a message, while your own log can still expose the address, phone number, template variables, and internal event name. The deletion checklist therefore has to name each storage surface, including dead-letter queues, tracing attributes, exported CSVs, and the reconciliation cursor. The API integration is the easy line in the diagram; proving that an old recipient cannot be selected again is the operational work.

The four-step implementation runbook

First, define the application contract. Normalize an event into an immutable ID, select a channel, and record why the recipient is eligible. Store a suppression reason such as hard_bounce, invalid_number, or manual_block; do not infer a permanent failure from a transient timeout.

Second, make the worker idempotent. Use the event ID plus channel as the deduplication key, and persist the decision before sending. A retry after an ambiguous network error should be able to ask the database whether the send was accepted. Provider-side idempotency helps, but it does not replace a consumer-side record.

Third, reconcile delivery state by polling the event surface. There are no webhook event pushes in either namespace, so the reconciler needs a cursor or time window, a bounded retry schedule, and a metric for state age. Do not page on a dashboard that is merely green; page on the condition that changes user impact, such as a growing unreconciled set or a suppression write that failed.

Fourth, verify deletion and rollback. Before launch, create a test recipient, produce a known invalid-recipient path, confirm suppression prevents a second send, and remove the test data from both application storage and provider-side records. Roll back by disabling the channel policy, not by replaying the queue. A rollback that leaves retries enabled is just another incident with a slower clock.

Here is the small polling adapter I keep close to the worker. It calls a verified read route, keeps the key outside source control, makes the HTTP method explicit, and treats rate limiting as an operating condition rather than a tight retry loop. It does not guess the provider response schema, so the application can store the raw event only under its own retention policy.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/event/list"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && retryAfter > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("event list failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("event list rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

The read example is intentionally narrow. A write adapter would also need a client-supplied idempotency key, but this route is enough to demonstrate the polling contract without inventing a send payload. The application still owns whether a retry is safe and whether a recipient is eligible.

Which boundary belongs to which product?

Choose a focused API when the system has a finite set of transactional events and the backend can own rules, retries, suppression, and reporting. Infrai is worth trying for that slice when you want to swap the service behind a plain REST capability without changing the application contract; its public discovery surface and consistent examples can lower the work of wiring a second capability, while one key and one common interface reduce the number of credential and SDK boundaries the team operates.

That recommendation has a hard edge and a clear limitation. Infrai is not the right choice when the workflow requires webhook-driven fallback sequencing, hosted email OTP, cancellation of scheduled email, or dynamic SMS template discovery. SMS geographic guardrails and country-based spend circuit breakers also remain application work.

Customer.io or Braze is the better choice when fallback sequencing, audience state, and multi-step engagement are the product rather than incidental code around a send call. Twilio is the stronger specialist comparison when SMS-specific country, sender, and abuse controls dominate the design. Resend is a sensible focused email comparison when the problem is transactional email and the team wants to evaluate email delivery behavior separately. OneSignal belongs in the shortlist when push is central; it should not be selected as a proxy for regional deletion guarantees across every channel.

Before choosing, ask each vendor the same four questions: which region processes the recipient and message, what retention applies to raw content and delivery metadata, how does deletion propagate, and which subprocessors touch the data? Put the answers beside the integration estimate. That is the decision record an on-call engineer can use at 3am.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the email template discovery documentation and validate the regional, retention, and deletion terms with the providers before sending production data.

References

  • Resend documentation
  • Customer.io documentation
  • Braze documentation
  • OneSignal documentation
  • Twilio SMS documentation
  • SendGrid documentation
  • Postmark documentation
  • Mailgun documentation
  • Infrai email template discovery

title: Keep file versions and observation dates separate when reading a CSV
description:
By The Sideline

A data file can have a release date that differs from the date of its observations. A download time is a third timestamp. Treating them as interchangeable can make a dashboard appear fresher than its inputs.

The Sideline's public five-row CSV sample provides a small example. It has sample_version and value_as_of fields, plus value_type to identify the modeled quantity. In the sample checked on November 2, 2026, the version is 2026-10-11 and the value-as-of date is 2026-10-05. Those are sample dates, not a claim that the file describes today's complete athlete dataset.

You can inspect the distinct values before joining or aggregating the file:

import csv

with open('sample.csv', newline='', encoding='utf-8-sig') as source:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(source))

for field in ('sample_version', 'value_as_of', 'value_type'):
    present = sorted({row[field] for row in rows if row[field]})
    missing = sum(not row[field] for row in rows)
    print(field, present, 'missing:', missing)

The point is to expose the distinction before analysis. Keep a file's version as provenance for the artifact. Use the observation date when stating the age of a value. Record the download time separately in your workflow. If future files contain multiple observation dates, do not flatten them into the newest one without explaining which rows are older.

Preserve the value_type label as well. An estimate remains an estimate after conversion to JSON or insertion into a database. A blank field should remain missing rather than silently becoming zero. A five-row sample demonstrates a format; it does not establish population coverage or grant rights to redistribute a full dataset.

Download the example: https://thesideline.co/samples/sideline-college-sports-data-sample.csv
Field-use and license context: https://thesideline.co/data/usage

Disclosure: The Sideline publishes the linked sample. This tutorial was prepared with AI assistance; its field names and distinct date/type values were checked against the public sample.

title: CSS view transitions in Laravel and Livewire
description:
Hi, I'm Aimantas. I build small web products, and the bit I've enjoyed most lately is tiny: tap a tile in Ball Quiz and it grows into the game board. Leave, and it shrinks back into the tile. The morph is plain CSS, on a Laravel and Livewire app.

It also stopped working on phones because of a two-pixel overflow, which is a story I'll get to. First, the fun part.

One rule turns page loads into transitions

Ball Quiz pages are ordinary documents. One at-rule asks the browser to animate between them, and a media query switches it off for people who ask for less motion:

@view-transition { navigation: auto; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  @view-transition { navigation: none; }
}

By default the browser snapshots the old page, loads the new one and crossfades. Browsers without support just load the page, so nothing is lost. I tuned it so leaving is quick (140ms) and arriving is a bit slower (260ms) with an 8px rise, which reads as "new page" without feeling like a slideshow:

::view-transition-old(root) { animation: 140ms cubic-bezier(.4, 0, 1, 1) both bq-vt-page-out; }
::view-transition-new(root) { animation: 260ms cubic-bezier(.16, 1, .3, 1) both bq-vt-page-in; }
@keyframes bq-vt-page-out { to { opacity: 0; } }
@keyframes bq-vt-page-in { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px); } }

Give the moving thing a name

The tile-to-board morph is one idea: put the same view-transition-name on an element on each page and the browser animates position and size between them. A name has to be unique on the page when the snapshot is taken, and the lobby shows lots of tiles, so every game gets its own. There are nine game modes, plus the daily and the sticker album, so eleven names. Here's Sprint:

.bq-play-tile[data-game="sprint"],
.bq-game-page[data-game="sprint"][data-game-active="true"] .desk-quiz {
  view-transition-name: bq-game-sprint;
}

::view-transition-group(bq-game-sprint) { animation-duration: 380ms; }

The data-game-active check matters: only a board with a round actually running claims the name, so a setup screen can't steal the morph.

A tile and a board aren't the same shape, so I crop the snapshots instead of letting them squash:

::view-transition-old(*), ::view-transition-new(*) {
  height: 100%; object-fit: cover; overflow: clip;
}

Decide what stays put

This was my favourite part. Motion only looks good when something holds still. The header gets its own name and a zero-length animation, so it stays pinned while the page changes under it. The active nav pill gets a name too, and slides to the next link over 300ms:

.desk-header { view-transition-name: bq-header; }
::view-transition-group(bq-header) { animation-duration: 0s; }

The bottom answer sheet gets the same treatment. Without its own name it would shrink into a tile it never belonged to, so it leaves on its own track, sliding down in 160ms:

.bq-game-feedback { view-transition-name: bq-sheet; }
::view-transition-old(bq-sheet) { animation: 160ms cubic-bezier(.4, 0, 1, 1) both bq-vt-sheet-out; }
@keyframes bq-vt-sheet-out { to { transform: translateY(100%); } }

When the next page is slow

The browser keeps the old page on screen until the new one is ready, which is lovely when that takes 50ms and awkward when it takes two seconds. So there's a small script on top. After 120ms it shows a progress bar along the top. After 350ms it drops in a skeleton shaped like the destination, and the tile morphs into that skeleton straight away. When the real page arrives, the cross-document transition morphs the skeleton into it. Trimmed down, the swap looks like this:

const swap = () => {
  morphFrom.style.viewTransitionName = 'none';
  skeleton.style.viewTransitionName = `bq-game-${morphFrom.dataset.game}`;
  main.prepend(skeleton);
};

document.startViewTransition(swap).ready.catch(() => {});

The tile gives up its name and the skeleton takes it, so the name stays unique. The catch is there on purpose: the browser skips a transition when the next page arrives first, and that's fine.

The two-pixel bug

On 12 October the tile-to-board morph was working on desktop and quietly not happening on phones. No error on screen, just a hard cut.

The reason: a view transition gets skipped (the browser throws InvalidStateError) if the area being snapshotted changes between the two pages. On mobile, any horizontal overflow widens the layout viewport. When the board is revealed it slides in with translateX(20px), and that overflowed the page by 2px. Two pixels were enough for the browser to drop the whole transition.

The fix is one line:

main { overflow-x: clip; }

I used clip rather than hidden on purpose. hidden turns main into a scroll container, which would break the sticky game bar. clip cuts the overflow and leaves everything else alone. I added a frontend test for it, because this is exactly the kind of bug that comes back quietly.

Small feedback inside a round

The same "motion shows what changed" idea carries into the game. A new question slides in 20px over 280ms, and the answer sheet slides up over 260ms. Both only run when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .desk-quiz-play   { animation: bq-question-in 280ms cubic-bezier(.16, 1, .3, 1) backwards; }
  .bq-game-feedback { animation: bq-sheet-up 260ms cubic-bezier(.16, 1, .3, 1) backwards; }
}
@keyframes bq-question-in { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateX(20px); } }
@keyframes bq-sheet-up    { from { transform: translateY(100%); } }

I use the same @view-transition rule on aimantas.com too, where it's a quiet crossfade, plus a scroll-driven reading bar with animation-timeline: scroll(root) and no scroll listener. The original post there has live demos you can tap.

If you want to try it

  1. Add @view-transition { navigation: auto; } and switch it off for prefers-reduced-motion. Best effect for the least code.
  2. Give an element on both pages the same unique view-transition-name. In a list, name each item.
  3. Decide what should stay still. A pinned header makes everything else look deliberate.
  4. Make leaving faster than arriving.
  5. Crop snapshots with object-fit when shapes differ, and check your phone for a stray pixel of overflow.

What I haven't checked

I've read the stylesheet and script and confirmed the same rules are on the live ball-quiz.com stylesheet (2 November 2026). I haven't tested the motion in every browser, and I haven't measured whether it changes how many rounds people play. It feels better to me. Whether it is better is a separate question, and I'd rather find that out than assume it.

If you try this in your own app, I'd like to hear what you ended up naming your first transition. I write up what I'm building, and what breaks, at aimantas.com.

title: CDN & Edge Compute: Serving Content and Running Code Close to Users
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Cut the 3,000-mile round trip by caching assets at the edge and running code close to users. The decisive skills: getting cache-control and TTL right, and handling invalidation, the genuinely hard part.

Contents

  • The 3,000-mile round trip
  • The mental model
  • The picture: a request through the edge
  • Where each kind of work belongs
  • Caching in practice: cache-control and a tiny edge function
  • Cache invalidation: the hard part
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The 3,000-mile round trip

Your origin server lives in one place, say, a data center in Virginia. A user in Sydney requests your homepage. That request crosses an ocean, hits your server, and the response crosses back. Even at the speed of light through fiber, that round trip is ~250ms before your app does any work. Add a few more round trips for images, scripts, and fonts, and the page feels sluggish, not because your code is slow, but because the data is simply far away.

A CDN (Content Delivery Network) fixes the distance problem by keeping copies of your content in hundreds of locations worldwide, so the Sydney user is served from a server in Sydney. Edge compute takes the next step: it lets you run small bits of code at those same locations, so even dynamic logic happens close to the user instead of 3,000 miles away.

📌 Who this is for: Developers and junior cloud engineers who ship a web app or API and want it to feel fast everywhere, not just near the origin. If you've heard "just put a CDN in front of it" and weren't sure what that actually does (or why your dynamic pages broke when you did), this is for you.

The mental model

A CDN is a globe-spanning cache that serves your content from wherever the user is; edge compute is the ability to run code in that same cache, so decisions happen near the user instead of at the origin.

In the real world In tech
The central warehouse holding all stock Your origin server, the source of truth
Local corner shops in every neighborhood Edge PoPs (Points of Presence) worldwide
Popular items kept on the shop shelf Cached assets (cache hit, served locally, fast)
Shop is out, so it phones the warehouse Cache miss, PoP fetches from origin, then caches
"Sell-by" date on each item TTL, how long the cached copy stays fresh
A clerk who can answer simple questions on the spot Edge function, small compute running at the PoP

A CDN is a chain of local corner shops, restocked from one central warehouse.

The whole game is moving work and data closer to the user. The further down the list you can answer a request, at the shop instead of the warehouse, the faster and cheaper it is.

The picture: a request through the edge

A user hits the nearest PoP. A cache hit returns instantly; a miss fetches from origin. An edge function runs at the PoP itself.

  1. User hits the nearest PoP: DNS (or anycast routing) sends the request to the geographically closest Point of Presence, not your origin. This is the first big latency win.
  2. PoP checks its cache: It builds a cache key (usually method + host + path, sometimes query string or headers) and looks for a fresh copy.
  3. Cache hit → served locally: If a fresh copy exists, the PoP returns it immediately. The origin never even hears about this request.
  4. Cache miss → fetch from origin: No fresh copy? The PoP requests it from the origin, streams it back to the user, and stores a copy for the next visitor, governed by the response's cache headers.
  5. Edge function runs at the PoP (optional): For requests that need logic, auth checks, redirects, A/B routing, personalization, a small function executes at the PoP, often without touching the origin at all.

Where each kind of work belongs

The edge is fantastic for some things and useless for others. The deciding question is almost always: can this be cached or computed without the origin's data? Here's the rough map.

Dimension At the edge (PoP) At the origin
Best for Static, public, read-heavy content Dynamic, private, write-heavy logic
Static assets (JS, CSS, images, video) Cache aggressively, long TTL, served from PoP Origin only on first miss
Dynamic / personalized HTML Risky, cache only with care (vary keys, short TTL) Default home, render per request
Edge function Auth gate, redirects, geo-routing, A/B, header rewrites Heavy business logic, transactions, ORM queries
Data access None or a tiny edge KV / read replica Full database, object store, internal services
Latency ~10-40ms (close to user) Tens to hundreds of ms (one location)
Cost driver Requests + egress; minimize origin trips Compute + DB time per request

What lives where, and why.

💡 Tip: Rule of thumb: cache what's the same for everyone, compute at the origin what's unique to one user. Edge functions sit in between, use them for fast, stateless decisions, not for your whole backend.

Caching in practice: cache-control and a tiny edge function

The CDN doesn't guess how long to cache, your response headers tell it. The single most important header is Cache-Control. Get it right and the edge does the heavy lifting; get it wrong and you either serve stale data or never cache at all.

response headers

# A static asset with a content hash in its name, cache forever.
# "immutable" tells the browser not to even revalidate.
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# An HTML page that can be served stale briefly while refreshing
# in the background (great for read-heavy pages).
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

# Private, per-user content, never cache at a shared PoP.
Cache-Control: private, no-store
  • max-age=N, how long (seconds) the copy is fresh. This is your TTL.
  • public vs private, public may be cached by shared CDN PoPs; private means only the user's own browser may cache it (never the edge).
  • no-store, do not cache anywhere. Use for anything sensitive or truly per-request.
  • stale-while-revalidate=N, serve the stale copy instantly for N extra seconds while fetching a fresh one in the background. Users never wait on the miss.
  • immutable, the content at this URL will never change (use with hashed filenames like app.9f3a2.js), so skip revalidation entirely.

Now a tiny edge function. This one runs at every PoP, redirects EU visitors to a regional path, and adds a security header, all without a round trip to the origin. The exact API varies by provider (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Lambda@Edge), but the shape is the same: read the request, decide, respond or pass through.

edge-function.js

// Runs at the PoP, milliseconds from the user.
export default {
  async fetch(request) {
    const url = new URL(request.url);
    const country = request.headers.get("cf-ipcountry") || "US";

    // Geo-redirect EU users, decided at the edge, no origin hop.
    const EU = new Set(["DE", "FR", "NL", "ES", "IT"]);
    if (EU.has(country) && !url.pathname.startsWith("/eu")) {
      url.pathname = "/eu" + url.pathname;
      return Response.redirect(url.toString(), 302);
    }

    // Otherwise fetch (cached) origin content and harden the response.
    const response = await fetch(request);
    const headers = new Headers(response.headers);
    headers.set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
    return new Response(response.body, { ...response, headers });
  },
};

Notice what this function does not do: it doesn't query a database, run an ORM, or hold state. Edge runtimes are deliberately lightweight (small CPU/memory budgets, short execution limits). That constraint is the point, it's what keeps them fast and cheap to run in hundreds of places at once.

Cache invalidation: the hard part

There's an old joke that the two hardest problems in computer science are naming things, cache invalidation, and off-by-one errors. Caching is easy; knowing when the cached copy is wrong is the hard part. You have three main tools.

  1. TTL expiry (let it lapse). The cleanest option: set a sensible max-age and let copies expire on their own. No action needed, but stale data lives for up to one TTL. Great for content that tolerates being a little behind.
  2. Cache busting (change the URL). Put a content hash in the filename (app.9f3a2.js). When the file changes, the URL changes, so the old cache entry is simply never requested again. This is why you can cache hashed assets immutable for a year, the standard trick for static builds.
  3. Active purge (tell the CDN to forget). Call the CDN's purge API to evict a specific path (or a tag, or everything) right now. Use it when you must force-refresh published content immediately, but it's slower to propagate and easy to over-use.

purge.sh

# Targeted purge of one path (fast, surgical), preferred.
curl -X POST "https://api.cdn.example/zones/$ZONE/purge" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{ "files": ["https://site.com/pricing"] }'

# Purge everything (the nuclear option), slow to repopulate,
# briefly hammers your origin on the cold cache. Avoid as routine.
curl -X POST "https://api.cdn.example/zones/$ZONE/purge" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{ "purge_everything": true }'

⚠️ Warning: Prefer cache busting over purging for assets, and TTL + stale-while-revalidate over purging for pages. Reach for active purge only for the genuine "I published something wrong, fix it now" case. A purge-everything on every deploy turns your CDN into a slow proxy.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Caching dynamic or private data. Serving a public-cached page that includes one user's name or cart means the next visitor gets their data. If a response varies per user, mark it private / no-store, or vary the cache key on the right header.
  2. No TTL strategy. Leaving headers to defaults means either nothing caches (every request hits the origin, you gained nothing) or everything caches too long (users see stale content for days). Decide a TTL per content type, on purpose.
  3. Heavy compute at the edge. Edge runtimes have tight CPU and time budgets. Pushing a full render, big dependencies, or chatty database calls to the edge gives you the worst of both worlds: slow functions far from your data. Keep edge logic small and stateless.
  4. Forgetting the Vary header. If a response legitimately differs by Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language, or auth, but you don't tell the CDN, it will serve one cached variant to everyone. Set Vary so the cache key includes what actually matters.
  5. Purging everything on every deploy. It feels safe, but it cold-starts the entire cache and stampedes your origin. Use hashed filenames so deploys need no purge at all.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • A CDN serves copies of your content from PoPs near the user; a cache hit never touches your origin.
  • Edge compute runs small, stateless code at those PoPs for fast decisions close to the user.
  • Cache-Control headers, max-age, public/private, stale-while-revalidate, immutable, are your caching policy.
  • Cache what's the same for everyone; compute per-user logic at the origin.
  • Invalidate by TTL expiry, cache busting (hashed URLs), or active purge, in that order of preference.
  • The edge wins for static, public, read-heavy content; the origin owns dynamic, private, write-heavy work.
  • The edge isn't a place to move your backend, it's a place to answer the easy questions before the hard ones reach home.

Where to go next

The edge is one layer of a fast, global system. Two siblings pair naturally with this one: the gateway that sits in front of your services, and a real-world case study of edge-scale delivery.

  • API Gateways & the Edge, the control point that authenticates, routes, and rate-limits requests as they enter your platform.
  • How Netflix Streams to 200 Million Devices Without Breaking, caching, edge delivery, and CDN strategy at planetary scale.
  • Build the foundations on the Cloud Engineer path, networking, latency, and global architecture in context.
  • Practice the request-path fundamentals in the networking lab and DNS lab.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: What a $200 Product/UX Diagnostic actually contains
description:
Most "UX review" offers describe the outcome and hide the document. This is the document, section by section, so you can decide whether it is the right first decision before you pay for it.

The Product/UX Diagnostic is the smallest engagement I sell: one user goal across up to five screens or states, 5–10 prioritized findings, and the three actions worth taking first, delivered next business day as a written report. No meeting, no revision round. Every report is written from the same template, and Josue reviews every deliverable before it is sent. Here is what that template forces the report to contain.

1. Client and scope

The report opens by restating what was agreed: the product, the one user goal, the screens or states inside the boundary, and the outcome you said matters. This is not filler. It is the contract the findings are judged against. If a finding is outside that boundary it does not appear, and if the boundary turned out to be wrong, the report says so instead of stretching.

2. Executive summary

Two things, and only two: a one-sentence diagnosis, and the three actions worth taking first. A founder or head of product should be able to read this section and act without reading the rest. Everything below it exists to justify these three lines.

3. Method and limits

This section states plainly what the diagnostic is and is not. It is an expert review of the supplied experience. It is not user research, usability testing, an accessibility certification, a legal or compliance review, or a guarantee of commercial results.

It lists the evidence that was used: the supplied URL, prototype or screenshots; the user goal and business outcome you gave me; direct inspection of the agreed experience. And it lists what was not assessed: analytics or behavioural data, competitor research, engineering feasibility or estimates, and any screens, roles or flows outside the agreed scope.

Why this matters to you: a review that hides its limits is asking you to trust its confidence. A review that states them is asking you to trust its evidence. Only the second kind is worth paying for.

4. Prioritized findings

Between five and ten findings, never more. Each one is written in the same four-part block:

  • Observation — what happens, described as your user would meet it.
  • Evidence — where in the supplied experience it is visible, so your team can go and look rather than take my word.
  • Why it matters — the cost to the user goal or the business outcome, in plain terms.
  • Recommended action — a concrete next move, bounded by what the evidence supports.

The cap is deliberate. A list of forty issues is a way of avoiding the ranking. Five to ten, in priority order, is a decision.

5. What to do next: Now, Next, Later

The findings are regrouped into three horizons. Now is what to fix in the current sprint. Next is what to plan for. Later is what to keep in view but not act on yet. This is the section your team actually works from.

6. Final quality gate and honesty footer

Before a report goes out it passes a written checklist, and it closes with an honesty footer that repeats the limits in one paragraph. If something could not be assessed because access was missing or the scope changed, that footer says it. The report never implies more coverage than it had.

How this relates to the deeper audits

The diagnostic answers one question: what should I fix first? If your question is different, the document is different. The \$350 teardown walks one complete booking, onboarding or checkout flow and returns the five leaks costing you most, ranked, in 48 hours. The \$550 critical-flow audit is the full single-flow review: every finding with severity, evidence, cost, fix and effort, an annotated walkthrough with timestamps, a "stop doing" list, and a recorded call. The sample report shows that format on a composite AI assistant. If you are not sure which depth you need, the diagnostic is the cheap way to find out, and the report will tell you honestly if it should have been something else.

Find the problems worth fixing first.

One user goal, up to five screens, next business day. Read the full offer and the intake before you decide.

title: Write the spec, then keep an independent human review of the change
description:
When an agent writes most of the code, your job is to turn a messy problem into a precise, repeatable solution in language, then keep an independent human review of the change. Laurie Voss said the best AI code review tools he has seen have like an 80% hit rate, and that this is not enough to put software into production. Write the spec, derive acceptance cases from it, let the agent implement, and have a person review the change plus anything that was never written down.

Laurie Voss, head of developer relations at Arize and a co-founder of npm, made that case on Chain of Thought in September 2026.

How do you write a spec an agent can execute?

Arrive at the precise version in language before any code is generated. Agents write code faster than we could ever have written code, so somebody else will type it. Get to the precise, repeatable solution in your thoughts. Pseudocode is fine if it helps.

Interview the stakeholder one question at a time. Domain experts usually lack the skill of figuring out what a stakeholder needs. They can say what they want one question at a time, but not how to make it work and repeatable. In his bakery example, you have no idea how to make the perfect croissant, and the person who runs the bakery has no idea how to write bakery software and is not interested in finding out. Making that precise and repeatable was a systems analyst's job in the 60s: translating business requirements into software requirements without writing any software. He expects that job back as a product engineer, who figures out the real requirements and works with agents to implement them, even if that person writes no code.

For each behavior, write down:

  • the user and the job they are trying to finish
  • the inputs they will have
  • the outcome that counts as done
  • the cases that must fail
  • what this change will not build

If a sentence still depends on an unstated habit, split it and ask one more question.

They could tell you probably, if you interview them one question at a time, what it is that they want to be able to do and what they want the software to be able to do, but they're not going to have any sense of how to put that together and how to make it work and how to be repeatable.

Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize, on Chain of Thought ep 74

AI Codes: Product Engineers De… - Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering - Apple Podcasts

Podcast Episode · Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering · September 22 · 56m

podcasts.apple.com

Where should a human still review agent-written code?

Put a review tool on the first pass and keep an independent human review of the change. The best code review AI tools he has seen have like an 80% hit rate. He said that is really good, and that it is not enough to put stuff into production.

He does not see anyone asking an agent to deploy a finished change, figure out what hardware it should run on, or connect those pieces. He expects agents to be good at that about 10 years from now. Deploying, refactoring, architecting, and scaling are tricky, subtle areas that need a lot of knowledge nobody wrote down. He called that tacit information and said agents will continue to be bad at it for the next five years. In the two to five year frame, senior code review and that operational work still sit with people.

I would say the best code review AI tools that I've seen have like an 80% hit rate. And an 80% hit rate is really good, but it's not enough to put stuff out into production, right? You can't mess up 20% of the time and ship that's not going to work out. So there's still scope for senior level code reviews, obviously AI assisted, you can get the 80% done and focus on the last 20%, which is very important given how much more code is being produced.

Laurie Voss, Head of Developer Relations at Arize, on Chain of Thought ep 74

How do you turn that spec into tests the code must pass?

Turn each behavior in the spec into a case the generated code must pass, and block the change on a failure. Do not loosen a case to match a surprise result unless the stakeholder's answers support that result. If the case was wrong, fix the spec, then run again.

A minimal sketch to adapt, not a drop-in library.

def cases_from_spec(spec):
    cases = []
    for behavior in spec["behaviors"]:
        cases.append({
            "name": behavior["name"],
            "given": behavior["given"],
            "action": behavior["action"],
            "expect": behavior["expect"],
        })
    return cases

def change_is_acceptable(spec, run_case):
    for case in cases_from_spec(spec):
        if not run_case(case):
            return False
    return True

run_case stands in for whatever runner you already trust. It does not review the deploy, the hardware plan, or the tacit rules.

FAQ

Is an 80% hit rate from an AI code review tool enough to ship?

No. He said that is not enough to put stuff into production. Have a person independently review the change.

Is a code-focused bootcamp still a good bet?

He is not sure he would advise spending 15 grand on a bootcamp anymore, because those programs center on a particular framework. He would pick a more theoretical course, including complexity and the business of software. Architecture, operations, scaling, complexity, and design can all be taught, he said, and people are already teaching them if you look carefully.

Does the retooling all have to happen this year?

He said you do not have to completely reskill overnight, and programming jobs are not all going to vanish overnight. Over the next five years, a lot of people do need to retool.

Takeaway

  • Interview the stakeholder one question at a time until each need is one testable behavior.
  • Write the precise, repeatable solution in language before the agent writes code.
  • Derive acceptance cases from that spec and block the change when a case fails.
  • Let review tools take the first pass, and keep an independent human review of the change.
  • Keep deployment, hardware, architecture, scaling, and unwritten operational knowledge with a person while agents are still weak there.

The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought.

Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one.
