title: A Tenant Leak Does Not Throw an Error. It Just Returns the Wrong Rows.
description:
Most bugs announce themselves. A tenant leak does not. The query runs, the status code is 200, the page renders, and somebody in one company is looking at another company's payroll.

That is what makes multi-tenancy different from the rest of the work. There is no stack trace to grep for and no error rate to alert on. The system is behaving exactly as written. It was written wrong.

This is how we build isolation into multi-tenant products so that a mistake has to get past three independent layers before it reaches a user, and so that every build actively tries to break it.

The two ways tenant data actually escapes

In every leak we have looked at, the cause was one of two things.

The first is a missing filter. Somebody wrote a query without the tenant predicate. Usually it is not the obvious code. It is the admin export, the cron job, the "quick" reporting endpoint, the findById helper that takes a primary key and nothing else.

// Looks harmless. It is the whole bug.
async function getPayslip(id: string) {
  return db.one('SELECT * FROM payslips WHERE id = $1', [id]);
}

An id is globally unique, so this never throws. It just returns whatever row matches, for whoever asks.

The second is a re-derived tenant. The request arrives with a verified tenant, and then forty lines deeper, some function reads the tenant again out of a request body, a query string, or a header, because that was convenient at the time.

// The tenant was already established. This throws it away.
async function listEmployees(req: Request) {
  const tenantId = req.body.tenantId ?? req.query.tenantId;
  return db.many('SELECT * FROM employees WHERE tenant_id = $1', [tenantId]);
}

Nobody writes this on purpose. It appears a year later, inside a feature that had a legitimate reason to accept a tenant parameter, and it is a direct object reference to every other tenant in the system.

Both of these are failures of discipline, and discipline does not survive a team of eight and a two-year roadmap. So the rules below are structural. They do not ask anyone to remember anything.

Rule 1: resolve the tenant once, at the edge, and carry it

Tenant resolution happens exactly once per request, as early as possible, from the authenticated session. After that it is read-only context. It is never re-derived from anything the caller supplied.

In Node, AsyncLocalStorage is the right tool for this, because it survives await boundaries without being threaded through every signature.

import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';

type RequestContext = { tenantId: string; userId: string };

export const context = new AsyncLocalStorage<RequestContext>();

export function tenantMiddleware(req, res, next) {
  const session = req.session; // already authenticated
  if (!session?.tenantId) return res.status(401).end();

  context.run({ tenantId: session.tenantId, userId: session.userId }, next);
}

export function currentTenant(): string {
  const ctx = context.getStore();
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('No tenant context on this execution path');
  return ctx.tenantId;
}

AsyncLocalStorage lives in node:async_hooks, was added in v13.10.0 and v12.17.0, and was marked stable in v16.4.0. getStore() returns undefined outside a run() call, which is exactly the behaviour you want: the throw in currentTenant() means any code path that somehow escaped the middleware fails loudly instead of quietly running unscoped.

Worth saying plainly: a background job, a queue consumer, or a migration script has no request and therefore no context. Those paths must open their own context explicitly, one tenant at a time. "It is only a cron job" is how the admin export got written without a filter.

Rule 2: let the database refuse, not just the application

Application-level scoping is layer one. It is also the layer most likely to have a hole in it, because it is the layer humans edit every day. Postgres row level security gives you a second layer that does not care how careless the query was.

ALTER TABLE employees ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE employees FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON employees
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);

Three details in there carry most of the weight.

Enabling RLS is fail-closed. The Postgres documentation is unambiguous: "If no policy exists for the table, a default-deny policy is used, meaning that no rows are visible or can be modified." So the dangerous state is not "RLS on, policy wrong". It is "RLS never enabled on the table somebody added last sprint".

FORCE is not optional. By default, "table owners normally bypass row security", and a table owner "can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY". Without FORCE, an application connecting as the owning role sails straight past every policy you wrote, and your test suite happily agrees that isolation works.

The second argument to current_setting is what makes it safe. With missing_ok set to true, the function returns NULL instead of throwing when the setting was never set. That matters because tenant_id = NULL evaluates to NULL, which is not true, so the policy returns no rows. Forget to set the tenant and you get an empty result, not an error and not everybody's data.

There is one more property that is easy to miss. A policy "will be evaluated for each row prior to any conditions or functions coming from the user's query". So a leaky user-defined function in a WHERE clause cannot see rows the policy already excluded.

Rule 3: set the tenant per transaction, never per connection

The natural-looking move is to set the tenant right after the connection is checked out of the pool. Do not do that. A pooled connection is handed to the next request when yours is done, and if anything short-circuits before the reset, the next request inherits your tenant.

Bind it to the transaction instead, so the database tears it down for you.

export async function withTenantTx<T>(fn: (tx: Tx) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  const tenantId = currentTenant();

  return db.tx(async (tx) => {
    // is_local = true  ->  dies with this transaction
    await tx.none("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)", [tenantId]);
    return fn(tx);
  });
}

set_config(name, value, true) is the function form of SET LOCAL: per the docs, "if is_local is true, the new value will only apply during the current transaction". There is no reset to forget, no finally block to get wrong, and a rollback cleans it up like everything else.

Where the connection pooler bites

If PgBouncer sits between the application and Postgres, the pooling mode changes what session state means. Its own feature map lists these as never compatible with transaction pooling:

Feature Session pooling Transaction pooling
SET / RESET Yes Never
LISTEN / NOTIFY Yes Never
PREPARE / DEALLOCATE Yes Never
WITH HOLD CURSOR Yes Never
Session-level advisory locks Yes Never

This is the strongest practical argument for rule 3. A session-level SET is listed as "Never" under transaction pooling, because the server connection underneath you can change between statements. Inside an explicit transaction the pooler holds one server connection for the life of that transaction, and SET LOCAL expires with it, so the tenant setting cannot outlive the work it belongs to. The PgBouncer docs do not call out SET LOCAL specifically, so if you run a pooler, verify this against your own configuration rather than taking it on trust.

Rule 4: the application role must not own the tables

This one is short and it undoes everything above when you get it wrong.

Superusers and roles carrying the BYPASSRLS attribute "always bypass the row security system when accessing a table". Table owners bypass it too unless you used FORCE. So the role your application connects as should own nothing, inherit nothing, and hold no BYPASSRLS.

CREATE ROLE app_runtime LOGIN PASSWORD :'pw' NOBYPASSRLS;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO app_runtime;

-- migrations run as a different role that DOES own the tables
CREATE ROLE app_migrator LOGIN PASSWORD :'mpw';

Then assert it, because a later migration can quietly change it:

SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolbypassrls
FROM pg_roles
WHERE rolname = 'app_runtime';
-- expect: f, f

Rule 5: USING hides rows, WITH CHECK stops you writing them

USING is the read filter. WITH CHECK governs rows being inserted or modified. If you give a policy only a USING clause, Postgres "implicitly provides a WITH CHECK clause identical to its USING clause" for the commands that need one, which is usually what you want.

Where this bites is a policy written only FOR SELECT. Reads are then isolated and writes are not, so an insert can create a row belonging to another tenant that the author of the insert can never see again. The row is real, it is in the other tenant's exports, and nothing in your logs points at it.

Write both clauses explicitly. It costs one line and it removes an argument from every future code review.

Rule 6: prove isolation on every build

The only isolation you can trust is the kind something actively tries to break. This test belongs in CI, not in a quarterly review.

test('tenant B cannot read tenant A rows by primary key', async () => {
  const a = await seedTenant('A');
  const b = await seedTenant('B');

  const row = await asTenant(a, (tx) =>
    tx.one('INSERT INTO employees (tenant_id, name) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id',
           [a, 'Ada']));

  const leaked = await asTenant(b, (tx) =>
    tx.oneOrNone('SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = $1', [row.id]));

  expect(leaked).toBeNull();          // not "throws", not "403" — no row
});

test('every tenant-scoped table has RLS enabled and forced', async () => {
  const bad = await db.many(`
    SELECT c.relname
    FROM pg_class c
    JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
    WHERE n.nspname = 'app'
      AND c.relkind = 'r'
      AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns
                  WHERE table_schema = 'app'
                    AND table_name = c.relname
                    AND column_name = 'tenant_id')
      AND (c.relrowsecurity = false OR c.relforcerowsecurity = false)`);

  expect(bad).toEqual([]);            // catches the table added last sprint
});

The second test is the one that pays for itself. Nobody forgets isolation on the table they are thinking about. They forget it on the table they added at 6pm on a Friday, and no amount of code review reliably catches a missing ALTER TABLE.

The part that is not about queries at all

Two operational facts tend to arrive late and expensively.

Migrations fan out. With a database per tenant, a schema change is not one migration, it is N of them, and it will fail somewhere in the middle. An all-or-nothing migration across hundreds of databases is neither atomic nor finishable, so the runner has to be resumable, idempotent, and able to report which tenants are on which version. Build that before you need it.

One tenant can stall another. A large export, an unbounded report, a runaway join — in a shared deployment these consume shared resources, and the tenant who did nothing wrong is the one who files the ticket. Reporting queries belong on a read replica, long jobs belong in a queue with per-tenant concurrency limits, and bulk imports should be idempotent and reversible because somebody will upload the same file twice.

A checklist before shipping a tenant-scoped feature

  1. Tenant resolved once, from the authenticated session only.
  2. No function anywhere accepts a tenant id as a parameter from the caller.
  3. New tables with a tenant_id have ENABLE and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.
  4. Every policy has both USING and WITH CHECK.
  5. current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) — the true is present.
  6. Tenant is set with SET LOCAL / set_config(..., true), inside the transaction.
  7. The runtime role is not a superuser, has no BYPASSRLS, and owns no tables.
  8. A cross-tenant read test runs in CI and fails the build.
  9. A catalog test asserts RLS on every tenant-scoped table.
  10. Background jobs open an explicit tenant context per tenant.
  11. Reporting runs on a replica; bulk imports are idempotent.

None of this is clever. That is the point. Isolation should be the boring part of the system, enforced in three places that would all have to fail together, and checked by something that runs whether anyone remembers to think about it or not.

We are the engineering team at INNERLUXES. We build multi-tenant platforms and integrate them with existing enterprise systems, which is where most of the above was learned the slow way.

title: Canary Historian vs TDengine: two historians that publish prices by tag count
description:
Canary and TDengine are two of the few historians that publish their prices, and both price by tag count. Canary is a classic process historian with its own lossless storage, store-and-forward collectors and unlimited Axiom and Excel clients. TDengine sells a time-series database plus an industrial data platform (TDengine All-in-One) that is free up to 5,000 tags, with an AGPL-3.0 open-source core.

What each one is

  • Canary: a process historian with its own storage, Axiom trending, Excel clients and store-and-forward collectors.
  • TDengine: a time-series database for Industrial IoT (TDengine TSDB) plus an industrial data management platform (TDengine IDMP), sold together as TDengine All-in-One.

Pricing (public pages, checked Nov 2026)

  • Canary prices by tag count, perpetual or annual subscription, with Enterprise licensing for unlimited tags. Example: 3,500 tags cost US$9,970 for the license plus US$1,795 CustomerCare perpetual (US$11,765), or US$3,980 per year as a subscription. There is no free tier on the pricing page.
  • TDengine prices by tag count, annual or perpetual, with high availability at +30% and over 500,000 tags on quote. It's free up to 5,000 tags, including small production use (optional support is US$3,375/year). Example: 10,000 tags cost US$15,500/year or US$38,750 perpetual; 100,000 tags cost US$46,000/year or US$115,000 perpetual.

Open source

  • Canary is commercial software under its own Software License Agreement.
  • TDengine's core database, clustering included, is open source as TDengine OSS under AGPL-3.0.

Data collection

  • Canary has collectors for OPC UA, OPC DA, MQTT Sparkplug B (or JSON), SQL and CSV, not separately licensed, and Store & Forward buffers data to disk during outages.
  • TDengine has zero-code connectors for MQTT, Kafka, OPC, PI System and more, plus edge-to-cloud replication, in all plans.

Analytics and clients

  • Canary includes unlimited Axiom and Excel clients; an ODBC connector is an upgrade.
  • TDengine includes SQL, stream processing, AI forecasting and anomaly detection, data modeling, dashboards, event management and an Excel add-in.

Managed cloud and deployment

  • Canary Private Cloud runs on US Azure, from US$12,320/year for 3,500 tags plus a US$1,500 one-time setup. Self-hosted, the historian server sits with collectors installed close to the data source.
  • TDengine Cloud runs on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, from US$970/month (Starter, 5,000 tags). Self-hosted, it ships Linux and Windows packages, Docker or Kubernetes, for edge, VM, on-prem server or cloud.

Quick fit check

Pick Canary if you want a proven process historian with lossless storage, unlimited trending clients and support included in the price, or your plant runs OPC and Sparkplug B sources and you want unlicensed collectors with store-and-forward.

Pick TDengine if you're under 5,000 tags and want a free production start, want an open-source core you can inspect, or want SQL, stream processing, AI analytics and PI System or Kafka ingestion in one product.

The full side-by-side table with every source link is on PlantWired: Canary Historian vs TDengine. Related: InfluxDB vs TDengine, Factry Historian vs Canary Historian, the TDengine profile, and Choosing a process historian.

Prices and licensing terms change, and our data comes from public vendor pages, so it surely has gaps. If you run either in production and something's wrong, tell us in the comments and we'll fix it.

PlantWired is a free, vendor-neutral map of factory software. A short weekly brief on new integrations is at plantwired.vercel.app.

title: 03/04/2026: Why Date Formats Put Calendar Events in the Wrong Week
description:
I make Yotei, a Windows and Mac app that is mentioned in this guide. Originally published at yotei.win.

"03/04/2026" is the third of April in most of the world and the fourth of March in the United States. A calendar has no way to know which one the sender meant, and neither does an app that reads a screenshot. Wrong dates are the most dangerous mistake a screenshot to calendar tool can make, because the event looks perfectly normal and sits in the wrong week.

This guide lists the ways a date on a screen can be read wrongly, what the reference sources say about each, and the habits that catch the errors. I also describe one bug I fixed in Yotei, because it shows the problem in practice.

Disclosure. I made Yotei, a screenshot to calendar app. The advice below applies to any app, or to typing the event yourself.

The short answer

  • Numeric dates have three orders in use around the world: day-month-year, month-day-year and year-month-day.
  • Only the year-first form, as in 2026-04-03, cannot be misread, which is why standards use it.
  • Time zone abbreviations are no safer. "CST" can mean three different zones.
  • Relative dates such as "next Friday" depend on the day the message was sent.
  • Whatever tool you use, read the weekday and the date together before you confirm.

Three date orders in daily use

Wikipedia's article on date formats by country describes three all-numeric orders: day-month-year (DMY), month-day-year (MDY) and year-month-day (YMD). In its country table and map, DMY is by far the most common, across Europe, Africa, Latin America and most of Asia and the Middle East. MDY is the form of the United States and a few territories, and it appears as one of several orders in Canada, Ghana, Kenya, the Philippines and some others. YMD is used in places such as China, Japan, South Korea and Bhutan. Several countries use more than one order in daily life.

The result is that any date where both the first and second numbers are 12 or below is ambiguous when written as digits. 03/04/2026 and 07/08/2026 can each be two different days. A date like 25/04/2026 is only valid as day-month, which helps a reader, but only on that one date.

Why it matters for you: a message from a colleague in another country, a booking confirmation from a US company and a school letter from your own country can all use different orders, and they can all land on the same screen.

The one order that cannot be misread

ISO 8601 writes dates as year-month-day, for example 2026-04-03. Wikipedia notes that it is meant to "harmonise these formats and ensure accuracy in all situations", that many countries have adopted it as their sole official date format, and that Canada's government recommends it for all-numeric dates. It reads the same everywhere because no real month number is above 12 and no year starts with a zero.

If you send dates to other people, write them as "Thu 3 Apr 2026" or as 2026-04-03. If you are the one reading, convert the date to words in your head before you trust it.

Time zone abbreviations are not safer

People often add a zone to avoid confusion, then use an abbreviation that is itself ambiguous. Wikipedia's list of time zone abbreviations gives "CST" as its example: China Standard Time (UTC+08:00), Cuba Standard Time (UTC-05:00) and Central Standard Time in North America (UTC-06:00). "IST" can be Indian Standard Time (UTC+05:30), Irish Standard Time (UTC+01:00) or Israel Standard Time (UTC+02:00). The same article states that these abbreviations "are not part of the international time and date standard ISO 8601".

A city name such as "Europe/Amsterdam" or an offset such as "UTC+1" leaves no room for doubt. There is more in calendar time zones explained.

"Next Friday" and the other relative dates

Messages are full of dates with no number in them: "tomorrow at 3", "this Thursday", "next Friday". Their meaning depends on the day the message was sent, which is often not visible in a screenshot. There is also a human ambiguity. On a Monday, some people mean the coming Friday by "next Friday" and others mean the Friday of the following week.

This was a real bug in Yotei. An early version resolved "next Friday" to a Saturday: the AI that reads the screenshot was working out weekdays itself, with no reference to check against. The fix is to give it the current weekday and a table of the next 14 days with every request, and to tell it to use that table for words like "Friday", "next Friday" or "tomorrow" instead of calculating. In a check on Monday 2 November 2026, "next Friday" then resolved to 6 November. That reads the phrase as the coming Friday, which is one of the two things people mean by it, so the review screen shows the resolved date and you can change it if you meant the week after. A tool that hides the resolved date from you takes that choice away.

Other traps worth knowing

  • 12-hour and 24-hour time. "7:00" could be morning or evening unless "am", "pm" or a 24-hour form is shown. Screenshots often crop that part.
  • Two-digit years. "5/6/27" can be read three ways. The year is usually 2027, but not every system agrees.
  • Ranges across midnight or across months. "Fri 31 Jan to Mon 3 Feb" is one event over four days, not two.
  • Dates in other languages. Month names change, and so does the order of day and month in a sentence. A reader that works well in English can slip in another language.

Habits that catch the mistakes

  1. Read the weekday with the date. If the message says "Thursday 4 March" and your calendar shows 4 March as a Wednesday, one of them is wrong. This single check catches most day-month swaps.
  2. Look at the sender's country. It tells you the likely date order and the likely time zone.
  3. Confirm the zone for anything cross-border. Ask for a city or an offset, not an abbreviation.
  4. Never skip the review step. Choose tools that show the result before it is saved, and use that screen. Why you should always review events explains what to look at.
  5. Write dates clearly yourself. "Thu 12 Nov, 14:00 CET" is hard to misread.

How I made this guide

The facts about date orders and time zone abbreviations come from two Wikipedia articles, "Date format by country" and "List of time zone abbreviations", read on 2 November 2026. Wikipedia is a secondary source, and the first article's country table was cut off when I read it, so I describe the pattern and do not give counts. The "next Friday" example comes from Yotei's own commit history and a live check on that date after the fix. I did not run a study of how often readers get dates wrong, and I will not claim one. I used no affiliate links. If something here is wrong, email support@yotei.win.

FAQ

Is 03/04/2026 the 3rd of April or the 4th of March?

It depends on the country. Most places read it as 3 April (day first). The United States reads it as 4 March (month first). Without context, it cannot be known from the digits.

Which date format is the safest to write?

The ISO 8601 order, year-month-day, such as 2026-04-03, or a form with the month in words, such as 3 Apr 2026.

Are time zone abbreviations like CST and IST reliable?

No. CST can mean China, Cuba or North American Central time, and IST can mean India, Ireland or Israel. Use a city or a UTC offset.

How do screenshot to calendar apps handle "next Friday"?

They have to know today's date and decide what the phrase means. Yotei is given the current weekday and the next 14 days and shows you the resolved date before it saves anything. Check any app's result the same way.

What is the quickest way to catch a wrong date?

Compare the weekday in the message with the weekday your calendar shows for that date. If they differ, the day and month were probably swapped.

title: Vector Collections and Fixed Dimensions: 3 Node.js Deduplication Invariants
description:
TL;DR: Treat a vector collection as an embedding-space contract: every record uses one model, one fixed dimension, and one declared chunking policy. For media deduplication, create a new collection and reindex when the embedding model changes. Do not put a new model's vector into the old collection merely because both arrays have the same length.

A collection is a set of same-shaped vectors plus their metadata. Fixed dimension is not a capacity knob. It is a property of the embedding model, and similarity is meaningful only among vectors produced within the same model's embedding space.

That gives us an operational rule too: reject contract mismatches before indexing, then monitor freshness while a replacement collection fills.

Shape first.

Why must a vector collection have one fixed dimension?

A similarity function compares coordinates position by position. If one vector has 768 coordinates and another has 1,536, there is no complete coordinate pairing. A collection fixes the shape so every stored vector can participate in the same comparison.

Equal length is necessary, but insufficient. Two models can both emit 768 numbers while assigning different learned meanings to coordinate 217. Their outputs produce a numeric score, but that score does not establish useful semantic similarity. The arrays share a shape, not a semantic coordinate system.

Picture the system as a short pipeline. Before: article text enters model A, which emits a dimension-D vector; the collection compares it only with model-A vectors. After a model change: the text enters model B, lands in a new collection, and is compared only with model-B vectors. Traffic moves after the required corpus has been reindexed.

Dimension describes shape, not room. A 1,536-dimensional collection does not hold twice as many articles as a 768-dimensional collection. Record count and dimension answer different questions.

Make the contract visible in Node.js

Suppose a publisher receives two versions of a wire story. Metadata such as storyId, desk, and publishedAt filters candidates; the vector represents the text used for semantic near-duplicate detection. Chunking belongs in the contract. Embedding a headline plus the first 400 words is a different policy from embedding every 400-word chunk, even if both use the same model and dimension.

This runtime guard catches the category error early:

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;

if (!apiKey || !baseUrl) {
  throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL");
}

async function getDiscovery(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/discovery", baseUrl), {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return getDiscovery(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`discovery_failed status=${response.status} body=${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

type Contract = {
  collection: string;
  embeddingModel: string;
  dimension: number;
  chunkingPolicy: string;
};

type StoryVector = {
  storyId: string;
  embeddingModel: string;
  chunkingPolicy: string;
  vector: number[];
  publishedAt: string;
};

function assertContract(contract: Contract, story: StoryVector): void {
  if (story.vector.length !== contract.dimension) {
    throw new Error(
      `dimension_mismatch expected=${contract.dimension} actual=${story.vector.length}`,
    );
  }
  if (story.embeddingModel !== contract.embeddingModel) {
    throw new Error(
      `model_mismatch expected=${contract.embeddingModel} actual=${story.embeddingModel}`,
    );
  }
  if (story.chunkingPolicy !== contract.chunkingPolicy) {
    throw new Error(
      `chunking_mismatch expected=${contract.chunkingPolicy} actual=${story.chunkingPolicy}`,
    );
  }
}

const contract: Contract = {
  collection: "wire-stories-model-a-v1",
  embeddingModel: "model-a",
  dimension: 768,
  chunkingPolicy: "headline-plus-first-400-words-v1",
};

const incoming: StoryVector = {
  storyId: "wire-2026-10-03-0042",
  embeddingModel: "model-a",
  chunkingPolicy: "headline-plus-first-400-words-v1",
  vector: Array.from({ length: 768 }, () => 0),
  publishedAt: "2026-10-03T08:30:00Z",
};

await getDiscovery();
assertContract(contract, incoming);

The discovery request lets the service inspect the live capability catalog before wiring a vector operation; it uses an environment-held key, an explicit method, status handling, and bounded exponential backoff for rate limits. The local guard is intentionally boring. Good. Count each rejection reason separately. A rise in dimension_mismatch points toward shape configuration; model_mismatch catches the subtler equal-length failure; chunking_mismatch reveals content-policy drift. Freshness needs another signal: measure the interval between a source update and successful indexing in the active collection. Also report the reindex backlog by collection generation. Those measurements stop a clean model migration from quietly producing stale duplicate judgments. Set alerts from the newsroom's publication deadline and ingestion objective, not an invented universal threshold.

Chunking and freshness set the useful boundary

For near-duplicate media records, collection design follows the unit that can be a duplicate. Whole-record embeddings are easier when records are short and similarly structured. Chunk embeddings can expose shared passages inside long articles, but create multiple candidates per story and need aggregation before the system labels two records duplicates.

There is a trade-off. Small chunks expose copied paragraphs; overly small chunks lose enough context that a routine topic match can resemble a duplicate. Choose a policy, version it, and test it against labeled duplicate pairs. Metadata cannot repair scores from mixed policies.

Media records also change. A correction or appended paragraph should be embedded under the same active contract and replace its current record. During migration, query generations deliberately: old vectors remain comparable with old vectors, and new with new. The replacement becomes authoritative only after its reindex reaches the completeness the application requires.

Short version: new model, new collection, reindex.

Compare products by the contract they expose

The mathematical boundary does not change with the vendor. The product question is where each system exposes it and how much surrounding infrastructure a team wants to own.

Option Contract surface Good fit Boundary
Pinecone Index creation includes vector dimension and metric. Teams wanting a managed vector database with explicit index shape. A model migration still requires a separate generation and reindex.
Qdrant Collection vector configuration declares size and distance. Teams valuing an open-source vector database and collection-level configuration. Self-hosting retains deployment and operational ownership.
Weaviate Collection configuration connects vectorization choices to objects. Teams wanting object-oriented schema and integrated vectorization options. Matching dimensions do not make different vectorizers compatible.
Infrai Search and RAG use a plain REST API under one key, without a required vendor SDK. Teams standardizing varied backend calls behind HTTP. Changing models still means a new collection and reindex.

No row wins universally. Pinecone's managed index, Qdrant's open-source deployment choices, and Weaviate's collection model imply different ownership. Infrai fits when a plain REST boundary and less client-library lifecycle work matter. That convenience does not alter the data contract.

A portable control follows: keep embeddingModel, dimension, chunkingPolicy, and collectionGeneration in pipeline configuration. The vendor resource then enforces a contract that your team can inspect independently.

What if two models return the same vector length?

They are still not comparable. Dimension says how many coordinates exist, not what the learned space means. This trap passes superficial validation because both payloads look structurally correct. Keep the model identifier in the write contract and reject a mismatch before upsert.

Must every experiment trigger a full production reindex? No. An experiment can use a separate candidate collection holding a representative evaluation set. Compare duplicate judgments there first. A production switch does require a new collection and reindex, because the existing corpus must be embedded into the candidate model's space.

Keep the phases distinct. During evaluation, report quality against labeled pairs. During migration, report indexed coverage and freshness. After cutover, report query outcomes and contract rejections. One average should not blur all three.

The durable mental model is compact: a vector collection is a comparison domain, not a bag of arbitrary arrays. Fix its shape, model, and chunking policy. Replace that domain as a unit when the semantic contract changes.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
  • Pinecone: Create an index
  • Qdrant: Collections
  • Weaviate: Collection definition

title: Compare spectrum snapshots without diagnosing the hardware
description:
Originally published on KeyboardTester.click: GPU vs PSU Coil Whine: How to Find the Source and Quiet It. This developer adaptation focuses on reading comparison data, not identifying a faulty computer component.

Photo: Elias Gámez / Pexels. The photo illustrates maintenance, not a new measurement.

An A/B spectrum screenshot invites a tempting shortcut: subtract two numbers and call the result a hardware diagnosis. The useful software boundary is narrower. A parser can validate the export, describe which relative quantities changed, and refuse to calculate a delta when the inputs do not support that comparison.

This exercise uses a versioned export containing saved A and B snapshots. You can run it entirely with the synthetic fixture below. It does not need microphone access, an account, a network connection or a particular GPU.

The input contract is smaller than the conclusion

The reference browser analyzer currently exports tool: "coil-whine-test", version: 1, readings, and microphone-processing metadata. Each saved reading has a boolean detected; a detected peak also carries frequency, level and prominence. An undetected snapshot uses null values for the absent peak fields. Additional metadata is retained in the original export, but this reader does not pretend it can establish microphone placement or gain from it.

The analyzer's search range is 1–18 kHz. Its 12 dB local-prominence gate is an implementation rule, not a universal equipment threshold. A 32,768-sample FFT at 48 kHz gives roughly 1.46 Hz bin spacing. As MDN documents, the FFT size specifies the analysis window. Bin spacing alone does not guarantee microphone accuracy or establish that nearby peaks share one physical source.

Three numbers deserve separate names:

  • Frequency: where the selected narrow peak sits.
  • Digital level: amplitude relative to digital full scale, in dBFS. This is not calibrated room dBA.
  • Prominence: contrast against the local spectral background. A quieter background can increase prominence even when the selected tone's digital level falls.

The last case is why the program prints both deltas and never emits a field such as gpu_is_faulty.

A complete standard-library reader

Save this as compare_tones.py. It accepts only the known tool/version, checks detected snapshots for finite numeric values, and handles missing detections explicitly. Python booleans require special care: bool is a subclass of int, but false is not a valid audio level or schema version here.

"""Describe a Coil Whine Test v1 export without diagnosing hardware (MIT)."""
import argparse
import json
import math
import sys


def finite_number(value, name):
    if isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, (int, float)):
        raise ValueError(name + " must be a number")
    if not math.isfinite(value):
        raise ValueError(name + " must be finite")
    return value


def reading(value, name):
    if not isinstance(value, dict) or type(value.get("detected")) is not bool:
        raise ValueError(name + " needs a boolean detected field")
    if not value["detected"]:
        return {"detected": False}
    result = {"detected": True}
    for field in ("frequency", "level", "prominence"):
        result[field] = finite_number(value.get(field), name + "." + field)
    if not 1000 <= result["frequency"] <= 18000:
        raise ValueError(name + " frequency is outside this tool's search range")
    if result["level"] > 0 or result["prominence"] < 0:
        raise ValueError(name + " has an invalid relative level")
    return result


def summarize(payload, same_setup=False, tolerance_hz=20.0):
    tolerance_hz = finite_number(tolerance_hz, "tolerance_hz")
    if tolerance_hz < 0:
        raise ValueError("tolerance_hz cannot be negative")
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        raise ValueError("export must be an object")
    if payload.get("tool") != "coil-whine-test" or type(payload.get("version")) is not int or payload["version"] != 1:
        raise ValueError("expected a coil-whine-test version 1 export")
    snapshots = payload.get("readings")
    if not isinstance(snapshots, dict):
        raise ValueError("readings must be an object")
    a, b = (reading(snapshots.get(key), key) for key in ("A", "B"))
    result = {"A": a, "B": b, "hardware_source": "undetermined",
              "same_setup_asserted_by_user": bool(same_setup),
              "warning": "Relative digital data only; no calibrated SPL, defect or hearing-safety conclusion."}
    if not same_setup:
        result["status"] = "setup_not_confirmed"
    elif not (a["detected"] and b["detected"]):
        result["status"] = "missing_detected_pair"
    elif abs(b["frequency"] - a["frequency"]) > tolerance_hz:
        result["status"] = "different_peak_frequency"
    else:
        result.update(status="relative_pair", tolerance_hz=tolerance_hz,
                      frequency_delta_hz=b["frequency"] - a["frequency"],
                      level_delta_db=b["level"] - a["level"],
                      prominence_delta_db=b["prominence"] - a["prominence"])
        result["warning"] += " Close frequencies do not prove the same physical tone."
    return result


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("export_file")
    parser.add_argument("--same-setup", action="store_true",
                        help="Assert that mic, distance, gain and workload comparison were controlled")
    parser.add_argument("--tolerance-hz", type=float, default=20.0)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        with open(args.export_file, encoding="utf-8") as source:
            payload = json.load(source)
        result = summarize(payload, args.same_setup, args.tolerance_hz)
    except (OSError, ValueError) as error:
        print("Cannot compare: " + str(error), file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, allow_nan=False))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

--same-setup is an assertion from the person conducting the comparison. It is not an automatic verification. Use it only after controlling the intended microphone, placement, distance, gain and workload comparison. The export cannot establish those conditions for you.

The default 20 Hz proximity tolerance is a conservative example setting for this reader, not a claim about auditory perception, resolution or hardware identity. Change it deliberately for your dataset. Even when two reported peaks fall within that tolerance, the output warns that they may not be the same physical tone.

Run a fixture that exposes the prominence trap

Create example.json:

{
  "tool": "coil-whine-test",
  "version": 1,
  "readings": {
    "A": {"detected": true, "frequency": 8000, "level": -55, "prominence": 20},
    "B": {"detected": true, "frequency": 8002, "level": -59, "prominence": 22}
  }
}

These are invented software fixtures, not recordings of a physical computer. Run:

python compare_tones.py example.json
python compare_tones.py example.json --same-setup

The first run returns setup_not_confirmed and no level delta. The second returns relative_pair, level_delta_db: -4 and prominence_delta_db: 2, while keeping hardware_source: "undetermined". The captured peak is lower in digital level yet more prominent against its neighboring bins. Collapsing those into one “noise score” would discard the distinction we wanted to preserve.

Change B's frequency to 9000: the status becomes different_peak_frequency, with no amplitude delta. Make A an undetected reading: the status becomes missing_detected_pair. Missing snapshots, the wrong tool/version, non-finite numbers, boolean numeric fields and invalid ranges produce a clear error instead of a plausible-looking result.

Fourteen deterministic tests were run for this exact implementation, including CLI success/error paths, tolerance boundaries, absent detections, validation and input immutability. They validate the reader's software behavior. They do not validate a microphone, GPU, PSU, physical repair or hearing-safety claim.

Input preflight belongs before the acoustic comparison

With real captures, first check which input reaches the browser. The SoundTesters microphone test provides a live input display and records a local sample for up to 30 seconds when started; listening requires an explicit playback choice. That is a useful way to discover a mistaken webcam-mic selection before interpreting an acoustic export. It is not a calibration or a coil-whine source detector.

Finish that input check, stop playback and live monitoring, and close the mic test before collecting acoustic snapshots. Speaker playback can contaminate a microphone measurement. Keep the acoustic analyzer visible beside the workload: the reference implementation stops capture when its tab is hidden. Record context in a separate note and repeat the pair rather than trusting a single screenshot.

No numeric reader can distinguish GPU from PSU solely because the pitch follows frame rate; both respond to load. Use manufacturer guidance for equipment questions, and stop using equipment with burning smells, sparks, crackling, shutdowns or damaged connectors.

Disclosure and reuse

The complete Python example is offered under the MIT license. It was prepared by an AI agent for this authorized publication and tested with synthetic fixtures. KeyboardTester.click and SoundTesters are owned by the same publisher; links identify the referenced export and input-preflight workflows, not independent endorsements. No new physical component diagnosis or repair result is claimed. The original guide covers the broader comparison method and its limitations.

title: Google Cloud Spend Caps Reach General Availability With an API and Live Costs
description:
TL;DR

  • A spend cap is a Google Cloud budget rule that pauses eligible services in a project once usage cost passes the budget's target amount, and it leaves the resources themselves in place.
  • Google made spend caps generally available on 30 October 2026, after a preview period.
  • The release adds three things: a spend caps API on the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API, live cost reports showing the estimated costs that triggered enforcement, and a monthly reset at the start of the next budget period.
  • The budgets API carries a spendCap object, and a spend cap budget accepts exactly three CURRENT_SPEND threshold rules at 50%, 80% and 100%, with FORECASTED_SPEND rules rejected.
  • A cap pauses usage for an eligible project or service once its budget is breached.
  • During the current budget period, an enforced cap can be lifted manually; Google also lifts it automatically at the start of the next budget period, and services might take up to one hour to return fully to normal after a lift.
  • Google recommends applying strict low-dollar caps to sandboxes and testing clusters first, and confirms the default alerts to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.
  • The guardrail controls spend inside a billing account and leaves the architecture decisions, such as which workload belongs on reserved capacity, to the people running it.

A budget is a monitoring object. It watches spend, sends alerts at thresholds you choose, and reports on what happened. A spend cap adds an action to that object: when usage cost crosses the target, eligible services in the project stop serving paid requests.

Capture of the Google Cloud announcement, cloud.google.com/blog/topics/cost-management/google-cloud-spend-caps-now-generally-available, taken 30 October 2026.

That distinction is the whole feature, and Google has now made it generally available with the controls a team needs to run it at scale. The announcement is dated 30 October 2026 and comes from Shruthi Nambi, a senior product manager on the cost management team, who says the feature protects workloads from runaway costs and leaves resources in place.

A spend cap is a budget rule that pauses eligible services when usage crosses the target

Every Cloud Billing budget answers the same question: what did this scope cost against the amount I expected. The budget carries a scope, an amount, a time period and threshold rules, and the alerts fire against those thresholds.

A spend cap budget attaches a spendCap object to that structure. When the target amount is crossed, services named as eligible in the project stop serving paid requests, and the resources stay where they are, which is the part operators notice first: the resources remain in place throughout enforcement.

Netics editorial visual: the three changes Google shipped with general availability.

Three changes came with the GA release: an API, live cost reports and a monthly reset

Google describes the preview feedback as the source of all three updates. The first is programmability: managing guardrails by hand across hundreds of projects creates a major operational burden. The second is visibility, since a cap that fires without an explanation costs the on-call engineer the same evening. The third is maintenance, since a cap that stays enforced until someone clicks a button becomes its own recurring task.

The release notes for each of those is worth reading in the order the engineering work happens: you create caps programmatically, you read the costs that triggered one, and you decide what should happen at the next period boundary.

The API reuses the Cloud Billing Budgets resource and adds a spendCap object

The spend caps API arrives through the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API, so a team that already creates alerting budgets has the client library and the IAM surface in place. Google's examples cover lifting, updating and deleting caps on the fly, and applying a cap at the moment a developer creates a new sandbox project.

The API reference documents the constraints that come with the field, and they matter for anyone writing the automation:

  • A spend cap budget needs exactly three threshold rules, on CURRENT_SPEND, at 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0.
  • FORECASTED_SPEND threshold rules are unsupported for spend caps.
  • notificationsRule must be set, with enableProjectLevelRecipients true, disableDefaultIamRecipients false or unset, and both pubsubTopic and monitoringNotificationChannels empty.
  • ownershipScope must be OWNERSHIP_SCOPE_UNSPECIFIED or ALL_USERS, and BILLING_ACCOUNT is unsupported.
  • A spend cap budget uses a month as its time period.
  • While the cap is ENFORCED, only spendCap.input_state can change in a patch request, and any other field change fails.

Those constraints describe a deliberately narrow resource. The three fixed thresholds encode Google's own alert ladder, the empty Pub/Sub topic rules out routing cap notifications through your own pipeline, and the monthly period rules out a quarterly cap. A team building a Terraform module around this should expect a thin object with strict validation.

Capture of the Cloud Billing API reference, cloud.google.com/billing/docs/reference/budget/rest/v1/billingAccounts.budgets, taken 30 October 2026.

Live cost reports show the estimated costs that triggered enforcement

Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage, and Google says they run on estimated live costs. The new cost report view shows the financial snapshot that triggered enforcement and gives the engineer immediate context for root-cause analysis.

For a team, this changes the sequence of an incident. The standard billing pipeline takes hours to settle net costs, so the initial conversation starts from a total.

Act on the estimate immediately; discounts and credits can leave the settled bill slightly different. Treat the report as the reason the cap fired, then reconcile the amount against the invoice when the billing pipeline closes.

Google Cloud's own product mock from the announcement, cloud.google.com/blog/topics/cost-management/google-cloud-spend-caps-now-generally-available: estimated and live costs by SKU, with the subtotal the cap evaluated.

How a cap treats pay-as-you-go, CUD-covered usage and ongoing fixed usage

Google's current documentation says enforcement pauses all new usage for the scoped service, including on-demand, pay-as-you-go usage and usage covered by commitments such as CUDs; persistent resources remain active and their ongoing fixed usage continues to accrue charges. In-flight requests run to completion.

That single sentence should drive the architecture conversation in any team that runs both models of capacity. Teams should map each cap to the workloads inside its project-and-service scope before relying on it during an incident. Test the pause behavior with a non-production workload and record the result in the runbook.

The failure mode to avoid is discovering the cap's workload boundary during an incident. Write down which workloads fall inside each project-and-service scope, keep that list beside the cap configuration, and classify every new AI workload before the first month closes.

Netics editorial visual: the requests a cap stops and the capacity that keeps serving, according to Google's own statement.

An enforced cap lifts manually during the current period or automatically at the next one

The announcement documents the automatic monthly reset, and the API reference explains the manual lift path; the operational risk is the gap between recovery at the next period boundary and a same-period recovery that requires manual action.

The announcement says automated monthly resets mean enforced caps reset and blocked services resume at the beginning of the next month, with the manual override kept for teams whose governance requires an audit first. The Billing documentation lists three spend cap statuses, and describes Enforced as services paused during the current budget period. A manual lift restores usage during that period; the automatic lift occurs at the start of the next period, and services might take up to one hour to return fully to normal after a lift. The API reference supplies the mechanism the announcement implies: while the cap is enforced, setting spendCap.input_state to AWAITING_NEXT_PERIOD lifts it, and the cap resets for the next budget period.

A team that plans a monthly automatic resume should verify the behaviour in one project before relying on it for a production workload, and should decide what happens to in-flight requests at the boundary. Google says services might take up to one hour to return fully to normal after a cap is lifted, so that delay belongs in the runbook.

Capture of the Cloud Billing budgets documentation, cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets, taken 30 October 2026.

Google recommends starting with non-production projects and three alert thresholds

Google's own deployment advice is the least surprising part of the release and the most useful. Apply strict, low-dollar caps to developer sandboxes, testing clusters and experimental AI agent playgrounds first, and treat production once the automation and the runbook exist.

The default alerts go to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100% of the cap, so the operational work is making sure those roles hold the right people. Spend caps permissions can be added to custom roles, which lets a platform team delegate cap management through a custom role.

The guardrail covers the bill and leaves architecture decisions to people

Google pairs spend caps with Early Anomalies Detection in its own playbook: the anomaly detector watches early cost signals daily and points at the SKU behind a trend, and the cap enforces once a budget is breached. Together, the two controls form a sequence: the anomaly detector flags emerging cost drift, then the cap enforces once the budget is breached.

The decision that created the exposure remains with the team. A cap stops paid requests after a project passes its target. The team then chooses the experiment's model size, the batch job's capacity model and the appropriate budget for the sandbox project.

A small team can use the following practical sequence. Attach a low cap to every sandbox project at creation, in the same automation that creates the project, which is exactly what the API enables. Set the three alerts to a role someone actually reads. Put the cap amount and the resume behaviour in the runbook next to the on-call instructions.

For further context, see Netics' overview of cloud infrastructure controls. The broader question of what a euro of cloud spend buys in Europe is also covered in a comparison of cloud sovereignty cost figures, and a spend cap is the instrument that keeps that comparison honest month to month.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: An OpenRTB bid floor keeps its own currency.
description:
A bid request can allow EUR responses while an impression's floor is still denominated in USD. If an integration reads the response currency list and silently applies it to the floor, its arithmetic can look correct while comparing different units.

The problem is easy to miss because both values are ordinary JSON numbers. Their meaning depends on the currency attached to each field.

This walkthrough uses OpenRTB 2.6's June 2026 specification snapshot. The examples focus on currency handling and are not complete bid requests or production pricing logic.

Follow the field that owns the currency

The request's cur field describes allowed bid response currencies. The impression's bidfloorcur describes the currency of that impression's floor. In the referenced snapshot, the latter defaults to USD when omitted.

Those are separate contracts. Setting cur to ["EUR"] does not rewrite an omitted bidfloorcur to EUR.

Consider this fragment:

{
  "cur": ["EUR"],
  "imp": [
    { "id": "video-1", "bidfloor": 3.20 }
  ]
}

For the impression floor, the omitted currency resolves to USD under the cited specification. A bid price expressed in EUR needs an explicit conversion before a numerical floor comparison makes sense.

There is another scope to review when deals are involved. A deal has its own floor fields. Inspect the applicable deal and exchange contract rather than applying an impression-level assumption everywhere.

Preserve the amount and currency together

Avoid passing a bare number called floor through several functions. Use a structure that carries the amount, currency and source. That makes it harder for a later step to lose the unit or confuse an explicit value with a default.

The following complete Node.js example performs a narrow comparison. The exchange rate is synthetic and is supplied by the caller:

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

function impressionFloor(imp) {
  const amount = imp.bidfloor === undefined ? 0 : imp.bidfloor;
  const currency = imp.bidfloorcur === undefined ? 'USD' : imp.bidfloorcur;
  if (!Number.isFinite(amount) || amount < 0) {
    throw new TypeError('invalid floor amount');
  }
  if (!['USD', 'EUR'].includes(currency)) {
    throw new TypeError('unsupported currency in this example');
  }
  return {
    amount, currency,
    currencySource: imp.bidfloorcur === undefined ? 'default' : 'explicit'
  };
}

function convertFloor(floor, target, rates) {
  if (floor.currency === target) return floor.amount;
  const rate = rates[`${floor.currency}:${target}`];
  if (!Number.isFinite(rate) || rate <= 0) {
    throw new Error('usable conversion rate missing');
  }
  return floor.amount * rate;
}

const request = { cur: ['EUR'], imp: [{ id: 'video-1', bidfloor: 3.2 }] };
const floor = impressionFloor(request.imp[0]);
const rates = { 'USD:EUR': 0.9 };
const floorInEUR = convertFloor(floor, 'EUR', rates);

assert.equal(floor.currency, 'USD');
assert.equal(floor.currencySource, 'default');
assert.ok(Math.abs(floorInEUR - 2.88) < 1e-12);
assert.equal(3.0 >= floorInEUR, true);
assert.equal(3.0 >= floor.amount, false);
assert.throws(() => convertFloor(floor, 'EUR', {}));
assert.throws(() => impressionFloor({ bidfloor: '3.20' }));
assert.throws(() => impressionFloor({ bidfloor: -1 }));
assert.equal(impressionFloor({ bidfloor: 0 }).amount, 0);

The two comparisons deliberately produce different answers. With this invented rate, a EUR 3.00 bid exceeds the converted EUR 2.88 floor. Comparing the same bid directly with the unconverted USD 3.20 number would reject it.

The example supports only two currencies so that unsupported inputs fail visibly. A production implementation needs a maintained currency set, a rate source and an explicit rounding policy.

Define the direction and age of the rate

A rate named 0.9 is incomplete. State that it means EUR per USD, record when it became effective and identify the source. Multiplying by an inverse rate can produce plausible values without immediately revealing the error.

Attach that metadata to the pricing decision or a retrievable rate snapshot. A later replay should use the rate policy that applied to the original decision, rather than whichever rate happens to be current when a developer investigates it.

Do not treat a missing rate as one-to-one conversion. Decide whether the application should skip the impression, stop the calculation or route the case for review. That decision is business policy and should appear in the diagnostic result.

Likewise, do not round a floor for display and reuse the displayed number in auction logic. Define the precision and comparison behavior required by your integration. Binary floating point, exchange rounding rules and boundary prices need deliberate treatment beyond this small example.

Test defaults and explicit values separately

An omitted currency and an explicit USD currency can lead to the same effective value while carrying different diagnostic meaning. Preserve which path was taken so you can find producers that rely on defaults unexpectedly.

Include fixtures for a missing floor, a zero floor, an explicit non-USD currency and a malformed numeric string. Zero must survive as zero. A truthiness check such as amount || fallback can replace a legitimate value.

Then add a request with multiple impressions and different floor currencies. This catches helpers that compute one request-wide currency and apply it to every impression.

For deal traffic, keep dedicated cases with the deal identifier and applicable floor fields. The test should establish which floor the integration selected before it tests the comparison arithmetic.

Debug a rejected bid with the normalized record

When a bid appears to clear a floor but is rejected, collect the matched impression or deal, raw floor amount, effective floor currency, response currency, conversion snapshot and final comparison value.

Check the units as well as the currency. OpenRTB pricing uses CPM conventions in these fields. An amount interpreted as a per-impression charge introduces a separate scale error that currency conversion cannot fix.

Finally, distinguish your local eligibility calculation from the exchange's auction result. Clearing this one floor check does not establish that the bid is otherwise valid or that it should win.

I maintain RTBlint. Its OpenRTB mistakes reference is useful for reviewing the surrounding request and response contract. Keep the currency decision in your own replay fixture so that a pricing investigation can reproduce the exact comparison.

Sources

  • OpenRTB 2.6-202606, BidRequest and Imp

Technical sources checked October 25, 2026. Drafted with AI; examples are synthetic unless explicitly stated otherwise.

title: Your API Errors Shouldn't Be a Guessing Game
description:
Imagine you're building a frontend application and an API request fails.

The backend returns:

{
  "message": "Something went wrong"
}

Great. But what went wrong?

Was it a validation error? A missing resource? A permission issue? Or something else?

Now the frontend has to guess what happened.

There's a better way to handle API errors, and it's already standardized.

The Problem With API Errors

Different APIs often return errors in different formats.

One endpoint returns:

{
  "error": "Invalid email"
}

Another returns:

{
  "message": "User not found",
  "code": 404
}

And another might accidentally expose an internal database error.

This makes frontend development harder because every endpoint needs different error-handling logic.

What if every API followed the same error structure?

Meet Problem Details

RFC 7807 introduced a standard format called Problem Details for HTTP APIs.

It was later replaced by RFC 9457, which is the current standard.

The idea is simple: return errors in a consistent, predictable format.

Here's an example:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient Funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Your balance is $40, but the total is $55.",
  "instance": "/checkouts/123"
}

Much better, right?

Every field has a purpose:

  • type: Identifies the kind of error.
  • title: A short description of the problem.
  • status: The HTTP status code.
  • detail: Explains what happened in this request.
  • instance: Identifies the specific occurrence of the problem.

The API should also return the appropriate HTTP status code and this content type:

Content-Type: application/problem+json

Now the frontend knows what kind of problem occurred without guessing from random messages.

What About Form Validation?

This is where it gets even more useful.

Imagine a registration form with invalid inputs.

Your API could return:

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 422,
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "email",
      "message": "Invalid email address"
    },
    {
      "field": "password",
      "message": "Must contain at least 8 characters"
    }
  ]
}

The errors array is a custom extension, not a required field in the standard.

Now the frontend can display each error beside the correct input.

No need to parse random error strings.

Handling Errors in JavaScript

Here's a simple example using fetch:

const response = await fetch("/api/register", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify(formData)
});

if (!response.ok) {
  const problem = await response.json();

  if (problem.type === "https://api.example.com/problems/validation") {
    console.log(problem.errors);
  } else {
    console.error(problem.title);
  }
}

In a real application, you should also handle network failures and responses that don't contain valid JSON.

The important part is that your frontend can rely on documented error types instead of matching message strings.

A Few Things Worth Remembering

Using Problem Details doesn't automatically solve every error-handling problem.

You still need to follow a few good practices:

  • Never expose stack traces, SQL queries, or internal secrets.
  • Keep error types stable so frontend code doesn't break.
  • Use appropriate HTTP status codes.
  • Use safe, user-friendly messages where appropriate.
  • Add a request ID when useful for debugging and support.

For localization, frontend applications can map stable error types to translated messages instead of relying on English error descriptions.

Final Thoughts

A good API isn't just about returning successful responses.

It's also about explaining failures clearly.

RFC 9457 gives us a standard way to do that.

No random error structures. No guessing from message strings. Just predictable errors that both frontend and backend developers can understand.

And the best part?

You don't need a new library or framework to get started. Just a consistent error format.

How are you currently handling API errors in your projects?

title: DOM (Document Object Model)
description:
DOM is a programming interface that allows javascript to access and change HTML elements, content, styles and attributes.
note: DOM connects HTML and JavaScript.

1.DOM works :

<h1 id="heading">Hello World</h1>

javascript can access and change that heading using DOM.

document.getElementById("heading").innerHTML = "welcome";

output: welcome //displays welcome instead of Hello World.

2.DOM methods:

  • getElementById() :select element by ID.

  • getElementByClassname() : select element by classname.

  • getElementByTagname() : select element by tagname.

  • querySelector() : select 1st matching element

  • querySelectorAll() : select all matching element.

3.Changing HTML content:

<p id="demo" >hello world</p>
<script>
document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML="para";
</script>

4.Changing CSS using DOM :

<h1 id="title">Hello</h1>

<script>
document.getElementById("title").style.color="red;
</script>

5.DOM events :
events are actions performed by the user, such as clicking, typing or moving the mouse.
Example code : Button click.

<button id="btn">Click Me>/button>
<script>
document.getElementById("btn").onclick=function() {
alert("Button Clicked");
}
</script>

Program You can try:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Document</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1 id="txt">0</h1>
    <button onclick="increament()">+</button>
    <button onclick="decrement()">-</button>
    <button onclick="reset()">Reset</button>

    <script>

        let count = 0;

    function increament(){
        const incBtn = document.getElementById("txt");
         count++;
         incBtn.innerText = count;

    if(count >=10){
        document.getElementById("txt").style.color="green";
        document.getElementById("txt").style.fontSize="60px";  //fontsize increase
    }
    else if (count >=5)
    {
        incBtn.style.color="blue";
        document.getElementById("txt").style.fontSize="40px";

    }
     else if (count <5)
    {
        incBtn.style.color="red";
        document.getElementById("txt").style.fontSize="30px";

    }
    else
    {
        document.getElementById("txt").style.color="black";

    }


    } 

    function decrement(){
        const decBtn = document.getElementById("txt");
        count--;
        if(count<0)
    {    count=0

    }
    // if(count>0)
    // {count--;} 

        decBtn.innerText = count;
        if(count >=10){
        document.getElementById("txt").style.color="green";
        document.getElementById("txt").style.fontSize="60px";  //fontsize increase
    }
    else if (count >=5)
    {
        decBtn.style.color="blue";
        document.getElementById("txt").style.fontSize="40px";

    }
     else if (count <5)
    {
        decBtn.style.color="red";
        document.getElementById("txt").style.fontSize="30px";

    }

    }

    function reset(){
        const rst = document.getElementById("txt");
        count=0;
        rst.innerText = count;
        rst.style.color="red";

    }

    </script>


</body>
</html>

title: Cloudflare DNS Zone Builder cuts peak memory 85% and halves build delay
description:
Originally published on ColdCaseTech.

Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.

Then vs. Now (News report): Then: Cloudflare announced on 2026-11-02 that a targeted build planner and a new scheduler for its DNS Zone Builder cut peak memory by 85% and halved the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver. Now: Cloudflare states that zone setting changes no longer rebuild zones with tens of millions of records, while timestamp-only updates still cause a full build until the caller and its purpose can be identified.

Cloudflare reported on November 2, 2026 that a targeted build planner and a new scheduler for its DNS Zone Builder cut peak memory by 85% and halved the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver (Cloudflare). The company set out the work in a blog post that follows its 2022 description of the DNS propagation pipeline (Cloudflare).

The Zone Builder now receives about 700 DNS record changes per second, up from about 250 in 2022, plus about 100 other events such as zone setting changes (Cloudflare). Some zones hold more than 20 million records, and the company expects them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions (Cloudflare).

Key Facts

Item Detail Source
Peak memory Cut by 85% Cloudflare
Change-to-Quicksilver time Halved Cloudflare
Record changes per second About 700 now, about 250 in 2022 Cloudflare
Largest zones More than 20 million records Cloudflare
Build types Five, from resources only to full zone Cloudflare

Timeline

  • 2026-11-02: Cloudflare published its account of the targeted build planner and scheduler for DNS builds (Cloudflare).

Details (as Reported)

A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver (Cloudflare). According to the company, the original Zone Builder rebuilt the desired state from the current database state and did not need to know why a zone changed (Cloudflare). A full build still reads, encodes and compares every record and holds the whole zone in memory, and for the largest zones the zone does not fit in memory at all (Cloudflare).

The new planner chooses the smallest build the company can prove is safe, and the scheduler combines work for the same zone (Cloudflare). Builds come in five types: resources only, resources and metadata, apex and metadata, purge, and full zone (Cloudflare). The rule is that every key a targeted build writes must be byte-for-byte identical to what a full build would write, and if that cannot be proven the system does a full build (Cloudflare).

To support targeting, the company changed the event producer to include changed zone fields and settings, with previous and new values when available (Cloudflare). Cloudflare stated that the extra memory headroom let it safely shorten waits the pipeline has always needed for resilience (Cloudflare). In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average, and 4,250 times faster on a test zone with one million records (Cloudflare).

Keep one backup somewhere else. A copy of critical data with a second provider means one compromised account or one regional outage cannot take everything down with it. See Contabo storage plans (affiliate link)

What Is Not Yet Confirmed

  • Some database functions only update a timestamp, and Cloudflare stated that such an update still causes a full build until it can identify the caller and its purpose (Cloudflare).
  • Missing details, unknown events, or any change that may affect records anywhere in the zone also lead to a full build, according to Cloudflare (Cloudflare).

Sources

  • Cloudflare, 2026-11-02

Tools related to this case

  • A standby server outside your main cloud for failover: Contabo dedicated servers
  • Routing optimizer for unstable or high-latency connections: GearUP
  • Keeps routers and home servers up through short power cuts: UPS battery backups
