title: How to find and fix slow PostgreSQL queries
description:
Originally published on the Hubfly space blog. By Octave, drafted with AI, tested on Hubfly space.

TL;DR

  • What you get: a repeatable way to find the queries that cost your database the most time, prove why they're slow, and fix them, with before-and-after numbers.
  • Who it's for: developers running Postgres for a real app who don't have a DBA.
  • Time needed: about 20 minutes, plus a few minutes for the database to start.
  • Cost: a Nano managed Postgres on Hubfly space is $2.02 a month (about $0.003 an hour). Delete the instance when you're done and following along costs well under a cent.
  • Checked on: PostgreSQL 18.6 on a Hubfly space Nano instance, October 2026.

Your app was fast in the demo. Now the orders page takes a second to load and nobody knows why. You could guess, add a few indexes and hope. Or you could ask Postgres which queries actually eat its time, fix the worst one, and measure the result.

In this guide you'll do exactly that. Slow queries cost you users, and on a small database they also cost you money, because the usual fix is to buy a bigger server. A missing index often costs more than an undersized server.

Try it on Hubfly space: the managed Postgres used here starts at $2.02 a month and every query-tuning tool in this guide is included at no extra cost.

How it works in one picture 

your app ──► Postgres ──► pg_stat_statements (counts every query shape)
                               │
                               ▼
              1. rank by total time  ──►  2. EXPLAIN ANALYZE the winner
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
              4. reset + measure again  ◄──  3. add the right index

pg_stat_statements is a Postgres extension that groups queries by their shape (WHERE customer_id = $1, not = 4242) and records how often each one ran and how long it took. That's the data you need, because the query that hurts you is rarely the slowest one. It's the one that's a bit slow and runs all the time.

Step 1: Create a Postgres database

If you already have Postgres with pg_stat_statements, skip to Step 3.

  1. In the Hubfly space dashboard, click Create Project, name it (for example shop), choose Managed service and click Create Project.
  2. Click Create a database, keep PostgreSQL 18 and the Nano size (0.25 vCPU, 512 MiB, 10 GiB storage).
  3. Name the instance shop-db and click Create database.

The price panel on the Create database form: $0.00277 an hour while running, $2.02 a month.

The instance usually reaches Running within a few minutes. Hubfly space managed Postgres preloads pg_stat_statements (SHOW shared_preload_libraries; returns it), so you don't have to restart anything to start collecting data. On a self-managed server you'd add it to postgresql.conf and restart first.

Step 2: Load some realistic data

You need enough rows for a slow query to be slow. Open SQL editor and switch off Read-only. The editor warns that writes change your data immediately and that there are no backups (automatic backups are still coming soon), so do this on a test instance, never on production. Paste this and click Run:

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO customers (email)
SELECT 'user' || g || '@example.com' FROM generate_series(1, 50000) g;

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status text NOT NULL,
  total_cents int NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status, total_cents, created_at)
SELECT 1 + (random() * 49999)::int,
       (ARRAY['pending','paid','shipped','refunded'])[1 + (random() * 3)::int],
       (random() * 20000)::int,
       now() - random() * interval '365 days'
FROM generate_series(1, 300000);

ANALYZE customers;
ANALYZE orders;

That's 50,000 customers and 300,000 orders. On a Nano instance the whole script takes about 12 seconds.

Note one thing that's easy to miss: Postgres creates an index for a PRIMARY KEY, but not for a foreign key. orders.customer_id has no index. That's the most common cause of slow pages in real apps.

Step 3: Run your app's queries

In real life your app does this part. Here, simulate it by running the three queries an order-history page and a dashboard would run. Paste the whole block into the editor and click Run six times:

-- "My orders" page, for five different customers
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 30001 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 999 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 25000 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Customer lookup
SELECT email FROM customers WHERE id = 4242;
SELECT email FROM customers WHERE id = 17;

-- Admin dashboard: last 30 days by status
SELECT status, count(*), sum(total_cents) FROM orders
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '30 days' GROUP BY status;

If your database already serves real traffic, skip this step. Real traffic is better data.

Step 4: Find the query that costs the most time

Open Query insights. Before you read it, click Reset statistics and run your workload again, so setup statements like the big INSERT don't drown out the real queries. Resetting only clears the counters; your data isn't touched.

Statement statistics before the fix: the orders lookup is 60% of all query time.

Read the Where the time goes chart from the top:

  • orders WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $2: 30 calls, mean 45 ms, total 1.36 s, 60%
  • orders WHERE created_at > now() - interval $1 GROUP BY status: 5 calls, mean 167 ms, total 836 ms, 37%
  • customers WHERE id = $1: 12 calls, mean 6.32 ms, total 76 ms, 3.3%

Your call counts and timings may differ slightly.

Sort by total time, not by mean. The dashboard query has the worst mean (167 ms), but the orders lookup runs far more often and costs more overall. Fix what costs the most first.

Prefer SQL? Query the view yourself

The dashboard reads pg_stat_statements for you. To query the view from psql or your own tools, install it in your database from the Extensions tab (find pg_stat_statements and click Install). Running CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements yourself fails with permission denied to create extension because the admin user isn't a superuser; the Extensions tab does it for you. Then:

SELECT round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
       calls,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms,
       rows,
       left(query, 70) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;

The admin user can read every user's statistics, but it can't call pg_stat_statements_reset(). Use Reset statistics in Query insights for that.

Step 5: Ask Postgres why it's slow

Copy the top query, put real values back in, and prefix it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS):

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, status, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

The plan before the fix: a sequential scan that reads 2,500 pages to return 8 rows.

Three lines tell the whole story:

  • Seq Scan on orders: Postgres reads the entire table.
  • Rows Removed by Filter: 299992: it throws away almost everything it read.
  • Buffers: shared hit=2503: it touched 2,503 pages (about 20 MB) to return 8 rows.

That took 15.8 ms here with the table already in memory. On a busy server, with a bigger table or a cold cache, the same plan takes far longer, and it gets worse every day as orders grows.

Careful: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement. For an UPDATE or DELETE, wrap it in BEGIN; … ROLLBACK; or use plain EXPLAIN, which only plans.

Step 6: Add the right index, without locking the table

The query filters on customer_id and sorts by created_at, so one index on both columns, in that order, serves both:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_id_created_at_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

CONCURRENTLY builds the index while your app keeps writing to the table. A plain CREATE INDEX blocks inserts and updates until it finishes, which on a large production table can mean minutes of failed checkouts. It took 1.02 s on 300,000 rows. Run it as its own statement: CONCURRENTLY can't run inside a transaction.

While you're here, give the dashboard query the obvious index too, one on created_at (Step 7 shows why it isn't enough on its own):

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_created_at_idx ON orders (created_at);

Now run the same EXPLAIN again:

The plan after the fix: an index scan, 14 pages, 0.161 ms.

Index Scan using orders_customer_id_created_at_idx, 14 pages instead of 2,503, and 0.161 ms instead of 15.8 ms. The separate sort step is gone too, because the index already stores rows in created_at DESC order.

Step 7: Measure again, then fix the next one

Click Reset statistics, run the same workload, and open Query insights again.

After the two indexes: total query time for the workload drops from 2.27 s to 409 ms.

The composite index took the orders lookup from a 45 ms mean to 0.10 ms over the same 30 calls. With both indexes in place, total time for the workload fell from 2.27 s to 409 ms. And notice what happened: the dashboard query is now 99% of the remaining time, still averaging 67 ms. That's normal. Each fix promotes the next problem to the top. Repeat Steps 5 and 6 on it.

When a normal index isn't enough

The plain created_at index from Step 6 didn't do much for the dashboard query. EXPLAIN shows Postgres using it (Bitmap Index Scan on orders_created_at_idx) but still visiting Heap Blocks: exact=2500, every page of the table, because 30 days of orders are scattered across all of it. It still took 95 ms.

The fix is a covering index: store the columns the query reads inside the index, so Postgres never visits the table.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_created_at_covering_idx
  ON orders (created_at) INCLUDE (status, total_cents);
VACUUM (ANALYZE) orders;
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_created_at_idx;  -- the plain index is now unused

Run each statement on its own. Because DROP INDEX removes an object, the editor asks "Run destructive statements?"; check the name and click Run anyway. The plan changes to Index Only Scan … Heap Fetches: 0, 125 pages instead of 2,570, and 6.7 ms instead of 95 ms. The VACUUM matters: index-only scans need Postgres's visibility map to be up to date, which autovacuum also does on its own schedule. Dropping the unused index matters too, because every index slows down writes a little.

Step 8: Catch the next slow query before users do

Query insights shows totals. To see each slow query as it happens, log it.

  1. Open Configuration, find log_min_duration_statement and set it to 250 (milliseconds; use a lower value like 50 while tuning).
  2. Click Review changes. The review shows the diff and says "These settings apply live without a restart." Add a note and click Apply live.
  3. Open Logs and search for duration:.

Every statement over the threshold appears with its duration and text.

Out of the box the instance logs statements slower than 1 second. Logs can contain query text and data values, so don't share them carelessly.

Then open Alerts and make sure you hear about trouble without watching the dashboard. Storage and connection thresholds are set to 85% and 90% (you can choose 50–99%). Instance down and Email me are off by default: turn both on and click Save changes.

Alerts with Instance down and email turned on.

What can go wrong

1. "relation pg_stat_statements does not exist"

The library is loaded, but the view only exists in a database after CREATE EXTENSION. Install it from the Extensions tab for each database you query from. Query insights works without this step.

2. "permission denied to create extension", or a permission error when you reset

The admin user isn't a superuser, so it can't create untrusted extensions or call pg_stat_statements_reset(). Use the Extensions tab to install and Reset statistics in Query insights to reset.

3. "CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block"

Some migration tools wrap every file in a transaction. Run the statement on its own, or mark that migration as non-transactional (for example disable_ddl_transaction! in Rails, or atomic = False in a Django migration). If a concurrent build fails, it leaves an INVALID index behind; drop it and try again.

4. You added an index and nothing changed

Run EXPLAIN again. If the plan still says Seq Scan, the column order may be wrong (put the = column first, the sort or range column second), the table may be too small for an index to be worth it, or the query wraps the column in a function (lower(email)) so you need an expression index. If it says Bitmap Heap Scan with every block visited, try a covering index as in Step 7.

Takeaway

Don't guess which query is slow. Rank by total time, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) the winner, fix it with an index built CONCURRENTLY, then reset and measure. Here, the composite index took the busiest query from 45 ms to 0.10 ms, the two indexes together cut total time for the workload by 82% (2.27 s down to 409 ms), and a covering index then took the next query from 95 ms to 6.7 ms. The cost of the database didn't change: the Nano instance is still $2.02 a month.

Finished experimenting? Delete the test instance from its Settings tab (Delete instance, then type its name to confirm). Storage is billed while an instance exists, even when it's stopped.

Next, read the docs on monitoring and operating a managed database for sessions, metrics and safe config changes.

Deploy this

Create a managed Postgres on Hubfly space, load your schema, and open Query insights. Query insights, logs, alerts and the config editor come with every instance at no extra cost.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Connect your app safely. Use the Apps tab to bind the database to a Hubfly space Cell app; it creates a dedicated user and a DATABASE_URL secret for you. See Databases.
  • Lock down access. Restrict connections to an allowlist of your IPs under Network. See Network access.
  • Give reporting tools a read-only user. Create one under Users & roles so a dashboard can never change data. See Users, databases and tokens.

title: Amazon RDS now supports per snapshot billing
description:
Starting today, Amazon RDS supports per snapshot billing for Amazon RDS snapshots. Per snapshot billing allows you to get the cost of each individual snapshot.

Previously, RDS snapshot charges were aggregated at the database instance level on the Cost and Usage report as well as the Cost Explorer. This meant that while understanding the snapshot charges, you could only see the aggregate view at the database instance instead of drilling down to each individual snapshot. Now, you can use cost allocation tags on your snapshots to see exactly how much each snapshot costs, giving you a better understanding of your backups spend and budgets. Per snapshot billing is enabled by default on all RDS snapshots for no additional charge.

Per snapshot billing is available for all Amazon RDS engines in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, please visit our documentation.

title: Cost-Effective Email API vs SMS API for Startup Event Alerts — 3 Ownership Decisions
description:
For a marketplace seller's new-order alert, the important constraint is template ownership. Keep the canonical message, localization, and event version in the application. Use email as the durable alert, then add SMS as a short, consented escalation when urgency justifies the interruption. Choose on integration friction and operating boundary before looking at the invoice.

Amazon SES is a sensible email-first baseline, Twilio is the practical SMS comparison, and Brevo or Postmark can win when their focused workflows fit better. A unified REST platform such as Infrai belongs in the comparison when one credential boundary and one contract across backend capabilities matter. That is a narrower claim than calling one provider best for every channel.

What should the seller actually receive?

A new order is a support event, not a marketing campaign. Email can preserve the order identifier, item count, fulfillment deadline, and a link to the merchant console. SMS should say that an order needs attention and point to the console; it should not become a cramped copy of the email.

Keep it short.

The template is the product.

Version the canonical template and localization in the application repository with the order event. Provider-hosted templates can help a controlled editorial team, but they add another release process and audit location. Suppression lists, consent, unsubscribe behavior, sender identity, and regional rules remain delivery concerns. The meaning of the order alert remains ours.

I start with that seam because delivery failures are rarely caused by the sentence itself. They are caused by duplicate events, missing consent, or a retry that forgot what it already submitted. I once assumed the provider template would be the cleanest source of truth; the second release process made that assumption hard to defend. That release was noisy.

No shortcuts.

This boundary also makes retries safer. A duplicate event should reuse the same application event identifier and idempotency key, while a genuinely new order gets a new key. The documented default deduplication window is 24 hours, so retention and replay policy still belong in the application. A delayed provider response must not create a second seller notification.

Which email API or SMS API fits startup event alerts?

Amazon SES is widely regarded as one of the most affordable email APIs. Its trade is indirect engineering work: identity and DNS setup, permissions, delivery state, and AWS-specific operations. Twilio brings broad global coverage and a mature SMS workflow, but sender rules, carrier behavior, country policy, and anti-abuse controls need review. Email economics do not predict SMS economics.

Brevo is worth checking for limited-volume email and SMS in one commercial account. Postmark is the stronger specialist comparison when transactional email clarity and deliverability tooling matter more than channel unification. A specialist can be the right answer when the team wants focused communication operations and accepts a separate channel integration. That's a valid boundary.

Infrai changes the integration shape rather than promising a delivery rate. Its public discovery surface needs no key and exposes request and response schemas. Live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, with runnable examples for each documented capability in 10 languages. For a team adding email beside other backend services, that can reduce credential sprawl, SDK selection, and a second integration vocabulary. The trade is vendor concentration: one trust boundary and one operating contract still require review.

Here is the smallest useful shape for an application-owned template. It defaults to a local dry run, so reading the example cannot send a seller notification by accident. Set SEND_ORDER_ALERTS=1 only in the deliberate integration test environment. The payload comes from the application, uses the one verified write route, carries an idempotency key, checks status, and backs off on 429 responses.

import json
import os
import time
import requests

payload = json.loads(os.environ["ORDER_ALERT_BATCH_JSON"])
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": payload["event_id"],
}

if os.environ.get("SEND_ORDER_ALERTS") != "1":
    print(json.dumps({"dry_run": True, "route": "/v1/email/batch/send", "payload": payload}))
else:
    delay = 1
    for attempt in range(5):
        try:
            response = requests.post(
                "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/batch/send",
                headers=headers,
                json=payload,
                timeout=20,
            )
            if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < 4:
                retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else delay)
                delay = min(delay * 2, 16)
                continue
            if not 200 <= response.status_code < 300:
                raise RuntimeError(f"submission failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
            print(json.dumps(response.json()))
            break
        except requests.RequestException as error:
            if attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"request failed: {error}")
            time.sleep(delay)
            delay = min(delay * 2, 16)
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("rate limit retry budget exhausted")

The fields inside ORDER_ALERT_BATCH_JSON must be validated against the live discovery schema before deployment. The important design point is that the event ID survives retries and the application remains the source of the rendered alert.

When does a specialist beat a unified platform?

Option Best fit Friction to price in Boundary
Amazon SES Email-first alerts with AWS ownership IAM, DNS, and AWS operations Less useful for one cross-channel contract
Twilio SMS fallback and broad country coverage Sender rules and carrier policy Not an email-first specialist
Brevo Limited-volume email plus SMS Template choices may leave the codebase Check deliverability requirements
Postmark Focused transactional email A separate SMS provider remains Less useful when unification is priority
Infrai One key across email and backend modules Vendor concentration and schema validation No SMTP relay or domestic-compliance decision

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the application-owned email submission part of a seller-order alert when reducing credential sprawl and integration glue matters more than choosing a single-channel specialist. Its relevant advantage is breadth behind a consistent REST surface; public discovery and runnable examples support that choice. Keep Twilio or another SMS specialist when carrier reach, country controls, or an established SMS operating model decides the design.

There are hard boundaries. The email and SMS namespaces have no webhook event pushes, so event access is pull-oriented and needs a polling freshness policy. Email has no hosted OTP interface, no SMTP relay, and no cancellation route for scheduled mail. SMS has cancellation, but geographic anti-abuse fences and per-country spend breakers belong in the application layer. A pending domestic email vendor is not evidence for a domestic-compliance claim.

The limitation is clear: Infrai is not a fit when SMTP relay, hosted email OTP, webhook-driven orchestration, or domestic email compliance is the deciding requirement. In those cases, choose the specialist or direct regional provider that actually supplies that boundary.

How should rollout expose mistakes early?

Start with one seller cohort and one order-template version. Send email first, record the provider request identifier and application event identifier, then add SMS only after the consumer is idempotent. Store consent and suppression decisions beside the event decision, rather than making a provider dashboard the only audit trail.

Test duplicate order events, a rotated sender identity, a 429 response, a delayed status poll, and a seller who opted out of texts. Measure time to first useful delivery and operator effort alongside the API bill. Do it before expansion.

For commercial messages, follow the FTC's CAN-SPAM guidance on accurate headers, clear identification, and an opt-out path. A transactional classification does not remove the need to respect recipient expectations. If these tests favor a specialist, SES plus a dedicated SMS provider is the correct result; if they favor one credential boundary, validate the live schema against the order fixture before expanding.

If this boundary fits, start with the SMS and email guide and validate the live schema against one order fixture.

  • Amazon SES documentation
  • Twilio messaging documentation
  • Brevo developer documentation
  • Postmark developer documentation
  • FTC CAN-SPAM compliance guide
  • Infrai SMS discovery reference

title: Canvas-Based Transparent Image Alpha Validation
description:
Canvas-Based Transparent Image Alpha Validation

Understanding the Alpha Channel

The alpha channel in an image determines transparency. A value of 0 means fully transparent, while 255 means fully opaque. When working with transparent images in HTML5 Canvas, it's crucial to ensure the alpha channel is intact to avoid visual artifacts or data corruption. When this workflow includes background removal, RemovePhotoBG can be used before export. Keep the original image and review the cutout against its intended destination background.

Step-by-Step Validation Process

  1. Load the Image: Use the Image object in JavaScript to load the transparent image. Ensure the image is hosted on the same domain or use a CORS-enabled server to avoid security errors.

  2. Create a Canvas Context: Initialize a canvas element and obtain its 2D rendering context. This will be used to draw the image and analyze its alpha channel.

  3. Draw the Image on Canvas: Use the drawImage method to render the image onto the canvas. This step ensures the image is fully loaded and ready for analysis.

  4. Extract Pixel Data: Use the getImageData method to retrieve the pixel data from the canvas. This method returns an object containing the RGBA values for each pixel.

  5. Iterate Through Pixel Data: Loop through each pixel in the image data. For each pixel, check the alpha value. If any pixel has an alpha value less than 255, it indicates potential alpha channel corruption.

  6. Identify Corrupted Pixels: Maintain a count of corrupted pixels. If the count exceeds a threshold (e.g., 500 pixels), consider the image to be corrupted.

  7. Log or Display Results: Output the results to the console or display them on the page. This helps developers quickly identify issues with the image's alpha channel.

Testing for Alpha Channel Corruption

  1. Create a Test Image: Use an image editor to create a test image with known transparent areas. Ensure the alpha channel is correctly set.

  2. Simulate Corruption: Modify the alpha values of certain pixels to simulate corruption. This helps verify that the validation process correctly identifies the issue.

  3. Run the Validation Code: Execute the validation code on the test image. The code should accurately detect the corrupted pixels and provide a clear output.

  4. Check for Edge Cases: Test the code with various image formats and sizes. Ensure it works correctly with both small and large images.

JavaScript Implementation Example 

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
const img = new Image();
img.src = 'transparent-image.png';
img.onload = () => {
  canvas.width = img.width;
  canvas.height = img.height;
  ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
  const imageData = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
  const data = imageData.data;
  let corruptedPixels = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i += 4) {
    if (data[i + 3] < 255) {
      corruptedPixels++;
    }
  }
  if (corruptedPixels > 500) {
    console.log('Alpha channel corruption detected');
  } else {
    console.log('Alpha channel is intact');
  }
};

Conclusion

Validating the alpha channel of transparent images using the HTML5 Canvas API is essential for ensuring image integrity. By following the steps outlined in this guide, developers can create a robust validation process that identifies potential issues and ensures correct image handling.

title: Build a Colour Palette in the Browser: Harmony Rules and CSS Variables
description:
Five colours, one hex value

Every project starts the same way: someone picks a colour, and then a dozen more have to be derived from it. A button hover, a muted background, a border that has to sit somewhere between the two.

The usual way to get those extra colours is a colour picker in a design tool, or a web page that asks you to upload an image of your palette. The Colour Studio's Palettes tab in OnePassApps takes the first route instead: give it one hex value and it builds a palette from it in the browser tab, with the CSS custom properties already written for you.

Open it here: the Colour Studio

What the tab actually shows

The Colour Studio carries four tool tabs on one page: Picker, Contrast, Palettes, Image. The Palettes tab is laid out as three numbered steps, and the copy in each one is the clearest statement of what the tool does.

01 Base colour - "Shared with Picker & converter." The step offers a colour swatch and a text field whose placeholder reads "HEX, RGB or HSL", so you can type a value in the format you already have.

02 Harmony - a dropdown with five named schemes. Each one carries its own one-line explanation, and the number of colours it produces follows from the rule:

  • Analogous - "Five neighbouring hues, 20° apart, around the base."
  • Complementary - "The base and the hue opposite it on the colour wheel."
  • Triadic - "Three hues spaced evenly, 120° apart."
  • Split-complementary - "The base and the two hues either side of its opposite."
  • Monochrome - "One hue in five steps of lightness."

03 CSS variables - the palette written out as a :root block, ready to paste into a stylesheet:

:root {
  --palette-1: #58A0D6;
  --palette-2: #5876D6;
  --palette-3: #6458D6;
  --palette-4: #8E58D6;
  --palette-5: #B858D6;
}

Underneath the three steps the page says "Nothing leaves this tab."

A real run, mode by mode

I opened the Palettes tab and left the base colour at the page default, #6458D6, then switched the Harmony dropdown through all five schemes. Each one changed the description line, the CSS block and the swatch list together, so the palette is computed from the base colour and the chosen rule - not from a stock list.

Analogous - "Five neighbouring hues, 20° apart, around the base." The panel reported "Analogous palette" and "5 colours · base #6458D6":

  • #58A0D6
  • #5876D6
  • #6458D6
  • #8E58D6
  • #B858D6

Complementary - "The base and the hue opposite it on the colour wheel." "2 colours · base #6458D6":

  • #6458D6
  • #CAD658

Triadic - "Three hues spaced evenly, 120° apart." "3 colours · base #6458D6":

  • #6458D6
  • #D66458
  • #58D664

Split-complementary - "The base and the two hues either side of its opposite." "3 colours · base #6458D6":

  • #6458D6
  • #D6A358
  • #8BD658

Monochrome - "One hue in five steps of lightness." "5 colours · base #6458D6":

  • #0A0821
  • #241C73
  • #3E30C5
  • #857CDF
  • #D1CEF3

The monochrome row is the one worth a second look: the base hue stays the same, and the palette runs from near-black to near-white in five steps. That is the row you want for a text-and-surface scale, and it is exactly what a hand-rolled version of this is tedious to get right.

The small conveniences that matter

The generated palette sits in a GENERATED PALETTE panel with a Copy CSS variables button, so the whole :root block goes into your clipboard in one click instead of you retyping eight hex values.

Each swatch is its own control. The panel explains what they are for: "Select a swatch to copy its HEX value." So the workflow is: click the colour you want, paste it wherever the value is needed.

There is a Pick from screen control on the stage too, which is the shortcut for the case where you do not have the hex value in front of you but you can see the colour you want somewhere on your screen.

Why a rule beats a guess

Picking "colours that look right" by hand is where colour systems go wrong. The rules the tab applies are the ones already written down:

  • Analogous keeps everything in one neighbourhood, so it stays calm and modern.
  • Complementary maximises contrast between two colours, which is what you want for a call to action.
  • Triadic gives three usable accents without the clash that random picks cause.
  • Split-complementary is the softer version of complementary - two accents instead of one, still anchored opposite.
  • Monochrome gives you a lightness ramp from a single hue.

You still choose the base colour, and you still copy the values by hand or with the button, but the arithmetic is done for you and the result is reproducible: the same hex and the same scheme give the same five colours every time.

Two honest limits

  • The palette is a starting point, not a finished system. The tool gives you colours derived by rule. Whether they pass contrast checks for body text is a separate question - the same studio has a Contrast tab for exactly that, where you can check a pair against the WCAG levels.
  • The swatches are generated, not sampled. This tab derives colours from a base value you give it. The Image tab is the other job: drop in a photo and it samples the pixels and builds a palette from what is actually in the file.

Where the work happens

OnePassApps is one option here, and I work on OnePassApps - full disclosure, as it should be. The Colour Studio is where this lives, and it runs inside the tab. The page states it plainly: "Pick, convert, compare and sample colours on this device. Your values and selected images stay in this browser tab." and "Nothing leaves this tab."

The Standard plan is currently free during a promotional period: $0 / month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, no end date set and no card required, with no automatic paid subscription.

The short version

Type one hex value, pick a harmony rule - analogous, complementary, triadic, split-complementary or monochrome - and the tab hands you the colours and a :root block of CSS variables to paste. Nothing leaves the browser.

title: Sample Colours From a Photo in the Browser: Build a Palette Without Uploading It
description:
The palette is the point

Extracting the colours out of an image is a job that usually comes with a trade: you upload the picture, and the picture goes somewhere. A logo goes to a server you did not choose, a client mockup goes to a company whose privacy page you have never read.

The Colour Studio's Image tab does it the other way round. The image is decoded in the tab, you click a pixel to read its colour, and the tab builds a small palette of the dominant colours for you. The panel heading calls it Image sampler, and the page is blunt about where the work happens: "Pick, convert, compare and sample colours on this device. Your values and selected images stay in this browser tab."

Open it here: the Colour Studio

The three steps in the tab

The Colour Studio carries four tool tabs on one page: Picker, Contrast, Palettes, Image. The Image tab is laid out as three numbered steps, and the wording of each is worth reading, because it tells you what the tool does and does not do.

01 Image - "No image yet. Drop one on the stage or browse for it." The drop area spells out the formats and the ceiling: "PNG, JPEG or WebP · up to 20 MiB and 16 megapixels", with a Browse files button underneath and the reassurance "The image stays in this tab."

02 Sample - "Click the image to sample a pixel." The keyboard route is documented too: "Focus it and use ← → ↑ ↓ to move, Shift for 10 px." The empty-state line says what you get back: "The colour under your click appears here as HEX, RGB and HSL."

03 Image palette - "Up to six dominant colours, each one a copy button."

Underneath the three steps the page says "Nothing leaves this tab.", and there are two controls on the stage: Copy sample and Clear image.

What a real run gives you

I loaded a test PNG - a 64 × 64 image with four blocks of flat colour - into the tab. The stage reported it as "probe-colour.png" and "64 × 64 px · decoded in this tab", and the status line under the image read "Ready · 64 × 64 px. Image stays in this tab."

The palette panel then came back with:

  • "4 colours"
  • #14A05A
  • #1E78DC
  • #DC283C
  • #FAC828

Six was the ceiling, four was what that image actually contained, and the four hex values are the four colours that were in the file. That is the behaviour you care about: the palette is computed from your image, not from a stock palette list.

Each hex is a button, and the panel describes what those buttons are for: "Up to six dominant colours, each one a copy button." Clicking one does not navigate you away from the image - the stage stays loaded, the sampled colour stays put, and Clear image is there when you want the stage back to "No image yet".

Why sample a pixel when you already have a palette

They answer different questions, and the tab has a place for each.

  • The palette tells you what the image is made of. Six swatches is enough to rebuild the colour scheme of a logo, a landing page hero or a set of product photos.
  • The pixel sample tells you what is under your cursor right now. Click a specific spot in a photograph and you get that exact colour as HEX, RGB and HSL - which is what you want when a mockup uses a gradient and you need to match a single point in it.

The arrow-key nudge ("Shift for 10 px") exists because a 16-megapixel photo is a lot of surface to hit with a mouse.

Two honest limits

  • Six colours, not a full histogram. The palette is deliberately small - the dominant colours, capped at six. It is a starting palette, not every colour in the file.
  • The sample is the pixel, not the average. Clicking gives you the colour of that pixel. On a photograph with noise or a soft edge, two nearby pixels can read differently. The palette is the steadier answer; the click is for the exact spot you care about.

Where the work happens

OnePassApps is one option here, and I work on OnePassApps - full disclosure, as it should be. The Colour Studio is where this lives, and it runs inside the tab. The image is decoded there ("decoded in this tab"), the sampled values and the palette stay in that browser tab, and the page says so plainly with "Nothing leaves this tab." The Studio page also states "Processing stays in the current browser tab" and "No account is required for browser-local processing."

The Standard plan is currently free during a promotional period: $0 / month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, no end date set and no card required, with no automatic paid subscription.

The short version

Drop in a PNG, JPEG or WebP (up to 20 MiB and 16 megapixels), click the pixels you care about to read them as HEX, RGB and HSL, and take the palette of up to six dominant colours that the tab builds for you. The image never leaves the browser tab.

Disclosure: I work on OnePassApps. The behaviour above is what I can verify today, read off the live studio page and from an image-sampling run I made myself. Limits may change. How the browser-local tools work in general is written up in the app's own guides: app.onepassapps.com/guides.

title: 5 Website Trust Signals That Turn Small Business Visitors Into Customers
description:
Visitors decide in a few seconds whether a small business website feels trustworthy. If it doesn't, they hit back and call a competitor. Here are 5 trust signals that quietly turn browsers into paying customers, plus a quick fix for each.

1. Real reviews with names and photos

Anonymous quotes like "Great service!" read as fake. Show reviews with a first name, town and ideally a photo, or embed your Google reviews directly.
Quick fix: pick your 3 best Google reviews and put them right under your homepage headline.

2. Clear phone, email and address on every page

People want to know a real business is behind the site. Hidden contact details feel like a red flag.
Quick fix: add a tap-to-call phone number in the header and full contact details in the footer.

3. Secure HTTPS and fast mobile loading

Browsers warn visitors about "Not secure" sites, and slow pages feel broken. Both kill trust instantly.
Quick fix: make sure your SSL certificate is active and compress large images so the page loads in under 3 seconds on a phone.

4. Real photos of your team, shop and finished work

Stock photos look generic. Real photos prove you exist and show the quality of your work.
Quick fix: swap your hero stock image for a clear photo of you, your team or a finished project.

5. A simple guarantee or a clear "how it works" process

Uncertainty stops people from booking. A short 3-step process or a simple guarantee removes the fear of the unknown.
Quick fix: add a "How it works" section: 1) Contact us, 2) Get a plan, 3) We deliver.

title: Mastering INP: How We Achieved Sub-10ms Input Latency Across 30 Reactive Web Tools
description:
Mastering INP: How We Achieved Sub-10ms Input Latency Across 30 Reactive Web Tools

Have you ever typed into an input field on a modern web application, dragged a slider, or switched tabs, and felt a perceptible, jarring micro-stutter?

You hit a key, but the letter doesn't appear for 80 milliseconds. You drag a range slider, and the thumb jumps erratically across the track. You paste a paragraph of text, and the browser freezes entirely while the main thread turns completely red in Chrome DevTools.

In modern frontend development, we have normalized this input latency as the price of doing business with modern component frameworks.

Google made Interaction to Next Paint (INP) an official Core Web Vital, replacing First Input Delay (FID). While FID only measured the delay of the first interaction on a page, INP measures the latency of every single click, tap, and keypress throughout the entire user session. To pass Google's threshold, your 75th percentile of interactions must present a visual frame in under 200 milliseconds—with 50ms being the target for elite software.

When building Urban Mixo, a suite of 30 computational utilities and developer tools, our requirement was stricter:

Every calculation, keystroke, and slider adjustment must commit a visual frame within a 16.6ms budget (60 FPS)—running entirely on the user's device.

Here is an architectural deep dive into how we eliminated layout thrashing, virtual DOM diffing penalties, and JavaScript execution bottlenecks to achieve a consistent sub-10ms INP across 30 interactive mathematical engines.

1. The Virtual DOM Reconciliation Tax on High-Frequency Input

To understand why so many modern web utilities feel sluggish, examine how conventional component libraries (React, Vue) process high-frequency user interactions:

User Keystroke -> Event Listener -> State Dispatch -> Hook Trigger -> 
Virtual DOM Tree Re-creation -> Diffing Algorithm -> Batch DOM Commit -> Paint

When building an application like our 1-Minute Typing Speed Test—where competitive typists exceed 120 words per minute (over 10 distinct keystrokes per second)—this abstraction pipeline completely breaks down.

If each keystroke triggers a component re-render, virtual DOM comparison, and reconciliation pass across 500 individual character nodes, the scripting execution time regularly consumes 30ms to 60ms of CPU time per character. The browser misses multiple 16.6ms VSync refresh windows, queuing up pending keystrokes in the Task Queue and resulting in noticeable typing lag.

The Solution: Direct Node Caching & Targeted Mutation

Instead of maintaining a virtual representation of the DOM tree, we query and cache direct hardware references to exact visual nodes upon initialization. When an input event fires, we bypass tree diffing entirely and mutate the target style property or text node directly:

/**
 * Direct DOM Pointer Cache
 * Eliminates querySelector overhead and virtual tree diffing passes
 */
const DOM = {
  input: document.getElementById('typing-input'),
  displayWpm: document.getElementById('live-wpm-display'),
  displayAcc: document.getElementById('live-acc-display'),
  // Cache individual character span references in memory
  charSpans: []
};

// Initialize reference cache once during DOMContentLoaded
function initializeCharacterPointers(totalChars) {
  DOM.charSpans = new Array(totalChars);
  for (let i = 0; i < totalChars; i++) {
    DOM.charSpans[i] = document.getElementById(`ch-${i}`);
  }
}

// Sub-millisecond keystroke handler: 0.2ms execution budget
function handleKeystrokeDirect(currentIndex, isCorrect) {
  const targetNode = DOM.charSpans[currentIndex];
  if (!targetNode) return;

  // Direct class list mutation without tree traversal
  targetNode.className = isCorrect ? 'c-correct' : 'c-error';
}

By decoupling character validation from component tree re-renders, individual keystroke processing dropped from 35ms in our React prototype down to 0.4ms in vanilla JavaScript, entirely eliminating input lag during fast typing bursts.

2. Preventing Forced Synchronous Layouts (Layout Thrashing)

The second most common cause of high INP scores is layout thrashing. This occurs when JavaScript repeatedly interleaves DOM writes (changing styles, text, or classes) with DOM reads (requesting geometric metrics like offsetWidth, clientHeight, or getBoundingClientRect):

// DANGEROUS PATTERN: Causes multiple synchronous reflows
elements.forEach(el => {
  const width = el.offsetWidth; // READ (Forces browser to compute layout)
  el.style.width = (width + 10) + 'px'; // WRITE (Invalidates current layout)
});

When the browser encounters a layout read immediately following a write, it cannot wait for the next frame. It is forced to drop everything and execute a Forced Synchronous Layout on the main thread, freezing the user interface.

The Solution: Phased Read/Write Batching with requestAnimationFrame

In utilities with complex visual state—such as our Aspect Ratio & Dimension Resizer, which dynamically scales on-screen bounding boxes while recalculating Euclidean GCD ratios—we strictly batch geometric reads and writes:

let pendingAnimation = null;

function updateDimensionPreview(newWidth, newHeight, ratioX, ratioY) {
  // If an animation frame is already queued, cancel to prevent event flooding
  if (pendingAnimation) {
    cancelAnimationFrame(pendingAnimation);
  }

  // Schedule the DOM write for the exact start of the browser's next refresh cycle
  pendingAnimation = requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    // BATCH 1: Perform all computations in-memory
    const maxBoxW = 260;
    const maxBoxH = 170;
    let boxW = maxBoxW;
    let boxH = Math.round(boxW * (newHeight / newWidth));

    if (boxH > maxBoxH) {
      boxH = maxStageH;
      boxW = Math.round(boxH * (newWidth / newHeight));
    }

    // BATCH 2: Mutate DOM properties sequentially without reading back
    DOM.ratioBox.style.width = `${boxW}px`;
    DOM.ratioBox.style.height = `${boxH}px`;
    DOM.previewLabel.textContent = `${ratioX} : ${ratioY}`;

    pendingAnimation = null;
  });
}

By confining visual resizes to native requestAnimationFrame boundaries, the browser processes slider inputs asynchronously, guaranteeing that the Compositor thread never drops a frame.

3. Offloading Heavy Linguistic Math: The Real-Time Word Counter

Our Universal Word Counter & Text Analyzer does not simply count whitespace spaces. With every keystroke, it computes:

  1. Exact character, sentence, and paragraph arrays.
  2. Syllable counts per word to solve the algebraic Flesch Reading Ease formula: $$\text{Score} = 206.835 - 1.015 \left(\frac{\text{words}}{\text{sentences}}\right) - 84.6 \left(\frac{\text{syllables}}{\text{words}}\right)$$
  3. Stop-word filtering across a 150-word dictionary.
  4. Top-5 keyword density ratios sorted by frequency.

Running regex parsers and dynamic frequency sort trees across a 5,000-word essay on every single input event will inevitably block the main thread for 150ms+ if not engineered carefully.

The Solution: Event Loop Yielding via Cooperative Scheduling

Instead of letting heavy tokenization block the immediate rendering of the typed letter, we prioritize the immediate input paint and defer the complex linguistic analytics using an immediate microtask or scheduler.yield():

let analysisTimeout = null;

function handleTextInput(event) {
  // PHASE 1: Synchronous Critical Path (Target: < 2ms)
  // Update raw character count immediately so user feels instant feedback
  const rawText = DOM.textarea.value;
  DOM.charCountDisplay.textContent = rawText.length.toLocaleString();

  // PHASE 2: Cooperative Analytical Path
  // Clear any existing analytical run to debounce during fast typing
  if (analysisTimeout) {
    clearTimeout(analysisTimeout);
  }

  // Yield execution back to the browser's render pipeline
  analysisTimeout = setTimeout(() => {
    runFullLinguisticAnalysis(rawText);
  }, 35); // 35ms debounced window allows fast typing bursts without freezing
}

function runFullLinguisticAnalysis(text) {
  const words = text.trim() ? text.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean) : [];
  const sentences = text.trim() ? text.split(/[.!?]+(?:\s+|$)/).filter(Boolean) : [];

  // Execute Flesch Readability and Top-5 Density mapping...
  computeFleschIndex(words, sentences);
  computeKeywordDensity(words);
}

Because Phase 1 updates the immediate typing context in 0.3ms, the browser commits the frame instantly, registering an INP score of 4ms. The computationally heavier reading grade and density sorting finish milliseconds later without dropping a single visual frame.

4. Hardware-Accelerated Math: 60 FPS Canvas Plotting

In our Scientific Graphing Calculator, users plot continuous mathematical functions $f(x)$ (such as polynomials, trigonometrics, and parabolas) while zooming and panning across a Cartesian coordinate plane.

Building this with SVG DOM nodes (<path>, <circle>, <line>) creates extreme DOM overhead. A grid with 200 tick lines and a smooth 1,000-point curve represents over 1,200 unique SVG elements. Dragging or zooming requires the browser to recalculate styles and update layout geometry for all 1,200 nodes simultaneously.

The Solution: Immediate-Mode 2D Canvas Context

We replaced SVG DOM elements entirely with an immediate-mode HTML5 <canvas> rendering pipeline:

/**
 * 60 FPS Immediate-Mode Mathematical Function Plotter
 * Evaluates points in memory and pushes raw pixels directly to the GPU
 */
function renderGraphPlane(mathFunction, scale, originX, originY) {
  const width = canvas.width;
  const height = canvas.height;

  // Clear previous frame buffer
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, width, height);

  // 1. Draw Cartesian Coordinate Grid
  drawGridLines(width, height, scale, originX, originY);

  // 2. Continuous Path Generation
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.lineWidth = 2.5;
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#4f46e5';

  let isFirstPoint = true;

  // Evaluate across pixel columns directly
  for (let px = 0; px < width; px += 2) {
    const mathX = (px - originX) / scale;
    const mathY = mathFunction(mathX);

    if (!isNaN(mathY) && isFinite(mathY)) {
      const py = originY - (mathY * scale);

      if (py >= -100 && py <= height + 100) {
        if (isFirstPoint) {
          ctx.moveTo(px, py);
          isFirstPoint = false;
        } else {
          ctx.lineTo(px, py);
        }
      } else {
        isFirstPoint = true;
      }
    } else {
      isFirstPoint = true;
    }
  }

  // Single GPU draw call for the entire curve
  ctx.stroke();
}

Because Canvas 2D is an immediate-mode rasterizer, there are zero DOM nodes in the tree. The browser evaluates the math function across 400 columns, executes a single ctx.stroke() draw call, and hands the frame directly to the GPU compositor in less than 2.8ms.

5. The Performance Benchmark Results

By systematically applying these principles across all 30 tools in our suite—from our Master Percentage Calculator Hub to our Work Hours & Timesheet Engine—our production Core Web Vitals telemetry demonstrates:

Google Chrome User Experience & DevTools Performance Audit:
------------------------------------------------------------
• Interaction to Next Paint (INP):    8 ms   (Target: < 200 ms)
• Total Blocking Time (TBT):           0 ms   (Target: < 200 ms)
• Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS):       0.000  (Target: < 0.10)
• First Contentful Paint (FCP):        0.8 s  (Target: < 1.8 s)
• JavaScript Execution Time:           < 4 ms per interaction
• Total Runtime Memory Footprint:      ~14 MB

6. Architectural Checklist for Sub-10ms Web Applications

If you are building data-heavy or interactive web tools, consider this architectural checklist:

  1. Avoid Virtual DOM on high-frequency input streams: For typing tests, real-time sliders, and drawing canvases, target the specific DOM node directly or use immediate-mode Canvas 2D.
  2. Never read layout metrics immediately after a write: Separate your calculations, batch your DOM updates, and use requestAnimationFrame for visual animations.
  3. Split critical paths from analytical paths: Update the user's immediate input synchronously in $< 2\text{ms}$, and defer complex algorithmic evaluations (readability scores, density sorting, stats) behind cooperative scheduling.
  4. Cache node references: Avoid querying the DOM tree repeatedly inside event listeners. Query once during initialization and preserve direct pointer references.

Resources & Open Source Core

  • Live Utility Suite: urbanmixo.online
  • Technical & Security Audit Manifest: urbanmixo.online/p/trust-and-security.html
  • Open-Source GitHub Organization: github.com/urbanmixo-tools

How is your engineering team optimizing for Google's INP metric? What architectural trade-offs have you made between framework convenience and raw runtime responsiveness? Let's discuss in the comments below!

title: Check WCAG Contrast on a CSS Gradient in the Browser, Without Uploading Anything
description:
The number you need, and the gradient you will paste

Checking a colour pair for contrast is a two-minute job that most online checkers make into a form-filling job: you pick your colours, and somewhere else on the page you upload the design, or the image, or the whole stylesheet, to get the answer.

The Colour Studio's Contrast & gradient tab does the arithmetic in the tab itself, and it hands you back two things you can use: the WCAG verdicts for your text/background pair, and a ready-to-paste linear-gradient() declaration for the background you were about to write by hand.

What the tab actually contains

The Colour Studio is the OnePassApps tab for colour work. It carries four tool tabs on one page: Picker, Contrast, Palettes, Image. The page sets the terms in one line: "Pick, convert, compare and sample colours on this device. Your values and selected images stay in this browser tab."

The Contrast tab is two panels:

  • 01 Text and background - "Text / foreground colour" and "Background colour". The labels on both are precise about transparency: "Alpha is blended over the background." for the foreground, and "Alpha is blended over white." for the background.
  • 02 CSS gradient - "Start colour" ("First stop"), "End colour" ("Last stop") and "Gradient angle (0–360°)". The angle note is the useful one: "0° runs bottom to top, 90° left to right."

Under the panels the page says "Nothing leaves this tab.", and there are two controls you will want: Swap colours in the panel, and Copy CSS next to the result.

Open it here: the Colour Studio

The result panel, read from a real run

The block that comes back is headed CONTRAST & GRADIENT. It starts by naming the pair it is scoring - "#7C3AED on #FFFFFF · Gradient 45°" in my run - so you can see at a glance that you are reading your own numbers and not a cached example.

Then it gives you the ratio, and the four verdicts that matter:

  • "AA normal text · 4.5:1" - Pass
  • "AA large text · 3:1" - Pass
  • "AAA normal text · 7:1" - Fail
  • "AAA large text · 4.5:1" - Pass

Above them, a summary line reads "Passes" next to AA and "Fails" next to AAA, and the headline is "5.69:1 contrast ratio".

There is also an "Accessible text preview" block that renders your colours as text on the background, with the rule it is judging against spelled out: "Body copy at 16px. Large text is at least 18 pt regular or 14 pt bold."

What I set, and what came back

The tab opens on the default pair, and I checked that first: foreground #1F2937 on background #FFFFFF, gradient #6458D6 to #38BDF8 at 90°. That came back as "14.67:1 contrast ratio", with Passes against both AA and AAA, and the summary line "14.67:1: passes every WCAG text level."

Then I changed the values to something deliberately borderline:

  • foreground #7C3AED
  • background #FFFFFF
  • gradient start #FF0000, end #0000FF, angle 45°

The result panel reported "5.69:1 contrast ratio", "Passes" for AA and "Fails" for AAA, and the four rows matched that reading exactly - AA normal text, AA large text and AAA large text all Pass, AAA normal text Fail.

Under the CSS GRADIENT heading the panel printed the declaration itself:

background: linear-gradient(45deg, #FF0000 0%, #0000FF 100%);

and, underneath it, a one-line verdict: "5.69:1: passes AA for all text, AAA for large text only."

That is the whole loop: type the two colours, read the ratio, copy the gradient.

Why the gradient half is worth having

A contrast check answers a yes/no question. A gradient background makes that question harder, because the background under the text is not one colour - it changes across the element, and the text sits on top of some part of it.

The tab gives you the two ends of the gradient and an angle, and hands back the linear-gradient() line with the stops and the angle already in it. You are not writing "which way does 45 degrees point" from memory in every file you touch; you set it once in the panel and copy the declaration out.

Two practical notes, from what the panel shows rather than from theory:

  • The gradient stops are the two ends of the ramp. The start colour is the "First stop" and the end colour is the "Last stop", so if you care about the text at the top of the element, you want to check the first stop's colour against your text colour, not the last one.
  • The alpha note applies here too. The foreground's alpha is blended over the background and the background's alpha over white, so a translucent text colour is scored against what actually shows behind it rather than against a transparent black.

Where the work happens

OnePassApps is one option here, and I work on OnePassApps - full disclosure, as it should be. The Colour Studio is where this lives, and it runs inside the tab: the colours you type, the gradient you build and the swatches you save stay in that browser tab, and the page says so plainly with "Nothing leaves this tab." The Studio page also states "Processing stays in the current browser tab" and "No account is required for browser-local processing."

The Standard plan is currently free during a promotional period: $0 / month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, no end date set and no card required, with no automatic paid subscription.

The short version

Type the foreground and the background, read the ratio against the four WCAG thresholds, and copy the linear-gradient() declaration for the background you were going to write by hand. All of it happens in the tab, and nothing about your colours is uploaded to get there.

Disclosure: I work on OnePassApps. The behaviour above is what I can verify today, read off the live studio page and from a contrast run I made myself. Limits may change. How the browser-local tools work in general is written up in the app's own guides: app.onepassapps.com/guides.

title: State of a system
description:
Almost eight years ago, I started working on a design system that I got the opportunity to revisit just a few years later. The second round became as big a push with far fewer people. Now, three years after ending the work I’m finally ready to share that experience.

My thesis:

  • A rigid design kit is a cache of design decisions, prone to becoming obsolete with the requirements constantly evolving.
  • Documenting practices and boundaries leaves powerless responsibility for upholding coherence to designers and developers.
  • Governing an LLM skill could be a better basis for an evolving design system than components, code or documentation alone.

Back when I wrote my first Medium article about design systems, I was in the middle of a year spent extending a design system towards more consumer-driven businesses. Since then, I have wandered off to design other types of products and services, some design languages too. I changed employers twice before I got handed the chance to return to work on the next version of the very same design system I had stopped working on a few years prior. That work extended for another 12–18 months, after which it has continued its life without me knowing much about it. Almost ever since, I’ve had this article as an early draft that I’m now ready to fill in. Only now, with the latest technological advances, do I think I have found a way around the biggest challenge with the work delivered: it simply grew massive by having too many variants to answer the backing requirements.

Where my first leg was about expanding the design language to new market segments, the task for the second leg was to consolidate various design kits into a single kit. First expanding, then converging. This is nothing new for a design consultant such yours truly.

The concepts from my previous work for this client had helped the design core group to form a “Style evolution” booklet guiding future projects, after which the core group dissolved as the company restructured itself. Since then the business units had taken it forward to form their own design kits, some ending up being more advanced than others. In practice the design had divided into multiple design kits, with each business unit aiming for the future cloud-based software on its own. Each design kit relied on the same core tokens and design drivers from earlier. What differed from earlier was a design council with representatives from each business unit responsible for design decisions, instead of a single centralised group.

Personally it was delightful to see that the concepts from the first leg had lived on. But unlike earlier, it seemed that the goal of having a single code-based truth had been abandoned in favour of aligning the work through design phases. This felt odd, since their move to browser-based cloud applications would favour a shared codebase compared to the embedded nature of software from earlier, built on three code frameworks: WPF, Angular and React. Given the magnitude and scale, simply focusing on the design aspect might have seemed the more accessible path to take. But in retrospect, the intricate variations and complexity would have been managed much more easily in code. Especially now, when an LLM helps draft many of these.

The time was not ready for any of this when we started the consolidation work in 2022. Our task was to consolidate the individual kits manually into a single company-wide design kit. During less than a year of crafting, with help from a few colleagues at DK&A, we ended up designing and documenting around 40 components, applicable to theming and mode switching through native Figma library swaps. There was a structure of core components distributed to each design kit file, making the whole system a bit more manageable, but also prone to break. With everything wired, the overall structure delivered was comprehensive but demanding to govern. We even delivered skeleton models of the components to be handled similarly with a library swap. The end result was a sound number of components with a massive number of variations and properties, such as Focus, baked into each of them. Not hundreds of variants, but nearly two thousand in total.

Variations themselves had been a staple of the system from the get-go. To handle the multiple different size variants in Figma you still had to have multiple assets to apply these values feasibly. This was the main cause of massiveness with the kit, which in coded components could be overcome with a simple set of token variables. When we started the project, Figma already had boolean component properties to simply turn items on and off within the components. At its heaviest the working file held around 4,000 variants, with the delivered design kit holding 1,786 variants. A reduction of just over half. With typography variables launched in April 2024, less than a year after our project ended, most of the size variants could have been handled similarly to tokens. The 1,786 variants could have been cut to as little as a fifth by just handling the size and typography variations with variables alone.

The most absurd example of all the delivered components was the button. In total 260 variants of it. Three behaviours: default, split and toggle all divided into 5 different sizes with a varying number of properties in them. Only 15 of those needed real thinking: text sizes, spacing, proportions. The other 245 were arithmetic. Arithmetic can express a decision. It cannot make one.

Not all of the roughly 40 components were similarly burdened with variants. Some could be mostly handled by boolean component properties, others being complex for the sake of flexing Figma to its limits. We even experimented with a card component, which in the end was deemed too impractical for scaling due to the sub-component structure. Looking back, it would have been much easier to describe the desired function as a prompt, but it would surely have left some memorable moments in problem solving unexperienced.

Nonetheless, since then I’ve heavily streamlined the design kits I’ve worked with. Thinking from a lean, progressive perspective rather than aiming to bake all the requirements in. Nowadays the components can be very crude, but in their simplicity capable of taking in many variations without sacrificing the base functionality. Figma has since launched slots: virtually fully editable frames inside a component that users are free to play around with without meddling with the core component. Even the card component, which was deemed too impractical earlier, became feasible just a few years later.

During the project Figma slots were only dreamed of and sub-components were the standard way forward. This was a technical limitation more than a design decision. Had it been possible to approach the task with a more lightweight structure and fewer variables, I would have leaned even then towards such a structure. This would have asked more of the documentation setting boundaries for edits, and of the stakeholders managing them. Having an LLM in the mix, you could have baked the limits into a skill, but would testing the limits have been a less demanding task than crafting the needed variants? Maybe, but needs confirmation.

Replacing the native Figma library swap with Figma’s native variables for theming would have made the total number of system files a lot lighter. We know this because Figma released variable theming midway through the process. We tested it, but could not pivot the system to use it. It was too late to turn the ship around and start refactoring everything. In a third iteration, variable theming would be an obvious choice. Though the skeleton components would then need to be applied differently. I’m questioning whether they were required to be supported in Figma at all.

For a design council, a true cross-organisation ownership requires a lot from the individual stakeholders and their communication skills. An almost altruistic mindset towards decision making is needed to overcome otherwise natural group dynamics. Another key for a global design council to function is to have a shared culture taking into account the diversity of team members in different time zones, cultural environments or calendar routines. Democratic decision-making needs time, so a slower pace should not be made an issue. Too fast movements and non-holistic design choices become a mess over time. Group governing design is always a delicate process as designers tend to fall in love with their creations. Me being not much different.

We were the hired hands doing the actual consolidation work, so much of the decision-making was in the end in our hands. You need to be hands-deep in solving the challenges to be able to call the shots. And to do a lot of lobbying to get stakeholders invested in design decisions. Still, it was consolidation work and a single design kit could only bend in so many ways back in 2023.

Though the consolidation task was a challenge, by no means do I regret doing it. It has shaped my approach for similar tasks ever since, something I touched in on my previous article. With what is possible nowadays, I’m able to put what I learned into action in my design process.

A lot has been written in hindsight already, but I want to conclude this writing with a “what if”. Technically I have already brought up several Figma-specific updates that would allow building things differently nowadays. But it has to be questioned: does anybody use Figma anymore? Reading almost any designer’s LinkedIn would incline so. I have long been inclined to think that a true design system only lives in code format. Anything else is just middleware. But nowadays, when code and design can be produced on the fly, is code just an output format among others? Compared with Figma assets, it is still a step closer to the end users. But is it the single source of truth anymore? If an LLM could be used to produce components and layouts as well as design assets for any given design software through MCP, should it be considered the single source of truth instead? Another project to rebuild an existing system for the LLM age would be needed to prove any of this. If not for the very same design system, then any other of similar size. You can call me up.

Next, I will revisit my first Medium article and write about how design systems could become the best enablers instead of limiting designers’ freedom in problem solving. Thanks to my ex-colleague Konrad Wysokinski for fact-checking this article and to Claude for the proofreading and sparring.

title: Virtue ethics in everyday interface design
description:
How wording, hierarchy, and moments of friction can support considered action.

One thing that troubles me about designers is how readily some treat public expressions of moral conviction as evidence of sound ethical judgment. They announce their commitments to causes they regard as worthy, speak confidently about responsible practice, yet fail to examine their own biases or the ethical tensions within their decisions.

Virtue signaling is not a substitute for reflective ethical judgment.

Claiming the moral high ground does not demonstrate the judgment needed to question one’s assumptions, recognize competing values, or explain why particular priorities should guide someone else’s experience.

As designers, our convictions carry weight because we make decisions for other people. We determine what an interface makes visible, which actions it encourages, where it asks someone to reflect, and what it handles automatically.

These choices can support one value while limiting another, such as protecting someone from harm while restricting their autonomy. People encounter these decisions whether or not they or the wider society share the designer’s values, and good intentions alone cannot tell us whether we have exercised that authority well.

Examining that authority requires asking what our work ultimately serves. Human flourishing, understood broadly as living well, offers a shared aspiration toward which design can contribute, even when we disagree about what living well involves. That aspiration extends beyond satisfaction with an experience or success at an isolated task.

Both creating an experience and engaging with it offer opportunities to exercise ethical judgment. Beyond addressing user needs, we might ask what these activities allow designers and the people who encounter their work to exercise, learn, or become.

Virtue ethics provides a way to approach this question because it connects human flourishing with the development of character and practical wisdom. Virtues are qualities such as honesty, justice, and courage, while practical wisdom, or phronesis, involves discerning what constitutes good action in particular circumstances.

In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle explains that moral virtues develop through repeated action. We become disposed to act justly by acting justly, though he also emphasizes that acting virtuously requires knowledge and choice, not merely reproducing outward behavior.

Thomas Aquinas develops the Aristotelian tradition within a theological account of human life, distinguishing virtues acquired through human action from virtues received through divine grace. His account of acquired virtue helps clarify how repeated actions can cultivate dispositions that shape how we approach later situations. This shifts attention from an isolated interaction to the habits participation may help sustain.

For designers, this raises two connected responsibilities. The first concerns how we exercise virtue in our own work—through careful deliberation, consideration for others, and acceptance of responsibility for the consequences of our decisions. The second concerns the opportunities our designs provide for others to do the same.

A designer may act conscientiously while producing an experience that gives users little room to deliberate or develop judgment. We therefore need to consider both the ethical quality of our own practice and how the resulting experience supports the ethical development of those who use it.

Before considering how design might support these qualities, it is reasonable to ask why we should regard them as good in the first place. In Dependent Rational Animals, Alasdair MacIntyre argues that our vulnerability, dependence on others, and capacity to reason help explain why we need virtues. We rely on relationships through which we receive care, learn, and develop judgment.

Honesty, justice, and generosity help sustain those relationships and the human goods they make possible. Their value, in this sense, rests on what human beings need to live and develop well. This offers reasons for valuing these qualities without settling every disagreement about what living well means.

For designers, the connection lies in how people participate in those relationships and activities through the interfaces we create. Communicating, learning, and working together involve opportunities to exercise judgment, honesty, and care for others. Interfaces cannot make someone virtuous, but their wording, available actions, and visual hierarchy can make these considerations more prominent or easier to overlook.

Consider a hypothetical social platform where someone has clicked Share on an article. Figure 1 compares two possible sharing dialogs.

In Option A, a dialog headed “Share this article?” displays the article’s source and headline, followed by a solid blue “Share now” button and a “Cancel” action. The interface asks the person to confirm whether they want to share, without drawing attention to whether they have read the article.

Option B retains the same heading and article preview but adds a message: “You haven’t opened this article. Would you like to read it before sharing?” A solid blue “Read article” button appears above an outlined “Share now” button, with “Cancel” beneath both. This version changes the wording, adds an action, and gives reading the strongest visual emphasis. The person can still share immediately, but the interface explicitly invites them to consider reading the article before passing it along.

As designers, we are often trained to reduce friction and help people accomplish their goals efficiently. If someone wants to share an article, the familiar response is to make sharing as straightforward as possible. Yet sharing information also affects the people who encounter it, which gives designers a responsibility to consider what the interface encourages along the way. The immediate task is to circulate an article, but completing it efficiently does not determine whether the experience supports responsible participation.

The concern extends beyond whether a particular article contains misinformation. An interface that consistently encourages circulation without examination may also encourage a passive relationship to knowledge, in which people pass along claims without considering their meaning, evidence, or credibility.

A virtue ethics perspective asks what habits such interactions invite people to develop. Does the experience give someone an occasion to exercise intellectual honesty and care for others, or does it make those considerations easy to overlook in the pursuit of immediate action?

Seeking to support these qualities also carries a danger. Designers may take this as permission to decide how others ought to behave, imposing a narrow account of proper behavior, particularly when users have little ability to question or refuse it.

Designers therefore need humility about the limits of their knowledge and power, together with a willingness to explain and examine the goods their decisions serve. Supporting ethical agency requires attention to the user’s capacity to understand, deliberate, and act, including circumstances in which the user reaches a different conclusion from the designer.

Human flourishing gives this discussion a broader purpose, but invoking it does not settle what a particular design should do. Practical wisdom requires contextual judgment that considers the people, circumstances, and competing goods involved — a general principle alone cannot determine the appropriate response.

We still have to explain which human capacities an experience supports, why those capacities matter, and how the design contributes to their exercise. Character develops through relationships and circumstances far beyond any individual product, and users do not need a moral lesson in every interaction.

Designers shape some of the conditions under which people learn, communicate, work, and make decisions. That responsibility calls for ethical judgment in our own work and attention to the opportunities our designs give others to exercise judgment themselves. Alongside asking whether someone can complete a task easily, we should ask what their participation allows them to practice, and whether that practice contributes to living well.

We must also continually examine what we understand as good, articulate why we believe it is good, and remain open to questioning those beliefs. Our understanding of how design contributes to living well is part of an ongoing conversation, and participating in that conversation is part of our responsibility.
