title: Building an Offline-First POS That Stays Consistent With an Online Store
description:
We just shipped a Windows point of sale for StoreFlux (a headless commerce backend) that keeps working with no internet connection and never drifts out of sync with the online store it's attached to. Wanted to write up the actual mechanics, since "offline-first" gets used a lot as a buzzword without the plumbing behind it.

An outbox of idempotent events, not a sync API

Every action at the till — a sale, a refund, a shift open/close, a stock adjustment, a product edit — gets written to a local SQLCipher database in the same transaction as the receipt and the stock change, plus one row in an outbox table. A background loop drains that outbox to the server in order. Each event carries a client-generated id, and the server only ever applies a given id once. That one property is what makes a retry safe: if the network dies mid-request and the register doesn't know whether the server got it, it just resends the same event with the same id, and worst case the server politely no-ops it instead of creating a duplicate order.

The register and the server agree on money, because they're tested against each other

The till logic is written in Rust (rust_decimal for the actual math), the server side in C#. Those are two different type systems making the same calculations — tax, split tenders, discounts, change — and if they ever disagree by a cent, that's a real bug, not a rounding quirk to shrug off. So there's a parity test that replays identical sales through both engines and diffs the totals, tax, and stock to the cent. It's already caught two real bugs this way: refund restock math that didn't match between the two sides, and offline refunds that were getting dated at upload time instead of at the actual time of the sale — which matters a lot once you're closing out a shift and the cash doesn't add up because a refund landed in the wrong shift.

Stock is server stock plus local deltas, not an independent count

A register doesn't keep its own authoritative stock number. It shows the last full stock pull from the server, minus whatever it's sold locally and hasn't uploaded yet. That sounds like a small detail but it's the difference between "two tills at two different shops double-selling the last unit of something" and not — because neither till is pretending to own the real count, they're both just showing a server snapshot plus their own pending deltas.

Counter sales can't be allowed to lie to the analytics

This was a design decision I almost got wrong early on: should a point-of-sale order "count" the same as a website order everywhere? No — specifically not in the conversion funnel. Every order carries a channel now. Counter sales count fully in revenue, tax, and average order value (they're real money), but the website's conversion-rate and cart-abandonment numbers only look at online orders. Otherwise a slow week online looks artificially fine because the shop next door had a good Saturday, and that's actively misleading for anyone trying to diagnose their actual storefront.

Every receipt is also a lookup key

The receipt number prints as a barcode (CODE128, with the module width picked based on paper size so it actually fits a 58mm roll) or a QR code depending on config. Scan that receipt back into the app — at the counter, days later — and it opens that exact sale for a reprint or a refund. It's a small thing but it removes an entire category of "customer lost their receipt, now what" friction.

Security assumptions for something that lives on a shop's PC, unattended

A register activates with a one-time code and gets back a token that's stored hashed and bound to that specific machine's fingerprint, not something that's portable if someone copies a config file. The local database's encryption key lives in the OS credential store, not in a config file next to the database itself. And a register that's been offline longer than a configured grace period locks itself until it can reach the server again — better a cashier has to wait a minute for connectivity than a stolen laptop keeps ringing up sales indefinitely with no way to revoke it remotely.

Live now if you want to see where it landed: storeflux.store/#pos

Curious if anyone else has built something similar — specifically interested in how other people have handled the "two independent codebases computing the same money math" problem. Parity testing felt like the obvious answer once we needed it, but I'd like to hear if there's a cleaner pattern.

title: The Cheapest Way to Sync API Data to PostgreSQL (2026)
description:
The cheapest way to sync Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero or Paddle data to PostgreSQL in 2026: free tiers, real prices and hidden costs for 8 options, compared.

By Ilshaad Kheerdali · 2 November 2026

You want billing data from an API (Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero or Paddle) sitting in your own PostgreSQL database on a schedule, and you want to pay as little as possible for it. Fair enough. Most of the tools that do this were priced for data teams moving hundreds of tables into a warehouse, not for a founder who needs invoices next to a users table.

The honest answer to "what is the cheapest way" is that it depends on three numbers, and at small volumes the cheapest option is often free. This post prices eight real options with 2026 figures taken from each vendor's own pricing page, shows which one is cheapest at each stage, and covers the costs that do not appear on those pages.

The Three Numbers That Decide the Price

Every pricing model in this space charges on some mix of three things. Know yours before you compare anything.

  1. How many rows move each month. Not the size of your account, the volume that actually gets synced. Some tools count only rows that changed; others count every row written on every run. That difference can be tenfold for the same data.
  2. How many sources you need. One Stripe account is a very different purchase from Stripe plus Xero plus a CRM. Several tools charge per connection, and free tiers often restrict which connectors you can use.
  3. How often it needs to run. Daily is cheap almost everywhere. Hourly moves you up a tier with most vendors, and every-few-minutes is where prices jump.

There is a fourth number that no pricing page shows: your time. A free tool you have to host, patch and debug is not free. More on that below.

Every Option, Priced (2026)

Option Cheapest paid entry Free option Pricing unit Fastest schedule at entry price
DIY script + cron $0 plus hosting Yes Your time Whatever you build
Stripe real-time Postgres sync $0.0025 a row, or $100 a month for 50,000 rows 5,000 row changes a month Rows synced Real time (public preview)
Fivetran Usage-based, $5 base charge per connection 500,000 MAR a month Monthly active rows 15 minutes on Free
Airbyte Core (self-hosted) $0 plus a server Yes Your infrastructure Whatever you configure
Airbyte Cloud Standard From $20 a month 14-day trial Credits 1 hour
Codeless Sync $19 a month (Starter) 1,000 rows a month, manual Flat plan with row allowance Daily (12-hourly on Business)
Skyvia $99 a month, or $79 billed annually 10,000 records a month Flat plan Once a day on Free and Basic
Stitch From $100 a month 14-day trial Rows Plan-dependent
Hevo $299 a month, or $265 billed annually 1M events, limited connectors Events 1 hour on Free

A few of those need unpacking, because the headline number is rarely the whole story.

DIY: a script and a cron job

The cheapest option on paper. A Node or Python script that calls the Stripe API, upserts into Postgres, and runs from cron on a server you already pay for. Direct cost: nothing.

The real cost is everything after the first version works: pagination, rate-limit retries, OAuth token refresh for QuickBooks and Xero, schema changes when an API adds a field, and noticing when it silently stops. The hidden cost of rolling your own prices that out properly. If your time is worth anything, DIY is rarely the cheapest option past the first month.

Stripe's own real-time Postgres sync

If your only source is Stripe, start here. Since October 2026, Stripe Data Pipeline can stream Stripe API data straight into a Postgres database you own, on any host, as a public preview. It is metered on rows synced, meaning each create, update or delete Stripe writes to your database: the first 5,000 a month are free, then $0.0025 a row, or $100 a month for 50,000. The initial backfill of each table is free, and Stripe says most businesses never pass the free allowance. For a Stripe-only setup that is the cheapest option in this post, and the only real-time one at $0.

It covers Stripe and nothing else, it is a preview with no announced post-preview pricing, and the meter grows with your payment activity rather than staying flat. Stripe Data Pipeline now syncs to PostgreSQL covers its limits in detail. Supabase users may also know Supabase's earlier open-source Stripe Sync Engine, whose code now lives in Stripe's GitHub; for a new setup, Stripe's hosted sync does the same job without running anything yourself.

Fivetran Free

This is the one most "cheapest ETL" roundups quietly skip, so say it plainly: Fivetran's Free plan gives you 500,000 monthly active rows, 15-minute syncs, unlimited users and no time limit. A monthly active row is a distinct row that changed that month, counted once however many times it syncs, so a small SaaS business will usually sit far below the limit. For low volumes, Fivetran can genuinely cost $0.

The catch is what happens at the edge. Fivetran notifies you at 350,000 and 500,000 MAR; exceed the limit a second time and it freezes your connections until you upgrade. The paid Standard plan adds a $5 base charge per connection and bills on a consumption curve with no published per-row rate, which is why Fivetran pricing is hard to forecast. Free is a real plan. Knowing what month two of paid looks like is harder.

Airbyte: Core and Cloud

Airbyte comes in two shapes. Core is the open-source version you host yourself: no licence fee, but you run the server, the upgrades and the monitoring. Cloud Standard starts at $20 a month with 5 credits included, and you can buy more. Per Airbyte's credit docs, API sources cost 6 credits per million rows, and incremental syncs only charge for added, edited or deleted rows. So the included credits cover roughly 830,000 API rows a month, with hourly syncs. On raw price per row, that is hard to beat.

Two caveats matter for billing data specifically. Airbyte's Xero source is listed as available on self-hosted Core only, not on any Airbyte Cloud plan, so Xero on the $20 plan is off the table. And the Paddle source is a Marketplace connector, meaning community-maintained rather than supported by Airbyte's core team. Stripe and QuickBooks are both Airbyte-supported and available on Cloud.

Codeless Sync

Flat plans with a published row allowance: Free is $0 for 1,000 rows a month with manual syncs, Starter is $19 a month for 25,000 rows, Pro $29 for 100,000 and Business $99 for 500,000. All four billing providers are on every plan, any PostgreSQL host works, and scheduled syncs (daily, weekly or monthly, plus 12-hourly on Business) start at Starter. Annual billing drops those to $190, $290 and $990 a year.

Rows here count every row written by a sync, not distinct changed rows, so the sync mode matters. A full sync re-reads everything each run. A fixed window (last day, 7 days or 30 days) only fetches records from that window, which keeps the monthly count small. For QuickBooks and Xero the window is based on when a record was last updated; for Stripe it is based on when a record was created. More on estimating that below.

Skyvia, Stitch and Hevo

Skyvia has connectors for all four billing providers and PostgreSQL. Its free plan allows 10,000 records a month on a once-a-day schedule, with two scheduled integrations whose schedules expire after 30 days. Basic is $99 a month, or $79 billed annually, for 5 million records, still once a day; hourly needs Standard at $199 a month ($159 annually).

Stitch starts at $100 a month with a 14-day trial and no ongoing free plan.

Hevo has a free plan of 1M events a month with hourly scheduling, but only on a limited set of connectors, so check your source is on it before counting on it. The Starter plan is $299 a month, or $265 a month billed annually.

All three are capable products. For one or two billing sources, they are priced for a bigger job.

The Cheapest Option at Each Stage

Putting the numbers against actual situations:

Your situation Cheapest sensible option Monthly cost
Stripe only, under 5,000 row changes a month Stripe real-time Postgres sync $0
One source, low volume, happy with a usage meter Fivetran Free $0
Just testing whether billing data in Postgres is useful Codeless Sync Free $0
One to four billing sources, want the same bill every month Codeless Sync Starter $19
Many sources beyond billing, comfortable configuring pipelines Airbyte Cloud Standard From $20
You need hourly on a budget Airbyte Cloud Standard From $20
You have a spare server and an engineer's time Airbyte Core or DIY $0 plus hosting and time

Codeless Sync does not win every row of that table, and it should not. If Stripe is your only source, Stripe's own sync is very likely cheaper. If Fivetran Free covers you and you are comfortable watching a meter, it is cheaper. If you need hourly syncs, Airbyte gives you that at a price Codeless Sync does not match, because Codeless Sync does not offer hourly to customers at all.

Where it does win is the combination most small SaaS teams actually have: Stripe for revenue plus QuickBooks or Xero for the books, a daily refresh, any Postgres host, and a bill that is the same number every month.

The Costs Free Tiers Don't Show

The sticker price is the easy part. These are what actually change the maths:

  • The overage cliff. Free usage tiers end in a freeze or an upgrade, not a gentle slope. Fivetran freezes connections on a second overage. Stripe's Postgres sync does not freeze, it simply starts billing per row, so a busy month shows up on the invoice. Codeless Sync pauses syncing at the plan's row limit too, but the ceiling is a number on the pricing page you chose in advance, and it resets each billing period.
  • Connector maturity. A connector existing is not the same as it being supported. Community or marketplace connectors can lag API changes, which costs you debugging time the pricing page does not mention.
  • Hosting. Self-hosted Airbyte and DIY scripts need a server, and a server that runs a sync reliably is rarely the smallest one on the menu.
  • Schema drift. When Stripe or Xero adds a field, somebody has to handle it. If that somebody is you, it is a cost. Why Stripe to Postgres syncs keep breaking covers the usual failures.
  • Frequency you do not need. Paying extra for hourly syncs of billing data is common and usually wasted. How often you should sync billing data argues that daily is the right default for almost everyone.

How to Estimate Your Row Count

The number that decides your plan with almost every vendor is rows per month, so estimate it before you sign up rather than after.

For a tool that counts every row written per run, the formula is simple:

rows per month = rows fetched per run × runs per month

A worked example: a SaaS business with about 2,000 customers, adding about 120 customers and raising about 400 Stripe invoices a month, syncing daily with a last-7-days window. Each run fetches roughly a week's worth of new records, around 30 customers and 100 invoices. That is about 130 rows per run, times 30 runs, or around 4,000 rows a month for Stripe. Add a Xero connection with a similar number of changed records and you are near 8,000, comfortably inside a 25,000-row allowance. The same setup on a full sync every day would re-read all 2,000 customers and every invoice each run, and blow through it in days. A windowed Stripe sync only picks up new records, so an occasional full sync is worth scheduling to catch older ones that changed.

If you already have some billing data in Postgres, a monthly count by creation date gives you a realistic baseline:

SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('month', created) AS month,
  COUNT(*)                     AS invoices_created
FROM stripe_invoices
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month DESC
LIMIT 6;

Invoices are usually the busiest table, so that number, plus your customers who changed something, is a good approximation of your monthly volume. For a usage-metered tool like Fivetran, it is also close to your monthly active rows.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the cheapest ETL tool for PostgreSQL?

For small volumes, a free tier: Fivetran Free (500,000 monthly active rows) or, for Stripe only, Stripe's own real-time Postgres sync (5,000 row changes a month free). For a paid plan with a fixed monthly bill, Codeless Sync Starter at $19 a month covers Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero and Paddle into any PostgreSQL host. Airbyte Cloud Standard starts at $20 a month and is cheaper per row, but its cost moves with volume.

Is there a free way to sync Stripe data to PostgreSQL?

Yes, several. Stripe's own Data Pipeline sync to Postgres is free up to 5,000 row changes a month on any host, though it is still a public preview. Fivetran's Free plan and Codeless Sync's Free plan both work with any PostgreSQL host, the first metered on changed rows and the second limited to 1,000 rows and manual syncs. A DIY script is also free in licence terms, but not in maintenance time.

Is Airbyte cheaper than Fivetran?

At small volumes Fivetran Free costs nothing, so no. Once you pass Fivetran's free limit, Airbyte Cloud is usually easier to predict, since it publishes its credit rates (6 credits per million API rows, with 5 credits included on the $20 Standard plan) while Fivetran asks you to use an estimator. Self-hosted Airbyte Core has no licence fee at all.

How much does it cost to sync Stripe to Postgres?

Between $0 and about $20 a month for most small SaaS businesses. Free tiers from Stripe itself, Fivetran and Codeless Sync cover the smallest cases. Codeless Sync Starter ($19) and Airbyte Cloud Standard (from $20) cover scheduled syncing at typical small-business volumes. Warehouse-grade tools like Stitch and Hevo start at $100 a month or more.

Is building my own sync cheaper than paying for a tool?

In direct cost, yes. In total cost, rarely. The first version of a Stripe sync script takes a day. Keeping it working through API changes, token expiry, rate limits and silent failures is where the cost sits, and it lands on whoever is on call.

Which option is cheapest for syncing QuickBooks or Xero?

Codeless Sync and Skyvia both cover QuickBooks and Xero on their entry plans, at $19 and $79 to $99 a month respectively. Airbyte Cloud supports QuickBooks, but its Xero connector is only available on self-hosted Airbyte Core. Fivetran Free can work if your volume stays under 500,000 monthly active rows.

Wrapping Up

If you can live on a free tier, do. Stripe's own Postgres sync and Fivetran Free are both genuinely $0 for the right setup, and there is no prize for paying when you do not have to.

When you outgrow free, the cheapest option is the one whose bill you can predict for the sources you actually use. For billing data from Stripe, QuickBooks, Xero or Paddle into any Postgres host, on a daily schedule, that is a flat $19 a month.

Start free with Codeless Sync, or compare the plans on the pricing page.

title: Why Does My SVG Icon’s Why Does My SVG Icon’s Handle Stay Black? Debugging a Sprite with DevTools
description:
Hover over the Search button. The word turns purple. So does the ring of the magnifying glass. Its handle stays black.

That ring is a useful clue. The button’s hover rule works, and its color reaches the icon. Before changing any CSS, look at what draws the handle.

Reproduce the two-color magnifier

Save this snippet as demo.html and open it in a browser. Hover over the button, or press Tab to focus it. The deliberately large icon makes the short black line easy to spot.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Find the black handle</title>
<style>
  button {
    display: inline-flex;
    align-items: center;
    gap: .4em;
    padding: .4em .7em;
    color: #111;
    background: white;
    border: 2px solid currentColor;
    border-radius: .4em;
    font: 2rem system-ui;
  }
  button:hover, button:focus-visible { color: #6932bc; }
  button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid currentColor; outline-offset: 4px; }
</style>
<svg width="0" height="0" aria-hidden="true" style="position:absolute">
  <symbol id="search" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
    <g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round">
      <circle cx="10" cy="10" r="6"/>
      <path d="M14.3 14.3 20 20" stroke="#111"/>
    </g>
  </symbol>
</svg>

<button type="button">
  <svg width="32" height="32" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#search"/></svg>
  Search
</button>
</html>

At rest, everything looks right because the button and the handle happen to use the same shade of black. The defect only appears when their colors should change together.

Follow the reference in DevTools

  1. Inspect the Search button. Under its visible SVG you’ll find <use href="#search">. That fragment points to the drawing shared by every instance of this icon.
  2. In the Elements panel, press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on macOS) and search for symbol#search. Expand the symbol and its group. The circle draws the lens. The short path draws the handle.
  3. Compare the two shapes. The circle has no stroke value of its own, so it inherits the group’s stroke. The path explicitly requests #111. Changing the button’s color can’t change that literal value.
  4. Double-click the path’s stroke="#111" attribute in the Elements panel, delete the attribute and press Enter. Move the pointer back over the button. The handle should now turn purple with the ring.

Keep the one-line fix

The DevTools edit disappears when you reload. Make the same change in the source that produces the sprite:

- <path d="M14.3 14.3 20 20" stroke="#111"/>
+ <path d="M14.3 14.3 20 20"/>

The group already defines the stroke for the whole magnifier. Removing the handle’s override lets both shapes follow the same rule. If your sprite is generated, edit the input icon and regenerate it so the next build keeps the fix.

Check the state that exposed it

Reload, then press Tab with the pointer away from the button. The focus outline, label, ring and handle should all turn purple. Move focus away and they should return to black. A screenshot of the idle button alone would look identical before and after the repair.

Apply this edit only to shapes intended to follow the text color. An amber status dot inside an otherwise monochrome icon may have a fixed fill for a reason.

For the steps that turn individual icons into reusable symbols, see our SVG sprite tutorial.

title: Postgres Major Upgrades Without Fear: A Practical Shadow-Testing Pipeline with pg_upgrade --check, pg_stat_statements and Query Diffing
description:
Tuần này trên Hacker News có một thread hơn 700 điểm: Postgres 19 bị trễ vì người ta tìm ra nhiều bug hơn hẳn trước đây, một phần nhờ các công cụ fuzzing và AI agent đi soi code. Nghe thì có vẻ đáng lo, nhưng mình thấy đây là tin tốt. Bài học mình rút ra cho team mình lại khác: nếu chính core team còn tìm ra bug ở những chỗ không ngờ, thì việc bạn nâng major version Postgres chỉ vì đã đọc release notes là quá mạo hiểm.

Mình từng nâng một cluster từ 14 lên 16 mà chỉ chạy test suite của app. Test pass hết, deploy xong thì có một report query chậm từ 200ms lên 9 giây vì planner chọn plan khác. Từ đó mình làm một pipeline nhỏ gọi là shadow testing: chạy chính các query thật của production trên cả version cũ và version mới, rồi so kết quả và thời gian. Bài này chia sẻ lại cách làm, dùng PostgreSQL 17 → 18 làm ví dụ, nhưng áp dụng được cho mọi lần nâng major version.

Tại sao test suite của app là chưa đủ

Unit test và integration test thường chạy trên database gần như trống, với vài chục dòng fixture. Những thứ hay vỡ khi nâng major version lại nằm ở chỗ khác:

  • Planner thay đổi: cost model, cách ước lượng selectivity, các tối ưu mới (ví dụ PG18 có skip scan cho B-tree index nhiều cột). Đa số trường hợp nhanh hơn, nhưng sẽ có vài query bị chọn plan tệ hơn.
  • Thay đổi hành vi: hàm bị deprecate, collation thay đổi, cast ngầm khác đi. Mấy thứ này chỉ lộ ra với data thật.
  • Extension: PostGIS, pg_partman, timescaledb... phải có bản build cho version mới, và không phải lúc nào cũng có ngay.
  • Statistics: sau pg_upgrade, ở các bản trước 18 thì optimizer statistics không được giữ lại, phải chạy ANALYZE lại toàn bộ. Nếu quên thì vài giờ đầu sau upgrade query nào cũng chậm. PG18 đã giữ lại được phần lớn statistics, nhưng extended statistics vẫn phải analyze lại.

Nên mục tiêu là: test với data thật (hoặc snapshot đã ẩn danh) và workload thật.

Kiến trúc pipeline 

flowchart LR
    A[Production PG17] -->|pg_stat_statements| B[Top N queries]
    A -->|snapshot / pg_dump| C[Clone PG17]
    C -->|pg_upgrade --check| D[Clone PG18]
    B --> E[Replay script]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Diff report: rows + timing + plan]

Ý tưởng rất đơn giản: lấy một snapshot, dựng hai bản giống hệt nhau, một bản giữ nguyên PG17, một bản nâng lên PG18. Sau đó replay cùng một tập query lên cả hai và so sánh.

Bước 1: Lấy workload thật và dựng môi trường

Đầu tiên, lấy các query quan trọng nhất từ pg_stat_statements. Mình lấy theo total_exec_time vì đó là những query ảnh hưởng nhiều nhất tới hệ thống:

# Export top 200 query theo tổng thời gian chạy
psql "$PROD_RO_URL" -At -F $'\t' -c "
  SELECT queryid, calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2), query
  FROM pg_stat_statements
  WHERE query NOT ILIKE '%pg_stat%'
    AND query ~* '^\s*(select|with)'
  ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
  LIMIT 200;" > top_queries.tsv

# Dựng 2 container từ cùng một snapshot data
docker run -d --name pg17 -p 5417:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=test \
  -v ./snapshot17:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17

# Kiểm tra trước khi upgrade thật (không đụng vào data)
pg_upgrade --check \
  -b /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin -B /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin \
  -d /data/pg17 -D /data/pg18

Vài lưu ý thực tế:

  • Chỉ replay SELECT/WITH read-only. Đừng replay UPDATE/DELETE trừ khi bạn chạy trong transaction rồi ROLLBACK.
  • pg_stat_statements đã normalize query thành $1, $2. Bạn cần sinh tham số thật, mình thường lấy từ log log_min_duration_statement hoặc viết vài sample value cho từng query.
  • pg_upgrade --check bắt được rất nhiều vấn đề sớm: extension thiếu, kiểu dữ liệu không tương thích, encoding lệch. Chạy nó trên clone trước, đừng chạy lần đầu trên production.
  • Sau upgrade, chạy vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages trên bản PG18 trước khi đo, không thì kết quả timing vô nghĩa.

Bước 2: Replay và diff kết quả

Đây là phần quan trọng nhất. Script Python dùng psycopg 3 (3.2+) chạy mỗi query trên cả hai server, so sánh hash của kết quả và thời gian chạy:

import hashlib, time, csv
import psycopg

OLD = 'postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5417/app'
NEW = 'postgresql://postgres:test@localhost:5418/app'
RUNS = 5

def run(conn, sql, params):
    timings, digest = [], None
    for _ in range(RUNS):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        rows = conn.execute(sql, params).fetchall()
        timings.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
    # Sort để không bị lệch do thứ tự khi query không có ORDER BY
    digest = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(map(repr, rows))).encode()).hexdigest()
    timings.sort()
    return digest, timings[len(timings) // 2], len(rows)

def main(cases):
    with psycopg.connect(OLD) as old, psycopg.connect(NEW) as new:
        for c in (old, new):
            c.execute("SET statement_timeout = '30s'")
        for qid, sql, params in cases:
            h1, t1, n1 = run(old, sql, params)
            h2, t2, n2 = run(new, sql, params)
            ratio = t2 / max(t1, 0.01)
            flag = 'RESULT_DIFF' if h1 != h2 else ('SLOWER' if ratio > 1.5 else 'OK')
            print(f'{flag:12} {qid:>22} old={t1:8.1f}ms new={t2:8.1f}ms x{ratio:.2f} rows={n1}/{n2}')

Mình dùng median của 5 lần chạy để tránh nhiễu do cache lạnh. Ngưỡng 1.5x là con số mình chọn theo kinh nghiệm, bạn tự chỉnh tùy SLA. Hai loại flag cần chú ý:

  • RESULT_DIFF: nghiêm trọng. Kết quả khác nhau thì hoặc query của bạn không deterministic (thiếu ORDER BY với LIMIT, dùng random(), now()), hoặc có thay đổi hành vi thật. Lần nào cũng phải điều tra.
  • SLOWER: lấy EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) ở cả hai bên rồi so.

Bước 3: So sánh plan khi query bị chậm

Với những query bị flag SLOWER, mình xuất plan dạng JSON rồi so node gốc để biết planner đổi chiến lược ở đâu:

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Script
    participant O as PG17
    participant N as PG18
    S->>O: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)
    S->>N: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)
    O-->>S: plan A
    N-->>S: plan B
    S->>S: so Node Type, Rows estimate vs actual

Thường gặp nhất là estimate rows lệch rất xa so với actual rows. Cách xử lý theo thứ tự ưu tiên:

  1. Chạy ANALYZE lại bảng liên quan (đôi khi chỉ do thiếu stats).
  2. Tăng default_statistics_target cho cột cụ thể: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET STATISTICS 1000;
  3. Tạo extended statistics cho các cột tương quan: CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies, ndistinct) ON col_a, col_b FROM t;
  4. Cuối cùng mới tính tới rewrite query hoặc thêm index.

Đừng vội tắt từng planner option như enable_nestloop = off ở cấp global. Đó là băng dán, sẽ làm hỏng các query khác.

Kết luận

Việc Postgres 19 bị trễ vì tìm ra nhiều bug hơn nhắc mình một điều: phần mềm càng được soi kỹ thì càng thấy nhiều chỗ chưa ổn, và database của bạn cũng không ngoại lệ. Vài điều nên làm ngay:

  • Bật pg_stat_statements ngay hôm nay nếu chưa có. Không có nó thì bạn không biết workload thật của mình trông ra sao.
  • Luôn chạy pg_upgrade --check trên clone trước, vài tuần trước ngày upgrade dự kiến, để có thời gian xử lý extension.
  • Shadow test với top 100-200 query theo total_exec_time. Thường chỉ tốn vài giờ setup nhưng bắt được những vấn đề mà test suite không bao giờ thấy.
  • Coi RESULT_DIFF là blocker, SLOWER là việc cần điều tra trước khi deploy.
  • Sau upgrade, chạy vacuumdb --analyze-in-stages và theo dõi pg_stat_statements trong 24-48 giờ đầu, so với baseline cũ.
  • Đừng nâng lên bản .0. Đợi tới .1 hoặc .2, nhất là với một release đã bị trễ vì nhiều bug như vậy.

title: From a GraphQL monorepo to FastAPI and React: the coupling changed
description:
Language Power is a vocabulary trainer I've built three times. The current version is a Python backend, FastAPI with PostgreSQL and Redis, and a React client, kept in two separate repositories and talking over REST. It runs as a private deployment I use every day and a public demo with strict limits. The version before it was a TypeScript monorepo with a GraphQL API and a shared schema.

I built the app for my own language learning, so what follows is about maintaining one developer's project over several years, not about a team or about traffic. Between the two versions I changed more than the repository layout: the language, the API style, the database, authentication and the deployment. So this isn't a controlled comparison of monorepos and separate repositories. It's an account of which dependency caused each cost, and what changed when that dependency went away.

v2: a monorepo while the app was taking shape

Version 2 ran from 2022 to 2025 (language-power-v2). It was a Yarn workspaces + Lerna monorepo with four packages:

Package What it held
server Apollo Server 4 on Express, MongoDB
front React 18 + Apollo Client, built with Webpack 5
ui The design system and the game components, documented in Storybook
shared The GraphQL schema, as .graphql files

I chose GraphQL because I planned to use the app while travelling and wanted each screen to ask for only the fields it needed. The monorepo followed from that: one schema, and every package generating its TypeScript types from it. The server, the front and the design system each have their own codegen config pointing at the same folder (server, front, ui):

schema: '../shared/schema',

During those years I was still working out what the app should be. I added games, rewrote the spaced-repetition scheduler, added Spanish with its verb conjugations and noun genders, and tried features I later dropped, such as tags and a speaking game. The schema changed often.

What the monorepo bought

  • Schema changes surfaced early. Codegen fails when a query in front asks for a field the schema no longer has, and the regenerated types turn stale field names into type errors. This was early feedback, not a guarantee: the production builds skip type checking (tsc --noCheck on the server, happyPackMode in the front's Webpack config), and CI ran lint, codegen and the server's tests, not tsc.
  • One change, one pull request. A new game meant a schema change, a resolver, a game component in ui and a page in front. All of it went into one PR.
  • End-to-end tests in the same repo. Cypress ran against the server and client from the same commit, so there was never a question of which server version a client build was tested against.
  • No package publishing. front imported @lp/ui straight from the workspace, so there was no version to bump between them.

While the schema changed every week, these were the properties I wanted.

What it cost

Upgrades

When I tried to upgrade Apollo on the server and check that it still returned the same data, codegen failed. As I remember it, the packages had ended up needing different codegen versions. I no longer have the error, so I can't say more about the cause than that.

Codegen and its plugins are declared separately in three packages. When upgrading that tooling, I had three configurations and their generated output to check rather than one central setup. Some changes could therefore spread beyond the package I originally wanted to upgrade.

Builds

Neither image can be built from its own package alone. Dockerfile-server copies packages/shared and runs yarn build:server, which runs codegen before compiling. The front image copies shared, front and ui (Dockerfile-front), because @lp/ui has no build step of its own: its main points at src/index.ts (package.json), and front's Webpack compiles the design system's source. A replacement for Webpack would have to handle that source and its build assumptions too.

None of this comes from the monorepo as such. A design system with its own build, or one codegen setup at the root, would have loosened it. I didn't need either when I set the repo up, and the coupling built up gradually.

The same setting, in two places

The incident I remember best was about a number.

Login used a JWT. The server signed it with a lifetime from its TOKEN_TTL variable (token.ts):

const tokenTtl = TOKEN_TTL || DEFAULT_TOKEN_TTL;
const token = jwt.sign({ id, role }, JWT_SECRET, {
  expiresIn: isDemo ? '1h' : `${tokenTtl}d`
});

The client didn't read the expiry from the token. It computed its own from its own TOKEN_TTL and used it to send me to the login page when the session ran out (auth-hook.tsx):

const tokenTTL = Number.parseInt(process.env.TOKEN_TTL || '7');
// ...
const TOKEN_EXPIRATION_PERIOD = isDemo
  ? 3600 * 1000
  : 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * tokenTTL;

I deployed v2 by hand to a small DigitalOcean droplet. Building the images on the droplet was too much for it, so I built them locally, pushed them to Docker Hub and only pulled them on the server. That put the two values in different places. The client's was a build argument in my local script (docker-prod.sh), compiled into the bundle:

--build-arg TOKEN_TTL=7 \

The server's was whatever I had typed into its environment on the droplet. I don't remember the exact values, but at one point they didn't match, and the result depended on which side was shorter:

  • Client shorter: I was logged out while my token was still valid.
  • Server shorter: the client still thought I was logged in, so instead of a redirect to the login page, every request failed with an error saying I had to log in.

Changing the client's side meant rebuilding the image, pushing it and redeploying—all for one number.

TOKEN_TTL wasn't the only setting split this way. When I archived v2, I added an ALLOW_SIGNUP flag so that people trying the Docker build could create an account (commit). It had to reach four places: the server's signup check, the client's sign-in and sign-up pages, the server's runtime environment and the client's build arguments. The compose file sets it twice.

The shared repository didn't cause this. Two packages each owned the same value, and nothing made them agree.

v3: separate repositories once the features settled

When I started v3 in 2026, I knew which features I wanted: six games, a scheduler I'd been using for years, and two languages. I was more interested in deploying, upgrading and changing each half on its own schedule. v3 is two repositories:

  • language-power-api: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, deployed to Google Cloud Run
  • language-power-client: React + TypeScript with Vite, deployed to Netlify, which proxies /api to the backend

The backend is a single process with feature modules (auth, words, games, dictionary). The two deployables are the backend container and the client's static build.

The contract is checked at runtime

A Python backend can't share TypeScript types directly. I could have generated them from FastAPI's OpenAPI document. I didn't, because I wanted the two repositories to stay completely separate, with nothing generated from one checked into the other.

Instead, the client describes each response in zod, and the wrapper every API call goes through parses the data before the app uses it (http.ts). Calls whose body isn't used, such as logout, pass schema: null and skip it.

const result = schema.safeParse(data);
if (!result.success) {
  // ...
  throw new ApiError("contract", message, response.status, result.error.issues);
}

A response that doesn't match becomes its own kind of error, "contract", and is reported to Sentry. New fields from the backend are ignored, so adding to a response is safe. A removed or renamed field fails on the first request that hits it.

Upgrading FastAPI doesn't touch the client's dependencies, and neither build needs a file from the other repo.

One owner for each setting

The TOKEN_TTL problem went away for a reason unrelated to the repositories: v3 uses server-side sessions instead of JWTs. The session lifetime exists in one place, session_ttl_seconds: a session lasts 30 days from login. The client doesn't know it. It asks /auth/me who the user is, and a 401 or 403 there means no one is logged in (api.ts). A 401 or 403 from any other endpoint makes the client check /auth/me again. Why I moved to sessions is a separate article.

For values the client does need, the backend sends them. GET /auth/config (router.py) returns the settings a logged-out visitor's screen depends on:

return {
    "signup_enabled": service.signups_open(),
    "signup_open_today": await service.signup_open_today(db),
    "use_mocks": service.mocks_enabled(),
    "account_ttl_hours": settings.account_ttl_hours,
    "searches_per_language": settings.searches_per_language,
}

signup_open_today couldn't be an environment variable at all. The demo allows a fixed number of new accounts per day, so the value comes from the database and changes during the day.

Changing an existing value, such as the demo's account lifetime, needs a backend deploy and no new client build. Adding a field is different: when I added the account lifetime and search limit, the backend change was the router and a test (commit), and the client needed a new release for the two schema fields and the notice that shows them (schemas.ts).

The client's application code reads environment variables only for Sentry (config.ts). The deployment needs one more input, API_ORIGIN, which Netlify uses to proxy /api to the backend.

What v3 gave up

  • Drift isn't checked automatically before deploy. If I rename a field in the API and forget the client, testing the two together locally would show it, but nothing in either CI does: neither runs the other side, and there's no contract test between them. Otherwise it fails on the first request in the deployed app, loudly and specifically.
  • Some rules are copied by hand. The password limits, the limits on a word's fields and the spaced-repetition settings limits exist in both repos. The client's copies say so in comments, such as "Mirrors the server's signup rules (auth/schemas.py)" (password.ts).
  • A cross-cutting feature is two changes in two repos. The demo limits were a set of backend commits and a set of client commits, tested separately, and the backend had to ship first.
  • The config isn't refreshed on its own. The client caches /auth/config with staleTime: Infinity (queries.ts). It's fetched again after a signup is refused with a 429 and cleared on logout, but otherwise an open page keeps the value it loaded with.

Keeping the repositories separate didn't remove the coupling between them. They still share field names, status codes and the /api prefix. Generating the client's schemas from OpenAPI would make the existing API dependency explicit and easier to check, at the cost of a generation step and its tooling. I accepted hand-written schemas as the simpler start, knowing they need keeping in sync.

What I take from it

For this app, the setup that suited each stage was different. While the schema changed every week, a single PR across the stack and shared types were worth the cost of upgrading packages together. Once the features settled, I changed the contract less often and cared more about upgrading and deploying each half on its own, and the runtime check has been enough for one developer and one client.

The most expensive problem in v2, the token lifetime, didn't depend on the repo layout. It came from the same value being owned in two places. A monorepo could have avoided it by having the client read the expiry from the token, and separate repositories could have repeated it. Before blaming the number of repositories, I'd now look for the specific dependency causing the pain.

Next steps

  • Generate the client's zod schemas from OpenAPI in CI, or add a contract test that runs them against the real API, so drift fails before deploy.
  • Give /auth/config a response model. It already appears in the OpenAPI document, but with an untyped response ({}), so generation couldn't reproduce its client schema yet.
  • Serve the validation limits from the backend instead of copying them.

Links

  • Live demo: language-power.netlify.app
  • v3 backend: language-power-api, with its architecture diagram
  • v3 client: language-power-client
  • v2 monorepo (archived): language-power-v2, with the Storybook still deployed
  • Professional contact: LinkedIn — Mariia Ganza

title: Best shadcn registries for ready-made blocks in 2026
description:
Checked against official sites on November 2, 2026.

You need a pricing section, a hero and a footer. The useful question is not which library has the most components. It is which registry gives you a complete section that fits your project, and what happens when your agent installs it.

My shortlist: shadcn/ui for free application layouts, Shadcnblocks for a broad marketing catalog, Tailark for marketing pages, VibeUI for a visual pick → AI instruction → install workflow, and Magic UI for animated details.

Disclosure: I build VibeUI. It is included below with its account requirement, free limit and paid restrictions. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a benchmark of installation speed or agent accuracy.

What a registry actually gives you

A shadcn registry distributes source files and their declared dependencies into your project. It can contain a small control, a section or several files for a page. The format does not guarantee a shared visual style, license or dependency list.

The official registry documentation describes the distribution model. Check the actual block and access terms before choosing a library for a client project.

Quick comparison

Registry Where I would start Free access Paid boundary Install route
shadcn/ui Sidebars, login screens, dashboard layouts Official blocks are free and open source No paid tier for the official blocks page shadcn CLI
Shadcnblocks Heroes, pricing, product and marketing sections Free blocks; Basic blocks require login Pro blocks and larger bundles Namespaced shadcn CLI; key for Pro
Tailark Marketing websites with a selected design style Free pages, blocks and snippets Premium blocks, illustrations and page collections Registry workflow; follow the selected block's instructions
VibeUI Pick a designed block and hand it to Cursor or Claude Code Free account: 20 different components per month PRO-only items and scenarios; unlimited copies with PRO Copy for AI or authenticated shadcn namespace
Magic UI Animated text, backgrounds and UI effects Public component documentation and source Separate Pro blocks and templates shadcn CLI

The rows describe different products. A background effect and a whole dashboard are both installable source, but they do not replace the same amount of work.

1. shadcn/ui: start here for application layouts

The official blocks page includes dashboards, collapsible sidebars and authentication layouts. It shows the files, preview and install command together.

For example, the documented dashboard command is:

npx shadcn@latest add dashboard-01

Choose it when: you want an application layout built around the shadcn system and are comfortable doing the product-specific design yourself.

Check first: the file list. A dashboard can add a page, several components and example data. An agent still needs instructions about where that page belongs and which sample data to replace.

2. Shadcnblocks: a wide marketing catalog

Shadcnblocks separates blocks, components and templates. Its categories include heroes, pricing, testimonials, product sections and dashboards. Free blocks are available, while Pro access and higher bundles cover more of the catalog.

The CLI guide documents the registry configuration and API-key authentication for Pro. Its example command is:

npx shadcn@latest add @shadcnblocks/hero1

Configure the registry as the guide describes before using the command.

Choose it when: you want many section variants to compare for a commercial site.

Check first: whether the exact block is free or Pro, and which primitive-library build matches your project. A large catalog is useful only if the chosen section installs into your actual setup.

3. Tailark: a marketing-site starting point

Tailark focuses on marketing sites, with blocks, pages and illustrations in multiple styles. It states compatibility with Radix UI and Base UI.

Its pricing page distinguishes free pages, blocks and snippets from premium blocks, illustrations and fuller page collections. Do not assume every page shown in a preview belongs to the free tier.

Choose it when: the design of a marketing page is the main decision, and you want to work within one of its styles.

Check first: access to the exact section and the installation instructions attached to it. I would select the hero and the following content section together before committing to a style.

4. VibeUI: visual selection with an agent instruction

VibeUI (vibeui.club) is a shadcn-compatible catalog of React/Tailwind components, landing blocks and animations. Each item has a Copy for AI instruction with the install command, dependencies, what to preserve and what can change.

The useful distinction is the handoff: choose a preview, give the instruction to the agent, and ask it to install that component. The instruction is intended to preserve the selected design; it is not a guarantee that an agent will follow every rule.

The installation guide covers Copy for AI and an authenticated namespace. Use the command generated for your account instead of copying somebody else's temporary link.

Choose it when: you already know which block you want and need to communicate that choice to an AI coding agent.

Check first: a free account allows 20 different components per month. Some blocks, animations and page scenarios need PRO. The English pricing page lists $9 for a month or $69 for a year, paid once with crypto and no automatic renewal. Those restrictions matter if you prefer open-source-only tools or another payment method.

5. Magic UI: add motion where it earns its place

Magic UI's installation guide uses the shadcn workflow. Its catalog includes animated text, backgrounds, marquees and other effects; Pro blocks and templates are offered separately.

The guide's example is:

npx shadcn@latest add @magicui/globe

Choose it when: the page layout is already settled and you need a specific animated element.

Check first: the selected component's dependencies and motion behaviour. A visual effect is an addition to the page, not a substitute for its structure or content.

How to hand a registry block to an agent

A bare URL leaves too much room for interpretation. I would send a brief like this:

Install the exact block using its documented command.
Read the registry files and dependency list before editing.
Put it on the existing landing page.
Keep its layout, spacing, typography and motion initially.
Replace only the copy, links and brand assets.
If installation or access fails, report the error before substituting another block.
Check the result on mobile and with reduced motion enabled.

For private registries, the shadcn namespace documentation supports authentication headers using environment-variable placeholders. Keep the actual token out of the prompt, repository and screenshots.

My selection rule

Start with shadcn/ui for the app shell. Compare Shadcnblocks and Tailark for marketing sections. Consider VibeUI when the design-to-agent handoff is the problem. Add Magic UI when you can name the effect the page needs.

Before paying or installing, check three things on the exact item: access, dependencies and license. Then install one representative block and inspect it in your project. That tells you more than the library's total component count.

title: Build an Incremental ETL Pipeline in Python Using PostgreSQL Watermarks
description:
Build an Incremental ETL Pipeline in Python Using PostgreSQL Watermarks

Incremental ETL avoids rereading an entire source table on every run. Instead, the pipeline remembers the latest source change it successfully loaded, then requests only records after that point. That remembered position is the watermark.

This tutorial builds a small but production-oriented pipeline that copies app.orders into warehouse.fact_orders. It uses PostgreSQL timestamps plus a primary-key tie-breaker as the watermark and performs idempotent upserts in Python.

Define the Watermark Contract First

A watermark is only reliable when its source column has a clear contract. In this example, each source row has:

  • updated_at: when the application last changed the row
  • id: a stable, unique primary key

The checkpoint is the pair:

(last_updated_at, last_id)

Rows are ordered lexicographically:

(updated_at, id)

For example, if the saved watermark is:

(2025-03-08 10:00:00+00, 42)

the next extraction includes rows where:

(updated_at, id) > ('2025-03-08 10:00:00+00', 42)

The id is important. Multiple rows can receive the same timestamp, especially when inserts happen in a batch. Without a tie-breaker, rows sharing the previous maximum timestamp may be skipped.

This design assumes:

  1. updated_at is populated by the database or application for every insert and update.
  2. updated_at is never intentionally moved backward.
  3. Source rows are not physically deleted without another way to represent deletion.
  4. The pipeline can safely reload a small overlap window.

The final assumption matters because timestamp watermarks are not a full change data capture system. We will revisit that limitation later.

Create Source, Target, and Pipeline-State Tables

For a small local example, use one PostgreSQL database with separate schemas. In a real system, the source and warehouse may be different databases, clusters, or services.

Run this SQL first:

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS app;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS warehouse;

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS app.orders (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
);

-- Ensure application updates refresh the watermark column.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.updated_at := clock_timestamp();
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS orders_set_updated_at ON app.orders;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_set_updated_at
BEFORE UPDATE ON app.orders
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION app.set_updated_at();

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse.fact_orders (
    order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
    source_updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    loaded_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse.pipeline_state (
    pipeline_name TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    last_updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    last_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
);

INSERT INTO app.orders (customer_id, status, total_cents)
VALUES
    (101, 'paid', 2599),
    (102, 'pending', 4999),
    (103, 'paid', 1200);

The target table retains source_updated_at. That field is useful both for observability and for preventing an older reprocessed record from overwriting a newer target version.

Understand the Pipeline Architecture and Transaction Boundaries

The pipeline has four logical components:

PostgreSQL source table
        |
        |  rows after saved watermark
        v
Python extraction and transformation
        |
        |  idempotent upsert
        v
PostgreSQL warehouse table
        |
        |  successful load only
        v
PostgreSQL pipeline_state checkpoint

The critical correctness rule is:

Advance the watermark only after the target rows have been written successfully.

If the process fails during loading, the saved checkpoint must not move. On the next execution, the same source rows are read again. That requires target writes to be idempotent: loading the same source row twice must produce the same final target state.

This example uses a transaction around target upserts and the state update. It also obtains a PostgreSQL advisory lock so two scheduler invocations cannot run the same pipeline concurrently.

The source extraction uses a REPEATABLE READ transaction. That gives the run a consistent source snapshot: the upper watermark and extracted rows describe the same view of the source table.

If you want a broader structured learning path after implementing this pattern, this data engineering roadmap is an optional next step.

Run the Incremental Python ETL Job

Install the PostgreSQL driver:

pip install "psycopg[binary]"

Set a connection string. This example uses the same database for source and target:

export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/analytics"

Save the following as incremental_orders.py:

import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import psycopg
from psycopg.rows import dict_row

DATABASE_URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]
PIPELINE_NAME = "orders_incremental_v1"

# Re-read recent changes to tolerate slightly late commits.
# Target upserts make this safe.
LOOKBACK = timedelta(minutes=10)

INITIAL_WATERMARK = datetime(1970, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)


def run_pipeline():
    with (
        psycopg.connect(DATABASE_URL, row_factory=dict_row) as source_conn,
        psycopg.connect(DATABASE_URL, row_factory=dict_row) as target_conn,
    ):
        # This transaction contains both target writes and state advancement.
        with target_conn.transaction():
            with target_conn.cursor() as target_cur:
                # Prevent concurrent runs of this exact pipeline.
                target_cur.execute(
                    "SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(%s))",
                    (PIPELINE_NAME,),
                )

                target_cur.execute(
                    """
                    SELECT last_updated_at, last_id
                    FROM warehouse.pipeline_state
                    WHERE pipeline_name = %s
                    FOR UPDATE
                    """,
                    (PIPELINE_NAME,),
                )
                saved_state = target_cur.fetchone()

                if saved_state:
                    # Intentionally overlap prior work. id=0 means all IDs at
                    # the overlap timestamp range are eligible for reload.
                    lower_updated_at = saved_state["last_updated_at"] - LOOKBACK
                    lower_id = 0
                else:
                    lower_updated_at = INITIAL_WATERMARK
                    lower_id = 0

                # Read a consistent source snapshot.
                with source_conn.transaction():
                    with source_conn.cursor() as source_cur:
                        source_cur.execute(
                            "SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY"
                        )

                        # Capture an upper bound from the same source snapshot.
                        source_cur.execute(
                            """
                            SELECT updated_at, id
                            FROM app.orders
                            ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC
                            LIMIT 1
                            """
                        )
                        upper_bound = source_cur.fetchone()

                        if upper_bound is None:
                            print("Source table is empty; nothing to load.")
                            return

                        upper_updated_at = upper_bound["updated_at"]
                        upper_id = upper_bound["id"]

                        source_cur.execute(
                            """
                            SELECT
                                id,
                                customer_id,
                                status,
                                total_cents,
                                updated_at AS source_updated_at
                            FROM app.orders
                            WHERE (updated_at, id) > (%s, %s)
                              AND (updated_at, id) <= (%s, %s)
                            ORDER BY updated_at, id
                            """,
                            (
                                lower_updated_at,
                                lower_id,
                                upper_updated_at,
                                upper_id,
                            ),
                        )
                        rows = source_cur.fetchall()

                # Upsert makes retries and overlap reads safe.
                if rows:
                    target_cur.executemany(
                        """
                        INSERT INTO warehouse.fact_orders (
                            order_id,
                            customer_id,
                            status,
                            total_cents,
                            source_updated_at
                        )
                        VALUES (
                            %(id)s,
                            %(customer_id)s,
                            %(status)s,
                            %(total_cents)s,
                            %(source_updated_at)s
                        )
                        ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE
                        SET
                            customer_id = EXCLUDED.customer_id,
                            status = EXCLUDED.status,
                            total_cents = EXCLUDED.total_cents,
                            source_updated_at = EXCLUDED.source_updated_at,
                            loaded_at = clock_timestamp()
                        WHERE warehouse.fact_orders.source_updated_at
                              <= EXCLUDED.source_updated_at
                        """,
                        rows,
                    )

                # Advance state only after all target upserts succeeded.
                target_cur.execute(
                    """
                    INSERT INTO warehouse.pipeline_state (
                        pipeline_name,
                        last_updated_at,
                        last_id
                    )
                    VALUES (%s, %s, %s)
                    ON CONFLICT (pipeline_name) DO UPDATE
                    SET
                        last_updated_at = EXCLUDED.last_updated_at,
                        last_id = EXCLUDED.last_id,
                        updated_at = clock_timestamp()
                    """,
                    (PIPELINE_NAME, upper_updated_at, upper_id),
                )

                print(
                    f"Loaded or reprocessed {len(rows)} rows. "
                    f"New watermark: ({upper_updated_at}, {upper_id})"
                )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_pipeline()

Run it:

python incremental_orders.py

Verify Expected Results and Incremental Behavior

After the first run, query the target:

SELECT order_id, customer_id, status, total_cents
FROM warehouse.fact_orders
ORDER BY order_id;

Expected result:

order_id customer_id status total_cents
1 101 paid 2599
2 102 pending 4999
3 103 paid 1200

The state table should contain one checkpoint:

SELECT pipeline_name, last_updated_at, last_id
FROM warehouse.pipeline_state;

Now simulate an update and a new order:

UPDATE app.orders
SET status = 'paid'
WHERE id = 2;

INSERT INTO app.orders (customer_id, status, total_cents)
VALUES (104, 'pending', 7500);

Run the Python job again. The pipeline will:

  • reread a small 10-minute overlap,
  • update order 2 from pending to paid,
  • insert the new order,
  • advance the state to the newest (updated_at, id) pair.

Because the load uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, overlap rows do not create duplicates.

Production Pitfalls That Watermarks Do Not Solve Automatically

Late commits can be missed without overlap. An application transaction may assign updated_at, remain open for several minutes, and commit after the ETL has already moved beyond that timestamp. The overlap window reduces this risk, but it is not a mathematical guarantee for arbitrarily long transactions.

Backdated timestamps break the contract. If an application sets updated_at from client-provided data or restores old timestamps during a migration, the row may fall behind the checkpoint and never be extracted.

Hard deletes are invisible. A query for changed rows cannot detect a row that no longer exists. Use soft deletes such as deleted_at, maintain a deletion tombstone table, or adopt change data capture (CDC).

Timestamp precision matters. PostgreSQL TIMESTAMPTZ supports microseconds, but a timestamp alone is still not a unique event identifier. The (updated_at, id) pair handles different rows with identical timestamps; it does not represent multiple distinct updates to the same row with the exact same timestamp.

Large batches need staging. executemany is appropriate for a small tutorial. For high volume, load into a staging table with PostgreSQL COPY, then perform a set-based INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT.

For stronger guarantees across long-running transactions, deletes, and every row-level change, use PostgreSQL logical replication/CDC or an application outbox rather than relying solely on an updated_at watermark.

Test the Pipeline as a State Machine

Test more than whether rows appear in the target. The state transition is the important behavior.

Useful integration tests include:

  1. Initial load: insert source rows, run the job, and assert target row count and state values.
  2. Idempotent retry: run the job twice without source changes; assert no duplicate target rows.
  3. Update propagation: update a source order, rerun, and assert the target reflects the new values.
  4. Same-timestamp ordering: insert multiple rows with a controlled identical updated_at; confirm all are loaded because id breaks ties.
  5. Failure before checkpoint: intentionally fail after extraction but before the state update, then rerun. Target data may be reprocessed, but no source change should be lost.
  6. Concurrent execution: start two jobs and confirm the advisory lock serializes them.

Keep test data small and inspect warehouse.pipeline_state directly. A pipeline can look correct in the destination while silently holding an incorrect checkpoint that causes future data loss.

Takeaway

A PostgreSQL watermark pipeline is built on a simple rule: extract rows after a durable checkpoint, load them idempotently, and update that checkpoint only after the load succeeds. Use a composite (updated_at, id) watermark, a bounded source snapshot, transactional target writes, and an overlap window. It is a practical pattern for mutable tables, but for strict handling of deletes and long-running transactions, move to CDC or an outbox-based design.

title: Where macOS keeps Contacts, Calendar, Reminders, Safari tabs and Voice Memos, and how to read them from a backup
description:
If you've ever needed one deleted contact or a lost Safari tab group back, you've probably found the advice is "restore the whole thing". Mostly that's because nobody writes down where the data lives. So here's the map, checked on macOS 26.6 in a VM with a real Time Machine backup, and on two public encrypted iPhone backups (iOS 15.3.1 and 17.3).

On the Mac

App Where it lives
Contacts ~/Library/Application Support/AddressBook/AddressBook-v22.abcddb, plus Sources/<UUID>/ per account
Safari tab groups ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.Safari/Data/Library/Safari/SafariTabs.db
Safari bookmarks and Reading List ~/Library/Safari/Bookmarks.plist
Safari history ~/Library/Safari/History.db
Calendar ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.calendar/Calendar.sqlitedb (not ~/Library/Calendars)
Reminders ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.reminders/Container_v1/Stores/Data-<UUID>.sqlite, one per account
Voice Memos ~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.VoiceMemos.shared/Recordings/ (CloudRecordings.db and the .m4a files)

All of these need Full Disk Access to read. Without it, every read fails with "Operation not permitted", and so does tmutil listbackups.

In a Finder iPhone backup

Backups store files under hashed names. Manifest.db maps them, so you look up by domain and relative path:

App Domain and path
Contacts HomeDomain Library/AddressBook/AddressBook.sqlitedb
Safari tabs HomeDomain Library/Safari/SafariTabs.db
Safari bookmarks HomeDomain Library/Safari/Bookmarks.db (Reading List is the hidden folder com.apple.ReadingList)
Calendar HomeDomain Library/Calendar/Calendar.sqlitedb
Reminders iOS 15: HomeDomain Library/Reminders/Container_v1/Stores/. iOS 17: AppDomainGroup-group.com.apple.reminders Container_v1/Stores/

Time Machine on macOS 26 has a trap

On an APFS destination the real backup is a volume snapshot called com.apple.TimeMachine.<date>.backup. The visible <date>.previous folder is a view of the latest backup. It looks like an incomplete backup, and it isn't one.

To get at the snapshots, run tmutil listbackups. That mounts them read only under /Volumes/.timemachine/<UUID>/, and the mount only appears after you've run it.

The good news is that the default exclusions are system paths and ~/Library/Caches, so every store above was in the snapshot, including the -wal and -shm files.

Things that will bite you if you read these yourself

Copy first, and copy the WAL. These are WAL-mode SQLite databases, and recent changes may only exist in the -wal file. Copy the database with its -wal and -shm to a private folder and open that copy. Real iPhone backups do this too: Manifest.db itself can be in WAL mode, which broke my first reader.

Dates are Cocoa seconds, counted from 1 January 2001, not Unix time.

All-day events end on the last second. In Calendar.sqlitedb a one-day event has end_date at start + 86399. iCalendar's DTEND is the day after, so a straight copy gives you the wrong end date.

Reminders lists are confusing. A list's name is in ZREMCDOBJECT.ZNAME2, while ZNAME is the account. iOS 17 and macOS 26 keep reminders in ZREMCDREMINDER, and iOS 15 keeps them all in ZREMCDOBJECT.

Safari's Frequently Visited folder isn't bookmarks. com.apple.FrequentlyVisitedSites sits in the same table, hidden. Filter it out, or your restore fills up with sites nobody saved.

Write vCard 3.0. Apple's CNContactVCardSerialization read 3.0 UTF-8 correctly in my tests, but garbled non-ASCII text in a 4.0 card ("Åse" became "√Öse"). It also cuts a URL at an unescaped semicolon.

Voice Memos can have rows with no audio. ZEVICTIONDATE means the audio was moved to iCloud, so the file isn't local. A row with no .m4a isn't corruption.

Getting things back in

  • Contacts: a .vcf opens in Contacts, which asks you to confirm before adding anything. Safe to try.
  • Calendar: same with .ics, with a confirmation dialog first.
  • Safari bookmarks: File > Import From > Bookmarks HTML File.
  • Safari tab groups: I found no safe way to write them back, so export them as a bookmarks folder and a URL list.
  • Voice Memos: open -a VoiceMemos file.m4a imports a file.
  • Reminders: I didn't find a reliable import, so treat this as export only.

What I didn't verify

To be straight about the gaps: the public iPhone images had no voice memos and no reminder items, so those paths are less proven. They also had no named Safari tab groups. My test Mac was a fresh install in a VM, so Bookmarks.plist didn't exist yet and that path comes from Apple's docs, and I didn't click through the Safari bookmarks import. Check your own files before trusting this for those.

Full disclosure: I sell a Mac app built on this research, NoteRescue. It does the comparison per item across backups, and the scan is free. You don't need it if you're comfortable with sqlite3 and the paths above.

Written with AI assistance. The paths come from my own test notes.

title: TanStack Table vs ReUI: picking a React data grid for a shadcn app
description:
If you build a data grid with TanStack Table in a shadcn app, most of the work is the grid UI, not the table logic. ReUI's data grid is that UI already written, on top of the same TanStack Table. So the useful question isn't which engine to use. It's how much grid UI you want to write, and how much of it you want to own.

I work on ReUI, so keep that in mind. I'll point out where plain TanStack Table is the better call.

What I checked

I compared @tanstack/react-table 9.3.1 with the ReUI data grid as the shadcn CLI served it on 3 Nov 2026. To see exactly what lands in a project, I ran npx shadcn@latest view @reui/data-grid and counted the files.

TanStack Table ReUI data grid
What you install one npm package 12 files in components/reui/data-grid
UI included none table, header menus, filters, pagination, virtual table, cell selection
Extra packages none TanStack Virtual, dnd-kit, Base UI or Radix
Who maintains the UI you you, once it's installed
License MIT MIT, free

TanStack Table gives you state, not a table

TanStack Table describes itself as headless, with "full control over markup, styles, and behavior". You get sorting, filtering, grouping, selection and pagination as state and row models. It renders nothing.

For a sortable, paged table that's ideal. You map rows into the shadcn <Table> you already have and you're done in an afternoon.

It gets heavier when the table has to behave like a grid: a menu on each column header, resize handles, pinned columns, keyboard focus moving between cells, virtualization (a separate package, TanStack Virtual), and copy and paste across a range of cells. TanStack Table leaves all of that UI to you on purpose.

ReUI's data grid is that UI, already written 

npx shadcn@latest add @reui/data-grid

That adds 12 files and a little over 11,000 lines of TSX to your project. The four biggest files:

File Lines (about) What it covers
data-grid-table.tsx 3,100 the table, sticky headers, pinning, row states
data-grid-cell-selection.tsx 2,600 range selection, copy, paste, fill handle
data-grid.tsx 1,300 the provider and shared state
data-grid-table-virtual.tsx 1,200 row and column virtualization

That number cuts both ways. It's a lot of grid work you skip. It's also a lot of code that now lives in your repo: you can change any line, and you also maintain every line.

One caveat on the cell selection file: a range selection you write yourself could be far smaller if you skip the edge cases (pinned columns, virtualized rows, translated labels). The count shows what a complete version covers, not what you'd have to write.

You still write the TanStack Table part. The grid renders it:

const table = useTable({
  features: dataGridFeatures,
  data,
  columns,
})

return (
  <DataGrid table={table} recordCount={data.length}>
    <DataGridContainer>
      <DataGridTable />
    </DataGridContainer>
    <DataGridPagination />
  </DataGrid>
)

Your columns, row models and state work the way they do in TanStack Table. Grid behaviour is turned on with tableLayout props instead of built by hand: headerSticky, columnsResizable, columnsPinnable, columnsDraggable, rowsPinnable, cellSelection. On top of that you get infinite scroll, tree and expandable rows, footer rows, inline editing, and one i18n prop for every built-in string.

Four of the free examples:

There are two versions, one on Base UI and one on Radix UI, so use the docs page that matches your project. What it doesn't have: pivot tables and Excel export.

Which one I'd pick

You need Pick
A sortable, paged table TanStack Table with the shadcn <Table>
Every pixel your own, and time to build it TanStack Table
Pinning, resizing and virtualization in your own design system ReUI data grid
Spreadsheet-style range selection and editing ReUI data grid

Docs and every example: https://reui.io/docs/components/base/data-grid?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=data-grid-comparison

If you've built a grid on TanStack Table, what took the longest: the column menus, virtualization, range selection, or something I didn't list?

title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
description:
Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs.

Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8

We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us.

Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed.

OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain.

In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts.

Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin.

- Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution.

- Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more.

- Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one.

- Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices.

We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer.

Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run:

- Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug

- Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug

- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug

- Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug

Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%.

Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench

Write-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench

Harness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench

We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up.

We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!
