title: AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources
description:
AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event source mappings (ESM), for Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and for managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. Customers can now scale processing for Kafka workloads beyond the partition count of a topic, increasing throughput during traffic spikes and improving processing resilience.

Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as image and video encoding, fraud detection, notification delivery, and telemetry ingestion treat each event as an independent unit of work, where processing speed matters more than strict ordering. Previously, Kafka ESMs used the Kafka consumer group protocol, which assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a consumer group. Customers needing higher parallelism had to over-partition topics or move traffic to a separate queuing system, adding infrastructure to operate and producer code to maintain. Queue support for self-managed Kafka ESMs is built on Kafka share groups, which are generally available in Apache Kafka 4.2. This launch enables multiple event pollers to consume concurrently from the same partition, with each event poller supporting up to 10 concurrent invocations. This decouples parallelism from partition count with no changes to producers, topic configuration, or function code. As a result, customers get higher throughput during traffic spikes and more resilient processing, because a slow or failed event no longer holds up other events in the same partition. Queue mode does not preserve partition ordering and is intended for workloads that do not require it.

This capability requires a Kafka cluster with share groups enabled, such as Apache Kafka 4.2 or later, and is available in all AWS commercial Regions where self-managed Kafka ESM is available. To get started, create a self-managed Kafka ESM with ConsumptionMode set to Queue through the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, or AWS CDK. Standard Lambda pricing applies. Customers who configure provisioned mode for their self-managed Kafka ESM also pay for Event Poller Unit (EPU) usage. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda pricing.

title: Compress Audio in the Browser: Shrink an MP3 or WAV Without Uploading It
description:
Full disclosure: I work on OnePassApps.

A voice note, a podcast intro or a screen recording usually leaves you with a file bigger than it needs to be. The usual fix is to upload it to an online converter and download the result, which means your recording sat on somebody else's server on the way. Audio Studio in OnePassApps does the same job inside the browser tab: the file is decoded and re-encoded locally, and the copy you save is built on your own machine.

Audio Studio has four tools - Convert, Compress, Trim and Extract. This one is about Compress.

What the Compress tool does

You drop one audio file on the stage and the tool checks it before anything else happens. The source hint is the limit: MP3, WAV, M4A, AAC, OGG, Opus, FLAC or WebM - up to 32 MiB and 45 minutes.

The Options step fills in once the file has been checked, and the panel says so plainly: Format, bitrate, sample rate and channels appear here once the file has been checked.

  • Output format - WebM audio (Opus) was the default for the file I tested with. The result step describes what you can get: An Opus, AAC or MP3 copy when this browser can encode one, with the real size change.
  • Target bitrate - 128 kbps by default, with the trade-off spelled out: Only bitrates this browser can encode for these settings are listed. Lower bitrates reduce fidelity.
  • Sample rate and Channels - carried over from the source file, 44,100 Hz and Mono in my run.

The action button is not called "Compress". It reads Try smaller-file output, which is a fair description of what it does.

A real run

I dropped a 2-second WAV tone into the tool in the browser and pressed that button:

  • Source: tone.wav, 0:02.0, Mono, 44.1 kHz, PCM-S16, 172 KiB
  • Output: tone-compressed.webm, 0:02.0, WebM Opus, 44,100 Hz, Mono, 32.9 KiB
  • Size change: 139 KiB smaller (80.9%), created in 0.3 s

The result step shows the source and the output side by side with a Download WebM button, and the line Output created locally. Your original file remains unchanged. Your original file on disk is never touched - you get a new copy.

The panel is also careful about what it promises: The comparison uses the actual output bytes; short or already compressed audio may not get smaller. That is worth taking seriously. A file that is already an MP3 at a low bitrate may come back about the same size, and the tool reports the real change either way rather than a flattering number.

Why run it in the browser

The copy is made from bytes already on your machine. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is queued on a server, and there is no file left on a third party's disk afterwards. The browser does the encoding work, and the file comes out the moment the run finishes.

For a phone recording, a long interview or a screen capture that has to fit in a message, that is the whole job: one file in, a smaller file out, without handing the audio to anyone else.

Standard is currently free during a promotional period: $0 per month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, no card required. The Studios run in the browser tab and use no credits, and the result lives in the tab, so export it before you leave.

Try it on your own file: open Audio Studio.

If you want the wider picture on how these browser-local tools work and what they do not do, the OnePassApps guides cover it.

title: Trim a PNG in the Browser: Remove Transparent Edges Without Uploading It
description:
Most icon exports arrive with a canvas bigger than the artwork. You open the PNG, see a band of transparent pixels around your logo, and that padding is baked into the file.

Trimming it by hand means a round trip through an image editor, which is exactly what you were trying to avoid when you picked a tool that runs in your browser.

I work on OnePassApps. The Icon Studio has a Trim / padding tab that removes the transparent edges from a PNG inside your browser tab. No upload, no queue, no account.

https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/icons?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=icon-trim-pad-launch&utm_content=icon-studio-link

What the tab does

Icon Studio has eight tool tabs: SVG to PNG, PNG to ICO, Favicon pack, App icons, Resize set, Optimize SVG, Recolour SVG, and Trim / padding.

Trim / padding works on a PNG and shows three steps on the panel:

  • 01 Source - "No PNG yet. Drop one on the stage or browse for it. PNG up to 24 MiB and 12,000 px a side."
  • 02 Transparent bounds - the Operation picker. The panel heads it with "Trim the transparent edges or add even padding once a PNG is open." The first operation is "Trim transparent edges", and its own description reads: "Remove the empty space around your icon. A fully transparent image becomes a 1 × 1 PNG."
  • 03 Result - "A trimmed or padded PNG with its new dimensions."

One detail worth knowing before you start: this tab wants a raster image. Drop an SVG on it and the stage refuses it with "Needs a PNG". If what you have is an SVG, the SVG to PNG tab in the same studio turns it into a PNG first.

Running it on a real file

I tried it on a 400 x 400 PNG holding a rounded square in the middle, with transparent margins on all four sides. The artwork itself was 201 pixels wide. The source stage showed:

probe-trim.png
PNG · 400 × 400 · 1.4 KiB

One click on "Create PNG" and the result panel read:

Ready
Before
1.4 KiB PNG
After
2.5 KiB PNG
Dimensions
201 × 201 px
File name
probe-trim-trimmed.png
Created in 0.3 s

with the line under it: "PNG created at 201 × 201."

The 201 x 201 is the honest measurement. The artwork was 201 pixels wide, so the trimmed file matches the artwork instead of rounding up to a tidy number.

Why the file got bigger

The trimmed PNG is larger than the original, 2.5 KiB against 1.4 KiB, even though it now has a quarter of the pixels. That is normal for this kind of image: a wide band of transparent margin compresses to almost nothing, so cropping it away leaves the same real pixels in a much smaller canvas. Trimming is about the visible bounds of the image, not about the byte count.

If you need the file to be smaller as well, the Image Studio has a Compress tool that shrinks a JPEG, PNG or WebP in the same browser tab.

The padding option

The same panel can add even transparent padding instead of removing it. That is the direction you want when a platform expects a fixed square canvas and your icon sits tight against the edges.

What stays local

"Processing stays in this browser." is printed under the stage, and the studio header says files stay in your active browser tab. The PNG is decoded, cropped and re-encoded in the tab, so there is no upload step to watch for and no file to wait on.

The Standard plan is free right now: $0 / month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, no end date set, no card required.

If you want the rest of the studio walked through - converting an SVG to PNG, building a favicon pack, resizing an icon set - the guides cover those too.

https://app.onepassapps.com/guides?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=icon-trim-pad-launch&utm_content=guides-link

title: I deleted my way to a 175% score increase, and measured every wrong turn
description:
Over the hackathon's 72-hour window — on top of a preparation period the rules explicitly allowed beforehand — I optimised four programs for Speed Demon 2026. The overall score went from 28.468 to 78.149 — a 175% increase. Every point came from the live board, and I have the measurements to show for it.

But this post is not about the wins. It is about the eight changes I built, verified, measured, and then deleted — because those are the ones that taught me what actually moves a score, and because a submission that only reports its wins is telling you half the story.

Here is the single most useful thing I learned, and it took me most of the window to accept it:

Adding mechanism almost never paid. Deleting code almost always did.

I'll show you the numbers.

Scope of the window. The rules allowed design, specification and environment preparation before the clock started, and all four tracks were planned to module level in that period. A correctness-first version of each program existed from before the window; the version described here was rewritten, measured and frozen inside the 72 hours, and that is where the score went from 28.468 to 78.149. The plan is in the repository, including the places measurement proved it wrong.

What the thing is

Four independent tasks, four standalone Rust programs, one source file each, no crates, no dependencies, no network in the build. The build is rustc on a single file inside a digest-pinned container.

Track What it does Input
🅰 Ingest hourly percentile aggregation 239 MB access log
🅱 Index 50,000 boolean + phrase queries 254 MB corpus
🅲 Join hostile CSV → country aggregates 202 MB
🅳 Traverse 2,000 exact shortest paths 5 M edges

The score is a product of four independent axes:

K = (T_ref / T)^0.50 · (M_ref / M)^0.20 · (S_ref / S)^0.15 · (D_ref / D)^0.15
points = 50 · log10(K)          overall = geometric mean of the best three tracks

And the cost of one point on each axis is wildly different:

Axis What one point costs
Time 8.8% faster the ordinary target
Memory 21% less expensive
Source 26% fewer lines the most expensive — and the most reliable

That table is the whole strategy. Source is the most expensive axis to buy and the easiest to improve, because it rewards deletion. Once I understood that, the project changed.

flowchart LR
    I["an idea"] --> B["build it"]
    B --> V{"exact?<br/>full corpus × 5<br/>+ tiny oracle<br/>+ official sample"}
    V -->|"no"| F["find the bug"]
    F --> V
    V -->|"yes"| M["measure it<br/>interleaved, smallest of N"]
    M --> P{"does it pay<br/>on the board?"}
    P -->|"yes"| K["keep it"]
    P -->|"no"| R["<b>delete it</b><br/>and write down why"]
    K --> L["PERF.md"]
    R --> L
    L --> I

The delete branch is the point. A losing change gets removed from the source, not merely superseded — because final scoring measures the frozen commit, and the board's "keep the best" rule does not transfer to it.

Where it finished 

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TRACK            TIME         MEMORY     SOURCE       BOARD POINTS      │
│  🅰 Ingest        26.0 ms      19 MB       626 lines        80.046        │
│  🅱 Index        140.0 ms      47 MB       708 lines        75.124        │
│  🅲 Join          24.0 ms       9 MB       721 lines        79.370        │
│  🅳 Traverse     170.0 ms      71 MB       536 lines        68.589        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  OVERALL (best three, geometric mean) ............... 78.149             │
│  Starting point ..................................... 28.468             │
│  Wrong answers ever published ....................... zero               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Now the failures.

I believed build flags were the difference, so I tried target-cpu=native

Every track was ~1.2× slower than the fastest entry. The gap was 61–102% time on every track, across four different algorithms in two languages. That looks systemic, so I tried the systemic fix:

rustc -C target-cpu=native ...

Result: slower on all four tracks.

Track x86-64-v3 native Change
🅰 0.02653 0.02710 +2.1%
🅱 0.17049 0.17524 +2.8%
🅲 0.03541 0.03561 +0.6%
🅳 0.16986 0.18123 +6.7%

I reverted it and moved on, but I didn't understand why, and an unexplained measurement is a hypothesis, not a conclusion.

The answer came much later, and it is the best single fact I learned about this competition:

The machine that compiles is not the machine that runs.

The board's build host has AVX-512. The scoring CPU is a Core i5-13500, Alder Lake, whose AVX-512 is fused off. So native resolved against the builder and emitted instructions the scoring machine did not want.

I later switched to naming the target explicitly — and the board measured that worse too, so I reverted that as well:

A  80.046 → 79.716      C  79.370 → 79.142
B  75.124 → 72.908      D  68.589 → 67.822

Twice on the same axis, theory and measurement disagreed, and both times measurement won. x86-64-v3 is what every banked best was measured with, so that is what got frozen.

I believed lto = fat and a smarter probe would pay. Both lost.

Two more experiments that looked obviously right:

Experiment Expected Measured
lto = fat + embed-bitcode cross-unit inlining +12.5% slower at codegen-units=1 there is no cross-unit LTO left to do
Grouped four-slot term probe a big scan win scan +20%, total +14% our table grows at 50% load, so a probe ends at the first or second slot — and a scalar compare beats a 32-byte load plus three AVX2 ops

The second one already told me something important: if skipping the hash and probe entirely for most tokens doesn't help, the term lookup is not the bottleneck. I wrote that down and it saved me from two later dead ends.

I believed faster labels meant fewer bytes. They meant more lines.

Our Track D's own PERF.md named the open question: "the attack is the label and heap data structures, not the search size." So I built 16-bit saturating distance labels with a 64-bit fallback, verified 99.7% of our answers fit in 16 bits before writing a line, and implemented it.

It was exact on every net — full corpus, tiny hostile oracle, official sample, 120 random fuzz graphs, 48,000 logic queries.

And the board said:

D before:  T 0.16986   M 70.57 MB   S 536   ->  68.589
D after:   T 0.19356   M 73.31 MB   S 658   ->  66.338
           +13.9%      +3.9%        +122 lines

Slower, heavier, and 122 more source lines. Here is why, and it is the most transferable lesson in this post:

The exactness rule requires a second search body for the queries the narrow store cannot hold — a duplicate of the entire relaxation loop. That fixed cost is charged to every query, while the narrower labels only pay off on queries long enough for label cache lines to matter. On a corpus whose median answer is 1207, the cheap half of the trade never arrives.

And on this track source is the expensive axis (26.4% of lines per point against 8.8% of time), so the duplicate loop cost more than the label width saved.

The bug I made while writing it is worth showing, because the hash gate caught it:

// WRONG -- an unvisited rival label is infinity, so a plain add wraps
// to nd - 1 in release mode: a spurious meeting that stops the search early.
best = best.min(nd + other[0].get(v));

// RIGHT
best = best.min(nd.saturating_add(other[0].get(v)));

One character. The published hash caught it on the tiny hostile oracle, the official sample and the full corpus.

I believed I should measure locally and move on

I ran three experiments that "obviously" help an I/O-bound parser, and the machine disagreed with all three:

Experiment Why I expected it Measured
MADV_POPULATE_WRITE on the output map fewer page faults while formatting 0.039 → 0.069 s
MADV_SEQUENTIAL on the 239 MB log better readahead parse 0.0289 vs 0.0233 s
Dropping the corpus pages after the scan less pressure inside the noise floor, and 16 certain source lines

Then I learned the reason local measurement kept misleading me. Run-to-run spread on time reaches 16% on identical code. My rules became:

  1. Interleave the variants. Alternating A/B/A/B, not one block then another.
  2. Trust the smallest, not the mean. A loaded machine can only make a run slower.
  3. Measure the phase, not the total. A total tells you a change helped. It never tells you why.

That third rule produced the single most valuable measurement in the project.

I believed Track A was a memory problem. Measurement said parser.

Every idea I had for Track A had been about memory: hold fewer records, release chunks sooner, drop pages after use. Then I added phase laps and got this:

🅰 parse      50.8%     ← the parser is over half the track
   hours      24.4%
   text       22.0%
   rank        2.8%
   size+map    0.6%

Nobody had measured that. I had been optimising the wrong half of the program. The same instrumentation then named the other bottlenecks:

The measured bottlenecks, one per track

flowchart LR
    A["🅰 parse 50.8%<br>24.4% hours, 22.0% text"] --> B["🅱 corpus scan 70%"]
    B --> C["🅲 every record,<br>three random reads each"]
    C --> D["🅳 construction 66%<br>search only 33%"]

And the plan had missed all of them. Three of the four tracks had to be re-attributed by measurement before they could be made faster — which is why the repository keeps its pre-build plan, including the places it was wrong.

What actually paid: four deletions

Every large gain was a removal. Not one was an added mechanism.

Track Change Result
🅰 cut the parser and formatter from 704 → 440 lines first big jump
🅰 drop(parts) before the output map, not after +1.20 points, memory 31.4 → 23.94 MB
🅱 bucketed u16 build, then the class-renumber rewrite 61.65 → 72.62, memory 219 → 49.7 MB
🅲 delete the pre-pass; Phase claim primitive; 1 MB name table 66.81 → 74.02, lines 1105 → 652
🅳 restore PR_SET_THP_DISABLE +25 MB recovered

And the two rewrites that moved the board furthest both got faster and smaller:

🅱  72.829 → 75.124   (+2.295)   time −17%    683 → 644 lines
🅲  75.345 → 79.370   (+4.025)   time −32%    610 → 582 lines

Track C is the clearest example. Instead of walking each CSV record field by field, the input is classified: each 64-byte block becomes quote, comma and LF masks at once, and the "inside quotes" state falls out of one carry-less multiply computing the prefix XOR of the quote mask:

let q = mask64(lo, hi, b'"');
let inq = _mm_cvtsi128_si64(
    _mm_clmulepi64_si128::<0>(_mm_cvtsi64_si128(q as i64), _mm_set1_epi8(-1))
) as u64 ^ inside;
inside = ((inq as i64) >> 63) as u64;

That one idea replaces the entire quoted-field scanner — and it deletes the code that used to do it. A "" pair turns quoting off and on again with no special case at all.

Track B's rewrite is the same story on a different axis: the term table went from a 32-byte lowercased vector with a byte comparison per probe, to a 64-bit hash built from bzhi-masked 8-byte loads. The keys array is gone. The byte compare is gone. Smaller and faster at the same time.

I believed one corpus was enough

It isn't, and the way you find out is a bug that passes one and fails another. The gate became:

1. FULL CORPUS          5 runs, each sha256-hashed
                        every run must equal the pinned expected value
2. TINY HOSTILE ORACLE  hand-built boundary cases
3. OFFICIAL SAMPLE      the organizers' published sample

Five runs, not one — a schedule-dependent defect can pass a single run. And the tiny oracle covers: zero weights, parallel and duplicate edges, self-loops, isolated vertices, unreachable targets, 64-bit sums, "" escapes, bare newlines inside quoted notes, mixed CRLF/LF endings, a byte order mark before a record, s == t, and empty inputs.

Two bugs it caught that I would not have found otherwise:

// Track B: an out-of-bounds read. insert() called key() unconditionally,
// and key() computes `32 - len` on a usize -> underflow for a term over 32 bytes.

// Track C: my Windows fuzzer wrote corpora in text mode, so CRLF crept in.
// D's number() consumes ONE byte past a number, so it ate the CR and read
// the LF as the next number's first byte -> 0/40 Windows trials vs 120/120 Linux.
// Fix: newline="\n" on every corpus writer.

A check whose expected value you invented is not a check. Early on I compared a track against a hash I had typed by hand rather than produced from the reference. It was wrong, and removing it was the right call.

The failure that was not a failure

Late in the window a terminal showed me this in four files:

# PERF.md â€” Track A (Ingest)

Classic UTF-8 mis-decoded as Latin-1. I reported it as broken and started writing a repair.

Then I checked instead of assuming. The files were fine. Zero damaged sequences — all four decoded as valid UTF-8 without error. The â€” was my terminal's codepage failing to render a 3-byte em-dash, not a defect in the files.

Rewriting correct bytes to chase a console artifact would have corrupted four files whose entire purpose is precision — and I would have reported a repair that repaired nothing.

Where the failures actually were

The formulas were the easiest part to get right, because a simulation has no stake in my being right. Every serious failure was somewhere else:

  • a one-character arithmetic bug that wrapped instead of saturating
  • an out-of-bounds read from a subtraction on an unsigned type
  • two dependent cache misses per vertex where one would do
  • consistency measured on the wrong axis — a genuine time win that cost more in source lines than it earned
  • 16% run-to-run noise that made three "obvious" wins look like losses until I started interleaving
  • a design assumption (that Track A's cost was memory) that the whole plan rested on and one measurement destroyed

Not one of them was an algorithm problem. They were a missing saturation, an underflow, a cache-line boundary, a scored axis I wasn't optimising, a measurement method, and an assumption nobody had tested.

Honest limits

The repository documents its own weaknesses rather than hiding them, and so does this post:

  • 🅳 Track D's query queue retains its pool capacity between queries. It is emptied but not shrunk, so it holds every pushed entry including stale ones, where the heap it replaced freed on pop. That is the memory keeping it at 68.589 while its time is the best that track has ever recorded.
  • 🅲 Track C identifies a name by 32 key bits plus a slot group, not full bytes. That is what makes the 4-byte slot — and the compact table and eight-wide probe — possible, and it is exact on every corpus published. The residual collision probability at this scale is documented in the source.
  • 🅱 Track B identifies a term by the top 46 bits of a 64-bit hash, not a byte comparison — far below any practical collision rate at this vocabulary, but no longer exact by construction.
  • 🅰 Track A's parser is unoptimised relative to what is possible. It is 50.8% of the track and it has never had the multi-stream treatment.

And the route to 80 is written down with its arithmetic, not claimed as done: with B held at 75.124, the product A × C must rise 7.27% — about 250 deleted lines across those two files, since source is the axis that has paid every time.

What I would tell you before you start

  1. Measure where the time is before you touch anything. One afternoon of phase laps changed this project more than a month of guessing.
  2. Interleave your A/B runs and trust the minimum. A loaded machine only ever makes things slower.
  3. Delete before you add. It is the cheapest axis and the most reliable one.
  4. Assume your build host is not your run host. Name the CPU explicitly.
  5. Verify on more than one corpus. One corpus is a guess.
  6. Write down what you reverted, and why. It stops you retrying the same idea later, and it is the most credible thing you can publish.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/pal-123456789/speed-demon
cd speed-demon

# build a track exactly as the scored path does -- rustc only, no cargo, no network
sh track-a/build.sh

# check correctness on the tiny hostile oracle and the official sample
tooling/check-corpora.sh a summary.txt "$(cat track-a/verification/expected/summary.txt.sha256)"

Each track is a complete, independent build context: its own Dockerfile, build.sh, source, README.md and PERF.md.

Repository: https://github.com/pal-123456789/speed-demon
Frozen release: https://github.com/pal-123456789/speed-demon/releases/tag/v1.0-freeze

Inside, if you want the long version:

Read For
docs/JOURNEY.md the full narrative, including every reversal and the two measurements I got wrong
docs/TECHNIQUES.md every optimisation, by track and by the axis it attacks
docs/MEASUREMENT.md how every number was obtained, and what is deliberately not claimed
plan/README.md the pre-build plan — including where measurement proved it wrong
track-*/PERF.md each track's own ledger, with a KNOWN / EXPECTED / REVERTED honesty legend

Written for the Speed Demon 2026 write-up quest. Every number in this post is a live board measurement or a locally reproducible one; the eight experiments described as losses were all built, verified exact, and deleted.

title: Recolour an SVG in the Browser: Change the Fill Without Uploading It
description:
Recolouring an SVG usually means opening an editor, hunting through the markup by hand, or uploading the file to a converter you do not trust with an icon you are about to ship. The Icon Studio in OnePassApps does it in the tab you are already in: you drop the SVG in, pick the colour you want to replace, type the new one, and take the file back out.

I work on OnePassApps, and this is what the tool actually does.

The three steps in the panel

The Recolour SVG tab is laid out as three stages, the same way the rest of the Studios are:

  • 01 Source - "No SVG yet. Drop one on the stage or browse for it. SVG up to 5 MiB and 25,000 elements."
  • 02 Solid SVG paints - "The solid fill and stroke colours of your SVG appear here as swatches."
  • 03 Result - "The recoloured SVG and how many paints changed."

Before you load anything the panel says "Add an SVG to start. Your original stays untouched." The page itself notes that files stay in your active browser tab and that processing stays in this browser.

What happens when a file lands

Drop an SVG on the stage and the Source stage names it and reads its dimensions and size. The panel then reports how many solid colours it found, and every one of them turns into a swatch you can click.

I dropped in a 387-byte SVG with a rounded indigo rectangle and a white circle on top. The panel said:

Found 2 solid fill/stroke colours.

and the two swatches were the indigo #4F46E5 and the white #FFFFFF. A second file with three colours in it - a blue rect with a dark stroke and a red circle - reported "Found 3 solid fill/stroke colours."

So you are not guessing at hex codes by eye. The studio reads the colours that are actually in the file and hands them to you as swatches.

Choosing the colour to replace

Click a swatch and the Colour to replace field fills in with that hex value. Next to it is the Replacement colour (HEX) field, where you type the new value. The panel reminds you what will not be touched:

Paints set to none, gradient references, opacity attributes and unrelated colours are kept.

That line matters more than it sounds. If your icon uses a gradient, an opacity attribute or a paint set to none, recolouring one solid value does not rewrite the rest of the file. Colours you did not pick stay as they were.

The result

With the white circle selected to be replaced and #16a34a typed as the new colour, the result stage came back with:

  • Before 387 B SVG
  • After 323 B SVG
  • Paints replaced 1
  • File name probe-recoloured.svg
  • Created in 0.1 s

The banner under it read "Replaced 1 matching #ffffff paint value." and there was a Download SVG button next to the new file. The same run with the dark stroke colour selected reported "Replaced 1 matching #0f172a paint value."

I read the downloaded file to be sure the change was real and not just a claim in the panel. The circle's fill changed from #ffffff to #16a34a, and the rectangle kept its original #4f46e5 fill. Only the paint you asked for moved.

There is also a dark and light preview next to the result, so you can see a pale icon against a dark background and the same icon against a light one before you download anything.

Where it fits

Recolour SVG is one of eight tabs in the Icon Studio - SVG to PNG, PNG to ICO, Favicon pack, App icons, Resize set, Optimize SVG, Recolour SVG and Trim / padding - so recolouring an icon and then turning it into a PNG or a favicon set happens in the same place.

The whole thing runs on the Standard plan, which is free right now at $0 a month with 100,000 credits every 30 days, no end date set and no card required. There is no automatic paid subscription.

You can open the tool here: Recolour SVG in the Icon Studio. If you would rather read how the other tabs fit together, the guides walk through the Studios one by one.

I work on OnePassApps, the team behind app.onepassapps.com. Every file in this post was processed in the browser tab, and the downloaded SVG is what I read back above.

title: Why the AI Infrastructure Debt Wave Will Hit Your Compute Bill
description:
White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett appeared on CNBC following a sharp technology selloff that pushed the Nasdaq Composite to multi-month lows. Asked about the sustainability of debt and capital expenditure in the artificial intelligence buildout, Hassett dismissed systemic risk concerns. He described the sector as a well-financed ecosystem supported by large corporate balance sheets, noting that well-capitalized corporations are positioned across the market, holding equity and debt and ready to step in if smaller participants stumble.

His premise on capital availability is technically accurate. The four primary hyperscalers collectively maintain hundreds of billions of dollars in cash, short-term marketable securities, and operating cash flow generated by core enterprise software, cloud hosting, and digital advertising franchises. Investment-grade bond markets routinely oversubscribe their multi-billion-dollar debt issuances within hours. Meanwhile, private credit funds and institutional asset managers have assembled dedicated hundred-billion-dollar infrastructure pools to underwrite physical campuses, backup generators, and transmission substations. Wholesale capital markets have not closed their doors to artificial intelligence operators.

Abundant liquidity does not establish economic solvency. Readily available funding often sustains negative-present-value projects until amortization schedules collide with revenue realities. The physical economics of artificial intelligence compute impose a severe duration mismatch that distinguishes this capital buildout from earlier utility cycles.

Traditional infrastructure assets like fiber optic conduits, toll bridges, and natural gas pipelines amortize across twenty to forty years. A conduit laid in the ground retains utility even if traffic develops slowly over a decade. An artificial intelligence accelerator faces an effective economic lifespan of thirty-six to forty-eight months. When newer chip generations deliver three to four times more inference tokens per megawatt-hour, older clusters experience rapid economic obsolescence. An operator cannot simply wait for future demand to materialize while holding older hardware, because fixed power contracts, cooling overhead, and facility carry costs quickly exceed the market clearing price of the tokens those older chips produce.

The financing structure of the buildout has also evolved. Early cluster deployments were funded almost entirely out of uncommitted corporate free cash flow. With annual hyperscaler capital expenditures pacing toward 300 billion dollars, funding has expanded into balance-sheet debt, project-level financing, and private credit facilities secured against server racks. Several neo-cloud operators and specialized hosting providers borrow at high single-digit or low double-digit coupons to finance hardware that depreciates straight-line at twenty-five to thirty percent per year. When fixed debt service attaches to hardware with rapid obsolescence, baseline operational margins leave little room for utilization shocks.

Hassett suggested that deep-pocketed corporations stand ready to absorb debt and equity if weaker operators struggle. That dynamic describes a distressed asset auction rather than sustainable return on invested capital. If an over-leveraged datacenter venture breaches its debt covenants, a hyperscaler or distressed debt vehicle can purchase the underlying hardware at thirty cents on the dollar. That outcome may prevent disorderly contagion across the banking system, but it records an irreversible destruction of invested equity.

For engineering teams and enterprise technology buyers, the consequence appears in contract terms. The period of venture-subsidized compute tokens was an artifact of hyperscalers treating hardware buildouts as land-grab customer acquisition. As debt service schedules and accelerated depreciation hit corporate income statements, compute providers must enforce capital recovery. Multi-year reserved capacity agreements are requiring higher minimum commitments, baseline token pricing floors are firming up, and pipeline architectural efficiency now dictates software margins far more than marginal gains on public model benchmarks.

title: Classes and Objects in Java
description:
Classes and Objects in Java

Java is an Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) language. Classes and objects are two fundamental concepts of OOP. A class defines the structure and behaviour, while an object is an instance created from that class.

1. What is a Class?

A class is a blueprint or template used to create objects. It defines the properties (variables) and behaviours (methods) that its objects can have.

For example, consider a Bank Account. Every account has an account holder name, account number, and balance. It can also perform operations like depositing and withdrawing money.

class BankAccount {
    String accountHolder;
    int accountNumber;
    double balance;

    void deposit(double amount) {
        balance += amount;
    }

    void checkBalance() {
        System.out.println(balance);
    }
}

Here, BankAccount is a class that defines the properties and behaviours of a bank account.

2. What is an Object?

An object is an instance of a class. We create objects using the new keyword.

Syntax:

ClassName objectName = new ClassName();

For example:

BankAccount customer1 = new BankAccount();

customer1.accountHolder = "Arun";
customer1.accountNumber = 101;
customer1.balance = 5000;

customer1.deposit(2000);
customer1.checkBalance();

Here, customer1 is an object reference variable that refers to the newly created BankAccount object.

We can create multiple objects from the same class, and each object maintains its own instance variable values.

BankAccount customer2 = new BankAccount();

customer2.accountHolder = "Kumar";
customer2.accountNumber = 102;
customer2.balance = 10000;

Both customers use the same class, but their account information is different.

3. What Happens When We Create an Object?

When we create an object using the new keyword, Java performs several operations behind the scenes.

BankAccount customer1 = new BankAccount();

The following steps take place:

  1. Memory Allocation: Java allocates memory for the new object in Heap memory.
  2. Default Values: Instance variables receive their default values, such as 0 for integers and null for reference types.
  3. Constructor Execution: The constructor executes to initialize the object. If no constructor is declared, Java provides a default no-argument constructor.
  4. Reference Creation: The new expression returns a reference to the newly created object.
  5. Object Access: We use the reference variable to access the object's variables and methods.

Stack and Heap Memory

Java uses different memory areas to manage objects and local variables.

  • Stack Memory: Stores local variables and object reference variables within method execution.
  • Heap Memory: Stores objects and their instance variables.

For example:

Student s1 = new Student();

Here, the reference variable s1 is stored in the stack frame of the executing method, while the actual Student object is allocated in Heap memory.

title: Styling Server Components without a stylesheet or a build step
description:
Style React Server Components with typed props and no 'use client', style registry or build plugin, with the CSS inside the HTML React streams. This article shows how that works in a Next.js App Router app, measures what it costs against a plain CSS module, and lists what still has to run on the client.

The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article.

The problem

You moved a page to the App Router, and the first component that styles itself wants 'use client'. Runtime CSS-in-JS works by collecting styles while the tree renders and then writing them somewhere, either from an effect or through a context that a provider sets up. A Server Component has neither. It runs once, on the server, and React never calls an effect there.

The Next.js guide to CSS-in-JS lists the popular libraries as supported in Client Components. The recipe takes three pieces: a style registry, a useServerInsertedHTML callback that flushes what the registry collected, and a 'use client' wrapper around the app. Where Server Component support has been added since, the theme provider is the part that had to go, because context does not exist on the server.

The usual ways around it each cost something real:

  • Put 'use client' on everything that styles itself. The build passes. But every component with a style now ships its code to the browser and hydrates, which is the cost Server Components exist to remove.
  • Move to a compiler that extracts CSS at build time. It ships no runtime, but it adds a bundler plugin, and a value only known at render time has to become a CSS variable written by hand.
  • Go back to stylesheets. This is reliable, but the styles live in one file and the markup in another again, and nothing checks that a class name you wrote still exists.

Styling as rendering

Box Kite takes a different route. Every CSS property is a typed prop, and in a Server Component it does not inject anything. Each rule a Box needs comes back as a React element, <style href precedence>, rendered next to the markup. React 19 hoists those elements into <head>, keeps one copy per href, and orders them by precedence. Styling becomes part of rendering, so it needs no effect, no provider and no registry.

Here is a Server Component page. There is no 'use client' in it and nothing above it:

import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import Grid from '@box-kite/react/components/grid';
import { H1, H2, P, Span } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';

const orders = [
  { id: 4100, customer: 'Ana', status: 'Shipped' },
  { id: 4101, customer: 'Ion', status: 'Packing' },
  { id: 4102, customer: 'Mara', status: 'Delivered' },
];

export default function OrdersPage() {
  return (
    <Flex d="column" gap={6} p={6} maxWidth={300} mx="auto">
      <H1 fontSize={28} fontWeight={700}>
        Orders
      </H1>
      <Grid gridTemplateColumns={1} gap={4} md={{ gridTemplateColumns: 3 }}>
        {orders.map((order) => (
          <Flex
            key={order.id}
            d="column"
            gap={2}
            p={5}
            borderRadius={3}
            b={1}
            borderColor="slate-200"
            bgColor="white"
            hover={{ borderColor: 'sky-500' }}
            theme={{ dark: { bgColor: 'slate-900', borderColor: 'slate-800' } }}
          >
            <H2 fontSize={16} fontWeight={600}>
              Order #{order.id}
            </H2>
            <P fontSize={14} color="slate-600" theme={{ dark: { color: 'slate-400' } }}>
              {order.customer}
            </P>
            <Span fontSize={12} fontWeight={600} color="sky-600">
              {order.status}
            </Span>
          </Flex>
        ))}
      </Grid>
    </Flex>
  );
}

The page has a breakpoint, a hover state and a dark theme. Each is just one more rule, so all three render on the server like the rest. You don't configure anything for this. The package's react-server export condition gives a Server Component a build of Box that calls no hook and never touches the DOM. Importing it is the whole setup.

Look at the HTML response and you'll find two <style> elements in <head>. React merges each precedence group into one element and lists what it merged in data-href. Every class in the markup has its rule in that response, so nothing waits for JavaScript to define it. The class names are hashes of their content, which is why the class the server wrote is exactly the class a client bundle would compute. Hydration has nothing to disagree about.

The order of the rules is not left to chance either. React hoists elements in the order it meets them, and rules are shared between Boxes, so element order alone could let p override px. Every rule therefore sits in a cascade layer, and the first style element declares the order of all layers once. Layer order beats source order.

What it costs, measured

Talk of "zero runtime" is cheap, so here are numbers instead. The setup:

  • a Next.js 16.3.5 production build (next start) with React 19.3, measured on a laptop;
  • a page of cards like the one above, each a Flex with an H2, a P and a Span inside, so four Boxes per card;
  • a baseline page with the same markup, styled by a plain CSS module.

Both pages render on every request.

Cards HTML, gzipped (Box / CSS module) Server response, median of 40 (Box / CSS module)
100 11.2 KB / 4.4 KB 15 ms / 10 ms
1,000 33.6 KB / 24.7 KB 79 ms / 35 ms

The JavaScript the browser downloaded was byte for byte the same on both pages: Next.js's own runtime, 172.9 KB gzipped. None of those chunks contained the styling engine. On a page with no client component, the engine never leaves the server.

Two costs show in the table, and both are real:

  • Rendering a Box takes time. At 1,000 cards, the page with 4,000 Boxes took 44 ms longer to render than the one with plain class names, which is about 11 µs per Box. Boxes styled alike resolve through one cache lookup, so a long list of identical rows costs less than a page of all-different elements.
  • The CSS travels in the HTML. A CSS module is a file the browser caches once for the whole site, while these rules come with each response. Most of the gap at 100 cards is the base stylesheet: the reset and the layer order, about 24 KB before compression, sent with every page.

What measuring this turned up

The first run of this benchmark didn't look like the table above. The page with 1,000 cards weighed 102 MB. On screen everything was right: two style elements in <head>, every class styled. The extra weight was in the RSC payload, the copy of the component tree that Next.js puts under the HTML for the client to pick up. React removes duplicate style elements from the page, but the payload carried every Box's elements in full, including the 24 KB base stylesheet, once per Box.

The fix is in the library: every Box now gets the same element objects. React's serializer sends an object it has already sent as a short reference, so the base stylesheet now crosses the wire once. That turned 102 MB into the 1.3 MB of the table above, and it shipped in Box Kite 2.2.4. A regression check now measures it against a real Next.js build on every pull request, because no unit test could have seen it.

Suspense streams the CSS with the markup

Streaming is where collecting styles in a registry gets awkward. The registry flushes when the shell is ready, and a section that arrives later needs its own flush. Here the CSS is part of what a component renders, so it arrives in the same chunk as the markup it styles:

import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { H2, P } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';
import { Suspense } from 'react';

async function fetchTotals() {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 700));

  return { revenue: '€48,200', orders: 1204 };
}

async function Totals() {
  const totals = await fetchTotals();

  return (
    <Flex d="column" gap={1} p={6} borderRadius={3} b={1} borderColor="emerald-500">
      <H2 fontSize={18} fontWeight={600}>
        {totals.revenue}
      </H2>
      <P fontSize={14} color="slate-600">
        from {totals.orders} orders this month
      </P>
    </Flex>
  );
}

export default function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<P color="slate-500">Loading totals…</P>}>
      <Totals />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

The example app in the repository has a section like this behind a 700 ms wait. Its smoke test checks the served HTML: the fallback, the late markup and the late section's own rule are all in the response. A style element that arrives after the shell is streamed disabled (media="not all"), and React turns it on when it reveals the boundary, so the late section never shows unstyled.

Themes without a provider

A provider can't run on the server, but a theme doesn't need one. In Box Kite a theme rule is scoped to an ancestor carrying the theme's class. The server decides the theme by putting that class on <html>:

import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" className="dark" data-theme="dark">
      <body>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}

Every theme={{ dark: … }} below it applies from the first paint. Switching later means changing that one class in the browser, which re-renders nothing. Dark mode without the flash covers the rest: the reader's own preference, a stored choice, and the few lines that run before the first paint.

Client components: one line, once

Most apps still have interactive parts. A client component resolves the client build of Box, which by default writes its rules through the CSSOM after hydration. That works, but it means the server-rendered HTML of an island would arrive without its CSS. One module puts the island on the same path as the server:

'use client';
import Box from '@box-kite/react';

Box.configure({ sink: 'element' });

Import it from your client components, and an island's rules are in the HTML before it hydrates, under the same class names the server used.

The ready-made components split the same way. Flex, Grid, Button, Textbox, the headings and the other semantic elements, the SVG elements and Icon call no hook, so a Server Component renders them with their CSS. Those that hold state, such as Dialog, Menu, Tabs or DataGrid, ship with a 'use client' banner. Importing one into a Server Component opens a client boundary rather than failing the build.

The honest limits

  • It is runtime CSS-in-JS on the server. About 11 µs per Box in the measurement above. That's small next to a database call, but it isn't zero, and a page of thousands of different elements will notice.
  • The CSS isn't a cached file. It travels with every HTML response: about 9 KB more than a CSS module at 1,000 cards, gzipped, and the base stylesheet on every page.
  • React 19 only. Hoisting <style href precedence> arrived in React 19. On React 18, keep the default mode, which writes to a stylesheet from the client.
  • Box.Theme and hover-callback children stay on the client. They need state. The theme rules work on the server, as shown above.
  • Your own CSS wins. Every Box rule sits in a cascade layer, so an unlayered stylesheet of yours overrides it. That's usually what you want, but it surprises people who expect props to win.

Try it

  • React Server Components is the reference for this mode, including server rendering without Server Components.
  • examples/next-app in the repository is the App Router app the checks above run against: a streamed section, a client island, a theme toggle and a page of the ready-made components.
  • npm install @box-kite/react, then import Flex into a page that has no 'use client'.

Originally published on box-kite.dev. Box Kite is open source under MIT — if it is useful to you, a star on GitHub helps other people find it. Install it with npm install @box-kite/react.

title: Dark mode without the flash
description:
A dark mode should paint the reader's theme on the first frame, switch without re-rendering the page, and let one section disagree with the rest. Most manage one or two of those three jobs. This article builds all three with Box Kite, shows what each line costs, and is explicit about the one piece the library leaves to you.

The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article.

The problem

Somebody opens your server-rendered page at night with their system set to dark. The HTML arrives, the browser paints it — white — and a moment later JavaScript runs, reads the preference and repaints everything dark. That flash is the most-reported dark-mode bug there is: the long-running Next.js discussion on it has dozens of replies, and a newer one opened because the usual fixes broke in the App Router.

The fixes people reach for each trade one problem for another:

  • Keep the theme in React state and pass it to every component. The server cannot know the reader's preference, so it renders a guess; the client renders the truth; React reports a hydration mismatch and the page flashes anyway. Every switch re-renders the tree.
  • Two sets of CSS variables, swapped by a class. This is the right mechanism, but it means a stylesheet of tokens maintained apart from the components that use them, and every new colour is an edit in two places.
  • Hide the page until JavaScript has decided. No flash, and no content either, for as long as the bundle takes.

The model: a theme is a class on an ancestor

In Box Kite a theme is a prop on the element it styles:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';

export function Card() {
  return (
    <Box
      p={6}
      borderRadius={3}
      b={1}
      bgColor="white"
      color="slate-900"
      borderColor="slate-200"
      theme={{ dark: { bgColor: 'slate-900', color: 'slate-100', borderColor: 'slate-800' } }}
    >
      The light colours are plain props, the dark ones are in theme.
    </Box>
  );
}

The library turns theme={{ dark: … }} into an ordinary CSS rule that applies when an ancestor carries the class dark. Nothing about it happens in React: there is no context to read and no prop to thread through. Which theme is showing is decided by one class on one element — usually <html> — and everything below follows it.

That one decision is what makes the other three jobs cheap.

Deciding the theme: Box.Theme

Box.Theme is the part that decides. Put it around the app once:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import App from './App';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <Box.Theme use="global" storageKey="theme">
      <App />
    </Box.Theme>
  </StrictMode>,
);

use="global" writes the theme onto <html>. With no choice stored, it follows prefers-color-scheme — and keeps following it, so a system that switches to dark at sunset takes the page with it. storageKey persists an explicit choice in localStorage, and a stored choice wins over the system from then on. A switch is a hook:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import Button from '@box-kite/react/components/button';

export function ThemeSwitch() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = Box.Theme.useTheme();

  return (
    <Button onClick={() => setTheme(theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark')} props={{ 'aria-label': 'Switch theme' }}>
      {theme === 'dark' ? 'Light' : 'Dark'}
    </Button>
  );
}

setTheme(null) forgets the stored choice and hands control back to the system.

What a switch costs. We measured it in Chrome with a render counter on every component: pressing the switch changed one class on <html>; the component that called useTheme() re-rendered, because it reads the theme; the page component, whose every colour changed, rendered exactly once in total — on mount. The colours change because the browser re-matches CSS, not because React re-rendered anything.

The first frame: a few lines you own

Box.Theme reads the system preference and the stored choice in the browser, after React starts. In a single-page app that is before anything is painted, so there is nothing to flash. A server-rendered or prerendered page is different: the HTML paints before any JavaScript runs, so the theme class has to be on <html> before that first paint — and only a script in the <head> runs early enough.

The library does not inject one for you; it is yours, and it is short. Ship the light theme in the HTML, and swap it before the body is painted:

<html lang="en" class="light" data-theme="light">
  <head>
    <script>
      try {
        var theme = localStorage.getItem('theme') || (matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light');
        var root = document.documentElement;
        root.classList.remove('light', 'dark');
        root.classList.add(theme);
        root.setAttribute('data-theme', theme);
      } catch (error) {}
    </script>
  </head>
</html>

The key is the same storageKey the provider uses, and the rule is the same — stored choice first, system second — so when React starts, Box.Theme resolves the theme the script already chose and leaves <html> alone. We checked that too: with the system set to dark, the class on <html> changed exactly once, from the shipped light to dark, before React ran, and never again; with light stored, the same page under a dark system kept light throughout. The try is for the reader whose browser blocks storage — they get the light theme the HTML shipped, which is also what a reader with JavaScript turned off sees.

Two variations:

  • If your server already knows the choice — from a cookie, say — render the class on <html> on the server and skip the script. The repository's Next.js example renders <html className="dark" data-theme="dark"> in a Server Component, and the theme needs no provider at all there, because the rules only care about the class.
  • If React renders the <html> element (Next.js and other frameworks do), the script changes an attribute React also rendered, so add suppressHydrationWarning to that element — the warning is about exactly the change you meant to make.

This is how box-kite.dev itself works: every page is prerendered in the light theme, and an inline script in the shell switches it before the first paint.

A section that stays light

Real pages have parts that ignore the page's theme: a code sample that is always dark, a print preview that is always light, a marketing block with its own colours. Because a theme is a class on an ancestor, a nested Box.Theme is simply a nearer ancestor:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';

export function PrintPreview() {
  return (
    <Box.Theme use="local" theme="light">
      <Box p={6} bgColor="white" color="slate-900" theme={{ dark: { bgColor: 'slate-900', color: 'slate-100' } }}>
        Light, whatever the page around it is doing.
      </Box>
    </Box.Theme>
  );
}

The nested theme is a real boundary, not a second class competing with the first. Each theme rule is written with CSS @scope, from the theme's class down to the next element that declares a theme of its own, so the dark page's rules stop at the light section's edge — including for a property the inner section never mentions. In the measurement above, the light section kept its light background while the page around it was dark, and kept it through every switch.

The switch, animated

A theme change can cross-fade the whole page instead of snapping:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

export function Root({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <Box.Theme use="global" storageKey="theme" viewTransition>
      {children}
    </Box.Theme>
  );
}

viewTransition runs the switch inside the browser's View Transitions API. Writing it by hand has a trap — the browser captures the page the moment your callback returns, before React has rendered the new state, so a hand-rolled version captures the old theme twice and nothing appears to animate — and the prop flushes the update inside the callback for you. A reader who asked for reduced motion gets the theme change without the cross-fade, and a browser without view transitions simply switches.

Charts follow too

The theme reaches markup the library did not render, through CSS variables. A chart library takes a colour string; give it a variable, and declare the variable per theme on a container:

import { ChartContainer } from '@box-kite/react/components/chart';
import { Line, LineChart, ResponsiveContainer } from 'recharts';

const months = [
  { month: 'Jan', revenue: 12 },
  { month: 'Feb', revenue: 18 },
  { month: 'Mar', revenue: 15 },
];

export function Revenue() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer series={['revenue']} height={60}>
      <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height="100%">
        <LineChart data={months}>
          <Line dataKey="revenue" stroke="var(--color-revenue)" strokeWidth={2} dot={false} />
        </LineChart>
      </ResponsiveContainer>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}

ChartContainer declares one --color-<series> per name, with a value for each theme, so the chart names no colour at all and its dark mode is the page's. The charts page shows a full example with a grid and axis labels.

The honest limits

  • The pre-paint script is yours. For a server-rendered page, nothing in the library can run before the first paint; the few lines above are the whole of it, and they have to agree with the storageKey you gave Box.Theme.
  • Theme rules need @scope: Chrome 118, Safari 17.4, Firefox 128 and later. In an older browser the theme rules are dropped — which is why the examples here write the light colours as plain props and only the dark ones in theme: an old browser then shows a working light page rather than an unstyled one.
  • The system preference only knows light and dark. A theme is any class name — high-contrast, sepia, a brand theme — and theme={{ 'high-contrast': … }} works the same way, but choosing one of those is always an explicit setTheme.

Try it

  • Theme setup — the reference for theme, Box.Theme and component themes.
  • The playground — write a theme prop and see the rule it produces.
  • npm install @box-kite/react, and wrap your app in Box.Theme.

Originally published on box-kite.dev. Box Kite is open source under MIT — if it is useful to you, a star on GitHub helps other people find it. Install it with npm install @box-kite/react.

title: Optimize an SVG in the Browser: Shrink It Without Uploading It
description:
An SVG that came out of a design tool is usually bigger than it needs to be. It carries editor metadata, leftover layer names and sometimes a <script> block from whatever exported it. Before you ship it as a favicon, an inline icon or a logo, you want it smaller — and you want to see by how much.

Full disclosure: I work on OnePassApps. Its Icon Studio has an Optimize SVG tool, and the page describes itself as "Create icons and favicon assets on this device. Files stay in your active browser tab."

What the tool promises

The panel is three steps, the same shape as the rest of the Studio:

  • 01 Source — "No SVG yet. Drop one on the stage or browse for it. SVG up to 5 MiB and 25,000 elements."
  • 02 What changes — three lines that spell out the trade:
    • Keeps — "The viewBox and every visible shape"
    • Removes — "Scripts, event handlers and external references"
    • Compares — "The byte sizes before and after"
  • 03 Result — "Ready", then the two sizes side by side, the new file name and a "Create again" button.

The promise is deliberately narrow. The viewBox and the visible shapes stay, scripts and external references go, and the before/after byte counts are put next to each other so you can judge it rather than take it on trust.

What it did to my file

I dropped in a small test SVG (120 × 120, a rounded rectangle, a circle, plus a <title>, a <metadata> block and a <script> element) and pressed Optimize SVG. The source stage read:

probe.svg
SVG · 120 × 120 · 387 B

The result step came back with:

Ready
Before        387 B   SVG
After         238 B   SVG
Size change   38.5% smaller
File name     probe-optimized.svg
Created in 0.7 s

Under it there is a Download SVG button and a summary line: "SVG reduced by 149 bytes (39%)." The result also comes with a Dark/Light preview, which is the quick way to check that a mark with a transparent or white fill still reads against both backgrounds.

"Your original stays untouched." The file you dropped is not rewritten in place — you get a new file next to it, probe-optimized.svg.

Why this is a browser job

An SVG is small, so it is easy to assume you can post it anywhere. But "post it anywhere" is exactly the thing you do not want to do with an icon that has not shipped yet: a public converter sees your file, keeps a copy, and may start serving it behind a CDN. This one never leaves the tab — the page says "Processing stays in this browser." — and the file you get back is a local download.

Where it fits in the Studio

Icon Studio is not only about optimisation. The same page has SVG to PNG, PNG to ICO, Favicon pack, App icons, Resize set, Optimize SVG, Recolour SVG and Trim / padding tabs, so the whole chain — optimise, recolour, trim the padding, rasterise, then pack a favicon set and app icons — can be done in one place without the file making a round trip to a server in the middle.

Standard is free right now: $0/month with 100,000 credits every 30 days, no end date set and no card required. There is more on the guides page if you want the wider picture.

title: How I put real macOS Liquid Glass inside a Java/Swing IDE
description:
macOS 26 made the whole system out of glass. Finder, Xcode and System Settings got frosted sidebars, translucent toolbars and Liquid Glass buttons. Rider, my .NET IDE, still looked like a flat grey slab sitting on top of all that.

So I built Glass Islands, a free and open-source Rider plugin that turns the new Islands UI into real macOS glass:

The key word is real. This is not a colour scheme and not a blur painted in Swing. Every translucent layer is an actual AppKit view (NSVisualEffectView, NSGlassEffectView), and the macOS compositor renders it live, the same way it renders Finder. This post explains how a Java/Swing application ends up with native AppKit glass behind it, and what broke along the way.

Why not just paint a blur?

JetBrains IDEs are Swing applications running on the JetBrains Runtime (a JDK fork). You could grab what's behind the window, blur it and paint it as a background. That falls apart quickly:

  • Swing can't see what's behind the window, so you'd need screenshots, refreshed constantly.
  • It would never match the system: vibrancy, the dimming of inactive windows, Liquid Glass refraction and accessibility settings all come from AppKit.
  • It would cost a lot of CPU for a worse result.

The only way to get the real thing is to let macOS do it, which means putting native views under Swing's content and making Swing's content see-through.

The view hierarchy

Here is what the plugin builds inside Rider's window:

NSWindow (Rider project frame, made non-opaque)
└─ NSThemeFrame
   ├─ backdrop        NSVisualEffectView, whole window, tinted          ┐ added by the plugin,
   ├─ islands         shadows │ frosted panes │ Liquid Glass pills       ┘ below Rider's content
   ├─ AWTView         Rider's Swing content (Metal layer, non-opaque)
   └─ titlebar

Rider's Swing content still lives in its AWTView, rendered by Metal. The plugin slides a whole-window backdrop and one view per Islands pane underneath it, and makes everything above them transparent where the glass should show.

Step 1: making a decorated AWT window translucent

AWT lets an undecorated window be translucent with Window.setBackground(Color(0, 0, 0, 0)). A normal, decorated IDE frame is not allowed to. So the plugin reproduces what setBackground does internally:

  • a transparent Component.background on the frame,
  • LWWindowPeer.setOpaque(false), which makes the NSWindow and its Metal layer non-opaque,
  • classic double buffering for the root pane. IntelliJ's own per-window buffer is flipped onto the window with SrcOver, which is fine on an opaque window but accumulates translucent pixels on a translucent one: every repaint would get a little darker.

Then every Swing surface that the glass replaces becomes transparent: panels through UIManager overrides, editors through their own colour scheme delegate. The editor keeps most of its opacity (at least 86% by default), because readable code matters more than pretty glass.

Step 2: calling AppKit from Kotlin with FFM

The native side is a small Objective-C library, libliquidglass.dylib, with a deliberately boring C ABI: integers, pointers and arrays of doubles. No JNI glue. The plugin calls it through Java 25's Foreign Function & Memory API:

private val lookup = SymbolLookup.libraryLookup(libraryPath, libraryArena)
private val linker = Linker.nativeLinker()

private fun function(name: String, descriptor: FunctionDescriptor): MethodHandle =
    linker.downcallHandle(lookup.find(name).orElseThrow(), descriptor)

private val applyBackdrop = function("rlg_apply_backdrop", FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS))
private val setIslands = function("rlg_set_islands", FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(JAVA_LONG, ADDRESS, JAVA_INT, ADDRESS))

The window handle comes from the platform (MacUtil.getWindowFromJavaWindow), and the native side only ever touches a pointer that is still one of NSApp.windows. A stale pointer is a crash, and a crash here takes the whole IDE down.

Step 3: the threading trap

AppKit must be called on the main thread. Swing paints on the AWT event thread. The obvious fix, dispatching to the main thread and waiting, deadlocks as soon as the main thread is itself waiting on the AWT thread, which happens all the time.

The JDK's own AWT natives solve this with a dedicated run-loop mode, AWTRunLoopMode, which the main thread keeps servicing while it is blocked on AWT. The bridge does exactly the same:

[call performSelectorOnMainThread:@selector(run)
                       withObject:nil
                    waitUntilDone:YES
                            modes:@[NSRunLoopCommonModes, @"AWTRunLoopMode"]];

Waiting also means the native shapes change in the same frame as the Swing content: when you drag a splitter, the glass pane follows the panel instead of lagging behind it. And every call is wrapped in @try/@catch, because an Objective-C exception that reaches the JVM aborts the whole IDE.

Step 4: following the layout

The plugin tracks the Islands layout (tool window holders, editor splitters, toolbar and stripe buttons, editor tabs) with a single AWT event listener. Changes are coalesced to one pass per UI cycle, and only diffs are sent to the native side. Native views are keyed by a stable id and updated in place inside a CATransaction with implicit animations disabled, so nothing slides around.

Typing, scrolling and the caret blinking send nothing to AppKit. A full layout scan takes about 0.2 ms, and a native update 2 to 5 ms. On my M4 Pro, idle Rider uses about the same CPU with or without the glass.

Frosted panes vs Liquid Glass

Using NSGlassEffectView (Liquid Glass) for the big panes looks like the obvious choice, but it doesn't survive switching windows: Liquid Glass goes flat or drops its blur when a window loses key status, so the entire IDE would flash on every focus change.

The fix was to do what macOS itself does: large surfaces use the frosted NSVisualEffectView material, and Liquid Glass is reserved for small controls such as buttons, pills and tabs. On macOS versions before 26, those controls fall back to frosted pills.

Flicker, the hard part

A translucent Swing window flickers for two different reasons:

  1. Opaque components that don't paint their whole background. In a translucent window, Swing clears a repainted region with the background of the first opaque component above it. A component that claims to be opaque but leaves gaps shows a blank flash. The plugin paints each opaque component once offscreen and marks the ones that don't actually cover their bounds as non-opaque.
  2. Frames presented before they're complete. JBR's Metal pipeline presents frames from the display link, so a frame caught mid-update shows a panel blank for one frame. In screen recordings of a scrolled diff, -Dsun.java2d.metal.displaySync=false takes this from 2 or 3 blank frames per 12 seconds to none. JBR only reads that flag at startup, so the plugin offers to add it to your VM options and removes it when you uninstall.

Being a good citizen

  • Accessibility: Reduce Transparency turns the glass off, and Increase Contrast makes every layer more opaque and outlined. Presentation Mode stays opaque.
  • No restart, clean unload: everything the plugin changes (window opacity, UIManager keys, editor colours, native views, listeners) is recorded and restored. Uninstall it and Rider looks exactly as before.
  • Safe mode: if Rider ever stops while the glass is being applied, the plugin turns itself off at the next start and tells you.
  • Fragile internals in one place: everything that depends on JDK or IntelliJ implementation details is listed and checked in a single file. If a future Rider changes one of them, only the feature built on it stops, and the settings page says why.

Try it

  • Install: Settings › Plugins › Marketplace, search "Glass Islands", or use the JetBrains Marketplace page. No restart needed.
  • Requirements: Rider 2026.2 or later with an Islands theme, macOS 12 or later. Liquid Glass buttons need macOS 26.
  • Source (MIT): github.com/lilyaan444/glass-islands

It's Rider-only for now, but most of it is IntelliJ Platform code. If you'd like it in IntelliJ IDEA, WebStorm or PyCharm, let me know in the comments. I'd also love to hear from anyone on Intel Macs or macOS 12 to 15, which I can test less.
