title: Fluid sizes with CSS clamp(): practical examples you can copy
description:
Media queries make values jump: 16px, then suddenly 20px, then 24px. Fluid values grow smoothly with the screen instead. In modern CSS, one line does it:

font-size: clamp(16px, calc(10.66667px + 1.48148vw), 32px);

This post shows how to read declarations like this, gives you ready-made examples, and covers the mistakes that quietly break them.

How to read a clamp() declaration

clamp() takes three arguments:

clamp(minimum, preferred, maximum)
  • minimum: the value never goes below this (16px above)
  • preferred: the part that changes with the viewport (calc(… + …vw))
  • maximum: the value never goes above this (32px above)

The example above means: 16px on a 360px screen, 32px on a 1440px screen, smooth growth in between, and it stays at 16px or 32px outside that range. No media queries needed.

The numbers in the middle look odd, but you don't need to touch them by hand. You decide the two endpoints, and the declaration follows from them.

Copy-paste examples

All of these scale between a 360px and a 1440px viewport.

Body text, 16px → 18px

font-size: clamp(16px, calc(15.33333px + 0.18519vw), 18px);

Headline, 28px → 56px

font-size: clamp(28px, calc(18.66667px + 2.59259vw), 56px);

Section spacing, 32px → 96px

padding-block: clamp(32px, calc(10.66667px + 5.92593vw), 96px);

Grid gap, 12px → 32px

gap: clamp(12px, calc(5.33333px + 1.85185vw), 32px);

Card corners, 12px → 24px

border-radius: clamp(12px, calc(8px + 1.11111vw), 24px);

Values that shrink on wider screens

Fluid doesn't always mean "bigger on desktop". Here's card padding that is roomy on phones (24px) and tighter on wide multi-column layouts (12px), between 375px and 1440px:

padding: clamp(12px, calc(28.22535px - 1.12676vw), 24px);

Note the minus before the vw part. That's what makes the value go down as the screen gets wider.

Three mistakes that break clamp()

1. Swapping min and max. The first argument must be the smaller value, even when it belongs to the wider screen. In the padding example, 12px comes first. If the minimum is larger than the maximum, clamp() always returns the minimum, and your value stops being fluid without any error.

2. No spaces around + and -. calc(10px+2vw) is invalid. calc(10px + 2vw) works. The browser drops the whole declaration if the spaces are missing.

3. Using px for text without thinking about it. Pixel values ignore the user's browser font-size setting: someone who set their default text to 20px still gets your 16px. For font-size, convert the px parts to rem (divide by 16) and leave the vw part as it is:

font-size: clamp(1rem, calc(0.66667rem + 1.48148vw), 2rem);

For width, gap or border-radius, plain px is usually fine.

What clamp() can't do: opacity

Try to make opacity fluid and you'll hit a wall. opacity needs a plain number like 0.6, but anything with vw in it is a length, and CSS won't convert one into the other.

The workaround is a tiny JavaScript function that returns the value for the current viewport width. Fading an overlay from 0.4 on small screens to 0.8 on large ones:

function getResponsiveValue(viewportWidth) {
  const minViewport = 320;
  const maxViewport = 1980;
  const minValue = 0.4;
  const maxValue = 0.8;

  if (viewportWidth <= minViewport) return minValue;
  if (viewportWidth >= maxViewport) return maxValue;

  const progress = (viewportWidth - minViewport) / (maxViewport - minViewport);
  return minValue + (maxValue - minValue) * progress;
}

const overlay = document.querySelector('.hero-overlay');
const update = () => {
  overlay.style.opacity = getResponsiveValue(window.innerWidth);
};

update();
window.addEventListener('resize', update);

Browser support

clamp() and calc() with vw work in all current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari. No fallbacks needed unless you support very old browsers.

Generate your own

The examples above cover common cases, but your design has its own sizes and breakpoints. I built a small free tool for exactly that: wresp.com. Pick a property, enter the values you want on a narrow and a wide screen, and it gives you the clamp() declaration, or the JavaScript function for opacity. A live preview slider shows how the value behaves at every width in between.

It's a side project, so feedback is very welcome. What would you want from a fluid-value generator that other tools don't do? Let me know in the comments. 👇

title: I built a hand-drawn React UI kit that's crooked on purpose and accessible anyway
description:
Most UI kits try hard to look neutral. PlopUI goes the other way: wobbly sticker buttons, washi-tape tags, a hand-lettered marker font, colors picked by instinct. The whole thing looks like it was drawn on the back of a receipt.

It has one rule: break the visual rulebook, never the accessibility one.

The drawing sits on top, never instead

A PlopUI button is a real <button>. A checkbox is a real checkbox. The hand-drawn outlines, shadows and doodles are decoration layered over native elements, so the browser and screen readers still know exactly what everything is.

That means the boring stuff just works:

  • Tab, Enter and Space do what you expect. Select and Menu also handle arrow keys, Home, End, type-to-jump and Escape.
  • Every interactive component has a keyboard test, and the docs site runs end-to-end tests in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
  • Status never relies on color alone. The error character (Bix) winces and sweats, so the meaning reads even if you can't tell red from green.

Crooked, but the same crooked everywhere

The hardest part of a "random" look is server rendering. If a button's tilt comes from Math.random(), the server draws one angle and the browser draws another. React complains about a hydration mismatch, and the button visibly jumps.

So nothing in PlopUI calls Math.random() while rendering. Every tilt, wobble and jitter comes from a seed:

// hashString is FNV-1a: it turns a string like "Post sketch" into a 32-bit number.

/** A deterministic random generator: same seed, same sequence, values in [0, 1). */
export function seed(value: string | number): () => number {
  let x = typeof value === "number" ? value >>> 0 || 1 : hashString(value) || 1;
  return () => {
    // mulberry32
    x = (x + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
    let t = x;
    t = Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 15), t | 1);
    t ^= t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), t | 61);
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}

/** A value in [-range, range], rounded so it serializes identically on server and client. */
export function seededTilt(value: string | number, range = 2.5): number {
  const n = seed(value)();
  return Math.round((n * 2 - 1) * range * 100) / 100;
}

Same seed in, same crooked line out, on the server and in the browser. The rounding matters too: two decimals means the number is written identically in the server HTML and in React's props.

Built for the App Router

The package never imports next/*, so it works in any React 19 app. In Next.js, every interactive component already carries "use client", and the static ones (a timeline, a plain tag) stay Server Components and ship no client JavaScript.

It's also light where it counts: everything is tree-shakeable, and a plain Button is about 5.6 kB gzipped.

The wobble knows when to chill

Every animation respects prefers-reduced-motion. Turn it on and the motion stops, while state changes still show, just instantly. Looping scenes pause while they're off screen, which took the docs site's idle CPU on a throttled phone from 12% to 0%. And the animated footer has a pause button, because anything that moves for more than five seconds should.

Three packages

  • @plop-ui/react: the components, hooks and characters.
  • @plop-ui/tokens: colors with measured contrast, type, motion and five paper surfaces as CSS variables. There's also a tokens.json for Figma (Tokens Studio).
  • @plop-ui/fonts: Sketchpop, the marker font, under the SIL Open Font License. Every letter is drawn three times and rotates through calt, so a word like "Shipped!" never repeats the same p twice.

Try it 

npm i @plop-ui/react @plop-ui/fonts

import "@plop-ui/fonts/fonts.css";
import "@plop-ui/react/styles.css";
import { PlopProvider, Button, toast } from "@plop-ui/react";

export function App() {
  return (
    <PlopProvider surface="poster">
      <Button buddy onClick={() => toast.success("Sketch posted", { buddy: true })}>
        Post sketch
      </Button>
    </PlopProvider>
  );
}

Or skip the install and play with it first: the Playground lets you stick components onto paper and copy the code.

What it's for

Creative tools, learning apps, games, portfolios, side projects: anything that should feel made by a person. It's not the right pick for a dense enterprise dashboard where every pixel has to stay quiet.

PlopUI is free and MIT-licensed: plopui.com · GitHub. Issues and pull requests are welcome, and a few are labeled "good first issue". If something breaks, tell me. I'll fix it and thank you by name.

title: Serverless applications on AWS with Lambda using Java 25, API Gateway and Aurora DSQL - Part 9 Using Container Image with SnapStart and priming approach
description:
Introduction

In part 8 of the series, we learned how to convert the sample application to one using a container image as a deployment artifact on AWS Lambda and measured the performance of the Lambda functions. We observed that the Lambda cold start times are quite high.

In this part, we'll enable SnapStart on the Lambda functions using a container image. We'll also apply priming techniques and measure the performance of the Lambda functions for all scenarios.

You can find the final version of our sample applications, which we can deploy on AWS Lambda as a container image, in the following GitHub repositories:

  • Sample application with JDBC and Hikari connection pool in the aws-lambda-java-25-aurora-dsql-as-container-image repository.
  • Sample application with Hibernate and Hikari connection pool in the aws-lambda-java-25-hibernate-aurora-dsql-as-container-image repository.

Besides the previous part, please read the following articles in this series to grasp the general concepts:

  • Part 3 Introducing Lambda SnapStart
  • Part 4 SnapStart and DSQL request priming
  • Part 5 SnapStart and full priming

The business logic required to implement the Lambda SnapStart priming approaches and the measurement design is the same. The changes that we need to make for each Lambda function in the SAM templates of both projects are the same as those we covered in part 8.

Measurements of cold and warm start times of our application with JDBC and Hikari connection pool using a Container Image

For the sake of completeness, we provide the measurements for the "No SnapStart enabled" approach from part 8.

Cold (c) and warm (w) start time with -XX:+TieredCompilation -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 compilation in ms:

Approach c p50 c p75 c p90 c p99 c p99.9 c max w p50 w p75 w p90 w p99 w p99.9 w max
No SnapStart enabled 1886 2047 2218 2568 2628 2629 4.90 5.24 5.63 8.00 131.40 380
SnapStart enabled but no priming applied, all 929 967 1021 1183 1275 1275 5.06 5.46 5.86 8.50 387 854
SnapStart enabled but no priming applied, last 70 918 953 1018 1180 1180 1180 5.08 5.46 5.86 8.50 387 854
SnapStart enabled and DSQL database request priming applied, all 587 624 998 1030 1133 1134 5.06 5.46 5.86 8.60 319 762
SnapStart enabled and DSQL database request priming applied, last 70 585 614 990 1024 1024 1024 5.04 5.41 5.82 8.57 318 762
SnapStart enabled and full priming applied, all 560 589 698 931 1092 1092 5.02 5.35 5.72 8.67 195 643
SnapStart enabled and full priming applied, last 70 558 579 641 921 921 921 4.98 5.33 5.72 8.57 194 422

Measurements of cold and warm start times of our application with Hibernate and Hikari connection pool using a Container Image

For the sake of completeness, we provide the measurements for the "No SnapStart enabled" approach from part 8.

Cold (c) and warm (w) start time with -XX:+TieredCompilation -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 compilation in ms:

Approach c p50 c p75 c p90 c p99 c p99.9 c max w p50 w p75 w p90 w p99 w p99.9 w max
No SnapStart enabled 3971 4150 4229 4660 4914 4914 5.46 5.86 6.30 8.20 203 398
SnapStart enabled but no priming applied, all 1091 1132 1287 1410 1417 1418 5.55 6.01 6.40 8.53 516 868
SnapStart enabled but no priming applied, last 70 1080 1099 1151 1236 1236 1236 5.61 6.05 6.50 8.60 513 744
SnapStart enabled and DSQL database request priming applied, all 938 982 1097 1230 1237 1238 5.59 6.00 6.45 8.46 332 678
SnapStart enabled and DSQL database request priming applied, last 70 931 969 1012 1202 1202 1202 5.61 6.00 6.43 8.43 316 646
SnapStart enabled and full priming applied, all 637 666 928 1119 1231 1231 5.61 6.03 6.48 8.77 185 590
SnapStart enabled and full priming applied, last 70 629 648 706 988 988 988 5.63 6.05 6.50 8.84 182 535

Conclusion

In this part, we enabled SnapStart on the Lambda functions using a container image. We also applied priming techniques and measured the performance of the Lambda functions for all scenarios. What we observe is that both cold and warm start times are very competitive when using the container image. Especially if we compare them to the measurements we did for the Lambda Java 25 managed Lambda runtime. See the results in the article SnapStart and full priming for comparison. I especially look for 90th-percentile measurements where the performance of the Lambda function with a container image is significantly better. What we also see is that the effect of the snapshot tiered cache is not so strong for the container images (see the last 70 measurements). With GraalVM Native Image, we have even higher cold and warm start times compared to container images. It also requires quite high effort to create and maintain the GraalVM Native images. For the container image, it is medium effort.

For the performance-sensitive Lambda functions, using the container image as the packaging format provides a very good solution. This is especially true when enabling Lambda SnapStart, which recently became available, and implementing priming. Please note that SnapStart charges apply to the container images, while SnapStart for supported Java managed versions remains free on AWS Lambda. So, gaining additional performance with SnapStart for container images comes at an additional cost. That's why choosing a managed Java version versus a container image becomes a cost-performance trade-off.

Please also watch out for another series where I use a NoSQL serverless Amazon DynamoDB database instead of Aurora DSQL to do the same Lambda performance measurements.

If you like my content, please follow me on GitHub and give my repositories a star!

Please also check out my website for more technical content and upcoming public speaking activities.

title: Goodbye :nth-child! How Modern CSS sibling-index() Works Under the Hood
description:
Ever found yourself writing endless lines of :nth-child(1), :nth-child(2), :nth-child(3) or injecting custom CSS variables via JavaScript just to stagger a list of entrance animations?

Modern CSS (Values & Units Module Level 5) introduces two native functions:

  • sibling-index() — Returns the 1-based index of the element among its siblings.
  • sibling-count() — Returns the total count of siblings under the parent.

Here is the complete video breakdown and live animation:

1. Staggered Delays in Pure CSS 

.card {
  animation: cardFadeIn 0.6s cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) both;
  animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 120ms);
}

2. Dynamic 360° Color Wheels with OKLCH 

.chip {
  --hue: calc((sibling-index() / sibling-count()) * 360deg);
  background: oklch(0.68 0.22 var(--hue));
}

3. Reverse z-Index Overlapping Avatars 

.avatar {
  margin-left: -14px;
  z-index: calc(sibling-count() - sibling-index() + 1);
}

🎯 60-Second Challenge: Can You Solve It?

Can you write a single calc() formula so the middle item in an odd list of bars gets the largest height/scale?

title: How I Earned $700 in AWS Credits as an AWS Community Builder
description:
I got $700 worth of AWS credits to play and learn across the AWS ecosystem, and you can follow the same path. Here's how.

TL;DR: Where the $700 comes from

Source Credits
AWS Community Builders Program $500
New AWS account bonus $100
"Explore AWS" tasks (5 × $20) up to $100
Total up to $700

Step 1: Join the AWS Community Builders Program

The program opens for applications once a year, usually around November/December. To get in:

  1. Join the waitlist and submit your interest.
  2. Share your engaging posts and community contributions, since these are what get you noticed.

Benefits include:

  • ✨ $500 in AWS credits for your projects
  • ✨ Exclusive sessions with AWS product teams
  • ✨ 50% discount on AWS re:Invent tickets
  • ✨ One year of free CloudAcademy access
  • ✨ A free AWS certification of your choice
  • ✨ A global network of 3,000+ AWS experts

Apply here:

  • 📌 Join the waitlist
  • 📌 Program details

Step 2: Get into the Builders portal and Slack

Once you're selected, you get access to the AWS Builders portal and the Community Builders Slack workspace. The Slack is active and worth joining for its own sake. Members post new things constantly, and you hear about upcoming AWS products before they launch.

Step 3: Claim your $500 credits

Watch the #cb-announcements Slack channel. When the time comes, the team posts a link to claim your $500 in AWS credits.

⚠️ Heads up: every member gets a unique credit link. Don't share it, and don't redeem it on a company account.

Step 4: Create your AWS account (+$100)

Use your personal credit link to create an account in the AWS Console.

  • You'll need an international credit card. AWS usually makes a $1 charge to verify the card, then refunds it.
  • As a first-year user, AWS gives you $100 in credits to experiment with.

Running total: $600

Step 5: Complete the "Explore AWS" tasks (+$100)

After sign-up, the console shows a new Explore AWS section covering popular services such as EC2, Serverless, RDS, Bedrock and Cost Alerts. Each task you complete earns $20, and with five tasks you can earn up to $100.

I've completed 4 of 5, which is $80 so far.

Step 6: Check your Billing page

Open the Billing page to see a full breakdown of every credit and where it came from.

Wrap-up

That's how you can reach $700 in credits in your first year as an AWS Community Builder. That's plenty of room to build, break and learn on AWS without worrying about the bill.

If you apply, I'd love to hear how it goes. Drop a comment below, and follow me for more AWS content. 🚀

Program terms and credit amounts can change, so check the official AWS Community Builders pages for the latest details.

title: Chasing milliseconds in Speed Demon 2026: lessons from a solo optimisation sprint
description:
The change I'm proudest of from this contest brought Track A's board memory down from 22.69 MB to 19.69 MB, with similar wall time. The change I was surest about looked faster on my test VM. On the real scoring machine its two runs averaged about 40% slower than the control, and I threw it away the same morning.

I entered Speed Demon 2026, organised by Hackathon Raptors, as team PeppaPig, a team of one. I wrote all four tracks in Rust with no crates, only the standard library. This post is about my method, and the many times my own measurements lied to me.

The contest and the score

There are four tracks. Each is a small, well-defined data job:

  • A: Ingest: parse a request log and write per-hour, per-endpoint latency summaries with percentiles.
  • B: Index: tokenize a document corpus and answer phrase and boolean queries.
  • C: Join: join a quoted CSV of records against a region table and aggregate.
  • D: Traverse: build a weighted graph and answer shortest-path queries.

Every output has to be byte-identical to the organisers' Python reference. Correctness is a gate, not a score component. Pass it, and you get a single number, K, built from reference-to-submission ratios for time, memory, source size and dependencies:

  • T, wall time (exponent 0.5). This is the big one. The board takes the mean of the middle 3 of 5 runs.
  • M, peak cgroup memory (exponent 0.2), taking the highest peak across the five runs. Output written to the tmpfs /out counts against you.
  • S, formatted code lines (exponent 0.15). That includes your Dockerfile.
  • D, 1 plus direct runtime dependencies (exponent 0.15). With no third-party runtime dependencies, my dependency factor was 1.

The memory ratio is capped at 50; the source and dependency ratios are capped at 1. Wall-time gains are uncapped.

The scoring run gets 6 P-cores and 12 threads on an Intel i5-13500. The input is pre-warmed into the page cache, so the timings focus on warm-cache processing.

S is subtle: while the source-size penalty applies, doubling S costs about 10% of K. Removing counted lines while preserving time and memory gives a predictable gain; a small measured speedup may disappear on the board.

My best board K per track: A 47.32, B 34.36, C 41.77, D 27.59. B's 34.36 came from the live board and is not yet in the repository log; the logged best for the submitted B code is 34.20.

The method

Be honest about who did the typing

A lot of the experimenting was done by AI coding agents (Hark, OpenAI Codex and Kiro) working side by side, with me directing. Each opened its own branches and pull requests, and every one had to beat production on the board like anything else. My job was to pick targets, set the rules of evidence, decide what shipped, and read every report. The agents worked in parallel on profiles, candidates, correctness checks and benchmark preparation. That let one person try far more ideas, and made a strict process vital: many plausible small wins in a night are a great way to fool yourself.

Profile on hardware that looks like the box

My laptop is ARM, so the serious work moved to an x86 cloud VM. I pinned the benchmarks to a fixed CPU set. Builds ran at low priority on separate cores. perf highlighted hot instructions through sampling, and a cgroup harness read memory.peak the way the board does.

One idea per agent, one lock per benchmark

Each agent got one idea and its own directory. Every timed run took a shared file lock, so agents never benchmarked at the same time.

Paired, interleaved, and repeated

A candidate never ran against a number from yesterday. It ran in repeated pairs against the current production build, in alternating order and across input seeds. Track B used profile-guided optimisation (PGO), so there I compared multiple separately trained PGO builds per side.

The board decides

The rule I settled on was to repeat promising candidates on the live board and judge them against a same-track control from the same period, not against my best-ever run. Some obvious losses stopped after one run; noisy candidates needed more repetitions. If the evidence supported keeping a change, it became production. Otherwise it was reverted, and the reason went into a per-track PERF.md log.

Four wins

1. Track A: redesigning the summary for memory

Profiling left me looking for small gains in the parse, but memory became the cheaper target. The old summary copied each hour's latencies into a per-worker scratch buffer. The new one reuses an existing record vector and does an in-place counting sort (American-flag style) to group records by endpoint in output order. Percentile selection happens within each group; the extra full-hour scratch buffer is gone.

On the board, peak memory fell from the control's 22.69 MB to 20.44 and 19.69 MB, with similar wall time. It tied the control on its first run (45.97 vs 45.97, M −2.2 MB) and won the rerun with 46.90, at M 19.69 MB. It shipped.

2. Track B: a collision-free term table, then 16-bit result lists

B spends most of its time tokenizing and looking up terms. The old linear-probe table could require multiple probes and unpredictable branches. The new version builds a hash-and-displace table once, after parsing the queries, for query terms of at most 16 bytes. Those query keys get distinct slots; a lookup uses a 16-bit bucket displacement and an exact two-word key comparison to reject nonmembers. Longer terms still use a HashMap.

On the board, production B had been sitting at about 30.4–30.9. The table scored 32.51, then 30.67 in a normal batch. Parallelising the setup on top of it (query parsing and interning on all 12 threads) gave 32.66 / 32.10, and that shipped.

Then came a tiny one. Storing the answer step's scratch result lists as u16 instead of u32 also trimmed scored S from 761 to 758. On the board it scored 33.62 / 33.80, with T down to about 120 ms from the ~150 ms I started the day with.

3. Track C: smaller buffers, lower M

C reads records.csv through per-thread pread buffers instead of mapping it. Shrinking the read buffer to 32 KiB and the event blocks to 512 entries brought M to 11.0 MB at the same T (22.9 ms). K went from a best of 39.94 to 41.13 / 41.08. Prewarmed input pages can remain charged outside the measured cgroup, but its peak still includes anonymous memory, kernel memory and tmpfs. Cached input is not categorically free.

4. Line trims with identical machine code

The cheapest wins in the contest were deletions, but I only trusted a deletion if I could prove it changed nothing that runs. For Track A, the agents removed selected #[inline(always)] attributes, dropped guards that were provably always true, and folded a few statements together. Then they diffed the disassembly function by function. For the attributes we removed, the hot code was instruction-for-instruction identical. Where removing an attribute did change the code, it stayed.

A's scored S went from 350 to 325. Its board runs averaged 46.96 against production's 45.97–46.90, and the S gain itself is deterministic. B got the same treatment, with scored S falling from 758 to 701: it scored 33.92 and 34.13 and was kept. An earlier D trim reduced S from 407 to 383, but its board K was 23.93 against the previous best of 24.11.

Failures, and what they taught me

VM wins that lost on the board. That opening story was Track A's compact endpoint dictionary using atomic slot publication. On the VM it looked faster. On the board it scored 38.74 and 39.73, with T at 32 and 30 ms. The control scored 45.97 at T 22.4 ms. A deferred-formatting change reduced board memory to about 18.1 MB but went the same way (40.79 / 45.78), and B's "24-byte slots, twice the table" faded over three runs (31.16 → 28.95 → 26.87). Early on, an allocator-tuning change sent A's board memory from about 22 MB to 65.6 MB. The VM is a filter, not a judge.

PGO variation can hide small wins. I compared multiple PGO builds per side before trusting small differences. Single-threaded training does not by itself guarantee identical binaries; that needs checking in the build outputs. (Adding a PGO stage to the Dockerfiles for A, C and D did not improve their logged board K, and those Dockerfile lines count in S.)

Benchmark order bias. One of our scripts biased the run order. For a while, that made a whole batch of comparisons unreliable. Balanced ordering fixed it, and now I don't trust any A/B number unless I know the order was alternated.

Board noise comes in batches. Running the same code again on the board can move K materially. Some batches are just slow: once, B's T jumped from about 150 to 195 ms with no code change. Worse, the tracks don't slow down together: in one batch B was slow while A ran normally, and in another A lost badly while B and D looked fine. "The other tracks were normal" cannot establish that yours was unaffected. So the rule became: repeat promising candidates, and compare against a control from the same track.

What the leaders did better

The evening before the freeze, I compared my numbers with the board leaders track by track. Those comparisons were not preserved in the per-track logs, so I can't substantiate the exact gaps here. My impression was that runtime remained the biggest opportunity; in C, memory also mattered. Board numbers alone couldn't tell me which techniques the leaders used. I treated faster hot loops and better parallel efficiency as hypotheses to test. CPU time divided by thread count is only an idealised work estimate; serial phases and scaling limit how close wall time can get.

Still, I used board results to decide what shipped, and the per-track logs record many of these trials. If you take one thing from this post: your benchmark is a hypothesis about the scoring machine, not a measurement of it.

Code and performance logs (including recorded run IDs, T, M, S, K) are in the team PeppaPig repository, one PERF.md per track.

title: Behavioral Design Unpacked: Nudges, Funnels & Persuasion | UX Unpacked #3
description:
Why This Matters to You

You've spent weeks designing a feature. You launch it—and nobody uses it.

The problem might not be bad design. It might be that you're missing how behavior actually works.

Over the past three articles in UX Unpacked, I've walked through the frameworks that explain why people do what they do online. But here's what I realized: these aren't separate tools. They're connected layers of the same system.

This fourth installment combines everything we've covered into one actionable framework:

  • Nudge Theory — How choice architecture shapes decisions
  • CREATE Action Funnel — Why users drop off before acting
  • Persuasive Technology — How products build lasting behavior change

By the end of this article, you'll see behavioral design as a cohesive whole—not isolated concepts.

Let's connect the dots.

The Big Picture: Three Layers of Influence

Think of behavioral design as three concentric circles.

The outermost layer is persuasive technology—the broadest category. It's any technology designed to change attitudes or behaviors through persuasion rather than coercion. Everything else sits inside this.

The middle layer is nudge theory—specific techniques for steering choices without forbidding options. Defaults, framing, social proof, simplification. These are tactical moves within a larger persuasive strategy.

The innermost layer is the CREATE Action Funnel—the moment-to-moment decision process where all of this plays out. Every nudge, every persuasive element, has to pass through these six gates to actually change behavior.

💡 Design Principle: Work from the inside out. If someone can't cross the CREATE funnel, no amount of persuasion or clever nudging will help. Fix the bottlenecks first.

Layer 1: CREATE—Where Behavior Actually Happens

Steve Wendel's CREATE Action Funnel describes the six stages before action occurs. Every product interaction passes through these gates.

Cue

The trigger that gets you thinking about taking a specific action.

LinkedIn sends push notifications. HomeAway sends follow-up emails. A red badge appears on an app icon. These are cues—and they exist whether you design them intentionally or not.

Most teams forget the cue entirely. They assume users will form habits spontaneously. That almost never happens.

Reaction

Your instinctive first response to the idea of taking the action.

"Oh man, better check what's happening." versus "Ugh, create a profile?!"

This happens before rational thought. Emotional. Automatic. Your design's tone, timing, and context set the stage here.

Evaluation

A more rational cost-versus-benefit analysis.

"I like LinkedIn's content—this time will be no different." versus "Will a 5-star rating matter when I barely use this platform again?"

Benefits must outweigh perceived costs. When they don't, users drop out.

Ability Check

Seeing whether you can even take the action right now.

"I definitely have the ability—just tap the icon." versus "Can I do this on my phone? Will it take five minutes?"

Friction kills momentum. The easier the path, the higher the conversion.

Time Pressure

Determining whether it's urgent to act now.

"I should see if there are trending topics today." versus "Dammit, this link expires soon."

Genuine urgency helps. Manufactured scarcity backfires. Know the difference.

Experience

The act of taking the action and the feelings that come with it.

"That was a productive two minutes." versus "The link expired anyway. Whatever."

This feeds back into future reactions. Good experiences build habits. Bad ones create avoidance patterns.

💡 Critical Insight: The funnel is cyclical. The experience informs the next reaction. First impressions aren't just important—they're permanent.

Layer 2: Nudges—Steering Without Pushing

Within each CREATE stage, you can deploy nudges—any aspect of choice architecture that alters behavior predictably without forbidding options or changing economic incentives.

Defaults at the Evaluation Stage

Pre-filled templates reduce decision paralysis. Opt-out donation systems tripled participation rates compared to opt-in. Set helpful defaults that align with user goals, not just business metrics.

Framing During Reaction

"90% success rate" lands differently than "10% failure rate." Positive framing activates approach motivation. Negative framing triggers threat response. Choose based on desired outcome.

Social Norms Across All Stages

"Most users complete setup in two minutes." Shows what others do. Leverages conformity drive. Builds trust through collective behavior.

Salience at the Cue Stage

Place important buttons in prime real estate. Make choices impossible to miss. Visibility precedes everything else.

Timing Within Time Pressure

Request ratings after task completion, not interruption. Ask when value is fresh, not forgotten. Context determines receptivity.

Simplification in the Ability Check

Reduce form fields from ten to three. Remove friction ruthlessly. Every extra step is a leak in your funnel.

Feedback Loops Reinforcing Experience

Show profile completion percentages. Track progress visually. Make invisible effort visible.

💡 Design Tip: Multiple nudges compound. Stack them carefully. Too many create pressure. Too few create indifference.

Layer 3: Persuasive Technology—The Engine Underneath

B.J. Fogg identified three ways technology functions persuasively. Understanding which role your product plays helps you design more intentionally.

Technology as Tools

Increase ability by making actions easier or restructuring them entirely. Installation wizards. Auto-categorization. One-click ordering.

When it works: Completion rates rise. Users accomplish more with less effort.

When it fails: Additional features add complexity instead of removing it.

Technology as Media

Use narrative and interactivity for rehearsing behavior, building empathy, exploring causal relationships. Simulation games. Visualizations. Procedural rhetoric through mechanics.

When it works: Users internalize lessons through experience rather than instruction.

When it fails: The experience feels manipulative or preachy.

Technology as Social Actors

Apply social influence through language, assumed roles, and presence. Embodied conversational agents. Helpful interfaces. Apologies and greetings that mimic human interaction.

When it works: Trust builds naturally. Users feel understood.

When it fails: Uncanny valley kicks in. Humanity feels manufactured.

💡 Critical Warning: Users respond to computers as social actors even when they shouldn't. This automaticity demands extra responsibility. The asymmetry—technology knows you, you don't know it—creates power imbalance.

The Audit: Eight Questions

Pick a behavior you're trying to encourage. Run it through this checklist.

1. Have I made the cue visible? Is the button above the fold? Do users know when to act? Is it clear what happens next?

2. What's their initial reaction? Am I assuming positivity or expecting skepticism? Tone and context matter more than I admit.

3. Do benefits outweigh costs? If I were the user, would I feel this was worth my time? Be honest about the trade-off.

4. Can they actually do it right now? How many clicks or taps? Does it interrupt their current flow? Friction compounds silently.

5. Is there genuine urgency—or manufactured scarcity? Countdown timers work once. After that, users recognize the pattern. Authentic constraints only.

6. What experience am I creating? Positive reinforcement or surveillance? Celebration or judgment? Trust builds slowly, destroys fast.

7. Which functional mode dominates? Tool, media, or social actor? Mixing modes without intention creates confusion.

8. Am I respecting freedom of choice? Can users opt out? Is the exit obvious? Is consent reversible?

Any answer feels unclear? That's where iteration starts.

Ethics: The Red Lines

Thaler and Sunstein emphasized two rules for libertarian paternalism:

Help people do what they already want to do. Preserve their freedom to choose.

Ask yourself: Would I be comfortable if everyone knew how I designed this choice?

Good practices:

  • Help people succeed at goals they hold
  • Preserve autonomy with obvious opt-outs
  • Build long-term trust over short-term engagement

Red flags:

  • Fake countdown timers creating artificial urgency
  • Hidden fees buried in checkout flows
  • Forced continuity trapping subscriptions
  • Confirm-shaming guilt-tripping opt-outs
  • Roach motel patterns easy to enter, impossible to leave

Dark patterns extract value at user expense. Ethical design creates mutual success.

💡 Final Word: With great power comes responsibility. The question isn't whether your design persuades—it's whether it does so transparently.

What Research Shows

Despite promising results, three challenges persist across all frameworks.

Technical limitations: Self-report systems carry bias and recall errors. Sensor-based monitoring struggles with ambiguity. Predicting human behavior remains difficult—especially for precisely timed interventions.

Measurement difficulties: True randomized controlled trials are rare. Most participants self-select, meaning they may already be adopting desired behaviors. Meta-analyses show evidence remains controversial. Long-term studies are hard but necessary.

Ethical uncertainty: Manipulating feelings and desires remains debated. Persuasive backfires—where technology triggers the bad behavior it was designed to reduce—are real risks. A weight-loss app obsessed with calories might trigger disordered eating patterns.

But some things do work consistently. Health coaching combining goal-setting, education, and progress tracking produces sustainable change. Feedback on electricity consumption typically yields 5-12% savings. Awareness of environmental, financial, and health benefits makes eco-friendly behaviors more attractive.

Case Study: LinkedIn Works, HomeAway Doesn't

Let's apply everything at once to two real examples.

LinkedIn succeeds because:

  • The cue is always visible (home screen icon)
  • Expectations are met consistently (relevant content)
  • Ability is nearly effortless (tap and scroll)
  • Urgency is subtle, not manufactured
  • Experience delivers value quickly (2-minute productivity)

Even after disabling push notifications, checking continues because the underlying value persists. The habit forms around the tool itself, not the interruption.

HomeAway fails because:

  • The cue arrives late (after vacation ends)
  • Initial reaction is frustration ("I already did this")
  • Benefits feel distant (rating matters someday, maybe)
  • Ability is uncertain (can I do this on my phone?)
  • Time pressure feels coercive (expiring links)
  • Experience disappoints (link invalidates)

Every CREATE stage had friction. Multiple nudges tried to compensate but couldn't overcome fundamental design failures.

The lesson: You can't nudge a broken funnel. Fix the foundation first.

Apply This Tomorrow

You don't need to rebuild your entire product.

Find one behavior you're struggling to encourage. Map it against all three layers:

Start with CREATE. Where do users drop off? Is it visibility? Friction? Motivation?

Add nudges at that specific bottleneck. Don't scatter tactics randomly. Target the leak.

Then consider which persuasive mode serves best. Tool for efficiency. Media for understanding. Social actor for connection.

Start small. Track changes. Iterate based on actual behavior—not assumed motivations.

Coming Next in UX Unpacked

This series continues building fluency in behavioral design:

Spectrum of Thinking Interventions—automatic nudges versus deliberate reflection. When to trigger System 1 versus System 2, and why choosing the wrong point backfires.

Behavioral Science Foundations—the interdisciplinary study of human behavior across psychology, sociology, and anthropology. How these principles enhance engagement, usability, and satisfaction in UX.

Each piece stands alone while connecting to the bigger picture.

Final Thought

Behavioral design doesn't promise transformation. But it does give you vocabulary for what already shapes every interaction.

You're always designing choice architecture. The question is whether you're doing it consciously.

Work from the inside out. Fix funnels before nudging. Measure before optimizing. Build trust before extracting value.

About the Author

I'm Ribin K Roy—software developer, UI/UX designer, and student learning in public. I document what I pick up along the way.

This series exists because I've found that the best way to solidify my own understanding is to write it down in plain language. If you're new to UX design or just want to brush up on fundamentals without wading through dense textbooks, welcome. You're in the right place.

If you found this helpful, subscribe or follow wherever you're reading. The next article drops soon.

Sources Cited

Wendel, Steve. A Method to Persuade. HelloWallet internal framework.\
Thaler, Richard H. & Sunstein, Cass R. Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness. 2008.\
Fogg, B.J. Persuasive Technology: Using Computers to Change What We Think and Do. Morgan Kaufmann, 2003.\
Nerlikar, Rajesh. Behavioral Science Crash Course: CREATE Action Funnel. Action Design ATX, 2019.

title: Feature-flag AI-suggested UI before it hits every user
description:
The first time we shipped an agent-written settings panel straight to main, it looked fine in staging. Then support got three tickets in an hour: a toggle that did nothing for free plans, a “Save” that double-fired on slow networks, and a new empty state that hid the only CTA half our users needed.

CI was green. Visuals looked close. The bug was product judgment the model never had — and we gave 100% of traffic that judgment on day one.

So we stopped treating “agent UI merged” as “agent UI live.” Feature flags became the default release valve for anything an agent touched in the UI layer.

The failure mode: merge = rollout

Agent PRs tempt you to skip the usual caution:

  • Diff is “just UI”
  • Screenshots look right
  • Playwright clicked through the happy path
  • Reviewer approved the code shape

None of that answers: does this layout work for the cohort that never sees premium fields? Does the new empty state break the onboarding funnel? Does the regenerated form still respect the old keyboard path power users rely on?

Those are traffic questions. Feature flags are how you ask them without a full revert.

What I flag (and what I don’t)

I flag user-visible surfaces the agent authored or heavily rewrote:

  • New panels, modals, empty / error / loading states
  • Regenerated forms and settings sections
  • Agent-refactored navigation / IA changes
  • Copy-heavy UI where tone or CTA placement shifted

I usually don’t flag:

  • Pure token / lint / type cleanup with no layout change
  • Test-only or Storybook-only diffs
  • Internal admin tools with a tiny known audience (still stage them; just don’t burn a flag name)

Rule of thumb: if a stranger on the free plan could hit it tomorrow, it gets a flag.

The default pattern we use

Keep it boring. One boolean (or percentage) per agent UI surface, named after the ticket, not the model:

// flags.ts — names are product, not “gpt-panel-v3”
export const flags = {
  settingsBillingV2: booleanFlag('settings-billing-v2', false),
  emptyProjectsAgentCopy: booleanFlag('empty-projects-agent-copy', false),
} as const;

In the route / component:

export function SettingsBilling() {
  const enabled = useFlag('settings-billing-v2');

  if (!enabled) {
    return <SettingsBillingLegacy />;
  }

  return <SettingsBillingV2 />; // agent-authored surface
}

Kill switch lives next to the flag definition, not in a Slack thread:

// ops: set settings-billing-v2 = false → instant revert without redeploy

If your stack is LaunchDarkly / Unleash / Statsig / a homegrown % cookie — same idea. The important part is default off for agent UI, not which vendor.

Rollout ladder (what we actually do)

  1. Internal / dogfood — flag on for the team only. Click the weird paths humans use.
  2. 1–5% — watch error rate, rage clicks, support tags for that surface.
  3. 25% → 50% — only if step 2 is quiet for a real workday, not twenty quiet minutes.
  4. 100% — then delete the legacy branch when you’re sure, not “someday.”

Agent UI fails differently than human UI: it often fails narrowly (one plan tier, one locale, one empty-state branch). Small percentages catch that before it becomes a Monday war room.

What I put in the agent prompt

Feature flags are a release policy. The agent still needs to build behind them:

Implement this UI behind flag settings-billing-v2 (default off).

Keep SettingsBillingLegacy working and unchanged.

Do not delete legacy routes/components in this PR.

Wire the flag at the route/section boundary, not inside every leaf.

Add a short “flag off = legacy” note in the PR body.

Without that, agents “helpfully” delete the old panel and leave you with a binary deploy rollback.

PR template checkboxes 

### Agent UI rollout
- [ ] New/changed user-visible UI is behind a named flag (default off)
- [ ] Legacy path still renders when flag is off
- [ ] Flag name matches the ticket / surface (not the model name)
- [ ] Rollout plan noted: dogfood → % → 100% (or “internal-only”)
- [ ] Kill switch owner named (who can flip it in prod)

Reviewers stop arguing “is this ready?” and start asking “who turns it on?”

Metrics I watch for the first day

Not vanity:

  • Error / exception rate on the flagged route
  • Support tickets tagged with that surface
  • Funnel drop at the new empty / CTA step
  • Accessibility smoke (keyboard + one screen reader pass on dogfood)

If any of those spike at 5%, you don’t “monitor overnight.” You flip the flag off and open a fix PR.

Review comments I leave

When the agent rewrote a panel with no flag:

This surface ships to every user on merge. Wrap it in settings-billing-v2 (default off) and keep legacy until we ramp. Agent UI doesn’t get a free pass on rollout.

When they deleted legacy in the same PR:

Don’t delete SettingsBillingLegacy here. Flag-off must still work. Removal is a follow-up after 100% + quiet metrics.

When the flag is hardcoded true “for testing”:

Hardcoded true is a silent 100% rollout. Use the real flag client; leave default false in prod config.

What I stopped doing

  • Merging agent UI straight to 100% because staging looked pretty
  • Naming flags after models (gpt-settings-rewrite) instead of product surfaces
  • Letting the agent delete legacy in the same PR that introduces the new UI
  • Treating “Playwright green” as “safe for everyone”

Feature-flagging AI-suggested UI isn’t distrust of the model — it’s admitting the model never saw your free-plan edge cases, your support queue, or your Monday traffic. Ship the code when it’s ready. Ship the exposure when the numbers say so.

title: The Board Is the Only Benchmark: 72 Hours of Speed Demon 2026
description:
Team ttimesai on four tracks in zero-dependency Rust: hashes instead of byte compares, memory you pay for without noticing, profiling through a file name, and a bug that showed up in 12 runs out of 30.

Speed Demon 2026, run by Hackathon Raptors, gave teams 72 hours (30 October 15:00 UTC to 2 November 15:00 UTC) to beat naive Python references on four tracks: A · Ingest (aggregate 3.1M log lines into per-endpoint, per-hour percentiles), B · Index (50,000 boolean and phrase queries over a 250 MB corpus), C · Join (parse a hostile multi-megabyte CSV and join it against regions), and D · Traverse (2,000 shortest-path queries on a 5M-edge weighted graph). The speed score per track is 50 · log10(K), where K is the product of four ratios against the reference, with exponents for wall time (0.50), peak memory (0.20), source lines (0.15) and dependencies (0.15); the "points" below are this speed score, and the track total adds the judged parts on top. The live board runs every push once on a 12-thread i5-13500 with turbo off.

Our repo: https://github.com/ttimesai-star/speed-demon (public from 2 November, after code freeze). Every number below comes from the board's own runs or from the PERF.md logs in that repo. Board results are from the public board on 31 October; the final scoring (five runs of the frozen commit on a hidden seed, on a machine with no other load) is run by the organisers and published with the winners on 13 November, after this post, so it is not in here.

How the code was written. Plainly: the code was written by Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant, in long sessions, and a human on the team set the goals and the rules. The assistant also read the board results, decided which experiments to run, and wrote this post from the repo logs. The rules it worked under were: check output hashes before every push, keep at least 15 minutes between pushes, trust only the board for speed and memory, and log failures as well as wins. Rule 06 of the hackathon allows this ("we do not gatekeep on how the code was produced"), and every track README says it. Rule 06 also asks that PERF.md shows a human understood what happened; the log in the repo is the evidence for that, and you can judge it. Every figure below was checked against the repo logs.

Where we ended up (public board, 31 October)

Track First scored run Best board run T, s M, MB Source lines Points Place
A · Ingest 0.132 s, 730.7 MB, 50.30 pts run-da36d3a4aa55 0.0292 27.2 216 80.84 6 / 86
C · Join 0.140 s, 21.7 MB, 59.76 pts run-ea8e26ca4156 0.0403 10.3 258 76.55 5 / 74
D · Traverse 0.909 s, 234.8 MB, 49.16 pts run-d27164d64d22 0.1757 79.3 439 68.36 6 / 76
B · Index 1.296 s, 232.5 MB, 46.52 pts — 0.4310 150.3 577 58.55 30 / 65

Our three best tracks summed to 225.8, and the board's overall ranking, which counts the best three tracks, had us 5th of 99 teams on 31 October. For scale, the reference takes 32.05 s on track A. The final scoring is the organisers' and comes later, as noted above.

1. You cannot benchmark this on your laptop

The first scored run of track A was the lesson that shaped the rest of the weekend. On our 2-vCPU CI runner the program peaked at 18.5 MB. The board measured 730.7 MB and 0.132 s (run-299ca5c2b1ad).

The cause was our own reservations: 12 threads × 72 hours × a "worst-case" vector. Our best explanation is that the board machine has transparent huge pages on and backed those reservations with 2 MB pages. Every touched huge page counted in full, and zeroing them ate most of the wall time. We could not reproduce the exact 730 MB in CI (with THP=always and 12 forced threads we got 55.5 MB), so that part is inference, not proof. The fix was to reserve for the mean hour and opt out of THP at start. Later we also pinned glibc's mmap threshold:

unsafe { prctl(41, 1u64, 0u64, 0u64, 0u64) }; // PR_SET_THP_DISABLE: small vectors, no 2 MB pages
unsafe { mallopt(-3, 1 << 16) }; // M_MMAP_THRESHOLD fixed at 64 KB: a freed hour's records leave M at once

The first line took A from 0.132 s / 730.7 MB to 0.0340 s / 29.8 MB in one push (run-ffe31d35df4b). The second line is subtler. glibc raises its mmap threshold after each large free, so the per-hour buffers we freed during output stayed in the arena and in peak memory. With the threshold fixed, M dropped from 29.0 to 26.8 MB at the same T (run-2e4a68da0bef). Track D got the same line later.

Our two test machines disagreed with the board in both directions:

  • Track D, hash tables instead of dense label arrays: CI was 4 % slower, the board 2.2× slower (run-a741c2a56a3e). Reverted.
  • Track B, a Bloom filter in front of the dictionary: PC −20 %, CI +2 %, board no change (run-9aa73a6479ad). Reverted.
  • Track B, PGO: board 0.6456 s against 0.6115 s without it (run-a6a09a082994). Reverted.
  • Track C, 32-byte inline name slots: slower on our PC, whose 96 MB L3 holds everything, and faster on the board's 24 MB L3 (run-20344632fbda, kept).

From ~20:50 UTC on day one we also had no CI: the private repo had used up its GitHub Actions minutes on A/B runs. From then on we checked correctness on a Windows PC build of the same logic and measured speed and memory only on the board.

2. Profiling a machine you can't log into

We needed phase timings from the board itself, but it only reports T, M and a short public failure string. So a profiling build writes its timings into the name of an extra empty file in /out:

let t0 = std::time::Instant::now();
let us = || t0.elapsed().as_micros();
// ... at the end of main:
let name = format!("A_nt{nt}_l{tl}_b{tp}_s{}-{}_e{}-{}-{}_j{tj}_g{tg}_w{tw}_f{}-{}-{}_x{}", st[0], st[nt - 1], en[0], en[nt / 2], en[nt - 1], fin[0], fin[nt / 2], fin[nt - 1], us());
fs::write(format!("{dout}/{name}"), b"").unwrap();

The run then fails on purpose ("/out must hold exactly …, found […]"). That failure text is public on the board, and T is still recorded. We checked separately on the PC that the real output was correct. These runs were measurements only and never counted toward a best score.

The first profile of A (run-5db9c3f80e78) showed: parse ends at 19.3 / 19.6 / 19.9 ms (first / median / last thread), output workers finish around 29.9 ms, and main returns at 29.97 ms of a 33.5 ms T. ~3.5 ms was process start and exit, mostly unmapping the 239 MB input in one thread. So each parse thread now drops its own pages as soon as it finishes:

// MADV_DONTNEED on the whole pages of d[a..b]: unmapped here in parallel, not at the exit in one thread
let (p, e) = (a.next_multiple_of(4096).min(b), b / 4096 * 4096);
unsafe { madvise(d.as_ptr().add(p.min(e)), e - p.min(e), 4) };

A control push without it ran 0.0356 s, against 0.0329 s with it (run-8c3d925f7fbd and run-3a49e8d76354), so it is worth about 2.5 ms. That is about 7 % of the program, for code that computes nothing.

The same trick works for ablations. On track C we pushed a build that skips setting the per-country bitset bits. The output is wrong on purpose, but the run is timed: T 0.0523 s, M 9.8 MB (run-138c8acedbb3). So the bitset costs about a tenth of T and 3.7 MB. That is less than per-thread buffers would cost in memory points, so it stayed.

3. The biggest single lever: stop comparing key bytes

The largest single jump of the second day came from one idea on two tracks. Identify a key by a 64-bit hash and never compare its bytes. On C, a perf profile of the first version had 23 % of the time in bcmp, comparing each name with its first occurrence at a random spot in a 202 MB mapping. Inline slots and arenas helped. Then we dropped the bytes entirely:

// Dense id of the name with hash h, shared by all threads. A slot holds the low 44 bits of h << 20 | id and its
// index is the top 17 bits of h, so names count as equal when all 61 bits match: with 100,000 names the chance
// that any two do is about 100,000^2 / 2^62, below 10^-8. An 8-byte slot per name keeps the table at 1 MB.
fn name_id(t: &[AtomicU64], h: u64) -> u64 {
    let (mut i, tag) = ((h >> 47) as usize, h & (1 << 44) - 1);
    loop {
        let mut v = t[i].load(Acquire);
        if v == 0 {
            let id = TOP.fetch_add(1, Relaxed);
            match t[i].compare_exchange(0, tag << 20 | id, Release, Acquire) {
                Ok(_) => return id,
                Err(w) => v = w,
            }
        }
        if v >> 20 == tag {
            return v & 0xFFFFF;
        }
        i = (i + 1) & (SLOTS - 1);
    }
}

No more random reads into the input to compare bytes, and the table shrank from 4 MB to 1 MB. Our profile had already shown C running 3.3× slower per thread on the board than on our PC, which we put down to cache misses on tables of ~9 MB. T went from 0.0481 to 0.0416 s, M from 13.4 to 10.5 MB: +2.7 points in one push (run-c21f5e3b4e84). On A the same change for endpoints gave 0.0294 s and +0.6 points (run-3b77efb47584). There, two of the 1,842 templates collide with a probability below 10⁻¹².

This trades exactness for a stated, tiny probability, and we documented the bound in PERF.md and the README. Every local dataset (published hashes plus the organisers' reference run on extra seeds) still matched byte for byte.

4. The bug that full-size runs never showed

That name_id function had a bug. The empty name hashes to 0. If it happened to be the first name inserted, it got id 0, and its slot then held exactly 0, which reads as "empty". The next empty name would claim a fresh id. Whether this happened depended on which thread got to the table first, so the output depended on thread timing.

Five runs of the full dataset all passed, and so did the board. The spec's tiny worked example, run 30 times, was wrong 12 times. On full data we estimated about one run in a hundred would fail. The final score is five runs on a hidden seed, so this could have cost us the whole track. The fix was one character:

-static TOP: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(0); // names (a lost race for a slot leaves an unused id)
+static TOP: AtomicU64 = AtomicU64::new(1); // names from 1, so no slot is 0 (the empty name hashes to 0); a lost race leaves an unused id

After the fix: 60/60 worked-example runs, 30/30 tiny, 20/20 sample, and all ten datasets matched the reference (commit ebb2a44). From then on every candidate version went through 30 repeated runs of each small dataset, not only the big ones. Small inputs make rare orderings likely. Big inputs hide them.

5. Memory on the graph track: 279 MB to 79 MB

Track D started at 279 MB peak. That was mostly 12 threads × dense label arrays plus a graph stored as 8-byte edges. The leaders were at 70–110 MB. The steps that got us there:

  • Free early. The parsed edge buckets are freed right after the first CSR, and the reverse CSR is built inside the old edge array: M 279 → 139 MB (run-783c571ed206).
  • Paged labels. Each thread keeps a pool of small pages of [u32; 2] labels instead of n labels per thread.
  • Pack the edges into 4 bytes. At full scale a node id needs 21 bits, which leaves 11 for the weight, and 99.93 % of weights fit: 
// A search graph: offsets, edges as head | weight << .3 (the head takes .3 bits; a weight that does not fit
// leaves the field's top value and is kept exact in .2, sorted by edge position). Weights are mostly below
// 2^11 and n is below 2^21 at full scale, so an edge is 4 bytes instead of 8.
struct G(Vec<u32>, Vec<u32>, Vec<(u32, u32)>, u32);

That cut M from 137 to 90 MB at the same T (run-a4daf0dfb2bb). A radix heap, prefetches in the BFS renumbering, and running queries in order of their source's new id brought T from 0.194 to 0.176 s. Final: 0.1757 s, 79.3 MB (run-d27164d64d22).

6. Where track B stalled

Track B never caught up: 0.43 s against about 0.27 s for the track leader on the night of 30 October. The cost sat in tokenizing and dictionary lookups. Only memory responded: the peak was held by 75,000 small allocations and per-thread term streams. One shared list buffer, u16 term ranks in the streams, and dropping the 75,000 offset vectors took M from 185 to 154 MB, and a later step reached 150 MB. B stayed out of our best three.

7. Noise: ±5–10 % on unchanged code

Track A ran anywhere from 0.029 to 0.041 s on identical code across the day. One push of a compacted track C read 0.0651 s; the same code pushed again read 0.0481 s. A D outlier of 0.1922 s re-measured at 0.1778 s. What we did about it:

  • Control in every push. The board re-runs every track on each push, and track B was unchanged for the whole second day, so its time showed how fast the board was in that hour. When an unchanged track ran 12 % slow in the same push as an experiment, we did not trust that push's verdict either way.
  • Compare within one push, never across hours.
  • Re-measure anything under ~5 % before believing it. Several "wins" were noise: prefetchw and an AVX2 byte search on C, and a compact key arena on A, all ended up inside the spread of unchanged code.
  • Pick finals by mean, not best. The board keeps your best run, but the final scoring takes five runs of the frozen commit on a hidden seed on a quiet machine. So pushing the same code again for a luckier number buys nothing. We chose final versions by the average of several board runs (A ≈ 0.0303 s, C ≈ 0.041 s, D ≈ 0.177 s).

8. Source lines are points too

S has a weight of 0.15, counted after rustfmt. Rewriting the same algorithm more compactly took C from 368 to 288 lines and D from 429 to 363, worth +0.5 to +0.8 points with no change in speed. The other side: 30 extra lines cost about as many points as 2–3 % of T, so a small speed tweak can lose more than it wins. We counted lines with the board's formatter rules before every push.

What we would tell the next team

  1. Get on the board in the first hour with something trivial. Our CI numbers predicted little about the board.
  2. Build a profiling channel into the board (a file name, an exit code, anything public) before optimising.
  3. Make serial work your first target. With 12 threads waiting, a one-thread sort of 200k country codes cost track C about a quarter of its time.
  4. Hash identities beat byte compares, if you state the collision bound and check every dataset you have.
  5. Repeat small inputs many times. Our worst bug lived in a 30-run test, not in a 3-million-line one.
  6. Log the failures. Dozens of our PERF.md entries are reverted or not-taken experiments, and they taught us more than the wins.

The code, every PERF.md row with its board run ID, and the reverted experiments are in the repo: https://github.com/ttimesai-star/speed-demon. Thanks to Hackathon Raptors for a board that told the truth, even when we didn't want to hear it.

title: Build headlines said 92x faster. I measured my own crate first.
description:
A few weeks ago the Rust corner of my feed lit up: a new toolchain promising dramatically faster builds, one benchmark, one headline number. I have seen this movie before: a number from somebody else's crate, somebody else's machine, and then a week of arguing about whether it applies to mine.

I did not want to argue about toolchains. I wanted a ruler: something that tells me, on my crate and my machine, where the seconds actually go (per crate, per build script, per link step), then tells me which fix is cheapest, and lets me verify the delta after I apply it.

So I built cargoscope. It measures. It recommends. It verifies. It never touches your toolchain.

The three commands

cargo cargoscope measure [--json out.json] shells out to cargo build --timings twice. The first build is timed; the second is a no-change rebuild. That second run is the trick: cargo omits fresh-skipped units from the timing report, so a build-script-run unit that still shows real duration in the no-change rebuild was genuinely executed again with no source changes. Its freshness is broken: typically a script that rewrites its own rerun-if-changed inputs. That is measured, not guessed from the script source.

The report shows wall time, top crates by compile time, build scripts that re-run on every build, and the codegen+link share of the final binary. On stable, the report is honest about what it cannot separate: "link step not separable on stable — the bin unit's duration covers codegen+link together."

cargo cargoscope recommend ranks fixes cheapest-first with exact config snippets: cargo check for the edit loop, fixing re-running build scripts, mold/lld linker, sccache, cranelift (gated behind --nightly-ok). It changes nothing. The snippets are yours to review and apply.

cargo cargoscope compare before.json after.json prints the measured delta and a verdict line. Only measured numbers; nothing is promised.

A real demo, honest numbers

The animated demo below is a real terminal recording on the repo's small fixture crate (verbatim transcript also in the repo). Watch the loop: measure flags a build script with RE-RUNS ON EVERY BUILD, recommend ranks the rerun-if-changed fix, I apply it, measure again, compare:


wall:   0.7s -> 0.7s  (-6.6%)
units:  5 -> 4
verdict: -6.6% wall time faster (0.7s -> 0.7s)

Small crate, small numbers, no hype. The re-run flag is gone; the per-crate deltas are printed, wins and losses. That is the whole point: the tool's job is to make the second measurement possible, not to impress you with the first.

The bug the nightly CI caught

To separate the link step, cargoscope parses nightly -Ztime stderr. While dogfooding on a real nightly toolchain I found that rustc 1.101-nightly removed -Ztime entirely (unknown unstable option). The old code set RUSTFLAGS=-Ztime whenever it detected nightly, and cargo forwards RUSTFLAGS into its own internal rustc probe, so measure broke completely on new nightlies (cargo exit 101).

The fix: probe first (rustc -Ztime --print=sysroot; --version short-circuits before -Z validation, so it cannot be the probe), set the flag only when the probe passes, and fall back gracefully otherwise. A nightly CI job now runs measure on a real nightly toolchain every night and asserts the graceful fallback. Finding your tool broken on a toolchain you claimed to support is the best possible use of a nightly job.

Where the rivals beat us

Honesty section, as always with my tools:

  • cargo-blaze wins if in-place recompilation fits your workflow: it actually makes rebuilds faster instead of measuring them. It is a young, invasive bet (replaces the compiler driver). cargoscope complements it: it can measure blaze's own delta.
  • cargo build --timings wins on zero install. The raw HTML timeline has everything cargoscope parses. cargoscope adds ranking, re-run detection, and before/after verification on top.
  • cargo-bloat answers a different question (binary size, not build time).

Honest limits

  • It does not speed up your builds. It measures. If you want the build itself to go faster without measuring first, this is the wrong tool.
  • Timing numbers are your machine's, your crate's, your profile's. A −6.6% here is not a claim about any other setup.
  • Link-step timing needs a nightly toolchain whose rustc still accepts -Ztime (removed by 1.101-nightly; support is probed, never assumed).
  • cargo --timings output format is not a stable API. The parser is defensive, records the tested cargo version, and fails loudly instead of guessing.

Try it

The npm package is not published yet, so install from source for now:

git clone https://github.com/techdevfun/cargoscope.git
cd cargoscope && npm install && npm run build
# then, inside any Rust crate:
npx cargo-cargoscope measure

Requires Node 20+ and a Rust toolchain (stable is fine). Zero runtime dependencies, MIT licensed.

Repo: github.com/techdevfun/cargoscope. Issues and PRs welcome; please include your measure output (redacted paths are fine) when reporting wrong numbers. Also listed in the TECHDEV catalog.

title: Building OrderCraft: A Local-First Financial Charting Terminal in a Single ~14MB Go Binary
description:
Modern financial charting platforms have converged on the same frustrating cloud SaaS model: lock basic technical analysis behind $15 to $60/month subscriptions, restrict free users to 2 indicators per chart, paywall multi-chart split-screen layouts, and force all your watchlists and layouts into their cloud.

On the flip side, developers who try to build hosted open-source alternatives hit two massive walls almost immediately:

  1. IP Rate Limits: Public exchange APIs (like Binance or Yahoo Finance) ban central server IPs within hours when multiple users request market data through a shared backend.
  2. Market Data Redistribution Licensing: Exchanges demand thousands of dollars per month the moment a central server redistributes market feeds to third-party users.

To solve both problems at the root, I built and open-sourced OrderCraft (v0.1.0, MIT License) — a high-performance, 100% local-first financial charting and technical analysis terminal built with Go, React 19, TypeScript, and Lightweight Charts (Apache-2.0).

ordercraft-hq / terminal

High-performance, local-first financial charting & technical analysis terminal built with Go, React, and Lightweight Charts.

OrderCraft

High-Performance Open-Source Financial Charting & Market Analysis Workstation

⚡ What is OrderCraft?

OrderCraft is a 100% original, permissive open-source financial charting workstation built from first principles with Go, React 19, TypeScript, and Lightweight Charts v5 (Apache-2.0).

Designed for active discretionary traders, quantitative developers, and financial analysts, OrderCraft runs as a single standalone binary with an embedded high-speed frontend (//go:embed), a local Docker container, or a PWA app. It features sub-millisecond multi-exchange WebSocket streams, multi-chart synchronized workspaces, pixel-perfect drawing primitives, vectorized indicator math, and complete local SQLite persistence.

🚀 Key Features

Capability Highlights
Multi-Provider Data Feeds Zero-config out-of-the-box public streams (Binance Spot & Futures, Bybit v5, Coinbase Advanced) and BYOK broker integrations (Alpaca Markets, OANDA v20).
Unified Single Binary Go backend embeds the React SPA (//go:embed) and runs standalone with --app-mode, --port,
…
View on GitHub

🏗️ How It Works: The Single-Binary Local-First Architecture

Instead of running in the cloud, OrderCraft compiles into a single standalone ~14.8MB executable (CGO_ENABLED=0) that runs directly on your machine (127.0.0.1). Because your machine connects directly to public market data feeds or your own brokerage API keys, there is no middleman server, zero telemetry, and no exchange redistribution bottleneck.

1. Zero-Dependency //go:embed Packaging

The entire frontend (React 19, TypeScript, Vite) compiles down into static assets and is embedded directly into the Go binary using //go:embed:

  • No Node.js, Python, or external database installation required for end-users.
  • Cross-compiles cleanly to standalone binaries for Windows (amd64), macOS (arm64 / Apple Silicon & amd64), and Linux (amd64 / arm64).
  • Running ./ordercraft --app-mode automatically detects Chromium, Brave, or Edge and launches the terminal inside a native, frameless desktop application window.

2. Concurrent Go WebSocket Fan-In / Fan-Out Coordinator

Financial charting requires sub-second tick updates across multiple symbols and timeframes simultaneously. In internal/server/hub.go and internal/datafeed/:

  • The Go backend manages upstream WebSocket streams and REST polling across Binance, Yahoo Finance, OANDA v20, Alpaca, and TwelveData.
  • Incoming ticks are normalized, aggregated into live OHLCV bars in memory, and fanned out over a local WebSocket hub to all subscribed chart panes in the browser.

3. Pure-Go SQLite Persistence (0600 Permissions)

All historical OHLCV candle caches, multi-pane workspace layouts, custom chart drawings, indicator templates, and BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) brokerage credentials are stored in a local SQLite database:

  • Historical bars are cached locally so switching timeframes or scrolling back in history is instantaneous.
  • API keys (OANDA, Alpaca, TwelveData) are stored strictly on your local disk with 0600 file permissions (0700 directory permissions) and are masked (AKIA••••••••1234) across all status endpoints so raw secrets are never exposed back to the browser.

4. Custom Canvas 2D Drawing Primitives (ISeriesPrimitive)

While lightweight-charts (Apache-2.0) provides fast HTML5 Canvas candlestick rendering, it does not ship with interactive drawing tools out of the box. We built a custom Canvas 2D drawing engine from scratch supporting:

  • Trendlines, Rays & Extended Lines (with OHLC magnet snapping)
  • Fibonacci Retracements with customizable levels
  • Parallel Channels & Shaded Rectangles
  • Long & Short Risk-Reward Position Calculators with interactive Entry, Take-Profit, and Stop-Loss drag handles
  • Multi-Pane Synchronized Workspaces: Split your screen into 1x1, 2V, 2H, 3, or 4-pane grids with synchronized crosshairs, symbols, and timeframes.

5. Hardening a 127.0.0.1 Server Against Cross-Tab Browser Attacks

One overlooked attack surface in local-first web apps is Localhost CSRF & Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking. If a local server sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * or skips WebSocket Origin checks, any malicious website open in another browser tab can query [http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/](http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/)* and read user data.

Before releasing v0.1.0, we hardened the Go HTTP/WebSocket server to enforce:

  • Strict loopback Origin validation (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]) on both REST preflight/mutation handlers and the WebSocket upgrader.
  • Upstream URL path and query escaping (url.PathEscape / url.QueryEscape) across all provider adapters to prevent SSRF/path traversal.
  • http.MaxBytesReader payload caps and Slowloris connection timeouts (ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout).

⚡ Try It Out in 10 Seconds

You can grab the prebuilt v0.1.0 binary for Windows, macOS, or Linux directly from our GitHub Releases page, or build from source:

git clone https://github.com/ordercraft-hq/terminal.git
cd terminal
# Run in native frameless desktop window mode:
./ordercraft --app-mode

Out of the box, it streams live crypto (BINANCE:BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, etc.) and equity data (AAPL, NVDA, SPY) with zero configuration or API keys required.

I'd love for you to check out the repository, give it a ⭐ on GitHub if you find local-first tools useful, and let me know in the comments (or in GitHub Discussions) what indicators or market data providers (IBKR, Polygon, local CSV/Parquet backtest replay) you'd like to see in v0.2.0!
