title: Spring Boot Best Practices That Should Fail Your Build
description:
Spring Boot best practices are useless if they live only in code reviews.

You probably know the story. The team agrees that field injection is bad. Everyone knows that @Transactional on a private method does not work with Spring proxies. Someone writes in Confluence that controllers should not call repositories directly. Then two months later, the same problems are back in the codebase.

That is why I created Spring Boot Code Guard. It converts Spring Boot best practices into Konsist checks that run as regular JUnit 5 tests. The test reads your Kotlin source code, checks annotations, package names, class names, and dependencies, then fails with a rule ID such as CodeGuard:noFieldInjection.

Let’s break down the rules that should fail your build before they reach code review.

Table of contents

  • 1. Spring Boot Best Practices Should Be Executable
  • 2. General Spring Boot Best Practices
    • Constructor Injection Instead of Field Injection
    • Proxy Annotations Must Not Be Placed on Private Methods
    • Use Structured Logging Instead of println and printStackTrace()
    • Configuration Classes Should Not Store Mutable State
    • @Bean Methods Should Live in @Configuration Classes
    • Custom Exceptions Should Not Extend Raw Exception
    • Kotlin Data Classes Should Not Be JPA Entities
    • JPA Entities Should Declare an Identifier
    • Repository Methods Should Return Concrete Types
    • @Transactional Belongs in the Service Layer
    • Domain and Entity Packages Should Not Depend on Spring
  • 3. Naming Rules
  • 4. Spring Boot Project Structure Best Practices
    • Positive Placement Rules
    • Exclusive Package Rules
  • 5. Spring Boot REST API Best Practices
    • Use Specific HTTP Method Annotations
    • Do Not Add Trailing Slashes to Mapping Paths
    • GET Endpoints Should Return Something
    • Do Not Expose JPA Entities Through REST APIs
    • Controllers Should Not Depend on Repositories
    • Services Should Not Depend on Web Types
    • Services Should Return DTOs, Not Entities
  • 6. How to Add Code Guard
  • 7. What This Does Not Replace

1. Spring Boot Best Practices Should Be Executable

Spring Boot gives you a lot of freedom. The official documentation even says that Spring Boot does not require a specific code layout, but there are best practices that help, especially around root packages and component scanning (Spring Boot: Structuring Your Code).

The reviewer should think about behavior, edge cases, business logic, security, and production risks. Repeating “please move this class to the service package” for the hundredth time is painful to watch.

Code Guard’s position is simple: if a Spring Boot best practice can be described structurally, it can be tested structurally.

2. General Spring Boot Best Practices

General Spring Boot best practices catch the small details that look harmless in a pull request and become annoying when they spread across the project.

Constructor Injection Instead of Field Injection

Spring supports field injection with @Autowired, but it also supports constructor injection, and a single constructor is used even when it is not annotated (Spring Framework: Using @Autowired).

Code Guard chooses constructor injection as the project rule:

// Bad
@Service
class PaymentService {
    @Autowired
    lateinit var repository: PaymentRepository
}
// Better
@Service
class PaymentService(
    private val repository: PaymentRepository,
)

Rule: CodeGuard:noFieldInjection

Why fail the build? Dependencies should be visible from the constructor. If a class has too many dependencies, you see it immediately.

Proxy Annotations Must Not Be Placed on Private Methods

Spring AOP proxying has a hard limitation: private methods cannot be advised because they cannot be overridden (Spring Framework: Proxying Mechanisms). The transaction documentation also explains that proxy-based transactions intercept calls coming through the proxy, not internal calls hidden inside the same object (Spring Framework: Using @Transactional).

This code looks meaningful, but the annotation is lying to you:

// Bad
@Service
class InvoiceService {

    fun createInvoice() {
        persistInvoice()
    }

    @Transactional
    private fun persistInvoice() {
        // no transactional proxy interception here
    }
}

// Better
@Service
class InvoiceService {

    @Transactional
    fun createInvoice() {
        persistInvoice()
    }

    private fun persistInvoice() {
        // transaction is opened on the public service method
    }
}

Rule: CodeGuard:noProxyAnnotationsOnPrivateMethods

The rule covers @Transactional, @Cacheable, @CacheEvict, @CachePut, and @Async. Same family of problem: a proxy annotation on code that the proxy cannot intercept.

Proxy Methods Must Not Self-Invoke Other Proxy Methods

Same root cause as the private-method case, different symptom. When a public proxy-annotated method calls another proxy-annotated method on the same instance, the call goes through this, not through the Spring-generated proxy. The second annotation is silently ignored (Spring Framework: Understanding AOP Proxies).

The transactional reference makes the same point about self-invocation bypassing the proxy and skipping any configured advice (Spring Framework: Using @Transactional).

// Bad
@Service
class ReportService {

    @Transactional
    fun generate(id: Long) {
        archive(id) // self-invocation, @Async never fires
    }

    @Async
    fun archive(id: Long) {
        // expected to run on a separate thread, but does not
    }
}

// Better
@Service
class ReportService(
    private val archiveService: ArchiveService,
) {
    @Transactional
    fun generate(id: Long) {
        archiveService.archive(id)
    }
}

@Service
class ArchiveService {
    @Async
    fun archive(id: Long) {
        // proxied call from another bean, advice runs
    }
}

Rule: CodeGuard:noSelfInvocationOfProxyMethods

The rule also flags proxy method calls from constructors, init blocks, and property initializers – the proxy is not in place yet during object construction, so even an external-looking call would still bypass it.

Use Structured Logging Instead of println and printStackTrace()

Spring Boot has a logging system with Logback as the default when using starters, and it pre-configures log output with levels, logger names, process IDs, and optional file output (Spring Boot: Logging).

This code bypasses it:

// Bad
@Service
class ImportService {
    fun importFile(file: File) {
        try {
            println("Importing ${file.name}")
        } catch (ex: IOException) {
            ex.printStackTrace()
        }
    }
}

// Better
@Service
class ImportService {
    private val log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(javaClass)

    fun importFile(file: File) {
        try {
            log.info("Importing {}", file.name)
        } catch (ex: IOException) {
            log.error("Failed to import {}", file.name, ex)
        }
    }
}

Rules:

  1. CodeGuard:loggerInsteadOfPrint
  2. CodeGuard:noStackTracePrint

Good practice here is not “never debug locally.” Good practice is not letting local debugging habits become production behavior.

Configuration Classes Should Not Store Mutable State

Spring documents @Configuration classes as sources of bean definitions, with @Bean methods used to instantiate and configure Spring-managed objects (Spring Framework: @Bean and @Configuration).

Code Guard enforces a stricter project rule: @Configuration classes should define beans, not behave like mutable state holders.

// Bad
@Configuration
class MailConfiguration {
    var retries = 0

    @Bean
    fun mailClient(): MailClient = MailClient()
}

// Better
@Configuration
class MailConfiguration {
    @Bean
    fun mailClient(properties: MailProperties): MailClient =
        MailClient(properties.host, properties.port)
}

Rule: CodeGuard:statelessConfiguration

There are intentional exceptions for @Value and @ConfigurationProperties fields. The rule is not against configuration values. It is against turning configuration classes into stateful objects.

@bean Methods Should Live in @Configuration Classes

Spring allows @Bean methods in non-@Configuration classes, but the @Bean javadoc calls that “lite mode.” In lite mode, inter-bean method calls are plain Java/Kotlin calls and are not intercepted through the CGLIB-enhanced configuration class semantics (Spring Framework @Bean javadoc).

Code Guard chooses the predictable rule:

// Bad
@Component
class ClientFactory {
    @Bean
    fun client(): HttpClient = HttpClient()
}

// Better
@Configuration
class ClientConfiguration {
    @Bean
    fun client(): HttpClient = HttpClient()
}

Rule: CodeGuard:beanMethodsInConfiguration

Yes, Spring can handle lite mode. No, I don’t want it used accidentally in the codebase.

Custom Exceptions Should Not Extend Raw Exception

Checked exceptions have their place, but many Spring Boot applications are cleaner when domain and application exceptions are unchecked and handled by controller advice. Code Guard enforces that classes ending with Exception extend RuntimeException, one of the well-known unchecked subtypes, ResponseStatusException, NestedRuntimeException, or another custom exception class.

// Bad
class PaymentFailedException(message: String) : Exception(message)

// Better
class PaymentFailedException(message: String) : RuntimeException(message)

Rule: CodeGuard:customExceptionStructure

This is a project convention, not a Spring Framework requirement. The point is consistency. If every service invents its own exception hierarchy, global error handling becomes a mess.

Kotlin Data Classes Should Not Be JPA Entities

Kotlin data classes automatically generate equals() and hashCode() from primary constructor properties, and data classes cannot be open (Kotlin: Data Classes). Hibernate explains that final entity classes prevent proxy creation for lazy loading unless you use special alternatives, such as proxying an interface (Hibernate ORM User Guide).

That is already enough to be paranoid.

// Bad
@Entity
data class UserEntity(
    @Id
    val id: Long,
    val email: String,
)

// Better
@Entity
class UserEntity(
    @Id
    var id: Long? = null,

    var email: String,
)

Rule: CodeGuard:noDataClassEntity

If you want deeper JPA entity design details, I wrote a separate guide: Spring Data JPA with Kotlin: Entities, Repositories, and Pitfalls.

JPA Entities Should Declare an Identifier

Hibernate’s user guide is direct here: every entity must define an identifier, and simple identifiers use the @Id annotation (Hibernate ORM User Guide: Identifiers).

Code Guard checks that an @Entity class, or one of its parents inside the same codebase, declares an @Id field.

// Bad
@Entity
class AuditLogEntity(
    var message: String,
)

// Better
@Entity
class AuditLogEntity(
    @Id
    var id: Long? = null,

    var message: String,
)

Rule: CodeGuard:entityId

Repository Methods Should Return Concrete Types

Spring Data JPA supports entity, interface, and DTO projections. It uses the declared return type to build the result (Spring Data JPA: Projections).

A repository method that returns Any or Object throws that contract away. Callers must guess the type or cast it themselves.

// Bad
interface AuditLogRepository : JpaRepository<AuditLogEntity, Long> {
    @Query("select a.message from AuditLogEntity a where a.id = :id")
    fun findMessage(@Param("id") id: Long): Any?
}

// Better
interface AuditLogRepository : JpaRepository<AuditLogEntity, Long> {
    @Query("select a.message from AuditLogEntity a where a.id = :id")
    fun findMessage(@Param("id") id: Long): String?
}

Rule: CodeGuard:repositoryReturnType

The rule also looks inside wrappers, so List<Any>, Optional<Any>, and Page<Any> fail too. Map<String, Any> and other multi-argument generic types remain allowed.

@Transactional Belongs in the Service Layer

Spring does not force you to put @Transactional only in services. It gives you the annotation and proxy infrastructure. Your architecture decides the boundary.

Code Guard’s rule is deliberately stricter: controllers should not own transaction boundaries. They should translate HTTP input into application calls and HTTP output back to the client.

// Bad
@RestController
class OrderController(
    private val orderService: OrderService,
) {
    @Transactional
    @PostMapping("/orders")
    fun create(@RequestBody request: CreateOrderRequest) =
        orderService.create(request)
}

// Better
@Service
class OrderService {
    @Transactional
    fun create(request: CreateOrderRequest): OrderResponse {
        // transactional business operation
    }
}

Rule: CodeGuard:transactionalPlacement

I covered more transaction details in Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Transactions and Manual Queries.

Domain and Entity Packages Should Not Depend on Spring

Code Guard also checks that classes in ..domain.. or ..entity.. packages do not import org.springframework.*.

Rule: CodeGuard:domainLayerIndependence

This one is not about pleasing a framework. It is about keeping the domain model portable and boring. Your entity should not know that the web layer exists. Your domain object should not need Spring to explain what it is.

3. Naming Rules

Naming rules are less exciting than transaction bugs, but they remove friction.

Code Guard checks:

  1. CodeGuard:serviceNaming: @Service classes end with Service.
  2. CodeGuard:repositoryNaming: @Repository classes and interfaces end with Repository.
  3. CodeGuard:controllerNaming: @Controller and @RestController classes end with Controller.
  4. CodeGuard:exceptionHandlerNaming: @ControllerAdvice and @RestControllerAdvice classes end with ExceptionHandler or Advice.
  5. CodeGuard:configurationPropertiesNaming: @ConfigurationProperties classes end with Properties.

Example:

// Bad
@Service
class PaymentProcessor

// Better
@Service
class PaymentService

This will not save your application on its own, but it saves attention. When a project has 50 services, 10 repositories, and 7 controllers, predictable naming matters.

4. Spring Boot Project Structure Best Practices

This is the strongest architecture section.

Spring Boot recommends a root package above the rest of the application so that component, entity, and configuration property scanning stay within your project, preventing accidental scanning of everything (Spring Boot: Structuring Your Code).

Java package names are conventionally lowercase, and Oracle’s Java tutorial explains the convention to avoid conflicts with class and interface names (Oracle Java Tutorial: Naming a Package).

Code Guard builds on top of these conventions with package rules.

Positive Placement Rules

These rules say where a type should live:

  1. CodeGuard:packageNaming: package names must be lowercase.
  2. CodeGuard:servicePackage: @Service classes must live in a ..service.. package segment.
  3. CodeGuard:controllerPackage: controllers must live in ..controller.. or ..web...
  4. CodeGuard:configurationPackage: @Configuration classes must live in ..config.. or ..configuration...
  5. CodeGuard:propertiesValidation: @ConfigurationProperties classes must live in ..property...
  6. CodeGuard:entityPackage: @Entity classes must live in ..domain.. or ..entity...
  7. CodeGuard:repositoryPackage: repositories must live in ..repository...

Spring Boot also recommends kebab-case canonical property names for configuration binding, and its documentation says the @ConfigurationProperties prefix must be kebab case (Spring Boot: Externalized Configuration).

Code Guard enforces that too:

// Bad
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "mailClient")
class MailProperties

// Better
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "mail.client")
class MailProperties

Rule: CodeGuard:configurationPropertiesPrefixKebabCase

Exclusive Package Rules

If a service must be in a service package, then a repository should not quietly move into the same package.

Code Guard checks package exclusivity:

  1. CodeGuard:onlyServicesInServicePackage
  2. CodeGuard:onlyEntitiesInEntityPackage
  3. CodeGuard:onlyControllersInControllerPackage
  4. CodeGuard:onlyConfigurationsInConfigPackage
  5. CodeGuard:onlyPropertiesInPropertyPackage
  6. CodeGuard:onlyRepositoriesInRepositoryPackage

The rules include practical exceptions for file-level helpers, nested helper classes, and JPA @MappedSuperclass, JPA @embeddable, and @IdClass support where relevant. The goal is not to punish normal Kotlin code organization. The goal is to stop architectural erosion.

5. Spring Boot REST API Best Practices

The web layer is where small shortcuts become public API problems.

Use Specific HTTP Method Annotations

Spring MVC documents @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, and @PatchMapping as shortcut variants of @RequestMapping, and says most controller methods should be mapped to a specific HTTP method (Spring Framework: Mapping Requests).

Code Guard turns that into a rule:

// Bad
@RestController
class UserController {
    @RequestMapping("/users")
    fun users(): List<UserDto> = emptyList()
}

// Better
@RestController
class UserController {
    @GetMapping("/users")
    fun users(): List<UserDto> = emptyList()
}

Rule: CodeGuard:httpMethodAnnotation

Do Not Add Trailing Slashes to Mapping Paths

Spring Framework 6 deprecated transparent trailing slash matching and favors explicit redirects through a proxy, servlet/web filter, or controller (Spring PathPatternParser javadoc).

Code Guard keeps URL mappings consistent:

// Bad
@GetMapping("/users/")
fun users(): List<UserDto> = emptyList()

// Better
@GetMapping("/users")
fun users(): List<UserDto> = emptyList()

Rule: CodeGuard:noTrailingSlash

GET Endpoints Should Return Something

A GET endpoint that returns Unit or void is suspicious. If the endpoint is a command, it probably should not be GET. If it is a query, it should return a meaningful response.

// Bad
@GetMapping("/reports/rebuild")
fun rebuildReport() {
    reportService.rebuild()
}

// Better
@PostMapping("/reports/rebuild")
fun rebuildReport(): RebuildReportResponse =
    reportService.rebuild()

Rule: CodeGuard:restControllerReturnType

Do Not Expose JPA Entities Through REST APIs

Returning entities from controllers couples your HTTP contract to your persistence model. It also makes it easier to accidentally expose fields that were added for database logic, not for clients.

// Bad
@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
fun user(@PathVariable id: Long): UserEntity =
    userService.getEntity(id)

// Better
@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
fun user(@PathVariable id: Long): UserResponse =
    userService.get(id)

Rule: CodeGuard:dtoSeparation

Related reading: Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Repositories Design Guide and Spring Data JPA with Kotlin.

Controllers Should Not Depend on Repositories

Controllers should call services. Services coordinate business logic and data access. Repositories should not appear as constructor parameters in controllers.

// Bad
@RestController
class UserController(
    private val userRepository: UserRepository,
)

// Better
@RestController
class UserController(
    private val userService: UserService,
)

Rule: CodeGuard:controllerRepository

Services Should Not Depend on Web Types

An @Service should model application work, not HTTP transport. Returning ResponseEntity, reading HttpServletRequest, or depending on a controller binds the service to the web layer.

// Bad
@Service
class InvoiceService {
    fun find(id: Long): ResponseEntity<InvoiceResponse> =
        ResponseEntity.ok(loadInvoice(id))
}

// Better
@Service
class InvoiceService {
    fun find(id: Long): InvoiceResponse =
        loadInvoice(id)
}

@RestController
class InvoiceController(
    private val invoiceService: InvoiceService,
) {
    @GetMapping("/invoices/{id}")
    fun find(@PathVariable id: Long): ResponseEntity<InvoiceResponse> =
        ResponseEntity.ok(invoiceService.find(id))
}

Rule: CodeGuard:serviceWebDependency

The rule covers Spring Web and HTTP types, the Jakarta and Javax Servlet APIs, and dependencies on controllers from the same project.

Services Should Return DTOs, Not Entities

CodeGuard:dtoSeparation stops REST controllers from accepting or returning JPA entities. This rule catches the leak one layer earlier: public @Service methods must not return entities.

// Bad
@Service
class UserService(
    private val userRepository: UserRepository,
) {
    fun find(id: Long): UserEntity =
        userRepository.getReferenceById(id)
}

// Better
@Service
class UserService(
    private val userRepository: UserRepository,
) {
    fun find(id: Long): UserResponse =
        userRepository.getReferenceById(id).toResponse()
}

Rule: CodeGuard:serviceEntityReturn

The rule follows common wrappers, so List<UserEntity>, Optional<UserEntity>, and Page<UserEntity> fail too.

6. How to Add Code Guard

The library is published to Maven Central, and the README shows this dependency:

implementation("dev.protsenko:spring-boot-code-guard:1.0.11")

Then add a JUnit 5 test, for example src/test/kotlin/SpringCodeGuardTest.kt:

import dev.protsenko.codeguard.spring.springBootRules
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test

class SpringCodeGuardTest {

    @Test
    fun `spring boot rules`() {
        springBootRules {
            all()
        }.verify()
    }
}

That is the aggressive mode.

For a legacy project, start smaller:

import dev.protsenko.codeguard.spring.springBootRules
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test

class SpringCodeGuardTest {

    @Test
    fun `spring boot rules`() {
        springBootRules {
            general {
                noFieldInjection()
            }
            jpa {
                entitiesHaveIdField()
            }
            naming {
                serviceNamingConvention()
            }
            packages {
                packageNamingConvention()
            }
            web {
                properHttpMethodAnnotations()
            }
        }.verify()
    }
}

If a rule is right but one old class needs time, suppress it explicitly:

@Suppress("CodeGuard:noFieldInjection")
@Service
class LegacyPaymentService {
    @Autowired
    lateinit var repository: PaymentRepository
}

If a rule does not fit your project, exclude it:

springBootRules {
    all()
    exclude(
        "CodeGuard:noFieldInjection",
        "CodeGuard:transactionalPlacement",
    )
}.verify()

The point is not to turn every team into my team. The point is to make Spring Boot best practices visible, executable, and impossible to forget silently.

7. What This Does Not Replace

Code Guard is not a replacement for code review. It is not a full architecture test suite. It will not tell you if your business rule is wrong, your SQL is slow, your transaction boundary is too wide, or your API design is confusing.

It catches repeatable mistakes before review:

  1. Wrong annotation placement.
  2. Wrong package boundaries.
  3. Wrong naming conventions.
  4. Entity leaks through REST.
  5. Repository usage from controllers.
  6. Spring proxy annotations cannot work.

That is enough to be useful. Humans should review code like humans. Tests should reject mechanical mistakes like tests. That is the real value of executable Spring Boot best practices.

The rules in this post come from my Spring Data JPA guide. Start with Spring Data JPA Best Practices: Entity Design Guide.

title: React 19 forwardRef Migration: ref as a Prop in TypeScript
description:
TL;DR

In React 19, function components receive ref as a regular prop, so you delete forwardRef, read ref from props (or let it travel in ...props) and type it with ComponentProps or Ref<HTMLInputElement>. forwardRef still works in React 19.3 and logs no warning, but React plans to deprecate it, and a library that supports React 18 has to keep it. The parts that need care are merged refs, which should pass on cleanup functions, and asChild, where the ref belongs on the child element.

Your components are full of forwardRef wrappers, displayName lines and ComponentPropsWithoutRef types, and React 19 says you no longer need them. The React 19 forwardRef change is small on paper: function components now receive ref as a regular prop. The work is at the edges. Props types that strip the ref, components that need the DOM node themselves, and asChild wrappers that hand the ref to a child all behave a little differently once the wrapper is gone. This tutorial migrates an input and a button, checked against React 19.3 and TypeScript 5.9, and shows the patterns we use in Wingo UI, whose source does not call forwardRef once.

What changed about forwardRef in React 19?

Function components get ref in their props, so the wrapper has nothing left to do. The React 19 release post says new function components "will no longer need forwardRef" and that React will "deprecate and remove forwardRef" in future versions. The forwardRef reference says the same: no longer necessary, deprecated in a future release.

So the React 19 forwardRef replacement is the ref prop itself. Four facts decide how you migrate:

  • forwardRef still works and stays quiet. We searched the development builds of react and react-dom 19.3.0 for a deprecation message and found none. Old components keep running while you migrate.
  • Class components did not change. A ref passed to a class still points to the instance and never shows up in its props.
  • element.ref is on its way out. React 19 still fills it, but reading it in development logs "Accessing element.ref was removed in React 19. ref is now a regular prop." Read element.props.ref instead.
  • React 18 strips ref from props. A library that still lists React 18 as a peer dependency has to keep forwardRef. Radix does: @radix-ui/react-slot 1.3.3 wraps its Slot in React.forwardRef and accepts React 16.8 through 19. Wingo UI requires React 19, so its components take ref as a plain prop.

How do you migrate a component from forwardRef to ref as a prop?

Delete the wrapper, type the props with ComponentProps, and let the ref travel in ...props. Here is the classic shadcn-style input before:

// components/ui/input.tsx (React 18)
import * as React from "react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";

const Input = React.forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"input">>(
  ({ className, type = "text", ...props }, ref) => (
    <input ref={ref} type={type} className={cn("h-10 w-full rounded-[10px] px-3", className)} {...props} />
  ),
);
Input.displayName = "Input";

export { Input };

And after:

// components/ui/input.tsx (React 19)
import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { cn } from "@/lib/utils";

export function Input({ className, type = "text", ...props }: ComponentProps<"input">) {
  return (
    <input
      data-slot="input"
      type={type}
      className={cn("h-10 w-full rounded-[10px] px-3", className)}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}

ComponentProps<"input"> already contains ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement>, so the spread hands it to the <input> and <Input ref={inputRef} /> works without one ref-specific line. A named function gives React DevTools its name, so displayName goes too.

For a whole folder, start with the official codemod from reactjs/react-codemod, on a clean branch so you can read the diff:

npx codemod react/19/remove-forward-ref --target components/ui

shadcn/ui made the same move when it switched to React 19. The shadcn Tailwind v4 guide lists the manual steps: replace React.forwardRef<...> with React.ComponentProps<...>, remove ref={ref}, add a data-slot attribute, convert to a named function and drop displayName. Their current Button types its props as React.ComponentProps<"button"> plus its variants and asChild. If your project still has the older shadcn forwardRef components with local edits, updating shadcn components without losing edits covers the merge.

To keep forwardRef from coming back, add a lint rule. As of October 2026, eslint-react's no-forward-ref is in its recommended presets, and Biome's noReactForwardRef (since Biome 2.2.5) is opt-in with an unsafe fix. Leave them off in packages that still support React 18.

How do you type ref as a prop in React 19 with TypeScript?

Most of the time you type nothing, because ComponentProps<"button"> includes ref. You add ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement> only when you write the props type yourself. The other type changes are deletions and renames:

React 18 pattern React 19 replacement
forwardRef<HTMLInputElement, Props>(...) ref?: Ref<HTMLInputElement> in Props, or ComponentProps<"input">
ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"input"> for a wrapper ComponentProps<"input"> (the old type strips the ref you now pass on)
ComponentPropsWithoutRef<typeof Root> plus ElementRef<typeof Root> ComponentProps<typeof Root>, and ComponentRef<typeof Root> when you need the node type (ElementRef is deprecated)
child.ref on a React element child.props.ref
useRef<HTMLInputElement>() useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) (an argument is now required)
ref={(node) => (el = node)} ref={(node) => { el = node; }} (a returned value now reads as a cleanup)

The last row trips people up the day they upgrade @types/react. Ref callbacks may return a cleanup function now, so an arrow function that implicitly returns the node fails with Type 'HTMLDivElement | null' is not assignable to type 'void | (() => VoidOrUndefinedOnly)'. Add braces and it compiles.

When the props are your own, declare the ref like any other prop:

import type { ReactNode, Ref } from "react";

type IconButtonProps = {
  label: string;
  icon: ReactNode;
  onPress?: () => void;
  ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>;
};

export function IconButton({ label, icon, onPress, ref }: IconButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button ref={ref} type="button" aria-label={label} onClick={onPress}>
      {icon}
    </button>
  );
}

Generic components get their type parameter back

Generic components gain the most from ref as a prop in React 19. forwardRef returns a component that is not generic, so a typed list needed a cast to get its <T> back:

// React 18: forwardRef drops <T>, so the signature is cast back on
export const List = forwardRef(ListInner) as <T>(
  props: ListProps<T> & { ref?: Ref<HTMLUListElement> },
) => ReturnType<typeof ListInner>;

Now it is a plain generic function, and T is inferred at the call site with the ref still typed:

import type { ComponentProps, ReactNode } from "react";

type ListProps<T> = Omit<ComponentProps<"ul">, "children"> & {
  items: T[];
  getKey: (item: T) => string;
  renderItem: (item: T) => ReactNode;
};

export function List<T>({ items, getKey, renderItem, ...props }: ListProps<T>) {
  return (
    <ul {...props}>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={getKey(item)}>{renderItem(item)}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// <List ref={listRef} items={customers} getKey={(c) => c.id} renderItem={(c) => c.name} />

Wrapper layers pass the ref without extra code

In our Button the ref never appears by name. ButtonProps is Omit<ComponentProps<"button">, "color" | ...> plus our props. The component reads them through useDefaults("button", buttonProps), which layers app-wide defaults from UIProvider under the props passed in, and spreads the rest onto motion.button. With forwardRef the ref would arrive as a second argument, and every layer between the caller and the element would need its own way to carry it. As a prop, it is one more key.

How do you merge refs in React 19?

Merge the two refs in a memoized callback ref that returns a cleanup. You need this when the component uses the DOM node itself and the caller wants it too. Our Input is the real case. It needs the node to clear the text with a real input event, put focus back after clearing and hear form resets, and your code needs the same node to focus the field after a failed submit. This is the pattern from components/ui/input.tsx, trimmed to a search field:

"use client";

import { useCallback, useRef, type ComponentProps, type Ref } from "react";

// hands the node to the caller's ref and returns the matching cleanup
function attachRef<T>(ref: Ref<T> | undefined, node: T) {
  if (typeof ref === "function") {
    const cleanup = ref(node);
    return () => (typeof cleanup === "function" ? cleanup() : ref(null));
  }
  if (ref) {
    const object = ref;
    object.current = node;
    return () => {
      object.current = null;
    };
  }
  return undefined;
}

// writes through the prototype setter so React sees the change, then fires the event onChange listens to
function clearValue(input: HTMLInputElement) {
  Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype, "value")?.set?.call(input, "");
  input.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", { bubbles: true }));
}

export function SearchField({ ref, ...props }: ComponentProps<"input">) {
  const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement | null>(null);

  const setRef = useCallback(
    (node: HTMLInputElement | null) => {
      inputRef.current = node;
      const detach = attachRef(ref, node);
      return () => {
        inputRef.current = null;
        detach?.();
      };
    },
    [ref],
  );

  return (
    <div className="flex items-center gap-2">
      <input ref={setRef} type="search" {...props} />
      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => {
          if (!inputRef.current) return;
          clearValue(inputRef.current);
          inputRef.current.focus();
        }}
      >
        Clear
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

Three details matter:

  • Cleanups. When the node goes away, React 19 calls the cleanup a ref callback returned, instead of calling the callback again with null. So attachRef runs the caller's cleanup if they returned one and falls back to ref(null) if they did not.
  • A stable callback. useCallback keeps setRef the same between renders. A new callback ref on every render makes React detach and reattach it each time. In a StrictMode test, an inline ref callback logged its cleanup and a fresh attach after a plain re-render, while the memoized one stayed attached.
  • A clear React can hear. clearValue goes through the native value setter and fires an input event, so the caller's onChange runs with an empty value, like after a keystroke. Assigning input.value = "" empties the field without telling React or a form library.

Textarea merges refs the same way, so it can measure its own node and grow with its content.

Using it from the outside is a normal ref:

"use client";

import { useRef } from "react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Input } from "@/components/ui/input";

export function SignupForm() {
  const emailRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

  return (
    <form
      noValidate
      onSubmit={(event) => {
        event.preventDefault();
        const email = emailRef.current?.value.trim() ?? "";
        if (!email.includes("@")) emailRef.current?.focus();
      }}
      className="flex flex-col gap-3"
    >
      <Input ref={emailRef} type="email" label="Email" placeholder="emma.carter@example.com" clearable />
      <Button type="submit">Create account</Button>
    </form>
  );
}

React Hook Form's register passes a ref the same way, so {...register("email")} reaches the <input> with no adapter. The React form components guide covers which fields need Controller instead.

Live demo: Input. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Press Continue with a short title: the demo's own ref moves focus back to the field. Then type and press Escape or tap the clear button: the Input's internal ref empties it and keeps focus). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Input docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add input

When you expose methods instead of a node, useImperativeHandle(ref, ...) works exactly as before, with ref from props. Our Pro Schema Builder hands out validate() and getJsonSchema() that way; see pricing for what Pro includes.

How does ref as a prop work with asChild and Slot?

Spread the props, ref included, onto Slot, and put the ref on the child when you need the child's type. Radix Slot composes the ref it receives with the child's own ref. In React 19 it reads the child's ref from element.props.ref, so neither one is lost and no warning fires.

The trap is TypeScript. A button component types its ref for <button>, so passing a link ref to the wrapper fails:

import Link from "next/link";
import { useRef } from "react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";

export function UpgradeLink() {
  const linkRef = useRef<HTMLAnchorElement>(null);

  // error: Type 'RefObject<HTMLAnchorElement | null>' is not assignable to type 'Ref<HTMLButtonElement> | undefined'
  return (
    <Button asChild ref={linkRef}>
      <Link href="/pricing">See plans</Link>
    </Button>
  );
}

Put the ref on the child. Slot merges it with its own, and the type is right:

"use client";

import Link from "next/link";
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";

export function UpgradeLink({ highlight }: { highlight: boolean }) {
  const linkRef = useRef<HTMLAnchorElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (highlight) linkRef.current?.focus();
  }, [highlight]);

  return (
    <Button asChild variant="outline">
      <Link ref={linkRef} href="/pricing">
        See plans
      </Link>
    </Button>
  );
}

Our Button renders asChild through motion.create(Slot), so two refs want the same node: motion's, for the press spring, and yours. Slot composes both. We mounted this Button in Chromium under StrictMode with a plain anchor as the child: the child's ref received the <a>, and the console stayed empty.

Live demo: Button. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (This Button has asChild on, so it renders a link: press it for the same spring dip, and Tab to it for the same focus ring). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Button docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add button

Two more things break asChild after a migration:

  • A child component that drops the ref. Slot passes ref, className and event handlers to the child, and a component that does not spread its props loses all three. Radix tooltips and popovers find their trigger through that ref, so the content has no element to position against.
  • A homemade Slot that reads child.ref. It still works at runtime, but logs the element.ref error in development, and @types/react 19 no longer declares ref on ReactElement, so TypeScript rejects it too. Read it from props, with a type argument because element props default to unknown in React 19: 
import { isValidElement, type ReactNode, type Ref } from "react";

type WithRef = { ref?: Ref<HTMLElement> };

// React 18 code read children.ref, which logs an error in React 19 development builds
export function getChildRef(children: ReactNode) {
  return isValidElement<WithRef>(children) ? children.props.ref : undefined;
}

What should you try next?

Install the two free components from this post and read how they handle refs in your own project:

npx wingo-ui@latest add button input

Both land in components/ui as source you own, along with the field, spinner and helpers they import, and none of those files use forwardRef. For the other half of the stack they target, browse the Next.js and Tailwind CSS guides, starting with Tailwind v4 design tokens.

Components in this post

  • Button (Free): The button every screen starts with: five variants, six tones, three sizes plus icon sizes, and a loading state that never jumps. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add button
  • Input (Free): The single-line text field: icons and addons inside the box, a clear button, a loading spinner, a counter and floating labels. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add input

FAQ

Is forwardRef deprecated in React 19?

Not formally. The React docs say forwardRef is no longer necessary in React 19 and will be deprecated in a future release. As of React 19.3 it still works and logs no warning, but new function components should take ref as a prop.

How do I type the ref prop in React 19 with TypeScript?

When you wrap one element, use ComponentProps<'button'>, which already includes ref. When you write the props type yourself, add ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>. Stop using ComponentPropsWithoutRef for wrappers, and replace ElementRef with ComponentRef.

Do I still need forwardRef if my library supports React 18?

Yes. React 18 removes ref from props before your component runs, so only forwardRef gives you the ref there. Keep it until React 18 leaves your peer dependencies; forwardRef components still work in React 19.

Does asChild still work without forwardRef?

Yes. Radix Slot reads the child's ref from its props in React 19 and composes it with the ref the Slot receives. Put the ref on the child when you want its real type, such as HTMLAnchorElement for a link rendered through a button component.

Is there a codemod to remove forwardRef?

Yes. The reactjs/react-codemod project ships remove-forward-ref: run npx codemod react/19/remove-forward-ref --target components/ui on a clean branch, then review the diff, especially generic components and props types that still use ComponentPropsWithoutRef.

Do class components get ref as a prop in React 19?

No. A ref passed to a class component still points to the component instance and is not passed in its props.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: React 19 forwardRef Migration: ref as a Prop in TypeScript. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Gemma 4 in Rust on TorchTPU: Hands On With Colab
description:
This article provides a step by step guide to running Gemma 4 E2B with the model written in Rust and every operation executed by TorchTPU, on a Colab v5e-1 runtime: one TPU v5e chip. A Rust crate reads the checkpoint, unpacks the 4-bit weights, runs the 35 layers and the ring cache, and drives the decode loop. Python hosts the backend and starts the engine. No JAX is involved.

https://github.com/xbill9/torchtpu-dev/tree/main/colab/rust

Rust writes the same tokens as compiled Python at about half the streaming speed and less than half the peak memory. Same chip, same checkpoint, same 19-token prompt, 64 greedy tokens, 33,024-token context:

One Colab v5e-1 chip Streamed tok/s Batched tok/s First call Peak memory
Rust, defer-and-fuse 14.7 to 15.7 15.2 to 16.0 82 to 84 s 7.75 GB
Rust, strict eager 4.8 to 5.0 4.8 23 to 25 s 8.62 GB
Python torch.compile 33.4 to 33.5 45.1 to 45.2 98 to 101 s 16.91 GB

Both Rust ways match the compiled Python model on all 64 tokens and on all three long-prompt answers.

What Is Being Measured?

TorchTPU (torch_tpu) is a PyTorch backend for TPUs. The question here is how far a model can move out of Python and still run on it. The Rust ways run on PyTorch 2.13.0 and the Python baseline on 2.14.1. The notebook swaps versions between them, for a reason Step 3 covers.

The model is Gemma 4 E2B in the W4A16 repack xbill9/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-w4a16-ct-text, with the per-layer table from its -text-emb4 twin. The Python baseline comes from notebook 05, the ring cache in PyTorch on TPU: Hands On With Colab.

Versions on the Colab image: Python 3.13.18, torch_tpu 0.2.0, libtpu 0.0.50, Transformers 5.20.2, compressed-tensors 0.19.0, rustc 1.99.1. Each way runs in a fresh Python process, so none inherits another's compiled programs.

Step 1 — Run the Notebook

Open notebook 06 in Colab, pick Runtime → Change runtime type → v5e-1 TPU, then Runtime → Run all. No Hugging Face token is needed. The notebook installs Rust and builds the crate on the VM:

Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 1m 44s
rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13)
Rust installed and crate built in 122 s

From a terminal, the Colab CLI runs it on a real v5e-1 and keeps the executed copy:

git clone https://github.com/xbill9/torchtpu-dev
cd torchtpu-dev/colab
make setup
python3 tools/verify_on_tpu.py 06_e2b_rust_on_torchtpu

OK: 06_e2b_rust_on_torchtpu ran clean on v5e1 -> runs/2026-11-01/06_e2b_rust_on_torchtpu_output.ipynb

1/1 notebooks verified

Step 2 — How Rust Reaches the Chip

TorchTPU 0.2.0 ships no supported C++ API, and it links libtorch_python, so Python has to host the process. Importing torch_tpu registers TorchTPU's kernels on libtorch's dispatcher. The tch crate calls that same libtorch, loaded once in the same process, so a Rust call on a tpu tensor lands on the TorchTPU kernel.

The bridge is a PyO3 extension. PyO3 0.30 builds the crate as a native Python module, torchtpu_rs, and turns Rust functions and structs into Python functions and classes. tch's python-extension feature converts a Python torch.Tensor to a tch::Tensor and back, in two small helpers, take and give. A function unpacks a Python tensor, runs ATen calls and hands the result back:

#[pyfunction]
fn matmul_sum(py: Python<'_>, x: &Bound<'_, PyAny>) -> PyResult<Py<PyAny>> {
    let x = take(x)?;
    give(py, x.matmul(&x).sum(Kind::Float))
}

Run on the chip:

Rust matmul then sum: 64.0 on tpu:0
built in Rust, moved: [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] on tpu:0
bf16 kept: torch.bfloat16

The result stays on tpu:0, and bf16 survives the trip.

🔎 Tip: tch Has No TPU Device

tch::Device has no tpu variant. type_as follows any tensor already on the chip, so the crate builds on the host and moves by example:

/// Host to device without naming the device: tch has no `tpu`, but `type_as` follows the tensor.
fn on(t: &Tensor, like: &Tensor) -> Tensor {
    t.type_as(&like.to_kind(t.kind()))
}

Python passes in torch.zeros(1, device="tpu") and every tensor follows it. Avoid Tensor::device() on these tensors for the same reason.

Step 3 — Pin PyTorch to What tch Generates

tch 0.26 is generated for PyTorch 2.13.0, and its bindings fail to compile on 2.14.1:

'qr' is not a member of 'torch'

So the crate builds against 2.13.0, which TorchTPU 0.2.0 supports, with LIBTORCH_USE_PYTORCH=1 pointing the build at the installed PyTorch:

[dependencies]
tch = { version = "0.26.0", features = ["python-extension"] }
torch-sys = { version = "0.26.0", features = ["python-extension"] }
pyo3 = { version = "0.30", features = ["extension-module"] }
safetensors = "0.8.0"
memmap2 = "0.9.12"

Step 4 — The Model in Rust

The crate is about 580 lines. weights.rs memory-maps the safetensors files and unpacks the compressed-tensors 4-bit format to bf16. gemma.rs holds the model: 35 layers, of which 15 own keys and values and 20 reuse them, the same layout as the Python ring.

The ring's attention masks every slot that is empty or out of the window, so a step is the same program at every position:

fn attend(&self, q: &Tensor, pos: &Tensor) -> Tensor {
    let scores = q.matmul(&self.k.tr()).to_kind(Kind::Float);
    let (kpos, qpos) = (self.kpos.unsqueeze(0), pos.unsqueeze(1));
    let mut keep = kpos.ge(0).logical_and(&kpos.less_equal_tensor(&qpos));
    if let Some(w) = self.window {
        keep = keep.logical_and(&kpos.greater_tensor(&(&qpos - w)));
    }
    let weights = scores.masked_fill(&keep.logical_not().unsqueeze(1), f64::NEG_INFINITY);
    // softmax, then the values

Python starts it with a directory and a tensor on the chip:

import torch_tpu
import torchtpu_rs

engine = torchtpu_rs.Engine(MODEL_DIR, EMB4_DIR, torch.zeros(1, device="tpu"), 33024)
tokens, read_s, decode_s = engine.generate(ids, 64, 1)

The last argument sets how often tokens come back to the host: 1 streams, 8 reads in batches of eight.

PyO3 is what makes Engine a Python class. The Rust model sits behind a #[pyclass], and its methods take and return plain Python lists and numbers, so token ids cross the boundary with no tensor at all:

#[pyclass(unsendable)]
struct Engine(gemma::Gemma);

#[pymethods]
impl Engine {
    // new, layout and logits omitted
    #[pyo3(signature = (ids, max_new, read_every=1))]
    fn generate(&mut self, ids: Vec<i64>, max_new: i64, read_every: i64) -> (Vec<i64>, f64, f64) {
        tch::no_grad(|| self.0.generate(&ids, max_new, read_every))
    }
}

#[pymodule]
fn torchtpu_rs(m: &Bound<'_, PyModule>) -> PyResult<()> {
    // the two test functions omitted
    m.add_class::<Engine>()?;
    Ok(())
}

unsendable makes PyO3 refuse calls on the engine from any thread but the one that created it.

Step 5 — Check It Against Transformers

Before any TPU time, the Rust engine runs on CPU beside Hugging Face Transformers, on PyTorch 2.13.0 with the real checkpoint:

load 6.8 (3, 12, 20, 1024)
top5 rust [818, 102500, 4420, 16520, 18318] [25.75, 18.875, 18.75, 18.5, 18.125]
top5 hf   [818, 102500, 4420, 16520, 18318] [25.625, 18.75, 18.625, 18.25, 18.0]
max abs diff 0.375 KL(hf||rs) 1.8714923498919234e-05
same 64 of 64
first diff None

The top five candidates are the same, the KL divergence is 1.9e-5, and all 64 tokens match. The layout line reads 3 full-attention rings, 12 sliding rings and 20 shared layers.

Step 6 — The Three Ways on the Chip

Final run of notebook 06:

way                       load s  first s  graphs  breaks  streamed  in batches  peak GB
Rust fused, torch 2.13      23.1     83.5       -       -      15.1        15.2     7.75
Rust eager, torch 2.13      23.8     22.8       -       -       4.8         4.8     8.62
Python compile, 2.14.1      25.9    101.1       2       0      33.5        45.1    16.91
Rust fused, torch 2.13: first 64 of 64 tokens identical to Python compile on 2.14.1
Rust eager, torch 2.13: first 64 of 64 tokens identical to Python compile on 2.14.1

Defer-and-fuse is the fast mode for Rust. torch.compile traces Python, so it cannot see Rust. TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1 works below ATen and needs no change to the crate. It takes Rust from 4.8 to 15.1 tokens per second streamed, about 3.2x, at the same tokens. In this run Rust fused streams at 0.45x the compiled Python step and batched Python reaches 2.97x Rust (arithmetic, evidence/arithmetic.txt).

Compiling costs Python more memory: its 16.91 GB peak against 7.75 GB for Rust fused is 2.18x, close to the chip's 16 GiB.

🔎 Tip: Don't Run torch.compile on 2.13 For This Model

The compiled Python ring needs 2.14.1. On 2.13.0 the same source behaves differently:

Python compile, 2.13        25.6     34.6      65      64      15.9        16.2    11.26
Python compile, 2.13: first 21 of 64 tokens identical to Python compile on 2.14.1

It splits into 65 programs with 64 graph breaks and writes a different reply from token 21. Changing Transformers and compressed-tensors versions made no difference, and changing the PyTorch version did. Its cause is untested. The Rust ways on 2.13.0 are unaffected and match 2.14.1.

Step 7 — Long Prompts

Notebook 05's prompts fill the context with numbered records, each with a random code, and ask about one record:

way                       prompt  read s read tok/s  decode   answer  found
Rust fused, torch 2.13        61     0.1        776    14.6   915965    yes
Rust fused, torch 2.13      4081     1.0       4172    14.8   610395    yes
Rust fused, torch 2.13     32761     8.0       4116    15.6   319550     no
Rust eager, torch 2.13     32761    28.5       1148     4.8   319550     no
Python compile, 2.14.1     32761     5.0       6555    45.1   319550     no

Rust fused reads the 32,761-token prompt in 7.6 to 8.0 s, the compiled ring in 5.0 s and Rust eager in about 29 s. All three ways give the same three answers. The third is wrong in every way, the same code the Python ring gives, so the limit belongs to the model at this depth. Decode speed holds steady at every depth, because each step attends over every slot of a cache of the same size.

Compare and Contrast

One v5e chip, Gemma 4 E2B Streamed tok/s Model code PyTorch Peak memory
Python torch.compile 🥇 33.4 to 33.5 Python 2.14.1 16.91 GB
Rust, defer-and-fuse 🥈 14.7 to 15.7 Rust 2.13.0 7.75 GB
Rust, strict eager 🥉 4.8 to 5.0 Rust 2.13.0 8.62 GB

So, Which One?

For speed on this chip, stay with the compiled Python ring on PyTorch 2.14.1: 45 tokens per second in batches and 33 streamed.

For a model in Rust, set TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1: about 15 tokens per second streamed, the same tokens and answers, and less than half the peak memory. TorchTPU marks that variable experimental, so it may change.

Keep strict eager for debugging, at about 5 tokens per second.

Summary

The goal of this article was to run Gemma 4 E2B on a TPU with the model written in Rust, through TorchTPU and without JAX. The key to the solution was tch sharing the one libtorch that TorchTPU registers its kernels with, so a Rust ATen call on a tpu tensor reaches a TorchTPU kernel, with PyO3 exposing the Rust engine to Python as a module. The Colab v5e-1 results were:

  • 🟢 Rust matches compiled Python on 64 of 64 tokens and 3 of 3 long-prompt answers
  • 🟢 Rust matches Transformers on CPU on 64 of 64 tokens, with a KL divergence of 1.9e-5
  • 🟢 One environment variable takes Rust from about 5 to about 15 tokens per second streamed
  • 🟢 Rust peaks at 7.75 GB against 16.91 GB for compile
  • ⚠️ Rust fused streams at 0.45x compiled Python, because torch.compile cannot trace Rust
  • ⚠️ tch 0.26 builds against PyTorch 2.13.0 only
  • ⚠️ Python still hosts the process, builds the prompts and tokenizes
  • ❌ torch.compile on PyTorch 2.13.0 splits this model into 65 programs and changes the reply

Scope: Gemma 4 E2B-it QAT only, text only, one Colab v5e-1 runtime per run on 2026-11-01, greedy decoding, one sequence at a time, four prompts, a 33,024-token context. Rust ranges cover three runs and compiled Python ranges two. The earliest Rust run used Transformers 5.21.0 and compressed-tensors 0.20.1, and the rest 5.20.2 and 0.19.0. The Rust ways ran on PyTorch 2.13.0 and the Python baseline on 2.14.1, one version apart. The 131,328-token context, a serving endpoint, a Rust Colab kernel, and where the time goes between Rust fused and compile were not run. The final crate formatting commit was built and checked on CPU, and the TPU runs used the source before it.

The strategy for running a Rust model on TorchTPU was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

title: Command Auditing in an SSH Terminal: What the Client Can See, and What Only the Server Can Enforce
description:
Originally published on MistLab. Part 6 of Building an SSH Terminal.

Part 6 of "Building an SSH Terminal". Code excerpts are from MistTerm v1.2.26, an open-source (AGPL) SSH terminal client by MistLab and from the server-side agent installer in the Mist server repository; they are trimmed, and comments are translated from Chinese.

TL;DR

A terminal sees keystrokes, not the command the shell finally runs. Line editing, alias and variable expansion, scripts and other SSH clients all bypass it. Client-side command checks are therefore advisory. Enforcement has to happen on the server, where processes start, for example by wrapping commands with sshd's ForceCommand. In-band markers in terminal output can be forged and should only be used for display.

Teams that share production servers often want a guard rail: warn before rm -rf /, require a second look before DROP DATABASE, keep a record of what was run. The obvious place to build that seems to be the terminal, because it sees every keystroke. It is a useful place to advise and the wrong place to enforce. MistTerm splits that: a local check that only warns, and enforcement on the server, where the process starts.

Why a terminal cannot know which command will run

Recall Parts 1 and 2. A terminal sends bytes and receives bytes. It does not see the remote shell's command line. It sees keystrokes going out and echo coming back. The command that actually runs differs from the keystrokes in many ways the terminal cannot model:

  • Line editing. Cursor movement, Tab completion, history recall (↑, Ctrl-R, !!), and readline or zsh widgets all change the line without any one-to-one mapping to keys.

  • Expansion. Aliases, functions, variables, globbing and command substitution happen inside the shell. $(echo rm) -rf x contains no rm -rf the terminal could match.

  • Indirection. Scripts, cron, sudo -s, tmux, a nested ssh hop, or a program reading commands from a file all execute commands that never pass through the terminal's input path.

  • Other clients. Anyone can connect with plain OpenSSH and bypass a terminal-side rule entirely.

So a client-side check is a best-effort hint for the person at the keyboard. Enforcement has to happen where the command executes: on the server, by the component that starts processes. MistTerm's design document for the team features states it the same way. The server-side check is the authority, and the local engine is a hint.

Where commands are checked: client hints vs. server enforcement

The client side: a local rule engine

MistTerm's client has a rule engine, CmdAuditEngine, whose policy is synchronized from the team service (/v1/teams/{team_id}/command-audit/sync, refreshed every 300 seconds). It is active only when a team policy is enabled. The evaluation order is fixed, and the first match wins:

// src/core/cmd_audit.rs — CmdAuditEngine::check (outline)
pub fn check(&self, command: &str) -> CmdAuditResult {
    let cmd = command.trim();
    if cmd.is_empty() || !self.is_active() { return allow_result(); }
    // 1. team custom rules, in order (an Allow rule short-circuits)
    // 2. built-in "read-dangerous"  → policy.dangerous_action
    // 3. built-in "read-sensitive"  → policy.sensitive_action
    // 4. built-in dangerous         → policy.dangerous_action
    // 5. built-in read-safe / safe  → allow
    // 6. otherwise                  → policy.unknown_action
}

The default policy maps dangerous matches to Block, sensitive matches to Confirm and unknown commands to Allow. Teams can change all three.

The engine is consulted wherever the client itself originates a command: snippets and saved commands sent to a pane, batch execution across hosts, and commands proposed by the built-in AI assistant. In those cases the client knows the exact text it is about to send, and the check is precise.

Typed commands: gating Enter

Commands typed by hand are the hard case. In v1.2.26 MistTerm checks them at the moment Enter is pressed. When a policy is active, the Enter key does not immediately send \r. The client first reconstructs the line from the keys it has sent since the last Enter, then runs the check:

/// Keyboard Enter: if a policy is active and the local line is trustworthy,
/// hand it to the host for auditing first; otherwise send `\r` as before.
fn submit_enter_key(&mut self) {
    if self.typed_enter_request.is_some() { return; } // previous Enter still being audited
    if let Some(line) = self.typed_enter_gate_line() {
        self.typed_enter_request = Some(line);
        return;
    }
    self.release_typed_enter(); // sends "\r"
}

The reconstruction is approximate on purpose, and the code says so by declining to gate when the line cannot be trusted:

fn typed_enter_gate_line(&self) -> Option<String> {
    if !self.typed_enter_gate || !self.connected { return None; }
    if self.terminal.is_alt_screen() || self.lrzsz.is_active() || self.transfer_progress.is_some() {
        return None; // full-screen apps (vim, less, …) and file transfers
    }
    let line = self.typed_line_buffer.trim();
    if line.is_empty() { return None; }
    if Self::looks_like_secret_prompt(&self.terminal.cursor_line_text()) {
        return None; // "password", "passphrase", … — never treat a secret as a command
    }
    Some(line.to_string())
}

The local buffer tracks printable input, Backspace, Ctrl-U and Ctrl-C (clear) and Ctrl-W (delete word). It does not model cursor movement, completion or history. For example, a line recalled with ↑ leaves the local buffer empty, so Enter is passed through rather than blocked. The source comment warns against the alternative: blocking whenever the buffer looked wrong would produce a terminal that "can move left and right but cannot press Enter".

If the check blocks, or the user declines a confirmation, the characters are already on the remote command line, because they were sent key by key. The client sends Ctrl-U (0x15) to clear the remote line and resets its own buffer:

pub fn discard_typed_line(&mut self) {
    self.typed_enter_request = None;
    self.typed_line_buffer.clear();
    self.pty_outbound_line_buffer.clear();
    let _ = self.send_pty_input(&[0x15]); // kill-line on the remote side
}

Ctrl-U is the default line-kill for both the kernel's canonical mode and readline. It is still a convention: a remote program with different key bindings would behave differently.

Where should command auditing be enforced? On the server

The Mist server repository ships an agent installer for team servers (deploy/agent/install.sh, installed with a one-line curl … | sudo bash). It is plain bash and curl, with no daemon. It registers the machine and installs an sshd ForceCommand wrapper. With ForceCommand, sshd runs the wrapper instead of whatever the client asked for, and passes the requested command in SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND.

What the wrapper does, read directly from the installer:

CMD="${SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND:-}"
LOGIN_SHELL="${SHELL:-/bin/sh}"

# Interactive login (no command): give a normal login shell; we must not exit,
# or people could not log in at all
if [ -z "$CMD" ]; then exec "$LOGIN_SHELL" -l; fi

# sftp subsystem is not a shell command: hand off to sftp-server
# …

# If the config is unreadable, do not audit; run as usual. The config holds this
# machine's secret and is readable only by root, so currently only the root
# account's commands are audited.
[ -r /etc/mist-agent/config ] && . /etc/mist-agent/config 2>/dev/null || exec "$LOGIN_SHELL" -c "$CMD"

RESP=$(curl -sS -m 5 -X POST "$MIST_API/server/command-audit/check" …)

Then:

  • If the service cannot be reached, the command runs, with a stderr notice that it was not checked and will not be recorded. That is fail-open.

  • If the result is block or confirm (or allowed: false), the command does not run, and a blocked record is sent. For confirm, the message explains that a plain ssh host cmd has no way to confirm interactively.

  • Otherwise the command runs and the result is reported.

Taken together, the default installer enforces policy on non-interactive commands (ssh host 'cmd', automation, CI) for root. An interactive login gets an ordinary login shell, and the wrapper sees nothing typed into it afterwards. That is an inherent limit of ForceCommand: it intercepts the session's initial command, not the commands a shell later runs.

The check endpoint (POST /v1/server/command-audit/check) returns allowed, action, the matching rules and a record id. It does not issue any approval token.

Interactive shells: an optional hook

Checking commands inside an interactive bash requires a hook inside bash. The MistTerm repository contains an optional script, scripts/fix-mist-agent-interactive.py, that installs one. It is not part of the default agent installer. It uses bash's DEBUG trap with extdebug:

shopt -s extdebug
trap mist_audit_preexec DEBUG

With extdebug set, if the DEBUG trap returns a non-zero status, bash skips the command about to run (bash manual, shopt / extdebug). The hook posts the command to the same check endpoint, with a 1.5 s timeout and fail-open, and prints a marker line for the client:

MIST_AUDIT  {"v":1,"action":"block","message":"…","rule":"…","command":"…"}

On block it returns 1, so bash skips the command. On confirm it prints the marker and returns 0, which means the command runs. The marker only lets the client show the rule to the user. A DEBUG trap is a convenience layer, not a security boundary: the user controls their own shell and can remove the trap, and other shells (zsh, fish, sh) are not covered.

The MIST_AUDIT marker line: printed by the optional bash hook, stripped by the client

Parsing an in-band marker

On the client, ServerAuditProbe sits between the session and the emulator. It holds back an incomplete line that might be the start of a marker, strips complete MIST_AUDIT lines from the display, and turns them into dialog events:

/// Feed one chunk of PTY data; returns bytes to display and parsed events.
pub fn feed(&mut self, chunk: &[u8]) -> (Vec<u8>, Vec<ServerAuditEvent>) {
    // for each complete line: parse_mist_audit_line → event, else pass through;
    // for a trailing partial line: hold it only if it could still become a marker
}

Holding back a partial line only when it could still become a marker matters for latency. The probe skips leading whitespace and escape sequences, and keeps bytes only if what remains is a prefix of MIST_AUDIT, or if the chunk ends inside an unfinished escape sequence. Ordinary echo goes straight to the screen.

An in-band marker shares the stream with everything else, so any output can contain one. cat a file with that line in it and the client will show a dialog. That is acceptable only because the marker carries no authority. The decision was already made on the server, and the dialog is informational.

One leftover in the client deserves mention. After a user confirms a server-side confirm, the client would first send MIST_AUDIT_APPROVE\t<token> if the marker carried a non-empty token field (src/ui/app.rs). The hook forwards a token only if the check response contains one, and the server's check response has no such field. So in current deployments that branch never runs. We note it so readers of the source do not take it as a working approval mechanism.

Summary

  • A terminal sees keystrokes, not commands. Editing, expansion and indirection make terminal-side checks advisory by nature.

  • MistTerm's client checks the commands it originates precisely, and typed commands approximately at Enter. When the local line is not trustworthy (alt screen, transfer, password prompt), it steps aside instead of guessing.

  • Enforcement belongs on the server. The default agent wraps non-interactive commands for root via ForceCommand and fails open if the service is unreachable. Interactive shells need an optional bash hook, which can block but does not hold a confirm.

  • In-band markers are forgeable by any output. Use them for display, never for decisions.

One later addition, outside the v1.2.26 excerpts above. From MistTerm v1.2.38 the same Enter path can append a local line to ~/.mist/logs/exec-history.jsonl. Preferences → Activity audit → "Check and record commands typed in the terminal" turns that off. With no team login the file is not written for typed commands anyway. Part 10 is that record. It does not move enforcement off the server.

FAQ

Can an SSH client reliably audit commands?

No. It sees keystrokes, not the final command, and other clients bypass it entirely. Client-side checks are best-effort hints.

Where should SSH command auditing be enforced?

On the server, where processes are started, for example by wrapping commands with sshd's ForceCommand.

Can in-band markers in terminal output be trusted?

No. Any program output can forge them. Use them for display, never for decisions.

title: Exporting a Solo site: fixing fonts, image paths and forms by hand
description:
Solo's Shutdown FAQ says the export ZIP holds "an HTML export of your website and a CSV file with links to your image assets, as well as your contact form and newsletter submissions". It also says: "Image source files are not included in the ZIP."

You can't just upload that ZIP to a static host. This post covers four problem areas: images, fonts and styles, page links, and forms. For each one, you get the code our Solo export tool uses (or what it doesn't do) and the manual steps.

A caveat first: we haven't seen a real Solo export. Solo doesn't document the file names or folder layout. Our tests run on a synthetic fixture, fixtures/solo-export-example-bakery-with-assets.zip, built by scripts/build_synthetic_export.py. It assumes a layout that matches what Solo's FAQ says the ZIP contains. The code is written to cope with a different wrapper folder.

The fixture 

solo-export-example-bakery-with-assets.zip
├── website/
│   ├── index.html
│   └── about/index.html
├── image_links.csv
├── contact_form_submissions.csv
└── newsletter_submissions.csv

index.html contains the kinds of references the code has to handle:

<link rel="icon" href="/favicon/favicon.ico">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/_next/static/css/x.css">
<script src="https://soloist.ai/_next/static/chunks/main.js"></script>
...
.hero{background-image:url(https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1542653285-7f095a1183e0?crop=entropy&cs=srgb&fm=jpg&q=60&w=1600)}
...
<a href="/example-bakery/about">About</a> · <a href="/about">About</a>
<img src="https://images.unsplash.com/photo-...?...&w=1080" srcset="...w=400 400w, ...w=1080 1080w, ...w=2400 2400w">
<script id="__NEXT_DATA__" type="application/json">{... "url": "https://images.unsplash.com/photo-...?crop=entropy\u0026cs=srgb\u0026fm=jpg\u0026q=85" ...}</script>

Image URLs show up in four places: src, srcset, inline CSS url(), and JSON. The JSON copy escapes & as \u0026.

1. Image paths

What the code does

lib/localize.ts scans every text file (html, htm, css, js, mjs, cjs, json, csv, txt, xml, svg) with one regex that tolerates both escapes:

export const IMAGE_HOSTS = new Set(["cdn.soloist.ai", "images.unsplash.com"]);

/** Matches http(s) URLs, including HTML `&` and JSON `\\u0026`. */
export const URL_RE = /https?:\/\/(?:[^\s"'<>()\\,]|\\u0026)+/g;

export function normalizeUrl(raw: string): string {
  return raw.replace(/&/g, "&").replace(/\\u0026/g, "&");
}

Then it collapses size variants so each image is downloaded once:

if (host === "cdn.soloist.ai") {
  const m = x.pathname.match(/^(.*)_(\d+)x(\d+)(\.\w+)$/);
  if (m) {
    const fetchUrl = `https://${host}${m[1]}_2048x2048${m[4]}`;
    return { key: host + m[1], fetchUrl, original: url, fallbackUrl: url !== fetchUrl ? url : undefined };
  }
}
if (host === "images.unsplash.com") {
  return {
    key: host + x.pathname,
    fetchUrl: `https://${host}${x.pathname}?ixlib=rb-4.0.3&fm=jpg&q=85&w=2400&fit=max`,
    original: url,
    fallbackUrl: url,
  };
}

A cdn.soloist.ai URL ending in _NNNxNNN maps to its _2048x2048 variant. Unsplash URLs are keyed by pathname, so all the w=400, w=1080 and w=2400 variants count as one image. If the upgraded URL fails, downloadOne() in lib/fetch-images.ts retries with the original URL.

Each file is saved as images/<sha1-prefix>.<ext>, with the extension taken from Content-Type. Then every match in every text file gets rewritten to a path relative to that file:

export function posixRelative(fromFile: string, toFile: string): string {
  // ...
  const rel = [...Array.from({ length: fromParts.length - i }, () => ".."), ...toParts.slice(i)].join("/");
  return rel || normalizedTo;
}

A root page gets images/abc.jpg. about/index.html gets ../images/abc.jpg.

In the browser, cdn.soloist.ai images can't be fetched directly. Our README notes they "have no CORS headers", so the tool routes them through a same-origin /api/img proxy. That proxy allows only cdn.soloist.ai over HTTPS and only passes image/* responses.

By hand

CORS only applies inside browsers, so a script or curl can download the images directly.

  1. Grep every text file for cdn.soloist.ai and images.unsplash.com URLs. Decode & and \u0026 before you dedupe.
  2. Dedupe on path, ignoring size suffix and query string. Download the largest variant.
  3. Replace every occurrence, including srcset entries, CSS url() and __NEXT_DATA__, with a relative path. Calculate the path from each file's own folder, not from the site root.

2. Fonts and styles

What the code does

The exported HTML links stylesheets under /_next/. lib/assets.ts only fetches static, non-JS files from that one prefix:

const JS_PATH = /\.(?:js|mjs|cjs)(?:$|[?#])/i;
const ALLOWED_STATIC_EXT =
  /\.(?:css|woff2?|ttf|otf|eot|svg|png|jpe?g|gif|webp|ico|avif)(?:$|[?#])/i;

export function isAllowedSoloStaticAsset(url: string): boolean {
  const u = new URL(url);
  if (u.protocol !== "https:") return false;
  if (u.hostname !== SOLO_ASSET_HOST) return false; // "soloist.ai"
  if (!u.pathname.startsWith(SOLO_PATH_PREFIX)) return false; // "/_next/"
  if (JS_PATH.test(u.pathname)) return false;
  return ALLOWED_STATIC_EXT.test(u.pathname);
}

captureSoloAssets() starts from each <link rel="stylesheet"> (or rel="preload" as="style"). It reads @import and url() from every CSS file it downloads and queues those references up to depth 4. Each file is saved under assets/ at its original path, so https://soloist.ai/_next/static/media/bakery.woff2 becomes assets/_next/static/media/bakery.woff2. CSS url() values are then rewritten relative to the saved CSS file. Our test asserts the result:

const css = new TextDecoder().decode(result.files["assets/_next/static/css/x.css"]);
assert.match(css, /url\(["']?\.\.\/media\/bakery\.woff2/);
assert.doesNotMatch(css, /https:\/\/soloist\.ai\/_next\/static\/media\/bakery/);

fetchAssetWithRetry() retries once on a 502 or a network error. Anything still missing gets one more sweep after a delay (ASSET_SWEEP_DELAY_MS = 2000). If it's still missing after that, it's listed as skipped in the report.

By hand

  1. Download each /_next/static/css/*.css the pages link.
  2. grep -o 'url([^)]*)' and @import in each file. Download those too, and repeat for any CSS they pull in.
  3. Keep the _next/static/... folder structure under one assets/ folder. Most relative url(../media/x.woff2) references then resolve without edits. Rewrite any absolute https://soloist.ai/_next/... references.
  4. Point the <link href> in each page at the local copy, relative to that page.

3. Scripts and page links

stripSoloNextScripts() removes <script src> tags and <link rel="preload" as="script"> tags pointing at soloist.ai. It leaves __NEXT_DATA__ alone, because that tag has no src. Once scripts are removed, the report says: "Interactive parts that relied on Solo's scripts may not work."

Links in the fixture use both /<handle>/about and /about. rootAbsoluteToRelative() maps both onto files in the flattened ZIP. These are the cases from tests/assets.test.ts:

rootAbsoluteToRelative("/example-bakery/about", "index.html", files)          // "about/index.html"
rootAbsoluteToRelative("/about", "index.html", files)                         // "about/index.html"
rootAbsoluteToRelative("/example-bakery/#menu-1", "index.html", files)        // "#menu-1"
rootAbsoluteToRelative("/example-bakery/#menu-1", "about/index.html", files)  // "../index.html#menu-1"
rootAbsoluteToRelative("/favicon/favicon.ico", "index.html", files)           // unchanged

The first path segment only counts as a handle if it isn't a known asset root (favicon, img, images, assets, static, _next, css, js, fonts), doesn't contain a dot, and doesn't match a file or folder in the ZIP.

By hand: delete the Solo <script> tags and script preloads. Then, for every root-absolute href, drop the handle segment and rewrite the rest to a relative path.

4. Forms

Our tool doesn't convert Solo forms. Our static-host guide says it plainly: "The tool strips Solo scripts, and a static host cannot send the form."

The code does handle the submissions data. lib/process-zip.ts treats every .csv (and manifest.csv / report.txt) as private and splits it into a second ZIP:

function isPrivateDataPath(path: string): boolean {
  if (path === "_rescue-data" || path.startsWith("_rescue-data/")) return true;
  const base = path.split("/").pop() ?? path;
  if (PRIVATE_DATA_BASENAMES.has(base)) return true;
  if (base.endsWith(".csv")) return true;
  return base.endsWith("_submissions.csv");
}

countFormSubmissions() in lib/solo/gaps.ts counts non-empty data rows in contact_form_submissions.csv and newsletter_submissions.csv. Its quote-aware CSV splitter keeps a multi-line message as one row.

By hand:

  1. Move every CSV out of the folder you deploy. Those files hold your visitors' names and emails.
  2. Replace the form markup with a mailto: link, or point it at a form backend you control. Static files can't receive a POST.

Output

From the README, the Example Bakery fixture with styles produces:

website-ready-to-host.zip
  index.html
  images/<hash>.jpg
  assets/_next/static/css/x.css
  assets/_next/static/media/...

private-form-data-do-not-upload.zip
  image_links.csv
  contact_form_submissions.csv
  newsletter_submissions.csv
  manifest.csv
  report.txt

Host only the first ZIP. If you'd rather not do this by hand, the free tool runs in the browser: https://site-export-rescue.pages.dev/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=solo-export-fixes

Written with AI assistance from our own source code and test exports, and checked against them.
