title: Constraining agent CSS to design tokens (without pasting the whole theme)
description:
I used to drop the entire tokens.css into the agent prompt so it “wouldn’t invent colors.” It still invented colors. Just prettier ones — #3B82F6 instead of blue, 14px instead of space.3, a one-off radius that almost matched radius.md.

Pasting the whole theme teaches the model what exists. It does not teach it that everything else is illegal. Agents treat big token dumps like a style moodboard, then freestyle.

Here’s the thinner constraint that actually stuck in our agent UI PRs.

The failure mode: theme dump

A prompt like this looks responsible and fails quietly:

Here is our full design token file (800 lines of CSS variables). Style this settings panel to match.

What came back:

  • Hex that “felt close” to --color-accent-primary
  • padding: 18px because “the mock looked about that”
  • A new --card-shadow-soft declared inline in the component
  • Tailwind arbitrary values (bg-[#0f172a]) next to token classes

The model saw the tokens. It optimized for “looks like our product,” not “uses only the legal surface.”

What “token-constrained CSS” means

I define it as four hard rules the agent can fail against:

  1. No raw values — no hex, rgb, hsl, or bare px/rem for color, space, radius, or shadow in changed CSS/JSX
  2. Import / reference allowlist — only named tokens from the published set (var(--space-4), theme('spacing.4'), tokens.space[4], whatever your stack uses)
  3. No local token invention — do not declare new --* custom properties in feature CSS unless the ticket says “new token approved”
  4. Closest-token rule — if the design asks for something off-scale, stop and name the gap; don’t invent a near-miss

If the prompt only says “use our design system,” the agent hears “make it pretty.” Name the bans.

The slim token pack I actually paste

Instead of the whole theme, I keep a token cheat sheet under ~40–60 lines and refresh it when the public scale changes:

## Legal tokens (CSS / Tailwind / JS — same names)

### Color
- bg.default, bg.subtle, bg.muted
- fg.default, fg.muted, fg.danger
- border.default, border.strong
- accent.primary, accent.primary-hover
Forbidden: raw hex/rgb, inventing --color-*, opacity hacks that bake a new tint

### Space
- 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 10 12 (map to --space-* or spacing.*)
Forbidden: 13px, 18px, 22px, “eyeballed” padding, gap: 7

### Radius
- sm | md | lg | full
Forbidden: border-radius: 10px, rounded-[10px]

### Shadow
- shadow.sm | shadow.md | shadow.lg
Forbidden: one-off box-shadow stacks in feature CSS

### Type
- font.size: sm | md | lg | xl
- font.weight: regular | medium | semibold
Forbidden: font-size: 15px, font-weight: 450

## How to reference (pick your stack)
- CSS: var(--space-4), var(--color-fg-muted)
- Tailwind: p-4, text-fg-muted, rounded-md (token-mapped utilities only)
- JS/CSS-in-JS: tokens.space[4], tokens.color.fg.muted

## Acceptance (must pass before PR)
- [ ] Zero hex/rgb/hsl in the diff
- [ ] Zero bare px for space/radius/type (layout hacks like 1px hairlines need a one-line NOTE)
- [ ] Zero new --* declarations outside tokens/
- [ ] Any off-scale design ask is listed as a blocker, not approximated

That’s the whole “theme” most feature tasks get. The full tokens.css stays in the repo for humans and for codegen — the prompt carries the decision surface.

Prompt shape that works

My default ask looks like this:

Style X using only the Legal tokens below.

Do not invent colors, spacing, radius, or shadows.

If a value isn’t on the scale, stop and name the missing token — don’t approximate.

Prefer existing utility / token classes over new CSS files.

When done, paste the Acceptance checklist with pass/fail and list every token you used.

I also add one explicit ban that cut a lot of noise:

Forbidden: Tailwind arbitrary values for color/space/radius (bg-[#…], p-[18px], rounded-[10px]). If the utility doesn’t exist, the token doesn’t exist for this task.

Arbitrary values are how agents smuggle freestyle CSS past a “we use Tailwind” rule.

A tiny CI gate that catches the same mistakes

Prompts leak. I pair them with a cheap lint on agent-touched paths:

# scripts/check-no-raw-css-values.sh — run on changed UI files
rg -n --pcre2 \
  '(#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b|rgba?\(|hsla?\(|\b\d+(\.\d+)?px\b|rounded-\[[^\]]+\]|bg-\[[^\]]+\]|p-\[[^\]]+\]|gap-\[[^\]]+\])' \
  src/components src/app \
  -g '!**/tokens/**' \
  -g '!**/*.test.*' \
  && exit 1 || exit 0

False positives happen (SVG path data, 1px hairlines). Allowlist those with a comment:

/* RAW_OK: 1px hairline separator — not a spacing token */
border-top: 1px solid var(--color-border-default);

The point isn’t zero exceptions. It’s that every exception is named, so agent PRs can’t quietly grow a second palette.

For Tailwind shops, eslint-plugin-tailwindcss with no-arbitrary-value (or a custom restrict) on src/features/** works even better — fail the PR when the model reaches for [#0f172a].

What I put in the PR template

A short checkbox beats another paragraph in the system prompt:

### Token compliance
- [ ] No raw color / space / radius / shadow values in the diff
- [ ] No new --* tokens outside tokens/
- [ ] Off-scale design requests called out (not approximated)
- [ ] `scripts/check-no-raw-css-values.sh` (or ESLint) passed

Reviewers stop arguing taste (“that blue is fine”) and start enforcing the scale.

Review comments I actually leave

When I see freestyle CSS in an agent diff:

Token miss: padding: 18px isn’t on the space scale. Use var(--space-4) / p-4 or stop and request a new token. Don’t approximate.

When the model invents a local variable:

New --card-shadow-soft belongs in tokens/ with a design OK, not in the feature file. Revert and use shadow.md or file a token RFC.

When Tailwind arbitrary values show up:

bg-[#0f172a] is a banned escape hatch here. Map to bg-subtle / bg-muted or name the missing token. Arbitrary color values fail the token gate on purpose.

What I stopped doing

  • Pasting the entire theme “for completeness”
  • Saying “match the design system” without listing banned value types
  • Trusting the model to “prefer tokens” without a lint gate
  • Letting one-off hex land because “it’s only in this panel”

Constraining agent CSS to design tokens is less about teaching every variable name and more about shrinking the legal alphabet. Give a short allowlist, ban raw values out loud, and fail CI when freestyle sneaks in. The full theme can stay in the repo — it just doesn’t need to live in every prompt.

title: The Effort to Reach: Designing for Fitts’s Law
description:
Originally published on ryanverwey.dev.

Fitts’s Law describes how movement time depends on the distance to a target and the target’s width. In comparable pointing conditions, a larger target or a shorter journey generally makes acquisition easier. For interface design, that means giving actions a usable hit area, separating competing controls, and placing the next step where the task makes it useful.

The interesting work starts when those goals compete.

An interface can have generously sized buttons and still make someone travel across the screen after every edit. It can put actions close together and make the wrong one dangerously easy to hit. It can enlarge an invisible click area without giving anyone confidence that the area is available.

This seventh installment of Applied Design Theory examines those tradeoffs. My central argument is that a target should be easy to acquire in the context of an intentional action. Size matters, but so do the path, the surrounding controls, and what happens after a mistake.

The previous article, The Cost of a Pause, looked at what happens after someone acts. Here, we move one step earlier: the effort required to make that action land.

What Fitts’s Law Actually Models

Paul Fitts’s 1954 paper investigated the relationship between movement and precision using controlled motor tasks, including repeated tapping between targets. The work connected the demands of movement with ideas from information theory. It preceded modern graphical interfaces; it was not a study of mobile checkout buttons. MacKenzie’s 1992 research review explains the original experiments and their later application to computer input.

The practical distinction is between reaching a known target and completing an entire task. Finding a control, interpreting its label, deciding whether to proceed, moving to it, activating it, and waiting for the result are different parts of an interaction. Fitts’s Law is especially useful for examining the movement component. It does not turn every delay into a target-size problem.

Consider a hypothetical account page with an unfamiliar icon labeled only by a tooltip. Increasing the button’s hit area might make it easier to select after someone identifies it. That change would not explain what the icon means. A clear label addresses a different obstacle.

That distinction connects to The Decision Tax: a well-placed target cannot compensate for an unclear choice. The user needs both a decision they understand and a control they can operate.

Read the Equation Without Inventing Precision

A common version used in human-computer interaction is the Shannon formulation:

MT = a + b × log₂(1 + D / W)

Here, MT is predicted movement time, D is movement distance, and W represents target width for the modeled task. The coefficients a and b are fitted from observations. They are not universal constants that can be copied into every product. MacKenzie’s 1989 paper develops this formulation; the added 1 distinguishes it from the familiar original logarithmic form.

The logarithmic term is the index of difficulty. We can use it to compare hypothetical geometry without pretending to know how many milliseconds a particular user will need.

Illustrative condition Distance D Width W log₂(1 + D / W)
Baseline 240 24 3.46 bits
Double the width 240 48 2.58 bits
Halve the distance 120 24 2.58 bits
Do both 120 48 1.81 bits

These are calculated examples in consistent arbitrary distance units, not measured user results. They show why size and placement deserve attention together. In this simplified comparison, doubling width and halving distance produce the same ratio. Neither calculation establishes a percentage improvement in task completion or conversion.

Figure 1. Two variables to inspect: the room available for landing and the distance to reach it. The illustration is schematic, not a scale drawing or measured performance chart.

Width Is More Specific Than Overall Area

A long, shallow button can occupy plenty of pixels while still demanding precise vertical positioning. In the basic one-dimensional model, width is measured along the movement axis. Real interfaces introduce two-dimensional shapes and different approach directions.

MacKenzie and Buxton’s 1992 experiment compared alternative ways of representing target width for rectangular targets. Their results support taking both dimensions seriously instead of automatically treating a rectangle’s horizontal length as its usable width.

For a design review, I would inspect the shortest dimension, the likely approach, and the entire interactive boundary. A wide text link with very little height should not receive a free pass because it looks substantial in a screenshot. Nor would I use the experiment’s fitted coefficients as a performance promise for a different device or audience.

Design the Hit Area, Then Make It Understandable

The visible symbol and the interactive region are separate design decisions.

Imagine an overflow menu represented by three dots in a table row. The dots might be visually small because they are a secondary action. That does not require making those few painted pixels the entire target. A real button can provide padding around the icon, an accessible name, and a visible interaction state.

The next question is whether people can recognize that larger area. Budiu’s Nielsen Norman Group article notes that invisible padding may leave users aiming cautiously at the visible symbol. My application of that observation is to make the button’s shape or surrounding treatment communicate its operable area, particularly for important actions.

Figure 2. The active region can extend beyond the icon. This conceptual comparison is not a pixel specification; verify the actual boundaries in the implementation.

Here is a small implementation example. It uses an ordinary button rather than attaching behavior directly to an icon:

<button class="row-action" type="button" aria-label="More actions for Quarterly report">
  <span aria-hidden="true">•••</span>
</button>

.row-action {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  min-inline-size: 48px;
  min-block-size: 48px;
  padding: 8px;
  border: 1px solid currentColor;
  border-radius: 8px;
  color: #173b3b;
  background: #fff;
}

.row-action:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #005fcc;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

The 48-pixel dimensions are an example design choice, not a value derived from Fitts’s equation. A production menu still needs appropriate expanded-state communication, menu behavior, and focus management. This fragment only demonstrates how the button owns its hit area. W3C’s CSS target-size technique similarly distinguishes a control’s size from its text or icon.

I would test the padded edges, not just the center. I would also check whether a parent clips the control, a neighboring link overlaps it, or a transparent overlay intercepts the click. A component’s declared dimensions are only useful if the resulting region actually activates the intended action.

For a design system, this belongs in the shared control. Fixing twenty individual icons independently creates twenty opportunities for the next screen to behave differently. This is the kind of implementation responsibility I discuss in my Atomic Design work: reusable components should carry dependable behavior as well as consistent appearance.

Size and Spacing Solve Different Problems

Size gives the intended action a larger landing region. Spacing helps keep a near miss from becoming another action. Increasing one does not automatically improve the other.

In our hypothetical table, suppose Edit and Delete sit side by side. Expanding both hit areas through overlapping invisible regions would make ownership ambiguous. Increasing padding within two distinct buttons, then giving the controls separation, creates a clearer result.

I would also question whether those actions belong together in that form. Frequent editing and occasional deletion may deserve different presentation. That is a task and consequence judgment, not a claim that Fitts’s Law prescribes a particular menu layout.

Spacing also has a cost. Pushing every control far apart can make sequential work tedious and force more scrolling. The goal is enough separation to distinguish actions while keeping related work reasonably close. Inspect the surrounding target boundaries instead of choosing a gap token in isolation.

What WCAG Requires, and What It Does Not

For web interfaces, two different target-size criteria are often confused:

WCAG criterion Level Size requirement before exceptions
2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA At least 24 × 24 CSS pixels
2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) AAA At least 44 × 44 CSS pixels

Under 2.5.8, an undersized target can satisfy the spacing exception when a 24-CSS-pixel-diameter circle centered on its bounding box does not intersect another target or the corresponding circle around another undersized target. Other exceptions cover equivalent controls, inline targets, unmodified user-agent controls, and essential presentation.

The enhanced criterion has its own exceptions, including equivalent controls and inline targets. It does not provide the same spacing exception.

These are requirements for pointer targets, not only touchscreens. CSS pixels also are not physical screen pixels. Passing one target-size criterion does not establish overall WCAG conformance, and a minimum is not a guarantee of comfortable operation.

For this example, I chose a roomier button because repeated table actions deserve more than a borderline pass. In another interface, I would evaluate density, user needs, and observed errors before choosing the component’s dimensions. I would record an exception when relying on one, rather than turning “there is some whitespace” into an accessibility claim.

Place Controls Along the Task

Distance only becomes meaningful when we identify a starting point.

In an illustrative form, a person completes the final field near the bottom, then travels back to a small Save control in the header. Placing a clearly labeled action after the fields offers a more direct continuation. That recommendation assumes the person is finishing the form in that sequence. It is not evidence that every page needs a fixed bottom bar.

Figure 3. A task-relative placement comparison. The alternative changes both placement and target size, so it cannot isolate the effect of either variable. These are invented layouts, not tested product results.

The distinction matters on complex screens. A report builder might have several entry points: editing a title, changing a filter, selecting rows, or inspecting a chart. There may be no single last field and no universal best location for Save.

I would observe the common sequences, identify the actions that follow each one, and preserve a predictable home for global controls. Contextual actions can appear near a selection when that relationship is understandable. They should not move unpredictably just because the cursor has moved.

A nearby action also needs enough context to be the correct action. If Save actually publishes changes immediately, the label and review flow deserve attention before celebrating a shorter pointer journey. Reducing travel should not remove a step that helps someone understand an important consequence.

Touch Does Not Give Us a Permanent Starting Cursor

On a desktop, pointer position can be observed. On a phone, the previous touch does not reveal where a hand is resting now or how the device is being held.

Hoober’s 2017 account of his touch research emphasizes variation in how people hold and interact with devices. His 2022 discussion challenges the assumption that a mouse-based starting position transfers neatly to touch.

My practical response is to test the actual task on devices, including changes of grip, scrolling, and use with the on-screen keyboard. A bottom action might help one sequence but become obscured or awkward in another. A convenient position in a static phone mockup is a hypothesis about use, not proof of reachability.

Screen Edges Need a Boundary That Really Stops the Pointer

The familiar edge advantage comes from a constrained pointer: if it cannot move beyond a display boundary, a target that reaches that boundary can be harder to overshoot in that direction. This is the desktop case described in Budiu’s explanation.

However, a card edge, browser content edge, or window edge is not necessarily a pointer barrier. Hoober’s touch-era discussion is useful here because it questions whether the assumed boundary exists at all. A neighboring monitor can also turn what appears to be a screen edge into a crossing point.

For a website, I would not defend a tiny corner control by calling it an “infinite target.” I would inspect the actual environment. The browser may have chrome around the page, the control may be inset, and touch interaction has no equivalent cursor clamp. A large enough close button remains a sensible design choice without a borrowed geometric excuse.

Make the Right Action Easier Without Making Mistakes Expensive

Fitts’s Law describes a relationship in movement performance. It does not tell a product team which behavior should be encouraged.

Imagine a cancellation page with a prominent Keep subscription button and a tiny, isolated cancellation link. The arrangement might make one action easier to acquire, but that does not make it a better experience for someone who came to cancel. My standard is that the person’s intended legitimate action should remain clear and operable.

Similarly, a destructive action should not be made inaccessible in the name of caution. I would preserve a usable target, distinguish the consequence, separate it from routine actions, and provide a suitable review or recovery mechanism. Confirmation should earn its interruption through the risk involved.

Input behavior matters too. W3C’s Pointer Cancellation guidance explains why activation on release, using ordinary click behavior where appropriate, supports cancellation. Executing an ordinary action immediately on pointer-down can remove that opportunity. Enlarging the button would not repair that interaction decision.

And if a task requires dragging, enlarging the handle is only one improvement. WCAG 2.2’s Dragging Movements criterion requires a single-pointer alternative without dragging, subject to its exceptions. Keyboard support alone is not necessarily that alternative. A reorderable list might offer clickable Move up and Move down actions as well as dragging.

These checks expand the review beyond whether the target can be hit. They ask whether an attempted action can be controlled and whether the task remains available through another workable interaction.

Walk Through One Complete Redesign

Return to our hypothetical report table. Each row has a report title, an Edit icon, and a Delete icon. The icons are tightly packed. Editing opens a panel whose Save control sits above a long form. A success message appears in a corner after saving.

I would begin with the task “update this report’s notes and return to the list.” That gives the review a definite purpose without assuming every table interaction has the same path.

First, I would make Edit an identifiable button with its own usable area. If the row title opens the report, I would keep that link distinct from the edit action. Making the entire row clickable while also placing several controls inside it would require careful interaction design; it should not be a shortcut for avoiding that distinction.

Second, I would separate deletion from routine editing. I might place it in an explicitly labeled actions menu, depending on how often it is needed. This is an example to test, not a universal endorsement of hiding secondary actions.

Third, I would place Save after the relevant fields or provide a stable action region that stays usable with zoom and the mobile keyboard. Validation messages should not move the button into the path of an already-started click.

Finally, I would return useful feedback near the work: identify which report was saved and preserve a clear way back to the list. That last decision connects target acquisition to the feedback concerns from the previous installment.

The redesign changes several things. If a usability session improves, I would not attribute the entire gain to Fitts’s Law. Labels, grouping, placement, and feedback all contribute. The law helped expose one class of friction; the finished task still needs evaluation as a whole.

Measure Successful Use, Not Just Faster Clicking

Before testing, define the question. Are you studying pointing movement under controlled conditions, or assessing a complete workflow? Both are useful, but they need different measurements.

For the report example, I would record whether people select the intended control, how often they activate a neighbor, whether they correct a mistake, and whether the requested edit is successfully completed. I would inspect task time alongside those outcomes. Faster completion of the wrong action is not a success.

If the specific question concerns geometry, vary size or distance while holding other features reasonably stable. If you change labels and layout together, report the result as a design comparison rather than isolating a motor-performance effect you did not measure.

MacKenzie’s research review documents how device, task, selection method, and treatment of errors complicate comparisons. That is a reason to describe test conditions carefully and avoid importing a coefficient from an unrelated experiment.

For practical product work, I would include people who use different input methods and people with relevant access needs, then test the interface in the states the task creates: validation errors, expanded menus, zoomed text, loading content, and an open keyboard. Automated size checks can find geometric failures. They cannot establish whether the action is understandable or whether the user can recover.

A Review You Can Use on the Next Screen

This is my proposed review sequence, not a validated research instrument:

  1. Name the intended action. What is the person trying to accomplish, and what makes the correct control recognizable?
  2. Trace the approach. What precedes this action? Is the assumed pointer or hand position supported by the task?
  3. Inspect the real target. Which pixels activate it? Check both dimensions, padding, clipping, and overlap.
  4. Inspect its neighbors. What happens after a near miss? Are adjacent actions distinguishable and sufficiently separated?
  5. Check the changing states. Does the target stay usable when content loads, errors appear, the viewport narrows, or the keyboard opens?
  6. Complete and recover. Can the person confirm the result, cancel an accidental attempt, and use an appropriate alternative input method?

A useful review ends with a specific change and a way to evaluate it. “Increase the Edit button’s interactive area and check adjacent-action errors in the row-edit task” is more actionable than “apply Fitts’s Law.”

My position is straightforward: let the interface absorb avoidable precision work. Give the intended action enough room, place it in a sensible sequence, and make its boundaries clear. Then watch someone complete the task. The value of the geometry is in the use it supports.

References

Budiu, R. (2022, July 31). Fitts's law and its applications in UX. Nielsen Norman Group.

Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 47(6), 381-391. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0055392. Historical discussion above also draws on MacKenzie's accessible 1992 review.

Hoober, S. (2017, March 6). Design for fingers, touch, and people, part 1. UXmatters.

Hoober, S. (2022, February 9). Fitts’ law in the touch era. Smashing Magazine.

MacKenzie, I. S. (1989). A note on the information-theoretic basis for Fitts' law. Journal of Motor Behavior, 21, 323-330. DOI.

MacKenzie, I. S. (1992). Fitts' law as a research and design tool in human-computer interaction. Human-Computer Interaction, 7(1), 91-139. DOI.

MacKenzie, I. S., & Buxton, W. (1992). Extending Fitts' law to two-dimensional tasks. In Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 219-226). Association for Computing Machinery. DOI.

World Wide Web Consortium. (n.d.-a). Understanding SC 2.5.2: Pointer cancellation.

World Wide Web Consortium. (n.d.-b). Understanding SC 2.5.5: Target size (enhanced).

World Wide Web Consortium. (n.d.-c). Understanding SC 2.5.7: Dragging movements.

World Wide Web Consortium. (n.d.-d). Understanding SC 2.5.8: Target size (minimum).

World Wide Web Consortium. (n.d.-e). Technique C44: Using CSS to ensure targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Fitts’s Law mean every button should be bigger?

It gives a reason to examine target geometry. A particular button may need more space, a clearer label, a different location, or a combination. Enlarging everything can create crowding and scrolling that deserve their own evaluation.

Does doubling target size cut interaction time in half?

No. The common model is logarithmic, and predicted movement time depends on fitted coefficients. Whole-task time also includes activities the equation does not model, such as understanding the choice and waiting for a result.

Is 44 pixels the WCAG 2.2 AA minimum?

No. The AA target-size criterion uses 24 × 24 CSS pixels with specified exceptions. The enhanced AAA criterion uses 44 × 44 with its own exceptions. Check the applicable criterion in full.

Can a small icon have a large touch target?

Yes. Make the surrounding control interactive, keep its area separate from neighboring actions, and communicate that it is a control. Test the actual padded region, not just the icon.

Should the main action always go at the bottom of a phone screen?

No. Placement should follow the task and remain usable across device states and input methods. A bottom position is a candidate to test, not a universal consequence of Fitts’s Law.

Do these illustrations show measured improvements?

No. They are original explanatory illustrations. The numerical table is a worked calculation, and the form and report examples are hypothetical. No conversion gains or participant results are claimed.

title: 🧠 Do Prompt ao RAG: como fazer um LLM responder sem inventar (e sem processo do cliente)
description:
E aí, dev que já viu uma IA inventar uma política de reembolso que não existe? Ou pior: prometer um recurso que o produto não tem, e você ter que explicar pro cliente que “a máquina se confundiu”?

Pois é. Colocar um LLM pra atender clientes é fácil. Difícil é fazer ele responder com precisão, manter o tom corporativo e não alucinar quando não sabe a resposta.

Foi exatamente isso que um experimento acadêmico que conduzi recentemente em minha Pós-Graduação em Engenharia de IA procurou descobrir: como diferentes estruturas de prompt impactam o comportamento do modelo num cenário real de suporte SaaS. E o resultado? O prompt ajuda – e muito – mas não é suficiente. A virada de chave vem com RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).

Neste post, vou te contar o que o experimento revelou, por que prompt engineering sozinho não resolve, e como implementar RAG na prática com Spring AI – do embedding ao vector store. Bora? 🚀

🔬 O experimento: 15 perguntas, 5 estratégias, 75 interações

O estudo simulou a CloudFlow, uma organização fictícia desenvolvida para o experimento, cuja proposta é oferecer uma plataforma SaaS de gestão de projetos para equipes remotas. O time de suporte recebe centenas de dúvidas diárias por chat e e-mail. A empresa queria usar um LLM para atendimento de primeiro nível, mas precisava entender como a estrutura do prompt afetava a qualidade, a consistência e a segurança das respostas.

Foram elaboradas 15 perguntas de clientes, cobrindo desde dúvidas simples (“Como altero a senha?”) até reclamações complexas (“Recebi uma cobrança duplicada”) e questões de conformidade (“Vocês armazenam dados em conformidade com a LGPD?”).

Cada pergunta foi submetida a 5 estratégias de prompt:

  1. Prompt Simples (Zero-Shot) – Sem contexto, sem papel, sem regra.
  2. Role Prompt – Define a persona: “Você é um especialista de suporte da CloudFlow. Seja profissional, educado e objetivo.”
  3. Estrutura Explícita de Saída – Força o formato: Saudação → Solução → Próximos Passos.
  4. Few-Shot – Fornece exemplos de como a resposta deve ser redigida.
  5. Restrições e Políticas (Guardrails) – “Nunca invente informações. Quando não souber, escale para um humano. Nunca prometa reembolsos.”

Cada execução foi repetida três vezes para medir consistência. No total, 75 interações avaliadas em clareza, completude, tom corporativo, segurança, consistência e risco de alucinação.

📊 O que o experimento revelou (e por que você deveria se importar)

A tabela abaixo resume os resultados médios:

Critério A (Simples) B (Role) C (Estruturado) D (Few-Shot) E (Políticas)
Clareza 3 4 4 5 5
Completude 2 3 5 4 5
Tom Corporativo 2 5 4 5 5
Segurança 2 3 4 4 5
Consistência 2 3 4 5 5
Risco de Alucinação Alto Médio Médio Baixo Muito Baixo

A conclusão é clara: o LLM é o mesmo, mas o comportamento muda completamente dependendo do contexto que você fornece.

  • Role Prompt resolveu o tom, mas não a estrutura.
  • Estrutura Explícita melhorou a completude, mas ainda deixava brechas para alucinação.
  • Few-Shot trouxe consistência cirúrgica.
  • Políticas (Guardrails) reduziram o risco de alucinação ao mínimo.

Nenhuma das estratégias, quando aplicada isoladamente, mostrou-se totalmente eficaz. Com base nos resultados obtidos, o estudo concluiu que a abordagem mais adequada é uma arquitetura híbrida, combinando Role Prompting, Estrutura de Saída, Few-Shot Learning, Políticas de Segurança e RAG para consultar informações do FAQ oficial.

RAG é a peça que faltava para evitar que o modelo “chute” quando não sabe a resposta.

🧩 O que é RAG (e por que ele resolve o problema da alucinação)

RAG significa Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Em português claro: em vez de confiar apenas no que o modelo aprendeu durante o treinamento, você recupera documentos relevantes de uma base de conhecimento e os injeta no prompt antes de pedir a resposta.

LLMs são treinados em grandes datasets, mas não são treinados nos seus dados privados. Treinar um modelo no seu domínio seria caro e demorado. Então, a alternativa é usar RAG para recuperar informações relevantes de um datastore e passá-las ao LLM junto com a pergunta.

O fluxo é mais ou menos assim:

Em vez de o modelo “inventar” a política de reembolso, ele consulta o documento oficial e responde com base nele. É a diferença entre um atendente que sabe a resposta e um que acha que sabe.

🛠️ Mãos à obra: RAG com Spring AI na prática

Vamos implementar o fluxo completo usando Spring AI. O artigo do meu parceiro Sivalabs me ajudou nessa missão.

1. Dependência e configuração

Adicione o starter do Spring AI para OpenAI (ou outro provedor):

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-openai-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-M1</version>
</dependency>

Configure a API key no application.properties:

spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}

2. Convertendo texto em embeddings

O EmbeddingModel transforma texto ou documentos em vetores:

@Component
class MeuComponente {
    private final EmbeddingModel embeddingModel;

    MeuComponente(EmbeddingModel embeddingModel) {
        this.embeddingModel = embeddingModel;
    }

    void converterTextoParaEmbedding() {
        List<Embedding> embeddings = embeddingModel.embed("Eu gosto de Spring Boot");
        List<Embedding> embeddingsDoc = embeddingModel.embed(new Document("Eu gosto de Spring Boot"));
    }
}

3. Armazenando e recuperando do VectorStore

O VectorStore é a interface que abstrai o banco vetorial. Para desenvolvimento, use SimpleVectorStore (em memória). Para produção, PgVectorStore (PostgreSQL com extensão pgvector).

@Configuration
class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    VectorStore vectorStore(EmbeddingModel embeddingModel) {
        return new SimpleVectorStore(embeddingModel);
    }
}

Uso:

@Component
class MeuComponente {
    private final VectorStore vectorStore;

    MeuComponente(VectorStore vectorStore) {
        this.vectorStore = vectorStore;
    }

    void armazenarERecuperar() {
        List<Document> documentos = List.of(
            new Document("A CloudFlow oferece integração nativa com Slack na versão Enterprise."),
            new Document("A política de reembolso é de 30 dias corridos após a compra.")
        );
        vectorStore.add(documentos);

        SearchRequest query = SearchRequest.query("Como funciona a integração com Slack?")
            .withTopK(2);
        List<Document> similares = vectorStore.similaritySearch(query);

        String contexto = similares.stream()
            .map(Document::getContent)
            .collect(Collectors.joining(System.lineSeparator()));
    }
}

O withTopK(2) limita a busca aos 2 documentos mais similares – evitando poluir o prompt com informação irrelevante.

4. Implementando o RAG com ChatClient

Agora o pulo do gato: recuperar os documentos, montar o prompt com contexto e chamar o LLM.

@RestController
class RAGController {
    private final ChatClient chatClient;
    private final VectorStore vectorStore;

    RAGController(ChatClient.Builder builder, VectorStore vectorStore) {
        this.chatClient = builder.build();
        this.vectorStore = vectorStore;
    }

    @GetMapping("/ai/suporte")
    String responderCliente(@RequestParam String pergunta) {
        // 1. Busca documentos relevantes
        List<Document> similares = vectorStore.similaritySearch(
            SearchRequest.query(pergunta).withTopK(3)
        );

        String informacao = similares.stream()
            .map(Document::getContent)
            .collect(Collectors.joining(System.lineSeparator()));

        // 2. Monta o prompt com contexto e política de segurança
        String systemPrompt = """
            Você é um agente de suporte sênior da CloudFlow.
            Use APENAS as informações abaixo para responder.
            Se a informação não estiver disponível, diga que não sabe e escale para um humano.
            Nunca prometa reembolsos ou ações que não pode executar.

            Informações:
            {informacao}
            """;

        // 3. Chama o modelo
        return chatClient.prompt()
            .system(systemPrompt.replace("{informacao}", informacao))
            .user(pergunta)
            .call()
            .content();
    }
}

Pronto. Agora o modelo não está mais “chutando” – ele está fundamentando a resposta em documentos reais e respeitando políticas de segurança. É a combinação de RAG (contexto recuperado) com guardrails (restrições explícitas).

📚 DocumentReader: de arquivos para embeddings

Em vez de criar Document na mão, você pode ler arquivos diretamente com os DocumentReader. O Spring AI oferece implementações como TextReader, JsonReader e PagePdfDocumentReader.

@Component
class CarregadorDocumentos {
    private final VectorStore vectorStore;

    @Value("classpath:faq-cloudflow.txt")
    private Resource resource;

    CarregadorDocumentos(VectorStore vectorStore) {
        this.vectorStore = vectorStore;
    }

    @PostConstruct
    void carregar() {
        var textReader = new TextReader(resource);
        textReader.setCharset(Charset.defaultCharset());
        List<Document> documentos = textReader.get();
        vectorStore.add(documentos);
    }
}

Na prática, você carregaria sua base de conhecimento (FAQ, políticas, manuais) uma vez e ela ficaria disponível para consulta em tempo real.

⚖️ Prompt Engineering vs. RAG: quando usar cada um

Abordagem O que resolve O que não resolve
Prompt Engineering Tom, formato, persona, consistência básica Falta de conhecimento factual; alucinação em perguntas específicas
RAG Falta de conhecimento; fundamentação em dados reais Tom e formato (precisam ser definidos no prompt)
Prompt + RAG Ambos Ainda requer guardrails e monitoramento

A grande sacada do experimento da CloudFlow é que prompt engineering é necessário, mas não suficiente. Você pode ter o melhor role prompt do mundo – se o modelo não tiver acesso à informação correta, ele vai inventar.

RAG resolve a falta de conhecimento. Prompt engineering resolve o comportamento e o tom. Juntos, eles formam a base de um atendimento automatizado confiável.

💡 Dicas quentes para implementar RAG sem sofrer

1. 🎯 Ajuste o topK com cuidado

Buscar 3 documentos é um bom ponto de partida. Muitos documentos poluem o prompt; poucos podem deixar informação de fora. Teste e ajuste.

2. 🧹 Faça chunking inteligente

Documentos muito longos devem ser divididos em pedaços menores (chunks) antes de virar embeddings. Senão, a busca por similaridade fica imprecisa.

3. 🔒 Sempre inclua guardrails

RAG não impede alucinação completamente. O modelo ainda pode ignorar o contexto e inventar. Políticas explícitas (“use APENAS as informações fornecidas”) são essenciais.

4. 🏭 Use pgvector em produção

SimpleVectorStore é ótimo para desenvolvimento, mas para produção use PgVectorStore (PostgreSQL + pgvector) ou outro banco vetorial. O pgvector suporta índices HNSW para busca eficiente em larga escala.

5. 📊 Monitore e avalie

RAG não é “configure e esqueça”. Monitore a qualidade das respostas, colete feedback dos usuários e ajuste o topK, os prompts e a base de conhecimento continuamente.

🎯 Conclusão

O experimento da CloudFlow mostrou que o comportamento do LLM é moldado pela engenharia de contexto. Role prompt, estrutura de saída, few-shot e guardrails fazem diferença – e fazem muita diferença.

A raiz do problema é simples: LLMs não possuem conhecimento nativo sobre os dados da sua organização. Eles desconhecem políticas internas, FAQs e detalhes operacionais específicos. Sem mecanismos para acessar essas informações, inevitavelmente produzirão respostas baseadas em suposições, abrindo espaço para alucinações

A solução é combinar o melhor dos dois mundos:

  • Prompt engineering para definir como o modelo se comporta (tom, formato, segurança).
  • RAG para garantir o que ele sabe (dados reais, recuperados de uma base confiável).

Com Spring AI, isso é mais fácil do que parece: EmbeddingModel, VectorStore, DocumentReader e ChatClient cobrem todo o fluxo, do documento à resposta.

Da próxima vez que sua IA inventar uma política que não existe, lembre-se: o problema não é o modelo. É a falta de contexto.

Já usou RAG em produção? Ou ainda está no mundo do prompt puro? Conta aí nos comentários! 👇

SpringAI #RAG #LLM #PromptEngineering #Java #InteligenciaArtificial

📚 Referências

  • Micro-capstone: Análise de Comportamento de LLM para Atendimento Corporativo (CloudFlow) – experimento com 15 perguntas e 5 estratégias de prompt.
  • Sivalabs: Spring AI RAG using Embedding Models and Vector Databases – implementação prática de RAG com Spring AI, EmbeddingModel, VectorStore e DocumentReader.
  • Spring AI Documentation: QuestionAnswerAdvisor e RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor para implementações prontas de RAG.

Quer mais? No próximo post vou mostrar como usar RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor para implementar RAG modular com Spring AI, incluindo re-ranking e filtragem de documentos. Até lá! 🚀

title: How I Built a Mac Cleaner in Rust
description:
CleanMyMac wanted $40 to renew. I cancelled, looked for a free alternative, and didn't find one that felt like a real Mac app. So I spent a few weeks writing my own. This is the story of SweepMac — and the parts that were genuinely interesting to build.

What it does

SweepMac is a native macOS cleaner. The usual surface: caches, logs, trash, leftover app data, browser privacy data, a disk-usage map, startup audit. Plus a menu-bar health monitor (RAM, CPU, disk, network, thermals) and malware scanning via ClamAV. Free, open-source (BSD-3), no telemetry, no accounts, no subscription. ~3.2 MB app.

The safety model (the part I'm most proud of)

Cleaning apps are dangerous software. One wrong click and you've trashed ~/Library. So before writing a single scanner, I spent time reverse-engineering CleanMyMac's guardrails using REA (a reverse-engineering toolchain). Here's what I found and rebuilt:

  1. Trash-first, always. The only remover in CleanMyMac is MoveToTrashFileRemover — everything goes to Trash, nothing is hard-deleted. SweepMac does the same: trash_paths() moves files to Trash, and the UI says "Undo from the Trash if needed."

  2. SIP check everywhere. CleanMyMac calls isFileProtectedByRootlessAtPath: from 10 different frameworks. I traced it — it forwards to Apple's own NSFileManager isFileProtectedByRootless:. SweepMac uses the public equivalent: stat flags & SF_RESTRICTED (0x80000). Every scanner walk skips restricted paths. Verified live against /System/Library/CoreServices → protected.

  3. Ignore list. CleanMyMac has an IgnorableNodeType framework with live publishers. SweepMac has a persisted set at ~/.sweepmac/ignored — per-item "Ignore" button, skipped by all scans.

  4. Pre-clean snapshots. CleanMyMac has SnapshotsStorage with makeSnapshot/restore. SweepMac writes a JSON manifest (~/.sweepmac/snapshots/.json) of every item before cleaning — and aborts the clean if the snapshot fails to save. Never clean what you didn't record.

  5. System-app data is never "orphan." CleanMyMac's orphan sweep flags any reverse-DNS folder over 1 MB under Library whose bundle ID isn't in the installed-apps set. But that set is built only from /Applications + ~/Applications — Apple's system apps live in /System/Applications and are never in the set. So com.apple.mediaanalysisd (428 MB), com.apple.Maps (13 MB) all qualified as "orphan" and were preselected for deletion. One click trashed live system data. Fix: skip com.apple.* keys (the same rule CleanMyMac's Protection module already uses).

  6. Space Lens can't trash user-data roots. SpaceLens lists top-level children of ~ (Library, Documents, Movies) — and showed the same "Clean selected" button as every other page. One checkbox + click = trashing ~/Library. Fix: disable the Clean button on that route entirely.

The architecture

Five crates, one process:

sweep-core — pipeline traits (Scanner), JunkItem, shared helpers (home, dir_size, file_size, trash_paths), ignore list, snapshots, SIP guard.

sweep-scanners — one file per feature: SystemJunk, TrashBin, Uninstaller, Privacy, Performance, Protection, Clutter, SpaceLens, Malware, ClamAV setup. Scanners enumerate only, never delete.

sweep-health — menu-bar sensors (raw syscalls + Mach APIs, std+libc only). 2s sampler thread, channels only.

sweep-shell — egui app, native menu bar (NSStatusItem/NSMenu via objc), updater, login items. UI state lives here, not in scanners.

sweep-helper — privileged worker scaffold (dev-only, never run privileged).

The interesting bugs

Pump deadlock. The Protection page's first-run ClamAV setup streams log lines. I ended setup mode only when a log line matched "Protected" / "already running" / "is up" / "failed" / "not found". But "Cannot write config files.", "cannot launch clamd: …", and "clamd started but not answering yet — retry shortly." (the expected first-run outcome) matched none. Busy stayed true forever — Scan, Clean, and "Set up protection" all disabled until restart. Fix: treat channel disconnect (sender dropping) as "done." Added 2 tests for the exact case.

240 subprocesses per second. update() runs on every input event (~120 Hz). Per frame: loginitems::status() spawned id -u + launchctl print, tray::menu_icon_enabled() read the config file, fda_granted() did two read_dir calls. Fix: 5s TTL cache with invalidation on toggle — same pattern as the clamd ping cache.

Clutter scanned the same trees 2–3×. Roots included /, /Users, /Applications, /Library, and ~/Downloads simultaneously, each walked 4 levels deep. ~/Downloads/old.dmg was found through / (depth 4), /Users (depth 3), and the Downloads root (depth 1) — three identical rows, tripled totals, cleaning failed twice with "No such file." Fix: dedupe output by path. Also added /Volumes to the skip list — external disks and NAS shares were being walked 4 levels deep.

Malware scan failures were invisible. Read errors and clamd errors only eprintln!'d; the item list stayed empty and the UI said "Nothing found — this area is clean." Fix: count failed files, show the count in progress, and never claim "clean" after an incomplete pass.

The ClamAV dance

ClamAV lives at /opt/homebrew/sbin/clamd (not in GUI PATH — find_bin covers it). First freshclam needs DatabaseMirror in the conf (Homebrew's default lacks it). clamd takes minutes to load signatures on first start — the ping loop waits 60s, don't shorten it. The setup flow handles all of this automatically: brew install clamav → generate configs → freshclam → launch clamd. No terminal commands for the user.

What I skipped

iCloud placeholder awareness — no cloud files are scanned, so nothing to guard.

Bulk scan progress/cancel — I excluded Protection from "Scan all" (opt-in) rather than adding a cancel button. Clutter stays in bulk but is much faster now with root dedup and /Volumes skip.

Snapshot restore UI — manifests are written and pruned to 10 newest. Restore is manual (open the JSON in ~/.sweepmac/snapshots/).

Intel build — Apple Silicon only. rustup target add x86_64-apple-darwin + release flag when someone asks.

Numbers

78 tests (was 70 before this audit round)

5 crates, ~3.2 MB app

0 new warnings (only pre-existing objc-macro cfg noise + libc deprecation notes)

17 audit findings fixed in one pass

Links

GitHub: https://github.com/ankushthakur2007/sweepmac

Latest release (DMG): https://github.com/ankushthakur2007/sweepmac/releases/latest

Update checks run against GitHub Releases (releases/latest) — no self-hosted feed

Happy to answer questions about the Rust/egui architecture, the ClamAV TCP protocol, or how I extracted CleanMyMac's safety checks.

title: Your AI Portal Isn't Ready Until a Stranger Can Recover from Failure
description:
A branded AI portal can look finished long before it is ready for real people.

The logo is crisp. The custom domain resolves on the founder's laptop. The home page has a polished banner and a generous catalog of models. Then the first outside user arrives, picks the wrong sign-in method, lands on a callback error, opens the pricing page on a phone, and asks a question the documentation never anticipated.

That is the awkward gap between configured and usable.

The usual response is to add more copy, more navigation, and more features. I think that is backwards. A portal becomes trustworthy when a stranger can recover from confusion without needing the person who built it. The most useful launch work therefore happens in the failure paths, not in the hero section.

Start with an incognito window, not the admin panel

Admins are terrible test users. Our browser remembers sessions, our DNS cache is warm, and we already know what every vague label is supposed to mean. Familiarity quietly fills gaps that a new visitor cannot cross.

Open the site in a private window and give yourself one simple job: sign in, find one service, understand its price, and locate the instructions for using it. Do the same on a phone. Better still, ask someone who has never seen the dashboard to try while you stay silent.

Watch where they hesitate. A pause before clicking is often more informative than a bug report. It may reveal that the main action has a clever name instead of a clear one, that the service catalog exposes internal terminology, or that the login page gives equal visual weight to methods your audience rarely uses.

Responsive design is not merely about squeezing a desktop layout onto a narrow screen. Content has to remain readable and controls have to work at the available viewport size. The responsive design guidance on web.dev is a useful baseline when checking the banner, navigation, pricing tables, and documentation on smaller screens.

Treat sign-in as a round trip

Seeing a login button is not evidence that authentication works. The real path leaves your site, passes through an identity provider, returns to a callback, creates or retrieves an account, and finally restores the user to a sensible location.

Test that whole loop while logged out. Then test cancellation, an expired session, a second browser, and a user who presses Back halfway through. Error messages should say what happened and what the person can do next without leaking account details.

This is also where security and usability meet. Generic authentication errors can reduce account enumeration risk, while throttling and logging help with automated attacks. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet explains the trade-offs more carefully than a UI-focused launch guide can.

A useful sign-in failure does not say OAuth error 400. It says the sign-in could not be completed, offers a safe retry, and points to support if the problem continues. The detailed provider response belongs in protected logs, tied to a request or correlation ID that support can use.

A custom domain is a chain, not a textbox

Adding a hostname in a dashboard is only one link. DNS must direct the name to the right target, the certificate must cover that hostname, the server must present the intended site, and redirects must not bounce users between old and new addresses.

CNAME records are commonly used to alias one hostname to another, but DNS behavior and restrictions still depend on where the record sits and how the provider handles it. Cloudflare's DNS record type reference is a helpful refresher before changing production DNS.

You can run a small smoke test without sending a credential anywhere:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

host="${1:?usage: ./probe.sh portal.example.com}"

echo "== DNS =="
dig +short "$host"

echo "== HTTPS response =="
curl --silent --show-error \
  --output /dev/null \
  --write-out 'status=%{http_code} remote_ip=%{remote_ip} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' \
  "https://$host/"

echo "== Certificate dates and names =="
echo | openssl s_client -connect "$host:443" -servername "$host" 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates -ext subjectAltName

This script does not certify the application. It simply separates a few layers. If DNS returns nothing, rewriting homepage copy will not help. If TLS fails, testing an API key is premature. If transport works but the page is wrong, you now know to inspect routing or host configuration.

Run the probe from another network as well. Your machine may still have an old answer cached, and DNS changes are not observed everywhere at exactly the same moment.

Pricing copy should survive a screenshot

Users do not see your internal cost model. They see a number, a unit, and whatever explanation fits near the button. If those three pieces do not make sense in a screenshot with no surrounding context, the pricing page is asking support to finish the interface.

Write down what triggers a charge, which unit is being purchased, whether displayed values include your adjustment, and where usage can be reviewed. Avoid mixing terms such as request, task, credit, second, and image unless their relationship is explicit.

Then test an intentionally small operation and reconcile the visible records. An HTTP success, a completed generation, a usage entry, and a billing entry are related events, but they are not interchangeable proof. Record each result separately. If a workflow is asynchronous, preserve the task ID rather than repeatedly creating new tasks when the browser appears idle.

This is less glamorous than tuning a margin slider, but it prevents the worst kind of pricing surprise: one where both the operator and the customer are looking at correct numbers and interpreting them differently.

Documentation should answer the question after the happy path

Most onboarding docs explain how to begin. Far fewer explain what to collect when beginning does not work.

A practical first page can be short. It should show where to sign in, how to reach the primary service, how pricing is measured, where usage appears, and how to contact support. The troubleshooting section should ask for a timestamp, a sanitized error, the affected route, and a non-secret request or task ID. It should explicitly warn people not to paste API keys, session cookies, or full authorization headers into tickets.

Screenshots help when they show decisions, but they age quickly when used as decoration. Crop them to the relevant control, add a sentence describing the expected result, and review them whenever navigation changes. Alt text should explain what the image contributes rather than repeat “screenshot of dashboard.”

The best documentation is usually written from actual support conversations. When the same question appears twice, improve the page. When a page never answers a real question, consider deleting it. A small, maintained guide beats a large museum of old interfaces.

Make launch evidence boring and easy to hand over

Memory is not a release process. Keep a plain-text record that another person can understand:

Audience and primary task:
Test time and network:
Desktop browser / mobile device:
Anonymous homepage result:
Sign-in round-trip result:
DNS / TLS result:
Service discovery result:
Price and unit understood:
Small usage test and record IDs:
Support route tested:
Open problem, owner, next check:

Use pass, fail, or not checked. Do not turn an empty field into an implied success. Store sensitive evidence somewhere appropriate and put only safe references in the handoff.

This record changes the launch conversation. Instead of “the portal seems ready,” the team can say which journey was tested, from where, at what time, and what remains unknown. That is a much stronger foundation for inviting users than another round of homepage polishing.

A branded portal does not earn confidence because every setting has a value. It earns confidence because the common journey is understandable and the broken journey is recoverable. Keep the first experience narrow, make the units unambiguous, test the domain in layers, and let real user confusion decide what to improve next.

References and further reading

  • Ace Data Cloud subsite settings guide
  • Responsive web design basics — web.dev
  • Authentication Cheat Sheet — OWASP
  • DNS record types — Cloudflare
