title: Next.js Doesn't Render Pages Anymore. It Streams Something Stranger.
description:
If you ask ten developers what the "use client" directive does in Next.js, at least eight of them will give you the same intuitive answer:

"Server Components run on the server. Client Components run in the browser. So 'use client' tells Next.js to run the component on the client."

It sounds completely logical. The directive is literally named use client. The mental model seems clean: two environments, two directives, a neat split between backend and frontend.

Except that is not how Next.js works at all.

If Client Components only ran in the browser, why does this code crash your server with ReferenceError: window is not defined?

"use client";

export default function UserProfile() {
  // 💥 Crashes during build or initial page load on the server!
  const screenWidth = window.innerWidth;

  return <div>Screen width: {screenWidth}px</div>;
}

If it were truly client-side only, window would be defined, the browser would evaluate it, and there would be no error on the server.

The truth is surprising to many developers: Client Components in Next.js also execute on the server.

The "use client" directive does not define where a component executes. It defines a module boundary that dictates what code gets packaged into your browser bundle.

To write fast, bug-free Next.js applications, you have to dismantle the "server vs. client execution" myth and understand what the rendering engine is actually doing behind the scenes.

The Core Misconception: Execution vs. Bundling

In the App Router, every file is a Server Component by default.

When you prepend "use client" to the top of a file, you are not saying "never run this on Node.js."

You are telling the bundler:

"Everything exported from this file, and anything it imports, needs to be compiled into a JavaScript bundle and sent across the network to the browser. Also, allow this sub-tree to use React hooks (useState, useEffect) and browser event listeners (onClick)."

When a user visits a route for the first time, Next.js performs Server-Side Pre-rendering (SSR) for your entire page—including your Client Components.

Here is what happens during that initial request:

  1. Server Components execute on the server. They can access databases, read files, read secret environment variables, and compute data. They output a stream of structured UI instructions called the RSC Payload.
  2. Client Components ALSO execute on the server. Next.js executes their render function once on the server to generate semantic HTML tags (<div class="profile">...</div>).
  3. The browser receives raw HTML immediately. The user sees the fully formed page almost instantly (First Contentful Paint).
  4. The JavaScript bundle downloads in the background. React runs in the browser, matches the JavaScript event listeners to the existing DOM nodes, and brings the page to life. This second step is called Hydration. 
                ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                │             INITIAL HTTP REQUEST              │
                └──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                         Next.js Server Execution
                                       │
        ┌──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                                             ▼
┌───────────────────────────────┐             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│       Server Component        │             │       Client Component        │
├───────────────────────────────┤             ├───────────────────────────────┤
│ • Runs ON SERVER ONLY         │             │ • Runs ON SERVER (Initial SSR)│
│ • Zero JS sent to browser     │             │ • Bundled into client JS      │
│ • Direct DB / Secrets access  │             │ • Re-runs in browser          │
│ • Emits: RSC Payload          │             │ • Emits: HTML + JS Bundle     │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘             └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                │                                             │
                └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                       │
                        Combined Server Response
                                       │
              ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
              ▼                                                 ▼
    Raw Pre-rendered HTML                          RSC Payload Stream
  (Instant paint on screen)                    (Virtual DOM data instructions)
              │                                                 │
              └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                              Browser Environment
                                       │
                        ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                        ▼                             ▼
                 Fast First Paint              React Hydration
              (Non-interactive HTML)         (Attaches events & hooks)

Once you see this diagram, the window is not defined error makes immediate sense. When Next.js pre-rendered your Client Component on the server to generate that initial HTML, Node.js evaluated window.innerWidth. Because Node.js has no browser window, it blew up before the HTML ever left the server.

What Actually Is the RSC Payload?

Most developers know what HTML is, and they know what JavaScript is. But Next.js introduces a third artifact that is the true backbone of the App Router: the React Server Component (RSC) Payload.

When the server evaluates your Server Components, it does not produce HTML directly. Instead, it generates a compact, streaming binary/JSON format representing the virtual tree.

Here is a conceptual look at what an RSC Payload stream contains:

  1. Rendered HTML-like UI descriptions of all Server Components (tags, attributes, text).
  2. Placeholders ("holes") where Client Components should go.
  3. References to JavaScript chunk URLs that the browser needs to load to fill those client holes.
  4. Serialized props passed from Server Components into Client Components.

Let's look at a concrete example. Suppose you have this page:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx (Server Component by default)
import Counter from './Counter';

export default async function DashboardPage() {
  const user = await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id: 1 } });

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Welcome back, {user.name}</h1>
      <Counter initialCount={user.savedItemsCount} />
    </main>
  );
}

And your counter component:

// app/dashboard/Counter.tsx
"use client";

import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Counter({ initialCount }: { initialCount: number }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount);

  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>
      Saved Items: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

When Next.js renders DashboardPage, it executes the database query on the server. The code for db.user.findUnique never leaves the server. The database driver is not in your browser bundle.

Next.js then serializes the result into an RSC stream that looks conceptually like this:

[
  "$", "main", null, {
    "children": [
      ["$", "h1", null, { "children": "Welcome back, Sarah" }],
      ["$", "$L1", null, { "initialCount": 5 }]
    ]
  }
]

Notice ["$", "$L1", null, { "initialCount": 5 }].

$L1 is a reference placeholder. Elsewhere in the stream, Next.js specifies:

1:I["./app/dashboard/Counter.tsx", ["chunks/counter.js"], "default"]

The server says: "At this spot in the tree, place the component exported from Counter.tsx. You will find its code in chunks/counter.js. And give it the prop initialCount: 5."

Why does Next.js stream this payload instead of just sending plain HTML?

Because when a user navigates between pages on the client (client-side routing), Next.js does not re-download a full HTML page. It requests only the new route's RSC Payload!

React merges the new RSC Payload directly into the existing browser DOM. Any client-side state in parent components (like an active dropdown, playing audio, or scroll position) stays preserved, while the server components update seamlessly.

The Boundary Rule: What Can Cross the Line?

Because Server Components run in an isolated server context and Client Components run across both environments, the border between them has strict physics.

1. Props Must Be Serializable

When a Server Component passes props to a Client Component, those props must travel across the network inside the RSC Payload.

That means props must be serializable to JSON (with React-extended support for Promises, BigInt, Date, and Set/Map):

// ❌ FAILS: Functions cannot be serialized across the network
<ClientButton onClick={() => console.log("clicked")} />

// ❌ FAILS: Classes with methods lose their prototype
<ClientUserCard user={new UserModel("Sarah")} />

// ✅ WORKS: Plain objects, strings, numbers, booleans, arrays
<ClientUserCard user={{ name: "Sarah", role: "admin" }} />

// ✅ WORKS: Server Actions (marked with "use server")
<ClientButton action={deleteAccountAction} />

If you try to pass an inline callback function from a Server Component to a Client Component, Next.js throws an error: Functions cannot be passed directly to Client Components unless you explicitly expose it with "use server".

2. The Import Flow Is One-Way Only

You can import a Client Component into a Server Component. But you cannot import a Server Component directly into a Client Component.

"use client";

// ❌ This does NOT work as a Server Component anymore!
import ServerSecretWidget from './ServerSecretWidget';

export default function ClientModal() {
  return (
    <div>
      <ServerSecretWidget />
    </div>
  );
}

Why? Because the moment you import a file into a file marked "use client", the bundler treats that imported file as part of the client bundle too!

If ServerSecretWidget used private database credentials, the bundler would either throw a compilation error or, worse, attempt to bundle backend modules into the browser.

The Slot Pattern: Putting Server Components Inside Client Components

If Client Components cannot import Server Components, how do you put a data-fetching Server Component inside a Client Component (like an interactive animated modal or collapsible sidebar)?

This is where the Composition Pattern (or Slot Pattern) comes in, and it is one of the most elegant architectural patterns in React.

Instead of importing the Server Component into the Client Component, you pass it as a children prop:

// components/CollapsibleSection.tsx
"use client";

import { useState, ReactNode } from 'react';

export default function CollapsibleSection({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(true);

  return (
    <section>
      <button onClick={() => setIsOpen(prev => !prev)}>
        {isOpen ? "Collapse" : "Expand"}
      </button>
      {isOpen && <div>{children}</div>}
    </section>
  );
}

Now, in your Server Component:

// app/page.tsx (Server Component)
import CollapsibleSection from '@/components/CollapsibleSection';
import HeavyDatabaseList from '@/components/HeavyDatabaseList';

export default async function Page() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Project Feed</h1>
      {/* HeavyDatabaseList stays a Server Component! */}
      <CollapsibleSection>
        <HeavyDatabaseList />
      </CollapsibleSection>
    </main>
  );
}

How does this work?

HeavyDatabaseList is evaluated on the server by Page.tsx. Its output is converted into the RSC Payload.

CollapsibleSection receives the already-resolved React elements as children. The code for HeavyDatabaseList never touches the browser bundle.

CollapsibleSection handles the interactive toggle in the browser without ever knowing or caring what rendered inside its slot.

Three Costly Mistakes Developers Make (And How to Fix Them)

Understanding the rendering pipeline protects you from the three most common performance killers and bugs in Next.js:

Mistake 1: Placing "use client" at the Root of a Feature

When developers need a single useState or onClick handler, they often slap "use client" at the very top of the page or layout.

// ❌ Anti-pattern: The entire subtree becomes client-side bundled
"use client";

import { useState } from 'react';
import HeavyChart from './HeavyChart'; // 120 kB bundled!
import LargeDataList from './LargeDataList'; // 85 kB bundled!

export default function AnalyticsDashboard() {
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("all");

  return (
    <div>
      <FilterDropdown value={filter} onChange={setFilter} />
      <HeavyChart filter={filter} />
      <LargeDataList filter={filter} />
    </div>
  );
}

The Fix: Push the client boundary down to the leaves.

Keep the container as a Server Component. Extract only the interactive input into a small Client Component:

// ✅ Better: Only the interactive trigger is a client component
// app/dashboard/FilterDropdown.tsx
"use client";

export function FilterDropdown({ current, onSelect }) { ... }

Keep heavy static presentation or data-fetching logic in Server Components to keep the JavaScript bundle lean.

Mistake 2: Accessing Browser APIs Outside of useEffect

Because Client Components render on the server during the initial request, accessing window, document, or localStorage during the render phase causes runtime server crashes:

"use client";

export default function ThemeWidget() {
  // 💥 Error: window is not defined during SSR
  const theme = localStorage.getItem("theme") ?? "light";

  return <div>Current theme: {theme}</div>;
}

The Fix:

Move browser API access into useEffect (which only executes in the browser after mount), or wrap it with a mount guard:

"use client";

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export default function ThemeWidget() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState<string>("light");

  useEffect(() => {
    // ✅ Safe: useEffect runs ONLY in the browser after hydration
    const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme");
    if (saved) setTheme(saved);
  }, []);

  return <div>Current theme: {theme}</div>;
}

Mistake 3: Hydration Mismatches from Non-Deterministic Values

If the HTML produced on the server differs from what the client produces during its first hydration pass, React emits a noisy console warning:

Text content does not match server-rendered HTML.

Common triggers:

"use client";

export default function Timestamp() {
  // ⚠️ Server renders at 12:00:00.000, browser hydrates at 12:00:00.120!
  return <span>Current time: {new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}</span>;
}

When React hydrates, it expects the server HTML and the initial client render tree to match character-for-character. If they disagree, React has to throw away the server HTML and rebuild the DOM tree from scratch, degrading performance.

For values that depend on the client's local time or random numbers, defer the dynamic rendering until after mounting, or use suppressHydrationWarning on individual tags where mismatches are intentional.

Quick Reference: Server vs. Client Components

Capability Server Component (Default) Client Component ("use client")
Initial Execution Server only Server (SSR) and Browser
Shipped to Client Bundle 0 kB JavaScript Full component code + imports
React Hooks (useState, useEffect) ❌ No ✅ Yes
Browser APIs (window, navigator) ❌ No ✅ Inside useEffect or events
Direct DB & Secret Key Access ✅ Yes ❌ No
Render Output RSC Payload (virtual stream) HTML string (SSR) + Client DOM
Primary Purpose Data fetching, security, zero bundle User interactivity, state, event handlers

The Mental Shift

Next.js does not split your application into two separate worlds. It weaves them together into a single continuous pipeline.

The next time you type "use client", remember:

You are not telling Next.js where to execute the code. You are drawing a line for the compiler, telling it where interactive JavaScript needs to begin, and allowing the server to hand off the user interface smoothly to the client.

Once you treat "use client" as a boundary rather than a location, the App Router transforms from a confusing maze of hydration errors into one of the most capable full-stack architectures in modern web development.

When you first started working with the Next.js App Router, what was the mental model hurdle that tripped you up the most? And what is your favorite pattern for keeping client bundles minimal?

References:

  • Next.js Official Documentation: Server Components
  • Next.js Official Documentation: Client Components
  • React Working Group: React Server Components Architecture
  • Dan Abramov: The Two Reacts

title: A Signed Mandate Is Not Authorization: A Rust SDK for AI-Agent Transactions
description:
A Signed Mandate Is Not Authorization: A Rust SDK for AI-Agent Transactions

An AI agent submits a $50 transfer request.

Its mandate has a valid Ed25519 signature. The signed scope permits transfers up to $100 per transaction. The requested amount is below that limit.

Would you authorize the payment?

Not yet.

The signature and the amount check establish useful facts. Neither establishes whether the delegation has been revoked, whether the agent has already exhausted a cumulative budget, or whether the request has been processed before.

That distinction matters when designing authorization boundaries for AI agents.

What can we actually verify offline?

Consider an issuer signing a mandate that identifies a principal, an agent, permitted actions, and transaction constraints.

A local verifier can check the issuer's signature against an explicitly trusted public key. It can then evaluate a specific transaction against the verified mandate.

For example:

  • Agent: agent:treasury-bot
  • Action: transfer
  • Per-transaction limit: USD 100.00
  • Requested amount: USD 50.00

If the signature is valid and the request satisfies the static constraints, the system can conclude that the request is eligible for an authoritative authorization check.

It cannot conclude that the payment should be executed.

There are at least three reasons.

Revocation: An issuer can revoke a delegation after signing it. The old signature remains cryptographically valid.

Cumulative budgets: An agent may have spent its total allowance across earlier requests. A local per-transaction check cannot establish the remaining distributed balance.

Replay: A request can be validly signed and still be submitted more than once.

These are mutable facts that require an authoritative source of current state.

Encoding that boundary in Rust

This distinction is central to FintechBear KYA, an open-source Rust SDK for AI-agent delegated authority verification and transaction policy evaluation.

The SDK separates a local policy result from a final authorization decision.

A successful local evaluation produces a PolicyOutcome. It does not produce an automatic Allow.

There is deliberately no From<PolicyOutcome> for Decision conversion.

Instead, the application must go through the authorize bridge and supply an OnlineAuthorizer that can make the authoritative decision.

The trade-off is deliberate: the SDK cannot independently authorize a payment. Applications need to implement the online authority.

That is a better failure mode than silently treating an offline check as permission.

A runnable example

The repository contains a Rust demo that exercises this distinction.

git clone https://github.com/fintechbear/fintechbear-kya-suite.git
cd fintechbear-kya-suite
cargo run -p kya-examples --example demo

The example:

  1. Configures an explicitly trusted issuer public key.
  2. Creates and verifies a genuinely signed Ed25519 mandate using a test-only signing key.
  3. Evaluates the USD 50.00 transaction against the USD 100.00 limit.
  4. Rejects a mandate whose signature has been modified.
  5. Denies a USD 100.01 request that exceeds the signed limit.
  6. Sends an eligible policy outcome to an example online authorizer that cannot establish approval.

The demo reports an eligible static outcome, but that result is not authorization.

Its failure cases include:

[4] in-scope transaction is ELIGIBLE (requires_online_authorization=true).

[5a] tampered signature rejected fail-closed:
     signature did not verify (VerificationSignatureInvalid).

[5b] over-limit intent denied by stage C:
     reason=AmountExceedsLimit (terminal, fail-closed).

The online-authority part of the demonstration also shows that an unresolved approval requirement or an unavailable authority does not become an Allow.

These are illustrative test transactions, not real payment executions.

You can inspect the full demo source and captured output.

Why exact money matters

Authorization constraints should not depend on floating-point rounding.

FintechBear KYA uses integer minor units with explicit currency information.

For USD, 10_000 minor units represent $100.00. The example's $100.01 request exceeds that limit by exactly one cent.

That makes the boundary explicit and testable.

It does not solve cumulative spending enforcement. Per-transaction limits and distributed budgets are different problems.

What the SDK does not implement

This is an early v0.1.0 pre-release.

The open-source core provides local evidence verification, deterministic static policy evaluation, and interfaces for the later authorization and execution stages.

It does not currently ship:

  • Agent proof-of-possession verification.
  • A concrete online revocation service.
  • Distributed cumulative-budget enforcement.
  • Global replay protection.
  • Payment execution enforcement.

Its AP2-style adapter is experimental; confirmed AP2 wire interoperability is not claimed.

The project has not undergone an independent third-party security audit and is not presented as a production-ready payment authorization system.

These boundaries are documented in the security limitations and threat model.

The engineering question

For a financial action initiated by an AI agent, signature verification and static policy are necessary parts of a possible design.

But where should the boundary between verified evidence and current authorization live?

FintechBear KYA puts that boundary explicitly in the API: local eligibility cannot be silently promoted to an authorization decision.

I'd be interested in how other Rust and security engineers approach this separation, particularly when the authoritative service is unavailable.

Source: https://github.com/fintechbear/fintechbear-kya-suite

Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance.

title: The fix for an empty state isn't filling it
description:
Last week I posted on Indie Hackers about a decision in my renovation cost tool: it ships with an empty price book. The model reads the floor plan, plain Python does the math, and any line without a real, sourced price stays "unpriced." I admitted the obvious cost. The first run feels like homework.

Within a day, seven people left real, specific suggestions. Not "great post." Actual designs. None of it is built yet. But reading them side by side taught me something I want to argue for:

The fix for an empty state is not filling it. It's making the blanks look like progress.

Here is how I'm sorting the ideas, including the one I'm turning down.

Keeping: show the blank as a step, not a failure

Three people (topapps, daiwik_builds and leadscout) landed on the same idea from different directions:

  • Show progress, like "7 of 12 lines priced," instead of a wall of blanks.
  • Label any total built from priced lines as partial, so nobody mistakes it for the full budget.
  • Ask for the lines that move the total the most first.
  • Next to every blank, say why it is blank and what to do next. Something like: "Unpriced: no quote yet. Request one from the package below."

What I like about this: it changes nothing about the numbers. The tool still refuses to invent a price. It just stops making the user feel like the tool is broken. An "unpriced" label with no next step reads as an error. The same label with a reason and an action reads as a to-do list.

The "biggest lines first" part is the one I'm least sure how to do honestly. To know which line moves the total most, you need some sense of its size before it's priced. Quantities alone (square feet of floor, length of wall) might be enough to rank by. A guessed price would not be allowed.

Keeping: let the price book fill itself through normal use

liranblumenberg pointed out that the tool already makes quote packages for contractors. So when a quote comes back, record it straight into the price book, with the source and the date attached. The empty book fills up as a side effect of doing the thing you were going to do anyway.

They added a detail I hadn't thought about: the UI should say clearly whether a quote can be reused on another project. A floor refinishing quote for one house is not a price for every house, and reusing it silently would be exactly the kind of quiet drift I'm trying to avoid.

Keeping: put scope next to the price

ska1296 suggested listing what each contractor's quote includes and excludes (debris removal, permits and so on) right next to the number. Two quotes for "refinish floors" are not comparable if one includes hauling and one doesn't. This is a small change that makes the real numbers more honest, which is the whole point of the tool.

Keeping: sanity check the one place the model touches numbers

gokulravi333 found the weak spot in my own argument. I say "no AI in the numbers," but the model reads the floor plan, and room dimensions are numbers. Their suggestion: check that room areas add up to the total, that dimensions fall in a plausible range, and flag "check this" when they don't.

This one stings a little because it's correct. Right now the safeguard is that a person has to confirm the overlay before outputs are treated as confirmed. A cheap arithmetic check before that step would catch the obvious misreads without asking the person to spot them.

Refusing: an AI estimate column with a confidence score

toptrack_software suggested a two column view: an AI estimate, clearly labeled, next to the real quotes, plus a confidence percentage.

I understand why. It directly fixes the homework feeling. A user opens the tool and immediately sees a number. And I suspect it's the version that would win in a side by side test of first impressions.

I'm still saying no, for two reasons.

First, anchoring. topapps replied in the same thread that if I ever add an AI number, it should be a wide range, kept out of the total, and visually secondary. I agree with that framing, and I think it shows the problem: the moment a number is on screen, it becomes the reference point. A buyer who sees "AI estimate" before any real quote arrives will judge the real quotes against a number nobody can trace.

Second, a confidence percentage looks like evidence. I have no way to say what "72% confident" means for a labor price in a specific city. If I can't explain where a number came from, I don't think the tool should show it, and a confidence score is a number too.

I could be wrong about this. It's the decision in this post I'm least comfortable with, because it trades a better first run for a principle.

What I learned from the thread itself

The post I wrote defended a decision. The comments didn't argue with the decision much. They redesigned the experience around it. That's a better outcome than agreement, and I wouldn't have gotten it if I hadn't written down the downside plainly. "The first run feels like homework" is the line people built on.

Everything above is a plan. The tool has still only been tested on fixtures, not real buyers, so I don't know yet which of these changes matters most in practice.

My question for you

If you've shipped a product that deliberately shows blanks or "unknown" instead of a guess, what made users accept it? Was it progress indicators, clear next steps, or did you eventually give in and add an estimate?

title: 🚀 Building Spring by Example V2: Completing Module 06 - Capstone Application
description:
When I started learning Spring, I noticed something about many of the tutorials I found.

They often showed how to use a feature, but not always why it worked or when you should choose one approach over another.

I learn best by building things and documenting what I discover, so I started a project called spring-by-example.

The idea is simple: instead of building one large application, I'm creating a collection of small, focused examples where each example explores a specific Spring concept with clear explanations, tests, and documentation.

I'm happy to say that I've now completed Module 06 - Capstone Application. 🎉

This module is a little different from the previous ones. Rather than focusing on individual Spring features, it brings together concepts explored throughout the project and demonstrates how they work together in complete applications.

The module covers:

  • Application Design and Architecture
  • Spring Boot
  • Spring Data and Persistence
  • REST APIs
  • Spring Security
  • Transaction Management
  • Modular Architecture with Spring Modulith
  • Application Testing
  • Integration Between Spring Technologies
  • End-to-End Application Verification

One of the most interesting parts of this module was exploring how to structure a Spring Boot application into well-defined modules.

Using Spring Modulith, I explored how to organize an application around business capabilities, establish clear module boundaries, manage dependencies, and communicate between modules using application events.

This helped reinforce an important architectural idea: even when building a monolithic application, you don't have to organize everything into one large, tightly coupled codebase.

I also explored how to test applications built with these technologies.

Testing individual components is important, but it is equally important to understand how those components behave when working together inside a running Spring application.

That led to the next example: integrating multiple Spring technologies.

For this example, I built an Order Management application using:

  • Spring Boot
  • Spring Data JPA
  • Spring Web
  • Spring Security
  • Spring Modulith
  • Transaction Management
  • Application Events

The application is organized into four business modules:

  • Catalog - manages product information.
  • Inventory - manages product stock and reservations.
  • Ordering - handles customer orders.
  • Audit - records important application events.

One of the workflows I particularly enjoyed implementing was order placement.

When a customer places an order, the application needs to coordinate several operations:

  1. Retrieve the requested product.
  2. Reserve the required inventory.
  3. Create and persist the order.
  4. Publish an application event.
  5. Record the resulting audit entry.

These operations also need to respect transaction boundaries.

For example, if there isn't enough inventory, the order should not be persisted and the inventory reservation should be rolled back.

I also explored how to use @TransactionalEventListener with AFTER_COMMIT to process an order event after the original transaction has successfully committed.

The Audit module then records the event in a separate transaction using REQUIRES_NEW.

This was a useful way to see how Spring transactions, application events, and modular architecture can work together in a realistic business workflow.

Finally, I completed the module with End-to-End Application Verification.

This example focuses on verifying a running Spring application through its externally exposed HTTP endpoints rather than testing its internal implementation directly.

Using Java's HTTP Client, Jackson, and JUnit, I built tests that communicate with the Order Management application as an external client would.

The verification covers:

  • Retrieving publicly accessible products.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Customer and administrator access restrictions.
  • Placing orders and retrieving order history.
  • Verifying inventory updates.
  • Preventing customers from accessing another customer's orders.
  • Verifying audit entries after successful order placement.
  • Handling invalid quantities, insufficient inventory, and nonexistent products.

I also added a dedicated GitHub Actions workflow that starts the Order Management application, waits for it to become available, and executes the end-to-end verification tests.

An important distinction I explored here is that end-to-end tests depend on a running application. They are therefore executed separately from the regular Maven build, which allows contributors to run the standard build without having to start the dependent application.

What I particularly enjoyed about this final module was seeing how the individual concepts explored throughout Spring by Example V2 come together.

Modular architecture helps organize the application. Spring Data JPA handles persistence. Spring Security protects endpoints. Transactions maintain consistency. Application events support communication between modules. Testing and end-to-end verification help establish confidence that everything works together.

The goal isn't just to know how to use individual Spring annotations or dependencies.

The bigger goal is to understand how these technologies complement one another when building real applications.

The project is open source, and I've been building it one focused example at a time:

🔗 GitHub: https://gith.ub/dsAQrAU5

🔗 GitLab: https://gitl.ab/gfDEyGH3

With Module 06 - Capstone Application complete, another important milestone in Spring by Example V2 has been reached. 🚀

Six modules completed, with each one building on the knowledge gained from the previous modules.

There's still more to explore, but I'm enjoying the process of turning what I learn into practical, runnable examples that others can learn from too.

If you've built applications with Spring, how do you approach modular architecture, transaction management, and testing workflows that involve multiple Spring technologies?

I'd love to hear about your experiences.

title: How a REST Client Should Handle 503 Service Unavailable: Retries with Backoff in Spring
description:
Your nightly job sends 50,000 articles to a partner's API, in batches of 1,000. At batch 23, the API answers 503 Service Unavailable. What should your client do? Give up, and the data is incomplete. Retry immediately, and you make an overloaded server even slower. This post shows how a REST client should handle a 503: which errors to retry, how long to wait, and how Spring Framework 7 does it with one annotation.

What a 503 Means

The HTTP status code 503 Service Unavailable says that the server can't handle the request right now, but probably will later. Common causes:

  • The server is down for scheduled maintenance.
  • The server is overloaded by too much traffic.
  • A service the server depends on, such as a database or another API, is failing.

The server may add a Retry-After header that says how long to wait. The important word is temporarily: a 503 is an invitation to try again later, not a final answer.

The Client Can't Control the Server

Business-to-business (B2B) integrations are a typical case. One company's application is the client, the other company's API is the server, and the client has no say in how the server is built, deployed or scaled.

The first version of our client caught the exception, wrote it to the log and continued with the next batch. The job finished "successfully", and 1,000 articles were silently missing. Somebody had to read the logs, call the partner company, and send the batch again by hand.

The opposite reaction is just as bad: retrying in a tight loop, three times in a row without a pause. A server that's overloaded receives even more requests, exactly when it can handle the fewest. If hundreds of clients do the same, they keep the server down.

Which Errors Should You Retry?

Retry only when the same request has a real chance of succeeding later:

Response Retry? Why
503 Service Unavailable Yes Temporary by definition
429 Too Many Requests Yes Wait until your limit resets
502 Bad Gateway, 504 Gateway Timeout Yes Usually a temporary network or proxy problem
Timeout, connection refused Yes The server may be restarting
400, 401, 403, 404, 422 No The same request will fail again
500 Internal Server Error With care Can be a bug, which a retry won't fix

Is the request safe to repeat? GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: sending them twice has the same effect as sending them once. Our request is a POST, but it's a search, so repeating it changes nothing. A POST that creates something, such as an order, is different: if the first attempt actually reached the server and only the response got lost, a retry creates a second order. APIs solve this with an idempotency key, a unique ID the client sends with the request, so the server can recognize a repeated request.

A Retry Loop with Backoff

A good retry waits longer after each failure (exponential backoff: 1, 2, 4 seconds...), adds a random part to each delay (jitter, so that many clients don't retry at the same moment), respects the server's Retry-After header, and gives up after a few attempts. Here it is with Spring's RestClient:

public class ArticlesClient {

  private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ArticlesClient.class);

  private static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4;
  private static final Duration INITIAL_DELAY = Duration.ofSeconds(1);
  private static final Duration MAX_DELAY = Duration.ofSeconds(30);
  private static final Set<Integer> RETRYABLE_STATUS_CODES = Set.of(429, 502, 503, 504);

  private final RestClient restClient;

  public ArticlesClient(RestClient restClient) {
    this.restClient = restClient;
  }

  public SearchResponse searchArticles(List<String> articleNumbers) {
    for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
      try {
        return restClient.post()
            .uri("/articles/search")
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .body(new SearchRequest(articleNumbers))
            .retrieve()
            .body(SearchResponse.class);
      } catch (RestClientException e) {
        if (attempt == MAX_ATTEMPTS || !isRetryable(e)) {
          throw e;
        }
        Duration wait = retryAfter(e).orElse(backoff(attempt));
        if (wait.compareTo(MAX_DELAY) > 0) {
          throw e;   // the server asks us to wait longer than we're willing to
        }
        logger.warn("Attempt {} of {} failed: {}. Retrying in {} ms",
            attempt, MAX_ATTEMPTS, e.getMessage(), wait.toMillis());
        sleep(wait);
      }
    }
  }
}

The helper methods decide whether and how long to wait:

private static boolean isRetryable(RestClientException e) {
  if (e instanceof RestClientResponseException responseError) {
    return RETRYABLE_STATUS_CODES.contains(responseError.getStatusCode().value());
  }
  return e instanceof ResourceAccessException;   // timeout, connection refused
}

// 1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to MAX_DELAY, each with random jitter between half and the full value
private static Duration backoff(int attempt) {
  long cap = Math.min(MAX_DELAY.toMillis(), INITIAL_DELAY.toMillis() << (attempt - 1));
  return Duration.ofMillis(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(cap / 2, cap + 1));
}

// Retry-After is either a number of seconds or an HTTP date
private static Optional<Duration> retryAfter(RestClientException e) {
  if (!(e instanceof RestClientResponseException responseError) || responseError.getResponseHeaders() == null) {
    return Optional.empty();
  }
  String value = responseError.getResponseHeaders().getFirst(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER);
  if (value == null) {
    return Optional.empty();
  }
  try {
    return Optional.of(Duration.ofSeconds(Long.parseLong(value.trim())));
  } catch (NumberFormatException notSeconds) {
    try {
      ZonedDateTime retryAt = ZonedDateTime.parse(value.trim(), DateTimeFormatter.RFC_1123_DATE_TIME);
      Duration wait = Duration.between(ZonedDateTime.now(), retryAt);
      return Optional.of(wait.isNegative() ? Duration.ZERO : wait);
    } catch (DateTimeParseException invalid) {
      return Optional.empty();
    }
  }
}

private static void sleep(Duration duration) {
  try {
    Thread.sleep(duration);
  } catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    throw new IllegalStateException("Interrupted while waiting to retry", e);
  }
}

The request and response are records:

public record SearchRequest(List<String> articleNumbers) {}
public record SearchResponse(List<Article> articles) {}
public record Article(String articleNumber, String name) {}

Don't Lose the Batches That Still Fail

Even with retries, a batch can fail, for example when the partner's API is down for an hour. Then the job must keep the data, not only a log line:

public List<List<String>> searchAll(List<String> articleNumbers) {
  List<List<String>> failedBatches = new ArrayList<>();
  for (int from = 0; from < articleNumbers.size(); from += BATCH_SIZE) {
    List<String> batch = articleNumbers.subList(from, Math.min(from + BATCH_SIZE, articleNumbers.size()));
    try {
      SearchResponse response = articlesClient.searchArticles(batch);
      save(response.articles());
    } catch (RestClientException e) {
      logger.error("Batch starting at {} failed after all retries: {}", from, e.getMessage());
      failedBatches.add(List.copyOf(batch));   // keep the data: retry later or report it
    }
  }
  return failedBatches;
}

The caller can store the failed batches in a table, send them again in the next run, or notify the team. In each case, nobody needs to search the logs.

Try It

I ran the client against a local test server that answers 503, then 503 with Retry-After: 2, then 200:

server: call 1 -> 503
WARN ArticlesClient -- Attempt 1 of 4 failed: 503 Service Unavailable: [no body]. Retrying in 618 ms
server: call 2 -> 503 (Retry-After: 2)
WARN ArticlesClient -- Attempt 2 of 4 failed: 503 Service Unavailable: [no body]. Retrying in 2000 ms
server: call 3 -> 200
result: SearchResponse[articles=[Article[articleNumber=4711, name=Potatoes]]]

The first wait is a random value from the backoff, and the second is exactly the 2 seconds the server asked for. In the other test runs, a 400 Bad Request failed immediately without a retry, a server that always answered 503 got four attempts with growing delays (0.8 s, 1.6 s, 2.1 s) before the client gave up, and a Retry-After of 120 seconds made the client stop instead of waiting.

To see a real 503 response, use the public test service httpbin.org:

$ curl -i https://httpbin.org/status/503
HTTP/1.1 503 SERVICE UNAVAILABLE
Content-Length: 0

The Spring Framework 7 Way: @Retryable

Since Spring Framework 7 (Spring Boot 4), retries are built into Spring itself, with no extra library. Enable them once:

@Configuration
@EnableResilientMethods
public class ResilienceConfig {
}

Then annotate the method:

@Service
public class ArticlesService {

  private final RestClient restClient;

  public ArticlesService(RestClient restClient) {
    this.restClient = restClient;
  }

  @Retryable(
      includes = {
          HttpServerErrorException.ServiceUnavailable.class,   // 503
          HttpServerErrorException.BadGateway.class,           // 502
          HttpServerErrorException.GatewayTimeout.class,       // 504
          HttpClientErrorException.TooManyRequests.class,      // 429
          ResourceAccessException.class },                     // timeout, connection refused
      maxRetries = 3,
      delay = 1000,
      multiplier = 2,
      maxDelay = 30_000,
      jitter = 250)
  public SearchResponse searchArticles(List<String> articleNumbers) {
    return restClient.post()
        .uri("/articles/search")
        .body(new SearchRequest(articleNumbers))
        .retrieve()
        .body(SearchResponse.class);
  }
}

In my test, this method also received 503, 503 and 200, with retries after about 1 and 2 seconds, and a 400 was not retried. The method itself contains no retry logic at all.

Which one should you use? @Retryable is shorter and keeps the business code clean, and it's the right choice in most cases. It can't read the Retry-After header, though, because it only sees the exception type. When an API sends Retry-After, typically with 429 and 503, the loop above respects it. On Spring Boot 3, the Spring Retry library offers a similar @Retryable.

Best Practices Checklist

  • Retry only errors that can succeed later: 429, 502, 503, 504 and timeouts.
  • Wait with exponential backoff and jitter, and respect Retry-After.
  • Limit the number of attempts and the longest wait.
  • Make sure a repeated request is safe; use idempotency keys for requests that create data.
  • Never lose data: keep failed requests for a later retry or a report.
  • On the server side, return Retry-After with your 503 and 429 responses. The rate limiting post shows how, and you can load-test it with concurrent clients.

"What happens when the service you call is down?" is a standard question in backend and system design interviews. Practice with real interview questions:

title: Mobile App Onboarding: A UX and Development Checklist for 2026
description:
Mobile app onboarding sits at the intersection of product design, authentication, permissions and application performance.

A new user may need to understand the app, create an account, grant access to a device capability and complete an initial task. Poor sequencing can turn these steps into unnecessary friction.

This article covers seven practical areas to consider when implementing an onboarding flow.

1. Define the first meaningful action

Before creating screens, define what a new user should accomplish.

Examples include:

  • Searching for a product.
  • Booking an appointment.
  • Creating a first task.
  • Starting a workout.
  • Adding an initial account.

Build the onboarding flow around this action instead of introducing every feature upfront.

2. Keep registration minimal

Separate required account information from optional profile data.

Use clear field labels, client-side feedback for usability and server-side validation for security. Handle network failures and authentication errors without losing the user's progress unnecessarily.

Where account creation is not required for the core experience, consider allowing guest access.

3. Request permissions contextually

Do not request every device permission during the first launch.

Map permissions to the features that need them. Explain why access is required and provide a sensible alternative when the feature can still work without it.

Apple's onboarding guidance and privacy guidance are useful design references.

4. Use contextual guidance

A short interactive hint near an unfamiliar control can be more useful than a long tutorial.

Keep guidance focused, dismissible where appropriate and available again through help or settings when users need it.

5. Optimise the first-session experience

Consider initial download size, image decoding, animation cost, network requests and memory usage.

Test on different screen sizes and hardware categories. Provide loading, empty, offline and retry states rather than leaving users with an unresponsive interface.

Refer to the Android core app quality guidelines when planning Android quality checks.

6. Design secure returning-user experiences

Onboarding also includes returning after reinstalling an app or changing devices.

Plan session management, credential recovery and restoration of user progress. Avoid insecure local storage or exposing authentication tokens in logs.

A relevant Android development change is Google's Zero-Tap Sign-In requirement, announced on 26 August 2026. From April 2027, eligible apps supporting sign-in will need to support secure sign-in restoration during device migration using the Android Restore Credentials API.

Review the official Android announcement and current Play technical requirements before implementation.

7. Instrument onboarding events

Measure the stages that matter, such as:

  • onboarding_started
  • registration_completed
  • permission_result
  • first_key_action_completed
  • onboarding_skipped

These are illustrative custom event names, not a prescribed platform event schema. Define event parameters consistently and avoid sending sensitive information.

Use the data to identify drop-off points, then validate possible causes through usability testing.

Implementation checklist

  • [ ] Define the first meaningful user action.
  • [ ] Keep required registration fields to a minimum.
  • [ ] Validate input on the server.
  • [ ] Request permissions when relevant.
  • [ ] Provide useful loading and error states.
  • [ ] Test across supported screen sizes and devices.
  • [ ] Plan secure account recovery and credential restoration.
  • [ ] Measure onboarding completion and key actions.
  • [ ] Review privacy and data-handling requirements.

Conclusion

A reliable onboarding flow requires more than a sequence of welcome screens. It needs a clear user goal, sensible permission timing, secure authentication and a responsive first-session experience.

Design the flow around what users need to accomplish, test it with real people and improve it using evidence.

For more mobile app and software development resources, visit Resynix.

title: I use an LLM to check fake citations, but I don't let it decide anything
description:
I'm building CiteWise, a tool that checks whether an academic reference points to a real paper. You paste a citation, it looks the work up in Crossref, DataCite, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PubMed and arXiv, and shows you which fields match and which don't.

The obvious way to build this in 2026 is "send the reference to an LLM and ask if it's real". I tried a version of that early on and it's a bad idea for the same reason people need this tool in the first place: LLMs are very good at producing things that look right.

So the LLM is in the pipeline, but it isn't allowed to decide anything. This post is about where that line sits, and about the bug in my first version that crossed it without me noticing.

The pipeline

Roughly:

Parse the raw string into fields (title, authors, year, journal, DOI...) with a rule-based parser.
Query the scholarly sources in parallel.
Score every candidate against the user's input, field by field.
Pick a status: verified, ambiguous, conflicting metadata, not found, and so on.

Step 3 is deterministic. Title similarity, author overlap, year, DOI equality, a penalty for contradictions. No model involved. If you run the same reference twice against the same source responses, you get the same score.

Where the LLM comes in

Some references are just messy. A student copies a citation out of a PDF and gets Smith J Lee K Deep learning for something 2019 Nature Methods 16 4 pp 1-9 with no punctuation. The rule parser gets half the fields, the search queries are bad, and nothing comes back.

That's the only case where the LLM runs: there's no DOI, and the first pass ended as not found or insufficient evidence. The model gets the raw string and tries to fill in the missing fields. Then we search again with those fields.

The bug

Here's a simplified version of what my first implementation did after the second search:

java
var enriched = llm.completeMissingFields(candidate);
var retry = resolver.resolve(enriched);
if (retry.score() >= first.score()) {
candidate = enriched; // <- this line
resolution = retry;
}

Looks reasonable. If the LLM-assisted search scores at least as well, use it.

The problem is what candidate means. It's the thing every candidate paper gets scored against. After this swap, the scorer was no longer comparing source records to what the user typed. It was comparing them to what the LLM thought the user meant.

So if the model guessed a plausible title, found a real paper with that title, and then the scorer compared the real paper to the model's guess, you'd get a high score. The user's original reference could have been wrong in exactly the way we're supposed to catch, and the result would say "verified".

The >= made it worse. A tie meant the LLM's version won.

The fix

The LLM output is now treated as search hints only. It can help us find candidates. It can't become the thing we compare against.

java
// Enrichment supplies retrieval hints only.
// It never becomes evidence about the user's input.
ResolutionResult resolveWithHints(Candidate original, Candidate hints) {
return resolve(original, retrieval.retrieve(hints));
}

Candidates are fetched using the enriched fields, then scored against the original parsed input. And the second pass only replaces the first if its score is strictly higher:

java
var selected = retry.score() > first.score() ? retry : first;

If the LLM found the right paper, it'll match the user's original fields better than whatever the first search returned, and the score goes up. If it found a plausible-but-wrong paper, the original fields won't match it, and the first result stands.

A smaller related change: the old code had a status called POSSIBLE_HALLUCINATION, assigned when the LLM had touched the input and nothing was found. That's a strong claim to make from "we didn't find it". New results never produce that status. Old records that have it are shown as "not found under the old rules".

The other thing I got wrong: treating silence as success

The second lesson wasn't about the LLM at all.

When a search returned no candidates, the old code decided between "not found" and "insufficient evidence" like this:

java
boolean searchCompleted = diagnostics.isEmpty()
|| diagnostics.stream().anyMatch(d -> d.ok());

diagnostics.isEmpty() counted as a completed search. So if something went wrong before any source reported back, we'd confidently tell the user their reference doesn't exist.

Now every check records which sources actually responded, and the result carries a separate completeness field: COMPLETE, PARTIAL or INCOMPLETE. For a reference with a DOI, Crossref and DataCite both have to answer. Without a DOI, at least two of the three general-purpose sources have to. If that doesn't happen, the result says so and suggests a retry, instead of saying "not found".

This also changed billing. A complete search that finds nothing still costs a check, because the search actually ran. A search where the sources were down doesn't.

What I'd tell someone building something similar
Decide up front which parts of your pipeline are evidence and which are search. Keep the LLM on the search side.
Be suspicious of >= when one side came from a model.
"No results" and "no response" are different outcomes. Make your types say so, or someone (me) will merge them by accident.
A tool that says "I couldn't check this properly" is more useful than one that guesses.

If you want to see it on a real reference, it's at citewise.dev. There are 10 free checks a month. I'm especially interested in references it gets wrong, so if you have a weird one, throw it at it and let me know in the comments.

title: Java Virtual Threads Aren't Free: 6 Hidden Costs to Check Before Production
description:
Java virtual threads make it cheap to run a huge number of concurrent tasks, but they don't make your system's limits go away. Memory, database connections, CPU cores, locks and observability all still cost something. Virtual threads were previewed in Java 19 (JEP 425) and became a standard feature in Java 21 (JEP 444). Here are six costs worth checking before you switch a production service over.

What do Java virtual threads actually change?

A virtual thread is a lightweight thread managed by the JVM rather than the operating system. When it blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (an ordinary platform thread), and that carrier picks up other work. That is why simple thread-per-request code can scale again without callbacks or reactive chains.

What doesn't change is everything the thread talks to.

1. Memory still adds up

Virtual threads are cheap, not weightless. Each one keeps its stack on the Java heap, and that stack grows with the depth of the call chain. Whatever a task holds (request objects, buffers, parsed payloads) stays reachable until the task finishes.

try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 500_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> processRequest());
    }
} // close() waits for every submitted task to finish

Starting 500,000 tasks like this takes a few lines. If each one holds even a modest payload while it waits, heap usage climbs quickly and the garbage collector has to work harder. A fixed thread pool used to act as an accidental throttle. With virtual threads that throttle is gone unless you add one yourself.

What to do:

  • Bound the incoming work with a queue, a rate limiter or a semaphore around the expensive step, instead of relying on thread count.
  • Keep per-task objects small and drop large buffers as soon as you're done with them.
  • Watch heap and GC behaviour under realistic load, not just a quick local test.

2. Your database pool becomes the real limit

Say 10,000 requests arrive at once and each one needs a query. Virtual threads will happily run all 10,000. Your connection pool might have 50 connections.

The other 9,950 requests wait. Waiting is cheap for a virtual thread, so the app doesn't fall over, but latency grows. If the wait is longer than your pool's timeout (connectionTimeout in HikariCP, for example), requests start failing with connection errors.

Making the pool bigger isn't the fix, because the database has its own ceiling. Size the pool for what the database can actually handle, set sensible timeouts, and fail fast when you're over capacity.

The same problem applies to anything rate-limited that has no pool of its own, such as a third-party API. A Semaphore is a simple way to cap concurrent calls:

private final Semaphore paymentApiPermits = new Semaphore(20);

PaymentResult charge(Order order) throws InterruptedException {
    paymentApiPermits.acquire();
    try {
        return paymentClient.charge(order);
    } finally {
        paymentApiPermits.release();
    }
}

You can have thousands of virtual threads, and still no more than 20 of them talking to the payment provider at any moment.

3. ThreadLocal caching stops paying off

ThreadLocal works fine on virtual threads. The trouble is a common pattern built on top of it: caching an expensive object per thread so it gets reused.

private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FORMAT =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));

With a pool of 200 platform threads, that's 200 formatters reused for the life of the application. With virtual threads you usually get a new thread per task, so you build a new formatter for every request and the "cache" saves nothing. Put something larger in that ThreadLocal, run a few hundred thousand threads, and it shows up in memory.

What to do:

  • Search your code (and check your libraries) for ThreadLocal used as an object cache. Swap in a thread-safe alternative, such as DateTimeFormatter instead of SimpleDateFormat.
  • Don't pool virtual threads just to keep ThreadLocal values alive. That defeats the purpose.
  • For passing request context down a call chain, look at Scoped Values, which became final in Java 25 (JEP 506) after previews in Java 21 to 24.

4. Pinning can stall carrier threads

A virtual thread is pinned when it can't be unmounted from its carrier while it blocks. During that time the carrier can't run anything else. The default scheduler has roughly one carrier per CPU core, so a handful of pinned threads can noticeably cut throughput.

On Java 21 to 23, the classic cause is blocking inside synchronized:

public synchronized void refreshCache() {
    loadFromRemoteService(); // blocking I/O while holding the monitor
}

Java 24 (JEP 491) fixed most of this: virtual threads can now block inside synchronized code and still unmount. Pinning still happens when a thread blocks inside a native method or a foreign function call, plus a few rarer cases such as class initialisers.

What to do:

  • Check which JDK you actually run in production. The advice differs before and after Java 24.
  • On Java 21 to 23, move blocking calls out of synchronized sections or switch those sections to ReentrantLock.
  • Record the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event with Java Flight Recorder to find real pinning instead of guessing.

synchronized isn't the villain here. Long blocking while pinned is.

5. CPU-bound work won't get faster

Virtual threads help when tasks spend most of their time waiting: database queries, HTTP calls, file and network I/O. They don't add CPU.

The default virtual thread scheduler is a ForkJoinPool sized to the number of available processors. On an 8-core machine, 100,000 virtual threads resizing images still share 8 cores, with extra scheduling overhead on top.

Workload Better fit
Database queries, HTTP calls, external APIs Virtual threads
Heavy computation (image processing, encryption, number crunching) Fixed platform thread pool sized to your cores
Divide-and-conquer data processing ForkJoinPool or parallel streams
Mixed workloads Virtual threads for request handling, with CPU-heavy steps handed to a bounded pool

6. Debugging at scale needs different tools

A thread dump with 200 threads is readable. One with 200,000 is not. The questions also change:

  • Which tasks are waiting for a database connection?
  • Are carrier threads being pinned?
  • Which downstream service is slowing requests down?

Tools that help:

  • jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file>: a thread dump format added in JDK 21 that includes virtual threads.
  • Java Flight Recorder and JDK Mission Control for pinning and latency events.
  • An APM tool or OpenTelemetry tracing, so you follow a request rather than a thread.
  • Structured logs with a request ID on every line.

Are Java virtual threads worth using?

For I/O-heavy services, yes. You get to write plain blocking code that scales well, and that code is far easier to read and debug than callback chains.

They're a poor fit for CPU-bound work, and they tend to move bottlenecks rather than remove them. Before you switch, check four things: your JDK version, your connection pool and downstream limits, your ThreadLocal usage, and your monitoring. Then load test with realistic traffic.

Virtual threads make concurrency easier to write. Good system design is still what makes it scale.

Written by the team at Solitaire Infosystems, a software development and IT training company in Mohali, India.

Have you moved a service to virtual threads yet? Which of these costs showed up first for you: the database pool, ThreadLocal, or pinning? Tell us in the comments.

title: A plan's day is one bar, and a slider can only grow into room that is free
description:
Nakodo emails creators and local businesses on a brand's behalf, and a plan buys a number of new conversations a day rather than a number of emails. Our pricing page publishes the numbers: Pro runs 5 campaigns at a time and contacts 25 creators or businesses each weekday, Business runs 25 campaigns and contacts 75.

Those two numbers together are the whole problem. Five campaigns and 25 a day means a busy campaign can eat the day by lunchtime and the other four get nothing, so each campaign has its own share, and the shares have to be editable in a way that cannot produce an invalid total. The screen that does it is 264 lines, and most of the thinking is in two of them.

One bar, not five numbers

The panel shows the plan's day as a single bar, with each campaign's share as a segment and what is left over as empty track.

<div className="flex h-2.5 gap-px overflow-hidden rounded-sm bg-paper-150" role="presentation">
  {parts.filter((p) => p.n > 0).map((p) => (
    <div
      key={p.id}
      className={cn("h-full transition-[width] duration-200 motion-reduce:transition-none", p.id === highlight ? "bg-cyano-700" : "bg-ink-400")}
      style={{ width: `${(p.n / Math.max(limit, total)) * 100}%` }}
    />
  ))}
</div>

The denominator is Math.max(limit, total), not limit. A total can exceed the plan's day, and it does so in one real situation: an account on Business with 25 campaigns downgrades to Pro, and the stored shares now add up to more than the smaller day. With limit as the denominator the segments would overflow their container and the bar would lie about its own scale. With max(limit, total) the bar stays full width and the sentence under it carries the problem:

{over > 0
  ? `${n(total)} set aside, ${n(over)} more than your plan's ${n(limit)} a day. Lower some to save.`
  : `${n(total)} of ${n(limit)} new emails a day set aside${total < limit ? `, ${n(limit - total)} free` : ""}`}

That paragraph is the accessible version of the bar, so the bar itself is role="presentation" and the sentence is aria-live="polite". Dragging a slider changes one number in a sentence a screen reader reads, instead of changing the width of a div a screen reader cannot see. The free remainder is only mentioned when there is one, because "0 free" is noise.

A share can always fall and can only rise into free room

Every change goes through one pure function, which is shared with the server:

export function clampShare(limit: number, shares: Record<string, number>, id: string, wanted: number): number {
  const current = shares[id] ?? 0;
  const others = Object.entries(shares).reduce((n, [k, v]) => (k === id ? n : n + v), 0);
  const n = Math.max(0, Math.round(Number.isFinite(wanted) ? wanted : 0));
  return n <= current ? n : Math.min(n, Math.max(current, limit - others));
}

The asymmetry is the point. Lowering is always allowed, raising is capped at what the others leave free. The naive version, Math.min(wanted, limit - others), is wrong in exactly the downgrade case: when the others already use more than the whole day, limit - others is negative, and a user trying to lower a share from 25 to 10 would be clamped to 0. Hence the Math.max(current, ...): the ceiling is never lower than where you already are.

The hook around it is six lines, and the clamp is inside the setter, so no component can set an invalid value:

export function useShares(limit: number, initial: Record<string, number>) {
  const [values, setValues] = useState(initial);
  const total = Object.values(values).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return { values, total, free: limit - total, set: (id, n) => setValues((v) => ({ ...v, [id]: clampShare(limit, v, id, n) })) };
}

Two screens use that hook: this panel, and the "Daily emails" step of the campaign setup flow, where one of the rows is the campaign being created.

The number box that shows what you typed

Sliders are fine for a rough split and useless for "make this one exactly 12". So each row has a slider and a number input, both driving the same clamp. A controlled number input over a clamping model has a known annoyance: type 30 when only 18 are free, and the field snaps to 18 under your fingers, usually mid-keystroke.

const [typed, setTyped] = useState<string | null>(null);
<Input
  type="number"
  value={typed ?? String(value)}
  onChange={(e) => {
    setTyped(e.target.value);
    const v = Number.parseInt(e.target.value, 10);
    if (!Number.isNaN(v)) onChange(v);
  }}
  onBlur={() => setTyped(null)}
/>

While the box has focus it shows the characters you typed; the model still clamps, so the bar and the sentence show the real value immediately. On blur the local string is dropped and the box falls back to the clamped number. You see your own typing, and you also see that the system disagreed, in the two places that matter.

The slider is the shadcn primitive with one addition, a thumbLabel prop, because a drag handle with no accessible name is a drag handle nobody can use:

<Slider value={[value]} min={0} max={limit} step={1} onValueChange={([v]) => onChange(v)} thumbLabel={`New emails a day for ${c.name}`} />

Saving the whole allocation as one field

The allocation is saved together or not at all, so the form posts a single JSON field through a Server Action:

<input type="hidden" name="shares" value={JSON.stringify(shares.values)} />

The Save button is disabled={shares.total > limit}, which is a convenience and not a guarantee, so the server runs the same rules again:

const parsed = shareMap.safeParse(parseJson(form.get("shares")));
if (!parsed.success) return sharesLost();
const { changed } = await withUserLock(user.id, (tx) => setShares(tx, user.id, values));

shareMap is z.record(z.uuid(), z.number()) with a 200-key limit. Inside the lock, setShares re-reads the plan and the campaigns, refuses ids that are not the user's, and runs the shared sharesProblem check that produces the same sentence the client shows. It also only writes rows whose value actually changed, and only writes an audit row if at least one did, so opening the panel and pressing Save changes nothing and records nothing.

One more rule lives on the read side. A campaign created before shares existed has null, which means "whatever the others leave":

const rest = Math.max(0, limit - set);
const each = unset.length > 0 ? Math.floor(rest / unset.length) : 0;
const odd = rest - each * unset.length;

The remainder goes to the oldest campaigns first, one each. And on an upgrade, stored shares grow in proportion rather than staying put, so 25 of Pro's 25 becomes 75 of Business's 75; a downgrade leaves them alone, because the clamp above can lower them whenever the user next opens the panel.

Details that only exist because of how the panel is opened

The panel is reachable from a link elsewhere in the app with ?manage on the URL, which means the component can be opened by navigation as well as by its own button. Closing it then has to clean up after the link:

const change = (next: boolean) => {
  setOpen(next);
  // Opened from a link (?manage): closing it drops that, so a reload doesn't reopen it.
  if (!next && new URL(window.location.href).searchParams.has("manage")) {
    window.history.replaceState(null, "", window.location.pathname);
  }
};

replaceState rather than a router push, because this is not a navigation anyone should be able to go back to. And the form inside is mounted only while the panel is open, so every time it opens it starts from the saved shares rather than from the numbers you abandoned last time.

The screen itself is behind sign-in, so the only way to see it is to have an account. What is public is the arithmetic it has to respect: the per-plan daily numbers and the campaign counts on pricing, including the line that says extra campaigns are paused rather than deleted if a plan gets smaller, which is the same downgrade case the clamp is written for. How it works covers where those daily conversations come from.

title: Article: Systemic Approach to Memory, Knowledge, and Context in Agentic AI Architectures
description:
The article argues that reliable agentic AI architecture depends on a context engine that selects, injects, compresses, and expires information before it reaches the model. It separates context, memory, and knowledge, and recommends tiered memory, curated knowledge, and token budgeting. It also covers common anti-patterns, such as context stuffing and stale data loops, with mitigations.

By Adi Polak

title: Time and Space Complexity
description:
Time complexity is the amount of time taken by an algorithm to run as a function of the length of its input. This is important cause:

  • Resources are limited.
  • Helps measure algorithms to make programs more efficient.

We are no calculating with a stopwatch. We're looking at how many operations did the CPU have to perform. Say for example:

We are running a function which takes a value 'N' and runs a loop 'N' times:

public static void runningLoop(int N){
    for(int i=0; i<N; i++){
        //ops
    }
}

Here, the loop is running N times which means Time Complexity is directly proportional to N.
Hence, we say the time complexity is O(N). We'll get to what O is.

Similarly,
Space complexity is the amount of time space by an algorithm to run as a function of the length of its input. Let's take examples.

Say #1:

int a = 1;
int b[5];

Here, since space is not variable but fixed => O(1)

Say #2:

int arr[] = new int[N];

Here, since space is variable => O(N)

Units of Complexity

  1. Big O: Upper Bound
  2. Theta θ: Average case
  3. Omega Ω: Lower Bound

Say:
We have to find an element in an array:

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

Omega is lowest bound which is the best case scenario.
If the element we're looking for is the first in the array then thats the best case scenario:
Ω(1)

Big O is highest bound which is the worst case scenario.
If the element we're looking for is the last in the array then thats the worst case scenario:
O(n)

Theta is average bound which is the average case scenario.
If the element we're looking for is the center in the array then thats the average case scenario:
θ(n/2)

Big O Complexities

1. Constant Time: O(1)

When only one operation is performed no matter what.
Doesn't grow with N.
Say for example:

int[] arr = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
System.out.println(arr[0]);

or

int sum = 10 + 20;

Regardless of what we do, whether the array contains 5 elements or 5 million elements, since we are accessing arr[0] that's one operation. Similarly, when adding two elements we are performing one operation. This makes the complexity O(1).

2. Linear Time: O(N)

When the number of operations increase with the value of N.
Grows ∝ N
Say for example:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(arr[i]);
}

If:

  • n=5 ~ Loop runs 5 times
  • n=100 ~ Loop runs 100 times
  • n=10000 ~ Loop runs 10000 times

and so on. This makes the complexity O(N).

3. Logarithmic Time: O(logN)

When after operation, the next set of operations are cut by half (More understood in Binary Search).
Grows very slowly.
Say for examples:

We are searching for an element in array of sizes:

16: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1
32: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1
64: 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1

4. Quadratic Time: O(N^2)

When the number of operations increase with the value of N and within these N operations you are performing a set of another N operations.
Say for example:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        System.out.println(i + " " + j);
    }
}

If:

  • n=5 ~ Loop runs 25 times
  • n=100 ~ Loop runs 10000 times
  • n=10000 ~ Loop runs 100000000 times

and so on. This makes the complexity O(N^2).
It's pretty bad XD

5. Cubic Time: O(N^3)

Similar to O(N^2) but worser.

Simplifying Expressions

There 3 main rules to simplifying Big O complexities:

Rule 1: Ignore constants.

Examples:
O(5N) = O(N)
O(100000N) = O(N)
O(3N + 2) = O(N)

Rule 2: Ignore the smaller terms since we're looking for worst case scenario.

Examples:
O(N^2 + N) = O(N^2)
O(N^2 + n + 10) = O(N^2)
O(logN + N^3 + 100000N) = O(N^3)

Rule 3: Add sequential operations and Multiply nested operations.


// Sequential Ops
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(arr[i]);
}

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(arr[i]);
}

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(arr[i]);
}

// Complexity: O(N + N + N) = O(3N) = O(N)

// Nested Ops
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(arr[i]);
    }
}

// Complexity: O(N * N) = O(N^2)

Order of Preferred Complexities

O(1) > O(logN) > O(rootN) > O(N) > O(NlogN) > O(N^2) > O(N^3) > O(2^N) > O(N!) > O(N^N)
<--- LEAST COMPLEXITY HIGHEST COMPLEXITY ---->

Practice Questions 


Question 1:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Answer 1: O(n)



Question 2:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    System.out.println(j);
}

Answer 2: O(N+N)=O(2N) => O(N)



Question 3:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        System.out.println(i + " " + j);
    }
}

Answer 3: O(N^2)



Question 4:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        System.out.println(i + j);
    }
}

Answer 4: O(n + n^2) = O(n^2)



Question 5:

for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Answer 5: O(logn)



Question 6:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) {
        System.out.println(i + " " + j);
    }
}

Answer 6: O(nlogn)



Question 7:

for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) {
    for (int j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) {
        System.out.println(i + " " + j);
    }
}

Answer 7: O(log^2 n)



Question 8:

for (int i = n; i > 0; i /= 2) {
    System.out.println(i);
}

Answer 8: O(logn)



Question 9:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) {
        for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
            System.out.println(i + j + k);
        }
    }
}

Answer 9: O(n^2 logn)



Question 10:

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
        System.out.println(i + " " + j);
    }
}

Answer 10: O(n^2)
