title: We call notFound() four times and never wrote the page it lands on, and the default has zero links
description:
Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages and tells you when a new listing appears. Its marketing site is 38 URLs of Next.js App Router, derived from four TypeScript arrays rather than typed out, and I have audited most of it in public by now.

Here is one I had not looked at. Four of those routes end like this:

if (!site) notFound();        // app/alerts/[site]/page.tsx
if (!article) notFound();     // app/guides/[slug]/page.tsx
if (!target) notFound();      // app/compare/[target]/page.tsx
if (!article) notFound();     // app/for/[audience]/page.tsx

Four deliberate throws into a page that does not exist in the repository:

$ find src -name "not-found*" -o -name "error*" -o -name "global-error*" -o -name "loading*"
$

Nothing. No not-found.tsx, no error.tsx, no global-error.tsx, no loading.tsx anywhere under src. Every one of those four calls, and every mistyped URL on the domain, is handed to the framework's built-in page. So I went and read what we have been serving.

What the default actually is 

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{size_download}\n" https://notifio.app/nope
404 13615

13,615 bytes. Measured in the loaded DOM:

/nope /help
<a> elements 0 18
<script src> 7 9
<title> tags 3 1
visible text 404 / This page could not be found. the page

Zero anchors is the one that matters. There is no nav, no footer, no link home, no link to the site hub, nothing. A visitor who follows a stale link, or who types a path with the wrong capital letter, gets two lines of text and a dead end, on a site whose whole job is to get them to a download button.

The three title tags are the framework and our root layout both doing their job and nobody refereeing. In the raw HTML there are two:

<title>404: This page could not be found.</title>
<title>Notifio – Rental Listing Alert Monitor</title>

After hydration the DOM has three, because the metadata from the root layout is applied again on the client. Browsers use the first one, so the tab says the 404 text, which is at least the honest half of the pair.

The site has one theme, and the 404 has two

The body element on that page carries our own classes:

bg-[#0a0a0a] text-[#fafafa] antialiased font-sans

And the computed background is rgb(0, 0, 0). Not our near-black, pure black. In a browser set to a light colour scheme it is white with black text. The reason is one style tag the framework injects:

body{color:#000;background:#fff;margin:0}
.next-error-h1{border-right:1px solid rgba(0,0,0,.3)}
@media (prefers-color-scheme:dark){
  body{color:#fff;background:#000}
  .next-error-h1{border-right:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.3)}
}

That is an unlayered element selector. Our background is a Tailwind v4 utility, which lives in @layer utilities, and an unlayered rule beats every layered one regardless of specificity. I have been bitten by exactly this before, in the other direction, when our own hand-written stylesheet outranked 514 utilities.

So the only page on the site that respects prefers-color-scheme is the one we never wrote. Notifio's site is deliberately one fixed dark theme, and the 404 is the single place where the design follows the operating system instead. The h1 on it renders in system-ui while the body font is still our self-hosted DM Sans, which is the kind of detail that makes a page feel like somebody else's website.

The first branded 404 I ever wrote was for another app, for this exact reason: the default painted the header the wrong colour. Then I shipped a second product and did not do it again.

Who actually lands there

Trailing slashes are not the problem, because the framework already handles them:

/pricing/                                308 -> /pricing
/alerts/kamernet/                        308 -> /alerts/kamernet
/guides/how-fast-do-rental-listings-go/  308 -> /guides/how-fast-do-rental-listings-go

Case is:

/Pricing           404
/Download          404
/alerts/Kamernet   404

Static paths and dynamic segments are both case sensitive, and a capitalised path is what you get when somebody types a URL from a slide, a printed flyer or a voice note. I wrote about one capital letter turning a path into a 404 on a sister product and the same thing is true here.

And then there is this one:

/for          404
/for/expats   200
/for/students 200
/for/amsterdam 200

Three pages live in a URL space whose index does not exist. That is a deliberate split between two URL spaces, audience pages under /for and guides under /guides, both rendered from one Article type, with one hub page listing both. The hub is at /guides, so the parent of /for/expats is a 404 with no links on it. Anyone who deletes the last segment out of curiosity, which is a thing people do, gets the dead end.

The page we did build

This is the part that annoys me. The site has one carefully made full-screen status page, and it is this:

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "Down for Maintenance",
  description: "Notifio is down for maintenance. Please try again in a little while.",
  robots: { index: false, follow: false },
};

It has a Nav, a Footer, a clock icon in a circle, a heading, a one-paragraph explanation from a shared constant, and a full-width Back to home button. It also has a comment on top saying when you can see it:

// Only reachable while MAINTENANCE is on; src/proxy.ts redirects it home otherwise.

That boolean has been true for a few hours in the life of this product. The 404 is reachable by every visitor, every crawler and every stale link, every day, and it got nothing. We built the rare page and skipped the common one, which I think happens because the rare page was a task ("we are taking the database down") and the common one is a default that already technically works.

The missing error boundary, and the honest reason it has not hurt

No error.tsx either, which means an uncaught render error anywhere in the tree lands on the framework's error page: the same typography, the same absence of links, plus a stack trace in development and a bare apology in production.

The reason this has not cost us anything is worth stating rather than glossing over. Nine of our page routes are force-static, and their data is a TypeScript array in the same repository, so a bad field is a build failure rather than a runtime one. Only three pages are force-dynamic: the home page, the download page and the pricing page, because all three resolve a visitor's currency from the request. Those are the three that can throw while somebody is looking, and they are also the three pages where a blank error screen costs real money.

There is no loading.tsx anywhere, and that one is correct by accident: a static page has nothing to stream, so a loading fallback would never render. I would still rather it were absent on purpose.

What I am doing about it

In order:

  1. app/not-found.tsx with the real Nav and Footer, a short line of copy, and four links out: the site hub, the guides hub, the help page and the download page. The nav and footer alone take the link count from zero to about twenty.
  2. app/error.tsx with a reset() button, scoped to the same chrome, so a currency lookup failing on the pricing page does not look like the site is gone.
  3. Either an index page at /for or a permanent redirect from /for to /guides. The redirect is one line in the config and I am inclined to take it, because the hub that lists both spaces already exists and a second hub would compete with it.
  4. A test that fails if src/app/not-found.tsx is missing. Our metadata test already walks src/app and reads every page file as text with readFileSync, which is a trick I wrote up for a sister app, so the cheapest version of this is three lines in a suite that is already looking at that directory.

The general lesson I will take from it: a framework default that renders without erroring is the hardest kind of gap to notice, because nothing in the build, the logs or the tests is unhappy. The thing that found this one was counting <a> elements on a page I had never thought to open.

You can check all of it yourself: notifio.app/nope is the before picture while it lasts, notifio.app/maintenance redirects home because the boolean is off, and the pages that do work are the alert site hub, including Kamernet and SpareRoom, with the guides at notifio.app/guides.

title: The Card-Update Page Gets One Visit. Design for That Visit.
description:
Here is a design constraint most teams never state out loud: the customer who lands on your card-update page will probably visit it exactly once. They are not browsing. They did not wake up wanting to explore your billing portal. They clicked a link in a message about a failed payment, they have their new card in one hand and their phone in the other, and they are giving you about ninety seconds. If the page works in those ninety seconds, you keep a subscriber. If it does not, no second email will fix it, because the moment of intent has passed.

Let us walk the page, screen by screen, the way that one visit actually happens.

The arrival

The visit starts before the page loads. The link in your email or text should be signed, expiring, and tied to the account, so the customer lands already identified — no login wall, no 'find your customer ID' treasure hunt. If your security model genuinely requires a login, say so in the message and keep the session alive through it; the classic failure is a customer who logs in and is deposited on a generic dashboard, their original destination discarded. Measure this transition like an engineer: what percentage of clicks become page views? That gap is pure loss, and it is usually authentication, not apathy.

The first screenful

At the top, answer three questions in plain text: whose account is this, what happened, and what will happen when they finish. 'The card ending in 4417 for your monthly plan was declined. Add a new card and we will retry the $24 payment today.' That one sentence replaces a page of reassurance. Show your product's name and logo exactly as they appear on the customer's statement, because a mismatch at this moment reads as phishing. Do not show navigation, promotions, upgrade offers, or a newsletter signup. This page has one job, and every other element is competing with revenue you have already almost lost.

The form itself

Ask only for what the processor needs: card number, expiry, security code, and a postal code if your fraud checks require it. Prefill the name from the account. Use the card-number input type so phones offer autofill and scanning, format the number in groups of four as they type, and detect the card brand silently instead of asking. Keep the form to a single column, keep labels visible above the fields rather than as disappearing placeholders, and make the submit button say what it does — 'Update card and retry payment' — not 'Submit'. For a fuller treatment of these choices, a card-update page guide built around the moment of intent collects the patterns in one place, and it is worth comparing against your current page field by field.

Errors, handled like a conversation

Inline validation should catch a mistyped digit before submission, and processor errors should come back translated. 'Your card was declined' tells a customer nothing; 'This card has expired — please check the date or use a different card' tells them exactly what to do next. Never clear the fields they already typed correctly. Never end at a dead end: if the new card also fails, offer the honest alternatives — try another card, pause the subscription, talk to a person — rather than looping them through the same form. Log every error code this page sees. Designers rarely get that data, and it changes decisions fast: one team I know discovered a third of their abandonments were a single address-verification rule, not the form at all.

The confirmation

The visit ends with certainty. As soon as the retry succeeds, say so, on the page and in a follow-up message: new card saved, payment completed, next renewal on this date. If the retry is queued rather than instant, say when it will run and how they will know the result. Ambiguity here generates support tickets and, worse, chargebacks from customers who re-subscribe or pay twice because they could not tell whether the first attempt worked.

Test it the way it is used

Finally, test the page under the conditions of the real visit: on a mid-range phone, on average mobile data, one-handed, with a physical card being read at the same time. Time it. If a motivated person cannot finish in ninety seconds, the page — not the customer — is the churn risk. These are the kinds of details gathered on Swipe Again's home page, where recovery is treated as a design discipline as much as a billing one.

You will not get a second visit to make a better impression. Design the one visit as if the subscription depends on it, because a measurable share of the time, it does.

title: Users Don't Hate Your App. They Hate These 7 Things About It
description:
Getting users to download your mobile app is a big achievement. But what happens when they uninstall it just a few days later?

The problem isn't always your app idea or its features. Sometimes, small issues like complicated onboarding, slow loading, confusing navigation, or too many notifications can frustrate users and push them toward alternatives.

Understanding why users uninstall apps is essential for developers who want to build successful mobile applications. A great app should do more than attract downloads. It should provide a smooth experience, solve real problems, and give users a reason to return.

In this article, we'll explore seven common reasons users uninstall mobile apps and practical ways developers can fix these issues to improve user experience and app retention.

1. Complicated App Onboarding

First impressions matter, especially when someone opens a mobile app for the first time. If users have to complete lengthy registration forms, verify multiple details, or grant unnecessary permissions before exploring the app, they may lose interest quickly.

For example, imagine someone downloads a shopping app but must create an account, verify their email, enter personal details, and provide several permissions before viewing products. Instead of enjoying the experience, they may simply uninstall the app.

To prevent this, developers should simplify the onboarding process by offering social login options, reducing unnecessary registration steps, and allowing users to explore essential features before requesting additional information.

A smooth onboarding experience helps users understand an app's value quickly, reducing one of the common reasons why users uninstall mobile apps and giving them a reason to keep using it.

2. Slow Loading and Frequent App Crashes

Nobody likes waiting for an app to load or dealing with unexpected crashes while completing an important task. Even if a mobile app offers useful features, poor performance can quickly frustrate users and damage their trust.

For example, imagine a user trying to make an online payment, but the app takes too long to respond or suddenly crashes during the transaction. After experiencing this problem repeatedly, they may switch to a more reliable alternative.

These app performance issues can result from inefficient code, poorly optimized APIs, excessive resource usage, or inadequate testing across different devices.

Developers can prevent these problems by optimizing app performance, reducing unnecessary background processes, monitoring crashes, and testing applications across different devices and network conditions.

A fast, stable, and reliable mobile app creates a smoother experience and gives users more reasons to keep using it.

3. Poor User Experience and Confusing Navigation

A mobile app should make everyday tasks easier, not more complicated. When users struggle to find features, understand buttons, or navigate between screens, they may become frustrated and stop using the app.

For example, imagine someone opening an AI-powered mobile app for food delivery but struggling to find the search bar, explore restaurant menus, or complete an order. Even if the app offers great services, confusing navigation can make users choose a competitor instead.

A poor mobile app user experience often results from cluttered layouts, inconsistent design elements, complicated navigation, and too many unnecessary steps.

Developers can improve the experience by creating simple interfaces, using clear navigation menus, maintaining consistent design patterns, and testing the app with real users. Collecting user feedback also helps identify usability problems that developers might otherwise overlook.

A well-designed mobile app user experience helps users complete tasks effortlessly, builds confidence, and gives them stronger reasons to keep using the app.

4. Too Many Push Notifications

Push notifications can help mobile apps keep users informed about important updates, offers, and activities. However, sending too many notifications or irrelevant messages can quickly become annoying.

For example, imagine someone receiving multiple promotional notifications from a shopping app every day, even when they haven't shown interest in those offers. Instead of encouraging them to open the app, these repeated interruptions may push them to disable notifications or uninstall the app completely.

This problem often occurs when developers focus more on increasing app engagement than understanding what users actually want to receive.

To avoid notification fatigue, developers should send relevant and timely notifications, allow users to customize their notification preferences, and avoid unnecessary promotional messages. Personalizing notifications based on user interests and activities can also make them more useful.

Relevant push notifications can strengthen user engagement, but excessive messaging can damage the user experience and reduce app retention.

5. Too Many Advertisements and Hidden Costs

Users expect mobile apps to provide value without constantly interrupting their activities. When an app displays too many advertisements, unexpected pop-ups, or unclear subscription charges, it can quickly lose users' trust.

For example, imagine someone using a free mobile app to edit photos. Every time they select a tool or save an image, another advertisement appears. If the app also hides important features behind unexpected payments, users may look for a better alternative.

These monetization practices can create frustration, especially when users don't understand what they're paying for or why certain features require additional charges.

Developers can prevent this by displaying advertisements responsibly, keeping subscription plans transparent, and clearly communicating which features are free and which require payment. Offering a smooth experience with fair pricing helps users feel more confident about using the app.

Transparent pricing builds confidence. When users understand what they're paying for, they're more likely to consider upgrading instead of uninstalling the app.

6. Privacy and Security Concerns

Users want to feel safe when sharing personal information through a mobile app. If an app requests unnecessary permissions, collects unclear amounts of personal data, or raises security concerns, users may hesitate to continue using it.

For example, imagine a simple calculator app requesting access to contacts, location, and photos without explaining why. Users may question whether the app actually needs that information or how their data will be used.

These privacy concerns can damage user trust and become another reason why users uninstall apps.

Developers can address these issues by requesting only essential permissions, explaining why specific data is needed, using secure authentication, and protecting sensitive information through appropriate encryption and security practices. Clear privacy policies and transparent data-handling practices also help users feel more confident.

When developers prioritize mobile app privacy and security, they improve what is user experience by building trust, protecting user information, and creating a safer environment that encourages long-term app usage.

7. Lack of Useful Features and Regular Improvements

Users download mobile apps because they expect them to solve a problem or make everyday tasks easier. If an app fails to deliver useful features or doesn't improve over time, users may eventually lose interest and uninstall it.

For example, imagine someone using a project management app that lacks task reminders, progress tracking, or useful collaboration features. If competing apps offer these capabilities, users may switch to an alternative that better meets their needs.

This problem often occurs when developers stop collecting user feedback, overlook changing expectations, or fail to update outdated functionality.

To prevent this, development teams should regularly analyze user feedback, monitor feature usage, fix reported issues, and introduce improvements based on actual user needs. Regular updates should focus on meaningful improvements rather than adding unnecessary features.

An app that continuously evolves with user expectations can improve engagement, build loyalty, and give people more reasons to keep using it.

How Developers Can Reduce App Uninstalls

Reducing app uninstalls requires more than fixing bugs or adding new features. Developers need to understand user expectations and continuously improve the overall mobile app experience.

Here are some practical ways to improve app retention:

  • Simplify onboarding: Make registration quick and allow users to explore essential features without unnecessary steps.
  • Improve app performance: Optimize loading speed, fix crashes, and test applications across different devices.
  • Focus on user experience: Create simple navigation, clean interfaces, and accessible features.
  • Send relevant notifications: Deliver useful updates instead of overwhelming users with promotional messages.
  • Maintain transparent pricing: Clearly explain subscriptions, in-app purchases, and paid features.
  • Prioritize security: Protect user data and request only necessary permissions.
  • Listen to user feedback: Regularly improve features based on user needs and app usage patterns.

Why App Retention Matters More Than Downloads

Getting thousands of app downloads might look like success, but downloads alone don't determine whether a mobile app is successful. What matters is whether users continue using the app after installing it.

For example, an app may attract thousands of downloads through marketing campaigns, but if users uninstall it within a few days because of poor performance or confusing features, those downloads won't create long-term value.

This is why developers and businesses should focus on mobile app retention rather than downloads alone. Retaining existing users helps build stronger customer relationships, encourage repeat engagement, and create opportunities for sustainable business growth.

By continuously improving app performance, understanding user behavior, and responding to feedback, development teams can create applications that users genuinely want to keep using.

Final Thoughts: Build Apps People Actually Want to Keep

Getting users to download your app is only the beginning. Keeping them engaged requires a smooth experience, reliable performance, useful features, and a strong focus on user expectations.

From complicated onboarding to privacy concerns, even small issues can influence why users uninstall apps. Developers should regularly evaluate their applications, listen to user feedback, and make meaningful improvements to create better experiences.

Remember, successful mobile app development isn't just about adding more features or attracting more downloads. It's about understanding what users need and building an application that consistently delivers value.

When users find your app useful, reliable, and easy to navigate, they have more reasons to stay rather than look for an alternative.

title: Onboarding Instrumentation: What to Actually Log Before You Redesign the Flow
description:
Most "redesign the onboarding" tickets start with opinions and end with a flow that's shorter but unmeasured, nobody can say if the new version converts better because nobody logged the old one in a way that answers the question. Before touching copy or screen order, the instrumentation needs to exist. Here's the minimum set that makes a before/after comparison possible.

Define "first value" as an analytics event, not a UI state

"Onboarding complete" is a UI state, it fires when the last screen closes, whether or not the user got anything out of it. First value is different: it's the first time the product actually does something useful for this specific user. A photo app's first value event is library_cleaned, not onboarding_dismissed. A budgeting app's is transaction_categorized, not account_created. If you can't name the event, you haven't found it yet, go compare retained users against churned users from the first few days and find the action that separates them.

The three metrics that matter, and why completion rate isn't one of them

  • Activation rate - percent of new users firing the first-value event within a defined window (7 days is common). This is the real top-line number.
  • Time to value - median time from first open to first-value event. Read it alongside activation rate; a shorter median among a smaller activated cohort is a trap, not a win.
  • Step-level drop-off - where people actually leave the flow, step by step. This is what tells you whether a step is disposable or load-bearing.

Completion rate (did they finish the flow) tells you almost nothing on its own. A 90% completion rate with a 40% activation rate means your flow is good at getting people through screens and bad at getting them to the thing that matters.

Sort every step with one question, logged against real data

  • Keep: would the product be unsafe, non-compliant, or non-functional without this step? -> identity verification, required consent, payment auth.
  • Defer: useful later, not required for first value? -> profile photo, notification prefs, invites.
  • Remove: serves the team more than the user? -> unused feature tours, duplicate confirmations, long surveys.

This only works if you can see step-level drop-off per cohort, don't sort from a whiteboard, sort from the funnel.

Permission requests: timing is an engineering decision, not a copy decision

Request permissions at the moment they're needed, not in a batch during onboarding, camera access when the user starts their first scan, notification permission after they've seen a reason to want alerts, not before. This isn't just better UX, it measurably changes grant rates, because the system prompt appears with context instead of as an abstract ask. If your onboarding flow currently front-loads permission requests, that's usually an easy first fix with a clear before/after in your grant-rate logs.

Deferred registration needs a technical answer to "what happens to this session if they bounce?"

Letting users try the product before creating an account (Duolingo's well-known move, worth roughly a 20% DAU lift in an early internal test, per the company's own account) means you need anonymous-session state that can later merge into a real account without data loss. If your backend can't cleanly convert an anonymous session into an authenticated one, deferred registration will cost you more in support tickets and lost progress than it gains in completion.

Regulated flows: the identity-check step isn't a UX problem, don't instrument it like one

If you're in fintech or insurance, step-level drop-off at an identity-verification gate will look terrible compared to everything else in the funnel, and that's often expected, not a bug. Signicat's 2022 survey across 14 European countries put financial-app abandonment at 68% in the prior year, with 21% citing excessive personal-data requests specifically. The fix there isn't removing the step, it's reducing abandonment around it: save-and-resume state, clear in-flow explanations of why each field is required, and collecting only what's legally mandated at account creation rather than front-loading optional fields into the same gate.

Varmeta's longer write-up on separating load-bearing onboarding steps from the ones that just add screens covers the product-and-design side of this in more depth. The condensed table version is on GitHub if you want the keep/defer/remove criteria and cited numbers without the narrative, closer to something you'd paste into an internal doc.

Discussion: if you've instrumented an onboarding flow properly, what ended up being your actual first-value event, was it the one the product team originally assumed?

title: Amazon CloudFront now supports self-service increases in AWS Service Quotas
description:
Amazon CloudFront now supports AWS Service Quotas, so you can view, monitor, and request increases for 28 CloudFront quotas from the Service Quotas console or API.

Until now, increasing a quota on resources such as distributions, cache policies, origins, or alternate domain names meant opening a support case and waiting for manual review. If you have AWS Business Support or higher, requests for limit increases within published thresholds are now approved automatically. For example, you can raise your distribution quota from 500 to 1,000, or the number of alternate domain names per distribution from 100 to 500, without opening a support case. Some quotas also publish usage metrics to Amazon CloudWatch every 5 minutes, so you can set alarms and request an increase before you reach a limit..

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudFront is supported.

To get started, visit the Service Quotas console to view and request increases for your CloudFront quotas. To learn more, see Amazon CloudFront quotas in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide.

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.
561666530 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Prometheus library to patch the following vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
564969400 Fixed an issue where variables initialized from an empty <Value/> element in AssignMessage (AssignVariable) were not treated as empty strings when referenced in message template functions such as replaceAll.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

Assured Workloads

Feature

The Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5) supports the following products:

  • Google Security Operations SIEM

Feature

The Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4) supports the following products:

  • Google Security Operations SIEM

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

New versions available for upgrades and new clusters.

The following versions are now available for new GKE clusters, and for manual control plane upgrades and node upgrades for existing clusters. For more information about versioning and upgrades, see GKE versioning and support and About GKE cluster upgrades.

Rapid channel

Note: Your clusters might not have these versions available. Rollouts are already in progress when we publish the release notes, and can take multiple days to complete across all Google Cloud zones.

(2026-R42) Security updates

This release includes new GKE versions that use updated Container-Optimized OS images. These updated images are cumulative, incorporating security fixes from all Container-Optimized OS versions released since the previous GKE release.

To identify the specific vulnerabilities that were resolved in each updated Container-Optimized OS image, see the Security release notes for that image. The following table includes links to the release notes for each updated Container-Optimized OS image:

GKE version Container-Optimized OS version Details

Issue

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.
  • Container-Optimized OS with containerd (cos_containerd) node pools on GKE versions 1.33 and earlier, 1.34 versions earlier than 1.34.6-gke.1154000, and 1.35 versions earlier than 1.35.3-gke.1389000.

Workaround: For cos_containerd node pools, upgrade the node pool to a version with the required kernel support (for example, 1.34.6-gke.1154000 or later, 1.35.3-gke.1389000 or later, or match the control plane). For ubuntu_containerd node pools, a fix is in progress. Alternatively, downgrade the control plane to a version earlier than 1.36.3-gke.1244000.

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the <namespace> segment in these queries.

Queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification. We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases.

Mitigation:

  • Recommended: Migrate to supported headless Service DNS records (<hostname>.<subdomain>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local).
  • Workaround: Ensure the <namespace> specified in the DNS query exists in the cluster.

Negative backend deadlines are deprecated

A negative backend deadline in an OpenAPI 2.0 x-google-backend extension or a gRPC BackendRule uses the default deadline, the same as 0. BigQuery offers TimesFM 3.0, a built-in time series forecasting model that implements Google Research's open source TimesFM model. You can use TimesFM 3.0 with the following functions:

Conversational analytics in BigQuery also supports using TimesFM 3.0 with these functions.

After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where node drain in maintenance mode did not wait for attached storage volumes to detach.
  • Added support in bgpadvertiser for advertising IPv6 addresses in addition to IPv4 addresses for bundled BGP control plane load balancing.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.36.100-gke.144:

  • Link to Vulnerability fixes for the list of security vulnerabilities addressed in this release.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster had a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where updating control plane configurations could cause transient Kubernetes API server downtime. After the fix, the update process strictly verifies that each API server is healthy before restarting subsequent control plane nodes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could stall indefinitely in the terminating state due to orphaned machine resources.
  • Fixed an issue where worker node pool creation could stall during provisioning in environments with strict network firewall policies. The node pool controller no longer waits for all inventory machines to be ready before declaring the node pool, eliminating a provisioning deadlock.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

The microVM sandbox type is now Generally Available (GA) with GKE Sandbox in clusters that run version 1.37.0-gke.4713000 and later. MicroVM sandboxes provide hardware virtualization and isolation for untrusted workloads, AI agent runtimes, and multi-tenant environments. GKE microVM sandboxes use Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor to provide this isolation while maintaining a full Linux kernel that includes standard Linux features

For more information, see the GKE Sandbox documentation.

You can enable this feature in a VPC Flow Logs configuration for a subnet (through the Network Management API), a VPC network, or an organization.

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Pay-as-you-go usage above quota must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, October 12, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent. To use Advanced Analytics, you must also enable whichever Conversational Analytics toggle corresponds to the content that you are querying (Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents). If both the Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents toggles are turned off, then Advanced Analytics cannot be enabled. If either Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents is enabled, Advanced Analytics can be enabled, but it is turned off by default.

The Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents settings inherit the enablement state of the Conversational Analytics setting in previous versions of Looker.

Conversational Analytics preview features can still be enabled selectively under the Enable Trusted Tester Features setting.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

Conversational Analytics data agents for both user-defined dashboards and LookML dashboards are now generally available.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

You can now apply themes to Looks in addition to internal dashboards.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where duplicating a scheduled plan could fail to retain the custom message value. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table visualizations now proportionally scale left-pinned columns during automatic sizing, which prevents unnecessary horizontal scrollbars. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where enabling subtotals on table visualizations did not automatically disable the Cell Visualizations option. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where previews for Looker charts in Slack integrations could fail to be displayed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where editing and saving a dashboard could cause the dashboard to reload indefinitely, forcing users to refresh the page. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table cell visualizations that included both positive and negative values could display unwanted scrollbars and hide value labels. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the BigQuery JDBC driver could fail to properly parse certain data types, such as BYTES, STRUCT/RECORD, and nested ARRAY structures. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where linked filters on a dashboard could fail to display autocomplete suggestions even when a parent filter is selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to ensure that phase timings (such as connection acquisitions, execution runtimes, and optimistic pivot fallback retry loops) are successfully captured for queries that fail or time out. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity Dashboard Diagnostics dashboard has been updated to fully support statistics, tile run counts, and performance recommendations for LookML dashboards. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the color palette popover in visualization settings failed to dynamically reposition when it expanded, causing controls to overlap or truncate. This feature now performs as expected.

Breaking

When you set up a connection, self-service modeling will now be available only if a role that grants create_self_service_from_table also selects it through that role's model set.

Fixed

The opacity for the comparison bar in short KPI visualizations has been reduced to increase legibility.

Memorystore for Redis

Feature

To help protect your data and provide a baseline level of persistence, RDB snapshots are enabled by default when you create an instance using the Google Cloud console. This feature is generally available.

VPC Service Controls

Feature

General availability support for the following integration:

  • Cloud Storage for Firebase

Feature

VPC Service Controls feature (Status: Preview): Support for automated remediation suggestions is available in the VPC Service Controls violation analyzer.

Remediation suggestions analyze access denial events and generate actionable, narrowly scoped configuration changes to resolve perimeter denials and adhere to the principle of least privilege. The remediation engine can automatically propose ingress rules, egress rules, VPC accessible services updates, and existing or new context-aware access levels.

For more information, see Resolve access denials with remediation suggestions.

Note: Near real-time sync upon Knowledge Catalog (KC) enablement isn't available for existing instances created before April 18, 2026. For more information, see the release note from October 14, 2026.

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running MySQL version 8.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 5, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) instances running Looker 26.18. Feature enablement for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Feature

Looker now includes built-in support for the Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) dialect. The Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) uses the bundled Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver, so that you don't have to install unpackaged custom JDBC driver JAR files. See the Dremio documentation page for more information.

Feature

The AI-Assisted Quick Starts feature, called Starter questions in the new Explore experience, is now generally available.

Feature

The new Diagnose & Repair tool evaluates your LookML project repository across eight diagnostic test checks in either your personal development environment or the shared production environment. When issues are found, Looker can automatically perform repairs (such as removing stale lock files, fixing file permissions, or repairing corrupted object indexes) or rebuild damaged repositories while safeguarding uncommitted changes on a dedicated recovery branch.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now includes the Style Validator, which enforces LookML coding standards, naming conventions, and structural best practices across your LookML project. You can run the Style Validator with the default built-in ruleset or customize rule severities, file exclusions, path overrides, and custom rules by adding an lkmlstyle.yaml configuration file to your project repository.

Feature

Now available in preview, Conversational Analytics agentic workflows support scheduled agentic workflows in addition to triggered agentic workflows. You can use scheduled agentic workflows to schedule recurring deliveries of AI-generated insights summaries, data tables, visualizations, and PDF reports to email or Slack by using natural language. Recipients can select Investigate in a workflow notification to open a private, persistent conversation with the data agent.

Users and admins can manage workflows on the updated Manage Workflows user page and Manage Workflows admin page, respectively, and Looker admins can monitor scheduled workflow runs and troubleshoot errors on the new Workflow Executions admin page.

Workflows that were created in versions earlier than Looker 26.14 appear on the Legacy Workflows tab and must be recreated.

Feature

Now available in preview, Looker Data Apps are freeform canvas dashboards that are built by local AI coding agents, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or Cursor, from natural-language prompts. Data Apps give you complete visual layout control (including absolute positioning, overlapping elements, and custom web components) while remaining bound to Looker's governed LookML semantic layer and user permissions.

Change

In Conversational Analytics, the default question mode is now Fast rather than Thinking. Fast mode is intended for answering quickly, and it directly maps your query to underlying LookML definitions without generating reasoning steps. You can still select Thinking mode from the question mode drop-down menu when asking complex, multi-step analytical questions about Explores or dashboards.

Change

The Modern User Interface preview feature toggle now defaults to ON.

Change

The Modern visualization theme now supports map charts (static map points and regions), word cloud charts, and donut multiples. While support for donut multiples was previously documented, it is now officially available with this release. These additions expand the range of visualization options that are available with the modern theme.

Feature

Looker now supports connections to the ClickHouse 26+ dialect. ClickHouse 26+ uses modernized JDBC drivers and introduces support for symmetric aggregates. See the ClickHouse documentation page for more information.

Feature

Enhanced observability metrics, including user engagement and estimated token usage data on the Token usage tab of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard, are now generally available (GA). This launch also adds a Daily Token Utilization visualization and supports token usage observability for Conversational Analytics data agents that are published to Gemini Enterprise. (Note: This item was added on October 20, 2026.)

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor includes enhanced prompt injection and jailbreak protection for Workspace data. This capability improves detection accuracy and minimizes false positives when screening Workspace content, such as emails, documents, and files.

This capability is available on multi-region endpoints in the US (us) and EU (eu) for templates and floor setting configured with filter version v3 or later, including the Stable and Latest aliases.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports global access. You can enable this feature when creating a Secure Web Proxy instance to make sure that clients from any Google Cloud region can connect to your proxy.

With global access, you can route your outbound traffic through specific regions to meet regulatory compliance or cost requirements. You can also use this option to simplify your network administration by managing outbound traffic from a centralized location.

This feature is available in Preview.

Security Command Center

Feature

Using gcloud CLI, the securitycenter REST API, or client libraries, you can configure Pub/Sub and BigQuery continuous export to receive notifications when findings are deleted from Security Command Center due to data retention policies.

For more information, see the following:

  • Enable finding notifications for Pub/Sub
  • Stream findings to BigQuery for analysis
  • Enable real-time notifications
  • Creating and managing Notification Configs

Sensitive Data Protection

Change

If you set InfoType.version to legacy when including the MEDICAL_ID infoType in your InspectConfig, Sensitive Data Protection now includes MEDICAL_RECORD_NUMBER findings as type MEDICAL_ID in the scan results.

Regular expression matchers in host and route rules in URL maps are now generally available (GA).

You can now use regular expressions (regex) matchers to configure more flexible and precise traffic routing rules within URL maps for Application Load Balancers. This feature allows you to leverage the power of RE2 syntax for matching on:

  • URL Paths: Using the regexMatch field within routeRules.
  • HTTP Headers: Using the regexMatch field within headerMatches in routeRules.

CodeMender updates (v0.14.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Better pull request scans: cm find --diff now catches removed security controls and gives large files more time (configurable with --diff-job-timeout).
  • Unified sessions: --deep and --diff scans now appear as a single session in cm session list, cm report, and cm stats.
  • Moved code in cm verify: cm verify now finds code that moved since cm find and updates the finding's location.
  • Guided activation: cm now opens the activation page and waits for activation instead of exiting.
  • New cm find flags: --deep-max-turns limits exploratory steps per file in --deep scans, and --enable-bash allows shell commands during scans.
  • Improved detection: More distinct findings per file and more precise CWE classification for weak hashing and randomness.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed scans of repositories reached through nested symbolic links.
    • Fixed findings for nonexistent files and over-merged findings.
    • Shell scripts created by cm verify are now executable.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Monitor response and playbook health with the Response Health Hub

Google SecOps now includes the Response Health Hub curated dashboard, a central location for monitoring playbook performance, execution latency, automation effectiveness, and integration health across environments.

Key capabilities include:

  • Volume and adoption tracking: Monitor total playbook execution volume, daily trends, completion success rates, and queued playbook backlogs.
  • Attachment and rerun insights: Track average and maximum playbooks attached per case or alert, and identify playbooks with high rerun counts.
  • Execution latency diagnostics: Compare end-to-end playbook execution time against active action execution time, and drill down into the 30 slowest playbook and action runs.
  • Playbook and integration health monitoring: Investigate the latest failed playbook runs, highest failure-rate and terminated playbooks, and integration action error reasons.
  • Automation effectiveness metrics: Compare automated versus manual case closure rates and Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR).

For more information, see Monitor response and playbook health.

If you have custom rules that still reference the legacy feeds, update them to use the GTI_IOC feed. For more information, see Migrate to GTI_IOC.

The update follows the standard Google SecOps rollout schedule. It starts on Monday, October 12, 2026 and rolls out to all regions during the week.

Workforce Identity Federation allows users to authenticate by using external identity providers without the need to manage individual Google Accounts. Administrators can select Workforce Identity as the primary authentication method when they create or edit an instance and, optionally, enable secondary Google OAuth for secure backup access.

Starting today, projects with producer VPC spokes linked to Network Connectivity Center hubs will reflect hourly usage fees. Charges on your future billing invoices are based on Network Connectivity Center pricing.

From a template revision, you can create, assess, and deploy applications directly, or publish the revision to your catalog to reuse it in other templates (Preview). BigQuery

Feature

The AI.AGG function is generally available (GA). You can use this function to semantically aggregate unstructured input data based on natural language instructions.

Feature

BigQuery generative AI functions now support the gemini-4-argon model. This model is generally available.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Cloud Service Mesh: networkservices.googleapis.com/AgentGateway

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend
  • Limitations of spend cap budgets
  • Configure a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

  • Using the Cloud Billing Budget API for spend cap budgets
  • Spend cap budget concepts and limitations
  • Create a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Feature

Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. Feature

Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud Storage

Feature

Object enrichments is now available in Preview. When you configure object enrichments, Cloud Storage applies Google's pre-trained machine learning models to eligible images and PDF documents in your buckets and attaches the resulting metadata to your objects as object contexts. You can inspect enrichments on individual objects or query them at scale in BigQuery by using Storage Insights datasets. For more information, see About object enrichments and Configure object enrichments.

Feature

Object contexts with extended data are available in Preview. Google services attach these contexts to your objects during automated analysis, such as machine learning labeling. To retrieve a context and its extended data, use the viewFullContext JSON API method.

Storage Insights datasets include the Object Contexts Catalog view (object_contexts_catalog_view), which you can use to analyze object contexts in BigQuery. For more information, see Object contexts catalog and Analyze object contexts.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.106.0 is available. This release adds support for flexible managed instance groups on static compute nodes, multiple network interfaces (multi-NIC) for Google Cloud Managed Lustre instances, and parallelism controls for Terraform to accelerate cluster deployment and teardown.

This release also introduces the cloud-build community module to build container images with Cloud Build.

Additionally, this release adds preflight checks for storage profiles when you submit jobs and cleans up gateways when you cancel jobs.

This update also scopes the --main-only flag in the gcluster job logs command to the main Pod and its default container.

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can query regional views of global Compute Engine project and OS image resources by using the regional read-only projectViews and imageViews endpoints. Querying regional views isolates your control-plane read requests to a specific region, helping your workloads stay available during global API disruptions. For more information, see Use regional views for resilient control-plane reads and Access global resources regionally for high availability.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. Gemini 4 Argon is supported in the web app and mobile app. For more information about turning on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Argon. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce

You can connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce to search data and automate actions across these third-party apps.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon is available in AlphaEvolve

AlphaEvolve experiments can generate candidate programs with Gemini 4 Argon in the global, us, and eu regions. To use it, specify gemini-4-argon in the models field of generationSettings. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Supported models and AlphaEvolve limitations.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Argon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-argon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation tokens on the GenerateContent API, and agentic video understanding in GA.

Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive (gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive), a version of Gemini 4 Argon for defensive cybersecurity use cases, is also available in GA behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

  • Known issue (long decodes): Long decoding (continuation_token) on the GenerateContent API (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path.
