title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

Read more

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster
description: Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 introduces native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, enabling the MCP data plane to run directly within your own Kubernetes cluster. This architecture ensures that AI agent request traffic and tool execution remain entirely inside your infrastructure while pulling configuration updates from the control plane. Developers can expose OpenAPI 3.0.x specifications as discoverable MCP tools, leverage existing security policies and API products, and trace end-to-end requests using W3C trace context headers.

title: Python vs Go vs Rust for a Vector Search API: the Language Explained 5% of the Throughput Variance
description:
Most "Python vs Go vs Rust" API benchmarks I have seen measure the HTTP layer with a trivial handler. A semantic-search API spends much of its time somewhere else: inside the vector store. So I built the same /search endpoint nine times, three languages times three stores, and ran all of it on tight hardware: one 8 GiB Mac mini, closer to an edge box or a small VM than to a database server. The question was not only which stack is fastest, but which one degrades first when memory and threads run short, and why.

Thesis: for a semantic-search API, the store you pick decides most of your throughput. The language decides much less.

Antithesis I expected to find: Python's JSON parsing on the same cores as the search should drag FastAPI down at high load, so the language should matter most exactly where it hurts.

What the data says, for this design on this machine: the store explains about two thirds of the variance in throughput, the language about 5% (method in Result 1). Which store was fastest depended on data size and k, not on the framework. And the two most consequential things I found were not speed rankings at all: a Go binding that crashes at a kernel thread limit, and an 8 GiB machine whose free memory moved pgvector's throughput by 4 to 7x.

The setup

The 3 x 3 factorial. One API contract, implemented three times:

API layer Framework Runtime
Python FastAPI 0.159.1 on uvicorn 0.54.0 (httptools, uvloop) CPython 3.13.12
Go net/http (stdlib ServeMux) Go 1.27.3
Rust axum 0.8 on tokio 1 rustc 1.99.1

Each one is backed by three stores:

Store Index Topology
pgvector 0.8.0 on PostgreSQL 17.11 HNSW, cosine separate server, unix socket
DuckDB VSS (DuckDB 1.5.6) HNSW embedded, in-process
LanceDB 0.40.0 IVF_HNSW_FLAT, one partition (a single HNSW graph) embedded, in-process

All three indexes use cosine distance and the same build parameters, HNSW M = 16 and ef_construction = 128. Only the search-time knob (ef) differs per store, and it is set by recall calibration (below), not by hand.

DuckDB is pinned to 1.5.6 in all three languages because the Rust duckdb crate has no 2.0 build yet, and one engine version across languages matters more than the newest one.

Deployment per language, fixed before any data. Go and Rust run as one process each. Python runs 6 uvicorn workers in front of pgvector (one per core the server was meant to use) and 1 worker in front of the embedded stores, because every extra worker would load its own copy of the index into 8 GiB. The Python handler parses the raw body with orjson and checks the vector length, like the Go and Rust handlers; it does not use a Pydantic model. pgvector connection pools hold 24 connections in total per server, and DuckDB gets 6 threads. An ablation swapped the Python process model (1 vs 6 workers for pgvector, 1 vs 2 for the embedded stores; 100k, recall 0.95, k 10, 3 runs each): the median MST was the same ladder step in both arms for all three stores (3,200, 1,600 and 400 rps). Postgres runs with shared_buffers 1 GB and effective_cache_size 3 GB, sized for 8 GiB.

Host. One Mac mini: Apple M2 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores), 8 GiB RAM, macOS 26.5.2, on AC power, kept awake with caffeinate. That constraint is what this study is about. No CPU pinning, because macOS has no affinity API on Apple silicon. The API server, Postgres and the load generator share all 8 cores. Everything is installed natively, no Docker.

Data. Cohere Wikipedia embeddings (768 dimensions) as packaged by VectorDBBench: 100k vectors, and a seeded 300k subset of the 1M set. Exact top-100 ground truth by brute force.

Equal recall, not equal parameters. Comparing stores at the same ef is misleading, because the same number buys different recall in different engines. Each store's search knob was calibrated on 200 queries to hit a target recall of 0.90, 0.95 or 0.99, and recall@k was then scored on held-out queries from the actual HTTP responses. Held-out recall landed within -0.011 to +0.044 of target in all 36 store, scale, k and target combinations (the +0.044 is pgvector at k 100, where the calibration grid starts at ef 100 so that every query can return 100 hits); the median deviation per store is +0.002 for DuckDB, +0.004 for pgvector and +0.013 for LanceDB (for example 0.971 at a 0.95 target at 300k). Overshooting costs throughput, so LanceDB's overshoot works slightly against it. The one undershoot worth naming is pgvector at 100k, k 10, target 0.90: ef 16 reached 0.901 on the calibration queries and 0.889 on the held-out ones. Those two configurations (ids only and ids plus text) hold the study's highest MST, 6,400 rps, so read that number as recall 0.89.

The metric. Max sustainable throughput (MST): the highest offered rate at which a 30 second open-loop step (vegeta) sends at least 98% of requests with at most 0.1% errors and p99 at or below 100 ms. Each run starts a fresh server process, warms up for 20 s at 50 rps (discarded), then climbs a doubling ladder on the grid 25, 50, 100 ... rps, with 3 s between steps, and stops at the first step that fails. The centre cell starts at 25 and adds three bisection steps. Elsewhere the ladder starts about four doublings below the centre-cell MST of the same language and store, and walks down if that first step already fails, so MST has 2x resolution and "the same" means "the same ladder step". A cell's value is the median MST of its 5 runs.

The design. 24 configurations (2 scales x 3 recall targets x top-k 10 or 100 x ids only or ids plus ~1 KB of text per hit) x 9 cells x 5 replicates, plus calibration, index builds and ablations: 1,543 runs over 88 hours. Run order follows a Williams design drawn at random per block (seed 20261022), so no cell always runs after the same neighbour. Warm cache everywhere except a cold-start ablation.

Result 1: the store dominates

Method. For each of the 24 configurations separately, I take the 45 runs (9 cells x 5 runs; a few cells have 4 after exclusions) and split the total sum of squares of log MST into store, language, store x language interaction and residual, the classic two-way ANOVA decomposition. A share is that term's sum of squares divided by the total. The table shows the median of each share across the 24 configurations. Medians are taken term by term, so the four rows do not add up to 100%.

Fact. The median variance shares are:

Source Share of variance in log MST
Store 69%
Language 5%
Store x language interaction 7%
Run-to-run residual 12%

The store explains more than the language in 23 of 24 configurations. The exception is a tie: 100k vectors, recall 0.99, k 10, ids only, where each explains 50%. Across configurations the store share ranges from 33% to 100% and the language share from 0% to 50%, with 22 of 24 configurations at 14% or less. Because MST sits on a doubling ladder, log MST takes few distinct values, so these shares are coarse. They describe this design (these stores, scales, recall targets and k values on this host), not every possible one.

At low load the result is even more one-sided. For p50 latency at about a quarter of each cell's MST, the store share is 79% and the language share 5% (main run).

Interpretation. Look at either panel of the chart and ask what moves a bar more: changing its colour (the store) or moving it sideways (the language). Within a language, the best store beats the worst by a median of 4x for Python and Rust and 2x for Go. Within a store, the best language beats the worst by a median of 2x for DuckDB and pgvector and 1x for LanceDB. On a 2x ladder, that is one step for the language and one to two steps for the store, and the store's steps show up in almost every configuration.

Why the language mattered so little here: the HTTP layer was not the bottleneck. With a stub store that returns fixed ids, every language sustains at least 12,800 rps (median of 5 runs, JSON in, k 100 plus text out included). No run with a real store in the whole study got past 6,400. FastAPI parsing a 768-float JSON body is not what limits a semantic-search service on this machine.

What the language layer actually does. Here is the pgvector /search path in each of the three APIs, copied from the benchmarked source and trimmed only with .... Each handler parses the JSON body, checks the vector length, makes one store call and encodes the result as JSON. The full sources are in the repo: https://github.com/firfircelik/vector-api-bench/tree/main/api

FastAPI (api/python/app.py):

@app.post("/search")
async def search(req: Request):
    body = orjson.loads(await req.body())
    vec = np.asarray(body["vector"], dtype=np.float32)
    if vec.shape != (DIM,):
        return Response(status_code=400)
    return jresp(await state["store"].search(vec, int(body.get("k", 10)), bool(body.get("doc", False))))

class PgVectorStore:
    ...
    async def search(self, vec, k, doc):
        async with self.pool.connection() as c:
            rows = await (await c.execute(self.sql_doc if doc else self.sql, (vec, k))).fetchall()
        r = {"ids": [x[0] for x in rows], "scores": [float(x[1]) for x in rows]}
        ...

Go net/http (api/go/main.go; write sets the content type and calls json.NewEncoder(w).Encode):

mux.HandleFunc("POST /search", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var q struct {
        ...
    }
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&q); err != nil || len(q.Vector) != dim {
        http.Error(w, "bad request", 400)
        return
    }
    ...
    res, err := st.Search(r.Context(), q.Vector, q.K, q.Doc)
    ...
    write(w, res)
})

func (s *pgStore) Search(ctx context.Context, v []float32, k int, doc bool) (*resp, error) {
    ...
    rows, err := s.pool.Query(ctx, q, pgv.NewVector(v), k)
    ...

Rust axum (api/rust/src/main.rs):

async fn search(State(a): S, Json(q): Json<Req>) -> Result<Json<Resp>, (StatusCode, String)> {
    if q.vector.len() != a.dim { return Err((StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, "dim".into())); }
    a.search(q.vector, q.k, q.doc).await.map(Json).map_err(|e| (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, e))
}
...
            Store::Pg { pool, sql, sql_doc } => {
                let c = pool.get().await.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
                let st = c.prepare_cached(if doc { sql_doc } else { sql }).await.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
                let rows = c.query(&st, &[&pgvector::Vector::from(v), &k]).await.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
                Ok(Resp { ids: rows.iter().map(|r| r.get(0)).collect(), scores: rows.iter().map(|r| r.get(1)).collect(),
                          docs: if doc { Some(rows.iter().map(|r| r.get(2)).collect()) } else { None } })
            }

That is the whole language layer: parse, one store call, encode. A wrapper this thin is consistent with the language explaining about 5% of the throughput variance, and with the stub-store floor of at least 12,800 rps in every language. Where the language does show up (Result 3), it is in the store client underneath that one call, not in these handlers.

Result 2: which store was fastest depended on the data, not the framework

Fact. Geometric mean of the cell medians across the 23 non-centre configurations:

Store All 69 cells 100k vectors (36 cells) 300k vectors (33 cells)
LanceDB 1,039 rps 1,295 rps 817 rps
pgvector 816 rps 1,831 rps 338 rps
DuckDB VSS 388 rps 544 rps 268 rps

Counting the fastest store per configuration and language (69 cells), with ties: LanceDB 51, pgvector 48, DuckDB 2. Without ties: LanceDB 20, pgvector 18, DuckDB 0. Ties are common (31 of 69 cells) because the ladder doubles.

The map splits cleanly:

  • 100k vectors, k 10: pgvector is fastest or tied in 18 of 18 cells (geo-mean 2,743 vs LanceDB 1,796 rps), up to 6,400 rps at the 0.90 target (held-out recall 0.89, see the setup).
  • 300k vectors, k 100: LanceDB is fastest or tied in 18 of 18 cells (geo-mean 544 rps vs DuckDB 224 and pgvector 121).
  • 300k vectors, k 10: close, LanceDB 1,330 vs pgvector 1,158 rps.
  • DuckDB VSS never wins a cell on its own. Its two shared wins are 400 rps ties at 300k, k 100.

Interpretation. pgvector is the fastest store here at 100k. At 300k it falls behind LanceDB, and at 300k with k 100 it is last (121 rps vs DuckDB 224). My reading is memory: at 300k the pgvector index is 1.23 GB, larger than the 1 GB shared_buffers I could afford on an 8 GiB machine, so part of it has to come from the OS page cache, which competes with everything else on the machine, and at k 100 each query plausibly touches much more of the graph and the heap. The memory-pressure section supports this: at 300k, pgvector's latency tracked free memory (r = -0.80), DuckDB's and LanceDB's much less. LanceDB lost 37% of its geo-mean from 100k to 300k, pgvector 82%. This is one host with 8 GiB, so I would not carry the 300k ranking to a server with 64 GiB without measuring it there.

Result 3: where the language does show up

The language effect is real in two places, and in both it is the store client, not the web framework.

DuckDB: the binding's cost per query. Without HTTP at all (6 concurrent direct client calls, 300k, recall 0.95), DuckDB answers 844 queries per second from Go, 615 from Rust and 573 from Python, at 7.0, 11.5 and 11.6 ms of client CPU per query. Through the API at the centre cell the CPU per request repeats the order: Go 3.7, Rust 5.6, Python 6.6 ms. Same DuckDB 1.5.6 underneath, same thread setting. The data does not tell me why the Go binding is cheaper.

pgvector: Python is one step lower in the fastest configurations. At 100k, recall 0.90, k 10, Python/pgvector reaches 3,200 rps where Go and Rust reach 6,400. My reading: that is where the API process does the most work per second and pgvector's server-side cost per query is lowest, so the API layer's own cost becomes visible.

LanceDB: the language makes no difference to the median (best/worst ratio 1.0x), until Go hits the wall in the next section.

The Go + LanceDB thread ceiling: the stack that broke

This one is not a throughput ranking. It is a failure mode, and it is the finding I would most want to know before shipping.

Fact. In the clean centre rerun (5 runs, 300k, recall 0.95, k 10):

  • Through 1,600 rps the Go/LanceDB server is healthy: p99 about 2 ms, 0 errors, and a flat 216 to 328 OS threads.
  • In the 3,200 rps step the process dies within about 4 seconds, in all 5 runs. In the four runs where the 2 second sampler caught the climb, the thread count reached 1,133 to 2,048 within about 2 seconds; the fifth died between samples, and its crash dump shows Go thread ids up to 1,501.
  • server.log shows the same sequence 5 times: runtime/cgo: pthread_create failed: Resource temporarily unavailable, then SIGABRT. Four of the Go crash dumps are complete. They list 1,517 to 1,765 goroutines, and all but one goroutine per dump is in state syscall inside the same cgo function, _Cfunc_simple_lancedb_table_select_query_ipc. The fifth dump is interleaved with other output but shows the same function. The highest Go thread id in the dumps is between 1,501 and 1,766.
  • The Mac's per-process thread limit is kern.num_taskthreads = 2048. Two of the five runs were sampled at exactly 2,048 threads.
  • The three bisection steps after the crash (2,262, 1,902 and 1,744 rps) measured a dead port: 100% instant errors. The Go/LanceDB MST of 1,600 is therefore a lower bound. The true ceiling is somewhere between 1,600 and 3,200 rps.
  • In the main run, 86% of Go/LanceDB runs (n = 117) ended their first saturated step with more than 90% errors. Every other cell had 0% such runs; they degraded with rising latency and timeouts instead.

The mechanism. The Go runtime documentation states it directly: GOMAXPROCS limits the threads executing Go code, but "there is no limit to the number of threads that can be blocked in system calls on behalf of Go code". A cgo call counts as one. The Go server calls lancedb-go's synchronous Execute once per request, and net/http starts a goroutine per request with no admission control. While a search runs inside the Rust core, its goroutine holds an OS thread, and the scheduler starts new threads for the goroutines that are still runnable.

That is harmless while the store keeps up. Measured without HTTP (300k, recall 0.95, 6 concurrent callers), LanceDB answers about 2,500 to 2,800 queries per second from any language. Offer 3,200 rps and the backlog grows. By Little's law, in-flight requests equal arrival rate times time in system; at 3,200 rps it takes only about half a second of queueing to have 1,500 calls in flight, and in Go each one is an OS thread. Go's own guard, debug.SetMaxThreads, defaults to 10,000 threads, far above the macOS limit of 2,048, so the kernel says no first and the runtime aborts the process.

Rust and Python use LanceDB's async API. A waiting request there is a future, not a thread, so they queue and slow down instead of crashing. Rust/LanceDB sustains 2,466 rps at the same cell, with bisection.

Interpretation. This is not "Go is slow". Through 1,600 rps the Go/LanceDB server was healthy, with p99 about 2 ms and 216 to 328 OS threads. During the 3,200 rps step the thread count climbed to the macOS limit of kern.num_taskthreads = 2048, pthread_create failed with EAGAIN and the process aborted. What is missing is a concurrency bound: unbounded goroutines making blocking cgo calls into the store turn every queued request into an OS thread, and on this host the thread limit runs out before anything else does. That makes MST 1,600 a lower bound; the true ceiling is somewhere between 1,600 and 3,200 rps, and on this host it was set by the thread limit, reached through this binding's blocking calls, rather than by the speed of Go code. The usual remedy is to cap in-flight store calls and let the excess wait or be rejected. I did not implement or measure that here, so I make no claim about what it would buy.

Two caveats. This is the lancedb-go cgo binding on Darwin; on a host with a higher per-process thread limit I would expect the same mechanism at a different threshold, which I did not measure. And the binding is young (its last tag is v0.1.2; I vendored a 2026 commit and rebuilt its core against LanceDB 0.40.0).

The memory-pressure lesson: how 8 GiB nearly wrote the wrong article

My first centre-cell numbers said pgvector was the slowest store in all three languages. They were low by a factor of 4 to 7.

Fact. Centre cell (300k, recall 0.95, k 10, ids), pgvector, median MST of 5 runs (rerun Python: 4, see below):

API First run (Oct 23) Clean rerun (Oct 27) Ratio
Rust 518 rps 2,933 rps 5.7x
Go 366 rps 2,690 rps 7.3x
Python 616 rps 2,466 rps 4.0x

How I noticed. Three things did not fit.

  1. In the first run, one replicate per language was already fast (Python 2,262, Rust 2,690, Go 1,037 rps) while the other four sat between 128 and 672 rps. A store that is bimodal on identical inputs is telling you about its environment.
  2. Across 45 pgvector 300k runs, p50 latency at 100 rps correlated with the memory available before the step at r = -0.80. For DuckDB it was -0.14 and for LanceDB -0.35.
  3. An A/A control (the same Rust/pgvector cell, 58 times between Oct 23 and Oct 27) split into a fast mode (26 runs, p50 1.9 ms at 388 rps) and a slow mode (32 runs, p50 8.6 ms).

In the main run, available memory before a step had a median of 2.7 GiB and a minimum of 0.7 GiB, and swap peaked at 10.9 GiB, while I was also using the Mac during the day.

How I tested it. I reran only the centre pgvector cells, plus the Go/LanceDB cell as a control, on the evening of Oct 27 (runs started between 18:46 and 20:50 TR), with a monitor sampling free pages, compressor pages, page-ins, page-outs, swap and per-process threads every 2 seconds. Nineteen of the 20 runs started with at most 0.34 GiB of swap, and all 14 pgvector runs among them landed in the fast mode. The remaining run, the very first one (Python/pgvector), started with 2.6 GiB of swap left over from the day and measured 258 rps. I excluded it, so the Python rerun median is over 4 runs. The Go/LanceDB control cell in the same rerun reproduced its original 1,600 rps.

What it changed. pgvector went from last to roughly level with LanceDB at the centre cell: Rust 2,933 vs 2,466 rps, Python 2,466 vs 2,466, and Go 2,690 against a Go/LanceDB value of 1,600 that is only the crash-bounded lower bound from the previous section. The clean pgvector rerun ran on a different, quieter evening than the LanceDB values, so this comparison crosses days, and I read it as level, not as a pgvector win. None of the main conclusions rests on the centre cell: they rest on the variance shares and on the scale flip in Result 2.

Then I checked the rest of pgvector. A one-replicate screen of all 69 pgvector cells moved 21 of them by more than 25%, 20 of them at 300k. I reran those 21 at 5 replicates. Their medians replace the originals in every table above. The pgvector geo-mean went from 1,039 to 816 rps; LanceDB and DuckDB did not change because they were not rerun.

Interpretation. On a machine where the index does not fit in the database's own buffer, throughput depends on how much page cache the rest of the system leaves you. That is not a benchmark artefact to hide; it is the production question "how much RAM does this index need" showing up in the numbers. But it means a single afternoon's run can be off by 5x without anything looking broken.

What I could not pin down

  • pgvector at 300k with k 100 is noisy at the bottom of the ladder. These cells now sit at 25 to 400 rps. The first run had several at 400 to 800 that I could not reproduce. I tested one obvious explanation, that the reruns started their ladder at 100 rps instead of 25 and so hit a cold first step. Four configurations, 3 runs per arm, starts alternated: the per-configuration medians were 200 vs 100, 200 vs 200, 100 vs 100 and 200 vs 400 rps (start at 25 vs start at 100). The geo-mean of those medians is 168 rps either way (150 vs 168 over all 12 runs per arm). The hypothesis is refuted, and the higher first-run values remain unexplained. I report the rerun values.
  • Some reruns overlapped daytime use. During the 5-replicate pgvector rerun, 10 of 105 runs showed swap-outs or page-in rates more than 4x their overnight level. Excluding them moves the pgvector geo-mean from 816 to 823 rps. With a stricter alignment of monitor samples to load steps, 14 runs are flagged and the geo-mean is 805. None of these changes a conclusion.
  • The centre comparison crosses days. The clean pgvector rerun ran on Oct 27; the LanceDB and DuckDB centre values come from Oct 23. The Go/LanceDB control in the rerun had the same MST but lower latency (p50 at 100 rps 2.6 vs 3.9 ms), which suggests the host was quieter on the evening of Oct 27 than on Oct 23. That is why I call the centre cell level rather than a pgvector win.

What this tells you about constrained hosts, and what it doesn't

This study ran on one 8 GiB Mac mini whose 8 cores were shared by the API, the store and the load generator. That is closer to an edge box or a small VM than to a database server, and that is the point: on tight hardware the interesting question is which stack degrades first, and how.

Specific to this machine, do not carry over:

  • The absolute MST values. Every rps figure above belongs to this host. On a bigger server with more cores, more memory and a higher thread limit I would expect them to be higher, but I have not measured that.
  • The exact Go/LanceDB ceiling. 1,600 rps is the last healthy step before the macOS limit of 2,048 threads per process stopped the process in the 3,200 rps step. It is a property of this host and this binding, not a speed of Go or of LanceDB.
  • The 300k pgvector numbers. A 1.23 GB index against 1 GB of shared_buffers on 8 GiB is a memory-bound setup. With room to cache the index, the 300k picture may look different, and I have not measured that.

What I expect to hold on other constrained hosts (expected, not shown here):

  • The store dominates the language. Store 69%, language 5%, store ahead in 23 of 24 configurations, and a stub store at 12,800 rps or more in every language: the HTTP layer was far from the limit.
  • The ranking flips with scale. pgvector led at 100k vectors (1,831 vs 1,295 rps), LanceDB at 300k (817 vs 338). Which side of the flip you are on depends on whether the index fits the memory you have.
  • Failure modes come from the host's limits. Thread exhaustion killed Go/LanceDB, and memory pressure moved pgvector by 4 to 7x. A larger machine moves these limits further out, but the mechanisms stay: unbounded blocking calls consume OS threads, and an index that outgrows its buffer depends on whatever page cache is left.

These are expectations from one host. Treat them as hypotheses to check on your own hardware, not as results.

Threats to validity, and what this does not show

Each point below is a limit of the design, with what the data says about it.

  • One host. Every number comes from one 8 GiB Mac mini (Apple M2, 4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, macOS 26.5.2). Nothing is pooled across machines. Absolute rps values belong to this host.
  • macOS, not Linux. Most production APIs run on Linux. The Go/LanceDB ceiling is tied to the macOS limit kern.num_taskthreads = 2048, and memory behaviour differs (macOS compresses and swaps memory before anything is killed). I did not measure Linux, so I make no Linux claim.
  • Load generator on the same host. vegeta, the API server and Postgres share all 8 cores, unpinned, because macOS has no CPU affinity API on Apple silicon. Load-generator CPU is recorded per step. No real-store step and no rerun step pushed it above 1.5 cores; only the stub-store steps at 25,600 rps did, which is why the stub floor is reported as "at least 12,800". The client still competes with the server for CPU, which is part of what a constrained host means.
  • Index parameters. All three stores build HNSW with the same M = 16 and ef_construction = 128 (LanceDB: IVF_HNSW_FLAT with one partition, its closest equivalent). The search knob is calibrated per store to the same recall target, not set equal. Other build parameters, quantization or per-store tuning beyond this were not explored.
  • Recall matching. Held-out recall from the actual HTTP responses landed within -0.011 to +0.044 of target everywhere; the largest undershoot (pgvector, 100k, k 10, 0.90 target, 0.889) is named in the setup.
  • Warm-up and cache state. Every run starts a fresh server process and discards 20 s at 50 rps. All reported numbers are warm. The cold-start ablation could not drop the macOS page cache without root, so it measured a fresh process, not a cold disk, and I do not report it as cold.
  • Repetitions. 5 runs per cell in a randomised Williams order (seed 20261022), cell value = median. Run-to-run residual is reported as its own variance share (median 12%). An A/A control of one cell repeated 58 times between Oct 23 and Oct 27 is one of the three signals that exposed the memory-pressure modes.
  • Ladder resolution. Outside the centre cell MST is a doubling ladder, so most ratios are 1x, 2x or 4x by construction, and a 1.5x real difference can show up as 1x or 2x.
  • Python deployment. Python ran 6 workers for pgvector and 1 for the embedded stores, decided before the data. Swapping that choice did not change the median MST in the ablation (see the setup).
  • Memory pressure. The main run had a median of 2.7 GiB available before a step, and pgvector at 300k was sensitive to it (r = -0.80 between free memory before the step and p50 at 100 rps, 45 runs). The affected cells were rerun: the centre cell on a quieter evening (judged by the Go/LanceDB control's lower latency), and the 21 pgvector cells that moved by more than 25% at 5 replicates. Flagging daytime-contaminated reruns moves the pgvector geo-mean between 805 and 823 rps against 816 reported.
  • Exclusions. A run counts as an outlier when its MST is at most a quarter of its configuration's median (or its first-step p99 is 5x worse, for short and cold modes). It is excluded only with a host-side cause: a host-gate timeout, swap of 6 GiB or more, swap growth of 0.5 GiB or more within a step, a crash, or the window when I was actively using the Mac. That gave 63 outliers and 45 exclusions (24 of 1,035 CORE runs, 2 of 45 centre runs). The rule was written after seeing the data, so here is its effect: exclusions change 3 of 216 cell medians and none of the store-level numbers above.
  • Invalid steps. The runner flagged 190 of 7,859 steps as invalid. All 190 were overload drains (a 10 s client timeout stretched the step), so they count as saturated. Zero steps were host stalls.
  • Statistics. The variance shares are descriptive. The protocol also planned permutation tests and bootstrap confidence intervals; I have not run them, so I make no significance claims.
  • Protocol deviations. The repo's protocol lists every deviation from the base plan (no CPU pinning, no 1M scale because a 1M DuckDB process would need about 10 GiB, a 2-worker instead of 6-worker Python arm for embedded stores in the ablation) and the runner settings as actually run.
  • A runner bug. The runner records a step's started timestamp when the step ends. Anything that aligns host-monitor samples to steps has to shift by one step. The thread chart and the stricter contamination check use the corrected alignment.
  • Reproduction. Versions are pinned in the repo, with the scripts, per-run summaries, the rerun's raw data and host monitor, the crash markers, and the commands that recompute every number and regenerate every chart in this article (README, section "Reproduce the article numbers and charts"), and a claim-by-claim map from each number to its source file (analysis/claims.md): https://github.com/firfircelik/vector-api-bench

The takeaway

If you are choosing a stack for a semantic-search API, my reading of this data is: choose the store first and size its memory second. On this constrained machine the language explained about 5% of the throughput variance and the store about two thirds. pgvector was fastest at 100k vectors and slowest at 300k with k 100, LanceDB lost the least from 100k to 300k, and DuckDB VSS never won a cell on its own. Pick the language your team ships best, and then check how its store binding behaves when the store falls behind, because that is where this Go and LanceDB setup went from 1,600 healthy requests per second to a dead process in four seconds.

title: Why Your Python Script Works Locally but Fails in Production
description:
Your code works perfectly on your machine. Then you deploy it, and everything starts breaking. Sound familiar?

There's a moment almost every Python developer experiences.

You've spent hours building a script. You've tested it several times. Everything works exactly as expected.

Then you move it to a server.

And suddenly:

  • The API stops responding.
  • A file can't be found.
  • A library behaves differently.
  • The application crashes without a useful error message.
  • A process that previously took 30 seconds now runs indefinitely.

The frustrating part?

You haven't changed the code.

So what went wrong?

The answer is usually simple: your local environment and your production environment are not the same.

And writing code that works is only the first step toward building software that works reliably.

Let's explore seven common problems that turn working Python scripts into production failures — and how to prevent them.

1. The Hidden Danger of Missing Timeouts

Let's start with something that looks completely harmless.

import requests

response = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/products"
)

print(response.json())

This code works perfectly when the API is available and responds quickly.

But what happens when the server stops responding?

By default, the requests library doesn't set a timeout.

That means your application could wait indefinitely for a response.

Now imagine this script is running as part of a scheduled job.

One unavailable API could block the entire workflow.

A better approach 

import requests

def fetch_products():
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            "https://api.example.com/products",
            timeout=(3, 10)
        )

        response.raise_for_status()

        return response.json()

    except requests.Timeout:
        print("Request timed out")

    except requests.RequestException as error:
        print(f"Request failed: {error}")

    except ValueError:
        print("Invalid JSON response")

    return None

Here, the timeout configuration specifies:

  • 3 seconds for establishing the connection.
  • 10 seconds for waiting between socket read operations.

One important detail: these timeouts are not a strict 13-second limit on the total request duration.

A server that continuously sends small amounts of data may keep the connection active much longer.

For strict execution deadlines, you need additional controls at the application or infrastructure level.

Lesson: External services are not guaranteed to respond, even when your code is correct.

2. Hardcoded Paths Work Until They Don't

Consider a script that saves data to a CSV file.

import csv

with open(
    "C:/Users/Developer/Desktop/products.csv",
    "w"
) as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(["id", "name", "price"])

This might work perfectly on your Windows laptop.

But what happens when you deploy it to a Linux server?

The directory doesn't exist.

The application fails.

This problem becomes even more common when working with Docker containers, virtual machines, or cloud environments.

Use pathlib instead

Python provides a much better way to handle filesystem paths.

from pathlib import Path
import csv

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

DATA_DIR = BASE_DIR / "data"
DATA_DIR.mkdir(
    parents=True,
    exist_ok=True
)

OUTPUT_FILE = DATA_DIR / "products.csv"

with OUTPUT_FILE.open(
    "w",
    newline="",
    encoding="utf-8"
) as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(["id", "name", "price"])

This approach is more portable and avoids operating-system-specific path separators.

However, there's another important production consideration.

The application directory might be read-only.

In containerized environments, you may also lose local files when a container is replaced.

For persistent data, configure an appropriate storage location or use an external storage service.

Lesson: Never assume that the production filesystem looks like your development machine.

3. Your Dependencies Are Part of Your Application

Here's a situation that can be surprisingly difficult to debug.

You develop a Python application using several libraries.

Everything works.

A colleague clones the repository and runs the same code.

It crashes.

Why?

Because your environments contain different dependency versions.

For example, your application might rely on behavior that changed between major versions of a library.

The wrong approach 

pip install requests beautifulsoup4 pandas

This installs available versions that satisfy the requirements at installation time.

But those versions may differ across machines or deployments.

A more reliable approach

For a simple project, you can maintain a dependency file with pinned versions.

requests==2.32.3
beautifulsoup4==4.12.3
pandas==2.2.3

These are example versions, not necessarily the versions your project should use.

Then install dependencies with:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

For larger applications, consider tools such as uv, Poetry, or pip-tools to generate and maintain lockfiles.

Also remember that dependency versions aren't the entire environment.

Python version, operating system, native libraries, and system packages can affect application behavior.

For example, a package with native extensions might work on one platform but fail on another.

Lesson: Reproducibility is a requirement, not a convenience.

4. Print Statements Are Not a Logging Strategy

During development, many of us debug code like this:

print("Starting parser")
print("Opening page")
print("Extracting products")
print("Done")

There's nothing inherently wrong with print().

For small scripts, it's often sufficient.

But imagine your application runs every 15 minutes on a remote server.

One

title: SQL Server'da yavaş sorgu nasıl hızlandırılır?
description:
POS hareketlerini listeleyen bir endpoint'imiz vardı. Tabloya her gün milyonlarca satır ekleniyordu ve ekranın en sık kullanılan hâli gün bazlı sorguydu: bir işyerinin belli günlerdeki hareketleri, sayfa sayfa. Bu sorgu dakikalar sürüyordu. CreatedDate kolonunda indeks vardı, ama sorgu onu kullanmıyor gibiydi.

Dört değişiklikle sorgu dakikalardan saniyelere indi. Bu yazı için o dört adımı 10 milyon satırlık sentetik bir tabloda yeniden ölçtüm. Ölçümlerden biri, o gün suçladığımız şeyin asıl suçlu olmadığını gösterdi.

Kısa cevap: SQL Server'da yavaş bir listeleme sorgusunu hızlandırırken önce indeksin gerçekten kullanılıp kullanılmadığına bak. Kolona uygulanan fonksiyonlar (CONVERT, DATEDIFF) indeksi devre dışı bırakır; filtrelediğin kolonlar için bileşik indeks gerekir. Derin sayfalarda OFFSET atlanan her satırı okur; cursor (keyset) sayfalama her sayfada aynı maliyettedir. Geniş listelerde önce yalnızca Id'leri seç, kolonları sonra getir. Join'deki bir CTE her satır için yeniden çalışabilir; ara sonucu temp tabloya almak bunu bir kez çalışır hâle getirir.

Ölçüm düzeneği

Gerçek tabloyu ve verisini kullanamam, o yüzden benzerini kurdum. PosHareketleri tablosunda 10 milyon satır var: 30 gün, günde yaklaşık 330 bin hareket. Yanında işyerleri (20 bin), terminaller (60 bin) ve iadeler (200 bin) duruyor. CreatedDate kolonunda tek kolonlu bir indeks var. Bizim tablomuz 30-40 kolondu; buradaki 10 kolon, yani gerçekte farklar daha da büyür.

Ortam SQL Server 2022 Express. Sorgular uygulamanın göndereceği gibi parametreli (sp_executesql), her biri iki kez çalışıyor ve ikincisi sayılıyor; yani önbellek sıcak.

Süreyi raporluyorum ama asıl baktığım sayı mantıksal okuma (logical reads): sorgunun okuduğu 8 KB'lık sayfa sayısı. Süre makineye, önbelleğe ve o anki yüke göre oynar; okuma sayısı oynamaz. İkisini de şöyle açarsın:

SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON;
-- sorgu
SET STATISTICS IO, TIME OFF;

Messages sekmesinde her tablo için logical reads ve sorgunun CPU ve geçen süresi görünür. Yanına gerçek çalışma planını (actual execution plan, SSMS'te Ctrl+M) açarsan hangi operatörün bu okumaları yaptığını da görürsün.

Tarih filtresi: kolona fonksiyon uygulamak

Gün bazlı sorguda tarih filtresi CreatedDate'i güne çeviriyordu:

WHERE IsyeriId = @isyeri
  AND CAST(CreatedDate AS date) BETWEEN @bas AND @bit

Bir kolona fonksiyon uyguladığında veritabanı genellikle o kolonun indeksinde arama (seek) yapamaz. İndeks CreatedDate'in kendisine göre sıralı; CAST(CreatedDate AS date) ya da CONVERT(char(8), CreatedDate, 112) sonucuna göre değil. Bu durumda her satır için fonksiyonu hesaplayıp sonucu karşılaştırmak zorunda kalır. Bu tür koşullara sargable olmayan (non-sargable) koşul denir.

Biz bunu düzelttik: gelen tarihleri bir gün kaydırıp aralık olarak yazdık.

WHERE IsyeriId = @isyeri
  AND CreatedDate >= @bas
  AND CreatedDate <  DATEADD(day, 1, @bit)

Bu yazı için ölçerken şunu gördüm: SQL Server CAST(... AS date) için bir istisna yapıyor. Kolonu date'e çevirmeyi tanıyor ve indekste yine aralık araması yapabiliyor. Tek günlük, ilk 50 satırlık sorguda dört farklı yazımın sonucu:

Filtre Okuma Süre
CAST(CreatedDate AS date) = @gun 203 ~1 ms
CreatedDate >= @gun AND CreatedDate < @gun + 1 gün 215 ~0 ms
DATEDIFF(day, CreatedDate, @gun) = 0 14.112 1.038 ms
CONVERT(char(8), CreatedDate, 112) = ... 169.934 2.066 ms

DATEDIFF indeksi baştan sona tarıyor, CONVERT bütün tabloyu okuyor. CAST ise aralıkla neredeyse aynı. Yani bizim sorgudaki asıl yük CAST değildi.

Aralıkla yazmak yine de doğru alışkanlık. CAST istisnası SQL Server'a özgü ve yalnızca date'e çevirmede geçerli; aynı kod başka bir veritabanında ya da başka bir fonksiyonla aynı şansı bulamaz. Aralık her yerde indeksi kullanır.

Asıl fark işyeri filtresinde çıktı. Aynı sorguyu bir işyeri ve yedi gün için üç farklı indeks durumunda çalıştırdım:

İndeks Okuma Süre
Yalnızca CreatedDate 169.934 454-611 ms
CreatedDate + ayrıca IsyeriId 2.044 2 ms
Bileşik (IsyeriId, CreatedDate) 215 1-2 ms

Yalnızca tarih indeksi varken yedi günlük aralık 2,3 milyon satıra denk geliyor. Optimizer bu kadar satır için indeksten tek tek tabloya gitmektense bütün tabloyu taramayı seçiyor; CAST'lı ve aralıklı yazımın ikisi de aynı taramaya düşüyor. Bileşik indekste önce işyerine, sonra o işyerinin tarih aralığına iniliyor ve sorgu yalnızca gösterilecek satırları okuyor.

Bileşik indekste kolon sırası önemli: eşitlikle filtrelenen kolon (IsyeriId) önce, aralıkla filtrelenen kolon (CreatedDate) sonra. Ters sırada indeks yine tarih aralığını tarar, işyerini her satırda ayrıca kontrol eder.

Derin sayfada OFFSET neden yavaşlar

Listede sayfalama vardı, ama yetersizdi. Klasik OFFSET ... FETCH sayfalaması şöyle görünür:

SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo
FROM PosHareketleri h
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
WHERE h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC, h.Id DESC
OFFSET @atla ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;

OFFSET 50000 "50 bininci satırdan başla" demek değil, "50 bin satırı oku, at, sonra 50 satır ver" demek. Veritabanının atlanacak satırların yerini bilmesinin başka yolu yok. Sayfa ilerledikçe okunan ve atılan satır sayısı artar.

Bir günün hareketlerinde (yaklaşık 330 bin satır) 50'lik sayfalarla ölçünce:

Sayfa Okuma Süre
1 215 2 ms
100 20.339 21 ms
1.000 203.269 176 ms
6.000 169.934 (tablo taraması) 918 ms

1.000. sayfada işyeri ve terminal tablolarından da 103'er bin okuma var: sorgu atlanacak satırlar için de join yapıyor. 6.000. sayfada optimizer indeksi bırakıp tabloyu taramaya geçiyor. Bizim tablomuz 30-40 kolon olduğu için atılan her satır daha pahalıydı.

Geçici çözümümüz cursor sayfalama oldu. Fikir, "kaçıncı sayfadayım" yerine "en son hangi satırda kaldım" bilgisini taşımak. İstemci bir sonraki sayfayı isterken önceki sayfanın son satırının CreatedDate'ini ve Id'sini gönderir; sorgu oradan devam eder:

SELECT TOP (50) h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo
FROM PosHareketleri h
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
WHERE h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit
  AND (h.CreatedDate < @sonTarih
       OR (h.CreatedDate = @sonTarih AND h.Id < @sonId))
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC, h.Id DESC;

Bu sorgu indekste doğrudan kaldığı yere iner ve 50 satır okur. Ölçümde her sayfa 220 civarı okuma ve 2-3 ms; 1. sayfayla 6.000. sayfa arasında fark yok.

Bedeli de var: kullanıcı "47. sayfaya git" diyemez, yalnızca ileri ve geri gidebilir. Listede toplam sayfa sayısı gösteriliyorsa onu ayrı bir COUNT ile hesaplamak gerekir. Hareket listesi gibi kullanıcının genellikle baştan aşağı kaydırdığı ekranlarda bu kayıp küçük.

GUID'li tenant'larda cursor

Bizde bazı tenant'ların Id'leri long, bazılarınınki GUID'di. GUID'li tenant'larda Id üzerinden büyüktür/küçüktür yapamıyorduk, o yüzden cursor'dan yalnızca long Id'li tenant'lar yararlanabildi. Aslında sıralama zaten CreatedDate'e göre; Id yalnızca aynı tarihli satırları ayırmaya yarıyor. Bu iş için Id'nin sıralı olması değil, tekil olması ve her seferinde aynı sırayı vermesi yeterli. SQL Server'da GUID'ler de kendi (tuhaf ama tutarlı) sıralarıyla karşılaştırılabildiği için yukarıdaki sorgu GUID'le de çalışır. Tek dikkat: son Id'yi uygulamada karşılaştırma, olduğu gibi SQL'e geri gönder; .NET'teki Guid sıralaması SQL Server'ınkiyle aynı değil.

Önce Id'leri seç, kolonları sonra getir

Cursor'ın kullanılamadığı tenant'lar için başka bir yol bulduk: önce olabildiğince filtreleyip yalnızca Id'leri seçmek, join'leri ve kolonları ikinci adımda yapmak.

WITH sayfa AS (
    SELECT Id, CreatedDate
    FROM PosHareketleri
    WHERE CreatedDate >= @bas AND CreatedDate < @bit
    ORDER BY CreatedDate DESC, Id DESC
    OFFSET @atla ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY
)
SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo
FROM sayfa s
JOIN PosHareketleri h ON h.Id = s.Id
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
ORDER BY s.CreatedDate DESC, s.Id DESC;

İç sorgu yine OFFSET kullanıyor ve yine atlanan satırları okuyor, ama bunu yalnızca CreatedDate indeksinde yapıyor. İndeks dar: içinde tarih ve Id var, 30-40 kolon yok. Join'ler ve geniş satırlar yalnızca seçilen 50 Id için yapılıyor. Bu kalıba deferred join de deniyor.

Grafik: bir günlük hareketlerde (yaklaşık 330 bin satır, 50 satırlık sayfa) sayfa numarasına göre süre. OFFSET: 1. sayfa 2 ms, 100. sayfa 21 ms, 1.000. sayfa 176 ms, 6.000. sayfa 918 ms. Önce Id, sonra join: 6.000. sayfa 28 ms. Cursor: her sayfa 2-3 ms.

6.000. sayfada OFFSET 918 ms'ten bu yazımla 28 ms'e iniyor, okuma 170 binden 998'e düşüyor. Cursor kadar düz değil ama sayfa numarasına göre gitme imkânını koruyor.

Join'deki CTE her satırda çalışınca

Filtrelenmiş Id'leri önce bir CTE'de toplayıp ana sorguya join'liyorduk. Planı incelediğimizde CTE'nin her satır için yeniden çalıştığını gördük ve temp tabloya geçmek zorunda kaldık.

Sebebi, SQL Server'ın CTE'yi bir ara tablo gibi saklamaması. CTE, sorguya gömülen bir alt sorgudur (inline). Optimizer onu nested loops join'in iç tarafına koyarsa, dış taraftan gelen her satır için o alt sorgu yeniden çalışır. Sentetik tabloda aynı şekli kurdum: bir işyeri aralığı ve bir haftalık hareketlerin Id'leri CTE'de, dışarıda join'ler ve iade toplamı.

WITH secilen AS (
    SELECT h.Id FROM PosHareketleri h
    WHERE h.IsyeriId BETWEEN @isyeriBas AND @isyeriBit
      AND h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit
)
SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo,
       (SELECT SUM(r.IadeTutar) FROM Iadeler r WHERE r.HareketId = h.Id) AS IadeToplam
FROM PosHareketleri h
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
WHERE h.Id IN (SELECT Id FROM secilen)
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;

Gerçek planda optimizer dış tarafta tarih indeksini sondan başa tarıyor ve CTE'nin PosHareketleri aramasını her satır için bir kez çalıştırıyor. Plandaki "Number of Executions" değeri 5.002.003. Sonuç 40,6 milyon okuma ve 9 saniye.

Temp tabloyla aynı iş iki adım:

SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate
INTO #secilen
FROM PosHareketleri h
WHERE h.IsyeriId BETWEEN @isyeriBas AND @isyeriBit
  AND h.CreatedDate >= @bas AND h.CreatedDate < @bit;

SELECT h.Id, h.CreatedDate, h.Tutar, h.KartMaskeli, i.Ad, t.SeriNo,
       (SELECT SUM(r.IadeTutar) FROM Iadeler r WHERE r.HareketId = h.Id) AS IadeToplam
FROM #secilen s
JOIN PosHareketleri h ON h.Id = s.Id
JOIN Isyerleri i ON i.Id = h.IsyeriId
JOIN Terminaller t ON t.Id = h.TerminalId
ORDER BY h.CreatedDate DESC
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 50 ROWS ONLY;

Filtre bir kez çalışıyor, sonuç #secilen'e yazılıyor. SQL Server temp tabloya istatistik de oluşturduğu için ikinci sorguda kaç satırla çalışacağını biliyor. İki adım toplam 0,85 saniye; CTE'li hâlin onda biri. Bizde de temp tablo sorguya özeldi; sorgu bitince düşüyordu, ayrıca indeks koymadık.

Temp tablonun bedeli, sorgunun artık tek bir ifade olmaması. ORM'in ürettiği tek bir SELECT ile yapılamıyor; ya ham SQL ya da stored procedure gerekiyor. Ara sonuç çok büyükse tempdb'ye yazmanın maliyeti de hesaba girer.

Kendi sisteminde nasıl fark edersin

Yavaş bir sorguyu SET STATISTICS IO ON ile çalıştır ve okuma sayısını, sorgunun döndürdüğü satır sayısıyla karşılaştır. 50 satır gösteren bir liste için yüz binlerce okuma görüyorsan sorgu ihtiyacından fazlasını okuyor.

Sonra gerçek çalışma planında iki şeye bak: indeks üzerinde Seek yerine Scan olan operatörler ve "Number of Executions" değeri 1'den çok büyük olan operatörler. İlki indeksin kullanılmadığını, ikincisi bir alt sorgunun ya da CTE'nin her satırda yeniden çalıştığını gösterir. EF Core kullanıyorsan önce üretilen SQL'i log'dan al; Include ve Select yazısında ORM tarafındaki karşılığını anlatmıştım.

Bizim sorguyu dakikalardan saniyelere indiren tek bir değişiklik olmadı. Ölçümde dört adımın ortak noktası aynı çıktı: ekranda gösterilmeyecek satırı okumamak.

Bu yazı ilk olarak huseyinbozdemir.com'da yayımlandı.

title: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite: Ein Vokabelquiz als erstes API-Projekt
description:
Google stellte Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite am 17. Juni 2025 als Vorschau vor. Am 22. Juli folgte die stabile Version. Innerhalb der Gemini-2.5-Familie lag der Schwerpunkt bei der Veröffentlichung auf Geschwindigkeit und Kosteneffizienz, etwa für Übersetzung und Klassifikation. [1][2]

Wer bereits eine einfache API-Anfrage senden kann, braucht als nächsten Schritt oft eine überschaubare Anwendung. Für diesen Versuch habe ich zehn vorbereitete Vokabelfragen über die Crazyrouter API an gemini-2.5-flash-lite geschickt. Daraus sollte eine einzelne HTML-Datei mit Antwortauswahl, Punkten und einer Wiederholung der falsch beantworteten Fragen entstehen.

Das Projekt hat einen klaren Übergang: Bis zur Antwort arbeite ich mit einer Modell-API, danach mit einer lokalen Webseite. Die erste Version enthielt die wesentlichen Abläufe; fehlende Details habe ich direkt in der Datei ergänzt.

Warum das mit Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite erstellte Quiz ohne API läuft

Ein Modell verarbeitet Eingaben und erzeugt Antworten. Eine Chat-App stellt dafür eine Oberfläche bereit; über eine API können andere Programme dieselbe Art von Anfrage stellen.

In diesem Projekt erzeugte Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite die HTML-Struktur, die Gestaltung und die Spiellogik. Crazyrouter war der verwendete API-Zugang. Der Browser führt die fertige Datei aus. Beim späteren Beantworten der Fragen findet keine weitere Modellanfrage statt.

Die HTML-Datei im Repository kann als index.html heruntergeladen und lokal geöffnet werden. Sie enthält einen festen Fragenkatalog. Ein Neuladen erzeugt keine neuen Aufgaben; Lernstände werden zwischen Besuchen nicht gespeichert.

Wer später Fragen bei jedem Durchlauf erzeugen lassen möchte, benötigt zusätzlich einen Aufruf auf dem Server, eine Prüfung der neuen Aufgaben und eine Begrenzung der Nutzung. Das wäre ein anderes Projekt als die hier geprüfte statische Datei.

Für die erste Version konnte ich mich deshalb auf die Datei konzentrieren: Fragen anzeigen, Antworten auswerten und eine neue Runde starten.

Laut Google kann das Modell Text, Bilder, Video, Audio und PDF als Eingaben verarbeiten. Die Ausgabe ist Text. Welche Formate und Parameter ein bestimmter Anbieter tatsächlich unterstützt, muss zusätzlich geprüft werden. Bilder verstehen zu können bedeutet bei diesem Modell also nicht, Bilder erzeugen zu können. [3]

Eine Webseite lässt sich trotzdem generieren: HTML, CSS und JavaScript bestehen aus Text. Daraus kann der Browser Fragen, Schaltflächen und eine Punkteanzeige darstellen.

Weitere mögliche Einstiegsaufgaben sind das Sortieren von Nachrichten, das Herausziehen bestimmter Angaben aus einem Dokument oder das Aufbereiten einer Mitteilung. Google nennt Klassifikation und einfache Datenextraktion als Einsatzbereiche. Diese Aufgaben wurden hier nicht mitgetestet; der konkrete Versuch betrifft nur das Vokabelquiz. [3]

Die Anfrage an Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite und die erzeugte Datei

Die Quiz-Demo enthält zehn englische Fragen mit jeweils vier Antwortmöglichkeiten. Eine richtige Antwort bringt zehn Punkte, eine falsche null. Nach einer Runde lassen sich die Antworten ansehen oder nur die Fehler wiederholen.

Die englischen Sätze üben unter anderem den Unterschied zwischen „borrow“ und „lend“. Fragen, richtige Antworten und Erklärungen standen vor der Generierung fest. Das Modell sollte diese Inhalte in eine Anwendung einbauen. Der Versuch bewertet deshalb nicht, wie gut es selbstständig neue Lernaufgaben erstellt.

Die ursprünglichen Anweisungen waren auf Chinesisch. Auch die Schaltflächen, Übersetzungen und Erklärungen der Demo sind weiterhin in vereinfachtem Chinesisch. „开始闯关“ startet das Quiz, „下一题“ führt zur nächsten Frage und „查看成绩“ zeigt das Ergebnis. Dieser Artikel ist keine zusätzliche Messung mit einem deutschen Prompt und keine deutsche Version der Spieloberfläche.

Für das Verhalten habe ich konkrete Regeln vorgegeben: Eine Frage darf nur einmal gewertet werden. Ohne Antwort darf man nicht weitergehen. Eine neue Runde muss den alten Punktestand löschen. Bei der Fehlerwiederholung sollen sich sowohl die Anzahl der Fragen als auch die maximal erreichbaren Punkte anpassen.

Aus „Baue ein Quiz“ wurde so eine Reihe prüfbarer Erwartungen. Wer drei Fragen falsch beantwortet, sollte anschließend drei Fragen mit höchstens dreißig Punkten üben können.

Am 2. November 2026 wurde eine Generierungsanfrage an die Chat-Completions-Schnittstelle von Crazyrouter gesendet. Das verwendete Modell war gemini-2.5-flash-lite. Die Antwort kam mit HTTP 200 zurück, der Abschlussgrund war stop, und die Ausgabe war nicht durch das Längenlimit abgeschnitten. Bis zur vollständigen Antwort vergingen rund 18,1 Sekunden.

Die Anfrage verwendete temperature mit dem Wert 0.3, max_tokens mit 9000 und stream mit false. Die gemessene Zeit gehört zu genau dieser einen Anfrage. Sie enthält keine anschließenden Korrekturen und ist keine Aussage über typische Antwortzeiten.

Nach dieser Antwort war die Generierung abgeschlossen. Ob der Punktestand beim Neustart verschwindet, musste sich anschließend im Verhalten der Datei zeigen.

Das Quiz von Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite: Rückmeldungen prüfen und ergänzen

Bei einem Quiz kann man den Zustand vor und nach jeder Aktion beschreiben. Vor der Antwort sind die Optionen verfügbar. Nach der Antwort ist die Entscheidung gesperrt, die Rückmeldung sichtbar und der Wechsel zur nächsten Frage möglich. Am Ende der Runde werden die gesammelten Antworten ausgewertet.

Die entscheidende Prüfung betraf danach die Anwendung. In den Skripttests ergaben zehn richtige Antworten 100 Punkte, zehn falsche null und sieben richtige siebzig. Die Wiederholung nach drei Fehlern umfasste drei Fragen mit einem Maximum von dreißig Punkten. Mehrfaches Auswählen derselben Antwort brachte keine zusätzlichen Punkte.

Die Zahlen stimmten in diesen Fällen. Bei der Rückmeldung an die Spieler fehlten jedoch noch vier Dinge:

Lücke in der ersten Version Lokale Korrektur
Die letzte Frage hatte weiterhin eine Beschriftung für „Nächste Frage“ Die Schaltfläche kündigt jetzt die Ergebnisansicht an
In der Rückschau fehlten die Erklärungen Jede Frage erhielt ihre zugehörige Erklärung
Bei einer perfekten Runde fehlte ein eindeutiger Hinweis Die Seite teilt mit, dass es keine Fehler zu wiederholen gibt
Die Rückmeldung nannte das richtige Wort nicht direkt in der Überschrift Das Lösungswort steht nun auch dort

Diese Änderungen erfolgten lokal, ohne eine weitere Modellanfrage. Zusätzlich wurden Zustandsprüfungen, die Tastaturbedienung und die Gestaltung für schmale Ansichten angepasst. Die verlinkte Demo enthält diese Korrekturen.

Danach bestanden alle elf automatisierten Prüfungen. Sie liefen mit jsdom, einer simulierten Umgebung für Seitenelemente und Skripte. Geprüft wurden unter anderem Punkte, wiederholte Eingaben, Neustart, Fehlerwiederholung und Erklärungen. Darstellung und Touch-Bedienung in echten Browsern sind damit nicht abgedeckt; diese Prüfungen sind noch offen.

Das Ergebnis zeigt eine brauchbare Grundlage für diese begrenzte Aufgabe. Es belegt weder eine fehlerfreie erste Generierung noch eine allgemeine Zuverlässigkeit bei größeren Anwendungen.

Interessant sind dabei auch Wiederholungen. Wenn ein Klick bereits gewertet wurde, darf ein zweiter Klick dieselbe Aktion nicht erneut auslösen. Wenn die Fehlerliste zu einer neuen Runde wird, muss der alte Punktestand verschwinden. Eine Funktion kann für sich betrachtet funktionieren und beim Übergang in die nächste Runde trotzdem falsche Daten übernehmen.

Das mit Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite erstellte Quiz schrittweise ändern

Für die nächste Version würde ich eine einzelne Änderung wählen und ihre Folgen beschreiben. Beim Austausch eines Wortes betrifft das die Frage, die richtige Auswahl und die Erklärung. Eine neue Spielregel kann zusätzlich den Punktestand oder den Neustart verändern.

Soll zunächst nur die Darstellung anders aussehen, können Fragen und Bewertung unverändert bleiben. Bei einer neuen Spielregel muss dagegen auch geprüft werden, ob die bisherigen Abläufe weiterhin passen.

Als kurze Kontrolle bietet sich eine Runde mit absichtlich falschen Antworten an: Sind nur diese Fragen in der Wiederholung? Passt die erreichbare Punktzahl? Beginnt eine vollständige neue Runde wieder bei null? Das sind Vorschläge für die eigene Prüfung, keine zusätzlichen Messungen dieses Versuchs.

Zugang zu Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite und Einrichtung der API

Die Verfügbarkeit hängt vom Zugangsweg ab. Am 2. November 2026 beschrieb die Dokumentation der Gemini Developer API einen Zugang für Nutzer, die die 2.5-Modelle bereits zuvor aktiv verwendet hatten. Die entsprechende Google-Cloud-Seite nannte dagegen den 20. Oktober 2026 als Einstellungsdatum und unterschied diesen Lebenszyklus ausdrücklich von dem der Gemini API. [3][5]

Für diesen Versuch wurde vor dem Aufruf geprüft, ob das Modell in der Liste des verwendeten Crazyrouter-Kontos enthalten war. Eine erfolgreiche Anfrage dieses Kontos ist keine Zusage für die Verfügbarkeit anderer Konten.

In einem Werkzeug mit frei einstellbarer OpenAI-kompatibler Verbindung werden drei Angaben benötigt: der API-Schlüssel aus der Crazyrouter-Konsole, die Basisadresse https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1 und der genaue Modellname gemini-2.5-flash-lite. [4]

Wer HTTP direkt verwendet, sendet eine POST-Anfrage an https://api.crazyrouter.com/v1/chat/completions und nutzt Bearer-Authentifizierung. Die Basisadresse eines SDK und der vollständige Endpunkt erfüllen unterschiedliche Zwecke; der Pfad sollte nicht doppelt angehängt werden. Die API-Dokumentation und das Anfrageformat beschreiben diese Verbindung. [4]

Übermittle den Fragenkatalog, die Regeln und die Anforderung einer vollständigen HTML-Datei zusammen als Nachricht in messages. Bei direkter Verarbeitung der Antwort findest du den erzeugten Text unter message.content im ersten Eintrag von choices. [4] Speichere nur den HTML-Inhalt, ohne einleitende Erläuterungen oder Markdown-Markierungen. Achte auf die Endung .html und prüfe danach die beschriebenen Abläufe.

Der Schlüssel bleibt im privaten Werkzeug oder auf dem Server. Er gehört nicht in die öffentlich geteilte Datei. Dass die Demo ohne Schlüssel spielbar ist, liegt daran, dass die Generierung bereits abgeschlossen ist.

Wenn eine Anfrage scheitert, prüfe Zugangsdaten, Endpunkt, Modellname und Kontozugang. Wenn die Anfrage erfolgreich war, aber das Spiel falsch zählt, liegt die nächste Untersuchung in der erzeugten Anwendung. Diese Trennung macht aus einem ersten API-Erfolg einen verständlichen Entwicklungsablauf.

Dieser Text wurde mit KI erstellt.

Quellen, geprüft am 2. November 2026:

[1] Google: Vorschau vom 17. Juni 2025.

[2] Google Developers Blog: Stabile Version vom 22. Juli 2025.

[3] Google AI for Developers: Dokumentation zu Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite.

[4] Crazyrouter: API-Dokumentation und Anfrage- und Antwortformat.

[5] Google Cloud: Modellspezifikation und Lebenszyklus.

title: How To Create Commandline Chat Server in Linux
description:
We have all used chat services such as Google Chat, Facebook chat, and WhatsApp. Linux's nc (netcat) command can also turn a machine into a very simple command-line chat endpoint with one command. The example below is useful for a quick lab test or a temporary conversation on a trusted LAN. It is not a replacement for a real chat service: there is no account system, encryption, or group-chat feature.

What is the nc command in Linux and what does it do?

nc is the command name used by many implementations of netcat, a networking utility often called a Swiss Army knife. It can read from and write to TCP or UDP connections, making it useful for debugging services, checking ports, transferring data, and temporarily listening on a port. This guide uses TCP, which is the default; do not add -u unless you deliberately want UDP.

The server and client addresses below are examples. Replace 192.168.0.7 and 192.168.0.15 with addresses on your own network.

Start the listener on the server

On the server (192.168.0.7), the traditional GNU netcat syntax is:

nc -l -vv -p 11119

The switches mean:

  1. -l: listen for an incoming connection instead of connecting to another host.
  2. -v: verbose output; -vv provides more detail.
  3. -p 11119: use local TCP port 11119 with this GNU-style listener.

You can replace 11119 with another unused, unprivileged port above 1024. Leave this terminal open.

Netcat is not one identical program on every Linux system. OpenBSD nc, which is common on modern distributions, normally takes the listening port as an argument instead:

nc -l -vv 11119

Ncat, from the Nmap project, is commonly invoked as ncat:

ncat -l -vv 11119

In particular, do not blindly copy GNU's -p listener syntax to OpenBSD nc; its -p option concerns a source port. Run nc -h or read man nc to identify the installed implementation and its supported options.

Connect from the client

On the client (192.168.0.15), connect to the server's address and port:

nc 192.168.0.7 11119

Type a line and press Enter on either terminal; the other terminal should display it. Press Ctrl+C to end the session. This is a direct, one-to-one pipe between two terminals, not a chat room.

Check the listener, route, and firewall

If the client cannot connect, check the server before changing random settings. In another server terminal, run:

ss -ltn | grep ':11119'
sudo ss -ltnp | grep ':11119'

Look for LISTEN. A listener on 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections; 0.0.0.0 means all IPv4 interfaces, which may be more exposure than you want. The second command can show the owning process, but process details may require sudo. If nothing is listening, the command may have exited or used syntax unsupported by your netcat variant.

From the client, a short TCP probe can distinguish a closed service from a network problem:

nc -vz -w 3 192.168.0.7 11119

-z performs a connection check rather than starting a chat, and -w 3 sets a timeout. Connection refused usually means nothing is listening on that port. A timeout more often points to a firewall, wrong address, disconnected network, or Wi-Fi client isolation.

On an Ubuntu-style host, inspect the firewall with sudo ufw status verbose. If UFW is active and you need a temporary exception, restrict it to your actual LAN prefix—for this example's network:

sudo ufw allow from 192.168.0.0/24 to any port 11119 proto tcp

Do not copy that subnet if yours differs, and do not create a router port-forward for this exercise. Firewalld users can inspect the active zone with sudo firewall-cmd --list-all. Remove a temporary UFW rule when finished:

sudo ufw delete allow from 192.168.0.0/24 to any port 11119 proto tcp

Limitations and LAN safety

Basic netcat accepts one connection and provides no usernames, message history, presence, delivery guarantees, or multi-user relay. Some versions have -k to keep listening after a disconnect, but that does not turn the session into group chat. Text is also plaintext: someone able to observe or intercept the network path could read it, and the client has no built-in proof of the server's identity. Never type passwords or sensitive information into this chat.

LAN-only use reduces exposure but does not make the connection trustworthy. A compromised laptop or an untrusted shared network can still observe traffic. Use a non-root account, a high port, a trusted LAN, and a narrowly scoped firewall rule; stop the listener when done. Avoid -e or similar “execute a program” options entirely for this recipe—they can turn a simple listener into an unintended remote shell.

Common mistakes

  • Address already in use: another process owns the port. Inspect it with ss and choose a different port rather than killing an unknown service.
  • The first client disconnects and later clients fail: restart the listener, or check whether your variant supports -k; neither approach adds group-chat semantics.
  • A connection succeeds but nothing appears: press Enter after typing, confirm that both ends use TCP and the same port, and make sure you did not leave -z in the chat command.
  • The listener command rejects -p: identify the variant and use its documented port syntax instead of adding more flags.

Safer modern alternatives

For remote administration, prefer SSH, which provides encryption and account authentication:

ssh user@192.168.0.7

SSH grants shell access, so it is not automatically a chat replacement; give accounts only the access they need. If you specifically need a netcat-like encrypted pipe, Ncat supports TLS with --ssl and certificate-verification options. Configure and verify certificates rather than treating encryption without identity checks as sufficient. For real private or group conversations, use a maintained messaging application with authentication and end-to-end encryption. A VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale can protect the network path, but it does not add chat identities, history, or group management to nc.

title: How to Setup a Firewall with UFW on an Ubuntu and Debian Cloud Server
description:
Introduction

A properly configured firewall is one of the important aspects of overall system security. Ubuntu associated with a firewall configuration tool named UFW i.e Uncomplicated Firewall. Its primary goal is to manage iptables easier.

Prerequisites

Make sure that you have logged into your server with a non-root user account with sudo privileges or with the root user. It's better to use sudo in place of Root to run Administrative commands.

Install UFW

By default UFW is installed in Ubuntu 18.04, if it is not installed on your system, you can install the UFW package by using below command.

"
**$ sudo apt install ufw**
"

Check UFW Status

Once the installation is completed you can check the status of UFW with the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw status verbose**
"

By default, UFW is disabled. You have to enable it by using below command.

"`
