$ sudo ufw enable

"`

Now it is activated.

## Using IPv6 with UFW

If your VPS is configured for IPv6, ensure that UFW is configured to support IPv6 so that will configure both IPv4 and IPv6 firewall rules. To do that, open the UFW configuration with this command:

"
**$ sudo vi /etc/default/ufw**
"

Then you have to set IPv6 to "yes" like this:

"
**IPV6=yes**
"

Save and exit then restart the firewall with below commands:

"
**sudo ufw disable
sudo ufw enable**
"

Now the UFW will configure the firewall for both IPv4 and IPv6.

## UFW Default Policies

UFW will lock all incoming connections and allow all outbound connections. This means that anyone trying to access your server will not be able to connect, if not you open the port. This means all incoming connections are restricted and allow all outgoing connections.

The default policies can be set by using below commands.

"
**$ sudo ufw default deny incoming**
"

And

"
**$ sudo ufw default allow outgoing**
"

If you want to be more restrictive, you can also deny all outgoing requests as well. This can be done by using below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw default deny outgoing**
"

## Allow SSH Connections

Before enabling the firewall we need to add a rule which will allow incoming SSH connections. To configure the UFW firewall, allow all incoming SSH connections by entering the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow ssh**
"

The syntax for adding this service is quite easy. For example, The below command allows a connection on port 22 using TCP protocol.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 22/tcp**
"

If your SSH server is running on port 2222, we could enable connections with below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp**
"

Enable UFW

So far UFW firewall is configured to allow all incoming SSH connections. Now we can enable it by entering the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw enable**
"

Allow connections on other ports

Depending on applications that run on your server, you will also allow incoming access to some other ports. How to allow incoming connections to some of the services are given below.

## Open port 80-HTTP

By using below commands HTTP connections can be allowed.

"
*$ sudo ufw allow http*
"

You can use port number 80 in place of http:

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 80/tcp**
"

Also you can use application profile like "Nginx HTTP" :

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 'Nginx HTTP'**
"

## Open port 8080

If you run Tomcat or any other application that listens on port 8080 to allow incoming connections to enter below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp**
"

## Allow Port Ranges

Instead of allowing access to single ports UFW allows us to access port ranges.

If you allow port ranges with UFW, you must specify the protocol, either tcp or udp.

For example, if you want to allow port from 7100 to 7200 on both tcp and udp then run below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow 7100:7200/tcp
$ sudo ufw allow 7100:7200/udp**
"

## Allow IP Addresses

To allow access on all ports from the home machine with IP Address of 64.63.62.61, Then use the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw allow from 64.63.62.61**
"

## Deny Connections

The default policy for all incoming connections is set to deny and if you haven't changed it, UFW will block all incoming connection unless you explicitly open the connection.

For example, you have opened the ports 80 and 443 and your server is under attack from the 23.24.25.0/24 network. To deny all connections from that IP addresses you can use the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw deny from 23.24.25.0/24**
"

If you want to deny access to ports 80 and 443 from that IP Address you can use the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw deny from 23.24.25.0/24 to any port 80
$ sudo ufw deny from 23.24.25.0/24 to any port 443**
"

Writing allow rules are also same as deny rules, only need to replace allow with deny.

## Deleting UFW Rules

There are two ways to delete UFW rules.

By rule number.

For example, To delete UFW rule by rule number is as below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw delete 2**
"

By specifying the actual rule.

For example, To delete UfW rule by specifying the actual rule is as below

"
**$ sudo ufw delete allow 8069**
"

## Disable UFW

If you want to stop UFW and deactivate all rules you can use below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw disable**
"

If you want to re-enable UFW and activate all rules, You can use below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw enable**
"

## Reset UFW

If you reset UFW, it will disable

and delete all active rules. To reset UFW, Enter the below command.

"
**$ sudo ufw reset**
"

## Conclusion

In this guide, we have explained how to install and configure the UFW firewall on Ubuntu 18.04 server. Be sure to allow all incoming connections that are necessary for proper functioning of your system.

title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts
description:
By Renchao Wu. Originally published on widechaos.cn.

For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-02.

All five point at the same thing: infrastructure for agents; retrieval, a knowledge base, a skills directory, an evolution loop, and one course that turns evaluation into a specification.

1. sahenjp/RustXNG ⭐ 471 · Rust

GitHub: https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG

In one line: A self-hosted search service that returns ranked results and page text in a single request, built to be an agent's retrieval layer.

What it is: Written in Rust, AGPL-3.0-or-later, a port of SearXNG with a SearXNG-compatible response shape and a browser UI on port 8888. The repository was created on 18 October 2026 and reached v0.26.0 in two weeks, with two releases on 1 November.

What stands out:

  • Text comes back with the results. With include_raw_content=1 it returns about 32,000 characters from the top five pages, so an agent can inspect extracted text without fetching every page separately. Extraction does not establish source accuracy, completeness or permission to republish it.
  • Several upstream engines with per-engine failure handling. 226 engine types, 352 settings entries, 180 enabled by default; each engine has its own timeout, failed engines are suspended with backoff, and engines that keep returning nothing are rested.
  • The project documents default SSRF checks. The documented policy restricts fetching to public addresses. I have not tested redirects, DNS changes or the full network boundary; it is not an independent security guarantee.
  • Ops surface included. /healthz, OpenMetrics /metrics, response cache, image proxy, bot rate limiting, and idle timeout for sidecars.

Compared with: The relationship to SearXNG is a port, not a fork in spirit; compatible interface, engines carried over, plus page-text fetching, SSRF protection and a ranking pass (term coverage, site authority, identifier match). Those additions are documented by the project; I did not re-check them against SearXNG item by item. Against hosted search APIs the difference is self-hosting and text volume: the README reports a 100-question comparison on one machine, hit@1 of 79–83 versus Exa 77 and Tavily 34; about 32,000 characters per request versus about 9,000 and about 1,200; 0.01 s for a repeated query versus 0.6 s and about 1 s. Those are the project's own numbers, not my tests, and it notes they move a few points between runs.

Recent updates: v0.26.0 (1 November) published a ghcr.io image and made the English README primary; v0.25.0 the same day repositioned the project as an agent retrieval layer. All three release notes are one line about checksums, so the substance is in the commit messages.

Who it's for: Anyone who wants to host an agent-search endpoint. The metasearch service still sends queries to enabled upstream engines and fetches third-party pages; self-hosting does not make retrieval offline or eliminate third-party data exposure. Two conditions apply: Google is unavailable in this build (the WML endpoint returns 403, the HTML endpoint needs JavaScript, headless browsers get detected), so replacement engines need testing; and the license is AGPL-3.0-or-later, whose exact terms should be checked for the intended deployment. The README specifically discusses source obligations for a modified network-service version; network access alone is not a complete licence analysis.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Collapsing "found it" and "got citable text" into one request is the right subtraction; whether it replaces an existing setup depends on results without Google.

Checked: README, three release notes, recent commits and docs/COMPARISON-EXA.md; not installed.

2. undefined-ui/second-brain-os ⭐ 1,170 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/undefined-ui/second-brain-os

In one line: A plain-Markdown knowledge base an agent maintains for you, plus a course and toolkit for building that agent.

What it is: 130 pages; a guide, a seven-module agents course and five handbooks; with a toolkit of 18 skills, 72 slash commands, 6 subagents, 4 scripts, a plugin and a starter vault. MIT. Obsidian is a viewer, not a dependency. It implements the llm-wiki pattern Karpathy published as a gist on 4 April 2026: the wiki is primary and raw sources are an archive; new sources get compiled into existing pages; three operations; ingest, lint, query.

What stands out:

  • Compilation, not side-by-side summaries. A concept page is rewritten and thickened by new sources instead of becoming a list of excerpts. That is a maintenance choice; I have not measured long-term accuracy or upkeep.
  • Maintenance is a command, not a reminder. 72 slash commands cover creating pages, merging, health checks and graph export; /metrics, /health and /graph-export run from scripts inside the vault.
  • Health has script-generated indicators. The health and graph-export entry points provide observable indicators. A health score or graph export does not by itself detect every contradiction or establish that stored claims are true.
  • The resource list is dated. Every entry in resources/ carries one line on why it belongs, and the README states it was checked on 1 November 2026 with stars from that day's API.

Compared with: The README compares this file-maintenance approach with memory servers and retrieval-based context assembly. This one is a methodology document plus a copyable vault plus a command set, and its bet is that an agent maintains files through fixed operations. It names Basic Memory 1.0, ai-memory 3.0 and Hindsight 1.0 and explains how it differs; that is its own account, and I did not read those repositories. The checkable dimensions are three: whether writes leave evidence, whether pages are compiled, and whether lint actually runs.

Recent updates: No releases; main-branch iteration. On 2 November the graph recommendation moved from Kuzu to Ladybug (Kuzu was archived in October 2025; the project describes Ladybug as a continuation with embedded CSV support; I have not independently verified migration compatibility), and the README was reorganised by level with a "new this month" section. A companion site went up on 14 October.

Who it's for: People already keeping file-based notes who want an agent to take over filing and linking. It assumes Claude Code's directory conventions (.claude/skills, commands, agents); another agent means changing how they load. If you want "install it and it organises itself", this is not that; it gives process and scripts, and you still feed it the first ten sources.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. The method matters more than the tooling, and here the method is written as executable commands.

Checked: README, the llm-wiki pattern document and recent commits; not installed.

3. ant-research/AntOmniEvo ⭐ 1,221 · Python

GitHub: https://github.com/ant-research/AntOmniEvo

In one line: A framework that treats a system's tunable parts as a directory of files, has a coding agent rewrite them from failure trajectories, and keeps the loop and the audit trail.

What it is: Python, Apache-2.0. The division of labour is "you define, the framework controls, AI does the work": you supply how to run the system, an evaluator, train/val data, a directory mapping for the tunable artifacts, and a starting point; the framework handles scheduling, budgets, selection and persistence; a coding agent acts as the Proposer. Tunable artifacts can be a skill's SKILL.md plus scripts, a pipeline's pipeline.json plus node code, or a single-file algorithm plus its description. The system being optimised need not contain an LLM; the Proposer must be able to write code.

What stands out:

  • Optimisation becomes file editing. Prompts, skills, DAG topology and node implementations all go through one mechanism because they share one property: they are files.
  • The scoring rule is the objective. The evaluator returns 0 to 1, train and validation are split, and the README insists on a held-out set rather than gains on the training split.
  • The design records edits alongside failure evidence. The deliverable includes lineage linking changes to the failure material used by the proposer. This records a rationale, not proof that the edit caused an improvement.
  • Candidate state is persisted for interruption and resumption. Candidates, runs, analyses and changelogs land in a CandidateStore. I have not tested crash recovery, partial external effects or exact replay behaviour.

Compared with: OpenEvolve is another evolutionary-code-optimisation project; its reported gains are tied to its own tasks and evaluation conditions, which I did not reproduce. This project widens the object to skills, prompts, pipeline configs and node code inside a directory, restricts the editor to a coding agent reading failure trajectories, and treats the change-to-failure mapping as part of the deliverable. These descriptions do not establish that the projects have mutually exclusive optimisation targets or that either is more effective. I only read both READMEs and ran neither.

Recent updates: No releases. On 29 October the visualiser gained an English/Chinese switch; on 28 October a trajectory-model document landed along with a note that the paper's experiment scripts and datasets will be open-sourced separately. The paper is Mara Chain (arXiv 2609.35855).

Who it's for: Teams with a repeatable, reasonably cheap evaluation whose optimisation target can be expressed as a directory of files. The docs are explicit about the mismatch cases: a handful of scalar parameters, an evaluation that is not repeatable or is very expensive, or output with strict compliance requirements (it edits files in a sandbox, so audit the permissions yourself).

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Treating auditability as a hard requirement is worth more than the evolutionary machinery itself.

Checked: README, docs/when-to-use.md, recent commits and the paper entry; not installed.

4. wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese ⭐ 407 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese

In one line: A Chinese-language course on engineering AI agents, built around Stanford CS329Z's public materials: 19 lessons, four exercises, readable offline.

What it is: 19 lessons, four hands-on exercises, Markdown sources, a single-file offline HTML reader, and scripts to build and verify publication. The order follows the engineering chain: agent landscape, LLMs for builders, RAG, tool use and function calling, orchestration, context management, memory architecture, multi-agent systems, system optimisation, evaluation engineering, data selection and quality, LLM judges, safety, coding agents, proactive agents, open problems. The README states plainly that this is an independent Chinese study guide, not an official Stanford translation, and that rights to the original course and code stay with their authors; open revisions live in a separate editorial-notes file. There is no license file at the repository root.

What stands out:

  • Evaluation is written as a specification. Lesson 13 formalises agent evaluation as a four-tuple; request, environment, stopping criteria, scorer; and lists four difficulties: non-unique solution paths, stateful environments with side effects, compounded non-determinism, and cost plus safety constraints.
  • Scaffolding is called out. The same model with a different token budget or tool set cannot be compared directly; realistic scaffolding needs controlled variables. That one line is useful when reading anyone else's leaderboard.
  • Dense per lesson. A lesson runs several thousand characters with stated learning goals, not a bullet outline.
  • Offline. The single-file HTML does not depend on the site.

Compared with: Among Chinese agent courses it chose to reproduce one course lesson by lesson rather than spread a roadmap wide; the cost is narrow coverage. Against the original English course the increment is Chinese phrasing and engineering organisation, and I did not compare coverage lesson by lesson. There is a practical constraint: the text is organised from public course materials, the repository carries no license, and rights stay with the original authors; public availability does not establish permission to redistribute or use the material commercially; check the applicable rights.

Recent updates: First release on 28 October, then per-lesson descriptions and Chinese search improvements on 31 October. Five days in: 407 stars, 45 forks.

Who it's for: Python developers who want to fill in agent engineering concepts systematically, especially evaluation and safety. If you want a runnable codebase, that is not the shape here; there are exercises, but the body is lecture material.

My take: ⭐⭐. Solid as a Chinese-language evaluation text; as an engineering reference it needs code alongside.

Checked: README, lesson 13, and the repository file list; did not run the build scripts.

5. heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills ⭐ 6,332 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills

In one line: A cross-vendor directory of agent skills; 388 entries; with six quality criteria attached.

What it is: An 82 KB README with 388 links in six languages, plus a companion site. Two halves: official and vendor directories (AI platforms and models, cloud and infrastructure, developer tools and frameworks, the Google ecosystem, business and marketing, security and web intelligence; six sections with 47 vendor groups), and community skills (16 groups covering vector databases, data and analytics, cloud storage, marketing and more). Its claim is to list skills real teams use rather than bulk-generated ones; the compatibility list names Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Windsurf.

What stands out:

  • Organised by who published it. Vendor-maintained skills come first, then third-party ones; a useful provenance distinction, not a substitute for inspecting the contents.
  • Six quality criteria. Unambiguous instructions, one focused task, a working example, documented trade-offs, SKILL.md under 500 lines, verified on the target agent. Usable directly as acceptance checks.
  • Translations are a pipeline. Commits show translated READMEs and site data synced from the main README rather than six hand-maintained copies.
  • Submissions pass an automated gate. Every pull request triggers a checker script: only README.md may change, changes must be additive, at most five lines per PR, a fixed line format, duplicate detection, the repository must exist and not be archived, it must contain a SKILL.md, have at least 20 stars and be at least 14 days old; failures get a needs-fixes label. Entries come from outside contributors, but code enforces the floor.

Compared with: Against a plain link list it adds two concrete things; six stated quality criteria and an automated gate that actually rejects submissions (the rules above are the script's rules); against each vendor's own marketplace it is a horizontal index, and its compatibility list names intended hosts. It does not establish that each listed skill was tested on every host or version. What the gate verifies is entry compliance and repository availability; it cannot verify a claim like "verified on the target agent", which still depends on the author or your own test.

Recent updates: On 2 November it synced multilingual READMEs and site data, tidied a triage batch, and added claude-code-skills-zh, motionboard, mobbin/skills and others (#641 to #647). Created on 29 December 2025; 6,332 stars since.

Who it's for: People looking for existing skills, or wanting acceptance criteria for their own. Start with the vendor sections; check third-party entries' maintenance yourself.

My take: ⭐⭐. Fine as an index, not as a quality endorsement.

Checked: README structure, the quality-standards section, the pull-request checker script and recent commits; installed no skills.

At a glance

Project What it is Most distinctive Who it's for Worth digging
RustXNG Self-hosted retrieval layer Results and page text in one request, SSRF-guarded Anyone wiring search for a local agent ⭐⭐⭐
second-brain-os Self-maintaining knowledge base Maintenance as 72 commands; a documented ingest/lint/query workflow People on file-based notes ⭐⭐⭐
AntOmniEvo Auto-evolution framework Every edit carries a failure trail, diffable and revertible Teams with a stable evaluation ⭐⭐⭐
cs329z-chinese Chinese agent course Evaluation taught as a four-tuple specification Anyone filling gaps in evaluation and safety ⭐⭐
awesome-agent-skills Skills directory A cross-vendor index with six stated acceptance criteria Finding skills, setting standards ⭐⭐

Notes from this issue

  • Agent infrastructure is being split into replaceable parts. Retrieval, knowledge bases, skill directories and evolution loops each have their own projects, and the interfaces look more like services an agent calls than interfaces a person uses. When choosing, ask about the interface shape before the feature list.
  • The projects make auditability part of their design. An evolution framework requires every edit to carry a failure trail; a knowledge base makes lint a mandatory operation. Those choices make changes easier to inspect; I have no evidence here about the authors' prior losses or the effectiveness of the checks.
  • Stating limits has become part of the documentation. One says outright that Google is unavailable in this build; another says the framework does not fit systems with only a few scalar parameters. Sentences like these help more than a performance table.

title: AWS HealthImaging: A Guide to DICOM Storage and Access
description:
Medical imaging systems generate large volumes of data, including X-rays, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and ultrasound studies. Managing these files requires scalable storage, reliable access, and strong data protection. AWS HealthImaging helps healthcare organizations manage medical imaging data in the cloud while supporting applications that retrieve and process Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) files.

In this guide, we explore how AWS HealthImaging works, how organizations can optimize DICOM storage and access, and which architectural practices support reliable imaging workflows.

What Is AWS HealthImaging?

AWS HealthImaging is a cloud-based medical imaging service from Amazon Web Services (AWS). It helps healthcare organizations store, manage, and access medical imaging data at scale.

Traditional imaging environments often rely on Picture Archiving and Communication Systems (PACS). These systems store medical images and support retrieval across clinical departments. However, growing imaging volumes can increase infrastructure, maintenance, and storage requirements.

AWS HealthImaging provides a managed cloud service for medical imaging data. Organizations can use it as part of an imaging architecture without managing every storage component themselves.

The service organizes imaging data into image sets. It also provides application programming interfaces (APIs) for importing, searching, retrieving, and managing imaging information.

Healthcare developers can use these capabilities to build applications such as:

Cloud-based medical imaging platforms.

Web-based diagnostic image viewers.

Radiology workflow applications.

Medical image research platforms.

Artificial intelligence (AI) imaging solutions.

Connected healthcare applications that use imaging records.

AWS HealthImaging can support imaging workflows across multiple facilities. Organizations should still design access, integration, and governance policies around their clinical requirements.

Understanding DICOM and Medical Imaging Workloads

Before optimizing storage and access, we need to understand the information that medical imaging systems handle.

DICOM is a standard for managing and exchanging medical imaging information. It defines how imaging systems structure, store, transmit, and identify medical images.

A DICOM study can contain multiple series, and each series can contain multiple images. For example, a CT examination may include hundreds of image slices.

DICOM files can also contain important metadata, including:

Patient and study identifiers.

Imaging modality and examination details.

Acquisition date and time.

Study and series descriptions.

Image dimensions and orientation.

Equipment and acquisition parameters.

This information helps imaging applications organize studies and retrieve relevant images.

Why DICOM Workloads Need Careful Optimization

Medical imaging workloads differ from ordinary document storage. A single examination can contain large files and thousands of individual image frames.

Radiologists may need to retrieve an entire study quickly. Other applications may request only selected frames or metadata.

Common workload patterns include:

High-volume imports: Hospitals transfer large imaging archives into centralized storage.

Frequent retrieval: Clinical applications request studies throughout the day.

Metadata searches: Users search for examinations using patient or study identifiers.

Concurrent access: Multiple clinicians may access the same imaging study.

Long-term retention: Organizations preserve imaging records according to operational and regulatory requirements.

AI processing: Algorithms retrieve image data for analysis and model inference.

An effective architecture must account for these patterns. It should balance storage requirements, retrieval performance, application needs, and operational costs.

How AWS HealthImaging Manages DICOM Storage

AWS HealthImaging provides a managed environment for storing medical imaging data. Its image set structure helps applications organize and retrieve imaging information.

Understanding this structure helps developers design efficient storage and access workflows.

Image Sets and Imaging Metadata

AWS HealthImaging organizes imported DICOM data into image sets. An image set represents a logical collection of imaging information that applications can manage.

The service provides APIs for accessing image set information and metadata. Applications can use these capabilities to identify relevant imaging records before retrieving image data.

This separation supports more targeted access patterns. For example, a viewer can search for a study before requesting its image frames.

Importing DICOM Data

Organizations often begin cloud imaging projects by transferring existing DICOM archives. AWS HealthImaging supports DICOM import workflows through its service APIs.

A typical import process involves:

Preparing the source DICOM files.

Uploading the files to an appropriate Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) location.

Starting an import job through the supported AWS HealthImaging API.

Monitoring the import job and reviewing its status.

Checking the resulting image sets and metadata.

Validating representative studies through application retrieval workflows.

Developers should validate source files before importing large datasets. This helps identify malformed files, missing metadata, and inconsistent identifiers.

They should also test import behavior with representative imaging studies. Different modalities and acquisition systems may produce different data patterns.

Managing Imaging Data at Scale

Storage planning should consider both current data volumes and future growth. Imaging archives can expand as organizations add facilities, modalities, and clinical services.

AWS HealthImaging can help reduce the operational burden of managing imaging storage infrastructure. However, organizations still need clear policies for data lifecycle management.

A practical storage strategy should address:

Expected daily and annual imaging volumes.

Historical archive migration.

Study retention requirements.

Data access frequency.

Duplicate and invalid study handling.

Backup and recovery expectations.

Regional data residency requirements.

These considerations help organizations build a storage model that supports clinical operations.

Optimizing DICOM Access and Retrieval Performance

Storage capacity alone does not determine imaging performance. Clinical applications also need predictable access to image data and metadata.

AWS HealthImaging provides APIs that allow applications to search and retrieve imaging information. Developers should design these workflows around actual user behavior.

Search Before Retrieving Image Data

A common inefficiency occurs when applications retrieve large imaging datasets before identifying the required study.

We recommend separating discovery from retrieval. Applications should first search for relevant image sets and examine their metadata.

Once users select a study, the application can request the required image data. This approach helps avoid unnecessary data transfers.

For example, a radiologist searching for a patient's previous CT scan may need only the matching study. The application should not retrieve unrelated imaging records.

Retrieve Only the Required Image Frames

Some imaging workflows require an entire study. Others need only selected images or frames.

Applications should request the smallest useful data set whenever the workflow permits. This can reduce network traffic and improve responsiveness.

A diagnostic viewer may initially load selected image frames. It can retrieve additional frames as users navigate through a study.

Developers should also consider image dimensions and rendering requirements. These factors influence how applications process and display retrieved data.

Design Efficient API Requests

Every API request adds processing and network overhead. Applications should avoid unnecessary repeated requests for identical information.

Useful optimization practices include:

Requesting only the metadata needed by the current workflow.

Reusing valid identifiers across related requests.

Avoiding repeated searches for unchanged records.

Managing concurrent requests carefully.

Applying controlled retry logic.

Monitoring API response times and error rates.

Caching can also improve application responsiveness. However, developers must define appropriate expiration and invalidation rules.

Patient information changes over time, so applications should not rely on stale metadata. They must also protect cached information through suitable access controls.

Improve Viewer Performance

Medical image viewers need to display studies efficiently. Poor retrieval design can cause delays during scrolling, zooming, and image navigation.

We recommend loading essential study information first. The viewer can then retrieve image frames according to user interactions.

Developers should test performance across different network conditions. They should also evaluate large studies and concurrent clinical sessions.

These tests help identify bottlenecks in retrieval, processing, and rendering.

Building a Scalable AWS HealthImaging Architecture

A healthcare imaging architecture usually includes more than a storage service. It connects data sources, ingestion processes, application services, viewers, and clinical workflows.

A typical architecture may include the following components:

Imaging sources: Modalities and existing PACS environments generate DICOM studies.

Ingestion layer: Import workflows transfer imaging data into the cloud environment.

AWS HealthImaging datastore: The service manages imported imaging data and image sets.

Application backend: Backend services manage authentication, application logic, and API requests.

Metadata and search services: Application components help users locate relevant studies.

Image viewer: A web or desktop application retrieves and displays imaging information.

Monitoring and security services: Operational tools track system health and access activity.

Connect Existing PACS Environments

Many healthcare organizations already operate PACS infrastructure. Replacing these systems immediately may not be practical.

A phased integration strategy can connect existing imaging environments with cloud services. Organizations can migrate selected datasets or workflows before expanding the architecture.

Developers should evaluate existing DICOM interfaces, export capabilities, and vendor restrictions. They should also define how applications handle records across cloud and on-premises environments.

Integrate with EHR and Clinical Applications

Medical images often need to appear alongside clinical records. Integrating imaging applications with Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems can help providers access relevant studies.

For example, an EHR workflow may display imaging study references within a patient's clinical record. An authorized user can then open the corresponding study in an imaging viewer.

Developers should coordinate patient identifiers and study references carefully. Incorrect mappings can associate imaging records with the wrong patient.

Support Multiple Facilities

Healthcare networks may operate hospitals, diagnostic centers, and specialist clinics across different locations.

A centralized imaging architecture can support shared access across participating facilities. However, developers must define access boundaries and organizational responsibilities.

The design should consider user identity, facility permissions, data ownership, and regional requirements. These controls help maintain appropriate access as the system grows.

Security and Compliance for Medical Imaging Data

Medical images often contain protected health information (PHI). Organizations must protect this information throughout ingestion, storage, retrieval, and sharing.

In the United States, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) establishes requirements for protecting electronic protected health information (ePHI).

AWS provides security capabilities that organizations can configure within their cloud environments. However, using a cloud service does not automatically make an application HIPAA compliant.

Organizations must implement appropriate technical, administrative, and physical safeguards.

Encryption and Data Protection

Encryption helps protect medical imaging information against unauthorized access. Organizations should use supported encryption options for data storage and secure communication.

They should also manage encryption keys through appropriate controls. Key access should follow organizational security policies.

Identity and Access Management

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) helps control access to AWS resources. Organizations can define permissions for users, applications, and service roles.

We recommend applying the principle of least privilege. Each application should receive only the permissions required for its specific workflow.

Healthcare applications should also enforce user-level authorization. A valid service credential should not automatically grant every user unrestricted patient access.

Audit Logging and Monitoring

Organizations need visibility into how applications access imaging records. Audit and operational logs can support security reviews and incident investigations.

Monitoring should cover:

Authentication and authorization events.

Imaging import and retrieval activity.

Failed API requests.

Permission and configuration changes.

Unusual access patterns.

Application errors and service availability.

Logs should avoid unnecessary exposure of PHI. Organizations should define retention, access, and review policies.

Network Security

Network controls help restrict communication between application components. Organizations can use suitable network isolation and access policies.

They should also review public endpoints, service permissions, and data transfer paths. Security testing should cover both application and infrastructure configurations.

Common AWS HealthImaging Implementation Challenges

Cloud imaging projects involve several technical and operational considerations. Planning for these challenges helps prevent avoidable delays.

Legacy DICOM Compatibility

Older imaging systems may produce files with inconsistent metadata or unsupported characteristics. Import validation helps identify these issues before migration.

Developers should test files from different modalities and vendors. They should also define procedures for handling failed imports.

Large-Scale Data Migration

Historical imaging archives can contain millions of files. Transferring these datasets requires careful planning around network capacity and import throughput.

Organizations should migrate data in controlled batches. They should monitor job status and validate imported studies before expanding migration.

Patient Identity and Metadata Consistency

Different systems may use different patient identifiers or metadata conventions. These differences can create duplicate records or incorrect associations.

A consistent identity-matching strategy helps reduce these risks. Teams should also establish data validation and reconciliation procedures.

Application Compatibility

Existing viewers may rely on specific DICOM interfaces or storage assumptions. They may require changes before working with a cloud-based imaging service.

Developers should review viewer capabilities early. They should also test retrieval, rendering, and clinical workflows before production deployment.

Cost Management

Cloud imaging costs depend on storage, data transfer, API usage, and other architecture choices. Organizations should evaluate expected usage before deployment.

Useful cost-management practices include:

Estimating storage growth by modality.

Reviewing data retrieval patterns.

Monitoring data transfer charges.

Avoiding unnecessary API calls.

Evaluating migration and operational costs.

Reviewing service pricing as requirements change.

Cost optimization should not compromise clinical availability or required retention policies.

Best Practices for Optimizing AWS HealthImaging Workloads

A structured implementation approach helps organizations balance performance, reliability, security, and cost.

We recommend the following practices:

Assess imaging workloads: Identify modalities, file volumes, access patterns, and retention requirements.

Validate DICOM files: Check representative datasets before large-scale imports.

Plan migration in phases: Move data in manageable batches and validate each stage.

Use targeted retrieval: Search metadata first and request only the required image data.

Optimize application requests: Reduce redundant calls and apply controlled retries.

Test real clinical workflows: Evaluate study search, image navigation, and concurrent access.

Secure every integration point: Apply encryption, identity controls, and appropriate permissions.

Monitor performance: Track import jobs, API errors, retrieval times, and application health.

Document operational procedures: Maintain integration specifications and recovery processes.

Review costs regularly: Compare actual usage with expected storage and retrieval patterns.

These practices create a foundation for reliable medical imaging applications. They also help organizations adapt as imaging workloads and clinical requirements change.

How AWS HealthImaging Supports AI and Advanced Imaging Applications

Healthcare organizations increasingly use AI to support medical image analysis and clinical research. These applications require reliable access to imaging data.

AWS HealthImaging can serve as part of an architecture that connects imaging storage with processing applications. Developers can build services that retrieve authorized image data for downstream workflows.

Potential use cases include:

AI-Assisted Image Analysis

AI models can analyze medical images to identify patterns or support clinical review. Applications can retrieve relevant imaging data and send it to authorized processing services.

Developers must validate model performance and maintain clinical oversight. AI-generated findings should not replace qualified medical judgment.

Medical Imaging Research

Research platforms often need access to large imaging datasets. Cloud-based storage can support research workflows across distributed applications.

Organizations must apply appropriate de-identification, consent, access, and governance controls. They should also follow applicable research and privacy requirements.

Connected Diagnostic Workflows

Imaging applications can connect with EHRs, reporting platforms, and clinical portals. These integrations help providers access relevant images within broader care workflows.

The architecture should maintain accurate patient and study references. It should also support appropriate access restrictions across applications.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is AWS HealthImaging used for?

AWS HealthImaging helps healthcare organizations store, manage, and access medical imaging data in the cloud. Developers can use its APIs to build imaging applications and retrieval workflows.

2. Does AWS HealthImaging support DICOM?

Yes. AWS HealthImaging supports workflows for importing and managing DICOM medical imaging data. Developers can use the service's APIs to access image sets and related information.

3. How does AWS HealthImaging differ from traditional PACS?

Traditional PACS platforms manage medical imaging storage and retrieval within healthcare environments. AWS HealthImaging provides a managed cloud service for medical imaging data. Organizations should compare their integration, workflow, and operational requirements before choosing an architecture.

4. Can AWS HealthImaging integrate with an EHR?

Yes. Developers can build integrations between AWS HealthImaging and EHR applications. These connections can help users access imaging studies through clinical workflows.

5. Is AWS HealthImaging HIPAA compliant?

AWS offers services and security capabilities that support eligible HIPAA workloads under applicable conditions. Organizations must configure their environments and applications appropriately. They must also meet their own HIPAA obligations.

6. How can we improve DICOM retrieval performance?

Start by optimizing metadata searches and avoiding unnecessary image transfers. Retrieve only the required data, manage API requests efficiently, and test viewer performance under realistic workloads.

7. Can AWS HealthImaging support AI medical imaging applications?

Yes. Developers can build architectures that connect AWS HealthImaging with authorized image processing and AI services. They must also address data security, model validation, and clinical oversight.

8. What should organizations consider before migrating imaging data?

Organizations should assess DICOM compatibility, archive size, network capacity, metadata quality, retention policies, and application dependencies. A phased migration with validation helps reduce operational risks.

Build Scalable Medical Imaging Solutions with Oodles

Medical imaging platforms need more than cloud storage. They require reliable data ingestion, efficient retrieval, secure access, and integration with clinical applications.

AWS HealthImaging can support these requirements within a carefully planned cloud architecture. The right implementation depends on imaging volumes, existing systems, user workflows, and long-term operational goals.

At Oodles, we work on healthcare technology solutions involving medical imaging, healthcare APIs, EHR and EMR integrations, and cloud-based application development. We help organizations evaluate technical requirements and design practical integration strategies.

title: How to Boot into rescue mode in RHEL 7 / CENTOS 7
description:
Rescue mode provides a convenient single-user environment and allows you to repair your system in situations when it is unable to complete a normal booting process. In rescue mode, the system attempts to mount all local file systems and start some important system services, but it does not activate network interfaces or allow more users to be logged into the system at the same time. In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, rescue mode is equivalent to single user mode and requires the root password.

If you are already logged in as root at a local console, you can enter emergency mode directly. Use the console rather than SSH because emergency mode deactivates network interfaces:

[root@linuxlab01 ~]# systemctl emergency

To enter rescue mode during boot instead, select a kernel on the GRUB 2 screen and press e to edit. Find the line starting with linux16 and append systemd.unit=rescue.target, then press Ctrl+X to boot.

When prompted, enter the root password. You can then perform maintenance tasks such as inspecting disks, editing files with vi, or checking an unmounted filesystem.

Rescue mode vs emergency mode vs single-user mode

These three get mixed up constantly, so it helps to know which one you actually want before you are staring at a broken boot:

  • Rescue mode (rescue.target) mounts your filesystems and starts basic services, but no networking. Use this when the system boots partially and you need to repair config files, reset a password, or run fsck.
  • Emergency mode (emergency.target) is even more minimal: only the root filesystem is mounted, and read-only at that. Use this when rescue mode itself will not start — for example when a bad fstab entry stops the boot.
  • Single-user mode is the older SysV term; on RHEL 7 and later, rescue mode is its systemd equivalent.

Booting into rescue mode from GRUB, step by step

  1. Reboot and wait for the GRUB menu. If it does not appear, hold Shift (BIOS) or tap Esc (UEFI) during boot.
  2. Highlight your normal kernel and press e to edit — this does not change anything permanently, only this one boot.
  3. Find the line starting with linux16 (or linux on newer releases) and add systemd.unit=rescue.target at the end, separated by a space.
  4. Press Ctrl+X to boot with that temporary parameter.

When prompted, enter the root password. You land in a root shell where you can edit files, check logs with journalctl -xb, or run filesystem checks.

The mistakes that cost people an hour

Forgetting to remount read-write. In emergency mode the root filesystem is read-only, so every edit fails until you run:

mount -o remount,rw /

A broken fstab is the most common reason you are here. If boot fails right after you edited mounts, comment out the new line in /etc/fstab instead of debugging anything else first. Adding nofail to non-essential mounts (USB drives, secondary disks) prevents this entire class of boot failure.

No networking in rescue mode is normal. ping will not work, and that is expected, not a new problem. If you need the network to download a package, boot normally with a working kernel instead.

Inspect the failure before changing anything

Start with evidence instead of running several repair commands and hoping one works:

systemctl --failed
journalctl -xb --no-pager
lsblk -f
findmnt

The first two commands show failed units and detailed boot messages. lsblk -f identifies block devices and filesystem types, while findmnt shows what is actually mounted. Before editing a configuration file, keep a backup, for example cp -a /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.before-rescue.

After changing /etc/fstab, run systemctl daemon-reload, then mount -a to test the entries. Read any error carefully; do not assume the repair worked just because a prompt returned.

Check filesystems safely

Never run a repair utility on a mounted filesystem. For a non-root ext4 filesystem, unmount it first and substitute the device name shown by lsblk:

umount /dev/sdb1
fsck /dev/sdb1

RHEL 7 and CentOS 7 commonly use XFS. For an unmounted XFS filesystem, use xfs_repair /dev/sdb1 instead of fsck. Do not use xfs_repair -L merely to bypass a log-related error; zeroing the log can cause data loss and should be a last resort after exhausting safer options.

You cannot unmount the root filesystem while running from it. To repair root, boot the matching installation media and enter its rescue shell without mounting the installed system. This installer rescue environment is separate from systemd's rescue.target.

Rebuild initramfs only when it is relevant

If boot messages point to missing storage drivers or LVM support after a kernel or storage change, regenerate the image for the kernel currently running in rescue mode:

dracut --force /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)

This overwrites that kernel's image, so verify the version first and retain a backup when possible. It does not repair every installed kernel.

A rescue shell has unrestricted root privileges. Use trusted consoles and boot media, and do not treat disabling SELinux or running chmod -R 777 as a repair. Those actions can create a second, security-sensitive problem while hiding the original one.

Getting back out

When repairs are done, simply:

exit
# or, to force a full restart:
reboot

Because the GRUB edit was temporary, the next boot uses your normal kernel parameters automatically. If the system comes up clean, consider making the fix permanent where appropriate (correcting fstab, rebuilding initramfs with dracut, or restoring a config you changed) — and take a snapshot or backup before the next experiment.

title: How to Analyze Real-Time Apache and Nginx Logs using GoAccess
description:
GoAccess turns Apache and Nginx access logs into an interactive terminal dashboard or a standalone HTML report. It is useful for checking traffic, popular URLs, status codes, referrers, browsers, and client addresses without first shipping logs to another service. Because it reads the access log directly, the web server must already be logging requests in a format GoAccess understands.

Install GoAccess and verify it

On Debian or Ubuntu, install the distribution package:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install goaccess

On Fedora or a RHEL-compatible system with a repository that provides GoAccess, use:

sudo dnf install goaccess

macOS users can install it with brew install goaccess. Distribution packages may not contain the newest upstream release, but they are usually the simplest way to receive security and packaging updates.

Confirm that the command is available:

goaccess --version

Running goaccess without arguments also prints its basic usage and options.

Find the real access log

GoAccess analyzes access logs, not error logs. Common paths are:

  • Apache on Debian/Ubuntu: /var/log/apache2/access.log
  • Apache on RHEL-compatible systems: /var/log/httpd/access_log
  • Nginx: /var/log/nginx/access.log

Virtual hosts often use separate files, so check the CustomLog directive in Apache or access_log directive in Nginx rather than assuming the default. Use sudo ls -l on the path if your normal user cannot read it. Prefer read-only group access for a dedicated reporting user over running a long-lived dashboard as root.

Check for the COMBINED format

A typical Nginx combined or Apache LogFormat ... combined entry contains the client address, request time, request line, status, response size, referrer, and user agent:

192.0.2.10 - - [17/Oct/2026:10:15:30 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 1024 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"

The built-in COMBINED setting matches this layout. It is not a universal option: if an administrator adds a virtual-host name, changes field order, or removes fields, you must supply a custom format instead.

Monitor logs in the terminal

For Apache on Debian/Ubuntu, run:

sudo goaccess -f /var/log/apache2/access.log --log-format=COMBINED

For Nginx, change the path:

sudo goaccess -f /var/log/nginx/access.log --log-format=COMBINED

The -f option selects the input file. The terminal dashboard parses the existing entries and updates as new requests arrive. Scroll through the panels to inspect requested files, 404s, visitor hosts, operating systems, and browsers; press q to exit.

Treat visitor numbers as an approximation, not a count of people. Network address translation, shared connections, changing addresses, and bots all affect the result.

Create HTML reports

For a static report, use -o with an .html filename rather than relying on shell redirection:

sudo goaccess -f /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  --log-format=COMBINED -o goaccess-report.html

Open the resulting file in a browser, or copy it to a suitably protected reporting directory. A static report does not refresh itself; rerun the command or schedule a carefully permissioned reporting job to update it.

GoAccess can also update HTML in real time:

sudo goaccess -f /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  --log-format=COMBINED --real-time-html \
  --addr=127.0.0.1 --port=7890 -o /srv/goaccess/report.html

This starts GoAccess's WebSocket service on loopback. Remote publication needs additional configuration: proxy both the report and WebSocket through an authenticated TLS endpoint and set --ws-url when the browser-facing address differs. Do not simply expose port 7890 to the internet.

Analyze multiple or rotated logs

To include yesterday's uncompressed rotation alongside the current Nginx log, pass both files, oldest first:

sudo goaccess /var/log/nginx/access.log.1 \
  /var/log/nginx/access.log --log-format=COMBINED

This is helpful when an incident crosses midnight or a rotation boundary. Only combine logs that belong together; merging several virtual hosts makes their traffic look like one site. Check rotations for overlap or missing periods, and do not assume every .gz file can be read by your particular build.

Use a custom log format

For an Nginx-style combined layout, the long-form equivalent is:

sudo goaccess -f /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  --log-format='%h %^[%d:%t %^] "%r" %s %b "%R" "%u"' \
  --date-format='%d/%b/%Y' --time-format='%H:%M:%S'

Here %h is the client host, %r the request, %s the status, %b the response bytes, %R the referrer, and %u the user agent. %d and %t parse date and time, while %^ skips unneeded text. If your server adds $request_time or another field, account for it in the format string. Test against a small sample before processing years of logs.

Troubleshooting and common mistakes

  • Permission denied: verify the path and grant read-only access; avoid making logs world-readable.
  • “Nothing valid to process” or zero parsed hits: the log, date, or time format probably does not match. Confirm you selected an access log, then test with sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/nginx/access.log | goaccess - --log-format=COMBINED.
  • Unexpectedly large or small totals: check for overlapping rotations, missing logs, health checks, and bot traffic.
  • A stale or disconnected HTML dashboard: static HTML never live-updates. For real-time HTML, check that GoAccess is still running and that the WebSocket is reachable through any proxy.

Protect reports containing visitor data

Access-log reports can reveal IP addresses, visited URLs, query strings, referrers, and user agents. Query strings may even contain reset tokens or other sensitive values. Treat the HTML as confidential operational data, not a public analytics page.

Keep reports out of an unauthenticated web root. Restrict file and directory permissions, require authentication and TLS when serving them, limit network access, and delete reports when they are no longer needed. Binding a real-time service to loopback and restricting direct access to its port prevents a protected web page from being undermined by an open backend.

Conclusion

GoAccess is a practical way to inspect web traffic directly on a server. Start with the correct access log and COMBINED format, move to custom parsing only when needed, and apply the same access controls to its reports that you would to the underlying logs.

title: Hardening SSH for Production Servers
description:
SSH is the gateway to your server, so it is the first service to lock down on a new machine. By the end of this guide you will have key-only logins, no direct root login, a short list of accounts allowed in, and fail2ban banning addresses that keep failing, with every change tested before you close your session. This is Part 1 of the Linux Server Baseline series (Part 2 covers file permissions, Part 3 covers cron). Commands target Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12, with RHEL differences noted where they matter.

Set up key-based login first

Once password logins are off, a key is the only way in over the network, so the key has to work before you touch the server config. Generate an ed25519 key on your workstation, not on the server:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"

Accept the default path (~/.ssh/id_ed25519) and set a passphrase. Then copy the public half to the account you will log in as:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub deploy@203.0.113.10

ssh-copy-id uses your password one last time and appends the key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Confirm the key works on its own by telling the client not to fall back to a password:

ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey deploy@203.0.113.10

If you get a shell, key authentication works. While you are logged in, run sudo whoami and confirm it prints root, because root login is about to be disabled and this account is how you will administer the box.

For the rest of this guide, keep one SSH session open and run every test from a second terminal. Reloading sshd does not drop established sessions, so the open one is your way back if a change goes wrong. Also, if your admin account has no local password (common on cloud images), set one with sudo passwd deploy so the provider's console login works if you need it.

Put your settings in a drop-in file

On Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12, /etc/ssh/sshd_config starts with Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf. For most keywords sshd keeps the first value it reads, and it reads the included files in lexical order before the rest of the main file. Cloud images often ship a file such as 50-cloud-init.conf, and it may contain PasswordAuthentication yes. If you add PasswordAuthentication no to the bottom of sshd_config, or to a file named 60-hardening.conf, the cloud-init value is read first and yours is ignored.

Check what is already there:

grep -rniE 'include|passwordauthentication' /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/

Naming your file 00-hardening.conf puts it ahead of everything else. Create it with sudoedit /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf:

PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
AllowUsers deploy alice
X11Forwarding no

What each line does:

  • PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no together stop password prompts. With UsePAM yes (the Debian and Ubuntu default), keyboard-interactive auth can still ask for a password through PAM, so both are needed. KbdInteractiveAuthentication is the current name; older guides call it ChallengeResponseAuthentication, which is now a deprecated alias.
  • PermitRootLogin no replaces the default prohibit-password, which still allows root in with a key. Admins log in as themselves and use sudo, so the logs show who did what.
  • PubkeyAuthentication yes is already the default. Stating it keeps the file self-explanatory.
  • MaxAuthTries 3 limits authentication attempts per connection (default 6). Every key the client offers counts as one attempt.
  • LoginGraceTime 30 disconnects clients that have not authenticated within 30 seconds (default 120).
  • AllowUsers refuses every account not listed, even with a valid key. On a box with many admins, AllowGroups sshusers is easier to maintain. Pick one: if you set both, a user has to pass both checks. Make sure your own account is on the list.
  • X11Forwarding no overrides the yes in Debian and Ubuntu's stock config. Servers rarely need it.

Validate and reload without locking yourself out

Test the syntax before anything else. No output means the config parsed:

sudo sshd -t

Then ask sshd for the effective configuration, which shows the value that actually won after all files were read:

sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

passwordauthentication no

Repeat the grep for permitrootlogin, kbdinteractiveauthentication, maxauthtries, and allowusers. If any shows the old value, an earlier file is setting it (see troubleshooting below).

Reload the service. It is called ssh on Ubuntu and Debian and sshd on RHEL and Fedora:

sudo systemctl reload ssh

Now, from a second terminal, log in again. Then confirm passwords are refused by disabling key auth on the client:

ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no deploy@203.0.113.10

deploy@203.0.113.10: Permission denied (publickey).

A login as root should fail the same way. If the new login does not work, go back to the session you kept open, move the file aside with sudo mv /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf /root/, reload, and work out what went wrong before trying again.

Change the port for less log noise

Moving SSH off port 22 cuts the volume of automated login attempts in your logs. It is not real security: a port scan of your address still finds the new port, and key-only auth is what actually protects you. Do it if the noise bothers you, and open the firewall before you move sshd.

sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp
sudo ufw status

Add Port 2222 to 00-hardening.conf and run sudo sshd -t. How you apply it depends on whether SSH is socket-activated, which is the default on Ubuntu 23.04 and later, including 24.04:

systemctl is-enabled ssh.socket

If that prints enabled, systemd owns the listening socket and generates its port from your sshd config, so regenerate and restart the socket:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ssh.socket

If it prints anything else, such as disabled on Debian 12, restart the service with sudo systemctl restart ssh. Either way, existing sessions stay up. Confirm the new listener:

sudo ss -tln | grep -E ':(22|2222)\s'

From a second terminal, run ssh -p 2222 deploy@203.0.113.10. To confirm the port is reachable from outside your provider's network, test it with the port checker. Only then remove the old rule with sudo ufw delete allow 22/tcp (or sudo ufw delete allow OpenSSH, depending on how it was added).

On RHEL, Rocky, and Alma, SELinux only lets sshd bind ports labelled ssh_port_t, and the firewall is firewalld. Label and open the port before restarting sshd:

sudo semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=2222/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

semanage comes from the policycoreutils-python-utils package.

Ban repeated failures with fail2ban

MaxAuthTries limits guesses per connection. fail2ban works across connections: it watches for failed logins and adds a firewall rule that blocks an address after too many. With passwords disabled it mostly saves log space and CPU, but it is cheap to run.

sudo apt install fail2ban python3-systemd

Leave jail.conf alone so package upgrades can update it cleanly, and put your settings in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local:

[DEFAULT]
ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 198.51.100.7

[sshd]
enabled = true
port = 2222
backend = systemd
maxretry = 5
findtime = 10m
bantime = 1h

An address that fails maxretry times within findtime is banned for bantime. Set port to your SSH port (use ssh if you stayed on 22), or bans will block a port nobody is using. Put your office or VPN address in ignoreip so you cannot ban yourself.

backend = systemd makes fail2ban read the journal instead of a log file. Default Debian 12 installs have no /var/log/auth.log because rsyslog is not installed, and without this line the sshd jail fails to start. It works on Ubuntu 24.04 as well. Restart and check the jail:

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

The output lists currently failed and total banned counts plus the banned IP list. If an address you need gets banned, release it with sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 198.51.100.23.

Troubleshooting common lockouts

Locked out completely

Use your provider's web console, serial console, or rescue mode. These log in locally without going through sshd or the firewall, which is why the local password matters. Once in, move the drop-in aside, run sudo sshd -t, and reload. If the firewall is the problem, sudo ufw allow 22/tcp gets you back.

Permission denied (publickey)

Check the username first. Cloud images create a distro-specific default user (ubuntu on Ubuntu, for example), and any account left out of AllowUsers is refused. Next, check file permissions. sshd ignores authorized_keys if ~/.ssh or the file can be written by other users, or if the home directory is group- or world-writable. The fix for an account named deploy:

sudo chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh

If octal modes are unfamiliar, Linux File Permissions and chmod, Explained covers what these numbers mean. The server log usually names the reason, such as Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes:

sudo journalctl -u ssh -n 30

Use -u sshd on RHEL. On the client side, ssh -v shows which keys were offered.

Too many authentication failures

With MaxAuthTries 3, an agent holding several keys can use up the attempts before it reaches the right one. Offer only the key you mean:

ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 deploy@203.0.113.10

A setting is ignored

If sshd -T shows the old value, another file sets it first. Find it with sudo grep -rni passwordauthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/, then remove the line or rename your file so it sorts earlier. On Ubuntu, a port change that does not show up in ss usually means daemon-reload and the ssh.socket restart were skipped. If the old port is still listed after both, run sudo systemctl restart ssh as well.

Checklist before you log out

  • Key login works from a fresh terminal, and password login is refused.
  • Your admin account has a local password for console access.
  • sudo sshd -t is clean and sudo sshd -T shows the values you set.
  • The firewall allows your SSH port and the port checker can reach it.
  • sudo fail2ban-client status sshd shows the jail running.

Next in the series, Linux File Permissions and chmod, Explained covers the modes that decide whether sshd trusts your key files.

title: DNS Propagation: What Actually Happens After You Change a Record
description:
You change an A record, and your phone loads the new server while your laptop keeps loading the old one. DNS has no mechanism for pushing a change out to resolvers. What people call propagation is resolvers everywhere holding cached copies of the old answer until each copy's TTL runs out. This guide shows where those copies live, how to inspect each one with dig, and a migration order that keeps the switchover short and reversible.

How a lookup actually works

When a program on Linux resolves a name, it calls the stub resolver in the C library. The stub follows /etc/nsswitch.conf, which normally checks /etc/hosts first and then asks the DNS server listed in /etc/resolv.conf. On Ubuntu 24.04 that is systemd-resolved at 127.0.0.53, which keeps its own cache and forwards to an upstream server.

The upstream is a recursive resolver: your router, your ISP, Pi-hole, or a public service such as 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, or 9.9.9.9. With an empty cache, it walks the hierarchy:

  1. It asks a root server, which refers it to the servers for the TLD (for .com, the gtld-servers.net set).
  2. It asks a TLD server, which refers it to the authoritative nameservers for example.com.
  3. It asks an authoritative server, which returns the record and its TTL.

The resolver caches every step: the list of TLD servers, the delegation for your domain, and the final answer. Until those entries expire, it answers from cache without contacting anyone.

You can do the walk yourself, skipping the resolver's cache for everything below the root:

dig +trace www.example.com

com.            172800  IN  NS  a.gtld-servers.net.
;; Received 1170 bytes from 198.41.0.4#53(a.root-servers.net) in 20 ms
example.com.    172800  IN  NS  ns1.example-dns.net.
;; Received 180 bytes from 192.5.6.30#53(a.gtld-servers.net) in 30 ms
www.example.com. 300    IN  A   203.0.113.10
;; Received 60 bytes from 198.51.100.53#53(ns1.example-dns.net) in 40 ms

That output is trimmed and your servers will differ. The Received ... from lines show which server gave each answer, which is useful when a delegation points somewhere unexpected. On Debian and Ubuntu, dig comes from the dnsutils package (bind-utils on RHEL and Fedora).

TTL decides how long old answers live

Every record carries a TTL in seconds. A resolver that fetched the record at 10:00 with a TTL of 3600 can serve that copy until 11:00 without checking again. Resolver operators can also configure minimum and maximum cache times, so a few resolvers keep answers for more or less time than the TTL says.

This is why lowering the TTL right before a change does not help. Resolvers only learn the new, lower TTL when they refetch the record, and they refetch when the old TTL expires. If a record had a TTL of 86400 (one day), lower it to 300 at least a day before you change the value. After that day, every cache holds a copy that expires within five minutes.

Negative answers are cached too

When a name does not exist, the resolver caches that as well (RFC 2308). The authoritative server includes the zone's SOA record with an NXDOMAIN answer (or a NODATA answer, when the name exists without that record type), and the negative result may be cached for the lesser of the SOA record's own TTL and the SOA MINIMUM field. If you query new.example.com before creating it, or a monitoring check does, resolvers can keep saying it does not exist after you add it.

dig example.com SOA +noall +answer

example.com.  3600  IN  SOA  ns1.example-dns.net. hostmaster.example.com. 2026091701 7200 3600 1209600 300

The fields after the contact address are serial, refresh, retry, expire, and minimum. Here the minimum is 300 and the SOA TTL is 3600, so negative answers live for up to 300 seconds. Querying a missing name typically shows that value on the SOA in the authority section, counting down if the answer came from a cache.

Why nameserver changes take longer

Moving to a new DNS provider means changing the nameservers at your registrar. The registrar sends the change to the registry, which updates the delegation (the NS records) in the TLD zone. Those delegation records have their own TTL set by the registry, and resolvers that cached the old delegation keep asking your old provider until it expires.

The value varies by TLD, so check yours. Find the TLD's servers, then ask one of them directly:

dig com NS +short

dig @a.gtld-servers.net example.com NS +norecurse

;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
example.com.  172800  IN  NS  ns1.example-dns.net.
example.com.  172800  IN  NS  ns2.example-dns.net.

For .com the delegation TTL is 172800 seconds (48 hours). The zone's own NS records at your provider carry another TTL that resolvers may also use. The practical rule is to keep the old provider serving a correct copy of the zone for at least the delegation TTL after the switch, and preferably longer.

Checking what resolvers actually see

Start with the source of truth. Ask the authoritative server directly, with recursion turned off:

dig @ns1.example-dns.net www.example.com A +norecurse

Look for aa (authoritative answer) in the flags line. The TTL in this answer is the configured value and never counts down. If this answer is wrong, fix the zone at your provider first, because waiting will not change it.

Providers run several authoritative servers, and they can briefly disagree after an edit. dig +nssearch prints the SOA serial from each one:

dig +nssearch example.com

Matching serials mean the servers have the same version of the zone. Next, compare public resolvers:

for r in 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9; do dig @"$r" www.example.com A +noall +answer; done

www.example.com.  187   IN  A  203.0.113.10
www.example.com.  300   IN  A  203.0.113.10
www.example.com.  2451  IN  A  198.51.100.20

The first two have the new address. The third still has the old one, cached with 2451 seconds left. Run the loop again a minute later and cached TTLs will have dropped by about 60. A TTL equal to the configured value usually means a fresh fetch. A large public resolver is many separate caches behind one address, so repeated queries can return different TTLs.

To see answers from resolvers in many regions at once, use the DNS lookup tool, which includes a global propagation map.

Caches on your own machine

dig sends queries straight to a DNS server. It ignores /etc/hosts and nsswitch.conf, so it can show the new address while your browser and curl still use the old one. To see what applications get, ask the system resolver:

getent hosts www.example.com

If that disagrees with dig, check /etc/hosts first. A test entry added during an earlier migration overrides DNS until someone removes it:

grep -n example.com /etc/hosts

Then check whether systemd-resolved is in use. It is the default on Ubuntu 24.04, while a default Debian 12 install does not include it:

resolvectl status

If the command is missing or fails with an error, there is usually no local cache to clear, unless you installed something like dnsmasq or nscd. If resolved is active, query through it and flush its cache:

resolvectl query www.example.com
sudo resolvectl flush-caches

Browsers keep their own short-lived host cache, and a browser with DNS over HTTPS enabled uses a different resolver from the operating system. Restarting the browser clears the cache. Also check its secure DNS setting when it disagrees with the rest of the machine. Your router or Pi-hole caches answers as well, and restarting its DNS service clears that layer. If you run split-horizon DNS at home, as in the home lab networking guide, your LAN will see different answers from the internet on purpose.

Why different locations see different answers

Answers vary by location for a few reasons. Public resolvers such as 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 use anycast: the same address is served from many sites, and each site has its own cache, filled at different times and expiring at different times. Some DNS providers use GeoDNS or latency-based routing, returning different records depending on where the query comes from, so a "wrong" answer in one region may be intended. And ISP resolvers fetched the record whenever their users happened to ask, so their copies expire on their own schedule.

When regions disagree, check the authoritative answer first, then check whether your provider has location-based rules on that record.

A safe migration playbook

This order works for moving a site or service to a new IP address.

  1. At least one old TTL ahead (a day is typical), lower the TTL on every record you will change to 300. Confirm with dig @ns1.example-dns.net www.example.com A +norecurse +noall +answer.
  2. Wait out the old TTL. Changing the record earlier leaves long-lived stale copies in caches.
  3. Change the record. Confirm the authoritative server returns the new value.
  4. Keep the old server running and serving correct content. Some resolvers enforce minimum cache times, and long-running programs may have resolved the name once at startup. Watch its access log (for example sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log) until traffic stops.
  5. Verify from the public resolvers above, from the DNS lookup tool, and with getent hosts on a client.
  6. Once everything is stable, raise the TTL back to your normal value, such as 3600.

If something goes wrong in step 5, revert the record. With a 300-second TTL, the rollback reaches most resolvers as quickly as the change did.

Common mistakes

Start with names that were never changed. The apex, www, mail, and API subdomains are separate records, and changing one does not change the others. Export or list the whole zone before a migration and check each name afterwards.

A CNAME at the zone apex is not allowed in standard DNS. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, and the apex always has SOA and NS records. Providers work around this with ALIAS or ANAME records or CNAME flattening, which answer with A and AAAA records.

In zone files, a name without a trailing dot is relative to the zone origin:

www  IN  CNAME  example.com     ; becomes example.com.example.com.
www  IN  CNAME  example.com.    ; what you meant

If dig returns example.com.example.com., a missing dot is the cause.

Changing nameservers and records at the same time makes failures ambiguous, because you cannot tell whether a resolver is asking the old provider or the new one. Copy the zone unchanged to the new provider, confirm dig @old-ns and dig @new-ns return the same answers, switch the nameservers, wait out the delegation TTL, and only then edit records.

A DNSSEC DS record left at the registrar breaks resolution when you change providers. The DS record points at the old provider's signing key, so validating resolvers (including 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, and 9.9.9.9) return SERVFAIL while non-validating ones still work. Diagnose it by comparing a normal query with one that disables validation:

dig example.com DS +short
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com A
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com A +cd

A SERVFAIL on the second query and an answer on the third points at DNSSEC. The safe order is to remove the DS record at the registrar, wait for its TTL to pass (check it at the TLD servers as shown earlier), switch providers, then enable DNSSEC at the new provider and add its DS record.

Before and after a DNS change

  • Note the current TTL of every record you will touch and lower it at least that far ahead.
  • Check the authoritative answer and dig +nssearch right after each edit.
  • Compare public resolvers and the DNS lookup tool map.
  • Look at /etc/hosts, the local resolver cache, and the browser before blaming DNS.
  • For provider moves, handle DS records first and change nameservers separately from records.

title: Cron Jobs Explained: Syntax, Pitfalls, and Logging
description:
Cron is still the simplest way to run a command on a schedule, and it is also where scripts tend to fail without anyone noticing. This guide covers the schedule syntax, where cron jobs live, the environment differences that break scripts that work in your shell, and how to log and debug jobs. It is Part 3 of the Linux Server Baseline series. Examples use the cron package on Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12; RHEL and Fedora use cronie, and the differences that matter are noted.

Read the five schedule fields

Every cron line starts with five time fields, followed by the command:

Field Allowed values
Minute 0-59
Hour 0-23
Day of month 1-31
