Month 1-12, or jan to dec
Day of week 0-7, where 0 and 7 are both Sunday, or sun to sat

Each field accepts * for every value, a list (1,15), a range (1-5), or a step (*/15 means every 15 units from the start of the range, so minutes 0, 15, 30, and 45). Ranges and steps combine: 9-17/2 in the hour field means 9, 11, 13, 15, and 17.

Expression Runs
*/15 * * * * Every 15 minutes
0 9 * * 1-5 09:00, Monday to Friday
30 2 * * * 02:30 every day
0 0 1 jan * Midnight on 1 January

Names are case-insensitive three-letter abbreviations. Debian's crontab(5) man page says ranges and lists of names are not allowed, so the documented way to write mon-fri there is 1-5. Paste any expression into the cron parser to see when it will run before you install it.

Instead of five fields you can use a shortcut: @hourly (0 * * * *), @daily or @midnight (0 0 * * *), @weekly (0 0 * * 0), @monthly (0 0 1 * *), and @yearly or @annually (0 0 1 1 *). @reboot runs once when the cron daemon starts at boot, which can be before services such as your database are ready.

When both day fields are set

If day of month and day of week are both restricted (neither is *), cron runs the job when either one matches. 0 9 1 * 1 runs at 09:00 on the 1st of every month and also every Monday. To run on the first Monday only, restrict the day of month and test the weekday inside the command:

0 9 1-7 * * [ "$(date +\%u)" = 1 ] && /usr/local/bin/monthly-report

date +%u prints 1 for Monday. The backslash before % is required in a crontab line, as explained below.

Where cron jobs live

Each user has a personal crontab. Jobs in it run as that user, and it has no user field:

crontab -e
crontab -l
sudo crontab -u deploy -l

crontab -e opens it in your editor and checks the syntax when you save. The files are stored under /var/spool/cron/crontabs, but always go through the crontab command. Be careful with crontab -r: it deletes your whole crontab without asking, and r sits next to e on the keyboard. Keep a copy with crontab -l > ~/crontab.bak.

System crontabs are /etc/crontab and the files in /etc/cron.d. These have a user field between the schedule and the command:

15 3 * * * deploy /usr/local/bin/app-cleanup

Cron picks up changes to these files on its own, but it checks them first. On Debian and Ubuntu, files in /etc/cron.d must be owned by root, must not be writable by group or other, and must have names made only of letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens. A file called app-cleanup runs. A file called app-cleanup.cron is ignored without an error. The last line in any crontab must end with a newline.

The /etc/cron.hourly, cron.daily, cron.weekly, and cron.monthly directories hold scripts with no schedule line. /etc/crontab runs them through run-parts (or anacron runs them, if it is installed), and the times are in /etc/crontab. The scripts must be executable, and on Debian and Ubuntu the same naming rule applies, so backup.sh is skipped. Check what will actually run:

run-parts --test /etc/cron.daily

The cron environment is not your shell

A command that works in your terminal often fails under cron because cron gives it a much smaller environment:

  • PATH is minimal, so commands in /usr/local/bin or /usr/sbin are not found by name.
  • SHELL is /bin/sh, which is dash on Debian and Ubuntu, so bash syntax such as [[ ]] or source fails.
  • No profile is loaded. Nothing from ~/.bashrc or ~/.profile exists, including variables you exported.
  • The working directory is the crontab owner's home directory, so relative paths resolve there.
  • % is special. Cron turns an unescaped % into a newline and sends everything after it to the command's standard input. Write date +\%F, not date +%F. Inside a script file this does not apply.

To see the exact environment on your system, add * * * * * env > /tmp/cron-env.txt to your crontab, wait a minute, read the file, and remove the line.

The fix is to use absolute paths and set the environment at the top of the crontab:

SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
MAILTO=ops@example.com

These lines are plain assignments. Cron does not expand variables in them, so PATH=$PATH:/opt/bin does not work.

Cron schedules jobs in the system time zone. Check it with timedatectl and look at the Time zone line. If you change it with sudo timedatectl set-timezone, restart cron with sudo systemctl restart cron so it uses the new zone. cronie on RHEL supports a CRON_TZ= line to schedule a crontab in a different zone. Debian's cron documents that it runs all jobs in a single time zone, so a TZ= line there only changes what the command sees, not when it runs.

Capture output and find the logs

Anything a job prints is mailed to the crontab owner, or to MAILTO. On a server with no mail transfer agent, Debian's cron logs No MTA installed, discarding output and the output is gone. Send it to a file instead:

0 * * * * /usr/local/bin/sync-files >> /home/deploy/logs/sync-files.log 2>&1

>> file 2>&1 appends both standard output and standard error. The order matters: 2>&1 >> file sends errors to the old standard output instead. The log path must be writable by the user the job runs as, which rules out /var/log for most user crontabs.

Cron itself logs a line each time it starts a job. On Ubuntu and Debian, read it from the journal:

sudo journalctl -u cron --since today

Sep 17 02:30:01 web1 CRON[48210]: (root) CMD (flock -n /run/lock/backup-app.lock /usr/local/bin/backup-app >> /var/log/backup-app.log 2>&1)

If rsyslog is installed, which is the case on Ubuntu 24.04 server but not on a default Debian 12 install, the same lines are in /var/log/syslog (grep CRON /var/log/syslog). On RHEL, use journalctl -u crond or /var/log/cron. A CMD line proves cron started the command. It says nothing about whether the command succeeded, which is why your own log matters.

A nightly backup with logging and locking

If a job can run longer than its interval, two copies end up running at once and writing the same files. flock -n prevents that: it takes a lock on a file and, if another process already holds it, exits immediately with status 1 instead of waiting. The simplest form is flock -n /tmp/job.lock command. For root jobs, /run/lock is a better home for lock files.

Here is a backup script at /usr/local/bin/backup-app:

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

DEST=/var/backups/app
stamp=$(date +%F-%H%M)

mkdir -p "$DEST"
echo "$(date -Is) backup started"
tar -czf "$DEST/app-$stamp.tar.gz" -C /srv/app data
find "$DEST" -name 'app-*.tar.gz' -mtime +14 -delete
echo "$(date -Is) backup finished"

set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first failed command, so a failed tar leaves a "started" line with no "finished" line after it, and old archives are not pruned. The % signs need no escaping because this is a script, not a crontab line.

Make it executable by root only. Mode 750 lets root run it while keeping it away from other users; Linux File Permissions and chmod, Explained covers what those digits mean.

sudo chown root:root /usr/local/bin/backup-app
sudo chmod 750 /usr/local/bin/backup-app

Run it once by hand with the lock, then check the log and the archive:

sudo flock -n /run/lock/backup-app.lock /usr/local/bin/backup-app

Then schedule it in /etc/cron.d/backup-app:

SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
MAILTO=""

30 2 * * * root flock -n /run/lock/backup-app.lock /usr/local/bin/backup-app >> /var/log/backup-app.log 2>&1

The next morning, tail /var/log/backup-app.log and ls -lh /var/backups/app tell you whether it worked. If the previous run still holds the lock, flock skips the new run and prints nothing, so a missing "started" line for a night means the job was skipped or never ran.

When a systemd timer fits better

systemd timers do the same job with two units. The service describes what to run:

# /etc/systemd/system/backup-app.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly application backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup-app

The timer says when:

# /etc/systemd/system/backup-app.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run backup-app nightly

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now backup-app.timer
systemctl list-timers backup-app.timer

Persistent=true runs the job at boot if a scheduled run was missed while the machine was off. Output goes to the journal (journalctl -u backup-app.service), and systemd will not start a second copy while the first is still running, so you need no flock or redirects. systemd-analyze calendar '*-*-* 02:30:00' checks an OnCalendar expression.

Cron is still fine for a one-line job on a server that is always on, for users managing their own jobs without root, and for images that do not run systemd.

Troubleshooting checklist

The job never runs

  • Confirm the daemon is up with systemctl status cron (crond on RHEL).
  • Look for a CMD line at the expected time. If there is none, the problem is the schedule or the file, not the command.
  • Check the expression and the system time zone.
  • For /etc/cron.d and run-parts directories, check the filename for dots, root ownership, and group or world write bits.
  • A user field in a personal crontab makes cron treat the username as the command. A missing user field in /etc/cron.d makes cron read the first word of the command as a username, and the job fails.
  • Make sure the file ends with a newline.

It runs by hand but not from cron

If the CMD line is there, cron did its part and the command failed. Read your job's log, then reproduce cron's environment:

env -i HOME="$HOME" LOGNAME="$USER" PATH=/usr/bin:/bin SHELL=/bin/sh /bin/sh -c '/usr/local/bin/sync-files'

The usual causes are a command not on PATH, an unescaped %, bash syntax running under sh, a relative path, or a variable that only exists in your login shell.

Too much email

Redirect output to a log file and set MAILTO="" at the top of the crontab. Avoid > /dev/null 2>&1 on jobs you care about, since it throws away the errors along with the noise.

Where to go next

Before you rely on a new job, confirm three things: the expression means what you think in the cron parser, a CMD line appears in the journal at the expected time, and the job's own log shows it finished. For the rest of the series, start with Hardening SSH for Production Servers.

title: How to spend a UTXO that has an inscription or rune on it (without burning it)
description:
A UTXO that carries an inscription or a rune is a normal Bitcoin output. It is spendable. Your wallet just refuses to spend it for you, so the plain sats behind it sit there as "unavailable balance". Here is how to move them yourself without destroying the collectible.

A 30-second recap of ordinal theory

Ordinal theory tracks individual satoshis by the order they were mined. An inscription attaches data to a specific sat; a rune marks a balance tied to specific outputs. In both cases the thing you care about lives on one particular sat (or range of sats) sitting inside one particular UTXO, usually a tiny one around 546 satoshis.

So "an inscription UTXO" is just a regular output that happens to hold a sat someone considers special. Spend the output carelessly and that sat can end up paid to a miner as a fee. That is the whole danger, and the whole reason wallets lock these.

Why the wallet won't just spend it

Ordinals-aware wallets (UniSat, Xverse and others) lock any output carrying a collectible so you do not accidentally spend it as a network fee. The protection is reasonable. The side effect is that the plain BTC in those outputs is frozen behind the collectible, and the normal Send flow will not touch it. For the full picture of that lock, see why UniSat shows "unavailable balance".

The rule that keeps the collectible safe

When you spend an inscribed UTXO, Bitcoin assigns the sats to outputs in order. The sats from the first input flow into the first output, and so on, with whatever is left over going to the fee. So the trick is simple:

  • Put the input that carries the collectible first.
  • Make the first output big enough to receive those collectible sats, pointed at an address you control.
  • Everything after that is plain BTC you can send wherever you like.

Get that order right and the collectible lands safely in your own output. Get it wrong and it can be swept into the miner fee and lost for good.

Doing it by hand, step by step

  1. Find the UTXO and what it carries. Get the exact txid:vout and check on an ordinals explorer where the inscription or rune sits inside the output.
  2. Order the inscribed input first. In your PSBT, that input is input #0.
  3. Size the first output to hold the collectible. Send those sats to an address you own. Then add a second output for the freed plain BTC.
  4. Pick where the plain BTC goes. An exchange deposit address or a plain wallet like Electrum, Sparrow or Ledger.
  5. Review and sign. Check every input and output amount, then sign and broadcast.

Important: if you send the freed sats to another ordinals wallet (UniSat, Xverse), they get locked again as unavailable balance. To treat them as plain Bitcoin, send to a non-ordinals wallet or an exchange.

Tools that will build this kind of transaction

Sparrow and Electrum, pointed at your address, can construct plain-BTC sweeps, though you have to be careful with input ordering and output sizing yourself. Across one UTXO it is manageable. Across dozens or hundreds of dust outputs it gets error prone fast, and one slip can cost a collectible.

Letting a tool handle the assembly

If you would rather not line up inputs and outputs by hand, Sat Rescue does exactly this part: it reads your UTXOs, separates the inscription and rune outputs from plain dust, orders the inputs so collectibles stay segregated, and builds the sweep transaction. You connect read only, your wallet shows you the transaction, and you sign it yourself. Keys never reach the site.

It is open source, so you can read the input-ordering logic before trusting it: github.com/OculusMans/sat-rescue. It takes a 17% fee on what it recovers, shown in your wallet before you sign, and skips the fee on amounts too small to matter. The manual route above is always free.

FAQ

Is a UTXO with an inscription actually spendable? Yes. On the blockchain it is an ordinary output. Ordinals wallets just choose not to spend it so you do not lose the collectible by accident.

What happens if I get the input order wrong? The collectible sats can land in the miner fee or in the wrong output and be lost. That is why the inscribed input goes first and the first output is sized to carry it.

Can I just send it to another ordinals wallet? You can, but it will be locked there again as unavailable balance. To treat the freed sats as plain BTC, send them to an exchange or a non-ordinals wallet.

Originally published at satrescue.app.

title: Your Abandoned Carts Just Got a New Rescue Route
description:
Shopify Messaging now supports WhatsApp marketing automations. Here’s what it means and how to set it up before Black Friday.

Think about the last time you left something in an online cart. Did you get an email? Probably. Did you open it? Maybe not.

Now think about the last WhatsApp message you got. You probably read it within minutes.

That gap is what Shopify is going after with its latest update. On October 28, 2026, Shopify announced that you can now create WhatsApp marketing automations inside Shopify Messaging. You can read the official post here: Create WhatsApp marketing automations in Shopify Messaging.

Let’s break down what’s new.

Three ready-made flows, one new home

The update is short and simple. You can now send well-timed WhatsApp messages to customers automatically. Shopify gives you ready-made templates for three common moments:

  • Abandoned browse: Someone looked at your products but didn’t add anything to their cart.
  • Abandoned cart: Someone added items to their cart but never started checkout.
  • Abandoned checkout: Someone started checkout but didn’t finish paying.

You can also add WhatsApp to your own custom automations, not just the pre-built ones.

To find it, open your Shopify admin and go to Messaging > Automations.

Your emails get buried. WhatsApp messages usually don’t.

Most stores already send abandoned cart emails. That’s good, but inboxes are crowded. Your message sits next to dozens of other promotions.

WhatsApp feels more personal. It’s where people chat with friends and family, so messages tend to get noticed fast.

It matters most if your customers live in places where WhatsApp is part of daily life, like India, parts of Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East.

The other big win is convenience. Before, many stores needed a separate app to run WhatsApp flows. Now it lives in the same place where you already manage your store.

Set it up in five simple moves

You don’t need to be a tech expert. Here’s a simple path.

  1. Open Messaging > Automations. This is the home of your WhatsApp flows. Follow the setup steps to connect your WhatsApp Business account.

  2. Start with abandoned checkout. These shoppers were the closest to buying. A friendly nudge here often brings the best return, so turn this one on first.

  3. Then add abandoned cart and abandoned browse. Once checkout is running, add the other two. Each one catches shoppers at a different stage.

  4. Test before you go live. Place a test order and check that the shopper name, product name, and cart link show up correctly. A broken link in a recovery message is worse than no message at all.

  5. Collect opt-ins. This one is important. WhatsApp requires customers to say yes to marketing messages. Add a clear opt-in checkbox at checkout or sign-up. Sending messages to people who haven’t agreed can get your number restricted.

Before you press “turn on”: four quick checks

Costs may apply. The Shopify changelog doesn’t go into pricing, so check the Shopify Help Center page on marketing automations before you launch. WhatsApp usually charges per message category, and marketing messages tend to cost more than service messages.

Don’t overdo it. One helpful reminder is great. Three pushy ones in a day will annoy people. Keep your tone warm and short, like a message from a friend who works at your store.

Keep email running. WhatsApp isn’t a replacement. Use both. Some customers will respond to email, others to WhatsApp, and having both gives you more chances to win the sale.

Check your account early. If your Meta business account has any issues, it’s better to find out now than in the middle of a sale.

Black Friday won’t wait for your setup

Black Friday and Cyber Monday bring lots of traffic and lots of abandoned carts. People compare prices, get distracted, and leave. Every recovered order during this period counts.

If you set this up today, you’ll have time to test, fix small problems, and start collecting opt-ins before the rush. If you wait until the sale starts, you’ll be fixing things while customers are already slipping away.

If you only do one thing this week

Shopify didn’t invent WhatsApp marketing. It made it easier. You don’t need extra tools or complicated setups to start. You need a few minutes, a connected WhatsApp Business account, and a clear opt-in process.

Turn on the abandoned checkout flow, test it, and let it run. A small message at the right moment can bring back a sale you thought was gone.

Read the official update here: Shopify Changelog: Create WhatsApp marketing automations in Shopify Messaging

title: A – Z Linux Commands – Overview with Examples
description:
There are a countless number of commands in Linux. We are bound to use a number of them on a daily routine or numerous times to perform common tasks than others. It is important to note that certain commands are "distro-based" - they can only be found in specific distros. While others are generic Unix/Linux commands that you'll find in all if not most mainstream distros.

In this article, we will introduce you a list of most frequently used Linux commands with their examples for easy learning. You can find the actual description of each Linux command in their manual page which you can access like this:

$ man command-name

adduser/addgroup Command

The adduser and addgroup commands are used to add a user and group to the system respectively according to the default configuration specified in /etc/adduser.conf file.

$ sudo adduser clinerds

agetty Command

agetty is a program which manages physical or virtual terminals and is invoked by init. Once it detects a connection, it opens a tty port, asks for a user's login name and calls up the /bin/login command. Agetty is a substitute of Linux getty:

$ agetty -L 9600 ttyS1 vt100

alias Command

alias is a useful shell built-in command for creating aliases (shortcut) to a Linux command on a system. It is helpful for creating new/custom commands from existing Shell/Linux commands (including options):

$ alias home='cd /home/clinerds/public_html'

The above command will create an alias called home for /home/clinerds/public_html directory, so whenever you type home in the terminal prompt, it will put you in the /home/clinerds*/public_html* directory.

anacron Command

anacron is a Linux facility used to run commands periodically with a frequency defined in days, weeks and months.

Unlike its sister cron; it assumes that a system will not run continuously, therefore if a scheduled job is due when the system is off, it's run once the machine is powered on.

For more information about anacron and cron read: Cron Vs Anacron: How to Schedule Jobs Using Anacron on Linux

apropos Command

apropos command is used to search and display a short man page description of a command/program as follows.

$ apropos adduser

apt Command

apt tool is a relatively new higher-level package manager for Debian/Ubuntu systems:

$ sudo apt update

apt-get Command

apt-get is a powerful and free front-end package manager for Debian/Ubuntu systems. It is used to install new software packages, remove available software packages, upgrade existing software packages as well as upgrade entire operating system.

$ sudo apt-get update

aptitude Command

aptitude is a powerful text-based interface to the Debian GNU/Linux package management system. Like apt-get and apt; it can be used to install, remove or upgrade software packages on a system.

$ sudo aptitude update

arch Command

arch is a simple command for displaying machine architecture or hardware name (similar to uname -m):

$ arch

arp Command

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is a protocol that maps IP network addresses of a network neighbor with the hardware (MAC) addresses in an IPv4 network.

You can use it as below to find all alive hosts on a network:

$ sudo arp-scan --interface=enp2s0 --localnet

at Command

at command is used to schedule tasks to run in a future time. It's an alternative to cron and anacron, however, it runs a task once at a given future time without editing any config files:

For example, to shutdown the system at 23:55 today, run:

$ sudo echo "shutdown -h now" | at -m 23:55

atq Command

atq command is used to view jobs in at command queue:

$ atq

atrm Command

atrm command is used to remove/deletes jobs (identified by their job number) from at command queue:

$ atrm 2

awk Command

Awk is a powerful programming language created for text processing and generally used as a data extraction and reporting tool.

$ awk '//{print}'/etc/hosts

For more Awk concepts (basic and advance) with simple and easy-to-understand, we've created a book that contains 13 chapters with a total of 41 pages, which covers all Awk basic and advance usage with practical examples: Awk Getting Started Guide for Beginners

batch Command

batch is also used to schedule tasks to run a future time, similar to the at command.

basename Command

basename command helps to print the name of a file stripping of directories in the absolute path:

$ basename bin/findhosts.sh

bc Command

bc is a simple yet powerful and arbitrary precision CLI calculator language which can be used like this:

$ echo 20.05 + 15.00 | bc

bg Command

bg is a command used to send a process to the background.

$ tar -czf home.tar.gz .
$ bg 
$ jobs

To learn more about bg command, read: Start Linux Command in Background and Detach Process in Terminal

bzip2 Command

bzip2 command is used to compress or decompress file(s).

$ bzip2 -z filename      #Compress
$ bzip2 -d filename.bz2  #Decompress

To learn more examples on bzip2, read: How to Compress and Decompress a .bz2 File in Linux

cal Command

The cal command print a calendar on the standard output.

$ cal

cat Command

cat command is used to view contents of a file or concatenate files, or data provided on standard input, and display it on the standard output.

$ cat file.txt

To learn more about cat command, read: 13 Useful Cat Command Examples on Linux

chgrp Command

chgrp command is used to change the group ownership of a file. Provide the new group name as its first argument and the name of file as the second argument like this:

$ chgrp clinerds users.txt

chmod Command

chmod command is used to change/update file access permissions like this.

$ chmod +x sysinfo.sh

chown Command

chown command changes/updates the user and group ownership of a file/directory like this.

$ chmod -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html

To learn more about chgrp, chmod and chwon commands, read: Managing Users & Groups, File Permissions & Attributes in Linux

cksum Command

cksum command is used to display the CRC checksum and byte count of an input file.

$ cksum README.txt

clear Command

clear command lets you clear the terminal screen, simply type.

$ clear

cmp Command

cmp performs a byte-by-byte comparison of two files like this.

$ cmp file1 file2

comm Command

comm command is used to compare two sorted files line-by-line as shown below.

$ comm file1 file2

cp Command

cp command is used for copying files and directories from one location to another.

$ cp /home/clinerds/file1 /home/clinerds/Personal/

date Command

date command displays/sets the system date and time like this.

$ date
$ date --set="8 JUN 2017 13:00:00"

dd Command

dd command is used for copying files, converting and formatting according to flags provided on the command line. It can strip headers, extracting parts of binary files and so on.

The example below shows creating a boot-able USB device:

$ dd if=/home/clinerds/kali-linux-1.0.4-i386.iso of=/dev/sdc1 bs=512M; sync

df Command

df command is used to show file system disk space usage as follows.

$ df -h

diff Command

diff command is used to compare two files line by line. It can also be used to find the difference between two directories in Linux like this:

$ diff file1 file2

dir Command

dir command works like Linux ls command, it lists the contents of a directory.

$ dir

dmidecode Command

dmidecode command is a tool for retrieving hardware information of any Linux system. It dumps a computer's DMI (a.k.a SMBIOS) table contents in a human-readable format for easy retrieval.

To view your system hardware info, you can type:

$ sudo dmidecode --type system

du Command

du command is used to show disk space usage of files present in a directory as well as its sub-directories as follows.

$ du /home/aaronkilik

echo Command

echo command prints a text of line provided to it.

$ echo "This is clinerds- Linux How Tos"

eject Command

eject command is used to eject removable media such as DVD/CD ROM or floppy disk from the system.

$ eject /dev/cdrom
$ eject /mnt/cdrom/
$ eject /dev/sda

env Command

env command lists all the current environment variables and used to set them as well.

$ env

exit Command

exit command is used to exit a shell like so.

$ exit

expr Command

expr command is used to calculate an expression as shown below.

$ expr 20 + 30

factor Command

factor command is used to show the prime factors of a number.

$ factor 10

find Command

find command lets you search for files in a directory as well as its sub-directories. It searches for files by attributes such as permissions, users, groups, file type, date, size and other possible criteria.

$ find /home/clinerds/ -name clinerds.txt

free Command

free command shows the system memory usage (free, used, swapped, cached, etc.) in the system including swap space. Use the-h option to display output in human friendly format.

$ free -h

grep Command

grep command searches for a specified pattern in a file (or files) and displays in output lines containing that pattern as follows.

$ grep 'clinerds' domain-list.txt

groups Command

groups command displays all the names of groups a user is a part of like this.

$ groups
$ groups clinerds

gzip Command

Gzip helps to compress a file, replaces it with one having a .gz extension as shown below:

$ gzip passwds.txt
$ cat file1 file2 | gzip > foo.gz

gunzip Command

gunzip expands or restores files compressed with gzip command like this.

$ gunzip foo.gz

head Command

head command is used to show first lines (10 lines by default) of the specified file or stdin to the screen:

# ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%mem | head

history Command

history command is used to show previously used commands or to get info about command executed by a user.

$ history

hostname Command

hostname command is used to print or set system hostname in Linux.

$ hostname
$ hostname NEW_HOSTNAME

hostnamectl Command

hostnamectl command controls the system hostname under systemd. It is used to print or modify the system hostname and any related settings:

$ hostnamectl
$ sudo hostnamectl set-hostname NEW_HOSTNAME

hwclock

hwclock is a tool for managing the system hardware clock; read or set the hardware clock (RTC).

$ sudo hwclock
$ sudo hwclock --set --date 8/06/2017

hwinfo Command

hwinfo is used to probe for the hardware present in a Linux system like this.

$ hwinfo

id Command

id command shows user and group information for the current user or specified username as shown below.

$ id clinerds

ifconfig Command

ifconfig command is used to configure a Linux systems network interfaces. It is used to configure, view and control network interfaces.

$ ifconfig
$ sudo ifconfig eth0 up
$ sudo ifconfig eth0 down
$ sudo ifconfig eth0 172.16.25.125

ionice Command

ionice command is used to set or view process I/O scheduling class and priority of the specified process.

If invoked without any options, it will query the current I/O scheduling class and priority for that process:

$ ionice -c 3 rm /var/logs/syslog

iostat Command

iostat is used to show CPU and input/output statistics for devices and partitions. It produces useful reports for updating system configurations to help balance the input/output load between physical disks.

$ iostat

ip Command

ip command is used to display or manage routing, devices, policy routing and tunnels. It also works as a replacement for well known ifconfig command.

This command will assign an IP address to a specific interface (eth1 in this case).

$ sudo ip addr add 192.168.56.10 dev eth1

iptables Command

iptables is a terminal based firewall for managing incoming and outgoing traffic via a set of configurable table rules.

The command below is used to check existing rules on a system (using it may require root privileges).

$ sudo iptables -L -n -v

iw command is used to manage wireless devices and their configuration.

$ iw list

iwlist Command

iwlist command displays detailed wireless information from a wireless interface. The command below enables you to get detailed information about the wlp1s0 interface.

$ iwlist wlp1s0 scanning

kill Command

kill command is used to kill a process using its PID by sending a signal to it (default signal for kill is TERM).

$ kill -p 2300
$ kill -SIGTERM -p 2300

killall Command

killall command is used to kill a process by its name.

$ killall firefox

kmod Command

kmod command is used to manage Linux kernel modules. To list all currently loaded modules, type.

$ kmod list

last Command

last command display a listing of last logged in users.

$ last

ln Command

ln command is used to create a soft link between files using the -s flag like this.

$ ln -s /usr/bin/lscpu cpuinfo

locate Command

locate command is used to find a file by name. The locate utility works better and faster than it's find counterpart.

The command below will search for a file by its exact name (not *name*):

$ locate -b '\domain-list.txt'

login Command

login command is used to create a new session with the system. You'll be asked to provide a username and a password to login as below.

$ sudo login

ls Command

ls command is used to list contents of a directory. It works more or less like dir command.

The -l option enables long listing format like this.

$ ls -l file1

lshw Command

lshw command is a minimal tool to get detailed information on the hardware configuration of the machine, invoke it with superuser privileges to get a comprehensive information.

$ sudo lshw

lscpu Command

lscpu command displays system's CPU architecture information (such as number of CPUs, threads, cores, sockets, and more).

$ lscpu

lsof Command

lsof command displays information related to files opened by processes. Files can be of any type, including regular files, directories, block special files, character special files, executing text reference, libraries, and stream/network files.

To view files opened by a specific user's processes, type the command below.

$ lsof -u clinerds

lsusb Command

lsusb command shows information about USB buses in the system and the devices connected to them like this.

$ lsusb

man Command

man command is used to view the on-line reference manual pages for commands/programs like so.

$ man du
$ man df

md5sum Command

md5sum command is used to compute and print the MD5 message digest of a file. If run without arguments, debsums checks every file on your system against the stock md5sum files:

$ sudo debsums

mkdir Command

mkdir command is used to create single or more directories, if they do not already exist (this can be overridden with the -p option).

$ mkdir clinerds-files
OR 
$ mkdir -p clinerds-files

more Command

more command enables you to view through relatively lengthy text files one screenful at a time.

$ more file.txt

mv Command

mv command is used to rename files or directories. It also moves a file or directory to another location in the directory structure.

$ mv test.sh sysinfo.sh

nano Command

nano is a popular small, free and friendly text editor for Linux; a clone of Pico, the default editor included in the non-free Pine package.

To open a file using nano, type:

$ nano file.txt

nc/netcat Command

nc (or netcat) is used for performing any operation relating to TCP, UDP, or UNIX-domain sockets. It can handle both IPv4 and IPv6 for opening TCP connections, sending UDP packets, listening on arbitrary TCP and UDP ports, performing port scanning.

The command below will help us see if the port 22 is open on the host 192.168.56.5.

$ nc -zv 192.168.1.5 22

netstat Command

netstat command displays useful information concerning the Linux networking subsystem (network connections, routing tables, interface statistics, masquerade connections, and multicast memberships).

This command will display all open ports on the local system:

$ netstat -a | more

nice Command

nice command is used to show or change the nice value of a running program. It runs specified command with an adjusted niceness. When run without any command specified, it prints the current niceness.

The following command starts the process "tar command" setting the "nice" value to 12.

$ nice -12 tar -czf backup.tar.bz2 /home/*

nmap Command

nmap is a popular and powerful open source tool for network scanning and security auditing. It was intended to quickly scan large networks, but it also works fine against single hosts.

The command below will probe open ports on all live hosts on the specified network.

$ nmap -sV 192.168.56.0/24

nproc Command

nproc command shows the number of processing units present to the current process. It's output may be less than the number of online processors on a system.

$ nproc

openssl Command

The openssl is a command line tool for using the different cryptography operations of OpenSSL's crypto library from the shell. The command below will create an archive of all files in the current directory and encrypt the contents of the archive file:

$ tar -czf - * | openssl enc -e -aes256 -out backup.tar.gz

passwd Command

passwd command is used to create/update passwords for user accounts, it can also change the account or associated password validity period. Note that normal system users may only change the password of their own account, while root may modify the password for any account.

$ passwd clinerds

pidof Command

pidof displays the process ID of a running program/command.

$ pidof init
$ pidof cinnamon

ping Command

ping command is used to determine connectivity between hosts on a network (or the Internet):

$ ping google.com

ps Command

ps shows useful information about active processes running on a system. The example below shows the top running processes by highest memory and CPU usage.

# ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%mem | head

pstree Command

pstree displays running processes as a tree which is rooted at either PID or init if PID is omitted.

$ pstree

pwd Command

pwd command displays the name of current/working directory as below.

$ pwd

rdiff-backup Command

rdiff-backup is a powerful local/remote incremental backup script written in Python. It works on any POSIX operating system such as Linux, Mac OS X.

Note that for remote backups, you must install the same version of rdiff-backup on both the local and remote machines. Below is an example of a local backup command:

$ sudo rdiff-backup /etc /media/clinerds/Backup/server_etc.backup

reboot Command

reboot command may be used to halt, power-off or reboot a system as follows.

$ reboot

rename Command

rename command is used to rename many files at once. If you've a collection of files with ".html" extension and you want to rename all of them with ".php" extension, you can type the command below.

$ rename 's/\.html$/\.php/' *.html

rm command

rm command is used to remove files or directories as shown below.

$ rm file1
$ rm -rf my-files

rmdir Command

rmdir command helps to delete/remove empty directories as follows.

$ rmdir /backup/all

scp Command

scp command enables you to securely copy files between hosts on a network, for example.

$ scp ~/names.txt root@192.168.56.10:/root/names.txt

shutdown Command

shutdown command schedules a time for the system to be powered down. It may be used to halt, power-off or reboot the machine like this.

$ shutdown --poweroff.

sleep Command

sleep command is used to delay or pause (specifically execution of a command) for a specified amount of time.

$ check.sh; sleep 5; sudo apt update

sort Command

sort command is used to sort lines of text in the specified file(s) or from stdin as shown below

$ cat words.txt

split Command

split as the name suggests, is used to split a large file into small parts.

$ tar -cvjf backup.tar.bz2 /home/clinerds/Documents/*

ssh Command

ssh (SSH client) is an application for remotely accessing and running commands on a remote machine. It is designed to offer a secure encrypted communications between two untrusted hosts over an insecure network such as the Internet.

$ ssh clinerds@192.168.56.10

stat Command

stat is used to show a file or file system status like this (-f is used to specify a filesystem).

$ stat file1

su Command

su command is used to switch to another user ID or become root during a login session. Note that when su is invoked without a username, it defaults to becoming root.

$ su 
$ su clinerds

sudo Command

sudo command allows a permitted system user to run a command as root or another user, as defined by the security policy such as sudoers.

In this case, the real (not effective) user ID of the user running sudo is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.

$ sudo apt update
$ sudo useradd clinerds
$ sudo passwd clinerds

sum Command

sum command is used to show the checksum and block counts for each each specified file on the command line.

$ sum output file.txt

tac Command

tac command concatenates and displays files in reverse. It simply prints each file to standard output, showing last line first.

$tac file.txt

tail Command

tail command is used to display the last lines (10 lines by default) of each file to standard output.

If there more than one file, precede each with a header giving the file name. Use it as follow (specify more lines to display using -n option).

$ tail long-file
OR
$ tail -n 15 long-file

talk Command

talk command is used to talk to another system/network user. To talk to a user on the same machine, use their login name, however, to talk to a user on another machine use 'user@host'.

$ talk person [ttyname]
OR
$ talk'user@host' [ttyname]

tar Command

tar command is a most powerful utility for archiving files in Linux.

$ tar -czf home.tar.gz .

tee Command

tee command is used to read from standard input and prints to standard output and files as shown below.

$ echo "Testing how tee command works" | tee file1

tree Command

The tree command is a tiny, cross-platform command-line program used to recursively list or display the content of a directory in a tree-like format.

$ tree

time Command

time command runs programs and summarizes system resource usage.

$ time wc /etc/hosts

top Command

top program displays all processes on a Linux system in regards to memory and CPU usage and provides a dynamic real-time view of a running system.

$ top

touch Command

touch command changes file timestamps, it can also be used to create a file as follows.

$ touch file.txt

tr Command

tr command is a useful utility used to translate (change) or delete characters from stdin, and write the result to stdout or send to a file as follows.

$ cat domain-list.txt | tr [:lower:] [:upper:]

uname Command

uname command displays system information such as operating system, network node hostname kernel name, version and release etc.

Use the -a option to show all the system information:

$ uname

uniq Command

uniq command displays or omits repeated lines from input (or standard input). To indicate the number of occurrences of a line, use the -c option.

$ cat domain-list.txt

uptime Command

uptime command shows how long the system has been running, number of logged on users and the system load averages as follows.

$ uptime

users Command

users command shows the user names of users currently logged in to the current host like this.

$ users

vim/vi Command

vim (Vi Improved) popular text editor on Unix-like operating systems. It can be used to edit all kinds of plain text and program files.

$ vim file

w Command

w command displays system uptime, load averages and information about the users currently on the machine, and what they are doing (their processes) like this.

$ w

wall Command

wall command is used to send/display a message to all users on the system as follows.

$ wall "This is CLINerds - Linux How Tos"

watch Command

watch command runs a program repeatedly while displaying its output on fullscreen. It can also be used to watch changes to a file/directory. The example below shows how to watch the contents of a directory change.

$ watch -d ls -l

wc Command

wc command is used to display newline, word, and byte counts for each file specified, and a total for many files.

$ wc filename

wget Command

wget command is a simple utility used to download files from the Web in a non-interactive (can work in the background) way.

$ wget -c http://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/wget/wget-1.5.3.tar.gz

whatis Command

whatis command searches and shows a short or one-line manual page descriptions of the provided command name(s) as follows.

$ whatis wget

which Command

which command displays the absolute path (pathnames) of the files (or possibly links) which would be executed in the current environment.

$ which who

who Command

who command shows information about users who are currently logged in like this.

$ who

whereis Command

whereis command helps us locate the binary, source and manual files for commands.

$ whereis cat

xargs Command

xargs command is a useful utility for reading items from the standard input, delimited by blanks (protected with double or single quotes or a backslash) or newlines, and executes the entered command.

The example below show xargs being used to copy a file to multiple directories in Linux.

$ echo /home/aaronkilik/test/ /home/aaronkilik/tmp | xargs -n 1 cp -v /home/aaronkilik/bin/sys_info.sh

yes Command

yes command is used to display a string repeatedly until when terminated or killed using [Ctrl + C] as follows.

$ yes "This is CLINerds- Linux HowTos"

youtube-dl Command

youtube-dl is a lightweight command-line program to download videos and also extract MP3 tracks from YouTube.com and a few more sites.

The command below will list available formats for the video in the provided link.

$ youtube-dl --list-formats https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iR

zcmp/zdiff Command

zcmp and zdiff minimal utilities used to compare compressed files as shown in the examples below.

$ zcmp domain-list.txt.zip basic_passwords.txt.zip
$ zdiff domain-list.txt.zip basic_passwords.txt.zip

zip Command

zip is a simple and easy-to-use utility used to package and compress (archive) files.

$ tar cf - . | zip | dd of=/dev/nrst0 obs=16k
$ zip inarchive.zip foo.c bar.c --out outarchive.zip
$ tar cf - .| zip backup -

zz Command

zz command is an alias of the fasd commandline tool that offers quick access to files and directories in Linux. It is used to quickly and interactively cd into a previously accessed directory by selecting the directory number from the first field as follows.

$ zz

That's it for now! As we mentioned before, there are a countless number of commands in Linux. The list is possibly longer than we can offer. Use the feedback form below to share any useful and frequently used commands missing in this list.

title: I built a terminal multiplexer for coding agents that works on my phone
description:
Disclosure: drafted with AI help from my own notes and posts, and checked against the repo.

I run a lot of coding agents at once, mostly Claude Code and Codex, across several projects. Running them was never the problem. The problems were everything around them: too many windows, agents leaving hung processes behind, no way to tell which one was waiting on me, and having to remote into my desktop or SSH into a single shell to deal with any of it from my phone. Even then, a terminal on a phone couldn't show me the frontend I needed to check.

I tried Orca and herdr. Both were better than what I had. Neither had a real markdown notes editor, and neither had a phone interface I could actually work in. So I built swe-mux.

What it is

A terminal multiplexer. It runs any shell or CLI in real terminals on your own machine and serves the same live sessions to your desktop and your phone. Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and oh-my-pi get a live status (working, done, or waiting on you), searchable history and resume. Anything else runs as an ordinary terminal with everything except the status.

It's the actual terminal, not a UI wrapped around the agent. You can use it as a plain terminal, or start claude in a shell and that pane becomes an agent session.

On the desktop it's tabs and panes of sessions, notes, files and dev-server previews. Shift+Enter, Ctrl+Backspace, paste and click-to-position behave the same in every agent, shortcuts come from tmux, VS Code, Vim or Emacs presets, and images paste straight from the clipboard.

Status

Status comes from three places: the CLI's hooks, its transcript, and the terminal itself. No single one of them reliably tells "waiting on you" apart from "busy in the background", so it uses all three. You pick which events alert you and how, a sound on the desktop and a push notification on the phone, with quiet hours and separate desktop and mobile settings.

The phone

The same sessions, over your own Tailscale network, installed as a PWA. The terminal with a usable keyboard and a key rail for the keys a phone keyboard doesn't have, git diff review, files, notes, and a push notification when an agent needs a decision.

A dev server bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host is proxied through swe-mux, so the phone opens it without another port being exposed. Being able to play-test and check a frontend on the phone is what closed the development loop there for a lot of my projects. I can work from anywhere now, and I do.

Your tailnet policy is the access control. There's no separate swe-mux login, so any device your tailnet admits gets a terminal on your machine. Treat it like SSH.

Two things I use constantly

A prompt queue, so the thing I think of mid-turn waits until the agent is actually done instead of interrupting it.

Messages between sessions, so a Codex session can ask a Claude session something. I don't want my workflow tied to one provider.

Notes

Notes, and any markdown file in a project, open in the same WYSIWYG editor on desktop and phone, and they autosave. No more notes scattered across different places.

Sessions survive updates

A separate supervisor process owns the terminals, so the daemon can restart and the app can update underneath them without killing anything. I update it several times a day. My own daemon started 615 times across the 98 days its log covers, so this was never optional.

It has limits. A reboot, a power loss or the supervisor itself crashing still ends the live processes. What survives those is the transcript and enough state to resume each agent.

Limits

It was built on Windows, which is where I use it every day and the only platform with a packaged desktop app. The installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen warns on first run; the PyPI install avoids that. macOS and Linux run the daemon and use a browser. CI runs all three, and I've tested Linux myself, but I haven't lived on macOS.

There's no swe-mux account, no server of mine in the path, and no telemetry. The agents still talk to their own providers, and there's a once-a-day update check you can turn off in Settings.

Try it

The demo is the real interface with simulated agents, nothing to install.

Install with uv tool install swe-mux (or pipx install swe-mux), then run swe-mux on Windows or swemux start elsewhere. It's Apache-2.0: github.com/jatoran/swe-mux.

I've put a lot of work into the first run. Where the install or the first hour goes wrong is the feedback I want most.

title: My load test had 1,000 players. None of them were late.
description:
Before the first event I ran 1 vs 100 against a thousand simulated players, and nothing broke. Then a lecture hall of real people broke it with a fraction of that. The test measured load correctly. It just never contained the one thing real people always do: arrive late.

I tested 1 vs 100 properly before anyone played it. A script opened a thousand simulated players over real WebSockets, started a question, and had all of them answer in the same instant: the thundering herd, the worst moment a live quiz has.

It held. No dropped connections, the question reached every player in tens of milliseconds, and the reveal came back in under half a second.

At the first real event, it broke anyway. Not under load. Under people.

What the test could not contain

Here is what the script did, in order: connect every player, wait until every one of them has joined, and only then press Start.

That is the one order a real room never follows. In a lecture hall, people are still scanning the QR code when the host decides the room looks full. The game had a rule for anyone who joined after Start: watch, do not play. My thousand bots never triggered it, because not one of them was late. Everyone in the real room after the first 45 or so was, and their phones showed every question and never let them answer. The rule and the fix are their own note.

The test was faithful about load and wrong about time. It measured how many people the server could hold, and assumed they would all arrive at once, on cue, and stay on the page. Real people arrive late, switch tabs and reload. None of that is load, and all of it is what broke.

The first ten minutes

The first people with the problem came to me, and I did not know what it was. I went around to them, reassured them, and opened my laptop next to them to look. Technically, nothing was wrong anywhere I could see. The server was healthy and the game was running.

I told them their answers were being counted. I believed it. They were not, and I did not know that yet.

When more and more people had the same problem, I went outside to deal with it properly, making phone call after phone call to understand what was happening.

Not starting again

After about ten minutes the event coordinator came out to find me and asked what was going on. Her suggestion was to start the entire event again.

I asked her not to. Restarting would have thrown away the game for everyone who was playing fine, to fix it for the people who were not. Instead I asked her to tell the crowd that anyone hit by the bug would go through to the next stage rather than be eliminated.

That kept the event moving and kept the people who had been wronged in the game. Meanwhile I changed the rule and deployed the fix while the event was still running, and the stranded players came back in at the next question.

What a load test is for

A load test answers one question well: can the server take this many people at once. It is worth running, and mine was right.

It cannot answer the question that decided the night: what happens when people do not behave like a script. That needs a different test, one that is written from watching a real room: people joining after the start, leaving the page, coming back. Measuring the wrong thing precisely felt like safety. It was only confidence.

First published on davidmashiah.com, with the rest of my notes on real-time systems, machine learning reliability and supply chains.

title: Shopify Just Opened Campaign Autopilot to Every Store: What Devs and Store Builders Should Know
description:
If you build or maintain Shopify stores, your clients are about to ask you one question: "Should I turn on Autopilot?"

On October 28, 2026, Shopify made Campaign Autopilot available to all merchants. It also added more channels and a new SEO feature. Here's the official post: More channels and features now available in Campaign Autopilot.

Let's break it down in plain words, with a developer's eye on what to check first.

What Campaign Autopilot actually does

The idea is simple. A merchant sets a budget and some guardrails. Autopilot then looks at the store, the products, and the customers, and builds a marketing campaign.

It also decides which channels to run on, how much to spend on each, and moves budget toward what's working. The merchant doesn't have to build separate campaigns on every platform.

The channels it can reach

According to the changelog, Autopilot can reach shoppers across:

  • Meta Ads
  • Microsoft Advertising
  • Snapchat
  • Shop
  • Shopify Messaging
  • X Ads (coming soon)

For anyone who has juggled several ad dashboards for one client, having this in one place is a big change.

The new SEO suggestions

This part is easy to miss. Autopilot now suggests SEO optimizations. The merchant reviews and approves them, so nothing goes live on its own.

Merchants can also ask for SEO updates directly in Sidekick, Shopify's built-in assistant.

If you've ever had a client who "doesn't have time for SEO," this gives them a low-effort place to start.

Where merchants find it

Autopilot lives in the Growth tab of the Shopify admin. You can jump straight there with the Growth tab link. For the full guide, see the Shopify Help Center.

What you can do for your clients before they turn it on

Autopilot builds campaigns from what's already in the store. The changelog says it looks at the store, products, and customers. So it's reasonable to assume the quality of that data affects the quality of the campaigns. Here's a short checklist you can run through.

1. Clean up the product catalog. Check titles, descriptions, prices, and images. Fix missing alt text, empty descriptions, and broken variants. Messy data in means messy ads out.

2. Review the storefront. Ads send people to your pages. Make sure product pages load fast, look right on mobile, and have a clear path to checkout.

3. Check tracking and analytics. Before spending money, confirm that orders and traffic sources are being recorded correctly. You can't judge a campaign you can't measure.

4. Help set sensible guardrails. Talk with the client about a starting budget and limits. Start small, watch the results, and raise it later.

5. Go through the SEO suggestions together. Read each one before approving. Some may not fit the brand voice, and a quick human review catches that.

Keep your own judgment in the loop

Autopilot is a helpful tool, but it isn't magic. A few habits will save you headaches.

  • Don't set it and forget it. Check performance in the first days and weeks.
  • Give it time to learn. A Common Thread Collective post on this update suggests allowing two to three weeks of learning time before peak traffic. That's one agency's advice, not a Shopify rule, but it makes sense for systems that optimize on their own.
  • Explain the limits to clients. Autopilot can pick channels and shift budget, but it doesn't know everything about the brand. Someone still needs to review what goes out.

Why the timing matters

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are just around the corner. Ad costs often rise during busy seasons, so stores that start early have more time to learn what works.

If your clients turn this on the week of the sale, you'll be fixing small problems while customers are already shopping. Starting now gives everyone room to test.

The takeaway

Campaign Autopilot doesn't replace good products or good store work. It takes over the repetitive parts of marketing: picking channels, splitting budget, and suggesting SEO changes.

If you do one thing this week, open a test store or a client store, look at the Growth tab, and see what Autopilot suggests. Then run the checklist above before anyone spends real money.

Official update: Shopify Changelog: More channels and features now available in Campaign Autopilot

Have you tried Campaign Autopilot yet? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Preventing Silent Schema Drift in Pydantic Model Inheritance: A Practical Guide to Type-Safe Validation
description:
Preventing Silent Schema Drift in Pydantic Model Inheritance: A Practical Guide to Type-Safe Validation

1. The Hidden Trap: Why Schema Drift Goes Undetected

In distributed microservice architectures and large-scale Python codebases, leveraging Pydantic model inheritance to share schemas across API boundaries, database entities, and domain representations is common practice. However, as systems evolve and multiple teams modify models over time, subtle contradictions inevitably surface:

  1. Implicit Nullability Reduction (Contravariance Violation): An optional field defined as str | None in a base model is narrowed down to str in a derived model. While this appears innocent during strict local instantiation, downstream ingestion pipelines will fail unpredictably with a ValidationError when missing or null data is encountered at runtime.
  2. Incompatible Type Mutation: An identifier defined as int in the base model is mutated to str in a subclass. Under Pydantic's default lax mode (coercion enabled), numeric strings might be auto-coerced, but in strict validation contexts (strict=True), serialization pipelines, or OpenAPI schema generation, behavior diverges sharply. This discrepancy makes debugging across staging and production environments notoriously difficult.

Relying solely on dynamic integration or property-based tests to catch these drift issues requires instantiating models across every possible permutation of field values, severely limiting test coverage. What is needed is a static, compile-time/test-time introspection mechanism that traverses class definitions and verifies the structural type integrity across inheritance hierarchies before runtime execution.

2. Architecture and Inspection Flow

This validation utility directly introspects Pydantic v2's internal metadata (model_fields), extracting field annotations from both base and derived classes to evaluate compatibility and coercion risks.

sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as "CI Pipeline"
    participant Det as "SchemaDriftDetector"
    participant Base as "Base Model"
    participant Derived as "Derived Model"

    CI -- "analyze_inheritance(Base, Derived)" --> Det
    Det -- "Fetch model_fields" --> Base
    Det -- "Fetch model_fields" --> Derived
    loop Each Common Field
        Det -- "Evaluate type safety" --> Det
        alt Risk Detected (Nullability reduction / Type mutation)
            Det -- "Generate DriftReport" --> Det
        end
    end
    Det -- "Return DriftReport list (JSON)" --> CI

3. Implementation

The following is a standalone, self-contained implementation of a schema drift detector built exclusively on standard library constructs (typing, types) and Pydantic v2 native primitives. For serialization performance, it prioritizes orjson when installed, falling back gracefully to standard json.

from typing import Any, Dict, List, Type, get_origin, get_args, Union, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# Graceful fallback for high-performance JSON serialization
try:
    import orjson
    HAS_ORJSON = True
except ImportError:
    import json
    HAS_ORJSON = False


class DriftReport(BaseModel):
    model_name: str
    base_model_name: str
    field_name: str
    issue_type: str = Field(..., description="Classification of drift or coercion hazard")
    base_type: str
    derived_type: str
    message: str


class SchemaValidatorConfig(BaseModel):
    strict_coercion_check: bool = Field(default=True, description="Enforce strict type equivalence")


def _get_type_name(tp: Any) -> str:
    if tp is None:
        return "NoneType"
    if hasattr(tp, "__name__"):
        return tp.__name__
    return str(tp)


def _is_none_type(tp: Any) -> bool:
    return tp is None or tp is type(None)


def _extract_union_types(tp: Any) -> set:
    """Extract constituent types from typing.Union and PEP 604 union expressions (|)."""
    origin = get_origin(tp)
    # Supports typing.Union and types.UnionType (Python 3.10+)
    if origin is Union or (hasattr(types := __import__("types"), "UnionType") and origin is types.UnionType):
        args = get_args(tp)
        return set(args)
    return {tp}


def _is_coercion_risky(base_tp: Any, derived_tp: Any) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """
    Determine whether altering a base type in a derived class risks
    data loss, parsing discrepancies, or validation failures.
    """
    if base_tp == derived_tp:
        return False, "TYPES_IDENTICAL"

    base_args = _extract_union_types(base_tp)
    derived_args = _extract_union_types(derived_tp)

    base_allows_none = any(_is_none_type(arg) for arg in base_args)
    derived_allows_none = any(_is_none_type(arg) for arg in derived_args)

    # 1. Nullability reduction: Removing None-tolerance triggers runtime validation errors
    if base_allows_none and not derived_allows_none:
        return True, "NULLABILITY_REDUCTION"

    # 2. Nullability expansion: Expanding to allow None is generally safe, recorded as structural drift
    if not base_allows_none and derived_allows_none:
        return False, "NULLABILITY_EXPANSION"

    # 3. Incompatible concrete type mutation (e.g., int -> str)
    base_non_none = {arg for arg in base_args if not _is_none_type(arg)}
    derived_non_none = {arg for arg in derived_args if not _is_none_type(arg)}

    if base_non_none != derived_non_none:
        return True, "RISKY_TYPE_MUTATION"

    return False, "TYPE_DRIFT"


class SchemaDriftDetector(BaseModel):
    reports: List[DriftReport] = Field(default_factory=list)

    def analyze_inheritance(self, base_model: Type[BaseModel], derived_model: Type[BaseModel]) -> List[DriftReport]:
        base_fields = base_model.model_fields
        derived_fields = derived_model.model_fields

        local_reports: List[DriftReport] = []

        for field_name, derived_field in derived_fields.items():
            if field_name in base_fields:
                base_field = base_fields[field_name]

                base_tp = base_field.annotation
                derived_tp = derived_field.annotation

                if base_tp != derived_tp:
                    is_risky, issue_type = _is_coercion_risky(base_tp, derived_tp)
                    report = DriftReport(
                        model_name=derived_model.__name__,
                        base_model_name=base_model.__name__,
                        field_name=field_name,
                        issue_type=issue_type,
                        base_type=_get_type_name(base_tp),
                        derived_type=_get_type_name(derived_tp),
                        message=(
                            f"Field '{field_name}' type changed from "
                            f"{_get_type_name(base_tp)} to {_get_type_name(derived_tp)} "
                            f"(Issue: {issue_type})."
                        ),
                    )
                    local_reports.append(report)

        self.reports.extend(local_reports)
        return local_reports

    def export_json(self) -> bytes:
        data = [report.model_dump() for report in self.reports]
        if HAS_ORJSON:
            return orjson.dumps(data, option=orjson.OPT_INDENT_2)
        else:
            return json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2).encode("utf-8")


# --- Demonstration & Execution ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    class BaseUser(BaseModel):
        id: int
        username: str
        email: str | None = None

    class V2User(BaseUser):
        # Intentional drift examples:
        # 1. id: int -> str (RISKY_TYPE_MUTATION)
        # 2. email: str | None -> str (NULLABILITY_REDUCTION)
        id: str
        username: str
        email: str

    detector = SchemaDriftDetector()
    detector.analyze_inheritance(BaseUser, V2User)

    # Export analysis output as JSON bytes
    json_output = detector.export_json()
    print(json_output.decode("utf-8"))

💡 For immediate deployment: The complete source code suite (ZIP) for this architecture is available on Gumroad for $0+ (Pay What You Want).

4. Key Architectural Considerations

1. Robust Union Decomposition via get_origin

To reliably evaluate Python 3.10+ union expressions (A | B) alongside traditional typing.Union[A, B], the _extract_union_types helper inspects the metadata via get_origin and get_args. By decomposing union arguments into sets, the detector isolates NoneType presence and accurately evaluates nullability differentials without false negatives caused by ordering differences (e.g., str | None vs. None | str).

2. Issue Categorization

Rather than triggering false alarms on harmless adjustments, drift is partitioned into actionable severity levels:

  • NULLABILITY_REDUCTION: A field that was previously nullable is redefined to reject None. When existing records or upstream microservices send payload instances with null fields, validation breaks immediately.
  • RISKY_TYPE_MUTATION: The underlying scalar type has been changed (e.g., int mutated to str), causing silent type coercion discrepancies or validation failures depending on Pydantic's strictness settings.
  • NULLABILITY_EXPANSION: Safe widening of the type domain; recorded for tracking changes but not flagged as an immediate failure.

3. Automated CI/CD Pipeline Enforcement

The JSON output produced by export_json() integrates cleanly into automated quality gates (e.g., GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or pre-commit hooks). By embedding this check in your test suite, pull requests introducing breaking schema mutations can be blocked before reaching deployment artifacts, ensuring true contract stability across services.
