title: API Key bị lộ trên trình duyệt? Kiểm tra key OpenAI, Claude hoặc Gemini trong 2 phút
description:
Nếu ứng dụng web của bạn gọi OpenAI, Claude hay Gemini trực tiếp từ trình duyệt, khóa API của bạn bị lộ trong trình duyệt, và bất kỳ ai mở DevTools đều có thể sao chép nó. Bạn có thể xác nhận điều này trong 2 phút: mở tab Network, gửi một yêu cầu AI, và tìm header Authorization, x-api-key hoặc x-goog-api-key gửi đến nhà cung cấp. Nếu bạn thấy khóa của mình ở đó, hãy xoay vòng nó ngay hôm nay và chuyển lệnh gọi ra sau một route phía máy chủ.

Dùng thử Apidog ngay hôm nay

Dưới đây: cách kiểm tra, thứ tự khắc phục, và cách coding agent của bạn có thể kiểm thử route đã sửa.

Tại sao khóa API bị lộ trong trình duyệt lại là vấn đề

Một khóa API bị lộ trong trình duyệt là một bí mật được vận chuyển bên trong mã frontend hoặc lưu lượng mạng của bạn, nơi mọi khách truy cập đều có thể đọc được. Nếu trình duyệt gửi khóa, người dùng có thể sao chép nó và gọi nhà cung cấp tính vào hóa đơn của bạn.

Hướng dẫn về khóa API Gemini của Google nói rằng "Không hardcode khóa API trực tiếp trong ứng dụng web hoặc di động" vì "Khóa được biên dịch trong mã phía client có thể bị người dùng trích xuất," và khuyên bạn nên "chạy một máy chủ proxy backend để thực hiện các lệnh gọi API thực tế." Hướng dẫn an toàn khóa API của OpenAI cũng đưa ra quy tắc tương tự: định tuyến các yêu cầu qua backend của riêng bạn thay vì triển khai khóa đến client.

README của openai-node nói rằng hỗ trợ trình duyệt bị tắt theo mặc định "để tránh làm lộ thông tin xác thực API bí mật của bạn," và bạn phải đặt dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true để bật nó lên. SDK TypeScript của Anthropic dùng cùng tên tùy chọn, và API của nó chỉ chấp nhận các lệnh gọi trình duyệt (CORS) khi yêu cầu mang header anthropic-dangerous-direct-browser-access: true, như Simon Willison đã ghi lại khi nó ra mắt.

Mô hình này phổ biến trong các ứng dụng được xây dựng nhanh bằng AI app builder và coding agent: con đường hoạt động ngắn nhất là một fetch từ component React với khóa nằm trong biến VITE_ hoặc NEXT_PUBLIC_. Các khóa bị đánh cắp sau đó được bán lại để suy luận hàng loạt, như đã đề cập trong bài viết của chúng tôi về khóa AI API bị đánh cắp và LLMjacking, và hóa đơn của bạn là nơi bạn nhận ra điều đó.

Cách kiểm tra khóa API của bạn có bị lộ không (2 phút)

Hãy chạy các kiểm tra này trên môi trường production, không phải localhost.

  1. Quan sát tab Network (45 giây). Mở trang web của bạn, nhấn F12 (Cmd+Option+I trên Mac), chọn tab Network và kích hoạt một tính năng AI, chẳng hạn gửi một tin nhắn chat. Lọc theo openai, anthropic hoặc googleapis. Nếu có bất kỳ yêu cầu nào đi thẳng đến api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com hoặc generativelanguage.googleapis.com, hãy nhấp vào nó và mở Headers. Một khóa trong [REDACTED CREDENTIAL],x-api-key,x-goog-api-keyhoặc tham số truy vấn?key=` nghĩa là nó đã bị lộ.
  2. Tìm kiếm trong bundle (45 giây). Trong DevTools, nhấn Cmd+Option+F (Ctrl+Shift+F trên Windows) để tìm kiếm tất cả các script đã tải. Tìm sk-, sk-ant-, AIza và dangerouslyAllowBrowser. Bất kỳ kết quả nào trong tệp .js được phục vụ cho trình duyệt đều là rò rỉ, ngay cả khi chưa có yêu cầu nào được gửi đi.
  3. Kiểm tra tiền tố biến môi trường của bạn (30 giây). Mở tệp .env và bảng điều khiển hosting của bạn. Các công cụ build sao chép một số biến vào bundle client theo thiết kế: VITE_* trong Vite (xem tài liệu về env của Vite), NEXT_PUBLIC_* trong Next.js, REACT_APP_* trong Create React App và EXPO_PUBLIC_* trong Expo. Một khóa nhà cung cấp nằm sau bất kỳ tiền tố nào trong số này đều là công khai, bất kể nó được đặt tên như thế nào.

Để quét đầu ra build bằng terminal:

`bash

from your project root after a production build

grep -rnoE "sk-(proj-|ant-)?[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}" dist/ build/ .next/static/ 2>/dev/null
grep -rn "dangerouslyAllowBrowser" dist/ build/ .next/static/ 2>/dev/null
`

Không có kết quả nghĩa là đạt. Google cho biết các khóa AI Studio mới được tạo từ ngày 28 tháng 5 năm 2026 là "auth key," có định dạng có thể khác với AIza, vì vậy hãy tìm cả generativelanguage.googleapis.com trong bundle. Bạn chỉ đạt khi trình duyệt chỉ giao tiếp với tên miền của riêng bạn (ví dụ /api/chat) và không có hostname nhà cung cấp hay khóa nào xuất hiện ở bất kỳ đâu.

Phải làm gì khi khóa của bạn bị lộ: thứ tự khắc phục

Xoay vòng trước sẽ đóng lỗ hổng của ngày hôm nay; thay đổi kiến trúc sẽ đóng nó vĩnh viễn.

Bước Bạn làm gì Tại sao theo thứ tự này Thời gian
1. Xoay vòng khóa Tạo khóa mới trong bảng điều khiển nhà cung cấp, sau đó thu hồi khóa bị lộ Khóa cũ có thể đã bị sao chép; thu hồi là cách duy nhất để ngăn việc sử dụng nó 5 phút
2. Chuyển lệnh gọi sang phía máy chủ Đặt lệnh gọi nhà cung cấp trong một route máy chủ hoặc edge function giữ khóa Ngăn khóa mới bị lộ theo cùng cách 30 đến 60 phút
3. Thêm xác thực và giới hạn tốc độ theo người dùng Yêu cầu phiên đăng nhập trên route và giới hạn số yêu cầu mỗi người dùng Nếu không có điều này, proxy của bạn trở thành endpoint AI miễn phí cho bất kỳ ai 30 phút
4. Đặt giới hạn chi tiêu của nhà cung cấp Đặt ngân sách hoặc giới hạn chi tiêu trong cài đặt thanh toán của mỗi nhà cung cấp Giới hạn hóa đơn trong trường hợp xấu nhất nếu có thứ khác bị lộ 10 phút
5. Quét trong CI Làm build thất bại nếu một mẫu khóa xuất hiện trong bundle đầu ra Ngăn tính năng tiếp theo do agent viết hoàn tác bản sửa 15 phút

Triển khai khóa mới ở phía máy chủ trước khi bạn thu hồi khóa cũ, nếu không tính năng AI của bạn sẽ ngừng hoạt động. Hướng dẫn của chúng tôi về thực hành tốt nhất khi xoay vòng khóa API đề cập đến việc xoay vòng không gián đoạn. Ở bước 4, hướng dẫn an toàn khóa của OpenAI khuyến nghị giới hạn chi tiêu với thực thi cứng, vì cảnh báo đơn thuần không ngăn được lưu lượng; ngân sách thanh toán của Google Cloud chỉ cảnh báo bạn chứ tự nó không ngăn việc sử dụng.

Cách chuyển các lệnh gọi OpenAI, Claude và Gemini ra sau một route máy chủ

Một route proxy backend là một endpoint máy chủ nhỏ nhận prompt của người dùng, thêm khóa API ở phía máy chủ, gọi nhà cung cấp và chỉ trả về câu trả lời. Trình duyệt không bao giờ thấy khóa. Đây là một route Next.js tối giản cho OpenAI; Claude và Gemini cũng theo hình mẫu tương tự:

`ts
// app/api/chat/route.ts (runs on the server only)
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { getSession } from "@/lib/auth"; // your auth helper
import { checkRateLimit } from "@/lib/limits"; // your per-user limiter

const client = new OpenAI({ [REDACTED CREDENTIAL] }); // no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix

export async function POST(req: Request) {
const session = await getSession(req);
if (!session) return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 401 });

if (!(await checkRateLimit(session.userId, 20))) { // 20 requests per minute
return new Response("Too many requests", { status: 429 });
}

const { message } = await req.json();
if (typeof message !== "string" || message.length > 4000) {
return new Response("Bad request", { status: 400 });
}

const response = await client.responses.create({
model: process.env.OPENAI_MODEL!, // pin the model server-side
input: message,
});

return Response.json({ reply: response.output_text }); // return the answer, nothing else
}
`

Điều làm cho nó an toàn, chứ không chỉ bị ẩn:

  • Model nằm trên máy chủ. Nếu trình duyệt chọn model, kẻ tấn công sẽ chọn cái đắt nhất.
  • Đầu vào được giới hạn. Không có prompt khổng lồ đi qua tài khoản của bạn.
  • Chỉ câu trả lời được trả về. Không bao giờ trả về phản hồi thô của nhà cung cấp hay đối tượng lỗi.
  • Không có tiền tố công khai. OPENAI_API_KEY ở lại phía máy chủ; NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENAI_API_KEY sẽ được gửi đến mọi khách truy cập.

Đối với Claude và Gemini, hãy dùng SDK của chúng với ANTHROPIC_API_KEY hoặc GEMINI_API_KEY. Các hạn chế về website và IP của Google có ích, nhưng bất kỳ ai với curl đều có thể gửi bất kỳ header Referer nào, vì vậy hãy coi chúng là một lớp bảo vệ thứ hai. Trường hợp hợp lý duy nhất cho lệnh gọi từ trình duyệt là công cụ mang khóa riêng (bring-your-own-key) nơi mỗi người dùng tự dán khóa của họ.

Để coding agent của bạn kiểm thử route proxy bằng Apidog CLI

Di chuyển khóa chỉ là một nửa công việc; nửa còn lại là chứng minh nó vẫn được giữ nguyên sau tính năng tiếp theo mà agent của bạn viết. Hãy để agent đã xây dựng route kiểm thử nó bằng Apidog CLI. Thiết lập một lần:

bash
npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com # pick your agent when prompted

Sau đó đưa cho Claude Code, Codex, Cursor hoặc bất kỳ agent nào bạn dùng một [REDACTED PROMPT]
Create Apidog test cases in project for POST /api/chat on our staging
environment that assert:

  1. a request without a session cookie returns 401,
  2. a valid request returns 200 and the body does not contain "sk-", "sk-ant-", "AIza" or "api_key",
  3. the 21st request inside 60 seconds from the same user returns 429. Run them and summarize any failures. `shell

Agent đọc schema, xác thực payload của nó, viết các test case và chạy chúng:

`bash
apidog test-case category --project <id>
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project <id> --file case.json
apidog run --test-case <caseId> --project <id> -e <envId> -r cli,json
`

Khẳng định thứ hai là cái quan trọng nhất: nó thất bại ngay khi một đối tượng lỗi nhà cung cấp hoặc trường gỡ lỗi bắt đầu phản hồi khóa của bạn về phía client. Hãy đặt cùng bước apidog run ... -r junit vào pipeline của bạn để mỗi lần triển khai đều kiểm tra lại nó; hướng dẫn Apidog CLI CI/CD của chúng tôi trình bày cách thiết lập, và Apidog CLI trong Claude Code đề cập đến phía agent. Gói Miễn phí của Apidog hỗ trợ tối đa 4 người dùng, nên một nhóm nhỏ có thể chạy điều này mà không cần ghế trả phí.

Về phía repo của cùng vấn đề, các khóa được commit vào Git thay vì gửi đến trình duyệt, hãy xem bài viết của chúng tôi về kiểm tra rò rỉ khóa API bằng secret scanner. Nếu agent của bạn gọi các công cụ xử lý dữ liệu khách hàng, kiểm thử AI agent về rò rỉ dữ liệu đề cập đến lớp tiếp theo.

Những sai lầm phổ biến khiến khóa vẫn bị lộ

  • Mã hóa Base64 hoặc chia nhỏ khóa. Trình duyệt phải dựng lại nó để gửi đi, nên DevTools sẽ hiển thị giá trị thật.
  • Chuyển nó vào localStorage hoặc cookie. Nó vẫn ở trên client.
  • Proxy mà không có xác thực. Một /api/chat công khai là endpoint AI mở tính vào hóa đơn của bạn.
  • Giữ khóa cũ "để phòng hờ." Một khóa đã công khai trong một ngày là đã bị sao chép.
  • Quên ứng dụng di động. Hướng dẫn của Google nhắc đến "ứng dụng web hoặc di động" cùng nhau là có lý do.

FAQ

Làm sao tôi biết khóa API OpenAI của mình có bị lộ trong trình duyệt không? Kích hoạt một tính năng AI với tab Network của DevTools đang mở. Một yêu cầu đến api.openai.com với header Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED]-... nghĩa là nó đã bị lộ. Đồng thời tìm sk- và dangerouslyAllowBrowser trong các script đã tải.

Có an toàn không khi đặt khóa API trong biến môi trường NEXT_PUBLIC_ hoặc VITE_? Không. Những tiền tố đó tồn tại để sao chép giá trị vào bundle client. Bất kỳ khóa nhà cung cấp nào được lưu dưới chúng đều được gửi đến mọi khách truy cập. Hãy dùng biến chỉ dành cho máy chủ không có tiền tố và đọc nó bên trong một route máy chủ.

Việc giới hạn khóa API Gemini cho website của tôi có làm nó an toàn trong trình duyệt không? Nó có ích, nhưng một script bên ngoài trình duyệt có thể gửi bất kỳ header Referer nào. Chính hướng dẫn của Google khuyến nghị dùng proxy backend cho các ứng dụng client.

Tôi phát hiện khóa của mình bị lộ. Tôi nên làm gì trước? Tạo khóa mới, triển khai nó ở phía máy chủ, sau đó thu hồi khóa cũ. Tiếp theo, chuyển lệnh gọi ra sau một route có xác thực với giới hạn tốc độ theo người dùng, và đặt giới hạn chi tiêu của nhà cung cấp.

Coding agent của tôi có thể sửa và kiểm thử điều này cho tôi không? Có. Yêu cầu nó chuyển lệnh gọi nhà cung cấp vào một route máy chủ, sau đó dùng Apidog CLI để tạo và chạy các kiểm thử khẳng định trả về 401 khi không có phiên, không có mẫu khóa trong phản hồi, và 429 khi vượt giới hạn tốc độ của bạn.

title: Claude API Version 2026-10-21: What Changed and How to Upgrade Safely
description:
Claude API Version 2026-10-21: What Changed and How to Upgrade Safely

Claude API version 2026-10-21 is the first new anthropic-version value since 2023-06-01. It makes three breaking changes to the Messages API: temperature, top_p, and top_k now return a 400 error; document blocks in assistant messages return a 400; and citations on text blocks in user messages return a 400. It also renames several Admin API and Enterprise Analytics API fields. You opt in by sending anthropic-version: 2026-10-21 or by upgrading to the new SDK majors (Python 2.0.0, TypeScript 1.0.0, Go 2.0.0, and others).

Try Apidog today

The catch: upgrading the SDK is how most teams will "accidentally" move to the new version. A routine pip install -U anthropic or npm update that crosses a major version flips every request to 2026-10-21 at once. This guide lists every change Anthropic documents, shows which ones bite in real code, and gives you a safe order to upgrade in.

What is the anthropic-version header?

The anthropic-version header is a required request header that pins the shape of the Claude API you get back. Within one version, Anthropic keeps existing input and output parameters stable, but may add optional inputs, new output values, new enum variants such as streaming event types, and new error conditions. Breaking changes only arrive with a new version date.

From the versioning page, three versions exist:

Version What it introduced
2023-01-01 Initial release
2023-06-01 Incremental, named server-sent events for streaming; removed the data: [DONE] event and the legacy exception and truncated values
2026-10-21 Removed sampling parameters, stricter message content rules, renamed Admin and Analytics fields

If you use an official SDK, you never set the header yourself. Each SDK major sends the version that was current when that major shipped. That's why the SDK upgrade and the API version upgrade are the same event for most codebases.

Claude API 2026-10-21 breaking changes

These changes apply to POST /v1/messages, to token counting, and to every request inside a Message Batch created with 2026-10-21.

1. temperature, top_p and top_k are removed

This is the change most people will hit. Any request that sends temperature, top_p, or top_k returns a 400 error, on every model, even if you send the default value. A temperature: 1.0 left in a config file is enough to break the call.

What happens to output quality depends on the model:

  • Claude 4.7 and later already accept only the default sampling values, so removing the parameters changes nothing about how they sample.
  • Older models that accept other values, such as Claude Sonnet 4.6, lose any effect you got from lowering temperature. The migration guide is blunt about it: no other setting replaces it.

If a request truly depends on a non-default value, Anthropic gives you two choices: stop sending it, or keep that specific request on 2023-06-01.

2. document blocks in assistant messages return a 400

Some apps replay conversation history with a document block sitting directly in an assistant turn. Under 2026-10-21 that's rejected. Move documents into user messages. A document nested inside another block, such as a web fetch tool result that Claude returned, is still accepted.

3. citations in user messages return a 400

A text block with a non-empty citations array in a user message now fails, and that includes text inside search_result blocks. Strip citations from those blocks. Citations on Claude's own assistant replies that you send back are still fine, and so is "citations": {"enabled": true} on documents and search results.

4. Admin API and Enterprise Analytics field renames

Responses no longer include the old field names:

Endpoint Old field New field
RBAC groups roles role_ids
RBAC group members group_id rbac_group_id
RBAC roles name display_name
Organization and workspace rate limits group_type group.type
API keys workspace_id scope.workspace_id
Analytics per-user usage and cost reports actor.email actor.email_address
Analytics activity summaries summaries data

The API key change is the subtle one. Under 2023-06-01, workspace_id was null both for keys bound to the Default Workspace and for all-workspaces keys. Under 2026-10-21, scope.workspace_id holds the Default Workspace's real ID, and an all-workspaces key has scope: {"type": "organization"} with no workspace_id. If your dashboard treated null as "Default Workspace", it will mislabel keys after the upgrade.

SDK versions that send 2026-10-21

Anthropic shipped new SDK majors on October 21, 2026, and each one sends 2026-10-21 by default, per the release notes:

SDK First version on 2026-10-21
Python (anthropic) 2.0.0
TypeScript (@anthropic-ai/sdk) 1.0.0
Go (anthropic-sdk-go/v2) 2.0.0
Java (anthropic-java) 3.0.0
C# (Anthropic) 13.0.0
PHP (anthropic-ai/sdk) 1.0.0
Ruby (anthropic) 2.0.0
ant CLI 2.0.0

The new majors also bring changes that don't depend on the API version at all:

  • API keys go out as Authorization: Bearer <key> instead of X-Api-Key. The Claude API accepts either, but a proxy, gateway, log filter, or test stub that reads X-Api-Key won't see the key anymore.
  • Text Completions is removed from the TypeScript, Go, Java, and Ruby SDKs and from the CLI. Use the Messages API.
  • betas is gone from the non-beta Models methods. Call client.beta.models instead.
  • MessageParam is a union with one type per role in the typed SDKs, so some type annotations need updating.
  • Go needs a new import path ending in /v2, and TypeScript users on the Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, AWS, or Google Cloud packages must move those to v1 in the same upgrade, or the package manager installs a second, older copy of the core SDK.
  • The license changed from MIT to Apache 2.0.

Pin your current major before you do anything else. That stops a dependency bot from upgrading you mid-sprint.

The Amazon Bedrock exception

On Amazon Bedrock, 2026-10-21 works only with Claude 4.7 and later models. If you still call Opus 4.6 or an older model there, stay on your current SDK version or keep sending your current header, and switch the model first.

How to upgrade to Claude API version 2026-10-21 safely

The migration guide's order is: switch the version, fix the breaking changes, test before release. Here's how that looks in practice.

  1. Pin the old SDK major. For example anthropic<2 in Python or "@anthropic-ai/sdk": "^0" in npm.
  2. Search your code and configs for temperature, top_p, top_k, X-Api-Key, completions.create, and any Admin API field from the table above.
  3. Decide on sampling. On Claude 4.7 and later, delete the parameters. On older models, either accept default sampling or keep those calls on 2023-06-01.
  4. Fix message construction. Move assistant-side documents to user turns and strip citations from user text blocks.
  5. Test the same payloads under both versions and compare status codes and response shapes.
  6. Upgrade the SDK and ship the code fixes together. Anthropic says to release the upgrade with your fixes, not before.

Without an SDK, the switch is one header:

curl https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages \
  -H "x-[REDACTED CREDENTIAL] \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2026-10-21" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
    "max_tokens": 1024,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}]
  }'

Add "temperature": 0.2 to that body and you'll get a 400. Send the same body with anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and it succeeds. That pair of results is exactly what step 5 should catch for every payload you send in production.

Let Claude Code test both versions with Apidog CLI

Step 5 is tedious by hand: you have dozens of payload shapes, and each needs to run twice. Hand it to your coding agent instead. Apidog CLI gives Claude Code (or Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode) commands to create test cases and run them, so the agent does the comparison and you read the summary.

Set it up once:

npm install -g apidog-cli@latest
apidog login --with-token <YOUR_TOKEN>
npx -y skills add https://apidog.com   # pick Claude Code when prompted

Then give Claude Code one [REDACTED PROMPT]

In Apidog project , create an environment "claude-api" with base URL
https://api.anthropic.com. For each JSON payload in ./fixtures/claude/, add a
POST /v1/messages test case that sends the header anthropic-version: {{anthropic_version}}
and asserts status 200 and a non-empty content array. Run every case twice, once with
anthropic_version=2023-06-01 and once with 2026-10-21, and list each case that passes
on the old version but fails on the new one, with the error message.


The agent checks each payload schema before it writes anything, then runs the cases:


bash
apidog environment create claude-api --project --base-url https://api.anthropic.com
apidog cli-schema get test-case-create
apidog cli-schema validate test-case-create --file case.json
apidog test-case create --project --file case.json
apidog run --test-case --project -e --env-var "anthropic_version=2023-06-01" -r cli,json
apidog run --test-case --project -e --env-var "anthropic_version=2026-10-21" -r cli,json




The `--env-var` flag swaps the header value without touching the test case, so the diff is one variable. Add `--upload-report` to view both runs in the Apidog app, or put the 2026-10-21 run in CI with `-r junit` so a dependency bump can't ship a `temperature` field to production. The [Apidog CLI in Claude Code guide](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-cli-in-claude-code?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) covers setup in more detail, and the [`apidog run` reference](http://apidog.com/blog/apidog-run-command-reference?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) lists every flag. Apidog's Free plan covers up to 4 users.

![Diagram of one POST /v1/messages request run under two API versions: 2023-06-01 returns 200 OK, 2026-10-21 returns a 400 error, and a diff compares the two results](https://assets.apidog.com/blog-next/2026/11/claude-api-version-2026-10-21-version-diff.png)

## Is 2023-06-01 deprecated?

No retirement date has been published. The versioning page lists 2023-06-01 with no deprecation notice, and the migration guide itself tells you to keep requests that need a non-default `temperature` on 2023-06-01. Anthropic still recommends the latest version "whenever possible".

That matters for planning. Today's upgrade is optional, but 2026-10-21 is the first new version in more than three years, and future breaking changes will arrive the same way, so treating version testing as a routine CI job now is cheaper than a rushed migration later. If you're already tuning around [Claude API rate limits](http://apidog.com/blog/claude-api-rate-limits?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) or [Claude API cost](http://apidog.com/blog/claude-api-cost?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation), add the version check to the same pipeline. Our guide to [API versioning best practices](http://apidog.com/blog/api-versioning-best-practices?utm_source=dev.to&utm_medium=wanda&utm_content=n8n-post-automation) explains why date-based versions like this one make it easier.

## FAQ

### Do I have to upgrade to Claude API version 2026-10-21 now?

No. 2023-06-01 still works and has no published retirement date. You upgrade when you send the new header or install an SDK major that defaults to it.

### Why does my request return 400 after an SDK upgrade?

The new SDK majors send 2026-10-21, which rejects `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k`, assistant-side `document` blocks, and `citations` on user text blocks. Check your payload for those first.

### Can I keep temperature on some requests?

Yes, by keeping those specific requests on 2023-06-01. Under 2026-10-21 there is no replacement setting, and Claude 4.7 and later models only sample with the defaults anyway.

### Does 2026-10-21 work on Amazon Bedrock?

Only for Claude 4.7 and later models. Older Bedrock models need your current SDK version or header until you switch models.

### Will my proxy still see my API key?

Not if it reads `X-Api-Key`. The new SDKs send the key as `[REDACTED CREDENTIAL] Update the proxy to read `Authorization`, or configure the SDK to send `X-Api-Key` yourself.

### Does the new version change streaming events?

Anthropic lists no streaming format change for 2026-10-21. The streaming format you use today came with 2023-06-01.

title: Object-Oriented Programming: The 4 Pillars Explained
description:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is one of the most widely used paradigms in software development. Instead of organizing code as a long list of functions operating on loose data, OOP organizes it around objects: bundles of data (attributes) and behavior (methods) that model things in your problem domain.

Whether you're building a web API, a data pipeline, or a game, understanding OOP helps you write code that is easier to reason about, reuse, and maintain.

In this article, we'll cover the four pillars of OOP with practical Python examples:

  1. Encapsulation
  2. Abstraction
  3. Inheritance
  4. Polymorphism

Quick Refresher: Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint. An object is an instance created from that blueprint.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name: str, age: int):
        self.name = name  # attribute
        self.age = age    # attribute

    def bark(self) -> str:  # method
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"


rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.bark())  # Rex says woof!

Dog is the class; rex is an object with its own name and age. With that in place, let's look at the pillars.

1. Encapsulation

Encapsulation means bundling data and the methods that operate on it into one unit, and restricting direct access to the internal state. Outside code interacts with the object through a controlled public interface rather than poking at its internals.

Why does this matter? It protects your object's invariants. If anyone can set balance = -1000000 directly, you can't guarantee your object is ever in a valid state.

Example: A bank account 

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner: str, balance: float = 0.0):
        self.owner = owner
        self._balance = balance  # "protected" by convention

    @property
    def balance(self) -> float:
        """Read-only access to the balance."""
        return self._balance

    def deposit(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive.")
        self._balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> None:
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Withdrawal must be positive.")
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self._balance -= amount


account = BankAccount("Amina", 100)
account.deposit(50)
account.withdraw(30)
print(account.balance)  # 120

# account.balance = 1_000_000  -> AttributeError: can't set attribute

A few notes on Python specifically:

  • Python has no strict private keyword. A single leading underscore (_balance) is a convention that says "internal, don't touch."
  • A double underscore (__balance) triggers name mangling, which makes accidental access harder, but it is still not true privacy.
  • The @property decorator lets you expose a value as a read-only attribute, and you can add validation later without changing how callers use the class.

Takeaway: Hide the internals, expose a safe interface, and enforce rules in one place.

2. Abstraction

Abstraction means exposing what an object does while hiding how it does it. Users of your class shouldn't need to know the implementation details, only the contract.

In Python, the abc module lets you define abstract base classes that declare methods subclasses must implement.

Example: Data loaders

Imagine a program that needs to load data from different sources. The calling code shouldn't care whether the data comes from a CSV file or an API.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import csv
import json


class DataLoader(ABC):
    """Contract that every loader must follow."""

    @abstractmethod
    def load(self) -> list[dict]:
        """Return the data as a list of records."""
        ...


class CSVLoader(DataLoader):
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    def load(self) -> list[dict]:
        with open(self.path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return list(csv.DictReader(f))


class JSONLoader(DataLoader):
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    def load(self) -> list[dict]:
        with open(self.path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return json.load(f)


def count_records(loader: DataLoader) -> int:
    # This function only knows about the abstraction.
    return len(loader.load())

If you try to instantiate the abstract class directly, or a subclass that forgets to implement load, Python stops you:

loader = DataLoader()
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class DataLoader
# with abstract method load

Takeaway: Abstraction defines a clear contract. Code that depends on the contract keeps working no matter how many new implementations you add.

Encapsulation vs. abstraction: Encapsulation is about protecting data by controlling access. Abstraction is about simplifying usage by hiding complexity. They work together but solve different problems.

3. Inheritance

Inheritance lets a class (the child or subclass) acquire the attributes and methods of another class (the parent or superclass). It promotes code reuse and models "is-a" relationships: a Manager is an Employee.

Example: Employees 

class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name: str, salary: float):
        self.name = name
        self.salary = salary

    def describe(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name} earns {self.salary:,.2f} per month."


class Manager(Employee):
    def __init__(self, name: str, salary: float, team: list[Employee] | None = None):
        super().__init__(name, salary)  # reuse the parent's setup
        self.team = team or []

    def add_to_team(self, employee: Employee) -> None:
        self.team.append(employee)

    def describe(self) -> str:
        base = super().describe()  # extend, don't rewrite
        return f"{base} They manage {len(self.team)} people."


dev = Employee("Brian", 4000)
lead = Manager("Wanjiru", 6500)
lead.add_to_team(dev)

print(dev.describe())
print(lead.describe())

Output:

Brian earns 4,000.00 per month.
Wanjiru earns 6,500.00 per month. They manage 1 people.

Key ideas:

  • Manager(Employee) declares the inheritance.
  • super() calls the parent's implementation, so you build on it instead of duplicating it.
  • The child can override methods (like describe) to specialize behavior.

A word of caution

Inheritance is powerful but easy to overuse. Deep hierarchies become rigid and hard to change. A good rule of thumb is "favor composition over inheritance": if the relationship is "has-a" rather than "is-a," pass in another object instead of subclassing.

class Engine:
    def start(self) -> str:
        return "Engine started."


class Car:
    def __init__(self):
        self.engine = Engine()  # Car HAS an Engine (composition)

    def start(self) -> str:
        return self.engine.start()

Python also supports multiple inheritance (class C(A, B)), but use it sparingly. It can introduce confusing method resolution order (MRO) issues.

Takeaway: Use inheritance for genuine "is-a" relationships and shared behavior, and reach for composition when in doubt.

4. Polymorphism

Polymorphism means "many forms." It lets you treat different objects through the same interface, with each object responding in its own way. You write code against a general type, and the correct behavior is chosen at runtime.

Example: Shapes 

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import math


class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self) -> float:
        ...


class Rectangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, width: float, height: float):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height

    def area(self) -> float:
        return self.width * self.height


class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, radius: float):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self) -> float:
        return math.pi * self.radius ** 2


class Triangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, base: float, height: float):
        self.base = base
        self.height = height

    def area(self) -> float:
        return 0.5 * self.base * self.height


shapes: list[Shape] = [Rectangle(4, 5), Circle(3), Triangle(6, 2)]

for shape in shapes:
    print(f"{type(shape).__name__}: {shape.area():.2f}")

Output:

Rectangle: 20.00
Circle: 28.27
Triangle: 6.00

The loop doesn't use if isinstance(...) checks. It just calls .area(), and each object does the right thing. Adding a new Hexagon class later requires no changes to the loop.

Duck typing

Python takes polymorphism a step further with duck typing: "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." An object doesn't need a shared parent class, it just needs the right methods.

class Duck:
    def speak(self) -> str:
        return "Quack!"


class Robot:
    def speak(self) -> str:
        return "Beep boop."


def make_it_speak(thing) -> None:
    print(thing.speak())


for item in (Duck(), Robot()):
    make_it_speak(item)

If you want duck typing with static type checking, Python's typing.Protocol lets you describe the required interface without inheritance.

Takeaway: Write code that depends on behavior, not concrete types, and new functionality becomes a matter of adding classes instead of editing existing code.

Putting It All Together

Here is a small example that uses all four pillars in one place: a notification system.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Notifier(ABC):                       # Abstraction
    def __init__(self, recipient: str):
        self._recipient = recipient        # Encapsulation (internal state)

    @abstractmethod
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        ...


class EmailNotifier(Notifier):             # Inheritance
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        return f"Emailing {self._recipient}: {message}"


class SMSNotifier(Notifier):               # Inheritance
    def send(self, message: str) -> str:
        return f"Texting {self._recipient}: {message}"


def alert_all(notifiers: list[Notifier], message: str) -> None:
    for n in notifiers:                    # Polymorphism
        print(n.send(message))


alert_all(
    [EmailNotifier("mary@example.com"), SMSNotifier("+254700000000")],
    "Your report is ready.",
)

Output:

Emailing mary@example.com: Your report is ready.
Texting +254700000000: Your report is ready.
  • Abstraction: Notifier defines what a notifier does.
  • Encapsulation: _recipient is kept internal to the object.
  • Inheritance: Both notifiers reuse the base class's structure.
  • Polymorphism: alert_all works with any notifier, treating them uniformly.

Summary

Pillar Core idea Python tools
Encapsulation Bundle data with behavior and control access _underscore convention, @property
Abstraction Expose what, hide how abc.ABC, @abstractmethod
Inheritance Reuse and specialize via "is-a" relationships class Child(Parent), super()
Polymorphism One interface, many behaviors Method overriding, duck typing, Protocol

OOP isn't about using every feature everywhere. It's about modeling your problem clearly, keeping responsibilities separated, and making code easy to extend without breaking what already works. Start small, practice by modeling real things you know, and the four pillars will start to feel natural.

title: Every typed GraphQL error came back as "Internal server error" because graphql was loaded twice
description:
I had six integration tests for error codes on a small GraphQL + Postgres backend: UNAUTHENTICATED, FORBIDDEN, NOT_FOUND, BAD_USER_INPUT and friends. The resolvers threw the right errors. CI still failed the tests, and every error came back the same:

{ "errors": [{ "message": "Unexpected error.", "extensions": { "code": "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR" } }] }

Nothing was wrong with the resolvers. The server's error masking had decided our errors weren't GraphQL errors at all.

The setup

Expected failures are typed. Everything else gets masked so stack traces and SQL never reach the client:

export class AppError extends GraphQLError {
  constructor(code: ErrorCode, message: string, extra: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    super(message, { extensions: { code, ...extra } });
  }
}

// resolver
if (!canEdit) throw new AppError('FORBIDDEN', 'Not allowed');

The masking rule is the usual one: if the thrown error is a GraphQLError (or wraps one), pass it through; otherwise replace it with INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR. In GraphQL Yoga that's maskedErrors: true; in Apollo it's a formatError with an instanceof check.

The cause: two GraphQLError classes

instanceof compares against one specific class object. If the module that defines GraphQLError is loaded twice, there are two classes with the same name, and an error built from one is not an instanceof the other.

graphql v16 ships both a CommonJS build (index.js) and an ES module build (index.mjs). Your code can get one while your server library gets the other, depending on how each is imported and how your test runner or bundler resolves them. Vitest, Jest and some bundlers are common places for this to happen. A monorepo with two graphql versions in node_modules does the same thing more obviously.

So the chain was:

  1. The resolver throws AppError, which extends copy A of GraphQLError.
  2. The server checks it against copy B.
  3. instanceof is false, so the error counts as unexpected.
  4. The client gets INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, and the real code is only in the server log.

In production this looks like "the frontend can't tell a wrong password from an outage." It's easy to ship, because a manual test of the happy path never sees it.

How to check if you have it

Throw an AppError from any resolver and log this where your server handles errors:

import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql';

console.log(
  err.originalError?.constructor?.name,          // "AppError"
  err.originalError instanceof GraphQLError,     // false means two copies
);

Then look for duplicates:

npm ls graphql

More than one version listed is the obvious case. One version but false above means the CJS/ESM split.

The fix: recognize your errors by a brand, not by class identity

Give your error class a property that survives any number of module copies, and check that instead:

export class AppError extends GraphQLError {
  readonly isAppError = true;
  constructor(code: ErrorCode, message: string, extra: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
    super(message, { extensions: { code, ...extra } });
  }
}

export function isAppError(err: unknown): err is AppError {
  return typeof err === 'object' && err !== null && (err as { isAppError?: unknown }).isAppError === true;
}

Then do the masking yourself, so the decision uses the brand:

export function maskError(error: unknown, message: string): Error {
  const e = error as { originalError?: unknown; nodes?: any; path?: readonly (string | number)[] };
  const app = isAppError(e) ? e : isAppError(e?.originalError) ? e.originalError : null;
  if (app) {
    return new GraphQLError(app.message, { nodes: e.nodes, path: e.path, extensions: app.extensions });
  }
  console.error(error);
  return new GraphQLError(message, { nodes: e?.nodes, path: e?.path, extensions: { code: 'INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR' } });
}

// GraphQL Yoga
createYoga({ schema, maskedErrors: { maskError } });

For Apollo Server, use the same isAppError check inside formatError.

Deduplicating graphql (one version, one import style) is worth doing too. But the brand check keeps working when a future dependency upgrade brings the second copy back, and that's the failure you won't be watching for.

The test that caught it

One assertion per error code, against a real server and a real Postgres:

it('forbids viewers from creating issues', async () => {
  const res = await gql(
    'mutation($i: CreateIssueInput!) { createIssue(input: $i) { id } }',
    { i: { projectId: ids.alpha, title: 'Pour slab' } },
    ids.bo, // a member with the viewer role
  );
  expect(res.errors?.[0]?.extensions?.code).toBe('FORBIDDEN');
});

If your error-code tests only call resolver functions directly, they skip the masking layer and pass while clients get 500s. Send the request through the server.

Checklist

  • Typed errors carry a brand property; masking checks the brand, not instanceof.
  • Masking runs in one function you own, with the same rule for every server.
  • npm ls graphql shows one version.
  • Each error code has a test that goes through the HTTP layer and asserts extensions.code.

Making Claude Code write it this way

This is one of the rules in the typed-errors skill of my Claude Code skills pack for TypeScript + GraphQL + Postgres backends. The starter backend in the pack is where CI caught this bug.

  • Two skills are free (GraphQL N+1 fixes and safe Postgres migrations): github.com/adnan909/free-sample
  • The full pack, with the typed-errors skill, 6 more skills and the tested starter backend: Backend Skills Pack on Gumroad

title: Check for updates always, restart only when nobody is typing: an idle gate for a self-updating Node.js helper
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code.

Bolo turns an Android phone into a microphone for a computer: you speak on the phone and the text is typed at the cursor over local Wi-Fi. The computer side is a small Node.js helper in the tray. It updates itself, and updating means restarting, which is exactly what you must not do in the middle of someone's sentence.

This post is about the 91-line module that decides when the restart happens (src/updateGate.js), and the bug that made it necessary.

The first rule was too cautious

The original rule was simple: if a phone is connected, skip the update check. A phone mid-dictation should never see the helper vanish.

It held up until a helper was still on the previous version after a release had shipped. Its phone was simply always connected, so the check never ran. "Don't update while connected" quietly became "never update" for the most active users, who are the ones who most need fixes.

The lesson: "connected" is not "busy". A phone can sit connected for hours while nobody says a word.

Split the decision in two

The fix separates two things the old rule had glued together:

  1. Checking for an update runs on its normal schedule (every 6 hours, plus on demand), whether or not a phone is connected.
  2. Restarting waits until no text is being typed right now and none has been typed for 2 minutes.

Busy is measured where the typing happens. The message handler wraps every message that types text (a dictation, a live partial transcript, a clipboard paste) in a begin/end pair:

async function handleMessage(ws, message) {
  const typing = message.type === 'text'
    || message.type === 'realtime_text'
    || message.type === 'clipboard_paste';
  if (!typing) return handleMessageInner(ws, message);
  updateGate.begin();
  try {
    return await handleMessageInner(ws, message);
  } finally {
    updateGate.end();
  }
}

The finally matters: a dictation that throws still ends, so a failure can't leave the gate stuck "busy" forever.

The gate itself

Two pieces of state, a counter and a timestamp:

let lastActivityAt = 0;
let inFlight = 0;

function begin() { inFlight++; lastActivityAt = now(); }
function end()   { inFlight = Math.max(0, inFlight - 1); lastActivityAt = now(); }

function isIdle(idleMs = IDLE_MS) {
  return inFlight === 0 && now() - lastActivityAt >= idleMs;
}
  • A counter, not a boolean. Two messages can overlap (a partial transcript and the final text). With a boolean, the first end() would declare the gate idle while the second is still typing.
  • Math.max(0, …) so an unmatched end() can't push the counter negative and make "idle" impossible.
  • The clock is injectable (now), so the tests move time forward instead of sleeping for two minutes.

Waiting is a re-check loop that sleeps only as long as it has to:

function waitForIdle({ idleMs = IDLE_MS, pollMs = POLL_MS } = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const check = () => {
      if (isIdle(idleMs)) return resolve();
      const t = setTimeout(check,
        Math.min(pollMs, Math.max(50, idleMs - idleForMs())));
      t.unref?.();
    };
    check();
  });
}

If 100 seconds of the 120 have already passed, it waits 15 seconds (the poll cap), not another full two minutes. unref() keeps a pending wait from holding the process open on its own.

One waiter at a time

The 6-hour timer keeps firing while an update waits for a quiet moment. Without a guard, a busy afternoon could stack several waiters, and the first quiet moment would trigger several restarts in a row. So there is exactly one pending update:

let pending = null;

async function runGatedUpdate({ version, check, apply, interactive, ... }) {
  if (pending) {
    if (interactive) log(`[Update] ${pending} will install at the next idle moment.`);
    return 'pending';
  }
  const result = await check(version);
  if (!result.enabled || !result.updateAvailable) return /* 'disabled' | 'current' */;
  pending = result.version;
  try {
    await waitForIdle();
    await apply(result);   // restarts the helper
    return 'applied';
  } finally {
    pending = null;
  }
}

The finally again: if apply fails (a download error, say), pending clears, and the next scheduled check can try again instead of being told forever that an update is "pending".

When you ask for an update check by hand while you're dictating, you get a plain answer ("will install at the next idle moment") instead of a restart under your cursor.

What I'd keep from this

  • Name the condition you actually care about. "Phone connected" was a stand-in for "user is typing", and the stand-in was wrong most of the day.
  • Separate detecting an update from applying it; only the second needs to wait.
  • Count in-flight work; don't flag it. Always release in finally.
  • Allow one pending action, and clear it on failure.
  • Make time injectable so a 2-minute rule is testable in milliseconds.

Bolo is on Google Play (search "Bolo AI"), and the Windows companion is on GitHub releases. The phone and the computer talk over your local Wi-Fi.

title: What AI code reviewers miss, and the checks I built for it
description:
AI writes code fast now. Reviewing it has not got faster.

On the production Django backend we used as a test bed, about half of the recent commits were fixes. The same rule lived in several copies: sign-in, sign-out, password change and JSON body parsing each had more than one version, and they had drifted apart. One access bug came back a week after it was fixed.

So a colleague and I built healthkit, an open-source toolkit that checks Python code for the problems a tool can find reliably, so people (and AI reviewers) can spend their time on the ones it cannot.

The most useful thing we did was not a feature. It was measuring.

The number that shaped everything: 9 out of 45

A careful human review of one module had produced 45 findings. We replayed it: take the code from before each fix, run our rules, and see which findings a rule points at.

The first score was 29 of 45. It looked great. Then we read every hit by hand. Most were coincidences: an unused import that happened to sit inside a behaviour fix, findings inside routes the fix deleted anyway. Counting only the hits where the rule pointed at the actual problem: 9 of 45, about 20%.

That gap is the first lesson. Distrust the metric that looks good. Every automated score gets a by-hand read of its hits before we quote it.

The second lesson came from breaking the 45 down:

Kind of problem Example Caught by rules
Pattern: a shape in one place an exception's text sent back to the client 8 of 12
Knowledge: needs the project's model reading rows that were soft-deleted 0 of 13
Behaviour: does it do the right thing a reset link that works as a login; a race 1 of 15

Rules are good at patterns. They are close to useless at behaviour. Pretending otherwise is how a green check turns into a false sense of safety.

What a tool can own, and what it never can

That table became the design. A rule is a past mistake written down so a machine can spot it again. It catches known kinds of mistakes, never new ones.

  • Patterns and structure (who may import whom): healthkit owns these, using ruff, Opengrep and import-linter with rule sets we measured.
  • Project knowledge: partly, through small guards each project writes in its own .healthkit/ folder.
  • Behaviour: never by rules. That is the job of tests, QA and people.

So the README says it plainly: healthkit can never judge whether the logic is right, whether it is secure, or whether the design is right. A clean run means "nothing it knows about", never "safe".

Five design decisions

1. AI is not in the gate. The pass/fail decision uses deterministic rules and tools only. AI review is advisory and never blocks. When AI spots a recurring problem, it becomes a rule, and the rule enforces it.

2. Check the lines you changed. healthkit review --base main checks only the lines your branch changed, so an old codebase does not bury you in history. scan and baseline exist for when you want the whole module.

3. The agent writing code cannot quietly change the referee. Most runs are done by AI coding agents before they hand over work. An agent that can edit the rules, add exceptions or exclude folders can make any check pass. So any change to the .healthkit/ settings, and any # noqa that switches a check off, is flagged as needs human approval, even when everything else is clean. We found the gap by hand: the default excluded everything under migrations/, so real code placed there would never be checked. The default now matches only Django's generated migration names.

4. Weak rules warn, they don't block. One rule found real bugs but was right only about half the time on code it was never tuned on (41% and 55% on two projects). It ships as worth a look:: printed and counted, but it never fails the run. A rule moves to blocking only after reaching 70% on unseen code from at least two projects.

5. "Could not check" is never a pass. Exit codes: 0 nothing found, 1 problems, 2 could not check, 3 only a settings change that needs approval. This came from a tool that reported zero unused functions on code with known dead code. Its verification step had timed out and it quietly withheld everything. "0 findings" can mean "did not run". Every adapter now surfaces the tool's own errors next to its findings.

Catching bugs nobody wrote a rule for

Behaviour bugs need a different approach. healthkit api sends good and bad input to every route of an API (via Schemathesis) and treats any server error as a finding. On the test project it found six real crashes, none of which had a rule.

It also answers a question rules can't: can this user see that data?

  • Multiple users: you give it one token per role, for example an admin, a plain user, and a user in another organisation. Every route is tested as each of them, and it checks that one user cannot read another's objects.
  • Access policy: you write down who must be refused where, and any successful answer is a finding: 
[[api.deny]]
user = "HK_TEACHER"
routes = ["GET /people/students", "GET /finances/**"]
reason = "a teacher sees only her own class"
  • The size of a leak: a finding says how much came back (got 200 (469 records) or got 200 (empty)), so a real leak stands out from an empty list. It shows only the count, never the data.
  • Read-only by default: it sends GET requests only, unless you add --allow-writes. We learned this the hard way: a sweep that wrote data deactivated the user that one crashing input needed, so the next sweep found 4 crashes instead of 6. Neither bug had been fixed.

Building it with AI agents: the lessons

healthkit was built with AI assistance under a written working agreement, one rule for each thing research says AI-written code tends to miss. Three lessons stood out:

  • An agent's "refuted" is not evidence. A verifier agent marked a real bug as not a bug by misreading the code it quoted. It had been asked to run a test and did not. A two-minute script proved the bug. Now any claim, from any agent, counts only with output that was actually run.
  • Verifiers drift to what is easy to confirm. Asked to try new ways around the gate, a verifier agent re-tested the gaps we had already closed and skipped the new ideas. The first new idea we tried by hand was a complete bypass. Now every verification brief lists the cases that must be tried, and the report is checked case by case.
  • Measure before building, and you may build less. We planned a similarity engine to find copied code. Measuring first, it found 1 of 4 real cases. Two cheap checks of about 110 lines did better, and found a rate-limit bug and a security helper copied with the opposite behaviour, neither of which any review had named.

Try it 

uv tool install git+https://github.com/paudelbaibhav/healthkit
healthkit review --base main

It works on any Python project, with extra checks for Django and web APIs. Output comes as text, JSON for agents, Markdown for pull-request comments, or GitHub annotations.

Code, decisions and every lesson we wrote down: github.com/paudelbaibhav/healthkit. It's MIT licensed, with about 220 tests.

What does your team rely on to review AI-written code: rules, AI reviewers, or people? I'd like to know what has actually worked for you.

title: New Windows program uses artificial intelligence to evaluate victims' stolen data
description:
Security researchers have discovered VOLTA-AUTODOXER, a new Windows infostealer that uses large language models to analyze stolen data.

The malware harvests credentials, session tokens, and crypto keys, then employs models via OpenRouter to rank the victim's financial worth before exfiltration.

The program, known as VOLTA, infiltrates computers and collects massive amounts of personal data. Specifically, it can steal saved passwords, digital browsing traces, payment details, digital cryptocurrency wallets, and login profiles from various applications.

How stolen data is organized

After collecting the data, the program searches the victim's emails for receipts from orders and purchases to confirm their home address. It then creates a folder with information that includes location, address, employer, card details, and an estimate of the value of the bills.

To process this data, the program connects to artificial intelligence services. It primarily uses the Claude system, while it has a mechanism for automatically switching to other systems, such as Kimi and Gemini, in case the first system refuses to respond. A special instruction text asks the artificial intelligence to act as an analyst, assessing the value of the victim and how careful he was with his safety.

How the data reaches the perpetrators

All data and analysis results are sent to the perpetrators via the Telegram application at three different stages of the process.

title: How to Learn React: A Simple Beginner Roadmap (Step by Step)
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

To learn React as a beginner, follow this order: be comfortable with HTML, CSS and modern JavaScript first, then learn components and JSX, then props and state, then events and forms, then fetching data, and finally routing and a framework such as Next.js — building one small project at each step instead of only watching tutorials. Most beginners who follow this sequence can build real React apps within two to three months of steady practice.

Step 0: The Skills React Assumes You Already Have

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, so it stands on three legs: HTML for structure, CSS for appearance, and JavaScript for behaviour. You do not need to be an expert in any of them, but three JavaScript ideas must feel friendly before React will make sense: arrow functions, array methods such as map and filter, and destructuring. These three appear in almost every React component ever written, and struggling with them inside React feels twice as hard as learning them in plain JavaScript first.

Give this foundation two honest weeks if it is new. Build one small static page, then make one tiny JavaScript app — a counter, a to-do list without a framework — so variables, functions and DOM updates are familiar territory. Skipping this step is the single most common reason beginners conclude that React is "too hard", when really the missing piece was never React at all. The official React Learn course itself opens by assuming this background, which tells you how universal the advice is.

Step 1: Components and JSX — Thinking in Pieces

React's central idea is the component: a small, reusable piece of interface written as a JavaScript function. A button, a card, a whole page — each is a component, and big interfaces are assembled from small ones the way a wall is assembled from bricks. Your first milestone is writing a component, displaying it inside another component, and passing it simple content.

Inside components you will write JSX, the HTML-like syntax that lives inside JavaScript. If JSX still feels like a stranger, our explainer on what JSX is in React walks through it with small examples before you go further. The screenshot in this article, from the official React Learn quick start, shows the pattern in its purest form: a MyButton component defined once and then nested inside MyApp with a single tag. That nesting — components inside components — is the entire architecture of every React app you will ever open, from a practice counter to the dashboard of a company you have heard of.

The official React Learn "Quick Start" page on react.dev — a component nested inside another component.

Step 2: Props and State — Data That Flows and Data That Changes

With static components under your fingers, learn the two words that run every React app. Props are data a parent hands down to a child — the title and price given to a product card. State is data a component remembers and changes itself — the count in a counter, the text in a search box — using the useState hook. When state changes, React redraws the component automatically, which is the moment the library stops feeling like markup and starts feeling alive.

Our detailed guide to React components, props and state is the natural deep-dive for this step, with examples of each idea separately. Practise with a small project that needs both: a list of books or products rendered from an array, where each card receives props, and a favourite button on each card keeps its own state. If you can build that without copying, you understand the heart of React — honestly, a large fraction of professional React work is this exact step wearing better clothes.

Step 3: Events, Forms and Lists

Next, make your interfaces respond. Handling a click with onClick, reading an input with an onChange handler and controlled form fields, and rendering lists with map plus a stable key for each item: together these turn static screens into working tools. Build a small expense tracker or a notes app at this stage. It will be ugly. It will also teach you more about state than a week of videos, because every bug in a form is a state lesson arriving exactly on schedule.

While building, adopt the habit that separates calm developers from frustrated ones: when something does not update, ask "which state should have changed?" before changing any code. In React, the screen is a reflection of state, so a wrong screen almost always means wrong or stale state — a debugging compass that will serve you in every project on this roadmap and beyond it.

Step 4: Fetching Data and Talking to APIs

Real apps display data they do not own, so step four is loading data from an API with fetch inside the useEffect hook, showing a loading message while waiting, and handling the bad day when the request fails. Public practice APIs offer free data about weather, movies, products and countries, so you can build a respectable little app without writing any backend at all.

The React installation guide is worth a visit around this stage too, because it explains how real projects are set up with modern tooling, instead of the single-file practice pages most beginners start with. Set your practice project up the proper way once — folders, components in separate files, a sensible structure — and later steps, especially sharing your work with employers, become dramatically easier.

Step 5: Routing, Next.js and the Road Beyond

Stage Learn Project to build
Foundation HTML, CSS, modern JavaScript A static page and a plain-JavaScript to-do list
Basics Components, JSX A personal profile page made of components
Core Props, state, useState A product list with favourite buttons
Interactive Events, forms, lists and keys An expense tracker or notes app
Real data useEffect and fetch A weather or movie search app
Beyond Routing, then Next.js basics A small multi-page blog or portfolio

Once single-page apps feel comfortable, learn routing — how an app shows different pages without reloading — and then meet Next.js, the framework built on React that adds routing, server rendering and structure out of the box. Our comparison of React vs Next.js explains what the framework adds and why learning plain React first makes Next.js feel like a helpful upgrade instead of a second mountain. After that, the road branches by taste: styling libraries, testing, TypeScript, or deeper state tools — all optional side quests once the main path is walked.

The Habits That Make the Roadmap Work

A roadmap is only paper without habits. Build something at every step, however small, because projects expose the gaps that tutorials politely hide. Type code yourself instead of copying it, and when an error appears, read it before searching it — React's error messages are unusually honest by industry standards. Finally, keep every project, even the embarrassing early ones, in Git repositories: six months from now, that visible trail from counter app to data-fetching app is the most convincing portfolio a beginner can show.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to learn React?

With the JavaScript foundation in place and steady practice of an hour or two a day, most beginners build comfortable, real projects in two to three months. Reaching job-ready depth takes longer, but the first working apps come quickly.

Should I learn React or JavaScript first?

JavaScript first — at least arrow functions, array methods and destructuring. React is written in JavaScript, so every gap in the language becomes a gap in React, only harder to see.

Is React hard for beginners?

The core ideas — components, props, state — are genuinely simple. Beginners struggle mainly when the JavaScript foundation is missing, or when they try to learn React, routing and a framework all in the same week.

Do I need Next.js to get a React job?

Not at the start. Employers expect strong React fundamentals first; Next.js is a valuable second skill that builds directly on them, which is why it sits at the end of this roadmap.

Conclusion

Learn React in the order it builds on itself: JavaScript foundations, components and JSX, props and state, events and forms, fetching data, then routing and Next.js — with a small, finished project proving each step. Follow that sequence patiently and React stops being a wall of new words, and becomes what it really is: a simple idea, applied one component at a time.

title: ParticleDB's Premature 'Full ACID' Claims Invalidated by Jepsen Testing Across Versions 1.1.4 to 1.1.18.11.rc-22
description:
Introduction

ParticleDB, a distributed database system, has boldly claimed "Full ACID" compliance—a promise that, if true, would ensure Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability in its data operations. However, recent testing by Jepsen across versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 has invalidated these claims, revealing that ParticleDB’s assertions were premature. Jepsen’s investigation uncovered critical discrepancies between ParticleDB’s marketing promises and its actual performance, raising concerns about the system’s reliability in mission-critical applications.

The core issue lies in ParticleDB’s inadequate implementation of ACID properties. For instance, Jepsen’s tests exposed scenarios where atomicity—the guarantee that transactions are all-or-nothing—failed under specific workloads. This failure occurred due to race conditions in the system’s concurrency control mechanisms, where simultaneous write operations caused partial transaction commits, leading to data inconsistencies. Additionally, isolation—the property ensuring transactions execute independently—was compromised, as read operations occasionally returned stale data, a direct result of oversights in ParticleDB’s testing and validation processes.

Compounding the problem is the miscommunication or overstatement of ACID compliance in ParticleDB’s marketing materials. While the system may handle certain ACID properties under ideal conditions, Jepsen’s tests revealed that these guarantees break down under stress. For example, high-throughput workloads triggered network partitions, causing the system to prioritize availability over consistency, a trade-off that violates ACID principles. This discrepancy between marketing claims and real-world performance risks eroding trust among users and developers who rely on ACID compliance for critical applications.

The stakes are high. If ParticleDB’s claims remain unaddressed, users could face data inconsistencies and system failures in production environments. For instance, financial systems relying on ParticleDB might process duplicate transactions or lose data, leading to financial losses. To mitigate this risk, ParticleDB must re-evaluate its implementation, strengthen its testing processes, and communicate its capabilities with transparency. Only then can it regain credibility in a market where ACID compliance is non-negotiable.

Methodology

Jepsen’s investigation into ParticleDB’s “Full ACID” claims spanned versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22, employing a rigorous testing framework designed to stress-test the database’s adherence to Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability guarantees. The process involved:

  • Tooling: Jepsen utilized its proprietary testing suite, which injects controlled chaos into distributed systems to expose inconsistencies. This included network partitions, latency spikes, and concurrent transaction workloads to simulate real-world stress conditions.
  • Criteria for ACID Evaluation:
    • Atomicity: Transactions were tested for all-or-nothing execution. Jepsen observed partial commits under high concurrency, where race conditions in ParticleDB’s concurrency control mechanisms allowed incomplete transactions to persist, deforming data integrity.
    • Consistency: The system failed to maintain a valid state post-transaction, with stale data returned during read operations. This was traced to oversights in ParticleDB’s validation processes, where read-write conflicts were not adequately isolated.
    • Isolation: Jepsen detected dirty reads and non-repeatable reads, indicating compromised isolation levels. This occurred due to insufficient locking mechanisms, causing concurrent transactions to interfere with each other’s state.
    • Durability: Under network partitions, ParticleDB prioritized availability over durability, leading to data loss in certain scenarios. The system’s failure to flush writes to disk before acknowledging transactions expanded the risk of data corruption.
  • Edge-Case Analysis: Jepsen specifically targeted high-throughput workloads and network partitions, conditions under which ParticleDB’s ACID guarantees broke down. For instance, network latency exceeding 500ms triggered a consistency-availability tradeoff, forcing the system to violate ACID principles to maintain responsiveness.

The testing revealed a causal chain: inadequate implementation of ACID properties → stress-induced failures → observable data inconsistencies. ParticleDB’s claims were deemed premature due to these systemic oversights, highlighting the need for robust testing and transparent communication in distributed database systems.

Findings: Jepsen’s Investigation Exposes ParticleDB’s Premature ACID Claims

Jepsen’s rigorous testing of ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 revealed systemic discrepancies between the database’s “Full ACID” claims and its actual performance under stress. Across six critical scenarios, ParticleDB failed to uphold Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability guarantees, exposing flaws in its implementation, testing processes, and marketing communications.

Scenario-Based Failures: Mechanisms and Observable Effects

  • Atomicity Failure (Race Conditions):

Under high concurrency, ParticleDB’s transaction manager failed to enforce all-or-nothing execution. Race conditions in the concurrency control mechanism allowed partial commits, where only subsets of operations were applied. This deformed transaction integrity, leading to data inconsistencies observable in financial ledger-like workloads (e.g., account balances mismatching transaction histories).

  • Consistency Failure (Stale Data Reads):

Read operations returned outdated data due to oversights in isolating read-write conflicts. ParticleDB’s validation process failed to lock shared resources during writes, allowing concurrent reads to access intermediate states. This expanded the window for stale data exposure, particularly in inventory management scenarios where stock counts fluctuated unpredictably.

  • Isolation Failure (Dirty Reads):

Insufficient locking mechanisms enabled dirty reads, where transactions observed uncommitted changes from concurrent operations. This occurred because ParticleDB’s isolation levels were not strictly enforced, allowing interference between transactions. In ticketing systems, for example, this caused phantom bookings where seats appeared available but were already reserved.

  • Durability Failure (Network Partitions):

During network partitions (>500ms latency), ParticleDB prioritized availability over durability. Writes were acknowledged before being flushed to disk, leading to data loss when nodes failed. This broke the durability guarantee, as critical updates (e.g., financial transactions) vanished post-recovery, violating ACID principles.

  • Edge-Case Breakdown (High-Throughput Workloads):

Under extreme throughput (>10,000 ops/sec), ParticleDB’s consistency-availability tradeoff mechanism heated up, forcing ACID violations to maintain responsiveness. Network partitions triggered a failover to eventual consistency, expanding the risk of stale data propagation. This was observable in real-time analytics systems, where dashboards displayed conflicting metrics.

  • Marketing Discrepancy (Overstated Compliance):

ParticleDB’s marketing materials claimed “Full ACID” without qualifying edge-case limitations. This miscommunication created a gap between user expectations and system capabilities, eroding trust. Developers relying on ACID guarantees for critical applications faced unforeseen risks, such as financial losses from inconsistent transaction processing.

Causal Chain and Optimal Remediation

The root cause of ParticleDB’s failures lies in inadequate ACID implementation, compounded by oversights in testing and validation processes. Stress-induced failures exposed systemic weaknesses, leading to observable data inconsistencies. To address these issues:

  • Re-evaluate Implementation: Strengthen concurrency control mechanisms to eliminate race conditions and enforce strict isolation levels.
  • Enhance Testing: Incorporate chaos-injection testing to simulate edge cases like network partitions and high-throughput workloads.
  • Transparent Communication: Clearly document ACID compliance limitations in marketing materials to manage user expectations.

Rule for Remediation: If stress-induced failures expose ACID violations, use chaos-injection testing to identify edge cases and re-architect concurrency control to enforce guarantees under all conditions.

Failure to address these issues risks systemic breakdowns in production environments, particularly for mission-critical applications. ParticleDB must act decisively to restore credibility and ensure data integrity.

Analysis: Why ParticleDB’s 'Full ACID' Claims Were Premature

ParticleDB’s assertion of "Full ACID" compliance crumbled under Jepsen’s scrutiny, revealing a cascade of technical oversights that rendered the claim premature. The root cause lies in the inadequate implementation of ACID properties, exacerbated by testing and validation processes that failed to simulate real-world stress conditions. This analysis dissects the causal chain, edge-case breakdowns, and practical implications for users and ParticleDB’s reputation.

Causal Chain: From Implementation Flaws to Observable Failures

The breakdown begins with ParticleDB’s concurrency control mechanisms, which failed to enforce atomicity under high-throughput workloads. Race conditions in the transaction manager allowed partial commits, violating the all-or-nothing principle of atomicity. For instance, in financial systems, this led to ledger mismatches where debits and credits failed to balance, a direct consequence of the system’s inability to handle concurrent transactions without interference.

Isolation failures further compounded the issue. Weak locking mechanisms permitted dirty reads, where transactions observed uncommitted changes from other transactions. This resulted in phantom bookings in ticketing systems, where seats appeared available but were already reserved, a clear violation of isolation guarantees.

Under stress, ParticleDB prioritized availability over consistency, a tradeoff that violated ACID principles. Network partitions exceeding 500ms latency triggered this breakdown, causing the system to acknowledge writes before flushing them to disk. This led to data loss post-recovery, as unpersisted changes were discarded during system restarts.

Edge-Case Breakdown: High Throughput and Network Partitions

ParticleDB’s claims faltered at the edges of operational capacity. At >10,000 ops/sec, the system defaulted to eventual consistency, propagating stale data in real-time analytics. This edge-case behavior was not documented in marketing materials, creating a trust gap between expectations and reality. For mission-critical applications, this discrepancy translates to unforeseen risks, such as financial losses from inconsistent transaction processing.

Practical Implications: Eroding Trust and Systemic Risks

The premature "Full ACID" claims have tangible consequences. Developers relying on ParticleDB for critical applications face data inconsistencies, system failures, and potential financial losses. For example, inventory systems experienced unpredictable stock counts due to stale data reads, while ticketing platforms suffered from overbookings. These failures stem from the misalignment between marketing promises and technical reality, a gap that erodes trust and undermines ParticleDB’s credibility.

Remediation: A Rule-Based Approach

To address these issues, ParticleDB must adopt a chaos-injection testing framework to simulate edge cases like network partitions and high-throughput workloads. This approach exposes systemic weaknesses before deployment. Additionally, re-architecting concurrency control to enforce strict isolation and eliminate race conditions is critical. A rule for remediation: If stress-induced failures expose ACID violations, apply chaos-injection testing and re-architect concurrency control to enforce guarantees under all conditions.

Transparent communication is equally vital. ParticleDB must clearly document ACID limitations in marketing materials, avoiding overstatements that create false expectations. This transparency rebuilds trust and ensures users understand the system’s capabilities and boundaries.

Conclusion: The Cost of Premature Claims

ParticleDB’s premature "Full ACID" claims highlight the dangers of overstating technical capabilities without rigorous validation. The causal chain—from implementation flaws to observable failures—underscores the need for robust testing and transparent communication. For users, the stakes are clear: unaddressed issues lead to systemic breakdowns in production, particularly for mission-critical applications. ParticleDB’s path forward requires not just technical remediation but a commitment to honesty and accountability in an era where data integrity is non-negotiable.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Jepsen’s rigorous testing of ParticleDB across versions 1.1.4 to 1.1.18.11.rc-22 has conclusively demonstrated that the database’s claims of “Full ACID” compliance are premature. The investigation uncovered systemic failures in Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability under stress, driven by flawed concurrency control and inadequate testing processes. These issues manifest as data inconsistencies, phantom reads, and durability compromises, particularly under high-throughput workloads and network partitions. The root cause lies in ParticleDB’s inability to enforce strict ACID guarantees when faced with edge cases, such as concurrent transactions exceeding 10,000 ops/sec or network latencies surpassing 500ms.

The causal chain is clear: inadequate ACID implementation leads to stress-induced failures, which in turn result in observable data inconsistencies. For instance, race conditions in the transaction manager cause partial commits, while weak locking mechanisms allow dirty reads, directly impacting mission-critical applications like financial ledgers and ticketing systems. The prioritization of availability over durability during network partitions further exacerbates the risk of data loss post-recovery.

Recommendations for ParticleDB

  • Re-evaluate Implementation: Strengthen concurrency control mechanisms to eliminate race conditions and enforce strict isolation. For example, replace weak locks with multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) to prevent dirty reads and ensure atomicity under high concurrency.
  • Enhance Testing: Adopt chaos-injection testing to simulate edge cases such as network partitions and extreme throughput. This will expose weaknesses in the system’s ACID guarantees and ensure robustness under real-world stress.
  • Transparent Communication: Clearly document ACID limitations in marketing materials. For instance, specify that the system defaults to eventual consistency above 10,000 ops/sec, avoiding overstated claims that erode trust.

Steps for Users to Ensure Data Integrity

  • Validate Claims Independently: Conduct stress tests using tools like Jepsen to verify ACID compliance under specific workloads. Focus on edge cases such as high concurrency and network partitions.
  • Implement Redundancy: For mission-critical applications, use external mechanisms like distributed locks or compensating transactions to mitigate risks of partial commits and data inconsistencies.
