  • Monitor for Anomalies: Deploy monitoring systems to detect anomalies like stale reads or phantom writes, which indicate ACID violations. For example, track transaction latency spikes as early indicators of stress-induced failures.

Professional Judgment

ParticleDB’s premature “Full ACID” claims highlight a broader industry issue: the gap between marketing promises and technical reality. To rebuild trust, ParticleDB must not only address the technical shortcomings but also adopt a culture of transparency and rigorous validation. The optimal remediation strategy involves a combination of re-architecting concurrency control, chaos-injection testing, and honest communication. Failure to act will result in systemic breakdowns, particularly in production environments where ACID guarantees are non-negotiable. The rule is clear: if stress-induced failures expose ACID violations, apply chaos-injection testing and re-architect concurrency control to enforce guarantees under all conditions.

title: E-commerce checkout: technical fixes that reduce drop-off
description:
Some people will always leave a checkout. They were comparing prices, or the shipping cost surprised them, or they got distracted. That part is about pricing and policy.

But a share of abandoned orders comes from things developers can fix: a slow page, a forced sign-up, a payment error nobody understands, a form that fights the customer. These are the cheapest sales to win back, because the customer had already decided to buy.

Here are the four areas I'd check first.

1. Load time on the checkout itself

Teams optimise the home page and product pages, then forget the checkout. It's often the heaviest page on the site, because it loads payment scripts, address lookups, fraud checks and every tracking tag marketing ever added.

  • Measure the checkout separately, on a mid-range phone over mobile data.
  • Remove scripts that don't belong. Chat widgets, heatmaps and review widgets rarely need to run on payment steps.
  • Load payment and address scripts when needed, not on page load if the customer won't reach that step for a while.
  • Never block the page on a slow third party. 
<!-- Load non-critical scripts without blocking the page -->
<script src="/js/address-lookup.js" defer></script>

2. Guest checkout

Forcing account creation before payment is one of the most common reasons people give up. They came to buy something, not to start a relationship with a password.

  • Offer guest checkout by default. Ask for an email for the receipt, nothing more.
  • Offer an account after the order, on the confirmation page: "Save your details for next time?" At that point it's a convenience, not a barrier.
  • Let returning customers sign in, but don't make it the first thing they see.

If your platform links guest orders to an account later by email, make sure that only happens after the customer verifies the address, so nobody can see someone else's orders.

3. Payment errors

A declined card is stressful. A declined card with the message "Error 402" or "Something went wrong" loses the sale.

  • Map payment provider error codes to plain messages that tell the customer what to do next.
  • Keep everything they typed when a payment fails. Don't make them re-enter their address.
  • Prevent double charges. Disable the pay button while the request is in flight, and use the provider's idempotency key feature so a retry doesn't create a second charge.
  • Log failures with the reason code so you can see whether a pattern is a customer issue or a configuration issue. Log the reason code and order ID, never card numbers or the security code. 
// Map provider decline codes to messages a customer can act on.
// Check the exact codes against your payment provider's documentation.
const DECLINE_MESSAGES = {
  card_declined: "Your bank declined this card. Try another card or contact your bank.",
  insufficient_funds: "Your card was declined for insufficient funds. Try another card.",
  expired_card: "This card has expired. Please check the date or use another card.",
  incorrect_cvc: "The security code doesn't match. Please check the 3 or 4 digits on your card.",
  processing_error: "We couldn't reach your bank just now. Please try again in a moment.",
};

function paymentErrorMessage(code) {
  return DECLINE_MESSAGES[code]
    || "Your payment didn't go through. Please try again or use a different card.";
}

const payButton = document.querySelector("#pay-button");

async function submitPayment(submitFn) {
  payButton.disabled = true;          // prevent double clicks
  payButton.textContent = "Processing…";
  try {
    const result = await submitFn();  // your provider's confirm call
    if (result && result.error) throw result.error; // some providers return errors instead of throwing
    // success: leave the button disabled and move to the confirmation page
  } catch (err) {
    showError(paymentErrorMessage(err.decline_code || err.code)); // showError: your own UI helper
    payButton.disabled = false;       // re-enable only after a failure
    payButton.textContent = "Pay now";
  }
}

4. Form validation

Checkout forms ask for a lot, so every bit of friction adds up.

  • Validate as people go, when they leave a field, not only when they press the final button.
  • Accept input the way people type it. Strip spaces from phone numbers instead of rejecting them, and use your payment provider's hosted card fields (they handle card formatting for you and keep card data off your servers). Don't force one postcode format for every country.
  • Use the right input types and autocomplete attributes so phones show the right keyboard and browsers can fill saved details.
  • Show errors next to the field, in plain words, and move focus to the first error. Put payment errors in a role="alert" area, and set aria-invalid="true" on fields with errors.
  • Don't ask twice. Default the billing address to the shipping address. 
<label for="ship-name">Full name</label>
<input id="ship-name" name="name" autocomplete="shipping name" required>

<label for="ship-postcode">Postcode</label>
<input id="ship-postcode" name="postcode" autocomplete="shipping postal-code" required>

<label for="ship-phone">Phone (for delivery updates)</label>
<input id="ship-phone" name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel" aria-describedby="ship-phone-error">
<p id="ship-phone-error" class="field-error" hidden></p>

<div id="payment-error" role="alert"></div>

<label><input type="checkbox" id="same-billing" checked> Billing address is the same</label>

// Tidy spaces, dashes and brackets when the customer leaves the field
const phoneInput = document.querySelector("#ship-phone");
phoneInput.addEventListener("blur", () => {
  phoneInput.value = phoneInput.value.replace(/[\s()-]/g, "");
});

How to know it worked

Before changing anything, set up a simple funnel in your analytics: cart, checkout start, shipping, payment, order complete. Note where people drop off. Then ship one fix at a time and watch the step it should affect. Combined with your payment failure logs, that tells you which fixes are paying for themselves and where to look next.

Checkout work isn't glamorous. But it's the one place on the site where every improvement lands on customers who'd already decided to pay.

Ahmed Vaseer is Founder & CEO - Ingenious Concepts. 80+ projects, ISO 27001 certified via Global CB.

title: Java learning series | Day- 4 Method, Constructor.
description:
What is Method?

Reusable block of code or instruction to perform a specific task with their name, when is called.
Methods allow you to write code once and reuse it across your application, making your program modular, readable, and easy to maintain.

Structure of Method in java

The method declaration consists of six components, 

Modifier returnType  methodName(parameterList){
// method code (line of code to execute)
return value ; (optional , based on returnType) 
}
  • Modifier --->Define the visibility or access type(eg.public private, protected.
  • Return type ---> The data type of the value(int , string) **returned by the method, or **void if the method does not return a value.
  • Method Name ---> The unique identifier used to call the method, typically returned in camelCase , the method name must be in verb as lowercase.
  • ParameterList ---> Input value passed into method while calling it will be received by parameterlist().
  • Method code ---> Actual code statement what the method to do , enclosed with curly braces{}.

1)Simple Method - No Return type and No Parameter, 

public class Greeting{

public static void main(String[] args){

Greeting Mygreet = new Greeting();
Mygreet.greet();
}

public void greet(){

System.out.println("Welcome");
}

}
  • void --> There is no need for return value we use void.

2) A method with return type and parameter, 

public class Calculator{

public static void main(String[] args){
Calculator myCal = new Calculator();
int result = myCal.add(10,20);
system.out.println("Addition :" result);

}
public int add(int no1 , int no2){
 return no1 + no2 ;
} 

}

Here the return type is int because the return value is int , if the return value is String the return type must be string.

Method overloading

same method name with different arugments or different type(data type) of arguments .
other name of method overloading is compile time polymorphism.

public class Calculator{

public static void main(String[] args){
Calculator myCal = new Calculator();
myCal.add(10,20);
myCal.add(10,30,40);
myCal.add(10);
myCal.add();

}
public int add(int no1 , int no2){
 System.out,println(no1 + no2);
} 

public int add(int no1 , int no2 , int no3){
 System.out,println(no1 + no2 + no3);
}

public int add(int no1){
 System.out,println(no1);
}

public int add(){
 System.out,println(no arguments);
}

what is constructor ?

  • A Special block of code that automatically executes when the object is created.
  • It initially asign a value to the non-static variable.
  • Called automatically when object is created.
  • Initializing object specific values

Rule of creating constructor:

  • same name --> constructor name must be in match the class name.
  • No Return type ---> It can't have return type (even void) .if we add any return type java will treats as regular function.
  • There is an default constructor with no arguments if we modified the default constructor with arugments were we want to create a new contructor for no arguments.

Types of constructor;

1) Default Constructor

  • Defined by java complier if you create an empty object with no arguments. 
public class Car{

public Car(){           # default constructor hide by java                                          

}

public static void main(String[] args){

Car myCar1 =  new Car();      
}
}
2) parameterized Constructor
  • Accepts arguments to dynamically initialize an object with distinct data at the moment it is created. 
public class Car{

String brand ;
int model;

public Car(String brand , int model){
this.brand = brand;
this.model = model;                                                  
}

public static void main(String[] args){

Car myCar1 = new Car("BMW", 2026);  


}
}
3) No-Argument constructor
  • Written explicitly by the programmer to assign custom default values, taking zero parameters.because once we modified an default constructor with parameters the default constructor is invalid. 
public class Car{

String brand ;
int model;

public Car(String brand , int model){
this.brand = brand;
this.model = model;                                                  
}

public car(){    #for no arguments
}

public static void main(String[] args){
Car myCar1 = new Car("BMW", 2026);   
car myCar3 = new Car(); 
}
}

Constructor overloading ;

  • Define multiple constructors in a single class as long as they have different parameter lists (different types, numbers, or order of arguments). 
public class Car{

String brand ;
int model;

public Car(String brand , int model){
this.brand = brand;
this.model = model;                                                  
}

public Car(int model ,String brand){
this.brand = brand;
this.model = model;                                                  
}

public car(){    #for no arguments
}

public static void main(String[] args){

Car myCar1 = new Car("BMW", 2026);   
Car myCar2 = new Car(2026 , "Bmw");
car myCar3 = new Car(); 
}
}

title: Our Capture Script Filmed the Test Harness, Not Lullwood
description:
When a video, a build or a report looks wrong, look at the artefact before you theorise about the code that made it. We relearned this on Lullwood, our free browser horror game built in three.js and Next.js. A short gameplay clip for Bluesky cost six agent working sessions and two failed reviews, and shipped nothing. Two source-cited root causes were both wrong. One frame pulled from the video showed the real problem: our capture script was recording a synthetic test scene, not the game.

The setup

Lullwood is built by Claude agents, so "a heartbeat" below means one working session of one agent. The clip was meant to be a short vertical video of a player holding still while a wolf sniffs past. A Playwright script drove headless Chromium against our own WebGL build and recorded the page. The capture tooling worked exactly as designed. The scene it was told to record was the problem.

Four takes, two failures

The first two takes were too short, and the captions we had written existed only in a text file next to the video, never in the pixels. Neither reached review.

The third take ran 23.8 seconds and opened on a flat, pale daytime gradient with no fog and no trees. That was qaWorld=micro, a test world that stands in for the night forest. The status bar had already spelled out the mechanic in text before the wolf appeared. Failed.

The fourth take ran about 23 seconds and fixed the empty world. It still opened on the full game HUD, then held a blown-out white band across the top of the frame for twenty seconds, with an untextured, motionless wolf sitting under it. Failed again. It had passed the length and resolution checks (about 23 seconds, 720x1280).

Two root causes, both wrong

Between those takes, two diagnoses went onto the ticket. Both were specific and both cited the engine source.

The first said the wolf could not see the player. At night its detection range plateaus at 6.16 units, and the staged hiding spot needed 6.3 to trigger. True as far as it went. The real culprit was a different setting, a test-world detection scalar that had nothing to do with the time of day.

The second said the hide camera was sitting inside the bush mesh, and that point-blank exposure was blowing out the picture. It came with a fix: re-stage the shot just before or after the hide beat. That would have bought a fifth take and a third failure. A single frame at the 22-second mark showed the player standing in open forest with no bush anywhere in shot, and the same white band still across the top.

Pulling that frame is one command, ffmpeg -ss 22 -i clip.webm -frames:v 1 frame.png. Our environment had no ffmpeg on the path, which did not help. Playwright ships a bundled binary.

What was actually wrong

The script called a QA hook built for engine tests. That hook throws out the real forest and rebuilds a small synthetic one from a short list of arguments: a bush, a wolf, nothing else. No argument puts real terrain, lighting or art into the frame, because it was never meant to. We were filming the test harness and calling it a shot of the game.

What nearly buried the answer was a healthy part of the pipeline. A 16:9 capture in the same folder was dark, foggy and exactly on-brand, which proved the renderer was fine. It was also filed as clip-wolf-16x9.webm, and it is the title screen. There is no wolf in it. Something that works is the best cover for something broken sitting next to it, and for most of an afternoon it argued for "this is a headless rendering limit".

Why this is not a game story

Every team that has trusted a green run over the thing the run produced has been here. The pipeline passed, the numbers matched the spec, and the artefact was still wrong. Reasoning about what a build should put on screen is still reasoning. It gave us two confident wrong answers in a row, and a wrong diagnosis costs more than no diagnosis, because it is actionable. "It's the bush" sends you to re-stage a shot that could never work. "I don't know yet" sends you to go and look.

What we changed

  • Footage for clips now comes from the live site or a production build, never the QA hook.
  • Before a root cause goes on a ticket, someone pulls the frame and looks at it. Container measurements come second.
  • The clip itself is cancelled.

We wrote the original, longer account on the Lullwood devlog. If you want the game behind the story, Lullwood is free in the browser and needs no signup.

We're one human founder plus a fleet of Claude agents building Lullwood in the open.

We filmed the QA harness, not the game: the Lullwood devlog post
Play Lullwood free in the browser

title: A 100% AI Eval Score Is a Red Flag, Not a Win
description:
A 100% AI Eval Score Is a Red Flag, Not a Win

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

In April 2026, a team at UC Berkeley's RDI lab ran an automated scanning agent against eight of the most-cited AI benchmarks in the industry — SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench, WebArena, FieldWorkArena, CAR-bench, GAIA, and OSWorld. The agent scored 100% on six of them. It didn't solve a single task. On SWE-bench Verified — the benchmark OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have used to compare their coding agents — the exploit was a pytest conftest.py hook that marks every test as "passed." The entire attack surface: the agent and the evaluator ran in the same container.

This is not a theoretical vulnerability. This is the evaluation infrastructure the AI industry currently relies on to compare billion-dollar models. And it's broken.

The demand signal for this piece came from three directions this week: an AI Engineer conference talk titled "If Your AI Scores 100%, Your Eval Is Wrong," OpenAI's own decision to retire SWE-bench Verified after finding 59.4% of audited tasks had flawed test cases, and Epoch AI's independent review rating the benchmark as "Flawed." When the benchmark creators, the benchmark users, and the benchmark auditors all agree the system is broken, it's not a controversy — it's a consensus.

The Berkeley Exploit: A Masterclass in Why Evals Fail

The UC Berkeley team — Hao Wang, Qiuyang Mang, Alvin Cheung, Koushik Sen, and Dawn Song — did not build a better AI model. They built an AI agent whose sole job was to find and exploit weaknesses in evaluation pipelines. The results are staggering:

Benchmark Tasks Exploit Score Method
Terminal-Bench 89 100% Replaced binaries with wrappers that fake pytest output
SWE-bench Verified 500 100% Pytest hook (conftest.py) marks all tests as passing
SWE-bench Pro 731 100% Container parser overwrite
WebArena 812 ~100% Read gold answers via file:// URLs; prompt injection against LLM judge
FieldWorkArena 890 100% Validator only checks if last message is from assistant — {} scores 100%
CAR-bench — 100% Hidden instructions injected into judge prompt
GAIA 165 ~98% Used publicly available answers
OSWorld 369 73% Downloaded gold files into evaluator paths

View the full Berkeley RDI research post →

The Hacker News thread on this research hit 588 points and 143 comments — the AI engineering community's reaction was immediate and pointed:

View the full HN discussion →

The root cause is simple and damning: most agent benchmarks run the agent and the evaluator in the same sandbox. The agent can tamper with the grader. It can overwrite the test harness. It can inject answers into the scoring pipeline. This is the evaluation equivalent of giving a student the answer key and a red pen.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Some benchmark maintainers argue these exploits don't reflect real-world model usage — no commercial lab would ship a conftest.py hack. That misses the point. The Berkeley team explicitly said they weren't accusing current leaders of cheating. Their point is that the loopholes are easy enough that an optimizer could stumble into them. When your gradient descent process is optimizing against a broken eval, you don't need malicious intent to get inflated scores.

The team also released BenchJack, an automated vulnerability scanner for benchmarks — essentially a penetration-testing agent for evaluation pipelines. If your benchmark can't survive BenchJack, it can't be trusted.

OpenAI Walks Away From Its Own Benchmark

In February 2026, OpenAI published a post announcing it would no longer report SWE-bench Verified scores. The reasoning was blunt: the benchmark's tasks come from public repositories that model providers train on. Gains increasingly reflect training exposure — memorization — rather than genuine coding capability. OpenAI's internal audit found that at least 59.4% of frequently-failed tasks had flawed test cases that reject functionally correct patches.

View the OpenAI post →

The Hacker News discussion hit 343 points and 208 comments, with one of SWE-bench's co-creators arguing the benchmark could still be trusted if contamination was accounted for — a position that found little support in the thread:

View the full HN discussion →

That's not a rounding error. More than half of the "hard" problems were hard for the wrong reasons — not because they tested real engineering skill, but because the test harness itself was broken. When your test suite penalizes correct answers, the benchmark isn't measuring what you think it's measuring.

OpenAI now recommends SWE-bench Pro as its successor, which uses rotating held-out problems and addresses some of the contamination issues. But the deeper problem remains: any public benchmark with a static task set will eventually be contaminated. The training data for frontier models now includes most of the internet, including the benchmark's problems and solutions. The half-life of a public eval is shrinking.

View the Epoch AI benchmark review →

Epoch AI, an independent research organization, rated SWE-bench Verified as "Flawed" in their benchmark review, concluding that its static task set means current and future models are likely contaminated. They join a growing chorus of voices arguing that the benchmark has outlived its usefulness.

Goodhart's Law Has Entered the Chat

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." — Charles Goodhart, 1975

The AI industry is living through one of the most expensive demonstrations of Goodhart's Law in history. Contrary Research reports that over $225 million has traded on Polymarket markets that are settled by Arena (formerly LMArena) leaderboard rankings. When that much money rides on a leaderboard position, the incentive to optimize for the metric — rather than the underlying capability — becomes overwhelming.

View the Contrary Research report →

Nick Heiner of Surge AI laid this out in his AI Engineer World's Fair talk, "When Will The Benchmaxxing Plague End?": AI benchmarking has drifted from real-world value because of weak methodology and poor incentives. The cost of building a rigorous large agentic coding benchmark runs into the millions — but the cost of gaming an existing one is near zero.

The benchmaxxing playbook is well-documented at this point:

  1. Data contamination: Train on the benchmark's problems. A January 2026 study measured contamination rates between 1% and 45% across popular benchmarks.
  2. Cherry-picking: Submit only your best-performing configuration. Report numbers from runs that happened to land high.
  3. Saturation: Top models now max out MMLU and SWE-bench while scoring near zero on ARC-AGI-3. The benchmark no longer discriminates between frontier models — it's a ceiling test, not a measure.
  4. Grader manipulation: As Berkeley showed, if your agent can touch the evaluator, it can fake the result.

Alex Duffy of Every.to captured this perfectly in "Benchmarks Are Memes": benchmarks spread like cultural memes, directing which capabilities labs invest in. When the meme is wrong — when it measures memorization instead of reasoning, or gaming instead of capability — the entire field optimizes in the wrong direction.

Andrej Karpathy has been vocal about the state of AI evaluation. His tweet about moving past toy LLM evals — "svg of a pelican on a bicycle" — toward generalized testing garnered 29K likes:

View original post on X →

His separate "Land or Water?" experiment — asking an LLM to classify 16,200 lat/long coordinates — demonstrates what creative, hard-to-game evaluation actually looks like. The models know the answer because they've compressed the internet. That's the point: a novel eval reveals what the model actually learned, not what it memorized from a test bank.

View original post on X →

ℹ️ The self-reported scores problem: When Moonshot AI published Kimi K2 with a roughly 50% score on Humanity's Last Exam, independent testers re-ran it and got 29.4%. Self-reported benchmark numbers from labs have a conflict of interest that's so obvious it would be disqualifying in any other field.

The Verification Crisis

Princeton's Sayash Kapoor has been documenting what he calls "The Missing Science of AI Evaluation" — a thesis presented at Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy. His core finding: flawed evaluation practices have produced overoptimistic accuracy claims in hundreds of published papers across fields from medicine to political science. Evaluation methods have failed to keep pace with deployment, creating a gap where lab performance fails to predict real-world utility.

View the evaluation crisis analysis →

This is the verification crisis. We have:

  • Models that score 100% on benchmarks they can trivially game (Berkeley RDI)
  • Benchmark creators who admit their own benchmarks are contaminated (OpenAI on SWE-bench)
  • Independent auditors who rate major benchmarks as "Flawed" (Epoch AI)
  • Financial markets that settle on leaderboard positions ($225M+ on Polymarket/Arena)
  • Self-reported scores that drop 20+ points under independent testing (Kimi K2)
  • An entire doctoral thesis arguing evaluation science is broken (Kapoor, Princeton)

And yet, companies are making million-dollar procurement decisions — which model to build on, which API to commit to, which vendor to trust — based on these numbers.

💡 The harness matters more than the model. We wrote about this when Dirac took Gemini 3 Flash from 47.8% to 65.2% on TerminalBench — a +17pp swing from harness engineering alone. If the wrapping around the model matters more than the model itself, then the eval's job is to test the system, not the weights. Most evals are still testing the weights.

What Actually Works: Building Evals That Survive Contact With Reality

The Berkeley team's recommendations read like a security audit checklist, because that's exactly what they are:

1. Isolate the evaluator from the agent. Never run them in the same container. Extract artifacts through a controlled channel. If your agent can import the grader, your eval is a theater prop.

2. Keep reference answers secret. Don't publish ground truth for leaderboard splits. Rotate instances. Consider held-out evaluation where the test set changes faster than models can train on it.

3. Test adversarially. Run a null agent (one that does nothing), a random agent, and a prompt-injection agent against your benchmark. A zero-capability agent should score at baseline. If it doesn't, your eval is measuring something other than capability.

4. Treat LLM judge inputs as untrusted. If your eval uses an LLM as a grader — and increasingly they all do — delimit agent content, strip injected instructions, and prefer extracted features over subjective judgments. The arXiv paper "Benchmarking is Broken" makes this case in detail.

5. Build private, held-out eval sets from your own traffic. This is the practitioner takeaway. Public benchmarks are useful for directional signal — they tell you roughly which tier a model is in. But for the ship decision — which model to deploy in production — you need an eval that no model has ever seen, built from your actual use cases, on your actual data distribution.

David Manheim of AI Evaluation Consensus made this point on the Future of Life Institute podcast: the path to reliable evaluation is the same path the security industry has already walked. Red-team your evals. Assume adversarial conditions. Build systems that fail gracefully when assumptions are violated.

What This Means for You

If you're an engineering leader choosing an AI model for production, here's the revised playbook:

Stop trusting single-number leaderboard scores. They are marketing assets, not engineering metrics. The gap between a self-reported 50% and an independent 29.4% should destroy your confidence in any number that hasn't been independently reproduced.

Triangulate across 3-4 diverse benchmarks, then build your own. Use public benchmarks to narrow the field to 2-3 candidates. Then build a private eval from 50-100 real examples from your production traffic. This eval is your actual moat — it reflects your use case, your edge cases, your data distribution. No lab can optimize against it because no lab has seen it.

Evaluate the system, not the model. If harness engineering can swing a score by 17 points on the same model, then model benchmarks are measuring the wrong thing. Evaluate your full stack — model + prompt + retrieval + tools + error handling — against real tasks. This is what the shift to harness leaderboards is about.

Treat "100%" as a bug report. Any eval where your system scores perfectly is testing the wrong thing. If your pass rate is 100%, your eval isn't challenging your system — it's congratulating it. As Ramakrishnan Lokanathan argued in his AI Engineer talk, a 70% pass rate is more informative than 100%, because it means the eval is actually stress-testing the boundaries of what your system can do.

Budget for eval maintenance. Evals rot. As models improve and train on more data, yesterday's held-out set becomes today's training example. Plan to refresh your eval set quarterly, just like you'd rotate encryption keys or update dependency versions.

The Moat Is Verification

The AI industry spent 2024-2025 racing to build the best model. It spent 2026 discovering that we can't agree on what "best" means. The next phase — and the real competitive advantage — is verification: proving that your system actually works on real problems, in production, under adversarial conditions.

The companies that build rigorous, private, continuously-refreshed evaluation infrastructure will make better model choices, catch regressions faster, and ship more reliable products. The companies that keep chasing leaderboard positions will keep getting surprised when their 100%-scoring model fails on the first real-world query.

Berkeley showed us what 100% looks like when the test is broken. The question is what your eval shows you when it's working.

Originally published at ComputeLeap

title: CVE-2026-105483: certificate SAN policy decides the risk
description:
CVE-2026-105483: certificate SAN policy decides the risk

The Node.js bug behind CVE-2026-105483 has a simple defensive lesson: a certificate is valid only for the identity type the client intended to verify. In affected Node.js 24.x and 26.x releases, a fullwidth-digit IPv4 host could be normalized and resolved as an address while tls.checkServerIdentity() evaluated DNS names and the Common Name. The result was a certificate trust decision for the wrong identity class.

Node.js fixed the problem in 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, 2026. The vendor rates it High. The advisory score is CVSS v3.0 7.4 with a network vector and high attack complexity. The CWE is 295, improper certificate validation.

DNS SAN and IP SAN are different promises

A DNS SAN says that the subject is identified by a DNS name. An IP address SAN says that the subject is identified by a literal IP address. Browsers and TLS libraries normally enforce that separation because an address and a name are different identities, even when DNS or an operating system resolver maps one to the other.

The affected Node.js path did not recognize the fullwidth-digit destination as an IP address. It normalized the destination to a normal IPv4 address and connected there. Verification then compared the normalized value with DNS names. A certificate carrying DNS:127.0.0.1 or an applicable DNS wildcard could satisfy that comparison.

The missing control was not a missing signature check. The chain could be trusted. The problem was that the signed identity did not describe the type of endpoint the client believed it was contacting.

Why public CAs and private PKI need separate review

High attack complexity reflects the certificate conditions. The attacker needs a chain trusted by the client and a certificate whose DNS identity matches the address representation used in verification. A public CA policy may restrict issuing DNS names that are numeric IP-looking strings, but an organization cannot assume that every CA in its trust store follows the same issuance profile.

Private PKI deserves direct attention. Internal CAs may issue certificates for test services, ephemeral hosts, or address-like names. Those certificates can be legitimate for their original scope while still becoming dangerous if they are accepted for an IP endpoint the client did not intend to contact.

Teams should inventory trust stores, intermediate authorities, and delegated issuance paths used by Node.js clients. That work is broader than this CVE, but the vulnerability provides a concrete reason to ask whether certificates with address-like DNS SANs are still necessary.

Application behavior that raises risk

The Node.js runtime flaw becomes a security incident only when an application reaches the affected verification path. Look for destinations that can be influenced by a tenant, administrator, integration, webhook, import, or configuration API. Also review connectors that accept an arbitrary endpoint and then attach credentials or sensitive data.

An application that always contacts a fixed DNS name has a smaller practical attack surface. An application that accepts a full URL, extracts its host, connects with Node.js TLS, and sends an API token has a much clearer identity dependency. The certificate certificate requirements still apply, but the attacker's ability to choose the destination representation matters.

Do not infer vulnerability from a hostname that happens to contain Unicode. Trace the exact value through URL parsing, validation, DNS resolution, and the TLS call. Record whether the application expects a DNS name, an IP address, or both, and whether the expected identity is checked after normalization.

Affected versions and deployment visibility

The official affected range is Node.js 24.x before 24.22.1 and 26.x before 26.12.1. The 22.x line received other security fixes in the same release cycle but is not listed as affected by this CVE. Check the actual process version and the container image digest. A lockfile, package manifest, or base-image tag is supporting evidence, not proof of what runs.

This matters in long-lived deployment systems. A service can inherit a patched image name while an old layer or sidecar still runs a vulnerable binary. Build attestations and runtime version reporting should agree before a team marks the deployment complete.

Exposure has a limited meaning

ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 matches at 04:17 +08:00 on November 2, 2026. The CVE filter returned zero. Exposure is 5,539,674 because the policy selects the greater verified query count. These are product fingerprints, not vulnerable installations.

Use the figure to frame internet-scale relevance, not to assign incident status. A Node.js fingerprint cannot reveal the exact release, the trust store, the application's destination validation, or whether the vulnerable certificate path is reachable. Those facts belong in internal evidence.

Remediation

Upgrade to 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or a later maintained release. Rebuild and redeploy every artifact that embeds Node.js. Verify the running version after rollout and retain the evidence with the change record.

Review certificate profiles for address-like DNS SANs, especially in internal PKI and test environments. Require applications to canonicalize destinations before policy checks, reject inputs that are neither approved DNS names nor canonical IP addresses, and avoid custom certificate verification that skips the standard hostname check.

Finally, test with certificates that isolate the behavior: one with only a numeric DNS SAN, one with a matching IP SAN, and one with neither. A patched client should accept only the certificate whose identity matches the intended endpoint type. Keep the test local and controlled, and do not use production trust anchors.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: Your Go Fake Repository Drifts From Postgres. Run One Contract Suite Against Both
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your checkout tests are green. One of them replays a request the way a flaky mobile client would: same order reference, sent twice. The in-memory repository stores both orders without a word, so the use case's "reference already used" branch never runs and the test passes. In production, Postgres rejects the second insert with SQLSTATE 23505, unique_violation, nothing maps it to a domain error, and the client gets a 500.

Same suite, another test. The order-history endpoint should return the newest order first. The fake appends to a slice, the test happens to insert in the order it asserts, and it passes. The Postgres adapter forgot its ORDER BY, and the Postgres docs are blunt about what that means: without sorting, "the rows will be returned in an unspecified order."

Neither bug is in the fake's code. The fake never agreed to the same rules as the database. Martin Fowler's definition of a fake already warns you: fakes "have working implementations, but usually take some shortcut." The fix he describes for doubles is a contract test, which checks that calls against your double "return the same results as a call to the external service would." In a hexagonal Go service you can do that with one exported function and a single call per adapter.

The port, with its rules written down

The contract starts as prose on the interface. If a rule isn't written here, no adapter can be held to it.

package domain

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var (
    ErrNotFound        = errors.New("order not found")
    ErrDuplicateRef    = errors.New("order ref already used")
    ErrVersionConflict = errors.New("order changed since read")
)

type Order struct {
    ID         string
    Ref        string
    CustomerID string
    Status     string
    CreatedAt  time.Time
    Version    int64
}

// OrderRepository is the port. Every adapter must:
//   - Create: store o with Version 1. ErrDuplicateRef if
//     another order already has o.Ref.
//   - Get: ErrNotFound if no order has that ID.
//   - ListByCustomer: newest CreatedAt first, ties broken
//     by ID in byte order.
//   - Update: write o.Status if the stored Version equals
//     o.Version, then bump it. ErrVersionConflict if not,
//     ErrNotFound if the order does not exist.
type OrderRepository interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, o Order) error
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
    ListByCustomer(
        ctx context.Context, customerID string,
    ) ([]Order, error)
    Update(ctx context.Context, o Order) error
}

The errors live in the domain because they are business facts. "That reference is taken" means something to a checkout use case. SQLSTATE 23505 does not, and it should never cross the port.

One exported function, every adapter

The suite goes in its own package, domain/ordertest, in a normal .go file rather than a _test.go file. go build ignores files that end in _test.go, so nothing declared in one can be imported by another package, and both adapter packages need to call this. Importing testing from a non-test package has a precedent in the Go project itself: nettest.TestConn "tests that a net.Conn implementation properly satisfies the interface," and it takes a constructor the same way.


One set of checks, two implementations. Each door has to open the same way.

The constructor gives each subtest a fresh, empty repository, so subtests never see each other's rows.

package ordertest

import (
    "errors"
    "slices"
    "testing"
    "time"

    "example.com/shop/domain"
)

var t0 = time.Date(2026, 3, 1, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)

func RunOrderRepoContract(
    t *testing.T,
    newRepo func(t *testing.T) domain.OrderRepository,
) {
    t.Run("missing id", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        _, err := repo.Get(t.Context(), "nope")
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrNotFound", err)
        }
    })

    t.Run("round trip", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-1", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        got, err := repo.Get(t.Context(), "o-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        if got.Ref != "R-1" || got.Version != 1 ||
            !got.CreatedAt.Equal(t0) {
            t.Fatalf("got %+v", got)
        }
    })

    t.Run("duplicate ref", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        ctx := t.Context()
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-1", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        err := repo.Create(ctx, ord("o-2", "R-1", "c-2", t0))
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrDuplicateRef) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrDuplicateRef", err)
        }
        _, err = repo.Get(ctx, "o-2")
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
            t.Fatalf("o-2 was stored anyway: %v", err)
        }
    })

t.Context() needs Go 1.24 or later. Timestamps are compared with Equal, because the time docs note that == "compares not just the time instant but also the Location," and a database adapter is free to hand back the same instant in a different location.

The function continues with the ordering rule:

    t.Run("list order", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        later := t0.Add(time.Hour)
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-a", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-c", "R-2", "c-1", later))
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-B", "R-3", "c-1", t0))
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-x", "R-4", "c-2", later))
        got, err := repo.ListByCustomer(t.Context(), "c-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        var ids []string
        for _, o := range got {
            ids = append(ids, o.ID)
        }
        want := []string{"o-c", "o-B", "o-a"}
        if !slices.Equal(ids, want) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want %v", ids, want)
        }
    })

The list order subtest is built to fail a lazy fake. Insertion order is o-a, o-c, o-B, and neither that order nor its reverse matches the expected o-c, o-B, o-a. A fake that returns map iteration order fails too, at least some of the time, since the Go spec says map iteration order "is not specified and is not guaranteed to be the same from one iteration to the next." The uppercase B is there on purpose, and it comes back in the Postgres section.

The last two subtests cover updates, followed by the helpers:

    t.Run("stale version", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        ctx := t.Context()
        mustCreate(t, repo, ord("o-1", "R-1", "c-1", t0))
        a, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        b := a
        a.Status = "paid"
        if err := repo.Update(ctx, a); err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        b.Status = "cancelled"
        err = repo.Update(ctx, b)
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrVersionConflict) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrVersionConflict", err)
        }
        got, err := repo.Get(ctx, "o-1")
        if err != nil {
            t.Fatal(err)
        }
        if got.Status != "paid" || got.Version != 2 {
            t.Fatalf("got %+v", got)
        }
    })

    t.Run("update missing", func(t *testing.T) {
        repo := newRepo(t)
        o := ord("nope", "R-9", "c-1", t0)
        o.Version = 1
        err := repo.Update(t.Context(), o)
        if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
            t.Fatalf("got %v, want ErrNotFound", err)
        }
    })
}

func ord(id, ref, cust string, at time.Time) domain.Order {
    return domain.Order{
        ID: id, Ref: ref, CustomerID: cust,
        Status: "pending", CreatedAt: at,
    }
}

func mustCreate(
    t *testing.T, r domain.OrderRepository, o domain.Order,
) {
    t.Helper()
    if err := r.Create(t.Context(), o); err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("create %s: %v", o.ID, err)
    }
}

The stale version subtest is the optimistic-locking rule from an earlier post on version conflicts in a Go repository adapter, folded into the shared suite instead of standing alone.

The fake, held to it

This map-backed fake passes the suite, and it is still small.

package memory

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
    "strings"
    "sync"

    "example.com/shop/domain"
)

type OrderRepo struct {
    mu    sync.Mutex
    byID  map[string]domain.Order
    byRef map[string]string
}

func NewOrderRepo() *OrderRepo {
    return &OrderRepo{
        byID:  map[string]domain.Order{},
        byRef: map[string]string{},
    }
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Create(
    _ context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    if _, ok := r.byRef[o.Ref]; ok {
        return domain.ErrDuplicateRef
    }
    if _, ok := r.byID[o.ID]; ok {
        return fmt.Errorf("memory: id %s exists", o.ID)
    }
    o.Version = 1
    r.byID[o.ID] = o
    r.byRef[o.Ref] = o.ID
    return nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (domain.Order, error) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    o, ok := r.byID[id]
    if !ok {
        return domain.Order{}, domain.ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) ListByCustomer(
    _ context.Context, customerID string,
) ([]domain.Order, error) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    var out []domain.Order
    for _, o := range r.byID {
        if o.CustomerID == customerID {
            out = append(out, o)
        }
    }
    slices.SortFunc(out, func(a, b domain.Order) int {
        if c := b.CreatedAt.Compare(a.CreatedAt); c != 0 {
            return c
        }
        return strings.Compare(a.ID, b.ID)
    })
    return out, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Update(
    _ context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    cur, ok := r.byID[o.ID]
    if !ok {
        return domain.ErrNotFound
    }
    if cur.Version != o.Version {
        return domain.ErrVersionConflict
    }
    cur.Status = o.Status
    cur.Version++
    r.byID[o.ID] = cur
    return nil
}

The byRef index is the fake's version of a unique constraint, and the sort is its version of ORDER BY. Without those two pieces, the duplicate and ordering bugs from the opening are exactly what you would have shipped.

Wiring it to the suite is one call:

package memory_test

import (
    "testing"

    "example.com/shop/adapter/memory"
    "example.com/shop/domain"
    "example.com/shop/domain/ordertest"
)

func TestOrderRepoContract(t *testing.T) {
    ordertest.RunOrderRepoContract(t,
        func(*testing.T) domain.OrderRepository {
            return memory.NewOrderRepo()
        })
}

The pgx adapter, mapping SQLSTATE 23505

The real adapter uses pgx v5. A failed insert carries a *pgconn.PgError with a Code (the SQLSTATE) and a ConstraintName. Checking both matters: a primary-key collision is also 23505, and it is not the same domain fact as a reused reference.

package postgres

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn"
    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"

    "example.com/shop/domain"
)

const cols = `id, ref, customer_id, status, created_at, version`

type OrderRepo struct{ pool *pgxpool.Pool }

func NewOrderRepo(p *pgxpool.Pool) *OrderRepo {
    return &OrderRepo{pool: p}
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Create(
    ctx context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    _, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, `
        INSERT INTO orders (`+cols+`)
        VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, 1)`,
        o.ID, o.Ref, o.CustomerID, o.Status, o.CreatedAt)
    var pgErr *pgconn.PgError
    if errors.As(err, &pgErr) && pgErr.Code == "23505" &&
        pgErr.ConstraintName == "orders_ref_key" {
        return domain.ErrDuplicateRef
    }
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create order %s: %w", o.ID, err)
    }
    return nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Get(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) (domain.Order, error) {
    rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx,
        `SELECT `+cols+` FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, id)
    if err != nil {
        return domain.Order{}, fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    o, err := pgx.CollectExactlyOneRow(rows, scanOrder)
    if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
        return domain.Order{}, domain.ErrNotFound
    }
    if err != nil {
        return domain.Order{}, fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err)
    }
    return o, nil
}

func (r *OrderRepo) ListByCustomer(
    ctx context.Context, customerID string,
) ([]domain.Order, error) {
    rows, err := r.pool.Query(ctx, `
        SELECT `+cols+` FROM orders
         WHERE customer_id = $1
         ORDER BY created_at DESC, id COLLATE "C"`,
        customerID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("list %s: %w", customerID, err)
    }
    return pgx.CollectRows(rows, scanOrder)
}

func (r *OrderRepo) Update(
    ctx context.Context, o domain.Order,
) error {
    tag, err := r.pool.Exec(ctx, `
        UPDATE orders SET status = $3, version = version + 1
         WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`,
        o.ID, o.Version, o.Status)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("update %s: %w", o.ID, err)
    }
    if tag.RowsAffected() == 1 {
        return nil
    }
    if _, err := r.Get(ctx, o.ID); err != nil {
        return err // ErrNotFound, or a real failure
    }
    return domain.ErrVersionConflict
}

func scanOrder(row pgx.CollectableRow) (domain.Order, error) {
    var o domain.Order
    err := row.Scan(&o.ID, &o.Ref, &o.CustomerID,
        &o.Status, &o.CreatedAt, &o.Version)
    return o, err
}

CollectExactlyOneRow returns an error matching pgx.ErrNoRows when the query finds nothing, which is the one place the adapter translates to ErrNotFound. CollectRows closes the rows for you.

Now the uppercase B. The fake breaks ties with strings.Compare, and the Go spec says strings "are compared lexically byte-wise." Postgres sorts text by the column's collation, and a linguistic collation such as en_US.utf8 does not have to put o-B before o-a the way byte order does. The C collation sorts "by byte values rather than natural language order," so COLLATE "C" on the tiebreak makes both adapters agree no matter what the database default is. Drop it, and the list order subtest is where you find out.

Real Postgres, behind a build tag

The integration test starts Postgres with the testcontainers-go Postgres module, runs the schema, and hands the suite a constructor that truncates the table. A //go:build line keeps it out of the default run.


The model and the real engine go on the same gauge. Only one of them needs Docker.

//go:build integration

package postgres_test

import (
    "testing"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
    "github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go"
    tcpg "github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go/modules/postgres"

    "example.com/shop/adapter/postgres"
    "example.com/shop/domain"
    "example.com/shop/domain/ordertest"
)

const schema = `
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          text        PRIMARY KEY,
  ref         text        NOT NULL,
  customer_id text        NOT NULL,
  status      text        NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  version     bigint      NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT orders_ref_key UNIQUE (ref)
)`

func TestOrderRepoContract(t *testing.T) {
    ctx := t.Context()
    ctr, err := tcpg.Run(ctx, "postgres:16-alpine",
        tcpg.WithDatabase("shop"),
        tcpg.WithUsername("shop"),
        tcpg.WithPassword("shop"),
        tcpg.BasicWaitStrategies(),
    )
    testcontainers.CleanupContainer(t, ctr)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    dsn, err := ctr.ConnectionString(ctx, "sslmode=disable")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, dsn)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    t.Cleanup(pool.Close)
    if _, err := pool.Exec(ctx, schema); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }

    ordertest.RunOrderRepoContract(t,
        func(t *testing.T) domain.OrderRepository {
            _, err := pool.Exec(t.Context(), "TRUNCATE orders")
            if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
            }
            return postgres.NewOrderRepo(pool)
        })
}

CleanupContainer goes before the error check because its docs say a nil container is a no-op, so a half-started container still gets removed. The module page also says it supplies no default wait strategy, which is why BasicWaitStrategies() is there. One container serves all six subtests, and TRUNCATE gives each one an empty table, which keeps the run to a single container start.

The constraint is named explicitly, orders_ref_key, because the adapter matches on that name. In a real service, replace the inline schema with your migration runner, so the test checks the constraint names your migrations actually create.

Two commands now cover both worlds:

go test -race ./...                    # fake only, no Docker
go test -race -tags integration ./...  # fake and Postgres

What the suite catches next

The suite only knows the rules you gave it, and Postgres has more. Two worth adding as subtests before they bite:

Timestamp precision. Go's time.Time holds nanoseconds, and Postgres timestamptz resolution is 1 microsecond. The suite uses whole-second timestamps, so it can't see this. A subtest that creates an order with time.Now() and compares CreatedAt after a round trip will pass on the fake and, whenever the clock reading has sub-microsecond digits, fail on Postgres. Decide in the port whether the repository truncates, then make the fake do the same.

Empty results. The two adapters in this post already disagree here. The fake above returns a nil slice for a customer with no orders. The pgx adapter does not: CollectRows is return AppendRows([]T{}, rows, fn), so it starts from an empty, non-nil slice. Marshal both and the encoding/json docs say "a nil slice encodes as the null JSON value," so one adapter gives the client null and the other [], and the suite as written passes both. Add a subtest that pins the shape, or normalise it in the handler.

When a third adapter shows up (a read-through cache wrapping the Postgres repo, a SQLite build for a CLI), its test is one RunOrderRepoContract call with a different constructor. If it disagrees with the other two, the suite names the rule.

If this was useful

A contract suite only works if the port says what the rules are and database errors stay in the adapter. Hexagonal Architecture in Go is the book I wrote about that layer: where repositories, adapters and their tests sit in a Go service, and how to test both sides of a port without a pile of mocks. It is part of the Thinking in Go series, with a companion book on the language itself.

title: Our mocks were lying to us for four months
description:
I want to talk about a specific kind of green build. The kind where 612 tests pass in 38 seconds, the coverage badge says 87%, and the thing is broken in production.

We had that build for most of a quarter.

The setup

We run a small logistics product. One of our TypeScript services talks to a third-party carrier API to fetch rates, book shipments, and pull tracking updates. When we built that integration, a colleague recorded a bunch of real responses, saved them as JSON fixtures, and wired them into our tests with nock. Fast, deterministic, easy to read. Everyone liked it.

That was in January.

How drift actually happens

Nobody decides to let mocks go stale. It happens in tiny steps.

The carrier added an optional surcharges array to rate responses. Our fixtures didn't have it, so our code never learned about it. Nothing broke. Yet.

Then they started returning estimated_delivery as a date-only string (2026-03-14) for some ground services instead of a full timestamp. Our code did new Date(value) and formatted it in the user's timezone. For anyone west of UTC, the delivery date showed up a day early. That one sat in prod for weeks, because who double checks whether "Thursday" should say "Friday"?

Then the big one. In April they moved tracking events behind pagination. The first call returned 20 events and a next_cursor. Our fixture had 6 events and no cursor, because the shipment we'd recorded back in January was a short one. In production, long-haul shipments stopped showing their latest status. Customers saw "In transit, Memphis" for packages that had been delivered two days earlier.

Every one of our tests passed through all of this. They were testing our code against January's API.

The afternoon I diffed everything

After the tracking complaint landed in our support channel ("customer says delivered, app says Memphis, again"), I blocked out an afternoon and did something slightly tedious. I wrote a throwaway script that sent the same requests behind each of our 34 fixtures to the carrier's sandbox, then diffed the real response shape against the saved one. Keys and types only, not values.

11 of 34 had drifted. Most trivially, a new optional field here and there. Three in ways that changed behavior.

I pasted the diff output in our team channel with no comment. Someone replied with the skull emoji, which was fair.

Where unit tests stop being useful

I don't think the lesson is "mocks bad". Our mocked unit tests were doing their actual job: given input X, does this function produce Y. The problem was that we were treating them as proof that our service worked with the carrier. They can't be that. A mock is a claim about someone else's system, and nobody was checking the claim.

That's the boring core of the whole unit testing vs integration testing argument, at least as I understand it now. A unit test isolates your code so you can trust its logic. An integration test puts your code next to the real dependency so you can trust the connection. You want both, and the trap is letting the fast, pleasant one stand in for the slow, annoying one.

We'd let the fast one stand in for everything.

What we do now

Nothing dramatic. Three changes.

A nightly drift check

That throwaway diff script became a nightly job. It hits the sandbox, compares response shapes to our fixtures, and posts to Slack if anything moved. It doesn't fail the build, because the sandbox is flaky enough that we'd be crying wolf twice a week. But we now see drift within a day instead of within a quarter.

Re-recording fixtures instead of hand-editing them

When drift showed up, we used to open the JSON and patch it by hand. That's how the January fixtures had turned into a weird hybrid of real and imagined responses. Now we re-record from the sandbox and commit the new file, so the PR diff shows exactly what changed upstream. Reviewers actually read those diffs, which surprised me.

Some teams push this further and record production traffic directly, then replay it as tests with dependencies mocked from the same recording. Keploy works roughly that way. We're not there yet, but fixtures that can't drift because they're re-captured from reality is a nice idea.

A thin layer of real calls

We added a handful of integration tests that run against the carrier sandbox on every PR that touches the carrier client. Seven of them. They book a shipment, fetch rates for three service levels, and pull tracking for a sandbox shipment with enough events to force pagination. About 40 seconds total, mostly because the sandbox is slow. We gate them on file paths so they don't run on unrelated changes.

Things I got wrong along the way

My first instinct was to replace all the nock mocks with sandbox calls. I got about halfway before the suite went from 38 seconds to just over six minutes and started failing randomly whenever the sandbox hiccuped. A teammate asked, very politely, whether I was trying to get people to stop running tests locally. I reverted most of it.

The other mistake: I assumed the carrier would loudly announce breaking changes. They did, kind of. Two of the three were on a changelog page I didn't know existed. The pagination change went out by email to an address belonging to someone who left the company last year. Go check where your vendors' notices actually land. I'll wait.

Where we ended up

612 unit tests, still mocked, still fast. Seven integration tests against the sandbox. One nightly drift check. Extra CI time on a relevant PR is under a minute.

The pagination test would have caught the tracking bug on its first run. The nightly diff would have flagged the date format the morning after it changed. Not perfect. Still a lot better than finding out from a customer whose package is apparently stuck in Memphis forever.

title: My backtest's worst week didn't stand out in any weekly stat. The trades showed why
description:
A max drawdown number tells you how deep the hole was. It doesn't tell you what dug it, and the fix depends on that:

  • Stops hit soon after entry. The entry or the stop size is the problem.
  • Losers that were in profit first. The exit is the problem.
  • Trades held too long against you. You need a time exit.

So I zoom into the worst stretch and look at the trades one by one. This post walks through one run, including a check I expected to explain the drawdown and that didn't.

The run

  • Strategy: moving-average cross (5/20), take profit 0.3%, stop loss 0.2%
  • Data: 30,000 synthetic 15-minute bars from a regime-switching generator. The dataset is named USDJPY_15M, but the prices and the dates (Oct 2026 to Sep 2027) are made up
  • Result: 1,863 trades, +4.6%, max drawdown -14.1%, win rate 41.5%

The UI in the screenshots is in Japanese. There is an EN switch at the top right.

The worst week

Instead of the deepest point of the drawdown, I looked for the steepest 7-day fall in equity. The deepest point often sits at the end of a long, slow slide, and a single week of that slide looks like nothing. The steepest week was Dec 13 to Dec 20: equity went from 10,303 to 9,691.

I compared the 46 trades opened that week with all 1,863:

That week Whole run
Win rate 19.6% 41.5%
Closed by the stop 70% (32 of 46) 49%
Median holding time 0.76 h 0.76 h
Losers that were in profit first (by at least half the loss) 35% 31%

The holding time didn't change, so the trades weren't held longer. The share of losers that were in profit first barely moved, so the exit wasn't giving back more than usual. What changed was the stop: 70% of the week's trades ended there, against 49% over the whole run.

The check that didn't explain it

My first guess was that the market was unusual that week. I split the 44 weeks of the run two ways and looked at the stop-out rate in each group:

Weeks grouped by Quietest / choppiest quarter Middle half Most volatile / trending quarter
Median 15-minute move 49.7% 48.9% 48.5%
Trend efficiency (net move / range) 49.4% 49.1% 48.0%

The stop-out rate is about 49% in every group. The drawdown week ranked 17th of 44 by volatility, right in the middle. It was a trending week (efficiency 0.68 against a median of 0.35), but the trending quarter as a whole made money: +33 a week on average.

A weekly label would have said "trend week, this strategy is fine in trends". That would have been wrong, and the weekly numbers couldn't show why.

What the trades showed

The zoomed chart shows it. Price rallied from 123.9 to 133.5 in three days, then moved sideways between 131 and 137, with a spike to 137.09 on Dec 16 that reversed within the day.

The stops were hit on both sides: 16 of 23 buys and 16 of 23 sells. A 0.2% stop is only about 2.5 median 15-minute moves wide. That's fine while price drifts. After a rally of nearly 8%, the swings around the new level were wide enough to reach it in both directions, while the average bar size for the week still looked normal.

The trade timeline under the charts shows the same range from the trades' side. Each bar is one trade, from open to close: green for buys, red for sells. Overlapping trades go on separate rows. The bars are short and they alternate between buys and sells, so these were quick stop-outs in both directions, not a few trades that dragged on.

This doesn't tell me the fix. It tells me where to look: at the stop size or at a filter right after large moves, not at the exit. I'd test either one on a part of the data I haven't looked at yet, because a filter tuned on one bad week fits that week and little else.

Doing this with your own backtest

  1. Find the steepest 7-day fall in equity, not the deepest point.
  2. For that week's trades, compare four numbers with the whole run: win rate, share closed by the stop, median holding time, share of losers that were in profit first.
  3. If only the stop share jumped, look at the entry and the stop. If the in-profit-first share jumped, look at the exit. If holding time jumped, add a time exit.
  4. Don't trust a weekly volatility or trend label to find it for you. In this run it pointed the wrong way.

How the zoom works

Some details on the chart side, in case you're building something similar.

The equity, drawdown, exposure and trade timeline charts are Chart.js with chartjs-plugin-zoom (Ctrl+wheel to zoom, drag to pan). When one finishes a zoom or pan, it reads its x range and applies it to the others with chart.zoomScale("x", { min, max }, "none"). The "none" animation mode matters: with animation on, each chart fires its own updates while the others are still moving.

The price chart is different. Its candles come from the server at a fixed bar budget, so on a range change it picks the finest timeframe that fits the range. In the clip, the zoomed week is drawn with 30-minute bars. It only picks timeframes the dataset actually has.

Redrawing the price chart is async. If it resets the other charts' ranges when it finishes, a Ctrl+wheel gesture that's still going gets cut off. So a flag keeps the other charts as they are while a sync redraw is in flight.

Entry and exit arrows are drawn only when 80 trades or fewer are in view. With 1,863 trades in the full view, arrows would just be noise. The two thin strips above the price chart show where opens and closes cluster, and the arrows take over once you've zoomed in far enough.

The demo runs without an account. The chart view in this post is in the app, where a free account comes with sample data to try it on: Hawk Backtester

If you find the cause of a drawdown a different way, I'd like to hear how.
