title: Your bank's CSV export is the messiest API you will ever consume
description:
I spent two weeks writing a bank-statement parser that runs inside the browser tab. No upload, no server, no account. Paste a CSV export from your card provider, get back the recurring charges hiding in it.

The part I underestimated was not the recurring-charge logic. It was the file format. Every bank invents its own dialect of CSV, and each dialect exists because someone in 2009 thought it was obvious. Here are the traps that broke my first parser, in the order they broke it, with the rule I ended up shipping.

1. The header is not on line one

Almost every export opens with a preamble: account holder, masked card number, statement period, a blank line, sometimes a marketing sentence. My first version assumed lines[0] was the header and produced zero rows on half of the samples.

The fix is to stop assuming and start searching. I scan the first ten lines, split each one, and ask whether it looks like a header: it needs a date-ish column, a description-ish column, and either an amount column or a debit/credit pair.

const DATE_ALIASES = ['date', 'transaction date', 'posted date', 'post date', 'trans date'];
const DESC_ALIASES = ['description', 'merchant', 'payee', 'name', 'memo', 'details'];
const AMOUNT_ALIASES = ['amount', 'transaction amount'];
const DEBIT_ALIASES = ['debit', 'withdrawal', 'withdrawals', 'charges'];
const CREDIT_ALIASES = ['credit', 'deposit', 'deposits', 'payments'];

One subtlety matters more than the aliases: a transaction line that appears above the header must be reported instead of being silently skipped with the preamble. If a row above the header parses as a date, I emit an issue pointing at that line. Quietly ignoring money is the worst possible parser behaviour.

2. The delimiter is not always a comma

European exports use semicolons. Some accounting tools use tabs. And the sample rule I first wrote, "look at the first line and count separators", fails for exactly the files that need it, because the first line is usually the preamble sentence and it contains no delimiters at all.

So the sniffing window is the first twenty lines instead of just the first one:

const sample = lines.slice(0, 20).join('\n');
for (const candidate of ['\t', ';', ',']) {
  const count = sample.split(candidate).length - 1;
  if (count > bestCount) { best = candidate; bestCount = count; }
}

Tab wins ties by virtue of being tested first. That is a deliberate choice: a tab-delimited file usually has no commas inside fields, while a comma file with a semicolon in a merchant name is common.

The splitter itself has to respect quoting, including the doubled-quote escape, or a merchant called "SMITH, J LLC" becomes two columns and the amount lands in the wrong place.

3. Negative money has at least four spellings

A charge is positive money leaving the account. Depending on the bank, the same refund looks like any of these:

  • -12.99
  • 12.99- (trailing minus, common in mainframe-era exports)
  • (12.99) (accounting parentheses)
  • a debit column and a credit column, where the sign lives in the column header

My parser normalises all four into integer cents before anything else touches the value. Integers instead of floats: 0.1 + 0.2 is a well-known way to make a totals column disagree with itself by a cent, and a subscription audit that is one cent off still fails the only test a user runs, which is whether the number matches their statement.

4. The same character means two different things

1,234.56 and 1.234,56 are the same amount. 12,50 and 1,250 are not, and they are both plausible inputs. The rule I ended up with:

  • if the string contains a comma and no dot, and exactly two digits follow the last comma, treat the comma as a decimal separator
  • otherwise strip every comma 
if (value.includes(',') && !value.includes('.')) {
  const parts = value.split(',');
  value = (parts.length === 2 && parts[1].length === 2)
    ? `${parts[0]}.${parts[1]}`
    : value.replace(/,/g, '');
} else {
  value = value.replace(/,/g, '');
}

Currency symbols, non-breaking spaces and stray letters get stripped before that check. If what remains does not match ^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$, the amount is rejected and the line is reported as an issue. Rejecting is cheap; guessing is not, because a misread amount corrupts every downstream total silently.

5. Dates are ambiguous, and guessing is worse than refusing

03/04/2026 is March 4th or April 3rd depending on where the file was produced. Six months of a subscription billed on the 4th can look like a monthly cadence or like two weeks of chaos.

The parser accepts ISO dates and short numeric dates, and exposes a single dayFirst flag. There is no automatic detection, because automatic detection here means inferring a locale from a file that does not declare one. A user who sees garbled dates can flip one switch; a user who does not notice they are garbled now has a wrong answer they trust.

6. Merchant descriptors are a compressed format

Raw descriptors look like this:

SP *SPOTIFY USA
PAYPAL *STEAM
SQ *BLUE BOTTLE
POS DEBIT 4821 WHOLEFDS MKT

They are written for a 22-character field, so payment processors prepend their own prefixes and banks append store numbers. Grouping by the raw string produces one subscription per location.

Normalisation does three things: strip known prefixes, unify punctuation, then drop trailing pure-digit tokens (store numbers) and truncate.

The prefix list has one hard constraint that cost me an afternoon:

// the separator is required, otherwise "SP\s*" eats the first two letters of SPOTIFY
/^SP[\s*]+/i

A permissive ^SP turns every Spotify charge into OTIFY USA, and it groups correctly by accident while being wrong about the merchant name. Requiring at least one separator after the prefix fixes it, and the same pattern applies to SQ, TST and PAYPAL.

7. Turning rows into cadence: why the median wins

Once every row belongs to a normalised merchant, recurrence is a question about intervals. I collect the positive charges, compute the day gaps between consecutive ones, and take the median.

Median because a single missed month should not move the answer. If a charge lands on the 3rd, the 5th, and then the 2nd of the month after a skipped cycle, the mean interval is inflated and a monthly subscription scores as irregular; the median still says thirty.

The classification is deliberately narrow:

  • monthly: median gap 25–35 days, at least 3 charges
  • annual: median gap 350–380 days, at least 2 charges
  • weekly: median gap 6–8 days, at least 4 charges
  • anything else: one-off

The counts are not decorative. Two charges 30 days apart are as likely to be a coincidence as a subscription, so monthly needs a third observation before it earns a row.

Confidence is a separate field, and it is where the honesty lives. Monthly is high confidence at four or more charges with every interval within five days of the median; annual needs three charges within ten days; weekly needs six within two. Everything else is medium. A high-confidence row is a claim the tool is willing to defend; a medium row is a hint.

The monthly equivalent is what makes an annual bill comparable to a monthly one: annual divided by twelve, weekly multiplied by 52 and divided by 12. Sorting by that number is the whole point of the audit, because it answers one question in a fixed order: which line costs the most per month.

8. What the audit refuses to claim

Two limits are worth stating, because users find them before you document them.

The first is aggregated billers. APPLE.COM/BILL and GOOGLE *... collapse an entire ecosystem into a single descriptor. The parser flags those rows, and the audit shows them as one line, because the statement does not contain the information needed to split them. Pretending otherwise would produce a confident, wrong breakdown.

The second is the trial that converts. A subscription billed once has one observation. Until the second charge arrives, it is a one-off, and the tool says so. There is no setting that makes it guess.

What comes out

The output is a priority list sorted by monthly equivalent, each row carrying the cadence, the last charge date, the next expected date (last charge plus the median interval), the annual equivalent, and the charge count. Two exports come with it: a CSV and a Markdown table of the same list, so the audit can be pasted into whatever the user actually uses to cancel things.

And a print stylesheet, because the moment this becomes real is the moment someone holds it next to a phone call.

The parser is about 500 lines and does not need a backend. If you want to try it on your own export, it runs on the statement audit page. Paste a redacted export; nothing leaves the tab.

If you have a bank export that this parser mangles, send me the header line and one broken row (with the amounts changed). Format bugs are the ones I can actually fix.

title: Auditing Node.js code for the CVE-2026-105483 TLS identity mismatch
description:
Auditing Node.js code for the CVE-2026-105483 TLS identity mismatch

A runtime patch closes CVE-2026-105483, but an audit can still reveal applications whose architecture makes the same identity mistake easy to repeat. The bug affected Node.js 24.x and 26.x before 24.22.1 and 26.12.1. A fullwidth-digit IPv4 host normalized and resolved as an address while tls.checkServerIdentity() evaluated it as a DNS name. A trusted certificate with a matching DNS SAN could authenticate the wrong IP endpoint.

Node.js rates the issue High. The GitHub advisory lists CVSS v3.0 7.4 and CWE-295. The audit should establish where destination identity becomes security-sensitive, then confirm that those paths run on a fixed runtime and use the intended identity type.

Start with the trust decision

Search the codebase for direct use of tls.checkServerIdentity(), custom checkServerIdentity callbacks, and TLS clients that accept destination values from outside the service. Include HTTP clients built on top of the standard TLS stack and integrations that create connections from user or administrator configuration.

The direct search is only a starting point. Many applications never name checkServerIdentity; they rely on a standard client to call it. Review the path that supplies the host value. Does it come from a fixed allowlist, a generated service name, a tenant configuration object, a callback URL, or a command-line argument? Each source has a different threat model.

For each sensitive path, write down four facts:

  • The expected destination type: DNS name, IPv4 address, or both.
  • The normalization performed before the connection.
  • The validation performed after normalization.
  • The trust store and certificate profile required by the server.

If the application expects an IP address but only validates a textual DNS-like value, the identity policy is incomplete even after the runtime update.

Review normalization at the boundary

Unicode presentation can change while the underlying destination meaning stays the same. Official Node.js guidance confirms that fullwidth-digit hosts normalized and resolved as IPv4 in the vulnerable path. Code reviews should therefore avoid comparing a raw host string with a canonical host and assuming both checks describe the same value.

Prefer a small, explicit destination policy. Accept approved ASCII DNS names through an allowlist, or accept a canonical IPv4 literal after parsing and validation. Reject ambiguous mixed representations instead of trying to normalize them into a broader destination language. The application's policy should be narrower than the parser's full input grammar.

This is a mitigation, not a replacement for 24.22.1 or 26.12.1. A patched runtime is the authoritative fix. The application restriction prevents new ambiguous inputs from reaching sensitive clients and makes future regressions easier to test.

Review custom verification callbacks

A custom callback can intentionally support private names, internal addresses, or application-specific identity metadata. It can also silently remove the standard checks. Inspect whether the callback:

  • Uses the parsed destination rather than the original unnormalized string.
  • Requires an IP SAN when the intention is to contact an IP address.
  • Accepts a DNS certificate only when the destination is an approved DNS name.
  • Rejects a mismatch instead of logging it and returning success.
  • Preserves all required certificate validation steps.

Any callback that returns success based only on an application label, a hostname substring, or a certificate Common Name is a candidate for redesign. This review should not rely on a text search alone because wrappers and helper libraries can obscure the TLS call.

Prioritize credential-bearing clients

The advisory assigns high confidentiality and integrity impact, but the operational severity depends on what crosses the connection. A metadata request can disclose service behavior. A signed API request can expose credentials or modify state. A management client can carry broader authority than its destination suggests.

Rank clients by the secrecy of the request, the authority of the response, and the attacker's ability to influence the destination. A low-volume internal integration that carries an administrative token may deserve more attention than a high-volume public read-only client.

Verify deployed artifacts

The affected versions are precise enough to make inventory feasible. Node.js 24.x before 24.22.1 and 26.x before 26.12.1 need to move to a fixed release. Check runtime output, container image layers, SEA packaging, and any embedded Node.js distribution. A source repository can be clean while a release artifact remains affected.

Record the runtime version before and after rollout. If the service exposes that information internally, compare it with the deployed image digest. If it does not, use the packaging and process inspection available to the operator instead of inferring the version from a package name.

Exposure and code evidence

At 04:17 +08:00 on November 2, 2026, ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 product matches and the CVE filter returned zero. The selected Exposure is 5,539,674 Node.js fingerprints, not confirmed vulnerable processes. Use the number to understand the technology population and internal code evidence to decide which services can reach the vulnerable path.

Completion criteria

Consider the audit complete when every sensitive TLS client has a documented expected identity type, an explicit normalization and allowlist policy, and a test that rejects a certificate with the wrong SAN class. Confirm the running runtime is 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or later, and retain the rollout evidence. A clean scan is useful only when the scanned artifact and the deployed process are the same one.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: Multi-Vendor Checkout: Splitting One Cart by Seller
description:
A multi-vendor cart looks like one purchase to the customer and is really three or four separate contracts underneath. Each seller ships from a different place, on a different carrier, with its own stock, its own return window and its own payout. Most marketplace bugs I have been asked to fix come from storing that as one order with a seller_id on each line, then trying to bolt on partial shipments, partial refunds and per-seller status later.

I run Loop Origin, where my team builds custom e-commerce and marketplace platforms, mostly on Laravel, Vue 3 and PostgreSQL. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every query and claim myself. The schema and code below are simplified from patterns I use in production.

How should a marketplace split one cart across multiple sellers?

Direct answer: Create one parent order for the customer's payment and one child order per seller for fulfillment. Quote shipping per seller group, allocate order-level discounts to child orders with a deterministic rounding rule, capture payment once, and let each child order move through its own state machine. Derive the customer-facing status from the children instead of storing it.

Three ways to model it

Model Payment Fulfillment and status Refunds Where it breaks
One order, seller_id per line One charge One status for all sellers Line-level math every time "Shipped" is false when one of three sellers shipped
Parent order + seller sub-orders One charge on the parent Independent per seller Scoped to a sub-order Needs allocation logic up front
Separate checkout per seller One charge per seller Independent Simple Customer pays three times, more card declines and fees

The second model costs more at the start and saves the most later. The rest of this post assumes it.

The schema 

CREATE TABLE orders (               -- what the customer paid for
  id               bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id      bigint NOT NULL,
  currency         char(3) NOT NULL,
  items_total      bigint NOT NULL,  -- minor units
  shipping_total   bigint NOT NULL,
  discount_total   bigint NOT NULL,
  grand_total      bigint NOT NULL,
  payment_intent   text UNIQUE,
  idempotency_key  uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE seller_orders (        -- what one seller must fulfil
  id               bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id         bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  seller_id        bigint NOT NULL,
  ship_from_id     bigint NOT NULL,  -- seller warehouse
  shipping_method  text   NOT NULL,
  items_total      bigint NOT NULL,
  shipping_total   bigint NOT NULL,
  discount_alloc   bigint NOT NULL,  -- share of order-level coupon
  status           text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (status IN ('pending','accepted','packed','shipped','delivered','cancelled','refunded')),
  accept_by        timestamptz NOT NULL,  -- seller SLA
  UNIQUE (order_id, seller_id, ship_from_id)
);

CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  id               bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  seller_order_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES seller_orders(id),
  sku_id           bigint NOT NULL,
  qty              int    NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price       bigint NOT NULL,
  qty_cancelled    int    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  qty_refunded     int    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

Two details carry a lot. The unique key includes ship_from_id, because one seller with two warehouses is two shipments, not one. And money is stored in minor units as integers, because the allocation step below has to add up to the exact cent.

Grouping the cart and quoting shipping

Group lines by seller and origin, then quote each group in parallel with a hard timeout. One slow carrier API should not block the whole checkout.

use Illuminate\Http\Client\Pool;
use Illuminate\Http\Client\Response;

$groups = $cart->lines->groupBy(fn ($l) => $l->seller_id.'-'.$l->shipFromId());

$responses = Http::pool(fn (Pool $pool) => $groups->map(fn ($lines, $key) =>
    $pool->as((string) $key)->timeout(3)->post(
        $this->carrierUrlFor($lines->first()->seller_id),
        $this->quotePayload($lines, $address)
    )
)->values()->all());

$quotes = $groups->map(function ($lines, $key) use ($responses) {
    $r = $responses[$key] ?? null;
    if ($r instanceof Response && $r->successful()) {
        return ShippingQuote::fromCarrier($r->json());
    }
    Log::warning('shipping.flat_rate_fallback', ['group' => $key]);
    return ShippingQuote::flatRate($lines->first()->seller);
});

Http::pool sends the requests concurrently, and a connection failure comes back as an exception object instead of a Response, which is why the check matters. The fallback is a business decision: a flat rate the seller agreed to in advance is better than a failed checkout, and the log line shows which sellers depend on it.

Show the customer one line per seller group ("Ships from Seller A, 3â€“5 days, Rs 250"). Splitting shipping per seller is honest and cuts disputes about why shipping costs more than expected.

Allocating discounts without losing a cent

An order-level coupon of Rs 500 across three sellers has to be split, because each seller's payout and each partial refund depends on it. Allocate in proportion to each seller's items total, then hand leftover units out by largest remainder:

function allocate(int $amount, array $weights): array {
    $total = array_sum($weights);
    $raw = array_map(fn ($w) => $amount * $w / $total, $weights);
    $alloc = array_map('floor', $raw);
    $left = $amount - array_sum($alloc);
    $rema = array_map(fn ($r, $a) => $r - $a, $raw, $alloc);
    arsort($rema);
    foreach (array_keys($rema) as $i) { if ($left-- <= 0) break; $alloc[$i]++; }
    return array_map('intval', $alloc);
}
// allocate(50000, [120000, 45000, 35000]) => [30000, 11250, 8750]

Store the result on seller_orders.discount_alloc at checkout and never recompute it. If you recompute after a line is cancelled, your refunds and payouts drift from what the customer actually paid.


AI-generated image.

One payment, many fulfilments

Capture once on the parent order, then record each seller's share in a ledger. I covered that side in detail in multi-vendor marketplace payments, ledgers and payouts; the important link here is that every ledger entry points at a seller_order_id, never only the parent.

Reserve stock per seller line at checkout with a short hold, and release it if payment fails. The hold-and-expire pattern is the same one in preventing double booking with locks, holds and expiry.

Each seller order then moves independently: pending â†’ accepted â†’ packed â†’ shipped â†’ delivered. The accept_by timestamp drives a scheduled job that auto-cancels and refunds a seller order that was never accepted, without touching the other sellers.

Deriving the customer status

Do not store a parent status. Derive it:

Child statuses Customer sees
All pending or accepted Processing
Some shipped, some not Partially shipped
All shipped or delivered (ignoring cancelled) Shipped
All delivered (ignoring cancelled) Delivered
All cancelled or refunded Cancelled

A stored parent status always ends up contradicting its children after a partial cancellation. A derived one cannot.

Failure modes and the trade-off each fix costs

Failure Symptom Fix Cost of the fix
One seller cannot fulfil Whole order cancelled Cancel only that seller order and refund its share Customer gets a partial order; notify clearly
Coupon recomputed after cancellation Refund larger than paid share Freeze discount_alloc at checkout Slightly unfair edge cases on minimum-spend coupons
Carrier quote timeout Checkout spinner, abandoned carts Timeout plus seller flat-rate fallback Occasional under- or over-charged shipping
Duplicate submit Two parent orders idempotency_key unique on orders One extra column and client-generated key
Return outside one seller's window Support escalations Store return policy per seller order at checkout Policy snapshot per order
Seller ships late Customer blames the platform accept_by and ship-by SLAs with auto-cancel Sellers must adopt the dashboard

Implementation checklist

  • [ ] Parent orders for payment, seller_orders per seller and origin for fulfilment
  • [ ] Money in integer minor units everywhere
  • [ ] Parallel shipping quotes with a timeout and a flat-rate fallback
  • [ ] Largest-remainder discount allocation, stored at checkout
  • [ ] Stock holds per line, released on payment failure
  • [ ] Ledger entries reference seller_order_id
  • [ ] Per-seller state machine with an acceptance SLA
  • [ ] Customer status derived, never stored
  • [ ] Return and cancellation policy snapshotted per seller order
  • [ ] Tests for partial cancel, partial refund and one-seller timeout

Frequently asked questions

Should the customer see one order number or several?

Show one order number and group shipments under it by seller. Customers think in purchases. Give each seller order its own suffix (for example 10452-A, 10452-B) for support conversations.

How do I handle free shipping thresholds with several sellers?

Decide whether the threshold is per seller or platform-wide, and say so at checkout. Per-seller is easier to fund, because each seller pays for its own shipping. A platform-wide threshold means the platform subsidizes the difference, which has to be booked in the ledger.

What if one seller's item goes out of stock after payment?

Cancel that seller order or just the affected lines, refund the line amounts minus their allocated discount, and keep the rest of the purchase moving. Never hold the other sellers' shipments.

Can sellers use different carriers in one order?

Yes, and they usually should. Shipping is quoted and tracked per seller order, so each can use its own carrier integration. A strategy-per-carrier pattern keeps that code clean.

How do taxes work when sellers ship from different places?

Tax often depends on where goods ship from and to, so calculate it per seller order, not per cart. Rules vary by country, so confirm them with an accountant before launch.

Is this overkill for a marketplace MVP?

The parent and child split is not. It is cheap on day one and painful to retrofit. You can skip the SLA jobs and parallel quoting until you have real sellers.

Follow & Connect

  • LinkedIn: Loop Origin
  • X: Muhammad Ali Mughal (@AliMughal887)
  • GitHub: Loop Origin (@LoopOrigin)

title: A Practical Approach to Evaluating Airflow Visualisation in GMP Cleanrooms
description:
Pharmaceutical cleanrooms depend on controlled airflow to protect exposed products, components and critical surfaces. In aseptic manufacturing, smoke studies help teams visualise airflow behaviour under defined operating conditions.

However, capturing a video of smoke movement is not enough. The observations must be assessed against predefined acceptance criteria to determine whether the airflow pattern provides the intended protection.

This article outlines a practical approach to reviewing airflow visualisation results in GMP cleanrooms.

  1. Define the Expected Airflow Behaviour

Before conducting a smoke study, identify what the test is intended to demonstrate.

The protocol should consider:

Cleanroom layout and equipment configuration

Critical process locations and exposed products

Intended airflow direction

Relevant operating conditions

Routine interventions and operator movements

Potential contamination pathways

The expected airflow behaviour should be clear enough for reviewers to compare actual observations with the predefined criteria.

  1. Capture Representative Operating Conditions

Airflow can change when operators interact with equipment or move materials through a critical area.

A study should therefore consider relevant operating conditions, rather than relying only on observations made in an unoccupied room.

Depending on the process, the protocol may include material transfer, equipment handling, component replacement and other representative interventions.

Video recordings should clearly show the test location, the activity being performed and the resulting smoke movement.

  1. Evaluate Airflow Observations Systematically

A structured review helps teams avoid relying on subjective impressions of whether airflow looks acceptable.

The following table summarises useful observation points.

Observation

What to assess

Airflow direction

Whether air moves in the intended direction

Product protection

Whether exposed products and critical surfaces receive appropriate protection

Turbulence and eddies

Whether local disturbances affect critical locations

Operator interventions

Whether activities disrupt the intended airflow pattern

Reversal or ingress

Whether air moves from less clean areas towards higher-grade areas

Smoke clearance

Whether slow-moving or stagnant patterns require further assessment

Not every visible disturbance represents a failure. Its significance depends on its location, duration, operating conditions and potential effect on product protection.

  1. Review Interventions and Local Disturbances

Operator movements and equipment arrangements can create local airflow disturbances.

For example, an intervention near an exposed product may influence the airflow pattern around that location. Reviewers should examine the video to understand whether the disturbance affects the intended protective airflow.

The assessment should record the observation, its location and the conditions under which it occurred. Where a potential contamination risk is identified, it should be evaluated and documented through the site's quality system.

  1. Establish Acceptance Criteria Before Execution

Acceptance criteria should be defined before the study begins. They should reflect the facility design, process requirements and contamination risks.

EU GMP Annex 1 addresses airflow visualisation and the need to demonstrate appropriate airflow protection in cleanrooms and critical areas. It does not establish one universal numerical pass/fail limit for every visible smoke pattern.

Manufacturers should therefore define and justify study-specific criteria through documented risk assessment and approved procedures.

  1. Maintain Traceable Study Records

A review is only useful when its conclusions can be traced back to the evidence.

Depending on the approved protocol, the study record may include:

Approved protocol and acceptance criteria

Test locations and operating conditions

Equipment configuration and relevant interventions

Smoke-generation details

Original video recordings

Annotated footage and observation logs

Assessment of observations against criteria

Deviations and investigations, where applicable

Review and approval records

Timestamps and location references can make it easier to connect a finding in the report with the corresponding video evidence.

  1. Distinguish Smoke Visualisation from Recovery Testing

Smoke visualisation and cleanroom recovery testing provide different types of evidence.

Smoke studies demonstrate visible airflow behaviour. They help teams understand airflow direction, local disturbances and the influence of interventions.

Recovery testing evaluates how quickly a cleanroom returns to a specified particle-cleanliness condition after a defined challenge.

Visible smoke clearance should not be treated as proof of particle recovery or restoration of the qualified cleanroom state.

Conclusion

A structured smoke study review connects airflow observations with predefined acceptance criteria and the protection required by the process.

By evaluating airflow direction, product protection, turbulence, interventions, potential ingress and supporting documentation, pharmaceutical teams can make more consistent assessments of cleanroom airflow behaviour.

The conclusions should always be based on the approved protocol, facility design and contamination-control requirements.

For a more detailed discussion of smoke study acceptance criteria and airflow risk assessment, see IncepBio's guide to smoke study acceptance criteria.

title: Routing WhatsApp Quick-Reply Buttons to Actions: Payloads, Retries, Edits and Double Taps
description:
Quick-reply buttons on WhatsApp templates ("Confirm", "Reschedule", "Pay deposit") are easy to send and easy to tap. Making each tap do something is where the design work is: knowing a tap from a typed word, keeping old messages' buttons working after the template changes, not sending two payment links when someone taps twice, and not letting a bot grab a chat a person is handling. This post builds a small button router in TypeScript, with tests for each case, and says where our own implementation got one of them wrong.

The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases shown.

What a tap looks like

A tap on a template's quick-reply button arrives as an inbound message with type: "button". Meta's webhook reference describes it: a button object with text and payload, and a context.id that is the ID of the message containing the button. A reply button on an interactive (non-template) message arrives differently, as type: "interactive" with an interactive.button_reply carrying an id and a title. A customer who types "Confirm" sends type: "text", which is not a tap at all.

// The parts of an inbound WhatsApp message a button router needs.
export type Tap = {
  wamid: string;
  from: string;
  payload: string;
  label: string;
  // ID of the message whose button was tapped, when WhatsApp sends it.
  tappedMessageId?: string;
};

type InboundMessage = {
  id: string;
  from: string;
  type: string;
  context?: { id?: string };
  button?: { payload?: string; text?: string };
  interactive?: { type?: string; button_reply?: { id?: string; title?: string } };
};

// Template quick replies arrive as type "button"; interactive reply buttons as
// type "interactive". Anything typed is "text" and is never a tap.
export const extractTap = (m: InboundMessage): Tap | null => {
  if (m.type === "button" && m.button?.payload) {
    return { wamid: m.id, from: m.from, payload: m.button.payload, label: m.button.text ?? "", tappedMessageId: m.context?.id };
  }
  const reply = m.interactive?.type === "button_reply" ? m.interactive.button_reply : undefined;
  if (m.type === "interactive" && reply?.id) {
    return { wamid: m.id, from: m.from, payload: reply.id, label: reply.title ?? "", tappedMessageId: m.context?.id };
  }
  return null;
};

Two things follow:

  • Match on the payload, never the label. The label is what the customer sees and can type. The payload is a value you control. If a typed "confirm" should also do something, that's a keyword rule, a separate decision.
  • Keep context.id. It tells you which message was tapped, which is what you need to stop a repeated tap from repeating a side effect.

Payloads: set them yourself

You can attach your own payload to each quick-reply button when you send the template, as a button component with sub_type: "quick_reply", the button's index, and a payload parameter. When you don't, don't count on the payload being anything but the label: Meta's own webhook example shows the same text in both.

We generate an opaque payload per button action (tba_ plus random hex) and store what it should do. The prefix makes our payloads recognisable, so a payload from another tool or an older template falls through to normal handling instead of being looked up.

The registry: payloads must outlive edits 

import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";

export type ActionType = "send_message" | "send_template" | "start_chatbot" | "send_payment_request";

export type ButtonAction = {
  payload: string;
  templateId: string;
  buttonIndex: number;
  type: ActionType;
  config: Record<string, unknown>;
  // Side effects that must not repeat for the same sent message, such as a payment link.
  oncePerMessage: boolean;
  active: boolean;
};

export type ButtonInput = { index: number; type: ActionType; config: Record<string, unknown>; oncePerMessage?: boolean };

export const PAYLOAD_PREFIX = "tba_";
const newPayload = () => `${PAYLOAD_PREFIX}${randomBytes(12).toString("hex")}`;

// Saving a template must not change the payloads of buttons that still exist:
// messages already sent carry the old payload and must keep working.
export const saveTemplateButtons = (store: Map<string, ButtonAction>, templateId: string, inputs: ButtonInput[]) => {
  const existing = [...store.values()].filter((a) => a.templateId === templateId);
  const byIndex = new Map(existing.map((a) => [a.buttonIndex, a]));

  for (const input of inputs) {
    const payload = byIndex.get(input.index)?.payload ?? newPayload();
    store.set(payload, {
      payload,
      templateId,
      buttonIndex: input.index,
      type: input.type,
      config: input.config,
      oncePerMessage: input.oncePerMessage ?? input.type === "send_payment_request",
      active: true,
    });
  }

  // Removed buttons are retired, not deleted, so a late tap is recognised.
  const kept = new Set(inputs.map((i) => i.index));
  for (const a of existing) if (!kept.has(a.buttonIndex)) store.set(a.payload, { ...a, active: false });
};

// The payloads to attach, by button index, when this template is sent.
export const payloadsForSend = (store: Map<string, ButtonAction>, templateId: string) =>
  [...store.values()]
    .filter((a) => a.templateId === templateId && a.active)
    .sort((a, b) => a.buttonIndex - b.buttonIndex)
    .map((a) => ({ type: "button", sub_type: "quick_reply", index: String(a.buttonIndex), parameters: [{ type: "payload", payload: a.payload }] }));

This is the part we got wrong. In WAPGROWAI, saving a template deletes its button actions and recreates them with new payloads. Messages already sent still carry the old payloads, so after any edit, taps on those messages stop matching: no action runs, and the tap goes through the normal pipeline like any other message. Nothing errors, so nobody notices until a customer says the button "didn't work".

The fix is in saveTemplateButtons: a button that still exists keeps its payload, and only new buttons get new ones. A removed button is retired, not deleted, so a late tap on an old message is recognised and sent to the inbox, where a person can answer it.

One trade-off: this keys a payload to the button's position. If someone swaps "Confirm" and "Reschedule", old messages' first button now runs the new first action. If your editor allows reordering, key by a stable button ID that moves with the button, not by its index.

The router 

import { extractTap } from "./taps.ts";
import { PAYLOAD_PREFIX, type ButtonAction } from "./registry.ts";

export type Outcome =
  | "duplicate_webhook"
  | "not_a_tap"
  | "not_ours"
  | "retired_button"
  | "already_done"
  | "left_for_agent"
  | "ran";

export type RouterDeps = {
  actions: Map<string, ButtonAction>;
  seenWamids: Set<string>;
  doneOnce: Set<string>;
  assignedToPerson: (customer: string) => boolean;
  runAction: (action: ButtonAction, customer: string) => Promise<void>;
  // The normal pipeline: keyword rules, an active chatbot, the inbox.
  fallback: (message: unknown) => Promise<void>;
  reply: (customer: string, text: string) => Promise<void>;
};

export const routeInbound = async (deps: RouterDeps, message: Parameters<typeof extractTap>[0]): Promise<Outcome> => {
  // WhatsApp retries webhooks; one tap must run its action once.
  if (deps.seenWamids.has(message.id)) return "duplicate_webhook";
  deps.seenWamids.add(message.id);

  const tap = extractTap(message);
  if (!tap) return deps.fallback(message).then(() => "not_a_tap");

  const action = tap.payload.startsWith(PAYLOAD_PREFIX) ? deps.actions.get(tap.payload) : undefined;
  // Another tool's button, or one without an action: treat it like any message.
  if (!action) return deps.fallback(message).then(() => "not_ours");
  if (!action.active) return deps.fallback(message).then(() => "retired_button");

  if (action.oncePerMessage && tap.tappedMessageId) {
    const key = `${tap.tappedMessageId}:${action.payload}`;
    if (deps.doneOnce.has(key)) {
      await deps.reply(tap.from, "We've already sent this. Scroll up to find it.");
      return "already_done";
    }
    deps.doneOnce.add(key);
  }

  // A person who has taken the chat owns it; a bot must not take it back.
  if (action.type === "start_chatbot" && deps.assignedToPerson(tap.from)) {
    return deps.fallback(message).then(() => "left_for_agent");
  }

  // The button wins: keyword rules don't also fire for this tap.
  await deps.runAction(action, tap.from);
  return "ran";
};

The order of checks is the design:

  1. Duplicate webhooks first. Meta retries deliveries, so the same tap can arrive twice with the same message ID. Record the ID, and in production put a unique index on it.
  2. Not a tap, or not ours: hand the message to the normal pipeline (keyword rules, an active chatbot, the inbox). A router that swallows everything it doesn't recognise turns buttons from other tools into silence.
  3. Retired buttons also go to the normal pipeline, so a person sees them.
  4. Once-per-message actions. A customer can tap the same button again, and for most actions that's fine: "Thanks, you're booked" twice is harmless. A payment request isn't: each tap would create another payment link. Key the "already done" check on the tapped message's ID plus the payload, so a new booking message gets its own link. Here the key is recorded before the action runs, which blocks a fast double tap; if the action fails, remove the key or store the failure so the customer can try again.
  5. People before bots. If a person has taken over the chat, a "Start chatbot" button shouldn't take it back. The tap goes to the inbox instead.
  6. The button wins. When a tap has an action, keyword rules don't also run for that message. Otherwise a rule listening for "confirm" fires alongside the button's own reply, and the customer gets two answers.

What the tests check

  • Parsing: template and interactive taps are read; a text message is not a tap.
  • Typed text: "Confirm" typed by hand goes to the normal pipeline, and no action runs.
  • Precedence: a tap runs its action, and the fallback (keyword rules) doesn't also run.
  • Webhook retries: the same message ID twice runs the action once.
  • Payment links: a second tap on "Pay" for the same message replies "already sent" instead of creating a second link; a tap on a new booking message creates its own.
  • Harmless repeats: a second tap on "Confirm" sends the thank-you again.
  • Edits: after saving the template again, button 0 keeps its payload, and a tap on a message sent before the edit still runs.
  • Removed buttons: a tap on a button that no longer exists goes to the inbox.
  • Human ownership: "Start chatbot" on a chat a person has taken over goes to the inbox instead.
  • Foreign payloads: a payload without our prefix falls through.
  • Sending: each active button gets a quick_reply component with its payload, by index.

Edge cases worth deciding

  • Payloads per send, not per template. A per-template payload can't tell you which campaign or recipient a tap came from. context.id can, if you store the WhatsApp message ID of every send. That also lets you report taps per campaign.
  • Actions outside the 24-hour window. A tap is a customer message, so it opens the customer service window, and the action can reply with free-form text. A follow-up that runs later, such as a reminder the next day, may need a template again.
  • Opt-outs. A "Stop offers" button should unsubscribe the contact through the same path as a typed STOP, so both are counted and respected in the same place.
  • Logging. Record every tap with its outcome (ran, already_done, left_for_agent and so on). "The button didn't work" is answerable in seconds when you can see the outcome.

Checklist

  • Match taps on a payload you set, never on the label.
  • Handle both button (template) and interactive.button_reply taps.
  • Keep context.id to know which message was tapped.
  • Keep payloads stable across template edits; retire removed buttons instead of deleting them.
  • Dedupe webhook retries by message ID.
  • Make side effects like payment links once per tapped message.
  • Don't let a bot take a chat back from a person.
  • Let a tap's action take precedence over keyword rules.
  • Fall through, don't swallow, for payloads you don't recognise.

WAPGROWAI is built by DI Solutions, a custom software and AI development company. This series covers what we've learned building WAPGROWAI on the WhatsApp Cloud API. Related: building a rules engine for WhatsApp automation and handling WhatsApp Cloud API webhooks in Node.js.

title: Reviewing accepted items does not reveal what a filter missed
description:
I released Rejected Check Audit, an offline tool for auditing denominators in multi-stage filters. It retains events rejected by earlier gates, keeps unknown labels separate from negative labels, and traces known misses to the stage where each event stopped.

Reviewing only the final releases can reveal errors among those releases. It does not reveal how many relevant events were rejected. Treating unreviewed events as negatives, or inventing downstream decisions for stages that never ran, changes the meaning of the reported metrics.

The repository contains twelve author-constructed events in three labeling views: complete labels, released-only labels, and a purpose-selected review subset. These are the same twelve identities, not thirty-six independent observations. When only releases are labeled, the auditor retains the original denominator and returns null for overall recall with an explanation. It does not extrapolate a selected review subset to the whole population.

The tool runs locally with the Python standard library and exports JSON plus stage, path and metric CSV files. A separate verifier, a frozen hand-counted contract and a CPU notebook are included. The final publication package passed fresh-directory execution and additional independent state-combination checks. Published HF file contents and the three searchable dataset views were also checked.

These results validate accounting behavior. They are not model-quality measurements or evidence that a filter improved. There are no production traces, model responses, inference calls or training runs. Real use still requires a defensible event identity, labeling rule, sampling design and stage semantics. Recall uses a conservative complete-label rule; sampling weights, population confidence intervals and partial-identification bounds are outside scope.

Dataset and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/WideChaos/rejected-check-audit

title: I Deleted My Scroll-Lock Library's Ugly Hack. `scrollbar-gutter` Replaces It.
description:
You open a modal. For one frame, before you can even read what it says, the page behind it flinches — the whole column of text shifts a few pixels to the right, like the browser flinched too.

Close the modal and it snaps back. Nobody styled that. Nobody asked for it. And if you build UI on Windows or Linux, you've shipped it to production without noticing, because on a Mac with the default trackpad scrollbars, it's nearly invisible. That's the part that makes this bug so sticky: the person who can see it and the person who has to fix it are usually not using the same operating system.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The standard explanation is that overflow: hidden on <body> — the thing every modal, drawer, and dropdown uses to stop the page scrolling behind it — also removes the vertical scrollbar. Removing the scrollbar hands its width back to the content. The content reflows into that space. The page shifts.

So people fix it the only way CSS used to allow: measure the scrollbar, then pay it back in padding.

function lockScroll() {
  const scrollbarWidth = window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth;
  document.body.style.paddingRight = `${scrollbarWidth}px`;
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden";
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.paddingRight = "";
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

This works. It's also the entire reason body-scroll-lock, react-remove-scroll, and half a dozen modal libraries ship their own copy of this exact measurement. Every one of them is solving the same problem: find out how wide the scrollbar would have been, then fake its presence with padding so nothing moves.

Before you keep reading — guess how many pixels of padding a 100-line copy-pasted "scroll lock" utility is usually off by, on the one OS nobody tested it on. The answer is almost always "enough to notice," because scrollbar width isn't a constant. It's roughly 17px on Windows across Chrome and Firefox alike, 0px on a Mac with overlay scrollbars — and the measurement has to run before you lock, every single time, or it reads the wrong number.

Why the shift happens at all

Here's the part the padding hack never actually fixes, it just hides: a classic scrollbar — the opaque kind with a visible track, standard on Windows and Linux — is laid out inside the element's content box. The browser treats it the same way it treats a sidebar: it eats width from whatever would otherwise render there. Turn the scrollbar off, and the content box grows back to full width. Turn it on, and the content box shrinks to make room. The content isn't "jumping" — it's being resized, every time, and resized fast enough that it reads as a flinch.

macOS's default overlay scrollbars don't do this. They float on top of the content without claiming any layout space, so toggling them on and off never changes anything's width. That's the whole reason this bug is invisible to a developer who only ever tests on their own Mac: the platform they build on structurally can't reproduce the thing their users are reporting.

The padding-right hack works around the resize by adding back exactly the width the scrollbar would have taken — but it only works if you already know the scrollbar is about to disappear, and you measured it correctly, before it does. It's compensating for a resize instead of preventing one.

scrollbar-gutter: stable: tell the layout to stop flinching

CSS has a property for exactly this now, and the name says what it does: reserve the scrollbar's gutter, stably, whether a scrollbar is currently needed or not.

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable;
}

Set this once, and the browser carves out the scrollbar's width in the layout permanently — for overflow: auto, scroll, and hidden. When your modal flips overflow to hidden to lock the page, the gutter is already reserved from before the modal ever opened. There's no width to give back, so there's nothing to resize, so there's nothing to flinch.

function lockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "hidden"; // that's it — no measuring, no padding
}

function unlockScroll() {
  document.body.style.overflow = "";
}

That's the whole fix for the layout-shift half of what a scroll-lock library does. You still need something to stop the page actually scrolling under a modal on touch devices — overflow: hidden alone doesn't catch every edge case there, and that part of a scroll-lock library can stay. But the width-measuring, padding-compensating dance that most of these libraries built their reputation on? scrollbar-gutter: stable makes it dead code.

There's a second value for layouts that center content and need symmetry on both sides:

html {
  scrollbar-gutter: stable both-edges;
}

both-edges mirrors the reserved gutter to the opposite inline edge, so if space is held open on the right, matching space opens on the left too — useful when a scrollbar appearing on only one side would visibly knock a centered layout off-center.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that's easy to get wrong: overlay scrollbars opt out of this too

Here's the honest asterisk, and it's the same one from earlier in reverse: scrollbar-gutter: stable only reserves space for classic scrollbars. MDN says it plainly — "When using overlay scrollbars, the gutter will not be present." On a system with overlay scrollbars, setting this property changes nothing, because there was never any layout space being given up in the first place.

That means you can't fully verify this fix by eyeballing your own Mac. You need a Windows or Linux machine, a Windows/Linux VM, or Chrome DevTools' device toolbar won't help either — it emulates viewport size, not the host OS's scrollbar rendering mode. The honest test is someone, or something, running an actual classic-scrollbar environment.

Is this safe to ship today?

Yes, with one small caveat worth knowing rather than discovering. Chrome and Edge have supported scrollbar-gutter since version 94 (2021), and Firefox since version 97 (2022) — this has quietly worked for most of your users for years. Safari was the holdout; it landed support in Safari 18.2, released in December 2024, which is also what pushed scrollbar-gutter to Baseline "newly available" that same month. If you need to support Safari versions older than 18.2, the property is simply ignored there — no error, no warning, the page just behaves exactly like it always did. That's a safe degrade, not a broken one, so there's no reason to gate this behind a feature query unless you want to show a different UI specifically for browsers that lack it.

The next time a modal makes your page twitch, you'll know exactly why — and now you know the one-line reason to stop paying JavaScript to measure a number CSS can just reserve for you.

Still carrying a scroll-lock library in your bundle for this exact problem? Go check what it actually does under the hood — there's a decent chance half of it just became unnecessary.
