title: Chrome Blocked 8 eMudhra CA Keys on Oct 17. A Node Release From Oct 14 Still Trusts Them.
description:
On Saturday, October 17, at 18:05 UTC, a researcher reported to the Chrome Root Program that the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates could be recovered by anyone. The keys had been generated with weak randomness. With one of them you can sign a certificate for any domain, and clients that still trust that intermediate will accept it.

Chrome blocked the keys 100 minutes later with a CRLSet push. Firefox blocked them the same day. Microsoft followed on the 20th, Apple on the 22nd, and Chrome removed the root above them, emSign ECC Root CA - G3, from its root store on October 27.

That covers browsers. Your backend is not a browser. It calls Stripe, sends webhooks and talks to your email provider through Node, Python or Go, and a lot of those don't read CRLSets. They check against a list of roots that shipped with the runtime or the package.

So I tested it. Same Debian 13 box, with the patched system ca-certificates (20250419+deb13u1) installed. A Node binary released on October 14 still connected to a site signed by a compromised intermediate.

What actually happened, briefly

  • Eight intermediates under emSign ECC Root CA - G3 had keys that could be recovered straight from the public certificates. eMudhra says it revoked all eight on October 18, that seven were never used in production, and that the one in production had issued zero certificates.
  • No abuse has been reported. Cloudflare said it found no exploitation on its services, and the test page below says plainly that nobody knows whether non-browser clients were targeted. Browsers also enforce Certificate Transparency, so a forged cert that was never logged fails there anyway.
  • Most non-browser clients check neither revocation nor CT. For them, the only fix is a trust store that no longer includes those roots.

Dennis Jackson from Mozilla put up a test page with live endpoints signed by the compromised intermediates, plus a list of which packages have shipped fixes. If your client connects and gets the text "That's bad!", it still trusts them. The -noct hosts use leaf certs that were never logged to CT, which is the case an attacker would actually use.

The test

A 13-line script that calls fetch() on the four test hosts:

// check-emudhra.mjs
const hosts = ['dv-g3b', 'dv-g3b-aaa', 'dv-g3b-noct', 'dv-g3b-aaa-noct'];
console.log(`node ${process.version}`);
for (const h of hosts) {
  const url = `https://${h}-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/`;
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) });
    const body = (await res.text()).trim().slice(0, 40);
    console.log(`${h.padEnd(16)} TRUSTED   ${res.status} "${body}"`);
  } catch (e) {
    console.log(`${h.padEnd(16)} rejected  ${e.cause?.code ?? e.message}`);
  }
}

Real output, run this morning:

node v24.22.1
dv-g3b           rejected  CERT_REVOKED
dv-g3b-aaa       rejected  CERT_REVOKED
dv-g3b-noct      rejected  CERT_REVOKED
dv-g3b-aaa-noct  rejected  CERT_REVOKED

node v24.22.0
dv-g3b           TRUSTED   200 "Your client successfully connected to th"
dv-g3b-aaa       rejected  UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY
dv-g3b-noct      TRUSTED   200 "Your client successfully connected to th"
dv-g3b-aaa-noct  rejected  UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY

The full body of that 200 is "Your client successfully connected to the site. That's bad!". Node 24.22.0 came out on October 14. Node 24.22.1 is the October 21 security release, which updated the bundled roots to NSS 3.131.1 and added a check that rejects chains containing blocked public keys. That second change is most likely where the CERT_REVOKED comes from.

I ran the same thing in Python with requests, which uses certifi's bundle and not the OS:

certifi 2026.10.23
dv-g3b           rejected  unable to get local issuer certificate
dv-g3b-noct      rejected  unable to get local issuer certificate

certifi 2026.07.22
dv-g3b           TRUSTED   200 'Your client successfully connected to th'
dv-g3b-noct      TRUSTED   200 'Your client successfully connected to th'

(The two -aaa hosts, which use Sectigo cross-signs, were rejected by every client on this box, old or new, so I've left them out here.)

curl on the same machine rejected all four, because it uses the patched system bundle. So the OS was fixed and two of the three clients on it weren't.

Why patching the OS didn't help

Node ships its own copy of the Mozilla root list inside the binary. requests reads certifi's cacert.pem out of your virtualenv. Updating ca-certificates touches neither.

One trap I didn't expect: node --use-system-ca didn't help on the old binary either. It still trusted the bad host. The Node docs say that flag uses the system store "along with" the bundled one, so the old bundled root is still there. --use-openssl-ca, which swaps the bundled store for OpenSSL's system store, did reject all four on the old binary. Upgrading Node is still the real fix. The flag just tells you where the trust is coming from.

Where the old copies are hiding

For a small SaaS or a side project, I'd check these:

  • Docker images built before October 21. The Node or Python inside is whatever was current at build time. If you pin node:24-slim by digest, it doesn't move until you move it.
  • Anything on Node 20. It's end-of-life, so it doesn't get the new root list at all. Vercel's advisory says the same thing and tells people to move to 22 or newer.
  • A pinned certifi in requirements.txt, poetry.lock or uv.lock. Patched from 2026.10.19.
  • CI runners and self-hosted cron boxes, which tend to drift.
  • Your Mac. As of the test page's October 28 update, the curl, git and python3 Apple ships still trust the compromised certificates.

The project you haven't touched since summer is the most likely to still have the old list. If that's you, I wrote a list of what to check first when you restart an abandoned side project, and an expired runtime is one of the items on it.

An 18-line check for any machine or image

This prints 1 if emSign ECC Root CA - G3 is still in the system bundle, in the node you're running, or in your certifi:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# roots-check.sh: 1 = root still trusted (bad), 0 = gone
NODE=${NODE:-node}; PY=${PY:-python3}
needle='emSign ECC Root CA - G3'

count_in_bundle() {
  openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile "$1" | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout \
    | grep '^subject=' | grep -c "$needle"
}

echo "system bundle:          $(count_in_bundle /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt)"
echo "node $($NODE -v) bundled: $($NODE -e '
  const { X509Certificate } = require("crypto");
  const hits = require("tls").rootCertificates
    .filter(pem => new X509Certificate(pem).subject.includes(process.argv[1]));
  console.log(hits.length)' "$needle")"
CF=$($PY -c 'import certifi; print(certifi.where())')
echo "certifi $($PY -c 'import certifi; print(certifi.__version__)'):     $(count_in_bundle "$CF")"

Output for the current versions and then the old ones:

system bundle:          0
node v24.22.1 bundled: 0
certifi 2026.10.23:     0

system bundle:          0
node v24.22.0 bundled: 1
certifi 2026.07.22:     1

To check a container, mount the script and run it inside, something like docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/c" your-image bash /c/roots-check.sh. Slim images often lack openssl or python, so just keep the line that applies (for a Node image, the node -e part is all you need).

Is your own site's certificate affected?

This is the other half, and for most indie sites the answer is no. If your cert comes from Let's Encrypt or Google Trust Services, like most small sites, nothing changes for you. It matters if you bought an ECC certificate that chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3. The University of Michigan, for example, had to replace certificates issued through CERTInext with ECC keys, and its sites behind Cloudflare in Full (strict) mode started returning 526 errors on October 20.

To see which root you're on, look at the issuer line and every row of the chain, not just the expiry date. openssl s_client -connect yourdomain.com:443 -showcerts shows them, or you can paste the domain into a free SSL checker that lists the issuer and the full chain. If "emSign" shows up anywhere in that chain, get a new certificate from a different CA before your visitors start seeing warnings.

The fix list

  1. Node: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 or later. Get off Node 20.
  2. certifi 2026.10.19 or later, and update the lockfile too.
  3. Rebuild images with --pull --no-cache so you don't reuse the old layer, then redeploy. Restart long-running processes too. A Node process that's been up since September is still running the old binary with the old roots.
  4. Run check-emudhra.mjs (or curl on the test host) from inside the deployed thing, not from your laptop. Cloudflare's write-up makes the same point: a passing browser test doesn't mean your background worker is fixed.
  5. If something starts failing with certificate errors after you patch, do not "fix" it with NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 or verify=False. That turns off the protection you just installed.

This is the second certificate change this month that only shows up when you check what's actually running instead of what the config says. The other one is Let's Encrypt moving to 64-day certificates, where the danger is hardcoded renewal thresholds.

If you pin your base image by digest (which you should for other reasons), what makes you rebuild it? A schedule, Renovate/Dependabot bumping the digest, or only when something breaks?

title: Why SQLite WAL Still Raises "database is locked" in Python
description:
You switch a small Python service to SQLite write-ahead logging, start two workers, and still see "database is locked." The obvious question is whether WAL is broken. Usually it is not. The mistaken assumption is that allowing readers and writers to overlap is the same as allowing multiple writers to commit simultaneously.

SQLite's WAL documentation makes the distinction explicit: readers can continue while a writer appends, but there is still only one active writer. That matters for webhook handlers, queue consumers, background jobs, and small web applications that share a single database file. A slow transaction can block a perfectly ordinary insert in another process.

This tutorial starts with a reproducible lock, then changes only the parts that actually control write contention. The examples use Python's built-in sqlite3 module, a local temporary database, and ordinary SQL. You do not need an ORM or a server installation.

WAL changes reader/writer overlap, not the single-writer rule

In the default rollback-journal mode, a reader can interfere with a writer's ability to complete a transaction. WAL stores new pages in a separate log first. A reader keeps using a consistent view of the database while the writer appends changes. That is a useful improvement for workloads that mix frequent reads with short writes.

However, the WAL still has one write stream. Two connections cannot both own the writer lock. The second writer must wait until the first transaction ends, or fail when its busy timeout expires. WAL is not a substitute for keeping transactions short.

A practical model is to separate three operations:

  • Reading a stable snapshot.
  • Owning the writer lock and committing a change.
  • Copying committed WAL content back into the main database during a checkpoint.

They have different concurrency behavior. Treating them as a single "SQLite is concurrent" setting hides the cause of most locking complaints.

Reproduce a blocked writer with two connections

Save the following as a standalone Python file and run it. It creates a temporary database, enables WAL, and opens two independent connections. Connection A deliberately keeps a write transaction open while connection B attempts another write.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import sqlite3

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    db = Path(folder) / "events.db"

    setup = sqlite3.connect(db, isolation_level=None)
    mode = setup.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL").fetchone()[0]
    setup.execute(
        "CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, message TEXT)"
    )
    setup.close()
    assert mode == "wal"

    writer_a = sqlite3.connect(db, timeout=0.2, isolation_level=None)
    writer_b = sqlite3.connect(db, timeout=0.2, isolation_level=None)

    writer_a.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    writer_a.execute(
        "INSERT INTO events(message) VALUES (?)", ("first",)
    )
    try:
        writer_b.execute(
            "INSERT INTO events(message) VALUES (?)", ("second",)
        )
    except sqlite3.OperationalError as error:
        print(type(error).__name__, str(error))
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Second writer unexpectedly succeeded")

    writer_a.execute("COMMIT")
    writer_b.execute(
        "INSERT INTO events(message) VALUES (?)", ("second",)
    )

    print(writer_b.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events").fetchone()[0])
    writer_a.close()
    writer_b.close()
~~~{% endraw %}

The expected observation is an OperationalError mentioning that the database is locked, followed by a row count of two. Connection B did not have corrupt data or a broken journal. It tried to write while connection A owned the writer lock. After A committed, B could proceed.

The small timeout is intentional. It makes the demonstration fast instead of leaving the program waiting. In a real service, choose a timeout from the request latency budget rather than copying this demonstration value blindly.

Notice the explicit BEGIN IMMEDIATE. It requests the write transaction at the start instead of letting the first write statement discover the contention later. That makes the critical section visible to the reader and to anyone inspecting logs.

## Set a bounded busy timeout, then measure it

Python's sqlite3.connect accepts a timeout parameter. Its documented default is five seconds. This controls how long a connection waits on a lock before raising an OperationalError; it does not promise that a lock will clear during that window.

SQLite also exposes PRAGMA busy_timeout, measured in milliseconds. You can inspect the configured value directly rather than guessing which connection settings are in effect.{% raw %}

~~~python
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect("app.db", timeout=2.0, isolation_level=None)
value = db.execute("PRAGMA busy_timeout").fetchone()[0]
print("Busy timeout in milliseconds:", value)

db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS jobs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)")
db.close()
~~~

The path here is illustrative; use a file inside your application's designated data directory. For tests, prefer a temporary directory. Keep a timeout small enough that one stuck worker cannot absorb an entire fleet of incoming requests. A longer timeout can smooth brief bursts, but it does not fix a writer that holds a transaction while waiting for network I/O.

A useful diagnostic log records transaction start time, time spent waiting to begin a write, commit time, and which operation ran inside the transaction. A simple error count without timing data will not tell you whether the cause is lock acquisition, a slow transaction, or a checkpoint interaction.

## Move network calls out of write transactions

This pattern causes unnecessary contention: begin a transaction, read a job, call a remote API, wait for a response, then update the row and commit. The database writer lock is now tied to unpredictable network latency.

The better boundary is usually a short claim transaction followed by the slow work outside it. A final short transaction records the result. If multiple workers may claim the same job, enforce the claim atomically with a conditional update, not a separate SELECT followed by an unconditional UPDATE.

The next example shows a claim that can be attempted by multiple connections. Each connection uses its own handle to the same local database.{% raw %}

~~~python
import sqlite3

def claim_job(db_path: str, job_id: int, worker: str) -> bool:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(
        db_path, timeout=2.0, isolation_level=None
    )
    try:
        conn.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
        changed = conn.execute(
            """
            UPDATE jobs
               SET status = 'claimed', worker = ?
             WHERE id = ? AND status = 'pending'
            """,
            (worker, job_id),
        ).rowcount
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
        return changed == 1
    except Exception:
        if conn.in_transaction:
            conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    finally:
        conn.close()
~~~{% endraw %}

This function intentionally does not perform the job itself. Its only responsibility is to claim it. The worker can then release the connection, execute the slow external task, and store completion in another short transaction.

A conditional claim is not a complete job queue. You still need an explicit policy for abandoned claims, visibility timeouts, retryability, and side effects. In particular, a failed network response must not automatically be interpreted as a failed remote operation. The database can prevent duplicate local claims without proving whether an external action happened.

## Make transaction ownership explicit

Connection behavior changed in modern Python: the sqlite3 module has an autocommit interface, while isolation_level controls the older implicit transaction behavior. Code copied from older tutorials may therefore use different transaction assumptions than your service.

The examples here deliberately set isolation_level=None and issue SQL BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK statements themselves. This is a simple way to make each critical section visible for teaching and testing. It is not a recommendation to mix implicit and explicit transaction models in an existing application.

If you use Python's newer autocommit parameter instead, choose a model once and test it against the exact Python version deployed. Do not assume that wrapping every operation in a with block fixes a transaction that begins too early. Confirm when the lock is actually acquired and when the database is free to accept the next writer.

A review of transaction boundaries should answer four concrete questions. Where does the transaction start? Which statement first needs the writer lock? Does any file, HTTP, model, or queue operation happen before commit? Does every exception path roll back or otherwise release the connection? If the answers are unclear, adding a timeout is only masking uncertainty.

## See what a long-lived reader does to checkpoints

A checkpoint copies content from the WAL back into the main database file. SQLite normally handles checkpointing automatically, so most small applications can begin with its defaults. That does not mean checkpoint progress is guaranteed under an endless stream of overlapping readers.

A reader holds a snapshot end mark. A checkpoint cannot advance past pages needed by that reader. If readers never finish, the WAL can grow even while new writes continue to succeed. This often appears as a growing database-wal file rather than as an immediate write failure.

You can inspect checkpoint status through PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE). It reports three values: whether the operation encountered a busy condition, the number of pages in the WAL, and the number of pages checkpointed.

~~~python
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db", timeout=2.0)
mode = conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode").fetchone()[0]
if mode != "wal":
    raise RuntimeError("Expected WAL mode")

busy, log_pages, checkpointed = conn.execute(
    "PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)"
).fetchone()

print({
    "busy": busy,
    "wal_pages": log_pages,
    "checkpointed_pages": checkpointed,
})
conn.close()
~~~

This is a diagnostic probe, not an instruction to force TRUNCATE after every request. A passive checkpoint may stop before completing without disrupting active readers. More aggressive checkpoint modes have different blocking behavior, so schedule them with knowledge of your workload rather than using them as a reflexive lock repair.

Also keep the database on a local filesystem suitable for SQLite WAL. Its shared-memory design does not support the ordinary cross-machine network-filesystem scenario described in SQLite's official documentation.

## Use a small contention test before tuning production

A reliable test needs at least two independent connections to the same file. A single connection running a loop cannot reproduce writer competition by itself. The most revealing test holds a transaction open on one connection, then measures how the other behaves with a known timeout.

Run the test in both directions: first with a deliberate hold that exceeds the timeout, then with a short hold that ends before the timeout. Confirm the expected failure and expected successful wait. Log elapsed time, not just the exception text.

After that, verify the application's own transaction length. A write query may take milliseconds while the surrounding transaction stays open for seconds. Look for synchronous HTTP calls, expensive serialization, long loops, or human input inside write transactions. Those are better targets for improvement than arbitrary PRAGMA values.

Keep the test separate from production records. A temporary directory and deterministic fixtures make the result repeatable and prevent a performance experiment from altering real work.

## A practical decision rule for small Python services

Start with WAL when the application has mixed reads and writes on one local machine and the mode is appropriate for its storage. Use a finite lock timeout and short write transactions. Have each process or worker create and manage its own connection according to the application's threading model. Avoid passing one Python connection around unrelated threads.

If a lock persists, measure the actual transaction boundary and write occupancy before increasing the timeout. If the database-wal file grows, inspect long-lived readers and checkpoint progress separately. These are two different symptoms with different interventions.

If the required write throughput depends on many simultaneous long write transactions, SQLite's single-writer design may be the wrong fit. That is an architectural decision, not evidence that WAL is malfunctioning.

The key result is reproducible: WAL lets readers overlap a writer; it does not let two writers own the write lock. Fix the time spent holding that lock, and the "database is locked" exception becomes a measurable contention signal rather than a mysterious configuration failure.

## Primary references

- [SQLite: Write-Ahead Logging](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html) — writer concurrency, checkpoints, and filesystem constraints.
- [Python: sqlite3 module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html) — connection timeout and transaction-control behavior.
- [SQLite: PRAGMA statements](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html) — busy_timeout and wal_checkpoint semantics.

The reproducer and claim function intentionally use built-in Python and SQLite features only; adapt transaction and recovery policy to the failure modes of your application.

---

Originally published on [Dispatch](https://dispatch-blog.hashnode.dev/why-sqlite-wal-still-raises-database-is-locked-in-python).

title: Cypress Email Tests Need a Freshness Gate
description:
An email test can find a message and still be wrong. This happens when a shared inbox contains an older verification email, the test selects the newest result without checking its age, and the browser follows a link that belongs to another run.

The result is especially confusing in Cypress. The command log shows that an email was found, the link was clicked, and the test failed later on a page that looks unrelated. A freshness gate makes the ownership question explicit: did this message arrive after this test triggered the email?

I use a temp mail so inbox for experiments when a real mailbox is not appropriate, but the provider is not the reliability strategy. The strategy is to record a boundary, reject stale messages, and preserve enough evidence to explain the next check.

Why the newest email can still be the wrong email

Suppose a password-reset test does this:

cy.request("POST", "/api/password-reset", { email });
cy.get("[data-testid=inbox-message]")
  .first()
  .click();

This looks reasonable until a retry, a local manual run, or another parallel worker leaves messages in the inbox. “First” is a sorting decision, not proof that the message belongs to this test.

A stale message may contain a valid link, so the failure is not always immediate. The link can open a reset page with an expired token, a session mismatch, or a state created by another test. Increasing Cypress retries can hide the collision for a while, but it does not fix the evidence boundary. The setup is a little more work, yet the diagnosis becomes much clearer.

Define freshness as a test contract

Capture the time immediately before the action that should cause delivery. Then make freshness one of the acceptance rules, along with recipient, subject, and a unique test marker when the application supports one.

const triggeredAt = new Date();

cy.request("POST", "/api/password-reset", { email }).then(() => {
  cy.pollInbox({ email, since: triggeredAt.toISOString() }).then((message) => {
    expect(message.receivedAt, "message freshness").to.be.greaterThan(
      triggeredAt.toISOString(),
    );
    expect(message.to).to.equal(email);
    expect(message.subject).to.contain("Reset your password");
  });
});

The exact mailbox API will vary. The useful part is the contract. since should be enforced by the query when possible, and checked again after parsing. Clocks can differ between services, so allow a small documented skew rather than pretending timestamps are perfect. If that detail is ignored, failures becomes hard to reproduce.

For teams that separate test signals from application behavior, using topic scores to keep automation work focused is a useful reminder: give each signal one clear job. Freshness proves timing and ownership; the UI assertion proves the browser flow.

A Cypress helper with an evidence trail

Keep polling, filtering, and diagnostics in a custom command or helper. The spec should say what the user is doing, while the helper explains why a candidate was accepted or rejected.

Cypress.Commands.add("waitForFreshMessage", (options) => {
  const evidence = [];
  const deadline = Date.now() + 45_000;

  function check() {
    return cy.mailbox(options.inbox).then((messages) => {
      const fresh = messages.filter((message) => {
        const isFresh = new Date(message.receivedAt) >= new Date(options.since);
        const isOwned = message.to === options.email;
        const hasSubject = message.subject.includes(options.subject);

        evidence.push({
          id: message.id,
          receivedAt: message.receivedAt,
          isFresh,
          isOwned,
          hasSubject,
        });

        return isFresh && isOwned && hasSubject ? message : null;
      }).find(Boolean);

      if (fresh) return cy.wrap({ message: fresh, evidence });
      if (Date.now() >= deadline) {
        throw new Error(`No fresh message found: ${JSON.stringify(evidence)}`);
      }
      return cy.wait(1_000).then(check);
    });
  }

  return check();
});

In production code I would also validate the timestamp format and cap the evidence size. The important behavior is that an old message is visible in the failure output instead of silently discarded. A burner email address can keep test data isolated, but isolation still needs a freshness check.

If CI stores the message body or headers, keep that artifact tied to the run id. Versioning email evidence by digest gives a practical way to compare what changed between retries without copying a whole mailbox into every log.

Triage stale-message failures

When the helper fails, I inspect the evidence in this order:

  1. Only old messages appear: check inbox reuse, worker cleanup, and the since timestamp.
  2. Fresh messages have the wrong recipient: check address allocation and application routing.
  3. Fresh messages have the wrong subject: check localization, template changes, or a different notification being selected.
  4. A message passes but the link fails: inspect token lifetime, session binding, and the browser state.

This order avoids changing the polling timeout before checking whether the test is reading the correct mailbox. A phrase like tempail may appear in search notes or a manual run, but it should never become evidence that a message is owned by the current test.

A repeatable checklist

Before merging a Cypress email test, verify:

  • the trigger boundary is captured immediately before the delivery action
  • each worker has an isolated inbox or a unique test marker
  • freshness, recipient, and subject are separate acceptance checks
  • rejected messages record ids and reasons
  • the deadline and clock-skew allowance are documented
  • CI saves the evidence when polling fails
  • the browser assertion runs only after the message passes the gate

If a team needs an external disposable email address generator for short-lived test data, keep its use inside non-production environments and document the data-retention assumption. The test should still be useful if the provider changes its inbox sorting.

Q&A

Is checking the newest message enough?

No. Newest is a relative ordering, not a relationship to the current test. Compare against the trigger boundary and verify ownership.

Should Cypress retry the whole test?

Usually not as the first response. Retry the bounded inbox observation while retaining the evidence from each attempt. A whole-test retry can make a stale-message problem look intermittent.

What if the provider has coarse timestamps?

Use a small, explicit clock-skew window and add a unique marker to the address or subject when possible. If neither is available, label the weaker guarantee in the test output.

A fresh-message gate does not make delivery instant. It makes the test honest about what it observed, which is a much better starting point when QA has to repair a red run.

title: Threat modeling the CVE-2026-105483 certificate bypass
description:
Threat modeling the CVE-2026-105483 certificate bypass

CVE-2026-105483 is best treated as an identity-binding failure. In affected Node.js 24.x and 26.x releases, tls.checkServerIdentity() could validate a fullwidth-digit IPv4 destination as a DNS identity. The connection normalized and resolved the destination to IPv4, while verification accepted a certificate with a matching DNS SAN. A client could therefore trust a server certificate for an endpoint it did not intend to contact.

The issue was fixed in Node.js 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 on October 21, 2026. Node.js rates it High. The advisory records CVSS v3.0 7.4 with high attack complexity and high confidentiality and integrity impact.

The vulnerable decision

TLS combines three operations that must remain aligned:

  1. Parse the requested destination.
  2. Establish a transport connection to the resolved endpoint.
  3. Verify that the peer certificate identifies that endpoint under the application's identity policy.

The vulnerable Node.js path separated the third step from the first two. The certificate chain could be signed by a trusted CA, yet the certificate identity could describe the endpoint as a DNS name rather than an IP address. This makes a generic statement such as "the certificate is trusted" insufficient. The relevant question is "trusted for what identity."

Build a concrete threat model

Start with the attacker's required position. The attacker needs to influence or impersonate the resolved endpoint, present a certificate trusted by the client, and supply a DNS SAN that matches the normalized address representation. High attack complexity in the CVSS vector reflects these coordinated conditions.

Next, identify where the client's destination comes from. A fixed, operator-controlled DNS name sharply limits who can select the fullwidth form. A tenant-provided callback URL, proxy setting, connector target, or imported integration can expose a wider population of potential attackers.

Then examine the data carried after the handshake. A health check may reveal little. A request with a bearer token, signed administrative operation, private file, or privileged database query can produce serious confidentiality and integrity impact.

Finally, examine certificate trust. A public trust store is only one source. Internal CAs, development roots, delegated intermediates, and application-specific trust bundles may create certificates that are valid for the client but outside the assumptions of public issuance policy.

Risk questions for each client

The following questions produce useful evidence:

  • Can any untrusted party choose a destination string?
  • Is the destination expected to be a DNS name or an IP address?
  • Does the application canonicalize the value before making a trust decision?
  • Does it require an IP SAN for an IP endpoint?
  • Which CAs can issue a certificate with an address-like DNS SAN?
  • What credentials or data are sent after the certificate check?
  • Can an operator detect a connection to an unexpected address?
  • Is the deployed Node.js runtime fixed?

A yes or no answer is less useful than an attached artifact: a code path, a certificate profile, a network policy, a runtime version, or a test result.

Separate exposure from compromise

ZoomEye Search app="Node.js" returned 5,539,674 product-fingerprint matches at 04:17 +08:00 on November 2, 2026. The CVE filter returned zero. The selected Exposure is 5,539,674, but the observable unit is a Node.js fingerprint, not a vulnerable process or a victim.

That evidence does not show that CVE-2026-105483 was exploited. It also cannot show whether an internet-facing service accepts user-controlled destinations. Use the count as background for why a Node.js estate matters, then rely on internal control evidence for incident decisions.

Prioritization

Prioritize clients that combine three properties: attacker-influenced destinations, a broad trust store, and high-value requests. Patch those systems first, then remove ambiguous destination inputs from their TLS path. Rotate credentials only if there is evidence that a connection reached an unintended endpoint; this CVE does not establish that event by itself.

For services with fixed destinations, upgrade on the normal critical-patch schedule while confirming the actual runtime. A fixed runtime is necessary even when the immediate exploit path looks narrow because configuration and integrations change over time.

Validation and response

Create an isolated test with a private CA and a certificate containing a numeric DNS SAN but no matching IP SAN. Verify that the patched client rejects the certificate for an IPv4 endpoint. Add a positive control with a matching IP SAN so the test distinguishes a correct rejection from a broken TLS client.

Monitor for failed identity checks after deployment, but do not assume silence proves safety. Existing clients may not log certificate identity details at the destination level. Combine runtime version evidence, destination-policy review, and controlled test results before closing the risk.

Remediation

Upgrade Node.js to 24.22.1, 26.12.1, or later. Rebuild packaged runtimes and redeploy images or single-executable applications that contain the old binary. Restrict user-controlled host inputs to canonical DNS names or canonical IP literals, require the matching SAN class, and avoid bypassing the standard certificate verification path.

The objective is to make one statement true across code, certificate policy, and deployment evidence: the identity being verified is the identity the application actually intended to use.

References

  • Node.js October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • Node.js 24.22.1 release notes
  • Node.js 26.12.1 release notes
  • GitHub Advisory GHSA-8h4p-qpcq-gq24
  • ZoomEye Search

title: 28 of 29 Reads of gymshark.com Described Its Checkout Host. The One That Didn't Had Next.js and Six Social Profiles
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali, and a dull part of that job is deciding who to write to. A clinic running Shopify with no consent banner is a different conversation from a hotel chain on Adobe. So one of the Apify Actors I maintain takes a list of domains and returns one flat row per website — CMS, e-commerce platform, framework, analytics, ad pixels, payments, CDN, consent tool, chat widget — plus the e-mails and social profiles it finds on the same page: Wappalyzer Scraper. No browser, no extension, no API key. $0.01 per website.

The input prefill is three domains, and my own health checks have been hammering that prefill since early October. Which means I now have something better than a demo: 29 runs between 6 October and 1 November 2026 on the same three domains, plus a panel I ran this morning on 20 well-known brands.

The 29-run panel said something I did not want to read.

The same domain, two completely different companies

Across those 29 runs, gymshark.com produced 29 rows and exactly two distinct values in the url field:

https://us.checkout.gymshark.com/     28 rows
https://www.gymshark.com/              1 row   (12 Oct 2026)

Here are the two stacks, side by side:

us.checkout.gymshark.com   Shopify · Cloudflare · AWS S3 · HTTP/3 · HSTS ·
                           Apple Pay · Shop Pay · Shopify Analytics
www.gymshark.com           Shopify · React · Next.js · Amazon CloudFront ·
                           HSTS · OneTrust · Apple Pay

Three technologies are shared. Everything else disagrees — including the CDN, which is Cloudflare on one page and CloudFront on the other, and the framework, which exists on one page and not the other. The readVia field says direct in both cases. No error, no retry, no warning.

And the contacts half of the row collapses completely:

rows with at least one social profile
gymshark.com     1 of 29
allbirds.com    27 of 27
notion.so       25 of 27

That single social-profile row for Gymshark is the 12 October row — the one that reached the home page, where the footer carries Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, YouTube and TikTok. A checkout page has no footer. So 28 of 29 times, this Actor truthfully reported that gymshark.com has no social presence, because the page it was handed does not.

Nothing here is a scraping failure. Gymshark's edge decides, per request, that my IP belongs on a checkout host, and HTTP 301 is not an error. The row is a correct description of a page nobody meant me to measure.

Where this goes wrong in practice

The input that sells this Actor looks like this:

{
  "domains": ["gymshark.com", "allbirds.com", "brooklinen.com"],
  "mustUse": ["shopify"],
  "mustNotUse": ["klaviyo"],
  "includeContacts": true
}

Read it out loud: Shopify stores that have not bought Klaviyo yet. Now feed it the checkout row. Shopify: present. Klaviyo: absent — because checkout pages carry almost no marketing tags. Gymshark survives the filter and lands in a prospect list of companies that "don't use Klaviyo", with no e-mail attached. A mustNotUse filter is only as honest as the page it was evaluated against, and I had not written that down anywhere.

The 20-brand panel: who gets redirected

This morning, one run, 20 brands, 9.1 seconds, $0.20. All 20 answered — 16 on a plain request, 4 only through a residential proxy. 128 technologies, median 6 per site, range 2 to 13.

Six of the 20 rows did not describe the bare home page:

gymshark.com  ->  https://us.checkout.gymshark.com/        (different host)
notion.so     ->  https://www.notion.com/                  (different domain)
lego.com      ->  https://www.lego.com/en-us
uniqlo.com    ->  https://www.uniqlo.com/us/en/
samsung.com   ->  https://www.samsung.com/us/
hm.com        ->  https://www.hm.com/entrance.ahtml?orguri=%2F

The technology counts line up with that list almost perfectly. The fat rows are direct-to-consumer stores that answer on their real home page: brooklinen 13, glossier 12, allbirds 12, decathlon 9. The thin rows are global brands: adidas 2, uniqlo 2, booking 2, zara 3, hm 3.

Adidas does not run two technologies. Four of those rows were header-only — every item in technologiesDetailed had foundIn: "header":

uniqlo.com    2   Akamai, HSTS
booking.com   2   Amazon CloudFront, HSTS
adidas.com    2   Akamai, HSTS
zara.com      3   Akamai, HTTP/3, HSTS

That is not a stack. That is "I reached a CDN and the document behind it told me nothing." The useful rule I now apply to my own exports: a row with ≤3 technologies and no foundIn: "page" evidence is a missing measurement, not a minimal stack. Drop it or re-queue it; do not count it in a market share tally. In this panel that is 4 of 20 rows — 20% of the bill, 0% of the signal.

One site answered three identical calls three different ways

I then ran only the four proxy-needing domains, three times, inside ten minutes. Three of them were stable down to the technology:

zara.com     3 techs, identical in all 3 passes
adidas.com   2 techs, identical in all 3 passes
asos.com     7 techs, identical in all 3 passes (jQuery, Akamai, HSTS,
             Mixpanel, New Relic, OneTrust, Optimizely)

hm.com was not:

pass 1   https://www.hm.com/entrance.ahtml?orguri=%2F   Akamai · ASP.NET · HSTS
pass 2   https://www2.hm.com/en_us/index.html           React · Next.js · Akamai · HSTS · Apple Pay
pass 3   https://www2.hm.com/it_it/index.html           React · Next.js · Akamai · HSTS · Apple Pay

Different host, different locale, and a poweredBy field that flips between ASP.NET and Next.js. Both answers are true: the region gate at entrance.ahtml is an old ASP.NET page, and the localized storefront on www2 is a Next.js app. Which one you get depends on the exit IP of the proxy that happened to answer. A fourth page, www2.hm.com/es_mx/index.html, came back when I passed the www2 host explicitly in the same hour.

So drift is not a property of the proxy. It is a property of the site: anything with a region gate in front of it will hand different machines different pages, and a technographic column built from one pass will quietly disagree with itself next month.

You cannot aim it at a deep page

Worth knowing before you try: this Actor normalises every input down to a host and reads that host's root. I fed it six deep URLs to prove the point:

input                                       actually read
https://www.uniqlo.com/us/en/men        ->  https://www.uniqlo.com/us/en/
https://www.booking.com/index.en-gb.html->  https://booking.com/
https://www.zara.com/us/                ->  https://www.zara.com/
https://www.adidas.com/us               ->  https://www.adidas.com/
https://www.gymshark.com/collections/all->  https://us.checkout.gymshark.com/

Path and www. are stripped, the root is fetched, and redirects take it from there. That is deliberate — when the input is 50,000 domains from a CRM export, the home page is the only URL you know exists — but it means this is the wrong tool for "what does this one landing page run". For that, point a browser-based crawler at the exact URL.

Calling it, and reading the answer honestly 

curl -s -X POST \
  "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~wappalyzer-scraper/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"domains":["allbirds.com","brooklinen.com"],"includeContacts":true}'

Three fields decide whether you trust the rest of the row, and I would read them in this order:

  1. url — is the host the one you asked for? Compare it to your input before anything else. If it drifted, the technologies belong to another page.
  2. readVia — direct or proxy. Proxy rows are geo-dependent, so for those the locale and sometimes the whole page can change between passes.
  3. technologiesDetailed[].foundIn — page, header or hint. Header evidence describes the edge (CDN, server banner, HSTS); page evidence describes the application. Market-share questions need page evidence.

The contacts half has its own honest limit. In the 20-brand panel, 13 sites gave at least one social profile and only 3 gave an e-mail — home pages mostly don't publish one. And Sephora's row contained age@3x.svg among its five addresses: a retina asset filename that satisfies an e-mail regex perfectly. I am tightening that filter, but the general point stands — e-mails harvested from markup need a verification step before anyone sends to them. I use a separate Actor for that rather than pretending a regex is enough.

What this is good for: counting platforms across a market, filtering a big list by platform before a human looks at it, spotting missing pixels or consent banners across a client portfolio, bulk enrichment at a tenth of a cent per field. What it is not good for: a specific page, exact version numbers, or anything injected only after JavaScript runs — there is no browser here, which is also why a thousand domains cost $10 and take minutes.

And the one line I should have put in the README on day one: the row describes the page the redirect gave you, not the company you typed.

title: Navigating Multi-Cloud Complexity: Introducing CloudCompass 🧭✨
description:
As enterprise architectures scale, managing multi-cloud resources and organizing local-first development workflows can get overwhelmingly chaotic. Distributed systems demand high visibility, intuitive interfaces, and streamlined diagnostic routing.

Enter CloudCompass—an open-source, theme-aware navigation framework and modular user interface suite engineered to simplify cross-cloud resource management and modern system architecture tracking.

🎥 Watch the Demo

Get a quick visual look at the responsive layout, dynamic switching, and clean navigational interface in action:

🎬 Watch the CloudCompass Demo Video

✨ Core Features & Highlights

CloudCompass bridges the gap between complex system design and clean developer UX. Here is a breakdown of everything packed inside the repository:

1. 🌐 Unified Multi-Cloud Navigation

  • Centralizes resource tracking across diverse cloud providers and hybrid environments into a single, cohesive dashboard.
  • Eliminates context-switching fatigue by organizing services, metrics, and environment targets in one intuitive interface.

2. 🎨 Theme-Aware Modular Interface

title: Let Claude Code read your production database — even a write disguised as SELECT gets refused
description:
Pointing an AI agent at a database is easy. Pointing it at production is where people stop.

dbboard is an open-source desktop database client with an MCP server that gives Claude Code read-only access to Postgres, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, Cloudflare D1, MongoDB and Firestore — enforced by the database, not by a keyword filter.

The usual guard is a keyword filter: reject anything that starts with UPDATE or DROP. It holds until the agent writes a CTE that deletes, a SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or two statements in one string. And the agent still needs the password, which now sits in its config and its transcript.

dbboard is built so that this question has a boring answer.

The one idea: the database says no, not only a filter

dbboard ships a separate MCP server, dbboard-mcp, that hands the connections you already have to Claude Code or Claude Desktop. Every read passes two checks.

First, the statement is parsed — a real SQL parser, not string matching — and anything that is not a single read-only statement is refused. Then it runs inside the database's own read-only mode, or through an adapter that cannot write at all:

Engine How a read is run
Postgres, Neon, Supabase, CockroachDB, Aurora DSQL BEGIN TRANSACTION READ ONLY
MySQL / MariaDB SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY
Turso / libSQL PRAGMA query_only
Cloudflare D1 no read-only mode exists, so the parser is the enforcement and fails closed
Cloud Firestore the adapter has no write path to reach: it implements the read endpoints and nothing else
MongoDB only six commands (find, aggregate, count, distinct, listCollections, listIndexes) and only their known options; the pipeline is walked for a $out or $merge hidden inside a $facet, $lookup or $unionWith

The second check is the one that matters. Here is dbboard-mcp against a local Postgres with fictional data, called exactly as an agent calls it:

run_read_query  DELETE FROM orders WHERE quantity = 1
→ query failed: not a single read-only statement: only read-only SELECT / WITH / EXPLAIN statements are allowed

run_read_query  WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM orders RETURNING id) SELECT count(*) FROM gone
→ query failed: not a single read-only statement: a data-modifying statement (in a CTE or set expression) is not read-only

run_read_query  SELECT nextval('orders_id_seq')
→ query failed: cannot execute nextval() in a read-only transaction

run_read_query  SELECT count(*) FROM orders
→ 180

The first two are caught by the parser. The third is a plain SELECT that still writes — it advances a sequence — so no parser flags it. Postgres refuses it, because the transaction itself is read-only. The table still has all 180 rows, and the sequence did not move.

Three more rules sit around that:

  • Passwords never reach the agent. They stay in the OS keychain. The agent sees { id, name, kind } for each connection, and no error message embeds a URL.
  • Writing is off until a person turns it on, per connection. Even then only an allowlist runs (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE, …). DROP of anything, TRUNCATE, GRANT / REVOKE and user or role changes are refused whatever the setting says.
  • Results are bounded, so one careless query cannot pour a whole table into the agent's context.

How to give Claude Code read-only access to your database

Download dbboard-mcp for your platform from the latest release (one self-contained executable), then:

# macOS
claude mcp add dbboard --scope user -- "$HOME/.local/bin/dbboard-mcp"

# Windows (PowerShell)
claude mcp add dbboard --scope user -- "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/dbboard/dbboard-mcp.exe"

The agent can then list connections and tables, describe a table, search a connection's schema by column name, follow foreign keys, and run read queries. Ask it "which orders in the last week have no shipment row?" and it finds the tables itself.

And for the person: one window

The desktop app is the same connections, for you:

  • Every database you look after in one sidebar — Postgres (Neon, Supabase, CockroachDB, Aurora DSQL), MySQL / MariaDB, Turso / libSQL, Cloudflare D1, Firestore and MongoDB. An SSH tunnel reaches the one behind a bastion; a colour and a tag on each connection show which one you are about to run against.
  • Leave the database name blank and one login lists every database it can open, with schemas and tables beneath.
  • Fix one value without writing an UPDATE: double-click the cell, type, save. Edits are keyed on the primary key, so a table without one stays read-only instead of guessing.

What it is not

Not a hosted service: nothing leaves your machine except your own queries to your own databases. Not code-signed either — a certificate is a recurring purchase this project does not make, so every release ships SHA256SUMS.txt to check instead.

Try it

  1. Download from the download page (Windows x64 / ARM64 .exe, macOS .dmg)
  2. Manage → Add connection, pick the database type, fill in the server
  3. Add dbboard-mcp to your agent as above

MIT-licensed. Bug reports and requests: Issues.

title: Compiling Customer Segments to SQL: OR Groups, Tenant Safety and Membership That Stays Current
description:
A WhatsApp campaign goes to a segment: "customers in Pune interested in the sale, or anyone in Mumbai". Behind that sentence is a small query compiler. It turns conditions a marketer picked from dropdowns into SQL that must never reach another tenant's contacts, never match everyone by accident, and treat 50%_off as text. Then there's keeping the membership current as contacts change. This post builds both in TypeScript against SQLite, with the cases that went wrong for us along the way.

The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the patterns, and each was run against the cases shown.

The shape: OR of ANDs

Segment builders almost always produce the same structure: boxes of conditions that must all match, and a contact in any box is in the segment. That's disjunctive normal form, and it stores well. Each condition row carries a group number; rows with the same number are ANDed, and the groups are ORed:

group field op value
0 city equals Pune
0 interest equals sale
1 city equals Mumbai

That's (city = Pune AND interest = sale) OR city = Mumbai, with no nested trees to store or edit. In WAPGROWAI it's a group_index column on the filter rows, added after segments already existed. Old segments had one group and a match-all/match-any switch, so a single group still respects that switch, and two or more groups ignore it.

The compiler 

// A segment is OR-of-ANDs: conditions sharing a `group` must all match,
// and a contact matching any one group is in the segment.
export type Op = "equals" | "contains" | "starts_with" | "ends_with" | "is_empty" | "is_not_empty";
export type Field = "name" | "phone" | "allow_campaign" | { attribute: string };
export type Condition = { field: Field; op: Op; value?: string; group?: number };
export type Compiled = { sql: string; params: (string | number)[] };

export class SegmentError extends Error {}

const NEEDS_VALUE: Op[] = ["equals", "contains", "starts_with", "ends_with"];

// `%` and `_` in a customer's search are text, not wildcards.
const escapeLike = (v: string) => v.replace(/[\\%_]/g, (c) => `\\${c}`);

const pattern = (op: Op, v: string) =>
  op === "contains" ? `%${escapeLike(v)}%` : op === "starts_with" ? `${escapeLike(v)}%` : `%${escapeLike(v)}`;

const textClause = (column: string, op: Op, value: string): Compiled => {
  if (op === "equals") return { sql: `${column} = ?`, params: [value] };
  if (op === "is_empty") return { sql: `(${column} IS NULL OR ${column} = '')`, params: [] };
  if (op === "is_not_empty") return { sql: `(${column} IS NOT NULL AND ${column} <> '')`, params: [] };
  return { sql: `${column} LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\'`, params: [pattern(op, value)] };
};

// Compare digits only, against both the full and the national number,
// so "+91 98200 11223", "919820011223" and "9820011223" all match.
const digits = (expr: string) => ["+", " ", "-", "(", ")"].reduce((e, ch) => `REPLACE(${e}, '${ch}', '')`, expr);

const conditionClause = (c: Condition): Compiled => {
  const value = (c.value ?? "").trim();
  if (NEEDS_VALUE.includes(c.op) && value === "") throw new SegmentError(`"${c.op}" needs a value`);

  if (typeof c.field === "object") {
    // Uncorrelated subquery: a join would repeat a contact once per matching attribute.
    const inner = textClause("value", c.op, value);
    return {
      sql: `id IN (SELECT contact_id FROM contact_attributes WHERE key = ? AND ${inner.sql})`,
      params: [c.field.attribute, ...inner.params],
    };
  }
  if (c.field === "allow_campaign") {
    if (c.op !== "equals" || !["yes", "no"].includes(value.toLowerCase())) {
      throw new SegmentError('allow_campaign only supports equals "yes" or "no"');
    }
    return { sql: "allow_campaign = ?", params: [value.toLowerCase() === "yes" ? 1 : 0] };
  }
  if (c.field === "phone") {
    if (c.op === "is_empty" || c.op === "is_not_empty") return textClause("national_number", c.op, "");
    const d = value.replace(/\D/g, "");
    const full = textClause(digits("country_code || national_number"), c.op, d);
    const national = textClause(digits("national_number"), c.op, d);
    return { sql: `(${full.sql} OR ${national.sql})`, params: [...full.params, ...national.params] };
  }
  if (c.field === "name") return textClause("name", c.op, value);
  throw new SegmentError(`Unknown field ${JSON.stringify(c.field)}`);
};

export const compileSegment = (accountId: string, conditions: Condition[]): Compiled => {
  const groups = new Map<number, Compiled[]>();
  for (const c of conditions) {
    const clause = conditionClause(c);
    const g = c.group ?? 0;
    groups.set(g, [...(groups.get(g) ?? []), clause]);
  }

  // No conditions must mean nobody: "everyone" is the expensive mistake.
  if (groups.size === 0) return { sql: "SELECT id FROM contacts WHERE 1 = 0", params: [] };

  const ors = [...groups.values()].map((and) => ({
    sql: `(${and.map((c) => c.sql).join(" AND ")})`,
    params: and.flatMap((c) => c.params),
  }));
  return {
    // The tenant check sits outside the parentheses, so no OR can widen it.
    sql: `SELECT id FROM contacts WHERE account_id = ? AND (${ors.map((o) => o.sql).join(" OR ")})`,
    params: [accountId, ...ors.flatMap((o) => o.params)],
  };
};

Each rule in there came from a real failure mode.

The tenant check goes outside the parentheses

The query every multi-tenant app should be afraid of looks like this:

SELECT id FROM contacts WHERE account_id = ? AND city = 'Pune' OR city = 'Mumbai'

AND binds tighter than OR, so the second group matches every Mumbai contact in every account. Wrap all the groups in one pair of parentheses and put the tenant check outside it. The test seeds a contact in another account who matches the first group, and checks they never appear.

No conditions means nobody

A segment whose conditions are all missing or half-filled has no filter left. If the compiler returns "all contacts in this account" for that, the segment silently becomes "message everyone", and a campaign to it costs real money. Ours did exactly this until we changed it: an empty segment now compiles to a query that matches nothing.

Refuse what you can't compile; don't drop it

A row like "name contains (blank)" or "opted in contains y" can't be turned into SQL. The tempting fix is to skip it. But dropping a condition always widens the result: skip one AND and the segment grows. For a campaign audience that's the dangerous direction, so the compiler throws, and the API returns a 400 the user can act on.

Values are parameters, and LIKE patterns are escaped

Every value goes in as a ? parameter. That stops SQL injection, but not LIKE wildcards: a search for 50%_off would match "50 people off" too. Escape \, % and _ before building the pattern, and say which escape character you used.

Phone numbers: compare digits

People type +91 98200 11223, 919820011223 and 9820011223, and the number is often stored with its formatting, split into a country code and a national number. Strip punctuation in SQL and compare against both the full and the national digits, so all three match. "Starts with 971" then finds UAE numbers.

Attributes: an uncorrelated subquery

Custom attributes live in their own table. A join repeats the contact once per matching attribute row, which breaks LIMIT/OFFSET on any paginated list that reuses the same filter. A correlated EXISTS works but has to name the outer table, and ORMs alias that table differently depending on what else the query includes. id IN (SELECT contact_id FROM contact_attributes WHERE …) avoids both, and the outer account_id check still scopes it.

One condition builder for every screen

The contacts list, the contacts export and the segment engine all filter the same table. Ours had three copies of this logic, and they drifted: a phone filter matched in a segment but not in the list, and % was a wildcard in one and not the other. Now there's one function that turns a condition row into a clause, and every caller uses it.

What we'd do differently: attributes need a key

The compiler above matches an attribute by key and value: city equals Mumbai. Ours doesn't. WAPGROWAI's attribute condition matches a value in any attribute, or an attribute's name. So "attribute equals Mumbai" also finds a contact whose notes say "asked about Mumbai store". The test covers that case: with the key, Meera, whose city is Pune, isn't in the Mumbai segment.

Matching any attribute felt simpler in the UI, with one dropdown fewer. It also makes segments wider than people expect, and it can't express "city is empty". Pick the key in the condition from the start.

Membership: computed once, read many times

You can evaluate a segment at send time, or store its members in a segment_contacts table and keep that up to date. Storing wins once segments show counts in lists, campaigns read them, and the same segment is used many times. But it means every change to a contact has to update the table.

import type { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";
import { compileSegment, type Condition } from "./compile.ts";

export type Segment = { id: string; accountId: string; conditions: Condition[]; isStatic: boolean };

// Full recompute for one segment: add who now matches, remove who no longer does.
export const syncSegment = (db: DatabaseSync, segment: Segment) => {
  if (segment.isStatic) return { added: 0, removed: 0 };
  const { sql, params } = compileSegment(segment.accountId, segment.conditions);
  const desired = new Set((db.prepare(sql).all(...params) as { id: string }[]).map((r) => r.id));
  const current = new Set(
    (db.prepare("SELECT contact_id FROM segment_contacts WHERE segment_id = ?").all(segment.id) as { contact_id: string }[]).map(
      (r) => r.contact_id,
    ),
  );

  const remove = db.prepare("DELETE FROM segment_contacts WHERE segment_id = ? AND contact_id = ?");
  // OR IGNORE: a per-contact sync running at the same time may have inserted it first.
  const add = db.prepare("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO segment_contacts (segment_id, contact_id) VALUES (?, ?)");
  let added = 0;
  let removed = 0;
  for (const id of current) if (!desired.has(id)) removed += Number(remove.run(segment.id, id).changes);
  for (const id of desired) if (!current.has(id)) added += Number(add.run(segment.id, id).changes);
  return { added, removed };
};

// Cheap path for "this one contact changed": check it against each segment.
export const syncContact = (db: DatabaseSync, segments: Segment[], contactId: string) => {
  for (const segment of segments) {
    if (segment.isStatic || segment.conditions.length === 0) continue;
    const { sql, params } = compileSegment(segment.accountId, segment.conditions);
    const matches = db.prepare(`${sql} AND id = ?`).get(...params, contactId) !== undefined;
    if (matches) db.prepare("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO segment_contacts (segment_id, contact_id) VALUES (?, ?)").run(segment.id, contactId);
    else db.prepare("DELETE FROM segment_contacts WHERE segment_id = ? AND contact_id = ?").run(segment.id, contactId);
  }
};
  • A full sync diffs the stored members against the current matches. It's the right tool when the segment's conditions change.
  • A per-contact sync checks one contact against each segment. It's the right tool for hot paths: a new contact from an inbound WhatsApp message shouldn't recompute every segment for every contact.
  • Static segments are never synced. "Everyone at Saturday's webinar" is a snapshot, and re-running its conditions would change it.

Every write path must sync

This is the part that's easy to get wrong. Membership is only as fresh as the code paths that call the sync. In WAPGROWAI, editing or importing contacts, the public API and new inbound contacts all sync. A chatbot node that saves an answer to a contact attribute doesn't, so a contact whose city a chatbot saved won't join "Pune" until something else triggers a sync. Campaigns read the stored membership, so that contact misses the campaign. List your write paths and test each one, or evaluate the conditions again when a campaign builds its recipient list.

Full re-syncs on every contact edit also get expensive: segments × contacts per edit. Use the per-contact path wherever you know which contact changed.

Don't soft-delete membership rows

We once made segment_contacts soft-deleting, with a unique index on (segment_id, contact_id). A soft-deleted row is hidden from the ORM but not from the index, so a contact who left a segment could never rejoin: the "is it already there?" check saw nothing, and the insert failed with a duplicate key. Membership is derived data; delete it for real. The test moves a contact out of "Pune" and back in.

Inserts must tolerate races

A full sync and a per-contact sync can run at the same time: an inbound message arrives while someone edits the segment. Both decide the contact should be added, and one insert hits the unique index. INSERT OR IGNORE (MySQL: INSERT IGNORE or bulkCreate with ignoreDuplicates) makes that harmless.

What the tests check

  • DNF: (Pune AND sale) OR Mumbai returns Asha and Ravi.
  • Tenancy: a contact in another account who matches the first group never appears.
  • Attribute keys: Meera's notes mention Mumbai, but she isn't in the Mumbai segment.
  • Empty segment: no conditions returns nobody.
  • Refusal: a blank value, or contains on the opt-in flag, throws instead of being dropped.
  • LIKE: 50%_ matches only the contact literally named "50%_off club".
  • Phone: three spellings of one number all match, and "starts with 971" finds the UAE contact.
  • Injection: a value like x' OR 1=1 -- matches nothing and never appears in the SQL.
  • Sync: a full sync adds two members and is a no-op when repeated; a contact can leave and rejoin; a static segment never changes.

Checklist

  • Store segments as OR-of-AND groups with a group number per condition.
  • Put the tenant check outside the parentheses.
  • Compile an empty segment to "nobody".
  • Refuse conditions you can't compile; never drop them.
  • Parameterize values and escape LIKE wildcards.
  • Normalize phone numbers to digits on both sides.
  • Match attributes by key and value, with an uncorrelated subquery.
  • Use one condition builder for lists, exports and segments.
  • Sync membership from every write path, and use the per-contact path for hot ones.
  • Hard-delete membership rows, and make inserts ignore duplicates.

title: PathoJev: Efficient Pathology Decisions from Shared Visual Context
description:
arXiv:2610.40752v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pathology workflows require multiple visual judgments about the same slide, from identifying tumor type to assessing grade and invasion. Generating and parsing a separate textual response for each structured question adds latency between visual evidence and usable decisions. Building on the System One paradigm, we introduce PathoJev, a pathology model that directly predicts answer probabilities for whole-slide and region-level assessment. PathoJev encodes each slide once and evaluates independent question suffixes in batches over the shared visual context. Reusing the hybrid backbone's recurrent states further limits the computation that grows with slide-context length for each additional question. Across three whole-slide benchmarks, the 9B and 27B models achieve mean accuracies of 77.2% and 78.1%, exceeding SlideChat by 5.4 and 6.3 percentage points. Both scales also maintain competitive accuracy on five ROI benchmarks. On WSI-Bench, the 9B model runs 9.1x faster than SlideChat. Shared context accelerates eight-question workloads by 6.9x and 5.9x over separate prefix encoding, rising to 11.2x and 8.9x for 64 questions. These results provide a reusable probabilistic interface for combining multiple visual judgments in whole-slide and local tissue assessment. Code: https://github.com/ChyaZhang/PathoJev.

title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.40754v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

title: Drone-PUR: From Visual Clue Discovery to Understanding and Reasoning in UAV Scenes
description:
arXiv:2610.40801v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.

title: EgoHSI3R: Online 4D Hand-Scene Interaction Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
description:
arXiv:2610.40832v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.

title: Spatial Atlas-Informed Loss Ensembles for Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT Metastasis Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.40834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing whole-body PSMA PET/CT prostate metastasis segmentation methods generally rely on images alone, without explicitly incorporating where metastases tend to occur. We investigate whether a population metastasis atlas can improve lesion detection when integrated into model training. We constructed voxel-wise mean and standard deviation maps from 375 expert-annotated training scans and used them to weight the cross-entropy loss of an nnU-Net. The additional penalties for missed lesions and false positives depend on spatial atlas statistics and diminish as predictions become confidently correct. Seven configurations were compared on validation data; three were combined by majority voting into SAILS (Spatial Atlas-Informed Loss enSemble). We compared SAILS with a baseline nnU-Net and inference-time atlas fusion on AutoPET~III (110 disease-positive cases) and Deep-PSMA (100 external cases). No atlas or registration is needed at inference. Results: On AutoPET~III, SAILS improved whole-body Dice (0.531 vs. 0.520; p=0.006), reduced missed-lesion volume (9.5 vs. 12.1 cc/case; p<0.01), and increased pooled lesion sensitivity (0.857 vs. 0.843; p=0.004). On Deep-PSMA, SAILS detected 126 additional reference lesions (sensitivity 0.769 vs. 0.751; p<0.001), without a significant whole-body Dice change (-0.009; p=0.36). High-risk bone Dice improved in both cohorts (0.576 vs. 0.552 and 0.667 vs. 0.653; both p<0.01). False-positive volume increased by 2.3 and 18.2 cc/case, respectively (p<0.001). Atlas-weighted training improves lesion detection, especially in high-risk bone, without test-time atlas registration, but increases false positives.

title: AquaProbe: Efficient Adaptation of Frozen Vision Models for Underwater Images
description:
arXiv:2610.40900v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable visual perception is essential for safe autonomous underwater exploration. Yet vision models pretrained on terrestrial images become less reliable underwater, where turbidity, backscatter, and wavelength-dependent attenuation alter scene appearance. Existing adaptation methods either spread adapters equally across the encoder depth or select layers using the divergence between two fixed domains. In this paper, we introduce AquaProbe for measuring how the location of the domain gap changes with water type and imaging range. AquaProbe separates newly introduced divergence from that accumulated through a frozen vision encoder using paired clean and physically rendered images and allocates a fixed LoRA budget according to the measured profile. The segmentation mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) for the proportional LoRA rank allocation, based on the measured profile, is 70.1; this is a better result than uniform LoRA rank allocation by 1.9 mIoU points while having the same parameter budget of 0.59 million adapter parameters. The three-way router, conditioned on estimated condition clusters, achieves 70.6 mIoU on the standard SUIM split and 63.4 AUDRC under held-out degradation.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Expert-Assisted Interpretation of Histopathology Foundation Model Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2610.40905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.

title: Coupled or Independent? Fault Coupling in Agentic Medical Vision Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.40913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language agents equipped with tools expose intermediate outputs for inspection and comparison with the model's reasoning, which may offer safety benefits over single-shot models. This paper tests that potential benefit when the sensor reading itself is untrusted, so that the tool and reasoning channels share a common visual fault. We consider a dermatology agent based on segmentation, contrastive retrieval, and an iterative vision-language reasoner and define a coupling taxonomy that distinguishes single-channel errors from joint errors that agree or disagree. On PAD-UFES-20, we show that typographic injection produces detectable directional retrieval capture, whereas physical corruption does not. Crop-first retrieval preserves the payload at a readable scale and produces 55% joint wrong agreement across all cases (71% of faulty cases); full-image retrieval produces 35% (43%). Under a binary decision, if both channels are wrong, their predictions must agree, so hard-label channel comparison cannot detect joint failures, limiting disagreement recall to 0.29 (crop-first) versus 0.57 (full-image). The direction of the order effect is reproduced on the independent HIBA test set.

title: Let LiDAR Decide Where to Look: Geometry-Measured Token Selection for Efficient Sparse Latent World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.40935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-centric autonomous driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, yet most depict sky, buildings, or empty road---content irrelevant to planning. Worse, these tokens dilute the planner's attention: we show that randomly discarding 75% of tokens already outperforms the dense model, because the planner can concentrate on the remaining driving-critical content. Building on this finding, we present Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), which uses LiDAR and radar point projections to select a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs. Because the selector operates on measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, the backbone encodes only the selected patches, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to $18\times$.
