title: 5 Email API Providers for High Deliverability Rates: Seller Template Control
description:
Short answer: Choose SendGrid for analytics-led deliverability work, Postmark for focused transactional mail, SES for AWS-centered systems, and Infrai when one REST credential can cover the order email and its generated receipt.

A marketplace order email has two separate ownership decisions: who sends it, and who owns the template that says what the seller sees. For a US welcome or transactional flow, I would choose the provider that lets the team keep that boundary explicit, then verify the sender domain with SPF and the provider's delivery tooling. If the same job also renders a PDF receipt, an aggregated REST surface can remove an awkward handoff between document generation and mail delivery.

Templates drift.

One bad default is enough.

This is a five-way checklist, not a claim that one provider wins every inbox. Deliverability is a sender reputation and compliance problem as much as an API problem.

1. Decide who owns the message before choosing an API

For a new order, the marketplace should own the template, version, locale, and event data. The email provider should own transport, suppression handling, and delivery evidence. That division keeps a provider migration from becoming a copy-editing project. It also makes review possible: a seller should receive the same order facts whether the backend sends through a specialist or a broader platform.

I would store a template identifier and a rendered version with the order event. The provider call then receives an already-approved subject and body, or a provider template identifier governed by the application. Do not let a dashboard-only template become the only copy of a customer-facing policy.

The domain setup still matters. SPF is documented in RFC 7208, and it is one part of proving that a sender is authorized. It does not guarantee inbox placement. Keep suppression state, opt-out policy, bounce review, and content changes in the application's operating model.

The receipt is a separate boundary.

2. Which email API providers fit high deliverability work?

The familiar shortlist has real differences. SendGrid is a reasonable fit when comprehensive analytics and ISP partnerships are central to the team's deliverability work. Postmark is aimed at transactional email, with speed and reliability as its focus. Amazon SES fits teams already invested in AWS services and looking for an email API that integrates with that environment.

Those are different operating choices, not three interchangeable logos. SendGrid gives the broader analytics story. Postmark is the more focused transactional specialist. SES makes the most sense when AWS identity, logging, and deployment are already part of the team's daily tooling. A specialist can also be the better answer when the team needs mature email-specific controls and does not want a combined platform to become another dependency.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main boundary
SendGrid Email API plus analytics tooling Teams working actively on deliverability signals More email-platform surface to govern
Postmark Focused transactional email API Operational messages where speed and reliability are the priority Less attractive for a broad backend capability set
Amazon SES Email API within AWS Services already organized around AWS More infrastructure decisions stay with the application
Infrai One REST API and key across capabilities Teams joining receipt generation to seller mail One vendor and one outage surface for both steps

Infrai is a different fit. It puts email and other backend capabilities behind one REST API and one key, so the integration team has one credential boundary and one bill to reconcile. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities and includes runnable examples in 10 languages, which is useful when a small team needs to get from an order event to a first useful request without installing another SDK.

The second advantage is inspectability. Discovery is public and self-describing, so an adapter can read a capability's request schema before a developer wires fields into a service. The live surface has 295 routes across 20 modules; that breadth is useful only when the application keeps a narrow, capability-specific adapter instead of treating the platform as an untyped toolbox.

My explicit recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for a marketplace backend that owns seller templates and also needs adjacent backend work, such as generating a receipt before sending the order message. The one-key boundary matters here because it removes credential and integration glue; it is not proof of superior inbox placement.

3. Keep the PDF-to-email seam inside one request model

The practical friction appears when an order email carries a generated document. With a Puppeteer plus Resend or SES stack, I would expect two signups, two credential sets, two vendor-specific SDK or HTTP surfaces, and glue to move the rendered bytes through a temporary bucket or another shared storage layer. That handoff needs cleanup, access control, and retry behavior.

An aggregated surface can make the ownership boundary easier to inspect: the order service uses the same Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY and the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base for the content-processing capability and the email capability. The exact request and response fields should come from public discovery, rather than from a guessed payload. This small Python helper makes that contract visible before the application wires its adapter:

import os
import requests

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}

paths = ["/v1/pdf/generate", "/v1/email/send"]
for path in paths:
    capability = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/discovery",
        headers=headers,
        timeout=10,
    )
    capability.raise_for_status()
    match = next(
        item for item in capability.json()["capabilities"]
        if item["path"] == path
    )
    detail = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/discovery/{match['id']}",
        headers=headers,
        timeout=10,
    )
    detail.raise_for_status()
    print(path, detail.json())

This is intentionally a contract inspection step, not a fabricated PDF payload or an invented email schema. The returned capability detail supplies the request schema and runnable examples. Build the adapter from those fields, then pass the PDF result to the email adapter without introducing a second vendor credential. Both operations should carry an idempotency key at the write boundary; standard retry logic must inspect the status, back off on 429, and surface a 4xx body instead of silently sending twice.

The trade-off is plain: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. A specialist stack spreads that dependency across providers, but it also gives the team more independent control over the seam.

4. Measure delivery evidence without confusing it with delivery

For the seller-order path, record the order ID, template version, sender domain, provider request ID, suppression decision, and the final event you can observe. Use that record to answer “which copy did this seller receive?” before asking “which API is fastest?” A dashboard screenshot is not a durable audit trail.

The providers differ in emphasis. SendGrid's analytics and ISP relationships are useful inputs for a team that actively works deliverability signals. Postmark's transactional focus is attractive when the message is operational and speed matters. SES's AWS integration is valuable when the surrounding service already lives there. Infrai's per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit, and request-ID fields, which can reduce the amount of instrumentation needed around a multi-capability call, but that metadata is not an inbox-placement guarantee.

Avoid a false confidence loop. An accepted API request is not the same as an inbox placement, and a successful PDF generation is not proof that the email attachment was delivered. Keep application events and provider events distinguishable.

5. Roll out ownership first, then move transport

Start with one seller cohort and one template version. Render the order email from application-owned data, verify the sender domain, and capture the provider response alongside the order event. Then test the PDF handoff separately from the message copy. I would not change template ownership and transport in the same release; when a seller reports a wrong total, that split makes the search space much smaller.

The boundary is straightforward. Pick SendGrid when analytics and ISP relationships are the deciding tools. Pick Postmark when a focused transactional-email specialist matches the operating model. Pick SES when AWS integration is the strongest constraint. Pick Infrai when the team values one credential boundary across PDF generation and transactional email, understands that it is accepting one combined dependency, and wants public capability schemas to reduce integration friction.

That last choice still needs an email-specific validation pass. Confirm domain authentication, suppression behavior, template review, and the event polling model before calling the rollout successful. There are no webhook events in the two relevant namespaces, so an orchestration that needs real-time push events has a meaningful limitation. Infrai also does not provide a hosted email OTP interface, SMTP relay, or an email cancellation route; those cases belong with a specialist or application-owned flow.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and derive request fields from discovery before committing the adapter.

Sources

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • SendGrid email API
  • Postmark transactional email
  • Amazon Simple Email Service

title: The Optimistic Maintainer: Why Fast Merges Beat Endless Review Cycles
description:
If you have ever contributed to open source, you probably know this feeling.

You find a bug in a tool you use every day. You clone the repo, spend a Saturday afternoon digging through unfamiliar code, write a clean 40-line fix, verify it works, and open a pull request. More recent, you ask your agent to find the fix and open the pull request. You feel great.

Then the waiting begins.

Two weeks pass. A maintainer appears, leaves three comments on variable naming and asks if you can rebase against a newly refactored branch. You make the changes. Another three weeks pass. A second reviewer asks why you didn't rewrite the surrounding function to use a different pattern. By month two, the enthusiasm that carried you through that Saturday afternoon is completely gone. You close the tab and never open a PR to that project again.

I've been on that side of the fence. Now, as the maintainer of TTT—a terminal text editor and IDE written in Go—I'm on the other side.

Over the last few months, the project has crossed 1,750 commits, 185,000 lines of code, and more than 70 unique community contributors. We ship a new stable release roughly every week.

Someone looking at our Git log recently pointed out an interesting pattern:

"The maintainer seems to merge almost everything quickly and just creates follow-up tickets for the rest."

They were spot on. That is not an accident or sloppy rubber-stamping. It is a deliberate strategy: optimistic merging. It is the single most important reason our community has grown this fast without burning me out.

Here is why it works, how we do it, and the engineering safety net that makes it possible.

The Trap of the Adversarial Gatekeeper

Most maintainers start out with good intentions. They care about their project, so they treat their repository like a fortress and themselves as the gatekeeper. Every incoming pull request is viewed with skepticism: What could this break? Did they follow all my implicit rules?

The problem is that open source contribution is discretionary effort. A contributor doesn’t work for you. When someone gives you a PR, they are giving you a gift of their free time. And even in modern times when opening a PR can be automated with an agent, they are opening the PR on your repository instead of somewhere else.

If you meet that gift with four rounds of nitpicking over inconsequential details, you aren't "maintaining high standards"—you are imposing friction. The contributor burns out, and you burn out from reading the same 30 lines of code across six weeks of back-and-forth.

Worse, when maintainers get paranoid about breaking things, they freeze. PRs pile up in the queue because the maintainer is afraid to merge them until they have a free weekend to manually test every edge case.

I wanted TTT to feel different: if you submit a working fix with tests, your code should be in main within hours, not months.

Step 1: You Need a Safety Net You Actually Trust

Here is the catch: you cannot practice optimistic merging if you don't trust your test suite. If merging a PR requires you to open the editor and manually poke at things to see if it feels right, you will inevitably become a bottleneck.

In previous posts, I wrote about how we built our --exec testing harness and how we used differential testing for our TextMate engine and Vim emulation.

Those weren't just academic exercises. They are the exact safety net that gives me the confidence to merge fast:

  1. 3,500+ Automated Tests: Across core algorithms, JSON-RPC LSP client communication, and buffer undo transactions.
  2. Deterministic UI Snapshots: Using our in-memory SimScreen and --exec scripts, CI tests actual visual layouts, tree widget expansions, and cursor goal-column math without needing a physical terminal.
  3. Automated PR Benchmark Comparisons: Every pull request runs scripts/bench-compare.mjs against main. It opens 64 MiB code files and 1 GiB logs. If a community PR introduces an accidental allocation loop or slows down rendering, CI tells us before I even open the review.
  4. Architectural Zones (ARCHITECTURE.md): Domain packages (internal/core/*) are strictly decoupled from the UI. They are forbidden from starting processes or touching terminal state.

Because the machine ruthlessly verifies that the invariants haven't broken, I don't have to spend my mental energy acting like a human compiler. Across 1,750+ commits, we have had exactly three reverts in the entire history of the project.

Step 2: The 90% Rule

When a contributor opens a pull request that solves 90% of a problem, passes CI, and includes tests, what do you do with the remaining 10%?

The gatekeeper demands that the contributor spend another week figuring out that last 10%.

The optimistic maintainer says: Merge the 90%.

Here’s what that looks like in practice:

  • The fix is solid, but missed a secondary edge case? Merge the PR, thank the contributor, and file a follow-up ticket: "Follow-up on #1284: handle ancestor tree preservation on collapsed roots."
  • The feature works, but needs a benchmark comparison? Don't make the contributor write a complex benchmark suite from scratch. Cherry-pick their commit, add the sub-benchmark alongside it, tag them with Co-Authored-By, and merge both.
  • Variable naming or a comment could be cleaner? Spend 30 seconds pushing a polish commit directly to main after merging, rather than making the contributor wait three days for another review cycle.

When contributors see their PR merged the same day they submitted it, the psychological shift is immediate. They don't feel like an outsider seeking approval; they feel like part of the team. Many of our most active contributors—people like Hao Chen, Jay Hemnani, Nandaleio, and Lzcwbcgs—started with a single small PR and kept coming back because the turnaround was fast and respectful.

Step 3: Defend Scope, Not Syntax

Optimistic merging does not mean accepting every feature anyone dreams up. If you merge every feature request into core, your binary will quickly turn into bloatware.

The distinction is: Be generous with code quality and bug fixes, but be strict about architectural scope.

Whenever a PR proposes something that doesn't belong in the core binary, I don't reject the contributor's idea—I guide it into our Lua plugin system:

  • A contributor built a great Linux desktop launcher integration into the core binary (#683). Core isn't the right place for desktop session launchers, so we agreed to package it as a featured Lua plugin (#1267).
  • A contributor submitted a port of the Catppuccin Mocha theme as a built-in Go theme. Rather than bundling dozens of themes into the core executable, we asked them to register it as a plugin manifest from ttt-plugins (#1240).

By pushing niche features into plugins, the core binary stays lean (single static Go binary, ~14 MB), while the community still gets the features they care about.

Step 4: Culture Encoded in Code

Most open source projects have a CONTRIBUTORS.md file that rots in the repository root. Almost nobody reads it, and bug reporters are never mentioned at all.

I wanted the culture of TTT to reflect that an editor is only as good as the people using it and reporting bugs. So we wrote a small script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/update-contributors.sh
set -euo pipefail

REPO="eugenioenko/ttt"
OUTPUT="internal/app/contributors.json"

contributors=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/contributors?per_page=100" --paginate \
  -q '.[] | select(.type == "User") | .login' | jq -R . | jq -s .)

reporters=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/issues?state=all&per_page=100" --paginate \
  -q '.[] | select(.pull_request == null and .user.type == "User") | .user.login' |
  sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr -k2,2 | awk '{print $2}' | jq -R . | jq -s .)

jq -n --argjson c "$contributors" --argjson r "$reporters" \
  '{contributors: $c, reporters: ($r - $c)}' > "$OUTPUT"

Before every release, this script fetches every person who contributed code and every person who opened an issue that led to a fix. It compiles them directly into contributors.json, which is embedded in the binary.

When you open Help > About inside TTT, you see this:

┌───────────────────────── About TTT Editor ─────────────────────────┐
│ Version: v1.10.0                                                   │
│ Website: https://tttedit.dev                                       │
│ GitHub:  https://github.com/eugenioenko/ttt                        │
│ ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ ttt is great because of everyone who contributes code, reports     │
│ issues, and uses it:                                               │
│                                                                    │
│ HaoChen · JayHemnani · Nandaleio · prime120 · Lzcwbcgs · ...       │
│                                                                    │
│ Thank you!                                                         │
│                                                            [Close] │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every bug reporter and every code author is literally baked into the application they helped build. It runs offline, makes zero network calls, and permanently credits the community.

The Takeaway

If you are maintaining an open-source project and feeling overwhelmed by PRs, consider flipping the model:

  1. Invest in automated safety nets first. If you don't trust your CI, build harness tests and benchmarks until you do. You cannot be a fast maintainer if you are a fearful maintainer.
  2. Stop holding PRs hostage over formatting. If the logic works and passes tests, merge it. Fix the variable name yourself in two minutes or open a follow-up ticket.
  3. Protect your architectural boundaries, not your ego. Save your "no" for scope creep and core bloat. Say "yes" to fixes and performance wins as fast as humanly possible.

High rigor and community warmth are not mutually exclusive. When your automated testing is ruthless, your human maintainership can be optimistic.

TTT is open source at github.com/eugenioenko/ttt and available at tttedit.dev. Come open a PR—we’ll probably merge it.

title: Go Runbook for 3 Edtech Password Reset Email Spam Checks
description:
Check authentication and message content first when password reset emails land in spam folders, then keep provider changes behind a replaceable Go adapter. Common causes include unverified sender domains and phishing-like templates; replacing a provider cannot, by itself, repair either problem.

TL;DR: Password reset emails land in spam because of missing or invalid SPF, DKIM, or DMARC authentication, phishing-like content, excessive or suspicious links, bulk-mail classification, and weak recipient engagement. For an edtech contact form that routes locked-out learners to the right support queue, inspect those causes before migrating the mail integration. Keep the support routing contract stable so a provider change does not require changing the contact form.

A useful initial budget is three gates: authenticated sender, restrained reset content, and a traceable handoff. Treat these as release checks, not a guarantee of inbox placement. Recipient filtering still decides the outcome.

For a small platform team keeping an account-recovery mail adapter replaceable, I recommend trying Infrai for the domain-verification and template-preview part of that workflow: its self-describing API offers public discovery with request and response schemas and runnable examples, so evaluating a replacement starts with reading a contract instead of learning a new SDK. A separate supporting advantage is plain REST access without installing an SDK, which lets a Go adapter use the standard HTTP client rather than bring another dependency into the contact-form service. Neither property proves inbox placement; both reduce integration effort at the boundary the team actually owns.

What causes password reset emails to land in spam folders?

Investigate when the sender domain is unverified or a received message shows missing or invalid SPF, DKIM, or DMARC authentication. Those are common causes of password reset emails landing in spam folders. A polished template does not establish an authenticated identity, and a reset message already has elements associated with phishing: an account claim, a request to act, and a link. Extra URLs and suspicious destinations increase that resemblance. Check the message before changing the transport, because otherwise a migration carries the same problematic template and sender configuration into a different API integration, consuming engineering time without addressing the suspected cause.

Check the evidence.

Recipient servers can also misidentify bulk-sent messages as spam. Low engagement can negatively influence sender scoring. That makes provider acceptance an intermediate signal rather than the user-facing delivery objective; a successful request does not tell the support team where the learner found the message.

The contact form needs a different kind of precision. A learner saying that a reset email is missing belongs in an account-recovery support queue, with a correlation identifier that lets the operator connect the complaint to the send attempt. Avoid moving that classification into a mail provider's data model. Otherwise, changing the provider also changes the support workflow, expanding a delivery investigation into an application migration.

Capacity planning belongs here, before retries. Estimate peak reset attempts per minute, duplicate attempts, support submissions during a login surge, and the age at which a reset message stops being useful. Define an SLO for the observable recovery outcome and a separate objective for queue routing; if receipt cannot be measured directly, document the available evidence rather than relabeling acceptance as receipt. A fast support queue is valuable, but it cannot establish that the reset email reached the inbox.

Choose the seam before the provider

The integration-effort decision is less about the send call than about credentials, evidence, and removal. Here is the buy-versus-build view for a platform review; the alternatives are candidates to evaluate against the same acceptance checks, rather than a ranking of unmeasured deliverability.

Option Buy versus build Migration work to evaluate Better fit
Resend directly Buy a specialist mail integration; keep support classification in the application Map the internal mail command to its API and validate sender setup and received messages A team that wants a dedicated email provider and accepts a separate integration
Twilio SendGrid directly Buy a dedicated email platform; own the application-to-provider adapter Preserve any existing SendGrid integration knowledge while keeping vendor identifiers out of support policy A team already standardized on SendGrid that would otherwise rebuild working integration code
Amazon SES directly Buy email delivery inside an AWS integration; own the support workflow Evaluate the application boundary alongside the team's existing AWS identity and operating practices A platform team whose AWS investment reduces the work of adopting SES
Infrai REST adapter Buy access through a self-describing REST surface; keep recovery policy in Go Read the discovery schema and runnable Go example, then map the same internal command into that contract A small team prioritizing contract inspection and fewer SDK dependencies

These are real choices. An existing, well-understood direct integration may require less work than introducing an abstraction, particularly when the on-call team already knows how to investigate sender authentication and inspect received messages with that provider. Choose a specialist directly when SMTP compatibility or a required real-time event integration is a deciding requirement; evaluate that requirement explicitly before adopting a broader REST platform. Do not infer those properties from a common API style.

The concrete portability claim is deliberately smaller: the application owns a versioned support-routing contract, and only an adapter depends on a provider's request and response shapes. Infrai's public discovery supplies full request and response schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go. That makes the adapter contract inspectable before implementation. It does not make different providers' email semantics identical, and it does not establish that a new sender will escape spam classification.

There is a trade-off: Infrai is not a good fit when a team needs its existing SMTP integration preserved; evaluate SendGrid or Amazon SES directly for that requirement. Infrai provides one API key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, so a team already using the platform can avoid adding another credential for the recovery adapter. A single API key reduces secret distribution work, while public discovery and plain REST reduce contract-learning and dependency work. These are different integration costs, and neither changes recipient filtering.

Keep the cost review secondary. Include adapter maintenance, credential rotation, evidence collection, and on-call investigation effort in the buy-versus-build decision, because removing an SDK does not remove responsibility for the recovery SLO.

Implement the handoff without leaking vendor types

Start by inspecting the domain-verification contract before implementing the mail adapter. The following Go program retrieves its public discovery document and prints the returned JSON; it does not send an email or claim to validate sender authentication. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with go run main.go using the Go standard library. Public discovery needs no key, but this example uses the environment-supplied Bearer header to show the authentication pattern used by the adapter.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/email.domain.verify", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            if !json.Valid(body) {
                return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned invalid JSON")
            }
            _, err = os.Stdout.Write(append(body, '\n'))
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
            delay = time.Until(deadline)
            if delay < 0 {
                delay = 0
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-timer.C:
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry limit reached")
}

The program performs a read, so it needs no write idempotency key. Its expected result is a discovery document with the capability's request and response schemas and examples; inspect those before constructing a verification request. It bounds rate-limit retries, honors both forms of Retry-After, and surfaces the status and response body for unsuccessful calls. It deliberately avoids guessing domain-verification request fields.

Keep a separate application-owned command with a version, request identifier, topic, and destination support queue. For example, a synthetic request learner-support-285 with topic password-reset-email-missing should route to account-recovery. A provider adapter can retain provider-specific message identifiers for investigation while the contact form continues to emit that command, so switching adapters does not also require teaching support agents a new category system. Require a request identifier and explicitly route unrecognized topics to the general learner queue. At a durable queue boundary, use the identifier to deduplicate processing.

Use the live discovery request schema and its runnable example when implementing the actual domain-verification or template-preview call. Review authentication, explicit methods, response-status handling, rate-limit backoff, and the capability's idempotency contract before enabling writes. Do not derive request fields from a route name, and do not assume previewing a template establishes delivery.

Preview isn't delivery.

Verify delivery and preserve rollback

Verification has three layers. First, inspect the received message's authentication results for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and resolve missing or invalid authentication rather than trusting a sender-setup checkbox alone. Second, review the exact reset template and its links: remove unnecessary URLs and investigate suspicious destinations or wording that resembles phishing. Third, follow a controlled account-recovery attempt through the mail adapter and support queue, recording what is actually observed about receipt and spam placement alongside the unchanged application correlation identifier.

Start small.

For the proposed routing contract, test a general learner question and confirm it routes to learner-general; leave the request identifier empty and require an explicit failure. During a provider evaluation, replay those same routing cases and compare the handoff fields. They should be identical across adapters. Then inspect newly received messages rather than extrapolating inbox placement from a contract check or discovery response. This separates an application regression from a sender-authentication or content problem without pretending that either check covers the other.

The rollback decision should have a narrow scope. Keep the previous adapter deployable, retain the required credentials through the observation window, and switch at the internal command boundary if routing or mail integration behavior violates the release criteria. Pause expansion before switching back, reconcile accepted attempts, and avoid sending the same reset message through both adapters merely to compare them. A duplicate mail stream contaminates the experiment and creates another support problem.

If authentication and content remain suspect, rolling back a provider is not a complete remediation. Keep the investigation attached to the account-recovery queue, and report the distinction between accepted attempts, observed receipt, and known spam placement. Choose the next integration on evidence and the effort of maintaining its adapter, not on a promise that changing vendors will repair every spam signal.

References

  • RFC 7208 Sender Policy Framework
  • RFC 6376 DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • RFC 7489 Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance
  • Resend documentation
  • Twilio SendGrid mail API documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation

If this contract boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai password reset email guide and use public discovery to inspect the adapter contract before implementation.

title: Three fewer graph passes, 12% more time
description:
Bounded Accord’s Speed Demon engineering notes, written on October 31, 2026 and updated after our last push on November 2. Live-board results are practice scores, separate from final judging.

The last graph-construction change in this account removed three complete reads of a five-million-edge array. It preserved the order of every adjacency list and left the shortest-path search unchanged. It passed the correctness checks. The measured program took about 12% longer.

That result came from our entry in Speed Demon, organised by Hackathon Raptors. Bounded Accord implements four tasks in Rust: log aggregation, Boolean and phrase search, a CSV join, and directed shortest paths. The entry repository contains the implementations and their performance records.

The comparisons below cover rejected changes, an officially scored storage improvement, and an input-partitioning change that reached the live board on the last day.

One graph pass can carry more expensive work

Track D stores the graph in two compressed sparse row structures: one for outgoing edges and one for incoming edges. Each row’s edges are contiguous. A forward search from the source and a reverse search from the target can then read their own adjacency arrays without searching the original edge list.

The accepted constructor first parses triples of source, destination and weight. For each direction, it counts degrees, computes row offsets, allocates edge storage, and scans the triples again to fill that storage. There are four full triple scans after parsing.

The candidate counts both degrees while parsing, then fills both adjacency arrays in one shared triple scan. Each edge still appears in its original relative order within its row. Parallel edges, exact duplicates, self-loops and zero weights remain intact. The input byte buffer is released before the edge arrays are allocated in both versions.

The following comparison includes reading, construction, all queries and writing the output:

Measurement Accepted constructor Fused constructor
Pinned-image process time 0.858853 s 0.960344 s
Peak native process RSS 192,388 KiB 185,220 KiB
Nonblank, non-comment source lines 281 286

Times are means of the middle three of five runs per version, after fixed warm-ups. Baseline and candidate runs were interleaved on the same Intel Core i5-12500H machine running Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL2. The images were pinned, six workers were used, and the published child timer excluded container startup. RSS came from separate native runs; it is not the official container-memory measurement.

The time ratio, baseline divided by candidate, was 0.894317. Memory fell by about 3.7%. Both timing spread checks passed, but the candidate missed our previously fixed efficiency requirements. We restored the accepted source and executable and checked the full output hash again.

The comparison establishes that this implementation was slower in this environment. It does not identify a cache-miss rate, a memory-bandwidth limit, or the cost of each added write. Counting loop passes supplied a hypothesis; it did not measure the cost of the resulting access pattern.

An exact small-key representation did pay

Track C joins CSV records to countries and counts distinct names per country. Splitting records at every newline would be wrong: a quoted field can contain a newline. In the officially scored pipeline, the producer carries quote parity across input blocks and dispatches only complete logical records. Six workers decode fields and accumulate numeric totals.

Distinctness spans all workers. The accepted design groups requests into 64 mutex-protected shards. Under a shard’s lock, the first occurrence of an exact (name, country) pair sets a membership bit and increments one worker’s count. Summing those counts is valid because the first-pair decision is shared.

The useful storage change was deliberately narrow. When there are at most 256 country groups, including the unmatched group, names of at most 16 bytes fit in two words plus a length. Four words hold the country-membership bits. The key contains every name byte; it is not a fingerprint used as identity. Length distinguishes a short name from a longer zero-padded value. Longer names and larger country tables keep the full-byte fallback.

Against the preceding accepted pipeline, this change reduced pinned-image time from 0.186579 to 0.152485 seconds and native peak RSS from 24,060 to 19,828 KiB. It passed its fixed adoption requirements. Its subsequent official run, run-52f0819fc621, recorded 55.455380 machine points, up from the previous best of 51.737524.

The tests targeted the representation’s boundaries: every inline-key byte position, lengths around 16 and 17 bytes, zero bytes, country-bit boundaries, tables through 513 countries, concurrent first-pair updates and reused scratch storage. Fast-path checks alone would have missed the fallback’s obligations.

A small time saving can lose the combined comparison

A later Track C candidate scanned each complete record for outside-quote commas and quote counts. That metadata let it derive decoded note lengths without visiting every note byte in the decoder. Unescaped names borrowed their input bytes; escaped names used scratch storage. Record framing and membership storage stayed unchanged.

It was correct across the tested cases, including split vector blocks, escaped quotes, embedded newlines, Unicode, BOM bytes and a two-megabyte note. It also reduced measured process time slightly:

Measurement Accepted parser Structural-metadata parser
Pinned-image process time 0.150447 s 0.147206 s
Peak native process RSS 20,060 KiB 20,016 KiB
Nonblank, non-comment source lines 393 458

The speed ratio was 1.022018, below our fixed 1.18 adoption requirement. Both timing spread checks passed. The source increase also mattered: Speed Demon’s coefficient charges for source size as well as time, memory and dependencies. Using our local RSS and line-count proxies gave a coefficient ratio of 0.988437, below our required 1.05. These counts differ from the host’s formatted-source and container-memory axes, so the ratio is an estimate, not a predicted official score.

We rejected this implementation before submission. Its shorter decoding path did not produce enough whole-program benefit to cover the measured trade-off.

Finding five boundaries without listing every record

A later input-partitioning change reached the local adoption threshold. The first version mapped the immutable CSV file read-only and divided it into six complete-record ranges. Workers borrowed those ranges directly, eliminating the producer’s owned buffers and channels. Its partitioner still scanned the entire input sequentially, collecting record-end offsets to choose just five internal cuts. That version saved memory but missed the time requirement.

The next version computes quote parity in six parallel byte ranges. A prefix XOR supplies the quote state at each proposed cut; a forward scan then finds the next newline outside a quoted field. An escaped quote contributes two quote bytes, so even a cut between them receives the correct starting state. Long quoted records may send several cuts to the same boundary, producing valid empty ranges. After partitioning finishes, six parsing workers borrow the resulting slices. The parser and shared membership tables stay unchanged.

This comparison uses a new fixed batch against the previously accepted producer pipeline:

Measurement Accepted producer pipeline Parallel-parity partitioning
Pinned-image process time 0.149709 s 0.124672 s
Container cgroup peak memory 20,582,400 B 18,612,224 B
Source-line proxy 409 491

The time reduction was 16.7%, and the measured memory reduction was 9.6%. The local coefficient ratio was 1.087865, above the fixed 1.05 requirement. That calculation uses time, memory, source size and direct runtime dependencies; image size is a separate build limit. Both implementations had a dependency-axis value of one.

Memory was read from the Docker cgroup with host data prewarmed and a common trusted holder keeping the cgroup available after the timer exited. This measures the container’s recorded peak, but it does not reproduce the host’s parent harness or isolation. The source count is also a local proxy. The baseline had one slower run; the predeclared middle-three mean excluded the fastest and slowest of five runs from each version, with all raw values retained.

Eleven Rust tests, seventeen validation groups and all fourteen image outputs passed. The checks included quote pairs split at every byte position, long records, Unicode, BOM handling and the final record without a newline. The source was frozen before fresh seeds 137 and 138 and reserved seed 139 were generated.

A separate diagnostic sampled the unchanged candidate twice. It captured 620 and 621 CPU events, with text decoding accounting for about 20% in each capture. The earlier producer pipeline also placed text decoding near 21%. These are exclusive CPU sample locations, not elapsed-time shares; they do not establish that a previously rejected parser change should be tried again.

The change's first live-board run, run-e08fc96bfae2, recorded 57.147738 machine points; the previous best was 55.455380. The board measured 0.160190 seconds instead of 0.187834, and 17,788,928 bytes of peak memory instead of 20,283,392. Formatted source grew from 401 to 483 lines. On the board the coefficient rose by a factor of 1.081, close to the local estimate of 1.088, although the two use different time, memory and source-size measurements.

The local winner that lost on the board

An earlier Track D experiment reordered vertices with breadth-first numbering. Its final local version remapped queries early enough to release the permutation before constructing the final adjacency arrays. The fixed native comparison improved from 0.849322 to 0.705578 seconds: about 16.9% less elapsed time. The RSS ratio was 0.997095, and the local coefficient proxy passed its gate.

The official trial was valid but scored 49.524627 machine points. The retained best was 50.424918. We restored the prior source.

Those official values are separate historical runs, not an interleaved experiment isolating the numbering change. The board observation was enough to reject that trial as an improvement over the retained best; it was not enough to explain the reversal. A later local diagnostic compared native and container execution contexts and still did not establish the cause.

This also changed how we described unchanged-source results. A repository push can run tracks whose source did not change. Our best recorded A and D values came from such runs. They belong in the measurement record, but their variation cannot be credited to a new algorithm. On the final day, the unchanged Track A source took 0.189345 seconds in one run and 0.146796 in the next, against its best of 0.130583.

Correctness evidence has a separate job

For the fused graph candidate, seven Rust property tests passed. One checked that parsing preserved the ordered rows in both directions. Another tested every directed three-node graph whose nine possible edges were absent, zero-weight or unit-weight: 19,683 graphs, with every source-target pair checked against Bellman–Ford.

The wider checks covered 117 adversarial and random graphs, repeated queries, large path sums, zero cycles and directed reachability. Seven host examples ran with one, two, six and twelve workers. Fresh tiny seeds 127 and 128 passed before reserved seed 129, with the source frozen. Published sample/full hashes and all fourteen measured or warm-up image outputs matched.

These checks made a performance comparison meaningful by ruling out the tested wrong-answer cases. They do not prove every possible input correct or turn a slower result into a useful optimisation. The graph invariants still have to hold: path sums remain 64-bit, reverse edges retain their own weights, and bidirectional search cannot stop merely because it found a meeting.

The entry at code freeze

Our last push before the November 2, 15:00 UTC code freeze was commit f00c64fca46bb4124462c053305a1395c596035f. It only updated the performance records; its source is the same as commit 29a57dc3752e417842e5bc2bf4796170c2ead170, which carried the parallel-parity change. The table lists the best live-board value for each track. The values come from different recorded runs, not a simultaneous four-track timing batch.

Track Process time Machine points Run
A: Ingest 0.130583 s 61.431366 run-8ed375c52049
B: Index 0.918916 s 55.479075 run-a9ce34cd1404
C: Join 0.159350 s 57.219847 run-596f68f709a3
D: Traverse 0.723518 s 50.424918 run-396084b71fdb

The A and D bests came from pushes that changed other tracks, with their own source unchanged. C's best came from the final, documentation-only push, which re-ran the parallel-parity source; its first run had scored 57.147738. These are practice-board machine results, not final judging or an award: final scoring reruns the recorded commit on a held-out dataset, and judges contribute 35% of each track total. The per-track PERF.md files retain the unsuccessful comparisons alongside the accepted changes; MEASUREMENTS.json binds the best values to run IDs and source hashes.

For the next graph-construction change, the missing evidence is where the modified access pattern spends time. For the CSV pipeline, the open question is whether the board's 8% coefficient gain holds on the held-out dataset.

The implementations, validation and this article were developed with Codex; Claude Code added the November 2 board results. Algorithm references, measurement limits and assistance disclosures are retained in the entry repository. Task definitions and the official scoring procedure are published by Hackathon Raptors.

title: How to Scrape Dribbble with Go: Designer Profiles, Shots, Collections, and a Portfolio Tracker (2026)
description:
Dribbble is where a lot of designers keep their portfolio, so it's a natural data source if you're scouting talent, studying which kinds of shots get attention, or keeping an eye on your own numbers. The first thing most people search for is "Dribbble API". There is one. It just doesn't do what most people expect.

So this post covers both: what the official Dribbble API gives you, and how to build a small Dribbble scraper in Go for the public pages it doesn't cover. The scraper uses the standard library plus golang.org/x/net/html, and it will:

  1. Respect robots.txt with a tiny matcher, and stop cleanly at bot challenges
  2. Read a designer profile: name, headline, bio, location, followers, skills
  3. Page through a designer's shots with likes, views, and publish dates
  4. List a designer's collections, and read the shots inside one
  5. Snapshot a few portfolios into CSV and report what changed

Everything below was run on October 30, 2026, and the output is real.

Before you start: Dribbble's Terms of Service list "copying, distributing, or disclosing any part of the Website ... by any automated or non-automated 'scraping'" as a prohibited activity. robots.txt allows the pages used here, but robots rules and terms are different things. Read the terms and weigh the legal risk for your use case before running anything, and prefer the official API wherever it covers what you need. Treat this as a learning project or small-scale research: keep request rates low, don't republish people's work, don't resell the data, and don't use it to mass-message designers. If you only need your own data, use the official API.

Is there a Dribbble API?

Yes: the Dribbble API v2 (https://api.dribbble.com/v2/, docs at developer.dribbble.com). You register an application, do the OAuth flow, and send Authorization: Bearer <token>. The limit is 60 requests per minute and 1,440 per day per authenticated user, with X-RateLimit-* headers and Link header pagination.

The catch is in the endpoint list. v2 has GET /user, GET /user/shots, GET /shots/:id, create/update/delete shot, projects, and jobs. All of them are about the authenticated user. The docs for "Get a shot" say it plainly: "This endpoint returns only shots owned by the currently authenticated user." The old v1 endpoints for any user's shots, followers, and popular lists are gone. Without a token, GET https://api.dribbble.com/v2/user returns 401, and /v2/users/simplebits/shots is a 404.

You want Use
Your own shots, profile, projects (e.g. to show your Dribbble work on your site) Dribbble API v2
Other designers' public profiles, shots, likes/views, collections The public website, which is what this scraper reads

How dribbble.com looks from a scraper's point of view

I checked the site with curl and with Go's HTTP client first. Here is what came back:

path                                            status  notes
/robots.txt                                     200
/simplebits                                     200     ~300 KB, shots embedded as JSON
/simplebits?page=2                              200     next 24 shots
/simplebits/about                               200     bio, location, skills, counts
/simplebits/collections                         200     6 collections per page
/simplebits/collections/4582-Data-Viz           200     24 shots per page
/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print             202     AWS WAF challenge, empty page
/shots/popular, /search/logo                    202     AWS WAF challenge
/shots/popular.rss                              202     AWS WAF challenge
/simplebits.rss, /shots.rss                     404     the old RSS feeds are gone

The status codes were the same with a Chrome User-Agent, curl's default, and Go's Go-http-client/1.1. So three findings shaped the code.

1. robots.txt is clear about what's off-limits. Profiles, collections, and shot pages are allowed. These are disallowed for every crawler:

Disallow: /*/followers$
Disallow: /*/following$
Disallow: /*/tags$
Disallow: /*/tags/*
Disallow: /shots/*/comments
Disallow: /shots/*/fans
Disallow: /shots/*/rebounds
Disallow: /shots/*/buckets
Disallow: /shots/week/*   (and /day/*, /month/*, /year/*)

So no follower lists, no who-liked-this lists, no comments. The scraper below checks every path against these rules before it sends a request.

2. Profile and collection pages are server-rendered, and the shots come as JSON. The profile page includes a <script> with var newestShots = [...], one object per shot in the grid:

{"id":27755136,"title":"Measure Twice Print","path":"/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print",
 "published_at":"September 23, 2026","is_rebound":null,"rebounds_count":0,
 "attachments_count":0,"view_count":"23.3k","likes_count":"108","liked":null,"ga":[]}

That's easier and sturdier than scraping the grid's CSS. Logged out, the page shows a "Sign up to continue" button where infinite scroll would be, but the classic ?page=2 link is still in the HTML and works.

3. Individual shot pages, popular, and search sit behind an AWS WAF challenge. They return HTTP 202 with x-amzn-waf-action: challenge and a small JavaScript page that a real browser solves. I didn't try to get around it, and you shouldn't either. Everything in this post comes from profile and collection pages, which already show titles, likes, views, and dates for every shot. The scraper treats a 202 as "stop", not "retry".

One more detail: the page's own config included "isRobot": true for my requests. Dribbble knows exactly what you are, so be polite.

Step 1: Project setup and a polite fetch helper 

mkdir dribbblescraper && cd dribbblescraper
go mod init dribbblescraper
go get golang.org/x/net/html

getHTML checks robots.txt, keeps at least two seconds between requests, backs off on 429/5xx, and returns ErrChallenged on a WAF challenge. The User-Agent is honest. Put your own contact URL in it.

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "regexp"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    base      = "https://dribbble.com"
    userAgent = "dribbblescraper/0.1 (+https://example.com/contact)"
)

var (
    client = &http.Client{Timeout: 25 * time.Second}

    // ErrChallenged means AWS WAF answered with a JavaScript challenge
    // (HTTP 202, empty-ish body, x-amzn-waf-action: challenge). We stop
    // instead of trying to solve it.
    ErrChallenged = errors.New("blocked by AWS WAF challenge")
    ErrDisallowed = errors.New("path disallowed by robots.txt")

    lastRequest time.Time
    minGap      = 2 * time.Second
)

// getHTML fetches a dribbble.com path after checking robots.txt, waits at
// least minGap between requests, and backs off on 429/5xx.
func getHTML(path string) (string, error) {
    if !robots.Allowed(path) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrDisallowed, path)
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if wait := minGap - time.Since(lastRequest); wait > 0 {
            time.Sleep(wait)
        }
        lastRequest = time.Now()

        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", base+path, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "text/html")
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", "en-US,en;q=0.9")
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 3 * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 8<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        switch {
        case res.Header.Get("x-amzn-waf-action") != "" || res.StatusCode == 202:
            return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrChallenged, path)
        case res.StatusCode == 429 || res.StatusCode >= 500:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "HTTP %d on %s, backing off\n", res.StatusCode, path)
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 15 * time.Second)
            continue
        case res.StatusCode == 404:
            return "", fmt.Errorf("not found: %s", path)
        case res.StatusCode != 200:
            return "", fmt.Errorf("GET %s: HTTP %d", path, res.StatusCode)
        }
        return string(body), nil
    }
    return "", errors.New("gave up after retries: " + path)
}

The robots matcher is about 50 lines. It reads the User-agent: * group and turns each rule into a regexp, so * matches anything and a trailing $ anchors the end:

// --- a tiny robots.txt matcher (User-agent: * group, * and $ wildcards) ---

type robotsRules struct{ allow, disallow []*regexp.Regexp }

var robots = &robotsRules{}

func loadRobots() error {
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", base+"/robots.txt", nil)
    req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)
    res, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    if res.StatusCode != 200 {
        return fmt.Errorf("robots.txt: HTTP %d", res.StatusCode)
    }
    inStar := false
    sc := bufio.NewScanner(res.Body)
    for sc.Scan() {
        line := strings.TrimSpace(strings.SplitN(sc.Text(), "#", 2)[0])
        k, v, ok := strings.Cut(line, ":")
        if !ok {
            continue
        }
        k, v = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(k)), strings.TrimSpace(v)
        switch {
        case k == "user-agent":
            inStar = v == "*"
        case inStar && k == "disallow" && v != "":
            robots.disallow = append(robots.disallow, robotsPattern(v))
        case inStar && k == "allow" && v != "":
            robots.allow = append(robots.allow, robotsPattern(v))
        }
    }
    return sc.Err()
}

// robotsPattern turns "/*/followers$" into ^/[^?]*?/followers$ style regexps.
func robotsPattern(p string) *regexp.Regexp {
    anchored := strings.HasSuffix(p, "$")
    p = strings.TrimSuffix(p, "$")
    parts := strings.Split(p, "*")
    for i := range parts {
        parts[i] = regexp.QuoteMeta(parts[i])
    }
    re := "^" + strings.Join(parts, ".*")
    if anchored {
        re += "$"
    }
    return regexp.MustCompile(re)
}

func (r *robotsRules) Allowed(path string) bool {
    // Match on the path without the query string for $-anchored rules.
    p, _, _ := strings.Cut(path, "?")
    for _, a := range r.allow {
        if a.MatchString(p) {
            return true
        }
    }
    for _, d := range r.disallow {
        if d.MatchString(p) {
            return false
        }
    }
    return true
}

A test pins down the rules we care about. It runs against the live robots.txt:

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "testing"
)

func TestRobots(t *testing.T) {
    if err := loadRobots(); err != nil {
        t.Skip("no network:", err)
    }
    cases := map[string]bool{
        "/simplebits":                     true,
        "/simplebits?page=2":              true,
        "/simplebits/about":               true,
        "/simplebits/collections":         true,
        "/simplebits/followers":           false,
        "/simplebits/following":           false,
        "/simplebits/tags":                false,
        "/shots/123-Foo/comments":         false,
        "/shots/123-Foo/fans":             false,
        "/shots/week/2026-10-01":          false,
        "/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-P": true,
    }
    for path, want := range cases {
        if got := robots.Allowed(path); got != want {
            t.Errorf("Allowed(%q) = %v, want %v", path, got, want)
        }
    }
}

func TestShotPageIsChallenged(t *testing.T) {
    if err := loadRobots(); err != nil {
        t.Skip("no network:", err)
    }
    _, err := getHTML("/shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print")
    t.Logf("shot page: %v", err)
    if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, ErrChallenged) {
        t.Errorf("unexpected error: %v", err)
    }
}

$ go test -v ./...
=== RUN   TestRobots
--- PASS: TestRobots (0.05s)
=== RUN   TestShotPageIsChallenged
    robots_test.go:37: shot page: blocked by AWS WAF challenge: /shots/27755136-Measure-Twice-Print
--- PASS: TestShotPageIsChallenged (0.07s)
PASS

Step 2: Small HTML helpers

golang.org/x/net/html gives you a parse tree but no selectors, so a few helpers go a long way. parseCount matters more than it looks: Dribbble shows views as 23.3k, and counts on the about page as 117,603.

package main

import (
    "strconv"
    "strings"

    "golang.org/x/net/html"
)

func parseDoc(s string) (*html.Node, error) { return html.Parse(strings.NewReader(s)) }

func attr(n *html.Node, key string) string {
    for _, a := range n.Attr {
        if a.Key == key {
            return a.Val
        }
    }
    return ""
}

func hasAttr(n *html.Node, key string) bool {
    for _, a := range n.Attr {
        if a.Key == key {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

func hasClass(n *html.Node, class string) bool {
    if n.Type != html.ElementNode {
        return false
    }
    for _, c := range strings.Fields(attr(n, "class")) {
        if c == class {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

// findAll walks the tree and returns every node matching pred.
func findAll(n *html.Node, pred func(*html.Node) bool) []*html.Node {
    var out []*html.Node
    var walk func(*html.Node)
    walk = func(n *html.Node) {
        if pred(n) {
            out = append(out, n)
        }
        for c := n.FirstChild; c != nil; c = c.NextSibling {
            walk(c)
        }
    }
    walk(n)
    return out
}

func first(n *html.Node, pred func(*html.Node) bool) *html.Node {
    if all := findAll(n, pred); len(all) > 0 {
        return all[0]
    }
    return nil
}

func byClass(c string) func(*html.Node) bool {
    return func(n *html.Node) bool { return hasClass(n, c) }
}

func byTag(tag string) func(*html.Node) bool {
    return func(n *html.Node) bool { return n.Type == html.ElementNode && n.Data == tag }
}

// text returns the whitespace-collapsed text content of a node (nil-safe).
func text(n *html.Node) string {
    if n == nil {
        return ""
    }
    var b strings.Builder
    var walk func(*html.Node)
    walk = func(n *html.Node) {
        if n.Type == html.TextNode {
            b.WriteString(n.Data + " ")
        }
        if n.Type == html.ElementNode && (n.Data == "script" || n.Data == "style" || n.Data == "svg") {
            return
        }
        for c := n.FirstChild; c != nil; c = c.NextSibling {
            walk(c)
        }
    }
    walk(n)
    return strings.Join(strings.Fields(b.String()), " ")
}

// parseCount turns "117,603", "23.3k", "1.2m" or "381" into an int.
func parseCount(s string) int {
    s = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(strings.ReplaceAll(s, ",", "")))
    mult := 1.0
    switch {
    case strings.HasSuffix(s, "k"):
        mult, s = 1_000, strings.TrimSuffix(s, "k")
    case strings.HasSuffix(s, "m"):
        mult, s = 1_000_000, strings.TrimSuffix(s, "m")
    }
    f, err := strconv.ParseFloat(s, 64)
    if err != nil {
        return 0
    }
    return int(f*mult + 0.5)
}

// leadingCount reads the number at the start of "223 Shots" or "117,603 followers".
func leadingCount(s string) int {
    f := strings.Fields(s)
    if len(f) == 0 {
        return 0
    }
    return parseCount(f[0])
}

Step 3: A designer profile

The /about page has everything: name, headline, bio, location, "Member since", Pro badge, skills, and follower counts. The trap is that there are (at least) two profile templates. On simplebits (Dan Cederholm, a Dribbble co-founder) the masthead shows "117,603 followers / 1,820 following / 46,450 likes". On Betraydan the masthead shows location and specializations instead, and there's no likes count at all. Both templates have a .profile-stats-section with count + meta spans, so the code reads followers from there and only takes likes when they're shown.

package main

import (
    "net/url"
    "regexp"
    "strings"

    "golang.org/x/net/html"
)

type Profile struct {
    Username    string   `json:"username"`
    Name        string   `json:"name"`
    Headline    string   `json:"headline"`
    Bio         string   `json:"bio"`
    Location    string   `json:"location"`
    MemberSince string   `json:"member_since"`
    Pro         bool     `json:"pro"`
    Followers   int      `json:"followers"`
    Following   int      `json:"following"`
    Likes       int      `json:"likes"` // 0 when the template doesn't show it
    Skills      []string `json:"skills"`
}

var usernameRe = regexp.MustCompile(`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$`)

// normalizeUser accepts "simplebits", "@simplebits" or "https://dribbble.com/simplebits/about".
func normalizeUser(s string) string {
    s = strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(s), "@")
    if u, err := url.Parse(s); err == nil && u.Host != "" {
        s = strings.Split(strings.Trim(u.Path, "/"), "/")[0]
    }
    if !usernameRe.MatchString(s) {
        return ""
    }
    return s
}

// fetchProfile reads /<user>/about, which has everything the main profile page
// has in its masthead plus bio, location, "Member since" and skills.
func fetchProfile(user string) (Profile, error) {
    p := Profile{Username: user}
    page, err := getHTML("/" + user + "/about")
    if err != nil {
        return p, err
    }
    doc, err := parseDoc(page)
    if err != nil {
        return p, err
    }
    p.Name = text(first(doc, byClass("masthead-profile-name")))
    p.Headline = text(first(doc, byClass("masthead-intro")))

    if p.Headline == "" { // the second profile template shows specializations instead
        p.Headline = text(first(doc, byClass("masthead-profile-specializations")))
    }

    // Dribbble has (at least) two profile templates. Both have a
    // ".profile-stats-section" with <span class="count"> + <span class="meta">
    // pairs; only one also has "N likes" in ".masthead-stats".
    if sec := first(doc, byClass("profile-stats-section")); sec != nil {
        for _, a := range findAll(sec, byTag("a")) {
            n := leadingCount(text(first(a, byClass("count"))))
            switch text(first(a, byClass("meta"))) {
            case "followers":
                p.Followers = n
            case "following":
                p.Following = n
            }
        }
    }
    if stats := first(doc, byClass("masthead-stats")); stats != nil {
        for _, st := range findAll(stats, byClass("stat")) {
            if t := text(st); strings.HasSuffix(t, "likes") {
                p.Likes = leadingCount(t)
            }
        }
    }

    var bio []string
    for _, b := range findAll(doc, byClass("bio-text")) {
        bio = append(bio, text(b))
    }
    p.Bio = strings.Join(bio, "\n")

    // The info section is rendered twice (small screens and large), so take the first.
    p.Location = text(first(doc, byClass("location")))
    p.MemberSince = strings.TrimPrefix(text(first(doc, byClass("created"))), "Member since ")
    p.Pro = first(doc, func(n *html.Node) bool { return hasClass(n, "info-item") && hasClass(n, "pro") }) != nil

    if sec := first(doc, byClass("profile-skills-section")); sec != nil {
        for _, a := range findAll(sec, byTag("a")) {
            if s := attr(a, "data-skill"); s != "" {
                p.Skills = append(p.Skills, s)
            }
        }
    }
    return p, nil
}

$ ./dribbblescraper profile simplebits
{
  "username": "simplebits",
  "name": "Dan Cederholm",
  "headline": "Making type \u0026 goods at SimpleBits®. Dribbble Co-Founder.",
  "bio": "Making type and goods at SimpleBits® since 2002.\nJoin my Secret Club™ for all my fonts, early releases, private community, discounts, and other good stuff.\nsimplebits dot com",
  "location": "Salem, MA",
  "member_since": "Jul 2009",
  "pro": true,
  "followers": 117603,
  "following": 1820,
  "likes": 46450,
  "skills": ["branding", "fonts", "icon", "illustration", "logo", "logo design", "type design", "ui"]
}

$ ./dribbblescraper profile https://dribbble.com/Betraydan/about
{
  "username": "Betraydan",
  "name": "Daniel Klopper",
  "headline": "Product Design, UI / Visual Design, Mobile Design",
  "location": "Cape Town, South Africa",
  "member_since": "Jul 2011",
  "pro": false,
  "followers": 19180,
  "following": 303,
  "likes": 0,
  ...
}

My first version only read the masthead and returned followers: 0 for Betraydan. Test against more than one profile before you trust a parser.

Two things you won't get logged out: social links and email. They sit behind "Get in touch", which opens a signup dialog. That's fine. That's the designer's choice.

Step 4: Shots, page by page

extractJSONVar finds var newestShots = and hands the rest of the page to json.Decoder. The decoder stops at the end of the JSON value, so there's no need for a fragile regexp to find the closing ].

Thumbnails are lazy-loaded: the <img src> is a 1×1 GIF, and the real URL is in data-src (and in a <noscript> copy). If your scraper saves src, you get 24 transparent pixels.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

// Shot is what the profile page ships in `var newestShots = [...]`,
// plus the thumbnail we read from the HTML grid.
type Shot struct {
    ID          int64  `json:"id"`
    Title       string `json:"title"`
    Path        string `json:"path"`
    PublishedAt string `json:"published_at"` // "September 23, 2026"
    Rebounds    int    `json:"rebounds_count"`
    Attachments int    `json:"attachments_count"`
    ViewsRaw    string `json:"view_count"`  // "23.3k" (rounded!)
    LikesRaw    string `json:"likes_count"` // "108"
    Views       int    `json:"-"`
    Likes       int    `json:"-"`
    Thumbnail   string `json:"-"`
}

func (s Shot) URL() string { return base + s.Path }

func (s Shot) Published() time.Time {
    t, _ := time.Parse("January 2, 2006", s.PublishedAt)
    return t
}

// extractJSONVar finds `var <name> = ` in a page and decodes the JSON value
// that follows. json.Decoder stops at the end of the value, so we don't need
// to guess where the array ends.
func extractJSONVar(page, name string, out any) error {
    marker := "var " + name + " = "
    i := strings.Index(page, marker)
    if i < 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("%q not found (markup changed?)", marker)
    }
    return json.NewDecoder(strings.NewReader(page[i+len(marker):])).Decode(out)
}

// fetchShotsPage reads one page of /<user>?page=N. Logged out, each page has 24 shots.
func fetchShotsPage(user string, page int) (shots []Shot, hasNext bool, err error) {
    body, err := getHTML(fmt.Sprintf("/%s?page=%d", user, page))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, false, err
    }
    if err := extractJSONVar(body, "newestShots", &shots); err != nil {
        return nil, false, err
    }

    // Thumbnails are lazy-loaded: src is a 1x1 GIF, the real URL is in data-src.
    thumbs := map[string]string{}
    if doc, err := parseDoc(body); err == nil {
        for _, li := range findAll(doc, byClass("shot-thumbnail")) {
            id := attr(li, "data-thumbnail-id")
            if img := first(li, byTag("img")); img != nil && id != "" {
                src := attr(img, "data-src")
                if src == "" {
                    src = attr(img, "src")
                }
                thumbs[id] = strings.Split(src, "?")[0]
            }
        }
    }
    for i := range shots {
        shots[i].Views = parseCount(shots[i].ViewsRaw)
        shots[i].Likes = parseCount(shots[i].LikesRaw)
        shots[i].Thumbnail = thumbs[fmt.Sprint(shots[i].ID)]
    }
    hasNext = strings.Contains(body, `class="next_page"`) && strings.Contains(body, `rel="next"`)
    return shots, hasNext, nil
}

// fetchShots pages through a profile until maxPages, an empty page, or no "Next" link.
func fetchShots(user string, maxPages int) ([]Shot, error) {
    var all []Shot
    seen := map[int64]bool{}
    for page := 1; page <= maxPages; page++ {
        batch, hasNext, err := fetchShotsPage(user, page)
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        added := 0
        for _, s := range batch {
            if !seen[s.ID] { // pages can overlap if a new shot is posted mid-crawl
                seen[s.ID] = true
                all = append(all, s)
                added++
            }
        }
        if added == 0 || !hasNext {
            break
        }
    }
    return all, nil
}

Step 5: Collections

Collections are curated sets of other people's shots. A designer's /collections page lists them 6 at a time, and ?page=2 gives the next 6. Each one is an li.shots-group-item with a name, a shot count, and a designer count:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/url"
    "regexp"
    "strings"

    "golang.org/x/net/html"
)

type Collection struct {
    ID        string `json:"id"`
    Name      string `json:"name"`
    URL       string `json:"url"`
    Shots     int    `json:"shots"`
    Designers int    `json:"designers"`
}

// fetchCollections reads /<user>/collections?page=N (6 per page, logged out).
func fetchCollections(user string, maxPages int) ([]Collection, error) {
    var all []Collection
    for page := 1; page <= maxPages; page++ {
        body, err := getHTML(fmt.Sprintf("/%s/collections?page=%d", user, page))
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        doc, err := parseDoc(body)
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        items := findAll(doc, byClass("shots-group-item"))
        for _, li := range items {
            c := Collection{ID: attr(li, "data-id"), Name: text(first(li, byClass("collection-name")))}
            if a := first(li, byClass("shots-group")); a != nil {
                c.URL = base + attr(a, "href")
            }
            c.Shots = leadingCount(text(first(li, byClass("shots-count"))))
            c.Designers = leadingCount(text(first(li, byClass("designers-count"))))
            all = append(all, c)
        }
        if len(items) == 0 {
            break
        }
    }
    return all, nil
}

A single collection page uses newer markup (shot2-item), 24 shots per page. Here the title and path are attributes on a <drb-shot-metadata> custom element, which is nicer than digging through text. The author is the profile link inside the details block.

type CollectionShot struct {
    ID         string
    Title      string
    URL        string
    Author     string // profile path, e.g. "Betraydan"
    AuthorName string
    Likes      int
    Views      int
    Thumbnail  string
}

type CollectionPage struct {
    Name      string
    Curator   string
    Shots     int
    Designers int
    Items     []CollectionShot
}

var collectionPath = regexp.MustCompile(`^/[A-Za-z0-9_-]+/collections/\d+(-[^/]*)?$`)

// fetchCollection reads one collection (24 shots per page) from a full URL.
func fetchCollection(raw string, maxPages int) (CollectionPage, error) {
    var out CollectionPage
    u, err := url.Parse(raw)
    if err != nil || !collectionPath.MatchString(u.Path) {
        return out, fmt.Errorf("want https://dribbble.com/<user>/collections/<id>-<slug>, got %q", raw)
    }
    seen := map[string]bool{}
    for page := 1; page <= maxPages; page++ {
        body, err := getHTML(fmt.Sprintf("%s?page=%d", u.Path, page))
        if err != nil {
            return out, err
        }
        doc, err := parseDoc(body)
        if err != nil {
            return out, err
        }
        if page == 1 {
            out.Name = text(first(doc, byClass("collection-page__title")))
            out.Curator = text(first(doc, byClass("curator__name")))
            for _, v := range findAll(doc, byClass("collection-page__meta-details-value")) {
                t := text(v)
                switch {
                case strings.HasSuffix(t, "Shots"):
                    out.Shots = leadingCount(t)
                case strings.HasSuffix(t, "Designers"):
                    out.Designers = leadingCount(t)
                }
            }
        }
        added := 0
        for _, it := range findAll(doc, byClass("shot2-item")) {
            id := attr(it, "data-id")
            if id == "" || seen[id] {
                continue
            }
            seen[id] = true
            added++
            s := CollectionShot{ID: id}
            if m := first(it, byTag("drb-shot-metadata")); m != nil {
                s.Title, s.URL = attr(m, "title"), base+attr(m, "path")
            }
            if img := first(it, byTag("img")); img != nil {
                s.Thumbnail = strings.Split(attr(img, "src"), "?")[0]
            }
            if d := first(it, byClass("shot2-item-details__user-container")); d != nil {
                if a := first(d, byTag("a")); a != nil {
                    s.Author = strings.Trim(attr(a, "href"), "/")
                }
                s.AuthorName = text(first(d, byClass("shot2-item-details__user-name")))
            }
            // Stats: the like count sits in [data-shot-like-count]; views are the
            // text of the last ".shot2-item-stats__item".
            stats := findAll(it, byClass("shot2-item-stats__item"))
            if lc := first(it, func(n *html.Node) bool { return hasAttr(n, "data-shot-like-count") }); lc != nil {
                s.Likes = parseCount(text(lc))
            }
            if len(stats) > 0 {
                s.Views = parseCount(text(stats[len(stats)-1]))
            }
            out.Items = append(out.Items, s)
        }
        if added == 0 {
            break
        }
    }
    return out, nil
}
