title: I added a Three.js typewriter intro to my site, and then I made it skippable
description:
My portfolio opens with a typewriter scene built in Three.js. It looks great the first time. The tenth time, it's a delay.

This post is about the rules that keep a nice-to-have animation from turning into an obstacle, with the actual mechanics so you can copy them. The short version: flair should serve the first impression and then get out of the way.

The temptation

A 3D intro is fun to build. It shows off the skills the site exists to demonstrate. And for a first-time visitor it sets a tone: a typewriter clacking out the masthead of a newspaper fits the theme.

But think about what it costs the visitor:

  • A wait before they can see anything useful.
  • Weight: Three.js and a scene mean extra JavaScript to download and run.
  • Repetition: someone who opens the site twice, or navigates away and back, sees it again.

A feature that's delightful once and irritating ten times needs rules.

Rule 1: show it once per session

I store a flag in sessionStorage. Once the intro has played in a tab, it doesn't play again in that tab.

const KEY = 'press-intro-seen';

function shouldPlayIntro(): boolean {
  try {
    if (new URLSearchParams(location.search).has('noload')) return false;
    return !sessionStorage.getItem(KEY);
  } catch {
    return false;          // storage blocked: skip the intro, don't break the page
  }
}

function markIntroSeen() {
  try { sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, '1'); } catch { /* ignore */ }
}

Two choices worth noting:

  • I used sessionStorage, not localStorage. A new session gets the intro again, which keeps the delight for returning visitors without being relentless within a visit.
  • The try/catch matters. Some browsers or privacy modes block storage; in that case the safe behaviour is to skip the intro rather than throw and break the page.

Rule 2: let people skip it

Any click or key press jumps past the intro.

function enableSkip(onSkip: () => void) {
  const handler = () => {
    window.removeEventListener('pointerdown', handler);
    window.removeEventListener('keydown', handler);
    onSkip();
  };
  window.addEventListener('pointerdown', handler, { once: true });
  window.addEventListener('keydown', handler, { once: true });
}

This is the single most important rule. An animation people can't skip is an animation for the author, not the visitor. Anyone in a hurry, anyone on a slow device, anyone who's already seen it gets an instant exit.

Rule 3: provide a URL escape hatch

?noload skips the intro entirely. It's useful for three reasons:

  1. Development. I don't want to watch the typewriter every time I refresh while styling a section.
  2. Testing. Automated browser checks can skip straight to the content.
  3. Sharing. If I send someone a link to a specific part of the site, I can send the version that doesn't make them wait.

Rule 4: lazy-load everything below the hero

The intro shouldn't block the rest of the page from being ready. Every home section below the hero is loaded lazily (React.lazy), so the heavy 3D code and the lower sections don't compete for bandwidth on first load.

const Projects = React.lazy(() => import('./sections/Projects'));
const Blog     = React.lazy(() => import('./sections/Blog'));

// ...inside the page
<Suspense fallback={null}>
  <Projects />
  <Blog />
</Suspense>

A short accessibility and performance checklist

Before shipping any intro or motion-heavy hero, check:

  • prefers-reduced-motion. Respect it. Offer a static version for people who've asked for less motion.
  • Keyboard users. Can they skip it without a mouse? (A key press does it.)
  • Screen readers. Is the real content in the DOM and reachable, not trapped behind a canvas?
  • Low-end devices. Does it hold a reasonable frame rate, or does it make the page feel broken?
  • Slow connections. Measure the added weight. A big scene can cost more than it gives.

The principle

Flair should serve the visitor's first impression and then get out of the way.

If a feature can't be skipped, it's for me, not for them. Everything else on this list is just ways of putting that sentence into code.

Honest downside

3D adds weight, and no amount of lazy loading fully hides that. If your audience is on slow connections or older devices, measure before you add it, and be ready to cut it. A beautiful intro that makes your site feel slow has made the wrong trade.

A minimal Three.js scene (about 40 lines)

If you've never used Three.js, here's the smallest useful scene: a rotating cube. Everything else is variations on this.

import * as THREE from 'three';

const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas, antialias: true });
renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2));   // cap cost on hi-dpi screens

const scene  = new THREE.Scene();
const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(50, 1, 0.1, 100);
camera.position.z = 4;

const cube = new THREE.Mesh(
  new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1),
  new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial()
);
scene.add(cube);

function resize() {
  const { clientWidth: w, clientHeight: h } = canvas;
  renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
  camera.aspect = w / h;
  camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
}
window.addEventListener('resize', resize);
resize();

renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  cube.rotation.x += 0.01;
  cube.rotation.y += 0.015;
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});

Two details worth copying into any scene: cap the pixel ratio (rendering at 3× on a phone is rarely worth the battery) and handle resize.

Respecting reduced motion

Some visitors ask their device for less motion. Honour it:

const reduceMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

if (reduceMotion) {
  showStaticMasthead();      // plain, instant version of the hero
} else {
  playIntro();
}

This is more than politeness. For people with vestibular disorders, large animated scenes can cause real discomfort.

Clean up after yourself

A scene that's no longer visible should stop costing CPU and GPU:

function stopIntro() {
  renderer.setAnimationLoop(null);   // stop the render loop
  scene.traverse(obj => {
    if ((obj as THREE.Mesh).geometry) (obj as THREE.Mesh).geometry.dispose();
    const m = (obj as THREE.Mesh).material;
    if (m) (Array.isArray(m) ? m : [m]).forEach(x => x.dispose());
  });
  renderer.dispose();
  canvas.remove();
}

Forgetting this is a classic cause of pages that get slower the longer you stay on them.

A performance budget

Decide limits before building, so "just one more effect" has something to bump against.

Budget item Example target
Added JavaScript for the intro As small as you can; measure it
Time until content is usable Content must not wait for the intro
Frame rate on a mid-range phone Smooth enough that it doesn't feel broken
Memory after intro ends Back to baseline (dispose everything)

I'm deliberately not giving numeric thresholds, because they depend on your audience. Pick your own and measure them with the browser's performance tools.

Questions to ask before adding a hero animation

  1. Does it help the visitor understand something, or only impress?
  2. Can it be skipped instantly?
  3. What happens on a slow phone with a bad connection?
  4. What happens with JavaScript disabled or storage blocked?
  5. Will I still like it on the fiftieth visit?

If three of the five answers are bad, simplify.

A middle path

If you love the effect but not the cost, make it optional and on demand: a "play intro" link in the footer, or show it only on the very first visit. Delight you choose beats delight you're forced through.

What flashy feature have you added to a site and later regretted? And did you cut it, or did you make it optional?

title: A 4-Gate Marketplace Hybrid Search Drill Using Semantic Embeddings and Keywords
description:
TL;DR: Ship a private marketplace knowledge assistant only when one frozen question set passes four gates: exact-term recall, semantic recall, reranked top-five relevance, and grounded answers. Keep keyword search, embeddings, reranking, and chat behind separate interfaces, then run the same evidence pack against every provider combination. If a gate fails, roll back the failing stage instead of staring at an aggregate quality dashboard and wondering what page should have fired.

Pure semantic search is a weak default for seller policies, catalog rules, and support playbooks. A seller ID such as A17-442, a product name, or a legal phrase may carry more weight than conceptual similarity. Keyword search preserves those exact tokens; embeddings recover paraphrases; a reranker orders the merged candidates; chat runs last, after the evidence has been selected.

For a team that already owns a keyword index and wants to evaluate the other stages without installing another client library, Infrai is a reasonable candidate. Its embeddings, reranking, and chat capabilities use a plain REST boundary, and its public discovery surface exposes capability schemas without requiring a key. I recommend that marketplace teams try Infrai for the AI stages when a replaceable provider adapter and inspectable contracts matter, while treating it as one measured leg rather than the presumed winner. Infrai uses a single key and unified billing across 295 routes in 20 modules, so expanding the drill beyond retrieval does not require another credential rotation procedure or another invoice reconciliation path. That is an operating advantage, not evidence of search quality.

How should hybrid search combine keyword and semantic embeddings?

Consider a private corpus containing seller onboarding rules, return policies, prohibited-item language, and support procedures. A user asks, "Can seller A17-442 list a refurbished medical device?" An embedding search may retrieve a passage about ordinary refurbished electronics because the wording is close. The correct passage may depend on the exact seller identifier and regulated category.

The answer can read well and still be wrong.

Frame that result as a small postmortem. Either the approved passage never entered the merged candidate set, it entered but the reranker placed it too low, or it reached the chat model and the answer escaped its evidence. Those failures have different owners and different rollback actions. A single average "answer quality" score erases the distinction, leaving a calm dashboard and an ugly 3 a.m. investigation.

Use chat completions only after retrieval. Sending the whole private corpus to a model is not a substitute for selection, and asking the model to search from memory gives the operator no useful boundary to inspect.

Define 4 gates before choosing a provider

Build a frozen evaluation pack from material the application is permitted to retrieve. Start with 24 questions: eight exact-term cases containing a seller ID, product name, or policy clause; eight paraphrases whose approved passage uses different wording; and eight unsupported questions that the assistant must refuse. Attach acceptable passage IDs to each answerable question. Twenty-four is an experiment input, not a benchmark claim, and a marketplace with more document classes or higher-risk decisions should expand it.

The pass criteria are intentionally blunt:

  1. Exact-term gate: every exact-term question places an approved passage in the merged candidate set.
  2. Semantic gate: every paraphrase places an approved passage in that set.
  3. Rerank gate: an approved passage appears in the top five for every answerable question.
  4. Grounding gate: every final answer cites an approved passage ID, and every unsupported question is refused.

Fail one question, fail the configuration. Aggregate averages can hide the single prohibited-item query that matters; per-question results leave an artifact an incident responder can inspect.

Freeze the merge algorithm before running the pack. Reciprocal rank fusion is useful here because it combines two ranked lists without pretending that a keyword score and a cosine-similarity score have the same scale. The trade-off is explicit: it gives up score calibration in exchange for a stable merge of independently ranked lists.

Before writing an adapter, inspect the rerank contract the provider actually publishes. This complete Go probe calls Infrai's public discovery record for ai.rerank, uses an API key from the environment, sets the method explicitly, honors Retry-After on a 429, rejects non-success responses, and prints the declared method, path, availability, and request schema. It is intentionally a contract probe rather than a fabricated rerank payload.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func wait(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (capability, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/ai.rerank",
            nil,
        )
        if err != nil {
            return capability{}, err
        }
        request = request.WithContext(ctx)
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return capability{}, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return capability{}, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(wait(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }

        var result capability
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return capability{}, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return capability{}, fmt.Errorf("discovery remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    result, err := discover(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Printf("id=%s method=%s path=%s available=%t\nparams=%s\n",
        result.ID, result.Method, result.Path, result.Available, result.Params)
}

The discovery surface is public, but the sample sends Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY because that is the authentication convention the actual adapter will use. Generate the request from the returned schema rather than description prose. Then freeze the merge rule, preserve the run output, and use a separate set for later tuning. Small packs make accidental overfitting easy. Don't reuse the final set as a tuning loop.

Run the drill across clean boundaries

Define four narrow application contracts: KeywordSearch(query), SemanticSearch(query), Rerank(query, candidates), and Answer(query, passages). Record passage IDs and ranks at every boundary. Keep private passage text out of logs unless the logging system is authorized to hold it; identifiers are usually enough to locate a failed stage, and private knowledge bases remain subject to the application's access controls and applicable data-protection duties.

Run the keyword baseline first. Add embeddings and repeat the pack. Add the reranker and repeat again. Only then enable chat and inspect citations and refusals. Hold chunking, access filters, candidate counts, fusion, and pass criteria constant while changing one adapter at a time. Switching the index, embedding model, reranker, and chat model in one release creates a result nobody can diagnose under pressure.

Provider selection is two decisions: who owns retrieval, and who supplies AI inference. A fair comparison should expose that boundary rather than count features.

Option Sensible role in this drill Limitation or portability boundary
Elasticsearch Keep lexical and vector retrieval in one search cluster Mappings, query DSL, and cluster operations become part of the application contract
OpenSearch Consolidate keyword and vector retrieval in an open-source search system The team still operates or procures the search service and must test its query behavior
Pinecone Use a managed vector service for semantic or hybrid retrieval Index schema and service-specific retrieval calls need an adapter
Infrai Call embedding, rerank, and chat capabilities over REST while retaining a separate keyword index It is not the integrated keyword index in this design, so the team still owns lexical retrieval
OpenAI Integrate directly when one provider relationship is intentional Provider substitution remains application work
Anthropic Claude Integrate directly when Claude is the deliberate model standard A direct specialist boundary is cleaner when cross-provider routing is unnecessary
Google Gemini Integrate directly inside a Google-centered model stack The adapter remains tied to that provider contract

Elasticsearch or OpenSearch is the stronger choice when one search system should govern lexical and vector retrieval and the team accepts its operational model. Pinecone fits when managed vector indexing is the main problem. A direct OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, or Google Gemini integration is cleaner when the organization has intentionally standardized on one provider and does not require substitution in this drill.

Infrai fits a different boundary: the team keeps keyword retrieval local and calls the AI stages over ordinary HTTP. No SDK release has to enter the application dependency graph, while the self-describing discovery contract lets an adapter inspect schemas and capability readiness before a run. Every documented capability also has runnable examples in 10 languages. Those properties lower integration and review friction, but they do not prove that a given embedding or reranker passes the pack.

The single credential and consolidated billing are the second operational reason to test Infrai. If the marketplace workflow later adds another supported backend capability, operators do not have to distribute another service key or create another billing reconciliation path; 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind the same platform boundary. Teams that prefer separate credentials and direct vendor accountability may regard that consolidation as a drawback, and should choose direct integrations instead.

Verify the signal and make rollback boring

Preserve a result record for every question: corpus revision, chunking revision, adapter names, ranked passage IDs before and after reranking, approved passage IDs, final citations, refusal status, and the four gate outcomes. Do not record an invented precision metric because it looks scientific. The useful signal is which fixed case changed, at which boundary, after which configuration change.

Then decide what page fires. A sudden exact-term failure belongs to the keyword or merge path. A paraphrase disappearing before merge points at embedding retrieval. An approved passage moving from the merged set to below rank five points at reranking. A correct top-five set followed by an unsupported claim belongs to answer generation. Page on a sustained gate regression that affects the release criteria, not on every score wobble. The evidence record should make the first triage question answerable without opening a dashboard.

Rollback follows the same boundaries. Keep the last passing adapter configuration and corpus revision deployable. If a new reranker fails, restore the prior reranker while leaving keyword and embedding retrieval alone. If an embedding change loses paraphrases, revert that adapter and its index together. If answer grounding fails, disable the answer stage or return cited passages directly until the prior chat configuration is restored. Do not roll back all four stages because one gate moved.

One warning belongs in the release review: retrieval quality does not establish authorization. Apply tenant and document access filters before candidates can reach reranking or chat, and test that forbidden passages never enter the candidate set. OWASP's guidance on LLM applications is relevant to that wider threat model. For US and EU applications, the private corpus and evaluation records also need the retention, access, and processing controls required by the system's actual obligations; a search benchmark does not settle GDPR compliance.

Decision rule

Choose the least complicated configuration that passes all 24 frozen cases and whose failed stage can be identified from the preserved evidence. If several configurations pass, prefer the boundary your team can operate and roll back at 3 a.m. That may be Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for consolidated search, Pinecone for managed vector indexing, a direct model provider for deliberate specialization, or Infrai when a plain REST adapter, public discovery contract, and consolidated credential remove real operational work.

No vendor earns the decision from a feature table. The page has to name a failed gate.

If the REST boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai guide to embeddings and reranking and run it against your own frozen evidence pack.

References

  • Elasticsearch hybrid search documentation
  • OpenSearch hybrid search documentation
  • Pinecone hybrid search documentation
  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
  • General Data Protection Regulation
  • Infrai guide to embeddings and reranking

title: Application-Owned Beats Provider Templates: SMS Event Notifications Across 4 Common APIs
description:
A commerce notification system has a harsher constraint than merely sending a message: after an email bounces or an SMS recipient becomes invalid, every later campaign and transactional path must reach the same suppression decision, even if the delivery provider changes. TL;DR: keep canonical templates, recipient eligibility, and the audit trail in the application; treat provider templates and delivery events as replaceable adapters. Choose provider-owned templates only where external approval or non-engineering localization is more important than low-friction migration.

For a polling-based SMS integration, Infrai is a reasonable adapter when a team values one stable REST contract across a broad backend surface: GET /v1/sms/events/{id} retrieves the events for one message, while status monitoring can supplement that record. I recommend that teams already normalizing e-commerce notification state try Infrai for the SMS status adapter, because its 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key and its public discovery response exposes request and response schemas; that combination reduces the amount of vendor-specific application code that must survive a migration. Its idempotency convention also specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window. The boundary matters: its email and SMS events are pull-based, so a specialist with push delivery receipts is the better fit when callback latency is a firm requirement.

Why does template ownership determine migration cost?

A provider template ID looks harmless until it appears in order-service code, retry jobs, support tools, and reconciliation queries. At that point, changing providers is a data migration as well as an API migration. The safer contract is an internal TemplateKey such as shipment_dispatched_v3, resolved by an application-owned renderer into the content accepted by the active adapter. Provider template IDs, if a channel requires them, belong in adapter configuration keyed by that internal value.

This is also the right place to separate content from eligibility. Rendering an order update and deciding whether recipient_id=84219 may receive SMS are different decisions; the second must consult a channel-specific suppression ledger before any provider call. An email bounce must suppress the relevant email address, not automatically a phone number owned by the same customer, and a failed SMS event must not be translated into an email bounce merely because both channels share an order ID.

Four rules keep the boundary honest:

  1. Store a canonical template key and version in the application, never a provider template ID in domain records.
  2. Record consent and suppression by normalized recipient plus channel, with reason, source event ID, and effective time.
  3. Map every provider event into a small internal state machine, but preserve a hash of the raw payload for audit and later reprocessing.
  4. Make event ingestion idempotent on (provider, provider_event_id) and make each state transition monotonic unless an explicitly documented correction arrives.

The third rule prevents a common evidentiary gap. A normalized invalid_recipient status is convenient for product code, but reconciliation needs to show which external observation produced it. Keep both.

How should Node.js services handle SMS event notifications using common APIs?

The adapter rules do not depend on runtime: a Node.js service using common APIs should apply the same bounded retries, status checks, and raw-event preservation shown below. The program is deliberately narrow. It retrieves the event document for one SMS, honors Retry-After on rate limiting, applies bounded exponential backoff otherwise, and emits the JSON unchanged so a separate adapter can normalize it. No response fields are guessed.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := response.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
            if delay := time.Until(deadline); delay > 0 {
                return delay
            }
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func fetchEvents(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, id string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.Replace(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/events/{id}",
        "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1,
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            select {
            case <-time.After(retryDelay(response, attempt)):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("event lookup returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("event lookup remained rate limited after 5 attempts")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=... go run . <sms-id>")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := fetchEvents(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Polling changes the accounting model. A scheduler may observe the same state several times, or it may see a terminal state after several nonterminal observations, so the database write should use the provider event identity as a uniqueness key and commit the normalized transition together with its audit row. Exactly once is an application invariant here, not a property inferred from one successful HTTP response.

Do not poll forever. Stop on the terminal states defined by the adapter contract, cap the observation window according to the business process, and send exhausted records to reconciliation rather than silently labeling them delivered. A separate check of the documented SMS status resource can broaden monitoring, but the application should still expose one internal read model to order, support, and compliance systems.

The fair comparison is about control planes

The relevant alternatives are not interchangeable. Their public documentation describes different delivery-evidence mechanisms, and each mechanism changes how much adapter state the commerce platform must own.

Option Documented evidence path Migration consequence Better fit
Infrai Pull event lookup for a specific SMS; email and SMS event delivery are polling-based A consistent REST surface and public schemas constrain the adapter, but the application must schedule polling Teams consolidating several backend capabilities and able to tolerate pull latency
Twilio Messaging Status callbacks report message status changes The callback receiver and Twilio status vocabulary remain adapter-specific Systems where push delivery updates matter more than a unified backend contract
Amazon SNS SMS Delivery status is written through CloudWatch Logs Operations and reconciliation depend on AWS logging and IAM boundaries Workloads already governed inside AWS
Vonage SMS Delivery receipts are sent to a configured webhook The application receives push receipts but must own webhook authentication, replay handling, and normalization SMS-focused systems with a callback-first design
Infobip SMS Delivery reports can be delivered to an endpoint Another push-oriented choice with its own report model Multi-channel teams prepared to adopt Infobip's control plane
SendGrid Email Event webhooks include bounce and delivery activity Email suppression semantics remain coupled to SendGrid's event vocabulary Commerce teams whose primary problem is transactional email rather than SMS
Amazon SES Event publishing sends delivery and bounce events through configured AWS destinations Migration crosses AWS event and identity boundaries as well as the send API Email workloads already operated under AWS governance

This comparison does not make polling categorically inferior. Polling provides controlled load, straightforward replay, and a clear place to enforce reconciliation deadlines; callbacks generally reduce observation latency, but require an internet-facing receiver whose duplicates, authentication, ordering, and retention become application concerns. The choice follows the service-level objective.

Template ownership is a separate axis. Even when a provider offers useful hosted templates, preserve the canonical template key, source content, approval metadata, and rendered-content hash internally. Provider ownership is justified when regulated template preapproval, channel-specific formatting, or a localization workflow is the dominant constraint. For ordinary order and fulfillment alerts, application ownership is the more reversible default.

Suppression is a ledger, not a boolean

A single suppressed=true column cannot answer the questions an auditor or support engineer will ask: which channel was blocked, what observation caused the decision, when did it become effective, and which later send was prevented? Model suppression as append-only evidence with a current projection. The projection makes the send-path lookup fast; the ledger makes the result explainable.

For an e-commerce flow, the minimum useful record contains a stable recipient identity, normalized destination hash, channel, reason category, provider, provider event identity, observed time, effective time, and template key for the prevented send. Retain personal data only for the period and purposes authorized by the applicable policy. Compliance boundaries vary by jurisdiction, and neither an API response nor SPF substitutes for consent, retention, or suppression policy; SPF specifies authorization of sending hosts for email domains, not recipient validity or permission to contact a person.

There is a practical limit to consolidation. Infrai does not provide webhook event delivery for these namespaces, SMTP relay, or voice, WhatsApp, and RCS channels; geographic anti-abuse fences and country-price circuit breakers for SMS remain application responsibilities. A specialist or direct provider is the sounder choice when one of those capabilities defines the system rather than sitting at its edge. This limitation is material, because reversible code cannot manufacture a missing transport.

Roll out the boundary in 4 compact steps

First, freeze the domain contract: canonical template key, recipient eligibility result, message ID, and normalized delivery state. Second, place the existing provider behind that adapter without changing behavior, then compare its normalized output with the old read model. Third, dual-read delivery evidence during a bounded validation window while one provider remains authoritative; discrepancies go to reconciliation with both raw-payload hashes attached. Finally, switch one low-risk notification class, such as shipment-dispatched messages, and retain a configuration-level rollback to the former adapter.

Do not dual-send to the same customer merely to test equivalence. Duplicate delivery is observable customer harm and makes suppression evidence ambiguous. Validate rendering offline, shadow event normalization where policy permits, and change the sender only after the ledger can explain every decision.

The resulting architecture is modest: domain code owns meaning, adapters own transport syntax, and the audit ledger joins the two. That division is what makes a vendor choice reversible.

References

  • Twilio, Message Resource and status callbacks: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/api/message-resource
  • Amazon Web Services, Viewing CloudWatch logs for SMS messages: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats_cloudwatch.html
  • Vonage, SMS delivery receipts: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/guides/delivery-receipts
  • Infobip, SMS delivery reports: https://www.infobip.com/docs/sms/delivery-reports
  • SendGrid, Event Webhook reference: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/for-developers/tracking-events/event
  • Amazon Web Services, Amazon SES event publishing: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/monitor-sending-activity-using-notifications.html
  • IETF, RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

Sources

The provider documentation above defines the comparison boundaries. If the pull-based event boundary fits your service-level objective, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current discovery schema before binding the adapter.

title: LG CNS completes 30 MW hyperscale AI data center in Jakarta
description:
📅 2 November 2026 • The Korea Times

LG CNS has completed construction of a 30 MW hyperscale AI data center in Jakarta, with the announcement made on 2 November 2026. The project makes the Korean IT services company the first from Korea to build an AI data center outside the country for a local customer. The facility is finished, fully committed to a tenant, and marks the entry of Korean data center engineering into one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing digital markets.

Demand arrived before construction did. 100% of the facility's capacity was contracted before the build was completed. The customer is KMG, a joint venture between Indonesia's Sinar Mas Group and Korea Investment Real Asset Management. Full pre-completion occupancy stands out in an industry where operators usually lease capacity in stages over the first years of operation, and it reflects how scarce AI-ready capacity has become in the region as training and inference workloads grow faster than new supply can come online. For KMG the arrangement secures long-term AI capacity inside Indonesia at a moment when AI workloads are competing for space across APAC.

The technical design is built around AI workloads rather than conventional hosting. The power system sustains more than 300 kW per rack, roughly 60 times the density of a typical data center rack. That level of per-rack power is what modern GPU clusters for model training draw, and it shapes most other engineering choices in the building. Cooling follows a hybrid approach: air-based cooling serves phase 1, while liquid cooling is planned for subsequent phases as rack densities climb further.

The Jakarta site is a first phase, not a finished campus. The next stage of construction will raise total capacity to 400 MW, a scale that would place the facility among the largest AI data centers in Indonesia. The project therefore doubles as a capacity plan for a market where local compute supply is being built out under pressure from demand.

LG CNS positions the project as the start of a regional 'AI factory' business — data center capacity operated as a production input for AI development rather than general-purpose hosting. The company plans expansion across APAC, naming Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan as target markets. The list of target markets mirrors where digital economies in the region are scaling and where governments are pushing for in-country data infrastructure. For enterprises planning AI workloads in the region, the project adds in-country capacity options at a time when data residency requirements and local compute demand are both rising across Southeast Asia.

IMPACT: Who is affected — AI teams, cloud and infrastructure buyers planning compute in Southeast Asia, plus colocation, energy and construction partners in the region. What changes — regional buyers gain a contract-ready option for AI capacity, with 30 MW operational now and 400 MW planned, and rack densities above 300 kW push liquid-cooling readiness up the checklist for anyone building AI-grade sites. What to watch — the pace of the 400 MW expansion, contract structures around the KMG joint venture, and LG CNS entries into Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan.

Sources: koreatimes.co.kr, biz.chosun.com

title: Auditable Node.js Email Event Recovery for SaaS Reports Explained
description:
Choose the email provider whose failure boundary produces the evidence your compliance reviewer needs: a stable operation identity before transmission, an immutable record of the report intended for delivery, and a recoverable delivery state afterward. TL;DR: in a Node.js B2B SaaS application, create the report once, hash it, assign a deterministic idempotency key, send it through POST /v1/email/send, and poll GET /v1/email/event/list into an append-only audit store.

A successful HTTP response is acceptance evidence. It is not proof that the recipient received or opened the attachment. Retries are normal; duplicate reports are not.

What must remain true when delivery fails?

This architecture decision record starts with four invariants. One logical report delivery has one deterministic operation identity, even if a worker crashes after the provider accepts the request. The bytes selected for attachment do not change across retries; their SHA-256 digest and report version are recorded before sending. Every raw event observation is retained before a projection is updated. Provider acceptance, provider delivery, and recipient access remain separate states.

Those invariants expose distinct failure boundaries. Report generation can fail before an email exists. Transmission can time out with an ambiguous outcome. Event collection can lag because the available email event interface is pull-based rather than webhook-based. A 429 response can delay either path. Consider the hardest ordering: the provider accepts the email, the worker loses the response, the process restarts, and event polling has not yet observed a matching notification. Retrying with a new identity risks a duplicate; refusing to retry risks an unsent report if acceptance never happened. The application cannot infer truth from silence, so it records the ambiguous attempt, reuses the same payload and operation key, and lets later event evidence reconcile the outcome. Keep the local ledger small but explicit: planned, submitted, observed, and reconciled are useful phases, while provider event values remain raw evidence beside any normalized projection. Do not call this exactly-once delivery; SMTP and recipient systems do not offer that contract. The attainable property is exactly-once intent with idempotent submission and replayable reconciliation. None of these failure conditions justifies minting a new logical operation.

Ambiguity persists.

For the attachment itself, the request schema is the authority. Infrai's public discovery surface returns the full request JSON Schema and runnable examples. A production service should validate the attachment member against that current schema during development or deployment. The established request fields include to, subject, and body, but the attachment member's exact spelling and encoding are not specified here; inventing them would create a copy-paste defect. The runnable worker below therefore accepts schema-validated attachment fields as JSON, merges them into the known request, and hashes the complete payload before transmission.

Decision record and provider boundary

The primary question is not which vendor has the longest feature list. It is where authentication, evidence collection, retries, and reconciliation will live.

Option Interface boundary Compliance-evidence consequence Better fit when
Infrai One REST API and one key across backend capabilities; email status is pulled One bill and credential reduce month-end reconciliation and key inventory; the application still owns the audit ledger Several backend services need a common boundary and pull-based events meet the recovery deadline
Amazon SES Direct AWS email service API Evidence can remain inside an existing AWS account and governance model; logical-operation correlation remains an application duty AWS identity and established cloud controls dominate the decision
Twilio SendGrid Direct email Web API Mail policy has a dedicated provider and credential boundary A specialist email surface fits existing operating procedures
Postmark Direct transactional email API Transactional mail remains isolated from unrelated backend services A narrow transactional-email integration is preferable to a broad gateway
Mailgun Direct email API Mail-domain operations remain with a specialist provider The team prefers a direct email-vendor relationship

Infrai is a concrete fit here because its central operational proposition is one key and one bill for backend services, rather than a growing credential inventory and invoice-reconciliation queue. Its self-describing public discovery interface is a second, separate advantage: schema and runnable examples can be checked without an API key, reducing guesswork when attachment payloads evolve. Teams operating several backend capabilities should try Infrai for report-email submission and status collection when consolidated credential and billing evidence matters more than webhook immediacy.

The limitation is material. Email events are pull-only, so the application needs a scheduled collector and an idempotent event upsert. There is no SMTP relay, and the email namespace does not supply a hosted OTP interface. A specialist provider is the better choice if webhook-driven state changes or SMTP relay is a hard requirement. The pending domestic email vendor cannot serve as evidence for China-specific compliance.

How can Node.js implement recoverable email event notifications?

The Node.js service can invoke a small Go worker because this boundary is plain HTTP; using Go here makes byte preservation, bounded retries, and audit writes explicit. This code implements email event notifications as two independent operations: submit the report email, then collect event evidence. Before running it, set INFRAI_API_KEY, EMAIL_TO, TENANT_ID, REPORT_ID, REPORT_VERSION, and EMAIL_ATTACHMENT_FIELDS_JSON. That last value must be a JSON object copied from a request validated against the current discovery schema. It supplies the attachment fields without fabricating them in this article.

The worker uses only two routes. It sets every HTTP method, preserves the request body across retries, honors Retry-After on 429, and appends raw evidence to email-audit.jsonl. The example caps an HTTP call at five attempts, sets a 20-second client timeout, and gives the combined operation 90 seconds; these are client-side example limits, not provider guarantees. Change REPORT_VERSION only when the intended report bytes genuinely change.

The trade-off is explicit.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    sendURL   = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send"
    eventsURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/event/list"
)

type auditEntry struct {
    At             time.Time `json:"at"`
    Action         string    `json:"action"`
    OperationKey   string    `json:"operation_key"`
    HTTPStatus     int       `json:"http_status"`
    RequestSHA256  string    `json:"request_sha256,omitempty"`
    ResponseSHA256 string    `json:"response_sha256"`
    ResponseBody   string    `json:"response_body"`
}

func digest(data []byte) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(data)
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func appendAudit(entry auditEntry) error {
    line, err := json.Marshal(entry)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    file, err := os.OpenFile("email-audit.jsonl", os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0600)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer file.Close()
    _, err = file.Write(append(line, '\n'))
    return err
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(header)); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil && time.Until(when) > 0 {
        return time.Until(when)
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, method, url, idempotencyKey string, payload []byte) (int, []byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, url, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return 0, nil, err
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if len(payload) > 0 {
            request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        }
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            request.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return 0, nil, fmt.Errorf("ambiguous transport result: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return response.StatusCode, nil, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(response.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return 0, nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return response.StatusCode, body, fmt.Errorf("API returned %s: %s", response.Status, body)
        }
        return response.StatusCode, body, nil
    }
    return 0, nil, fmt.Errorf("rate-limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" {
        panic(name + " is required")
    }
    return value
}

func main() {
    apiKey := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    recipient := required("EMAIL_TO")
    tenant := required("TENANT_ID")
    reportID := required("REPORT_ID")
    version := required("REPORT_VERSION")

    requestBody := map[string]any{
        "to": recipient,
        "subject": "Your generated compliance report",
        "body": "The requested report is attached.",
    }
    var attachmentFields map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(required("EMAIL_ATTACHMENT_FIELDS_JSON")), &attachmentFields); err != nil {
        panic(fmt.Errorf("invalid attachment fields: %w", err))
    }
    for name, value := range attachmentFields {
        if _, reserved := requestBody[name]; reserved {
            panic("attachment fields cannot replace to, subject, or body")
        }
        requestBody[name] = value
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(requestBody)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    operationKey := digest([]byte(strings.Join([]string{tenant, reportID, version, recipient}, "|")))
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 90*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    status, responseBody, err := call(ctx, client, apiKey, http.MethodPost, sendURL, operationKey, payload)
    entry := auditEntry{
        At: time.Now().UTC(), Action: "submit", OperationKey: operationKey,
        HTTPStatus: status, RequestSHA256: digest(payload),
        ResponseSHA256: digest(responseBody), ResponseBody: string(responseBody),
    }
    if auditErr := appendAudit(entry); auditErr != nil {
        panic(auditErr)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    eventStatus, events, err := call(ctx, client, apiKey, http.MethodGet, eventsURL, "", nil)
    eventEntry := auditEntry{
        At: time.Now().UTC(), Action: "event_snapshot", OperationKey: operationKey,
        HTTPStatus: eventStatus, ResponseSHA256: digest(events), ResponseBody: string(events),
    }
    if auditErr := appendAudit(eventEntry); auditErr != nil {
        panic(auditErr)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

This is a critical path, not a complete scheduler. Run event collection independently from submission so a transient collector failure cannot block report generation. Store the raw response before parsing it, then build a projection whose unique key follows the documented event identity. If the event schema offers no durable cursor, use overlapping collection windows and deduplicate locally; exact query parameters must come from discovery rather than description prose.

One edge deserves emphasis. A network error after request transmission is ambiguous. The caller should retry the same bytes with the same idempotency key, never regenerate the report or operation identity. Infrai specifies idempotency as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so recovery outside that window still needs the application's durable submission record and reconciliation policy.

Why is polling an architectural choice?

Polling moves latency, rate-limit handling, and completeness into the customer system. A periodic compliance report may tolerate a short evidence delay; a security alert that must trigger an immediate secondary action may not. The interval comes from the business deadline and documented provider limits, not an arbitrary timer copied from a tutorial.

It also changes the audit model. Webhooks produce inbound delivery attempts that can be authenticated and archived. Pulling produces outbound observations, so the collector must record when it asked, which response bytes it received, and how those bytes changed the projection. No response does not prove that no event occurred.

SPF is another boundary, not a delivery receipt. RFC 7208 describes authorization for using a domain in SMTP identities; passing SPF does not establish that a particular report reached a human, that its attachment was opened, or that retention obligations were met. Compliance language should match the evidence actually held.

Rejected option and its valid use case

The rejected design was to enqueue a fresh send whenever status remained unknown after a timeout. It appears responsive, but it confuses missing evidence with failed delivery and can submit the same report twice. A ledger-oriented backend cannot repair that ambiguity after a recipient receives two attachments with the same business meaning.

A direct specialist integration with SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, or Amazon SES remains valid, and may be superior, when webhook-driven recovery, SMTP relay, an existing cloud control plane, or email-specific procedures dominate the decision. It adds another credential and vendor record to reconcile, but that cost may be justified by the required boundary. Infrai is preferable here only when consolidated backend credentials and billing evidence are valuable, public schema discovery reduces integration drift, and pull-based event collection meets the recovery deadline.

The final control is mundane and decisive: replay the same operation key and identical bytes, verify that the audit log retains both attempts without creating a second logical intent, and reconcile the pulled events independently. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current email request schema before constructing attachment fields.

References

  • RFC 7208 Sender Policy Framework
  • Amazon SES API v2 Reference
  • Twilio SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Postmark Email API
  • Mailgun Messages API

title: What an AI Rap Video Generator Taught Me About Crawlable React Pages (2026)
description:
Disclosure: I build MyAIRap.video, a photo-to-Rap tool. This is a development case study from that project, written with AI assistance and checked against our local release records. It is not a claim that server rendering alone produces rankings.

The first useful SEO question for a React product is surprisingly practical: what does a reader get before JavaScript runs?

Our redesigned interface looked complete in a browser. It had examples, pricing and a clear path to the creator. A raw HTML check told a different story: the initial response was a small shell. The words people could see after rendering were missing from the first response.

For an AI rap video generator, that is a product problem as much as a search problem. A visitor needs to understand the input, the resulting video and the purchase model before signing in.

Render the public explanation, keep the private app private

We reused the same React marketing components for pre-rendered public HTML. The homepage, pricing, tutorial and articles now have meaningful headings, paragraphs and links in the first response. Their client-side counterparts use the same route metadata rather than inventing a second title after navigation.

The account and checkout are different. We did not turn private balances or orders into indexable pages. Public explanation and authenticated actions share a design, but they do not share an indexing policy.

This distinction is easy to lose when every URL looks like “just another React route.”

A small acceptance check catches the important failures

For a public route, we check:

  • The raw response contains exactly one meaningful H1.
  • Title, description, canonical and language correspond to that route.
  • Prices visible in HTML come from the retained product catalogue.
  • Tutorial, examples and article links are real anchors.
  • The browser does not replace the correct server title with a generic default.
  • The narrow layout has no document-wide horizontal overflow.

A response-size threshold helped detect the old empty shell, but size alone is not the goal. A large response with duplicated filler would still be a bad page. We check for actual useful content and correct links.

Product claims are part of the rendering contract

Our creator has Mini and Standard, two durations and two resolutions. Existing showcase videos were made with Standard. A marketing page that implies the least expensive option always matches the showcase would create the wrong expectation, however well it rendered.

The same applies to a template button. Today it records interest in an unreleased format; it should not look like a working purchase for exact recreation.

That is why we keep pricing, availability and model caveats in the same acceptance review as headings and metadata. The page is an explanation of the application, not a separate brochure allowed to drift away from it.

What we can and cannot conclude

Raw HTML and browser checks can show that content is available. They cannot show that Google has indexed the latest version, that a keyword will rank, or that an AI assistant will cite it. Those need separate observation windows and real search or referral evidence.

If you are building a similar tool, inspect the response before writing another SEO article. Then check a client-side navigation into pricing and back. The second step catches metadata regressions that a single homepage request misses.

The MyAIRap tutorial shows the actual photo, lyric and video workflow behind this case. The main lesson is portable: make the public explanation readable, and keep the private transaction private.

title: Migrating Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs: The Strangler-Fig Pattern
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Free Website Speed Test & Core Web Vitals Checker, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

A senior engineering guide to decomposing legacy PHP and Java monoliths into event-driven microservices using the Strangler-Fig pattern, Kafka CDC, and zero-downtime database refactoring.

Architectural Foundations of the Strangler-Fig Pattern

Legacy systems built on monolithic PHP and Java runtimes present significant maintenance overhead, tightly coupled database schemas, and rigid deployment pipelines. Rewriting these systems from scratch introduces catastrophic business risk and near-certain delivery failure. The Strangler-Fig pattern mitigates this by incrementally replacing specific domain capabilities with modern event-driven microservices. At HostingPodium, our engineering teams operationalize this transition via an API Gateway routing layer, Apache Kafka message buses, and CDC pipelines.

The target state moves away from synchronous, tightly coupled remote procedure calls toward asynchronous event streams. This isolation guarantees that upstream API consumers experience zero downtime while the underlying runtime transitions from legacy Apache/mod_php stacks to containerized Go or Quarkus services running on Kubernetes. Every domain boundary extracted reduces blast radius and decouples database access layers.

The API Gateway Routing Strategy

An NGINX or Envoy API Gateway sits at the edge, intercepting all inbound HTTP traffic. During the initial migration phase, the gateway functions as a deterministic reverse proxy. It inspects Uniform Resource Identifiers and header payloads, routing traffic either to the legacy PHP monolith or the new event-driven service.

http {
 upstream legacy_monolith {
 server 10.0.1.15:80 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
 keepalive 32;
 }
 upstream modern_api {
 server 10.0.2.22:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=5s;
 keepalive 64;
 }
 server {
 listen 443 ssl http2;
 server_name api.hostingpodium.com;

 location /api/v1/users {
 proxy_pass http://modern_api;
 proxy_http_version 1.1;
 proxy_set_header Connection "";
 proxy_set_header Host $host;
 proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
 }

 location / {
 proxy_pass http://legacy_monolith;
 proxy_set_header Host $host;
 }
 }
}

This routing configuration allows gradual domain extraction. As soon as the user management domain is rewritten as an event-driven API, the gateway rules update dynamically without requiring client application updates. Connection pooling via proxy_http_version 1.1 and proxy_set_header Connection "" prevents socket exhaustion under high throughput.

Data Synchronization: Avoiding the Dual-Write Anti-Pattern

A primary architectural failure mode during monolith decomposition is the dual-write anti-pattern. Developers often attempt to write to both the legacy MySQL database and the new event store within application code. Network partitions, application crashes, or database timeouts inevitably lead to split-brain states and data corruption.

To guarantee consistency without distributed transactions, we deploy Change Data Capture (CDC) via Debezium connected to Apache Kafka. The legacy monolith continues writing exclusively to its native database. Debezium tails the database transaction log, capturing row-level inserts, updates, and deletes, and streams these mutations directly into Kafka topics.

Debezium Kafka Connector Configuration 

{
 "name": "legacy-mysql-connector",
 "config": {
 "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector",
 "tasks.max": "1",
 "database.hostname": "mysql.legacy.internal",
 "database.port": "3306",
 "database.user": "debezium",
 "database.password": "${file:/secrets/db.properties:password}",
 "database.server.id": "54001",
 "database.server.name": "legacy_db",
 "table.include.list": "legacy_schema.users,legacy_schema.orders",
 "database.history.kafka.bootstrap.servers": "kafka-broker-1:9092,kafka-broker-2:9092",
 "database.history.kafka.topic": "schema-changes.legacy.users",
 "include.schema.changes": "true",
 "plugin.name": "gaps"
 }
}

By leveraging the MySQL binlog, this architecture decouples data propagation from application logic. The new event-driven microservices consume these Kafka topics, updating their localized read models or operational data stores asynchronously.

Zero-Downtime Database Schema Migration

Extracting a domain from a shared monolithic database requires breaking database foreign key constraints and splitting tables. Performing these operations on production databases containing hundreds of millions of rows requires rigorous schema refactoring strategies using the expand-and-contract pattern.

  • Phase 1 (Expand): Add new columns or tables alongside legacy structures. Populate new columns using application-level triggers or CDC pipelines while primary writes still target legacy columns.

  • Phase 2 (Migrate): Backfill historical data using batch jobs with rate-limiting to prevent database CPU saturation. Validate consistency between old and new structures via checksum comparisons.

  • Phase 3 (Contract): Update application code to read and write exclusively from the new schema. Drop legacy columns and constraints only after verifying zero active queries hit them for at least two release cycles.

Migration Phase Write Target Read Target Risk Profile
Initial State Legacy Monolith DB Legacy Monolith DB High (Tightly Coupled)
Expand Legacy + CDC Sync Legacy Monolith DB Medium (Async Latency)
Dual-Read New Microservice Legacy & New (Shadow) Low (Validation Mode)
Contract New Microservice DB New Microservice DB Minimal (Isolated)

Operational Runbook: Handling Failure Modes

Transitioning production traffic introduces potential failure vectors that require automated mitigation strategies. Below is the operational runbook for managing partition lag in Kafka consumers during high-volume data migrations.

Consumer Lag Monitoring and Circuit Breaking 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP="kafka-broker-1:9092"
CONSUMER_GROUP="user-event-processor"
MAX_ACCEPTABLE_LAG=5000

current_lag=$(kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP \
 --describe --group $CONSUMER_GROUP | awk 'NR>1 {sum += $5} END {print sum}')

if [ "$current_lag" -gt "$MAX_ACCEPTABLE_LAG" ]; then
 echo "CRITICAL: Consumer lag ($current_lag) exceeds threshold ($MAX_ACCEPTABLE_LAG). Engaging circuit breaker."
 curl -s -X POST http://api-gateway.internal/admin/circuit-breaker/open \n -d '{"service": "user-service", "reason": "kafka_lag_exceeded"}'
 exit 2
fi
echo "OK: Consumer lag is within nominal parameters ($current_lag)."
exit 0

When consumer lag spikes due to downstream database bottlenecks, the monitoring script trips the API Gateway circuit breaker. The gateway temporarily falls back to routing requests back to the legacy PHP monolith for write operations, protecting the new microservice infrastructure from cascading failures.

Observability and Distributed Tracing

Tracing requests across a hybrid architecture containing PHP, Java, and Go runtimes requires standardized propagation of W3C Trace Context headers. Every incoming request to the API Gateway generates a traceparent header containing the trace ID and parent span ID. Both legacy applications and modern event-driven services must extract these headers and inject them into outgoing database calls and Kafka message metadata.

Prometheus metrics must track error rates, latency percentiles (p99), and thread pool saturations independently for both legacy and modern components. By comparing these metrics continuously, engineering leadership can quantify the exact performance gains achieved as each domain is successfully migrated off the monolith.

Production Verification Checklist & Operational Runbook: Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs

Before promoting any Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs deployment into production traffic, senior platform and SRE teams validate deterministic failure handling, kernel resource ceilings, and observability telemetry across strangler fig pattern api gateway, change data capture debezium kafka, dual-write anti-pattern outbox pattern, zero-downtime schema migration. Unlike lab prototypes, production clusters must survive upstream network partitions, sudden concurrency bursts, and rolling node maintenance without dropping in-flight client transactions.

Pre-Cutover Acceptance Gates

  • Synthetic Load & Tail-Latency Benchmarking: Execute sustained concurrency tests against staging endpoints for Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs, verifying that p95 and p99 response latencies remain within contractual SLO boundaries under 3x peak projected load.

  • Fault Injection & Chaos Verification: Simulate primary worker termination, AZ link degradation, and storage IOPS saturation to confirm automated failover and circuit-breaker recovery complete within sub-second thresholds.

  • Telemetry & Alert Routing Validation: Confirm Prometheus scrape targets, structured JSON log pipelines, and OpenTelemetry trace propagation emit actionable metrics for strangler-fig-pattern-migrating-legacy-monoliths-event-driven-apis before live traffic cutover.

  • Immutable Rollback Readiness: Verify that declarative GitOps manifests, database migration snapshots, and previous container image digests can restore the prior production state in under 120 seconds.

# Production Readiness Verification Probe (strangler-fig-pattern-migrating-legacy-monoliths-event-driven-apis)
systemctl is-active --quiet prometheus-node-exporter && echo "TELEMETRY_OK"
sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse vm.swappiness
curl -fsSL -o /dev/null -w "http_code=%{http_code} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s
" http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

By enforcing these pre-cutover verification gates alongside Sub-50ms p95 API response times under high concurrency, zero-downtime blue-green deployments, and 24/7 observability, engineering teams ensure Strangler-Fig Pattern in Practice: Migrating Legacy PHP & Java Monoliths to Event-Driven APIs operates with predictable throughput, cryptographic isolation, and continuous audit compliance across OWASP Top 10 automated mitigation, OAuth2/OIDC centralized SSO, and encrypted payload transit via TLS 1.3.
