title: useSyncExternalStore: test snapshot identity and the initial SSR value
description:
An external store can notify its subscribers without changing the screen rendered through useSyncExternalStore. After the same snapshot object was mutated in this experiment, the screen still displayed 0 following the notification.

The Hook needs a subscription notification and a snapshot that represents the change. With SSR, the initial client read must also receive the value used to generate the server HTML.

The notification arrived with the same snapshot reference

This test store includes both replacement and a deliberately incorrect mutation for comparison. The mutate method is not a recommended application pattern.

export function createCounterStore(initial) {
  let snapshot = initial;
  const listeners = new Set();
  return {
    getSnapshot: () => snapshot,
    subscribe(listener) {
      listeners.add(listener);
      return () => listeners.delete(listener);
    },
    replace(count) {
      snapshot = { count };
      for (const listener of listeners) listener();
    },
    mutate(count) {
      snapshot.count = count;
      for (const listener of listeners) listener();
    },
    listenerCount: () => listeners.size,
  };
}

replace creates a new object. mutate changes only count on the existing object. Both call the registered listeners.

The screen reads count from useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getSnapshot).

Operation Count in the store Count on screen Recorded values passed through the display component
Initial 0 0 0
Mutate the same snapshot and notify 1 0 No additional invocation
Replace with a new snapshot and notify 2 2 2 added

Checking only whether a notification was sent misses this difference. The value returned by getSnapshot must represent the change when compared with Object.is. The official reference describes the contract: return the same snapshot while data is unchanged, and a new immutable snapshot when it changes.

The test observed the mutation without an unrelated parent-state update or other rerender. It did not check what the display would show after a rerender triggered elsewhere.

Returning a new object on every read violates the contract too. The documentation describes that pattern as causing an update loop, but this experiment did not execute that loop. It checks a store that reuses a snapshot until the next change.

Include unsubscription in the store contract

subscribe returns a function that removes the listener as well as registering it. The experiment recorded one subscription after mount and 0 after unmount.

The same store-provided subscribe function is reused. This does not measure resubscription caused by creating a new function on every render or performance with many subscribers.

SSR needs a matching initial snapshot as well as a current value

The server generated this HTML with renderToString:

<output id="store-count">0</output>

The client store intentionally starts with a newer current value of 1. The server's initial { count: 0 } is passed through window.__BOOTSTRAP__ and read during hydration.

import React from 'react';
import { hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { createCounterStore, StoreCounter } from './external-store.mjs';
const bootstrap = window.__BOOTSTRAP__;
const store = createCounterStore({ count: 1 });
const record = { serverSnapshots: [], renders: [], errors: [] };
function getServerSnapshot() {
  record.serverSnapshots.push(bootstrap.count);
  return bootstrap;
}
const root = hydrateRoot(document.getElementById('root'),
  <StoreCounter store={store} getServerSnapshot={getServerSnapshot} rendered={value => record.renders.push(value)} />,
  { onRecoverableError(error) { record.errors.push(error.message); } });
window.readHydration = () => ({ ...record, count: document.getElementById('store-count')?.textContent, subscribers: store.listenerCount() });
window.unmountHydration = () => root.unmount();

record and rendered are instrumentation. They record snapshot reads and component invocations, while onRecoverableError captures mismatches. The HTML and bootstrap data contain fixed numbers only; this is not an example of embedding user data.

Initial value passed to the client Sequence of count values read by the component Hydration mismatch
0, matching the server 0 → 1 None
2, differing from the server 2 → 1 Present

With the matching bootstrap, the component first read the server's value and then moved to the client store's current value. Both cases eventually displayed 1, so inspecting only the final display would miss the mismatch. These records capture component invocations, not the number of frames for which 0 was visible.

Omitting getServerSnapshot and rendering the same component through renderToString threw an error requiring the initial snapshot. The SSR documentation requires the same data during server rendering and hydration.

The Hook does not replace the storage implementation

In this example, createCounterStore stores the value. The Hook connects its subscription and snapshot to React. The experiment does not move all application-local state into an external store.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152. Notification behavior used a production build; hydration used a development build. Neither used Strict Mode or React Compiler. Server rendering used Node.js renderToString. Tearing during concurrent rendering and streaming SSR were outside the test scope.

The store and display component, SSR input, and browser results let you inspect notifications, snapshot references, and server initial values separately.

title: State Explorer: A Zoomable Timeline for React
description:
I turned an old Azure visualization idea into an open-source React component. The useful part is the little window at the bottom.

Imagine an API that was healthy all morning, degraded for five minutes, then healthy again. On a chart showing six hours, that five-minute interval is easy to skim past. A table gives you the exact timestamps, but makes it harder to see how that incident fits into the rest of the day.

I wanted both views at once: the whole story and a close look at the interesting bit.

The lower timeline keeps the full history in view. Drag its blue window to move through time, or resize an edge to zoom into the detail chart above.

Try the live demo — move the window, pull its left or right edge, and hover an interval. The demo has service health, build pipelines, and device states, all using the same component.

The zoom window

The bottom overview shows the full time range. The blue window inside it selects the period shown in the larger chart above. Drag the middle to move to another period without changing its duration. Drag either edge to widen or narrow the period. The upper chart updates so you can inspect state changes that were hard to make out at full scale.

It feels a little like sliding a magnifying glass over the timeline. Except the magnifying glass has handles, and thankfully doesn’t roll off your desk.

Hover or focus a state interval to see its state and original start and end times. Reset view takes you back to the starting range. The window also has keyboard controls, so dragging isn’t the only way to navigate.

An idea from 2015

In 2015, I joined an internal Azure project that collected logs, metrics, and errors from resources such as virtual machines. We needed an availability page, and I kept coming back to the same question: how do you show a full day of history and still let someone investigate a brief outage?

I spent a lot of time on that question. I even missed a Thanksgiving trip to California with friends while working through the design. Eventually I built a two-level timeline with jQuery and D3.js: full history below, selected detail above. The project later moved to Angular, and I rebuilt the component for it.

The earlier Availability Explorer. I kept a simplified standalone version and its demo on GitHub.

In 2021, I heard that the component was still being used. That was a lovely surprise. The code had changed, but the interaction had proved useful for years.

State Explorer is a new implementation of that idea, built for more than availability data. Its TypeScript core handles time intervals and projection; its React package renders the SVG timeline and overview navigator. Your app supplies the entities, state intervals, and colors.

Try it

Install the two packages in a React 18 or 19 application:

npm install @state-explorer/core @state-explorer/react

Here is a small example with one five-minute degraded interval:

import { useState } from "react";
import { StateTimeline } from "@state-explorer/react";
import type { Entity, StateInterval, TimeRange } from "@state-explorer/core";

const at = (time: string) => Date.parse(`2026-09-10T${time}:00Z`);
const domain: TimeRange = { start: at("08:00"), end: at("14:00") };
const entities: Entity[] = [{ id: "api", label: "API" }];
const intervals: StateInterval<"healthy" | "degraded">[] = [
  { entityId: "api", start: at("08:00"), end: at("10:20"), state: "healthy" },
  { entityId: "api", start: at("10:20"), end: at("10:25"), state: "degraded" },
  { entityId: "api", start: at("10:25"), end: at("14:00"), state: "healthy" },
];

export function Example() {
  const [viewport, setViewport] = useState<TimeRange>({
    start: at("10:00"), end: at("12:00"),
  });
  return (
    <StateTimeline
      entities={entities}
      intervals={intervals}
      domain={domain}
      viewport={viewport}
      onViewportChange={setViewport}
      label="API state history"
      getStateAppearance={interval => interval.state === "healthy"
        ? { fill: "#167d73", label: "Healthy" }
        : { fill: "#b87916", label: "Degraded" }}
    />
  );
}

The overview covers 08:00–14:00 UTC; the detail chart starts at 10:00–12:00. The five-minute change is at 10:20. The viewport is controlled by your app: moving or resizing the window calls onViewportChange, and the chart follows the range you pass back. You can also constrain or reject a proposed range. See the checked Quick Start for a larger two-entity example.

Scope and limits

State Explorer is useful when several entities move through discrete states over time: healthy/degraded/down, queued/building/deployed, online/offline, and similar histories. It doesn’t fetch data or decide what a gap means. You provide the intervals; it shows them on a shared time axis. There is no aggregation or virtualization yet, and the 0.1.x API is experimental. Large-data performance, physical touch devices, other browser engines, and real screen readers still need broader validation.

I would love to hear where a view like this helps, and where it gets in the way. Play with the demo, explore the source and docs, or open an issue with a real use case.

title: Dissecting the 4-Hop Cloudflare Tunnel Latency Trap & Hybrid Edge Mesh Architecture — Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh)
description:
I am Duong Phuc Khanh (Vietnamese: Dương Phúc Khánh, known across the engineering community as khanhdp or Kido, @khanhduong22, born 1995 in Da Nang, Vietnam — verified entity on Google Knowledge Graph /g/11zyg5zq1c, Wikidata Q141718572, ORCID 0009-0005-7192-2664, and featured in Báo Đà Nẵng for winning First Prize at Startup Runway 2018 and Smart Mobile Ordering Innovation).

In an effort to eliminate cloud compute bills, software engineers frequently attempt to repurpose high-core personal workstations or home servers (12–16 physical CPU threads, NVMe SSDs, residential fiber) as production hosts using Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) to bypass ISP Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) and dynamic WAN IPs.

However, as documented across Kido Engineering Blog and Episode 142 of Kido Chronicles, placing consumer hardware behind a standard Cloudflare Tunnel on the synchronous client request path introduces a severe architectural bottleneck: The 4-Hop Submarine Trombone Latency Trap. In this monograph, Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh) presents the transport math, WSL2 ext4.vhdx failure modes, and the Tier-1 Hybrid Edge Mesh architecture combining a regional Cloud Caddy Gateway with an encrypted Tailscale WireGuard mesh.

1. Executive Summary & Architectural Comparative Matrix

Because non-enterprise edge tiers terminate ingress tunnels at centralized regional Point-of-Presence (PoP) hubs (Singapore or Hong Kong in Southeast Asia) rather than local domestic exchange nodes, every HTTP request between an in-country user and an in-country home server is forced to traverse international submarine fiber cables twice per round-trip. This inflates Network Time To First Byte (TTFB) from ~28ms to 140ms – 220ms (a 5x–7x degradation).

The matrix below summarizes the three architectural tiers evaluated by Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh):

Architectural Tier Routing & Storage Mechanism Architectural Advantages (Pros) Critical Flaws & Failure Modes (Cons) TTFB & Availability SLA Recommendation
Option A: Naive Baseline (Cloudflare Tunnel to Home Server) Outbound QUIC tunnel via cloudflared terminated at regional edge PoPs; Docker on Windows WSL2. Zero router configuration; immune to WAN IP changes; $0 external hosting invoices. 4-Hop Submarine Trombone Loop: TTFB explodes to 140ms–220ms. High risk of ext4.vhdx corruption upon power loss; PPPoE lease resets cause downtime. • TTFB: 140ms – 220ms
• Uptime: 97.0% – 98.5%
• Data Durability: Fragile		 ❌ Premature Cost Optimization (Avoid)
Option B: Residential Router Port Forwarding + Dynamic DNS Direct ingress port 443 on residential router; automated DNS record synchronization upon IP drift. Low domestic latency (~15ms); exploits multi-core workstation CPU for zero extra cost. 1. Periodic PPPoE lease renewals yield 502 Bad Gateway for 30–60s.
2. Blocked behind ISP CGNAT.
3. Zero hardware power or dual-BGP network redundancy.		 • TTFB: 15ms – 30ms
• Uptime: 98.0% – 99.0%
• Operational Risk: High		 ⚠️ Suitable for Ephemeral Staging Only
Option C: Tier-1 Production (Hybrid Edge Mesh: Cloud Gateway + Private Tailscale) • Critical Path Tier: Regional Cloud VPS at Tier-3 Datacenter running Caddy Reverse Proxy on static IPv4 (99.99% SLA).
• Heavy Compute Tier: Residential workstation connected via private Tailscale mesh (100.x.x.x) acting as async CI runner and 3-2-1 cold backup vault.		 • Production workloads remain 100% available at deterministic 28ms TTFB.
• Eliminates idle remote VPS waste.
• Residential workstation offloads CPU-intensive workloads without risking client traffic.
• Zero router port exposure.		 Requires one low-cost regional Cloud VPS instance (~$4.5/mo) acting as entry gateway. • API TTFB: 28ms – 35ms
• Edge Cache HIT: 12ms
• Uptime SLA: 99.99% 		🏆 Tier-1 Production Standard

2. Naive Baseline & The Premature Home Server Illusion

When bootstrapping backends on local hardware, the standard docker-compose.yml pairing cloudflared with an application server and PostgreSQL looks deceptively clean:

# ❌ Naive Baseline: docker-compose.yml running production on a local workstation
version: "3.8"
services:
  cloudflared:
    image: cloudflare/cloudflared:latest
    restart: always
    command: tunnel run --token ${CLOUDFLARE_TUNNEL_TOKEN}
    network_mode: host

  app_server:
    image: enterprise/app:latest
    restart: always
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/production
      - NODE_ENV=production
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

  db_postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - ./pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data # Virtualized onto WSL2 ext4.vhdx
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

While this avoids router NAT configuration and masks the residential IPv4 address, it violates physical transport locality and storage durability invariants.

3. Scale Bottlenecks & The 4-Hop Trombone Latency Breakdown

3.1. The 4-Hop Submarine Trombone Latency Loop

Cloudflare Tunnel establishes long-lived outbound-only QUIC/HTTP2 connections from cloudflared to regional PoPs (principally Singapore — SIN or Hong Kong — HKG for non-enterprise Southeast Asian routes). Every transactional HTTP request suffers a 4-hop submarine penalty:

  1. Hop 1 (Ingress): A client in Hanoi, Da Nang, or Ho Chi Minh City sends an HTTP request $\rightarrow$ Packet crosses the submarine cable to Cloudflare Singapore (~35ms).
  2. Hop 2 (Tunnel Ingress): Cloudflare Singapore encapsulates the request into the QUIC tunnel and routes it back across the submarine cable to the residential cloudflared daemon in Vietnam (~35ms).
  3. Hop 3 (Tunnel Egress): The local application queries PostgreSQL and sends the HTTP response back through the tunnel to Cloudflare Singapore (~35ms).
  4. Hop 4 (Egress Delivery): Cloudflare Singapore forwards the response back across the submarine cable to the client in Vietnam (~35ms).

The physical wire latency alone is deterministic:
$$\text{Latency}{\text{network}} = T{\text{VN}\rightarrow\text{SIN}} + T_{\text{SIN}\rightarrow\text{Home}} + T_{\text{Home}\rightarrow\text{SIN}} + T_{\text{SIN}\rightarrow\text{VN}} \approx 4 \times 35\text{ms} = 140\text{ms}$$

Adding TLS handshakes and application serialization pushes empirical API TTFB to 160ms – 240ms. By contrast, hosting the application server directly inside a Tier-3 Singapore datacenter cuts the path to a single 2-hop round-trip:
$$\text{Latency}{\text{direct}} = T{\text{VN}\rightarrow\text{SIN}} + T_{\text{SIN}\rightarrow\text{VN}} \approx 2 \times 28\text{ms} = 56\text{ms}$$

3.2. Power Instability and WSL2 Virtual Disk (ext4.vhdx) WAL Corruption

On Windows workstations, Docker executes inside a Hyper-V virtual machine (WSL2) backed by a monolithic virtual disk image (ext4.vhdx):

  • Memory Ballooning (vmmem): WSL2 dynamically claims host RAM during container spikes without promptly releasing freed pages back to the host OS.
  • Unrecoverable WAL Truncation: During sudden residential power loss or forced OS reboots, in-flight PostgreSQL fsync calls flushing Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) segments to ext4.vhdx are severed mid-write, corrupting virtual disk metadata and preventing WSL2 partition mounting on reboot.

3.3. Residential PPPoE WAN Lease Renewals

Residential fiber connections renegotiate PPPoE dynamic IPv4 leases every 24–72 hours, dropping WAN connectivity for 30–90 seconds and causing batch request failures during peak morning traffic windows.

4. Tier-1 Production Architecture: The Asian Hybrid Edge Mesh

To achieve deterministic 28ms TTFB and 99.99% uptime while still harnessing 12–16 local workstation CPU threads, Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh) architected the Hybrid Edge Mesh around strict blast-radius isolation:

  1. Critical Path Production Tier (Singapore Datacenter — 99.99% SLA):
    • Runs stateful production workloads: PostgreSQL 19 on native NVMe ext4, Valkey Cache, and Core API handlers.
    • Served via Caddy 2 Reverse Proxy on a static IPv4 address with direct BGP peering (~28ms).
  2. Heavy Compute Worker Tier (Residential Workstation — Private Mesh):
    • Completely decoupled from synchronous user requests.
    • Runs self-hosted GitHub Actions CI runners (3x faster Docker builds across 12 CPU threads), internal staging environments, and 3-2-1 encrypted cold backups.

4.1. Caddy Reverse Proxy & Encrypted Tailscale WireGuard Bridge 

# /etc/caddy/Caddyfile - Cloud VPS Gateway (Singapore) — Duong Phuc Khanh (khanhdp)
{
    email admin@khanhdp.com
    admin off
}

# 1. Production API & Core Services: Directly hosted on Singapore VPS (TTFB ~28ms)
api.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:4000 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
    }
}

# 2. Heavy Staging & Operational Backends: Securely proxied via immutable Tailscale IP
staging.example.com {
    # 100.64.0.10: Tailscale mesh node address (RFC 6598) assigned to the residential workstation
    reverse_proxy 100.64.0.10:3000 {
        header_up Host {host}
        header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
        transport http {
            dial_timeout 3s
            response_header_timeout 30s
        }
    }
}

# 3. Static Assets: Served directly from high-speed NVMe storage with Edge Cache headers
cdn.example.com {
    root * /var/www/static
    file_server
    encode zstd gzip
    header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"
}

4.2. Automated Asynchronous 3-2-1 Cold Backup Over Tailscale Mesh 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup_production_to_home.sh — Duong Phuc Khanh (Dương Phúc Khánh · Kido)
set -euo pipefail

BACKUP_DATE=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S")
REMOTE_HOST="edge-gateway-sgp" # SSH alias resolving over Tailscale private mesh
BACKUP_DIR="/mnt/storage/cold-backups"
ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE="/etc/backup/encryption.key"

mkdir -p "${BACKUP_DIR}"

echo "🔄 [$(date)] Initiating PostgreSQL production backup from Singapore..."
ssh "${REMOTE_HOST}" "docker exec db_postgres pg_dump -U postgres -d enterprise_prod -Fc" \
  | openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pbkdf2 -pass "file:${ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE}" \
  > "${BACKUP_DIR}/prod_${BACKUP_DATE}.dump.enc"

# Retain rolling 30-day snapshot history
find "${BACKUP_DIR}" -type f -name "*.dump.enc" -mtime +30 -delete
echo "✅ [$(date)] Backup completed successfully: prod_${BACKUP_DATE}.dump.enc ($(du -h "${BACKUP_DIR}/prod_${BACKUP_DATE}.dump.enc" | cut -f1))"

5. Empirical Benchmarks & Production Proof (5,000 Concurrent Requests)

title: Advanced JavaScript Module Systems and Bundlers: Webpack, Rollup, and More
description:
JavaScript development has evolved tremendously with the rise of modern frameworks, large codebases, and complex dependencies. At the core of managing this complexity lie module systems and bundlers — crucial tools that help developers organize code, manage dependencies, and optimize delivery for browsers and servers.

This post dives into modern module systems, particularly CommonJS and ES Modules (ESM), and explores popular bundlers like Webpack and Rollup that bring these systems together for efficient application builds.

A Quick Recap: JavaScript Module Systems

Before bundlers, JavaScript had no native module system, leading to global namespace pollution and maintenance nightmares. Over time, these patterns emerged:

  • CommonJS: Introduced primarily for server-side with Node.js, CommonJS loads modules synchronously using require() and exports functionality with module.exports. It's simple but geared towards backend environments due to blocking behavior.
  • ES Modules (ESM): The official JavaScript module system introduced in ES6 with import and export syntax. Modules load asynchronously, support static analysis for optimization, and are natively supported on modern browsers and recent Node.js versions. ESM facilitates features like tree shaking, removing unused code for leaner bundles.
Feature CommonJS ES Modules (ESM)
Loading Synchronous Asynchronous
Syntax require, module.exports import, export
Support in Browsers No (needs bundling) Yes (native support)
Tree Shaking No Yes
Use Cases Server-side (Node.js) Client & Server

Why Do We Need Bundlers?

Modern JavaScript applications consist of hundreds or thousands of modules. Browsers historically didn’t support module semantics natively or loading numerous separate files created performance bottlenecks due to multiple HTTP requests.

Bundlers tackle this challenge by:

  • Combining all modules and dependencies into one or more optimized files
  • Supporting various module formats (CommonJS, ESM, AMD)
  • Performing code transformations (transpiling, minification)
  • Enabling advanced optimizations (code splitting, tree shaking)
  • Managing static assets (images, stylesheets) alongside JS

Popular Bundlers: Webpack and Rollup

Webpack

Webpack is a highly configurable, versatile bundler widely used in modern web development.

Strengths:
  • Supports multiple module formats.
  • Handles complex dependency graphs.
  • Rich plugin ecosystem for features like hot module replacement (HMR).
  • Integrates with loaders for CSS, images, TypeScript, etc.
  • Supports code splitting for lazy loading. Use case: Large applications requiring fine-grained control over the build process, such as React, Angular, or Vue apps.
Rollup

Rollup is designed primarily for bundling JavaScript libraries and is favored for its efficient tree shaking and smaller bundles.

Strengths:
  • Focuses on ES modules with static analysis.
  • Generates highly optimized, minimal bundles.
  • Simpler configuration compared to Webpack.
  • Ideal for library authors and smaller projects. Use case: JavaScript libraries or smaller apps where minimizing output size is critical.

How Bundlers Work: A High-Level View

  • Entry Point: The bundler starts from an entry module specified by the developer.
  • Dependency Graph: It builds a graph by recursively resolving all imported modules.
  • Transforming: The bundler applies loaders and plugins to transform code (e.g., transpiling with Babel).
  • Optimizing: Removes dead code (tree shaking), minifies output, and splits bundles if configured.
  • Output: Generates bundled file(s) for deployment or development.

Choosing Between Webpack and Rollup

Criteria Webpack Rollup
Project Size Large-scale, complex apps Libraries & smaller apps
Configuration Effort More complex, more options Simpler, more straightforward
Tree Shaking Supported but sometimes limited Excellent, ES modules based
Plugin Ecosystem Extensive Growing but smaller
Build Speed Slower on large projects Generally faster
Asset Handling Excellent (CSS, images, etc.) Basic, but extendable

Final Thoughts

Advanced module systems like ES Modules and CommonJS underpin modern JavaScript application structure. Bundlers like Webpack and Rollup bring modular code together, optimize it, and prepare it for production environments with sophisticated features. Selecting the right bundler and understanding module systems is key to efficient, scalable frontend and backend JavaScript development.

Stay tuned for more insights as you continue your journey into the world of web development!

Check out the YouTubePlaylist for great JavaScript content for basic to advanced topics.

title: My First Merged PR in Zalando Logbook: What I Built and What the Review Taught Me
description:
In my last post I wrote about why I started open source. This post is about the first PR that got merged for me in a big project: Zalando Logbook.

What is Logbook?

Logbook is a Java library from Zalando that logs HTTP requests and responses. If you work with REST APIs, you know why this matters. When something breaks in production, the first thing you want to see is what request came in and what response went out.

What I worked on

My PR added two things to Logbook:

  • StatusCodeBasedSink: a sink that makes decisions based on the HTTP status code of the response.
  • LevelBasedHttpLogWriter: a log writer that uses the status code to pick the log level.

The simple idea behind both: a 200 response and a 500 response should not be treated the same. Errors should stand out, and normal traffic should not fill your logs with noise.

It got merged in May 2026. You can see the full PR, the code and the review here: zalando/logbook #2301

How I approached it

I did not start by writing code. I started by talking to the maintainers on the issue, so I knew what they wanted before I built anything. Then I kept the change small and focused, wrote tests, and signed my commits.

Looking back, that order saved me a lot of pain. Writing code first and asking later is how PRs get stuck.

What the review taught me

Maintainers read very carefully. They do not only check if your code works. They ask:

  • Does this fit the style of the project?
  • Will this break anyone who is already using the library?
  • Is the naming clear for someone who has never seen this code?

Answering those questions made my code better than my first version. Reviews are slow sometimes, but they are free teaching from people who know the codebase far better than I do.

The part I did not expect

After my PR was merged, another contributor found a gap in my own work. The ECS sink did not follow the same status code behavior, so he opened an issue and then a PR to fix it.

My first feeling was a little embarrassing. But then I thought about it properly: this is exactly how open source works. Nobody ships perfect code. So instead of rushing to send a competing PR, I reviewed his one and left comments on the threshold behavior and on the docs checklist. You can read that discussion here: zalando/logbook #2379

That was a good lesson for me: reviewing someone else's PR is also a contribution, and it teaches you how others think.

What I would tell someone starting out

  1. Read the issue and talk to the maintainer first.
  2. Keep your PR small. A small diff gets reviewed faster.
  3. Take every review comment seriously, even when it feels strict.
  4. If someone finds a gap in your work later, treat it as part of the process, not as a failure.

What is next

In the next post I will write about my PR in the Adyen Java API Library, which shipped in SDK v42.0.0, and how it felt to see my change in a real release.

Proof of my work

Everything I write about here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • zalando/logbook #2301: StatusCodeBasedSink and LevelBasedHttpLogWriter (merged)
  • adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: merged after review
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and likes to collaborate, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments if you work with Logbook or want to contribute to it, I am happy to share what I learned.

Your Terraform state is not your inventory
description:
A state file knows what went through Terraform. It does not know the VM someone created from the console during an incident, the database a contractor set up in a second project, or the cluster another team deployed from a repo you have never seen. All of it runs in your accounts and all of it is on the invoice.

Control Cloud reads your clouds through the provider API with read-only credentials. If it exists, the API returns it, and it shows up, no matter who created it or how.

One list, read live

On this demo organization: six providers and an on-prem rack, 24 instances, 19 running and 5 stopped. Per provider: totals, cores, memory, storage, and the time of the last read, so you know how fresh the number is. Below it, All Resources: instances, clusters, networks, volumes and databases in a single list you can filter.

Why not just tag everything

Tags are a policy; the inventory is a fact. A policy that requires an owner tag stops the next untagged resource. It does nothing for the ones already there, and it never applies to what was created by hand before the policy existed. You still need to list what exists and compare it with what you think you own. That comparison is the whole job.

No agents, no state to trust

Nothing is installed on your VMs and nothing depends on a state file being complete. The read is the provider API, the same source the console uses, with a credential that can only read.

Free plan: 1 operator, 1 provider, no card. Public clouds and on-prem on one surface, read-only API access.

title: GitHub Open-Sourced Replica. Now Break Your Prototype’s Perfect Data.
description:
GitHub open-sourced Replica on October 28, giving teams an AI prototyping tool guided by their existing components, patterns, and documentation. A familiar design system can make a proposed feature feel credible quickly. The next useful move is to challenge the data behind the screen. A directory that looks effortless with six complete records may tell you very little about choosing from incomplete results on a phone.

Disclosure: This article was generated and fact-checked with AI using the public sources linked here. It was published through an automated workflow and has not been reviewed by Keith.

Replica supports interactive prototypes alongside a Copilot conversation and an optional self-hosted Hub for sharing and feedback. The release is an opportunity to make experiments easier to inspect, not evidence that a generated prototype has validated a product’s real inputs. The fixture set still shapes what a reviewer can discover.

The AfroTech Guide case study provides a concrete setting. The community-built guide combines approved people and event records with curated Houston dining recommendations. Public website features and connected AI capabilities have different release scopes; real-device and AI-host acceptance remain separate checks. It is an independent community resource, without a claim of official event affiliation.

The official AFROTECH speaker profile describes Building AfroTech.guide as an idea-to-launch walkthrough. For that kind of build discussion, showing which inputs shaped an interface can be as instructive as showing the finished screen. The exercise below is a proposed prototype review, not a claim that the guide uses Replica or has the problems described.

Give the reviewer a task the fixtures can challenge

Suppose the prototype asks someone to compare dining options near a planned stop. Begin with an ordinary task: inspect the available context, compare two candidates, and decide whether there is enough information to choose. Avoid defining success as “click the highlighted card.” That mostly tests whether the reviewer follows the route already chosen for them.

Build a small synthetic fixture set around the information the decision requires. Include a venue name long enough to wrap, a record without an image, and a description that does not fit neatly into one sentence. Keep those records fictional and visibly marked as prototype data. Inventing a restaurant’s hours or accessibility details would add misinformation rather than useful variation.

Then leave a decision-relevant field unknown. Ask the reviewer what they think the screen knows. If the layout makes an absent value look like a confirmed “no,” the feedback has exposed a meaning problem that the polished version concealed. A blank cell, a placeholder, and an explicit “not provided” can lead to different interpretations.

Keep the task and fixture version stable while comparing interface revisions. If every AI edit also changes the sample names, completeness, and result order, a calmer second attempt may owe more to easier data than better design. Record what changed so the reviewer can connect an observation to the experiment that produced it.

This does not require simulating the entire production directory. Select a few cases that could change the person’s decision, and preserve enough surrounding information to make the choice plausible. The goal is useful friction, not a page filled with arbitrary edge cases.

An empty list and a failed lookup need different reviews

A prototype often returns results immediately because the records are bundled with the screen. That is fine for exploring layout. It can hide a second question: what does the person believe when records have not arrived?

Provide a controlled way to hold a lookup in progress, return a genuine empty result, and produce an unavailable response. These are proposed prototype states, not reported failures in AfroTech Guide or Replica. The important comparison is whether the reviewer can tell what happened and choose a reasonable next step.

For an empty result, the screen can accurately say that the completed query found no matches within its stated scope. An unavailable lookup has not established that conclusion. If both states show the same cheerful empty card, the person may abandon a useful search because the interface implied there were no options.

Observe the next action before explaining the state. Do they revise a filter, wait, retry, or assume the directory has nothing relevant? Record the visible behavior and the reviewer’s interpretation separately. Their explanation can reveal an unclear message even when they eventually reach the expected button.

When comparing revisions, replay the same state transition and keep the task wording consistent. Note which behaviors are mocked. A clickable retry button in a prototype does not establish that the production service can recover, and a convincing loading sequence is not a measured latency result.

There is a tradeoff in prototype fidelity. Adding real service dependencies can make feedback more representative but slow the experiment and introduce unrelated failures. Controlled fixtures make a narrower question repeatable. State what the prototype is intended to teach, then reserve operational acceptance for the working integration.

For a community guide, useful feedback concerns whether someone can make a sound choice with the information actually available. Replica makes it easier to put an idea in front of a team. Giving that idea imperfect, clearly labeled data helps the team learn something beyond how convincing the demo looks.

title: Context Optimization Is Not Stream Recovery: Integrating context-mode Without Hiding Failures
description:
Your production agent fails at 3:47 AM. The on-call engineer opens the transcript: thirty-two thousand lines of test output, followed by a cheerful "I've analyzed the failures and here's my recommendation." The model never saw the actual error. It hit the context ceiling three tool calls ago and has been operating on stale summaries since.

This is not a conversation-history problem. A five-turn chat consumes maybe 8,000 tokens. A single pytest run with verbose output can return 50,000. One file search across a monorepo can yield 200 results. The agent keeps working, the streaming UI keeps typing, and nothing alerts you that the decisions being made are now based on truncated evidence.

mksglu/context-mode attacks that specific failure mode by sandboxing tool output, enforcing routing through MCP hooks, and persisting session memory outside the immediate inference context. The project reports 98% output reduction across 17 platforms. I have not reproduced those measurements.

As an external integrator, I evaluated one narrower question: Can a tool-output boundary reduce model input without making streamed responses misleading when the transport fails?

That requires keeping context management and stream delivery architecturally separate.

Put the reduction boundary before inference

The architecture splits into two paths.

The agent execution path routes tools through context-mode's supported mechanisms. Large outputs stay outside the model's immediate context; the model receives bounded, semantically selected information. Session memory maintains continuity across turns.

The presentation path takes the resulting conversation, invokes inference, and streams assistant output into React using the Vercel AI SDK.

Do not insert a generic truncator between those paths. Cutting a pytest log at 8,000 characters preserves setup noise while removing the actual failure line. Cutting serialized messages can corrupt tool-call relationships, leaving the model with a reference to a result that no longer exists in context.

Instead, enforce an application-level contract: the conversation submitted for inference must already contain bounded, relevant tool results. Preserve a reference to complete output wherever the execution environment supports later retrieval. Context-mode's configuration and retrieval semantics are deployment-specific; they are not interchangeable with AI SDK transport settings.

This matters because smaller input does not make delivery reliable. A proxy can still buffer output, a browser can disappear, and a user can cancel mid-sentence.

A bounded streaming route

The following Next.js App Router handler is the inference boundary, not a replacement for context-mode's MCP integration.

Install the compatible AI SDK 5 family: ai@5, @ai-sdk/openai@2, and @ai-sdk/react@2 for the client. Commit the lockfile. Set B_LOST_API_KEY and MODEL_ID in the server environment. The model identifier must be supported by your configured endpoint.

B-Lost's OpenAI-compatible relay at https://b-lost.com/v1 is the gateway in this topology. Whether its complete deployment path delivers unbuffered SSE is something to measure, not assume.

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import {
  convertToModelMessages,
  streamText,
  validateUIMessages,
} from "ai";
import { createOpenAI } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

export const runtime = "nodejs";
export const maxDuration = 60;

const MAX_INPUT_BYTES = 120_000;

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const apiKey = process.env.B_LOST_API_KEY;
  const modelId = process.env.MODEL_ID;

  if (!apiKey || !modelId) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Inference configuration is missing." },
      { status: 503 },
    );
  }

  // Also enforce a body-size limit at the ingress proxy.
  const body = await request.text();

  if (new TextEncoder().encode(body).byteLength > MAX_INPUT_BYTES) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Reduce tool output before requesting inference." },
      { status: 413 },
    );
  }

  let messages;
  try {
    const payload = JSON.parse(body);
    messages = await validateUIMessages({
      messages: payload.messages,
    });
  } catch {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Invalid UI message payload." },
      { status: 400 },
    );
  }

  const provider = createOpenAI({
    apiKey,
    baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1",
  });

  try {
    const result = streamText({
      model: provider.chat(modelId),
      messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
      abortSignal: AbortSignal.any([
        request.signal,
        AbortSignal.timeout(55_000),
      ]),
      maxRetries: 0,
      maxOutputTokens: 2048,
    });

    return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse({
      headers: {
        "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
        "X-Accel-Buffering": "no",
      },
      onError: () => "Generation interrupted. Retry explicitly.",
    });
  } catch {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Unable to start generation." },
      { status: 502 },
    );
  }
}

The byte limit is an admission guard, not a token budget. It runs after reading the body, so ingress must enforce its own limit. Neither this guard nor message validation constitutes authentication or tenant authorization.

The 55-second deadline leaves headroom below the route's 60-second deployment allowance. Platforms impose different limits. The abort signal requests cancellation; propagation of browser disconnects through hosting infrastructure still needs testing.

Diagnose the boundary that actually failed

Use useChat from @ai-sdk/react with its default transport pointed at /api/chat. This route emits the AI SDK UI-message stream protocol. A raw OpenAI SSE parser is the wrong consumer.

That distinction explains a common integration failure: the network tab shows incoming bytes, but the UI never updates because the client expects a different event format. Do not manually split arbitrary network chunks on newlines; chunk boundaries need not match SSE frames or UTF-8 character boundaries.

For buffering diagnostics, compare upstream first-byte time, route first-byte time, and the browser's first rendered text. Run curl -N against the deployed route with a valid message payload. If curl receives periodic events but React updates in bursts, investigate rendering pressure. With the AI SDK 5 React hook, experimental_throttle can reduce update frequency; rendering expensive Markdown on every delta can otherwise dominate the main thread.

If both curl and the browser receive one final burst, investigate the relay and hosting path. X-Accel-Buffering: no is advisory, not a universal buffering override.

Keep interruption visible

The deliberate trade-off here is rejecting oversized conversations rather than silently degrading them. The agent must return to its context-management layer and select better evidence.

Disabling automatic retries avoids treating a second generation as continuation of the first. It sacrifices some transient-error recovery for predictable UI semantics.

After cancellation or transport failure, keep partial assistant text visibly incomplete. Do not promote it into persistent session memory as a completed conclusion. Context-mode can reduce what enters inference; the application still owns whether an interrupted answer becomes durable agent history.

The hardest operational dilemma: you can reduce what enters the model, or you can retry failed streams automatically, but doing both without losing signal fidelity requires explicit session-state reconciliation that most frameworks do not provide. When your agent's context budget runs out mid-task, do you surface the failure to the user, retry with reduced context and risk nondeterministic behavior, or persist partial work and rely on the next turn to recover? How are you handling context exhaustion and stream interruption in production agent systems?

title: 三丰云免费云服务器实测：7天手动续期，稳如老狗
description:
上一版提到“零事故”，这个表述确实太绝对了。严格来说，我是每7天登录控制台手动点一次续期，累计三十多次，中间靠手机日历提醒才没断过。修正后的事实更平淡，但更真实：不是平台自动兜底，而是你愿意为它花30秒点一下按钮，它就真的给你稳稳跑着。这种“主动维系”的使用方式，反而让我对稳定性有了更清晰的体感。

从第一次开通到现在，配置一直是1核1G、5M带宽。跑的项目也没变：FastAPI + PostgreSQL后端、Nuxt3 SSR前端、Redis缓存。CPU偶尔冲到75%~80%，内存常驻600MB左右，5M带宽扛日常访问绰绰有余。它不会因为你是免费用户就在高峰期限速或降权——流量统计和nginx日志始终对得上，没有暗扣。

真实使用节奏：7天一续，断断续续

很多人问为什么不能“一次开通管半年”。答案很简单：规则写得很明白，免费资源是有有效期的，到期不续就回收。我设了每周六上午10点的日历提醒，雷打不动。每次点完续期，有效期立刻刷新，IP不变、数据不丢、服务不中断，连SSH会话都不用重连。

这种“可预期的确定性”，比那些号称“随时可能改规则”的平台踏实太多。中间确实有过一次忘记设置提醒，晚了一整天才续上，虽然没被回收，但那种心跳感让我立刻改回了强制提醒。对于个人开发者来说，这点时间成本几乎可以忽略不计，换来的是长期的稳定可用。

配置方面，Docker、Node.js、Python环境照常可用。我之前在另一台机器上用免费虚拟主机托管静态页面，体验也不错；但既然要跑PostgreSQL和Redis，云服务器才是正解。系统日志、磁盘使用率、网络吞吐都在监控面板里实时可见，数据透明，没有隐藏指标。

为什么愿意每7天点一次续期？

  • 成本为零，心理负担也为零：不用绑卡、不用签到、不用发帖，纯手动点击，30秒搞定
  • 续期机制透明可靠：没有隐藏条件，没有“连续登录X天才可续”之类的套路
  • 服务与续期解耦：即使某次晚了几小时续期，也不会立即删机，有缓冲余地
  • 数据始终安全：三十多次续期，数据库、配置文件、Docker卷从未丢失或损坏
  • 运维体验一致：无论第1次还是第30次续期，控制台响应速度、功能完整性完全一样
  • 信任是攒出来的：正是这一次次成功的续期，让我敢把笔记同步、代码托管这类日常任务放上去
  • 比“自动续费”更让人安心：主动操作意味着掌控感，知道服务还在、自己还能用
  • 适合轻量长期项目：不适合高可用生产环境，但作为个人技术栈的实验场+备用基础设施，完美匹配
  • 客服依然在线：期间提过两次工单（一次VNC黑屏、一次防火墙规则疑问），都在两小时内解决
  • 生态没缩水：文档更新及时，社区问答也有回应，FAQ能覆盖大部分常见问题

实测细节：负载与故障自救

说实话，75%~80%的CPU占用并不是平时维持的，而是在特定场景下出现的。比如我写了个定时任务，每天凌晨用cron触发一个数据同步脚本，同时后端在处理批量写入，这时候CPU会短暂冲高。内存方面，PostgreSQL和Redis常驻一起，600MB是个比较稳定的区间；如果偶尔飙升到800MB，通常是因为我在调试接口，开了几个后台进程。

5M带宽在这个场景下绰绰有余。Nuxt3 SSR出来的HTML体积不大，图片都走CDN或本地存储，所以流量曲线很平滑。没有遇到过因为带宽打满导致的服务不可用，这一点比很多同类产品要实在。

有一次遇到个小麻烦：SSH连上去发现某个容器状态异常，日志里全是OOM Killed。排查后发现是Redis配置里maxmemory-policy设错了，导致大Key加载时内存瞬间撑爆。重启容器、修正配置后恢复正常。这次经历让我意识到，免费资源虽好，但监控告警还是得自己搭，不能全靠平台盯着。好在三丰云的控制台给了基础的监控图表，足以发现异常。

适合谁这样用

如果你能接受每7天花30秒点一下续期，并且用途是学生课设、Linux学习、博客/简历托管、API调试、个人网盘、笔记同步、跑点小脚本这类轻量场景——那三丰云的免费云服务器就是目前最稳妥的选择之一。它不承诺“永久”，但兑现了“只要你愿意续，我就一直给”。

想试的自己搜“三丰云”官网，实名后创建实例。新手建议先从虚拟主机上手，再过渡到云服务器，体验更平滑。记住，这是实验场，不是生产环境；心态放平，折腾起来才从容。

title: Java Virtual Threads vs Kotlin Coroutines: Suspension Models and the Shifting Bottleneck
description:
The usage and internals of Java virtual threads and Kotlin coroutines are already widely covered.

Rather than explaining each technology separately, this post compares how their different ways of implementing suspension change how code is written and operated.

It is written for JVM server developers who have adopted or are evaluating virtual threads, and it focuses on where the costs that virtual threads keep out of the code show up at runtime.

In a thread-per-request server, the number of threads is the concurrency limit.

With a pool of 200 threads, the 201st request waits until one of the 200 finishes.

Yet many of those 200 threads are not computing anything. They are simply blocked, waiting for a response from a database or an external API.

An expensive resource stays tied up while doing nothing, and that is not a small problem.

The fix is simple in principle: release the OS thread while waiting.

Doing this by hand, however, changes the structure of the code. The function has to end at the point where it would wait, and the work that follows the result has to move into a separate callback.

Reactive chains exist for the same reason.

Code split up this way may behave correctly, but it is hard to read and modify.

So there is one more requirement: release the thread, but keep the code readable from top to bottom.

Java virtual threads and Kotlin coroutines were both designed to solve this problem, but they are implemented differently.

Both follow the same procedure. They suspend execution and release the thread, and when the wait is over, they continue from the suspension point. What differs is how they keep the suspended state.

A virtual thread saves its stack and later restores it (stackful). A coroutine returns from the function and later calls the same function again (stackless).

For virtual threads, the runtime does this work. For coroutines, the compiler transforms the code to do it.

This difference carries over into the code: virtual threads hide suspension points from the code, while coroutines mark them in the code.

Hidden does not mean gone. Both approaches only lower the cost of waiting; neither increases the total amount of resources.

The resource bottleneck does not disappear. It moves to a less visible place, and with virtual threads, unlike coroutines, that place does not appear in the code.

1. Suspension Mechanics - Saving the Stack vs Calling the Function Again

Virtual Threads - Saving the Stack and Unmounting from the Carrier

Virtual threads, a final feature since Java 21, leave no marker in the code.

In the two snippets below, the business logic is identical. Only the code that creates the executor differs.

// Conventional: one OS thread per request - limited to 200
try (var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200)) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            String data = fetchFromDb(); // the thread blocks here
            process(data);
        });
    }
}

// Virtual threads: same logic, each of the 10,000 tasks runs on its own virtual thread
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            String data = fetchFromDb(); // identical to the code above
            process(data);
        });
    }
}

The diagram below shows what happens while fetchFromDb() waits for a response.

Suspension and resumption of a virtual thread

Virtual thread VT-1 is mounted on a carrier (the OS thread that actually runs virtual threads) (①) and runs user code (②).

When VT-1 requests data from a socket (③) and the data has not arrived yet (④), the runtime registers the socket with the kernel's epoll, saves VT-1's entire stack to the heap, and unmounts VT-1 from the carrier (⑤-⑦).

The released carrier immediately runs another virtual thread, VT-2 (⑧).

When the kernel reports that the socket is readable (⑨), the runtime remounts VT-1 (⑩), restores its stack from the heap, and continues from the line after read() (⑪, ⑫).

Between ⑦ and ⑪, read() never returns. The call stack stays intact; it is only off the OS thread for a while.

The carrier's activation bar runs unbroken from ① to the end, while VT-1's bar stops at ⑦ and resumes at ⑪.

The point of this diagram is that the waiting is now done by a cheap virtual thread instead of an expensive OS thread.

Aspect Carrier (= platform thread) Virtual thread
What it is OS thread Object on the JVM heap
Count Number of CPU cores Hundreds of thousands to millions
Stack Fixed size (about 1 MB) Stored on the heap, only as large as used
Creation/switch cost High Very low

Coroutines - Returning from the Function and Keeping the Continuation

Coroutines make suspension points explicit in the source code.

A function that can suspend must be declared with suspend, and a suspend function can only be called from another suspend function or inside a coroutine builder.

// Markers such as 'suspend' and 'launch' are required
suspend fun handleRequest() {
    val data = fetchFromDb()        // this function must be suspend as well
    process(data)
}

runBlocking {
    repeat(10_000) { launch { handleRequest() } }
}

The diagram below shows how a coroutine suspends and resumes.

Suspension and resumption of a coroutine

When a dispatcher thread calls the function, execution starts at the label 0 block (①②).

At the suspension point, the function saves its local variables and the next label value to a Continuation object on the heap (③), then starts the asynchronous I/O (④).

The function then returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED and actually exits (⑤).

The stack unwinds, and the released dispatcher thread runs other coroutines (⑥).

When the I/O completes, the result is delivered through resumeWith() (⑦), the resumption is dispatched (⑧), and the same function is called again from the top (⑨).

This time it jumps to the saved label 1, restores its local variables, and continues after the suspension point (⑩).

Here, the dispatcher plays the role of the carrier described earlier.

A coroutine also runs on ordinary OS threads managed by a dispatcher and releases the thread when it suspends. Unlike with carriers, however, the developer chooses which thread pool to run on.

Dispatcher Default threads Use
Dispatchers.Default Number of CPU cores (at least 2) CPU-bound work. Used when no dispatcher is specified
Dispatchers.IO 64 or the number of cores, whichever is larger Blocking I/O only. Many threads, since most of them wait
Dispatchers.Main 1 (UI thread) UI frameworks such as Android

The Point of Divergence

Putting ⑦ of the virtual thread next to ⑤ of the coroutine makes the difference clear.

At ⑦, the stack is saved to the heap and set aside for a while. At ⑤, the function actually returns and its stack frames are gone.

Only the Continuation object saved at ③ remains. Resumption (⑨) does not pick up the old execution either: it calls the same function again and jumps (goto) to the saved label.

A Continuation is an object that holds what to do once the current computation finishes.

Normally that information exists only implicitly in the call stack and cannot be accessed. Passed as an argument, it becomes a value, so it can be stored on the heap and picked up later on any thread.

Passing "what to do next" as an argument is called continuation-passing style (CPS), and it is the basis on which coroutines implement suspension without a stack.

2. Suspension Markers - Transparency vs Function Coloring

With virtual threads, the JDK is what actually performs the suspension.

When a blocking primitive such as a socket read detects that it is running on a virtual thread, it registers with the kernel and suspends itself.

This works because the entire stack is saved.

Since the whole call stack at the moment of suspension is saved with it, the library frames in between do not have to do anything, and the suspension is not visible to those frames.

Because the JDK reworked the blocking primitives at the bottom (sockets, locks, sleep, and so on), most blocking libraries built on top of them scale without modification.

In coroutines, suspension has to propagate up the call chain, so every function in the chain must be marked suspend.

A suspend function can only be called from a suspend context, so the code splits into a suspend world and a regular world. This is called function coloring.

Function coloring - markers in the same call chain

This is the practical difference between the two, and it is where the earlier statement holds: virtual threads hide suspension from the code, while coroutines make it explicit.

Neither is superior; it is a difference in design philosophy.

What is hidden, however, does not go away. Removing the markers from the code has a cost, and that cost shows up elsewhere.

3. Hidden Costs

(1) The Shifting Bottleneck

Virtual threads can raise the number of concurrent requests, but the size of the DB connection pool stays the same.

If the HikariCP pool size is 20, only 20 requests use the database at a time, even with a million virtual threads. What determines throughput, the bottleneck, is this 20, not the number of threads.

The remaining requests wait for a connection.

In the thread pool model, the number of requests waiting like this has an upper bound.

If the wait queue is bounded, requests that arrive after it fills up are rejected. Clients get an error response immediately, and the error rate jumps at that moment.

Virtual threads have no upper bound on the number of threads.

No request is rejected; every request is accepted and waits for a connection.

With no errors, the error rate stays at its usual level. Only the response time changes.

Errors appear only once wait times start exceeding the timeout, and by then a large number of requests are already waiting.

The bottleneck has moved.

The shifting bottleneck - where waiting accumulates

The bottleneck moved from acquiring a thread to acquiring a connection. It did not disappear.

What disappeared is not the bottleneck but the rejections that used to show up in the error rate.

A connection pool is a counting semaphore that limits concurrent use to 20.

A request waits until one of the connections in use is returned, and connectionTimeout is the upper bound on that wait. It corresponds to Semaphore.tryAcquire(timeout).

So a timeout does not mean the setting is too small; it is a signal that the load has exceeded what the database can handle.

Increasing the pool size removes the signal, but the extra load goes straight to the database. That is why simply enlarging the pool is usually the wrong response.

Use timeouts as the basis for rejecting requests that cannot be served early (load shedding), and size the pool to what the database can actually handle, not to a rule of thumb such as cores x 2.

Coroutines face the same connection pool limit, and the cap of 20 concurrent connections does not appear in the code either.

However, blocking calls have to be wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.IO), so the places that call the database can be found in the code.

(2) Changes to the ThreadLocal Premises

ThreadLocal is storage that keeps a separate value for each thread. Reading the same variable gives a different value on each thread.

Even if developers never use it directly, server code already relies on ThreadLocal.

Logging MDC, Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder, and transaction synchronization all store per-request values this way.

This approach rests on two premises.

First, one request holds one thread until it ends. Second, a thread is reused across many requests.

With virtual threads, the second premise no longer holds, because a new thread is created for each request and discarded when the request ends.

Two ThreadLocal premises - how threads map to requests

As a result, of the two uses of ThreadLocal, one loses its effect and the other keeps it.

The one that loses its effect is using ThreadLocal as a cache.

It keeps one expensive object per thread and reuses it, so it falls apart when threads are not reused.

With a pool of 200, only 200 objects are created, and they are reused across a million requests, so the hit rate is effectively 100%.

With virtual threads, the same million requests create a million objects, each used once and thrown away. The benefit of the cache is gone, and only the creation cost remains.

Not a single line of code changes, and the increased number of allocations shows up only at runtime.

The use that keeps its effect is ThreadLocal as context.

In this case, however, the cost appears in memory.

The MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) used for logging is a typical example.

Put the request ID in once at the entry point with MDC.put("requestId", id), and every log line written while handling that request includes the ID. The functions in between do not take the request ID as a parameter.

This use needs only the first premise. If one thread handles only that request until it ends, looking up a value by thread is the same as looking it up by request.

Whether the thread is discarded or reused for the next request afterwards does not matter here.

On pooled threads, a missing MDC.clear() lets values from the previous request leak into the next request's logs.

A virtual thread is discarded when its request ends, so nothing is left to clear and no such leak occurs.

Without any code change, MDC becomes more accurate.

In exchange, a map is created for every virtual thread, and with InheritableThreadLocal the parent's values are copied as well, so memory usage grows with the number of threads.

This, too, does not appear in the code; it appears only in the heap.

ScopedValue was introduced as an alternative.

A scoped value is discarded when its scope ends, so nothing is left to clear, and it is shared with child threads without copying, so no extra maps are created. It is a final feature as of JDK 25.

Use Thread pool Virtual thread
Cache (reusing an expensive object per thread) Effective (200 objects reused across a million requests) Ineffective (a new object per request)
Context (per-request values such as MDC) Effective (leaks into the next request if MDC.clear() is missed) Effective (no leaks, memory grows with the thread count)
Premises that hold Premises 1 and 2 Premise 1

A coroutine can resume on a different thread at each suspension point. The first premise, which still holds with virtual threads, does not hold here.

Values stored in a ThreadLocal do not survive a suspension.

Per-request values therefore go into the CoroutineContext, and using MDC requires explicitly adding an element such as MDCContext.

With virtual threads, things work without code changes and the costs appear only at runtime. With coroutines, the code has to change; otherwise the request ID disappears from logs written after a suspension.

(3) Blocking Without Suspension

In both approaches, suspension does not happen if the layer underneath does not support it.

With virtual threads, suspension does not happen when calling native code through JNI, or when blocking inside a synchronized block on older Java versions (before JDK 24). At that moment the virtual thread cannot release its carrier thread (pinning).

For that interval, it effectively behaves like the old thread pool model.

There are only as many carriers as cores, so even one unreleased carrier reduces total capacity by that much. The scheduler does not automatically add a thread to replace a carrier that is not released.

Pinning - one carrier held

With coroutines, suspension does not happen when a coroutine makes a blocking call (plain JDBC, Thread.sleep(), and so on). The compiler transforms only suspend functions, so the real thread underneath simply blocks.

To actually release the thread, the entire I/O stack must be suspend-based. If a blocking call is unavoidable, move it into withContext(Dispatchers.IO) so that it runs on threads reserved for blocking.

The two problems surface in different places.

With coroutines, the blocking call stays visible in the code, so it can be caught while writing or reviewing.

With virtual threads, code that pins still compiles and passes functional tests. The cause gets traced only after throughput falls short of expectations under load.

Pinning caused by synchronized was resolved in JDK 24, so upgrading removes that cause.

Pinning caused by JNI remains regardless of version, so it has to be checked at runtime.

A few other cases besides JNI still cause pinning, so they are worth checking as well.

4. Measurement and Choice

Side-by-Side Comparison

Virtual Thread Kotlin Coroutine
Category Stackful (handled by the runtime) Stackless (transformed by the compiler)
Suspension marker None (transparent) suspend (explicit)
Function coloring No Yes
Where it can suspend Anywhere in the call stack Only at marked points
Saved on suspension The entire stack A Continuation object
How it resumes Restores the stack and continues Calls the function again and jumps to the label
Existing blocking code Scales as is, without changes Must be rewritten on a suspend basis
Cancellation Thread.interrupt() CancellationException (first-class)
Scope Thread abstraction Extends to Flow / Channel / Multiplatform
Introduced Java 21 (2023) Stable since Kotlin 1.3 (2018)

It is not strictly either/or. A coroutine dispatcher can also run on virtual threads.

val dispatcher = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()

Monitoring Targets

Check two JFR (Java Flight Recorder) events.

jdk.VirtualThreadPinned records remaining pinning. jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed records cases where a request to start or resume a virtual thread could not be submitted to the scheduler (for example, due to resource exhaustion).

Version Choice

Version Released Relevant changes
Java 21 (LTS) 2023-09 Virtual threads final. synchronized pinning remains
Java 24 2025-03 JEP 491 - synchronized pinning resolved
Java 25 (LTS) 2025-09 Current LTS. Structured concurrency API reworked (preview)
Java 26 2026-03 JEP 525 - structured concurrency, sixth preview (minor API changes)
Java 27 2026-09 Latest release. Structured concurrency, seventh preview

If you plan to use virtual threads seriously, JDK 25 LTS is a better choice than JDK 21 LTS, because it is the first LTS release with the synchronized pinning issue resolved.

Structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope) is still in preview as of JDK 27, so it is too early to use it in production code.

Selection Criteria

If the goal on the JVM is purely I/O concurrency, virtual threads are now often enough. Being able to keep existing blocking code as is is a major advantage.

On the other hand, if you need expressive asynchronous streams such as Flow, Channel-based designs, fine-grained cancellation, or Kotlin Multiplatform, coroutines are still the better fit.

There is no reason to migrate code already written with coroutines to virtual threads.

Whichever you choose, the conclusion of this post applies equally.

Both approaches only lower the cost of waiting; neither increases the total amount of resources.

Virtual threads hide that fact from the code, and coroutines expose it.

So when evaluating adoption, first measure the resources that requests wait on: connection pools, external API quotas, and disks.

References

  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
  • JEP 505: Structured Concurrency (Fifth Preview)
  • Virtual Threads After JDK 24: What Changed for Production Java (InfoQ)
  • Virtual Threads After JEP 491: The Bottleneck Moved
  • Java 24 - Thread pinning revisited
  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads
  • Virtual Threads - Oracle Java 21 Core Libraries Guide
  • JEP 506: Scoped Values
  • Scoped Values: A Better Alternative to ThreadLocal for Virtual Threads
  • ThreadLocal vs. Scoped Values: The Virtual Thread Migration No One Warned You About

This post is an English version of my original post in Korean.

title: Implementing 2026 Seller Compliance Practices for Retrying Failed Email API Calls
description:
TL;DR: Retry a failed email API call only when the response is plausibly transient, use capped exponential backoff with jitter, and write an immutable attempt record before each sleep. For a B2B marketplace order, the useful artifact is not merely sent=true; it is a chain showing which order was notified, which policy decision was made, what the transport returned, and when the next attempt became eligible.

The decision rule is deliberately boring: classify first, schedule second, send third, and record every transition. A 429 or a temporary 5xx can justify a later attempt. A malformed request, an authentication failure, or a permanent recipient rejection should go to review or a dead-letter path instead. Replaying every error at increasing intervals creates duplicate messages, obscures the real failure, and makes compliance evidence harder to defend.

That is the failure boundary.

What evidence does a seller notification actually need?

The scenario is a marketplace seller receiving notice of a new order. The notification service owns delivery attempts; the order service owns the order itself. Keep those responsibilities separate. The attempt record should contain an order identifier, notification identifier, recipient address or a privacy-preserving reference to it, policy version, attempt number, decision, response class, and UTC timestamps. Store the provider response body only under a retention rule reviewed for personal data.

A useful record distinguishes accepted, retry_scheduled, permanent_failure, and cancelled. It should preserve the idempotency key used for the request. That key does not make an arbitrary remote API idempotent by magic, but it gives a compatible transport a way to suppress an accidental replay and gives an investigator something concrete to correlate.

Record it.

Email has several layers. An HTTP API may accept a submission while later mail processing produces a bounce or delivery event. SPF is an authorization mechanism for hosts sending mail for a domain; it is not proof that a mailbox accepted a message. Record API acceptance as one fact, and downstream delivery or bounce evidence as another.

What are sound practices for retrying failed email API calls?

Start with the response class, not the number of attempts. A 429 Too Many Requests response is a rate signal; honor Retry-After when present and parseable, while still applying an operational maximum. A 5xx response generally indicates a server-side problem, but the remote contract is the authority. Transport timeouts and connection resets are ambiguous: the request may have reached the remote system before the client lost the response, so retry them only with an idempotency strategy and a bounded budget.

Do not retry a 400 caused by invalid payload data, a 401 or 403 caused by credentials or policy, or a confirmed permanent recipient rejection. A retry loop cannot repair bad data. It can multiply traffic and delay the queue behind a message that should have been quarantined.

Bound it.

For attempt n, a common schedule is base * 2^n, capped at a maximum, then randomized with jitter so a fleet does not wake every worker on the same boundary. The base and cap belong in capacity planning: model worst-case retry volume against API quota, queue depth, worker concurrency, and the notification SLO. As concrete policy inputs, a 30-second request deadline and a 15-minute retry horizon can be useful starting values for review, but they are not universal constants; measure queue age and dependency behavior before adopting them.

The queue math is easy to underestimate. Suppose 500 workers each hold one retryable job and the dependency returns 429 for two minutes. If every worker wakes at the same second, the second wave recreates the rate-limit event, and a queue that looked healthy before the incident can become a second source of load. Full jitter turns that synchronized wave into a distribution, while a cap prevents a single seller notification from consuming capacity indefinitely. Capacity planning should include the initial send plus every eligible retry, the number of workers that can become runnable during the same interval, the API quota's refill behavior, and the delay introduced by a database lease. The operational record should show the chosen delay, the cap, and the policy version so an auditor can reproduce the decision without guessing what the worker knew at the time.

Here is the policy boundary in Go. It has no vendor-specific endpoint, so the decision can be tested without network I/O.

package retry

import (
    "math/rand"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Decision struct {
    Retry  bool
    Delay  time.Duration
    Reason string
}

func Next(status int, retryAfter string, attempt int, base, cap time.Duration, r *rand.Rand) Decision {
    if attempt < 0 || base <= 0 || cap < base {
        return Decision{Reason: "invalid retry policy"}
    }
    if status != 429 && status < 500 {
        return Decision{Reason: "non-retryable response"}
    }
    delay := base
    for i := 0; i < attempt && delay < cap; i++ {
        if delay > cap/2 {
            delay = cap
            break
        }
        delay *= 2
    }
    if parsed, ok := parseRetryAfter(retryAfter); ok && parsed < cap {
        delay = parsed
    }
    if r != nil && delay > 0 {
        delay = time.Duration(r.Int63n(int64(delay) + 1))
    }
    return Decision{Retry: true, Delay: delay, Reason: "transient response"}
}

func parseRetryAfter(value string) (time.Duration, bool) {
    seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value))
    if err != nil || seconds < 0 {
        return 0, false
    }
    return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second, true
}

This treats Retry-After as a scheduling input, not permission to wait forever. A production implementation should accept an HTTP-date if its contract requires it, reject values above the policy cap, and record that a malformed header was ignored. The policy is only one part of the design; the evidence model and queue transaction matter just as much.

Where should the attempt record sit in the send path?

Persist the notification job before a worker can claim it. A worker claims one job with a lease, creates an attempt record with a monotonically increasing attempt number, sends with the stable idempotency key, then records the result and next state. The lease timeout must exceed the expected request deadline but remain short enough to recover a crashed worker without creating overlapping sends.

The awkward case is the important one: the remote service accepts the request, then the worker dies before recording the response. On lease expiry, the next worker cannot know whether the message was accepted. That is why the idempotency key, the remote event history when available, and a bounded reconciliation state are more valuable than an aggressive retry count. Marking the job unknown_delivery is honest evidence; pretending it failed is not.

type Attempt struct {
    NotificationID string
    OrderID        string
    Attempt        int
    IdempotencyKey string
    StartedAt      time.Time
    FinishedAt     time.Time
    HTTPStatus     int
    Decision       string
    NextAttemptAt  *time.Time
    PolicyVersion  string
}

Write the attempt and job transition in one database transaction when both live in the same store. Publish a wake-up message after commit, or use an outbox table so a crash cannot leave the database saying retry_scheduled while the queue knows nothing about it. The outbox is easy to inspect, replay, and explain during an audit.

Buy or build the delivery boundary?

The decision is about control and operational load, not a race to the smallest invoice. A managed transport can remove SMTP operations and expose delivery events, while a self-hosted boundary brings deeper routing control at the cost of reputation management, patching, feedback loops, and on-call work.

Boundary Evidence you can usually own Capacity and SLO concern Main trade-off
Managed email API Request IDs, submission status, event callbacks, policy records Quota behavior and callback lag must be measured Less transport toil, more dependency on contract and retention limits
Self-hosted SMTP relay Local queue, logs, configuration, delivery attempts IP reputation, queue growth, and receiving-domain behavior become SLO inputs More control, much larger operations surface
Hybrid boundary Application audit trail plus selected transport events Two failure domains require reconciliation and alerting Stable application evidence with limited transport ownership

Define minimum evidence before selecting an implementation. Ask how long request and event records remain available, whether callbacks are signed, how rate limits are communicated, and how deletion requests affect immutable audit records. A buy decision that cannot answer those questions is an unpriced compliance dependency.

How do you verify and roll back safely?

Unit-test every response class, malformed Retry-After, cap boundary, attempt limit, and clock conversion. Use a fake transport that can return a timeout after accepting the request; the expected result is an explicit unknown-delivery path, not an unbounded replay. Then run a small canary with synthetic seller addresses and a separate mailbox, checking that attempt record, queue state, and downstream event agree.

Watch retry rate by status class, age of the oldest queued notification, queue depth, lease expiry count, duplicate-suppression count, callback lag, and the percentage of jobs ending in unknown delivery. Set an SLO for notification freshness and another for evidence completeness. A system can meet a send-latency target while quietly losing the records needed to prove what happened.

Rollback should disable new retries through a configuration flag while leaving in-flight records readable. Drain or quarantine scheduled jobs according to their policy version; do not rewrite history to make a dashboard look healthy. Keep the previous classifier available until no remaining jobs use its rules.

The practical endpoint is modest: a retry policy that is bounded, observable, and explainable. Exponential backoff protects a struggling dependency, but the audit trail protects the business decision around a marketplace order. Treat both as part of delivery design.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, including status codes and Retry-After: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463
  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes, including 429: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585

title: Do not treat image complete as a successful decode result
description:
HTMLImageElement.complete can be true for a broken image. It can also be true when the element has no source, so it cannot establish that an image loaded successfully.

For an image-processing step, handle the operation you actually need. If the next step requires decoding, await decode() and handle rejection before replacing the preview. Keep the selected job identifier available when your application allows another file to be chosen during that wait.

The following is an illustrative boundary around an existing image element:

async function requireDecodedImage(image) {
  await image.decode();
  return image;
}

Handle rejection in the caller. A rejected promise should leave the previous preview intact when that is the intended interface behavior. Do not label an export ready merely because an earlier complete check returned true.

Keep load or decode status separate from the later canvas drawing and export result. Successful decoding does not establish that every subsequent operation will succeed. Name the failing stage in the interface so a missing image and a failed export are distinguishable.

Reference: MDN complete.
