title: What happens to your training job when GPU capacity runs out?
description:
When GPU capacity runs out before a training job starts, the job fails with a capacity error or waits in a queue; when it runs out mid-run, you lose everything since your last checkpoint. Nodus handles both cases: a job with no matching capacity waits in Queued for up to 24 hours by default, and a reclaimed job resumes from its latest checkpoint on new capacity. How much a reclaim costs you comes down to how often you save.

This post prices one reclaim on a 10-hour, 8 x H100 run, lists the warning each major cloud gives before it takes a machine back, and gives a rule for choosing a checkpoint interval.

What happens if there is no GPU free when you launch?

On a raw cloud account, the launch call fails and retrying is your job. Amazon EC2 returns InsufficientInstanceCapacity when it lacks the On-Demand capacity you asked for, and its advice is to wait a few minutes or ask for fewer instances per request. Google Compute Engine returns ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED and suggests another zone or trying later.

A script that launches one instance type in one zone stops right there. Teams usually end up writing a retry loop over zones and instance types, which is the start of a scheduler.

On Nodus a job asks for hardware, not for a zone, and a run with no matching capacity stays Queued until something fits. It is placed as soon as capacity appears, up to placement.queueTimeout (24 hours by default), and only then fails with CapacityUnavailable. The Jobs guide lists the levers that make it start sooner: accept more GPU types or regions, allow interruptible capacity, or raise the maximum hourly rate.

nodus describe shows every offering that was considered and why each one was rejected, so a queued job is never a mystery. If the run spans several clouds you own, we covered the setup in how to run training jobs across multiple GPU clouds.

What happens when your machine is reclaimed mid-run?

Interruptible capacity can be taken back at any time, and the warning you get is short. These are the published windows for the three largest clouds:

Platform Warning before the machine goes What restarts your run
Amazon EC2 Spot 2 minutes (120 seconds, interruption notice) You
Google Cloud Spot VMs 0 seconds of notice by default (configurable to 120 seconds), then a best-effort shutdown period of up to 30 seconds You
Azure Spot VMs Up to 30 seconds, best effort, through Scheduled Events You
Modal An interrupt signal runs your exit handler within its grace period Modal restarts the Function on the same input
Nodus Urgent checkpoint on the reclaim notice Nodus, from the latest committed checkpoint

Sources linked in the table; Nodus behavior from Attempts and recovery. Checked November 1, 2026.

By default, two of the three largest clouds give you 30 seconds or less to save a run.

Modal states that all of its Functions can be preempted by default, and its nonpreemptible option is not supported for GPU Functions. Modal does restart the input, but your training code still has to save and reload its own state.

How much does one reclaim cost you?

Take a 10-hour fine-tune on 8 x NVIDIA H100. The H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page, so the node costs 8 x $2.60 = $20.80 per hour and a clean run costs 10 x $20.80 = $208.00.

Now the machine is reclaimed at hour 7.5. We ignore restart time here, so the numbers are a floor.

  • With no checkpoints, all 7.5 hours are lost and the run starts again. You pay 17.5 hours, or $364.00, which is 75% more than the clean run.
  • With a checkpoint every hour, the last save was at hour 7, so 0.5 hours are lost. You pay 10.5 hours, or $218.40.

One reclaim without checkpoints costs $156.00 of repeated work; hourly checkpoints cut it to $10.40.

This arithmetic is ours, from the listed rate. The point holds at any price: the cost of a reclaim is the time since your last save multiplied by what the whole node costs per hour.

How often should a training job checkpoint?

Pick the interval from the loss you can accept per reclaim, not from habit. Our rule: worst-case loss per reclaim equals the checkpoint interval times the node's hourly cost. At $20.80 per hour, a 30-minute interval caps it at $10.40, and a 15-minute interval at $5.20.

The reclaim warning only helps if your save fits inside it. If writing model and optimizer state takes three minutes, a 30-second or 2-minute notice cannot save the run, and the periodic checkpoint is your real protection.

The other side of the trade is time spent saving. On Nodus, interval: auto sets the cadence from how often the capacity your job runs on is interrupted and how long a save takes. Per the checkpoints guide, a job gets at least four checkpoints over its expected run time, and checkpointing takes no more than about a tenth of it. Nodus also saves when the capacity gives notice, whatever the interval.

recovery:
  continuity: Checkpointed      # restore the latest checkpoint into each new attempt
  checkpoint:
    paths: [/nodus/state]       # up to 64 absolute paths, all saved in one checkpoint
    interval: auto              # or a fixed interval from 1m to 6h

That block is copied from the checkpoints guide. Your program still writes its own model, optimizer and step files under /nodus/state and loads them on start; Nodus saves and restores the directory, never process memory. We walk through the training-loop side in automatic checkpointing and resume for training.

How does Nodus move a reclaimed run to new capacity?

Nodus recovers make-before-break. On a reclaim notice it asks your run for an urgent checkpoint and, at the same time, prepares a replacement machine. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, so two copies of your run never write over each other.

A machine that simply goes silent is handled the same way. After 20 seconds without heartbeats a replacement is prepared, and after 60 seconds an attempt on shared capacity is declared lost and replaced. Each new attempt gets a higher epoch number, and Nodus accepts checkpoints only from the current one.

From the command line, the request names hardware and a spend cap:

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

nodus get attempts -l nodus.dev/job=<name> then lists every attempt of the run, and nodus describe shows the placement, the latest checkpoint, cost and events.

When does a run still fail?

Recovery is bounded, so a broken job does not loop forever on your money. Per the recovery docs, a run fails with a typed reason when two attempts in a row make no progress (NoProgress), when the same checkpoint fails to restore twice (RestoreFailed), or when it uses up recovery.maxAttempts. That limit is 8 recoveries by default and 3 for distributed jobs.

Failures caused by your own command, such as a non-zero exit or running out of memory, fail fast and are not retried. A preemption after real progress never counts against the NoProgress rule.

When is it better not to rely on failover at all?

Recovery reduces lost work; it does not make a reclaim free. If your run cannot tolerate any restart, for example a short benchmark whose timing must be uninterrupted, run it on capacity that is never reclaimed. On Nodus that is --interruptible never; elsewhere it means on-demand or reserved instances.

Reserved capacity is also the better choice when you need the same large cluster for weeks. A queue that waits for capacity does not help when you need 64 GPUs on a fixed date. On Nodus, Reserved Compute (Beta) holds capacity for an agreed configuration and reservation window.

For everything else, the cheapest setup is interruptible capacity plus checkpoints sized to the loss you can accept. We collected published interruption numbers in how often spot GPUs are interrupted.

FAQ

Will Nodus move my run to another region when capacity runs out?

Only to the regions you allow. Set placement.regions to region classes such as us or eu and the run waits rather than landing elsewhere; capacity with no reported location never satisfies a non-empty list.

Can I make a run fail instead of recovering?

Yes. Set recovery.onInterruption: Fail and the first interruption ends the run with Preempted or NodeLost. That suits work you would rather rerun by hand.

Do multi-node training jobs recover the same way?

They recover from a collective checkpoint. A stateful multi-node Nodus job uses recovery.checkpoint.format: Dcp, every rank saves at the same step, and a new gang restores the committed checkpoint. Distributed jobs get 3 recoveries by default instead of 8.

What if the old machine comes back after a replacement was prepared?

The replacement is released and your run continues where it was. Per the recovery docs, you are not charged for the replacement in that case.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: st-core.fscss Charts: Dynamic Updates in Modern Frameworks
description:
st-core.fscss draws area, line, and spider/radar charts with pure CSS — clip-path: polygon() and custom properties, no SVG path builders, no canvas, no chart runtime on the critical path.

That design has a practical consequence for apps: updating a chart is rewriting CSS variables. Reactive frameworks already do that well. You do not need a JS chart instance, a virtual DOM subtree for every point, or a third-party wrapper’s internal state.

This article covers:

  • How data maps to CSS variables
  • Smooth transitions when values stream in
  • Patterns for Svelte, React, Vue, and plain JS

Requires FSCSS ≥ 1.2.3 and st-core@v2.

Source: github.com/fscss-ttr/st-core.fscss

How dynamic updates work

Linear charts

@st-chart-points(array) writes inverted Y positions on the host:

--st-p1, --st-p2, … --st-pN

Fill, line, and dots only read those variables. Change the variables → the polygon and markers move.

Spider / radar charts

@st-spider-points(array, rmax) writes polar coordinates:

--st-sx1 / --st-sy1 … --st-sxN / --st-syN

Same rule: points write, renderers read. Multi-series means one host per series so variables do not collide.

What you update at runtime

Chart Variables to set
Linear --st-p1 … --st-pN as percentages (top = 0%)
Spider --st-sxN / --st-syN via calc() + sin / cos

Geometry length (number of vertices) is fixed when FSCSS expands the mixins. Streaming updates should keep the same point count as the compiled polygon, or recompile with a new array length.

Smooth transitions

Because the visible shape is clip-path (and dots use top / left), the browser can interpolate on the compositor:

.chart-fill,
.chart-line {
  transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
}

.chart-dot-1,
.chart-dot-2,
.chart-dot-3,
.chart-dot-4,
.chart-dot-5,
.chart-dot-6,
.chart-dot-7,
.chart-dot-8 {
  transition: top 0.3s ease, left 0.3s ease;
}

/* Spider markers */
.spider-dot-1,
.spider-dot-2,
.spider-dot-3,
.spider-dot-4,
.spider-dot-5,
.spider-dot-6 {
  transition: top 0.3s ease, left 0.3s ease;
}

Note: Add transition: clip-path 0.3s ease, top 0.3s ease; (and left where needed) on the selectors that own the geometry. When new data points stream in, motion stays native and typically hits 60fps without a JS animation loop.

Optional:

.chart-fill,
.chart-line {
  transition: clip-path 0.35s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);
}

Helper: write variables from JS

Linear (0–100 scores → CSS %) 

/** @param {number[]} values scores 0–100 */
export function linearVars(values) {
  return values
    .map((v, i) => `--st-p${i + 1}: ${100 - v}%`)
    .join(";");
}

// host.style.cssText = linearVars([40, 55, 30, 70, 60]);
// or: host.setAttribute("style", linearVars(values));

Spider / radar 

/** @param {number[]} values scores 0–100 @param {number} rmax radius % of box */
export function polarVars(values, rmax = 42) {
  const n = values.length;
  return values
    .map((v, i) => {
      const ang = (i * 360) / n;
      const r = (v / 100) * rmax;
      return (
        `--st-sx${i + 1}: calc(50% + (${r} * 1%) * sin(${ang} * 1deg));` +
        `--st-sy${i + 1}: calc(50% - (${r} * 1%) * cos(${ang} * 1deg));`
      );
    })
    .join("");
}

Call these when props/store data change. No chart library, no requestAnimationFrame required for the interpolation itself.

Dynamic updates in modern frameworks

Because st-core operates on standard CSS variables, reactive frameworks can pass dataset values straight into the host’s style (or a style binding) without re-mounting chart components or syncing third-party chart state.

Svelte

Compile FSCSS once (CLI or runtime). In the component, bind variables when data changes:

<script>
  export let data = [40, 55, 30, 70, 60, 45, 80, 50];

  function linearVars(values) {
    return values.map((v, i) => `--st-p${i + 1}: ${100 - v}%`).join(";");
  }

  $: chartStyle = linearVars(data);
</script>

<div class="chart" style={chartStyle}>
  <div class="chart-fill"></div>
  <div class="chart-line"></div>
  {#each data as _, i}
    <div class="chart-dot-{i + 1}"></div>
  {/each}
</div>

<style>
  .chart-fill,
  .chart-line {
    transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
  }
  :global([class^="chart-dot-"]) {
    transition: top 0.3s ease, left 0.3s ease;
  }
</style>

Stream updates:

data = await fetchLiveSeries(); // same length → smooth morph

Spider host:

<div class="spider" style={polarVars(skills, 42)}>
  <div class="spider-grid"></div>
  <div class="spider-spokes"></div>
  <div class="spider-fill"></div>
  <div class="spider-line"></div>
  {#each skills as _, i}
    <div class="spider-dot-{i + 1}"></div>
  {/each}
</div>

React 

import { useMemo } from "react";

function linearVars(values) {
  return values.map((v, i) => `--st-p${i + 1}: ${100 - v}%`).join(";");
}

export function AreaChart({ data }) {
  const style = useMemo(() => linearVars(data), [data]);

  return (
    <div className="chart" style={parseCssText(style)}>
      <div className="chart-fill" />
      <div className="chart-line" />
      {data.map((_, i) => (
        <div key={i} className={`chart-dot-${i + 1}`} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

/** cssText → React style object for custom properties */
function parseCssText(cssText) {
  return Object.fromEntries(
    cssText
      .split(";")
      .filter(Boolean)
      .map((pair) => {
        const [k, v] = pair.split(":");
        return [k.trim(), (v ?? "").trim()];
      })
  );
}

Or set the host with a ref (avoids parsing):

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export function AreaChart({ data }) {
  const ref = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!ref.current) return;
    ref.current.style.cssText = linearVars(data);
  }, [data]);

  return (
    <div className="chart" ref={ref}>
      <div className="chart-fill" />
      <div className="chart-line" />
      {data.map((_, i) => (
        <div key={i} className={`chart-dot-${i + 1}`} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

Keep transition rules in your global or CSS-module sheet imported once with the st-core output.

Vue 3 

<script setup>
import { computed } from "vue";

const props = defineProps({
  data: { type: Array, required: true },
});

function linearVars(values) {
  return values.map((v, i) => `--st-p${i + 1}: ${100 - v}%`).join(";");
}

const chartStyle = computed(() => linearVars(props.data));
</script>

<template>
  <div class="chart" :style="chartStyle">
    <div class="chart-fill" />
    <div class="chart-line" />
    <div
      v-for="(_, i) in data"
      :key="i"
      :class="'chart-dot-' + (i + 1)"
    />
  </div>
</template>

<style scoped>
.chart-fill,
.chart-line {
  transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
}
</style>

Vue accepts a CSS text string on :style for custom properties in modern builds; if your toolchain expects an object, split the same way as the React parseCssText helper.

Plain JS / live metrics 

const host = document.querySelector(".chart");

async function tick() {
  const series = await api.latestWindow(); // length N
  host.style.cssText = linearVars(series);
}

setInterval(tick, 2000);

With the transition CSS above, each tick morphs the area/line without tearing down nodes.

Multi-series

Each series needs its own host (same rule as static st-core):

<div class="series-a" style="/* --st-p* for A */">
  <div class="fill-a"></div>
  <div class="line-a"></div>
</div>
<div class="series-b" style="/* --st-p* for B */">
  <div class="fill-b"></div>
  <div class="line-b"></div>
</div>

elA.style.cssText = linearVars(seriesA);
elB.style.cssText = linearVars(seriesB);

Spider multi-series: one polarVars(...) per host, distinct --st-accent / opacity tokens as needed.

Checklist

  1. Compile st-core mixins for a fixed N (array length).
  2. Render host + fill/line/dots (dots need real DOM nodes).
  3. Add transition: clip-path (and top / left for dots).
  4. On data change, set --st-p* or --st-sx* / --st-sy* only.
  5. Keep N stable while streaming for smooth morphs.

Why this stays lightweight

Typical chart lib st-core + framework
Chart instance + diff CSS variables on a host
Re-render path / SVG Same DOM, new custom properties
Animation tween in JS Optional CSS transition
Heavy dependency FSCSS output + your existing UI framework

Reactive frameworks already schedule updates when props or stores change. st-core simply consumes those updates as style, which is why dynamic dashboards stay small and predictable.

Further reading

  • st-core.fscss — API, linear + spider examples
  • Dual-pass strokes and clip-path bands — same variables drive both fill and line

Smooth transitions note:

transition: clip-path 0.3s ease, top 0.3s ease; (plus left for polar dots) on your chart selectors gives native, high-frame-rate motion whenever new data points stream in — no chart animation API required.

Thanks for reading

title: Bespoke Web Design For Consultancies
description:
Bespoke Web Design For Consultancies

In the realm of digital presence, consultancies often find themselves at a crossroads, torn between the ease of standard off-the-shelf templates and the unique needs of their bespoke services. The consultancy sector, by its very nature, is built upon the foundation of tailored advice and solutions, making the adoption of generic web design templates a mismatch for their brand identity and service offerings.

Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail to capture the essence and uniqueness of consultancy services for several reasons. Firstly, they lack the personal touch and customized approach that consultancies embody. These templates are designed to fit a broad spectrum of businesses, resulting in a lack of differentiation and a failure to convey the specialized expertise that consultancies bring to the table. Secondly, generic templates often come with limitations in terms of flexibility and scalability, which can hinder the growth and evolution of a consultancy's online presence. Lastly, the use of generic templates can lead to a loss of credibility, as potential clients may perceive the consultancy as unoriginal or lacking in depth.

From an engineering standpoint, there are several key takeaways for consultancies looking to establish a strong online presence through bespoke web design:

  1. Customized User Experience (UX): A bespoke web design allows for the creation of a tailored UX that aligns with the consultancy's brand and service offerings. This can include personalized navigation, content presentation, and interactive elements that reflect the consultancy's unique approach and values.
  2. Flexible and Scalable Architecture: A bespoke web design can be engineered with flexibility and scalability in mind, allowing the consultancy's online presence to grow and evolve alongside the business. This includes the use of modular design principles, responsive layouts, and content management systems (CMS) that can be easily updated and expanded.
  3. Integration of Unique Selling Propositions (USPs): Bespoke web design provides the opportunity to prominently feature the consultancy's USPs, showcasing their specialized expertise and differentiators. This can be achieved through custom-designed sections, interactive elements, and storytelling techniques that highlight the consultancy's value proposition and resonate with their target audience.

In conclusion, bespoke web design is not just a luxury for consultancies, but a necessity for establishing a credible, unique, and effective online presence. By moving away from standard off-the-shelf templates and embracing custom design solutions, consultancies can better communicate their value, differentiate themselves from competitors, and attract clients who are seeking specialized advice and services.

title: Inside hex: A Deep Dive into Local Voice Dictation
description:
Hex

Hex is local voice dictation for Mac, Windows and Linux. Hold a key, speak, and it pastes.

The Core Engineering Challenge

Hex addresses the need for local voice dictation solutions across multiple operating systems while ensuring user privacy and responsiveness. By processing speech entirely on the device, it eliminates the latency and privacy concerns associated with cloud-based alternatives.

Architectural Blueprint & System Internals

Hex's architecture is built on Rust, leveraging its performance and safety features. The application operates by holding a shortcut, speaking, and releasing the key, which triggers transcription that is pasted into the active application. Notably, the first run downloads a speech model, and subsequent uses do not require internet access. Experimental features are available in a dedicated Labs section.

Recent Changes and Trending Status

The latest release, tagged @kitlangton/hex@0.3.1, published on 2026-09-26, introduced significant performance improvements. The update optimized the handling of model progress and dictation levels using shared bounded SSE framing. This enhancement prevents failures when processing large transport chunks and improves the responsiveness of event dispatching.

Developer Experience (DX) & Implementation

Installation is straightforward across platforms:

  • Homebrew: brew install --cask anomalyco/tap/hex
  • AUR: yay -S hex-bin
  • Linux Install Script: curl -fsSL https://anoma.ly/hex/install-linux.sh | sh
  • Nix: nix profile install github:anomalyco/hex

Further documentation is available in the docs/ directory, which provides insights into usage and contribution guidelines. However, the project does not accept pull requests, encouraging users to open issues instead.

Technical Trade-offs & Performance Bounds

While Hex offers robust local processing and privacy, there are limitations. For instance, community feedback highlights the challenge of integrating custom speech models, as the current design restricts dictation to verified models. Additionally, users have reported issues with shortcut changes in Gnome that require manual resets, indicating potential friction in usability.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Real-world feedback indicates both appreciation for Hex's capabilities and areas for improvement. For example, users have expressed a desire for support for custom speech models (see Issue #648). Furthermore, concerns about shortcut management on Linux have been raised, showcasing the importance of user-friendly design in cross-platform applications.

The Verdict

Hex provides a compelling option for developers seeking a local voice dictation tool that prioritizes privacy and performance. Its architecture, built on Rust, ensures efficient processing, while community feedback continues to shape its development path.

title: React: errores de email que sí ayudan
description:
Un formulario de email no termina cuando la persona pulsa Enviar. En ese momento empieza una conversación pequeña entre la interfaz y el usuario: ¿qué ocurrió?, ¿qué parte debo corregir?, ¿se perdió lo que ya había escrito?

Un mensaje como “Email inválido” responde muy poco. Puede ser técnicamente correcto, pero no ayuda a recuperarse. En una interfaz accesible, el error debe ser visible, anunciable por un lector de pantalla y suficientemente concreto para que el siguiente intento tenga más posibilidades de funcionar.

Este detalle importa especialmente en formularios de registro, inicio de sesión y verificación. La misma lógica que usamos para un mejor throwaway email en pruebas también sirve para evaluar la experiencia: un dato aislado no vale mucho si no podemos entender qué pasó con él.

El error no debe ser otro obstáculo

Antes de escribir JSX, separo tres preguntas:

  1. ¿Dónde está el problema? El campo debe tener un estado visual claro.
  2. ¿Qué debe hacer la persona? El mensaje necesita una instrucción breve.
  3. ¿Cómo se enterará de que cambió el estado? El contenido debe estar conectado al campo y anunciarse cuando corresponda.

Por ejemplo, “Escribe un email válido, como nombre@ejemplo.com” es más útil que “Formato incorrecto”. Si el sistema también comprueba que el dominio puede recibir mensajes, conviene explicar esa regla por separado. No mezcles un error de sintaxis con un problema de entrega, porque cada uno pide una acción distinta.

También hay que conservar el valor escrito. Borrar el campo después de un error hace que la corrección sea más lenta y puede hacer pensar que la aplicación perdió información. A veces el usuario solo necesita corregir un carácter, no empezar de nuevo.

Qué debe explicar un buen mensaje

Un buen mensaje de error contiene una causa observable y un siguiente paso. No hace falta convertirlo en un párrafo:

  • “Falta la parte después de @” indica qué revisar.
  • “Este email ya está registrado. Prueba iniciar sesión” ofrece una ruta alternativa.
  • “No pudimos enviar el código. Espera unos segundos y vuelve a intentarlo” distingue un fallo temporal.

Evita cambiar el mensaje mientras la persona todavía está escribiendo. Validar cada tecla puede producir una pantalla nerviosa. Una estrategia más amable es validar al salir del campo y volver a validar al enviar. Si el mensaje aparece demasiado pronto, si conviene darle al usuario un poco más de control sobre el ritmo.

En una sesión de pruebas puede aparecer texto como temp gamil com o dummy e mail. Son entradas que ayudan a comprobar que el componente no depende de ejemplos perfectos. El objetivo no es juzgar el texto, sino devolver una orientación consistente.

Un componente React pequeño y relacionable

La relación entre el input y su error puede ser explícita con aria-describedby y aria-invalid:

function EmailField({ value, error, onChange }) {
  const errorId = "email-error";

  return (
    <div className="field">
      <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
      <input
        id="email"
        name="email"
        type="email"
        value={value}
        onChange={onChange}
        aria-invalid={Boolean(error)}
        aria-describedby={error ? errorId : undefined}
        autoComplete="email"
      />
      {error && (
        <p id={errorId} className="fieldError" role="alert">
          {error}
        </p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

aria-invalid comunica el estado del campo. aria-describedby conecta la explicación con el control, de modo que la ayuda no queda flotando fuera del contexto. role="alert" debe reservarse para un cambio que realmente necesita atención inmediata; no lo pondría en una ayuda estática que aparece antes de cualquier acción.

Después de enviar un formulario con varios errores, el foco puede ir al primer campo inválido. Ese movimiento ahorra una búsqueda visual larga, pero hay que hacerlo con cuidado: no robes el foco mientras la persona sigue editando. Este patrón parecen simple, aunque marca una diferencia grande en teclado y móvil.

Para un estado de error global, usa un resumen con enlaces a los campos afectados. Cada enlace debe llevar al control correcto y el texto del enlace debe describir el destino. Los estados de carga y error tiene que seguir una secuencia comprensible: enviando, enviado o necesita corrección.

CSS: visible, estable y fácil de escanear

El color rojo no puede ser el único indicador. Combínalo con un icono, un borde, texto y una estructura que siga funcionando con zoom. La interfaz deberia conservar espacio para el mensaje, porque si el error empuja todo el formulario de forma brusca puede provocar que la persona pierda el lugar donde estaba.

.fieldError {
  margin: 0.4rem 0 0;
  color: #9b1c1c;
  font-size: 0.95rem;
}

.field input[aria-invalid="true"] {
  border: 2px solid #9b1c1c;
  outline: 3px solid transparent;
}

.field input:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #155eef;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

Comprueba el contraste con el fondo, el foco visible y el comportamiento en pantallas estrechas. No escondas el texto con overflow: hidden para conservar la altura del diseño. Un mensaje truncado no ayuda a nadie.

Para ver cómo encajan estos estados con una experiencia completa, vale la pena comparar estados de email accesibles y medibles. Si el formulario depende de un entorno de pruebas, también resulta útil observar un buzón de pruebas observable, no solo verificar que una petición devolvió 200.

Cómo probar la recuperación

No pruebes únicamente que el error aparece. Prueba que desaparece cuando la entrada se corrige y que el texto anterior no contamina el siguiente intento. Una matriz pequeña puede cubrir mucho:

  • enviar vacío;
  • escribir un formato incompleto;
  • pegar espacios antes o después del valor;
  • corregir con teclado sin usar el ratón;
  • repetir el envío mientras el servidor responde;
  • simular un fallo de red y volver a intentar.

En cada caso, revisa el DOM con un lector de pantalla, navega con Tab y observa el foco después del envío. También mide el tiempo hasta que la persona puede corregir el campo; no todos los errores necesita una solución distinta, pero sí una respuesta que no la bloquee.

Checklist final

Antes de publicar un formulario de email, confirma:

  • el campo tiene una etiqueta persistente;
  • el error identifica el campo y explica el siguiente paso;
  • aria-invalid y aria-describedby cambian con el estado real;
  • el color no es la única señal;
  • el foco es visible y se mueve solo cuando tiene sentido;
  • el valor escrito se conserva;
  • la solución funciona con teclado, zoom y una pantalla estrecha.

Un error bien diseñado no intenta esconder que algo salió mal. Reduce la incertidumbre y permite continuar. En React, eso suele requerir pocas líneas de código, pero una decisión clara sobre el estado, el contenido y la recuperación.

title: Built a duplicate file finder in Java, here's how it works
description:
So I've been working on this little project called DupeLens. It's basically a Java CLI that finds duplicate files in your folders and generates an HTML report.

Nothing crazy, just something I thought would be useful.

Why I made it

I wanted a simple way to check which files were duplicated without worrying about accidentally deleting something important.

So I built one myself.

How it works

It's pretty straightforward.

First, it checks file sizes. If two files have different sizes, there's no reason to compare them further.

For files with matching sizes, it uses SHA-256 to check whether their contents are identical.

Once it's done, it shows the duplicates in the terminal. You can also generate an HTML report if you want something easier to look through.

And that's about it. It doesn't delete, move, or modify your files.

Wanna try it?

You'll need Java 17 or newer.

Download the JAR from GitHub and run:

java -jar dupelens.jar ./your-folder --html report.html

Then just open report.html in your browser.

What's next?

Just released v1.0.0, so it's still pretty early.

I'm thinking about adding exclusion patterns and JSON output, but I'm open to other ideas too.

If anyone wants to check out the code or suggest improvements, that'd be cool.

GitHub: https://github.com/illusionoftalha/dupelens

It's open-source and MIT-licensed.

title: I kept losing my Claude Code sessions, so I wrote ccctl
description:
I use Claude Code all day, which means a lot of sessions: one per project, sometimes three, spread over terminal windows, tabs, tmux panes and multiple screens. Two questions kept coming back. Where is that session I had? And didn't I already talk this through with Claude, a few weeks ago, in some other project?

So I started writing small shell helpers. They grew, they got slow on big sessions, and now they are a single Go binary: ccctl, Claude Code control.

Where is that session?

ccctl ps lists every running Claude Code session with its title and state. ccctl focus brings one to the front - the iTerm2 tab, the Terminal.app window or the tmux pane. Tab completion knows the running sessions by title, so I never type a session ID.

Didn't I already have a session on that?

ccctl find searches every conversation in every project. My own history is 1.5 GB from eight months of work, and a search takes about a second. No index yet - that comes next.

Or all of it in one place

ccctl ui shows projects, sessions and the running ones on one screen. Enter resumes a session, or jumps to it while it runs. I really like k9s, so it works the same way, with :views, j/k and Enter.

The one I needed most

Renaming a project directory used to cost me its Claude Code history. ccctl move <dir> <new-path> renames the directory and takes its sessions, memory, settings and prompt history along. --dry-run shows the plan first, and it refuses while Claude Code still runs in there.

The honest part

ccctl is unofficial and not affiliated with Anthropic. It reads the files Claude Code writes under ~/.claude/, and those are not documented. A Claude Code update can change them, and then ccctl needs a fix. I test it with Claude Code 2.1.316 on macOS and Linux. No Windows.

Of course this was written with Claude Code, but I helped a little bit.

Try it 

brew install crux/tap/ccctl
# or
go install github.com/crux/ccctl/cmd/ccctl@latest

Code, docs and releases: github.com/crux/ccctl. MIT licensed. Issues and ideas welcome - I use it every day, so I will see them.

title: Transform Logs with Vector By DataDog
description:
Introduction

Managed platforms make deployment easy, but they decide where your logs can go. If the destination you need is a custom HTTP endpoint, that decision can leave you stuck.

This article shows how to get past it with Vector, an open-source data pipeline maintained by Datadog. The example is DigitalOcean App Platform forwarding its logs to a custom HTTP endpoint, App Platform sends logs the way it would to Datadog, Vector reshapes them, and your endpoint receives them in the format it expects.

The same idea applies well beyond App Platform. Wherever a managed service exports logs in a fixed format or to a fixed set of destinations, Vector can sit in the middle and reshape them:

  • AWS: CloudWatch Logs can stream through Amazon Data Firehose, which delivers to an HTTP endpoint in its own wrapper format. Vector has a Firehose source that unpacks it.
  • Google Cloud: Cloud Logging sinks can export to Pub/Sub, and Vector can read from a subscription.
  • Azure: Azure Monitor can stream logs to Event Hubs, which exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint that Vector can read.
  • Heroku, Render, and Vercel: their log drains and log streams send to an endpoint you choose, and Vector can receive them.

Check each provider's current documentation for the exact format. The rest of this article follows the App Platform example.

The limitation: a fixed list of log destinations

App Platform can forward runtime logs only to a fixed list of providers, and a custom HTTP URL is not one of them. According to DigitalOcean's "How to Forward Logs in App Platform" documentation (last updated 13 Jul 2026), the supported destinations are:

  • DigitalOcean Managed OpenSearch
  • OpenSearch
  • Datadog
  • Better Stack (formerly Logtail)

The same page notes that dedicated egress IP addresses cannot be used for log forwarding, so you cannot allowlist the sender by IP.

The usual workarounds each have a cost. Running OpenSearch just to relay logs means operating a stateful service as a pass-through. Shipping logs from the application itself means handling batching and retries yourself and missing anything outside the logger. There is a better option, and it hinges on one detail: the Datadog and OpenSearch destinations both let you supply your own endpoint URL.

What Vector is

Vector is a single long-running process that moves logs, metrics, and traces from one place to another and reshapes them on the way. You describe a pipeline in YAML using three kinds of component:

  • Source: where data comes in, such as a port Vector listens on.
  • Transform: code that reshapes each event, written in VRL, the Vector Remap Language.
  • Sink: where processed data goes out, such as another HTTP endpoint.

Vector can also buffer events to disk, so a short outage downstream does not mean lost logs.

The idea: Let App Platform believe it is talking to Datadog

Configure a Datadog log destination in App Platform, but point its endpoint at a server you control. App Platform POSTs its logs there, with the api_key value in a DD-API-KEY header, and never checks who is on the other end.

That server runs Vector, which accepts the request and translates it into whatever your real endpoint expects. The api_key becomes a shared secret between App Platform and your relay, so App Platform keeps using a supported destination while the translation lives in one small config file you own.

Architecture overview 

App Platform (Datadog log destination)
   |  HTTPS POST, api_key in the DD-API-KEY header
   v
+-- Your server -------------------------------------------------------+
| Nginx: TLS and shared-secret check (401 if the secret is wrong)      |
|    |  proxy to 127.0.0.1:8282                                        |
|    v                                                                 |
|   +-- Vector (systemd service) ----------------------------------+   |
|   | Source: http_server   accepts the JSON, no schema check      |   |
|   |    v                                                         |   |
|   | Transform: remap      VRL builds a new event                 |   |
|   |    v                                                         |   |
|   | Sink: http            one event per POST, disk buffer        |   |
|   +--------------------------------------------------------------+   |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  POST to your endpoint URL
   v
Custom HTTP endpoint (any URL that accepts JSON)

Nginx authenticates the request, Vector reshapes it, and your endpoint receives an ordinary log POST.

Building the relay, step by step

These steps assume a Linux server with Nginx and a TLS certificate already working for a domain such as logs.example.com. Vector slots in as one extra Nginx route.

1. Generate a secret and install Vector

App Platform cannot be allowlisted by IP, so a shared secret is the only authentication between it and your relay. Generate one, then install Vector:

openssl rand -hex 32
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSfL https://sh.vector.dev | bash
cp ~/.vector/bin/vector /usr/local/bin/vector
mkdir -p /etc/vector

2. Configure Vector

Create /etc/vector/vector.yaml. The transform is where you match your endpoint's schema, so adapt its output fields.

sources:
  app_platform:
    type: http_server
    address: 127.0.0.1:8282
    path: /api/v2/logs
    decoding:
      codec: json

transforms:
  reshape:
    type: remap
    inputs: [app_platform]
    source: |
      level = "info"
      if exists(.status) {
        level = downcase(to_string!(.status))
      }

      . = {
        "level": level,
        "message": .message,
        "service": .service,
        "raw": .
      }

sinks:
  custom_endpoint:
    type: http
    inputs: [reshape]
    uri: https://your-endpoint.example.com/logs
    method: post
    request:
      headers:
        authorization: "Bearer YOUR_ENDPOINT_TOKEN"
        content-type: "application/json"
    encoding:
      codec: json
    framing:
      method: newline_delimited
    batch:
      max_events: 1
      timeout_secs: 1
    buffer:
      type: disk
      max_size: 536870912

Two choices matter here: the plain http_server source rather than datadog_agent, and . = { ... }, which replaces the whole event. The first avoids the extra date field that App Platform sends, which the Datadog-specific source rejects. The second stops the original fields travelling alongside the new ones. The framing and content-type lines make each request a single bare JSON object, which many endpoints expect. Because the file holds a credential, run chmod 600 /etc/vector/vector.yaml.

3. Add the Nginx route

Inside the existing TLS server block, check the secret and proxy to Vector:

location /api/v2/logs {
    if ($http_dd_api_key != "YOUR_SHARED_SECRET") {
        return 401;
    }
    client_max_body_size 10m;
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8282;
}

Reload with nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx.

4. Run Vector under systemd 

cat > /etc/systemd/system/vector.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=Vector
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/vector --config /etc/vector/vector.yaml
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now vector

Pointing App Platform at the relay

Add a log_destinations block to the app component in the spec:

log_destinations:
  - name: custom-endpoint
    datadog:
      endpoint: https://logs.example.com/api/v2/logs
      api_key: YOUR_SHARED_SECRET

Or set the same values in the console: open the app, go to Settings, click Edit under Log Forwarding, choose Datadog, and fill in the destination name, endpoint, and API key. Make sure the right components are selected, then save. No redeploy is needed, and the same screen is where you rotate the secret later.

To test, deploy any app that writes to stdout, since App Platform forwards whatever the process prints, then watch the relay with journalctl -u vector -f. Events should reach your endpoint within seconds, along with health checks and request logs.

Reusing the relay for other apps

A second app can use the same relay without touching the server: add the same destination in its settings. All its logs then reach the same endpoint, which is fine unless you need to tell apps apart.

To keep them separate, give each app its own Nginx location with its own secret and its own Vector instance. Alternatively, keep one instance and have Nginx tag each request with a header that the transform uses to choose the target.

Conclusion

App Platform's log forwarding is limited to four named providers, but its Datadog destination accepts any endpoint you give it. Putting Vector behind that endpoint turns the limitation into a small translation problem: accept the payload, reshape it with a few lines of VRL, and forward it to the system you actually use. The same pattern fits any managed service that offers a configurable Datadog or HTTP destination.

Sources

  • DigitalOcean, How to Forward Logs in App Platform, the source for the supported destinations and the egress IP constraint.
  • Vector documentation, for sources, transforms, sinks, and VRL.

title: I built the same iOS & Android app five times to measure what sharing code really costs
description:
Most "should we go cross-platform?" debates are fought with opinions. I wanted numbers.

So I built the same app five times. Each version is an iOS app and an Android app with the same product, data and screens. The only thing that changes is how code is shared between the two platforms:

Shares UI on iOS / Android
Native baseline nothing SwiftUI / Compose, written twice
Rust + UniFFI logic SwiftUI / Compose
Swift, cross-compiled for Android logic SwiftUI / Compose
React Native logic + screens React Native views
Skip Lite logic + screens SwiftUI / real Jetpack Compose

The app is a UFC betting app (I know). It's built on two real, finished events, so every odd, result and settlement in the test fixtures is a fact rather than an invention. All the code, build scripts and measurement tools are open source: github.com/daniboybye/fightdeck.

The rule I started from: the app stays native

I left out anything that draws its own UI on a canvas. That isn't about taste. A canvas loses the system, not the pixels: accessibility, text selection, the input method editor, gestures, Dynamic Type and Liquid Glass all have to be re-implemented instead of inherited.

The rule was this: the host app stays SwiftUI and Compose, each feature ships as its own SDK, and the cross-platform technology hides behind that SDK. You keep new platform APIs from day one. You can mix technologies in one app, or swap one out. And you pay for what you mount, not for what exists. A hundred desktop features shouldn't ship their runtime into a phone.

The rule has a price, and it's better to know it up front: lost consistency, coordination between SDKs, diamond dependencies, some duplicated logic, and the testing illusion that every SDK passes on its own while the integration still breaks.

What it costs to ship

Release builds, arm64:

iOS .app Android download Fixed runtime (iOS / Android)
Native 1.96 MB 1.47 MB —
Rust 2.83 MB 2.17 MB ~0.55 / ~0.4 MB
Swift 1.97 MB 7.76 MB 0 / ~6.2 MB
React Native 23.32 MB 6.70 MB ~21.2 / ~5.2 MB
Skip Lite 2.07 MB 4.83 MB 0 / ~3.3 MB

The interesting column is the last one. Each further feature costs every approach roughly 0–100 KB. The runtime is what separates them, and you pay for it once. Swift and Skip cost nothing on iOS because the Swift runtime ships with the OS. React Native pays on both platforms.

What it costs to write

Host code vs. baseline Adapters Total hand-written Generated
Native — — 4,492 —
Rust −27% 64 4,878 8,473
Swift −28% 569 4,743 1,152
React Native −25% 733 5,531 282
Skip Lite −46% 216 4,524 2,785

The surprise: no approach writes less code in total than writing everything twice. Sharing moves lines out of the apps and into shared code, adapters and generated code. What you gain is one copy of the logic to change and test, not fewer lines.

What each technology actually felt like

Rust + UniFFI: where I'd start a new headless core in 2026. UniFFI, started by Mozilla, generates both sides of the bridge. Not one line of wrapper is written by hand: 8,473 generated lines leave 64 lines of adapter in the apps. You still design the API boundary, but with far fewer constraints than C++. Option and Vec arrive as Optional and Array. Records are copied on every crossing, so prefer a few coarse calls over many fine ones. The rough edge: the generated Swift isn't yet ready for Swift 6 strict concurrency, so it lives in its own Swift 5 target.

Swift on Android: free on iOS, Android pays. With the official Swift SDK for Android and swift-java's jextract, the Compose app really does run the same Swift, and the bridge is generated. But Android carries its own Swift runtime (+6.2 MB download, the largest install of all). You write a facade by hand. Iteration is slow, and you can't debug Swift from Android Studio. Even so, this is the approach where I needed the fewest iterations to finish, because Swift is what I read and review best. Familiarity is a real cost factor.

React Native: mature, cheap per screen, not invisible. One Hermes runtime serves every feature SDK. The next screen is just more JS in the same bundle, and the host never imports React Native. With the New Architecture, JSI and Codegen give typed calls in place of the old message bridge. The seam still shows, though: these are React Native widgets, not Liquid Glass or Material 3. Yoga's flexbox replaces platform layout, and types and component libraries you already have natively get re-implemented in JS. It also has the most adapter code (733 lines) and the most configuration.

Skip Lite: real Compose, but read the fine print. Skip transpiles Swift and SwiftUI to Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. On Android there's no Swift at all, and you debug ordinary Kotlin in Android Studio. It's the only approach that empties the host apps (−46%). The catch: the generator translates the declaration, not the platform's behaviour. Some failures are loud: an unsupported API breaks the build. Most are silent and only show up on a device: a view that doesn't render, a missing icon, or the keyboard not lifting content, because SwiftUI does that implicitly and there's no call to translate. The Android job changes from "write Compose" to "read Compose".

The takeaways

  1. Keep the app native and make the SDK the variable. It's the only setup where you can change your mind later.
  2. Logic shares well. UI shares less than it promises. Even in a demo with almost no business logic, sharing logic empties the apps by about a quarter, whatever the language, and that share grows with every rule you add.
  3. Choose by fixed cost and by where the seams show, not by how the first feature looks.
  4. Every approach moves the cost; none removes it. C++ pays in wrappers, Rust in generated code, Swift in Android tooling, React Native in runtime and visible seams, Skip in the limits of transpilation.

Two caveats, and they pull in opposite directions.

First, I set up the demo to penalise UI sharing: it targets iOS 26 and Android 17, and new design languages land in SwiftUI and Compose first.

Second, and more important: it's a demo with almost no business logic. The screens are most of the code, so sharing only logic looks modest here: about a quarter of the host code. A real app is different. Pricing, validation, settlement, sync, offline rules and caching pile up in the layer below the UI, and that layer is exactly what Rust and Swift for Android move into one shared copy. The fixed runtime is already paid and each extra feature costs ~0–100 KB. So the more logic the app has, the larger the share of code that Rust or Swift-for-Android share, while the UI stays fully native. In a production app I'd expect these two to share a much bigger part of the codebase than this demo shows.

The full write-up, with methodology and the rough edges per approach, is in FINDINGS.md. Every number can be reproduced with tools/ci-local.sh. If you've shipped one of these in production and your experience differs, I'd love to hear where. And if the repo saved you a week of evaluation, a ⭐ helps others find it.

This is the written version of my talk "Share Code, Keep Your Native iOS & Android UI".

title: Local and Smart Bookkeeping that stays on your Mac
description:
My accounting data lives on my Mac. Not in some cloud.

As a freelancer, I spent a long time looking for a tool that combines invoicing, time tracking, and taxes without a subscription and without storing my financial data on someone else’s servers. I couldn’t find one. So I built it myself.

Midnight is an open-source app for freelancers and self-employed professionals in Germany:

  • Invoices as PDF, XRechnung, or ZUGFeRD
  • Time tracking with projects, budgets, and one-click billing
  • Income, expenses, and receipts tailored to German EÜR accounting
  • Tax forecasts for the current year
  • An MCP server that allows AI agents to work directly with your own data

Everything runs locally in an SQLite database. Built with Rust, Tauri, and React.

jannikmenzel / midnight

Local bookkeeping for freelancers and the self-employed in Germany

Midnight

Local bookkeeping for freelancers and self-employed in Germany.


Features

Area What it covers
Overview Income, expenses, profit and open items for the selected period, unbilled time
Income & expenses Paid invoices as income, expenses with receipts, extracting name, amount and date from PDF receipts, CSV export
Categories Custom expense categories, pre-filled with typical items for the German EÜR (cash-basis profit statement)
Invoices Number sequences, line items, VAT and discounts, small business scheme under § 19 UStG, PDF export via LaTeX, e-invoices (ZUGFeRD/Factur-X EN 16931 and XRechnung 3.0), duplicating, saved products

title: Parley: A Private Messenger Template You Can Brand
description:
Plenty of organizations want their own messenger and can't use WhatsApp for it. A hospital that needs staff chat it controls. A company that wants messaging inside its product, under its brand, with no third party reading along. A community that doesn't want to live on someone else's platform. Building a secure messenger from scratch is a long project: the encryption protocol, multi-device sync, push, calls, media, groups and moderation are each a project of their own.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Parley is that messenger, finished. It's the second of this week's templates, after Skirmish, and like the others it comes as one Java project with the app, the server and the admin console. Pick the messaging template in the Initializr and you have it. The source is under MIT-0: brand it, sell it and keep your changes private.

Chats, groups and channels.
An encrypted conversation.
Voice and video calls.

What you get

Part What's in it
Messaging One-to-one chats, groups of up to 256 with invite links, broadcast channels, replies, forwards, edits and delete for everyone
Media Photos, video and voice notes, encrypted on the device before upload
Calls Voice and video calls over WebRTC, peer to peer
Privacy Disappearing messages, safety numbers, app lock, screen security, and controls for last seen, profile photo, read receipts and typing
Devices Linked devices, including a browser as another device
Bridges Optional Telegram and WhatsApp bridges, clearly marked in every conversation that uses them
Operations An admin console with a dashboard, users, reports and bridges
Reach iOS, Android, desktop and the browser from one project, in five languages including right-to-left Hebrew

The server can't read your users' messages

Parley uses the same design as Signal: X3DH to agree on keys and the Double Ratchet to rotate them with every message. It uses P-256 ECDH, which every platform's native crypto supports, with HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-256-GCM. Each message has its own key, and a key that leaks doesn't expose earlier messages.

The server stores and forwards envelopes: sender, target device, header, and ciphertext. It never sees the payload, so a breach of your server is a breach of ciphertext. Attachments are encrypted on the device with a fresh key before upload. On the phone, the history is sealed with a key held in the platform keystore.

The code that does this is short and readable, because the primitives are part of Codename One. This is the start of a session, from Ratchet.java:

```java {class="cn1-no-try"}
KeyPair ephemeral = KeyGenerator.ec(256);
PrivateKey me = Identity.privateKey();
byte[] dh1 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(me, pub(signedKey));
byte[] dh2 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(identity));
byte[] dh3 = KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(signedKey));
byte[] secret = x3dh(dh1, dh2, dh3,
oneTime == null ? null : KeyAgreement.ecdh(ephemeral.getPrivateKey(), pub(oneTime)));




`KeyAgreement`, `KeyGenerator` and `Hkdf` are new in `com.codename1.security`, added for Parley. They work on every platform, on the backend too, and Thursday's post covers them along with the WebRTC API.

## Calls that never touch your server

Calls use WebRTC with DTLS-SRTP, directly between the two devices. The Parley server rings the other side, relays the offer, answer and ICE candidates over the live WebSocket channel and hands out STUN and TURN credentials. The audio and video never pass through it, so a call costs your server almost nothing and stays private.

## Make it yours

The look starts at the top of `theme.css`:



```css
--brand: #0a7d6b;  /* White on the teal reads at 5:1. */
--brand-contrast: #ffffff;

Change the brand color and every screen follows, with dark mode variants beside it. The name, icon, languages, push and SMS providers, database and hosting work the same way they do in Wayline. A few directions to take it:

  • An internal company messenger: run your own TURN relay for calls (parley.ice.turn) and leave the bridges out, so nothing leaves your infrastructure.
  • Messaging inside your product: a marketplace that lets buyers and sellers talk, a clinic that talks to patients, a coaching app that talks to clients. The chat screens are ordinary Codename One forms, so they fit into another app.
  • A community app: channels for announcements, groups for members and the admin console for moderation.
  • Your own crypto choices: the curve and the cipher are in one class, Ratchet, if your compliance team has opinions.

Privacy settings.
Dark mode.
The admin dashboard.

Moderation without reading messages

An encrypted messenger still needs moderation. The admin console only sees what the server sees: accounts, message counts, conversation types and busy hours. When a user reports a conversation, their phone attaches the messages they chose to report, so content reaches an admin only through the people in that conversation. That keeps the privacy promise while still letting you handle abuse.

Try it

The development profile runs with nothing installed. Start the server, open two simulators, sign in as alice@parley.example and bob@parley.example, and message yourself. The server can also host the browser build, so a laptop browser becomes a linked device. The Parley page has the overview, and the user's guide and implementor's guide cover the rest.

title: What makes up your AWS NAT gateway cost
description:
Your AWS NAT gateway cost is the price of the service that lets servers without a public IP address reach the internet. According to AWS pricing on 28 October 2026, a gateway in us-east-1 costs USD 0.045 an hour, or about USD 33 a month. Every gigabyte it handles adds another USD 0.045, traffic to S3 included. In Frankfurt, used in the examples below, both rates are USD 0.052, and one gateway with its public IPv4 address comes to about USD 42 a month before the first byte goes through it.

In Cost Explorer, filter to EC2-Other, group by Usage type and compare NatGateway-Hours with NatGateway-Bytes. Outside us-east-1 both names start with a Region code, EUC1- in Frankfurt. If the hours cost more, look for gateways to delete; if the bytes do, look for the server sending the most data.

A NAT gateway costs money before the first byte

AWS bills every hour a gateway is provisioned and available, and a partial hour counts as a full one. In Frankfurt that is about USD 38 a month. The gateway's public IPv4 address adds USD 3.65 a month.

For production, AWS recommends a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone whose resources need the internet. Across three zones that is about USD 125 a month before any traffic.

A gigabyte to the internet costs USD 0.142 through the gateway

AWS applies the USD 0.052 processing fee to every gigabyte that passes through the gateway, whatever its source or destination. Traffic to the internet is then charged standard data transfer on top: USD 0.09 per GB in Frankfurt once the 100 GB of free transfer each month is used up. That gigabyte ends up at USD 0.142.

A server in a different Availability Zone from its gateway pays another USD 0.01 per GB for the traffic between them. Traffic within one zone is free, so keep data-heavy servers in their gateway's zone.

The chart for this part is in the original post.

Finding what sends traffic through the gateway

To find which gateway carries the traffic, compare the gateways' CloudWatch metrics BytesOutToDestination and BytesInFromDestination with the Sum statistic.

The server behind it shows up in VPC Flow Logs. According to AWS re:Post, it is enough to send them from the gateways' network interfaces to CloudWatch Logs. They are billed and record nothing from before you enable them, so leave them on for a few working days, then switch them off.

In CloudWatch Logs Insights, run the article's query on that log group. Replace the example addresses with your gateways' private addresses, listed under NAT gateways in the VPC console, and your VPC's CIDR range.

filter (dstAddr in ["10.0.1.25", "10.0.2.25", "10.0.3.25"]
  AND isIpv4InSubnet(srcAddr, "10.0.0.0/16"))
  OR (srcAddr in ["10.0.1.25", "10.0.2.25", "10.0.3.25"]
  AND isIpv4InSubnet(dstAddr, "10.0.0.0/16"))
| stats sum(bytes) as bytesTransferred by srcAddr, dstAddr
| sort bytesTransferred desc

In the top rows, look up the address that is not a gateway under Network Interfaces in the EC2 console, which also lists ECS tasks and Lambda functions.

Traffic to S3 in the same Region can bypass the gateway through a gateway endpoint, which has no charge. My post on EC2-Other shows how to add one and what to check in bucket policies first. The same endpoint also takes most of an ECR image pull off the gateway, because according to the ECR documentation the image layers are downloaded from S3. If the endpoint has its own policy, it must allow the ECR layer bucket.

NAT gateways nobody uses

Since November 2025 Compute Optimizer has flagged NAT gateways that have had no traffic for 32 days, and since February 2026 Trusted Advisor has done the same. Trusted Advisor's cost checks, though, are not included in the Basic or Developer Support plans, so on those plans use Compute Optimizer, which you opt in to once per account.

Without those tools, check two CloudWatch metrics over the last 32 days: the maximum of ActiveConnectionCount and the sum of BytesOutToDestination. The first counts only TCP connections, so only zero on both means nobody is using the gateway.

Before you delete a gateway, point the route tables that use it at another gateway or remove those routes; otherwise they stay as blackhole routes and those subnets lose their way out to the internet. AWS also does not release the gateway's Elastic IP address from your account, so it keeps costing USD 3.65 a month as an idle address. Release it once you know nobody has it on an allowlist, for example at a payment provider.

NAT instance vs NAT gateway

An EC2 instance can do the gateway's job, but the NAT AMI from AWS runs on Amazon Linux 2018.03, unsupported since 2023, so build your own on Amazon Linux 2023 and turn off its source/destination check. AWS's comparison recommends the gateway for availability and less upkeep, but an instance is billed only by type and hours, with no per-GB processing charge. Internet and cross-zone transfer cost the same either way.

In Frankfurt, a gateway with its public address costs about USD 42 a month without traffic, and a t4g.micro instance with its address and disk about USD 11. With 1 TB a month through it, the gateway comes to about USD 95, while the instance stays at about USD 11.

A single instance has no automatic failover, so if it stops, your private servers lose internet access until someone restarts it. Small t4g instances reach full network speed only in short bursts on network credits; once those run out, they drop back to their baseline bandwidth. Patching the system is also your job, and every reboot cuts your private servers off the internet.

An instance suits test and development environments, or a few servers with little outbound traffic. If losing outbound internet access would stop orders or payments, keep the gateway in production. Either way, move S3 traffic to the free gateway endpoint first, because that needs no extra server.

What it means for a small team

Delete idle gateways together with their addresses first. When NatGateway-Bytes grows, find the source with the query above before adding an endpoint for the AWS service that receives the most data.

Instead of clicking through Cost Explorer, you can load an export of the whole bill grouped by Usage type into the CSV analysis. When NAT and transfer are a significant part of the bill, it shows gateway hours, processed data and internet transfer separately.

Every gateway that has carried nothing for 32 days is about USD 42 a month in Frankfurt that you get back by deleting it and releasing its address.

Originally published on codelevel.pl. Prices are net, for businesses. AWS, Hetzner and OVH are trademarks of their owners; CODELEVEL is not a partner, reseller or representative of any of them.

title: Building Mawared: An Egypt-Focused HR and Payroll Platform
description:
I recently completed Mawared, a cloud-based HR platform designed around the day-to-day needs of companies in Egypt.

The idea came from a common operational challenge: employee records, attendance, leave requests, approvals, expenses, and payroll calculations can easily end up spread across spreadsheets and disconnected processes. When information is separated, it becomes harder for HR teams and managers to track what is happening and understand how one process affects another.

Mawared brings these workflows together in one connected system.
A connected view of HR operations
The platform is designed around several core areas:

  • Command Center: A dashboard for tracking attendance, payroll readiness, and operational exceptions.
  • Employee profiles: A central employee record connected to the company’s branches, departments, job titles, financial details, and documents.
  • Attendance and shifts: Attendance tracking with shift rules, grace periods, and GPS-based geofencing.
  • Approvals and leave management: A unified workflow for leave requests and other employee approvals.
  • Finance and expenses: Tools for managing advances, installments, expenses, and company custody items.
  • Governance and audit history: Role-based permissions and an audit trail to make actions and changes traceable. The goal is to make these modules work together instead of treating each one as a separate tool. Payroll designed for the Egyptian context Payroll was one of the most important parts of the project. The system’s payroll workflow accounts for items such as salary components, attendance-related deductions, advances, insurance, and income tax.

A payroll simulation helps make the calculation easier to follow by showing how the final net salary is reached. The design also includes a payroll readiness check to help identify missing or unresolved data before processing a payroll run.

Once a payroll period is locked, its records are protected from direct changes. Later adjustments can be handled as recorded settlements, keeping a clear history of what changed and when.

The platform also includes export formats for salary transfers to Egyptian banks, including CIB, QNB, National Bank of Egypt, and Banque Misr.
What I learned
Building Mawared pushed me to think beyond individual screens and features. The bigger challenge was connecting the workflows:

  • How can attendance exceptions affect payroll?
  • How can an HR manager spot missing information before payroll is processed?
  • How can approvals, expenses, and employee records remain traceable?
  • How should the product support companies with multiple branches? Working through these questions helped me think about the product from the perspectives of employees, HR teams, finance teams, and company managers.

Mawared is a project about bringing everyday HR operations into one clearer workflow, with the needs of the Egyptian market in mind.

title: Does PNG to ICO keep transparency? A measured alpha test at 16, 32 and 48 px
description:
Does PNG to ICO keep transparency? A measured alpha test at 16, 32 and 48 px

Yes. A PNG with an alpha channel, converted to ICO, keeps alpha = 0 in every transparent pixel at all three sizes tested. Below is the pixel-by-pixel proof.

The question

When you save an image as JPEG, the alpha channel is gone — JPEG has no transparency. If your icon source was a JPG, renaming the file extension to .ico does not bring alpha back; the pixel data simply doesn't contain it.

But if your source is a PNG with an alpha channel, does the ICO conversion preserve it? I ran a measurement to find out.

Source image

A test PNG with a gradient alpha channel: at 16×16, every row steps through alpha values 0, 64, 128, 255 — four columns of each. The image has 64 fully transparent pixels (alpha = 0), 128 partially transparent pixels (alpha 64 and 128), and 64 fully opaque pixels (alpha = 255). At 32×32 the pattern scales up to 256/512/256. At 48×48 the anti-aliasing produces a richer distribution but the transparent count is 528.

The ICO file produced from this PNG is 625 bytes total, containing three frames: 16×16 (138 bytes), 32×32 (151 bytes), 48×48 (282 bytes). Pillow independently decoded each PNG entry inside the ICO to verify the pixel data.

Method

  1. Open the PNG in the converter at icoforge.com/png-to-ico-transparency-test.
  2. Convert to ICO and download the output file.
  3. Decode each frame inside the ICO using Pillow's Image.open().
  4. Count pixels at each alpha value: 0 (transparent), 1–254 (partially transparent), 255 (opaque).

Results

Size (px) Frame bytes Alpha 0 (transparent) Alpha 1–254 (partial) Alpha 255 (opaque)
16 138 64 128 64
32 151 256 512 256
48 282 528 1,248 528

ICO total: 625 bytes. Source SHA-256: a6286835afc613468120d32d780b3d954bfb5b85e983cc0ea845617b8eb04e7a. Output ICO SHA-256: 33d026fca2ea106d6e46b51c944f20531f16105dd40797b155295b1e56715903.

Every number in this table comes from the measurements at icoforge.com/png-to-ico-transparency-test, where the source PNG and output ICO are also available for download.

Why alpha = 0 at the transparent pixels means transparency survived

The source PNG has 64 pixels at alpha = 0 in the 16×16 frame. If the ICO conversion had flattened the image — filling transparent areas with white or black — those pixels would show alpha = 255. Instead, the ICO frame contains exactly 64 pixels at alpha = 0, matching the source. The same holds at 32×32 (256 pixels at alpha 0) and 48×48 (528 pixels at alpha 0). The transparent regions are preserved.

The partially transparent pixel counts also match: 128 at 16×16, 512 at 32×32, 1,248 at 48×48. These are the pixels where the source alpha is 64 or 128 — and the ICO preserves those intermediate values exactly.

What about JPEG sources?

JPEG does not store an alpha channel. A JPG file contains only RGB data. If you convert a JPG to ICO, the result has no transparency — not because the converter dropped it, but because the source never had it. Changing a .jpg filename to .ico doesn't change the pixel data inside.

Data and sources

All measurements were taken on 2026-10-26 using Chrome's canvas rendering pipeline and verified with Pillow. The raw measurements JSON is available at:

  • /samples/png-alpha-test/measurements.json — frame byte counts, alpha value distributions, and SHA-256 hashes for source and output.

The source PNG and output ICO files are downloadable from the PNG to ICO transparency test page.

title: Rounding is a promise when you show a player their odds
description:
Development covered 23 Sep 2026 to 24 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

A player in Myriad Immortal Sect read "Tribulation success chance: 100.0%", pressed the button, and failed. The underlying chance was 99.96 percent. Nothing was wrong with the roll. The number on the screen had been rounded to the nearest tenth, and 99.96 rounds to 100.0.

To a programmer that is a formatting detail. To the player it is the game lying and then punishing them for believing it. This window turned into a small campaign about how odds are displayed, and the rules that came out of it are short enough to steal.

Round towards the outcome you cannot promise

The first rule is about direction. Rounding to nearest is the default everywhere, and for odds it is wrong at both ends.

Near the top, anything below certainty must never display as certainty. The odds card, the result card and the chronicle line now all round down, so 99.96 reads 99.9 and only a true certainty shows 100.0. Near the bottom, the mirror case: a chance that is possible but tiny used to print "0.0%", which says impossible. It now reads "<0.1%". The dispatch board's chip, which shows whole percentages, keeps anything uncertain inside 1 to 99, so a 99.7 percent errand shows 99 and a 0.3 percent one shows 1.

The principle is that the display should never claim more certainty than the roll has, in either direction. A player can live with "99.9% and I failed". They will not forgive "100% and I failed".

One number, one formatter, everywhere

The second rule is about agreement. The same probability appeared on three surfaces: the odds panel, the result card, and the guidance card on the main screen. The guidance card rounded to a whole number, so it said "The Tribulation is open at 100%" directly beside a panel showing 99.6.

Two screens showing different numbers for the same fact are worse than either number alone, because the player now has to decide which one the game believes. Every place that shows a tribulation chance now goes through one display function. The chronicle also writes odds in the player's own number format, since a decimal comma and a decimal point are not interchangeable to someone reading in their language.

If you are preparing for a crossing yourself, the codex entry for the Transcendence Pill covers one of the items made for that moment.

Bonuses cannot pass the ceiling

The third rule came from the list of ways to improve your odds. A talisman adds fifteen points. At 88 percent it was still advertised as plus fifteen, which would make 103. Now each lever is capped at the headroom left under 100, so at 88 the talisman says plus twelve. That is a tiny change and it removes a whole class of "the numbers do not add up" confusion.

The dispatch board got the same scrutiny from the other side, since its chip was only recently relabelled after it turned out to be a power ratio rather than a probability. The guide to dispatching disciples on errands explains what that board is for.

The third question a return screen should answer

A different kind of number from the same window. When you come back after time away, the summary used to answer two questions: what happened while you were gone, and what changed. It never answered the one players act on, which is what they can now afford.

Time away pays levels, levels pay insight, and insight buys skill tree nodes. So after a gap that paid levels, the return toast and the panel now say how many nodes are within reach, using the same check the tree itself uses to decide whether a node can be bought. "You can now learn four nodes" is a reason to open the game's most important screen. A list of totals is not.

A smaller promise in the text

One more broken promise, of a different sort. Onboarding lets you pick a name and a face, several of the faces are women, and it never asks your gender. Eighteen quest strings still called the player a woodcutter's son, a village boy, him. They now say child, youth, novice, them. The Chinese text keeps its own narrator idiom, which reads differently there. The keystone nodes guide is a good next read if those newly affordable nodes made you curious.

The short version

Round odds towards uncertainty at both ends. Format them in exactly one place. Cap every bonus at the ceiling it can actually reach. And when a screen reports what happened, end with what the player can do about it now.

Check the odds yourself before your first storm: it is free to play in the browser.
