title: Getting My App Ready for iPhone Duo
description:
iPhone Duo folds. That means one app has to feel right on a short outer screen, a big inner screen, and every angle in between.

Here is what I learned doing this for ForkMesh.

The One Big Idea

You don't design a screen for each pose. You make one app that resizes well, and you let controls move to the side.

On Duo, tabs and toolbars leave the top and bottom and stand in a column under the camera.

The outer screen. The empty column by the camera now holds the controls, and the list gets the height back.

How the Side Column Works

A Live Activity can grow out of the camera and take space. When that happens, less important buttons move into the … menu.

Keep your main action and anything with a badge visible longest.

Use System Bars First

This was my biggest lesson.

I planned to draw this column by hand, then read that iOS moves standard toolbars and tab bars for you. Custom bars stay where they are.

When I put real toolbar items on a screen in ForkMesh, they moved into the column as real Liquid Glass.

If your app has a custom tab bar like mine, try this before you build anything.

The Big Screen Is Not a Stretched Phone

Held upright: The inner screen is the one pose that keeps normal top and bottom bars. There is enough height for them.

Respect the Fold

System sheets, alerts and menus move away from the fold by themselves. For custom views, use ReservedRegion.

Checklist

  • Build with the latest Xcode. Otherwise your app won't use the full screen.
  • Use size classes, not fixed widths. In my test, the outer screen reported compact width.
  • Measure the window, not the screen. A fold can resize your app at any moment.
  • Keep state when folding. I found code that closed the open page on fold. Typed text and open pages must survive.
  • Keep the same features in every pose. Only the layout should change.
  • Give every toolbar item an icon and a title. Items with only text or a custom view won't move to the column.
  • Test short screens. The outer screen clipped my onboarding headline behind a button.
  • Check Split View. On the left half, controls move to the left edge.

Prompt You Can Use

Paste this into your AI coding tool, inside your project.

iPhone Duo Prompt 

Make this iOS app work well on iPhone Duo. Work in small steps and show me each result.

First, read the code and tell me:
- how the app handles navigation, tab bars and toolbars
- which bars are custom and which are system
- any fixed widths, screen-size checks or device checks
- any code that resets state when the window resizes

Then follow these rules:

1. Build with the latest Xcode and test on the iPhone Duo simulator.

2. Prefer system containers: TabView, NavigationStack, NavigationSplitView and .toolbar. Test one screen first, because custom bars do not move to the side.

3. If a custom bar must stay, use toolbarVerticalEdge to find the side and ReservedRegion to avoid the camera and fold.

4. Use size classes and safe areas. Remove fixed sizes and do not use the device model for layout.

5. Outer screen: one pane, controls in the side column. Back at the top, then page actions, then overflow. Tabs stay at the bottom.

6. Inner sideways: show list and detail together, with controls on the same side as the outer screen.

7. Inner upright: keep normal horizontal bars.

8. Half open: keep buttons out of the fold and let it divide the panes. Scrolling content may cross it.

9. Keep state through every fold and resize: open page, scroll position, typed text and running tasks.

10. Give each toolbar item an icon and a title. Set visibility priority so the main action and badged items stay visible longest.

11. Keep the same features in every pose. Keep other iPhones unchanged.

12. Check every screen for clipped text and for controls hidden by the side column, including onboarding, sheets and Split View.

At the end, list what you verified, what you could not test, and anything I should check by hand on Duo.

title: Building Mintu: A Privacy-First Desktop AI Companion with Tauri 2, Rust, and Local LLMs (v0.2.1 Release)
description:
Most desktop AI tools today suffer from two fundamental problems: they rely entirely on remote cloud APIs—raising serious privacy concerns—and they require constant context-switching between separate application windows.

To address both issues, I built Mintu, an open-source, local-first desktop companion that integrates directly into your screen as a native Dynamic Island. With today's v0.2.1 release, Mintu expands its platform footprint and core capabilities.

Here is a breakdown of what Mintu is, how its architecture works, and what is new in version 0.2.1.

The Core Philosophy: Complete Local Privacy

Mintu does not send prompts, conversation logs, or telemetry to external servers. All text generation and processing happen entirely on the user's hardware.

Key architectural pillars:

Zero Telemetry: No analytics beacons, tracking cookies, or external error reporters.
Local LLM Inference: Powered by llama.cpp, running quantized GGUF models (e.g., Qwen 2.5) directly on your CPU/GPU.
Local Persistence: Conversations, settings, and memory fragments are persisted strictly within a local SQLite database (mintu.db).
Offline-First: Network access is only used when the user explicitly downloads a new model or checks for GitHub releases.
The Tech Stack

Building a persistent, low-overhead desktop island that stays reactive required a stack optimized for memory efficiency and cross-platform native execution:

Core & System Integration: Rust via Tauri 2
Inference Runtime: llama.cpp bindings for quantized GGUF models
UI / Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, Modern CSS
Database: SQLite (local embedded storage)
OCR & Vision: Windows Media OCR / native image pipeline

Tauri 2 allows the application to maintain a minimal memory footprint compared to traditional Chromium-based wrappers, while Rust provides the concurrency and safety needed for background LLM inference and system monitoring.

What is New in Version 0.2.1

The v0.2.1 release focuses on workstation flexibility, productivity tooling, and multi-platform distribution:

  1. Multi-Monitor Display Management

Users with multi-monitor workstations can now freely anchor and move the Dynamic Island across displays without layout disruption or window clipping.

  1. Quick Scratchpad

An inline, accessible note-taking interface integrated directly into the island, allowing developers to dump code snippets, thoughts, and quick tasks without leaving their IDE or current window.

  1. Dedicated Audio Engine

A lightweight, zero-dependency sound pipeline designed for subtle auditory feedback during focus timer transitions and background system alerts.

  1. Native macOS Universal Package

In addition to Windows 10 and 11 (64-bit), Mintu now officially supports macOS across both Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) and Intel architectures, integrating with Apple Keychain and native window management.

  1. Direct Web Distribution

Users can now download both Windows installer packages (.exe) and macOS universal archives directly from the official website without relying solely on GitHub release mirrors.

Verification and Security

Because Mintu is a community-driven open-source project without commercial code-signing certificates, we publish full SHA-256 checksums for every build so users can independently verify binary integrity before execution:

Windows Installer (Mintu_0.2.1_x64-setup.exe): 670E600D8F80606C87AE949F88EB65599DFDA8825804821873F10F1D0237A5BA
macOS Universal (Mintu-v0.2.1-macOS.zip): 3C24988419EA9869AA9F76FBE2D924DA40F75C5D4F75963ED48390C2E38B5ED5
Try It Out and Contribute

Mintu is 100% free and licensed under the permissive MIT License.

Website: https://mintudev.netlify.app/
GitHub Repository: https://github.com/HuseynDeveloper/Mintu

Feedback, bug reports, and pull requests are welcomed. If you find the project interesting, consider starring the repository on GitHub.

title: Transparent Image Fallback System with Canvas API
description:
Transparent Image Fallback System with Canvas API

Understanding the Need for a Fallback System

Transparent images are essential for creating layered designs on the web. However, not all browsers or environments support full transparency, which can lead to unexpected rendering issues. A fallback system ensures that even when transparency is not supported, the image still displays correctly with a default background. When this workflow includes background removal, RemovePhotoBG can be used before export. Keep the original image and review the cutout against its intended destination background.

Building a Fallback System with Canvas API

The Canvas API allows developers to draw images and handle transparency programmatically. By using the Canvas API, we can create a fallback system that handles transparent images and provides a default background when necessary.

  1. Check Image Support: Before rendering an image, check if the browser supports transparent images. This can be done by examining the image's format and the browser's capabilities.

  2. Create a Canvas Element: Use the Canvas API to create a drawing surface where the image will be rendered. This allows for greater control over the image's display and fallback behavior.

  3. Draw the Image: Draw the image onto the canvas. If the image has transparency, it will be displayed correctly. If not, the canvas will default to a solid background.

  4. Handle Fallback: If the browser does not support transparency, the canvas will automatically fall back to a solid background. This ensures that the image is still visible and maintains the intended design.

TypeScript Example with Failure-Case Tests

Here is a TypeScript example that demonstrates how to implement a transparent image fallback system using the Canvas API:

const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
const img = new Image();

img.src = 'transparent-image.png';

img.onload = () => {
  if (ctx && img.complete) {
    canvas.width = img.width;
    canvas.height = img.height;
    ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
    document.body.appendChild(canvas);
  }
};

img.onerror = () => {
  console.error('Failed to load image');
};

To test this system, you can simulate different browser environments and check if the fallback behavior is triggered correctly. This ensures that the system is robust and handles all edge cases.

Ensuring Robust Image Display

By implementing a fallback system with the Canvas API, developers can ensure that transparent images are displayed correctly across all browsers. This approach provides a reliable solution for handling image transparency and maintaining the intended design.

Conclusion

A transparent image fallback system with the Canvas API is an essential tool for web developers. By understanding the need for a fallback system and implementing it correctly, developers can ensure that images are displayed correctly and maintain the intended design across all browsers.

title: Building a third-party embed that survives any host page
description:
We publish Regime Map, a country-by-country register of gambling regulation. The people who write about the subject, lawyers and journalists mostly, need the same picture we already draw: which countries license online casino and which don't. So we made the map embeddable. Paste a snippet, get the map.

The hard part of a third-party embed isn't drawing the thing. It's that you ship code into pages you will never see. Somebody's WordPress theme sets svg { max-width: 50% }. Somebody else's news site has a strict Content-Security-Policy. A third one is a React app that adds your element after your script has already run. And the reader on a cheap phone didn't ask for your 200 KB of JavaScript.

This post is the list of decisions we made so the embed survives all of that, and so it can't damage the host page in return.

The contract is the markup

What a site pastes is the whole public interface:

<div data-regimemap="map" data-lang="en" data-region="world" data-theme="light">Interactive map: online casino regulation by country.</div>
<p>Map: <a href="https://regimemap.com/gambling-regulation-map/">Regime Map</a></p>
<script async src="https://regimemap.com/embed/v1/embed.js" referrerpolicy="no-referrer"></script>

Three rules follow from treating that as an API:

  • Everything lives under /embed/v1/. Inside v1, anything may change as long as pasted code keeps working. New options arrive as new data- attributes with defaults. A breaking change would be /embed/v2/, and v1 keeps running.
  • The text inside the <div> is the no-JavaScript fallback. If the script is stripped or blocked, the reader still gets a sentence and the link below it.
  • Nothing ever goes blank. If we retire the embed, or switch it off for one site, it renders a short card instead of an empty box.

Load almost nothing up front

The script tag points at a loader of 2.4 KB gzipped. It does four things:

  1. Finds its own origin from document.currentScript, so the same file works in any environment with no configuration.
  2. Reserves each embed's height straight away, from the region's aspect ratio or a card's usual height, so the host page doesn't jump when the map arrives.
  3. Waits for an IntersectionObserver with a 200 px margin. A map in the footer of a long article costs the reader 2.4 KB until they scroll near it.
  4. Shares requests. Two maps and three cards on one page fetch each file once. Pasting the script tag twice is harmless; the second copy just rescans.

Everything else is plain ES5 with no framework, no dependencies and no web fonts. The renderers get content-hashed names and a one-year immutable cache; the loader is cached for an hour and names the current pair. Translated strings travel in the per-language data file, not in the renderer, so one renderer serves all seven languages and stays cacheable.

piece gzipped
loader 2.4 KB
map renderer, including the world geometry 33.4 KB
map data, per language 2.5–3.3 KB
map, total ≈ 39 KB
country card, total ≈ 8 KB

Single-page apps get one global, window.RegimeMapEmbed.scan(), to call after they insert an element. Each element mounts once; to change options you replace the element (in React, a new key).

Shadow DOM, but carefully

Each embed renders into an open shadow root. That stops the host's selectors from matching our elements, but it does not stop inheritance: font, color, line-height, letter-spacing and friends still flow in from the host. So the first rule is:

:host { all: initial; display: block; }

and then the stylesheet sets every property it relies on, including box-sizing. We tested against a page with deliberately hostile rules on *, div, a, table, svg and button.

Two details mattered more than we expected:

  • Styles arrive as a constructable stylesheet (adoptedStyleSheets). Where that API is missing, a <link> to a CSS file inside the shadow root takes over. Hosts with a strict style-src then only need to allow our origin.
  • There is no style="" attribute anywhere in the output. Sizes are set through the CSSOM instead. A host with style-src-attr 'none' still renders the embed. Inline style attributes are the first thing a strict policy kills, and they're easy to add without noticing.

Under a strict CSP the script form needs our origin in script-src and connect-src (plus style-src for the fallback path). The iframe form needs frame-src. That's it.

Credit without touching the host page

The embed is free. The one condition is a visible credit line under it, and that line is the host's own HTML, outside anything we render. The host may add rel="nofollow" to it, and the terms say so plainly.

The embed checks for it: a visible link to our domain in its parent element or one of the next two siblings. A hidden or zero-opacity link doesn't count. If there is none, the embed draws its own credit bar inside its own frame.

What it never does is inject a link into the host page. A widget that adds links to other people's pages from JavaScript is exactly what search engines describe as link spam, and it would also be rude. Every link the embed renders itself opens in a new tab with rel="nofollow noopener".

When scripts aren't allowed

Plenty of platforms strip <script>. For those there is an iframe form with the same options as query parameters. Two lessons:

  • Iframe height has no good answer without postMessage resizing, which we chose not to depend on. The map frame keeps a 16:10 ratio with a 420 px minimum, because at 320 px wide 16:10 alone is too short for the header, map and legend. Country cards get a fixed height that the configurator measures for that country and language at 360 px, so a phone never cuts them off.
  • Some platforms take neither scripts nor iframes, Medium and Substack among them. There the honest answer is a screenshot with a caption that credits and links the source.

Switching off one site without naming it

Sometimes an embed shows up somewhere it shouldn't. Every data file carries an off list of 32-bit FNV-1a hashes of hostnames (lower case, without www.). The embed hashes its own host, or an iframe's parent, and on a match shows "not available on this site" with no link.

Hashes, so the public file doesn't list anyone. And FNV-1a rather than SHA-256 because crypto.subtle only exists in secure contexts, and plenty of host pages are still plain http. The change reaches every embed within the hour, which is the data file's cache time.

Accessibility is part of "survives"

A map that only works with a mouse doesn't survive a keyboard user. The SVG is aria-hidden and a sentence summarises it. The map is one tab stop with a roving tabindex: arrow keys move from country to country, Home and End jump to the ends, Enter goes to the country's link, Esc closes. There's a full table view. Touch targets are 44 px, and small states are drawn as dots so they can be found and tapped at world scale. prefers-reduced-motion removes the transitions.

A checklist, if you're building one

  • Treat the pasted markup as a versioned API, with a no-JS fallback inside it.
  • Ship a tiny loader; lazy-load the rest near the viewport; reserve the height first.
  • Shadow DOM plus :host { all: initial }, then set everything you inherit.
  • No inline style attributes. Constructable stylesheets with a <link> fallback.
  • Never inject links or markup into the host page.
  • Offer an iframe form, and say honestly where neither form works.
  • Have a way to switch off one site without publishing a list of sites.
  • Make the keyboard and table views first-class, not an afterthought.

The configurator, with a live preview of the map and the country cards, is at regimemap.com/data-api. How we count where the embed appears without logging the people who read it deserves its own post; that's next.

title: Redesigning Solitaire for one thumb (and A/B testing where the deck goes)
description:
Most of the people who play Solitaire on our site do it on a phone, held in one hand, often on the sofa in the evening. Many of them are over 60. Until this week our Klondike layout on phones was simply the desktop layout squeezed into a tall screen: the deck in the top corner, the buttons in a toolbar at the top, and the cards small.

On a 6.5" phone held in one hand, the top of the screen is the hardest place to reach. And the deck is the thing you tap most in Klondike. So we rebuilt the portrait layout around the thumb.

What changed

A bottom bar instead of a top toolbar. Settings, New game, Hint and Undo now sit in a bar at the bottom, as big icon buttons with a label under each one. Undo is on the right, where a right thumb rests. Time, moves and score stay in a slim strip at the top, because you read them but never tap them.

The deck can live at the bottom. In the settings sheet you can choose Deck position: Top / Bottom. At the bottom, the deck and the waste pile sit just above the bar, so drawing a card is a short thumb move instead of a stretch. A small badge shows how many cards are left in the deck.

Left or right hand. A Hand setting mirrors the deck and Undo to the other side. It's a small thing, but without it a left-handed player has to reach across the whole screen for every card.

Draw 1 or Draw 3, from the next deal. The choice used to be buried in a menu. It's now the first row of the settings sheet, and it applies from the next deal so a game in progress never changes under you.

Columns use the whole height. In portrait there's a lot of empty felt under the columns. Long columns now fan down into that space before the cards start to overlap more, and face-down cards squeeze first so the face-up ones stay readable.

Dragging feels lighter. While you drag, the card lifts slightly around your finger, every legal drop shows a soft glow, and the one under your finger glows stronger. Tapping a card still sends it to the best place, so dragging is optional.

Landscape and desktop keep the original layout. The whole portrait mode is one class on the body, so the CSS stays scoped and nothing else moves:

portraitLayout() {
  let on = false;
  try { on = matchMedia('(orientation: portrait) and (max-width: 700px)').matches; } catch (e) {}
  document.body.classList.toggle('np-sol-portrait', on);
  this._portrait = on;
}

Top or bottom? We don't know yet, so we're testing it

My guess was that the bottom deck is better. But players who have used Solitaire for 30 years expect the deck in the top corner, and "easier to reach" doesn't always mean "feels right".

So players who never touched the setting get one of the two positions at random, once, and keep it. An explicit choice in the settings always wins over the test:

let ab = null;
try { ab = localStorage.getItem('np-sol-ab'); } catch (e) {}
if (ab !== 'top' && ab !== 'bottom') {
  ab = Math.random() < 0.5 ? 'top' : 'bottom';
  try { localStorage.setItem('np-sol-ab', ab); } catch (e) {}
}
// logged once per player as an event, so we can compare the two groups

What we'll compare per variant: how many people leave in the first 10 seconds, how many games get finished, how many are won, play time, and how many come back the next day. Finished games matter more to us than taps: if the bottom deck makes people quit fewer games, that's the answer.

The test started today, so there are no results yet. I'll post a follow-up when there's enough data to say something honest.

Small things we learned on the way

  • Put a word under every icon. A gear or a lightbulb is obvious to us; it isn't to everyone. "Settings" and "Hint" cost a few pixels and remove the guessing.
  • Don't change the rules mid-game. Draw 1 / Draw 3 applies from the next deal, so a game in progress never changes under you, and daily puzzles and duels keep the rules everyone else plays with.
  • Keep the bar out of the system gesture area. On phones with a home indicator, the bar needs env(safe-area-inset-bottom) padding, or the Undo button fights with the swipe-home gesture.

If you want to try it, it's at nitroplayer.com/games/solitaire. It works best on a phone, held in one hand. I'd love to hear where you'd put the deck.

title: Single Page Application (SPA) WorkFlow
description:
Let’s explain how we'd build the same todo application as a Single Page Application (SPA) using React.js, focusing on data and state management. Let's start
with a high-level overview and then dive into the details.

First, let's visualize the structure of our React SPA todo app:

graph TD
    A[App Component] --> B[TodoList Component]
    A --> C[AddTodo Component]
    B --> D[TodoItem Component]
    D --> E[Edit Todo]
    D --> F[Delete Todo]
    D --> G[Toggle Complete]

    H[State Management] --> A
    H --> B
    H --> C
    H --> D

In this React SPA structure, we have a main App component that contains child components for different parts of our application. The key difference from the MPA
version is that all of these components exist within a single page, and React manages the rendering and updating of these components based on user interactions
and state changes.

Now, let's talk about data flow and state management in this React SPA:

  1. State Management: In React, we typically keep the state at the highest necessary level and pass it down to child components as props. For a simple app, we might keep all state in the App component. For more complex apps, we might use a state management library like Redux or Recoil.
  2. Data Storage: Unlike the MPA where data was primarily stored on the server, in an SPA we keep a copy of the data in the client-side state. We still persist data to a server via API calls, but the immediate source of truth for the UI is the client-side state.
  3. CRUD Operations: These are typically handled by updating the client-side state and making asynchronous API calls to sync with the server.

Let's walk through a typical workflow:

  1. Initial Load:
    • React app loads and mounts the App component
    • App component fetches todos from the server (e.g., via a REST API)
    • State is updated with the fetched todos, causing a re-render
  2. Add Todo:
    • User inputs new todo in AddTodo component
    • On submit, state is updated with new todo
    • An API call is made to add the todo on the server
  3. Edit Todo:
    • User clicks edit on a TodoItem
    • TodoItem switches to edit mode (managed by local state)
    • On save, parent state is updated and an API call is made
  4. Delete Todo:
    • User clicks delete on a TodoItem
    • Todo is removed from state, causing an immediate UI update
    • An API call is made to delete the todo on the server
  5. Toggle Complete:
    • User clicks to toggle todo status
    • State is immediately updated, reflecting the change in the UI
    • An API call is made to update the status on the server

Now, let's look at a simplified code example for our main App component:

import React, { useState, useEffect } from "react";
import TodoList from "./TodoList";
import AddTodo from "./AddTodo";
import { fetchTodos, addTodo, updateTodo, deleteTodo } from "./api";

function App() {
    const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchTodos().then(setTodos);
    }, []);

    const handleAddTodo = (title) => {
        const newTodo = { id: Date.now(), title, completed: false };
        setTodos([...todos, newTodo]);
        addTodo(newTodo);
    };

    const handleToggle = (id) => {
        setTodos(todos.map((todo) => (todo.id === id ? { ...todo, completed: !todo.completed } : todo)));
        const todoToUpdate = todos.find((todo) => todo.id === id);
        updateTodo({ ...todoToUpdate, completed: !todoToUpdate.completed });
    };

    const handleDelete = (id) => {
        setTodos(todos.filter((todo) => todo.id !== id));
        deleteTodo(id);
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <h1>My Todos</h1>
            <AddTodo onAdd={handleAddTodo} />
            <TodoList todos={todos} onToggle={handleToggle} onDelete={handleDelete} />
        </div>
    );
}

export default App;

In this React example:

  1. We use the useState hook to manage our todos state.
  2. useEffect is used to fetch todos when the component mounts.
  3. CRUD operations are handled by functions that update the state and make API calls.
  4. The UI automatically updates when the state changes, thanks to React's reactivity.

The key differences from the MPA approach are:

  1. Single Page: Everything happens within a single page load. React handles updating the UI.
  2. Client-Side State: The immediate source of truth is the client-side state, not the server.
  3. Asynchronous Updates: API calls happen asynchronously, allowing for immediate UI updates.
  4. Component Structure: The UI is broken down into reusable components.

This approach provides a more fluid user experience, as most interactions don't require a full page reload. However, it also means we need to carefully manage
state and keep it in sync with the server.

Is this helpful in understanding the SPA approach? Would you like me to elaborate on any specific part of this workflow or dive deeper into how React manages
updates?

title: How do you run training jobs across multiple GPU clouds?
description:
You run training across several GPU clouds by putting one scheduler in front of all of them: a job names the hardware it needs, and the scheduler decides where it runs and where it goes when a machine disappears. Nodus does this for you: it places each job on the cheapest capacity that can start it, spends the credits in the cloud accounts you connect first, and restores the run from its last checkpoint on another machine if one is reclaimed. The other two options are an open-source orchestrator you operate yourself, or a script per cloud, which works until the first preemption at 3 a.m.

Why would you spread one team's training over several clouds?

The usual reason is money you already have, not a grand multi-cloud strategy. A small AI team often holds AWS credits from an accelerator program, a GCP grant, and a prepaid balance on a GPU provider such as RunPod or Lambda. Each pile expires on its own schedule, and none of them alone has the right GPU free every time you need it.

The second reason is availability. The GPU you want is often sold out in one place and free in another, and interruptible capacity gets reclaimed. We collected the published numbers in how often spot GPUs are interrupted.

A job that can only run in one account waits or dies. A job that can run in any of five has five chances to start.

The cost of doing this by hand is coordination: five consoles, five quota limits, five ways to launch a machine, and no single place that says which run is where and what it cost.

What are the three ways to do it?

Each approach moves the same three jobs (choosing a location, falling back, recovering a run) to a different owner.

Approach Who picks where a job runs Who handles a lost machine Who runs the control plane
A launch script per cloud You, by hand You, by relaunching Nobody
Open-source orchestrator (SkyPilot, dstack) The orchestrator, from a search space you define The orchestrator, with your checkpoint code You (or a hosted tier)
Nodus Nodus, from your connected accounts and its own capacity Nodus, restoring the last committed checkpoint Nodus

Sources: SkyPilot overview, SkyPilot managed jobs, dstack docs, Nodus cloud accounts. Checked November 1, 2026.

Our decision rule: if you have one cloud and one GPU type, a script is fine. Once you have two credit balances or you use interruptible capacity, you want a scheduler, and the real question becomes whether you want to operate it.

How does Nodus decide which cloud a job runs on?

Nodus places each run on the cheapest offering that fits the request, has a machine free and stays inside your limits, according to the placement docs. If that offering cannot be used, the next cheapest takes the run. You can switch the trade-off with a placement profile: Balanced (the default), Cost for the lowest expected cost to completion including lost work, or Speed for the fastest finish within 1.5 times the cheapest expected cost.

Deadlines and money filter the list before anything is picked. Offerings whose p90 finish is later than your deadline are dropped, and so are offerings whose expected cost exceeds your remaining budget. If nothing is left, the job waits in Queued and the estimate says why, for example ExceedsRemainingBudget. nodus describe then shows the chosen offering, the fallbacks in order and every rejected offering with its reason.

From the command line, a job asks for hardware, not for a cloud:

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

That example is copied from the nodus run reference, which also documents --profile and --interruptible.

How do you spend credits in your own cloud accounts first?

You connect each account once and give it a credit limit, and Nodus places your Jobs, Workspaces and other single-node work there before its own capacity. This is a Beta feature, turned on per organization, and the cloud accounts guide lists AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes and API-key providers including Lambda, RunPod, Nebius and DigitalOcean.

Here is a setup for a team with AWS credits and a RunPod balance. The commands are copied from the nodus cloud connect reference, with --priority added to set the order:

nodus cloud connect aws aws-main --credit-limit 500 --priority 1
printf '%s' "$RUNPOD_API_KEY" | nodus cloud connect runpod my-runpod --credit-limit 200 --priority 2

Work goes to priority 1 first, then 2. Accounts with the same priority, or none, go to whichever has the cheapest machine for the work. The credit limit is spent at the Nodus list estimate, which can differ from what your cloud bills you, so the docs advise setting it a little below the credit you actually hold.

What happens when an account is full or out of credit is your choice, set with --burst:

--burst When the account cannot take the job
Allow (default) The job runs on Nodus capacity at Nodus rates
Approve The job waits until you approve it with nodus request approve-burst
Deny The job waits for your account

One honest limit: multi-node runs and Sandboxes use Nodus capacity, not your connected accounts. If your plan is an 8-node gang inside your own AWS account, this feature does not do that today.

What does a run cost each way?

Take one 8 x H100 run of 10 hours, which is 80 GPU-hours. In your own connected account, the job estimate shows a Nodus route fee of $0.02 per device-hour, so the Nodus charge is 80 x $0.02 = $1.60. Your cloud bills the machine and disk separately, against your credits.

If your accounts are full and the run bursts to Nodus capacity, the H100 SXM 80 GB is listed at $2.600/hr on the Nodus pricing page, so the same run costs 80 x $2.600 = $208.00, all in.


The route fee is all Nodus adds in your own account; the machine itself is paid from your cloud credits.

The two numbers are not a like-for-like price comparison, because the first excludes your cloud's bill. They show what you pay Nodus in each case, which is the number to plan around when your credits run out mid-project.

If the job bursts, these are the other rates you would see on the same page:

GPU Listed Nodus rate per GPU-hour
NVIDIA B200 180 GB $5.500
NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB $3.593
NVIDIA H100 SXM 80 GB $2.600
NVIDIA A100 80 GB $1.090
NVIDIA L4 24 GB $0.430

Prices checked November 1, 2026 on the Nodus pricing page.


A burst to an L4 or A100 is cheap; a burst to B200 for a long run is where a budget cap matters most.

What happens when a machine in one cloud disappears mid-run?

A run survives a lost machine only if it saves checkpoints, whichever scheduler you use. On Nodus, a machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds, and after 60 seconds of silence an attempt on shared capacity is declared lost and replaced, per the attempts and recovery docs. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, so two copies never write the same checkpoint.

A Checkpointed run loses at most the work since its last committed checkpoint. Recovery has limits: by default 8 recoveries per run, and 3 for distributed Jobs. Failures caused by your own code, such as a non-zero exit or out of memory, fail fast and are not retried. The checkpoint guide shows the save and resume pattern in Python.

With a connected AWS account, one extra rule helps across clouds: if AWS refuses a machine because your GPU quota for that family is used up, Nodus skips that family in that region for an hour and runs the work elsewhere.

Where is an open-source orchestrator the better choice?

SkyPilot or dstack is the better choice when you need things Nodus does not do in your own accounts today, or when you want to own the control plane.

Pick SkyPilot if you run multi-node training inside your own clouds, Kubernetes clusters or Slurm, because it combines them into one pool with automatic failover across the search space you give it, per its overview. Its managed jobs recover from preemptions, GPU errors and node crashes, and clean up resources when done. It is open source, so nothing sits between you and your cloud bill.

Pick dstack if you want a self-hosted control plane across GPU clouds, Kubernetes and on-prem clusters, described in its docs as a unified interface for development, training and inference.

The trade is operating it. You configure each cloud's credentials and quotas, keep the controller running, and write the checkpoint and resume logic your jobs need. Pick Nodus when you would rather not run that layer, want one prepaid bill with per-job cost caps, and are happy for multi-node runs to use Nodus capacity.

How do you move an existing training script onto this?

Keep your script, make it write checkpoints to the checkpoint path, and launch it with a GPU request instead of a cloud name. The quickstart runs a script from your own directory with this command:

nodus run --name cli-quickstart --gpu L4 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --max-cost 1 --timeout 10m --no-warm --dry-run \
  --output metrics=/nodus/outputs/metrics.json -- python train.py

Drop --dry-run once the estimate looks right. Connect your cloud accounts afterwards; nothing in the job changes, and Attempts › Ran on on the job page shows whether each attempt ran in your account or on Nodus capacity. For multi-GPU code, our PyTorch multi-GPU training guide covers the torchrun side.

FAQ

Does connecting a cloud account let Nodus change my existing machines?

No. Viewing an account is read-only and does not create, change or delete resources. Running work is a separate, explicit upgrade, and Nodus then creates, labels and deletes only its own machines there.

Can one training run span two clouds at once?

Not by default. A multi-node run is placed with network: Colocated, which keeps every node in one location on one network. Regional and Global placement are possible, and the placement docs note that relayed paths between nodes have lower bandwidth, so most distributed training should stay in one place.

What does it cost to run CPU work in my own account?

CPU work has no Nodus routing fee; your cloud provider bills the machine and disk within your account's spending cap. The $0.02 per device-hour route fee applies to own-account GPU Jobs.

How do I stop using a connected account?

Disconnect it in Nodus first. Nodus stops placing work there, moves running work to the next source and terminates the machines it started, and only then should you remove its access on the cloud side.

title: React Fiber
description:
An Overview of Fiber Trees and Reconciliation

Unlocking the Power of Web Scraping for Data Collection and Analysis

React Fiber is a revolutionary feature in the React library that aims to significantly enhance the performance and rendering efficiency of React applications.
At the heart of Fiber lies the reconciliation process, a powerful mechanism that efficiently updates the user interface based on changes in application state.
In this blog, we will delve into the concept of Fiber trees and explore how the reconciliation process works.

Reconciliation Stack

Before the release of React 16, React employed a stack-based reconciliation algorithm known as the "stack reconciler" to compare the old and new virtual trees
and update the DOM accordingly. While suitable for simpler scenarios, the stack reconciler faced challenges as applications grew in complexity.

The synchronous nature of the stack reconciler caused updates to block the main thread, leading to janky and unresponsive user interfaces, especially with large
virtual trees or slower devices. Additionally, changes to the virtual tree were delayed until the reconciler completed its work, affecting overall performance
and responsiveness.

The Fiber Reconciler

To address these challenges and improve React's performance, React 16 introduced the Fiber reconciler, a complete rewrite of the previous stack-based algorithm
with several significant benefits.

How React Fiber Works

When a React application undergoes an update triggered by user interactions or events, the reconciliation process is initiated. Its goal is to efficiently
determine the parts of the user interface that require updating and apply these changes to the real DOM.

Fiber Trees - Current and Work in Progress

The reconciliation process involves two sets of virtual DOM trees: the "current" tree and the "work in progress" tree, also known as the Fiber tree. The
"current" tree represents the existing state of the virtual DOM, while the "work in progress" tree is a replica that incorporates the updates to be performed.

Render Phase

The reconciliation process begins with the render phase, where React traverses the component tree and creates fiber nodes, special data structures representing
different portions of the virtual DOM.

During the render phase, React compares the fiber nodes in the "current" and "work in progress" trees to identify parts of the virtual DOM requiring updates.
Leveraging a work loop, React breaks rendering work into smaller units that can be interrupted and resumed, prioritizing important updates to maintain a
responsive user interface.

Commit Phase

After completing the render phase and applying the necessary updates to the "work in progress" tree, React enters the commit phase. Here, React takes the
updates from the "work in progress" tree and applies them to the real DOM, making the changes visible to users.

React optimizes the performance by batching updates during the commit phase, reducing unnecessary reflows and repaints for a smoother user experience.

A New Horizon for Concurrency and Batching

React Fiber, the new reconciliation architecture introduced in React 16, not only improves rendering efficiency but also unlocks powerful features for
concurrency and batching. This allows React to break free from the limitations of synchronous updates and enables the library to handle complex user
interactions more intelligently.

| Concurrency and Batching

In traditional synchronous rendering, React updates the entire component tree before reflecting changes in the real DOM. This approach can lead to unnecessary
processing, causing performance bottlenecks and affecting user experience. React Fiber introduces the concept of concurrency, which enables asynchronous
rendering and prioritization of tasks.

With concurrency, React can pause, resume, or abort rendering work as needed, and even divide the rendering process into smaller, more manageable chunks. This
fine-grained control empowers React to prioritize essential updates and respond faster to user interactions, making the user interface feel more responsive and
fluid

New Functionality in React Fiber

To leverage the benefits of concurrency and batching, React introduces several new functionalities:

useDeferredValue;

The useDeferredValue hook allows developers to defer the processing of non-essential updates, optimizing performance by prioritizing high-priority work. For
example, in a search input, we may want to defer the rendering of search results until the user pauses typing. This way, React can focus on more critical tasks
like handling user input, ensuring a smoother experience.

import { useDeferredValue } from "react";

const Search = () => {
    const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

    // Defer the processing of non-essential updates
    const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

    const handleChange = (e) => {
        setQuery(e.target.value);
    };

    // Rest of the component logic
};

useTransition;

The useTransition hook allows developers to create smoother transitions during rendering updates. It helps to manage complex interactions by defining specific
points in the rendering process where React should wait for a transition to complete before displaying the changes.

import { useTransition, useEffect, useState } from "react";

const ExpensiveComponent = () => {
    const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

    // Simulate a time-consuming rendering process
    useEffect(() => {
        startTransition(() => {
            // Code to render the expensive component
        });
    }, []);

    if (isPending) {
        return <p>Loading...</p>;
    }

    // Return the fully rendered component
    return <div>Expensive Component Content</div>;
};

Suspense Component

The Suspense component is a powerful tool that allows developers to handle loading states and fallback UIs in an elegant and straightforward manner. It is
especially useful when dealing with asynchronous data fetching or code-splitting.

import { Suspense } from "react";

const MyComponent = () => {
    return (
        <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
            {/* Asynchronously load and render the lazy component */}
            <LazyComponent />
        </Suspense>
    );
};

Conclusion

React Fiber's reconciliation process, powered by the concept of Fiber trees, plays a pivotal role in driving React's remarkable performance. By intelligently
managing virtual DOM updates and efficiently applying them to the real DOM, React ensures that user interfaces remain snappy and responsive, making React a
popular and powerful choice for building modern web applications. The introduction of React Fiber marks a significant milestone in React's evolution, paving the
way for even more efficient and responsive applications.

Thanks for reading ❤️

title: React Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
description:
React makes it easy to manipulate data using forms.

One of the most common patterns you’ll see in React when dealing with forms is that we need to make React aware of changes to the form inputs when the user
types. This means that the component containing those input elements typically needs to keep track of the text in the input elements using state.

React supports two types of components: controlled components and uncontrolled components. Let’s uncover the main differences between controlled and
uncontrolled components.

Controlled Component

Unlike the uncontrolled component, the input form element in the controlled component is handled by the component rather than the DOM. It takes its current
value through props. The changes are notified through useState Hook. Let’s consider an example to understand it in a better way.

import { useState } from "react";
export default function ControlledComponent() {
    const [name, setName] = useState("");
    const [age, setAge] = useState();
    const [hairColor, setHairColor] = useState("");
    return (
        <form>
            <label htmlFor="name">
                Name
                <input name="name" type="text" placeholder="Name" value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />
            </label>
            <label htmlFor="age">
                Age
                <input name="age" type="number" placeholder="Age" value={age} onChange={(e) => setAge(Number(e.target.value))} />
            </label>
            <label htmlFor="haircolor">
                Hair Color
                <input name="haircolor" type="text" placeholder="Hair Color" value={hairColor} onChange={(e) => setHairColor(e.target.value)} />
            </label>
            <button type="submit">Submit</button>
        </form>
    );
}

The input field is Controlled because React sets its value from the state.

<input value={value} />

Whenever we type into the input field, the onChange handler updates the state with the input’s value accessed from the event object. The value state variable is
the source of truth. When we need to access the value entered by the user into the input field, we have to read the value from the state variable. The
Controlled components can help access the value of any input field.

Uncontrolled component

Similar to the traditional HTML form inputs, the uncontrolled component can be written using a ref to get form values from the DOM. Thus there is no need to
write an event handler for every state update and the HTML elements maintain their own state that will be updated when the input value changes.

import { createRef } from "react";
export default function UncontrolledComponent() {
    const nameInput = createRef();
    const ageInput = createRef();
    const hairColorInput = createRef();
    const handleSubmit = (e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        console.log(nameInput.current.value);
        console.log(ageInput.current.value);
        console.log(hairColorInput.current.value);
    };
    return (
        <div>
            <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
                <label htmlFor="name">
                    Name
                    <input name="name" type="text" placeholder="Name" ref={nameInput} />
                </label>
                <label htmlFor="age">
                    Age
                    <input name="age" type="number" placeholder="Age" ref={ageInput} />
                </label>
                <label htmlFor="haircolor">
                    Hair Color
                    <input name="haircolor" type="text" placeholder="Hair Color" ref={hairColorInput} />
                </label>
                <button type="submit">Submit</button>
            </form>
        </div>
    );
}

Conclusion

Both the controlled and uncontrolled form fields have their merit. Evaluate your specific situation and pick the approach — what works for you is good enough.

title: Lessons from Auditing Ethereum Fusaka (EIP-7594 PeerDAS & EIP-7825) Across 14 EL & CL Clients
description:
Why Multi-Client Differential Auditing Beats Single-Repo Code Review

Ethereum's upcoming Fusaka upgrade (combining the Osaka Execution Layer hardfork and Fulu Consensus Layer hardfork) introduces EIP-7594 (PeerDAS), EIP-7825 (Transaction Gas Limit Cap = 16,777,216), EIP-7883 (ModExp Gas Increase), and EIP-7934 (RLP Execution Block Size Limit).

When you read a single client in isolation, subtle deviations from the specification look intentional. When you compare all 7 Execution Layer clients (go-ethereum, reth, nethermind, besu, erigon, ethereumjs, ethrex) and all 7 Consensus Layer clients (lighthouse, prysm, teku, lodestar, nimbus-eth2, grandine, ethlambda) side by side against the official specification, discrepancies jump out immediately.

Case Study 1: engine_getBlobsV2 Pre-Osaka Error Code & Syncing Checks

According to execution-apis/src/engine/osaka.md#engine_getblobsv2:

  1. Clients MUST return -38005: Unsupported fork if the head block timestamp has not reached Osaka.
  2. Clients MUST return null when syncing.
  3. Clients MUST operate in all-or-nothing mode: if any requested versioned hash is missing or belongs to a v0 sidecar without 128 cell proofs, the entire response must be null.

By building a 7-client conformance matrix, we verified how each client handles > 128 hashes (-38004: Too large request), BlobSidecarVersion1 cell proof counts (CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB = 128), and pre-Osaka fallback behavior.

Case Study 2: PeerDAS DataColumnSidecar Inclusion Proof & Custody Group Sorting

In specs/fulu/das-core.md:

  • get_custody_groups(node_id, custody_group_count) increments a uint256 counter modularly (UINT256_MAX -> 0), deduplicates group indices modulo NUMBER_OF_CUSTODY_GROUPS (128), and returns sorted(custody_groups).
  • Every DataColumnSidecar gossip message on data_column_sidecar_{subnet_id} must verify both the depth-4 Merkle inclusion proof against signed_block_header.message.body_root (generalized index 27) and the proposer signature before entering fork-choice data availability checks.

Differential matrices turn specification text into deterministic assertions across Go, Rust, C#, Java, Nim, and TypeScript.

title: xrun: smoke-test on a free Kaggle GPU, train on vast.ai, let the agent read the metrics
description:
I train 3D computer vision models, and classical ones at hackathons. For a long time every run came with the same chores: vastai create instance, scp the data up, start the script, check on it, scp the checkpoint back, remember to destroy the instance. Kaggle had its own version of that with kaggle kernels push. I wanted to hand the whole loop to an agent: launch on whichever platform fits, smoke-test on a free Kaggle GPU before paying for the real training, and collect metrics the same way everywhere, so the agent can read them and decide what to do next.

That became xrun, a Rust CLI with a Python Textual TUI on top. One YAML manifest describes a run: where the GPU comes from, what to upload, what to run and what to bring back. xrun rents the instance, uploads the data, starts training, follows stages and metrics, pulls the checkpoints and destroys the instance when it's over. It supports six vendors: vast.ai, Kaggle, Lightning AI, Google Colab, your own server over SSH, and the local machine.

A manifest 

name: resnet50_baseline
vendor: vast                    # vast | kaggle | lightning | colab | ssh | local

vast:
  image: pytorch/pytorch:2.4.1-cuda12.1-cudnn9-devel
  gpu: { type: "RTX 4090", count: 1 }
  price: { max_per_hour: 0.55 }

data:
  - src: data/train.h5
    dst: /workspace/data/train.h5

run:
  cmd: python train.py
  args:
    --lr: 5e-4
    --epochs: 30

artifacts:
  patterns: ["checkpoints/best*.pt"]

policy:
  on_idle_minutes: 30           # no output for 30 minutes: destroy
  early_stop:                   # metric plateau: pull the best, then destroy
    metric: val_f1
    patience: 5

And the day-to-day loop:

xrun launch exp/resnet50.yaml --detach --max-cost 5
xrun events <id> --follow
xrun metrics <id> --key val_f1 --ascii
xrun pull <id> --ckpt best --into models/

The smoke test is a second manifest with vendor: kaggle and a small config. The training script and the metrics code stay the same, so if it survives a few epochs on Kaggle, I launch the vast.ai one.

A copy of the manifest is stored with the run, and its hash is part of the run's identity. I can edit the original freely and xrun rerun <id> still reproduces exactly what ran. For hyperparameters, xrun sweep exp/base.yaml --grid run.args.--lr=1e-3,5e-4 --launch writes out one manifest per variant.

Built for an agent to drive

Every read command (ls, show, events, metrics) has --json, and whatever the TUI can do, the CLI can do too. xrun show prints each metric's last value and step, so a score logged once at the end of a cross-validation run is visible without plotting anything. xrun install skill --claude (or --codex) installs a skill that teaches Claude Code or Codex to use xrun instead of hand-rolled vastai and ssh calls. So the agent can rerun the last experiment with a different learning rate, or pull the checkpoint of the run with the best val_f1 from the last day, through the same commands I would type.

Metrics come from a small hook in the training script:

from xrun_hook import stage, metric, metrics, done, notify

with stage("train"):
    for ep in range(epochs):
        loss = train_one_epoch(model, loader)
        metric("train_loss", loss, step=ep)
        metrics({"val_loss": v.loss, "val_f1": v.f1}, step=ep)

notify("training", f"best val_f1 = {best:.3f}")
done()

The hook writes events.jsonl and metrics.jsonl, and a background poller picks them up. On Kaggle xrun injects the hook into the kernel by itself. An uncaught exception gets recorded as an error event.

A billing instance is never left alone

xrun launch --detach leaves that poller running. It counts the spend and destroys the instance when the run finishes, fails, goes silent, hits a metric plateau or runs into --max-cost / --max-hours. If the destroy call fails, you get a push saying the instance is still billing. The poller can't report its own death, so xrun watchdog runs from the OS scheduler every five minutes: no heartbeat from the poller while the instance is alive means a notification and a respawned poller. It also catches instances that no run record knows about.

Notifications go to ntfy, Telegram, a webhook (Slack, Discord) or desktop toasts. Replying /stop <id> to the Telegram bot kills a run.

The run history lives in a local SQLite database, with no tracking service or account involved. MLflow and W&B plug in as mirrors if you want their charts.

Rough edges

xrun_hook isn't on PyPI yet, so outside Kaggle it travels with your code. Kaggle shows metrics mid-run only when an MLflow server is configured; without one you see the start and the end. Lightning AI was smoke-tested live on a CPU Studio only, and for Lightning and Colab xrun doesn't know the price, so --max-cost doesn't apply there.

Try it

macOS and Linux:

curl -sSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Gerrux/xrun/master/install.sh | sh

Windows (PowerShell):

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Gerrux/xrun/master/install.ps1 | iex

xrun doctor and then xrun launch exp/templates/quickstart.yaml check the whole chain locally with no credentials, GPU or data. The code is on GitHub under MIT: Gerrux/xrun.

If you run training on one of these vendors, a report of what broke is the most useful thing you could send me. Each of their APIs has its own habits, and half of the fixes so far came from exactly that.

I built xrun together with my AI sidekick, Claude Code (Opus 5.5), and this post was written with its help too.

title: Building Browser-Only Calculators for Real-World Tasks: 6 Lessons from MendNook
description:
Building Browser-Only Calculators for Real-World Tasks: 6 Lessons from MendNook

A rectangular screen frame has a width, a height, and two diagonals. Calculating the theoretical diagonal is easy. Helping someone understand whether that number is useful for a real repair is much harder.

That's the kind of product-design problem behind MendNook, a collection of home measurement guides and browser-based calculators. The site includes tools for checking screen-frame diagonals, planning screen materials, recording blind measurements, and comparing door-bottom gaps.

This post isn't a walkthrough of our production source code. Instead, it's a practical breakdown of six design principles for small browser-based tools, with illustrative JavaScript examples.

1. Separate the calculation from the decision

A diagonal calculator can use the Pythagorean theorem:

function rectangularDiagonal(width, height) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(width) ||
      !Number.isFinite(height) ||
      width <= 0 || height <= 0) {
    return null;
  }

  return Math.hypot(width, height);
}

rectangularDiagonal(30, 24);
// Approximately 38.42 inches

But the output should say theoretical diagonal, not your frame is square.

A calculation assumes ideal rectangular geometry. It cannot detect cracked corners, bent rails, or poor installation.

The transferable lesson: don't let an accurate formula imply a conclusion it cannot support.

2. Validate the meaning of an input

JavaScript has a surprising behavior:

Number("") // 0

That is usually not what someone expects from an empty measurement field.

A better starting point:

function parsePositiveMeasurement(raw) {
  const trimmed = raw.trim();

  if (trimmed === "") return null;

  const value = Number(trimmed);

  return Number.isFinite(value) && value > 0
    ? value
    : null;
}

A production form should also display a clear field-level error, explain units, and distinguish an absent optional measurement from an invalid required one.

If the interface accepts decimal inches, say so. If users cannot enter fractions such as 35 1/8 directly, explain how to enter 35.125.

3. Don't turn a conditional guideline into a universal rule

Consider an inside-mount blind measurement helper.

A user might record widths at three positions:

const widths = [35.25, 35.125, 35.0];

const narrowestWidth = Math.min(...widths);
// 35 inches

But the correct height rule can vary depending on the product and manufacturer.

A useful interface can report the shortest and longest measured heights without incorrectly declaring either the final ordering dimension.

The calculator organizes evidence. Manufacturer-specific instructions determine the final decision.

This principle applies beyond home improvement: finance, shipping estimates, insurance, and many other domains where a single formula cannot describe every rule.

4. Make the no-JavaScript experience honest

An interactive calculator might require JavaScript, but its explanatory content should remain useful when scripts are unavailable.

A progressive-enhancement fallback can provide:

  • The formula and its assumptions
  • A clearly labeled worked example
  • Manual measurement instructions
  • An explanation of what the calculator cannot determine

Never present a static sample value as though it was calculated from the user's inputs.

5. Minimize unnecessary data collection

Most measurement calculators need only numbers and a formula, not a user account.

MendNook's public tools are browser-based and do not require registration or a paywall.

Local arithmetic can reduce friction and make it easier to explain how entered measurements are handled.

However, a browser-based calculator is not automatically private. Developers still need to examine third-party scripts, analytics, storage, and network requests before making privacy claims.

6. Test edge cases, not just the happy path

For a rectangular diagonal calculator, useful tests include:

Test Expected behavior
30 × 24 inches Approximately 38.42 inches
Empty width Ask for a measurement
Negative height Show a validation error
Invalid numeric input Reject the value
Unequal measured diagonals Show the difference without inventing a universal tolerance
JavaScript disabled Keep educational instructions available

These checks can matter more to users than sophisticated component architecture.

The wider lesson

A useful real-world calculator is not simply:

Input → Formula → Output

It's closer to:

Input → Validation → Contextual calculation → Limitations → Next action

For an example, explore the MendNook frame diagonal calculator. It explains the formula and, importantly, what the result cannot prove.

What's one UX guardrail you've added because a mathematically correct result could still mislead users?

I'd love to hear how other developers handle this challenge.

Code snippets are illustrative examples, not excerpts from the production source.

title: Inside the Block: How Solana Validators Actually Order Transactions Post-Alpenglow (Empirical Study)
description:
Why "Higher Priority Fee = Earlier Block Position" Is Only Half True on Solana

Most Solana developers assume that setting a higher SetComputeUnitPrice guarantees an earlier position inside a block. When we measured live post-Alpenglow Solana Mainnet blocks across Agave CentralScheduler, Agave UnifiedScheduler, Jito-Solana Block Engine, and Frankendancer/Firedancer Pack tiles, we found a much more nuanced reality.

Full reproducible code & dataset (docker compose up --build): https://github.com/duongynhi000005-oss/solana-inside-the-block-scheduler-analyzer

1. The Priority Score Formula Inside Agave's Scheduler

In Agave (prio_graph_scheduler.rs), transactions are not ranked by raw priority fee. They are ranked by reward per requested Compute Unit (CU):

Priority_Score = (ComputeUnitPrice_MicroLamports * Requested_CU_Limit + Base_Fee)
                 / (Requested_CU_Limit + Signature_And_Account_Lock_Overhead_CU)

If your swap only consumes 22,000 CU but you leave the default 200,000 CU limit without calling SetComputeUnitLimit(25_000), your effective scheduler priority is diluted by up to 6x during write-lock contention.

2. Write-Lock Contention vs. Multi-Thread BankingStage Racing

Across our Mainnet sample (slots 464182838–464182886):

  1. Uncontended Transactions: Packed in parallel across 4 non-vote banking threads, achieving a Spearman rank correlation of 0.74 to 0.89 between CU price and intra-slot entry index.
  2. Multi-Thread Flush Inversions (18% of pairs): When two non-conflicting transactions arrive in the same 50ms window on different worker threads, the thread executing a lighter batch frequently flushes to the PoH Recorder 1–3 entries ahead of a higher-fee transaction whose thread was finishing a heavy CPI instruction.
  3. Hot Writable Account Chains: Transactions writing to the same AMM pool state account are chained sequentially inside PrioGraph, delaying lower-priority writers while non-conflicting low-fee transfers sail through on adjacent threads.

3. Reproducing the Measurements in One Command

We packaged our entire telemetry collector and analyzer into a read-only Docker Compose suite (zero private keys required, dry-run by default):

git clone https://github.com/duongynhi000005-oss/solana-inside-the-block-scheduler-analyzer.git
cd solana-inside-the-block-scheduler-analyzer
docker compose up --build
